## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, and also with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; and enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, commented on the text of each individual book of Scripture. An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

### Second series

*The Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.*

# Notice

Like certain authors of the Middle Ages, our Haymo, when citing Scripture, frequently introduces verses that have been slightly altered, or at times even truncated. This occurred either because he often wrote from memory, with the Bibles far from his eyes; or because he interpreted the sacred books from the Hebrew or Greek text; or finally because he drew his verses from an old version unknown to us. Whatever the case may be, according to our usual practice we have respectfully preserved Haymo’s writings intact, as we have those of the others, whenever their meaning did not plainly appear erroneous to us. This notice should be entirely sufficient to prevent the attentive and intelligent reader from being disturbed whenever he perceives some difference in our edition from the Vulgate. Let this notice apply to the preceding volume, as well as to the present and the following one.

# Continuation of the first part of the works of Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt

[Col. 0009]

# Exposition on the Twelve Minor Prophets

[Note: We reprint this according to the Cologne edition of the year 1529. At the end of the book one reads: “Cologne, at the house of Eucharius Cervicornus, under the supervision of Master Godefrid Hittorp, [Col. 0010C] citizen and bookseller of Cologne, on the day before the Nones of August in the year 1529, with Adolph Rinch and Arnold Segen as consuls.”] (G)*

## To the candid reader

[Col. 0009A] Among the latter prophets—commonly called the twelve minor prophets—there is a difference from the greater prophets not so much in the subject matter and course of their prophecy as in their manner of expression and the structure of their statements. For what the greater prophets, stimulated—as I may put it—by the more vehement goad of the divine power, poured forth in lengthy verbal periods, with various figures of riddles and frequent changes of persons, these minor prophets too, who are believed to have been visited by a gentler prompting of grace, have contained within narrower periods and through shorter byways of obscurity.

Moreover, prophecy is not brought forth by the human mind by its own natural power through human wisdom; rather, the Holy Spirit dictates it by the grace of the one who speaks, as Sedulius says. For, if we listen to Suidas, it is peculiar to prophets “to offer the tongue as an instrument to the grace of the Spirit.” Hence no one can expound the prophets unless he is stirred by a certain divine inspiration; just as no one utters prophecy unless he burns with the fire of the Holy Spirit.

In Plato, [Col. 0009B] Socrates argues that poets are moved by *enthusiasm*—ἐνθουσιασμῷ, “inspiration”—not only so that they may compose outstanding poems, but also that interpreters of poets may disclose their hidden meanings, point out their figurative expressions, arrange the sequence of their histories, and carefully and diligently explain the miracles of nature, the practices of life, and the adornments of morals that have been shadowed forth under the allurements and coverings of fables.

How, then, could an interpreter explain without God’s special inspiration the divine oracle which the prophet himself could not utter without the impulse of the divine presence? Isaiah testifies that the visions are the words of a sealed book. If it is given to one who knows letters and he is told, “Read,” he will answer, “I cannot,” for it is sealed. If it is given to one who does not know letters and he is told, “Read,” he will answer, “I do not know letters.” John says that he saw a book written within and without and sealed with seven seals; no one could open it, and no one could release its seals. Hosea, acknowledging the obscurity of his volume, wrote: “Who is wise and will understand these things, intelligent and will know them?” Jeremiah echoes him, saying: “Who is the wise man who understands this, and to whom the word of the Lord’s mouth has come, so that he may proclaim it?”

If no one releases the sealed book of prophecy except the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David; if prophecy does not arise from a private interpretation of Scripture, as Blessed Peter says; if prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke inspired by the Holy Spirit—who does not see that composing commentaries on the prophets is not only especially arduous but also dangerous?

For in these writings, just as an inelegant heap of words first presents itself to the reader, so, in extracting the meaning, immense labor—liable to error and slippery—continually confronts the interpreter. The words of the persons change repeatedly; the order of the history is confused; threats are tempered by consolations; anger is softened by appeasements; blows are soothed by remedies. Thus the joining together of the statements relating to the prophet’s purpose is difficult and full of danger.

For this reason it has come about that few have devoted labor and effort to expounding the prophets, while some have even rushed into their explanation “with unwashed hands,” as the saying goes. Among the Greeks, Blessed Jerome testifies that Apollinaris of Laodicea left little commentaries on the prophets, but of such a kind that they touch more upon the meaning of what they explain. Origen and Didymus also composed books on the prophets, but of such a kind that they did not satisfy Blessed Jerome’s palate.

After Jerome, many among the Latins undertook this task, but not with equal learning and judgment, nor with equal success and outcome. Among them is Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt. If anyone compares him with the others, he will admire the holiness of the man, commend his diligence, welcome his learning, kiss his piety, and scent the prophetic spirit with which the rhapsodists and expositors of the prophets must be imbued.

As regards the truth of the history, he investigated it with skill; as regards allegory, he strengthened it with the firmest testimonies of Scripture; as regards the confused order, he clarified it in the clearest sequence; as regards the coverings of historical events, he unfolded them with an extraordinary art; and finally, as regards the tangles of words and knots of statements, he untied them both learnedly and successfully.

He separated threats from consolations, distinguished consolations from calls to return, and differentiated what was impending for the two tribes—that is, the Jewish people—from what the ten tribes, or the Israelite people, were awaiting. He clearly distinguished the matters referring to the true body of Christ—namely, the incarnation, birth, flight into Egypt, [Col. 0010C] preaching, passion, ascension, and so forth—from those foretold concerning Christ’s mystical body: the Church, the calling of the nations, the attack of heretics, the severity of the final judgment, the reward of the blessed, and the eternal punishment of the damned.

Who, then, would be ashamed or reluctant to learn these things from the Minor Prophets? Let such a person buy this book for a small coin and, as that writer says, “hunt for the most precious possession of wisdom”—σοφίας κτῆμα τιμιώτατον. Farewell.

# On the Prophet Hosea

[Col. 0011]

## Chapter One

[Col. 0011A]

> “The word of the Lord which came to Hosea, son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.”

By “the word of the Lord” we must understand that Word of which John says at the beginning of his Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word.” This Word is not said to have been made in its nature, but to have been begotten by God the Father before all ages. Therefore, when it is said here, “The word of the Lord was made to Hosea,” it must be understood as follows: the word of the Lord was made—that is, the word of God the Father came to speak to Hosea. By speaking the word of the Lord to Hosea, he made him a god and savior of his people.

For Hosea is interpreted as “savior,” since by teaching and by the example of holiness he endeavored to save the people to whom he was sent. The fact that Hosea and the other prophets, to whom this word came, are called gods is made clear by the Lord in the Gospel: “If,” says the Lord, “he called them gods to whom the word of God came,” and so forth.

Thus, just as God makes human beings gods by speaking to them, so the Savior himself makes them saviors. The saints are called gods and saviors by grace, while by nature there is one Savior and God.

Here it should be noted that it does not say, “The word of the Lord was made *in* Hosea,” lest the meaning be that through him the word is spoken to someone else. Rather, it says, “to Hosea,” to show that the word is properly directed to the one to whom it is addressed.

For, as Blessed Jerome explains, it is one thing for the Lord to speak *in* Hosea and another for him to speak *to* Hosea. In Hosea, Hosea himself does not speak; rather, through Hosea the word is directed to others, just as the Prophet says in the psalm:

> “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me, for he will speak peace to his people.”

This shows that through the one who was speaking these words, God would speak to others. When he speaks to Hosea, however, he shows that the prophecy belongs specifically to him, when he says to him: “Go, take for yourself a wife,” and so forth.

He prophesied during the same period as Isaiah, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, and Jonah. This is clearly demonstrated by the names of the kings who are included in the titles of those prophets. Hence we understand that he prophesied both before and after the captivity. He foretold the captivity of the ten tribes, which he afterward mourned when he saw it.

[Col. 0011D]

> “Son of Beeri.”

The Hebrews report that wherever the names of the fathers or grandfathers of prophets are given, those fathers or grandfathers too were prophets. Thus it is established that Beeri was a prophet, whose son is reported to have been Hosea.

Hosea is interpreted, as we have said, as “savior,” and therefore signifies the Lord Christ, who is truly the Savior of the world. Hence he is also called Jesus, and the things that follow pertain to him.

Hosea is therefore called the son of Beeri, whose name is interpreted as “my well.” God the Father himself also says through the Prophet:

> “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water.”

The difference between a well and cisterns is that a well has perpetual waters flowing from a living spring, whereas a cistern possesses water from outside, water that is brought in and temporary.

Of this fountain the Prophet says:

> “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain.”

[Col. 0012A]

> “In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.”

Uzziah is the same man who elsewhere is called Azariah. He reigned in Jerusalem over the two tribes called Judah for fifty-two years. Jotham succeeded him, reigning for sixteen years. After him came his son Ahaz, who also reigned for sixteen years. In his eleventh year the ten tribes were led into captivity, into the mountains of the Medes and Persians, by Shalmaneser, king of the Chaldeans.

After Ahaz, his son Hezekiah reigned for twenty-nine years. From this it is evident, as we said above, that Hosea prophesied both before and after the captivity, and concerning the captivity itself as it was approaching.

“In the days of Jeroboam son of Joash.” We must not suppose that this Jeroboam was the first king of the ten tribes, who is said to have been the son of Nebat. This man, as is mentioned here, was the son of Joash and great-grandson of Jehu. Jehu had killed Jezebel, that most wicked queen, and two most wicked kings: Joram, son of Ahab and king of Samaria, together with his seventy brothers, and Ahaziah, king of Judah. It had been promised him that his sons would reign to the fourth generation.

Nevertheless, because they returned to the sins of the kings of the sons of Israel, they soon lost the kingdom.

[Col. 0012C]

> “The beginning of the Lord’s speaking in Hosea.”

These words can be understood in two ways: either because the captivity of the ten tribes was first announced to this man, before Isaiah and the others who were his contemporaries in prophesying; or because the first word spoken to him by the Lord was the one that follows, concerning the union with a promiscuous woman.

Accordingly, it immediately continues:

> “And the Lord said to Hosea: Go, take for yourself a wife of prostitution, and have children of prostitution, because the land will commit prostitution, prostituting itself against the Lord.”

Although some insist that these things happened literally, excusing the prophet from the guilt of prostitution on the grounds that he obeyed God’s commands in this matter, they fail to consider that God has never commanded anything unjust or shameful.

It should nevertheless be understood in the better way, according to the mystical meanings, just as what was said to Ezekiel:

> “You shall sleep on your left side for three hundred and ninety days, and you shall not turn to the other side; then again you shall sleep on your other, right side for forty days.”

Likewise, Jeremiah, while shut up in prison, was commanded to go to the neighboring nations hostile to the Israelite people and to the Euphrates, and there to hide the loincloth he possessed. Yet he could not go out even among his own people to sell his field; he went there like a traitor and informer against his fellow citizens, was captured and bound by them, and placed in prison—especially since Jerusalem was already besieged and surrounded on every side by the enemy.

As far as the literal meaning is concerned, a wife of prostitution is a woman who, being adulterous, is open to the lust of many men and brings a stranger upon her husband. Children of prostitution are those born from such a union.

[Col. 0013A]

> “And he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore a son.”

Since all these things, as was said above, must be understood spiritually, Hosea, whose name is interpreted as “savior,” signifies the Lord Jesus Christ. Coming through the mystery of the Incarnation, he took a wife of prostitution, namely the Jewish people, which, by abandoning the one true God, worshiped various apparitions of demons.

From her he begot children of prostitution, because he showed that all were under sin. Hence the wife of prostitution is appropriately called Gomer, a name interpreted as “perfect” or “consumed”—namely, in an evil deed—which no one doubts belongs to that same people.

Accordingly, she is also fittingly said to be the daughter of Diblaim, which is interpreted as “pleasure,” since she always sought to follow her own pleasure. She bore a son—that is, a people strong for evil.

If, however, we wish to examine this more deeply and interpret it in a favorable sense, the son born from the Israelite people is understood as the Lord Jesus Christ, because he who had joined that same people to himself through divinity wished to be born from it through humanity.

The interpretation of the name by which the son is commanded to be called agrees with this meaning, for Jezreel is interpreted as “seed of God.” Hence it follows:

[Col. 0013C]

> “And the Lord said to him: Call his name Jezreel, because in a little while I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu.”

Jezreel is interpreted as “seed of God.” As far as the literal meaning is concerned, it was a metropolitan city in the kingdom of the ten tribes. There we read that Naboth was killed, and on account of avenging his blood Jehu was raised up; he destroyed the house of Ahab and of Jezreel.

But because Jehu himself became the avenger of righteous blood, while his sons did evil in the sight of the Lord, the blood of Ahab was poured upon his house—that is, it returned upon him—when his sons were led into captivity and killed. And not long afterward both came to an end, that is, both the kingdom and the kings ceased.

For after Jeroboam, Jehu’s great-grandson, died—under whom Hosea began to prophesy—his son Zechariah succeeded to the kingdom. In the sixth month of his reign, Shallum, born from another line, killed him. Immediately the Assyrian kings captured Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, which were beyond the Jordan; then Naphtali; and finally all the remaining tribes.

From Zechariah until Hosea, under whom all ten tribes were led into captivity, there were only forty-nine years. For this reason it is said here: “In a little while I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu.”

Spiritually, Jehu, through whom the blood shed at Jezreel is said to be visited, signifies the Jews, by whom the blood of Christ was shed. We have already indicated that Christ is signified by the name Jezreel. His blood was visited upon them when they were killed by the Romans and carried throughout all the lands, and to this day remain exiles from their own land.

[Col. 0014A]

> “And I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to cease, and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.”

Above we said that Jezreel was the metropolitan city of the ten tribes. Near it lies a valley of enormous breadth, extending for more than ten thousand paces. In a battle fought there, Israel of the ten tribes was struck down by the Assyrians; their strength is here expressed under the name “bow.”

According to the mystical meanings, however, all who think wrongly about Christ—such as heretics, who have departed from the house of David, that is, from the Church—are understood in this passage under the name Israel. They are broken in the valley of Jezreel, that is, in the humility of the seed of God, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

[Col. 0014B]

> “And she conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said to her: Call her name No Mercy, because I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them; and I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God. I will not save them by bow, sword, war, horses, or horsemen.”

Once all strength has been taken away from the Jews, they are no longer called by the masculine sex but by the feminine, as fragile and weak. Hence that people is rightly called a daughter, because it had a womanish mind when it abandoned God and began to worship empty idols in place of God.

She is without mercy and delivered over to oblivion because to this day they serve the kings of Persia, and their captivity has never been completely ended.

The house of Judah, together with the two tribes joined to it, obtained mercy when, because of the confidence they had in God, an angel was sent and struck down 185,000 of Sennacherib’s army.

“And I will save them,” he says, “by the Lord their God”—that is, by the protection of myself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit. This is like the statement, “The Lord rained from the Lord,” that is, the Son from God the Father.

“And I will not save them by bow and sword, war and horses”—that is, not by any hope or human strength, nor by a multitude of horsemen, but rather by the Lord their God, who will send his angel to kill all their enemies.

If, however, this is referred to those who were found at the Lord’s coming, they too are rightly called a daughter and not a son, because they pursued the softness of their pleasure when they even invoked the blood of the seed of God, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

Therefore they too, having become without mercy, were handed over to the Romans, condemned to perpetual servitude, and delivered to oblivion.

But the house of Judah, whose name is interpreted as “confession”—that is, the apostles and the others, whether believers or teachers, who confessed faith in the name of Christ—were saved not by sword and bow, that is, not by any human help, but in the Lord their God, namely Christ, who chose them by his grace.

We may also understand by the name “daughter” the heretics, who follow doctrines of vanity and corrupt the perfect and strong meanings of Sacred Scripture. Endeavoring to soften them, they are handed over to the devil, whose eternal condemnation weighs upon them without mercy, forever forgotten by God.

But the house of Judah, that is, the Catholic Church, which faithfully confesses the faith of the Holy Trinity in inseparable unity, will be saved in the Lord its God, not in the multitude of armies or in the strength of its own powers.

[Col. 0014D]

> “And she weaned the one who was without mercy.”

One who is weaned departs from the mother and no longer feeds on the parent’s milk, but is sustained by other nourishment. It was the custom of the ancients to hold a feast for all their neighbors and friends on the day infants were weaned, that is, separated from milk.

Hence Samuel’s mother, when her husband was going up to the temple of the Lord, said that she would not go until the infant was weaned—that is, until he reached the age at which she could remove him from milk.

In Sacred Scripture milk signifies simple understanding. The Jews were nourished, in a certain sense, with milk so long as they remained within their own Law and continued to read the other Scriptures. But after they were led into captivity, they began to feed on the foods of the nations and to eat things sacrificed to idols.

Thus they reached the misery of losing even the small amount of knowledge they seemed to possess, so that they no longer understand even the surface of the Law itself.

[Col. 0015B]

> “And she conceived and bore a son, and he said: Call his name Not My People, because you are not my people, and I will not be your God. And the number of the sons of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured and cannot be counted. And in the place where it will be said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it will be said to them, ‘Sons of the living God.’”

These words can refer both to those who at that time were seized by the Assyrian kings and led into captivity, and to those who after the Lord’s coming were dispersed by the Romans throughout all the nations.

The former rejected God through the worship of idols; the latter through the denial and betrayal of the Son of God. For, not having the Son, they cannot have the Father.

For this reason God also rejected them, so that they would not be his people but would become servants of the devil. It would be said to them: “Because you are not my people, and I will not be your God.” I will judge you unworthy of possessing my inheritance and presence; I will reject you forever.

This can also be understood of heretics, who, rejecting God by thinking perversely about him, are completely driven away from him, lest they be able to say with the elect: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.”

“And the number of the sons of Israel shall be as above.” Although those Jews were then oppressed, or are now subjected to the harshest captivity, they are nevertheless innumerable to human beings. Of them Isaiah says:

> “If the number of the sons of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

This can be understood as fulfilled at the Lord’s coming and as truly destined to be fulfilled at the end of the age. For after the people of Israel has been dispersed throughout the whole world, and the multitude of the people has exceeded every reckoning, then Israel, which is now captive, will have its freedom.

[Col. 0016A]

> “And in the place where it will be said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ as above.”

We must understand the place where these things were said to be Jerusalem. There it is now said to them, “You are not my people”; there, in the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, it will be said to them, “Sons of the living God.”

This was fulfilled in the apostles and in the other faithful. For, as John says:

> “To all who believed in Christ, he gave power to become sons of God.”

If we wish to refer these words to the Jews who exist today, the place where it is said to them, “You are not my people,” is understood as the whole world, because among all the nations the Jews are now proved to be servants not of God but of the devil.

When they have believed through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, they will be called sons of God by all the nations.

[Col. 0016B]

> “And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one head.”

By Judah are signified those two tribes joined together—namely, the tribe of Benjamin and the priestly tribe, that is, Levi. Since the kings who ruled those tribes originated from the tribe of Judah, the two tribes themselves were also designated by the name Judah.

The ten tribes, being the larger part, retain their former name, Israel, because before the division into ten tribes and two, all were generally called by that name.

Thus, although they had been divided, it is promised that they will be gathered together into one by the Lord. At the time of the Lord’s Incarnation and Resurrection, many who had returned from captivity were living in Judea, both from the ten tribes and from the two, and many of them believed in Christ.

Of them it is said here:

> “The sons of Judah and the sons of Israel will be gathered together,”

that is, believers from the two and the ten tribes will come together in one fold of Christ.

[Col. 0016C]

> “And they will appoint for themselves one head”

—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom Ezekiel says:

> “There will be one prince in their midst, David my servant.”

Alternatively, by Israel we can understand the Gentiles and by Judah the believing Jews; or by Israel the heretics and by Judah the Catholics. All of these, converted to the unity of Christian faith, will appoint for themselves one head, Jesus Christ.

> “And they will go up from the land”

—that is, from earthly ways of thinking and from the lowliness of the letter that kills—and they will be raised to spiritual and life-giving understanding,

> “because great is the day of Jezreel.”

Here we should understand “day” as the entire period extending from the Lord’s birth to the end of the age, concerning which we sing in the psalms:

> “This is the day that the Lord has made.”

This day is great—that is, this period is great—in which forgiveness of sins is granted to believers and the door of the heavenly kingdom is opened.

# Chapter Two

> “Say to your brothers, ‘My people,’ and to your sister, ‘She who has obtained mercy.’”

If we wish to refer this solely to the Jews, he urges the people of Judea not to despair of the salvation of the ten tribes, but every day, by word, desire, and writing, to call them to repentance, because they are called their brother and sister.

They are called “brother” because it says, “My people”; “sister” because she is called “she who has obtained mercy.”

[Col. 0017A]

If we wish to refer it to the nations, they are told to say to the others who remain in unbelief: “They will be my people if they wish to believe in me and, rejecting the old way, wish to pass over to newness of life.”

Or you who believe in me, and adorn perfectly by your works the faith you possess, say to the other believers: “They will be my people if they wish to believe in me, remain in the faith to which they have been called, and strive to adorn it with works.”

Say also to your sister—that is, to the same people believing in Christ—that she has obtained mercy by believing in me.

[Col. 0017B]

> “Judge your mother, judge her, because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.”

This is said to the apostles and to the other believers, so that they may judge—that is, rebuke—their mother, the Synagogue, which, having been made a wife from a prostitute, does not abandon her former ways.

But again they are to rebuke their mother because she has once more prostituted herself with her lovers. The patience and clemency of this husband should be considered: he again exhorts his sons to rebuke their mother, because while they believed she remained in unbelief.

This was fulfilled at the time when Peter said to the weeping Jews:

> “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized,”

and so forth.

“Show her,” he says, “that she is not my wife and I am not her husband.” Since she rejected me, I too will reject her, so that I may not be her husband.

Christ is the husband of the Church, concerning whom the heretics say to that same Church: “Her husband is not in her house.”

[Col. 0017C]

> “Let her remove her acts of prostitution from her face and her adulteries from between her breasts.”

In sacred speech, prostitution or adultery is understood in two ways: both as uncleanness of the flesh and as idolatry, concerning which it is written:

> “You will destroy all who prostitute themselves away from you.”

A woman prostitutes herself or commits adultery when she is open to the lust of many men or brings a stranger upon her husband.

Since God is the husband of the soul, the Israelite people had subjected itself to many acts of prostitution, because, having abandoned Almighty God, it worshiped the apparitions of many demons.

Therefore it is now said: “Let her remove her acts of prostitution from her face”—that is, let her remove the worship of gods from her love and presence, because she was open to the lust of many, worshiping the gods of all the nations.

Let her also remove her adulteries from between her breasts—that is, from her heart, where an evil deed is first conceived. The heart is between the breasts, and, as the Lord makes clear, evil thoughts come forth from it.

They first conceived evil in their heart, and only afterward brought their thoughts forth into a wicked deed. Therefore the divine word urges her to remove all these things from herself, lest, because of the crimes she has committed, she lose the good things divinely bestowed upon her.

“Lest perhaps,” he says, “I strip her naked and set her as on the day of her birth.” The garment with which that same people was clothed is understood as God’s help, the teaching of the Law and the Prophets, and the protection of the angels. Almighty God threatens to take all these away from her unless she repents of the crimes she has committed, so that she may become naked and full of shame, just as she once was. And I will set her, he says, as on the day of her birth—that is, so that she may be deprived of all these things, as she once was while dwelling in Egypt.

“And I will make her like a wilderness, and set her like an impassable land.” A house is reduced to a wilderness when it loses its rightful master. This people was reduced to a wilderness when Almighty God withdrew from it because of its sins. Hence the Prophet says: “I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance,” and so forth. In the Gospel he himself threatens them that he will leave them, saying: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” It also became like an impassable land, because, having lost the straight path of faith, it lost God the Father and also lost his Son, who says: “I am the way.”

“And I will kill her with thirst”—that is, through deprivation of every good, or with the thirst of which the prophet Joel says: “I will send upon them hunger and thirst,” not hunger for bread or thirst for water, but hunger to hear the word of God. Alternatively, we may understand the water that was taken from them as the grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning which he himself speaks in the Gospel, inviting everyone to come to him and receive this water: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink, and rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

All these things may also be applied to the Jews who deny Christ, to heretics who abandon the true faith, and to those who follow various doctrines of error in heart, word, and deed. Unless they repent, stripped of all the virtues they received in the Church, they will be reduced to the condition of their day of birth; having become a wilderness and an impassable land, they will suffer thirst or the aridity of Sacred Scripture, so that even what they seemed falsely to possess may be reduced to nothing.

“And I will not have pity on her children, for they are children of fornication, because their mother has fornicated.” When the Jews went out from Egypt, the Lord, angered against their fathers, killed them in the wilderness. But he had pity on their children, preserving them for life and giving them the land he had promised to their fathers. Now, however, he threatens that he will not act in the same way, saying: “I will not have pity on her children.” Rather, they will go into captivity together with their fathers, die there, and no longer see the land of their birth, because they are children of fornication—that is, they were born in the worship of idols. For whatever faith their fathers held, that they taught their children.

Hence it is also added: “Because their mother has fornicated.” Just as a viper gives birth to a viper, so that same people produced children of the same kind as itself. “She was put to shame”—that is, she was stunned and filled with amazement—“who conceived them” and made them children of the devil.

“For she said: ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.’” The Jews said this while worshiping the gods of various nations. “I will go,” she says, “after my lovers”—that is, I will follow the gods in faith and affection, or imitate the nations whose gods I worship; they give me bread and water, and so forth. For everything good that this people had received from heaven from God, it thought it possessed from the demons and attributed everything to them.

This may also be understood spiritually of those who denied the Son of God, choosing Barabbas, the author of sedition, for themselves, and crucifying the Son of God, the giver of every good thing. Therefore they were put to shame, and not only they but also their descendants were punished by the worst of curses, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

In its literal exposition, these things may also be understood of heretics, who are put to shame; their children as well, begotten by evil teaching, blush together with them. The reason for their shame is made clear when it follows: “For she said: ‘I will go after my lovers’”—that is, I will follow the various doctrines of the heretics, whose bread is perpetual mourning. Their water is perverse and foolish teaching, by which they even destroy those who have been baptized. Contrary to this water is that of which it is written: “Deep water from the mouth of a man.” By wool and flax their feigned holiness and purity are represented. Warning that such people must be avoided, the Lord says: “For they will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.” By oil their flattery is understood, concerning which the Prophet says: “But may the oil of the sinner not fatten my head.” Their drink, too, is understood as Sacred Scripture, which they make turbid by interpreting it wrongly.

“For this reason, behold, I will hedge your way with thorns, and hedge her with a wall, and she will not find her paths.” By thorns the pricks of suffering and the harshness of adversity are expressed; by the wall, an obstacle is meant, preventing her from finding what she sought. “I will hedge your way,” he says, “with thorns”—that is, I will entangle your actions in the hardest labors. I will also hedge you with a wall, so that you will be unable to reach even what you desire. What follows, “and she will not find her paths,” has the same meaning. But, in prophetic fashion, the wording varies, so that it suddenly passes from one person to another.

“And she will follow her lovers,” the Assyrians or Chaldeans, seeking help from them while oppressed by the greatest tribulation. “And she will not overtake them”—that is, she will not obtain their help; indeed, she will be seized by them and led away captive. “And she will seek them and not find them” favorably disposed toward her.

“And she will say: ‘I will go and return to my first husband.’” That is, I will return to Almighty God, who once betrothed me through the Law he gave. “For it was better for me then,” as long as I obeyed his commandments, “and better still now,” when I am afflicted by various tribulations because of the worship of idols.

That Israelite people, raised up by prosperity, often withdrew from God by worshiping idols. Then, afflicted by calamities, it returned to God, who raised up a savior for them and delivered them. These words also apply to us both generally and particularly: raised up by prosperity, we sometimes transgress God’s commandments. Then, crushed by afflictions, we return to ourselves, recognize that we have sinned, and flee to the mercy of him under whose protection we remember that we were well off.

This often happens to those who, living in the world, desire its riches and honors. When they cannot attain them, they are so distressed by various tribulations that, willingly or unwillingly, they leave the world. Setting aside temporal concerns, which they cannot obtain according to their desire, they take refuge in a monastery. Those who were previously saddened because they did not possess everything they wanted rejoice to be content, according to the Apostle, with food and clothing and to serve God in poverty—those who had previously served the world and its desires.

“And she did not know that I gave her grain and wine and oil, and multiplied silver for her, which they made into Baal.” It was said above that the Israelite people attributed to idols all the temporal goods it had received from God, not knowing that Almighty God had caused it to abound in all these things. Therefore, having abandoned God, they made from the gold and silver they had received for ornament and adornment an idol of Baal of the Sidonians, which the prophet Ezekiel describes more fully in his book.

If we wish to understand these words spiritually, by grain we should understand the Law, by which they ought to have been nourished; by wine, spiritual joy, which they ought to have possessed not in temporal goods but in God; by oil, illumination of understanding; by silver, the brightness of eloquence, concerning which it is written: “Silver tested by fire: the words of the Lord are pure words”; and by gold, the commandment to love God and one’s neighbor. Although they ought to have glorified God in all these things, they preferred to worship demons rather than God.

“Therefore,” says the Lord, “I will turn”—namely, from my clemency to severity—“and take away my grain in its time, and my wine in its time.” The time of these crops is when, brought to maturity, they are gathered and stored in cellars to provide food throughout the year. If, however, at that time—when maturity is at hand—they are taken away from those who ought to have gathered them, the people are afflicted with the greatest grief. He threatens that he will take these things away from the Jews, so that they may suffer famine throughout the year. For often, because of human sins, God sends storms at harvesttime and at the vintage, taking away the fruits prepared for gathering.

“And I will free my wool and my flax, which covered her shame.” Some manuscripts falsely read *librabo* (“I will weigh out”); therefore *liberabo* (“I will free”) must be read. It is as though they held the flax and wool under their own servitude, although they themselves were servants of the devil. Therefore God says: “I will free my flax and my wool,” so that they may not be possessed by wicked masters. The shame that these things covered is understood as their idols, whose altars they adorned with the varied ornament of garments.

Spiritually, these garments signify God’s help and the protection of the angels. God removes all these things from them, so that those who had not recognized the giver through them may be handed over, abandoned in their iniquity, to the devil to be eternally tormented.

“And then I will reveal her folly in the eyes of her lovers.” He calls the idols that they had placed in the temple “folly.” By her lovers he means the Chaldeans, Assyrians, and Idumeans, with whom they had long maintained peace. The folly of the Jews was revealed in their eyes when Jerusalem was captured and the temple destroyed, and when these same enemies saw the images of the Cherubim and the idol of Baal. They began to say: “Behold, the Israelites, like all nations, worship idols; therefore, deservedly because of their iniquity, they are subjected to our power.”

“And no man will rescue her from my hand.” That is, she will not be able to escape from my hand through anyone’s strength or power. Rather, I will hand her over to the enemies by a just judgment and cause her to be led into captivity.

“And I will cause all her joy to cease.” This was fulfilled in those who were led captive by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, where they lost all their joy. It was fulfilled afterward in those who heard from the Lord: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you,” and: “Your house will be left to you desolate.”

“Her solemnity, her new moon, her sabbath, and all her festivals of the seasons”—the words “I will cause to cease” are understood. When he says “solemnity,” he uses one term for all. Or certainly, by this particular name he wishes the festival of Passover to be understood, which they used to celebrate honorably in memory of their liberation. He calls the new moon the renewal of the moon, because at the beginning of each month they joyfully observed such a festival. On the Sabbaths they also devoted themselves to leisure and feasting. They had other festivals as well: Pentecost, the solemnity of Tabernacles, the dedication of the temple, and others like them. All these were taken away from them when, placed in captivity, they were neither permitted to celebrate the aforesaid festivals joyfully according to their rite nor to devote themselves to leisure. All these things, taken away from them then, are now celebrated spiritually in the Church.

“And I will corrupt her vine and her fig tree”—with hail, drought, and frost, so that she may have no fruitful tree. Spiritually, by the vine he signifies joy of heart; by the fig tree we must understand sweetness and pleasantness. These were taken away from them, and therefore they remain in grief and bitterness. Concerning them he said: “These are my wages, which my lovers gave me.” He gives the reason why he had previously taken away the goods mentioned: she said, “These are my wages,” and so forth. For she thought that these things had been given to her by the demons as payment because she worshiped idols.

“And I will make her into a forest,” so that she may no longer have fruit-bearing trees but may be utterly reduced to solitude. This was partly accomplished by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, but it is known to have been fulfilled more completely by the Romans, who devastated their land and reduced it to solitude, making the people themselves exiles from their land through the final captivity.

Hence what follows: “And the beast of the field will devour her”—that is, the Roman army. Concerning this beast the Psalmist says: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it.” Alternatively, we may understand this beast as the devil, who devoured them when he drew them into his worship, for which they afterward suffered destruction.

What has been said about the Jews may also be understood of heretics. When they leave the Church and are abandoned by God, their folly is revealed to those who were formerly their lovers. Handed over to the beast—that is, the devil—and torn by his bites, they are punished by everlasting death.

“And I will visit upon her the days of the Baals, when she burned incense, adorned herself with her earring and her necklace, went after her lovers, and forgot me, says the Lord.” He still preserves the character of a prostitute, who adorns herself with gold and jewels to please her lovers and acquires by art whatever beauty she does not possess by nature.

“I will visit,” he says, “upon her the days of the Baals”—that is, in return for the days on which she worshiped Baal, I will bring upon her the affliction of tribulation. Here visitation is understood in a negative sense, namely, as the distress of tribulation, slaughter, and captivity that came upon the Jews because of their worship of idols. Elsewhere visitation is used in a positive sense, as in: “The dawn from on high has visited us,” and: “Visit us with your salvation.”

“I will visit upon her,” unquestionably meaning Judea, “the days of the Baals,” namely, the days on which she burned incense not to God but to demons. *Baal* is the singular form, while *Baalim* is the plural form for these same idols, in the masculine gender. Wherever the syllable *-im* occurs at the end of a Hebrew word, it indicates the masculine plural. Where *-oth* occurs, as in *Sabaoth*, it indicates the feminine plural. Thus *cherubim* and *seraphim* are masculine plurals, whereas *Sabaoth*, interpreted as “of armies,” “of hosts,” or “of powers,” is feminine plural.

Therefore *Baalim* is masculine plural, although some incorrectly read it as feminine. The Jewish people adorned its ear and its necklace to please its lovers, that is, the demons. It ought to have adorned its ears so that it might conceive God’s spiritual commandments in its heart, and its neck so that it might proclaim them to others. But it did these things because, following demons, it forgot God, who ought to have been its husband.

Heretics, however, offered incense to the Baals when they followed the perverse doctrines that they themselves fashioned for themselves as idols. They adorn their ears, by which words are heard, and their neck, by which they are uttered, so that through the beauty of their speech they may please those whom they have captured. By necklaces, too, divine words are understood, concerning which it is said to the Church: “Your neck is like necklaces.” They would not do these things unless they had forgotten God.

“For this reason, behold, I will allure her, and lead her into the wilderness.” Because the Lord is merciful and compassionate, although he threatened the foregoing evils, so that this same people might not despair he promises it salvation, saying: “For this reason”—namely, because I am merciful—“I will allure her,” that is, I will speak gently to her so that she may return to me. Hence it is said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near”; and: “Come to me, all you who labor,” and so forth.

“And I will lead her into the wilderness”—that is, I will free her again from captivity, just as I previously led her out of Egyptian slavery. And just as then I led them through the wilderness, protecting and delivering them from every enemy, so I will act when I bring them back from the land of their captivity to the soil of their own birth.

“And I will speak to her heart”—that is, I will speak gentle and consoling words to her, so that I may relieve her sadness with joy. This is what “speaking to the heart” means. Hence it is said: “Shechem spoke to Dinah’s heart”; and Joseph, after he was recognized by his brothers, is said to have spoken to their hearts. This was fulfilled when the Son of God, who speaks here through the Prophet, appeared in the flesh and said to the apostles—or rather, to all his disciples from that people who believed in him: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends.” He also calls them children, saying: “Little children, I am still with you.”

“And I will give her vine-dressers from that same place.” Isaiah shows what this vine is when he says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” David likewise says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” Vine-dressers were given to this vine, first when it came out of Egypt: Moses and Aaron, and the others who at that time cultivated the same vineyard through good work in word and example. Then, when it returned from Chaldean captivity: Zerubbabel, Jesus, and Nehemiah, together with Ezra and the other prophets, who proved to be its good cultivators.

Afterward, at his coming, he gave it the best vine-dressers: namely, the apostles, who were all from the same place—that is, from the same Israelite people.

“And the valley of Achor for opening hope.” Here we must recall the history of old. We read in the Book of Joshua son of Nun that, when the children of Israel had captured Jericho, Joshua placed it under the ban, together with everything in it. Achan son of Carmi, seeing among the spoils of the city certain things that pleased him, took them from what had been devoted to destruction. When the children of Israel could not withstand their enemies and had consulted the Lord about this, the Lord answered that they had been handed over because of what Achan had done. Joshua therefore had him stoned by all the children of Israel. The place of his killing was called the valley of Achor, that is, the valley of trouble, because Joshua had said: “Because you have troubled us, may the Lord trouble you on this day.”

After his death, hope of future victory was opened to the children of Israel. They went on and captured the town of Ai, killing its inhabitants; their sorrow was turned into joy, and they received hope precisely where there had been despair.

But since this event, as has been said, is known to have occurred, let us see what the prophetic words mean, since he prophesies these things as future, saying: “And the valley of Achor for opening hope.” We must therefore understand that, just as at that time the Jews took hope of conquering their enemies after Achan had been killed and were not disappointed in it, so, after Jerusalem had been destroyed by the Romans, the temple burned, and the Jews themselves killed and scattered captive throughout the whole world, hope of victory was opened to the apostles and the other believers. For they subjected the whole world to the faith of Christ, and they turned into spiritual understanding what had gone before in shadow—that is, that temple and the observance of all the ceremonies—as is now practiced in the Church by the faithful.

This was their hope of victory, of which it is said here: “And the valley of Achor for opening hope”; “I will give” is understood.

“And she will sing there as in the days of her youth and as in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt.” Here too he preserves the likeness of the historical account. In Exodus we read that, after Pharaoh and his cavalry had been submerged in the Red Sea, the children of Israel sang a song to the Lord, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord,” and so forth.

That period is called the days of her youth because at that time the same people grew in faith and worship of God; previously they had worshiped idols, namely, the calves of the Egyptians. Later they fashioned a calf and said: “These are your gods, Israel,” and so forth.

It is appropriately said: “As in the days of her ascent from the land of Egypt,” because Egypt lies on a plain while the land of promise is mountainous. Therefore, when they went from Egypt to Judea, they are said to have ascended, just as the Lord frequently says to them: “I caused you to ascend from the land of Egypt.”

But let us now examine the mystery. Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness” or “sorrow,” signifies the unbelief of the Jews. The Red Sea signifies baptism, which is consecrated by faith in the Lord’s Passion. Pharaoh and his army, submerged in the Red Sea, signify the devil and original sins, which are submerged in baptism. That wilderness through which they passed after the Red Sea, where they were fed with manna and water from the rock and finally reached the land of promise, represented the present life. In it the faithful receive manna and water from the rock—that is, the body and blood of Christ, or the teaching of the divine word.

The land of promise signifies the heavenly homeland, to which one reaches after baptism and the labor of this life. The Synagogue of believers is therefore promised that, just as then the children of Israel, after the destruction of Pharaoh, sang a song to the Lord when they had believed and come out of Egypt, so it too, having come out of the darkness of unbelief after the death of the devil and the crushing of vices, will pass with spiritual joy and gladness to the heavenly homeland, where the land of the living is.

They are rightly said to ascend as they go from Egypt, because we ascend well when we strive to pass from earthly things to heavenly things and from vices to virtues.

[Col. 0024D] “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that every man will call me ‘my husband,’ and will no longer call me Baalim. And I will remove the name of Baalim from her mouth, and she will no longer remember their name.” Concerning the name Baalim, according to the literal sense, this must be said: Belus was the father of Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians. Ninus named after himself the city which he built, Ninus, which the Hebrews and our people call Nineveh. Making his father Belus into a god, he made an image which he wished to be called Bel and worshiped by all. By this name he is called by the Babylonians, as is read in Daniel; by the Sidonians and Phoenicians, however, Baal; but by the Hebrews he is called Beelzebub, because of the filth and dirt of sacrificial blood—that is, “lord of flies,” or “having flies.” Because he was worshiped in many places, he is therefore designated in the plural as Baalim.

But now let us see what these words of the Lord signify, spoken concerning the faithful people: “She will no longer call me Baalim.” Baalim, as we have said, is the same as Baal and means “having”; Baalim means “having me.” Hence Hebrew and Syrian women call their husbands by this name, saying, “My Baal,” that is, “the one having me”; and the sense is, “having me in marriage.” There is another name in the same language with the same meaning, namely Is, which likewise means “man” or “husband.” Hence a woman is called Issa by them, as though “woman from man,” because she was taken from her husband. Therefore women who do not wish to say Baal or Baalim of their husbands call them by the other name, “my Is,” that is, “my husband,” namely, the one having me in marriage. What the Lord therefore says here—“she will not call me Baalim, but will call me my husband”—must be understood thus: wishing to show me as her husband, she will by no means call me Baalim, though that could properly be said, but will call me Is, that is, “my husband.” God so greatly hates the names of idols that he does not even wish his elect to remember their names. Therefore he says of the faithful people: “She will no longer call me Baalim,” because of the ambiguity of the word, lest, while saying one thing, she remember another, and, in naming a husband, think of an idol. Hence it is added: “And I will remove the names of Baalim from her mouth, and she will no longer remember their name.”

“And I will make a covenant with them in that day, with the beast of the field, with the bird of the air, and with the creeping thing of the earth.” Here the union of Jews and Gentiles in the unity of Christ’s faith is openly described; before his coming they were at odds with one another. Thus the Jews excluded the Gentiles from their fellowship; but afterward, assembling into Christ’s one fold, they now glory in possessing peace and brotherly love in the one faith of Almighty God. Hence Isaiah says to the same people: “Your former stranger will be joined to you,” so that he may no longer be a stranger but be recognized as a brother. Under the names of beasts, birds, and serpents are denoted the Gentiles, who worshiped these as gods. Purified from this, however, they are no longer called by these names but rational human beings. Thus, when Peter saw the sheet sent down to him from heaven, in which beasts, birds, and serpents were shown, and heard that he ought to kill and eat them, he replied: “Far be it from me, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” He was told: “What God has purified, do not call common.”

[Col. 0025D] “And I will break bow and sword and war from the earth.” That is, I will grant supreme peace and tranquillity on earth, that is, in the Church. Although many wars rage on earth, nevertheless, in comparison with that time there is great peace among human beings, especially among the elect, among whom no seedbed of discord finds a place. Isaiah says of this time: “Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they train any longer for war.” “And I will make them sleep in confidence,” that is, I will make them rest securely in my faith and peace. Or certainly, this sleep means the repose of the elect, who now sleep peacefully in hope of the future resurrection.

“And I will betroth you to myself forever; and I will betroth [Col. 0026A] you to myself in righteousness and judgment, and in mercy and compassions; and I will betroth you to myself in faith; and you shall know that I am the Lord.” It should be observed that he promises three times to betroth the same people to himself. First he betrothed her in Abraham, to whom he gave the seal of circumcision, that it might be a sign forever between God and his seed; or also when he led her out of Egypt. Second, on Mount Sinai, when he gave her the Law. Hence in the second place it is said: “I will betroth you to myself in righteousness,” that is, in observance of the Law, “and in judgment” of my commandments, so that you might both live righteously and know discernment between good and evil; “and in mercy and compassions,” so that, if because of your sins you were handed over into captivity and repented, you might again obtain mercy. Third, at the coming of the Son of God, whence it is also said here: “And I will betroth you to myself in faith,” namely, in faith in the holy Trinity. Of this betrothal the Apostle says, speaking of Christ: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” Again, speaking in the person of Christ, he says: “He betrothed to himself the Church, not having spot or wrinkle.”

But the Synagogue, betrothed three times by the Lord, made every betrothal void. Since, betrothed in Egypt, she did not keep the first betrothal and there committed fornication by worshiping foreign gods, she is again taken up through the Law and the sacred Scriptures of the prophets of the Old Testament, so that, strengthened as though by a second betrothal, she might no longer depart from the embrace. Thirdly, Jesus Christ the Son of God wished to unite her to himself through the grace of the holy Gospel; but, while few believed, the greater part of them, disregarding the offered betrothal gifts, remained in unbelief, as blessed Stephen reproaches them, saying: “You always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did.” But those who received his faith were joined to him by the bond of love, believing that he was Christ God, whom they had formerly denied. Among these were those who believed at the preaching of blessed Peter—five thousand on one day and three thousand on another.

“And it shall be in that day: I will hear, says the Lord, and I will hear the heavens, and they will hear the earth, and the earth will hear the grain, the wine, and the oil, and these will hear Jezreel.” According to the letter, the words may be understood thus: the Lord promises these temporal goods to those who believe in him. Spiritually, the heavens are the apostles, of whom the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God,” and so forth. These heavens were heard at the time of the Lord’s incarnation, when they prayed for the Canaanite woman and for Peter’s mother-in-law. These heavens now hear the earth, that is, the people dwelling in the Church; and this earth hears the grain, that is, it brings forth the plain teaching of the Old and New Testament, so that the Lord’s saying may be fulfilled: “Blessed is that servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of grain in due season.” It hears the wine; that is, it imparts spiritual understanding so that its teaching may gladden the hearts of its hearers. For the speech of teachers ought to be shaped according to the capacity of their hearers. [Col. 0027A] It also hears the oil, because in bishops and presbyters it gives the faithful the grace of the Holy Spirit. This is the heaven and the earth: namely, the apostles and the universal Church. And these will hear Jezreel—that is, they will bring the seed of God’s Word to the effect of action, so that that seed may yield fruit, one hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold. But what follows:

“And I will sow her in the lands.” This applies especially to the apostles, who were sown from Jerusalem, so that by their preaching and miracles they might make the land—that is, the hearts of their hearers—fruitful. Of them it is written: “These are the seed whom the Lord has blessed.” For the apostles themselves are both seed, because they were scattered throughout the whole world, hearing from the Lord, “Go into the whole world,” and so forth; and sowers, according to the saying: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” and so forth. “And I will have mercy on her who was without mercy,” that is, on the Synagogue now believing in me, which previously, while it wandered amid many demonic wonders and worshiped them as gods, was without mercy.

“And I will say to the one who was not my people: ‘You are my people’; and he will say to me: ‘You are my Lord.’” This is what he himself says to his faithful from that same people: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom.” And he says: “You are my God,” as Peter too says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”; and Thomas: “My Lord and my God.” [Col. 0027C] These words can be referred both particularly to the ten tribes and generally to all Israelites, namely, to those who believed.

CHAPTER III.

“And the Lord said to me: Go again, love a woman beloved by her friend and an adulteress, just as the Lord loves the children of Israel, while they look to foreign gods and love grape cakes.” By these two women—namely, the former harlot, who is called Gomer, and this one, who is called an adulteress—we should understand Israel and Judah: that is, the ten tribes, which were in Samaria under King Jeroboam, who was of Ephraim; and Judah, which reigned in Jerusalem from the line of David. Ezekiel describes these two women under the names of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah. If we wish to distinguish them more carefully, we may understand the ten tribes by the first, who is called a harlot, and Judah by the second, who is called an adulteress. Yet, generally, the whole Israelite people, as will also be shown in what follows, may be understood by both the one and the other.

According to the letter, what he says, “Go again,” and so forth, must be understood thus: the sense is this: you indeed love her, but she does not love you in the due return; rather, neglecting your love, she is an adulteress because she is joined to another husband and loves him more than you. What these things concern is made clear when it is added: “Just as the Lord loves the children of Israel.” That is, just as you love that woman, though she loves another more than you, so the Lord loves the children of Israel with the highest love; but they, despising him, “look to foreign gods”—that is, they venerate and worship them—“and love grape cakes.” He calls grape cakes what we call grape skins, that is, the husks of grapes thrown away from the press after they have been squeezed.

Spiritually, however, by these grape cakes are understood demons, who, so long as they were in their dignity, were in some manner grapes, that is, filled with the richness of the Holy Spirit. But after, in their pride against God, they wished to become like him, emptied of the grace of the Holy Spirit, they became barren and, as though useful for nothing, were cast down from heaven; withered in their old dryness, they possess nothing of their former grace. So too the Jews, abandoned by God because of unbelief, love demons emptied of every sweetness of goodness. Or by grape cakes we may understand the traditions of the scribes and Pharisees, wholly empty of the meaning of truth and full of superstition; the Jews loved these, abandoning the traditions of God for human traditions.

“Then I dug her for myself for fifteen silver pieces, a homer of barley, and half a homer of barley, and I said to her.” The Seventy translators, as blessed Jerome says, rendered what our translation has as “I dug” by “I hired,” which certainly pertains to the woman, since she is hired for this purpose: that she might keep faith with her husband and not join herself to another while he is alive. But when he says, “I dug her for myself as a woman,” he shows that he wishes to signify a vineyard, which—as the prophet testifies—is the house of Israel, concerning which it is written: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt.” This woman, therefore, is dug and hired for fifteen silver pieces, a homer of barley, and half a homer of barley—that is, for forty-five *modii*, since a homer contains thirty *modii*, while half a homer contains fifteen. Having been hired for this payment, she heard from the Lord: “For many days you shall wait for me; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man.” That is: “You shall neither prostitute yourself shamefully to lovers nor join yourself to me, the legitimate husband by whom you were hired. And do not think that an injustice has been done to you, because I said, ‘You shall wait for me’; I shall repay you in kind, because ‘I also shall wait for you.’”

Mystically, the fifteen denarii refer to the fifteenth day of the first month, that is, Nisan, on which the Jews went out of Egypt after the firstborn of the Egyptians had been struck down. On that very day, the fifteenth lunar day, the Lord brought them out of Egypt and hired them into his own service, freeing them through the slaughter of the lamb from the plague inflicted upon the Egyptians. He began to instruct them, ordering that five silver shekels be contributed as an offering to the house of God in place of the firstborn of their sons, who had not suffered the common plague. Then, on the forty-fifth day—represented by the forty-five *modii* of barley—they reached Mount Sinai. On the following day Moses was commanded to sanctify them for three days, to abstain from women, and to prepare themselves to receive the Law. After the three days had passed, on the fiftieth day Moses received the Decalogue of the Law. Since, therefore, they reached on the forty-fifth day the place where they received the Law, it is rightly reported that they were hired for forty-five *modii* of barley.

What follows—“For many days you shall wait for me”—refers to the present time, during which the Jewish people, once hired for fifteen silver pieces and forty-five *modii* of barley, await, after the incarnation of the Lord, that is, of the same bridegroom, the coming of their husband, until—as the Apostle says—“the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and so all Israel is saved.” But when he says, “You shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man,” he shows that meanwhile the people neither serve idols nor yet possess God; they have been stripped both of their lovers and of their husband. And because they have no husband, they do not now eat the food of human beings, that is, grain, but the barley of irrational beasts, since they do not grasp the life-giving spiritual sense but follow the letter that kills. What is added—“but I also shall wait for you”—pertains to those who await the time when, at the end of the age, believers from among the Jews will be received into Christ’s embrace, when from Jews and Gentiles there will be one flock with one shepherd, who says of himself: “I am the good shepherd.”

“For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without an ephod, and without *theraphim*.” The Jews refer all these things to the seventy years of their captivity. But it is better, as blessed Jerome says, to understand what is said as referring to the present time, or to the Jews’ final conversion. For these words already contain what was said above: “For many days you shall wait for me; you shall not commit fornication.” Now the Jews sit—that is, they dwell—contracted and bent down, because they have lost the uprightness of their condition. They are without the king Christ, who says: “But I have been appointed king by him”; and without a prince, that is, without the Savior himself, or also without the pontiff and priest of whom it is written: “You shall not curse the prince of your people.”

They are also “without sacrifice and without an altar,” because, having lost the place where they had possessed the temple and altar, concerning which the Law commanded them, “In the place that the Lord will choose, you shall sacrifice to him, and not in every place,” they no longer offer lawful victims. “And without an ephod.” Properly, *ephod* is called the shoulder-garment, but here it is taken for every garment. At times it is also used for linen clothing, as we read concerning Samuel, because he was dressed in a linen ephod. *Theraphim* properly means figures and images. In the present passage, however, it cannot refer merely to cherubim and seraphim, or to the other things ordered to be made as ornaments in the temple; rather, let us understand it here as referring to every priestly ornament.

After the Jews lost all these things, they were given to us spiritually in the Church. We have Christ as the true king and priest, who “is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” We have the true sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood. We also have the ephod, that is, the garment of innocence and simplicity, since we ourselves have been made priests and kings, according to what Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.” We also have the *theraphim*, that is, the sign and expressed remembrance of God in our hearts, according to what we sing to him: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us.”

“And after this the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king.” “After this,” that is, after all these things have been fulfilled, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the children of Israel will return through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch. They will seek the Lord their God and David their king, that is, the Father and his Son Jesus Christ, confessing with heart, mouth, and deed that his Son is the one God.

“And they shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the last of the days.” This means the Holy Spirit, who is not outside the Father and the Son but, together with the Father and the Son, is one God. Of him he says to his disciples: “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him!”

## CHAPTER IV

“Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a judgment with the inhabitants of the land.” These words properly concern those who were found at the coming of the Son of God, although in the literal sense they can also be applied to those who at that time were dwelling among the ten and two tribes. To them the prophet speaks these words, showing that God was not angry without cause when he threatened and inflicted the grievous punishments described above, so that they would be without a king and without the other things in which they had hitherto gloried.

But because they were without truth, without mercy, and without the knowledge of God, and because curse, falsehood, murder, and many other things had inundated them, all these things were taken away from the inhabitants of that land by God’s just judgment, and they themselves were handed over to captivity, adding sins to sins and piling old offenses upon new ones. As we have said, these words refer especially to those who saw and heard God in the flesh but refused to believe in him, and also to their descendants.

He says to them: “Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, for the Lord has a judgment with the inhabitants of the land,” that is, with the Jews who always desire earthly things. Opposed to them are those who are called heavenly, who, considering themselves pilgrims and strangers in this life, strive toward heavenly things. With these inhabitants of the land he conducts judgment—that is, he promises to hand them over to eternal condemnation.

He explains why he will do this, adding: “There is no truth,” but each person speaks falsehood with his neighbor. Or there is no truth because the one who says of himself, “I am the truth,” does not dwell in their hearts. “And there is no mercy,” because they persecute their subjects and show no compassion to the orphan and the widow. Hence they did not spare Christ himself, but like the most rabid dogs they opened their mouths against him, saying, “He is guilty of death,” and, “Crucify him, crucify him!”

“And there is no knowledge of God.” That is, faith in and knowledge of God’s name are not in the hearts of those who have taste only for earthly things. Or it means the knowledge—that is, the wisdom—of God the Father, who says of himself through Solomon: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present among learned thoughts.” Concerning him the Apostle says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.” He does not dwell on earth, that is, he does not rest in the minds of those who are alienated from faith in him. Concerning them it continues:

“Curse, falsehood, murder, theft, and adultery have inundated.” “Curse” refers to the insults and reproaches of those who raged against God, saying, “You have a demon,” and, “You are a Samaritan,” and other things of this kind. “Falsehood” refers to what they said: “He is guilty of death,” and, “This man is a glutton and a wine-drinker.” “Murder” refers to the fact that they handed him over to death, as well as all the prophets, as he himself reproaches them, saying: “And you fill up the measure of your fathers. Behold, I am sending you prophets and wise men and scribes,” and so forth. Blessed Stephen likewise says: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become.”

“Theft” refers to the fact that they robbed themselves and their children, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Or it refers to the time when they secretly bought Christ for thirty pieces of silver. “Adultery” refers to impurity or idolatry. All these things had inundated the Jews, that is, had abounded among them. By the word “inundation” he displays the enormity of their crimes.

“And blood has touched blood.” Blood touches blood when murder is joined to murder and sin is increased by sin. For the name “blood” signifies sin, as in the passage: “Deliver me from bloodshed.”

“Therefore the land shall mourn, and everyone who dwells in it shall grow weak, together with the beast of the field and the bird of the sky; and the fish of the sea shall also be gathered together.” “Therefore,” because the vices mentioned above have inundated the place of good works, the land shall mourn. The land appears to mourn when it remains uncultivated after its inhabitants have been removed, and when it begins to produce brambles and thorns though previously it brought forth joyful fruits of its own.

Thus, in this passage the desolation of the ten and two tribes is expressed when it says, “The land shall mourn.” Or by “the land” we can understand the Jews themselves, seeking the earth and having an earthly mind. Hence it immediately follows: “And everyone who dwells in it shall grow weak,” that is, everyone who remains there through love and desire. When they were seized by their enemies, they mourned and grew weak because they were losing the things they had loved with the greatest love and in which they had gloried.

“With the beast of the field and the bird of the sky.” It is natural, as blessed Jerome says, that if the land is abandoned by its inhabitants, the beasts and birds should also depart from it. In a higher sense, by the beasts of the field he signifies savage peoples, weighed down by beastlike stupidity. By the birds we can understand the proud, haughty, and frivolous, such as the Jews themselves were—boasting of the dignity of their merits and despising others. By the fish of the sea, they may appropriately be understood who lived in the depths of vices and in the darkness of sins. Or by the fish we may understand the philosophers of the world, laboring to investigate the profound questions of temporal matters.
