“The fish of the sea shall be gathered together,” implicitly, for death. Hence another translation has: “The fish of the sea shall fail.”

“Nevertheless, let no one judge, and let no man be reproved.” Above, he had summoned them to judgment so that they might recognize that they had been judged according to truth and not oppressed by God’s power, but handed over to their enemies because of their past sins. But because they had become worse, they were so lacking in understanding that even when convicted they felt no shame. He forbids the unjust to be judged and reproved by the just, because they are unworthy to receive correction.

“Let no just person,” he says, “judge the unjust, and let no pious man reprove the impious,” since, given the enormity of their crimes, the impious and unjust do not deserve this. “For your people are like those who contradict the priest.” The meaning is: Just as the common people are disobedient to the priest, refusing to obey his commands, and just as a disciple is disobedient to his teacher, so your people contradict the words of my mouth. Therefore they are not worthy to be reproved either by the prophet or by any just person.

“And you shall fall today, and the prophet also shall fall with you.” Above he spoke to the prophet about the people; now he turns his speech to the people themselves, namely, the ten tribes, saying: “You shall fall today,” that is, in the present time, or certainly in the clear light and before everyone’s eyes you shall be led into captivity.

“And the prophet also shall fall with you.” We can understand “prophet” here in two ways: either a false prophet—for the word is ambiguous—or the prophetic dignity itself, because we do not read that the ten tribes had a prophet after the captivity. For as long as the ten tribes had not been captured, they had the prophets Elijah and Elisha and the other sons of the prophets, who prophesied in Samaria. The two tribes, moreover, had prophets during the captivity itself and afterward. But after the ten tribes had been transferred to the Medes and Persians, no prophet is reported to have existed among them. Therefore it is said to them: “The prophet also shall fall with you,” that is, the prophetic dignity shall perish from you; or the false prophets who were explaining false prophecy to you shall perish together with you.

“And I have made your mother silent by night.” “Mother” refers to the Jewish people in general. The children of this mother are either the individual members of the people or those who were scattered through the towns and villages. Therefore, in the night—that is, in the darkness of captivity, sorrow, and oppressive distress—I made your mother silent, because she did not dare mourn her misfortune before her enemies.

“My people has become silent because it has had no knowledge.” That is, after being seized by their enemies, they wasted away in silence, not daring to resist them. The reason is given why this happened to them: because they had no knowledge of the Law of God and had not kept God’s commandments, so as to serve him and despise idols. Because they had previously closed their mouths against the praises of God, they justly came to this misery, that they did not even dare to lament their misfortune among their enemies.

“Because you rejected knowledge, I shall reject you, so that you shall not serve as priest to me.” The people themselves rejected knowledge—that is, God—when, with a most foolish mind, they began to worship the work of their hands. Abandoning the Maker of heaven and earth, they venerated golden calves at Dan and Bethel. Therefore they were rejected, so that there would be no priests from among them in the house of the Lord, but rather in the shrines of idols.

“And you have forgotten the Law of your God,” which forbids the worship of foreign gods. “I also shall forget your children,” handing them over to eternal captivity and showing them no mercy, as I once showed mercy to their fathers in the wilderness. For whoever does not know shall not be known.

All these things can also be referred to heretics, who abandoned the house of David and Jerusalem, that is, Christ and the Church. Therefore, covered by eternal night, they are silent regarding the praises of God, as it is written: “But in hell, who will confess you?” This is because they did not have the knowledge of God, that is, Christ, so as to believe his true faith. Hence they are rightly rejected by the Lord, so that they may not serve him as priests.

They are rejected from his priesthood because such people are often removed from this life by premature death and perish eternally, lest, unworthily handling the Lord’s body and blood, they become an occasion of stumbling to others, or, by living longer, become the cause of the destruction of many through their evil teaching. Their children are also said to be forgotten by God—that is, those generated by their perverse teaching—because they will be handed over to perpetual condemnation together with their fathers.

“According to the multitude of them, so they sinned against me.” That is, as many people as Israel had, so many altars it built for demons, and in the sacrifices offered upon them they sinned against me.

“I shall change their glory into shame.” He calls their idol their glory, in which they gloried and in whose worship they rejoiced. It was then changed into shame, because for that very crime they were led into captivity together with it.

“They shall eat the sins of my people.” This sentence is to be understood in two ways. “The priests shall eat the sins of the people,” that is, the sacrifices offered for human sins. For the sacrifices that were offered then, or that are now offered in the temple of the Lord, pass into the use of the priests. Hence the canons also say that laypeople should not eat of consecrated things.

But those who eat the alms of others, unless they pray worthily for them, are also like the Jews. Those who pray worthily for them live by the works of their hands. Or “the priests shall eat the sins of the people” because, when they flatter those who do evil, they take their sins upon themselves. Whoever consents to another’s sins becomes a participant in those sins. For when they see others sinning, they not only fail to reprove them but also exalt the sinners with praises. Hence it follows: “And they shall lift up their souls toward their iniquity.”

While the people were serving sins, the priests lifted up their souls, saying: “You are the people of God; you have descended from the race of Abraham. Because of his friendship, God will spare you if you sin against him.” Taking confidence from these words, the people sinned boldly, lifted up in pride. Or the priests deceived sinners by false flattery, saying: “Your sins have been forgiven.” Thus they lifted up their souls, because the people believed their words more than their own consciences and, although they were sinners, considered themselves just. Hence the saying: “My people, those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you.”

“And it shall be: like people, like priest.” That is, because they sin equally, they will equally endure the sentence of the indignant God. These priests, to whom the Lord predicts that evils will come just as they will come upon the people, were not from the tribe of Levi. Rather, coming from any tribe, they filled their hands with gold or silver, gave gifts to the kings of the ten tribes, and became priests in the temples of idols.

Any priest or prelate who takes the evils of others upon himself by flattering them likewise becomes their equal, and therefore will be condemned together with them. “And I shall visit his ways upon him”—that is, upon the priest. I shall punish all his works, because here “I shall visit” means affliction and torment. “And I shall repay his thoughts to him,” because they will pay the penalty not only for evil deeds but also for the worst thoughts by which they planned to do such things.

The meaning concerning heretics is straightforward: the more numerous they were, the more they sinned against the Lord, and according to their number they multiplied various doctrines of error. Their glory—that is, the dignity of wisdom and Christianity—is changed into shame when, by God’s just judgment, they are allowed to fall into various errors on account of their past sins, and are finally handed over to eternal punishments for them. Concerning them the Apostle says: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting.”

They eat the sins of the people when they speak pleasing words, deceive the hearts of believers through sweet speeches, and devour widows’ houses. When they see others sinning, they say: “God seeks nothing else but the truth of faith. If you preserve that, he does not care what you do,” misunderstanding the Lord’s saying: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” While they say these things, they lift up the souls of sinners in their iniquities, so that they not only fail to repent or humble themselves but even rejoice in their crimes and walk with their necks held high. Thus people and priest—that is, those who were taught and those who taught—will be bound by the same judgment, when the due punishments have been repaid to them not only for their deeds but also for their evil thoughts.

“And they shall eat, and shall not be satisfied,” that is, they shall practice evil works and shall not be filled, because the lustful and the greedy will never be satisfied with their wickedness. By contrast: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” These are the ones concerning whom the Prophet says: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied.”

For just as righteousness satisfies, so iniquity, having no substance, deceives those who eat through empty fraud and leaves the bellies of those who devour it empty. That is, “They have committed fornication, and they have not ceased.” “To commit fornication” is understood. The skins of perverse people fail in fornication, and the desire to commit fornication does not cease. And because they did not hear, “You have sinned; be still,” they will hear on the day of judgment: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

The ten tribes also committed fornication with idols under Jeroboam son of Nebat, and afterward did not cease worshiping idols. Why was this? “Because they abandoned the Lord by failing to keep him.” The meaning is that, by failing to keep him, they worshiped idols, because they abandoned the Lord their God, unable to serve two masters at once. “By failing to keep him” means, implicitly, failing to keep his commandments, by which he had ordered: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.”

“Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart,” that is, they overturn the human sense and understanding. The meaning is: just as wine and drunkenness make one who drinks excessively incapable of governing his mind, so fornication—whether bodily or spiritual—perverts the understanding, weakens the soul, and turns a rational human being into a brute animal, so that he pursues brothels and haunts of lust, and thinks that wood and stones are gods, worshiping the works of his hands.

“My people”—implicitly, “once”—“inquired of its piece of wood, and its staff announced it.” This was a form of divination performed with wood and staffs, by which they sought omens concerning future events. Hence we read in Ezekiel that “when Nebuchadnezzar was going against Ammon and Jerusalem, he stood at a crossroads, where, among other divinations, he mixed arrows, and among the others one came out against Jerusalem.”

Perhaps these people acted similarly, asking what would be more beneficial for them: whether they should worship God or idols. And because they were so perverse that, abandoning truth, they followed falsehood, God justly abandoned them, and through the response of the staff they were led astray by the devil. Hence it follows: “For the spirit of fornications deceived them, and they committed fornication away from their God,” that is, through idolatry they withdrew from their God.

The spirit of fornications is understood as the devil, who persuades human beings to depart from God and to venerate him in wooden and stone images. The beginning of this fornication is the formation of idols.

These things can also apply to heretics. They are never satisfied with their errors and do not cease from the shame of fornication. Practicing bodily impurity and failing to keep the Law and the other Scriptures, they abandon God, rave and become drunk, and, having lost the vigor of their minds, worship the idols they have fashioned from their own hearts and possess the spirit of fornication.

“They sacrificed on the tops of the mountains and burned incense on the hills.” The children of Israel, following their pleasures and the desires of the flesh, abandoned God and despised his temple. They sacrificed to idols on mountains and hills and burned incense to them—that is, incense of sweetness. There, because of the pleasantness of the places, they ate, drank, slept, and indulged themselves, and they called those same places the high places.

They did these things because they did not have the Most High God. Concerning these high places we read in the Books of Kings: “Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places. For the people were still sacrificing on the high places.” Or they are said to have done these things in high places because they worshiped on the roofs of their houses, following, I think, the custom of the serpent raised up on a pole.

“Under the oak, the poplar, and the terebinth”—“they sacrificed” is understood—“because its shade was good.” The Jews had lost the truth, and therefore they did these things. The Lord had commanded in the Law that sacrifice should be offered only in the place he had chosen. But they, on account of their pleasures, as was said above, sacrificed to idols in delightful places among groves and mountains, making altars under the shade of trees. Attracted by the pleasantness of these places, they practiced the impurity of their flesh. Hence the Lord had forbidden a grove to be planted near his altar.

“Therefore your daughters shall commit fornication.” “With foreigners” is understood; or, abandoning the Lord, they shall worship idols. “And your brides shall commit adultery,” that is, abandoning their own marriage bed, they shall join themselves to others.

“I shall not visit your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery.” Israel had committed fornication by departing from the Lord its God. Therefore its daughters committed fornication and its brides adultery, and they were left to their crime without any punishment, so that through their own grief they might understand God’s grief. He was so angry that he did not strike the offenders.

“I shall not visit your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery,” that is, I shall not punish them for their fornication and adultery, but shall permit them freely to serve their pleasures, so that through the injury done to you you may recognize my injury. I shall not avenge their evils except through the final captivity.

“For they themselves consorted with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men.” He gives the reason why he says that he will not avenge the iniquities of the daughters and wives of the people of Israel. The number of the children of Israel was so great that vengeance had abandoned hope of correction. “They consorted with prostitutes,” he says, “and sacrificed with effeminate men,” practicing shameful acts with women and men in the temples of their gods.

“And the people without understanding”—understanding God or their own sin is implied—“shall be beaten,” that is, worn down by blows and lashes through captivity.

If we wish to understand these things of heretics, their daughters and brides signify the souls whom they generated in error and betrothed to their doctrines. Such people are unworthy of God’s correction, because all their worship is fornication, and the shameful are joined to the shameful. Therefore they will be beaten, so that those who abandoned the Lord may eventually come to their senses through their blows.

“If you commit fornication, Israel, at least let Judah not sin.” As has often been said, “Israel” in this passage signifies the ten tribes, while “Judah” signifies Benjamin and the priestly—that is, the Levitical—tribe joined to it. The prophetic word now exhorts this tribe not to abandon God through the worship of idols, as Israel, that is, the ten tribes, had done by worshiping the idols Jeroboam son of Nebat had made for them.

“If you commit fornication,” he says, “Israel,” which mingled with prostitutes so completely that anyone who filled his hand—whether his own or the king’s, by giving gifts—could become a priest of idols. “At least you, Judah,” who possess Jerusalem and have priests and Levites according to the Law, together with the temple and its lawful ceremonies, do not sin by imitating Israel in worshiping idols.

“And do not enter Gilgal.” Gilgal is the place where the children of Israel, after crossing the Jordan, first pitched their camp. There, after receiving a second circumcision, they purged the idols. Now the tribe of Judah is forbidden to worship them when it is said: “Do not go up to Gilgal,” with the implicit meaning, “to worship gods there, as the Israelites—that is, the ten tribes—do.”

“And do not go up to Beth-aven.” Beth-aven is Bethel, which was formerly called Bethel, that is, “house of the Lord.” But after the worship of idols arose there and Jeroboam placed calves there, it was called “useless house” and “house of the idol.” Hence the Seventy use *domoon*—that is, “house of useless things”—for Beth-aven, because one of the golden calves had been placed there by Jeroboam.

“Do not,” he says, “go up to Beth-aven to sacrifice there,” because it is no longer the house of God but the house of idols.

“Nor shall you swear, ‘As the Lord lives.’” Those who had become worshipers of idols and whose mouths were polluted by praises of demons are forbidden to swear in the Lord’s name. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.” The Lord had commanded in the Law that the Jews should not swear by the names of idols or foreign gods, while permitting them to swear by his own name. For everyone by whom he swears, he either loves or venerates.

Therefore, lest they love or venerate idols, they were forbidden to swear by the names of idols, lest, by mentioning them, they should be enticed into loving and worshiping them. Instead, keeping the name of their God always in their mouths, they were to worship and adore him. But because the Jews themselves had now abandoned God and were worshiping idols, they are forbidden to swear, “As the Lord lives.” This was an oath among them, as Elijah said: “As the Lord lives, before whose presence I stand.” We read very often that they used this oath.

“Nor shall you swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’” as if he were saying: “I do not want mention of me to be made by your mouth, since it has been polluted by the worship of idols.”

“For Israel has turned aside like a wanton cow; now the Lord shall pasture them like a lamb in a broad place.” A wanton cow is called proud because of excessive fatness; it refuses to accept the yoke and, goaded by the gadfly, leaves the straight path of the furrow. So Israel—that is, the ten tribes—shook the yoke of the Law from its neck and, stirred by a demonic spirit, seized the broad road by following its pleasures, concerning which the Lord says: “Broad is the way that leads to destruction.”

“Now he shall pasture them,” as above. Here the prophet’s voice speaks about the same people. Since he had begun to speak of the wanton cow, he preserves the metaphor in what follows, saying that in the broadness of the fields God would pasture the Israelites like a lamb.

“Now,” he says—that is, in the present time, while the spirit governs these limbs, while I am still alive—the Lord shall pasture them in a broad place like a lamb. That is, they shall be led by the Assyrians into captivity, and there, in captivity, they shall be scattered through the breadth of the land and remain there for a long time.

Allegorically, the heretics are called Israel, while Judah signifies any ecclesiastical man who confesses God. To them it is said: “If you commit fornication, Israel”—that is, if you, O heretic, depart from God through false teaching—“let Judah not sin”; that is, let the ecclesiastical man not follow the doctrines of your perversity.

And let him not enter Gilgal—that is, the assemblies of heretics, where everyone’s sins are exposed and where they roll about like pigs in the mud of vices. For Gilgal is interpreted as “revelation” or “a place of rolling.” Nor should he go up to Beth-aven—that is, to the arrogant fabrications of false doctrines, because there is not the house of God there but the house of idols.

Those stained by such crimes are also forbidden to swear in the Lord’s name. They pollute his majesty by thinking evil things about him. Like a wanton cow struck by a gadfly, they have been struck by the burning arrows of the devil and have abandoned knowledge of the Law. Therefore they will pasture on the broad and spacious road that leads to death.

“Ephraim is a partner of idols.” In this passage Ephraim refers to the ten tribes after their separation from the house of David under Jeroboam, who was from the tribe of Ephraim, to whom Jacob had given the blessing of kingship. At times they are also called by the name Joseph, because Joseph was the father of Ephraim.

Ephraim, therefore—that is, the ten tribes—were partners of idols because they had become like the idols they worshiped as gods after fashioning them with their hands. Thus the Psalmist says: “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them.”

“Leave him alone.” “O Judah,” is understood: that is, do not despise the prophet’s words and do not follow the impiety of Israel, which is a partner and friend of idols, whose worship, religion, and food are separated from your banquet. Hence it follows:

“Their banquet has been separated,” that is, the sacrifice of idols has been separated from yours, because you offer to the almighty God, while they offer to demons.

“They have committed fornication upon fornication.” The repetition of the expression is a confirmation. It is as if he were saying: “Every day they commit fornication and love their fornication; they continually increase fornications by fornications.” First they worshiped the idol Jeroboam son of Nebat had made for them, and then the gods of all the nations.

“They loved to bring shame upon her protectors.” The protectors of the Israelite people are called Jeroboam and its other kings, who ought to have instructed them in the way of righteousness and defended them from their enemies. They loved to bring shame upon them, that is, idolatry. Through their action the wretched people adopted the worship of idols. Those who ought to have been their leaders on the way of salvation became leaders of error and eternal destruction.

“The spirit bound him in its wings.” Among the Hebrews, spirit and wind are expressed by one word, *ruaḥ*. Here “spirit” signifies demons, who bound them—and without doubt also bound the kings and the people subject to them—in their wings, that is, under their shadow, so that they suffered blindness of mind and could not freely proceed wherever they wished. The spirit itself bound him when it joined and united itself to him, so that he did not yet worship it, but already adored it in images. [Col. 0039A]

“And they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices.” That is, when they have been seized by their enemies, they will be confused and blush with shame, recognizing that this punishment has been inflicted upon them because of the sacrifices that they had previously offered to idols. In a higher sense, this too refers to heretics, who became participants in idols when they worshiped their various doctrines. Therefore the prophet exhorts the ecclesiastical man to abandon and despise their madness and to reject all association with them, because their sacrifice has been separated from the sacrifice of the faithful: they do not rightly celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, and therefore they commit fornication by following various errors and serving the uncleanness of the flesh. [Col. 0039B]

They love to bring shame, that is, they rejoice in offering their hearers vain and superfluous traditions. The spirit—that is, the devil—binds them, so that they do not remain steadfast in the Church but are “carried to and fro by every wind of doctrine.” They are truly put to shame in their sacrifices, because their bread—that is, their reward—will be perpetual mourning.

## CHAPTER V

“Hear this, you priests, and pay attention, house of Israel; listen, house of the king: for judgment is against you, because you have become a snare at the watchtower and a net spread over Tabor.”

He addresses the priests of the ten tribes and summons their kings to judgment—not because they were priests from the tribe of Levi, but because they were called priests by the people. Israel too, that is, the people, is summoned to judgment, and no one is excepted, so that the priests, the people, and the kings—who had led the people astray and appointed such priests for them—might hear together what they had done and why they were handed over to their enemies. [Col. 0039C]

“Hear this, all of you, and listen,” that is, receive it with the ear of the body and retain it with the understanding of the mind, “because judgment is against you,” that is, condemnation threatens you deservedly because of your iniquity, “for you have become a snare” of captivity and slaughter. I had indeed appointed you as watchmen and leaders over the people, so that you might govern them when they went astray. But you became a snare; therefore you are now called not watchmen and leaders but hunters. And just as a net is spread over Mount Tabor to catch birds, so by your teaching and example you captured the people and led them to death. [Col. 0039D]

Tabor is a mountain situated in the plains of Galilee, rounded and lofty, ending equally on every side. Concerning it the Psalm says: “Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name.”

“And you turned the sacrifices toward the depths.” Sacrifices are turned toward the depths when they are offered to demons. The people of the two tribes caused the sacrifices that they offered to almighty God to ascend above, that is, toward heaven. Israel, however, because it sacrificed to idols, caused its sacrifices to descend into the depths, that is, into hell.

In the moral sense, the Lord’s sacrifices are the praises of believers, the repentance of sinners, and the tears of prayers, concerning which it is written: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.” Yet there are some who, after tears and repentance for their sins, return to the sins they have already committed. These, clearly, turn the repentance they had practiced for their former sins toward the depths, because they become worse. Of such people it is written: “The dog has returned to its vomit.” [Col. 0040A]

According to the mystical sense, priests and leaders signify heretics, while the people signify their disciples and subjects. Both the leaders and the people are rebuked and brought to the judgment of condemnation, because those who ought to have been teachers of the peoples seized them through perverse teaching and led them into error. These same heretics also spread a net over Tabor—which is interpreted as “coming light”—when they set their snares within the Church, by which they capture birds, that is, souls flying toward heavenly things, through their perverse doctrines. [Col. 0040B]

They turn sacrifices toward the depths when they persuade people to sacrifice to demons, dragging them into their errors through their enticements, so that they may never repent of their evils and raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things.

“And I am the teacher of them all.” So that the peoples and their teachers—that is, the leaders and priests—would not despair of being able to return to pardon, the Lord mercifully declares that he will be the teacher of them all, saying: “And I am the teacher of them all.” It is as though he said: If they wish to repent and cease serving the gods whom they have hitherto worshiped, let them not despair, because I am their teacher. I will teach them what they ought to do; I desire to correct, not to punish, and I seek to save, not to destroy. [Col. 0040C]

“I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me.” By the name Ephraim he includes Jeroboam, son of Nebat, and all the kings descended from the same tribe. I also formed the peoples subject to those kings. Since, therefore, they are my creation and I behold all their deeds, let them not despair, but repent, and I will receive them.

“For Ephraim has now committed fornication.” That is, their kings, in the present time, have withdrawn from the worship of God and begun to commit fornication by worshiping golden calves. “And Israel has been defiled.” Since the people followed the fornicator king, they completed equal impiety with equal zeal. This must be joined to what precedes: “and this I know.”

“They do not direct their thoughts toward returning to their God, because the spirit of fornications is in their midst, and they have not known God.” Although the Lord mercifully declared above that he was their teacher, knowing the intention of their hearts he adds: They will not direct their thoughts toward returning to their God—that is, they will not repent of their evil thoughts, lest they carry out the evil deed they have conceived. And he gives the reason, saying: “The spirit of fornications”—that is, the devil—“is in their midst.” “And they have not known God,” that is, they have not understood him so as to worship and adore him with worthy reverence.

Because the devil dwelt in their hearts, he had blinded them so that they could not return to the true light and know God—that is, understand that he alone is to be worshiped. [Col. 0041A] Thus it is said of the sons of Eli: “Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they did not know the Lord.”

God also knows the leaders of perverse doctrines—that is, heretics—and the people subject to them, because he considers all their deeds and even their hidden thoughts; nothing among them can escape him. And because their subjects too have been defiled by their perverse teaching, they will not direct their thoughts toward repentance and returning to God, because they have been seduced by the spirit of fornication that moves among them. Therefore they do not know God.

“And the arrogance of Israel will answer to his face.” The arrogance—that is, the pride—of Israel was the swelling with which it rose up against God and despised his worship, venerating idols in insult to the Creator. [Col. 0041B] This arrogance will answer to his face when, deservedly because of his iniquity and the worship of idols, he is handed over to captivity, so that he will not go unpunished but his defiance will be humbled by his enemies.

“And Israel and Ephraim shall fall in their iniquity,” that is, the subject people and the kings who inclined them toward the worship of idols shall fall together and become weak, so that those who were strong in crime may be compelled, in their weakness, to return to God.

“Judah also shall fall with them.” These words show that the tribe of Judah too was already worshiping idols. He does not say that this will happen only to Israel and Ephraim—that is, to the ten tribes and their kings, who will be led into captivity—but also to Judah, that is, to the two tribes that ruled in Jerusalem. They too will follow the steps of the captives, so that those whose crimes they imitated may also share their punishment. [Col. 0041C]

The same applies to heretics: their arrogance answers to their face when, because of the pride with which they always boast that they know higher things, teachers and disciples alike fall together. Judah too—that is, the man instructed in ecclesiastical teaching who remains in the Church bodily but not in mind, possesses the same erroneous knowledge as the heretics, and vainly professes the ecclesiastical name—must himself be punished with the heretics.

“With their flocks and with their herds they shall go to seek the Lord, but they shall not find him.” This may be understood both of the ten tribes and of the two. The meaning is: When Israel, Ephraim, and Judah are oppressed by their enemies, then, led by belated repentance, they will go to seek the Lord with their gifts, eager to appease by offerings him whom they had previously offended by their transgressions. But they will not find him, because when they withdrew from divine worship, he too withdrew from them. Hence it follows: “He has been taken away from them.” [Col. 0041D]

They will not therefore experience him as a present helper, nor will they be able to appease him with their gifts, especially since the Psalmist says: “I will not accept calves from your house”; and: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls?” and so forth.

“They have acted faithlessly against the Lord,” namely, when they worshiped idols instead of God, “because they have begotten foreign children,” that is, having joined themselves to idols, they begot children not for God but for demons. Foreign children are understood as those generated in the error of idols, or those whom they consecrated to idols by passing them through fire.

“Now the month shall devour them with their portions.” Because, he says, they have done this, the enemies will come not after a long time but in the present: the Assyrians and the Chaldaeans will come and devour them with their portions, that is, with their possessions, which they received by lot and by boundary cord. Hence the Septuagint translated: “Rust shall devour them with its ivy.” The meaning is: Month after month the enemy will come and lay waste everything belonging to them; some he will kill, and others he will lead into captivity. How this happened is shown by the history of the Books of Kings and Chronicles, which records that this same people was taken captive not once or twice but many times. [Col. 0042A–B]

Heretics, however, suppose that they please God by the multitude of their sacrifices, while Judah—that is, ecclesiastical people—supposes that by giving alms they redeem their sins, even while remaining in them, although every sacrifice ordinarily wipes away past sins, not present crimes. Such people certainly do not find God, because he will be taken away and withdraw far from them. They act faithlessly when they neglect God’s commands and beget foreign children through demonic works. Therefore they are condemned daily and individually with their portions—that is, with the evil deeds they have committed—and hasten toward the destruction of eternal condemnation.

“Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; howl in Beth-aven.” A horn is made from the naturally curved horn of an animal, while the trumpet is commanded by the Law to be made of bronze or silver; it resounds in wars and in solemn celebrations. [Col. 0042C]

Gibeah and Ramah are neighboring cities in the tribe of Benjamin. This is the Gibeah in which Saul was born. Ramah is the city that the king of Israel attempted to occupy, as we read in the Book of Kings, in order to close the exit and entrance of the tribe of Judah and Benjamin. Beth-aven, moreover, is in the tribe of Ephraim; it was formerly called Bethel.

Since he had earlier foretold the captivity of the ten and the two tribes, saying, “Now the month shall devour them with their portions,” he exhorts them, as though captivity were already near at hand, to sound their horns and trumpets, encouraging one another to common mourning. The meaning is: Do not lament your captivity in a subdued voice; sound the horns and trumpets, so that all who are around may hear. [Col. 0042D]

This meaning agrees well with the interpretation of Gibeah as “hill” and Ramah as “height.” Thus he says to them: “Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah,” that is, climb the mountains and hills and loudly lament the captivity threatening you. “Howl also in Beth-aven,” where one of the golden calves is located, for whose worship its inhabitants will now be handed over as captives. And he appropriately adds: “Behind you, Benjamin.” For where the tribe of Benjamin ends, this city was founded not far away in the tribe of Ephraim, on the farther side of Benjamin.

“Ephraim shall become desolate on the day of correction.” In this passage, the name Ephraim designates both the kings descended from his stock and the people of the ten tribes themselves. He calls the time when they were handed over to their enemies because of their sins the day of correction, so that those who had refused to serve God in prosperity might endure correction, afflicted by the various miseries inflicted by their enemies. On that day both the kings and their subjects became desolate, when some were killed, others were led into captivity, and their land was left empty of its inhabitants. [Col. 0043A]

“In the tribes of Israel I have shown faithfulness.” The Septuagint has: “In the tribes of Israel I have shown faithful things.” The past tense is used there for the future: “I have shown” for “I will show.” It is as though he said: When the things that I previously spoke through the prophets come to pass, I will show faithfulness; that is, I will manifest that my words are faithful and true, because whatever I foretold concerning their destruction will be fulfilled in deed.

Heretics too dwell in Gibeah and Ramah—that is, in the swelling of proud knowledge—while they suppose that they possess lofty wisdom. There they worship idols, that is, the false doctrines they have fabricated from their own hearts. Therefore they are commanded not to conceal their evil in silence but to make it openly manifest to all. [Col. 0043B]

They are also commanded to howl in Beth-aven, which means “house of worthlessness”: that is, in their hearts, which formerly, through right faith, were Bethel, “house of God,” but have now been made worthless through various errors. It is fitting that Beth-aven is remembered as being behind Benjamin.

Benjamin means “right hand” and signifies the saints who will come to the right hand, that is, to the prosperity of the heavenly kingdom. Because of their eternal joys, they keep all the advantages of the present life behind their backs, since they set aside all transient things, saying with the Apostle: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, we pursue the prize of the heavenly calling.” [Col. 0043C]

Heretics, however, are behind Benjamin because they eagerly desire and delightfully pursue the things of the present life, which the saints regard with contempt. They place all their hope in transient matters. Though they previously appeared to be Ephraim, that is, “fruitfulness,” when the day of correction—that is, of judgment—comes, they will become desolate. Stripped of all the goods in which they seemed to abound, naked and empty, they will be handed over to unquenchable fire.

Then too the Lord will show faithfulness in their condemnation, demonstrating that his words are faithful and true, when he fulfills by his deed what he had foretold concerning their destruction. This may appropriately be applied not only to heretics but generally to all the reprobate. [Col. 0043D]

“The princes of Judah became like those who move a boundary.” They ought to have wept and exhorted their people to withdraw from the worship of idols, lest they themselves suffer similar things. Instead, they began to rejoice because their land would lie open to them more widely for possession. They became like those who move Israel’s boundaries, crossing their borders and desiring to enlarge their own kingdom and possession within the former kingdoms of the Israelites.

Therefore it follows: “Upon them I will pour out my wrath like water.” That is, the Babylonians will come upon the princes of Judah and will seize them like a rushing flood. Through them I will abundantly bring upon them complete captivity and death, because they will do this not by their own strength but through my indignation. [Col. 0044A] The language of pouring signifies the abundance and magnitude of the matter in question.

He also speaks to the princes of Judah—that is, of the Church—saying that they ought not to rejoice or regard the destruction of the reprobate as their own salvation, but rather to mourn that the others have perished, remembering their own condition. Hence the Apostle warns ecclesiastical men not to boast over the breaking of the Jewish branches but rather to fear lest they too be broken.

But because some rejoice in the destruction of the reprobate and therefore think themselves secure if others fall, the Lord pours out his wrath upon them like water. For often, while people rejoice at the fall of others, they themselves fall into the same evils for which they mocked those others, and thereby incur God’s wrath. [Col. 0044B] They also move the boundaries established by their fathers when they change truth into falsehood and preach something different from what they received from the apostles.

“Ephraim suffers oppression, crushed by judgment.” The Israelite people, still persisting in hardness of heart, said that they had been crushed by judgment and unjustly oppressed by their enemies. They said: Since we are descended from the race of Abraham, God’s friends, we ought not to have been handed over to people worse than you—that is, to the uncircumcised and idolaters, wholly alien from the worship of God.

He calls the affliction inflicted upon him by his enemies “oppression”; he said that he was crushed by judgment, that is, he confessed that he had been condemned unjustly and without any fault. [Col. 0044C] Therefore, so that he might recognize that he suffered this for a reason, it follows: “For he began to follow after filth.” It is as though he said: They were not handed over to the Chaldaeans because those who oppressed them were more righteous, but because the Jews, formerly my people, abandoned me and began to follow after filth—that is, after idols.

Thus they are compared to filth and uncleanness, and he justly pronounces sentence, showing that Ephraim—that is, Jeroboam—suffers oppression and is handed over to worse people because he began to follow idols and abandon God. For he himself made the golden calves that the people later worshiped.

The meaning concerning heretics is also clear: by their sophistries and dialectical skill they have oppressed the Church. But when they have done this, they follow not the purity of true faith but the filth of falsehood. [Col. 0044D] When they see themselves condemned with the devil and his angels, they seem to themselves to suffer oppression and to have the truth of judgment broken against them. The same should be understood of all the reprobate.

“And I shall be like a moth to Ephraim and like decay to the house of Judah.” A moth eats clothing, while decay or rot consumes wood. The meaning of these words is this: Just as a moth consumes clothing and decay or rot consumes wood, both over the passage of time, so I, after granting the ten tribes and then the two tribes a long period for repentance and calling them to salvation, will hand them over to condemnation.

Here it should be noted that the moth is referred to Ephraim, while decay is referred to the house of Judah. A moth consumes clothing more quickly than decay or rot consumes wood. Thus it is shown that the captivity of the ten tribes occurred first and that of the two tribes afterward. [Col. 0045A]

Since he also declares that he will consume all Ephraim like a moth, but, speaking of the tribe of Judah, says, “And I shall be like decay to the house of Judah,” he indicates in these words that he will preserve a certain part of them. That remnant later returned, and from it Christ took his origin; to it the promise was reserved, as Jacob says: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.”

After the heretics, who are understood under the name Ephraim, have been punished, Judah too—that is, those who remain in the Church yet are infected by the vices or errors of heretics—will be subject to the same sentence, because it was necessary that those who imitate their deeds should suffer the same punishment as they do. [Col. 0045B]

“And Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his bond; and Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king.” Ephraim—that is, the kings of the ten tribes—recognized his sickness, that is, his weakness, and Judah recognized his bond, that is, understood that captivity threatened him because he had joined the ten tribes in sin. He sent to Assyria, because he sought help not from God, who could release both sin and captivity, but from the king of the Assyrians.

We read in the Book of Kings that under Manahem, who ruled the ten tribes, Israel sent gifts to the Assyrians so that he might free him from the Damascene enemies. Judah too, under King Ahaz, sent presents to Tiglath-pileser so that he might free him from the oppression of Pekah, king of Damascus. [Col. 0045C]

Although they then saved them from the hands of their enemies, afterward they themselves conquered them and became avengers of God’s injuries—those who had previously been their liberators. Hence it follows: “But he will not be able to heal you, nor release your bond from you.” Since God was opposed to them, the Assyrians could neither free them from themselves nor release the bond of captivity.

According to the tropological sense, Ephraim and Judah may refer to heretics and ecclesiastical men. When they see their bond—that is, when they see themselves subject to sins, concerning which it is written, “Everyone is bound by the cords of his sins”—they seek not God’s help but the devil’s. He is the avenger of all sins, concerning whom it is written: “That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger.” [Col. 0045D]

Because they do not beseech the true helper and judge, they are forced to remain in their pains and in the various errors of their sins. The devil cannot heal them or rescue them from the bonds of sin, since by God’s just judgment they will perish together with him.

“For I shall be like a lioness to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah.” The meaning is: Although they went to Assyria and sent gifts to the avenging king so that he might free them, he could not heal them or release the bond of their captivity. I will show that, when I oppose it, all human help is vain.

“I shall be like a lioness to Ephraim.” The Septuagint translated “lioness” as “panther,” which in Greek is likewise called *panthera*. According to blessed Jerome, nothing is swifter than this animal. [Col. 0046A] Therefore the Lord rightly says, speaking against Ephraim—that is, against the ten tribes—that he will become like a panther, signifying the swift captivity by which the Assyrians would soon bring about their destruction.

Against Judah, however, he says that he will be like a lion, which is the strongest of beasts. This indicates that their captivity would occur somewhat later, through the very powerful kingdom of the Chaldaeans. The Lord compares himself to beasts for their condemnation, so that they may recognize in his indignation whatever is most savage.

“I will seize and go away and carry off, and there will be no one to rescue.” Since he had said above that he would be like a panther or a lion, he preserves the metaphor in what follows, saying: “I will seize”—understand, through my ministers. The Chaldaeans and Assyrians did not seize them by their own strength; almighty God, because of their iniquities, would take hold of them. [Col. 0046B] Hence even the enemies themselves could not spare them while the Lord was angry.

“I will seize,” that is, I will cause them to be seized by their enemies; “and I will go away with them,” so that even in captivity they might endure the presence of my vengeance, against whom they had sinned. “And I will carry them away from their own soil, and there will be no one to rescue,” that is, no one who can snatch them from my power. No one can rescue anyone from God’s hand unless the one held captive chooses to flee from it by his own will, as the betrayer Judas did.

“Going away, I shall return to my place until you fail and seek my face.” We should understand God’s place as his magnificence and majesty. Alternatively, we may refer these words specifically to the Son of God, through whom the entire dispensation of prophecy is carried out: his place is God the Father, according to what he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” [Col. 0046C]

“Going away,” he says, “I shall return to my place,” that is, when you have been handed over to your enemies, I will sit secure in my majesty—or in the Father—and will not descend to you to experience human emotions, whether to become angry with you or to pity you while forgetting your evils. Instead, I will allow you, whom I formerly protected, to remain subject to your enemies and will extend no help of compassion, until you fail and, compelled by servitude, seek my face in repentance.

The same may be understood of heretics and sinful ecclesiastical men. Because of the magnitude of their sins, almighty God, although most merciful, turns into the ferocity of wild beasts; he takes away from them their prey—that is, their disciples whom they seized from the Church—and causes them to return to the true faith. [Col. 0046D] There is no one who can rescue them, because no one can deceive the person whose heart God himself has illumined.

While he does this, he withdraws from the assemblies of the perverse and dwells in the Church of believers; he despises and rejects them until they waste away in their impieties and fail in their iniquity, seeking the presence of the one by whom they had been abandoned, saying: “Shine upon us, Lord, with your face, and we shall be saved.”

## CHAPTER VI

“In their tribulation they will rise early to me.” These words may in part refer to those who, pressed by the tribulation of captivity, began to repent and seek God, whom they felt to be absent and angry. And in the morning—that is, in the light of repentance—they said to one another: “Come, let us return to the Lord.” [Col. 0047A]

In general, these words apply to all Christians who believe in Christ. Afflicted by various tribulations, when the light of truth had arisen for them, at Christ’s coming they rose in the morning—that is, in the light of faith—from the darkness of unbelief and error, and began to exhort one another, saying: “Come, let us return to the Lord.”

Those who returned from captivity out of the two tribes, not content with their own salvation, exhort one another, saying: Come with the steps of love and faith; let us return to the Lord, whom we abandoned by sinning and by whose just judgment we were abandoned. [Col. 0047B]

“For he seized us,” by leading us into captivity through Nebuchadnezzar; hence it was said above: “I will seize.” “And he will heal us,” by bringing us back from captivity like a father bringing back his children. “He will strike us,” by chastising us with various tribulations and blows. “And he will heal us,” from the wounds of sins, if after the scourging we perform worthy repentance.

“After two days he will revive us.” This properly refers to believers, who, called and illumined by the faith of Christ, urge one another to return to the Lord. They had once withdrawn from his worship and, by worshiping various portents of demons, had deserved his absence.

“For he seized us,” he says, when the Word became flesh. Hence Paul says: “He took hold of the seed of Abraham.” [Col. 0047C] “And he will heal us,” because the heavenly physician, after the pain of wounds and sins, will give us complete salvation. Thus, when the Lord was going to heal the paralytic, he first cleansed him in soul and then relieved him in body from the distress of infirmity.

“He will strike us”—understand, in various ways—and after the striking he will heal us, according to the saying: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves.” Hence he also says to one who had been healed: “See, you have become well,” and so forth.

“After two days he will revive us.” Blessed Jerome says that the Hebrews vainly dream of salvation for themselves after a cycle of a thousand years, since the salvation of believers was promised on the third day, because the Lord rose from the dead. They refer the second day to the advent of their Christ and the third day to his coming for judgment, when those who are to be saved will be saved. [Col. 0047D]

But when they say these things, they ought to answer why they accept the second day. Those who accept the second and third testify that they have lost the first, because the second and third cannot exist without the first. Since they will not be able to answer concerning the first, let us refer all these things to the first and second advents of Christ, in which the salvation of believers was fulfilled.

Let us therefore take the first time of God to be the day of Christ’s first advent. After that day he will revive us through faith, though we were dead through unbelief; or, certainly, he revived us in the hope of resurrection, according to the Apostle’s saying: “He made us alive together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ.”

“On the third day he will raise us,” because when he rose from the dead, we too rose together with him; by his resurrection he signified our resurrection, since just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too will rise with him. [Col. 0048A]

Alternatively, let us understand the first day as Christ’s coming in humility, the second as his coming in glory, when he will be seen by all, and the third as the time when, after judgment has been completed, he will reveal to the elect the greater glory of his radiance. For God the Father ordained that the universal quickening and resurrection of all the saints should take place through the Son.

Or, for us, the first day is when we are reborn through the water of baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, passing from darkness into light, according to the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” The second is the repose of souls, and the third is the universal resurrection. [Col. 0048B]

“And we shall live in his sight,” when, as John says, “we shall see him as he is.” Or, if we wish to refer this to the present time, we live in his sight because “in him we live and move and are.”

“We shall know and follow in order to know the Lord.” We shall know him—that is, believing, we shall recognize the majesty of his divinity and perceive his Trinity in persons and unity in majesty. We shall follow him by imitating his footsteps or by ascending to heaven. Hence it follows: “In order to know the Lord.”

This will truly be fulfilled when we contemplate face to face what we now see through a mirror and in an enigma. Hence it is written: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

“His going forth has been prepared like the dawn.” Dawn is called the small light of day, by whose rising the darkness of night is driven away and the brightness of day begins to appear. The meaning is therefore this: Just as when dawn rises the darkness of night is driven away and the light of day is revealed, so when Christ was born in the flesh the darkness of our sins was dispersed, and the sun of righteousness rose for us. [Col. 0048C] By illuminating our blindness, he opened the eyes of our mind and revealed the brightness of our heavenly homeland and the light of true knowledge.

His birth is beautifully called his “going forth,” concerning which the Psalmist says: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.” Like a bridegroom he came forth from his chamber when he assumed an immaculate body from the incorrupt womb of the Virgin and appeared, born in the flesh.

Concerning his birth it rightly follows: “And he will come to us like the early and late rain upon the earth.” Literally, he calls the early rain the rain given by God to the land of Palestine after the seeds have been sown, by which the seeds, once watered, grow together. He calls the late rain that which brings the same crops to maturity. For the Promised Land does not receive rain from heaven as frequently as ours does, but only twice a year. Hence the Lord promises the same people through the prophet: “I will give you the early and late rain.” [Col. 0048D]

Spiritually, Christ is our early rain when we receive the foundations of his faith, by which, rooted in good works, we may abound. He is the late rain when, with the crops already prepared for harvesting—that is, when good works have been completed—we are stored in the Lord’s granaries. [Col. 0049A]

Or he is now our early rain while we know only in part. He will be the late rain when that which is perfect has come. Therefore the Jews, who did not receive the early rains and harvested without rain, will not receive the fruit of the seed at the end of time.

“What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah?” It is as though he said: How can I hand you over to your enemies without sorrow of heart, or what medicine can I apply to restore you to health?

“Your mercy is like a morning cloud and like the dew that passes away early,” that is, just as, when the sun comes, the cloud that had made the night gloomy passes away, and as the dew that rises at dawn dries up when the sun has risen, so the mercy with which I was accustomed to have mercy on you has passed away. [Col. 0049B] The time of your captivity is also near, and it will soon come through the Assyrians and Babylonians.

“Therefore I hewed them down through the prophets.” Lest the Jews, seeking an excuse, should say, “We were deceived by false prophets who promised us peace, and therefore we sinned,” the Lord testifies that he had previously slain the prophets, so that, recognizing that those who had been the cause of their error had been killed by the Lord, they might turn them into an occasion of salvation. Hence we read in the Books of Kings that four hundred and fifty prophets, and another innumerable multitude, were killed by Jehu, who overthrew the house of Ahab. Therefore it is also added: “And I killed them by the word of my mouth.” Elijah was the mouth of the Lord, for he ordered them to be killed. Alternatively: “Therefore”—that is, because mercy had withdrawn from those acting wickedly—“I hewed them down,” that is, I foretold through the prophets, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the others, that they were to be hewn down; and by my terrifying words I threatened them, so that those who despised the merciful one might fear him when offended. “And I killed them by the word of my mouth,” so that sinners might be punished by the terror of words before captivity drew near. But all these things, as my judgments by which I will judge you, “shall go forth like the light,” that is, they shall become manifest. Since I often rebuke you, yet you remain unrepentant, you will be condemned in the open light and before many nations. Or certainly my judgments shall go forth like the light because no one will doubt that you justly suffered what you endure.

These same words can also be referred to heretics or to the men of Judah, whom the Lord calls to mercy and desires to return to salvation. But when they remain unrepentant, the cloud or dew—that is, the prosperity of this world—will be taken away from them, as happened to that rich man dressed in purple, who learned that everything he had enjoyed passed away like a cloud or dew. The Lord also continually kills the prophets of heretics when he threatens them with eternal punishments. Their judgments will become manifest when, with everyone looking on, they are condemned together with the devil and his angels.

“Because I desired mercy, and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than a burnt offering.” The Jews, sinning in various ways, thought that they could be cleansed through the offering of sacrifices. But the Lord shows that he would rather have mercy: first, that they should have mercy on themselves, according to the saying, “My son, have mercy on your soul by pleasing God”; then on the poor; and that they should have knowledge of the true faith together with knowledge of themselves, rather than burnt offerings, because without faith and mercy it is impossible to please God.

“But they, like Adam, transgressed my covenant.” It is as though he said: They will not be able to be cleansed through sacrifices, as they suppose, because just as Adam, by tasting the fruit of the forbidden tree, despised God’s commandment, so these people, transgressing the divine law, act against the commandment of God, who said to them, “You shall not make foreign gods for yourselves.” And just as Adam lost paradise, so they too will lose the land that they had received as an inheritance. “Where”—that is, in Adam, or also in paradise—“they transgressed against me,” in accordance with what the Apostle says: “In whom all sinned.”

Every day, too, the Lord calls to repentance and to mercy and knowledge of the true faith both those within the Church who sin and those who dwell outside the Church, saying: “I desire mercy,” and so forth. Such people appear to offer gifts to God, to pursue humility, and to give alms—things that would be called sacrifices if they proceeded with upright faith and good intention. But since both groups reject mercy and the true knowledge of God, they boast in vain that they possess the other members while the head of faith has been cut off. For they have transgressed God’s covenant in the Church, just as Adam did in paradise; and therefore, just as he was expelled from paradise, so they will be expelled from the Church.

“Gilead is a city of those who work an idol.” Gilead is the name of a city or mountain, but here it is used for a city. It lies beyond the Jordan, in the tribe of Gad. In this city an idol was first consecrated, because it was inhabited by priests. It was also a city of refuge; but the more celebrated and authoritative it was, because it had been assigned to the portion of the priests, the more it became the beginning of idolatry and of every evil. And because these people first consecrated idols, they were the first to be captured by the Assyrians and led into captivity.

“Trampled down by blood.” We read in the Book of Kings that Jehu, anointed king at Ramoth-gilead, destroyed, according to the Lord’s command, the entire house of Ahab—that is, his seventy sons—and the others who had consented to him in evil. Therefore the city itself is said to have been trampled down—that is, humbled—by blood; or also because the vengeance for the blood that it shed, as we shall see in what follows, came upon it.

“And like the throat of men who are robbers.” The throats of robbers are caves and other hidden places in which, concealed, they strip and kill passersby. Habitations of this sort existed in that same region. Hence Gilead is said to be like the throat of robbers: just as those men, lying in wait, stripped and killed people, so the priests of Gilead, lying in wait for the simplicity of the people, stripped them of faith and killed them in mind. Those whom they could not deceive they deprived of their clothing and killed bodily. This is what follows: “A participant in the priests who kill those passing along the road from Shechem.”

Shechem is a city on the boundary between the ten tribes and the two tribes; today it is called Neapolis. The Israelites passed through it on their way to Jerusalem, where alone it was permitted to offer victims. Therefore, at the three times when, according to the commandment of the Law, the people had to go up to the temple of God, the priests of the idols placed robbers along the road to lie in wait for those traveling, so that they might worship the golden calves in Dan and Bethel rather than the Lord in Jerusalem. Those whom they could not turn back they killed on that same road. Gilead was a participant in these priests, because its priests entered into conspiracy and agreement with those mentioned above, and likewise through their ministers they killed those traveling to Jerusalem. Hence it follows: “Because they committed crime”—understand, in killing those people, or in idolatry.

Even now, wicked teachers lie in wait for those traveling along the road—that is, along the path of the present life—toward the heavenly Jerusalem, and they kill as many as they can at Shechem, that is, in good works, by turning them back to the wickedness of their own conduct through perverse teaching or bad example. For Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder.” In the shoulder, however, work is understood. Hence we also read of Issachar that he placed his shoulder beneath the work.

“In the house of Israel I saw a terrible thing.” “Terrible” is sometimes used for fear, as in the statement: “It is terrible to fall into the hands of the living God”; at other times it means something squalid or filthy, as in: “You did not abhor the womb of the virgin,” that is, you did not regard it as filthy. Here, therefore, “terrible” refers to the fear of idolatry. The prophet was terrified when he saw the idol that the Israelites had made after abandoning God, and therefore he says: “In the house of Israel”—that is, in the assembly of the ten tribes—“I saw idolatry.” For what is more terrible than ten tribes suddenly turning to the worship of idols?

“There are the fornications of Ephraim; Israel has been defiled.” It was said above that Ephraim signifies Jeroboam, namely, the first king of the ten tribes, while Israel signifies his entire kingdom. Thus it is said that there, that is, in the house of Israel where something terrible appeared, are the fornications of Ephraim—that is, of Jeroboam from the tribe of Ephraim, who, abandoning God, began to worship idols. A person commits fornication when, abandoning the Creator, who is the husband of the soul, he is joined to the adulterer, that is, the devil. And when Jeroboam fornicated, Israel was defiled—that is, the people subject to him, since he possessed, to a large extent, the common name Israel. Hence the discourse immediately turns to Judah, when it adds:

“But Judah too, prepare a harvest for yourself.” The meaning is: Do not think yourself safe because Israel is being led into captivity. You too, prepare grainfields for yourself to be reaped—that is, beget sons who will be cut down by Nebuchadnezzar and his army. For not much later you will be led captive into Babylon, and the time of your harvest—that is, of your slaughter—will come. “When I restore the captivity of my people”—understand, you will see it.

This was fulfilled under Cyrus, king of the Persians, when the Jews returned to their land through the agency of Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and Nehemiah, in the sight of many who had lived during the time when that captivity had taken place. When they saw the return of those who had been born in Chaldea, they returned together with them. Note, however, that Judah’s captivity and return are prophesied together; concerning Israel nothing is said, because while these people returned after seventy years, the others remained perpetually captive.

In the house of heretics, too, something terrible appears when they follow perverse doctrines and think wrongly about Christ; through the error of their fornication, the people deceived by them are also defiled. Judah—that is, men of the Church—is likewise commanded to prepare a harvest of cutting down, to be reaped because of their sins on the day of judgment by the one who is said in the Apocalypse of John to hold a sharp sickle in his hand. This, however, is not said as the wish of one desiring it, but as the prophecy of one announcing it. For if these people repent, they too will see their conversion from evil to good.

## CHAPTER VII

“When I wished to heal Israel”—understand, from the idolatry that they had practiced in Egypt or in the wilderness, when they cast the calf’s head in a mold, saying: “These are your gods,” because I preferred the sinner’s repentance to his death. “The iniquity of Ephraim was revealed”—that is, the idolatry of Jeroboam, who, suddenly established as king over the Israelite people, made golden calves; “and the wickedness of Samaria”—that is, the wickedness of the subject people who followed the impious king—“was revealed.” For “they”—both king and people—“practiced falsehood,” that is, the idol. Just as falsehood is opposed to truth, so the idol is opposed to God.

Or certainly they are said to have made falsehood in this respect: they spoke falsely when, prostrate before the gods, they said, “These are your gods,” transferring God’s glory to images. “And the thief entered, stripping; the robber is outside.” The difference between a thief and a robber is that the thief seeks the night and acts wickedly in secret, whereas the robber openly uses force. In this passage we should understand the thief, or robber, as Jeroboam, who entered the house of Israel like a thief, stole them from God, and, like a robber, stripped the wretched people of God’s protection. The meaning is: When I wished to erase the ancient sins of my people because of their longstanding idolatry, Ephraim and Samaria discovered new idols.

It can also be understood in this way: when the Lord and Savior wished to heal the sins of the Church, both of Jews and of the nations, Ephraim—that is, the abundance of false doctrines—suddenly arose. Many favoring it practiced falsehood against Christ, and through them the thief and robber—that is, the devil—entered the Church. Or we may understand the thieves and robbers as the heretics themselves, of whom the Lord says: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up by another way, is a thief and a robber,” and, “All who came before me are thieves and robbers.” Hence he significantly says that the robber strips from outside. They cannot deprive those whom they have taught of Christ’s garment unless they first lead them outside the Church and make them walk along the road of their doctrines.

“And lest they should say in their hearts that I have remembered all their wickedness, now their inventions have surrounded them.” Lest, he says, they should say in their hearts, “He is punishing us for ancient sins, and we are paying for the offenses of our fathers,” according to the saying: “Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge.” Now—that is, at the present time—“their inventions have surrounded them”; that is, I am not punishing them for the offenses of their fathers, as they think, nor for ancient iniquities, but for their present ones. They thought that their iniquity was hidden from God, although unquestionably God sees everything. Hence it is added: “They have been committed before my face”—that is, I always behold their evil deeds, which they commit in my presence without fearing my face.

The wicked, too, are condemned not only because of past sins, but because they add new impiety every day to their former deeds. Although they think they can conceal themselves from the Lord, they cannot escape his eyes, because it is written: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

“In their wickedness they made the king rejoice,” giving their consent to King Jeroboam so that they might worship idols according to his will, “and in their falsehoods,” by which they said: “These are your gods.” “The princes”—understand, made him rejoice—because the princes themselves consented to the king.

It should be noted that he now explains what they did before his face. Everyone who serves a perverse work or thinks wrongly about Christ, like Arius and the others, makes the king—that is, the devil—rejoice. And in the falsehoods of wicked doctrines they make the princes rejoice—that is, the devil’s satellites, who are called the princes of the devil’s darkness. For the hostile powers take great delight in our sins.

“All adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker.” He speaks this also against those who made the king rejoice in their wickedness and the princes in their falsehoods. “All adulterers”—that is, those who depart from their own husband, God—are like an oven heated by the baker. Just as an oven is kindled so that it may bake bread, so they were set ablaze by the wickedness of Jeroboam and by the fire of idolatry.

“For a little while the city rested from the mixing of the leaven, until the whole was leavened.” After he had fashioned the idols, Jeroboam did not use force against the people to make them worship them, lest, if some resisted for the sake of God and religion, their worship should be rendered ineffective. Therefore the city rested for a little while, until the people consented to the king of their own will: first the princes, then their attendants who favored the king and the princes, and finally the entire people were corrupted. This is what he says: “Until the whole was leavened.” What is done voluntarily lasts a long time; what is done under compulsion is quickly undone. Considering this, Jeroboam preferred that the people voluntarily submit to the new worship of idols rather than be compelled.

Leaven is used both in a good sense and in a bad sense. In a good sense, as the Lord says in the Gospel, when a woman took leaven and hid it in three measures of flour. Here, however, it is used in a bad sense, for the corruption of the people through the worship of idols. Heretics likewise conceal their wicked intention for as long as they can, covering falsehoods with truths, until those subject to them willingly obey their will and until the hearts of the deceived swell with the leaven of their perverse teaching, about which the Lord says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees.”

“The day of our king.” After the entire mass of the people had been kindled with devotion to the calves, they began saying at the doors of King Jeroboam: “This is the day of our king”—understand, this is the day that our ruler has made a festival for us. We celebrate it; in it we rejoice; in it we worship the golden calves.

“The princes began to rage from wine.” While the people shouted, “This is the day that our king has established as sacred,” the princes, who ought to have been rulers of the people, were not only not angry but, losing the understanding of their minds, began to rage from wine—that is, to suffer the madness of luxury and idolatry.

“He stretched out his hand with mockers, because they had brought their heart near like an oven while he was lying in wait for them.” When the king saw the people shouting what we have described, and the princes also drunk and submerged in the wine of idolatry, he stretched out his hand with the mockers—that is, with the princes who wickedly mocked the people and led them far from their God by blessing and giving thanks, or by consenting to their errors. For they had brought their heart near like an oven, so that he might set them ablaze and make them burn with the flames of idolatry. He therefore applauded and gave thanks to the people together with the princes because he understood that they had turned with all the effort of their minds toward error. He did this while lying in wait for them, so that they would not go up to the temple of the Lord but worship the calves that he himself had made. For he had craftily fashioned those calves so that the people of Israel, when going to the temple of God at Jerusalem, might not take the opportunity to reconcile themselves with the king of Judah.

“All night long he slept, baking them; in the morning he himself was kindled like a flame of fire.” After he had put the fire of wickedness into their hearts and saw them raging, with no one resisting his will, he slept all night long—that is, he lay secure, dwelling in darkness and baking them in the fire of impiety. In the morning, himself kindled by the flames of his own crimes, he came to offer sacrifice.

“They were all heated like an oven,” because, when they were no longer passing secretly but shamelessly from the worship of God to the ceremonies of idols, they were all set ablaze by the wickedness of their iniquity. “And they devoured their judges”—that is, those who did not wish to consent to them but rather rebuked them, and whom they killed. Or certainly they spiritually killed those who had previously been their judges, by drawing them into their wickedness.

When those people remembered the Lord’s religious observances and saw the king, the princes, and the entire people devoted to idolatry, they began to say: “What shall we do? Look, the king and his princes, and the whole people, worship gods. Now, since we live among them, we cannot fail to do the same, lest perhaps, stripped of all our possessions, we also lose our lives.” While they were saying these things, they too fell into the crime of idolatry.

“All their kings have fallen.” From this Jeroboam, that is, to the last Josiah, all the kings of the Israelites fell into idolatry or eternal destruction and walked in the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin. “There is none among them who calls to me”—that is, no one is found among the kings or among the subject people who calls to me and, abandoning idols, turns to God.

Blessed Jerome refers all these things to heretics and their disciples. Intoxicated by the wickedness of the devil, who is king over all the wicked, they celebrate the king’s day—that is, the festival day of each of their leaders, for example Marcion, Arius, Eunomius, and the rest—abandoning the Church and trampling on the truth of the faith. Hence those who preside over the others applaud them because they see their hearts filled with wickedness and infused with the wine of iniquity, concerning which Solomon says: “Princes must not drink wine, lest they forget wisdom.” They also go mad from wine. Concerning this Moses says: “The fury of dragons is their wine,” and so forth.

As for the statement that Jeroboam slept all night, this is shown by the fact that heretics, while dwelling in the darkness of unbelief, cannot perceive the light of the true sun. Those who sleep sleep at night, because their understanding has been oppressed. Their hearts are known to be heated by anger, greed, and the other vices. They themselves devour their judges—that is, if any possess virtue in their mind, or the faculties by which evils are distinguished from good things, they draw them away from such people. And all the princes of such people have fallen in God’s predestination, nor is there anyone among them who calls upon the Lord, so that, invoking the name of the Lord, he may be saved.

“Ephraim himself mingled among the peoples.” Here Ephraim signifies not only the kings, as above, but the entire people of the ten tribes. Ephraim, therefore—that is, the whole kingdom of the ten tribes—“mingled among the peoples,” meaning that it became like the nations that worship idols.
