“Ephraim became a cake baked under the ashes, which is not turned.” A cake that is not turned is full of dirt on every side. Ephraim became such by failing to repent; remaining unconverted, it was surrounded on every side by the ashes of sins. If it wished to turn from its iniquities, it could certainly be cleansed.

“Foreigners have devoured his strength, and he did not know it.” By “strength” he means the princes and all the strong men of the people, or certainly the treasures in which they trusted. Foreigners, therefore—those alienated from God, or even from the Jewish people, namely their enemies, the Chaldeans and Assyrians—devoured his strength by killing the princes, claiming their possessions for themselves, and consuming whatever power he could possess. Ephraim was so foolish that he did not know his God, or else did not understand the reason for which he had been handed over to those devouring him, considering himself righteous.

[Col. 0056A] “Gray hairs have also been poured out upon him, and he did not know it.” Human gray hairs are sometimes understood in a good sense, as in Solomon’s saying: “Gray hairs are the understanding of a person, and the age of old age is an unblemished life.” Here, however, they are understood in a bad sense, showing that wickedness persisted among this people until the end of the kingdom. “Gray hairs,” he says, “have been poured out upon him”—that is, they remained abundantly in wickedness until old age and the end of the kingdom. And he himself did not know that the end of his kingdom was near.

“And the pride of Israel will be humbled before his face.” Israel had raised itself against the Lord and trusted not in him but in the multitude of its army. And because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble,” the Prophet now says: “The pride of Israel will be humbled”—that is, its princes and army, in which it gloried, will be killed by the Assyrians and Chaldeans. And this will not happen after a long time, but now and in the present. For this is what he says: “Before his face.”

“They have not returned to the Lord their God, and they have not sought him in all these things.” What he had stated above somewhat obscurely, saying, “Ephraim became a cake under the ashes that is not turned,” he now states more clearly: “They have not returned,” he says, “to the Lord their God, and they have not sought him in all these things.” If they had returned to the Lord their God, they would certainly have heard the Lord speaking through Jeremiah: “Return to me, and I will return to you.” Following idols, they did not seek him amid all these adversities, so that they might believe perfectly in him and act rightly.

If we refer these things to heretical or impious leaders, Ephraim mingles among the peoples whenever any wicked leader draws others into his own likeness and becomes like them, according to what was said above: “As the people, so the priest.” Or Ephraim mingles among the peoples because all heretics differ in nothing from the error of the Gentiles. And the one who had once been a leader of the Church becomes like a cake under the ashes, surrounded on every side by the ashes of sins, and does not return to the Lord, remaining in the error that he began. Its strength—that is, the power of its virtues and understanding—is taken away by demons, the worst enemies of Christians. Yet it does not know this, while it considers as friends those whom it experiences as devourers. Gray hairs are also poured out upon it, while the foolishness of its heart persists in it until the end of life. For just as gray hairs signify the wisdom of a righteous person, so they signify the foolishness of an impious person. Yet it does not recognize the old age of its wickedness, of which it is written: “What grows old and ages is near destruction.” Although their pride is humbled every day by Christ, they do not repent and do not return to the Lord.

“And Ephraim became like a dove deceived, without a heart.” The dove is understood in a good sense, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves,” so that we may neither harm others nor suffer the snares of others, but by innocence and prudence present the balanced human being. For prudence without innocence is cunning, and innocence without prudence is foolishness.

In this passage, therefore, the dove signifies the foolishness of the Jewish people, who trusted in a human being rather than in God, calling upon Egypt and going to the Assyrians. The one who sought Egypt’s help—Egypt, which Isaiah calls a broken reed—was led captive by the Assyrians. Ephraim thus became like a dove deceived by the devil, without a heart—that is, without understanding of mind.

It should be noted that he compares them not to an eagle, hawk, raven, or any other bird, but to a dove, which is so weak that it cannot protect its own young. So too these people, when captured by their enemies, did not have the strength to defend themselves.

“They were calling upon Egypt”—understand, for help, or by worshiping their gods. “They went to the Assyrians,” not willingly but as captives. “And when they have gone away, I will spread my net over them”—that is, so that they may realize that, although they change their location, they cannot escape my sight. When they have gone into captivity, I will spread my net over them—that is, I will display my power over them, so that they cannot freely return to their land as they suppose, until I myself will it.

“I will bring them down like birds of the sky”—that is, just as a bird is drawn down from the height of the sky by a net spread over the waters, so I will bring them down from the height of their pride. “I will strike them according to the report of their assembly.” The meaning is: Just as they worshiped all the idols by common counsel, and, after fashioning them, all deliberated together to withdraw from me, so, when I am angry, they will all be devastated together, when I strike them collectively, from king to beggar.

These words can also be referred to the time of the Lord’s Passion. Just as they deliberated together about the Lord’s death, shouting to Pilate, “Crucify him, crucify him,” so they were collectively seized, beaten, and killed by their enemies during the Paschal festival.

“Woe to them”—that is, eternal condemnation will follow the present tribulation—“because they have departed from me,” by worshiping idols; “they will be devastated”—by their enemies, that is—and will be wretched. “Because they have transgressed against me,” worshiping the golden calves and transgressing my commandment, in which I said: “You shall not make foreign gods for yourselves.” “And I redeemed them” from Egyptian slavery and led them out with an exalted arm; “but they spoke lies against me,” making idols and saying: “These are your gods, Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt.”

“And they did not cry to me in their heart,” with which they loved idols. “But they howled in their dens,” imitating the voices of wolves or dogs in their praises of demons. Scripture calls the songs that they sang in praise of demons a howl. They had lost the rational understanding of their minds and had become like senseless beasts.

The meaning is readily understood concerning heretics, upon whom everlasting woe threatens because they have departed from God and transgressed his commandments—he who redeemed them with his blood. They speak lies against God, composing impious doctrines of falsehood. They do not cry to the Lord in their hearts but continually howl in their assemblies, which are called lairs of wild beasts, imitating the howling of wolves and the sound of irrational animals.

“They were ruminating over wheat and wine.” To ruminate is to vomit back up. Animals take what they eat during the day and bring it back from their innermost organs to the throat and jaws during the night; then, by chewing it more finely, they make it return to the stomach. The meaning is: Because they had an abundance of everything, which is encompassed in wine and wheat, they therefore fell away by departing from me, as Ezekiel also recalls happened in Sodom and Gomorrah.

It should be observed that, to show them to be like beasts of burden, he did not say “they were eating” but “they were ruminating.” They are also said to have ruminated in the sense that they did not understand spiritually the nourishment of the divine utterances. “They departed from me,” despising the worship of my religion and submitting themselves to the slavery of the devil. “And I instructed them”—that is, I taught them through Moses and the other faithful. “And I strengthened their arms”—that is, I gave them strength for battle, as happened in the times of Joshua and the Maccabees. “And they devised wickedness against me,” transferring my power to idols and saying that I was not God, but that the calves they themselves had made were gods. “Can they do anything or harm me?” The only thing they were able to do was to devise evil against me.

“They returned so that they might be without a yoke”—that is, just as formerly, before I called them through Abraham, then through Moses and the others, they were without a yoke and without knowledge of the Law and mingled with all the nations, so now they returned to their former state, running headlong without a yoke or the reins of God as they followed their desires.

“They became like a deceitful bow”—that is, a perverse bow, bending the arrow back against its lord. They had been made strong and stretched by God so that they might strike adversaries and enemies; but those whom God had stretched against their enemies turned against their own Lord, shooting arrows of blasphemy against him.

“Their princes will fall by the sword because of the fury of their tongue.” Just as the princes who deceived the wretched people were the head of wickedness, so now they themselves will first be truly disgraced because of the fury of their tongue. Having become mad, they dared to call the golden calves gods, doing in the land of promise what they had learned in Egypt. For the fury of their tongue signifies madness and blasphemy.

“This is their mockery in the land of Egypt”—that is, what they are now doing by mocking and ridiculing me through the worship of idols is not something new, because what they did in Egypt and afterward in the wilderness they also maintain now. There they began to worship idols, and to this day they persist in the same wickedness.

Spiritually, however, through wheat and wine we can understand the mysteries of Christ’s body and blood, or also sacred Scripture, which supplies food in its more obscure passages and drink in its clearer ones. Heretics fall upon this wheat or wine, unworthily receiving the Lord’s body and blood and interpreting divine Scripture with a perverse understanding. By reading continually and meditating on the Law and the other Scriptures, they pretend to eat what they ruminate by understanding it badly. In doing this they depart from the Lord, who taught them in the Church and gave them strength to fight against their adversaries. They themselves devise wickedness against God, constructing the most impious heresies; they become like the nations and are brought to nothing. Such people become like a deceitful bow when, through their own opinions, they inflict eternal death upon themselves.

Hence the princes of heretics are struck by the sentence of the true Judge because of the insanity of their tongue, since they blaspheme the Lord. In the false-named church they do the same things that they previously did when they dwelt in Egypt—that is, in the darkness of unbelief and ignorance.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Let there be a trumpet in your throat.” This is God’s voice to the prophet. He is commanded to raise his voice so that it may resemble a trumpet, so that many may hear him crying out, because many have sinned. Finally, he immediately adds what he ought to say with his raised voice: “Like an eagle over the house of the Lord.”

In this passage Nebuchadnezzar is called an eagle, coming against Jerusalem and the temple of God that stood in it. He is compared to an eagle because of his extraordinary speed or rapacity, since he imitated the flight of an eagle hastening swiftly toward its prey. Hence Ezekiel speaks of him figuratively: “A great eagle with great wings, with long-limbed reach, came to Lebanon.” Ezekiel calls the very temple of God, over which the prophet is commanded to announce the eagle’s coming, Lebanon. Hence Zechariah also says: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars.”

“Because they have transgressed my covenant and violated my law.” This verse also belongs to what precedes. The prophet is commanded to cry out in a loud voice that the eagle is over the house of God. The meaning is: What I tell and command you, O prophet—“Let there be a trumpet in your throat,” that is, announce in a loud voice that the king of the Chaldeans is coming—I command for no other reason than that they have transgressed my covenant by making idols and violated my law, in which I said: “You shall not make for yourselves gods of gold or silver.”

“They will call upon me: ‘My God, we have known you, Israel.’” When, he says, captivity has come and, pressed by anguish and compelled by necessity, they call upon me, seeking help and mercy, they will say: “We have known you, Israel”—that is, we who are called Israel and preserve the ancient name of Jacob, who pleased you, know and acknowledge you; and because of the knowledge of you that we possess above all the nations, deliver us.

“Israel has cast away the good; the enemy will pursue him.” This is the response of almighty God to what they had said: “We have known you, Israel.” The meaning is: How can you be called by the name Israel, which is interpreted as “a man who sees God,” when you have cast away the good—that is, the Lord God, from whom Jacob was called Israel?

“The good” that Israel cast away is understood as God, concerning whom it is written: “No one is good except God alone.” Israel therefore cast away the good—that is, it abandoned and regarded its God as nothing. Therefore, when it cries out, I will not hear it because of the false name Israel. Rather, the enemy—that is, the Assyrian, or even the devil—will pursue and seize it, because, having abandoned me as king, they asked for a king of their own, like the other nations. Hence he immediately adds:

«They themselves made kings, and not from me; they appointed princes, and I did not acknowledge them.» If we wish to refer this to their first king, Saul, a question arises as to why the Lord says, “They themselves made kings, and not from me,” and so forth, since the Lord chose him and appointed him king by lot. For after that king had been appointed, Samuel also said: “Surely you see whom the Lord has chosen.” Hence he brought him out from hiding in the house, and before his arrival had revealed it to Samuel. But it must be understood that Almighty God sometimes permits something to happen which he does not will, as plainly happened in the matter of this election. He saw that their hearts were inclined toward the choice of a king, and therefore permitted it to happen according to their request, against his own will. This is clearly shown by the thunder and lightning that occurred in summer, contrary to the custom of that land. Hence Samuel, knowing that God did not will this, foretold to them the right of the king, to whom they would be subjected in the harshest servitude, so that they might return to the Lord, the most merciful king.

But if we refer these words to Jeroboam, who later ruled over the ten tribes, and to the other princes who succeeded him in the kingdom, we plainly understand that this was done against God’s ordering. For although God, angered by Solomon’s sin, wished to divide the kingdom, nevertheless the people of Israel chose Jeroboam against God’s will. They ought, in accordance with the commandment, to have consulted God whether he wished this to happen, and then to have chosen a king by lot, rather than according to their own will. For necessary circumstances often arise which cannot be avoided; yet because people in such matters attend not to God’s will but to their own, they sin gravely. Thus, for example, it is said of the Lord and Savior that the Son of Man must be handed over, die, and be buried, and so forth; afterward it is added: “Woe to that man by whom he is to be handed over.” For Judas did not consider in the Lord’s death our necessity or God’s will, but rather followed his own desire. Therefore, although God had foreordained before the ages that this should happen, Judas, by carrying it out, was condemned to everlasting death.

“They themselves made kings, and not from me; they appointed princes, and I did not acknowledge them”—that is, I did not choose them, and therefore I reject them. To know, in God’s usage, means to choose; not to know means to reject.

“They made their gold and their silver into idols for themselves, so that they might perish”—that is, because they abounded in these things, they neglected God, who had given them these possessions for adornment and an abundance of delights, and made idols for themselves against their own soul, so that they might perish. For the gods they had made became the cause of death and destruction for them.

Spiritually, what is said here about Nebuchadnezzar can be referred to the devil, who in many places of Holy Scripture is called an eagle. Hence we read: “Although you exalt yourself like an eagle, from there I will bring you down,” says the Lord. This eagle came upon the gatherings of heretics, because they had once been houses of God. Since they transgressed God’s law and invoke God in vain with words while remaining far from knowledge of him in their deeds, and since, having rejected God through false teaching, they choose kings for themselves against God’s will—namely, princes and authors of perverse doctrines—God does not acknowledge them, because they are not worthy of his knowledge. Whatever gold and silver they possessed—that is, whatever they had in the brilliance of eloquence or the splendor of spiritual meanings—they perversely turn into idols, which they have fashioned from their own hearts. Because they did this, they therefore perished.

“Your calf has been rejected, Samaria.” Samaria is the name of a city and a province; here, however, Samaria, which was the metropolis of the ten tribes, is used for all the cities of that kingdom. For the golden calves were not in Samaria itself, but rather in Dan and Bethel, which, as has been said, are included within Samaria. We should understand one calf as referring to two, recognizing the singular number used for the plural, something that happens very frequently in Scripture.

“Your calf has been rejected,” he says—that is, the temple of the idol has been destroyed by the Assyrians. The calves themselves too were rejected, melted down, and carried into captivity. Hence it immediately adds: “My anger has burned against them”—meaning that I have taken vengeance upon them, whether upon the calves or upon those who worshiped them.

“How long will they be unable to be purified?” It is as though he said: What madness is this—that while I give them an opportunity for repentance, they refuse to return to soundness? Then, explaining what this calf was, from whose filth they would be unable to cleanse themselves, he adds:

“For it is from Israel itself.” That is, they did not receive the calf from elsewhere, as the Sidonians had Baal and Astarte, the Moabites Chemosh, and the Ammonites Moloch; rather, they and their king Jeroboam made the calf.

“An artisan made it”—that is, either Jeroboam, the inventor of wickedness, or certainly some artisan commissioned by him. This shows that the object whose form an artisan’s hand produces is not God, but an image.

“What will the calf of Samaria become? It will be like a spider’s web”—that is, just as spiderwebs, struck by the wind, are dissolved and brought to nothing, so its calf will be reduced to nothing. Here too he uses one calf for two.

[Col. 0061D] “For they will sow the wind, and reap the whirlwind.” “They will sow” is used for “they have sown,” the future for the past, as often happens in Scripture. “They will sow the wind,” he says—that is, they will perform empty works, manufacturing an idol utterly devoid of divinity; and therefore they will reap the whirlwind, namely captivity, storm, and misery.

“A standing stalk is not among them; the sprout will not produce flour.” When seeds scattered are corrupted by the wind and lose their inner substance, stalks cannot be produced from them from which flour might be made. The meaning is this: just as seeds corrupted by the wind do not yield fruit, so no fruit of good work can be found in them, nor can they possess any appearance of fruitful action. Hence it adds:

“And even if they produce anything, foreigners will eat it”—that is, if they should manage to possess some power for a time, or if they should do some good, foreigners—that is, the Assyrians—will take it all away; or else the demons, of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel, saying that the birds of heaven ate the seeds that had been sown.

“Israel has been devoured”—by enemies who killed them, or by demons who took away all their good. “Now he has become among the nations”—that is, he has become like the nations that worship idols. Hence it adds: “Like an unclean vessel.”

An unclean vessel, in the literal sense, is one that we customarily use for receiving and removing excrement. They themselves were stained with the excrement and filth of idols, becoming a vessel not for honor but rather for dishonor; therefore, like unclean things, they were cast away by the Lord. For what can be more unclean than a spirit possessed by a demon?

All this can also be applied to heretics, who pursue empty things and therefore depart empty-handed; sowing in the flesh, they will reap from the flesh the shame of corruption. In them the stalk of ecclesiastical doctrine may appear to stand, insofar as they have been baptized and celebrate the mysteries of Christ’s body; yet it will not produce flour—that is, it will not reach the fruit of good works—because all their activity is empty and worthless. Even if they accomplish anything, foreigners will eat it, because, exalted by human approval, they will lose all their good, and therefore will lack the fruit of reward in the future. They too are very often devoured by enemies—that is, by demons—and become an unclean vessel, becoming like pagans and even losing the name of Christianity.

“For they themselves have gone up to Assyria,” not proceeding willingly, but rather enduring the misfortune of an unwilling captivity.

“Ephraim is a solitary wild ass for himself.” A wild ass is a forest donkey, which does not seek domestic pastures as sheep do, but wanders freely through various places and loves a solitary dwelling. Such became the Jews when they departed from God, running according to their own desire after various idols and fashioning different gods for themselves. Abandoned by God, they became solitary. Of them it further says:

“They gave gifts to their lovers”—that is, to the Assyrians, with whom they had once been joined in friendship. This occurred in the time of King Menahem or Hoshea, as was said above.

“But they also hired nations with a payment,” supplying the words “for their assistance,” as was shown above where it says that Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king.

“Now I will gather them,” supplying “for battle,” so that all may be led captive together.

“And they will rest for a little while from the burden of king and princes.” It is as though he said: Until now they loved to give gifts to their adversaries, whom they loved. But now I will make them cease for a little while, so that, while they are being taken into captivity, they will not even pay tribute to their own kings and princes, until they reach Assyria. There they will no longer pay taxes and stipends as though they were free, but will be reduced to the most extreme slavery.

“For Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning; altars have become for him a cause of guilt.” He shows why they suffer captivity and cease for a little while from giving gifts to kings and princes: namely, because Ephraim—that is, Jeroboam, or certainly the entire people of the ten tribes—multiplied altars on which they might join sin to sin. They sinned all the more because they worshiped idols not only in Dan and Bethel, but also on mountains, in sacred groves, and in various places.

These altars—that is, shrines—were turned into a cause of guilt for him, because the more numerous they were, the more they sinned there.

“I will write for him the many laws of mine.” Since they regard as worthless the law that I gave them through Moses, worshiping idols in different places, although I commanded that there should be one altar in Jerusalem, I will impose upon him many laws by which he may be corrected. But again, emphasizing their wickedness, he adds that even these laws “were counted as something foreign.” It is as though he said: Since they despised the law that they had previously received, what benefit is there in writing further laws for them?

“They will bring sacrifices, slaughter the meat, and eat it.” Here it is shown that they made many altars for this reason: to bring sacrifices and slaughter various offerings there, where they might fill their bellies, not to please the Lord. Therefore it also adds: “The Lord will not accept them.” For the offerings were made not to him but rather to demons. They did not sacrifice them to the Lord, but to their own belly and throat. Their whole concern was that they themselves should eat the sacrifices, not that through them they should please the Lord.

Heretics likewise multiply altars for themselves when, abandoning the truth, they devise various doctrines, not to appease God but to provoke him. The altar of the holy Church is one, although many altars are built in different places throughout the world, just as there is one faith and one baptism, according to the teaching of the apostle Paul. When heretics abandon this, they incur a graver offense. Hence they do not deserve to receive God’s laws, because they have despised those they previously received. They abandon the one true offering of Christ’s body and sacrifice various victims, eating and consecrating Christ’s mysteries according to their own desire. Therefore, whatever they do—whether almsgiving, humility, chastity, or other works of virtue—is regarded by God as worthless. Nor will the Lord accept anything from such sacrifices, because in these things they seek not God’s glory but their own.

“Now he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins.” There is a distinction between iniquity and sin. Iniquity is whatever is committed before divine knowledge; sin, however, is what is perpetrated after the law has been given, and is regarded as more serious. Hence we read: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.”

When people remain in their offenses, the Lord remembers their iniquities, which they committed before the law, but he punishes their sins. Therefore, because these people sinned after the law had been given, it is now said—that is, in the present time—he will remember their iniquities, in order to avenge them, and he will visit their former sins through scourges and the torment of misery and captivity.

“They themselves will return to Egypt.” This can be understood in three ways. They returned to Egypt first in mind, by worshiping their gods; then by seeking assistance and not trusting in God’s protection; and finally, when God had commanded them not to return again to Egypt, they despised God and returned there even bodily, taking up residence there.

“And Israel forgot his Maker and built sanctuaries.” By the name Israel, as has often been said, the entire people of the ten tribes is understood, retaining its former name from the greater part. Having forgotten the worship of their God, they worshiped Baals and Astartes and other idols on mountains, hills, and beneath shady trees, and built sanctuaries there—that is, they constructed temples for the gods.

“And Judah multiplied fortified cities.” By Judah the two tribes are understood, namely Judah and Benjamin, together with the priestly tribe. When they saw that Israel had departed from the love of God and that Israel’s sins had been visited, they did not return to the Lord, but built fortified cities for themselves as a defense. Yet this profited them nothing, because, as the history of the Kings relates, in the fortieth year of Hezekiah Sennacherib came up, destroyed all the fortified cities, and captured them. Hence it adds:

“And I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour his houses.” Sennacherib is called fire, for he destroyed and burned with fire the cities and houses—that is, both public and private dwellings.

If we apply this, like the rest, to heretics, then the iniquities that had been forgiven them in baptism, as well as the new sins they committed after baptism, are charged against them, and vengeance is repaid to them because they have returned to Egypt—that is, to the darkness of unbelief from which they had departed through their confession of Christ. They have forgotten their God and devised various sanctuaries—that is, doctrines of falsehood.

Judah too—that is, the ecclesiastical man—builds fortified cities for himself through evil works or perverse interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, relying not on God’s help but on the craftsman’s deceit. Misunderstanding Scripture, he seeks to support his errors with divine testimonies. The Lord will set these ablaze with the fire of his Spirit and reduce them to nothing.

## CHAPTER IX

“Do not rejoice, Israel; do not exult like the nations, for you have committed fornication against your God.” The nations, ignorant of the knowledge of God and worshiping various monstrous forms of demons, rejoiced in their condition. The Israelites saw this and likewise began to rejoice in the worship of their gods, because they had become like the nations, supposing that they enjoyed peace as the other nations did.

Therefore it is said to Israel: “Do not rejoice,” because you have departed from me. You will not have peace for long, as you suppose; rather, you will be led into captivity, so that your sins may be punished. You wished to pay me the tribute of servitude, yet you became like the nations that do not know me and that rejoice and exult in their gods. Do not therefore rejoice, because you have committed fornication against your God, and do not suppose yourself to be like the other nations, since one who does not know God is punished in one way, whereas one who departs from God is punished in another. “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten severely.”

“You loved payment above all threshing floors of grain.” By threshing floors and grain we should understand an abundance of all things, which that people enjoyed and which they thought had all been given to them as payment because, after abandoning God, they had begun to worship idols. Everything they had received from God they attributed to idols. Therefore, by God’s just judgment, all these things are threatened with being taken away from them, when it adds:

“Threshing floor and winepress will not feed them”—that is, I will send them the poverty of famine, so that no grain will be found on the threshing floors and no wine in the winepresses. This is known to have happened in the time of Elijah and Elisha, when mothers, compelled by famine, fed upon the corpses of their own children.

“And wine will fail them”—that is, it will run out, and there will be none in the vineyards or winepresses, as they had supposed.

The same is said to heretics: Do not rejoice, thinking yourselves like the nations while you depart from the unity of the Church, for those who sinned without the law will perish without the law, while those who depart from the true faith after knowing God will be punished more severely. Although they abound in temporal goods, they are not satisfied by the threshing floor and winepress—that is, by Christ’s body and blood—because, while eating unworthily, they prepare for themselves perpetual mourning and eternal torments.

“They will not dwell in the land of the Lord.” They will suffer not only the scarcity of famine in the land that they received from the Lord, but they will also be led into captivity and will be unable to dwell in the land that they polluted by their crimes.

“Ephraim has returned to Egypt”—supply “in heart,” or, as was said above, by worshiping their gods.

“And in Assyria he ate what was polluted.” Just as they ate food sacrificed to idols in their own land, so, after being led into captivity, they fed in Assyria upon sacrifices to demons; when these were offered to idols, they became polluted.

“They will not pour wine for the Lord,” but for demons, “and they will not please him.” For, placed in Chaldea, they could not pour wine for the Lord, since they had neither temple nor altar at which they could perform these rites.

“Their sacrifices will be like the bread of mourners. All who eat it will be defiled.” Among the Jews, when a sacrifice was offered for the dead, whoever ate from it became unclean, as did the sacrifice that had been offered. The sacrifice itself is called the bread of mourners because it had been offered for a dead person, whose parents mourned his death.

Alternatively: It was customary among the Jews to mourn the dead for seven days. As long as this lamentation continued, whatever was done in the dead person’s house during those seven days in which they mourned him was unclean. Anyone who ate from that house or touched anything became unclean. Therefore they ate elsewhere until the seventh day. On the first day they mourned the dead person while he still lay in the same house. After his burial, the bier was placed in the middle, and they lamented as though the dead person were still present.

According to this custom, the prophet says: “Their sacrifices will be like the bread of mourners,” and so forth. The meaning is this: just as the things in a dead person’s house became unclean during the seven days in which they mourned him, and whoever ate or drank from them became unclean, so the sacrifices of those who sacrifice to idols are unclean, both the sacrifices themselves and those who offer or eat them.

“For their bread is for their own life”—supply “prepared,” that is, for this purpose they offer bread and other things to idols, so that they may be satisfied and rejoice in the present life. Here “soul” means the present life, as commonly occurs in divine discourse. Hence we read: “He who loves his life will lose it.”

“It will not enter the house of the Lord,” because it is offered not to the Lord but to demons. It should be understood that “bread” is used for every kind of food and sacrifice.

The meaning concerning heretics is clear. They do not dwell in the house of the Lord—that is, in the Church of the faithful, which, because of the firmness of its faith, is often called “land.” Hence John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” They will return to Egypt, imitating the works of unbelievers. Thus, among the Assyrians, they eat polluted food when they are satisfied by their pleasures in the company of demons. They do not pour wine for the Lord because spiritually they do not rejoice in him. Therefore they will not please him, but everything they do will be regarded as unclean.

They will not be able to enter the house of the Lord, because everything they do will be turned into mourning. They perform good works in order to offer their hearers the words of preaching, which are called bread, so that they may rejoice in the present, despoiling widows’ houses through their deception; those who eat this bread become defiled, because those who receive the doctrine of heretics become unclean. The gatherings of heretics are not houses of God but are called dens of robbers.

“What will you do on the solemn day, on the feast day of the Lord?” By the solemn day or feast day of the Lord we should understand the time of captivity and misery, when he exercised vengeance against his enemies and adversaries. Although all days belong to the Lord, that day is said to be especially his on which he is compelled to exact vengeance.

When, he says, the day of captivity comes and the most savage enemy breaks in, what festival is there for me—a festival that I regard as acceptable because it avenges me upon my enemies and puts an end to injustice? What will you do? Answer.

When they remain silent, he answers himself; indeed, he sees with divine eyes what they are going to do. Hence it adds:

“For behold, they have gone away from devastation.” Here the past is used for the future, according to the customary manner of Holy Scripture. “They have gone away” means “they will go away,” because, when the Assyrians and Chaldeans press upon them with misery and devastation and wish to bind them as captives, they will flee to Egypt in order to escape the hands of their enemies.

Hence it adds: “Egypt will gather them; Memphis will bury them.” This should be understood of the remnant of the two tribes who, after killing Gedaliah with Jeremiah, contrary to the Lord’s command, entered Egypt while fleeing from the Chaldeans. There they were later killed by Nebuchadnezzar, as the book of that prophet testifies.

Memphis, whose inhabitants buried the Jews who had been killed there, was the metropolitan city of Egypt before Alexandria.

“Their desirable silver, the nettle and the bur will inherit; the bur will be in their tents.” These words signify a long devastation, because where there had once been exceedingly beautiful houses, there arose burs and nettles. By that silver is understood what is purchased with silver, namely villas and fields, which prolonged devastation reduced to solitude.

The same is said to heretics: When the day of the Lord’s festival comes—that is, the day of judgment, when he will restore life to his friends—what will you do? For behold, you have been devastated by enemies, namely demons, who have stripped you of every virtue; you have imitated the works of unbelievers and become like the other nations.

Therefore Memphis will bury you there. Memphis is interpreted as “from the mouth,” because you will be condemned according to the judgments and blasphemies of your mouth, and you will experience in punishments what you uttered. Then the nettle will inherit your desirable silver—that is, whatever you possessed in the brilliance of eloquence and false doctrines—and perpetual fire will possess it, consuming you with eternal heat. There will also be bur in your tents—that is, the consciousness of sins and of your former way of life, and cares of this kind will torment you.

[Col. 0067C] “The days of visitation have come; the days of recompense have come.” In this passage “visitation” means affliction and torment. Elsewhere it is used in a good sense, as in: “He has visited us, the dawn from on high.”

“The days of visitation have come,” he says—the days of which he had said above: “What will you do on the solemn day and feast day of the Lord?” The days of recompense have come, so that they may receive what they have done.

“Know yourself, Israel: a foolish prophet, a madman, a spiritual man.” The Israelite people called the true prophets of God mad. Hence we read that the leaders at Ramoth-gilead said to Jehu: “What did that madman say to you?” He replied: “You know the man and what he said.”

Therefore it is said: O Israel, now recognize your own words. You called the prophet who spoke the truth to you and prophesied by the Holy Spirit foolish and mad. Know, then, that you are foolish—that is, without understanding—and that you called the prophet mad, you who despised my words. You thought yourself to be a spiritual man and believed that through the Spirit you saw things that would benefit you.

Alternatively: “Know yourself, Israel, to be a foolish prophet,” because you promised yourself peace, yet it did not come according to your false expectation. Know also that you are a mad prophet, because you despised my words, thought yourself to be a spiritual man, and believed that through the Spirit you saw things that would benefit you.

“Because of the multitude of your iniquity and the multitude of your madness.” That is, because of your countless sins you have also incurred great madness, so that, having lost your proper understanding, you did not know what you were doing. Hence you could neither foresee the adversities that were going to come upon you nor listen to those who had been taught by the Holy Spirit and were proclaiming these things to you; moreover, you called them mad and insane.

The day of vengeance will also come for the reprobate, when the Lord comes to judgment and they are visited for punishment, receiving according to what they have done. While they lived, they claimed to be Israelites—that is, men who see God—although they were not, failing to recognize their own foolishness. They said that the Son of God was a created thing, denied the Holy Spirit, and again asserted that one god was good while another was the creator of the world. Their madness is manifold, as are their many iniquities.

“Ephraim is a watchman with my God; the prophet has become a snare of ruin upon all his ways.” The prophet’s voice: “Ephraim is a watchman,” supply “with my God.” That is, Jeroboam, who is understood by the name Ephraim, was appointed by my God as a watchman for this purpose: that he and his successors might be kings and watchmen over God’s people, provide for their good, and govern and instruct them according to God’s will.

For the rulers and prophets of that people were called watchmen. Hence it is said to Ezekiel: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel.” Thus Jeroboam, together with his followers, was given to the people as a watchman and as a prophet, so that they might correct the people when they sinned and recall them to the right path.

But the one who ought to have instructed them became a snare of ruin in all his actions. Through his power and perverse persuasion he caused them to worship idols. The one who ought to have been a prophet, showing God’s people the proper worship, taught them idolatry. Hence it adds:

“Madness”—that is, an idol—“is in the house of his God,” that is, in Bethel, where previously there had been the house of God. There he established a golden calf to be worshiped.

“They sinned deeply, as in the days of Gibeah.” Here the prophet recalls the crime of the children of Israel that was once committed at Gibeah, when they killed the Levite’s wife, who was returning from Bethlehem, through an unlawful sexual assault. In this way he says that in their own time the Israelites had been plunged into an abyss of impiety so deeply that they surpassed the crime once perpetrated at Gibeah.

We may also understand “the days of Gibeah” as referring to the time when, in place of God, they chose Saul as king from the city of Gibeah. These people sinned more grievously, because the former merely abandoned God by choosing a human king to rule over them, whereas these not only chose Jeroboam son of Nebat as their king against God’s will, but also departed from God by worshiping the calves he had made.

“He will remember their iniquities,” supply “which he was thought now to have forgotten,” “and he will visit their sins,” supply “through captivity unto death.” God does not at any time suffer forgetfulness; rather, he is said to remember when he is known to repay sinners with vengeance.

These words can also be referred to those who had been placed over the Church, namely bishops and presbyters. But by teaching perverse doctrine, they became for others a snare of destruction.

[Col. 0069A] “Like paths [Alternatively: grapes] in the desert I found Israel, like the first fruit of the fig tree.” That is, when all the nations were deserted by God and did not possess knowledge of him, I found the people Israel like a path in the wilderness; and just as newly discovered fruit is eagerly gathered and eaten, so, with all the nations left in the desert, I chose them.

This is what follows: “Like the first fruit of the fig tree,” supply “which is delightful and gathered with affection.”

“On its summit I saw their fathers.” That is, at the beginning of that people, through the grace of my mercy, I chose Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob because they pleased me, adhering to faith and good works. To see, in God’s usage, means to have mercy.

“But they themselves went to Baal-peor,” that is, to the idol of the Moabites, “and became alienated”—that is, they departed.

“In their excess,” supply “of themselves,” “and they became abominable”—that is, worthy of rejection.

“Like the things they loved,” according to what is written in the Psalm: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.” Thus not only are idolaters so named, but the idols themselves are also called by this designation.

If we apply these words to the faithful people, then in the wilderness of this age—that is, while the whole world was held in sin and the nations were ignorant of God—the Lord first found among the apostles and apostolic men the Christian people, who saw God in their minds, and he was satisfied with their sweetest fruits.

But heretics, who usurp the name of Christianity for themselves, went to Baal-peor, serving lust. For it is difficult, as blessed Jerome says, to find a heretic who loves chastity, although he habitually parades it with his mouth: he says one thing with his lips, but his conscience preserves another and his deeds fulfill it. Therefore they too become abominable and unclean, like the things they loved.

“Ephraim flew away like a bird.” That is, the people of the ten tribes, quickly losing their own land, went into captivity. The prophet called him a bird in order to show the swift passage into Babylon.

“Their glory flew away from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception”—supply “flew away.” The people of the ten tribes gloried in the multitude of their children and armies, and considered themselves greater than their brother Judah, because Ephraim ruled ten tribes while Judah ruled two. They therefore had very many children in whom they gloried; all of them were either led into captivity or killed, and their entire glory in which they had boasted of their children suddenly departed.

Hence it adds:

“And even if they rear their children, I will make them childless among men”—that is, if they gather a multitude of children and have the opportunity to raise them, it will profit them nothing, because they will be handed over to slaughter. I will prevent them from boasting in them, because they will see them killed and captured by enemies. While the other nations rejoice in the propagation of children, they will be childless.

“But woe to them when I depart from them.” Because they departed from me, I too will depart from them. Then they will experience woe—that is, eternal condemnation—when they have lost all my help.

[Col. 0070A] “Ephraim, as I saw him, was like Tyre, founded in beauty.” Tyre was a distinguished city of great wealth, situated in the midst of the sea. It was called a marketplace because all kinds of riches for purchase were found there, and it abounded in a great multitude of inhabitants.

Therefore Ephraim—that is, the ten tribes, boasting in the multitude of their wealth and people—thought himself like Tyre, founded in beauty, that is, in the honor and splendor of abundant riches.

The meaning is this: Ephraim, who is now desolate, was so beautiful and was so fortified by God’s help that he was like Tyre, which is surrounded by the sea and disregards the storms and whirlwinds of the winds. Just as Tyre does not care about the waves rising against it, so they, protected by God’s help, regarded all who rose up against them as worthless.

“Ephraim will lead his children out to the slayer.” By the slayer we should understand Hazael, king of Syria, who besieged Samaria for a long time, until, compelled by famine, they went out to him, judging it preferable to perish at once by the sword rather than through prolonged hunger.

In the tropological sense, heretics are understood by Ephraim. Like unstable and wanton people, they depart from the Church and glory in the multitude of children whom they beget for themselves through perverse doctrine. The Lord threatens to punish these children even if they have been raised, because they were born from fornication. Thus the fathers are made childless when both disciples and their perverse teachers perish together. Of them it also adds: “Woe to them when I depart from them.”

At the same time it repeats what Ephraim was like. When, he says, he was in the Church amid the temptations of this age, he was beaten by the sea’s waves like Tyre, yet no adversity could prevail against him because he had Christ as his foundation, upon which a house built cannot be overthrown.

But now he leads his children out to the slayer—that is, to the devil, who eternally slaughters perverse souls. And fittingly he said, “he leads them out,” meaning that he causes them to be taken outside the Church.

In the moral sense, we may call the children of Ephraim his worst thoughts and doctrines opposed to the truth. The Lord destroys all these and does not allow such sinners to retain their children; abandoning them eternally, he punishes them together with their perverse doctrines and wicked thoughts. Hence it is said: “On that day all their thoughts will perish.”

[Cols. 0070D–0072B]

“Give them, Lord. What will you give them? Give them a womb without children and breasts that are dry.” Lest we misuse for evil those things that God gave for a blessing, and lest we turn to the contrary anything given by him, it is expedient that they be taken away from us. Thus, since we have been given a tongue for praising God and speaking what is good, if anyone abuses it for blasphemy, the Psalmist prays against him: “Let deceitful lips become mute,” and so forth. Since Ephraim therefore gloried in the womb, conception, and childbirth, and in the multitude of peoples, by which he was puffed up and swollen with pride, when instead he ought to have humbled himself and given thanks to God, who had multiplied them, the prophet speaks to the Lord, saying: “Give them, Lord,” and answers himself: “What will you give them?” Immediately, imprecating and inciting God against them, he adds: Give them a barren womb and dry breasts, so that they may have no causes for pride, and so that in the very thing in which they are accustomed to glory, they may be brought to shame. For their pride consisted in the multitude of their children; therefore he says: Give them a barren womb, so that they may not bear children, and give them dry breasts, so that, even if they bear children, they may have no means by which to nurse them.

“All their wickedness is in Gilgal, because there I hated them.” In Gilgal Saul was anointed king, when Samuel announced God’s anger to the people. There, he says, I hated them, because there, in asking for a human king, they withdrew from my rule. Alternatively: We read in the book of Joshua son of Nun that the Israelite people were circumcised a second time at Gilgal; there also, afterward, they first began to worship idols, supposedly in the cause of religion, and in their worship committed every crime. But since Gilgal is interpreted as “revelation” or “rolling-place,” the wickedness of heretics is rightly said to be in Gilgal, because their deeds are to be made manifest and they themselves are to be rolled down into hell. They truly deserve hatred, because they speak lies against God.

“Because of the wickedness of their inventions.” That is, because of the worship of idols, which they wickedly devised against me, “I will drive them out of my house,” that is, from Bethel, which is called “the house of God.” Or we can understand the house of the Lord as heaven, from which they were expelled, because, when they fail in the body, they also perish eternally in soul.

“I will no longer love them.” It is clear that the Lord did not continue to love them, and therefore they have remained in captivity to this day. “All their princes are departing”—the words “they are” being understood. By “princes” in this passage we should understand the kings of the ten tribes, all of whom withdrew from God through idolatry, and none of whom turned wholeheartedly to God. We can refer all these things to the time of Christ and understand them of the two tribes, which at his coming were expelled from the house of God so that they would not be saved, in order that Israel—that is, the Christian people—might be saved. Hence in the Gospel we read that the Lord made a whip of cords and drove them from the temple, because they had made his Father’s house a house of commerce.

“Ephraim has been struck down”—by God, who handed them over to their enemies—“their root has dried up; they will bear fruit no more.” He takes the metaphor from a tree: if its roots have dried up, it cannot bear fruit; and if it produces any for a little while, it will immediately dry up in the flower itself. But what root of the Israelites should we understand except their good fathers, from whom they took their origin according to the flesh? Yet because they were unwilling to hold fast to their faith and imitate their examples, their root dried up in this respect: it could not help them or free them from the impending evil. Or certainly we should understand the root as God almighty, in whom they had been founded, and who, as he had created all peoples, protected them and made them increase. This root, then, dried up in them because he no longer protects or defends them. Hence it follows: “They will bear fruit no more,” that is, they will not beget children, or they will have no good works.

“And even if they should beget children, I will kill the beloved ones of their womb.” That is, if it should happen that they have children against my will, it will profit them nothing, because I will kill their offspring, whom they love exceedingly. This is what he said above: “Even if they should raise children, I will leave them without children.”

“My God will reject them, because they have not listened to him, and they will be wanderers among the nations.” They follow various forms of worship in different places because they were unwilling to be steadfast in the worship of the one true God. We can understand this generally of all the Jews: because their princes withdrew from the Lord and moved the people to seek his death, he expelled them from his house and no longer continued to love them. Their root, struck and dried up, means that they have lost the understanding of the heart and do not understand sacred Scripture with sound judgment; therefore they produce no fruit of good works. And even if they do so—that is, if they appear to meditate upon sacred Scripture and the Law, and, as though they loved their children exceedingly, bring forth from themselves some knowledge and teaching—the Lord’s opposition will cut them down. For the God of all the prophets rejected them because they did not listen to him, and they were wanderers among the nations, possessing neither an altar, nor a temple, nor a city of their own. Hence David also says in the psalm: “Do not kill them, lest my people at some time forget; scatter them,” and so forth.

## [Cols. 0072C–0079B] CHAPTER X

“Israel was a leafy vine”—the words “in the saints” being understood—when it abounded in good works. Hence: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” “Its fruit was made equal to it.” For, possessing good shoots and fruitful branches, it produced many clusters, and the abundance of grapes equaled the greatness of its branches. For in proportion to the multitude of its peoples it abounded in good works—in the patriarchs, prophets, and other good men.

Another translation has: “Israel is a watery vine,” which we understand in a negative sense. For a watery vine, if it is not pruned by the vinedresser, grows entirely into foliage and squanders the moisture that it ought to have turned into wine through the vain display of leaves and branches; such a vine is harmful to the cultivators. Israel was such a vine: it grew in the multitude of its peoples but did not return fruit to God the cultivator, because, when it ought to have produced grapes, it produced wild grapes. Of these it is written: “Their vine is a vine of Sodom.” They devoted their labor not to good works but to the abundance of foliage.

“In proportion to the multitude of its fruit, it multiplied altars for itself.” That is, however many people there were, so many altars they had. What had previously abounded in good works afterward turned the abundance of its fruit into an offense, multiplying it, so that the more peoples it had, the more altars it built. Hence he adds: “According to the abundance of its land, it overflowed with images,” that is, in proportion as their land was more fertile than all other lands, so among all nations they produced more images there—that is, images of dead human beings or animals—until even the abundance of the land was surpassed by the excess of idols.

So also heretics, while they were planted in the Church, were called the Lord’s vineyard and produced exceedingly abundant fruits. But afterward, departing from the good altar—that is, from the unity of the faith—they built many altars of their error; and in proportion to the abundance of their land—that is, according to the sharpness of their understanding and the force of their ardent intellect—they overflowed with images. For out of their profoundest understanding kings and peoples worshiped golden calves and agreed in impiety, which captivity overtook.

The last king of the ten tribes was Hoshea, of whom it is written that he did evil in the sight of the Lord, but not like the kings who had been before him, because he allowed them, if they wished, to go to the temple of the Lord, which was in Jerusalem. But because, despite being given permission, they did not wish to go to Jerusalem, in the ninth year of Hoshea, Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, came, captured the people of Israel, led them away into Assyria, and settled them beside the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes.

It may be asked why they were not captured under the worst kings, but under one who had begun in some measure to turn toward better things. The answer is that under the other kings the people excused themselves, saying: We obey the commands of our kings and cannot resist tyranny; therefore we worship the calves that we are compelled to adore, and we cannot go up to the temple of the Lord. But in the days of Hoshea, the same king commanded that the calves should not be worshiped with such devotion, but that anyone who wished could go to Jerusalem and sacrifice in the temple. The people opposed this decree, and this is what he now says:

“Their heart is divided,” that is, the will and understanding of king and people. Therefore he now says, since no excuse remains: “Now they will perish,” and will be handed over to eternal captivity. As soon as the people dissented from the king, destruction and captivity arrived—destruction that the prophet Hosea not only foretold, as has been said, but also saw and mourned after seeing it. Therefore he says: “Now”—that is, at the present time—“he himself will smash their images; he will devastate their altars.” This is said of God almighty, not because he did it with his own hand, but because his will was fulfilled through the Assyrians, among whom he will devastate—that is, ravage and destroy—their altars.

The understanding of heretics is divided among themselves, since they think variously about Christ; therefore they will perish, that is, they will be condemned to everlasting punishment, when he himself—that is, God almighty—has devastated the images and altars, that is, the various doctrines that they fashioned from their own hearts.

“For now they will say.” “Now” is used in place of “then,” namely in the ninth year, when Hoshea was captured by Shalmaneser, who is himself Sennacherib, and was placed in prison. After the Lord has smashed Israel’s images, they will say: “We have no king,” namely, no one to defend us, because our king and all our princes have been captured and killed. Finally, explaining why their king and princes have been taken from them, they add: “For we did not fear the Lord.” As though they were saying: We have lost the human king who ought to have defended us because we did not fear the true King, God.

“And what will the king do for us?” The meaning is: If we had had a human king, what could he have done for us? That is, how could he have defended us, when God almighty is offended with us, and no one can resist his will? As though they were saying: It would have profited us nothing to have had a king.

“Speak words of an empty vision.” The prophet’s voice is the speech of God mocking those who promised themselves that peace and prosperity would come. Speak, he says, words of an empty vision; that is, promise yourselves prosperity and dream various dreams that declare that everything will turn out beneficially for you, just as you have done until now. Everything that seemed prosperous to you has been turned into its opposite. Hence it follows: “And you will make a covenant,” not with God, but rather with falsehood, saying: “There will be peace for us.” “And judgment will sprout like bitterness,” that is, the very falsehood in which you trust will not produce for you fruits of complete peace with which you can be satisfied, but the force of bitterness—namely, captivity and slaughter—“upon the furrows of the field,” that is, upon your earthly hearts, from which you have produced evil fruits, according to the saying: “From the heart come evil thoughts.”

The disciples of heretics, when their lies have been crushed, will likewise say too late: “We have no king,” that is, no teachers who previously ruled us, and through whose deceptions we did not fear God. “And what will the king do for us?” As though they were saying: What profit was there in following those whose help we do not experience in our time of need? They will say these things while seeking various excuses, so that they may appear to have gone astray not by themselves but through their teachers. Hence the words and visions of heretics are useless. They will make a covenant not with God but with the judgment of bitterness. Concerning this judgment the Lord says in the Gospel that some will receive a greater judgment: when the day of judgment comes, those who have sown falsehood in the furrows of the field of the heart will reap condemnation, while those who have sown in tears will reap in joy. It follows:

“The inhabitants of Samaria worshiped the cows of Beth-aven.” Beth-aven is Bethel itself, and it is interpreted as “the house of the idol”; there Jeroboam placed the golden calf that he had made. He mockingly calls the calves “cows,” as though he were saying: Israel has fallen into such great misery that it worships not only calves but even cows. The inhabitants of Samaria are understood to mean all the inhabitants of the ten tribes, whose metropolis was that same city.

“Because its people mourned over it.” To show that by the cows of Beth-aven the calf that was in Bethel must be understood, he did not say, “The people mourned over them,” but “over it.” It is called its people because they worshiped that golden calf, which evidently mourned when, as we find in what follows, it was carried away as a gift to the avenging king. “And its temple-attendants”—that is, its priests—“exulted over it,” because their deception had not been detected. For, as the Hebrews relate, they made bronze and gilded calves in place of the golden calves and put them in the same location.

When, therefore, the people mourned in the time of distress because the calves themselves had also been carried off by Sennacherib, king of Israel, the priests exulted because their deception could not be accused or detected. “In its glory.” Its glory—that is, the glory of the people—is what the calf itself is called, in which they gloried because they possessed golden calves. “Because it will depart from it.” He shows why they exulted in the glory of the people: because, he says, it departed from it—that is, from the people. Hence it follows:

“For even it has been carried into Assyria as a gift to the avenging king.” Sennacherib himself is the avenger because he took vengeance for the injury done to God against those who worshiped idols in place of God. Note that he expresses the misery and condemnation of the people by saying that what they seemed to value most highly they gave as a gift.

“Ephraim’s shame will seize him, and Israel will be ashamed of his plan.” We read in the Book of Kings that Menahem, king of Israel, sent a thousand talents of silver to the Assyrian king Pul, “so that his hand might be with him,” that is, so that he might provide him assistance. Some think that among these gifts the calves, which they supposed to be golden, were also sent. When the deception of the gilded calves was detected, the king of Israel was informed by letter; and by the very means through which they wanted to make him favorable to them, they offended and provoked against themselves the men to whom they had sent the gifts, since they supposed that this had been done not through the theft of the priests but through the king’s deception and plan. For when he discovered that the calves were bronze, he became exceedingly angry, thinking that they had wanted to mock him. For this reason he came and conquered them.

Therefore it is said: “Ephraim’s shame”—that is, destruction—“will seize him, and Israel will be ashamed”—that is, will blush—“of his plan,” namely, the plan by which he sought help from a foreigner.

“Samaria has made its king pass away like foam upon the face of the water,” that is, just as foam and a bubble of water quickly dissolve, so the kingdom of the ten tribes will quickly come to an end. It was said above that Hoshea wished and commanded them to return to the temple of the Lord; but because the inhabitants themselves were unwilling to listen to him, they caused him to perish, just as foam on water passes away and perishes in a time of rain or drought.

“And the high places of the idol will be destroyed.” Concerning these the Books of Kings often say: “Nevertheless, the people sacrificed on the high places.” What these high places of the idol are is made clear when he adds: “The sin of Israel”—the words “the same high places” being understood. For they sinned greatly when, having abandoned the temple of God, they worshiped idols on mountains, in groves, and in other pleasant places.

“Thistle and thorn will grow upon their altars.” This is a sign of the final desolation, when thistle and thorn grew up in their shelters because of the long abandonment. “And they will say to the mountains: Fall upon us; and to the hills: Cover us.” We can refer this not only to the captivity of the ten tribes but also generally to the time of the Romans and to the whole Jewish people. The Lord also makes this clear when he says in the Gospel: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves.” Or, even on the day of judgment, they will say to the saints, who are called mountains because of the heights of their virtues: “Fall upon us,” that is, cover our evils with your prayers. The passage also literally indicates the immense terror of sinners, who, when the day of judgment is imminent, would wish, if they could, to escape the presence of God and perish temporarily rather than perish eternally.

“From the days of Gibeah Israel sinned,” that is, from the day when Benjamin, through unlawful intercourse, shamefully and cruelly killed the Levite’s wife in the city of Gibeah. From that time, the people—Israel—sinned against me. Or it may mean from the time when they expelled God, so that he would not rule over them, and chose Saul as king. “There they remained,” that is, they persevered in those very sins.

“War will not overtake them in Gibeah because of the sons of iniquity.” That is, they did not perish in the battle at Gibeah because they rose up against the sons of iniquity—that is, against Benjamin—and destroyed it; rather, because they took vengeance against a human being but did not avenge the injury done to God, allowing the idol to remain in Micah’s house, battle will overtake them. They ought first to have exercised God’s vengeance by overthrowing Micah and his house and reducing the idol to nothing, and afterward to have avenged the Levite’s injury. Since, therefore, they took vengeance against a human being and not against God, and did this more for the sake of a human being than for God, and moreover refused to avenge the sacrilege against their God, battle will overtake them.

“According to my desire I will discipline them,” that is, I will hand them over to their enemies according to my will. “And peoples will gather against them,” namely, the multitudes of the Assyrians, “when they are disciplined for their two iniquities.” We can understand the two iniquities as their avenging a human being while neglecting the injury done to God. Or they committed two iniquities because they first sinned through Micah’s idols and second through Jeroboam’s calves. Or, certainly, by the two iniquities we may understand the two calves of Samaria, one in Dan and the other in Bethel. Or they perpetrated two iniquities because, abandoning God, they worshiped idols.

Jeremiah speaks of these two iniquities: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns that cannot hold water.” These two iniquities broke out against the two commandments of the Decalogue, in which it is said: “I am the Lord your God,” and “You shall have no other gods before me.”

“Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing.” Here he touches upon the custom of the Promised Land, where heifers, together with the other animals, were accustomed to thresh grain. When they have been wearied by the very heavy labor, they usually leave the threshing floor; but then, because they love the threshing floor since they eat the grain there—for it is written, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing”—they return of their own accord to the threshing floor. Thus Ephraim is like a cow or heifer because it learned to thresh the floor, and not only learned this but also, through yearly habit, began to love what it had been taught, although threshing entails labor.

So also the Israelite people, although they were frequently afflicted and suffered many adversities because of idolatry, nevertheless, desiring to follow their own pleasures and the greed of their belly, returned voluntarily to idols. Morally, we can refer this to those who turn from a secular way of life to the monastic religion and willingly return to the exercise of earthly labor. Although they are worn out by prolonged affliction from heat and cold, they nevertheless endure voluntarily all those things that they had formerly experienced.

“And I passed over the beauty of his neck.” That is, I will break his pride, by which, with a thick neck, he did not accept my yoke. “Passing over,” especially when it is said of God, always signifies blows and adversities. Thus the destroyer is also said to have passed through Egypt. The meaning is: Since Ephraim does not wish to receive the yoke of the Law, I passed over the beauty of his neck, and, having imposed a yoke, I subdued the swelling muscles of his neck. Hence it follows: “I will mount Ephraim,” that is, against him, so that the contentious and wanton heifer may learn to labor at what it does not wish to do.

Or we can understand the yoke as the condemnations of all the nations, since the Lord promises that he will remove it from his place, so that in this way he might return to him.

“Judah will plow; Jacob will break up the furrows for himself.” By Judah understand the two tribes. When they saw Israel being taken captive by its enemies, they began to cultivate their hearts and constrain themselves to the worship of God. By Jacob understand those alone who were left from the ten tribes and were summoned to the worship of the true religion. Once all hardness of heart had been removed, they began to produce fruits of good works. Concerning them it is written in Isaiah that Hezekiah sent them books and brought them to Jerusalem, so that they might worship God there in his temple, doing penance for their worship of idols.

According to the allegorical sense, this can be understood as referring to Ephraim, who had been instructed in the Law of God so that he might thresh the field of Scripture and meditate upon it day and night. He began to cast off the yoke of the Law and contend against ecclesiastical teachers for the ruin of those who listened. Therefore the Lord will either press down with a yoke the neck that has been raised and promises itself lofty things, or, passing over him, will trample him under his feet and mount upon him, so that he may know that he has God.

Judah—that is, the ecclesiastical man—will plow the earth, persevering in the work begun at the inception of his undertaking. Jacob, too, whose name is interpreted as “supplanter,” will break up the furrows of vices: he will crush the clods of history and the hardness of the letter into parts and divide them spiritually, so that they may produce spiritual fruits.

“Sow righteousness for yourselves in truth.” He preserves the agricultural metaphor once begun. He said that Ephraim was a heifer trained to love threshing, and that he would mount upon its neck in order to plow Judah and break up Jacob’s furrows. Now he commands them to sow in righteousness—that is, in the observance of the legal commandments.

“And reap in the mouth of mercy,” that is, in the grace of the Gospel. Hence: “Repent,” and so forth; and: “Do good to those who hate you”; and: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also.”

“Renew the fallow ground for yourselves,” that is, make your heart new, saying with the Psalmist: “Create a clean heart in me, O God.” Literally, fallow ground is a field when it has first been cut open by the plow.

“The time for seeking the Lord”—the words “will then be” being understood—“will be when he comes who will teach you righteousness,” that is, in the time of the Lord’s incarnation and passion, when all the things by which the faithful are justified will be openly revealed. Hence: “Seek the Lord while he may be found.” He gives the reasons why they should sow, why they should reap, and why they should renew their joyful fallow ground. The time for seeking the Lord, he says, is when Christ and Savior comes, who will teach you the righteousness that you now hope for in the Law. “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who does what is good.”

Likewise, those who have separated themselves from the Church and assumed the false name of Christians are commanded to do penance and receive both Testaments: in the Old they should sow righteousness, in the New they should reap mercy; thus they should renew for themselves the fallow ground of good works and seek God, who can teach them true righteousness.

“You have plowed wickedness; you have reaped iniquity.” The meaning is: Although I urged you to sow in righteousness and reap in the mouth of mercy, so that you might make me glad with your joyful fallow grounds, you instead plowed wickedness—that is, you devised iniquitous plans in order to withdraw from me. For it is the greatest iniquity to withdraw from God and worship idols in place of God. Therefore you reaped iniquity—that is, you caused captivity and death to come upon you because of your sins; you deserved to receive evil crops from evil seed.

“You have eaten the fruit of falsehood,” that is, you have received the recompense of falsehood. You dreamed of good things for yourselves, and adversity came upon you justly. So also heretics plow wickedness when they teach iniquity. Therefore they will reap iniquity and eat the fruit of falsehood when they are condemned according to the merit of their iniquity and falsehood. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.

“Because you trusted in your ways,” that is, in idols, in whose worship you walked, “in the multitude of your mighty men,” that is, in kings and princes, placing your confidence not in God but in the strength of armies.

“Tumult will arise among your people,” that is, the sound of the Assyrian army will come upon you, and, when they cry out, “all your fortifications will be devastated,” and those things that you considered fortified and secure will lie open to the enemy. Hence it is written in Isaiah that Sennacherib came up and captured all the fortified cities of Judah.

“As Salmana was devastated by the house of him who avenged Baal on the day of battle, a mother dashed to pieces upon her children, so Bethel has done to us because of the wickedness of your iniquities.” The history of Judges is recalled here. We read that an angel appeared to Gideon and said to him: “Go in this strength of yours, and you will deliver Israel from the hand of Midian.” First, however, he urged him to destroy the grove and the altars of Baal. For this reason he was called Jerubbaal, because his father said to him: “Let Baal avenge himself upon him who has demolished his altar.”

He therefore went with three hundred men, carrying torches in pitchers, and killed the army of the Midianites, who were advancing with everything they possessed and who seized and devoured everything belonging to Israel. The meaning is: Just as Salmana, prince of the Midianites, was devastated—he was killed by the house, that is, the family, of Gideon, who avenged, that is, condemned, Baal by destroying his altar on the day of battle—so Bethel, in which you placed the golden calf, will act against you because of the wickedness of your iniquities, for which you will be handed over to your enemies and perish.

When he says, “a mother dashed to pieces upon her children,” this refers to what the same history relates: after Gideon had captured Zebah and Salmunna, the princes of Midian, he said to them: “What were the men like whom you killed at Tabor?” Salmunna replied: “They were like you, and one of them was like the son of a king.” He said to them: “If you had spared them, I would not kill you,” and so forth. Then, concluding, he said: “As your sword made women childless, so shall your mother be childless.” He struck him and killed him.

Thus the mother was dashed upon the children, either because she was broken by excessive grief at the death of her sons, or certainly because she was killed together with them. For it could have happened that she was there and was dashed to pieces together with them, since, as was said above, they were advancing toward the land of Israel with everything they possessed.

## [Cols. 0079C–0081C] CHAPTER XI
