“As morning passes, so the king of Israel passes away.” He explains the same meaning through different figures, which he had expressed above: “Samaria has made its king pass away like foam upon the face of the water.” He presents the same matter under another comparison: just as morning, when the sun arrives, quickly passes away, so the king of Israel, Hoshea, passed away, because he was captured by the enemies. Morning is the rising of dawn, from the end of night until sunrise.

“Because Israel was a child, and I loved him.” He explains the benefits that God had bestowed upon him. Israel, he says, was a child, worshiping idols in Egypt and thinking like a child, and I loved him in the patriarchs and the other holy men.

“And from Egypt I called my son,” the words “through Moses” being understood. For he himself said to Pharaoh: “Thus says the Lord: Let my firstborn go, so that he may sacrifice to me in the wilderness.” And elsewhere: “My firstborn is Israel.” And again: “I have nourished and raised children.”

If we wish to refer these words to Christ, who is the Son of the Father, he called him from Egypt when, as Matthew says, at the command of the angel he was brought back by Joseph, together with his virgin mother, into the land of Israel. Spiritually, however, Egypt, which is called “darkness,” signifies this world. God therefore called his Son from Egypt when, through the glory of the Ascension, he lifted him from this world and placed him in heaven.

“They called them.” Although Israel is spoken of in the singular, it is understood in the plural, like “people” and “nation.” He rightly passes from the singular to the plural: “They called them”—that is, Moses, Aaron, and the others called all the Jews—to follow them as they went out from the land of Egypt and to fulfill God’s command and will.

“So they departed from their presence,” that is, when called by them, they withdrew quickly in this manner from their teaching, turning their backs on them and displaying hardness of mind when they said to Aaron: “Make gods for us who will go before us.” For Moses, they said, we do not know what has happened to him. And they went on to cry out: “These are your gods, Israel,” and so forth.

“They sacrificed to the Baals and offered sacrifices to images.” It had not been enough for them to despise those who called them unless they also sacrificed to Baal in the time of Ahab, who received the idol from the Sidonians because he had married Jezebel, the daughter of the king of the Sidonians. Baal himself is Beel-phegor. They also sacrificed to images, worshiping idols not only in Dan and Bethel but also on mountains, in groves, and in other pleasant places, adoring various images.

The interpretation concerning heretics is straightforward. Their king—that is, the devil, or any heresiarch—will pass like the dawn. When they were infants, when they believed and were little ones and were reckoned by the Christian name, God loved them and called them from the tribulation and darkness of Egypt. He called them through the apostles and teachers of the Church; when called by them, they withdrew from their presence and worshiped Beel-phegor—that is, serving their own vices and lusts, they sacrificed to the images that they had fashioned for themselves. For each of the heretics had his own gods, and whatever he imagined he worshiped as a carved or cast image.

“And I was like a nurse to Ephraim.” He recounts with what love Israel was loved when he called it from Egypt, according to the passage in Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God carried you, as a man is accustomed to carry his little son,” and so forth.

“I carried them in my arms,” that is, in my strength. As though he were saying: I, who was their father, became their nurse, and I myself carried my little one in my arms, so that he would not be harmed in the wilderness and would not be terrified either by the heat during the day or by the darkness at night. By day I was a cloud; by night, a pillar of fire.

“And they did not know that I was caring for them,” that is, when they had sinned and made a calf’s head for themselves, I gave them an opportunity for repentance, but they did not understand that I wished to heal them—that is, to cleanse them from their idols.

“With the cords of Adam I will draw them,” that is, with the affection of love with which I loved Adam. For just as I made him holy, so I also wished to sanctify them and make them clean. Hence it follows: “with the bonds of love,” that is, with the highest affection of love. Hence another translation has: “With the cords of men I will draw them.” The meaning is: With the love by which I loved and bound Abraham, Isaac, and the other holy men to myself, I will join these people to myself as well.

“And I was to them like one who lifts the yoke over their cheeks,” that is, I will take the yoke of the Law away from them, so that they do not perish beneath its very heavy burden, which says: “Whoever makes an idol, and whoever sacrifices to Moloch, shall surely die.” Because I desire mercy rather than vengeance, I will lift the yoke of the Law, lest they succumb beneath its weight. Or, alternatively, I will remove from them the yoke of captivity and domination imposed by all the surrounding nations.

“And I bent down to him so that he might eat,” that is, I gave him food, manna in the wilderness, so that he might be nourished. The phrase “I bent down to him” must be understood in this way: I caused food to bend down toward him.

We can also refer these words to the coming of the Lord’s incarnation. I loved them so much, he says, and was such a merciful shepherd that I myself carried the sick sheep upon my shoulders. But they did not understand that I was healing them through my passion, and that, because I am a lover of human beings, I would draw them to faith with the bonds of love, according to the saying: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” They thought my yoke, which is light, to be exceedingly heavy; and I bent down to them, abandoning the kingdoms of heaven, so that I might live among them after assuming human form; and I gave them the food of my body.

“He will not return to the land of Egypt.” Under Menahem, king of the ten tribes, the people of Israel wanted to flee to Egypt from before Sennacherib, seeking aid. Against this the Lord speaks here, saying: “He will not return,” he says, “to the land of Egypt,” so that they may have Pharaoh as king; “but Assur himself is his king,” that is, Sennacherib. Henceforth he will be his king, because, having been captured, he will be led into captivity, and he will rule over him by the right of the victor. Why they suffer such things is made clear when he adds: “For they were unwilling to return”—through repentance—because they trusted in a human being rather than in God.

“The sword began in his cities and will consume his chosen ones.” Consider the weight of their miseries: not fields, possessions, and rural estates are ravaged, but the enemy enters the cities themselves. The sword began, he says, in his cities—“to kill” being understood—“and will consume his chosen ones,” namely, his princes and the stronger men of his armies, “and will devour their heads.” This signifies the princes themselves, who by the right of the head rule the others.

“**And my people will hang upon my return**”—that is, when the time of captivity comes, and the sword has consumed all his warriors, and he can find no defense, then my pitiable people will repent too late. While the enemies lay everything waste, they will await my return, sigh, and seek an opportunity to turn back; but it will do no good, because once they were my people, but now they are not. “**And a yoke will be imposed upon him at once, which will not be removed.**” For even to this day they remain slaves in the mountains of the Persians and Medes. This may also be referred to the times of the [Col. 0081D] Romans, because it was then that the Jews were condemned to their final and perpetual captivity.

“**How shall I give you up, Ephraim? How shall I protect you, Israel?**”—that is, you are not worthy of protection. Here the Lord speaks to Israel in the manner of a compassionate father. “How,” he says, “shall I give you up?”—that is, how can I hand you over to captivity without suffering myself? How shall I protect you, and what shall I do with you, and by what means shall I correct you, and how shall I strip you of my help without the greatest anguish of heart? For here he speaks as a compassionate father. “**How shall I give you up? Like Admah**”—supply: I shall give you up; “**I shall make you like Zeboiim**”—that is, although not without grief, nevertheless I shall hand you over, reduce you to dust and a vast desolation, and destroy you down to ashes and embers, just as I destroyed Admah [Col. 0082A] and Zeboiim and the remaining cities of the Sodomites.

It should be noted that when the Lord speaks through the prophets against the two tribes, it is not Admah and Zeboiim that are mentioned, but Sodom and Gomorrah. Thus we read in Isaiah: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; heed the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.” And in the Gospel the Lord says to the disciples: “It will be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah than for the city that will not receive you.” And to Jerusalem Ezekiel says: “Sodom was justified in comparison with you.”

But when he speaks to the ten tribes, it is not Sodom and Gomorrah that are mentioned, but the other cities subject to them. This is evidently because, although the ten were greater in number, the two surpassed them in a certain dignity through the temple and the priesthood. Therefore they sinned more gravely [Col. 0082B] than the ten, who lacked all these things and were moreover far removed from Jerusalem. Likewise, Sodom and Gomorrah were greater in wickedness, because their depravity surpassed that of the others. The subordinate cities followed them, and therefore their punishment will be more severe. Similarly, it will be more severe for the two tribes, who even worshiped idols in the temple of the Lord, than for the ten. For the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows.

Thus ecclesiastical men, if they are held guilty of the same crimes as heretics, will in no way be subjected to the torments of Admah and Zeboiim, which are lesser, but to those of Sodom and Gomorrah, which represent greater crimes.

“**My heart has turned within me altogether; my repentance is troubled.**” That is, my will [Col. 0082C] has been shown by paternal affection. As soon as I spoke of evil against you and pronounced a harsh sentence, pity touched me, mercy prevailed, and my compassion was stirred, just as the pity of a father softens the severity of a judge. As soon as I said that I would make Ephraim and Israel like Admah and Zeboiim, my inward parts were moved, and I regretted destroying forever the people who had once been mine. For the Lord speaks here as follows: It is as though one of you were to say, “I shall kill you,” and immediately, moved by regret, were to add, “My fault, because I spoke against you in such a way.”

“**I will not carry out the fury of my anger**”—that is, I will not be changed from my clemency so as to destroy Ephraim, if he repents toward me. Hence it follows: “**I will not [Col. 0082D] turn back**”—that is, from my clemency to cruelty—“**so as to destroy Ephraim**,” that is, the people of the ten tribes. For I do not strike in order to destroy forever, but in order to correct. My severity is an occasion for repentance and compassion.

“**For I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst.**” A man strikes in order to destroy; he becomes angry in order to avenge, and his judgment is punishment. God, however, corrects in order to reform and chastises in order to correct.

What follows—“**the Holy One in your midst**”—is to be understood in this way: If you wish to repent, I will be in your midst, I will dwell with you, and I will save you, “**and I will not enter the city**”—that is, in order to punish, as judges do, because I am not one of those who dwell in cities and live according to human [Col. 0083A] laws.

The Jews understand this passage as follows: If you repent, I will not enter the city of the nations, but I will remain with you.

Alternatively: We often read of two cities, one begun by Cain and the other by Abel. One belongs to the wicked, the other to the righteous. He therefore says that he will not enter the city built by the murderer, the city constructed from crime, but will remain forever in the city of Abel.

We can also refer these things to heretics and to the people deceived by them. Heretics are told that, unless they repent, they will be made like Admah and Zeboiim, so that they will have no hope of salvation. Again, the most merciful Father says that he changes his sentence and regrets having spoken such words, so as to call them also to repentance and conversion.

[Col. 0083B] “I will not act,” he says, “in my fury; I will not destroy Ephraim”—as far as lies in me, as far as I desire, if he corrects his error with truth, if he loves me more than the leaders of heresy. For I am God and not man: I will extend my hand to the fallen and call the erring to salvation. And because I am holy, I will not enter the gatherings and cities of heretics. I gladly receive those who come out of their cities; I will not enter their cities.

“**They will walk after the Lord.**” This is the prophet’s voice, as though he were saying: Because the Lord’s mercy is so great that he promises forgiveness even to sinners and promises prosperity, “they will walk after the Lord”—that is, once converted, they will imitate him.

[Col. 0083C] “**He will roar like a lion; for he himself will roar, and the sons of the sea will tremble.**” When a lion suffers hunger, it usually emits a great roar; at its voice all beasts and birds are terrified and stand frozen in their tracks. The Lord’s roar, therefore, was the threat of captivity, when he said: “I will make you like Admah and like Zeboiim.” Amos also speaks of this: “The Lord will roar from Zion and from Jerusalem he will give his voice.”

Or the terror inflicted upon the nations may be understood as his roar, so that the captivity of the Jews might be brought to an end. His roar was also heard when, present in the flesh, he said: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” At this voice, when the true lion roared, even the false lion—which, according to the apostle Peter, is our adversary—immediately fell silent. He roared again when he said: “Then the king will say to those who are on his [Col. 0083D] left: Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” His roar will be complete and manifest when, coming to judgment, not only human beings but even the angels will tremble.

Hence it follows: “**And the sons of the sea will tremble**”—that is, the sons of this age. For the sea often signifies the present age.

“**And they will fly like a bird from Egypt and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I will settle them in their houses.**” The Jews still await all these things as future. But because we know that they have already occurred, let us say that from Egypt and from Assyria—that is, from the east and west, the north and the south—the faithful fly together to the faith of Christ, imitating the dove’s simplicity and innocence. Thereafter they may [Col. 0084A] fly away from the power of demons and be settled in their houses, that is, in the heavenly dwellings, specifically in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

If, however, we wish to refer this especially to heretics, then, hearing the lion’s voice and the threat of its condemning judgment, those who were born from the bitter waters of heretics will take up wings and fly like a bird, or like a dove, from the land of Assyria—that is, from demons—or from Egypt, that is, from the sorrow of tribulation. Freed from these things, they will dwell in their houses, that is, in the faith of the Church.

“**Ephraim surrounded me with denial, and the house of Israel with deceit.**” That is, Ephraim denied me—namely, Jeroboam, who worshiped idols and did not render me the honor due to divinity. Israel also wished to mock me by making idols, as though there were some divinity in them.

“**But Judah descended as a witness with God and with the holy faithful.**” The Hebrews relate that when the children of Israel were leaving Egypt, with a very high mountain on one side, the Red Sea on another, and enemies on the third, they were trapped. While the other tribes were hesitating and wished to return to Egypt, [Col. 0084B] Judah—that is, the two tribes who inhabit the temple and possess the Law and the prophets—as a witness to the Lord’s words, whose commandments he kept, descended with God. That is, humbling himself, he followed the Lord’s footsteps. He did this with the holy faithful, that is, with those who crossed over at the end, or certainly with the patriarchs whose works he imitated.

Heretics surround the Lord with falsehood, [Col. 0084C] or rather with denial. Whatever they say, they deny; indeed, it is falsehood. They surround him with deceit, that is, with the impiety of the house of Israel, while they construct everything they pretend by artful speech and speak impiously against God.

Judah, however—that is, the ecclesiastical man—does not grow proud or become swollen with heretical conceit, but humbles himself with God and remains faithful with the choir of the saints. Or he is a faithful and steadfast witness, building his house upon the rock, which no storm can shake.

## CHAPTER XII

“**Ephraim feeds on wind and pursues the scorching wind.**” History relates that Manahen, king of Israel, after making peace with Assyria, sought aid from the Egyptians. This, then, is what is meant here [Col. 0084D] by “Ephraim feeds on wind”: he is deceived by a vain hope, placing his trust in man. “And he pursues the scorching wind”—that is, he proceeds to Egypt, which lies in the southern part of the world.

“**All day long he multiplies falsehood and devastation.**” “All day long,” that is, at all times, he multiplies falsehood—that is, idols—and devastation, namely calamity and affliction, for himself, and prepares ruin for his cities.

“**And he made a covenant**”—namely, “**with the Assyrians**,” Manahen, as was said above. He sent them—that is, the Assyrians—gifts, so that they might make a treaty with him.

“**And he carried oil into Egypt.**” After making a treaty with the Assyrians and being unable to join Sennacherib to himself, but learning that Sennacherib was coming against him, he sent [Col. 0085A] gifts to Pharaoh. Among them he also sent oil, which is produced in the finest and most precious form in Samaria but is not found in Egypt.

Let us attempt to apply these same things to heretics. “Ephraim feeds on wind”—that is, by his works he makes demons rejoice. “And he pursues the scorching wind,” which is hostile to flowers and destroys everything that germinates. Hence the Septuagint also render it “scorching wind.” “All day long falsehood”—that is, false doctrine—and “devastation”—that is, destruction—he multiplies for himself and his own, since he is not content with his own error but gathers many disciples of vanity around himself.

They also make a covenant with the Assyrians—that is, they are at peace with demons, whose will they obey. And they carry oil into Egypt, because, although they are in the darkness of error, they falsely claim to possess knowledge of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0085B], whom those outside the Church do not deserve.

“**Therefore the judgment of the Lord is against Judah.**” This means captivity and misery. After the ten tribes were taken captive for their sins, Judah did not repent but acted still worse, to such an extent—as the prophet Ezekiel makes clear—that he surpassed his sisters in crimes.

“**And visitation**”—that is, the greatness of torments, scourges, and punishments—“**is upon Jacob**,” that is, upon the two tribes who arose from his seed. “**According to his ways and according to his deeds he will repay him**”—that is, he will receive what he did. For he did not merely fall by chance or through human weakness; he deliberately sought out and discovered the things in which he would sin.

[Col. 0085C] “**In the womb he supplanted his brother.**” Here he recalls the ancient history so that God’s mercy toward Jacob and Jacob’s hardness against God may be recognized. While he was still in Rebecca’s womb, he supplanted his brother Esau—not, of course, by his own strength, but by God’s disposition, since God judged that he would become faithful to him and a future patriarch.

“**And in his strength he was made strong with the angel.**” This occurred when he was sent by his father to Mesopotamia, or when the angel wrestled with Jacob all night beside the stream. Receiving a blessing from him, Jacob heard: “If you were strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men?”

“**And he prevailed against the angel**”—obtaining by [Col. 0085D] prayers that the angel would give him a blessing.

“**And he was strengthened.**” He was strengthened by the blessing of the one whom he had overcome, when it was said to him: “You will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel will be your name.”

“**He wept and entreated him.**” This was when he said: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” This, then, is the struggle he carried on with the angel: he held him fast by prayers so that he might bless him, not by the force of physical action.

“**He found him at Bethel.**” The order is inverted. Earlier, after following the counsel of his father and mother while fleeing from his brother, he saw the angel at Bethel, when he placed a stone under his head and fell asleep. There he saw the angels of God ascending and descending, and he heard the Lord, leaning upon the ladder, say to him: “Jacob, Jacob, do not fear. I am the Lord, the God of your fathers. Go down, and I will be with you; I will bring you back [Col. 0086A].”

For this reason he called that place Bethel, that is, “house of God.” “**And there he spoke with us**”—namely, in our father, saying to him: “The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your offspring.”

“**The Lord, God of hosts; the Lord is his memorial.**” He gave him this memorial of his name, so that he would be called Israel, that is, “a man seeing God.” His sons retain this name to the present day. For by the name given to him by the angel he always remembers the name of God, by whom he is also called thus.

“**And you shall return to the Lord your God.**” The prophet turns aside to Judah: “When these things are so,” he says, “you, Judah, will return to the Lord your God,” by practicing repentance and believing faithfully in him. This was fulfilled when [Col. 0086B] three thousand believed in one day, another five thousand on another, and thereafter many thousands.

“**Keep mercy and judgment, and hope in the Lord your God always.**” First, show mercy to yourself, according to what is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God.” Then strive to show mercy to others as well, according to the saying: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” and so forth. Then also preserve the judgment of discernment between good and evil, God and the devil. When you have done both, hope in the Lord your God, advancing continually toward greater things through good works.

We can refer these same words spoken about Judah to any ecclesiastical man who is reproached by the Lord because he does not remember his former benefits, but joins sins to sins every day. The passage explains what those benefits [Col. 0086C] are: “When,” he says, “the Church was giving birth to you at your birth, you supplanted Esau”—supply: the Jewish or gentile people—“having received his birthright, and in your strength you were made strong against the angel,” either conquering evil spirits or being strengthened by the angel’s blessings. “And you prevailed against the angel,” that is, by prayers you made him your helper, so that you might also prevail against men.

After you had gained the victory, you wept and entreated the angel of the Lord. Remembering your former sins, you found him at Bethel, that is, in the house of God, which is the Church, or, according to the Septuagint, in the house of “Oven,” that is, of pain, tears, and repentance.

And so that we might know who this Judah is, he says: “There,” [Col. 0086D] that is, in the Church, “he spoke with us,” that is, with us Christians. From that time onward we are counted by the name of Christ and are corrected under his direction.

Therefore, ecclesiastical man, who is called Judah, “confessing,” return daily through repentance to your God. If you should happen to sin, return to your God, as the prophet did when he cried: “I am weary with my groaning.” Keep God’s commandments as well; show mercy to others, so that you too may obtain mercy. Hope also in the Lord your God always—or draw continually nearer to God, advancing in virtue at all times and always approaching your God.

“**Canaan, with a deceitful balance in his hand.**” Above, he had admonished Judah to return to the Lord his God and, keeping mercy and judgment, to hope always in the Lord his God. Now the speech turns to Ephraim, that is, to the ten tribes, who are called Canaan—not by nature, but by imitation—according to what Daniel says to the elder, who certainly was of Jewish stock: “Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you.” And in Ezekiel we read that it was said to Jerusalem: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.”

[Col. 0087A] Ephraim has a deceitful balance, contrary to the command: “Let your measure be fair and your sextarius just.” “**He loved oppression**”—that is, he not only had an unjust and deceitful balance, but also loved oppression, namely the exploitation of the poor, whom he stripped by his power.

[Col. 0087B] “**And Ephraim said: Nevertheless, I have become rich.**” He now states more plainly who this Canaan is: the ten tribes who said, “I have become rich,” that is, “I abound in all temporal goods.” The meaning is: “I do not care from where I have gathered these things, so long as I have something to possess.”

Many suffer from this disease, because they do not distribute their riches to the poor, nor give thanks to God for them. Of such riches it is written: “The riches that have been gathered will be burned by fire.” They do not become redemption for them, although Scripture says: “A man’s riches are the ransom of his soul,” and the Lord says in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.”

“**I have found an idol for myself.**” He calls the riches by which he was nourished an idol. Just as the belly is a god for gluttons [Col. 0087C], so gold is an idol for the greedy. Or they say this literally, because they worshiped idols instead of God.

“**All my labors will not find in me the iniquity that I have committed.**” The meaning is: “Whatever I may have done wrong, because I have possessed riches, it will not be counted against me by those who need my help. Since they depend upon my goods, they will not accuse me of my sins; rather, I will be praised by them,” as it is written: “And the one who has acted wickedly will be blessed.”

These two things—riches and the ambition of servants—are without accusation. For the rich man has very many friends.

All these things apply to heretics, in whose hand is a deceitful balance, because they fraudulently deceive as many as they can. They also love oppression, while they persecute the innocent and [Col. 0087D] crush them by their power. After deceiving others, they are accustomed to say: “We have become rich through the multitude of disciples who follow us.”

“We have found an idol for ourselves.” Heresies are composed especially for this reason: to devour widows’ houses—those who are always learning but never arrive at knowledge of the truth. And he aptly says: “I have found an idol for myself.” For all the fabrications of heretics are idols and differ in no respect from the impiety of the nations. They are therefore accustomed to say: “Whatever I do, whatever I undertake, cannot be counted against me. I have my riches, the arguments of the philosophers; I have a multitude of people, and whoever sees it will not think that I am sinning.”

“**But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt.**” [Col. 0088A] The meaning is: While you rejoice in your crime and boast in the multitude of your riches, to the point of saying, “I have become rich; I have found an idol for myself,” although you have sinned gravely, I, the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt when you served Pharaoh and built cities from mud and straw, still grant you a place for repentance.

Hence it follows: “**I will still make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the festival.**” He calls the festival “the Feast of Booths,” which is celebrated in the seventh month after Passover. In remembrance of their departure from the land of Egypt, the children of Israel lived in tents.

“As,” he says, “at that time I freed you from Egypt and made you dwell in tents for forty years, so now I will do likewise, leading you out of captivity, so that even during the days of the Feast of Booths you may sit in tents, in the manner of your fathers, if only you do what I have commanded.”

[Col. 0088B] “**And I spoke through the prophets**”—that is, through Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the others.

“**And I multiplied visions.**” Hence Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne.” And Daniel says: “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man was coming.”

“**And I was represented in the hands of the prophets.**” Adam bore his image when, falling asleep, he had Eve formed from his side, just as Christ formed the Church on the cross. So also Jonah, concerning whom the Lord says: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster”; and David, who struck down Goliath; and Isaac, in whose place a ram was sacrificed.

These words are also addressed to those who followed heretics, so that they may return to God [Col. 0088C], who desires the sinner’s repentance rather than his death. They must believe that it was he who led them out of Egypt—that is, out of the darkness and error of the nations.

And lest perhaps, remembering their sin, they should delay returning, he says: “I will still make you sit in tents, as in the days of the festival,” so that what baptism accomplished, repentance may also accomplish, and they may dwell in the tents of the Savior—that is, in the churches—of which it is said: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God.”

And lest they suppose that the leaders of heresy and the princes of their error spoke by the Spirit of God, he says: “I am the one who spoke to the prophets, not to your teachers; I multiplied visions, and I was represented in the hand of the prophets who have been established in the Church.”

“**If Gilead is an idol, then they have wandered in vain, sacrificing [Col. 0088D] cattle at Gilgal.**” Gilead is both a mountain and a city situated beside that same mountain, across the Jordan in the tribe of Gad. Concerning it we read above: “A city of those who work idols, overturned with blood.” Gilgal, however, is in the tribe of Judah near Bethel; concerning it it was said above: “All their wickedness is at Gilgal.”

Since both the ten tribes, represented by Gilead, and the two represented by Gilgal worshiped idols in those places, it is rightly said: “If Gilead is an idol,” and so forth. That is: If the ten tribes worship idols, although they lack a temple, priests, and the worship of God, then you, Judah, have nevertheless abandoned God in vain and worship idols at Gilgal, even though you possess a temple, a priesthood, and the other things belonging to the true rite.

Moreover, by “cattle” [Col. 0089A] he means calves.

“**For their altars will also be like heaps upon the furrows of a field**”—supply: they will remain and be abandoned without cultivation after they have been led into captivity, like mounds made by gathering stones and sand.

“**Jacob fled to the region of Syria.**” The prophet seems to touch upon the history in Genesis, speaking of Jacob’s flight when he fled to his maternal uncle Laban in the region of Syria. Above he had also said concerning him: “In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was made strong with the angel.”

“**And Israel served**”—that is, Jacob himself—“**for a wife**,” that is, for Rachel, feeding the flocks of his uncle for seven years. “**And he served for a wife**,” that is, for another wife, for another seven years.

[Col. 0089B] “**But through a prophet the Lord brought him out of Egypt, and through a prophet he was preserved.**” Because he had begun to weave together the history of Jacob and Israel, he joins the sons to their father, saying: “Through a prophet the Lord brought him out of Egypt”—namely, through Moses, at whose urging they departed from the land of Egypt.

Or, if we wish to understand these words more deeply, the Lord—that is, God the Father—through a prophet, that is, through Christ, led his people out of the darkness of unbelief. Moreover, the same people were preserved through the prophet when, because of the sin of the calf, while the Lord’s anger raged, Moses fell prostrate before him and said: “Either forgive them, or erase me from your book,” and so forth, until the answer was given to him: “I have forgiven according to your word.”

[Col. 0089B] He will not be mistaken who says that Jacob the supplanter and Israel the seer of God preceded as a type of the Lord, and that Rachel, initially barren and beautiful, whom Jacob loved greatly, signifies the Church, while Leah, with dim eyes but fruitful, displays the mysteries of the Synagogue. He may also say that Christ himself led the people of believers out of the darkness of this age and brought them to the bright waters of the Jordan, that is, to baptism.

“**Ephraim provoked me to anger with his bitternesses.**” The meaning is: After I had freed Ephraim—that is, all ten tribes—from Egyptian slavery and granted him many good things, he provoked me, although I am by nature most sweet, through his bitternesses. That is, he made me bitter and compelled me to exact vengeance.

“**His blood will come [Col. 0089D] upon him**”—that is, he himself will be the cause of his death. Because of his sin he will be led captive and killed by his enemies, according to what David says to the man who announced that he had killed Saul: “Your blood be upon your head.”

“**And the Lord your God will repay him for his disgrace**”—that is, the vengeance for the blasphemy in which you said, “These are your gods who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” the Lord will bring upon you.

Heretics always provoke the most merciful Lord to anger. They compel the one who desires the sinner’s repentance rather than his death to punish them because of the hardness of their hearts. Their blood, by which they have shed both their own blood and that of many others, will come upon them, and the Lord their God will repay them for the insults [Col. 0090A] with which they blasphemed the Lord—not because he is their Lord, but because he was once their Lord.

## CHAPTER XIII

“**When Ephraim spoke, terror seized Israel.**” When Ephraim—that is, Jeroboam, son of Nebat, of the tribe of Ephraim—spoke and commanded that idols be worshiped, terror, that is, extreme fear, seized Israel, to such an extent that it abandoned God and sacrificed to idols.

Hence it follows: “**And he sinned against Baal**”—the idol of the Sidonians, which is also Bel—“**and he died**,” losing him through unbelief who says: “I am life.” For it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die.”

[Col. 0090B] “**And now they have added [Col. 0090B] to their sinning.**” Joining sin to the sin of idolatry, “**they made for themselves a cast image**”—that is, a calf—“**from their silver**,” so that they too might have their own calves, “**like the likeness of idols.**” Since the king had golden gods, they—that is, the subject people—made gods of silver for themselves according to their means, in the likeness of those gods.

“**It is all the work of craftsmen**”—that is, the work of man, not of God.

“**To these they say: Sacrifice human beings, while worshiping calves.**” Thus Manasseh and many others acted, concerning whom it is written: “They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons.” It is as though he were saying openly: You worshipers of idols, because sacrificial victims are lacking, sacrifice your sons and daughters, who worship the idols along with you, that is, to the calves.

But if, as some wish, the [Col. 0090B] demons are speaking to the people—“Sacrifice human beings”—while they offer calves, the greed of those who feed on the blood of victims and the smoke of burnt offerings is revealed. When victims fail, they desire human beings to be sacrificed, and they rejoice not only in their destruction but also in their blood.

“**Therefore they will be like a morning cloud and like the morning dew that passes away; like dust swept up by a whirlwind from the threshing floor and like smoke from a chimney.**” Because, he says, they sacrificed human beings to calves—or rather, to one calf—and worshiped calves, therefore they will be like a cloud, and so forth. All these things appear for a time and quickly cease to exist. Clouds and dew are dispersed and dried up when the sun arrives; dust swept up from the threshing floor and smoke from a chimney are likewise dissolved into thin air.

Hence the saying [Col. 0090D]: “As smoke disappears, so they will disappear.” The meaning is: Just as these four things suddenly dissipate, so they will suddenly be led away to the Assyrians. Hence it was said above: “As morning passes, so the king of Israel has passed away.”

Heretics are compared to the morning cloud, the dew, and the dust. Concerning them we read in the Catholic Epistle: “These are clouds without water.” They have the appearance of prophets and of the apostolic clouds to which God’s truth came, but they do not have water, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

“**But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt.**” Supply: I have been, ever since I brought you out of Egypt. “**And you shall know no God besides me, and there is no savior except me.**” He now recounts [Col. 0091A] what he did for them when he brought them out of Egypt by the hand of Moses, when he said to them: “Take heed lest you eat and be satisfied; lest you forget your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” and so forth. For there is no other God besides me, and there is no one else who can save.

“**I knew you**”—that is, I loved you. Just as God’s not knowing means rejecting, so knowing means loving and choosing. Hence it is also said to Moses: “I know you by name,” that is, I have chosen you especially above others.

“**In the wilderness, in a land of desolation**”—supply: I knew you there, where there were neither harvests nor vineyards, nor even fruit-bearing trees, but scarcity of everything.

“**According to their pastures they were filled**”—that is, although there was a lack of every good thing there, I gave them [Col. 0091B] manna from heaven and brought forth springs of water from the hardest rock.

“**And when they were filled, they lifted up their heart.**” That is, filled with manna, meat, and spiritual drink, they raised themselves up in pride.

“**And they forgot me**,” whose benefits they ought to have remembered, according to what is written: “The beloved grew fat and kicked.”

For throughout such a vast wilderness, where not only crops but also trees and vines fail to grow, where not even grass is produced and no waters temper the sun’s heat, Israel could not have reached the land of the Jordan in forty years unless the Lord had provided everything.

The Lord also led heretics out of the darkness of unbelief, where they served Pharaoh and his leaders. In the Church he commanded them to know no god other than the one who is the [Col. 0091C] Creator of all peoples and knows how to save those whom he made. He himself knew them and fed them in the land of desolation, so that they might say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing.”

He gave them the bread from heaven, which they had never eaten in Egypt, and water from the rock that followed them; the rock, according to the Apostle, was Christ. Filled with the bread of the riches of Scripture and satisfied, they lifted their hearts against the Creator and fashioned another god for themselves, forgetting God, who had gone before them so that they might bind the words of the Law before their eyes and have them in their hands, lest they ever forget their God.

“**And I will be to them like a lioness and like a leopard on the road of the Assyrians.**” A lioness is fiercer than all beasts when her cubs have been taken from her; a leopard, though variegated, is no less [Col. 0091D] savage. The meaning is: When they have been handed over to their enemies and led into captivity, I, who have always been most merciful toward them, will exercise against them the ferocity of all beasts.

Hence it immediately follows:

“**I will meet them like a bear deprived of her cubs, and I will tear open the inner parts of their liver.**” Those who have written about the nature of beasts say that among all wild animals nothing is more savage than a bear when she has lost her cubs or is in need of food.

The meaning is: Because in their hearts they conceived blasphemies while raging against me and uttered them against me, I will become for them all the beasts—that is, every form of ferocity. I will destroy and crush them through the Assyrians, and I will tear open the inner parts of their hearts, that is, I will remove the vital organs of their hearts.

“**And I will consume [Col. 0092A] them there**,” as a lion devours its prey; “**the beast of the field will tear them apart.**” It is as though he were saying: They are so wicked that, even when placed in captivity, they deservedly experience my savagery. “I will therefore consume them there,” as a lion devours its prey; “the beast of the field will tear them apart”—namely, Sennacherib, or the devil dwelling in the wilderness of this age.

It should be noted that the one who speaks in the Gospel to believers—“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened,” and so forth, up to “my burden is light”—now becomes, through the prophet, a lioness, a leopard, a bear, and a lion to unbelievers who refuse to repent.

“**Your destruction, Israel, is from yourself; only in me is your help.**” That is, you yourself are the cause of your destruction. Another translation has: “May you perish, Israel, who have descended into such a depth [Col. 0092B] of impiety that you can be saved only by the mercy of God.” For your help is only in me, if you repent, not from yourself.

“**Where is your king? Let him save you now in all your cities.**” The divine word is spoken ironically against those who, contrary to God’s will, chose a king for themselves and, relying upon his strength, boasted that they would be victorious.

“Where,” he says, “is your king?” Jeroboam, certainly, or even Saul, concerning whom you said to Samuel: “Appoint a king for us, so that he may judge us.” When he opposed this, you answered: “No, but there shall be a king over us; he will go before us and fight for us.”

Of the one about whom you had promised yourself that he would fight your wars, let him now save you in all your cities, now that the Assyrians are already threatening. Let him come to your aid in the face of the impending [Col. 0092C] danger. But you do not have a human king, because you do not have as God the one whom you cast away.

“**And your judges**”—that is, your companions and the other princes—“**of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and princes’**”—supply: Where are they?

“‘I will give you a king in my fury, and I will take him away in my indignation.’ I will give you a king—namely Saul—in my fury, to such an extent that in the days of harvest I would display rain contrary to the nature of the promised land; and I will take away in my indignation Zedekiah, whom, after putting out his eyes, I will lead to Babylon. Alternatively: I will give you a king—that is, Jeroboam—in my fury, and I will take away in my indignation Hosea, the last king of the ten tribes.

“‘The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up,’ that is, just as what is preserved in a sack is tied up and does not perish for the one who tied it, so all the iniquity with which Ephraim sinned against God has been bound to him and remains until the time of captivity. Hence it adds: ‘His sin is hidden.’ Not from God, to whom everything is naked and open, but from Ephraim himself, who wished to acknowledge it only at the time of captivity.

“‘The pains of a woman in labor will come upon him.’ That is, when the day of vengeance and captivity comes, and his iniquity is revealed and made manifest to everyone, then he will be shaken by sudden pains, just as a woman in labor is afflicted and groans. ‘He himself is an unwise son.’ Ephraim was a son of God, according to what is written: ‘Israel is my firstborn son’; but he was unwise because he did not recognize the true Father, God, and instead worshiped idols. ‘For now he will not stand in the crushing of sons,’ that is, when the day of labor and captivity arrives, he will not be able to endure the evil and bear the crushing of his sons, who will be killed while their fathers are present; or, they will not stand because they will be led away as captives.

“‘From the hand of death I will deliver them; from death I will redeem them.’ The almighty God speaks to those whom he deigns to deliver by his grace. ‘From the hand,’ he says, ‘of death I will deliver them,’ that is, from the work of sin, which draws one toward death. Because a work is performed by the hand, the hand of sin rightly signifies the very work by which the soul is killed. Hence it is written: ‘Death and life are in the power of the tongue’; or certainly by the hand of sin the power of the devil is understood. ‘From death I will redeem them,’ that is, I will deliver from hell all believing Jews and Gentiles. Hence it follows: ‘I will be your death, O death; I will be your sting, O hell.’

“He was death’s death because by his own death he destroyed death, leaving none of his own there. He stung it when he delivered one part—namely, his elect—but left another part, the reprobate, there. For when we bite, we consume one part and leave another; or by death and hell the devil is understood, whom Christ stung so that he would lose his power, though he would not thereby cease entirely to exist. The difference between death and hell is this: death is the separation of the soul from the body; hell is the place in which souls are confined, either for refreshment or in punishments according to the quality of their merits.

“[Col. 0093C] ‘Consolation is hidden from my eyes.’ The most merciful Father, seeing that we all die under the sentence pronounced against Adam, says: ‘Consolation is hidden from my eyes,’ because I behold the whole human race perishing. Or again, the prophet, considering that all die and descend into hell, and knowing beforehand that he himself would come to them, says: ‘Consolation is hidden from my eyes.’ The sense is: I cannot be consoled; nor can I ease my grief by anything I conceive in my mind, while I consider the unavoidable necessity of death.

“‘For he himself divides between brothers.’ He himself—that is, hell—divides between brothers, when it receives one who has been taken from this life and leaves the other alive. In this passage understand that all affection is absent, since mother is separated from daughter, father from son, and brother from brother. Therefore whatever divides the unity of brotherhood and sows discord is rightly called hell. Some, following the history of that time, understand the two brothers divided from each other by death as Judah and Israel, so that what was then represented in part might then be experienced in the whole.

“‘The Lord will bring a scorching wind ascending from the desert.’ We should understand this scorching wind as the one of which Habakkuk says: ‘God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran.’ For God the Father brought the scorching wind—that is, his Son—taking away sins from the desert of the human race, in which the devil, seeking rest, could not find it; or from the womb of the virgin, who conceived without the moisture of male seed. Hence: ‘How will this happen, since I do not know a man?’ Beautifully, both in Isaiah and in the present passage, the ascending flower or wind is said to rise, because from the lowliness of the flesh he ascended to the heights and led us with him to the Father, saying in the Gospel: ‘When I have been lifted up, I will draw all things to myself.’

“‘And he will dry up its veins,’ that is, its sins of death. We rightly understand the sins of death as its veins: once these have been dried up through Christ, death itself also will be dried up. ‘And he will lay waste its spring,’ that is, the devil, of whom he himself says: ‘Now the ruler of this world will be cast out.’ ‘And he himself will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel.’ This is understood in two ways. Desirable vessels are the saints, of whom Paul says: ‘We have this treasure in earthen vessels’; or, alternatively, those whom the devil desired to hold forever as vessels—Christ himself, coming, plundered from his power and led with him into paradise as exceedingly precious vessels.

## CHAPTER XIV

“‘Let Samaria perish, because she provoked her God to bitterness.’ We have often said that the ten tribes are called Samaria, after the metropolis Samaria, which is now called Augusta, that is, Sebaste, from the name of Augustus. Why the city was called Samaria we read in the Book of Kings. Here, therefore, the prophet speaks not as expressing a wish but as making a prediction, saying: ‘Let Samaria perish, because she provoked her God to bitterness,’ although he was most sweet to those who worshiped him, and forced him to repay their sins with vengeance, ‘by the sword,’ namely, the sword of the Assyrians. ‘Let it perish: let its little ones be dashed to pieces,’ that is, crushed against the ground; ‘and let its pregnant women be ripped open,’ that is, let pregnant women be cut open by the sword unto death. We must believe that all these things happened to it at the time of captivity and distress, when they lost their homeland and those who escaped the sword were led into perpetual slavery.

“‘Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have fallen through your iniquity.’ As far as history is concerned, these words were spoken to the ten tribes called Ephraim, who abandoned the Lord their God and worshiped the calves that Jeroboam had made. Spiritually, however, they can be referred to every sinner who, departing from his Creator, submits himself to an idol—that is, to every falsehood—and hopes to be saved by Assur, that is, by the devil, who is the author of falsehood, as is his father also. Let us therefore speak briefly of both meanings, giving both the historical interpretation and the spiritual application to each person.

“Above, the prophet foretold to the ten tribes to whom he was speaking the calamities and miseries that threatened them. Now he addresses them, exhorts them, and gives them counsel about how they should entreat the Lord: by setting aside idols and turning to God. ‘Return, Israel, to the Lord your God,’ from iniquity to righteousness through confession of sins and the performance of good works, ‘because you have fallen through your iniquity,’ by making idols and worshiping demons. You fell through idolatry; rise again through the worship and fulfillment of the religion of your God. Each one of us ought to act in this way. We have become weak and fallen into sin; let us rise to repentance, producing fruits worthy of repentance, as John the Baptist proclaimed, and let us turn back from our wicked deeds.

“‘Take words with you,’ O people of the ten tribes, ‘and return to the Lord, and say to him.’ The prophet does two things: he urges them to repentance and teaches them from what they should formulate their prayers to the Lord. ‘Take,’ he says, ‘words with you,’ that is, bring forth prayers and confession of sins, and return to the Lord in words as well as in deeds. For the person truly and sincerely turns from his iniquity to perform good works who proclaims with his mouth and fulfills in deed what he believes and holds in his heart.

“‘Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good, and we will repay the calves of our lips.’ Every believer ought to say such things: ‘Take away all iniquity,’ that is, cleanse us from all sins, according to the words: ‘Cleanse me from my hidden faults.’ ‘And receive what is good,’ namely confession, sincere prayers, and thanksgiving. When the prophet adds, ‘We will repay the calves of our lips,’ he speaks wonderfully. Who has ever had calves on his lips, unless a portion has been taken for eating? He does not command the offering of calves, sacrifices, and victims such as the Jews used to offer in the temple. Rather, by ‘calves of our lips’ we should understand praises and acts of thanksgiving, according to the Psalmist: ‘Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High’; and again: ‘A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit.’

“Thus each one of us offers calves—that is, praises—to almighty God when he confesses that he believes in God the unbegotten Father, the begotten Son, believing him true God and true man, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son; and that the Trinity possesses distinction of persons and unity in the power of the Godhead. In doing this he fulfills the Apostle’s statement: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’

“‘Assur will not save us; we will not mount upon horses.’ Blessed Jerome says that it is a Jewish tradition that in the days of Menahem, king of Israel, that king himself and the people of the ten tribes sent a thousand talents of silver to Pul, king of the Assyrians, so that he might be on their side, maintain peace with them, and provide assistance against the Egyptians. Among these gifts they also sent the two calves that their priests had made of bronze and gilded in place of the golden calves made by Jeroboam. The priests themselves, without the people’s knowledge, had transferred the gold to their own uses and made bronze calves in their place. Concerning these calves the prophet said above: ‘He himself’—that is, the calf—‘was carried to Assur as a gift to the avenging king,’ using the singular number for the plural.

“Therefore the prophet, speaking in the person of the people, said: ‘Assur will not save us.’ It is as though he were saying in other words: We can place our hope in the Assyrians, so that they may protect us, but we are not safe or protected by them. Now, therefore, we no longer have confidence in a human being but in you, who are our God, because cursed is the person who trusts in a human being and whose heart departs from the Lord. What he adds—‘We will not mount upon horses’—shows that they had trusted in the Egyptians, who possessed extremely swift horses. The meaning is: We will not mount upon horses; that is, we no longer place our hope in the Egyptians, but our refuge will be in you.

“Allegorically, if we wish to understand this, by Assur we can take the devil, and by the horse his pride. If one of us therefore places his trust in Assur, appeasing him with gifts—namely, wicked works in which he delights—in order to mount the horse, that is, to rise upon his arrogance, what the Lord says in the Gospel will happen to him: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.’

“‘Nor will we say any longer, “Our gods,” to the works of our hands,’ that is, we will no longer regard the golden calves that we ourselves made as gods, nor will we ask them for help. ‘For you will have mercy on the people who are in you.’ This means the people of Israel, concerning whom you had said: ‘Israel is my firstborn son.’ ‘You will have mercy,’ he says, ‘on that people who are in you through faith and repentance, although they had once departed from you by sinning; after they have returned through repentance, you will have mercy on them.’

“‘I will heal their wounds; I will love them freely.’ Because, having turned to God through repentance, they had said: ‘Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good,’ recognizing the Father whom they had abandoned, the Lord replied: ‘I will heal their wounds,’ that is, I will forgive them the sins by which they had been severely broken and wounded. ‘I will love them freely,’ that is, willingly. ‘Because my anger has turned away from them,’ since they have done penance.

“‘I will be like dew, and Israel will blossom like a lily.’ For I who was angry with them on account of their sins will now, because of my mercy, have compassion on them. I will be like dew to them, because by my mercy I will remove from them the heat of burning fire and desire; and they themselves will blossom like a lily, because they will abound and grow in the beauty of virtues and in the fragrance of good works. Hence Paul says: ‘We are the good aroma of Christ to God.’ The elect blossom—or rather, flower—like a lily, imitating the Lord their God, who says in the Song of Songs: ‘I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.’

“‘And his root will burst forth like Lebanon,’ that is, good will will be brought to the accomplishment of good works. Lebanon is a mountain whose very lofty trees extend their tops toward the air and sink their roots just as deeply into the earth, so that they are shaken by no storm but stand firm in a stable mass.

“‘His branches will spread,’ that is, they will advance from virtue to virtue, ‘and his glory will be like an olive tree.’ Because he had said, ‘His root will burst forth like Lebanon,’ lest we think that he is speaking of a holy man converted to the Lord as though from unfruitful trees, he compares him to a fruitful olive tree. Oil signifies mercy, which works through love and through all good works. He therefore says: ‘His glory will be like an olive tree,’ that is, he will be enriched by works of mercy, so that, when the lamp has been kindled, he may shine in the darkness and offer others an example of good works.

“‘And his fragrance will be like Lebanon.’ Among the Greeks and Hebrews, Lebanon is the name both of a mountain and of incense. Here it is used for incense. Just as we delight in the fragrance of incense, so we delight in the reputation of a righteous person.

“‘They will return, sitting in his shade.’ Those, namely, who had departed from God the Father by sinning will return to him. After they have returned, they will receive the reward of their conversion, so that they may sit beneath the shade—that is, dwell under his protection—and may say with the Church: ‘Under his shadow, which I had desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.’

“‘They will live on grain, and they will blossom like a vine.’ When, he says, they sit beneath his shade, those who had been dead will live on grain; that is, they will abound in good works, or in the body and blood of the Lord. Or certainly they will live on grain because through Christ, who is the true grain, they will rise from death to life. Hence: ‘Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone.’ He himself is also the vine, who makes those who believe in him drunk with spiritual wine. Hence the Psalmist says: ‘You visited the earth and intoxicated it.’ And the Lord himself says to his disciples: ‘Eat, friends; drink and become drunk, beloved.’

“The elect will therefore blossom like a vine because they will imitate their Lord through good works, according to what the Lord himself says: ‘Whoever serves me must follow me.’ ‘His remembrance will be like the wine of Lebanon.’ We can understand the wine of Lebanon as mixed wine, seasoned with various spices, so that it has an exceedingly sweet fragrance. The meaning is: just as spiced wine gives off a pleasant fragrance to human beings, so the memory of a righteous person who imitates the Lord’s works is pleasant and sweet.

“We can also understand the wine of Lebanon as that which was offered to the Lord in the temple, concerning which Zechariah says: ‘Open your doors, O Lebanon,’ and so forth. For just as almighty God delighted in the wine that was offered to him, so he rejoices and is glad in the fragrance of the faithful, who make the reputation of their faith and good works rise from themselves.

“‘Ephraim, what have I any longer to do with idols?’ The unspoken verb is: ‘What do you still set before me?’ The meaning is: Since you are about to receive such great blessings, because through repentance you have begun to become mine, why do you still wish to worship idols? ‘I will hear him and direct him when he does penance and cries out to me.’ ‘I will direct him,’ that is, I will make him walk along the right path. The way is Christ, through whom access to the Father is made.

“‘I am like a green fir tree’—the unspoken verb is ‘I have given him’—so that he might possess the verdure of faith and action and might always seek heavenly things with the gaze of his mind. ‘From me his fruit has been found,’ that is, all his activity and his observance of both the Old and the New Testament proceeded from my gift, without which you can do nothing.

“It should be understood—as we have often already said—that the salvation of Israel, its return to God, and its redemption from captivity are not to be understood in a fleshly manner, as the Jews dream, but are fulfilled spiritually and most truly.

“[Col. 0098B] ‘Who is wise and will understand these things; intelligent and will know them?’ In these words the prophet demonstrates the obscurity of the book and the difficulty of its explanation. Who, unless taught by Christ, can know what Jezreel signifies, what is meant by his sister who did not obtain mercy, what by his third brother, ‘not my people,’ what by the prostitute joined to Hosea, and the other things narrated in the chapter; or what is meant by the scorching wind and so forth at the end?

“Considering, therefore, the obscurity of these matters, he says: ‘Who is wise and will understand these things?’ But if the very person who wrote the book confesses that it is difficult or impossible, what can we do, who, with eyes clouded by disease and obscured by the filth of sins, cannot look upon the brightest rays of the sun? Or should I say what is written: ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways!’

“‘For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them.’ The ways of the Lord are understood as the commandments of the Old and New Testament. The righteous walk in them when they fulfill them in deed, saying to God with the Psalmist: ‘Make my steps firm in your paths.’ ‘But transgressors will fall in them.’ By transgressors are understood Jews, heretics, and false Christians who transgress the commandments of the Lord. They will fall in them because those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. And the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows.

## ON THE PROPHET JOEL

[Col. 0097]

[Col. 0097D] Joel is interpreted as “beginning.” Bringing forth a prophecy concerning Judea and Jerusalem, at the beginning of his book, after mournful banquets, he calls Jerusalem to mourning and foretells its destruction. He also prophesies the calling of the Gentiles and the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the gathered believers.

## CHAPTER ONE

“‘The word of the Lord that came to Joel the son of Pethuel.’ Joel is interpreted as “strong one of God.” Pethuel means “opening” or “word of the Lord.” The word of God, which was always with the Father, came to Joel.

[Col. 0098D] “‘Hear this, elders, and perceive with your ears, all inhabitants of the earth.’ The elders are so called not because of age but because of merit; the inhabitants of the earth are those who are weighed down by earthly works. There is a great difference between hearing and perceiving with the ears. Presbyters—that is, spiritual people—hear more sacredly; those who inhabit the earth perceive with their ears, but more humbly. ‘If this happened in your days or in the days of your fathers, tell it to your sons; and your sons to their sons, and their sons to another generation.’ What I am about to say is known to memory; a new matter requires new hearers. For new wine is put into new wineskins. [Col. 0099A] In this brief statement he has woven together the whole human race.

“‘What the locust left, the caterpillar consumed; what the caterpillar left, the grub consumed; and what the grub left, the rust consumed.’ What is signified by the caterpillar, which crawls upon the earth with its entire body, except lust? What is expressed by the locust, which flies up in leaps, except empty glory? What is represented by the grub, whose entire body is almost gathered into its belly, except gluttony? What is indicated by rust, which burns whatever it touches, except anger?

“Therefore the locust consumes what the caterpillar left, because often, when the vice of lust has departed from the mind, empty glory follows, when a person boasts as though holy because of his chastity. Thus, while vices succeed vices, another pest devours the field of the mind as another leaves it.

“Again, in another interpretation: the Assyrians under Shalmaneser, the Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus of Syria, and the emperor Vespasian of the Romans devastated Judea. Again, in another interpretation: these four pests signify four kinds of vices by which human souls are corrupted; for people fear, desire, grieve, and rejoice.

“‘Awake, drunkards, and weep, and howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.’ Those who trust in the love of this world and do not perceive the evils they suffer are called drunkards. What, then, does ‘Awake, drunkards, and weep’ mean, except: Shake off the sleep of your insensibility, and amid the devastation of the heart, with so many successive pestilences of vices, meet them with watchful lamentation?

[Col. 0099C] “‘For a strong and innumerable nation has come up over my land; its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of a lion’s cub.’ The strong and innumerable nation signifies demons, which have come up not over heaven—that is, over spiritual people—but over the earth, that is, over the carnal.

“‘It made my vine a desert, and stripped the bark from my fig tree; it laid it bare, utterly despoiled it, and cast it away; its branches have become white.’ The vine is called the Lord’s people, while the fig tree signifies the Israelite people. The devil stripped the bark from the fig tree because he stripped that Jewish people of all glory. Its branches became white because its priests and teachers appear outwardly white through hypocrisy.

“‘Mourn like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of your youth,’ O unhappy people, or soul, which had been joined in marriage to your bridegroom—that is, to Christ—as to a husband, but violated by demons and made adulterous: mourn like a virgin, that is, do penance.

“‘The sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of the Lord; the priests, the ministers of the Lord, have mourned.’ By the house of the Lord he means the Jewish people, or the soul, which, having been plundered by hostile powers, has been stripped of every sacrifice of righteousness.

“‘The land has been devastated; the earth has mourned, because the grain has been destroyed, the wine has been confounded, and the oil has languished.’ This is what David says: ‘There is none who does good, not even one.’ Grain, wine, and oil signify the gifts of the charisms, which through a degenerate life have been scattered by the devil among the Jewish people or in other souls.

“‘The farmers are confounded; the vinedressers have howled over the grain, the wine, and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished.’ The farmers or vinedressers are angels, or teachers and instructors, who, seeing the souls entrusted to them serve carnal passions, now mourn. The harvest signifies the human race.

“‘The vine has been confounded and the fig tree has languished; the pomegranate, the palm, the apple tree, and all the trees of the field have dried up, because joy has been confounded among the children of human beings.’ The vine or fig tree signifies the same thing as above: the Jewish people. The pomegranate and the other trees signify the various gifts of the charisms, which hostile powers take away from the human race through vices.

“‘Gird yourselves and mourn, priests; howl, ministers of the altar. Enter, lie down in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of our God.’ This is an exhortation to the leaders of the Church, so that through the instruction of the people entrusted to them they may lament these things as their own. He calls the Church the house of God, or the soul from which the gifts of God have perished through negligence of life.

“‘Sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the elders, all the inhabitants of the earth, into the house of our God, and cry out to the Lord: Alas, alas, alas, for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and like devastation from the Mighty One it will come.’ This means: Sanctify your fast by joining it to the other virtues. By the elders and inhabitants of the earth he means teachers and hearers, who are to be gathered into the Church through faith. The day of the Lord is called the day of judgment.

“‘Has not food perished before your eyes, joy and exultation from the house of your God?’ For as vices and sins increase, mourning succeeds joy. The house of God is understood as the Church, or the soul.

“‘The beasts have rotted in their dung.’ For beasts to rot in their dung is for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of lust. ‘The granaries have been demolished; the storehouses have been scattered, because the grain has been confounded.’ The granaries or storehouses signify the minds of the faithful, in which the grain of righteousness and the wine of prudence were accustomed to be stored.

“‘Why did the animal groan? Why did the herds of cattle bellow? Because they have no pasture; and the flocks of sheep have also perished.’ By the animal and the cattle he indicates learned people who do not know the teaching of God; by the sheep he signifies the Gentiles. The pastures have failed because the barrenness of the word of God possesses everything, and, when its rains have ceased, all things have dried up. The flocks have perished because there are no shepherds of the sort who teach sound doctrine.

“‘To you, Lord, I will cry out, because fire has consumed the beautiful things of the desert, and flame has burned all the trees of the countryside; even the beasts of the field, like a thirsty field longing for rain, have looked to you, because the springs of water have dried up, and fire has devoured the beautiful things of the desert.’ Fire signifies the devil; the desert, this world; the beautiful things of the desert, human beings or the glory of this age; the trees of the countryside, the Gentiles who have been consumed by the devil. The beasts of the field signify the Gentiles who, after evil deeds, have turned to God and implore his mercy. The springs of water signify knowledge of the law, which has dried up in the Jewish people through unbelief.

## CHAPTER TWO

“‘Blow the trumpet in Zion; howl on my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the earth be troubled, because the day of the Lord is coming, because the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and storm.’ The clear voice is the preaching of the Gospel; Zion is the Church or the soul. By the inhabitants of the earth he means carnal people, all of whom it terrifies and calls to repentance. The day of judgment will be such for those who are to suffer punishments that he compared it to a day of darkness and gloom because of the condemnation of the reprobate. Yet, because all things previously done will then be revealed by the justice of judgment, he compared it to the light of the sun.

“‘Like morning spread over the mountains, a numerous and strong people; there has been none like it from the beginning, nor will there be after it, throughout the years of generation after generation.’ The numerous and strong people signify the multitude of demons and the ungodly. Once they have been destroyed in judgment, from the beginning—that is, from Adam—to the end of the world, they will not exist forever, because after that same day of judgment there will be no ascent and descent, as Origen wished to say.

“‘Before its face is a devouring fire, and behind it a burning flame.’ Wherever it has entered, the army of demons immediately makes a desert and burns up all the flowers of the virtues.

“‘The land is like a garden of delight before it, and behind it a deserted wilderness; there is no one who escapes it.’ Before a person sins through its persuasion, while he is without sin, he becomes like a garden of paradise. But once it has seized him and led him into sin, it makes him a solitude and a desert, so that there is no one—or only rarely anyone—who can escape its snare.

“‘Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and they run like horsemen.’ The horse is the human being; the horseman is the devil. ‘Like the appearance of horses’ means the appearance of the wicked, through whom the devil persecutes the righteous. The devil’s four-horse chariot consists of the four passions that he describes under the name of pests at the beginning of this book.

“‘Like the sound of chariots they will leap over the tops of the mountains; like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble, like a strong people prepared for battle.’ The stubble signifies light and fruitless people, consumed by the devil’s fire.

“‘Before its face the peoples will be tormented; all faces will be turned into a pot.’ This means that when the peoples begin to be dragged with it into punishment and the devil begins to hold them under his own power.

“‘They will run like strong men; like warriors they will climb the wall.’ Wretched is that city—that is, the soul—which is captured by such an enemy. When he has entered it, he gladly runs upon and attacks the wall of the virtues; and when he has entered the house of conscience, if he finds anything good in it, he destroys everything.

[Col. 0102A] “‘Each man will walk in his ways, and will not turn aside from his paths. No one will crowd his brother. Each will walk in his own path. Yet they will also fall through the windows and will not be demolished. They will enter the city; they will run upon the wall; they will climb into the houses.’ When the devil has justly received power over certain people, he enters them through the senses of the flesh as through windows, removes what he finds within, and plunders it. But if someone prevents him from entering, he is not permitted to demolish that person’s structure of good works. ‘They will enter through the windows like a thief,’ that is, demons will secretly enter through our senses like thieves.

“‘Before its face the earth trembled; the heavens were shaken; the sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness.’ Before the face of this diabolical people, or even of the Antichrist, the earth trembled—that is, sinners; the heavens were shaken—that is, spiritual people. The sun and moon were darkened because under the Antichrist the faith of Christ and of the Church will fail in the hearts of some.

“‘And the Lord gave his voice before the face of his army, because his camps are exceedingly numerous, because they are strong and carry out his word.’ This is because divine preaching will precede the coming of the Antichrist. The camps of demons are called the Lord’s camps because, in every necessity, they serve his authority both for the testing of the righteous and for the condemnation of the reprobate.

“‘For great is the day of the Lord, and exceedingly terrible; and who will endure it?’ In Scripture, ‘who’ is always understood in two ways: either ‘no one’ or ‘few.’

“‘Now therefore, says the Lord: Return to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning.’ This is the Lord’s exhortation, calling the human race to repentance, first through fasting, because fasting is the foundation of repentance. The companions of fasting are weeping and mourning.

“‘And tear your hearts, and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, because he is kind and merciful, patient and of great mercy, ready to relent from evil.’ He speaks this against those penitents who promise repentance by their clothing but do not display it in their hearts. So that the sinner will not despair because of the greatness of his vices, he promises him the Lord’s kindness and mercy, because he does not immediately punish those who sin but gives them an opportunity for repentance.

“‘Who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him? A sacrifice and a libation for the Lord our God.’ He promises forgiveness for the sin of each person in uncertain terms, lest he make the penitent negligent; and he may leave behind a blessing. First, a blessing that drives away the curse; then sacrifice and libation, that is, good works pleasing to God.

“‘Blow the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast; call an assembly; gather the people. Sanctify the Church; assemble the elders; gather the little ones and those nursing at the breast.’ He repeats the same things so that they may be converted to God through hearing frequent instruction. The gathering of the people is the collection of the faithful in the Church through Christ; the diversity of ages is a distinction of merits.

[Col. 0103A] “‘Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room. Between the vestibule and the altar the priests, the ministers of the Lord, will weep and say.’ The bridegroom is Christ, who went forth publicly for the human race from his chamber—that is, from the bosom of the Father. The bride is the flesh of that same Christ, coming forth from the womb of the virgin Mary as from her bridal room. The bridegroom is the divine Word; the bride is the faithful soul. The priests, the ministers of the Lord, are the apostles, intervening on behalf of the sins of the people.

“‘Spare, Lord; spare your people, and do not give your inheritance over to disgrace, so that nations may rule over them.’ This means: so that he might send one who would deliver it. He did send one and spared his people; that is, at Christ’s coming he granted remission of sins, so that nations—that is, demons—would not rule over them.
