“‘Why should they say among the peoples, “Where is their God?” The Lord has been jealous for his land and has spared his people.’ He is said to be jealous because wherever jealousy is present, it is a sign of love. The Lord’s response is his promise, given through the books of the law and the prophets.

“‘Behold, I will send you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be filled with them, and I will no longer make you a disgrace among the nations.’ The grain is Christ, who in Zechariah is called the grain of the elect; the wine is the grace of the Holy Spirit; the oil is the charisms, which are poured by Christ through the gift of the Holy Spirit into the hearts of the elect. This means: by my blessing I will wipe away the ancient curse.

“‘And I will drive far from you the one who is from the north, and I will expel him into a land impassable and deserted.’ He calls the devil the north; by the impassable and deserted land he calls all the reprobate in whom he reigns.

“‘His face will be toward the eastern sea, and his rear toward the western sea.’ The devil does not have his face turned toward the sun of righteousness; wherever he looks, he always looks toward the sea of this age. The eastern and western seas signify the beginning and the end of his ruin.

“‘And his stench will rise, and his decay will rise, because he has acted arrogantly.’ When that same devil has been slain at the end of the world, then his stench—that is, what he is like—will appear to everyone.

“Do not fear, O land; rejoice and be glad, because the Lord has done great things. Do not fear, animals of the countryside, because the beautiful places of the wilderness have sprouted.” This means his purpose, which he arranged for the salvation of the human race, namely that the Son of God should assume flesh from their substance. The one whom he had previously called accursed he now says is restored by God’s blessing. “Animals of the countryside” means the nations, to whom the Word of power—that is, Christ—sprouted through the Virgin. “Because the tree has borne its fruit, the fig tree and the vine have given their strength. And you, sons of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, who has given you a teacher of righteousness and will cause the early rain to descend upon you.” The tree is Christ; the fig tree is understood as representing the Holy Spirit; the vine is likewise Christ among the people of the faithful. The sons of Zion are called the sons of the Church, established in the contemplation of faith. The teacher of righteousness is Christ, chosen by God the Father for his Church. By the early and the late rain he means the blessing of both Testaments, divinely bestowed in Christ.

“And the threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the winepresses will overflow with wine and oil”—that is, in Christ, or at the beginning of the spiritual kingdom, the Church’s threshing floors will be filled by believing peoples; or the hearts of the elect will overflow with various virtues through the rain of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“And I will restore to you the years which the locust, the young locust, the blight, and the caterpillar consumed. My great army, which I sent among you.” These four pests signify four disturbances through which the devil devours the human race, namely desire, fear, joy, and grief.

“And you will eat, eating, and be satisfied, and you will praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders with you.” For all who read the Scriptures carnally, like the Jews, and do not attain spiritual understanding, are eating but never reach satisfaction. “And you will praise the name of the Lord your God”—that is, if you have obtained God’s mercy through spiritual understanding. “And my people will not be put to shame forever, and you will know that I am in the midst of Israel”—that is, in the midst of those who see God through faith. “And I am the Lord your God, and there is no other, and my people will not be put to shame forever.” I am Christ, and I am your Lord: the same Christ, and no one besides Christ.

“And it will happen afterward that I will pour out my spirit [Col. 0104C] upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams, and your young men will see visions.” By the old men he means the prophets, and by the young men the apostles.

“But also upon my male servants and my female servants in those days I will pour out my spirit.” This was most clearly spoken and fulfilled according to the historical sense. By “my male servants” he means spiritual men and teachers; by “female servants,” churches, or the souls of believers.

“And I will give wonders in heaven and on earth, blood, fire, and vapor of smoke.” The Lord promises to give wonders in heaven—that is, among the saints—and on earth—that is, among sinners. And what are wonders except signs and the destruction of sinners, which were revealed at the coming [Col. 0104D] of the Holy Spirit? Blood signifies the killing of souls; fire, the heat of the body or the anger of the heart; and vapor of smoke, harmful thoughts that seethe in the hearts of human beings. According to both history and prophecy, all these things were fulfilled at the time of Christ’s Passion.

“The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.” This means that the radiance of certain believers, failing in the final tribulation, will be darkened, and the Church will be stained with the blood of martyrs.

“And it will happen that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” To call upon and confess the Lord must be demonstrated not merely by the voice, but by conduct and its result. [Col. 0105A] “For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the survivors whom the Lord will call.” We understand Mount Zion and Jerusalem as the Church, in which there will be salvation, as he has said.

## CHAPTER III

“For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem”—which previously did not exist. The first are the holy apostles, or the other believers from the circumcision; the survivors are those coming from the nations.

“And I will gather all the nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and there I will contend with them.” Jehoshaphat is interpreted as “the Lord’s judgment.” This, then, is what he says: When I have shown mercy to those who are judged by the confession [Col. 0105B] of my name, then I will bring all my adversaries down into the valley of judgment. By “all the nations” he either designates all the unbelieving peoples, or he means all the demons. “On account of my people and my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations and divided my land.” This means: I will not oppress them on the day of judgment, nor will they merely experience the authority of my power; rather, through the reasoning of justice, or even through their own confession, they will recognize that they are worthy of punishments.

“And they cast lots over my people.” This means that they strove competitively to rule over each individual. “They placed a boy in a brothel and sold a girl for wine, so that they might drink.” Here he complains about their casting of lots: they emasculated even the strongest sex—the age that could have grown toward virtue—through their injustices, and the soul that had been strongest was subjected to lust and pleasures.

“But what have I to do with you, Tyre and Sidon, and all the boundaries of the Philistines? Will you perhaps repay me with vengeance?” Tyre means “tribulation” or “distress,” while Sidon means “hunting”—that is, the demons. The Philistines mean “those falling through drunkenness.” All this should rightly be understood of heretics, through whom the devil separated God’s people from the Church; by their eloquence, as though by gold and silver, they lead the simple out of the Church and sell them under sin to the sons of the Greeks—that is, of the gentiles. “And if you take vengeance against me, I will quickly and swiftly repay you with retribution upon your head. For you took my silver and my gold, and you brought my desirable and most beautiful things into your shrines, and they sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of Greece, so that you might remove them far from their borders”—that is, under sin—“so that they might make them far from the faith of the Church.”

“Behold, I will raise them up from the place where you sold them, and I will turn your retribution upon your head.” I will raise them up as though they were lying fallen: those who were torn away from the foundation of the Church I will restore to their former condition of faith. And upon your head—that is, upon the head of you heretics who led them astray—I will return vengeance.

“And I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah”—that is, those whom you will possess away from the Church I will raise up against you, and your sons and daughters—that is, your disciples—I will bring under their authority through the preachers of the Church. “And they will sell them to the Sabeans, a distant nation, because the Lord has spoken.” Sheba is interpreted as “conversion,” while Judah means “confession.” The Sabeans are therefore called a distant nation because the saints who rule over heretics will live forever.

“Proclaim this among the nations; consecrate war; rouse the strong.” O princes—that is, teachers—proclaim it to those subject to you, because the day of judgment will come. “Let all the men of war approach and ascend.” Let the foot soldiers approach and the horsemen ascend. Horses mean impious human beings, while horsemen mean the devil or demons. These are called men of war because they habitually defeat the human race through vices.

[Col. 0106B] “Beat your ploughshares into swords and your pruning-hooks into spears; let the weak man say, ‘For I am strong.’” “Remove,” says the Lord, “O demons, all peace into sedition, and let everyone rise up for war.” “Let the weak man say, ‘For I am strong.’” In the Scriptures, to say something means to bring it to completion by deed. And when you have done all these evils and come with every strength to fight against my elect, then on the day of judgment I will overthrow all your strength.

“Break forth and come, all nations; gather from every side. There the Lord will cause your strong men to fall.” This makes clear that when the day of the Lord arrives and the end of the world draws near, Satan will pour out all his power in the time of Antichrist and fight more fiercely to test and overthrow souls.

“Let the nations rise and ascend into the valley of Jehoshaphat.” These are not judged in the mountains, nor on the plains, but in a depth and a lower place, so that the place of judgment itself may immediately be a punishment. “For there I will sit to judge all the nations round about.” God’s sitting means that he displays the state and authority of judging.

“Send out the sickles, for the harvest has ripened.” He says this to the angels: the reapers are angels, while the harvest is the peoples. In a sense the angels descend from their sublimity when they undertake the duties of executioners. “Come and descend, for the winepress is full; the winepresses overflow, because their wickedness has multiplied.” The world—or the winepress—is already overflowing [Col. 0106D] with iniquities; it can no longer contain the wickedness of the human race.

“Peoples, peoples, in the valley of slaughter, because the day of the Lord is near in the valley of slaughter.” He did not say “judgment,” lest he appear to leave the sentence in doubt; instead he used “slaughter,” from which nothing can remain.

“The sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness.” The sun is Christ; the moon is the Church. Christ’s stars, however, withdrew their brightness from those who will be tormented. For those who go into punishment will not deserve to see the light of righteousness.

“And the Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice, and heaven and earth will be shaken”—that is, from the Church of the saints, or from the heavenly Jerusalem. Just as all animals are terrified by a lion’s roar, so everyone will fear his voice. “And the Lord is the hope of his people and the strength of the sons of Israel. And you will know that I am the Lord your God”—that is, the God of believers and of those who see God through faith—“dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain.” The holy mountain means either the heavenly Jerusalem or, certainly, the Son himself. “And Jerusalem will be holy, and foreigners will no longer pass through it.” Whether it means the heavenly Jerusalem or the Church, they no longer have power within it. They are understood as the foreigners.

“And it will happen on that day that the mountains will drip sweetness, and the hills will flow with milk, and waters will go through all the streams of Judah.” He calls the saints mountains and hills according to the diversity of their merits; sweetness means the utterances of the Scriptures; streams, the hearts of the elect. Water signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. “And a fountain will go forth from the house of the Lord and will water the torrent of thorns.” The fountain is the manifest divinity of the Son of God, or the Holy Spirit; the torrent of thorns is the sins of the human race, which are burned away by their grace and purified for the future.

[Col. 0108A] “Egypt will be a desolation, and Edom a wilderness of destruction, because they acted wickedly against the sons of Judah and shed innocent blood in their land.” Egypt is interpreted as “darkness”—that is, the demons or sins. Edom means “bloody,” or “earthly,” that is, all earthly things belonging to the pleasure of flesh and blood. These will be laid waste on the day of judgment because, through their boundless wickedness, they deceived the sons of the Church in this world.

“And Judah will be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation. And I will cleanse their blood, which I had not cleansed, and the Lord will dwell in Zion.” Judah—that is, the house of confession—will be inhabited forever. But because it is not innocent in this life and has been stained by certain sins, although minor ones, I will cleanse everything through the abundance of my mercy, which they themselves did not cleanse by their own virtues. Zion is interpreted as “watchtower.” Therefore the Lord will dwell on high—that is, in the Church, in which he also reigns forever.

## ON THE PROPHET AMOS

[Col. 0107]

Amos, whose name is interpreted as “good,” prophesied in Samaria and Jerusalem, describing three and four crimes of the nations under the image of the whole world. He proclaims the coming of Christ in the Lord’s own voice as follows: [Col. 0107C] “I am the one who establishes thunder, creates the spirit, and announces Christ to human beings.” The remaining matters that he says about Amaziah and Jeroboam, or Israel, are to be referred tropologically to heretics.

## CHAPTER I

“The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.” Amos is interpreted as “a people torn away”; Uzziah as “rule” or “the strength of the Lord”; Jeroboam as “indication,” or “the cause of the people,” or “division of the people”; Joash as “the Lord’s memory,” or “temporality.” Tekoa, which is interpreted as “trumpet,” signifies the prophecies of the prophets.

[Col. 0107D] “And he said: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice. And the beautiful places of the shepherds will mourn, and the summit of Carmel will dry up.” From Jerusalem, where the temple and the worship of God were located, Christ arose and, like a lion, uttered his voice through evangelical preaching. The beautiful places of the shepherds are the Jewish people; the summit of Carmel is the temple, or the kingdom, or the priesthood of the Jews.

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke it, because they threshed Gilead with iron threshing carts. And I will send fire upon the house of Hazael, and the Lord will devour Ben-hadad.” The three and four crimes of the nations, which the sequence repeatedly sets forth, are these. The first crime is that all die in Adam. The second is that, having forgotten reason through the law implanted in nature, they did not understand. The third is that of those who do not obey the law that was given. The fourth, impossible to overcome, is that of those who did not believe in Christ. After the crimes of the nations, he reproves Judah in the seventh place for transgressing the law, and Israel in the eighth for the ungodliness they practiced against Christ. Or certainly the three and four crimes are: to think, to consent, to act, and not to repent; or else to think, to speak, to act, and to defend one’s sin. The first sin is to have thought what is evil; the second, to have assented to one’s thoughts; the third, to have committed it in deed; the fourth, not to have done penance after one’s sin. Hazael is interpreted as “the work of God.”

“And I will break the bar of Damascus, and destroy the inhabitant from the plain of the idol, and him who holds the scepter from the house of pleasure; and the people of Syria will be transferred to Cyrene, says the Lord.” Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood,” or “testing blood,” a figure of this world.

[Col. 0108D] “Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not revoke it, because they transferred a complete captivity in order to shut it up in Edom. And I will send fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it will devour its houses; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Ashdod and him who holds the scepter from Ashkelon. And I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the remnants of the Philistines will perish, says the Lord God.” Gaza is interpreted as “his strength.”

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not revoke it, because they shut up a complete captivity in Edom and did not remember the covenant of [Col. 0109A] brothers.” Tyre is interpreted as “tribulation” or “one who constricts.” It signifies the doctrines of the heretics’ perverse teaching, which seeks to seize the truth and confine it within earthly understandings.

“And I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it will devour its houses.” The fire seems to signify the impiety of the heretics, which devours their gatherings—represented as a wall or houses—that is, their consciences. It can also signify the future condemnation.

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not revoke it, because he pursued his brother with the sword, violated his mercy, continued his anger, and preserved his indignation to the end.” Edom, whose name is interpreted as “bloody” or [Col. 0109B] “earthly,” signifies the Jewish people and heretics who persecute their brother—that is, Christ in his members.

“I will send fire upon Teman, and it will devour the houses of Bozrah.” The Lord will send fire upon Teman—that is, upon desolate and dry Judea—so that, when the whole meaning of the letter collapses, the Church of Christ the Lord may be built upon his foundations.

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not revoke it, because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory. And I will kindle fire upon the wall of Rabbah, and it will devour its houses amid wailing on the day of battle and amid the whirlwind on the day of upheaval. And Milcom will go into captivity, he and his princes together, says the Lord.” [Col. 0109C] Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Since the whole congregation of the Church, gathered together through confession, serves as a testimony to the truth, Gilead appropriately expresses the Church, which by the work of all the faithful bears witness to what is true concerning God. Pregnant women are called souls that conceive an understanding of the Word from divine love; if they reach the proper time, they will give birth to the understanding they have conceived by displaying it in their works. Thus the heretics cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory, because they destroy by perverse preaching the minds of the faithful who already perceive something of the understanding of truth. They extend their own reputation for knowledge when they cut with the sword of error the hearts of the little ones already pregnant with the conception of the Word, and thus create for themselves a reputation for teaching.

## CHAPTER II

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not revoke it, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes. And I will send fire upon Moab, and it will devour the houses of Kerioth; and Moab will die amid a tumult, at the sound of the trumpet. And I will destroy the judge from its midst, and I will kill all its princes with him, says the Lord.” Moab, whose name is interpreted as “from the father”—that is, from the devil. Kerioth, or Kiriath-jearim, is rendered in our language as “village of forests,” because the Jews or heretics, whose figure this Moab represented, crush the bones of the king of Edom—that is, Christ’s elect—or the spiritual meanings in the divine books through carnal understanding, and reduce them to ashes.

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not revoke it, because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments. For their idols deceived them, after their fathers had gone away. And I will send fire upon Judah, and it will devour the houses of Jerusalem.” What is said about Judah refers to the Church, which is the true confession. It is reproved for having despised the law of the Lord and not having done his commandments.

“Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke it, because he sold the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals; they crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble.” This is rightly understood of Christ, whom the Jews sold for silver. The Jews and heretics turn the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth because they crush the understanding of humble believers within an earthly interpretation. They turn aside the way of the humble—that way of which he said, “I am the way and the truth and the life”—because they disdain to walk along it. “And a father and his son went to the girl, in order to profane my holy name.” The father is the Jewish people; the son is the Christian people. The one who enters the girl with his father is the person who, coming to the Church, wants to preserve the law together with the Gospel, and thereby commits fornication and profanes the name of God.

[Col. 0110C] “And they lay beside every altar upon garments taken in pledge, and they drank the wine of the condemned in the house of their god.” Such was the contempt for God among the Jewish priests that they stretched out their garments—garments in which they had slept or in which they had committed fornication—beside the altar with cords fixed to the ground and made coverings of them, so that no one could see those fornicating in the temple behind them.

“But I destroyed the Amorite from before them, whose height was like the height of cedars and who was strong like an oak. I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below. I am the one who brought you up from the land of Egypt and led you through the wilderness for forty years, so that you might possess the land of the Amorite. I raised up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men. Is this not so, sons of Israel? says the Lord. Yet you gave the Nazirites wine to drink and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘Do not prophesy.’” This was fulfilled according to the historical sense at that time, when, after the seven nations had been uprooted from the land of the Canaanites, the Jewish people took possession of their settlements.

“Behold, I will creak over you as a cart creaks when loaded with hay.” Since hay is the life of carnal people, as it is written, “All flesh is hay,” the Lord testifies that, in bearing with the life of carnal people, he bears that life as a cart bears hay. For him to creak under the weight of the hay is to complain of the burdens and iniquities of sinners.

[Col. 0111A] “Flight will perish from the swift; the strong man will not retain his strength; the mighty man will not save his life; the one holding the bow will not stand; the swift-footed man will not be saved; the rider will not save his life; and the strong-hearted man among the mighty will flee naked on that day, says the Lord.” This was fulfilled according to the truth of history when, on account of the merit of their sins, they were handed over to the Assyrians and other nations for plunder. In general, however, this threat will come upon all offenders on the day of judgment.

## CHAPTER III

“Hear the word that the Lord has spoken concerning you, sons of Israel, concerning the whole clan that he brought up from the land of Egypt, saying: ‘I have known only you from all the clans of the earth; therefore I will visit all your iniquities upon you.’” This is to be understood not only of the Jews but of all the elect, whom almighty God chastises in this life like a father chastising his children.

“Will two walk together unless they have agreed?” These two who agree with one another and walk together on Christ’s way are to be understood as the two peoples: those from the circumcision and those from the uncircumcision.

“Will a lion roar in the forest unless it has prey? Will a lion’s cub give voice from its den unless it has seized something?” The lion is the devil; the lion’s cub is the multitude of unclean spirits seizing prey—namely, the souls of the reprobate [Col. 0111C] who lose the unity of faith through discord and drag them with themselves into the abyss of condemnation.

“Will a bird fall into a snare on the earth without a bird-catcher? Will the snare be removed from the earth before it has caught something?” The snare of the earth, or of the bird-catcher, is to be understood as the devil, who catches the elect like birds through earthly actions or through the discord of disunity.

“If the trumpet sounds in a city, will the people not be afraid? If there is evil in a city, has the Lord not done it?” Whatever in the holy Scriptures is a threatening trumpet is meant. But the evil that the Lord does in a city is not contrary to virtue; it signifies the affliction and sufferings of human beings.

“For the Lord God will do nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets.” [Col. 0111D] This does not mean that God reveals to the prophets everything he will do in heaven, or everything he has already done, but only what he is going to do on earth.

“The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?” I know that someone left in his commentaries the statement that the roaring lion should be understood as the devil, roaring at those who are destined to perish. But God, who speaks through the prophets, should be referred to God the Savior, so that, just as they hear the lion’s roar in an evil sense and are seized for death, so the saints may hear God commanding in a good sense and be saved.

“Make it heard in the houses of Ashdod and in the houses of the land of Egypt, and say: ‘Gather upon the mountains of [Col. 0112A] Samaria and see the many insanities in its midst and those suffering oppression within it; they do not know how to do what is right,’ says the Lord God, ‘storing up iniquity and plunder in their houses.’” Ashdod is interpreted as “fire.” He exhorts the people of the nations to gather against the Jewish people, so that they may see the evils that the Jewish people themselves committed, and so that the Jewish people may not think that they have just complaints against God because he handed them over to plunder. They also suffer oppression within its inner chambers, or every simple believer is oppressed, while heretics desire falsehood in the name of truth and do not know how to do what is right at all, because they have lost the path of truth and do not believe in the one who says, “I am the truth.”

[Col. 0112B] “Therefore thus says the Lord God: The land will be afflicted and surrounded; your strength will be stripped from you, and your houses will be plundered.” Heretics, too, being earthly in their thinking, will either be afflicted on the day of judgment, all their strength will be weakened, and what they had acquired by plunder will be taken away, so that the peoples whom they deceived may be set free. Or certainly they are daily afflicted by ecclesiastical men through the testimonies of Scripture, and the strength of their syllogisms and sharp words—the means by which they had fortified their doctrine—will be stripped from them, so that those who had been snatched away from the Church may return to the Church.

“Thus says the Lord: Just as a shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs or the tip of an ear, so the sons of Israel who dwell in Samaria will be rescued, on the edge of a bed and on the couch of Damascus.” According to the historical sense, there is no doubt that this was fulfilled among the Jews at the time of their devastation. According to the tropological sense, it is to be understood of the calling of the nations, whom “the good shepherd, who lays down his life for his sheep,” rescued from the mouth of the lion—that is, the devil. The legs signify teachers; the tip of the ear signifies hearers.

“Hear and bear witness in the house of Jacob, says the Lord of hosts, that on the day when I begin to visit the transgressions of Israel upon him, I will also visit the altars of Bethel; the horns of the altar will be cut off and fall to the ground. I will strike the winter house together with the summer house; the ivory houses will perish, and the many houses will be destroyed, says the Lord.” According to the historical sense, we believe that this was fulfilled among the Jews; [Col. 0112D] according to the anagogical sense, it is to be understood of heretics, who, having set aside the Lord’s altar, which is the unity of faith, build many altars for themselves, not for God. By the winter house and the summer house he prefigures Israel and Judah, or at least the Jewish people and the heretics.

## CHAPTER IV

“Hear this word, fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the needy and crush the poor, who say to your masters, ‘Bring it, and we will drink.’ The Lord God has sworn by his holiness: Behold, days will come upon you, and they will lift you up on poles, and your remnants in boiling pots.” [Col. 0113A] By the fat cows he means the princes of the Jews or the rich of this world. Spiritually, however, Samaria, which is interpreted as “watch,” signifies the pride of heretics, who falsely claim to be guardians of God’s commandments. As for what he says, “They will lift you up on poles,” this happened historically to the Jewish princes. Tropologically, it represents heretics joined to ecclesiastical men through divine judgments, or certainly indicates future condemnation.

“And you will go out through the breaches, one opposite another, and you will be cast into Harmon, says the Lord.” According to the historical sense, this was fulfilled among the Jews when they were led away divided into captivity. Spiritually, however, it signifies heretics who withdraw from the unity of faith and, divided into various sects against one another, are cast through pride into [Col. 0113B] destruction.

“Come to Bethel and act impiously at Gilgal; multiply transgression. Bring your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes every three days; sacrifice praise from leavened bread, call for voluntary offerings, and proclaim them. For this is what you desired, sons of Israel, says the Lord.” According to the historical sense, he speaks ironically against the Jews, so that they should not commit crimes but, according to their transgression, heap sins upon sins, for which they may be punished more severely. Heretics, however, come to Bethel—that is, to the house of God—and act impiously when they offer to the devil the sacrifice owed to God alone. They also invite others to their impiety by proclaiming it, while from the leaven of false doctrines they seek human favor [Col. 0113C].

“Therefore I also gave you dullness of teeth in all your cities and lack of bread in all your places, yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” For if someone eats a sour grape—which signifies iniquity—his teeth will become dull, so that he will make poor use of the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, eating the grape while it is unripe and without sweetness.

“I also withheld rain from you when three months still remained until the harvest. I rained upon one city and did not rain upon another city. One part received rain, and the part upon which I did not rain dried up. Two or three cities came to one city to drink water, but they were not satisfied, and you did not return to me, says the Lord.” The Lord also withholds from the Jews and from heretics spiritual rains, all the dew of divine knowledge, and the knowledge of the Holy Trinity. The Lord rains upon one city—the Church of true confession—and does not rain upon another, which is found in the assemblies of heretics. Two or three cities go to one city in which the waters of hope, faith, and charity abound; but they are not satisfied because they come to seek divine grace not willingly but out of necessity.

“I struck you with scorching wind and blight among the multitude of your gardens and vineyards. The caterpillar will eat your olive groves and your fig trees, yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” Heretics have gardens and vineyards, olive groves and fig trees—that is, false virtues—which the caterpillar or the devil’s other pests undoubtedly gnaw away and consume.

“I sent death among you as in the land of Egypt; I struck your young men with the sword, even to the captivity of your horses; I caused the stench of your camps to rise into your nostrils, yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” Thus the Lord sends death upon Jacob so that we may put our members to death on earth. He also handed over the horses into captivity, lest they fall headlong into hell, so that they may recognize their sins, sense their foulness, and cease to sin.

[Col. 0114B] “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire, yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.” Therefore Israel and all the heretics who possess the works of Sodom and Gomorrah are overthrown and, like a brand snatched from the fire, are freed through God’s grace.

“Therefore this is what I will do to you, Israel. And after I have done this to you, prepare to meet the Lord your God, O Israel, for behold, I am the one who forms the mountains, creates the wind, announces his word to human beings, makes the morning mist, and walks upon the heights of the earth; the Lord of hosts is his name.” “After I have done to you,” he says, “the things that I testify I will do, prepare to call upon the Lord your God, or prepare to meet your God.” The spirit of which he speaks here is not the Holy Spirit, as heretics suppose; rather, we understand it as wind or the human spirit. After Christ has been announced, the light of truth is opened to us, though not perfectly, because now we see in part and know in part. By the mountains, or the heights of the earth, he means the apostles or all spiritual men, beneath whom the Lord walks. By the morning mist he means either his incarnation or, certainly, evangelical preaching, which, because it is not believed by unbelievers, is scarcely seen.

## CHAPTER V

“Hear this word, which I raise over you as a lament: The house of Israel has fallen; it will not rise again. The virgin of Israel has been cast upon her land; there is no one to raise her up.” [Col. 0114D] As far as the literal sequence is concerned, the ten tribes called Israel, led into captivity, never afterward returned to their land. Figuratively, however, he reproves both the Jews themselves and certain sinners in the Church who, after committing wickedness, do not wish to return to repentance.

“For thus says the Lord: From the city from which a thousand went out, a hundred will be left in it; and from the one from which a hundred went out, ten will be left in the house of Israel.” This is what Isaiah says: “If the number of the sons of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be converted from them.”

[Col. 0115A] “For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me and you will live; and do not seek Bethel, and do not enter Gilgal, and do not cross over into Beersheba, because Gilgal will surely be taken captive, and Bethel will be useless.” “Do not seek,” he says, “Bethel, where there was a golden calf; and do not enter Gilgal, which was devoted to idolatry; and do not cross over into Beersheba—that is, to the well of the oath—where, whenever the tribe of Judah went astray, it was accustomed to worship idols.”

“Seek the Lord, and live, lest perhaps he burn like fire—the house of Joseph—and it be consumed, with no one to extinguish it. Bethel, you who turn judgment into wormwood and abandon justice in the land.”

This is the fire kindled not by anyone else but by sinners themselves, concerning which the Lord says elsewhere: [Col. 0115B] “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled.”

“Who makes Arcturus and Orion, who turns darkness into morning and changes day into night, who calls the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth—the Lord is his name.”

According to the truth of the historical account, the Lord, who is the Creator of all things, threatens the future captivity of Samaria and brings devastation upon a powerful kingdom. Understand Arcturus and Orion, however, as the Church, or all the saints. The Lord turns darkness into morning when he leads the Gentile people from the error of unbelief into the light of faith. He also changes day into night, because he abandoned the Jewish people, who presumed upon their own righteousness, in the blindness of their heart.

[Col. 0115C] “Who smiles upon devastation over the strong and brings destruction upon the powerful.”

The description of God as smiling signifies that he is angry, because when we ourselves are angry, we sometimes smile.

“They hated the one who reproved at the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke with integrity.”

What is the gate at which the prophet reproves sinners, if not the entrance of vices? Or certainly, the prophet himself stands at the gate, at the beginnings of the virtues, and is hated by those whom he reproves. For whoever does not receive the prophet does not receive the one who sent him. It is beyond doubt that “the one who spoke with integrity” is to be understood as Christ the Lord.

“Therefore, because you plundered the poor and took a choice portion from him, you will build houses of hewn stone [Col. 0115D] and will not live in them; you will plant most beautiful vineyards and will not drink their wine, because I have known your many crimes and your mighty sins.”

It is not absurd to understand the poor man as Christ in his members: heretics attempt to plunder him through hidden snares.

“Enemies of the righteous, accepting a bribe and oppressing the poor at the gate. Therefore the prudent man will keep silent at that time, because it is an evil time.”

The enemies of the righteous are understood as all the enemies of Christ. Heretics, however, are proved to be worse than all the others, for they attempt to oppress the humble members of the Church at the gates of faith.

“Seek good and not evil, so that you may live, and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said. [Col. 0116A] Hate evil and love good, and establish judgment at the gate; perhaps the Lord God of hosts will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.”

For if you seek good, you immediately repel evil. Good, however, is the Lord himself. To establish judgment at the gate is, after evil has been rejected, to receive the truth. Or certainly, to establish judgment at the gates is for the leaders of the churches, within the holy Church—which is the gate of the kingdom of heaven—to teach the people, with true discernment, what is good and what is evil.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the ruler: In all the streets there will be lamentation, and in all the places outside it will be said, ‘Woe, woe!’ They will call the farmer to mourning and those who know how to lament to lamentation, and in all the roads there will be mourning, because I will pass through your midst, says the Lord.”

He prophesied the devastation [Col. 0116B] of the Jews, not only in their dwellings but also in everything that was outside them. Those who will have been in the Church will not hear “woe,” for this is the final punishment; but if they should sin, lamentation will be taken up over them. The farmers and those who know how to lament are ecclesiastical men, who call sinners to repentance before the coming judgment.

“Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you want it? The day of the Lord is this: darkness and not light.”

The Jews, like heretics, and likewise many members of the Church who rely upon their own righteousness, claim to desire the day of the Lord—that is, the day of judgment—as though secure despite their crimes, although they ought to fear it.

“As when a man flees from the face of a lion and a bear meets him, and he enters a house, leans his hand against the wall, and a serpent bites him.” [Col. 0116C]

The lion, the bear, and the serpent are to be understood here as the devil. The house, moreover, is each sinner’s own conscience, in which he is not well.

“Will not the day of the Lord be darkness and not light, gloom and not brightness in it? I hate and reject your festivals, and I will not accept the fragrance of your assemblies. If you offer me burnt offerings and gifts, I will not look upon them, and I will not accept the vows of your fattened animals. Take away from me the tumult of your songs; I will not hear the music of your lyre. Judgment will be revealed like water, and righteousness like a mighty torrent.”

He speaks of the sacrifices of the Jews and the offerings of heretics, [Col. 0116D] which are not approved by God. He also calls the songs of the Levites, with which they praised God, a tumult and a confused sound, and likewise those of the heretics. The judgment and righteousness of God, by which he will judge his people, will be manifest to all; and, like a very powerful torrent, it carries away with it whatever it seizes and does not permit whatever resists it to stand.

“Did you offer me victims and sacrifice in the wilderness for forty years, O house of Israel? You carried the tents of Moloch, your idol, and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves. And I will cause you to migrate beyond Damascus, says the Lord God of hosts is his name.”

Because the Israelite people had been enticed by the allure of idolatrous worship, [Col. 0117A] and because what they offered to God they did not offer willingly but under compulsion through fear of punishment, it was reckoned as though they had not offered it. By “the star” he means the star once worshiped by the unbelieving Saracens.

## CHAPTER VI

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria, nobles and chiefs of the peoples, entering pompously into the house of Israel.”

By the wealthy in Zion he means the leaders of the Jews, or the teachers of the heretics, who presume upon their own righteousness, trusting as though in Mount Samaria. According to another edition, these are the ones who despise Zion—that is, the Church of God—the Lord says.

“Cross over to Calneh and see; go from there to great Hamath, and descend to Gath of the Philistines, and to the best of these kingdoms.”

Historically, he rebukes the leaders of the Jews, or the wealthy of the Church, who live dissolutely and follow the broader paths of this world, along which unbelievers walk. What David did in the worship of God, they themselves do according to their own desire and luxury. For they have been set apart for an evil day—that is, the day of judgment—from the fellowship of the saints.

“Is their territory broader than your territory, you who have been separated for an evil day and have approached the throne of iniquity? You who sleep on ivory beds and indulge yourselves on your couches; you who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; you who sing to the sound of the psaltery, who have thought that they possess instruments of song like David; you who drink wine from bowls and anoint yourselves with the finest [Col. 0117C] ointment, and suffer nothing over the ruin of Joseph.”

In its tropological sense, the prophetic word is directed against heretics, who have been separated on an evil day—that is, either in the present time or on the day of judgment—from the fellowship of the Church. They suppose that their songs, that is, their false teachings, are the preaching of Christ. The divine word urges them to consider in their minds the philosophies of all the nations and to discover that their boundaries are narrower than the boundaries of the Holy Scriptures.

“Therefore now they will migrate at the head of those who migrate, and the faction of the luxurious will be removed. The Lord God has sworn by his own life, says the Lord God of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob and hate his house.”

According to the historical account, he speaks of the Jews [Col. 0117D] who were carried away into captivity.

“I will hand over the city with its inhabitants. If ten men should remain in one house, they too will die; and their relative will take him and burn him, to carry the bones out of the house. He will say to the one who is in the inner rooms of the house, ‘Is anyone still with you?’ And he will answer, ‘It is finished.’”

According to the historical testimony, we know that this was fulfilled among the Jewish people when Jerusalem was devastated by the Romans. Tropologically, it is to be understood of the heretics, in whose gatherings, if ten men should remain, they will all die the death that leads to Tartarus. Their relatives and household members will bury the bones of the righteous, concerning whom it is said: “Let the dead bury their own dead.” [Col. 0118A] The one who is outside and does not enter the house, but rather casts the dead outside, commands the one who burns the dead, dissolves them into ashes, and crushes their bones to keep silent and not defile the pure name of God with a dead mouth.

“And he will say to him: ‘Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord,’ because, behold, the Lord commanded, and he will strike the larger house with ruins and the smaller house with fissures.”

They think that the larger house and the smaller house signify the Jewish people and the Church gathered from the Gentiles. If this Church should ever sin and be struck with the fissures of heretics, it will be torn apart just as the Jewish people were shaken into ruin.

[Col. 0118B] “Can horses run over rocks, or can one plow with buffaloes? For you have turned judgment into bitterness and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood.”

Since wild oxen are untamed because of their ferocity and do not wish to have the earth split by the plow, while you are proud and lifted up, you have changed the worship of God, even though horses and buffaloes cannot change their nature, so that you might make what is sweet bitter.

“You who rejoice in nothing, who say, ‘Have we not taken horns for ourselves by our own strength?’ Behold, I will raise up against you, O house of Israel”—says the Lord God of hosts—“a nation, and it will crush you from the entrance of Hamath to the torrent of the wilderness.”

## CHAPTER VII

“This the Lord God showed me.”

[Col. 0118C] This is the voice of all the proud, who, relying upon their own strength, ascribe to their own power rather than to God the temporal authority they could possess only because they had received it from God.

“And behold, a maker of locusts at the beginning of the late rain; and behold, the late rain after the shearing of the flock. And it happened that, when it had finished eating the grass of the land, I said: ‘Lord God, be merciful, I beg you. Who will raise up Jacob, because he is small?’”

God is the maker and creator of the locusts. They come at the beginning of the late rain—that is, in spring, when everything is green. An innumerable swarm of young locusts followed these locusts. It came after the late rain and was called the shearer, or the shearing of the flock. There is no doubt that these signify the two kings of the Assyrians and the army of the Chaldeans, who devastated [Col. 0118D] the Jewish nation.

Alternatively: Gog, the king of the locusts, who is presented according to the translators of the Septuagint, is interpreted as “roof.” This signifies a certain proud and arrogant power of the Antichrist, who, coming at the end of the world with an innumerable multitude of unbelievers, will consume, as though in the late rain, all the grass of the earth—that is, everything weak and tender in the human race. Hence the prophet intercedes with God for the people of Israel, because they are small in understanding, asking that, with the sentence changed, at least a remnant of them might be saved.

“But the Lord had mercy concerning this. ‘It will not happen,’ said the Lord. This the Lord God showed me: and behold, the Lord God was calling judgment to the fire, and it devoured the great abyss, [Col. 0119A] and it consumed the portion at the same time. And I said: ‘Lord God, cease, I beg you. Who will raise up Jacob, because he is small?’ The Lord had mercy concerning this. ‘But this also will not happen,’ said the Lord God. This the Lord God showed me.”

Judgment is called to the fire when the sentence of righteousness is revealed for the punishment of eternal burning. It devours the great abyss because it burns the wicked and incomprehensible minds of human beings, which now shine before men even through the wonders of their proud works. The portion of the house is consumed because Gehenna also devours those who now boast that they are, as though through holy deeds, among the number of the elect.

[Col. 0119B] “And behold, the Lord was standing upon a plastered wall, and in his hand was a mason’s trowel. And the Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said: ‘A mason’s trowel.’ And the Lord said: ‘Behold, I will place a trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I will not continue to pass over him any longer. The high places of the idol will be demolished, the sanctuaries of Israel will be laid waste, and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.’”

The mason’s trowel signifies the Lord’s protection, which he removed from his people Israel as though from a former building. The adamant, a very hard, untamable, and unattractive stone, prefigures our Lord and Savior, “who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” He stands upon the adamantine wall—that is, upon the incorruptible building of the Church.

[Col. 0119C] “And Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: ‘Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot endure all his words. For thus says Amos: “Jeroboam will die by the sword, and Israel will migrate captive from his land.”’ And Amaziah said to Amos: ‘You who see, go away; flee to the land of Judah, and eat bread there, and prophesy there. You shall no longer prophesy at Bethel, because it is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom.’”

Everything contained in this prophecy concerning Amaziah, Jeroboam, and Israel is to be transferred tropologically to the heretics. Their priest Amaziah sometimes sends to Jeroboam, the king and patron of the heretics, and accuses holy men and heralds of the faith before him. He orders the teachers not to preach in Israel, lest they act against the king’s will, because Bethel—that is, the house of God, the false Church—is the king’s sanctuary and the house of the kingdom. For they are accustomed to say: “The emperor communicates with us, and if anyone resists him, he immediately brings accusations against him. Therefore you are acting against the emperor; you despise the commands of the Augustus.” [Col. 0120A]

“And Amos answered and said to Amaziah: ‘I am not a prophet, and I am not the son of a prophet, but I am a herdsman, plucking sycamores. The Lord took me when I was following the flock, and the Lord said to me: “Go, prophesy to my people Israel.”’”

Some explain the sycamores as sycamines, a kind of tree that grows in the plains of Palestine and produces wild fruit. If these trees are not plucked, they produce extremely bitter figs, and the watery sap is spoiled. But for us, since the solitude in which Amos lived produces no such trees, it seems more likely that he means brambles, which bear mulberries and relieve the hunger and want of shepherds. [Col. 0120B] Others maintain that sycamores signify all fruit-bearing trees.

“And now hear the word of the Lord: You say, ‘You shall not prophesy against Israel, and you shall not drip words upon the house of the idol.’ Therefore thus says the Lord God: ‘Your wife will prostitute herself in the city, your sons and your daughters will fall by the sword, your land will be measured by a measuring line, you will die in a polluted land, and Israel will migrate captive from its land.’”

This is what Scripture records the apostles doing when the scribes and Pharisees warned them not to teach in the name of Jesus, and they answered, saying: “We must obey God rather than men.” We know that the prophet Amos did the same.

Let Amaziah too, who now boasts [Col. 0120C] in the power of the priesthood, die in a land polluted by idols, and let him not die before he sees the people whom he had deceived serving and held captive. Amaziah, whose name is interpreted as “strong” and “rigid,” because he is rebellious and fierce, forbids an ecclesiastical man and true prophet to proclaim the word of God and to correct the wandering people. There is no doubt that he displayed the arrogance of the heretics. The wife of these heretics—that is, the false Church—will be shown to all the faithful to be an adulterous people; and her sons and daughters, whom she wickedly brought forth into error, will be struck either by the Lord’s indignation or by their own impiety. Her land also, and all her possession, will become a portion of the demons, and they themselves will die in a polluted land that does not have God as its inhabitant.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0120D] “This the Lord God showed me: and behold, a hook for fruit. And the Lord said: ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said: ‘A hook for fruit.’”

(At this point all the copies available to us lack Haymo’s words in chapters VIII and IX.)

## ON THE PROPHET OBADIAH

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119] The Hebrews say that Obadiah was a prophet who, under Ahab, king of Samaria, and Jezebel, the most wicked queen, fed one hundred prophets in caves—those who had not bent their knees to Baal—and that he was among the seven thousand whom Elijah is accused of not knowing. His tomb, together with the mausoleum of the prophet Elisha and of John the Baptist, is still held in great veneration at Sebaste, which was formerly called Samaria. It is read that, after he had fed one hundred prophets, he received the spirit of prophecy; and from being a commander of the army he became a commander of the Church. In him was fulfilled what the Lord says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward.” At that time he fed a small flock in Samaria; now he feeds Christ’s Church throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER I

“The vision of Obadiah.”

It may be asked why it is called the vision of Obadiah, since we do not read in what follows that he saw anything, but that he heard. It should be understood, however, that “vision” is used here for understanding, because what he heard he saw—that is, he understood—in the manner of the prophets. There are three kinds of visions: one is bodily, as with stones; another is spiritual, as when in dreams we see horses running and men fighting; and the third is intellectual, through which the holy prophets spoke. For they understood spiritually whatever they said.

“Thus says the Lord God to Edom.”

Edom himself is Esau and Seir; his region is likewise called by three names. He was called Esau from the eating of lentils, because he sold his birthright for the reddish food of lentils. Edom means “red.” He is also called Seir, that is, “hairy,” because he was bristly. His region was also called Idumea, Seir, and Teman.

Hence Amos says: “For three crimes of the children of Edom, and for four, I will not turn him back.” Isaiah says: “Seir cries out to me, ‘Watchman, what of the night?’” And Jeremiah says: “Is there no longer wisdom in Teman?” and the rest through the end of the prophecy.

The children of Israel were therefore enemies of the children of Edom, just as their father had once been an enemy of his brother Jacob.

The prophet speaks: “We have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy to the nations.”

He joins himself to the other prophets who spiritually proclaim the divine sentence against Idumea. For in Hebrew it is called Edom, and in Greek Idumea. “We have heard a report,” he says, “from the Lord”—that is, I and the other prophets like me who had written against Edom. And he sent an envoy to the nations—that is, his Son, who is certainly the Word of God the Father—to Nebuchadnezzar and his army, so that they might come against the Idumeans and destroy them.

Concerning this envoy the Lord speaks through Haggai: “I will shake all the nations, and the Desired One of all the nations will come.”

“Rise, and let us rise together against him for battle.”

The envoy who was sent to the nations says this: “Rise,” he says, “you who are sleeping, and do not regard the battle as difficult or unusual. You will have me first in the line of battle. I am also your leader, who appeared to Jesus son of Nun holding a sword. Therefore let us rise together against him for battle, because victory will be easy.”

Jeremiah likewise speaks in a vision against Edom: “I have heard a report from the Lord, and an envoy has been sent to the nations,” and so forth.

“Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are exceedingly contemptible.”

Jeremiah likewise says: “Behold, I have made you small, contemptible among men.” [Col. 0122A] In comparison with the other nations dwelling around him he was small, but he was lifted up in pride even though he was contemptible—that is, exceedingly despicable.

“O Edom,” he says, “although you are the least among all the nations around you, and small in number compared with the other peoples, you lift yourself beyond your strength in pride.” Hence it follows:

“The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock and exalt your throne, you who say in your heart…”

The land of the Idumeans lay in the southern region, and therefore, because of the excessive heat of the sun, they lived in caves in the earth or rock. The meaning is this: although you live in grottoes or rocky caverns, humble and extremely poor, and possess no lofty roofs of buildings, because of the excessive hardness or pride of your heart you strive to exalt your throne or kingdom as though you were omnipotent, and you say in your heart:

“Who will bring me down to the earth?”—that is, no one.

For “who” is sometimes used for “rarely” and sometimes for “no one,” as here and in the psalm: “God, who will be like you?”

“Though you should be exalted like an eagle, and though you should place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.”

“You,” he says, “swell with pride and, like an eagle, which flies higher than the other birds, rise aloft, so that you could even penetrate beyond the limits of nature; and, to say more, even if you placed your nest—that is, your dwelling—among the stars, from there I will bring you down to the earth, just as it often suddenly casts itself into the depths of the sea from the great height of the clouds.”

Even those who have written about the nature of birds have handed down that the eagle flies higher than all birds. It is said to possess such keen sight that, while it is carried motionless over the seas on unmoving wings and is not visible to human eyes, from such a great height it sees little fish swimming; and when they are near the shore, it descends like a missile, seizes its prey, and carries it on its wings to the shore.

What is said against Edom can be referred spiritually to the heretics, who, although they are small and contemptible, rise in pride against the Church, trusting in the secrets of their mysteries. The Lord threatens them that if, lifted up by mental arrogance, they should be exalted to heaven, he will bring them down from there.

“If thieves had entered upon you, if robbers by night, how would you have kept silent?”

What he says means this: if thieves and robbers, who customarily break into houses by night and seize what is in them, had entered upon you and, concealed by darkness, had gone around the corners of your houses, how would you then have kept silent? So, by implication, you will be silent when Nebuchadnezzar comes with the Chaldeans, Assyrians, and the other nations, unable to resist them.

“Would they not have stolen enough for themselves?” That is, would they not have taken whatever they thought could be sufficient for themselves?

“If grape-gatherers had entered upon you, would they at least have left you a cluster?” That is, if grape-gatherers had entered your vineyard and wished to ravage it like enemies, would they at least have left you a cluster?

It is as though he were saying: certainly they would have, because although their work had been careful, they would nevertheless have left clusters hidden among the branches, together with the vines’ leaves. But these grape-gatherers are understood as the Babylonians with their leader, who, at the Lord’s command, gathered in and killed that people, plundered them, and left nothing hidden that could have escaped their notice.

Hence the astonished prophet adds:

“How they have searched out Esau and investigated his hidden places!”

The Chaldeans searched all his secrets, caves, and the holes of the caverns in which they lived, and they were unable to hide anything from them. This is exceedingly remarkable, since that entire southern region of the Idumeans contains dwellings in caves, and, because of the excessive heat of the sun—for it is a southern province—makes use of underground huts.

[Col. 0123B] “They have driven you out to the boundary.”

That is, when Nebuchadnezzar came, not merely some portion of your region was taken captive; rather, reaching the boundaries of your kingdom, they expelled you from your throne.

“All the men of your covenant have mocked you; the men of your peace have prevailed against you.”

He speaks of the Moabites, Midianites, and the other neighboring peoples, who had formerly been allied with him but afterward joined the Assyrians and mocked those with whom they had once been confederated. They prevailed against them, leading into captivity those with whom they had formerly lived in peace while guarding their cities.

“Those who eat with you will set an ambush against you.”

That is, those who now enjoy such peace and friendship with you that they eat bread with you will, when the enemies arrive and join forces with them, set an ambush against you, taking care that none of those belonging to you can escape.

“There is no prudence in him.”

Not the kind of prudence he ought to have had, since he hopes in those who will become his adversaries. He says that Edom has no prudence in this respect, because he did not foresee that those with whom he was at peace would become his enemies.

“Will I not, on that day, says the Lord, destroy the wise men from Idumea and remove prudence from Mount Esau?”

That is: when your enemies possess your borders, all the men of your covenant have deceived you, and they have prevailed against you, I will destroy the wise philosophers of Idumea. Edom in Hebrew is called Idumea in Greek. I will also remove prudence from Mount Esau, so that his cunning may be shown to be folly, and so that they may find no plan by which they can escape the evil that overtakes them.

He rightly says that he will then remove prudence from the mountain, either because the city of Idumea is situated on a mountain, or because that entire region toward the south rises in steep mountains.

“Your strong men will fear from the south, so that a man from Mount Esau may perish.”

Another translation has: “Your warriors will be terrified from Teman.” Teman means “south.” Just as we read that Esau was called by three names, so the region of that land which extends toward the south is called by three names: Darom, Teman, and Negeb. According to Ezekiel, these names signify the south, the southwest wind, and the south.

The meaning is this: after you begin to hear that enemies are approaching and they begin to mock you, in whose peace you now trust, your kingdom’s strong men who dwell in the south will be terrified, so that the man from Mount Esau will perish—the man who had formerly been accustomed both to fight for the city and to give prudent counsel.

“Because of the slaughter and the iniquity against your brother Jacob.”

He explains why the wise men will perish from Idumea and the prudent from Mount Esau: because of slaughter and impiety, since he killed and acted wickedly against his brother Jacob when, while the Babylonians were devastating Jerusalem, he was their ally.

The hatred that Esau held against Jacob because of the blessing that Jacob had taken from him was likewise held by these people and their children forever. They grieved that they had lost the goods which the Jews had received. For this reason, when Nebuchadnezzar first came to Jerusalem, while the Chaldeans and Babylonians were devastating it, they joined them and killed the Jews together with them. Because of this sin the Lord speaks to them, saying:

“Shame will cover you, and you will perish forever.”

They were indeed put to shame after they were captured by their enemies, and they perished forever because they were condemned to perpetual captivity.

“On the day when you stood against him.”

That is, at the time of the manifest captivity, when Jehoiakim and Daniel were captured and the other boys were led into captivity—namely, at the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar in Jerusalem—when you stood against your brother.

“When foreigners”—foreign to God and to the offspring of the Jews—“were taking away his army, and strangers were entering his gates,” that is, the gates of the city of Jerusalem.

“And over Jerusalem,” that is, over its spoil, “they cast lots,” so that they might divide its plunder among themselves, each seeking to determine what he would take.

“You too were like one of them.”

Therefore these things will happen to you, because you, who ought to have been their guardian and helper, became their killer.

“And you will not look down upon your brother on the day of your brother, on the day of his exile; and you will not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction.”

The prophetic word now openly threatens Edom. When the man from Mount Esau has perished and eternal shame has covered him because of the slaughter and impiety against his brother, he will certainly not do what he previously did against his brother. It is as though he were saying: when the second and third captivity of the Jews comes, you will not look down upon them or rejoice on the day of their destruction, as you have done until now, because you will already be held captive by your enemies.

For, as has been said, Nebuchadnezzar first came to Jerusalem under Jehoiakim, when Ezekiel was taken with that king to Babylon; and the third time under Zedekiah, whom he led captive into a prison after gouging out his eyes. Therefore, during the second or third captivity of the Israelites, the Idumeans did not rejoice, because they themselves were already held captive.

Hence it follows:

“And you will not magnify your mouth on the day of distress,” saying: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations in it,” as you did at first.

Therefore the psalmist speaks in the voice of one invoking punishment, saying: “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem.”

When the two tribes that reigned in Jerusalem and were called Judah had been captured by the Chaldeans for the second or third time, the Idumeans did not magnify their mouths as though they were allies of the victors in their brother’s distress.

“Nor will you enter the gate of my people on the day of their ruin; nor will you look down upon his sufferings, you too, on the day of his devastation.”

That is, you will certainly not walk triumphantly through the gate of Jerusalem on the day of the devastation and ruin of my people, because, having been handed over to their hands, you will suffer similar things.

“And you will not be sent against his army on the day of his devastation,” as once you sent an army against him.

“Nor will you stand at the exits”—that is, on the roads—“to kill those who have fled; nor will you shut up his survivors” in prison and hand them over to their masters, “on the day of tribulation.”

That is, when they begin to flee by the roads and byways familiar to them toward the wilderness, you will not stand at the fork in the road or wait for them at the crossroads in order to kill those who have escaped, capture the others, and either take them yourself or preserve them for the captivity imposed by the enemy.

“For the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations.”

That is, the day of the Lord’s vengeance will come upon all the nations. The meaning is: when all the nations have felt the vengeance of God’s anger and drunk the cup of his fury, will you be left untouched as though innocent? As if he were saying: you will not be innocent, but you will drink all the more from this vengeance that comes upon all the nations.

Jeremiah speaks under the metaphor of a cup offered to all the nations: “Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, making all the nations drunk.”

According to Herodotus, the Assyrians and Babylonians subjected all the nations as far as the Propontis, the Scythian Sea, and the Ionian or Aegean Sea.

“As you have done, so it will be done to you.”

That is, just as you, having become an enemy, killed the Jews, so you too will be killed by enemies.

Hence it follows:

“Your recompense will be turned back upon your head.”

What you have done, you will receive. In this same sense the prophet invokes punishment against Babylon:

“Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is the one who repays you with the repayment with which you repaid us.”

“For just as you drank upon my holy mountain, Zion, so all the nations will drink continually,”

That is, just as you rejoiced with the Assyrians and Babylonians upon my holy mountain, where my temple and the altar of burnt offerings were, so all the nations that are now with you, supporting the Babylonians, will drink—that is, will rejoice—over you:

“they will drink, they will swallow, and they will be as though they did not exist.”

That is, they will not merely rejoice in your destruction; they will also swallow you up by killing you, so that the Idumeans will be as though they did not exist.

Or certainly, when he says “they will be as though they did not exist,” he refers to all the nations about which it was said above: “The day of the Lord is upon all the nations.” Whoever does not cling to him who is “I am” is as though he did not exist. Hence we also read in Esther: “Do not hand over your scepter, Lord, to those who do not exist.”

Or perhaps he says that all the nations are nothing because they were devastated and swallowed up by one another. For vengeance proceeded in such a cycle: just as the Idumeans killed the Jews, so they themselves were killed by the Assyrians and Chaldeans; the Assyrians and Chaldeans by the Medes and Persians; the Persians by the Macedonians; and the Macedonians by the Romans, whose kingdom was destroyed by the empire of Christ.

“But on Mount Zion there will be salvation, and it will be holy.”

The words of this prophecy were fulfilled when, after seventy years, under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, the tribes that had returned to Judea enjoyed the salvation of freedom. The mountain of the Lord’s temple was holy because of the priests, sacrifices, offerings, and the other things by which the people of God were sanctified through worship.

“And the house of Jacob will possess those who had possessed them.”

After Idumea had been overthrown and devoured by the hostile nations with whom it had earlier made a covenant against Jacob, there would be salvation on Mount Zion, and a remnant would remain. The house of Jacob, having returned from captivity, would possess those who had possessed it as an inheritance. For when they returned, many from the Medes and Persians followed them, and Jacob possessed them through religion and fellowship in the faith.

“And the house of Jacob”—that is, the two tribes together with the tribe of Levi—“shall be fire, and the house of Joseph”—that is, the ten tribes—“flame, and the house of Esau stubble.” The meaning is this: just as fire and flame devour stubble, so the two kingdoms, namely those of the two and of the ten tribes, joined together into the union of a single rod, according to Ezekiel, will lay waste to Idumea and devour it. For the ten tribes are designated by Joseph, on account of Joshua and Jeroboam. For many also of the ten tribes returned together with the two tribes, and they fought against the Idumeans in equal battle. Hence it follows: “And they shall kindle among them and devour them, and there shall be no remnant of the house of Esau.” Not even one person from that people will remain who could announce the destruction of their enemies to the neighboring nations. Hence the Septuagint also says: “There shall be no grain-carrier of the house of Esau.” For those whom they now call couriers, the ancients called grain-carriers.

Why all these things would happen is made clear when it follows: “because the Lord has spoken”—whose saying is his doing—this being applied to the Babylonian army. But all these things that we have said, and that we are going to say, the Jews, dreaming up false notions for themselves, refer to the time of Antichrist; and whatever we have interpreted against Idumea, they dream as applying against the Roman Empire. We, however, say that this either happened historically under Zerubbabel, or certainly is fulfilled mystically every day in the Church. But when it happened, or when it is to happen, he himself knows who commanded these things through the prophets.

“And those who are in the south shall inherit Mount Esau, and those in the lowlands, the Philistines.” When Judah had returned to his kingdom, those who are in the south—that is, the two tribes who lived in the southern part of the promised land according to the division made by Joshua son of Nun—shall inherit Mount Esau, so that they may not be confined even within narrow boundaries, but may also possess the mountainous regions [Col. 0127A] that Edom had formerly possessed. And those among the same two tribes who lived in the lowlands, namely in Lydda, on the hill of Diospolis, and in Nicopolis, shall possess the five cities of the Philistines—namely Gaza, Ascalon, Azotus, Ekron, and Gath—and the whole region that, according to the Acts of the Apostles, is called Sharon, so that they may reach as far as the seacoast and bring the Philistines under their rule, whom they had not previously subjugated.

“And they shall possess the region of Ephraim and the region of Samaria.” For the territory of the children of Israel will be extended so far that they will reach Ephraim; and their enemies will possess not only the kingdom of other nations but also the kingdom of the ten tribes, whose capital is Samaria.

[Col. 0127B] “And Benjamin shall possess Gilead.” Gilead was a city, or a mountain, in the tribe of Gad. Through this city or mountain, however, all Arabia is signified—the region formerly called Gilead and now named Gerasa—which Benjamin possessed in its entirety. His boundaries immediately beyond Jerusalem toward the north were thus expanded. Whether this actually happened, God will see.

For it can have been fulfilled in part over the course of five hundred years, up to the coming of Christ, and it is fulfilled and confirmed daily in the Church, while those who dwell in the true light inhabit the plains and lowly places—namely, the disciples of him who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.” They possess Mount Esau and the Philistines, by whom we may understand the philosophers of the nations, on account of the height of their eloquence; [Col. 0127C] they will also possess the region of Ephraim and Samaria, by which—as we often read in Hosea—the heretics are represented. Moreover, Benjamin—that is, “son of the right hand,” namely the Christian people—will possess Gilead, [Col. 0128A] which is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” that is, believing Jews, from whom we have received the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets.

“And the migration of this army of the children of Israel shall possess all the land of the Canaanites as far as Sarepta.” That is, those who return from captivity out of the ten tribes shall possess all—meaning all the regions—of the Canaanites as far as Sarepta. They will possess not only what lies to the south, west, and north—the Idumeans of Cilicia, the Palestinians, Mount Esau, and Samaria—but will also rule toward the east over all that belongs to the land of the Canaanites, as far as Sarepta of the Sidonians, where the widow once fed Elijah.

“And the migration of Jerusalem, which is in Bosphorus, shall possess the cities of the south.” By “in Bosphorus” he means in the boundaries or confines. Hence the Septuagint gives Sapharad, which is interpreted as “boundary” or “place.” The meaning is this: those who, having been transferred from Jerusalem itself, the metropolitan city, lived in Saphara—that is, in the borders of the Babylonians—will return and possess the cities of the south, which are in the tribe of Judah. For, living in their own city, they will obtain the places adjoining the city.
