“And saviors shall ascend Mount Zion.” Such as Zerubbabel and the others, as once there was Othniel and the other deliverers whom the Lord sent, down to Saul, and from him down to Zedekiah, “to judge Mount Esau.” They will ascend from captivity in order to judge and discern Mount Esau, as one subjected and enslaved to them—that is, the Idumeans together with their land. [Col. 0128C] “And the kingdom shall be the Lord’s.” When all have been subjugated, the kingdom will belong to the Lord, because he will make his own people reign in various places.

## ON THE PROPHET JONAH

[Col. 0127]

[Col. 0127] The Hebrews relate that Jonah was the son of the widow of Sarepta, whom Elijah raised after he had died. When Elijah had restored him to his mother, she worshiped him and said: “Now by this I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.” For this reason he was called the son of Amathi. Amathi is interpreted as “truth,” and because Elijah spoke the truth, he was called the son of truth. They say that his tomb is in Gath, which is in Ophir. Others say that he was both born and buried in Lydda—that is, Diospolis.

The Book of Tobit mentions this prophet, where the father, as he was dying, spoke to his son: “The destruction of Nineveh is near, for the word of the Lord has not failed.” First, we understand that the Ninevites were converted through Jonah’s preaching, repented, and received forgiveness from the Lord; afterward, however, they fell back into their former evils and, as had been foretold, were overthrown, when Josiah was reigning among the Hebrews and Astyages among the Medes.

## CHAPTER ONE

“And the word of the Lord came to Jonah son of Amathi, saying: ‘Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it, because its wickedness has risen before me.’” When it says, “its wickedness has risen before me,” or, according to the Septuagint, “the cry of its wickedness is revealed before me,” this is because they sinned shamelessly and without any reverence or fear. The same is meant by what is said concerning the Sodomites: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has come to me.” Sin accompanied by a voice is hidden sin; sin accompanied by a cry is manifest and public sin.

Mystically, Jonah, whose name is interpreted as “dove,” signifies Christ in his simplicity and gentleness, upon whom the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. Jonah is also interpreted as “grieving,” because he grieved over Jerusalem, which was destined to perish. That he signifies Christ is attested by the Lord himself in the Gospel, saying: “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.”

He is the son of Amathi, that is, of God, because God is truth. He is sent to Nineveh, which is interpreted as “beautiful” and signifies the world, than which we see nothing more beautiful with our bodily eyes. Hence in Greek it received its name from adornment: κόσμος (*kosmos*) means “world.” Since, therefore, the Jews had despised God’s commandments, Jonah—that is, Christ—is sent to Nineveh, that is, to the nations, so that the whole world, believing in him, may be saved. The wickedness of Nineveh that rises to the Lord is the will ever inclined toward evil, and especially the worship of idols, to which the world, having abandoned the Creator, devoted itself with the greatest zeal.

“And Jonah arose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.” He did not flee because he begrudged the Ninevites salvation, but because he did not want the Jews, his own people, to perish. For he knew that the repentance of the nations would be the ruin of the Jews. Moreover, he saw that other prophets had been sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to summon the people to repentance, and therefore he grieved that he had been chosen to be sent to the Assyrians, the enemies of Israel. He also knew through the prophetic Spirit that, when the nations received knowledge of God, Israel would be rejected. What he knew would happen at some time, therefore, he feared might happen in his own time; and for this reason he wanted to flee to Tarshish, just as Cain fled from the presence of the Lord.

Josephus thinks that Tarshish was the city of Tarsus in Cilicia, from which the apostle Paul came and from which he was called Tarsian. The Hebrews, however, say that Tarshish generally means “the sea.” The prophet therefore did not wish to flee to any particular place, but, having boarded a ship, intended to hurry wherever he could, without caring where chance might take him. A fugitive does not choose the place to which he will flee. And because it is written in the psalm, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel,” he thought [Col. 0129C] that he could flee from the God who was known only in Judah. But after he recognized through the storm that God was present there also, even in the sea, he confessed and said: “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

Mystically, our Jonah—that is, Christ—flees to Tarshish because he left his homeland, heaven; and, having taken on flesh, he came into the sea of this world. He loved the people from whom he assumed flesh to such an extent that he did not refuse suffering, lest, when Nineveh—that is, the gentile people—was saved, the Synagogue should perish. Hence he said to the Father: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” And, placed upon the cross, he prayed for those who had cried, “Crucify, crucify,” saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

[Col. 0129D] “And he went down to Joppa, and found a ship going to Tarshish.” Joppa is a port of Judea, to which Hiram, king of Tyre, transported timber from Lebanon on rafts; from there it was brought overland to Jerusalem. Jonah, therefore, coming from the mountainous regions of Judea to the maritime and level regions, is rightly said to have gone down.

“And he paid the fare to them, and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord”—that is, he paid the price of transportation. He is said to have gone down into the ship to show that, like a fugitive, he penetrated into the ship’s interior, seeking hiding places. Tarshish is interpreted as “contemplation of joy,” and Joppa as “beautiful.”

Mystically, Jonah—that is, Christ—leaves the mountains and goes down to Joppa because, when he was being persecuted in Judea, he passed, as we read in the Gospel, into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, which are cities of the Gentiles. Since these regions had been assigned to the portion of Israel, they are rightly signified by Joppa, that is, “beautiful.” The Lord therefore comes to Tarshish—that is, to the contemplation of joy—because he contemplated the salvation of the world, which he had predestined before the ages. The world’s salvation is his joy.

He goes down to Joppa because, with his passion near, he was accomplishing the salvation of the beautiful Gentile people. But because he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he does not wish to give the children’s bread to dogs. He therefore gives the fare to the passengers, whom we think signify the Gentiles—that is, the pledge of the salvation to be hoped for—so that he may first save the Jews, to whom he had come, and afterward save the Gentiles, as the inhabitants of the sea. Hence he is also said to have gone down into the interior and to have slept while the sea raged, as though neglecting them, because he seemed to neglect the Gentiles, whose salvation he was nevertheless accomplishing while sleeping on the cross and descending to the underworld, as though to the lowest part of the ship.

“The Lord, however, sent a great wind upon the sea, and a great storm arose on the sea, and the ship was in danger of being shattered.” Jonah had thought that it would benefit him if he boarded the ship and fled; but, on the contrary, both he and the ship were endangered because of him, so that it was in danger of being shattered. For what is thought prosperous against God’s will is turned into destruction, and nothing is secure when God opposes it.

Mystically, that storm signifies the fury of the Jews, who were seeking him for death and crying, “Crucify, crucify.”

[Col. 0130C] “And the sailors were afraid, and the men each cried out to his own god, and threw into the sea the objects that were in the ship, so that it might be lightened for them.” The sailors, ignorant of the one true God, called upon their gods, yet knew that nothing happens without divine providence. From this we understand that God is feared and sensed by every person, although people are led away from the one true God to many gods by false religions.

They throw the objects into the sea, as is done in extreme danger, so that, once the ship has been lightened, it may more easily ride above the waves.

“And Jonah went down into the interior of the ship and slept in a deep sleep.” While the sailors were troubled and calling upon their gods, Jonah remained secure and tranquil in mind, to such an extent that he slept. In this he displays the patience of a strong man standing unmoved both amid prosperity and amid adversity. It can also be said that, knowing he was fleeing, he did not dare to look upon the waves that were avenging his flight. Or perhaps he slept because he was overcome with weariness, just as we read that the apostles, during the Lord’s Passion, were overcome by sleep on account of their sorrow.

“And the helmsman approached him and said: ‘Why are you overcome by sleep? Arise, call upon your God; perhaps God will think of us, and we will not perish.’” It is natural for each person to hope more from another in times of danger. Therefore the helmsman, who ought to have consoled the others, awakens the sleeping Jonah so that he may call upon his God; and since their danger was shared, their prayer might also be shared.

Tropologically, this signifies that before Christ suffered, many gods were worshiped by the Gentiles; but after Christ died and the storm of the world was calmed, one God is now worshiped, and spiritual sacrifices are offered to him.

“And one man said to his companion: ‘Come, let us cast lots.’” Because they saw that the storm was greater than usual, they understood that it had not arisen naturally. For they could not have been ignorant of the patterns of winds and waves, having sailed for so long; and therefore, having cast lots, they sought the cause of the shipwreck.

When they say, “so that we may know why this evil has come upon us,” we must understand “evil” as affliction and calamity, in accordance with what is said in the Gospel: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil”; and what is said through the Prophet: “Is there evil in a city that the Lord has not done?” Otherwise, evil is used of what is opposed to virtue.

“And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah. And they said to him: ‘Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your work? What is your land, and where are you going? Or from what people are you?’” The one whom the lot had exposed, they compelled to confess in his own words. They ask about his person, his region, his journey, and his city, so that the cause of the danger may be known from these details.

“And he said to them: ‘I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven.’” Hebrew is interpreted as “one who passes over.” He does not say “Jew,” the name by which they began to be called after the ten tribes were divided from the two, but “I am a Hebrew”—a pilgrim and stranger—according to the Psalmist, who says of the same people: “They passed from nation to nation.”

“I fear the God of heaven,” he says—not the gods whom you invoke, who cannot save. “Who made the sea,” in which I am fleeing, “and the dry land,” from which I am fleeing: that is, I fear the one who is the maker of the universe. He feared God with servile fear, from whom he wished to flee. This fear can also be understood as worship. “I fear the God of heaven,” he says—that is, I worship him.

“And the men feared with a great fear, and they said to him: ‘Why have you done this?’ For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because Jonah had told them.” If you fear God, why do you flee, when you know that you cannot escape his power? They do not rebuke him but question him, because they had heard that he was a Hebrew and worshiped the God of heaven; and therefore, as though asking a holy man, they seek from him a remedy for so great an evil.

“And they said to him: ‘What shall we do with you, so that the sea may become calm for us? For the sea was advancing and swelling.’” “Because of you,” they say, “the sea rises against us, because we have taken you on while you are fleeing. What, then, shall we do with you? Shall we kill you? But it is wrong to kill a worshiper of God. What, then, do you command us to do? You yourself order what we should do, by which we may appease your God, whose anger we recognize through the storm.”

The sea, he says, was advancing toward vengeance, pursuing the fugitive prophet. It was swelling—that is, it was being raised into ever-greater waves—as though unwilling to delay the Creator’s punishment.

“And he said to them: ‘Take me and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become calm for you; for I know that on my account this great storm has come upon you.’” “The storm,” he says, “is rising against me. Throw me into the sea, so that you may live through my death.” The courage of the fugitive should be observed: he does not conceal or deny anything, but, having confessed, embraces his punishment lest the others perish because of him.

Let us refer all these things mystically to the Lord Christ, against whom the Jewish storm rose during his Passion. The sailors who asked what they should do with him are the apostles, who abandoned him during his Passion and, in a certain sense, left him amid the waves. The Lord seems to say: “The world sees me sailing with you to Tarshish—that is, toward the contemplation of joy—so that I may lead you to the joy where I am. Therefore death rages and desires to devour me, not knowing that, just as a fish is caught on a hook, so it will die through my death. Take me, therefore, and throw me into the sea. You throw me. For we ought not to inflict death upon ourselves, but willingly endure it when it is inflicted by others.”

“And the men rowed in order to return to the dry land, but they could not, because the sea was advancing and swelling against them.” Even though the prophet ordered them to throw him into the sea, they did not dare to lay hands upon a worshiper of God. Mystically, too, while the Jews, who had been God’s people, sought Christ’s death, the Gentiles did not wish him to die. For they wanted, as it were, to row toward dry land, thinking that the world could be saved without the sacrament of the Passion, whereas Jonah’s submersion—that is, Christ’s Passion—was the ship’s liberation, meaning the liberation of the world.

“And they cried out to the Lord and said: ‘We beseech you, Lord, let us not perish because of this man’s life, and do not charge us with innocent blood, because you, Lord, have done as you wished.’” As though they were saying: “We do not wish, Lord, to kill your prophet, but you, Lord, have done as you wished. Your will is being fulfilled through our hands. Therefore do not charge us with innocent blood.”

This speech of the sailors seems to be Pilate’s confession. After taking water, he washed his hands and said: “I am innocent of the blood of this man.” All these things were happening by the Father’s will, as it is said in the psalm: “To do your will, my God, I desired.”

“And they took Jonah and threw him into the sea.” “They took” means that they carried him with a certain service and honor; they did not hurl him violently, but placed him in the sea.

“And the sea ceased from its raging.” It was as though, having found the one it was seeking, it were like someone pursuing a fugitive at the fastest pace: once he has caught up with him, he stops and holds the one he has seized.

Mystically, before the Lord’s Passion, the world was endangered by the waves of diverse errors; but after his death we see all things tranquil, and the whole world rejoices in the secure unity of faith and knowledge of the truth. It is as though, when Jonah was thrown into the sea, the sea ceased from its raging.

“And the men feared the Lord with a great fear, and they sacrificed sacrifices to the Lord, and made vows.” Before the Lord’s Passion, people cried out to their gods; after the Passion, they fear the Lord and venerate him not with a small but with a great fear, in accordance with what is commanded in the Law: that he be feared and loved with all the heart and with all the soul.

They offered sacrifices—not animals, which literally they did not have with them amid the waves—but spiritual sacrifices, namely thanksgivings and praises. “Offer,” says the Psalmist, “a sacrifice of praise to God”; and the Prophet says: “Take away all iniquity, and accept what is good, and we will repay the calves of our lips.”

## CHAPTER TWO

“And the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow Jonah.” In place of “great fish,” the Lord in the Gospel said “sea-monster,” explaining the matter more briefly. As for the fact that he prepared it, this may mean that he prepared it from the beginning, when he created it, as the Psalmist says: “This dragon whom you formed”; or “he prepared it” may mean that he caused it to come alongside the ship, so that it might receive Jonah, who was thrown into its maw.

Mystically, the Lord God the Father commanded the underworld, which is the most savage dragon, to receive Jonah—that is, Christ—without recognizing the hook of divinity concealed within the bait of flesh. Therefore, as greatly as it rejoiced in devouring him, so greatly did it mourn when it vomited him forth, according to the prophecy of Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O underworld.”

“And Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights.” The Lord himself explained that this was fulfilled in him. It may be asked how he is said to have been in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights. We must understand this synecdochically—that is, the whole by a part—a figure very common in the divine Scriptures.

For the Lord was crucified on the day of Preparation at the sixth hour, and at the ninth hour he gave up his spirit. In the evening his body was taken down from the cross and placed in the tomb. There he lay during that night and the following Sabbath day, and during another night belonging to the following Sunday; thus he rose in the morning on the first day of the week, as Mark testifies. He therefore lay in the tomb for thirty-six hours.

Three days, however, comprise seventy-two hours. But if we count the day of Preparation—that is, Friday, on which he died—as one day, the Sabbath together with its night as another, and the night belonging to Sunday as belonging to the beginning of Sunday, the period somehow appears to consist of three days. Yet this must not be thought to be without a profound mystery. For thirty-six is to seventy-two as one is to two.

Our death is indeed double, because we die in the soul through sin and in the body through punishment. Christ’s death, however, was single, because he could die only in the body; in his soul he never admitted death, because he never sinned.

“And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the belly of the fish, and said:” Once the prophet had been received into the sea-monster’s womb and realized that he was safe, he did not despair of God’s mercy but turned his whole being toward supplication, knowing that the Lord is especially present in tribulations, as he himself promises the righteous man: “I am with him in tribulation; I shall deliver him.” The same Prophet says:

“I cried out to the Lord from my tribulation, and he heard me.” When he says in the past tense, “I cried out,” this means that, when he saw the sea-monster and the great mass of its body, he cried out as the waters receded and gave room to his voice. Or he cried out with the whole devotion of his heart, according to the Apostle who says: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father.”

He called the belly of the sea-monster the belly of the underworld, which was so vast that it swelled to the likeness of the underworld. These words can be referred allegorically to Christ, who says through David: “You delivered my soul from the lowest underworld.” He was himself alive in the underworld, free among the dead.

“From the belly of the underworld I cried out, and you heard my voice; and you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the sea, and the river surrounded me.” Literally, it is clear that he was enclosed in the belly of the sea-monster in the midst of the sea and surrounded by streams. In the mystical sense, however, he says what had been foretold through the Psalmist: “I am sunk in the mud of the deep, and there is no solid ground.”

In comparison with the heavenly dwelling, in which perfect peace reigns, of which it is said, “His dwelling has been established in peace,” every earthly habitation is full of waves and storms. The heart of the sea signifies the underworld, for which the Lord says “the heart of the earth,” because, just as the heart is in the middle of an animal, so the underworld is said to be in the middle of the earth.

Or the Lord complains that he was cast into the heart of the sea—that is, into the midst of temptations—but he did not feel the bitter waters, because, as the Apostle says, “He was tempted in every way according to our likeness, without sin.” For he does not say that he was surrounded by the water of the sea but by a river—that is, by sweet water—because he could be tempted externally, but the delight of sin did not wound his mind.

He says that he was cast down, just as he is also said in the psalm to have been struck, and the Apostle asserts that he was handed over by the Father. “All your whirlpools and your waves have passed over me.” The whirlpools and waves are temptations and blows, which never occur without God’s permission and will. Yet these whirlpools and waves did not overwhelm Christ; they passed over him. He himself endured and broke all the storms by which the human race was tormented, so that afterward we might sail securely behind him.

“And I said: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” Christ says this in the person of his humanity. For he who had assumed the form of a servant also uses its voice, saying that he had been cast away from the eyes of the Father. As though he were saying: “When I was with you, O Father, and I was light in your light, I did not complain that I had been cast away. But after I came into the deep and was surrounded by flesh, I endure human feelings and say that I have been cast away, in order to lead back to you those who had justly been cast away, so that where I am, they too may be with me.”

“Nevertheless, I shall again see your holy temple.” Literally, Jonah either says this in desire or confidently promises himself that he will return again to Jerusalem and see the Lord’s temple. Tropologically, the Son of God, placed in the disgrace of the Passion, promises himself the glory that he always had in and with the Father. Hence in the Gospel he said to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.”

Or he longs for the Father’s dwelling, because just as the Father is the temple of the Son, so the Son is the temple of the Father. For he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” And elsewhere: “I came forth from the Father and came.” Because he is both God and man, he asks in the form of a servant and promises in the form of God.

“Waters surrounded me up to my soul; the abyss enclosed me; the sea covered my head.” By the abyss he means the opposing powers, which have been consigned to the deepest regions of the underworld, that is, Tartarus. The demons feared going there, asking the Lord in the Gospel not to send them into the abyss. Thus the abyss enclosed Christ when the rulers of the underworld believed that they had seized him in death.

[Col. 0135B] “I descended to the extremities of the mountains; the bars of the earth closed me in forever.” Literally, by the extremities of the mountains he means the depths of the earth, by which the globe of the earth is sustained by God’s will as though by bars, as it is said in the psalm: “I have established its pillars.”

Mystically, the head of the Lord is the soul that rules the body. The sea covered his head when the weight of tribulation and death burdened the soul that he assumed for our salvation. By the extremities of the mountains he means the rulers of the underworld, who, cast down from heaven and deprived of freedom, were covered by the waves of punishments and enclosed by the abyss. The soul of the Redeemer descended to those places, not to be held there, but to rescue his own from them.

They are also the bars of the earth, as though the bolts of the deepest prison and punishments, always wishing to retain the souls they had once received. The Lord was enclosed by these bars; but, as he had foretold through Isaiah, he shattered the bronze doors and broke the iron bars.

What follows—“and you will raise my life from corruption”—refers to Jonah, who, although he ought to have decayed and been digested in the belly of the sea-monster, and his limbs ought to have been dispersed through the fish’s veins and body, came out safe and whole. Hence, with the affection of one who flatters, he says: “My Lord God,” calling the God common to all his own and personal God, whom, because of the greatness of such a benefit, he had especially experienced as God and Lord.

Mystically, however, the soul of Christ is raised from corruption because his flesh did not see corruption—that is, it was not dissolved by decay in the tomb—according to what he had foretold through the Psalmist: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption.” Blessed Peter interprets this concerning Christ in the Acts of the Apostles: “He did not see corruption,” glorified by the swiftest resurrection.

But it may be asked why he says elsewhere: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” There, “corruption” refers to the wounds and blows by which Christ’s flesh was disfigured, as though he were saying: “What benefit is there if I am afflicted with nails and wounded, if the Jews are not saved?” Here, however, “corruption” refers to putrefaction and dissolution.

“When my soul was fainting within me, I remembered the Lord.” “When,” he says, “I hoped for no other help, remembrance of the Lord was my salvation.” So also the Psalmist says: “I remembered God, and I rejoiced.” From this we learn that, when our soul fails while we are placed in some tribulation, or when it is torn away from the body, we ought to keep God in mind and turn every thought toward him, who is the God of body and soul.

“So that my prayer may come to you, to your holy temple.” “For this reason,” he says, “I remembered the Lord, so that my prayer might ascend from the extremities of the mountains to your holy temple”—that is, to heaven. For although God is everywhere, there he enjoys eternal blessedness in the presence of the angels who attend him.

He speaks as a priest who asks that the prayers of the people may ascend through him to God’s temple. Likewise, our Redeemer in his Passion prayed: “Father, if it is possible”—saying, “let this cup pass from me.” And, placed upon the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

[Col. 0136B] “Those who observe worthless things in vain abandon your mercy.” The prophet displays remarkable courage: in the belly of such a great beast, he discusses human frailty. God, merciful by nature, is ready to show mercy to all. We, however, through our own fault, willingly lose the clemency that offers itself to us.

It should be noted that he did not say “those who do worthless things.” No one exists who does not do vain things—that is, who does not sin—since “every living person is altogether vanity.” Rather, he says “those who observe,” that is, love them and pass over into the affection of their heart. Such people abandon their own mercy—that is, God—for it is said of him: “The Lord is compassionate and merciful”; and elsewhere: “My God, my mercy.”

He does not say that they are abandoned by his mercy; rather, they themselves abandon the mercy that is prepared and offers itself freely. This is said especially of the Jews, who, observing vanities—that is, the utterly vain precepts of the Pharisees—abandoned God, who had always shown them mercy.

“But I shall sacrifice to you with the voice of praise; whatever I have vowed, I shall repay to the Lord for my salvation.” The prophet, encouraged by good hope and already confident of his deliverance, promises that he will offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and fulfill all his vows.

Likewise, Christ the Lord, who died for our life, certain that God would raise him swiftly, joyfully promises in the voice of confession that he will offer himself as a sacrifice to the Father. “Our Passover,” says the Apostle, “Christ has been sacrificed.” He is both the priest and the sheep sacrificed for all, so that everything the Father gave him may not perish forever.

“And the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto the dry land.” God the Father commands the great sea-monster, the underworld, to restore the Savior to the earth—that is, to solid and immortal life—for “having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death will no longer rule over him.” The word “vomited” shows that Christ, alive, came forth from the deepest recesses of death, as though from the innermost vital organs of the sea-monster.

## CHAPTER THREE

“And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, [Col. 0137A] saying: ‘Arise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it the preaching that I speak to you.’” He is not rebuked, nor is he asked, “Why did you not do what I commanded?” The correction through the extremely harsh experience of shipwreck and devouring had been sufficient. For after blows, a servant is not charged with what he has done.

Mystically, our Lord, who had been sent to save Nineveh—that is, the Gentiles—and who in a certain sense wished to flee, refusing the Passion and saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” is now, after those for whose sake he did not wish to suffer had cried, “Crucify, crucify,” and “We have no king but Caesar,” returned from the belly of the sea-monster—that is, raised from the dead—and is sent again to Nineveh, so that after the Resurrection he may preach what had been commanded him by the Father before the Passion.

Everything here that he is commanded to do, that he obeys, that he does not wish to do, and that he is compelled once more to wish to do, must be referred to the form of a servant.

“Then Jonah rose and went to Nineveh according to the word of the Lord.” He rose, it says, without making any delay, but immediately girded himself for obedience. “Now Nineveh was a great city, a three-days’ journey.” The city of Nineveh was founded by Ninus, son of Belus, the first king of the Assyrians. They say that it was of such great circumference that it could be traversed around in a journey of three days. But Jonah, now corrected and mindful of the shipwreck he had endured, completed the three-days’ journey with the haste of a single day. Some think that he preached in only a third part of the city, and that in this way the word of the preaching reached everyone. The Son of God also rose from the dead and went forth in the apostles to Nineveh—that is, to all the ends of the world—in a journey of three days, because he commanded that the nations be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Yet this three-days’ journey is one way, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. Hence the sacrament of baptism is performed not in the names but in the name of the Trinity, which is one God—not so much by the apostles as by the Lord, whom Jonah prefigured. It should also be noted that, when the three days are mentioned, no night is referred to, because in the holy Trinity there is nothing obscure, nothing dark.

“And Jonah began to enter the city on a one-day’s journey, and he cried out and said: ‘Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.’” The number forty is appropriate to sinners in fasting and affliction. Thus Moses and Elijah also fasted for that many days, and the Lord himself, the true Jonah, sent into the world to preach, consecrated this fast for us. Attention should be paid to the fact that it says, “he cried out.” We read something similar about the Lord, because standing in the temple he cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Every saying of Christ is a great cry, because he announces great things.

“And the men of Nineveh believed in the Lord, and they proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least.” The older generation believed in the Lord, proclaiming a fast, and they clothed themselves in sackcloth. The first—the fast—was hidden; the second—the sackcloth—was visible. Such food and such clothing are appropriate to penitents, and most fittingly so: those who had offended God through luxury and the ambition of costly garments now seek to appease him through fasting and sackcloth. The older generation begins, and the younger follows, because no one is without sin—not even an infant of a single day whose life is upon the earth.

“And the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose from his throne, cast off his clothing, clothed himself in sackcloth, sat in ashes, and cried out and said in Nineveh, from the mouth of the king and his nobles, saying: ‘Let neither human beings, nor animals, nor oxen, nor sheep taste anything; let them not feed, and let them not drink water. Let human beings and animals be covered with sackcloth; let them cry out to God with all their strength; and let each man turn from his evil way and from the wickedness that is in their hands. Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and turn back from the fury of his anger, so that we may not perish?’”

We should understand the king of Nineveh as the philosophers of the nations—Plato, Aristotle, and the others—who are, as it were, kings of human beings, and whose teachings they observe as though they were divine oracles. The word reached these men only at the end, because they were the last, and the more difficult, to believe. They thought it foolish that God could become human and die. Yet even these men, although they received the Lord’s faith late, nevertheless began, after laying aside the ornaments of rhetoric and the pomp of secular doctrines, to follow the simple and rustic teaching of fishermen.

“Human beings and animals” are understood as both rational and irrational, because every kind of human being—both those who use reason and those who lived like brute animals—was converted to repentance and faith in Christ. Or they clothed themselves in sackcloth, that is, in mourning and sorrow, which they assumed while grieving over the losses of their former life. That sackcloth signifies mourning is shown by the Psalmist, who says: “You have torn off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness.” Strictly according to the literal sense, those who say, “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” speak ambiguously for this reason: being uncertain about their salvation, they may practice repentance more earnestly and provoke God more strongly to mercy.

“And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way; and God had compassion concerning the evil that he had spoken of doing to them, and he did not do it.” Just as then God threatened the Assyrian city, Nineveh, so every day he threatens the whole world with destruction for this purpose: that they may repent. For if the world turns, the Lord turns; and when sinners change their life, he changes his sentence. Here, as above, “evil” must be understood as affliction and punishment.

## CHAPTER IV

“And Jonah was afflicted with a great affliction, and he became angry.” Seeing the fullness of the nations entering in and what had been foretold in Deuteronomy being fulfilled—“They provoked me with one who was not God, and I will provoke them with one who is not a people”—he despairs of Israel’s salvation. Therefore he grieves and is sorrowful, not because he begrudged the salvation of the nations, but because Israel was perishing. Our Lord also wept over Jerusalem as it was perishing, and he does not wish to give the children’s bread to dogs; and the apostles are commanded first to preach to Israel. Thus he is sorrowful unto death, grieving that the people for whom he suffered should perish.

“And he prayed to the Lord and said: ‘I beg you, Lord, was this not my word when I was still in my own land? For this reason I hastened to flee to Tarshish. For I knew that you are a gracious and merciful God, patient and of great compassion, and forgiving concerning evil.’” Jonah partly prays and partly complains, saying that he did not wish to flee. Yet, beginning with a supplication, he moderates his complaint. “I beg you,” he says, “Lord, was this not my word when I was still in my own land?” “I knew,” he says, “that you were merciful; I did not wish to announce you as savage and cruel, and for this reason I wanted to flee.” Likewise, when Christ the Lord saw the Jews obstinate toward their own destruction, he seemed to say to God the Father: “Did I not know that this would happen—namely, that Israel would perish—when I was still with you, Father?” And through Isaiah he had said: “I have labored in vain; without cause I have spent my strength.”

“And now, Lord, please take my life from me, because death is better for me than life.” “Because I could not save the one nation, Israel, let me die, and the whole world will be saved.”

And the Lord said: “Do you think you are right to be angry?” Jonah had become angry either because he seemed to have been shown to be a liar before the Ninevites, or because he understood that Israel would perish. The Lord does not say, “You are wrong to be angry,” lest he appear to rebuke one who was grieving; nor does he say again, “You are right to be angry,” lest he contradict his own judgment. He therefore asks him the reasons for his sorrow, so that he may answer—or, if he remains silent, so that by his silence he may confirm God’s judgment.

“And Jonah went out from the city and sat east of the city. He made himself a shelter and sat beneath it in the shade, until he might see what would happen to the city.” When a city is understood negatively, it signifies confidence in earthly hope and worldly desire. For Cain, who stained the world with fratricide, is first said to have built a city. Jonah therefore goes out from the city—he who is called “dove” or “sorrowful”—because every simple person who grieves over his sins makes himself foreign to the desires of the world and places no hope in worldly vanities. He dwells facing east, awaiting the rising and the vision of the true sun. He dwells in a shelter, that is, in the guardianship of his mind; he rests, as it were, in a tabernacle, awaiting and contemplating what will happen to the city of Nineveh—that is, what will happen to the world. Concerning this city the Lord says through Hosea: “In your midst I am holy, and I will not enter the city.” And in Deuteronomy one of the cities of refuge is called Ramoth, which is interpreted as “vision of death.” For whoever is expelled from Jerusalem, which is “vision of peace,” dwells in Ramoth, that is, in the vision of death.

Mystically, before the sun rose and the ivy withered—that is, before the Gospel flashed forth, the world was redeemed, and the Jewish people rejected—our Jonah, that is, Christ, was under the shadow, because the truth had not yet appeared, but everything took place in types and figures. He is said to have sat in the posture of a judge, because sitting belongs to one who judges, or because he had humbled himself and contracted the majesty of his divinity into a certain smallness. For one who sits appears shorter than one who stands. As for the statement that he wished “to see,” let us refer it to the effect of human understanding. He sees everything before it happens.

“And the Lord God prepared an ivy plant, and it rose over Jonah’s head to provide shade over his head and protect him, for he had labored. And Jonah rejoiced over the ivy with great joy.” The nature of ivy is to creep over the ground in wandering curves and not to climb to higher places without supports or trellises. By the weak ivy, unable to accomplish anything by its own strength, the Jewish people may be signified: growing quickly and promising to do everything that God commanded, but soon growing weak and failing to fulfill the commandments. Once it protected Jonah, that is, Christ, by the hope of their salvation, and brought him no small joy; but it quickly withered after being struck, because it had no firm root of faith. It was like a tent-cover, presenting the appearance of a house but lacking a foundation. Concerning this Isaiah says: “The daughter of Zion will be left like a shelter in a vineyard.”

The locusts in the Gospel are rightly believed to have signified this people: a small creature that rises from the earth by leaping, but cannot fly higher, because the Jews, hearing the law, said: “Everything that the Lord our God commands us, we will do, and we will obey him.” But soon they turned into a crooked bow and did not keep God’s covenant.

“And God prepared a worm at the rising of dawn on the following day, and it struck the ivy, and it withered.” In the psalm entitled “For the morning’s assumption,” the Lord calls himself a worm, saying: “But I am a worm and not a man.” A worm arises from the earth without seed; it creeps humbly, moves without sound, and Christ was born from virgin earth, humble amid insults and not protesting in his passion. Therefore, before the sun rose—that is, before Christ rose again—the ivy was green and Judaea flourished. But after he rose and Nineveh—that is, the world—cast off the shadow of error and received the light of truth, the prepared worm struck the ivy of the Jewish people, and it withered, deprived of God’s help. This happened at the rising of dawn, because Christ rose in the morning on the first day of the week.

“And when the sun had risen, the Lord commanded a hot and burning wind, and the sun struck Jonah’s head, and he grew faint from the heat.” That is, even after Christ’s resurrection and the rejection of the Jews, the mind of the Lord and Savior still burned with a desire for Israel’s salvation, commanding the apostles and saying: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria.” Therefore he also commanded that the preaching begin from Jerusalem, saying: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise again, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

“And Jonah asked for his life, that he might die, and said: ‘It is better for me to die than to live.’” In baptism with Israel, so that in the bath they might recover the moisture that they had lost by denying Christ. Hence, when people asked Peter what they should do, he said: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized.” As for what we have said—that he wished to die in baptism—it is supported by the apostle’s statement: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.” Some understand the worm and the burning wind as the Romans, who, after Christ’s resurrection and ascension, completely destroyed Israel.

[Col. 0141B] “And the Lord said to Jonah: ‘Do you think you are right to be angry over the ivy?’ And he said: ‘I am right to be angry, even unto death.’” Earlier, when the people of Nineveh had already been saved through repentance, Jonah was questioned in the same words. He said nothing, although he saw that what he had foretold had not happened; by his silence he confirmed the Lord’s question. For he knew that the Lord was most compassionate and of great mercy. Now, however, when through the drying up of the ivy he understood Israel’s rejection, he answered most boldly: “I am right to be angry, even unto death.” For I did not wish the Ninevites to be saved in such a way that the Jews would perish; nor did I wish to win foreigners in such a way that I would lose my own people. According to the allegory already begun, in Jonah we understand Christ, who mourns Jerusalem as it perishes, and mourns unto death—not his own death, but that of the Jews, who were blinded so that the eyes of the nations might see, and died so that the nations might live, believing in the Son of God.

“And the Lord said: ‘You grieve over the ivy, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow; it came into being in one night, and in one night it perished.’” Jonah did not labor over the ivy, nor did the Savior labor as much over the Jews as over the nations. For as soon as they had been led out of Egypt, they cast away the idols and served the Lord to some extent. But he labored greatly among the nations: for their sake he became human, although he was God; for their sake he endured slaps, spitting, a crown of thorns, and death; he descended to the underworld so that they might ascend to heaven. Hence, when the prodigal son returned to his father, the elder brother became angry and complained to his father, saying: “Look, for so many years I have served you, and you never gave me a young goat so that I might feast with my friends.” Israel bore with great resentment that the nations, after squandering their substance with prostitutes, should receive their former grace again.

When God says, “The ivy came into being in one night,” the night signifies the time before Christ’s coming. When it adds, “and in one night it perished,” the night again signifies the time in which they denied Christ, when the true Sun of righteousness set for them.

“And I,” he says, “will I not spare Nineveh, the great city?” Nineveh, the great city, is the Church, gathered from the universality of the nations. It is truly great, because the multitude of the faithful from all the nations is much larger than the twelve tribes of Israel. When it says, “in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand human beings who do not know their right hand from their left, and many animals,” according to the literal sense it indicates the innocent and simple age of little children and infants, so that from this one may infer how great the number of adults must have been if the number of children was so large. Or certainly, in that city there was an immense multitude that, before repentance, did not know what was between good and evil. Good is understood by the right hand, and evil by the left.

But in the Church, as in a great house, there are vessels both for honor and for dishonor; there are carnal people and spiritual people; and there is an innumerable multitude of animals, that is, of those who are irrational and serve their bellies, who look toward the earth—do they ever look toward heaven? Of such the Psalmist says: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless animals and became like them.”

Nor should it be passed over that more than one hundred and twenty thousand human beings are said to have been in Nineveh. This number contains a great mystery within itself. For one hundred and twenty results if, beginning from one, you continually add the following natural numbers to the sum: add two to one, and you get three; add three, and you get six; add four, and you get ten. If this is continued through fifteen, preserving the sequence of natural numbers, one hundred and twenty is found.

Upon so many believers the Holy Spirit came on the day of Pentecost. The number fifteen consists of seven and eight: seven and eight make fifteen. There were that many steps in the temple of the Lord, and there are also that many psalms bearing the title “A Song of Ascents.” Paul is also read to have spent that many days with the apostles and to have discussed the Gospel with them. The multitude of the Church therefore rightly shines forth with such a number, in which the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments are revealed, as well as the squared hundred and the cubic thousand—that is, solid perfection.

# ON THE PROPHET MICAH

[Col. 0141]

## CHAPTER I

“The word of the Lord that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.”

The prophet Micah, whose name is interpreted as “Whatever” or “Who,” as though signifying “Humility,” is sixth in the order of the twelve prophets. Therefore we should expect profound mysteries from him, since he is placed in the middle, as it were in the heart, of the prophetic order. He was from Moresheth, which is a village of Palestine. Moresheth is interpreted as “inheritance.” Fittingly, Micah, whose name means “humility,” is born from the hope of inheritance: whoever strives to hold fast the virtue of humility for God’s sake will deserve to be an heir of God and a co-heir of Christ, who humbled himself for us and invites us to imitate the form of his humility, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.”

This prophet threatens Samaria with the anger of God and captivity, and announces the destruction that will come upon the people of Israel, because, having abandoned God, they serve idols. He also plainly announces the place of Christ’s birth. It is known that, when Hezekiah son of Ahaz was reigning, the ten tribes were led captive by the Assyrians; later, when Zedekiah was reigning, the two tribes called Judah were captured with their king, and Jerusalem was destroyed. Therefore the prophet’s title is arranged according to the order of the captivities: first, as has been said, Samaria, the capital of the ten tribes, was captured; afterward Jerusalem, the capital of Judah. Samaria is presented as a type of heretics, and Jerusalem as a figure of the Church.

“Hear, all you peoples, and let the earth and its fullness attend; and let the Lord God be witness to you, the Lord from his holy temple.” It should be noted that the peoples are commanded to hear, while the earth is commanded to attend. By “the people,” ecclesiastical men are meant; by “the earth,” heretics, whose teaching is earthly. The Apostle also lists heresies among the works of the flesh. Therefore those who are in the Church, if they listen, and those who are outside, if they attend, can escape what the prophetic word threatens.

The prophet therefore wishes God to be their witness—not from elsewhere, but from his holy temple, that is, the Church, through which God bears witness to the truth; or the temple of God is the Son himself, in whom the Father dwells and through whose mouth he speaks.

[Col. 0143C] “For behold, the Lord will go out from his place, and he will descend and tread upon the high places of the earth; and the mountains beneath him will be consumed, and the valleys will be split like wax before the fire, like waters rushing down a precipice. All this is for the transgression of Jacob and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what are the high places of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?”

The place of God is mercy, because by nature he is gentle and compassionate. But he who is gentle and merciful toward us when we sin is somehow compelled to change his nature. He goes out from his place and assumes the role of cruelty, which he does not possess by nature. His descent is the movement of his majesty toward lower things. To tread upon the high places of the earth is to crush the powerful of the earth.

“And the mountains beneath him will be consumed, and the valleys will be split.” By the mountains we understand rulers, and by the valleys subject peoples. “As,” he says, “wax melts near a fire, and as waters are carried headlong by a downward course, so all the pride of the wicked will dissolve and fail when the Lord comes.”

This will happen because of the crimes of the ten tribes, which he calls Jacob, or Samaria and Israel, and because of the transgression of Judah. For among the ten tribes the capital was Samaria, which is now called Sebaste; and in Judah Jerusalem ruled.

In the tropological sense, the holy places of God are those of which he says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them.” From these holy places, therefore, the Lord goes forth—not abandoning them, but through them preaching and announcing punishments for the wicked and rewards for the righteous. For we read that “the word went forth from the Lord.”

He descends and treads—not upon humble earth, that is, not upon those who are below, but upon the high places of the earth, that is, upon the saints, who understand the majesty of the one who comes. Although they are holy, they will nevertheless be shaken, that is, they will fear his presence. The valleys, however—that is, sinners and those who do not seek the things of God—will not be able to endure his presence. Whatever is hard within them will be split, and they will flow away like water.

This will be because of the impiety of Jacob, that is, of heretics, and because of the sin of Judah, that is, of those who are placed in the Church and confess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds.

According to another interpretation, the Lord went out from his place: he abandoned the Jews, among whom he had once dwelt, because of the sin they committed against Christ, just as he himself threatens them: “Your house will be left deserted.” He trod upon the high places of the earth: he came to the nations, which through his grace were made high and deserved to be raised up from earthly things. The mountains were shaken, that is, the doctrines of philosophers and the power of kings were disturbed; and, after all impiety in them had been consumed, righteousness grew. Pride was destroyed, and humility was raised up.

“And I will make Samaria like a heap of stones in a field where a vineyard is planted; I will drag its stones down into the valley, and I will uncover its foundations. All its carved images will be shattered, and all its wages will be burned with fire; and I will make all its idols a ruin, because they were gathered from the wages of a prostitute.”

Because Samaria—that is, the ten tribes—sinned first, and after abandoning the temple of God made golden calves for itself, it was the first to be destroyed when the Assyrians came. “I will make,” he says, “Samaria like a heap of stones.” Because the city of Samaria was situated on a mountain, it is fittingly said to be turned into heaps of stones, so that not only its walls and buildings but also its foundations, down to the last stone, may be overturned. The carved images and idols that they worshiped, together with the accumulation of their various works, are also proclaimed to be burned with fire.

When he says, “And they will return even to the wages of the prostitute,” this means that, just as they committed fornication with the idols they made in their own land, so they will go to another land of fornication—that is, to the Assyrians—and there likewise worship idols.

“Over this I will mourn and howl; I will go stripped and naked. I will make mourning like that of dragons, and lamentation like that of ostriches, because her wound is incurable, because it has reached Judah; it has touched the gate of my people, even Jerusalem.”

Up to this point he has spoken about Samaria; now he foretells evils for Judah, which had sinned through a similar error. The prophet therefore assumes the emotion of one who mourns. “I will make mourning like that of dragons,” as above. Just as dragons, when they are defeated by elephants, resound with a terrible hissing, and just as ostriches—which, because of the shortness of their wings, cannot fly far—make lamentation instead of song when they forgetfully leave their eggs in the sand to be trampled by the feet of beasts, so I too, says the prophet, will go stripped and naked, having lost my children and seen them led into captivity.

“Because her wound is incurable”—that is, the wound of Samaria—and the same sin and the same punishment by which Samaria had been overthrown has touched Judah and reached the gate of Jerusalem. For just as Samaria was overthrown by the Assyrians, so Jerusalem will be overthrown by the Chaldeans.

All these things must be referred mystically to heretics, whom God threatens with a beneficial overthrow, so that, when their various doctrines have been destroyed and consumed by the fire of which the Lord says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth,” they may mourn their errors and loosen the sandals from their feet—that is, cast away dead works.

They mourn especially because they also wished to introduce their error into Judah—that is, among Catholic men—but could not. For it reached the gates, that is, the ears, of the people of God, but could not penetrate the city; that is, it could not deceive the mind established firmly in faith.

“In Gath do not announce it; with tears do not weep. In the house of dust, sprinkle yourselves with dust.” Gath is one of the five cities of the Philistines, and Goliath the Gittite was from there. We know that the Philistines were always enemies of the Jews. The prophet therefore says: Do not announce in Gath the evil that I foretell is coming, lest your enemies rejoice. “With tears do not weep”: although your breast feels sorrow, conceal your weeping lest your enemies rejoice. “In the house of dust”—that is, in what is about to fall and be reduced to dust—sprinkle yourselves with dust there, not in the public squares, lest your enemies see and rejoice.

[Col. 0145C] “And pass over for yourselves, you inhabitants of Shaphir, in confusion and disgrace.” In place of “beautiful,” the Septuagint used the Hebrew word itself, *scaphir*. In both Syriac and Hebrew, *scaphir* means “beautiful”; by this name Samaria is called because it was situated in a most beautiful and fertile place. Therefore it is said to it: O beautiful and fertile Samaria, because you have been confounded in disgrace, pass over and proceed into captivity in such a way that, if possible, even the foreign enemy may not perceive it.

“She who dwells in the outlet has not gone out.” Here too the Hebrew word itself is used, namely *senna*. *Senna* is interpreted as “outlet,” signifying that captivity is already at the exit and at the doors. When he says, “She has not gone out,” he signifies that she was led into captivity not freely or willingly, but under compulsion and against her will.

“The house next door will receive mourning from you, the house that stood by itself.” Here too the Septuagint has the Hebrew word itself, namely *Azel*. The order is: “The house of Azel will receive mourning from you.” *Azel* is interpreted as “nearby” or “at the side.” By the house of Azel, therefore, he means the house of Judah, which was near Samaria and, as it were, at its side. It received mourning when it heard of Samaria’s disaster; yet this house of Azel, that is, Judah, stood by itself—that is, after Samaria had been taken captive, it remained in the condition of its kingdom, protected by God because of Hezekiah.

“Because she was weakened for good”—with “her own good” understood—that is, because she was humbled for her benefit, when Rabshakeh blasphemed the living God. “She who dwells in Ramoth,” that is, in bitterness. For this is the meaning of *Ramoth*. In bitterness and sorrow the people dwelt with King Hezekiah while Sennacherib besieged them.

“Because evil has descended from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem.” For the king of the Assyrians, after devastating Samaria, came against Jerusalem. At that time Rabshakeh was sent from Lachish to Hezekiah, urging him to surrender to the Assyrians, insulting the Lord and saying: What if he could rescue his people from the hand of the Assyrians?

“A tumult of chariots, a terror to the inhabitant of Lachish.” Lachish is a city of Judah. It was the first of the ten tribes to receive idols, and through it idolatry reached Jerusalem. The sense is: O Lachish, the cavalry and tumult of the Assyrians will reach you also and turn you into terror.

“She was the beginning of the sin of the daughter of Zion,” because—in other words, “in you”—the crimes of Israel were found; and through you, as through a gate, the impiety of the ten tribes migrated to Jerusalem.

“Therefore he will send messengers against the inheritance of Gath: the house of falsehood, for the deception of the kings of Israel.” Not only, he says, will chariots and tumult come against Lachish, but also against Gath, which is the capital of Palestine. By “messengers” he means marauders whom the king of the Assyrians sent against Gath. It was a house of idolatry and a city of falsehood, and had been used to deceive the kings of Israel.

“Even now I will bring an heir to you, who dwell in Mareshah,” that is, in “inheritance.” By “heir” he means the arrival of the enemy. God therefore says through the prophet that he himself will bring the Assyrians, who will possess Gath as an inheritance, because it had been used to deceive the kings of Israel.

“Even to Adullam the glory of Israel will come.” Adullam was a most distinguished city among the cities of the Jews, and he says that the hostility of the Assyrians will reach it also.

Some manuscripts read, “The glory of Israel,” so that the sense is: That captivity will come from Gath as far as Adullam, which is understood to be a city of Israel’s glory. Or it may be taken ironically, so that the sense is: The evil from Lachish, Mareshah, and Gath will reach Adullam. Here the division should be made, and the words “It is glory”—that is, “It is the disgrace and dishonor of the Israelite people”—should be added ironically and in a somewhat subdued voice.

These things concern the literal sense. Let us briefly see what mystery they contain. Gath is interpreted as “winepress.” It signifies heretics, who exalted themselves, claiming to possess the wine of Soreth, that is, of spiritual and divine knowledge, whereas their wine—that is, their doctrine—was from the vineyard of Sodom and the outskirts of Gomorrah.

They are also the house of dust, because they savor earthly things, and they are food for the serpent, that is, for the devil, to whom it was said: “You will eat earth all your days.” The prophet urges them not to exalt themselves but to repent, saying: “In the house of dust, sprinkle yourselves with dust.” Otherwise, when the time of vengeance arrives and the house that seemed beautiful to you has fallen, you will perish together, and your empty labor will provide laughter to those who see it.

“She has not gone out, because she dwells in the outlet”: that is, the Church, which dwells at the outlet, in the hope of receiving the heavenly kingdom, has not gone beyond the end of the divine Scriptures, nor transgressed the ordinances of the Fathers.

“The mourning of the neighboring house will receive from you.” The neighboring house is the Church. Heretics are not in that house, but they are near it. “They went out from us,” the Apostle says, “but they were not of us.” The house of heretics is therefore near the house of the faithful Church, but, being built upon sand, it has no foundation.

The sense is: O heretics, who are so near the Church but are always raised up against her, mourn for yourselves, because the enemy and avenging devil will receive mourning from you. That is, you will be the cause of your own destruction, and from you the devil, to whom you have been handed over, will receive the material for punishment.

“She who stood by herself, because she was weakened for her own good”: this must be joined to what precedes, where it says, “She has not gone out, who dwells in the outlet, who stood by herself.” The Church stood by itself because it remained stable in the truth. It was weakened—that is, afflicted by various tribulations—but this was for its good, because the more it was weakened, the stronger it became in faith, according to the Apostle, who says: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” Hence the Psalmist says of the same Church: “She was weakened, but you perfected her.”

This same Church dwells in Ramoth, that is, in bitterness, because, pressed by the weight of persecution, it has nothing sweet in the present life. Evil descends from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem, that is, the plots of heretics reach the hearing of the Church. But they cannot penetrate the Church, because inwardly it remains within the guardianship of the mind and does not go outside, lest it be violated, just as Dinah once went out, of whom it is said that she went out to see the women of that region.

Evil is said to descend from the Lord because nothing happens except by the Lord’s permission. He allows heretics to exist in the Church for this purpose: either that they may test or that they may exercise the faithful.

It follows: “A tumult of chariots, a terror to the inhabitant of Lachish,” and so forth. Lachish, which is interpreted as “a walk” or “a wandering,” signifies those heretics who wander and roam through various doctrines of error, and who are carried about by every wind of teaching. Of them it is said: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses,” and so forth.

These, therefore, became the leaders of the sin of the daughter of Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” because every calamity, every error, and every sin of the Church proceeded from heretics.

“Therefore I will send messengers against the inheritance of Gath.” The messengers are demons or visible enemies, who are sent by God’s just judgment against Gath, which is interpreted as “winepress”—that is, against heretics, who think they possess the wine of the purest truth, but are a house of falsehood and deceive whomever they can.

As for what follows, “He will yet bring heirs to you, who will dwell in Mareshah”: *Mareshah* in Latin means “inheritance,” signifying those who had been transferred from Christ’s inheritance—that is, from the fellowship of the Church—to the heretics. They are therefore promised that, if they wish to convert, the Lord will bring them heirs: holy teachers who, after separating them from their errors, will lead them into the inheritance of the Lord and into fellowship with the Church.

“Even to Adullam the glory of Israel will come.” *Adullam* is interpreted as “testimony of drinking” or “of exhaustion.” Let the heretics not boast, he says: the glory of Israel will come. The boasting of the heretics will reach Adullam—that is, the testimony of their exhaustion, or the judgment, when they will drain and drink down the measure of their deeds.

“Shave yourselves bald and cut your hair for the children of your delights; enlarge your baldness like an eagle, for they have been led away captive from you.” This is said specifically of Samaria—that is, the ten tribes—and generally of the whole people of Israel, who were led away captive. They are therefore commanded to shave themselves bald, as was customary in mourning, and to cut their hair and weep for their children. And just as an eagle at a fixed season loses its feathers and remains bare and featherless, so Israel should lay aside all the glory with which it was formerly surrounded and mourn its children, who have been captured by enemies. Even in our own time we see the Jewish people shaven bald, and all the grace with which it formerly flourished has entirely departed from it.

Mystically, this is said to the sinful soul: O soul, which once enjoyed paradise and flew like an eagle in contemplating heavenly things, assume the garb of penitence and mourn your children—that is, the works you have performed—because they have been taken captive under the law of sin.

## CHAPTER II

“Woe to those who devise what is useless and practice evil in their beds. In the morning light they carry it out, because their hand is against God.” Woe to the Jewish people, and woe also to all who devise what is useless—that is, who deliberate how they may offend God—and practice evil in their beds, meaning that they plan to do evil. The determination of the will is here taken for the completed action. Whatever evil they have considered during the night, as though it could not be postponed, they hasten to complete in action as soon as the morning light has appeared. They do not consider that their hand is against the Lord and that they are resisting him. The prophet continues, explaining what it is that they devise and do, and says:

“They coveted fields and seized them by violence; they robbed houses; they oppressed a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.” These things were being done then and, regrettably, are also done by many now. Therefore just retribution immediately follows:

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am devising evil against this family, from which you will not remove your necks, and you will not walk proudly, because the time is exceedingly evil.” Because, he says, you devised what is useless, I too am devising evil against you—not because God’s scourge is evil, but because it seems evil to those who endure it. And the evil will be such that you will not be able to raise your necks, weighed down by the burden of captivity.

“On that day a proverb will be taken up against you, and a song will be sung with sweetness, saying: ‘We have been utterly devastated by devastation.’” This will be repeated as a song and adopted in place of a proverb. As for what follows, “The portion of my people has been exchanged,” it signifies the Temple, which was holier than all nations and has been changed into ruin. “How will he depart from me”—the Assyrian is understood—“when he returns, the one who will divide our regions?” These are, as it were, the words of a frightened people. For when Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, was coming against Jerusalem, he heard people say of Tharaca, king of Ethiopia: “He has gone out to fight against you.” Then he withdrew from Jerusalem, but as though he intended to return after his victory. The people, therefore, who knew that he had withdrawn said: How can you say that the Assyrian will depart from us, when he will soon return to distribute our fields by lot?

“For this reason you will have no one casting a lot-line for you in the assembly of the Lord.” Because, he says, you have done the things mentioned above, O family of Israel, against whom I am devising evil, you will have no portion in the assembly of the Lord—that is, in the inheritance of the righteous. This may also be referred to the final captivity inflicted by Titus: they suffered all these things because they grew arrogant against God and condemned Christ to the cross.

These words may also be understood morally of the sinful soul, which devises evil in the secrecy of its heart and completes it in action. Therefore the Lord devises evil against us, an evil because of which we cannot raise our necks and walk uprightly. For this reason apostles are sent to mourn over us with Jeremiah, to take up a proverb against us, and, with the Apostle, to grieve over many of those who have sinned and have not done penance. The portion of the Lord’s people is also divided by a lot-line, when souls departing through various vices are divided by demons: one extends the lot-line of greed, another the line of lust, into the inheritance of the Lord and the field of holiness, fragrant with the scents of virtues, according to what Isaac said: “Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field.” They have been handed over to the king of the Assyrians and Babylonians—that is, to the devil.

O Israel, “do not speak, speaking thus: ‘It will not rain upon these people; shame will not overtake them,’ says the house of Jacob. Has the spirit of the Lord been shortened, or are these his thoughts?” O house of Jacob, do not deceive yourselves by presuming excessively upon God’s mercy, and do not say what many still say: God is good and merciful; the evil of captivity that we fear will not come upon us. For he who is abundant in mercy toward all will also be gentle toward us, and his goodness will not be shortened on our account alone. His thoughts are not such as human thoughts are, so that, like a human being, he should suddenly be provoked to anger. These are, as it were, the words of those to whom it is said: “Do not speak, speaking thus.”

“Are not my words good with the one who walks uprightly? And, on the contrary, my people have risen up as an enemy.” He introduces the Lord as replying and saying: I am good, as you say, and my words proclaim mercy—but toward those who walk uprightly together. You, however, not only do not act uprightly, but rise up against me and oppose me with a tyrannical spirit. Then he recalls what they were doing: “You stripped off the cloak from above the garment,” that is, you robbed them of clothing or of divine assistance, “and those who were passing simply”—and harmlessly—“you turned into war.” Or else, you turned those who were submitting to the authority of others into war, so that they would not receive the commands of their teachers and would not believe their instructors.

But morally we are also instructed not to think that we please God merely by reading his words in Scripture. The Lord’s words are good and beneficial to those who read them only when they are fulfilled in action, when heart and lips agree. Tunic and cloak are garments of faith and virtues, as the Apostle says: “Put on, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassion, humility,” and so forth; or they signify divine help and protection. Heretics or wicked priests remove all these things from the people entrusted to them by living wickedly.

“You have driven the women of my people from the house of their delights; from their little ones you have taken away my praise forever.” You have done not only the things I have mentioned, he says, but have also made formerly delicate matrons go into captivity. Or else, you have laid cities waste, driving out or killing their inhabitants, whom he metaphorically calls women or daughters. When the cities were laid waste, therefore, no one remained—not even a child—to sing psalms and praises to God.

“Rise, therefore, and go”—captivity is understood—“because”—in this land is understood—“you have no rest; because of its uncleanness,” that is, because of its crimes and impieties, “it will be corrupted”—your land is understood—“with the worst corruption.” Your captivity, he says, will not be brief, but will endure for a long time, and the land will be corrupted with the worst corruption—that is, Babylonian or Roman captivity.

Morally, wicked leaders of the Church drive women—that is, simple souls, weak in themselves—from their houses by their evil examples—that is, from the Church—and send them into the outer darkness. Therefore they too are told to rise and go, because they have been corrupted with the worst corruption, namely, a long habit of sinning, through the corruption of soul and body.

“If only I were not a man possessing the Spirit, and would rather speak falsehood! I will drip wine and drunkenness upon you; and this people will be one upon whom it is dripped.” O Jewish people, to whom the promises were made and from whom Christ was born according to the flesh, do not think that I wish to speak or that I willingly proclaim these evils to you. If only I were not a man possessing the Holy Spirit, but spoke instead with a demonic spirit, were counted among the false prophets, and the things I say were not true, so that the evils I foretell would not come. But because I am a prophet and speak by the Holy Spirit, I will drip wine upon you, so that you may become drunk on my words as though on unmixed wine and fall. While I drip, this people will receive drops of my prophecy and, whether willing or unwilling, will endure what I say.

But so that you do not think that I prophesy only adversity, I will announce prosperity to you. He therefore introduces the Lord himself speaking and making good promises:

“With a gathering I will gather Jacob.” I will come, he says, through myself; I will be born of a Virgin; and I will gather Jacob—that is, I will gather believers from the Jews to my faith. Or, in another sense: Because you were unwilling to believe in me in the humility of the flesh, I will come at the consummation of the age in majesty. Then I will drip upon you—that is, I will give you to drink the wine of the Holy Spirit, the wine of the divine word with which the apostles were made drunk on the day of Pentecost, and of which the Psalmist says: “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction.”

“I will gather all of you together, Jacob; I will assemble the remnant of Israel; I will place him together like a flock in a fold, like a herd in the midst of its enclosure”—that is, I will join believers from both peoples together in the fold of eternal rest. “They will tumult from the multitude of human beings.” He now plainly shows of which sheep or flocks he was speaking. They will tumult—that is, they will cry out—praising the good shepherd who will go before them and open a path ahead of them. He himself will lead them to himself. Hence it follows:

“For he will go up, opening the way before them; they will divide and pass through the gate, and they will go out through it; their king will pass before them, and the Lord at their head”—the prince and guide of the heavenly pastures are understood.

## CHAPTER III

“And I said: Hear, princes of Jacob and leaders of the house of Israel. Is it not yours to know judgment, you who hate what is good and love what is evil, who violently strip off their skins from them and their flesh from their bones, who have eaten the flesh of my people, stripped off their skin from them, broken their bones, and chopped them up as though in a cauldron and like meat in the middle of a pot? Then they will cry out to the Lord, and he will not hear them; he will hide his face from them at that time, just as they acted wickedly in their devices.”

Under the metaphor of lions or robbers, the cruelty of the leaders of the Jews is described. They stripped the poor and killed them, and, like savage beasts, crushed their flesh and bones. Just as meat is cooked in a pot, so in the city of Jerusalem they afflicted an innumerable multitude. Therefore he threatens them with the evil of captivity, either Chaldean or Roman; and although they cry out to him, he will not hear them, but will repay them according to how wickedly they acted in their devices—that is, in the crimes they were always inventing anew.

“Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace; and if anyone gives nothing into their mouths, they consecrate war against him. Therefore night will be your vision, darkness your divination; the sun will set upon the prophets, and the day will grow dark over them.
