Those who see visions will be confounded, and the diviners will be confounded; they will all cover their faces, because there is no answer from God.”

At that time there were false prophets among the people of Israel who, so that they might receive gifts from them, proclaimed a peace that had not been given to them. This is what he means by “biting with their teeth”: he shows the greed of those who receive. But if anyone gave them nothing, even if he was holy, they foretold that God’s wrath would come upon him. Hence he says that their speech was not prophecy but divination, and possessed not light but darkness and error. When what they had promised failed to occur, then their sun would set and they would be covered with confusion, because it would become known that their message was not an answer from God but a fraud of demons wishing to deceive human beings.

“Yet I am filled with the strength of the Spirit of the Lord, with judgment and power, to declare to Jacob his crime and to Israel his sin.” The prophet now speaks about himself. While the false prophets utter false predictions and are covered with confusion, he speaks under the impulse of the Holy Spirit and announces the Lord’s judgment and truth. He does not proclaim peace as they do in order to receive something, but announces to Jacob his crime and to Israel his sin, because they worshiped idols instead of God and because they crucified Christ.

These words may be applied to the worst teachers, who, by flattery, overthrow God’s people, saying: Have faith; it will save you. You do not need to live chastely. They do this in order to receive earthly advantages and to devour those people, either by taking their possessions or by spiritually killing their souls. Over such prophets the Sun of righteousness will set; then they will be confounded, and their faces will be covered with confusion.

“Hear this, princes of the house of Jacob and judges of the house of Israel, who abominate judgment and pervert everything that is right, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. Her princes judged for gifts, her priests taught for payment, her prophets divined for money, and they relied upon the Lord, saying: ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evil will not come upon us.’”

Because a threat had earlier been directed against the judges and false prophets, the discourse is now addressed generally to them, to the priests, and to all who flattered themselves with their knowledge of God. They are reproved because they not only fail to practice judgment but even abominate it and pervert what is right; because they build their houses with blood and the city of Jerusalem with iniquity—namely, with the plundering of the poor, the slaughter of the innocent, and the killing of the saints. Moreover, the princes judge after receiving gifts, the prophets prophesy for rewards, and they sell God’s favor. While doing all these things, they rely upon the Lord, saying: We are God’s people; the Lord is in our midst; evil will not come upon us.

For all these things the prophet—or rather, the Lord through the prophet—threatens them and says:

“Therefore, on your account, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the Temple a wooded height.”

He teaches that the Temple of God, which formerly shone with gold and precious stones, is to be reduced to utter ruins. All these things happened to the Jews because of what has been said above, and especially because of the shedding of the Lord’s blood.

These words may be applied morally to the Church, for she is the house of Jacob and the house of Israel. He therefore speaks of the perverse teachers and leaders—or judges—of the Church, who, although they themselves do all the evil they can, rely upon the Lord and promise themselves prosperity from his mercy in a vain hope, saying: “Evil will not come upon us.”

## CHAPTER IV

“And it will be: in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the summit of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills, and peoples will flow to it, and many nations will hasten and say: ‘Come.’”

Because the leaders of the Jews abominated judgment and built Zion with blood, the Lord’s mountain—that is, Christ—was raised in place of Mount Zion. This mountain was shown in the last days, that is, at the end of the ages, when, in the final period of the world, the Savior appeared through the saving sacrifice and took away the sins of the world.

“It will be prepared,” he says—that is, it will be made manifest—though previously it had been hidden for so many thousands of years. It will be prepared not only among the mountains but above the summits of the mountains. The mountains are the holy prophets. Although they wrote everything holy and pertaining to human salvation, nevertheless, in comparison with this prophecy, in which they prophesied the Savior’s coming, all else is lowly and does not reach the summits of the mountains.

This mountain has been exalted above the hills because the man assumed by the Word of God surpassed the grace and merit of all the saints. Because he humbled himself even to death, God the Father exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.

All nations will be gathered to this mountain—or, as the Septuagint says, will flow to it—and innumerable peoples will come together in the manner of rivers, believing. We already see that people from all the nations known to the Roman Empire have believed in Christ and flowed by faith to this mountain.

But what do they say as they come? “Let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” Ascent is necessary if we wish to come to Christ, “and to the house of the God of Jacob,” that is, to the Church, which is the house of God, according to the Apostle, “the pillar and foundation of the truth.” He calls Christ the God of Jacob.

They add why they should come: “He will teach us his ways,” through the teachers and shepherds who preside over the Church, whom John calls angels in the Apocalypse, or through the Scriptures, which show the way of the Lord—that is, Christ, who says: “I am the way.” “And we will walk in his paths,” that is, we will follow and imitate his apostles, who are his paths, through whom we believe in him.

“Because from Zion”—that is, from the primitive Church—“the law will go forth,” the spiritual law, namely, the preaching of the Gospel to the nations. “And the word of the Lord”—that is, the Son of God the Father, who is his Word—“from Jerusalem,” that is, from Judea, from which he assumed flesh.

“And he will judge among many peoples.” For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” “And he will rebuke strong nations even from afar,” that is, the wise men and philosophers of the world, whom he catches in their craftiness. He judges peoples by distinguishing who are worthy of salvation and who are unworthy.

“And they will beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into hoes. Nation will not take up the sword against nation, and they will no longer learn to wage war. And a man will sit beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, and there will be no one to frighten him.”

All zeal for warfare, he says, will cease when he comes and will be transferred to peace. Such will be the rest that not only in cities but also in villages and fields there will be complete security, so that each person may sit beneath his vine, as above.

“For the mouth of the Lord of hosts has spoken.” Let us read the histories, and we will find that before Christ’s coming the whole world was fighting against itself. Everything was inflamed by both foreign and civil wars, and no one could pass safely from one nation to another. But after Christ, at his coming, prepared the Roman Empire for the apostolic preaching by the proclamation of the Gospel, the world became accessible.

Tropologically, the cutting up of swords and spears signifies the end of the anger and persecution with which unbelievers formerly raged against the holy preachers. These weapons were changed into agricultural instruments, so that, when the darts of insults had been melted down, spiritual fruits might grow.

These things will happen because the Lord has spoken, whose every word is true and for whom to say is to do.

“For all peoples will walk, each in the name of his god; but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and beyond.” All other nations, he says, after their error, but we who have ascended the mountain of the Lord will walk in the name of the Lord our God, Jesus Christ, because he himself is the true mountain and God, and we are called Christians from his name.

“In that day”—that is, when the true sun has shone—“says the Lord, I will gather the lame; I will gather the one whom I had driven out; I will console the one whom I had afflicted; I will place the lame among the remnant, and the one who had labored among a strong nation.”

This means the Jewish people, crushed and unable to walk with an upright step, driven out and rejected. It will be gathered for this purpose: to be received and placed among the remnant and among a strong nation. This is what Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”

This happened through the preaching of the apostles, when it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Three thousand believed in one day, five thousand on the next,” and afterward many thousands. It will be fulfilled more fully at the end of the age, because when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

“And the Lord will reign over them”—that is, over those who have been gathered—“on Mount Zion,” that is, in the Church, which is situated in the contemplation of the spiritual life, “from this time forth and forever,” that is, from the present age into the future.

“And you, mist-covered tower of the flock, daughter of Zion, to you it will come; and the former dominion will come, the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem.”

By the mist-covered tower of the flock he means a place which, because shepherds gathered there, is called *Adher*—that is, “tower of the flock.” It is one mile east of Bethlehem. In this place an angel appeared to three shepherds and announced that God had been born; they are also buried there in an honored resting place. He calls the tower mist-covered because of the obscurity of the heavenly mysteries that were revealed there.

The first power signifies the angelic powers, which joyfully sang together, “Glory to God in the highest.” It is also the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem—that is, of the heavenly city, where the angelic powers contemplate the God of hosts.

Allegorically, the mist-covered tower is the Israelite people, or the Temple of God built by Solomon in Jerusalem. Of this tower Isaiah says: “He built a tower in the midst of it,” that is, in the midst of the vineyard. This tower—that is, the Jewish people—as long as it had a wall, meaning the protection of angels, and a winepress, meaning the altar, was inaccessible to the devil and was not mist-covered; rather, it was the city of God, which, situated on a mountain—that is, in the height of virtues—could not remain hidden.

But after it polluted itself with the Lord’s blood, it is called mist-covered and squalid. To it came the first power, that is, the Son, who speaks in the Apocalypse: “I am the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end,” and who, in the person of the man assumed, says: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways.” This power is the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem.

The first power therefore came into this world in order to make a second power. For it cannot be called first unless there is a second. Thus he made the apostles a second power, so that just as, from Christ who is light, they are called light, and from Christ who is the living bread they are called bread—the Apostle Paul saying, “We, though many, are one bread in Christ”—so, from the first power, they might be called power and kingdom.

“Now why are you drawn together in grief?” Since, he says, the first power is to come to you, why are you drawn together in grief and humbled?

“Is there no king for you, or has your counselor perished, because pain has seized you like a woman in labor?” By questioning, he confirms that she is rightly grieving and mourning, because her king, Christ—who is also the counselor and angel of the great counsel—has perished for her, that is, has been crucified by them. So far as they were concerned, he perished; and those who, according to the Gospel parable, killed the heir after casting him outside the vineyard were themselves also devastated by the Roman army. As a woman in labor cannot escape her pain, so that people could not avoid the danger and devastation impending over them.

“Be in pain and labor, daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor, because now you will go out from the city and dwell in the countryside; you will come as far as Babylon. There you will be delivered; there the Lord will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.”

The daughter of Zion—that is, the often-mentioned people—is commanded to grieve and go out from the city and dwell in the countryside, because God’s sentence requires that she go into captivity, and his judgment cannot be changed. She is therefore admonished to endure patiently and to come as far as Babylon, knowing that, if she bravely endures the scourge, she will soon be redeemed from the hand of her enemies. Once delivered, she will be able to say: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; though I have fallen, I will rise again,” and, with the Psalmist: “The Lord will not be angry forever, nor will he threaten for eternity.”

It is clear according to the literal sense that this people, led into captivity, was delivered and returned after seventy years under Joshua, Zerubbabel, and Ezra.

Morally, the soul, expelled from the city—that is, the Church—because of sin and handed over to the enemy for the destruction of the flesh, is commanded to come to Babylon, that is, to the confusion of its vices and its humiliation, so that, after performing worthy penance, it may be freed from the captivity of sin and, having returned to its father’s house, may deserve to be received by its most merciful Father.

According to blessed Gregory as well, it often happens that the soul called the daughter of Zion, which ought to contemplate God, is devastated by some spiritual and hidden vice—for example, pride or envy. In his mercy, God sometimes permits it to fall into an open sin of the flesh and, as it were, to come to Babylon—that is, to confusion—so that, confounded by the disgrace of its open crime, it may be freed from the captivity of the hidden vice.

“And now many nations have gathered against you, saying: ‘Let her be stoned, and let our eye look upon Zion.’” The prophet’s voice: O Jerusalem, to whom I am announcing the captivity that threatens, while it is still to come, many nations have already gathered against you. As though speaking of an adulterous woman, they say: Let her be stoned, and let our eye look upon Zion—that is, against Zion—so that we may insult her and rejoice in her misfortunes. And they say:

“But they did not know the Lord’s thoughts, nor did they understand his counsel, because he gathered them like hay on the threshing floor.” He caused them to be gathered for this purpose: that you might crush them like hay and straw on the threshing floor.

“Rise, therefore, and thresh, daughter of Zion, because I will make your horn iron and your hooves bronze”—that is, invincible strength. “And you will crush many peoples, and you will devote their plunder to the Lord, and their strength to the Lord of the whole earth,” so that they may be consecrated to the Lord your God.

For the Lord delights in such a sacrifice. What he says about the horn and hooves is to be understood metaphorically, from enemies threshing grain.

Morally, multitudes of spiritual wickedness gather against the Church of God and insult and reproach her for the deaths of her children. They do not know the Lord’s counsel or his thoughts, because he allows them to prevail for a time, so that the patience of the one may be rewarded and the wickedness of the others punished. The Lord gathers them so that they may be crushed, and so that their just condemnation may advance the Creator’s praise; their plunder and strength are turned into a sacrifice to the Lord.

## CHAPTER V

“Now you will be laid waste, daughter of a robber. They have laid siege against us; with a rod they will strike the cheek of the judge of Israel.”

I had promised you, the prophet says, that you would thresh and crush all the nations that had gathered against you and offer their plunder to the Lord your God. But because this will not happen now, but when the fullness of the nations enters at the end of the age, in the meantime you are being laid waste according to your merits. Therefore I no longer call you my daughter, but the daughter of a robber—that is, of the devil, who is always ready to plunder.

“They have laid siege against us.” This is the voice of God the Father speaking to the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Trinity of persons is plainly shown. The Jews laid siege against the Son of God when they plotted against him, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful.” For they were, as it were, besieging him while they planned to seize him. But because an insult to the Son is an insult to the Father and the Holy Spirit, it is therefore said in the plural, “against us.”

What follows, “With a rod they will strike the cheek of the judge of Israel,” shows that the soldiers struck the Lord’s head with a reed, and that this insult to the Son rebounded upon the whole Trinity. Because of these crimes, therefore, I will no longer delay vengeance, and now, in the present, you will be laid waste by the Assyrians or Romans.

“And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, small among the thousands of Judah, from you one will go forth for me who will be ruler in Israel.”

The prophet speaks in the person of God the Father, promising the incarnation of his Son and designating the place of his birth. And you, Bethlehem, formerly called Ephrata, are so small that, compared with the thousands of Judah, you are scarcely regarded as a little village. From this small town Christ will go forth, the one who will be ruler in Israel.

And so that you do not think that he is merely of David’s lineage—for he is indeed seen as a true human being—he adds: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” Before the ages he was begotten from my substance, because “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread,” because there was born the bread that descended from heaven. Ephrata is rendered “fury,” which pertains to Herod, who, when he learned that he had been mocked by the Magi, became exceedingly angry.

“For this reason he will give them”—the Lord is understood—“until the time when the woman in labor gives birth, and the remnant of his brothers will return to the children of Israel.”

For this reason, he says, he will give them—that is, the Jews—and allow them to retain their dominion until the time when the virgin who is to give birth will give birth in a new manner. After she has given birth, and the child born has fulfilled the task of the dispensation he assumed, while the Jewish people are captive or killed, the remnant of his brothers—that is, the apostles, who are the Lord’s brothers—will return to the faith of the patriarchs and prophets.

This may also be understood as follows: He will give them—that is, he will permit the Jews to observe the shadow of their law—until the time of the woman giving birth, that is, until the Church, the mother, spiritually generates the Gentile people to faith; until the barren woman gives birth to many, and she who had many children becomes weak. When the fullness of the nations has entered, at last all Israel will be saved. Then the remnant of his brothers will return to the children of Israel; when Elijah preaches, the hearts of the fathers will return to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers; the last people will be joined to the first. Then they will truly be children of Abraham, believing in the one whom Abraham saw and rejoiced.

“And he will stand and shepherd in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God. And they will return, because now he will be magnified to the ends of the earth.”

When, he says, the woman in labor has given birth and Christ, the Sun of righteousness, has filled the whole world, then the Lord himself, who previously walked as a human being, will stand, when all believe and worship him as God. He will shepherd them—that is, believers—“in the strength of the Lord,” meaning in the power of divinity. They will be able to say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing.”

He will also shepherd in the majesty of the Lord’s name, in accordance with what he prayed to God the Father when his passion was near: “Holy Father, keep them in your name.” They will turn back from the love with which they loved Christ carnally and will begin to love him as God. Or they will turn back in the sense that they will begin to seek spiritual and eternal things, whereas previously they sought earthly and temporal things. For Christ has been magnified to the end of the earth, and now his sound has gone forth to the ends of the world.

“And this one will be peace when the Assyrian comes into our land and when he treads upon our houses.”

When the Assyrian—that is, the devil—comes upon the land of the Church and wishes to devastate the religion of those whom the Lord shepherds, and when he treads upon our houses—that is, when he rises against and crushes the bodies that are dwelling places of souls—then he himself, Christ, will be peace in us, because no tribulation or distress will be able to separate the elect from his love.

For example, the Assyrian had come upon Paul’s land and had trodden upon his house when he was amid many labors, deaths, and the other things he himself recounts. But because in all these things he prevailed through him who loved him and who was his peace [Note: [Col. 0157D] Something appears to be missing.].

“And we will raise up against him seven shepherds and eight leaders of men.” God the Father is introduced as speaking and promising good things. “We”—I, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—“will raise up against him,” that is, against the Assyrian, seven shepherds, meaning the patriarchs and prophets who observed the number seven of the law, that is, the Sabbath; “and eight leaders,” meaning observers of the New Testament, who are raised up by the Lord in the Church from the apostles down to the present age.

The number seven pertains to the Old Testament because of the Sabbath; the number eight to the grace of the New Testament because of the Lord’s resurrection, which took place and was completed on the eighth day. Hence Solomon also says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.”

“And they shall pasture the land of Assyria with the sword”—the word of God is understood, concerning which the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.” This sword was sent by him who came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and so forth. They shall also pasture “the land of Nimrod with his spears,” and he will deliver us from Assyria when he comes into our land and treads upon our borders—that is, the land of Assyria, in which Nimrod, the mighty hunter before the Lord, reigned. Nimrod is interpreted as “descending temptation,” and signifies the devil, who fell from heaven through pride. His land—that is, the people whom he had possessed—those shepherds and leaders, namely the prophets and apostles, shall pasture. “With spears” means, implicitly, with divine preaching. Thus, after Assyria has been overcome and pierced through, and the land of Nimrod reduced to nothing, the Lord Christ will deliver us from the hand of Assyria, which had come to trample our land.

“And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like dew from the Lord, and like drops upon the grass.” After we have been delivered from Assyria, whose name means “directing”—that is, from the devil, who directs all his followers toward destruction—the remnant of Jacob, namely the apostles, or all the communities of the primitive Church, shall be in the midst of the peoples like dew falling from the Lord, cooling the heat of the vices by which all the nations were scorched and extinguishing the flaming darts of the devil. For it is also said that, into the blazing furnace in which the three youths had been thrown, an angel descended and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew. This, then, is what he says: the apostles’ teaching shall be in the midst of all the nations like dew from the Lord and like drops upon the grass. For heavenly preaching is compared to drops falling from rooftops. But when it says, “which does not await a man and does not wait for the children of men,” it signifies that the nations were awaiting no teacher or preacher who might pour the dew of preaching upon them and cultivate them with the ploughshare of spiritual teaching.

[Col. 0159C] “And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest and like a lion’s cub roaring among flocks of sheep; when he passes through, tramples, and seizes, there is no one to rescue. And your hand shall be exalted over your enemies.” Christ is the lion, as it is said in the Apocalypse: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered.” He is also the lion’s cub, of whom it is said in Genesis under the person of Judah: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son.” He, therefore, who is the lion, granted to the apostles that they too should be lions when he said to them: “Go, teach all nations,” and so forth. And just as no one can resist a lion, so they, delivered from the hand of the Assyrians, received power to seize the beasts—that is, irrational people deprived of the reason of God’s word. “When a man was in honor, he did not understand,” and so forth. They will seize them, not in order to tear them apart, but in order to separate them—that is, divide them—from unbelievers. No persecutor will be able to resist them, and the hand of the Lord will be exalted over those who had afflicted either the Lord himself or his apostles. “And all your enemies shall perish,” not so that they may be destroyed, but so that from enemies and unbelievers they may become friends and believers.

“And it shall be on that day”—when your hand, O Israel, has been exalted over your enemies—“I shall remove your horses from your midst,” that is, all the wanton impulses of the mind, concerning which it is said: “Do not become like a horse and a mule.” “And I shall destroy your chariots, and I shall destroy the cities of your land, and I shall demolish all your fortifications.” I shall also remove your wagons and chariots—that is, the crimes in which you gloried as though triumphing. And I shall destroy the cities of your land—that is, the confidence you placed in earthly riches, setting your hope with Cain, who first built a city on earth. And I shall remove all your fortifications—namely, the byways and displays of the world, the eloquence of rhetoricians, and the sophistries of dialecticians. “And I shall remove sorceries from your hand, and divinations”—demonic divinations is understood—by which you were deceived and deceived others. “They shall not be found in you.” Or by “divination” he calls the teachings of the ignorant, who wish to teach what they do not know and, as though divining, teach uncertain things as certainties.

“And I shall cause your carved images to perish,” that is, all false presumption and perverse doctrines. “And your statues from your midst; you shall no longer worship the works of your hands. And I shall uproot your sacred groves from your midst, and I shall crush your cities”—that is, the superstition of false religion and observance. Hence the Law also forbids a sacred grove to be planted in the temple of the Lord. And concerning the badly constructed cities, which shortly before he had called the cities of the land, he threatens that he will crush and consume them.

“And I shall execute vengeance in fury and indignation upon all the nations that have not listened.” Because they refused to receive the dew of my word, I shall execute vengeance in fury and anger upon the nations that wished to listen—that is, to obey.

## CHAPTER VI

“Hear what the Lord says: Rise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice; let the mountains hear the Lord’s judgment.” The prophet speaks and commands us to hear what the Lord says. By “mountains” he metaphorically calls the powerful and the rich; by “hills,” those who are subject and less powerful. Then the Lord himself speaks to the prophet: “Rise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.” Again the prophet, as he had been commanded, speaks to the mountains, and also to “the strong foundations of the earth,” and gives the reason why he compels them to listen: “because the Lord’s judgment is with his people, and he will be judged with Israel.”

The mountains and hills may also signify the angels, to whom the administration of human affairs has been entrusted. For the Apostle calls angels ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. “Contend,” he says, “in judgment with the mountains”—that is, with the angels—so that, if they are found not to have administered human beings worthily, the blame may be removed from the people and referred to their leaders, or to me, who appointed such beings over humanity. In the Apocalypse we read that the angels—that is, the overseers of the churches—are either praised or censured on the basis of the lives of those over whom they preside. God, therefore, who, as God, could inflict punishments for the crimes of a sinful people, does not wish to exercise power but justice; and he compels the people of Israel, in the presence of the angels and of every creature, to say whether they have anything to allege, so that, according to the Psalmist, God may be justified in his words and prevail when he is judged.

[Col. 0161A] “My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I wearied you? Answer me, for I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and freed you from the house of slavery, and sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before you.” God speaks to Israel, summons him to judgment, and grants him permission to argue against him. “What,” he says, “have I done that I ought not to have done, or in what have I wearied you by burdening you with hardships? Did you perhaps regard my benefits as insults, grieving because you had lost the melons and Egyptian pots? With a strong hand I brought you out of the house of slavery; I gave you teachers through whom you might know my will. And lest these things seem insignificant,

“My people, remember, I ask, what Balak king of Moab planned and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you might know the Lord’s acts of justice.” Shittim is a place in the desert, named after the trees that grow there in great numbers. They resemble the tree we call white thorn. Gilgal, however, is the place where, after the death of Moses, the people were circumcised by Joshua. Hence that place was called Gilgal, that is, “the hill of foreskins.” “Through all,” he says, “the places of the desert I have already journeyed with you, moving the camps, and I have always seen you. From Shittim, where Israel fornicated with the Midianites, to Gilgal—that is, until you had Saul as king, who was first anointed at Gilgal—throughout this entire journey and all that time I did not abandon you. And although you were always blaspheming me, I did not permit Balaam to curse you; rather, I caused him to bless you instead.”

[Col. 0161C] These things are understood according to the literal sense, but they may also be referred morally to us who are in the Church. The Lord therefore argues against us and reproves us by handing over his Son to death for our sake. He sent Moses before us—that is, the Law—and he sent Aaron, whose name is interpreted as “mountain of strength,” that is, Christ, who is the great high priest. He also sent Miriam, that is, the prophecies of the prophets. At the time when Balak—whose name is interpreted as “choosing,” that is, the devil, who seeks to devour everyone—who is the king of Moab, interpreted as “from the father of all,” namely those to whom it is said, “You are from your father the devil,” wished to deceive you through Balaam, whose name is interpreted as “vain people,” and who is the son of Beor, which can be interpreted as “in the skin,” signifying those devoted to dead works of the flesh, God did not permit him to harm us. Indeed, he turned Balaam’s curse—that is, the curse of a vain people—into a blessing. For the people of the nations are vain, born from him who is “in the skin,” that is, from one who always remains in his pleasures. Their curses and reproaches have been turned into blessing, because now they glorify those whom they once persecuted and killed.

“What worthy thing shall I offer the Lord? Shall I bend my knee before the exalted God? Shall I offer him burnt offerings and year-old calves? Can the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams, or with many thousands of fat goats?” God had summoned the people to judgment, but the people, knowing that they had sinned, does not wish to enter into judgment with God and instead turns wholly to prayers. Yet even in those prayers it has no confidence, because there is nothing that can worthily be offered to God for sins. For it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of goats and calves. “Shall I give my firstborn for my crime?” This is what the Book of Kings records Moab as having done: when he was besieged by the Jews, he went up onto the wall and sacrificed his son in the sight of all. “The fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul.” Likewise Jephthah, who offered his daughter for a rash vow.

But we too, when doing penance, should know that we can give nothing worthy to appease God; we can be saved only through the blood of the spotless and unique Lamb, provided that we imitate his Passion, so that we are prepared to die for him. For when the Psalmist had asked, “What shall I render to the Lord?”, he answered himself: “I shall receive the cup of salvation, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord.” If he who is God died for us without sin, then we, who are human beings and sinners, must always be prepared to die for him.

“I shall show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: surely, to do justice and to love mercy.” This is said not only to the people of one nation but generally to all human beings: “Since you doubt, human race, what you might do for your sins to appease God, I shall tell you what God seeks: namely, to do justice,” and so forth. Moses also said something similar in Deuteronomy: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, except that you love the Lord your God, walk in his ways, and love him,” and so forth.

God seeks from us that we make our own salvation: to do justice, so that we do nothing without counsel and reason; to love mercy, so that we do not show mercy as though compelled or forced, but with a willing spirit, because God loves a cheerful giver. “And to walk attentively with God,” so that we are never secure but always await the coming of the master of the household—or, certainly, so that we do not turn away from his commandments but diligently follow in his footsteps. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked.

“The voice of the Lord cries to the city, and salvation shall be for those who fear your name.” According to the historical sense, the voice—that is, the words—are those of Micah as he prophesies. The meaning is: the Lord’s threat is directed against Samaria, so that when the people of Judah hear of the punishments of these people, they may fear and attain salvation. But sinners generally, too, when they fear the punishments they see others suffering, are corrected by their example, and what is written is fulfilled in them: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser.”

“Hear, O tribes, and who will approve it? Even now there is fire in the house of the wicked, treasures of iniquity, and a diminished measure full of wrath.” O ten tribes, which are called Samaria, hear what the Lord testifies. And who has approved it—that is, who is rare—who wishes to act according to what the Lord commands? Even now there is fire—that is, iniquity—in the house of the wicked, and treasures of impiety are in the royal house. Then he describes individually the evils by which it would be laid waste. “A diminished measure,” that is, injustice, “full of wrath,” that is, provoking God’s anger. An unjust scale and differing weights, so that they sell merchandise at one weight and buy it at another; and, what is worse, it is not the poor who do this out of necessity, but the rich, who are fuller of iniquity than of possessions. Hence it follows:

“Shall I justify the wicked scale and the deceitful weights of the purse? In them its rich men are filled with iniquity, and its inhabitants speak falsehood.” Falsehood is added to riches, because the hand accustomed to gathering wealth possesses a deceitful tongue. Although your rulers were doing these and other things, I did not wish to destroy you immediately; I continued to wait and gradually began to strike with blows, as though warning you to correct yourselves. I sent among you hunger, thirst, diseases, devastation, the hostile destruction of crops, and the barrenness of vineyards. Yet you continually served idolatry and observed the ceremonies established by the most wicked king Omri, together with every work of the house of Ahab and Jezebel. Therefore I was compelled to give you over to hissing and to make you bear the reproach of my people, while enemies mocked that God’s people had been captured and overcome by enemies—for my name is blasphemed through you.

“And their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. Therefore I also began to strike you with destruction because of your sins. You shall eat, but you shall not be satisfied; your humiliation shall be in your midst. You shall seize, but you shall not save; and those whom you save I shall give to the sword. You shall sow, but you shall not reap; you shall tread the olive, but you shall not anoint yourself with oil; and you shall make new wine, but you shall not drink wine. You have kept the ordinances of Omri and every work of the house of Ahab, and you have walked in their pleasures, so that I might give you over to destruction, and all who dwell in it to hissing; and you shall bear the reproach of my people.”

## CHAPTER VII

“Woe is me, for I have become like one gathering grape clusters in the autumn harvest. There is no bunch to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe figs.” Now he foretells the captivity of Judah and Israel—that is, of the ten tribes and the two—and laments that there is no righteous person in this people who can withstand the wrath of God. “In vain,” he says, “I spoke, foretelling the evils that threatened; in vain I wished to convert some people from the ruined city and gather, as it were, the remaining clusters of a vineyard already harvested.” And when I found no clusters, I wished at least to eat unripe figs—that is, the large, immature figs—because I found no good ripe ones. It is as though someone were to say: “Because I found no bread, I wished to eat refuse and bran because of the severity of my hunger.” The prophet himself explains this comparison, saying:

“The holy person has perished from the earth, and there is no upright person among human beings. All lie in wait for blood; each man hunts his brother to death. They call the evil of their hands good.” They not only do these evil things but also defend them, and in a perverse order call what is good evil and what is evil good.

“The ruler makes demands, and the judge is intent on repayment.” For they do not receive gifts from those who offer them voluntarily but compel their subjects to give. The judge, therefore, is intent on repayment, because he judges another in the way in which he himself is judged by another, so that they may protect one another through mutual favor. “And the great man speaks the desire of his soul.” Whoever is great among them and most learned in the Law speaks not God’s will but his own. “And they have troubled it”—that is, the city or land of which he said, “The holy person has perished from the earth.”

“He who is best among them is like a buckthorn,” pricking and wounding anyone who approaches him. “And he who is upright is like a thorn from a hedge,” so that pain is felt precisely where help was expected. “The day of your watchfulness, your visitation, has come; now their devastation shall be.” He calls the day of watchfulness the devastation of Samaria or Jerusalem, which he foretells as future. He calls that devastation a visitation. “Now their devastation shall be”—that is, the devastation of the inhabitants. Therefore do not believe the words of any prophet, nor lend your ear to the flatteries of deceivers. For if faith is rare among friends and relatives, how much rarer is it among those who lie in flattery in order to gain something? Do not, therefore, believe a friend, because Ahithophel lied to his friend David, and Judas betrayed Christ. “And do not trust in a leader,” as the people of Shechem trusted in Abimelech, whom they themselves had made king and by whom they were killed.

“Guard the doors of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom,” lest you suffer what Samson suffered from Delilah. “For the son dishonors his father,” as Absalom did David by committing incest with his father’s concubines. “The daughter rises against her mother,” examples of which occur daily. “The daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law,” as Esau’s wife acted against Rebekah. “A man’s enemies are his household,” and his own family. Since these things are so, do not believe false prophets, O citizens of Samaria or Jerusalem.

“But I”—I do not trust in their false promises—“shall look to the Lord” and his mercy. “I shall await God my Savior,” and I am certain that “the Lord my God will hear me. Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise. When I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light. I shall bear the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him, until he judges my case and executes my judgment. He will bring me into the light; I shall see his righteousness, and my enemy shall look upon me, and shame shall cover her who says to me, ‘Where is the Lord your God?’ My eyes shall see her; now she shall be trampled like the mud of the streets.”

This is the voice of Jerusalem against Babylon and the other nations that rejoiced in her ruin: “O Babylon, my enemy, do not rejoice; do not exult over me, because I have fallen deservedly. For after I have borne the Lord’s anger, I shall rise, because he is my light amid the darkness of tribulations. I know that my God will lead me out of distress, and my eyes shall see his righteousness”—that is, the vengeance he will soon execute. Now, in their presence, they shall be trampled upon and devastated by the Medes and Persians.

Thus far the voice of Jerusalem, or of the prophet speaking in the person of the people. Now the discourse is directed to Jerusalem herself:

“O Jerusalem, the ‘days’ have come”—that is, the time—“for your walls to be built,” the walls that had been destroyed by the Chaldaeans.

“On that day”—that is, at that time—“the law shall be far removed,” namely, the command by which they ordered you to serve them, and you shall no longer be subject to Babylonian rule. “On that day”—that is, at the time when your walls shall be built—“Assyria shall come as far as you, and as far as the fortified cities, and from the fortified cities to the river, and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain, and the land shall become a desolation because of its inhabitants.” That is, the fleeing Assyrians shall come even from the fortified cities they had abandoned, as far as the river—that is, as far as the Jordan—and to the nearby Dead Sea; from the Red Sea to Mount Zion; from the mountain—that is, from the mountainous regions of the Persians and Medes, to whom Israel had previously been transferred. And the land of the Chaldaeans shall be desolated by its inhabitants, “and because of the fruit of their thoughts”—that is, their evil deeds, which are the fruit of evil thoughts.

These things may also be referred morally to the faithful soul, which is Jerusalem and in which the temple of God is—or which itself is the temple of God. When, because of its sins, it is either permitted to be tested by the devil or is worn down by various tribulations, it ought not to despair of mercy but rather to rise against its enemies—that is, the demons who mock our falls—and say: “I shall rise, because the Lord is my light; he himself will lead me from darkness into light.” For every tribulation in the present seems not to be joyful but will afterward yield the most fruitful fruit of righteousness to those who have been disciplined by it. When, therefore, the Lord has done this and delivered us from many tribulations, the enemies of the soul—the evil spirits of Babylon, that is, the satellites of confusion—will see it, blush with shame, and be trampled and held in contempt, while the saints rejoice and exult in their deliverance and in the enemies’ just condemnation.

“Pasture your people with your rod, the flock of your inheritance.” This is the voice of God the Father speaking to his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the good shepherd; he is commanded to pasture the people with the rod and the flock of his inheritance. By speaking distinctly, he shows that the people are one thing and the flock another, as the Psalmist also does when he says: “But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture.” Those who use reason and know how to distinguish truth from falsehood are called the people; the simple are called sheep, because they need to be governed by teachers. When, therefore, he says, “Pasture the people and the flock of your inheritance,” he shows that both people and sheep need the rod, so that they may be governed by the Lord, just as Moses, when he was sent to Pharaoh, was told: “You shall take the rod of God in your hand.”

“Dwelling alone in the forest.” They must therefore be pastured and governed with the rod because they dwell alone in the forest. Here we understand those who separate themselves from the Church and dwell in the forest of the nations, enjoying their friendships; or those who, because of pride, withdraw themselves from the fellowship of other human beings in order to appear holier. We read that many among the nations did this: detesting communion with the human race, they dwelt in the forest of vices and were trampled by beasts—that is, by demons. The holy hermits, for their part, were alone, but they did not dwell in a forest; they dwelt amid the beauty of virtues. Therefore those who are alone and dwell in the forest of vices must be pastured and governed with the rod. For the good shepherd does not abandon such people but recalls and corrects them. Hence it follows:

“In the midst of Carmel they shall pasture in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old, according to the days of your departure from the land of Egypt; I shall show him wonders. The nations shall see and shall be ashamed of all their strength.” Carmel is a very fertile mountain. Carmel is called *Carmelus* in Greek and Latin, and *Chermel* in Hebrew. Carmel is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision”; Bashan as “confusion”; Gilead as “migration of testimony.” Thus the peoples of the nations, who previously had been without a shepherd and wandered in the forest of error, will be transferred to Carmel—that is, to knowledge of true circumcision—and will serve the Lord in spirit. Understanding their error, they will be ashamed with a beneficial shame that leads to glory, which is what Bashan signifies. And when they have thus been ashamed of their sins, they will pasture in Gilead, which is interpreted as “transmigration of testimony”; that is, they will return to the Church, to which the testimonies of the old Law have migrated.

This will happen according to the days of old, concerning which Moses also says: “Remember the days of old,” and so forth. Those will remember the days of old who do not look upon present things but upon the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. He will also show them wonders, “which eye has not seen and ear has not heard.” Then all the nations that once afflicted God’s people will see and be ashamed of all their strength by which they prevailed against God’s saints. The good, however, will experience this shame because they will understand their sins.

“They shall place their hands over their mouths,” and they shall have no freedom to speak. They are said to place their hands over their mouths because the hand signifies action; ashamed of their evil deeds, they will remain silent. By contrast, the righteous open their mouths with their hands, because from good works they receive the ability to speak with the Lord. “Their ears” also “shall be deaf,” because they refused to hear the voice of Christ; like deaf asps, they stopped their ears so as not to hear the voice of the one enchanting—that is, wisely preaching—Christ. Of them it is further said:

“They shall lick the dust like serpents; like reptiles of the earth they shall be disturbed from their houses.” Serpents walk upon their bellies, and as they move across the earth they drag themselves along and eat the earth itself. Such are the reprobate, doing earthly works and eating earth, because they feed upon earthly allurements. They walk upon their bellies because they serve their belly and their appetite, and their belly is their god. They drag themselves toward the day of vengeance and God’s just judgment. Then they will be disturbed from their houses—or, in their confinement—when they see themselves shut in and hemmed about. They will fear not the Lord their God but ours, because they do not yet deserve to have him as their God. “They shall desire the Lord our God, and they shall fear you.” When he had been speaking of the third person, he suddenly turned by apostrophe to Christ and says: “They shall fear you.” For this reason they will fall silent and endure the other things that have been mentioned: so that they may fear you, O Christ, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

“Who is a God like you, who takes away iniquity and passes over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance?” The prophet understands that the Lord is angry with the nations in order to trouble and confound them, and that, once troubled and confounded, he may spare them, take away their sins, and grant them salvation. He therefore marvels at and praises God’s goodness, saying: “Who is a God like you?”—none is understood—“who takes away iniquity and passes over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance?” Just as once in Egypt the destroying angel, seeing blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over and did not harm them.

“He shall not continue to be angry, because he is one who willingly shows mercy. He will return and have mercy on us. He will cast away our iniquities and throw all our sins into the depths of the sea,” that is, he will not remain angry forever but will at some time have mercy on the Jewish people, just as he had mercy on the nations. For God willingly shows mercy because he is merciful, and therefore he will return in mercy to those whom he had rejected. He casts our sins into the depths of the sea so that they may no longer appear.

“You will give truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, which you swore to our fathers from the days of old.” You will give believers from both peoples, he says, the truth that you promised to your servant Jacob and the mercy that you pledged to your beloved Abraham. For by Jacob, whose name means “supplanter,” the ancient people of the Jews is understood; by believing in Christ, it supplanted unbelief. To them, therefore, he will give the truth of the rewards that he promised them. Through Abraham, whose name is interpreted as “father of many”—many nations is understood—the multitude of the nations is signified. By believing in Christ they became children of Abraham, and to them he will give mercy most graciously, justifying them from sins by his own merit. All these things you swore—that is, immutably promised—to the fathers of the true faith: that from the whole multitude of human beings you would save some by truth and others by mercy. “For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.”

## ON THE PROPHET NAHUM

[Col. 0167]

[Col. 0167C] The prophet Nahum, like Jonah, prophesied the destruction of the great city Nineveh. In accordance with his name, which is interpreted as “comforter,” he comforts the captivity of the ten tribes, whom the Assyrians had already transferred to Nineveh, while Hezekiah was reigning in Judah. For it was no small consolation both to those already serving the Assyrians and to those who were being besieged in Judah under Hezekiah to hear that their enemies, the Assyrians, would be captured by the Chaldaeans.

## CHAPTER I

“An oracle concerning Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elchesite.” Among the prophets, wherever it is used, “oracle” designates a heavy burden of misery, indicating that it weighs upon the one against whom it is spoken and does not allow him to lift his neck. As for the phrase “Nahum the Elchesite,” it refers to a little village in Galilee, now utterly destroyed and scarcely showing the traces of its buildings. What some say—that he had a father named Elchesaeus—is false. It is called “the book of the vision” because he did not speak in ecstasy, as the heretics claimed, as though unaware of what he was saying in the manner of those possessed; rather, he saw—that is, understood—everything he said.

Morally, the prophet speaks in the consolation of the saints about the destruction and end of the world, which is signified by Nineveh, whose name is interpreted as “beautiful” or “splendid.” And we see nothing more beautiful than the world, insofar as all should despise perishable and worldly things and prepare themselves for the day of judgment.

“A jealous God, and the Lord who takes vengeance.” The prophet praises the Lord because he is the avenger of his people against the Assyrians; or, in a higher sense, because he hears the groaning of the saints and, at the end of the age, inflicts fitting punishments upon their adversaries. He is called “jealous” in the sense of one who is zealous. Zeal is sometimes understood positively, as when Paul says: “Be zealous for the greater gifts,” and the Lord himself says in the Psalm: “Zeal for your house has consumed me.” God is zealous for the salvation of those whom he regards as worthy, so that those whom clemency does not save may be corrected by chastisement. Hence the angry Lord speaks through Ezekiel to Jerusalem, which persisted obstinately in its sins: “My zeal has departed from you; I shall not be angry with you any longer.”

It follows: “The Lord who takes vengeance, and who possesses fury; the Lord who takes vengeance on his enemies and is angry with his adversaries.” The Lord cannot experience any movement of the soul or any fury, since he is gentle and serene in complete tranquility. But metaphorically he is said to possess fury when he avenges evils, because that is how it appears to those who suffer them. The Lord is therefore angry in order to remove from us what is opposed to him; and once the things that displease him have been removed, corrected human beings return to their former state. For it is written: “He scourges every son whom he receives.”

“The Lord is patient and great in strength.” The one whom he had earlier called jealous and said possessed fury, he now calls patient: for he long endured the sins of the Assyrians and, by his forbearance, summoned them to repentance. But because they despised God’s goodness, he does not permit them to remain unpunished as though innocent. We can also say this about ourselves in the moral sense: God’s kindness awaits us for repentance. Let us therefore not despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance, lest—God forbid—we store up wrath for ourselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment.

“And cleansing, he will not leave the guilty innocent.” Thus he mercifully cleanses from sins, yet justly punishes what they have done badly. For just as he abandons no good deed that he will not reward, so he leaves no sin that he will not condemn. By cleansing, therefore, he makes innocent, because through scourges he cleanses, lest the one whom he cleanses consider himself innocent.

“The Lord’s ways are in tempest and whirlwind, and clouds are the dust of his feet.” For the miracles by which human hearts were shaken as though by the terror of a whirlwind, the Seventy more precisely used “commotion” instead of “whirlwind,” to show that human minds were stirred by extraordinary and unheard-of miracles. [Col. 0169B] The Lord’s feet signify his coming to judgment. Clouds and dust signify the hidden and inscrutable judgments of God, by which he will judge the world. The clouds are therefore the dust of the Lord’s feet, because what is now hidden and wrapped in the densest obscurity will then burst open and be dissolved into dust, so that it may be revealed to all.

“Rebuking the sea and drying it up, and reducing all the rivers to a desert.” According to the literal sense, God’s power is described, and it is shown that it is no great thing for him to destroy the Assyrians, since he can also alter the elements. This may also refer to the end of the world, because when the Lord comes to judgment he will dry up the sea and the rivers, according to the statement: “And the sea shall be no more.”

In a higher sense, the Lord rebuked the sea and dried it up, or by his transformation destroyed every bitterness and saltiness of unbelief. He dries up the rivers—that is, he reduces to nothing the knowledge falsely so called, which exalts itself against the truth. “Bashan and Carmel have languished, and the flower of Lebanon has withered.” Metaphorically, through the languishing of Bashan and Carmel, which are exceedingly fertile regions, and through Mount Lebanon, which bears cedars and very tall trees, it is shown that the Assyrian nation, once most powerful and ruling many peoples, will be laid waste when God is angry. These things may also refer to the last day, when the powerful, the noble, and those abounding in riches will languish and perish.

Bashan is interpreted as “confusion” or “disgrace”; Carmel as “knowledge of circumcision.” He therefore intimates that everything deserving of confusion and disgrace will languish on the day of judgment. Those also who seem to possess knowledge of true circumcision and presume upon their knowledge of God’s Law, boasting that they are whitened with holiness and flourishing in virtues—those signified by Lebanon, whose name is interpreted as “whitening”—will tremble and languish when the Lord comes to judgment.

“Mountains are shaken by him, and the hills are laid waste. The earth trembles before him, and the world, and all who dwell in it.”

This may be understood simply as referring to the consummation of the world, when both mountains and hills will be shaken at the Lord’s coming. For if, at his Passion, the sun was darkened and the earth trembled, how much more, when he comes in his majesty, will all things be disturbed and shaken. Figuratively, however, he declares that every power or eminence—“mountains,” that is, human beings—will either here be cast down through repentance, or at the judgment through strict severity.

“Before the face of his indignation, who can stand? And who can resist the anger of his wrath?”

You should understand: either few, or none. For there will be no soul that does not tremble at God’s judgment, since even the stars are not clean in his sight: “His indignation is poured out like fire, and the rocks are dissolved by him.” His indignation was poured out for this purpose: that the rocks—that is, the hard hearts of human beings—might be crushed and softened into repentance, might begin to possess a contrite and humbled heart, and might become God’s sacrifice, since “the sacrifice of God is a troubled spirit.”

“The Lord is good and strengthening in the day of tribulation, and knows those who hope in him.”

This final phrase, ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [Col. 0170B]—that is, by a common construction—is also joined to what precedes. The Lord is good to those who hope; he strengthens those who hope in him; and he knows those who hope in him. When he begins to be angry with the nations and to lay waste their most powerful kingdoms, he will know those who belong to him—that is, he will have mercy on them. For God’s “knowing” means choosing or showing mercy. By “the day of tribulation” he means the day of judgment.

“And in an overflowing flood he will make a complete end of its place, and darkness will pursue its enemies.”

God is good by nature and is goodness itself, nor will he be angry forever. But even if human wickedness increases and all flesh corrupts its way, he will bring a flood—that is, a scourge—not one that remains, but one that passes away. He himself will bring about the completion and end of its place—that is, of the flood—so that the Lord’s anger may pass away, [Col. 0170C] and mercy alone may appear.

This may specifically be referred to Israel: when enemies have devastated him and flooded the whole land as though with a deluge, God will bring captivity to an end and restore him to his own settlements, while he will afflict the Assyrians, his enemies, with darkness. The same must be understood of the saints and their persecutors: after God has afflicted the saints in the present, he will have mercy on them in the future; but darkness will seize the persecutors, the darkness they chose, where there will be perpetual “weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

“What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will bring about an end. A double tribulation will not arise.”

The Hebrews explain this passage according to the literal sense: “O Jews, why are you plotting evil, as though two tribes are to be captured in the same way as the ten tribes were captured? A double tribulation will not arise, so that these may be captured as those were, because the Assyrians, who are now intertwined like thorns, will be struck down by the angel of the Lord.” This happened when, in a single night, the angel struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand of them.

As for what follows—“From you will come one who plots evil against the Lord”—they wish it to be understood of Rabshakeh, whom the king of the Assyrians sent to blaspheme the living God. Indeed, where the Hebrew text has, “A double tribulation will not arise,” the Seventy, as though explaining it more openly, said, “The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing”; and this is the wording commonly repeated by everyone.

The prophet therefore says: “What are you plotting against the Lord?” Marcion the heretic [Col. 0171A] invented two gods: one of the Old Testament, evil, cruel, and delighting in human punishments; the other good, belonging to the New Testament, whom they say will bring about the consummation of the world. Against these the prophet says: “What are you plotting against the Lord?” The one who created the world will also bring about its consummation. Nevertheless, know that a double tribulation will not arise, nor will they be judged twice, because, among those whom present tribulation afflicts, it does not allow a future condemnation to arise. For this reason God inflicts punishments on sinners in the present, so that they may not perish eternally.

“For as thorns embrace one another, so is their banquet of those drinking together. They will be consumed like stubble full of dryness.”

He is speaking especially about heretics, whose banquet—that is, their fellowship and bonds of friendship—is like thorns embracing one another. Or by their banquet he means the altar and the Lord’s table, which they boast that they possess, but whose sacraments tear the soul as thorns tear bodies. When they speak against the Lord and intoxicate themselves with the wine of error, they certainly drink together; and for this reason they are consumed in the eternal fire of Gehenna, like stubble full of dryness.

“And from you will come one who plots evil against the Lord, devising transgression in his mind.”

Most openly, all heretics plot evil against the Lord when Arius says that the Son of God is a creature, not begotten from the substance of the Father but made; when Sabellius says that there is one person in the Trinity; and when Mani—deliriously—claims that Christ did not have a true body but a phantom body. [Col. 0171C]

“Thus says the Lord: Even if they are complete, and thus many, even so they will be shorn, and he will pass away.”

According to the literal sense, he speaks of the Assyrians: even if they are complete and strong, even if they increase in number beyond all the nations, nevertheless, when the angel of the Lord lays waste to them, they will be shorn—that is, diminished—as hair is very easily cut off with scissors. “And he will pass away”—you should understand, Assur: he will cease to exist, or, after his army has been destroyed, he will return to his own land.

“I have afflicted you, and I will not afflict you again.”

You should understand: at this time, by these enemies by whom you are now besieged. For afterward they were very often afflicted by others. Hence the text adds:

“And then I will break his rod from your back, and I will tear apart your bonds”—that is, all the power he possesses and in which he boasts, or the bonds he was preparing in order to bind captives.

In a higher sense, if the wicked become complete in evil and increase in number, they will be shorn through death, pass away, and perish, so that they no longer exist. As for what follows—“I have afflicted you”—it is spoken to the Church, and he promises her that after the affliction of the present life there will follow the consolation of eternal happiness.

“And the Lord will command concerning you, and no one will be sown any longer from your name.”

“O Assur, do not think that what you are about to suffer happens by chance. The Lord will command against you, because at his command you will endure the evils that have been foretold. ‘No one will be sown from your name,’” that is, no one will be born from you who will be called by your name or called your heir.

For, as the Book of Isaiah makes clear, as soon as Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, fleeing the plague that the angel of the Lord had inflicted around him, he was killed by his sons while worshiping in the temple of his god Nesroch. This is what follows: “From the house of your god I will kill you,” so that you may be punished in the very place from which you hoped for help.

“I will make your carved image and cast image your grave, because you are dishonored,” so that your wicked blood may be poured out among altars, idols, and couches.

Let us refer these things morally to heretics. It is foretold of them that, after they have suffered the things that have been described, the souls of those whom they deceived will no longer receive names from their errors, nor will they spread seeds of falsehood any further. “And from the house of your god I will kill you”—that is, from the churches of the wicked—“the carved image and cast image,” that is, all the idolatry of perverse doctrine. [Col. 0172B] For if money is the god of the greedy person, and the belly is the god of the glutton, then their own error, which heretics have fabricated from their hearts, can likewise be called an idol and a carved image.

“Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of one who evangelizes and announces peace. Celebrate your festivals, Judah, and fulfill your vows, because Belial will not continue to pass through you; he has been utterly destroyed.”

## CHAPTER II

“He has gone up who will scatter before you, who will guard the siege.”

We read in the Book of Chronicles that, while Sennacherib was besieging Jerusalem, the inhabitants of Jerusalem could not celebrate Passover in the first month—that is, April. But after his army had been struck down by the angel and Sennacherib’s death had been announced, they celebrated the Passover in the second month, that is, May, with rejoicing.

The prophet therefore says: “O Judah, do not be anxious and do not fear, because your enemy has been killed. Behold, a messenger is coming to you; he swiftly crosses mountains and hills and announces to you peace and the city’s deliverance from Sennacherib’s rule. Therefore celebrate your festivals and fulfill your vows with rejoicing, because the Lord has saved you, and all of Belial has perished”—that is, the whole army together with its king.

Belial is interpreted as “without a yoke.” Mystically, the Church is commanded—she whom the devil had oppressed with the heaviest yoke of idolatry—to celebrate festivals after being liberated through the Lord’s Passion, and to offer the Lord vows of praise together with the angels, when Belial has been slain: “For what fellowship has Christ with Belial?” The same must be said whenever he liberates the Church from persecutors and adversaries: she is to celebrate the feasts of spiritual joy and return a vow of thanksgiving to the Lord.

“Observe the road, strengthen your loins, fortify your strength greatly, because the Lord has repaid the pride inflicted against Jacob, and likewise against Israel, because destroyers have devastated them and have ruined their branches.”

The prophet’s speech is again directed to Nineveh, and he says to her: “Without doubt Nebuchadnezzar will come to destroy you, O Nineveh, and to devastate your fields. Since an unavoidable war threatens you, I foretell this to you: carefully observe the road and path by which the executioner will come; gird your loins; strengthen and encourage the power of your army, because just as the Lord avenged Judah—that is, the two tribes—against the pride of Sennacherib, so he will avenge Israel—that is, the ten tribes—which are being held captive in Nineveh.”

This is what he says: “As the Lord repaid the pride inflicted against Jacob”—that is, the pride that the Assyrians had exercised against Jacob, namely Judah—“so he will repay the pride inflicted against Israel,” that is, the pride that those same Assyrians had exercised against Israel, namely the ten tribes.

In the mystical sense, we are commanded to observe the road on which we are going to walk—that is, to direct the eye of the mind toward the faithful way by which we may come to him who says, “I am the way.” Next, we are commanded [or: “we are ordered,” according to a conjectural reading] to hold our loins, so that we may put to death within us all illicit desires of the flesh. Third, we are commanded to strengthen our courage, so that we may be able to fight against the devil.

[Col. 0173B] “His mighty men’s shield is fiery; the men of his army are in scarlet; the reins of the chariots are fiery on the day of his preparation, and the drivers are stunned; they are thrown into confusion on the roads.”

According to the historical sense, the army of the Chaldeans is described as it comes against Nineveh, and the pomp of those preparing themselves for war is narrated.

“His mighty men’s shield is fiery,” he says—that is, flashing and seeming to sparkle like lightning. “The men are in scarlet,” that is, in garments of scarlet color, so that the very similarity of their clothing might present the terror of fire and the appearance of blood. “The reins are fiery,” because of the extreme haste of those preparing themselves for battle.

“The drivers are stunned.” “It is not surprising,” he says, “that they come so swiftly, since the drivers”—that is, the rulers of either Israel or the Assyrians—“are stunned.” The speech is woven together in a mixed manner: [Col. 0173C] at one point it speaks of what Israel has suffered, at another of what the Assyrians have done, and at another of what the Babylonians intend to do against the Assyrians.

“His chariots collide in the streets.” “Such,” he says, “is the multitude of the mingled ranks that the chariots collide in the streets, since amid such a crowd they cannot find a way.” “Their appearance”—that is, the appearance of the Babylonians—“is like lamps, like darting flashes of lightning,” so that by their appearance alone they terrify their adversaries before striking them with the sword.

“He will remember his mighty men; they will fall along their roads. They will swiftly climb his walls, and the shelter will be prepared.”

Then, he says, the Assyrian people will remember their mighty men and seek those who have already fallen along the roads. They will swiftly climb the wall of Nineveh to defend it, and because of the length of the siege they will prepare a shelter for themselves to ward off the heat.

“The gates of the rivers are opened, the temple is thrown down to the ground, the army is led away captive, and its maidservants moan like doves, murmuring in their hearts.”

“What,” the prophet says, “was the reason that they did these things, since no one can resist God’s arrangement?” When Nineveh was captured, the gates of the rivers were opened—that is, of the many peoples—for that city had a multitude of citizens like rivers. By “the temple” he means the kingdom, which was to be destroyed. By “the captive army” he means all those generally who were led away to Babylon; by “maidservants,” the smaller cities, fortresses, and villages, or the women who were led away captive.

When he says, “Moaning like doves,” he shows that the terror was so great that grief did not even burst forth in sobs or groans; rather, they mourned silently among themselves, imitating the cooing of doves.

All these things may be referred to the end of the world, when all the armor of the devil will perish. Then the chariots will collide in the streets—that is, on the broad roads of the world, constrained by the narrowness of time and the imminence of judgment. The gates that had been closed will be opened, that is, all things that had been hidden will be revealed. Then the army—that is, the devil, the ruler of this world—together with the maidservants, that is, the souls subjected to him through sin, will be driven captive into hell.

The maidservants may also be understood in a favorable sense as simple and faithful souls [Col. 0174B], who will be led away rejoicing and praising God with the dove-like murmur of confession.

“And Nineveh is like a pool of waters—its waters; but they themselves have fled. ‘Stand, stand!’—but there is no one who turns back.”

He shows that, after the smaller cities—which he had earlier called daughters—were captured, Nineveh herself, the metropolis that had so many peoples that they could be compared with the waters of a pool, remained to be conquered; and that such a multitude was of no use to her, since no one was present to resist the enemy.

When the city itself cried, “Stand, stand!”—“Close the gates; climb the wall”—there was no one to hear; instead, everyone turned their backs and abandoned the city to be plundered. Therefore it is said to the Babylonians: “They have fled; you plunder silver, plunder gold, and there is no end” [Col. 0174C] “of the riches and treasures from all desirable vessels,” which had been amassed over so long a time. Those who plundered could not plunder as much as the booty offered itself to them.

Mystically, we have said that Nineveh signifies the world. Its waters are said to resemble neither the waters of the sea, nor rivers, nor springs, but the waters of a pool—waters that do not flow continually, but are supplied by rain and confined within a short limit. So too the doctrines of heretics, as though fallen from heaven and outside the fountain of the Church, appear great and heavenly even though they promise such things.

“They have fled,” withdrawing from the Lord and unwilling to return through repentance, although the Lord urges them to repentance and says: “Return, returning children, and I will heal your wounds.” Their riches—that is, their boast in knowledge—will be plundered and reduced to nothing.

“She has been scattered, split apart, and torn to pieces; her heart is melting, her knees are dissolving, there is weakness in all her loins, and all their faces are like the blackness of a pot.”

Under the figure of a scattered and torn woman, the condition of Nineveh at the time of its captivity is described: her heart melting, her knees dissolved, and, because of the enormity of their terror, their faces disfigured by pallor, seeming like a burned pot. Although all these things were literally fulfilled in Nineveh when it was captured by Nebuchadnezzar, they are nevertheless believed to await the wicked at the future judgment.

“Where is the dwelling of lions, and the pasture of the lion cubs?”

By “the dwelling of lions” he means Nineveh, [Col. 0175A] once a royal court and a place where lions—that is, the most powerful and cruel men—had lived.

“To which the lion went, to enter there, the lion cub.”

The lion is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon; the lion cub is his subordinate ruler. “And there is no one who terrifies him”—no one who resists him.

“The lion seized enough for his cubs,” that is, Nebuchadnezzar, as victor, possessed everything by right. “And he killed for his lionesses,” that is, he handed over his cities—or, certainly, his wives—as captives into slavery. “And he filled his caves with booty and his lair with plunder,” that is, he filled his cities and fortresses, or his treasuries, with gold, silver, and every precious possession.

According to the tropological sense, when Nineveh has been devastated—that is, when the world, which is set in wickedness, has passed away—then the saints will say in exultation: “Where is the dwelling of lions,” that is, of demons, “and where is the pasture of the wicked spirits’ cubs,” who roar in order to snatch away and seek food for themselves from God?

“To this Nineveh went the lion,” that is, the devil, “and the lion cub,” the Antichrist, of whom the Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion,” and so forth. Before Christ’s coming there was no one to terrify this lion, until one stronger than he came upon him, bound the strong man, searched his caves—that is, the hidden places of hell—and took his plunder—that is, the human beings he held—from his power.

“Behold, I am against you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will burn your chariots to smoke; the sword will devour your lion cubs; I will exterminate your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers will no longer be heard.”
