“O Nineveh, you will suffer all the things foretold, not through anyone else but through me. ‘Behold, I am against you,’ I who am the author of all these things. I will burn them to smoke,” that is, to the consummation; for when fire fails and the wood is consumed, smoke remains. “And the sword will devour your cubs,” that is, your nobles and subordinate rulers. “I will exterminate your prey from the earth,” so that you may no longer devastate it or exact tribute.

All these things that are spoken of Nineveh will come upon the devil and his accomplices at the judgment.

## CHAPTER III

“Woe to the city of blood, wholly full of falsehood and tearing apart; plunder will not depart from you.”

The power of the city of Nineveh is described, and its cruelty is condemned under the form of a lamentation. “Woe,” he says, “to the city of blood and murder, in which there is no truth but every kind of falsehood, full of plunder and the tearing apart of spoils, from which plunder never departed.”

“The sound of the whip, the sound of the rushing wheel, the snorting horse, the racing chariot, the mounted rider, the flashing sword, the glittering spear, the multitude of the slain, and the heavy collapse.”

He uses “sound” for noise. This is a most beautiful description of an army preparing itself for battle. “There is no end of their corpses,” because they will lie prostrate in the city. “And they will fall upon their bodies”—either in their own multitude, when they are packed too closely together, or among the corpses of those who have been slain.

“Because of the multitude of the fornications of the beautiful and pleasing prostitute who possesses sorceries, who sold nations through her fornications and families through her sorceries.”

He calls Nineveh a prostitute, either because of her idolatry or because she was the marketplace of all the nations and received their commerce and merchandise. Therefore she fornicated with all the nations and served the idols of all the nations. For this reason she is called a beautiful and pleasing prostitute who possesses sorceries. They devoted themselves to magical arts and held many nations under their authority.

In a higher sense, Nineveh signifies the world, in which much blood of the righteous is poured out, and in which heretics kill human beings with the sword of their tongue. The sounds of whips are heard in it, because the righteous suffer many tribulations. Therefore they will fall upon their bodies, when through excessive lust they weaken their bodies; or they fall in their own bodies because, as the Apostle says, “those who fornicate sin against their own body.” There they fall, and there they acquire the condemnation of eternal death.

“Behold, I am against you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will uncover your shame before your face; I will show your nakedness to the nations and your disgrace to kings; I will cast abominations upon you, I will treat you with contempt, and I will make you an example.”

God continues to threaten Nineveh, saying that he will show her disgrace to the nations, so that those who fornicated with her will themselves despise her and treat her with contempt, and she will become an example to all. This is a metaphor of an adulterous woman who, once discovered, is brought out into the open, condemned before everyone’s eyes, and made an example for the other women.

These things can also be referred tropologically to the world, whose shame the Lord will uncover before its face when he makes it see its errors. He will also show its nakedness to the nations, so that they may understand that this world is to be condemned: while it is thought to be possessed, it flees; and it keeps faith with none of its lovers, but, after deceiving wretched human beings, it delivers them to eternal destruction.

“And everyone who sees you will recoil from you and say: ‘Nineveh has been devastated.’”

Whoever sees Nineveh devastated and set up as an example to all, he says, will recoil from her, fearing to be involved in a similar punishment, [Col. 0176D] and will pity her, saying: “Who will shake his head over you? From where shall I seek a comforter for you?” Who will be your comforter, when, while you were prosperous, you pitied no one and prepared no companion for yourself in grief, as though you could always be happy and always remain mistress?

But we too, when we consider the frail nature of the world and how all its glory passes with the swiftest course, recoil from it—that is, we withdraw ourselves from love of it. We hate its desires, which plunge people into destruction, and we begin to desire the things that are eternal.

“Are you better than Alexandria of the peoples, which dwells among the rivers? Its waters surround it; the sea is its wealth; the waters are its walls.”

Ammon is interpreted as “the people of Alexandria,” and the site of Alexandria is described. For in Hebrew Alexandria is called Nōʾ-Amon. The prophet therefore speaks to Nineveh: “Are you better or more powerful than the peoples of Alexandria, which is situated upon the Nile and the sea and is surrounded on every side by rivers?” “Its waters surround it”: on one side it is enclosed by the Nile, on another by Lake Mareotis, and on the third by the sea.

“Ethiopia was its strength, and Egypt, and there is no end. Africa and the Libyans were your help, but she too was led away into migration and captivity.”

The geographical position of the provinces itself shows what support Ethiopia, Egypt, and the other nations he describes provided for Alexandria. “But she too,” he says, “will be led away into migration.”

“Her little ones were dashed to pieces at the head of every road; they cast lots over her illustrious men, and all her nobles were fastened in fetters. And you too will become drunk, and you will be despised, and you too will seek help from the enemy.”

The prophet describes these things, showing what evils—and how cruel—victors inflict on the vanquished: they spare no age, sex, or condition. Since Alexandria, a most powerful city, is going to suffer these things, why are you surprised, O Nineveh, if these same things also happen to you? You too will drink from the same cup and will come to such disgrace and distress that you will even ask help from your enemies.

“All your fortifications are like figs with their early figs; if they are shaken, they will fall into the mouth of the eater.”

“All the defenses of your wall,” he says—that is, your warriors—“will be like the early figs commonly called grossi. When these are lightly shaken, they fall from the tree and into the eater’s mouth. In the same way you will be captured very easily, and the soldiers will have little difficulty in taking you.”

This is according to the literal sense. According to the allegory, since Ammon is interpreted as “peoples,” the meaning may be as follows: Consider the peoples of the Church, situated upon prophetic streams and having around them the rivers of teachers. Its beginning is from the sea—that is, from the bitter law of the Old Testament, which no one could fulfill without the law of Christ.

It has Ethiopia as its defense: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 67); Ethiopia is also represented by Egypt, since before the knowledge of Christ she lived in darkness. [Col. 0177D] It also has the peoples of sandy and barren Libya, scorched by the heat of the sun—that is, the same Gentiles, who at first were squalid, without the moisture of spiritual grace and the washing of baptism.

Although it possesses all these things, if it does not nevertheless guard its heart with complete diligence, it too will be led away captive; its little ones, inexperienced in faith, will be dashed to pieces and plunged into sin; and its enemies—that is, its spiritual adversaries—will annihilate its splendid virtues.

“Behold, your people are women in your midst. The gates of your land will be opened wide to your enemies; fire will devour your bars. Draw water for yourself because of the siege; build your fortifications; enter the mud and tread it, kneading the clay. There fire will consume you; you will perish by the sword; it will devour you like a bruchus. Gather like a bruchus; multiply like a locust. You have multiplied your commercial dealings beyond the stars of heaven. The bruchus has spread itself out and flown away; your guards are like locusts, and your little ones like locusts of locusts, which settle on hedges on a cold day. The sun rose, and they flew away, and the place where they had been was not known.”

The speech is still directed to Nineveh. “It is not surprising,” he says, “that your overthrow is so easy, like the shaking off of early figs, since all your people have become effeminate and cannot resist. Therefore the gates will be opened, not to friends but to enemies. The bars by which they were closed will be consumed by fire.

“Since the siege will be long, draw water for yourself and take care that the besieged do not lack drink. Fortify your towers; enter the mud”—you should understand, with bare feet—“and tread it”—you should understand, kneading it, that is, softening and compacting it. When you have made bricks from it, hold them and repair the breaches in the walls. For the siege is near.

“But when you have done all these things, rejoice in your works; the sentence is defective here, before the comparison, ‘as swiftly as a bruchus devours the grass of the earth.’ Even when you have gathered an immense multitude of warriors, so that it can be compared with the densest bruchi and locusts, and when you have amassed all your treasures and riches, which cannot be counted any more than the stars of heaven can, you will lose all these things in a moment of time, just as locusts, bruchi, or ateleboi fly away when warmed by the sun and cannot be found.”

For there are three kinds of locusts: the larger, flying locust; the bruchus, a locust without wings; and the atelebos, the smallest and chirping kind, between the locust and the bruchus, crawling rather than flying on small wings. It is the nature of all locusts to be sluggish in the cold and to fly in the heat.

Tropologically, the people of Nineveh are worldly human beings, so emasculated by the passions and enticements of the flesh that they are compared with women and possess nothing manly. Therefore their gates—that is, the senses of the body—will be opened to their enemies, namely demons.

They do, however, possess reason and understanding as though they were very strong bars, by which they could close their senses. But fire will consume these bars, because they are overcome by the devil’s fiery arrows. Hence such people are commanded to draw up the water of divine speech. For Solomon calls speech from a man’s mouth deep water, and there they will find some remedy of salvation.

They are also commanded to take mud, knead it, and make bricks, so that they may remember that they were fashioned from mud and have assumed a mortal condition. But they should temper the mud itself with the water of God’s word, so that they may make bricks with which a fortification can be built, lest the enemy be able to enter again through the gates. That is, they should be instructed by the examples of Scripture, so that they may know how to resist the devil’s temptations.

Next they are commanded to multiply like a bruchus—that is, to grow and increase in the number of their virtues—so that, just as they formerly multiplied worldly business dealings, they may match the multitude of their sins with a multitude of virtues.

“Your shepherds slumber, king of Assur; your princes will be buried. Your people have hidden themselves in the mountains, and there is no one to gather them.”

“When your people have become effeminate and as weak as women,” he says, “it is not surprising that your shepherds”—that is, your princes and subordinate rulers—“have fallen asleep. And if they have been subdued or killed, although they ought to have been the first to stand in the battle line, your people have been scattered through fear of the approaching Nebuchadnezzar. For once the princes had been killed, the remaining multitude, unfit for war, was scattered in the mountains, and there is no one to gather the fugitives and compel the army to resist.”

“Your destruction is not obscure; your wound is grievous”—that is, it is not small and cannot be concealed, and no physician can heal it. “All who heard news of you clapped their hands over you.”

It is clear that whoever hears that Nineveh has been overthrown and that her once most powerful king has been cast down will be astonished and stunned at the magnitude of such an event, and will press his hands together as people do when they are amazed—or else, rejoicing and mocking your ruin, they will clap their hands.

Why this happens he shows by adding: “For over whom has your wickedness not passed continually?” “For this reason,” he says, “no one can grieve for you or shed tears over your wound, because there is no one over whom your wickedness has not passed. He does not say ‘stood,’ but ‘passed,’ because the wickedness and pride of the Assyrians were transitory and fleeting and could not endure forever.”

Tropologically, these words can be referred to the ruler of the world, who once boasted: “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven.” Rebuking him, the prophet also says: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning!”

He is therefore addressed by apostrophe: “O Assur, your shepherds slumbered at the coming of Christ the Lord, because they fed human beings not for salvation but so that, fattened with every impurity and iniquity, they might devour them more greedily. Your people, who once worshiped you, have departed from you and fled to the mountains, to the protection of the apostles and teachers.

“And now all who had been deceived by you mock you, because there is either no one or very few whom you have not at some time deceived, and over whom your wickedness has not passed. For one over whom wickedness stands cannot mock it. But when wickedness has passed away and goodness has followed, then they will mock the devil and, as though clapping their hands, will make a noise of good works against him.”

## ON THE PROPHET HABAKKUK

Habakkuk the prophet, who among the Hebrews is called Chabacuk, prophesied after Judah—that is, after the two tribes had been led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar. We can know this from the Book of Daniel. Daniel was one of the captives of Judah; while he was placed in the lions’ den, this prophet was carried from Judea by an angel together with a meal.

Chabacuk is interpreted as “embracing” or “embrace,” either because he was beloved of the Lord or because he wrestled with the Lord and embraced him, as it were, in a kind of contest. For none of the prophets dared so boldly to challenge the Lord to a debate and say: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry out?” and so forth.

## CHAPTER I

“The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.”

Wherever “oracle” is placed in the prophets, the burden of miseries and affliction is signified. Attention must be paid to what follows: “that Habakkuk the prophet saw.” He saw—that is, he understood—the things he was saying, unlike the heretic Montanus, who raves that the prophets did not know what they were saying and, in the manner of madmen, produced sound without understanding.

“How long, O Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? I will cry aloud to you, suffering violence, and you will not save?”

The prophet speaks full of grief and argues against the Lord: why had he allowed the temple consecrated to him and the city of Jerusalem—which was once called especially the city of God—to be destroyed by the Chaldeans; why he did not hear the people crying out to him, nor save those who shouted because of the violence of their enemies.

“Why have you shown me iniquity and toil, to see plunder and injustice against me?” Why, he says, have I lived and been brought to this point, so that I should see iniquity and toil—that is, the affliction which I endure from enemies? The prophet said this, disturbed by the anguish of his mind, and as though doubting that anything happens without God’s providence, like one unaware that the saints are tested and advance through tribulations, just as gold advances toward brilliance in the fire.

But it can also be said that the prophet speaks such words not in his own person, but in the person of the imperfect—those who, ignorant of God’s hidden judgments, when they see the wicked exalted and the good oppressed, dare to complain against the Lord, who knows what is fitting for whom and when. The Psalmist likewise laments something of this kind, saying: “Behold, these are the sinners, and those who abound in the world,” and so forth. Job, too, after enumerating the felicities with which the reprobate are surrounded in the world, concluded as follows: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.”

“And judgment came to be, and contradiction became stronger. Therefore the law was torn apart, and judgment did not reach its end, because the impious prevails against the just; therefore perverse judgment will go forth.” The prophet—or the people, in whose person he speaks—grieves because judgment was rendered against them not by truth but by power, and because they endured everything not through the law but by force; hence judgment itself reached no conclusion. For the end of judgment is to judge justly.

He shows why he has said these things by adding: “Because the impious,” that is, Nebuchadnezzar, “prevails against the just,” that is, Judah. Necho, the impious king of Egypt, prevailed against holy Josiah. Daniel and the three boys, martyrs, serve the most wicked king Nebuchadnezzar. This may also be referred to the saints, who complain why persecutors prevail against them, why a most impious judge, after accepting bribes, condemns the innocent and acquits the guilty.

[Col. 0181A] “Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astonished, because a work has been done in your days which no one will believe when it is recounted.” This is the voice of the Lord responding to the prophet’s complaint that an innocent people had been overcome by the impious. “Behold,” he says, “this iniquity, which you think was done only in Israel, see it being done among other nations. For not only Judah and Jerusalem were handed over to the Chaldeans, but all the surrounding nations.”

He also says that Nebuchadnezzar will possess such power and strength that, if anyone reports it, the magnitude of the event will make it seem unbelievable. What this work is, he shows when he says:

“For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation, proceeding over the breadth of the earth, [Col. 0181B] to possess dwellings not its own.

“It is dreadful and terrible.” That the nation of the Chaldeans was exceedingly warlike and powerful is testified by Trogus and Pompeius [Note: He introduces two writers from one and the same source], as well as by the others who wrote barbarian histories. Not content with its own borders, it roamed here and there, ranging over the height of the earth, living by plunder and the sword, and possessing cities that were not its own.

“From itself its judgment and its burden will go forth. Its horses are swifter than leopards and faster than evening wolves, and its horsemen will spread out. Indeed, its horsemen will come from afar; they will fly like an eagle hastening to eat. They will all come for plunder.” This means that he will appoint rulers and judges from his own nation and will not have attendants from other nations. Or certainly, his judgment will go forth from that nation itself, so that, just as it acted, so it may receive, and just as it devastated others, so it may itself be devastated.

“Its horses are swifter”—that is, faster—“than leopards,” an exceedingly swift animal distinguished by beautiful markings. He also compares their horses with evening wolves, because wolves are said to be fiercer as night approaches, driven mad by the hunger of the day. They are likewise compared with eagles, which hasten with the greatest speed to devour.

It follows: “Their faces are like a burning wind, and he will gather captives like sand; he himself will triumph over kings, and tyrants will be his laughing-stock. He will laugh at every fortification, heap up a siege-ramp, and capture it. Then his spirit will be changed, and he will pass on and fall.”

Just as all growing things wither at the breath of a burning wind, so at their appearance everything will be devastated. The number of plundered persons and captives will be so great that it could be compared with the sand of the sea—though this must be understood as hyperbole.

“He himself,” that is, Nebuchadnezzar, “will triumph over kings,” understood as the kings of other nations. “And tyrants will be his laughing-stock”: while triumphing, he will make them precede his chariot. He will be so proud that he will strive to surpass nature.

Finally, Nebuchadnezzar, wishing to capture the city of Tyre, situated in the midst of the sea, threw immense masses into the sea and heaped up such a siege-ramp that he almost made the sea itself into an island, establishing a land route across the waters. “He will laugh,” he says, “at every fortification,” as though it could be captured with the greatest ease. He will heap up a ramp of stones and earth and capture it—that is, the fortification.

“Then his spirit will be changed,” understood as “his spirit”: that is, he will be lifted up in pride, believing himself to be God. Hence he also erected a golden statue for himself and ordered all nations to worship it. And when he has done this, “he will pass on,” that is, he will lose human understanding, be expelled from human society, and afterward “he will fall,” that is, he will cease to exist.

“This is the strength of his god.” This should be read ironically, so that the meaning is: “This is the strength that Bel, his god, gave him.” For his strength was of the same kind as that of his god Bel.

Tropologically, the Chaldeans, whose name is interpreted as “demons,” signify wicked beings through whom God exercises vengeance. For God sends indignation, wrath, and tribulation through evil angels. They are a bitter nation because they spare no one; swift through the subtlety of their spiritual nature; proceeding over the breadth of the earth, that is, through the spacious paths of the world.

“From itself its judgment will go forth,” because it will be handed over to punishment according to its deeds, and the impious are permitted to its power, as were Philetus and Hermogenes, whom the Apostle handed over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme.

“Are you not from the beginning, Lord my God, my Holy One, and shall we not die?” The prophet understands from the words of the Lord’s response that Nebuchadnezzar received power against Judah—or the devil against the just—by a just judgment. But the fact that we live and have not been killed by him is due to your mercy.

“Lord, you appointed him for judgment,” that is, Nebuchadnezzar; through his power you judge justly and correct sinners. [Col. 0182C] For this is what follows: “And you established the strong one in order to correct,” that is, you gave him such great and solid strength for this purpose, so that through him you might correct those who transgress.

What is said here literally about the Chaldeans and their king can also be referred to the devil, whom God appointed for judgment, as it were a most powerful executioner, so that through him he might subject the wicked to punishments, while testing the good through their afflictions.

“Your eyes are pure, so as not to see evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity.” I know, he says, Lord, that you do not willingly look upon evil and injustice, and no one can doubt your justice. Nevertheless, why do you permit the Babylonians to do such things and allow just Israel to be oppressed by the impious Nebuchadnezzar?

“Why do you not look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent while the impious devours one more just than himself?” We call Israel just, not because it is perfectly just, but because, in comparison with the impious oppressor, it appears just.

“And you will make human beings like the fish of the sea, and like a creeping creature without a ruler.” Just as, he says, the fish of the sea, irrational beasts, and creeping creatures are without a ruler; the weaker are devoured by the stronger; and whoever possesses the right of force dominates another, so among human beings reason has no power, but everything is accomplished by strength. And although all things are governed by your providence, I cannot understand why the impious conquers and the just is conquered. He says this not because he actually thinks so, but because he assumes the form of human impatience.

[Col. 0183A] “He will lift it all up with a hook; he dragged it in his net and gathered it into his seine. Because of this he will rejoice and exult; therefore he will sacrifice to his seine and offer sacrifice to his net, because through them his portion has become fat.”

Because he had said, “Human beings will be like the fish of the sea,” he preserves the metaphor of fish. Just as, he says, a fisherman casts a hook, a net, and a seine, so that what he cannot catch with the hook he may seize with the net, while what escapes the net is surrounded by the wider seine, so the king of Babylon, after devastating everything and capturing all nations through war and, as it were, through snares, will rejoice and sacrifice to his seine and his net—that is, to the idol Bel, or to the golden statue which he erected in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. To it he will offer, as though they were the fattest victims, all the nations he had conquered, compelling them to worship it. For through those idols his portion has become fat, and through them he believed that he possessed all riches.

“And his food is choice; therefore he spreads his seine, and never ceases to kill nations”—that is, rulers and kings, whom he caught like great fish and subjected to his dominion; and for that reason he does not cease attacking and slaughtering all nations.

According to the tropological interpretation, the devil, whom the king of Babylon signifies, cast a hook and first dragged the human being from paradise. He surrounded him with seines and manifold deceptions, and through him made all human beings sinners. “And his food is choice,” because he disdains to tempt only the lowly and worldly; he also attacks the holy and perfect, and never ceases to persecute and deceive the human race.

## CHAPTER II

“I will stand at my watch and fix my step upon the fortification; I will contemplate, to see what he will say to me and what I will answer to the one reproving me.”

At first the prophet had complained, and the Lord had answered him, saying: “Look among the nations,” and so forth. In response to the Lord’s answer, he moderated his question, as though repenting of what he had previously said, and, speaking with conciliatory words, said: “My holy God, we shall not die.” Nevertheless, he asked the same question, though with a certain reverence: “Your eyes are pure, so as not to see evil. Why do you not look upon those who act unjustly?” and so forth.

Now he says that he is waiting to see what the Lord will answer, so that what has been said may be announced to everyone. “I will stand at my watch,” that is, in the height and elevation of my prophecy, so that after the overthrow of the temple and the city and the captivity of the people I may see what will follow.

“And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision and make it clear upon tablets, so that the one who reads it may run through it, because the vision is still for a distant time; it will appear at the end and will not deceive.”

In accordance with what the Lord had said through Isaiah—“While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, I am here’”—the Lord now answers and commands the prophet to write the vision, that is, the prophecy, and to make it clear, that is, to write it carefully and plainly upon the tablets of the heart, in accordance with the Apostle, who says to the Corinthians: “You are our letter, written in our hearts.”

And this is because the vision is still far off, reserved for its appointed time; when the end of events arrives, the vision will be shown to have been true. This prophecy plainly concerns the coming of Christ, and the question the prophet had asked—why the wicked should rule—has been resolved: iniquity would indeed reign in the world for so long, and the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar would capture human beings like fish, until he comes through the incarnation.

“If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come; it will not delay.” If, he says, because of your eagerness for the vision to be fulfilled, the one who is to come seems to you to be delaying, do not despair, but wait patiently, because he will surely come and will not delay.

“Behold, the one who is unbelieving will not have a rightly disposed soul within him. But the just will live by his faith.” [Col. 0184B] If anyone is unbelieving concerning this promise and wavers, doubting that what he sees delaying will come, his soul will not be rightly disposed but will be corrupted by the strength of unbelief. Another translation says: “My soul will not be pleased,” that is, “he will displease me.” But if the one who does not believe displeases him, then the just person who believes my promise will live by his faith.

“And just as wine deceives the drinker, so will the proud man be; he will not be adorned, who has enlarged his soul like the underworld, and like death he is not satisfied. He will gather all nations to himself and heap all peoples to himself. Will not all these take up a parable against him and a saying of riddles against him? And it will be said: Woe to him who multiplies what is not his.”

Here the destruction of Nebuchadnezzar is now clearly proclaimed. Just as, he says, wine intoxicates the drinker, so that neither foot nor mind performs its proper function, so the proud man—either all such men in general or Nebuchadnezzar in particular—will not be adorned and will not bring his desire to fulfillment. For death and the underworld are not satisfied with the slain, and, seizing everything, he places no end to his greed.

“How long does he burden dense mud against himself?” The statement is directed specifically against Nebuchadnezzar and generally against all the greedy. Every greedy person multiplies what is not his, because the riches which he gathers by right and wrong cannot remain with him but pass to other possessors. Beautifully, he called excessive riches “dense mud,” because they confuse the soul’s purity and weigh down the mind with the heaviest burden of iniquity.

“Will not those who bite you suddenly arise, and those who tear you apart be awakened, and you become their prey? Because you plundered many nations, all who remain of the peoples will plunder you, because of human blood and the iniquity of the land, the city, and all who dwell in it.”

He indicates the Medes and Persians, who, rising against the kingdom of the Babylonians, first bit them by attacking their luxury, and afterward tore and rent them apart, killing Belshazzar and scattering all the leaders of the kingdom. Then the devastator of the whole world became their prey, and he was plundered by all the peoples who had been able to escape his cruelty.

“This will come,” he says, “because of the blood of man,” that is, of Judah, “and the iniquity of the land”—understand, of Israel—“of the city,” that is, Jerusalem, “and of all who dwell in it,” designating the whole people.

The “how long” placed above is either the voice of one reproving, or it refers to the prophet’s desire, which longs for the swift destruction of wickedness and pride.

“Woe to him who gathers evil greed for his house, so that he may set his nest on high and think himself able to escape from the hand of evil.” He continues to speak against the impious king, who gathers evil greed for his house and does not understand that riches acquired through evil are the cause of his own ruin. At the same time, he is accused of pride because, after the manner of birds, he has placed his nest on high, thinking that he can escape from the hand of evil—that is, that he will never fall into the power of his enemies.

He calls the greed for money and riches “evil,” because there is also a good greed, that is, desire for the spiritual riches of wisdom and knowledge of God, although the word “greed” is rarely, or perhaps never, found used in a good sense.

“You have planned confusion for your house.” While, he says, you place your nest on high, you have done nothing except plan confusion for yourself and your descendants, because this solicitude will end in disgrace.

“You have cut down many peoples, and your soul has sinned. For a stone from the wall has cried out, and the wood that is between the joints of the buildings will answer.”

In this, he says, that you have killed very many, you have raged against your own soul, and you have burned with such cruelty that the stones of destroyed cities and the wood of overturned and burned [Col. 0185C] walls cried out against your cruelty.

Historically, the wood between the joints designates the timber customarily placed in the middle of a structure to hold the walls together. It should be noted that in the Septuagint it is written: “The scarab will cry out from the wood,” literally designating a fly, which in winter or during storms is accustomed to hide in the joints of walls. The meaning is therefore: Even flies hidden in the holes of the wood will cry out against your pride and greed.

“Woe to him who builds a city in blood and prepares a town in iniquity.” The discourse continues against Nebuchadnezzar, and he is told: Woe to him because he built Babylon in blood and deaths and constructed its walls in iniquity.

[Col. 0185D] “Are not these things”—understand, the things that are being said—“from the Lord of hosts?” Let no one, he says, consider the person speaking, lest, because of the advantage or status of the person, they should think that what is said ought to be despised. The words spoken by the prophets belong to the Lord.

“For peoples will labor in a great fire, and nations for nothing, and they will fail.” When Babylon has been burned, they will labor in vain to extinguish the fire and strive toward nothing. The Chaldean peoples will fail and grow weary, and they will not be able to extinguish the fire once it has been kindled.

“For the earth will be filled so that it may know the glory of the Lord, as waters cover the sea.” When Babylon has been overthrown, God’s power will become manifest to everyone. And just as waters cover the depths of the sea, so the whole earth [Col. 0186A] will be filled with the glory of the Lord.

In some manuscripts it is read negatively: “These things are not from the Lord of hosts.” The meaning is: Such a building, which is made in blood and iniquity, is not from the Lord.

“Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbor, pouring out his gall and making him drunk, so that he may look upon his nakedness.” The Hebrews relate at this point a story more fabulous than true. Zedekiah, they say, was captured by Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, which is Antioch, and after his eyes had been torn out he was led to Babylon. There, one day, when Nebuchadnezzar was celebrating a banquet with royal luxury, he ordered a cup to be given to Zedekiah which would loosen the drinker’s bowels into a flux. Thus brought in and compelled before the faces of the drinkers, he was defiled with the filth of his bowels. This, they say, is what is meant by: “Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbor,” [Col. 0186B] and so forth: namely, that a once exceedingly powerful king had been reduced to such disgrace.

Therefore God threatens him that he too will drink such a potion. But it is better to understand this not of a purgative drink, but of the evils that Nebuchadnezzar was to suffer. For in the Scriptures a cup or drink commonly signifies suffering or affliction.

The prophet therefore attacks the impious king because, forgetting his condition and acting as though he himself were not human and could not suffer what he inflicted on others, he intoxicated all human beings with the gall and bitterness of evils, so that he might look upon their nakedness—that is, their disgrace—and magnify his own power through their misery.

This is a metaphor for a drunken man: just as a drunkard is stripped naked and his disgrace is exposed, so Nebuchadnezzar [Col. 0186C] intoxicated everyone with the cup of fury, left them all stripped, and reduced those who had once been glorious to the lowest slavery. This is what is meant by “he was filled”—understand, “the neighbor.”

“Dishonor instead of glory. You too, drink and fall asleep; a cup from the Lord’s right hand will surround you, and a vomit of dishonor will come upon your glory.” Because, he says, you intoxicated very many, drink also from the Lord’s cup. You will be intoxicated by the cup—that is, by the punishments of the Lord’s right hand—and you will disgorge everything that you had swallowed, and from lofty glory you will come down to the worst evils.

“For the iniquity of Lebanon will cover you.” Lebanon stands for the temple, which was built from the woods of Lebanon. Hence another prophet says: “Open your gates, Lebanon.”

He therefore says that the iniquity of Lebanon—that is, [Col. 0186D] the overthrow of the temple and the devastation of the sanctuary—will despoil and destroy him. He preserves the metaphor because, having used Lebanon for the temple, he introduces animals for sacrifices and offerings, saying: “And the devastation of animals”—that is, the destruction of the sacrifices offered in the temple—“will terrify them,” that is, the Babylonians, because the violation of the temple and of the sacrifices, which had already ceased to be offered, terrified and destroyed them.

“Because of the blood of human beings,” that is, because of the slaughter of human beings, “and” because of “the iniquity of the land” of promise, “and of the city,” Jerusalem, “and of all who dwell in it.”

According to the tropological interpretation, heretics are rebuked because they intoxicate everyone with bitter and perverse teachings, giving their friend—that is, their companion in the faith—a drink not from the spring of Siloam, that is, from the “sent one,” namely Christ, whom God the Father sent into the world, but from the stream of Egypt, of darkness and grief. Hence that stream is rightly called Sior, that is, “turbid and muddy.”

They are therefore told that they too will be filled with dishonor instead of glory, when their perverse doctrine has been exposed and condemned by ecclesiastical judgment. The devastation of Lebanon will cover them. For Lebanon in Greek means “frankincense.” By frankincense the purity of prayer is expressed. The devastation of Lebanon will therefore cover them because their prayer—which is the special sacrifice of God—will be turned into their condemnation, in accordance with what the Psalmist said concerning Judas: “Let his prayer become sin.”

“What profit is there in a carved image, since its maker carved it; in a molten image and a false likeness, since its maker trusted in what he fashioned, in order to make mute idols?” The prophet marvels at the folly of King Nebuchadnezzar, because he ordered a golden statue to be made and trusted in the image he had fashioned, although it could in no way profit him.

There is this difference between a carved image and a molten image: a carved image is made of wood or marble, whereas a molten image is made of metals that can be dissolved and cast by fire. This may be understood not only of idolaters but also of heretics, whose carved images are the wicked doctrines they devise and revere and whose falsehood they worship as truth.

“Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ and, ‘Rise!’ to a silent stone. Can it itself teach?” This is said generally against all who venerate idols. Eternal woe will be his who worships wood, stone, or any metal as a god and, invoking it, says: “Awake!” although it is merely an inanimate form.

For eidos in Greek, or idea, means “form”; hence, diminutively, idolum is called a “little form.” Can the stone itself which you invoke teach you and foretell the future?

“Behold, this one is covered with gold and silver.” It is as though he were pointing something out: Behold, idolater, this stone which you worship is covered and overlaid with gold. “And there is no spirit”—that is, no vital breath—“in its inward parts,” that is, in the idol or stone.

“But the Lord,” whom we, true worshipers, adore, is “in his holy temple. Let all the earth be silent before him.” This does not mean, understand, a temple made by human hands, but either heaven or each of the saints, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”

Or “the Lord is in his holy temple” means the Son is in the Father; or “in his temple,” that is, in the whole universe, containing and governing all things. “For in him we live and move and are.” God is therefore in the world, not enclosed in a place, but filling all things without being confined by place through his majesty, running through all things and encompassing all things.

“Prayer of the prophet Habakkuk for ignorances.” Because he had previously complained rashly against the Lord, saying: “How long, Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear?” and shortly afterward: “Why do you not look upon those who act unjustly?”; and because he had heard the Lord respond and had learned that Nebuchadnezzar—or even the devil—had been appointed and perhaps established for this purpose, so that sinners might be judged and punished through them, he now repents and laments that he had spoken rashly. He asks forgiveness for his ignorance, and this is what is written in the title: “For ignorances.”

David, too, asks the Lord: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances.” Some think that the phrase “for ignorances” indicates that the prophet is praying to God for human errors and ignorance, so that when the darkness of error has been removed, the true light may be revealed.

## CHAPTER III

“Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid.” By “report” he means the voice which he heard inwardly in his mind. The same is found in Isaiah: “Lord, who has believed our report?” and elsewhere: “The Lord God opened my ear.”

“Lord, I heard your report.” I heard, he says, with the ear of my mind the punishments which you prepared for Nebuchadnezzar—or for the devil and his members—and five times threatened them with eternal woes. “And I was afraid”: I feared your most hidden judgments.

“Lord, your work”—understand, “I heard”—that is, the mystery of your incarnation. The work of God is, as blessed Augustine says, “the Word made flesh.” This may also be understood of his resurrection. I heard your work, he says, so that you who deigned to die for us might rise from the dead.

“In the midst of the years revive it,” that is, fulfill what you promised in the fullness of time. For you said: “The vision is still for a distant time, and it will appear at the end.” Therefore, when the time appointed by you has come, revive your work, so that your word may not die but be fulfilled in deed.

“In the midst of the years you will make it known.” When the time comes and you have completed the works you promised, then you will show that what you promised was true.

“When you are angry, you will remember mercy.” This does not mean that God, according to human custom, forgets in anger and afterward remembers mercy; rather, when we are placed in affliction, he seems to forget us when he does not quickly help those who suffer, as the Psalmist says in tribulation: “How long, Lord, will you forget me forever?”

At the same time, God’s clemency must be considered. He does not say, “After you have inflicted punishments,” but “When you are angry, you will remember mercy.” For the one who is angry does not always strike but merely threatens. The Apostle says something similar: “The wrath of God is revealed against all impiety of human beings.” He said “is revealed,” not “is inflicted,” but it is revealed in order to terrify and to spare those who have been corrected.

Another translation says: “In the midst of two animals you will be known.” We understand these two animals as the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. Some think that the two animals are the two cherubim who look toward one another and have between them the oracle or mercy seat. Others think that the two animals are the two thieves, between whom the Lord was crucified and recognized. Some say that they are the two Testaments, Old and New, which are animate and visible, and in whose midst Christ is recognized. Many understand Moses and Elijah, between whom the Lord appeared transfigured on the mountain.

[Col. 0189A] “God will come from the south.” Some wish “God will come from the south” to be understood as Bethlehem, which is situated in the southern region and in which city Christ was born.

“And the Holy One from Mount Paran.” Paran is a mountain near Mount Sinai, on which the law was given. The Holy One is said to come from there because through the law there is knowledge of God. This is according to the literal sense.

Or “God will come from the south,” that is, from midday—from those who are sons of light and of day. The Lord will therefore come from the south and is to be awaited by those who are fervent in love and faith. Hence in the Song of Songs the bride also asks: “Tell me where the one whom my soul loves pastures his flock, where he lies at midday.”

“And the Holy One from Mount Paran.” Paran is interpreted as “the mouth of the seeing one,” and truly from the mouth—that is, from the speech—of an educated and seeing person, that is, one who understands and is filled with the light of knowledge, comes the knowledge of God.

*(Diapsalma.)* “His glory covered the heavens.” At the Lord’s birth, heaven was filled and, as it were, covered with glory, while the angels proclaimed: “Glory to God in the highest.”

“And the earth is full of his praise,” because his coming poured peace back upon the earth, while the angels sang: “And on earth peace to people of good will.”

It should be noted that when it says, “His glory covered the heavens,” it shows that what is covered is less than that which covers it. Therefore the glory is greater than the heavens which are covered. We may also understand the heavens as the saints, who bear the image of the heavenly one and proclaim the glory of God. These heavens he covers—that is, he illumines—with the glory and majesty of God. “The earth is full of his praise,” because, according to the Psalmist’s voice: “His name is wonderful in all the earth.”

“His splendor will be like the light,” because the brightness of his miracles shone forth with manifest light. Nor should the difference of tenses trouble us. He says in the past tense, “His glory covered the heavens”; in the present, “The earth is full of his praise”; and in the future, “His splendor will be like the light.” For divine Scripture is bound by no law of time, since it surpasses all time.

“Horns are in his hands,” that is, the banners and trophies of the cross. It should be noted that although the Lord’s hands were fastened to the horns of the cross, he does not say, “The Lord’s hands are in the horns,” but “The horns are in his hands.” For he held the cross itself—or rather death itself—in his power, as he says: “I have authority to lay down my life.”

“There his strength is hidden.” There, that is, in the horns, his strength and the power of his divinity were hidden, because although he existed in the form of God and was equal to God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and humbling himself before the Father unto death, even death on a cross.

His strength was therefore hidden on the cross when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” We may also understand the horns as royal power. For it is the custom of the Scriptures to use “horn” for strength and power, as the Psalmist says: “In you we will scatter our enemies with the horn.” And the mother of holy Samuel says: “He will give power to his king and exalt the horn of his Christ.”

The horns were therefore in his hands because, although he suffered for us, he did not lose his royal power; indeed, through the cross he extended his dominion.

“Death will go before his face.” Death means the devil, the author of death, concerning whom John says: “And his name was Death.” Death therefore went before his feet because, immediately after he had been baptized in the Jordan, it encountered him, tempting him after a fast of forty days, before he had either preached or revealed himself as God through miracles.

Hence it follows: “The devil will go forth before his feet,” because he met him as he came out of the waters. Another translation says: “Resheph will go forth before his feet.” The Hebrews relate that Resheph is the name of a demon who holds primacy among the others, like Beelzebub. They say that he entered paradise in the form of a serpent and through it deceived the first human being.

Hence he received his name from the curse by which the Lord condemned him. For Resheph is interpreted as “crawling on the belly.” It had been said to the serpent—or rather to the devil who was in the serpent: “You shall walk upon your breast.”

The devil therefore went forth before the Lord’s feet because, as soon as he had been baptized and the Father’s voice had thundered over him at the descent of the dove, the devil, disturbed by these things, appeared to tempt him, wishing to test whether he was the Son of God.

“He stood and measured the earth.” To stand belongs to divinity, just as to pass over belongs to humanity. Standing, therefore, the Lord measured the earth, because the power of his divinity, arranging all things, measured the earth—that is, the hearts of earthly human beings—discerning and foreseeing who would be worthy to be chosen and who would rightly be rejected.

“He looked and dissolved the nations.” The Lord’s gaze is the divine power by which he foresees all things, arranging each according to place and time. He looked, therefore, and dissolved the nations—that is, he scattered them so that they would no longer be nations but, reborn through faith and baptism, would become sons of God.

“And the mountains of the age were crushed.” When the nations of the age had been dissolved, the mountains were crushed—that is, all the power of demons was broken. He calls them “mountains of the age” because of the swelling of their arrogance.

Or by “mountains of the age” he means the princes and powerful ones of this world, who were crushed in the hardness of their pride when they saw the brilliance of Christ’s miracles.

He calls them “mountains of the age” because there are other mountains which do not belong to the age: namely, the holy apostles and apostolic men, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains,” and so forth. These are not mountains of the age [Col. 0190D] but mountains of God, “mountains rich in milk,” that is, filled with spiritual grace.

“The hills of the world were bowed down by the paths of his eternity.” Those who are mountains are also hills: the powerful and those equal to them, whose pride no one had been able to humble before Christ’s coming. They were crushed and bowed down by the paths of his eternity—that is, of God—because the eternity of his divinity deigned to come to us.

His paths are from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, from the womb to the manger, from the manger to baptism, from baptism to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb again into heaven.

The mountains may also be understood as the stronger demons, who are in heretics and apostates and exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. The hills, however, are demons of lesser power, who are in worldly people who glory in riches, strength, beauty, nobility, and the other goods of the body.

These mountains and hills were crushed and bowed down at Christ’s coming because, when such people were converted and accepted the example of Christ’s humility, the demons who had been in them were confounded, and their opposing power was reduced to nothing.

“Because of iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia.” The Ethiopians are exceedingly black men, who are said to feed on the flesh of dragons; therefore they signify demons, black with wickedness, whose sweetest drink is human beings possessing a serpent’s disposition and always ready to do harm. The tents of the Ethiopians are those very human beings who, by laboring to acquire riches, become their tents. The prophet expressed this iniquity in a single phrase: “For every rich man is either himself wicked or the heir of a wicked man.” Thus the prophet says, “I saw”—that is, understand: human beings made tents of Ethiopia because of iniquity, namely greed, by which they never cease accumulating riches. Once they have acquired them, they surrender themselves to luxury and pleasures and to every kind of iniquity, and thus become lodging for demons, though they ought to have been the temple of God.

“‘The skins of the land of Midian will be thrown into confusion.’” What he called “tents” above he now calls “skins”; and what he called “Ethiopians,” he now calls “the land of Midian.” Midian is a region near Ethiopia. Midian is interpreted as “from judgment,” that is, destined for condemnation. Thus the skins of the land of Midian will be thrown into confusion—that is, the people who made themselves dwellings of demons by acquiring riches and worldly honors through injustice and iniquity. They will indeed be thrown into confusion because, terrified by the awareness of their sins and driven by fear of eternal punishments, they will always live in dread and, while still alive, will endure with daily terror the severe torments that await after death.

“‘Are you angry, Lord, with the rivers, or is your wrath against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea?’” The prophet questions the Lord and speaks as if in doubt: O Lord, when you made the river Jordan turn backward, and when you divided the sea to make a way for your people, were you angry with the rivers, or was your indignation against the sea? For the insensible elements had done nothing to offend you or deserve your indignation. Therefore, just as you then fought on behalf of your people, so now, mounting your horses and taking up your bow, you will grant salvation to your people.

It must be understood, however, that there are good rivers and evil ones, and likewise a sea that is good and sweet, as well as one that is utterly bad and bitter. The river is used in a good sense when the Psalmist says: “The river’s stream makes glad the city of God”; but in an evil sense when Pharaoh says through Ezekiel: “The rivers are mine, and I made them.” The sea too is used in a good sense where the psalm says: “The earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof. He founded it upon the seas.” The evil rivers, then, are the doctrines of heretics, which, like rivers, flow with frothing eloquence and run against the truth. The Lord is angry with these, and his wrath is against them. The sea, however, signifies the souls of those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine and are always in the depths. The Lord’s indignation is present in such people because they favor perverse teachers; yet his wrath has not fully kindled against them, but they are given time to recover from their errors.

“‘You who mount your horses, and your chariots are salvation.’” God’s horses are the souls of the saints, upon which the Lord mounts in order to possess them and direct them from the byways of error to the path of truth. One of these horses was the man who said: “I became like a beast before you.” The prophet Elisha is surrounded by these horses and chariots, which he also showed to his frightened servant. For Scripture says in the Book of Kings: “He looked, and behold, the mountain was full of fiery horses and fiery chariots around Elisha.” It should also be noted that among so many thousands of horses and chariots, no rider is seen. For the rider and charioteer was the one to whom the Psalmist sings: “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself.” God mounts such horses, and his chariots are salvation; or, as another translation says, “Your cavalry is health.” God’s cavalry is the multitude of all the righteous and the salvation of the whole human race, because, riding among the saints, he has traversed and saved the entire world.

“‘Awakening, you will awaken your bow’”—that is, what you promised in the Old Testament you will fulfill in the New. For by the bow, which is stretched between two horns, the two Testaments are understood. Hence what follows explains what the bow is: “‘The oaths that you spoke to the tribes.’” “You will awaken,” he says, “the bow”—the oaths that you spoke to the tribes of Israel concerning the coming of your Son, once they have been fulfilled.

*(Diapsalma.)* “‘You will split the rivers of the earth; the mountains saw you and writhed.’” The rivers of the earth are the hearts of earthly people, which were split open and laid bare through repentance when the apostles preached, so that they might receive the seed of God’s word. At the Lord’s Passion also the rocks were split, signifying that the hard hearts of the nations had to be broken open through faith. The mountains saw this—that is, the hostile powers—and writhed with envy at the salvation of the nations. Or the mountains are the lofty kingdoms of the earth and the exalted powers of the world. They saw the faith of Christ grow and spread, and they writhed, raising a most grievous persecution against the saints.

Hence it follows: “The torrent of waters passed by.” The torrent of waters is the mighty storm of persecution; it passed by, that is, subsided, after the mountains—that is, the powers of the world—acknowledged Christ. Or, in another sense, the torrent of waters is the preaching of the apostles, which passed through the world once it had been proclaimed to all its boundaries.

“The abyss gave its voice”—that is, the profound preaching of the apostles resounded throughout the world. “The height will lift its hands”—that is, divine power manifested itself through miraculous works; for lifting the hands means performing wonders. Alternatively: “The abyss gave its voice”—that is, the underworld, overcome by Christ, praised the conqueror of death. “The height lifted its hand”—that is, the angelic height, dancing as though in applause, praised Christ.

“The sun and moon stood in their dwelling.” According to the literal sense, as Isidore says, after the day of judgment the sun and moon will not set by descending beneath the earth, but will always remain visible above the earth: the sun in the east and the moon in the west, visible to the whole world. They will not descend beneath the earth, lest they display their light to the underworld.

In a deeper sense, “the sun and moon stood in their dwelling,” because Christ, who is the true sun, rose from the dead and ascended to heaven, his dwelling; while the moon—that is, the Church—remained steadfast and unwavering in the faith it had received. Another translation expresses this more clearly: “The sun was lifted up at its rising, and the moon stood in its order.”

“In the light of your arrows they will go, in the splendor of your flashing spear.” The order of the words is: “Your arrows and your spears will go in light and in the splendor of your flashing spear.” God’s arrows and spears are the apostles, because just as arrows and spears shine and wound, so the apostles shone through miracles and wounded through their preaching, announcing eternal punishments to sinners.

Alternatively: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling.” O God, the sun and moon and every splendor of signs by which you had previously illumined your people had been covered by the weight of evils and by a kind of horror of darkness; but when you appeared, they stood in their dwelling—that is, they recovered their splendor and power. Therefore the faithful peoples will undoubtedly go “in the light of your arrows and in the splendor of your flashing spear”; that is, they will walk through the path of this life in the light of your commandments, which, like arrows or spears, wound for salvation and terrify in order that they may amend their ways.

“In tumult you will trample the earth.” In the terrible preaching of the apostles you will trample the earth—that is, you will crush the hearts of earthly people—“and in fury,” that is, through the threat of judgment.

“You will make the nations”—earthly kingdoms and every power of the world—“stand amazed.” For “you have gone forth,” O God the Father, “for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your anointed,” that is, with your Son, whom above all the saints you anointed with the chrism of singular grace. As the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

“You struck the head from the house of the wicked.” The head is the ruler of this world; his house is the world, or the sinner’s soul, in which he rests as in his own lodging. Thus the head is struck from the house of the wicked so that, once it has been struck, the house may become God’s house and the dwelling of righteousness.

“You stripped the foundation as far as the neck.” You revealed to the faithful all the cunning and secret counsels of that wicked one, as far as the neck—that is, as far as the one who is himself the head and prince of spiritual wickedness, namely the Antichrist. For just as the neck is joined beneath the head, so he is subordinate to the devil’s wickedness and, as it were, its administrator of deception. Hence the Apostle says: “That we may not be outwitted by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his designs.”

*(Diapsalma.)* “You cursed his scepters.” A scepter is a royal insignia, and therefore the royal power is indicated by the scepter. God cursed the scepters of that wicked one—that is, his kingdom and power. According to the treatment of the preceding prophecy, we may understand “the wicked one” in a particular sense as Nebuchadnezzar, or more generally as every adversary of God’s people, or even the devil himself.

Concerning him it continues: “The head of his warriors”—understand, “you cursed.” “Not only,” he says, “his scepters, but also the very head whom you had struck, you cursed.” The head of his warriors is the devil, the head of those who persecute the Church, such as Nero, Domitian, and the others who imposed public persecution upon the Church.

“‘When they came’”—that is, those who were coming—“‘like a whirlwind,’” like a storm with immense terror, “‘to scatter me’”—that is, the unity of the holy Church. “Their rejoicing”—that is, the rejoicing of the persecutors—“was like that of one who devours the poor in secret.” Just as a plunderer rejoices when he strips a poor man while no one sees or comes to his aid, so the persecutors of the saints rejoiced as though God neither saw nor knew whom they were afflicting. This may also be said of every perverse person who rejoices when he sins with impunity, thinking that he can remain hidden from God and that God does not know what he is doing.

“You made a way in the sea for your horses.” God’s horses are the apostles and the other preachers, for whom God made a way in the sea—that is, in the world—so that they could travel throughout the earth. They could not, by their own strength, have reached so many savage nations to preach among them, unless he had made the way by reconciling the diversity of peoples under the single rule of the Romans.

“In the mud of many waters”—that is, in the idolatry of many nations you made a way for your preachers, so that they might reject it and proclaim it to be trampled underfoot like mud.

“I heard”—not with the bodily ear, but with the understanding of the mind. And what did he hear? Those things, namely, which were spoken by the Father to the Son concerning his birth and Passion, through which he was to redeem the world.

“And my belly was troubled”—that is, my understanding: I wondered why I had dared to criticize God’s judgments, since even the Son of God himself, who had no sin, endured so many things, and such unworthy things, from the unworthy.

“At the voice”—understand, “of this hearing”—“my lips trembled,” so that I would no longer dare to speak or complain about why the righteous suffer in the world.

“Let rottenness enter my bones, and let it seethe beneath me.” The prophet, now certain that the saints are trained by adversities in this life so that they may be led to true rest in the next, says that he willingly wishes to suffer every adversity. He desires to be tested and afflicted by bodily illness like Job, saying: “Let rottenness enter my bones,” so that not only the flesh but even the marrow of his bones may decay. “And let it seethe beneath me”—that is, let it boil with a multitude of worms. By this he shows himself ready to endure every most severe and final punishment.

And why? “That I may rest in the day of tribulation”—that is, on the day of judgment, when there will be tribulation such as there has never been before—and “that I may go up to our girded people.” The order is: “that I may go up to our girded people,” that is, to the people equipped and prepared to resist spiritual enemies.

“For the fig tree will not blossom.” The fig tree signifies the Jewish people, to whom the Lord came seeking the fruit of righteousness and found none; immediately he cursed it, saying: “May fruit never come from you.” Thus, foreseeing that the Jews would remain in their unbelief, the prophet, full of sorrow, says: “The fig tree will not blossom”—that is, the synagogue of the unbelieving Jews will produce neither the flower of faith nor the fruit of good works.

He did not say this about everyone, but about those who were blinded, most of whom perished. When the fullness of the nations has entered, then this fig tree will blossom, and all Israel will be saved.

“And there will be no bud on the vines.” We learn from many passages of Holy Scripture that the people are called a vine; one such passage is: “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” This vine, planted in the patriarchs and nobly cultivated in the prophets, bore fruit most acceptable to God, but when the Lord appeared it degenerated. When it ought to have produced grapes, it produced wild grapes; that is, when it ought to have believed in Christ, who had been promised and sent to it, it instead denied him and demanded his death, saying: “We have no king but Caesar,” and, “Crucify him, crucify him.”

Foreseeing this, the holy prophet laments, saying: “There will be no bud on the vines”—that is, no root of good works in the Jews.

“The work of the olive will lie.” Anyone who has read the Apostle Paul discussing the broken branches of the olive tree and the wild olive grafted into the good olive can recognize that the olive signifies the synagogue. The work of this olive was anointing, because in the Old Testament kings and prophets were anointed with visible oil. The prophet foretells that this anointing will cease at Christ’s coming, just as Daniel says: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing will cease.”

Or in this way: “The work of the olive will lie”—that is, the Jewish people will prove false, though they had promised to fulfill everything the Lord commanded, saying: “All that the Lord our God has commanded we will do, and we will obey him.”

“And the fields will not yield food.” He designates earthly Jerusalem by the name of fields, that is, plains. Although it was situated on mountains, and it had been said of it: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains,” after it refused to receive the Son of God it is called low-lying and level, having fallen from the height of virtue. Thus the fields will not yield food, because the Jewish people will now produce no harvest of faith or good works.

“The flock will be cut off from the fold”—that is, from Jerusalem, in which it dwelt like a flock in a fold. The undifferentiated multitude of the people will be cut off, destroyed by Titus and Vespasian through the sword, famine, and captivity.

“And there will be no herd in the stalls”—that is, the priests, scribes, and other rulers who, like fat bulls, presided over the subject peoples as over herds and indulged themselves as though in full stalls. Thus there will be no herd in the stalls, because once Jerusalem was overthrown, all that dignity of the rulers was abolished, and what the Lord had said was fulfilled: “Your house will be left to you desolate.”

“But I will rejoice in the Lord, and I will exult in God my Jesus.” After the destruction foretold for the people, the rulers, and the whole city, the prophet speaks in his own person and in that of all the apostles and saints: “I will rejoice in the Lord,” he says, not in riches and not in the glory of this world, “and I will exult in God my saving Jesus.” For Jesus is interpreted as “savior” or “saving one,” but the translator preferred to retain the Hebrew word itself, because the name Jesus, sweet and full of joy, is always delightful to hear.

“God the Lord is my strength.” Christ, who is my God, is all my virtue and all my righteousness.

“And he will set my feet like those of deer.” It is the nature of deer to abandon level and low places, climb the steep heights of mountains, and even kill serpents drawn from their caves by their breath. So the saints abandon earthly and lowly things, strive toward heavenly realities, and through their preaching drive the malice of the ancient serpent from human hearts.

The prophet therefore says: “God the Lord will set my feet”—that is, my actions—“like those of deer,” making me, by his grace, despise what is fleeting and desire what is eternal.

“And he will lead me upon my heights, singing psalms to the victor.” He will lead me upon my heights—that is, to that heavenly homeland prepared for me and for all the saints before the ages. Therefore I confidently say: “Upon my heights.” He himself will lead me, because this is not my power but his grace.

He will lead me singing to the victor—that is, to Christ, triumphant over death and the devil. He will therefore lead me upon the heights, that is, to the blessed assembly of the heavenly city, which consists of angels and holy human beings, so that, joined and united with them, I may sing with the angels to the victor: “Glory to God in the highest.” I will also sing in psalms of praise, joining my song with the psalmist David: “The king will rejoice in your strength, O Lord.”

# ON THE PROPHET SOPHONIAH

The prophet Zephaniah, who is ninth in the order of the Twelve Prophets, is interpreted as “watchtower” or “the Lord’s secret.” He sees the captivity of the city of Jerusalem, whose overthrow was already imminent during the reign of Josiah, the most righteous king, under whom Zephaniah also prophesied. He proclaims the devastation of other nations and thunders forth the day of judgment.

# CHAPTER ONE

“The word of the Lord that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.”

The Hebrews relate that whenever a prophet’s father or grandfather is mentioned in a title, those ancestors too were prophets. Therefore Zephaniah here was born from a prophetic line through his grandfathers and ancestors. Zephaniah had Cushi as his father, Gedaliah as his grandfather, Amariah as his great-grandfather, and Hezekiah as his great-great-grandfather.

Zephaniah, as was said, is interpreted as “watchtower” or “secret.” The prophets were watchmen, as is said to Ezekiel: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel.” The Lord’s secrets were also revealed to them, as it says in Amos: “The Lord God does nothing without revealing his word to his servants the prophets.”

This watchman, then, was the son of Cushi, whose name is interpreted as “humility” or “my Ethiopian.” His grandfather was Gedaliah, whose name means “greatness of the Lord”; his great-grandfather was Amariah, interpreted as “the word of the Lord”; and his great-great-grandfather was Hezekiah, whose name is rendered as “the strength of the Lord.”

Thus from the strength of the Lord is born the word of the Lord; from the word of the Lord, the greatness of the Lord; and from the greatness of the Lord, humility is generated, because the more someone ascends toward the perfection of virtue, the more he humbles himself, saying with the prophet: “I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord,” and so forth.

He will also confess himself to be God’s Ethiopian, since Cushi is interpreted as “my Ethiopian”; that is, he will acknowledge himself to be a sinner and say with the Apostle John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves,” and so forth.

Such a great and remarkable man is rightly said to have lived in the days of Josiah, the most holy king, whose name is interpreted as “the elevation of the Lord.” Thus, in the time of elevation, the son of humility arose, because through humility we are raised to heavenly elevation.

“‘Gathering I will gather everything from the face of the earth,’ says the Lord, ‘gathering man and beast, gathering the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea.’”

For a long time the Lord had awaited sinful Judah under wicked kings. They might even have had some excuse and said: “We wish to serve the Lord, but we are prevented by our kings.” Therefore he gave them the most righteous king Josiah, who wished by his example and admonitions to bring them back to the worship of God; yet they nevertheless persisted in idolatry.

Accordingly, the overthrow of Jerusalem, the captivity of the people, and the victory of Nebuchadnezzar are rightly prophesied against them.

“Gathering I will gather everything.” “I will no longer,” he says, “wait for repentance, but, gathering everything, I will consume it.” No human being, no beast, no birds, and no fish will remain; even the irrational animals will feel my anger. Since everything was created for the sake of humanity, the killing of human beings is rightly followed by solitude and the scarcity of beasts.

“And the ruins of the wicked will be.” This same prophecy may also be referred to the first coming of the Lord, when some were gathered from Jews and nations through faith: some like human beings endowed with reason, others like simple and uneducated cattle, others light like birds, and others curious like fish that search the depths of the sea.

“And the ruins of the wicked will be.” The ruins of the wicked will exist not only at the final judgment, when they hear, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire,” but this also occurred at the first coming, when the Lord came for the downfall of those who stood wickedly, so that those living in sin might die and begin to live in righteousness. Or, more simply, at Christ’s first coming there were the ruins of the wicked who denied Christ and refused to receive his faith.

“And I will destroy human beings from the face of the earth, says the Lord, and I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” The stretching out of the hands displays the gesture of one striking.

“And I will destroy from this place the remnants of Baal”—that is, his worshipers, who had remained in Judah after the slaughter of the enemies. For they had reached such great impiety that they placed a statue of Baal in God’s temple and worshiped God and idols in the same sanctuary. Ezekiel calls this image the “idol of jealousy.”

“And the names of the shrine-attendants together with the priests.” Shrine-attendants are doorkeepers, that is, guardians of buildings; in Hebrew they are called *Nethinim*. Here, however, he contemptuously calls the priests shrine-attendants, just as we call people devoted to a shrine—that is, a temple—“fanatics.” He therefore threatens to destroy both the shrine-attendants and the former priests of God.

“And those who worship upon the roofs the host of heaven, and worship and swear by the Lord, and swear by Melchon.” Standing upon the roofs, that is, on the rooftops, they worshiped the sun, moon, and other stars; and at the same time they swore by the name of the Lord and by the name of Melchon, which is interpreted as “king.”

“And those who turn away from behind the Lord, and those who have not sought the Lord nor searched him”—understand, “I will destroy” them: those who, turning away from the worship of the Lord, worship the host of heaven, swear by the names of idols, and worship Baal and the idol of the Sidonians.

In the tropological sense, Jerusalem signifies the Lord’s Church. At his coming he will destroy from it all idolatry and the remnants of the Baals, a name interpreted as “in higher places,” that is, empty glory and the pomp of false admiration. He will also destroy those who swear by the Lord and by Melchon—that is, those who think they can serve both God and the world, although the Lord says the opposite: “No one can serve two masters.”

They turn away from behind the Lord—that is, by inclining toward evil works, they abandon the path by which they ought to have followed the Lord. “Behind the Lord” may also signify his bodily coming, by which he was visible, just as his face may signify the divinity that cannot be seen as it is by any creature. Hence it was said to Moses: “There is a place by me, and you shall stand upon the rock. When my glory has passed by, I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back.”

Those who withdraw from behind the Lord are those who either do not believe that he became incarnate or despise his commandments.

“Be silent before the face of the Lord God, because the day of the Lord is near.” Let him be silent, show reverence, and tremble. Literally, we understand the day of the Lord as the time of captivity and vengeance upon the Jewish people. Spiritually, it is not unreasonable to understand it as the day of the final judgment.

“For the Lord has prepared a sacrifice; he has sanctified his invited ones.” By the prepared sacrifice he means the people, who at the time of vengeance were to be slaughtered like a sacrificial victim. “He has sanctified his invited ones,” as though they had been invited to a solemn banquet. Those holding a feast customarily sanctified themselves—that is, washed and put on more splendid garments.

We should understand the invited ones as Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, whom he himself summoned to punish sinners; for through his servant Jeremiah he says: “I have summoned Nebuchadnezzar my servant.”

Some understand the day of the Lord, when he prepared his sacrifice, as referring to his first coming, when the singular sacrifice—that is, Christ the true Lamb—was offered. They understand the invited and sanctified ones as the apostles and those who came to faith through them.

“And it will be on the day of the Lord’s sacrifice: I will visit the princes and the sons of the king.” The day of the Lord’s sacrifice is the time of the Jewish captivity, when the whole people was to be sacrificed by its enemies.
