At that time the Lord visited the princes and the sons of King Josiah, all of whom are known either to have been taken captive or killed. Or, more generally, he calls the royal offspring the sons of the king.

“And upon all who are clothed in foreign clothing”—that is, exotic and costly clothing—or upon those who worshiped idols in place of the worship of God.

“And I will visit everyone who arrogantly crosses the threshold on that day”—that is, those who once, in the pride and haughtiness of their dignity, climbed the steps or threshold of the temple. In the Hebrew truth it reads: “Those who cross the threshold,” which is what the worshipers of Dagon do: they do not tread upon the threshold of that temple, but cross over it.

“Who fill the house of the Lord their God with iniquity and deceit”—that is, with riches acquired through iniquity.

In the tropological sense, heretics are clothed in foreign garments. Having abandoned the garment of Christ that we received in baptism, they assume impiety in place of piety and falsehood in place of truth. They too arrogantly cross the threshold, those who despise the simplicity of faith and fill the Church with iniquity and deceit through their preaching of error.

“And it will be on that day, says the Lord, a voice of outcry from the Fish Gate, and a howling from the Second Gate, and great destruction from the hills.”

Literally, he calls the Fish Gate the gate that was nearer the sea and led toward Diospolis and Joppa. What follows, “A howling from the Second,” refers to the gate of the second wall on the same route toward the sea. We also read of a Second Jerusalem in the Book of Kings: “He sent to the prophetess Huldah, the wife of Shallum, who lived in Jerusalem in the Second.”

“Destruction from the hills” designates the disturbance from Mount Zion, that is, from the higher part of the city; once it was captured, the descent toward the lower areas was easier.

In the tropological sense, the Fish Gate expresses the sense of sight; the Second Gate, the sense of hearing. For sinners will chiefly be judged through these two senses—hearing and sight—through which the delight of sin flows into the remaining senses. There will be great destruction from the hills because everything that had been exalted will be crushed. For the voice of the Lord is against every proud and arrogant person, and he will be humbled.

Some understand the two gates as baptism and repentance. From the first gate there will be the voice of those who did not preserve what they promised in baptism; from the second gate, the howling of those who did not repent of the sins they committed after baptism.

“Howl, inhabitants of the Mortar; the whole people of Canaan has fallen silent.” Here we must understand “mortar” as a vessel in which grain is pounded—that is, beaten—and the first syllable is long. For there is another word, with the first syllable short, meaning a ball with which children play.

He therefore calls Jerusalem a mortar, for just as grain is struck from above with force and impact by a pestle, so the army of the Chaldeans or Romans will pour down from the Fish Gate, the Second Gate, and the hills and crush everything.

He calls the people the people of Canaan because they were committing the impieties of the Canaanites. Daniel too calls the lewd old man “a seed of Canaan.” When the enemies come, they will fall silent through excessive fear and, driven by the awareness of their crimes, will not even dare to invoke the God whom they have offended.

“All who were wrapped in silver have perished”—namely, those who trusted in riches and considered themselves, as it were, wrapped and surrounded by vast wealth, and therefore despised the poor.

It should be noted that he did not speak in the future tense, saying, “Canaan will fall silent” or “They will perish,” but in the past tense: “It has fallen silent” and “They have perished,” because what was certain to come he foresaw as though it had already come.

Nor will only those who glory in their riches perish; so too will those who are puffed up by worldly dignities, swollen with empty nobility, beauty, or bodily strength, and exalted by the other vanities of the world.

“And it will be at that time: I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will visit the men who are fixed upon their dregs.” “When,” he says, “the Chaldeans or Romans come and capture Jerusalem, then I will search every place in the city with a lamp, wherever they may be able to hide, even sewers and dark caves, so that no one can escape.”

Anyone who has read how Jerusalem was overthrown by the Romans will find that this happened exactly so. He will also visit the men fixed upon their dregs—that is, those who trust in their bodies. For he contemptuously calls bodily strength “dregs.”

Or he calls sinners fixed upon their dregs because, through the habit of sinning, they are fixed in their pleasures and do not wish to be cleansed from them by repentance. Such are those “who say in their hearts: ‘The Lord will do neither good nor evil’”—that is, he will neither repay good to the good nor repay evil to the evil.

In the tropological sense, on that day—that is, at the consummation of the world—God will search Jerusalem, meaning the Church, with a lamp, that is, in the judgment of Christ, who consists of humanity and divinity, just as a lamp consists of clay and light. Through him God the Father will execute all judgment.

He will visit the men fixed upon their dregs—that is, he will take vengeance upon those who delighted in their sins while defending their evils, blaspheming God as though he had made them such people, and removing God’s providence so that doing good would neither benefit them nor doing evil harm them.

Thus the Lord will search Jerusalem with a lamp: he will bring all hidden things into the light. An account and punishment will be demanded not only for deeds but also for idle words and the most subtle thoughts.

“And their strength will become plunder, and their houses a desolation; they will build houses but will not inhabit them; they will plant vineyards but will not drink their wine.”

This is plainly said of the Jews, whose strength and entire army were given over to plunder at the time of the captivity, whose houses were destroyed and whose fields and vineyards were devastated. The vengeance was neither delayed nor did God’s patience wait any longer; rather, he swiftly repaid them what they deserved.

But according to the tropological sense, on the day of judgment all the strength of the wicked will be given over to plunder. They built houses not upon rock but upon sand, and they planted not a choice vine but the vine of Sodom and Gomorrah. Such a planting will therefore perish.

“The great day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery.”

Literally, all these things are spoken either of the Babylonian or of the Roman captivity. Then they experienced the bitter day, those who had provoked God to bitterness. The strong and powerful were troubled there. That day was a day of wrath, for although they had often endured God’s anger before, they had not endured it at the consummation. This wrath was their end, because they lost their place, kingdom, and nation and were scattered throughout all the regions of the world.

These things may also be referred tropologically to the consummation of the age, when there will be a bitter voice addressed to those who are on the left: “Go into the eternal fire,” and so forth. The strong man will be troubled there, because even the saints will be shaken with fear and the powers of heaven will be moved. It will also be a day of wrath, tribulation, and distress, when all the nations will mourn and there will be no place of escape; no one will help another.

It will be “a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind.” Darkness must pursue those who, while doing evil, hated the light.

It will be “a day of trumpet and blast,” which, as the Apostle says, will be the judgment that takes place “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.”

All these things will be “against the fortified cities”—that is, against every confidence and presumption of the world—and “against the lofty battlements” (*angulos excelsos*; the source’s *angelos* is evidently corrupt), namely, against perverse works that turn aside from the Lord’s straight path.

“And I will distress the people, and they will walk like blind men, [Col. 0201D] because they have sinned against the Lord; their blood will be poured out like earth, and their bodies like dung. Their silver and gold will not be able to save them on the day of the Lord’s wrath and fury. In the fire of his jealousy the whole earth will be devoured, because he will make a swift end of all the inhabitants of the earth.”

It is clear that Jerusalem endured all these things because they sinned against the Lord Christ by handing him over to death. Then they walked like blind men, not knowing what they were doing; and because they had shed the blood of the prophets, and the blood of him who is the Lord of the prophets, therefore their blood was poured out like earth, and their bodies lay unburied like dung. Their riches also, acquired through iniquity [Col. 0202A] and excessive anxiety, will not be able to save their masters and possessors, because the fire of the Lord’s wrath will devour them and the whole land of their kingdom. The Lord, however, will make a swift end. For in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion, Jerusalem was taken by the Romans, and the end came swiftly.

But at the end of the world also the wicked will be distressed—that is, carnal people and those who have lived according to human standards—and they will walk like blind men because they have lost the true light. As for what follows, “Their blood will be poured out like earth,” blood will not be able to be poured out on the day of judgment, since their bodies will already be immortal. Therefore, by the name “blood” we should understand that by which the soul is nourished and lives, namely faith, [Col. 0202B] hope, love, and the other virtues in which the soul’s life consists. Whoever, then, has poured out this blood of the soul—that is, whoever has killed a person through a bad example or perverse teaching—will have his blood poured out on the day of judgment; that is, if anything vital seemed to exist in his good works, he will be compelled to lose it.

## CHAPTER II

“Gather yourselves together, assemble, nation not worthy of love.” After the evils just described, which they were going to suffer, the prophet summons the people to repentance: “Gather yourselves together, assemble in the unity of love, you who were scattered by sins. ‘Nation not worthy of love,’” that is, unworthy of God’s love.

“Before the vision gives birth to a day passing like dust, before the anger of the Lord’s fury comes upon you,” that is, before what has been foretold is fulfilled—things that will come so easily unless you forestall them by repentance, as dust is carried away by the slightest wind. Here one should consider how great God’s mercy is: he summons them to mercy lest he do what he has threatened. Tropologically, this is a general exhortation to everyone: let them gather into the fellowship of the Church and forestall God’s wrath through repentance, so that the day of judgment may not find them unprepared.

“Seek the Lord, all you meek of the earth, who have practiced his judgment.” The prophet’s voice is addressed to the saints: O saints and elect, who fulfill the Lord’s commandments, who, placed on earth, have heard the voice saying, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess [Col. 0202D] the earth,” and have imitated his meekness and practiced justice, seek the Lord by loving and worshiping him. And as though someone asked who this Lord is, the answer follows:

“Seek the just one, seek the meek one, if perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury”—that is, Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment. The meek are therefore commanded to seek the meek one, so that what is lacking in them may be perfected by him who is the end of all virtues. It must also be said that, while speaking to the just and the meek, he says, as though uncertainly, “If perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury.” What, then, will become of sinners?

“For Gaza will be destroyed, and Ashkelon will become a desert. [Col. 0203A] Ashdod they will drive out at noon, and Ekron will be uprooted.” Such, he says, will be the strength of the Chaldean army that even the most powerful cities of the Philistines, which had always resisted us in equal combat, will be seized by the same captivity.

Mystically, Gaza, which means “his strength,” signifies those who trust in bodily strength and worldly power. They will therefore be destroyed and reduced to nothing. Ashkelon means “weighed” or “murderous fire”; it signifies sinners who will be judged according to the measure of their crimes, and it will be repaid to them by the same measure with which they measured others—those who burned with the desire to shed blood and with zeal to scandalize and kill souls. They will be led into a desert and handed over to the fires of Gehenna.

Ashdod, which means “fire of generation,” signifies those who burn with a free and unrestrained fire in these matters. They will therefore be driven out at noon—that is, in the open and clear light—into the outer darkness, when the saints receive complete radiance.

Ekron, which is called “sterility” or “uprooting,” figuratively signifies those who have no fruits of good works and who, through perverse teaching, tear many away from the love of God. They too will be uprooted from the land of the living.

“Woe to those who inhabit the seacoast, nation of the lost.” After naming the four great cities of Palestine, the prophetic word is now directed against the whole province, and it foretells that those who lived beside the sea would also be devastated. What follows—“The word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the Philistines; I will destroy you so that there will be no inhabitant”—shows [Col. 0203C] that the Philistines were Canaanites, and the prophet threatens them with such devastation that their strongly fortified cities will be turned into shepherds’ folds:

“And the seacoast will become a resting place for shepherds and sheepfolds, and the seacoast will belong to the remnant of the house of Judah,” that is, of Canaan or Philistia. “There they will pasture; in the houses of Ashkelon they will lie down in the evening.” When the sons of Judah return from captivity under Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and Nehemiah, the entire land of the Philistines, who were held in captivity, will become their possession. It will be so deserted that shepherds from the remnant of the Jews will make their flocks lie down after midday in Ashkelon, once a most renowned city. This will happen “because the Lord their God will visit them and turn away their captivity [Col. 0203D].”

This is the historical meaning. In the spiritual sense, however, the cities of the Philistines whose destruction is foretold signify the pride of the Gentiles, according to the interpretation of their names given above. They are “those who inhabit the seacoast,” because they are battered by the various waves of error. Once their pride has been destroyed, the house of Judah—that is, the true confession of the Church—begins to dwell in their places: piety succeeds impiety, justice drives out injustice, and humility brings pride beneath itself.

“I have heard the reproach of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon, by which they reproached my people.” After the predicted calamity of the Philistines and the destruction of the cities of that land, the prophet now turns against Moab and the sons of Ammon [Col. 0204A] and foretells evils that will come upon them because they aided the Babylonians against God’s people, helping them overthrow the city and the Temple, and because, while mocking the captive Jews, they blasphemed God.

“I have heard the reproach of Moab.” This city belongs to Arabia and is now called Areopolis, that is, “the city of Mars.” “And the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon,” which is also a city of Arabia and is now called Philadelphia. The same name is used for both the region and the city. “And they have magnified themselves over their borders”: after expelling the former inhabitants, they enlarged their boundaries in their land.

“Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Moab will be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah.” How this was fulfilled literally cannot be explained. These cities were not overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, nor was their land burned by clouds of sulfur and turned into ashes and embers. Cities are still inhabited there, although their names have changed, and the region is cultivated. We must therefore have recourse to the spiritual meaning.

Moab and Ammon were sons of Lot, born from incestuous unions. Lot means “one who turns aside”; Moab means “from the father”; Ammon, “my people.” These therefore signify heretics and all inventors of wicked doctrines, who, turning aside from the true Father God, have become sons of the devil and hear from the Lord, “You are from your father the devil.” They are no longer God’s people, having been born in a dark cavern.

They therefore mock the simplicity of the Church and magnify themselves over its borders, acting against what Solomon says: “Do not transgress [Col. 0204C] the boundaries established by your fathers.” Under a solemn declaration, he threatens them that, just as those cities were physically overthrown, so they will be overthrown by eternal condemnation, and that fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms will be their portion in the cup.

“Dryness of thorns, heaps of salt, and a desert forever.” Heretics are rightly called “dryness of thorns,” because, like thorns, they continually wound and tear apart the unity of the Church, withering through their impiety and fit for nothing except to be cast into the eternal fire. They are also “heaps of salt,” because, like tasteless salt, they are thrown out of the Church and trampled by everyone.

Therefore, “the remnant of my people will plunder them, and the survivors of my nation will possess them.” This will happen to them because of their pride, [Col. 0204D] because they blasphemed and magnified themselves over the people of the Lord of hosts. “The Lord will be terrible against them, and he will waste away all the gods of the earth, and men will worship him, each from his place, all the islands of the nations.” This refers to teachers and preachers of the truth, who destroy the false knowledge of heretics and plunder their impious doctrines.

“But you also, Ethiopians, will be slain by my sword; and he will stretch out his hand toward the north and destroy Assyria. He will make the beautiful city a desolation, an inaccessible place, and like a desert; flocks will lie down in its midst, all the beasts of the nations, and the onocrotalus and the hedgehog will dwell on its thresholds.”

All these things said about Philistia, Moab, and the sons of Ammon [Col. 0205A] the Jews refer to the advent of their Christ, whom they think will come at the end of the world, rebuild Jerusalem, free the Jews from the power of all nations, and be worshiped by everyone, according to what was said above: “Men will worship him from their place, and all the islands of the nations.” They believe that he will overcome not only the nations mentioned above, which are neighbors of the Jews, but also the Ethiopians and Assyrians, and that he will reduce Nineveh itself to a desert so that it becomes a dwelling place for beasts.

This is what is meant by the statement that “the beautiful city will be reduced to a desert,” because by “Nineveh” he understands Babylon, especially because of the similarity between the monsters, the onocrotalus and the hedgehog, which the prophet Isaiah describes as having been in Babylon after its devastation.

It should be known that there are two kinds of onocrotalus: one aquatic and the other belonging to the desert. It is called *onocrotalus* because the Greeks call a cymbal *crotalon*; since this bird has no voice, it strikes its beak together in the manner of cymbals and produces something resembling a voice. When it is said, “the voice of one singing in the window, a raven on the threshold,” they either wish demons to be understood, or the cries of various birds that usually remain in deserted cities, such as owls, horned owls, and screech owls, together with many others—all of which are signs of desolation.

“For I will weaken its strength,” that is, I will diminish the strength of Nineveh or Babylon. “This is the glorious city.” The prophet speaks as though mocking it after its ruin and saying, “This is the glorious city,” “dwelling in security, which said in its heart: I am, and there is no other besides me.” [Col. 0205C] It not only spoke this with its mouth but also thought in its heart that it was so.

“How has it become a lair for beasts? Everyone who passes by it will hiss and shake his hand.” The statement that monstrous beasts lived in the deserted city was either literally true, or, under the figure of beasts, it indicates that the different nations were transformed.

Tropologically, the Ethiopians are unbelievers who have not yet laid aside the horror of the old person like blackness. He therefore threatens those who refuse to turn toward better things and wash away the blackness of their sins: they will be slain by his sword, namely by the exceedingly sharp sword of God’s word. Thus, if they repent like the Ninevites, sin will die in them and righteousness will live.

The Lord himself threatened this, but now the prophet speaks about God [Col. 0205D] in the third person: “And he will stretch out his hand toward the north and destroy Assyria.” The north wind is exceedingly cold, and it is also called “the right hand.” It signifies the devil, who rests in the hearts of those in whom love has grown cold. The bride also wishes him to depart from the garden of the Church, saying, “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind.” He is called “right” by those who take pleasure in his coldness, although in his work he is left-handed.

After he has stretched out his hand toward the north, he will destroy Assyria, whose name means “directing,” or rather “rebuking.” It signifies the same devil, who directs all his followers toward death, and who afterwards rebukes those to whom he suggests sins and exacts punishment from them. The Lord Jesus will therefore kill him [Col. 0206A] with the breath of his mouth.

Then beautiful Nineveh—that is, the world—will perish with its prince, so that no one will pity it. Nor is it inappropriate to understand “the beautiful city” as the Church, which at the end of the world, under the persecution of Antichrist, when iniquity has increased and love has grown cold, will be placed in desolation, with only a very few remaining who truly and not falsely confess themselves to be Christians. It will be handed over to beasts and filled with the monsters of vices.

The onocrotalus, which loves the desert, signifies those who cut themselves off from the Church and prefer their own assemblies to her, producing the hiss or crash of false doctrines rather than a voice. The Septuagint has “chameleon” instead of *onocrotalus*. A chameleon is an animal that changes its colors from moment to moment, signifying those who change through different vices—now through lust, now through greed, now through cruelty, sometimes through sadness, sometimes through useless exultation.

The hedgehog is a thorny and timid animal that curls itself into a ball so that it cannot be caught. It signifies those who are surrounded by the thorns of sins, defend the sins themselves, and refuse to confess their crimes to anyone. The raven, an unclean and tearing bird, signifies those who, though unclean with vices, slander others and speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts.

## CHAPTER III

“Woe to the provoking and redeemed city, the dove that did not hear the voice and did not accept discipline. She did not trust in the Lord; she did not draw near to her God.” [Col. 0206C]

After the captivity of the various nations described above, the prophet returns to the Jews, and all his speech is directed against Jerusalem. “Woe,” he says, “to you, city, once a dove, generated by the Law for the preservation of innocence, often sinning, taken captive, and again redeemed. Woe to you, provoking city”—that is, bringing God to bitterness through your crimes; or “provoking,” because, after receiving knowledge of piety, you turned toward impiety.

To provoke God is to sin knowingly. She did not hear the Lord’s commandment, and, when reproved, refused to accept discipline. Nor, when oppressed by evils, did she trust in the Lord. Although the Lord says, “I am God who is near, and not God who is far away,” she nevertheless refused to draw near to him.

[Col. 0206D] “Her princes are in her midst like roaring lions.” The prophet describes what kind of princes, judges, or priests she had. “Her princes,” he says, “were always turning toward prey like lions and were inclined to shed the blood of their subjects.”

“Her judges are evening wolves; they leave nothing for the morning,” not leaving to others anything that they could seize.

“Her prophets are mad”—that is, insane—“men without faith,” because they spoke as though from the mouth of the Lord, but brought forth everything foolish and false. “Her priests polluted the sanctuary; they acted unjustly against the Law,” committing sacrilege in the place of the sanctuary and claiming to act according to the Law while doing everything contrary to it. Because they acted unjustly,

[Col. 0207A] “the Lord is just in her midst; he will not do iniquity,” but will repay her what she deserves. “Morning by morning”—that is, openly—“he will bring his judgment to light, and it will not be hidden. But the wicked man did not know shame.”

He did these things so that the reproved city might turn toward better things, but Israel did not know shame.

“I destroyed nations, and their corners were scattered. I made their roads desolate, so that no one passed through them. Their cities were laid waste, with no man remaining and no inhabitant. I said: Surely now you will fear me; you will accept discipline, and her dwelling will not perish because of all the things for which I visited her. Yet rising early, they corrupted all their thoughts.”

“Because,” he says, “I could not correct them through punishments, I wanted them at least to be converted through benefits and to do penance. I therefore destroyed for you, O Judah, the nations hostile to you; for your sake I laid their cities waste and made their roads impassable, so that no one would travel through them. After this I sent prophets to warn you and summon you to repentance. I did all these things so that you would fear me and accept discipline. If you had done so, your dwelling—that is, the Temple—would not have perished because of the crimes you had committed.

“While the Lord was doing these things, they rose early, as though deliberately and defiantly, to fulfill their own thoughts. They should have hastened to return to God; instead, they hastened to carry out the evil they had conceived in their minds.”

These things may also be referred tropologically to the Church, which is rightly called a dove because she has faithful people who are simple and without malice. But because within her are those who profess to know God while denying him by their deeds—such as heretics and wicked Christians—therefore it is said: “She did not hear the voice of the Lord.”

The wicked princes and judges of this Church—that is, its teachers and masters—are compared with lions and evening wolves. The Lord will scatter their ways—that is, their perverse actions—and will destroy their cities, that is, the confidence they place in perverse doctrines. He will also bring his judgment to light when the night of this world has ended. It will not be hidden when he begins to demand from his servants the money entrusted to them. Then their corners will be scattered—that is, their perverse pleasures, which turn aside from the straight path.

Although he does these things, the Lord nevertheless does not depart from her, but admonishes her to fear him and accept [Col. 0207D] discipline. Yet because he is just, he does not spare sinners but repays them what they deserve.

“Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection in the future, because my judgment is to gather the nations and assemble the kingdoms.” The Jews and those among us who Judaize refer this to the times of Antichrist. They think that he will gather together all the kingdoms of the world under his single rule, and that then all people will speak one language, namely Hebrew, as occurred before the Flood.

We, however, following blessed Jerome, should refer this to the present times of the Church. “Wait for me,” he says, “on the day of my resurrection”—that is, prepare yourself for the time of my resurrection. When, after sins and vices, which are the death of the soul, we are prepared for a good life, Christ rises in us. Since he himself is the head and all the elect are his members, he is rightly said both to die and to rise together with his members, and also to sit with them on his throne, according to what he promised in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers I will grant to sit on my throne.” The Apostle likewise says: “He made us alive together and made us sit together in the heavenly places.”

It may also be understood in this way: “Wait for me on the day of my resurrection,” that is, at the time of the final judgment, when all will rise and I, together with my rising members, will rise; then the nations will be gathered and the kingdoms assembled—that is, the powers of the world, or the teachers of perverse doctrines.

“And I will pour out upon them my indignation and [Col. 0208B] all the anger of my fury.” The Lord’s indignation is poured out upon those who have sinned less; they are signified by the nations. But upon those who are powerful in evil and are founders of heresies, all the anger of the Lord’s fury is poured out.

“For in the fire of my jealousy the whole earth will be devoured”—that is, whatever is earthly and belongs to the works of the flesh. Therefore, the threat made above is not cruelty but mercy, since indignation and fury are poured out for the purpose of burning away the earth, that is, the rust of sins.

“For then I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip, so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder.” Then, he says—that is, when they have laid aside their errors—I will restore to them a chosen lip, the ancient speech of my confession.

This will occur when, according to the Apostle, every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth bows at the name of Jesus, and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. For this is what is meant by “They will serve him with one shoulder”: with equal devotion they will accept the yoke of his dominion, which is easy, and his burden, which is light.

“Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants, the children of my dispersed ones, will bring me an offering.” The word order is: “O daughter of my dispersed ones, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia they will bring an offering.” He calls the Synagogue the daughter of the dispersed, once a daughter whom he has now scattered through nearly the whole world.

The meaning is: O Israel, O once-daughter Synagogue, now scattered and captive, although you are tormented by jealousy and envy the salvation of the Gentiles, nevertheless, against your will, from Ethiopia—that is, from the Gentile world, black with sins and dark with unbelief—they will bring offerings to me. Now also the queen of Sheba, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, will come to hear the wisdom of the true Solomon. Hence the Psalmist says: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God.”

Literally, he calls the rivers of Ethiopia the Nile, which is divided into seven rivers. Spiritually, the rivers of Ethiopia are the peoples of the Gentiles, who have brought to the Lord sacrifices of thanksgiving and offerings of faith and devoted hearts.

“On that day,” he says—that is, at the time when the multitude of the Gentiles believes—“you will not be confounded,” O daughter of my dispersed ones, “over all your inventions by which you transgressed against me,” choosing Barabbas and crucifying the Son of God. [Col. 0209A]

“For then I will remove from your midst those who speak boastfully in the pride of your arrogance”—that is, the Pharisees, scribes, or priests who speak great things against the Lord. “You will no longer exalt yourself on my holy mountain”—that is, in the Church of the faithful—boasting of the nobility of your lineage and the election of your fathers.

This happened when, after the Lord’s resurrection, three thousand believed on one day through the preaching of the apostles, five thousand on another day, and many thousands thereafter; many also from the priestly class obeyed the faith.

“And I will leave in your midst a poor and needy people, and the remnant of Israel will hope in the name of the Lord.” When the Lord has removed the arrogant boasters from the midst of his people, the poor and needy will remain—namely, the apostles, uneducated men who relied on none of the world’s riches—and they will hope in the name of the Lord.

They are the remnant of Israel, of whom Isaiah says: “The remnant will be saved.” This remnant “will not do iniquity, nor will they speak” against the Lord “a lie; no deceitful tongue will be found in their mouth,” so that they say one thing with their words while plotting another in their hearts. “For they will pasture,” nourished by the food of the divine word, and they will be able to say with the Psalmist: “The Lord shepherds me, and I will lack nothing.”

“And they will lie down” securely; they will rest in the pastures of the Church, “and there will be no one to terrify them,” because the faith of believers will overcome all the savagery of persecutors.

These things may also be referred to the second advent of the Lord, when he has abolished every principality and power, and when, at last, the enemy death has been destroyed. Then the elect, free from all corruption and fear of death, will lie down securely in the pastures of the blessed vision of God.

“Praise, daughter of Zion; rejoice aloud, Israel. Rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem.” The daughter of Zion is the holy Church of the elect, which stands upon a watchtower—that is, in contemplation of the Lord. The Holy Spirit addresses her, so that she may praise and give thanks to Christ the Lord, the King of Israel, who redeemed her and who was made for her by God “righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.”

She is also the daughter of Jerusalem, which sees true peace, since Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” The present Church is the daughter of that Jerusalem which is above and which is our mother. He therefore urges her to exult, not with any kind of exultation, but with all her heart. The reason why she should rejoice and exult follows:

“The Lord has removed your judgment; the King of Israel has turned away your enemies.” This means condemnation, which he removed when he forgave the iniquity of his people and redeemed them with his precious blood. More fully, he will remove her judgment at the end of the world, when he redeems her from destruction and strengthens her in mercy.

He will also turn away her enemies—that is, all persecutors, or even the hosts of demons—and everything contrary to the peace of eternal rest. “The Lord is in your midst; you will no longer fear evil.” He himself said: “I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them.” The Son himself also promises, saying: “We will come and make our dwelling with him.” Since he dwells with us and in our midst, we will no longer fear evil.

“On that day it will be said to Jerusalem: Do not fear.” On that day—that is, at the end of the world—it will be said to Jerusalem, the free mother of the saints, either by angels or by the Holy Spirit: “Do not fear.” It will also be said to “Zion,” that is, to the Church herself, who happily contemplates God: “Let not your hands grow slack,” because you will no longer do anything for which you must repent. He shows where such security comes from by adding:

“The Lord your God is in your midst; the mighty one himself will save you. He will rejoice over you with gladness,” and “he will be silent,” not reckoning your sins against you, “in his love,” that is, in the love with which he freely loved you. “And he will exult over you with praise,” either by making you worthy of praise or by causing you to praise him with exultation.

“I will gather the *nugas*, those who had withdrawn from the Law,” that is, the useless and frivolous, who had withdrawn from your bosom by transgressing the Law. “Because they were from you, so that you may no longer bear reproach over them.” According to the Apostle, God did not reject his people whom he foreknew. I will therefore gather these people and bring them back to you, freeing them from the power of demons, so that you may no longer suffer reproach over their destruction.

It should be known that *nugas* is a Hebrew word used among the Latins. From this we can understand that the Hebrew language is the mother of all languages.

“Behold, I will kill all those who afflicted you at that time, and I will save the lame, and I will gather the one who had been cast out.” This is an open consolation of the Holy Spirit addressed generally to the Church, or specifically to each faithful soul.

There are many who reproach and mock either the whole Church or every holy soul when they see a holy man despising worldly things and seeking heavenly ones. They usually say: “He is insane; he does not live as we do; he avoids human gatherings, despises the pleasures of the world,” and other things of this kind.

Unbelievers reproach him for the cross of Christ; and if they see him in some temptation, they say what the relatives of the holy Tobias also said: “Where are the righteousness and almsgiving that you used to practice?”

The Lord therefore promises that he will take vengeance on such people: “Behold,” he says, “I will kill all those who afflicted you at that time, and I will save the lame”—either the afflicted Church or the faithful soul, which in the present life, pressed by the persecution of the devil or his members, wavers amid the storms of the world, yet walks with a firm step and a solid tread of faith.

He will therefore save this lame and afflicted one, and gather the outcast. The Church is cast out, and every faithful soul is cast out in the eyes of lovers of the world, as the saints often complain and say in the Psalms: “But now you have rejected and confounded us.” This is not surprising, since the Son of God himself, in respect of his humanity, also says to the Father: “Yet you have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ.”

“And I will make them a praise and a name in every land of their shame, at that time when I bring you back and at the time when I gather you. For I will give you a name and a praise among all the peoples of the earth, when I turn your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord.”

Whom will he make a praise and a name, except the children of the outcast and lame woman—Peter, Paul, and the other saints, whose names are magnified in glory throughout the churches spread across the whole world?

This will happen when he brings and receives the children of the afflicted woman, when they are placed in glory, and when the Lord is glorified in their victory and triumphs, just as he was glorified in Job’s endurance against the devil. Then those whom people presently thought miserable will be seen to be happy. Then they will see their captivity brought back to the heavenly Jerusalem in eternal glory, while they themselves rise to eternal shame.

## ON THE PROPHET HAGGAI

[Col. 0211]

[Col. 0211A] The prophet Haggai is interpreted “festive” or “solemn.” [Col. 0211B] He prophesied the restoration of the Lord’s temple, the overthrow of the nations, and the shaking of the world; and under the figure of Zerubbabel he foretells Christ’s coming. He was one of those who had recently returned from the captivity of Babylon under Zerubbabel, the priest Jeshua, and Ezra, when Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord had not yet been rebuilt. The people lived in hollow and lowly houses; therefore the word of the Lord was not addressed to them. For they were unworthy that it should be addressed to them, since they took no care to rebuild the temple, were content with a low-lying, level habitation, and were subject to Darius, king of the Persians. His name is interpreted “generation not made,” or “those who have been,” and he signifies those who serve the works and lust of the flesh. Such a king was deserved by a people who were without God’s temple and lived below rather than on Mount Zion.

## CHAPTER I

“In the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of the prophet Haggai.” The number two is very frequently used in an unfavorable sense. For it divides the primal unity and therefore signifies either the marriage bond or discord. In Genesis likewise, although at the completion of all the other days it is said, “God saw that it was good,” this is not found at the end of the second day. Nor is there any legal solemnity in the sixth month, as there is in the others, because it signifies servile works and labors. Rightly, therefore, in the second year of Darius and in the sixth month, the word of God comes to Haggai [Col. 0211D] for the reasons stated above: because they had no temple, lived in hollow places, and, under Darius, served works of the flesh. But because the altar had already been built and the foundations of the temple laid, the word of the Lord came on the first day of the month, so that, leaving behind Darius’s second year, they might return to the unity of God. The statement, “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai,” shows that he had good works and that the word of God rested in those deeds. Haggai is interpreted “festive.” This suggests that the person who strives to celebrate the Lord’s feasts not in the leaven of malice and wickedness but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth can receive God’s word.

“To Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, leader of Judah, and to Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, saying.” This Shealtiel, [Col. 0212A] whose son Zerubbabel is said to have been, was the son of King Jeconiah, who was taken to Babylon. [Col. 0212B] Zerubbabel is interpreted “adjacent flow,” or “set forth,” or “born in Babylon,” or “prince in Babylon.” He signifies Christ Jesus, who built a temple for God the Father out of living stones, that is, the faithful of both Testaments. He himself has been set forth for us to drink as the stream of a most abundant spring. But in order that we may drink him, we must ask this of God, as is suggested by his father Shealtiel, whose name means “God’s request.” He was born in Babylon, and Christ, the Son of God, appeared incarnate amid the confusion of this world, so that he might rescue us who were held captive by sin and lead us back to the land of promise. The word of the Lord came to Zerubbabel and also to Jeshua the high priest. Historically they were two men, one of the tribe of Judah and royal stock, the other of the priestly tribe. Mystically, however, they signified the one and same Christ, who is the true king and great priest. Zerubbabel bore his type insofar as he was king; Jeshua, son of Jozadak—that is, “the Lord is righteous”—bore his type insofar as he was priest. For God the Father is righteous and holy, and his Son is Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: This people says, ‘The time has not yet come for the Lord’s house to be built.’” It was not Zerubbabel or Jeshua the high priest who said this, but the people who had returned from captivity and were still under Darius. In the spiritual sense, everyone who serves fleshly pleasures does not wish any longer to build within the seat of his heart a temple for the Lord of chastity. This may also be referred to the Jews of the present time, who await Antichrist in place of Christ and say that the time of the Church has not yet come, because Christ has not yet come.

“And the word of the Lord came through the prophet Haggai, saying: ‘Is it time for you yourselves to dwell in paneled houses, while this house lies desolate?’” In response to what the people were saying—“The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built”—the Lord’s answer is given. Therefore, neither is it time for you to dwell in well-appointed and ornamented houses, which are intended not merely for use but for luxury. And you say that the time has not yet come for my house to be built, in which were the Holy of Holies and the Cherubim, and which now lies foul in desolation, scorched by heat and drenched by rains.

“And now, thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways.” Since, he says, you are saying, “The time has not yet come for the house of the Lord to be built,” consider what you have done and what you have suffered. For none of all your labor has been able to yield any profit.

“You have sown much, and brought in little,” and you have gathered far less than you sowed. Yet you cannot say: “Hunger followed because the farmer ceased cultivating the land.” “You have eaten, but have not been satisfied; you have drunk, but have not been intoxicated; you have clothed yourselves, but have not been warmed. And whoever gathered wages put them into a pierced purse” [Col. 0213B]. Yet you cannot say that the fast was voluntary, but rather that you had gathered only small fruits into your barns. You drank wine, but not enough to gladden the hearts of those drinking. The garment itself could neither drive away the cold nor warm you. If anyone had gathered wages, whether through commerce or hired labor, he labored in vain, because all the money flowed away as though it had been put into a pierced purse.

Spiritually, those set their hearts upon their ways who do nothing without the judgment of discernment, who always have the lamp of God’s word before the eyes of their mind. He sows much but gathers little who labors constantly in the work of preaching, yet receives only the smallest harvest from the faith and conduct of his hearers, since he shows them to have been scandalized by word and example. He eats and is not satisfied; he drinks and is not intoxicated, who does not practice the right things he knows. Hence Solomon says: “The righteous eats and fills his soul, but the belly of the wicked is insatiable.” He puts gathered wages into a pierced purse who performs works of virtue for the sake of displaying empty glory, or who gives alms to the needy from plunder. He is clothed but is not warmed by the heat who receives divine wisdom, by which he might be adorned and defended from the cold of wickedness, but, carrying it out lukewarmly and sluggishly, is deprived of its warmth.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways. Go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house” [Col. 0213D]. Consider, he says, all that you are doing; abandoning concern for your own houses, go up to Mount Lebanon, cut wood, and build my house. “And it will be acceptable to me, and I will be glorified, says the Lord.” Why he commands only wood, and not stones, to be brought is explained by what the Hebrews say: after the temple had been burned, the walls remained, and therefore only wood was needed for the roofing. Mystically, to ascend the mountain is to climb to the height of divine contemplation through progress in virtue, and, by seeking the testimonies of Scripture, to cut them out so that from them an acceptable temple may be built for the Lord.

“You looked for more, and behold, it became less” [Col. 0214A], “and you brought it home, and I blew it away.” I shall tell you, he says, another thing that has happened to you. When the time for reaping was already approaching, and you thought that you were holding grain in your hands, you harvested empty stalks and gathered barren straw without grain. And even what had been selected as a small amount from great heaps—when you had brought it into your houses—I blew away, and by my power it was scattered and reduced to nothing.

Spiritually, those look for more and receive less who, boasting of their works, falsely promise themselves an eternal reward from the Lord. “For what reason,” says the Lord of hosts, “because my house is desolate, while each of you hastens to his own house” [Col. 0214B]. Mystically, those hasten to their own house while the house of God lies desolate who, captured by worldly desires and occupied with earthly affairs, neglect to build the temple of God.

“Therefore, because of you the heavens have been restrained from giving dew, and the earth has been restrained from giving its produce.” He says: Not only did the heavens fail to give rain, but not even the morning dew, so that the parched fields might at least be moistened by a little humidity. Typologically, the heavens are the apostles, pouring the dew and rain of heavenly teaching into the earth—that is, into the hearts of their hearers. The heavens were restrained from giving dew when, because the unbelieving Jews despised the word of salvation, the apostles were commanded to go into the whole world and preach to the Gentiles.

“And I summoned drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the grain, and upon the wine, and upon the oil, and upon everything that the soil produces, and upon human beings, and upon animals, and upon all the labor of human hands” [Col. 0214C]. Drought is summoned first upon the land, then upon everything the soil produces, and finally upon human beings and animals, because, when famine has preceded, death certainly comes upon human beings and animals; thus the same sword consumes whatever human hands had labored over.

“And Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel heard, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and all the remnant of the people, the voice of the Lord their God and the words of Haggai the prophet, just as the Lord their God had sent him to them; and the people feared before the Lord.” It must be carefully observed that neither Zerubbabel nor Joshua the priest is said to have feared, but the people feared before the Lord [Col. 0214D]. For both signify Christ, who is king and priest in two natures, divine and human, and one person. When therefore Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest heard the words of the Lord, only the multitude, which had not yet attained to a perfect man, feared before the Lord—that is, before his indignation—for the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.

“And Haggai, the messenger of the Lord, one of the messengers of the Lord, spoke to the people, saying.” From this passage some have derived an error, supposing that Haggai was an angel by nature and, through some divine dispensation, assumed a human body, because it says: “Haggai spoke, the messenger of the Lord.” They hold the same opinion about Malachi and John the Baptist. But it must be understood that by nature they were human beings, while in office they were angels—that is, messengers—who announced God’s will to the peoples. Thus this prophet is called a messenger, that is, an angel, because he bore the type of the Lord and Savior, who himself is also called the Angel of Great Counsel. When it says, “the messenger of the Lord, one of the messengers of the Lord,” this means as though it said, “a prophet among the prophets.” “I am with you, says the Lord.” He does not say this to Zerubbabel or to Joshua, but to the people who had feared before the Lord. They are understood as representing Christ, as has been said, and the Lord was always with them and in them. The Lord therefore strengthens the people, saying: “I am with you; I will be your helper.”

“And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people.” The spirit of Zerubbabel and the spirit of Joshua were stirred up so that they might build the temple through kingship and priesthood. The spirit of the remaining people was stirred up—that is, their devotion of mind and willingness—so that they might do what the Lord had commanded. “And they entered and worked on the house of the Lord of hosts, their God.” They entered because they had gone outside—that is, they had forgotten themselves—like the prodigal son, of whom it is said that he came back to himself when he resolved to return to his father.

## CHAPTER II

“On the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius.” They began to build in the same year mentioned above and in the same month, but not on the same day. Above, the first day of the month is given; here, however, the twenty-fourth day is given. From this we understand that between the first day, on which the Lord spoke through Haggai, and the twenty-fourth, on which they began to work, there were twenty-two intervening days. Among the Hebrews there are twenty-two letters. This shows that the people needed to be taught and to learn the elements of God’s word.

Mystically, as long as we are in this life, we live as though under Darius, because the flesh struggles against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; and we live in the sixth month, in which number God completed all things perfectly, and in the second year, in which number the restoration of offspring is signified. Therefore we must fear before the Lord, enter, and do the works of the Lord—that is, build a temple for the Lord within us from virtues [Col. 0215D]. The twenty-fourth day, which contains the number twelve twice, signifies the faithful who are to be gathered from both peoples, Jewish and Gentile, and who are to build the spiritual temple. This too must be said: three times eight makes twenty-four; for circumcision, which took place on the eighth day, and the building of the spiritual temple are grounded in faith in the Holy Trinity.

“On the twenty-first day of the seventh month,” “the word of the Lord came through Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying” [Col. 0216A]. It was in the same year as above—that is, the second year of Darius—but also in the seventh month and on the twenty-first day of the month, that the word of the Lord again came through Haggai. The seventh month was entirely festive and solemn. Rightly, therefore, the word of the Lord comes to Haggai—that is, “festive”—in the seventh, that is, festive, month, and on the twenty-first day of the month, with three weeks completed and the mystery of the Trinity fulfilled. For three times seven is twenty-one.

“Who is there among you who is left who saw this house in its former glory? And what do you see it to be now? Is it not, in your eyes, as though it were nothing? And now, be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, high priest; and be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord of hosts; and act, because I am with you, says the Lord of hosts, according to the word by which I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt” [Col. 0216B]. The Lord most graciously consoles the people who had seen the former house in its glory, in comparison with which this one seemed as though it did not exist. Do not despair, he says; do not let your hands sink. I am with you. I, the Almighty, have spoken; for with me, to speak is to accomplish, and I shall fulfill those things that I covenanted with you when I brought you out of Egypt.

“And my Spirit”—that is, the divinity of my majesty, or the Holy Spirit, whose work is all consolation, and hence he is also called the Paraclete—“shall be in your midst.” Here the whole Trinity is mentioned. The Father is the one who says, “I am with you”; the Son is “the word by which I covenanted with you”; the Holy Spirit is “my Spirit,” he says, “which shall be in your midst.”

“Do not fear, for thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth and the sea and the dry land, and I will shake all the nations.” When the Covenant was first given on Mount Sinai, I shook heaven, when I spoke to you from heaven; I shook the earth, when my presence was seen amid cloud, darkness, and storm; and, as the Psalmist says, “God, when you went forth before your people,” and so forth. I shook the Red Sea when I divided it and provided a way for the passing people. I also shook the dry land when I led the people for forty years through a trackless, uncultivated, and arid wilderness.

Therefore I, who then did those things, will again shake the elements themselves; and this was certainly accomplished at the Lord’s coming [Col. 0216D]. For at the time of his passion heaven was shaken, when the sun was darkened and darkness came from the sixth hour until the ninth. The earth was shaken when the rocks were split, the tombs opened, and the earth itself trembled. The sea of the present age was shaken, stirred into rebellion by the blasts of demons, when the dragon too was slain—that is, the devil was overcome, the one who lay in the sea of this age. He also shook the dry land: the barren and unfruitful hearts of the Gentiles.

With the whole universe therefore shaken, all the nations were moved when the apostles preached, because their sound went out into all the earth. “And the one desired by all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts” [Col. 0217A]. It is clear that Christ’s coming is foretold. He was desired and awaited so that he might redeem the nations; concerning him the Apostle says: “Into whom angels long to look.” After he came, therefore, the glory of the Lord’s house was fulfilled—that is, the Church, which is the house of God built from living stones. For if the house built by a servant was glorious, by as much as a servant is inferior to the Lord, so much better is the house over which the Lord presides than the one over which the servant presided.

“Mine is the silver, and mine is the gold, says the Lord of hosts. The glory of this latter house will be greater than that of the former, says the Lord of hosts.” It is as though he said: Do not doubt that I can fulfill what I promise. I am the one who created all things; silver and gold and all riches are in my hand. I shall give everything necessary for building or adorning the temple.

According to the mystical sense, gold is the spiritual meaning and understanding hidden in the Scriptures, concerning which Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” Silver, however, is the clear speech of the Scriptures, whence the Psalmist says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver,” and so forth. The Church is adorned with these metals and becomes more splendid than the Synagogue formerly was.

“And in this place I will give peace, says the Lord of hosts.” Since we know of nothing more useful for building a renowned house than peace, he promises peace itself. Once it has been granted, the other blessings will follow more easily. But in the allegorical sense, the Lord gives peace in the present Church by restraining the plots of the evil enemy [Col. 0217C] and calming the battles of vices; in the future he will give true and eternal peace.

“On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Haggai, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man carries sanctified flesh in the fold of his garment, and with the edge of it touches bread or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, will it be sanctified?” It must be noted that above it was always said, “The word of the Lord came through Haggai”; here, however, it says, “The word of the Lord came to Haggai.” Above, because he had works that were clean but had not yet received full wisdom in his heart, and because there were among them people who did not wish to build a temple for the Lord [Col. 0217D], the word of the Lord is said to have come through his agency. Now, because the foundations of the temple have already been laid, and the people together with their leaders are already carrying out the work of the Lord’s temple, the word of the Lord comes to Haggai.

The word comes in the ninth month because he is about to speak of the uncleanness of the sinful people. For the number nine is never used in a good sense in the divine Scriptures. But because time was still being granted them for doing penance, the word of the Lord comes to the prophet on the twenty-fourth day of the same month, a number in which twelve—the sacred number everywhere—is doubled.

“Ask the priests about the law.” For it is their task to know the law, and when questioned they ought to answer from the law. The prophet Haggai therefore questions them in the person of the Lord, saying: “If a man carries sanctified flesh.” Sanctified flesh was the flesh of a sacrifice offered upon the altar, although there was great diversity even among the sanctified meats, as is fully explained in Leviticus. A person was called unclean in soul if he touched a corpse. As long as the soul is in the body, the human body is not unclean, since it has a soul made in the image and likeness of God. But as soon as the soul has left the body, the body becomes unclean, being earthly and formed from the pleasure of the flesh. We say this with regard to nature; otherwise, the bodies of the saints, whose death is precious, are holy because of the merit of the holy soul that inhabited them.

The prophet asks whether any man, whoever he may be, takes sanctified flesh and binds it in the edge of his garment, and whether the edge of the garment then touches bread or any other food: can that food be sanctified by touching the garment in which the holy flesh has been bound? “The priests answered and said: No.” A second question is then posed, and the prophet asks:

“And Haggai said: If one who is unclean in soul touches”—that is, one who has become unclean through touching a dead human being—“any of these things, will it be defiled?” And the priests answered and said: “It will be defiled.” And Haggai answered and said: “So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord; and so is all the work of their hands, and whatever they offer there—it will be defiled.”

The prophet says nothing about the first question but answers the second, showing why he had posed these questions. Whoever is unclean in soul and has touched a corpse will render unclean everything he touches or offers. The meaning is this: O people, who, when only the altar has been constructed and my house still lies in ruins, offer sacrifices upon the altar and think that you are sanctified by these meats, know that you are not so much sanctified by the sacrifices you offer in my ruined temple as all that you do is defiled, because you neglect my house while carefully building your own houses.

“And now, set your hearts from this day onward, before a stone was placed upon a stone in the temple of the Lord, when you approached a heap of twenty measures and there were ten; when you entered the winepress to press out fifty jars and there were twenty” [Col. 0218D]. O people of Israel, look back upon former days, and from this twenty-fourth day of the ninth month in the second year of Darius, consider and weigh whatever happened previously: how much you endured when the temple was not yet being built, and how much prosperity has come to you since its construction began. He himself now enumerates what those things were.

Before you began to build the temple of the Lord, when you approached a heap of barley or wheat in which you thought you could have twenty measures, you scarcely found half that amount. Similarly, when you came to the winepress and expected to obtain fifty amphorae from it, you scarcely found twenty. He shows why this happened.

“I struck all the work of your hands with blasting wind, mildew, and hail” [Col. 0219A], “and there was none among you who turned back to me, says the Lord.” This is a blight of crops, named from its golden color. I did these things, he says, so that at least, afflicted, you might return to me; but not even then was there anyone among you who returned to me.

Therefore, as long as the Lord’s temple lay destroyed and its rebuilding was postponed, everything contrary happened to them. But after they began to rebuild the temple, prosperity flowed in every respect. From this it is understood that anyone offers gifts to the Lord in vain, and wishes to please God with alms or offerings, as long as he does not build a temple for the Lord within himself. First, a person must make himself a temple of God by making progress; then he will be able to offer on the altar of faith gifts acceptable to God.

[Col. 0219B] “Set your hearts from this day and into the future, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the foundations of the Lord’s temple were laid. Set your heart upon this. Is the seed already in the sprout, and has the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree not yet blossomed?”

The ninth month among us is November, since we begin the year in March; among the Hebrews, however, whose first month is Nisan—that is, April—December is counted as the ninth month. In that month the seeds lie hidden in the earth, and it cannot be conjectured whether sterility or fertility will follow. Since it was therefore the ninth month, the prophet asks: “Is the seed already in the sprout?” Or, as another translation says more clearly, “in the husk,” that is, in the shell of the grain. Or have the fig tree and the other plants already produced a blossom, so that abundance may be discerned from the flower?

At present, therefore, I do not make a prediction based on flowers; rather, by the prophetic spirit I announce to you the future abundance of all things, because you have begun to build the temple of the Lord.

Mystically, the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month signifies the end of evil works. For the number nine, as has been said above, is always used in an evil sense, because it lacks the unity which, when added, completes the perfection of ten. Whoever brings evil within himself to an end, and, as though at the end of the ninth month, begins to build the house of the Lord—that is, to dedicate himself to divine worship—will abound in the fruits of the vine, fig, and olive. In other words, he will be filled with the grace and blessing of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, having attained the spiritual joy, refreshment, and illumination of the Holy Trinity [Col. 0219D].

But these things—the vine, fig, and olive—will be found where the pomegranate had been. This tree is so called because its fruit is filled with a multitude of seeds, arranged in separate chambers within composed membranes and enclosed by a single crimson rind. Hence it is also called the Punic apple, and for this reason it signifies the innumerable multitude of holy peoples united under the fellowship of one faith, as though gathered within the womb of a single rind.

“And on that day I will bless you.”

“And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month, saying.” It must be observed with the greatest care that the word of the Lord is said to have come a second time on the same day as above, namely the twenty-fourth, but the ninth month is not named, because the prophet is about to speak of Christ’s coming and his kingdom, all of which is prosperous and full of joy. Nor does he say, “through Haggai,” as at first; nor “to the prophet Haggai,” as in the fourth vision; but simply, “to Haggai”—that is, to the one celebrating the feast—who no longer foretells the one who is to come but points him out as already coming, so that he may see him.

“Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah.” The prophet is commanded to speak to Zerubbabel alone, who bore the type of Christ, because what is said is typical and pertains to the consummation of the world. What these things are is subsequently shown in the historical sequence:

“I will shake heaven and earth.” These future events are spoken to Zerubbabel alone, whom we have said bears the person of Christ, according to the human nature assumed. I will shake heaven and earth, he says—that is, I will change them for the better, so that there may be a new heaven and a new earth. For in this way the form of this world passes away while its substance remains [Col. 0220B].

Then it follows:

“And I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms and shatter the strength of the kingdoms of the nations,” that is, I will destroy every principality, power, and force, or the opposing forces of spiritual wickedness, so that the destruction of their kingdoms may benefit not only the nations but also the kings who ruled over them.

“And I will overthrow the chariot and its rider, and the horses and their riders will descend,” that is, every eagerness for warfare; once this has been removed, peace follows. The prophet Zechariah clearly shows that this was fulfilled in Christ, saying of Christ: “Behold, your king comes to you, meek, himself poor, riding upon a colt, the foal of an ass”; and immediately he adds: “And he will destroy the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem.”

“A man will rise up with the sword against his brother.” The Apostle says: “Take up the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” The sword, therefore, is the speech of heavenly teaching, cutting away and destroying all perverse doctrines. By this sword a man is separated from his brother, a son from his father, a daughter from her mother, a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies are those of his own household.

“On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord, and I will set you like a signet, because I have chosen you, says the Lord of hosts.”

It was said above that Zerubbabel bears the type of Christ. The Father calls him a servant because of the form of a servant that he assumed. The Apostle says of the same one: Since God the Father has subjected all things to the Son, then the Son himself will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him. For when all things have been subjected to him, he too will appear subject.

When this has been fulfilled, God the Father will take him and place him like a signet in his hand. For he is the image of the invisible God and the form of his substance. Hence the Son himself says of himself: “For this one the Father, God, has sealed.” We seal those things that we wish to preserve as uniquely beloved. The Father therefore specially sealed this one—that is, he chose him and endowed him with singular grace according to his humanity, so that, just as he was truly human, he might also be truly God.

With this signet or ring, whoever believes in him and strives to please him through good works is sealed. Amen.

# ON THE PROPHET ZECHARIAH

[Col. 0221]

[Col. 0221A] Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, almost the last of the twelve prophets, was a contemporary of the prophet Haggai. For they prophesied together under Darius, in the second year of his reign. Zechariah began to prophesy in the eighth month, which among the Hebrews is November, while Haggai began in the sixth month, which among them is likewise September, on the first day of the month. For this reason Zechariah is rightly placed tenth in order, while Haggai is placed eleventh.

This Darius was the son of Hystaspes, ruling over the Persians and Medes as the fourth ruler after Cyrus. For Cyrus destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans and transferred it to the Medes and Persians. In the first year of his reign, in accordance with what Isaiah had foretold, he sent back to Judea nearly fifty thousand captives from Babylon [Col. 0221B]. He also returned the vessels of the Lord’s temple that Nebuchadnezzar had taken and ordered the temple to be rebuilt in Jerusalem under Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest.

Cyrus was killed by Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae, who threw his head into a wineskin full of blood, saying: “Drink the blood for which you have always thirsted!” His son Cambyses succeeded him in the kingdom. Cambyses was followed by two brother magi; after they were killed, this Darius, son of Hystaspes, was established as king of the Persians. In his second year Zechariah began to prophesy.

Thus, from the first year of King Cyrus to the second year of Darius, forty years are counted. During these years only the altar had been built and the foundations of the temple laid, while neighboring nations, at the command of King Cambyses, prevented them from building either the temple or the city [Col. 0221C].

## CHAPTER I

“In the eighth month, in the second year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, the prophet.” Note that Zechariah is called the son both of Berechiah and of Iddo. It is established that this Iddo is the one who, as the Book of Kings indicates, was sent to the very wicked King Jeroboam, when the altar was destroyed and the king’s hand withered, and when, at the prayer of the man of God, it was restored.

According to the allegorical sense, the eighth month, which among the Hebrews is November, is the beginning of winter and has no solemn feast. Because the people had not yet been completely brought back from captivity and the temple of God had not yet been built [Col. 0221D], the prophet is said to have prophesied in a month that had neither solemnity nor joy.

Nevertheless, they remembered the Lord and retained the memory of the former temple and worship. This is shown by Zechariah, whose name means “memory of the Lord.” Therefore they were worthy of the Lord’s blessing—which is the meaning of Berechiah—because they had as witness of their devotion the Lord himself, before whom all things are naked and open, as is indicated by Iddo, whose name means “testimony of the Lord.”

Every person who strives to be mindful of the Lord is rightly called the son of Berechiah, that is, of the Lord’s blessing, and the son of Iddo, that is, of the Lord’s testimony, because whoever confesses Christ before human beings, Christ himself will confess before God the Father who is in heaven.

“The Lord was exceedingly angry with your fathers, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will return to you, says the Lord of hosts. Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried, saying” [Col. 0222A].

When the Lord is said to be angry, it must not be thought that any disturbance of mind enters into him. Rather, this indicates that those to whom these words are spoken are deserving of anger and punishment. Nor does one who is angry take vengeance when he rebukes for the purpose of correction. Hence it follows: “Return.” For if he is angry, why does he urge them to return?

He therefore commanded those who had returned from Babylon to turn back, so that the sons might not suffer what their fathers had suffered. The Lord of hosts, called *sabaoth* in Hebrew, is so named because beneath him is the army of the heavenly host. Both Haggai and Zechariah very frequently call the Lord “of hosts,” so as to give confidence to those who were building the Lord’s temple against the command of the Persian king and in defiance of Cyrus.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn back from your evil ways and from your most wicked thoughts, but they did not listen or pay attention to me, says the Lord. Where are your fathers and the prophets? Will they live forever? Yet my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? And they turned back and said: As the Lord of hosts had determined to do to us according to our ways and according to our deeds, so he has done to us.”

These words depend upon the preceding chapter, where it says: “Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Turn back from your ways,” and so forth. Therefore Zechariah does not say this in his own person, but in the person of the earlier prophets who cried out with the voice of the Lord, saying: “Turn back,” and so forth. Isaiah, Hosea, Jeremiah, and the others in succession cried this out, so that they might turn from evil works and wicked thoughts [Col. 0222D]. But, hardened and almost despairing, they did not listen, as the holy Daniel also confesses the same thing when praying to the Lord for the deliverance of his people.

“On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Shebat, in the second year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, the prophet.” The eleventh month, Shebat, is called February among us. Shebat is interpreted as “rod,” because of the severity and harshness of winter weather [Col. 0223A]. It was the twenty-fourth day, when the moon is already faintly luminous and nearly waning.

Since the prophet Zechariah was speaking to a people still for the most part exiled among the Assyrians, it is fitting that in the second year, in the eleventh month, and on the twenty-fourth day of the month—when the moon was already failing and the horror of darkness increasing—he is said to have prophesied the things that follow.

“I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse; and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the depth, and behind him were red, dappled, and white horses.”

He says that he saw by night, not by day, as Moses did when God spoke with him face to face, and as Isaiah did when he said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne.” For the people were still held in the distress of servitude as though in night, and therefore the prophet says that he saw at night the things he saw on their behalf [Col. 0223B]. Spiritually, the night in which the vision is seen signifies the obscurity of mystical vision. Hence the Psalmist says: “He”—there is no doubt that he means God—“made darkness his hiding place.”

“And behold, a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the depth.” The Hebrews understand the rider of the red horse literally as the archangel Michael. He was red because he is the avenger of the iniquities of that people, over whom he has special charge. “The myrtle trees that were in the depth” they understand as the prophets and saints who lived amid the captive people.

“The red, dappled, and white horses” that followed the man—that is, Michael—signify kingdoms, or the angels who preside over those kingdoms, though the order has been rearranged.
