The white horses signify the Medes and Persians, who were kind toward the Jews; under them the captivity was released and the temple restored. The dappled horses signify the Macedonians, some of whom were pious toward the Jews, while others were their persecutors. The red horses signify the kingdom of the Romans, cruel and bloodthirsty, which overthrew the temple and destroyed the nation.

Some understand four kingdoms together, in the order in which they are mentioned here. They say that the red horse on which the man sat, together with the red horses that followed him, signifies the Assyrians and Chaldeans, bloodthirsty and cruel: the Assyrians led the ten tribes into captivity under Shalmaneser, while the Chaldeans led the two tribes into captivity under Nebuchadnezzar, after burning Jerusalem and overthrowing the temple. They consider the third and fourth—the dappled and white horses—to be the Medes and Persians, some of whom were merciful, such as Cyrus, Darius, and Ahasuerus, while others were cruel, such as Cambyses.

“Then I said, ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the angel who spoke within me said to me, ‘I will show you what these are.’ And the man who stood among the myrtle trees answered and said.” Seeing horses of different colors, he asks what they are. For he knew that something else was signified under the appearance of horses. Then the angel who spoke in him promised that he would explain it. But when that angel remained silent, the man who stood among the myrtle trees explained what he had asked: “These are the ones whom the Lord sent to traverse the earth,” and to subject it to his authority.

“And they answered the angel of the Lord who stood among the myrtle trees.” Then the angels who presided over the individual kingdoms came [Col. 0224A] to no one other than the man who stood among the myrtle trees—that is, to the angel. “And they said, ‘We have traversed the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.’” As though they were saying: “All the kingdoms are yours and at peace, and none is oppressed by distress.”

“And the angel of the Lord answered and said, ‘Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is already the seventieth year.’” From this response, that angel who interceded for Israel, taking the opportunity to implore the Lord on behalf of the people, said: “O Lord, when the whole earth is inhabited in security, why do you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah—especially since, according to your promises, the time of captivity has been completed?”

[Col. 0224B] “And the Lord answered the angel who spoke within me with good words,” concerning the promise of future things; “with words of consolation,” concerning the necessity of present things. This is the literal interpretation. Allegorically, the man who mounted the red horse is the Lord and Savior. The red horse signifies the mortality of our flesh, which he assumed for us; to him Isaiah says: “Why is your garment red?” It should be noted, however, that the one described here as sitting on the red horse appeared in the Apocalypse of John seated in a white garment upon a white horse. For he who was red in the Passion was white in the resurrection. Hence the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy.”

The myrtle trees that were in the depths, among which the man is described as standing, are the angelic [Col. 0224C] powers that attended him and ministered to him even when he was present in the flesh. By the red, dappled, and white horses we should understand the apostles and apostolic men who traversed the whole world by preaching. Some were red because they were crowned with martyrdom; others were dappled because they were distinguished by doctrine, works, and the diverse variety of signs; others were white because they were illustrious for the brightness of virginity, the integrity of faith, and the purity of a clean heart. These were sent by the Lord to fill the whole world with evangelical preaching. Hence the Lord also says to Job: “Will you send forth lightning, and will they go, and on their return say to you, ‘Here we are’?”

The man stood among the myrtle trees—or, as another translation says, among the mountains—that is, Christ distinguished between the peoples of the two callings, those to be saved and those to be condemned. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are perishing and among those who are being saved.”

That the angel asks God to have mercy on the people because the seventieth year had already arrived signifies that Jerusalem—that is, the Church—will by no means attain perfect freedom before the true Sabbath, that is, rest, is fulfilled. The seventieth year signifies this, a number completed by multiplying ten by seven. This peace begins in the present when we cease from the battles of vices; but it will be perfected in the future, when we attain the vision of the Creator.

“And the angel who spoke with me said to me: ‘Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been zealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great zeal, and I am angry with great anger [Col. 0225A] against the wealthy nations, because I was angry only a little, but they helped toward evil.’” The good and consoling words that the Lord answered above are now commanded to be proclaimed by the prophet: “I have been zealous for Jerusalem—not with a small zeal, but with a great zeal.” Here “zeal” means fury and indignation. And because Jerusalem and Zion—since they are one—had committed great sins, they had incurred the great anger of God. But now, he says, “I will be angry with great anger against the wealthy nations, which rest in prolonged peace and abound in every good thing,” whom the red, dappled, and white horses signified above. He also explains the cause of such great anger, saying: “Because I was angry only a little, but they helped toward evil.” For God handed the Jews over to the nations for correction, as a father hands over a son to a tutor; but they showed them no mercy and raged against them with every cruelty.

“Therefore thus says the Lord: ‘I will return to Jerusalem with mercies, and my house shall be built in her,’ says the Lord of hosts.” This was under Zerubbabel and Joshua. “And the measuring line”—that is, the builders’ line—“shall be stretched over Jerusalem.”

Spiritually, Jerusalem is the Church, seeing peace and concord. It is also Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” since it contemplates not lowly or earthly things but heavenly ones. If it sins, or if charity grows cold within it, the Lord hands it over to persecutors for purification, like gold or silver in a furnace. But the adversaries to whom it is handed over for testing add evil, because they use cruelty in the name of discipline. [Col. 0225C] Therefore he threatens them with anger, while promising his Church peace and mercy; and he says that a measuring line, or cord, will be stretched over it—that is, he distributes the measures and ranks of the individual members who are in the Church, assigning them to their proper places and times according to the quality of their merits.

“Cry out again, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘My cities shall again overflow with good things, and the Lord shall again console Zion, and he shall again choose Jerusalem.’” The prophet is commanded to cry out, not with a loud voice but with the intention of his mind. “My cities,” he says, “which you now see burned to ashes by the fire of the Chaldeans, shall again abound in every good thing, so that their former misery may be consoled by present happiness.” But mystically, those good things are also promised to the Church, of which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

“And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns. And I said to the angel who spoke within me, ‘What are these?’ And he said to me, ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah and Israel and Jerusalem.’” The Lord himself explains that the four horns which scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem are four nations, saying: “These are the horns,” and so forth. Daniel too, under the figures of a lioness, a leopard, a bear, and another beast which he does not name explicitly, clearly describes four kingdoms: the Babylonian, Median-and-Persian, Macedonian, [Col. 0226A] and Roman kingdoms. It is very customary in Holy Scripture for horns to signify the power of a kingdom, as in: “He will exalt the horn of his Christ”; and again: “He has raised up a horn of salvation for us.”

These horns scattered, or dispersed, Judah and so forth. For the Jews suffered many evils from these nations, especially from Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes—that is, “appearing above”—because he wished to be called a god. Finally, the Romans devastated them with such a disaster that they dispersed them almost man by man, so that none of them could lift his head, crushed beneath the heavy burden of evils.

“And the Lord showed me four craftsmen, and I said, ‘What are these coming to do?’ And he said: ‘These are the horns that scattered Judah, each man by himself, so that none of them lifted his head; and these have come to blunt them, to cast down the horns of the nations that lifted up a horn over the land of Judah in order to scatter it.’”

The Lord himself explains what the craftsmen are and what they are coming to do. The prophet did not see them by himself; the Lord showed them to him. We understand these craftsmen to be angels obedient to God’s command, coming for the purpose of rebuilding what the nations had destroyed. The angels came to blunt them—that is, to dull and weaken the horns—so that they would no longer be able to scatter Judah. Some manuscripts read “to terrify them,” that is, to put the horns in fear, so that, laying aside their cruelty, they might submit their necks to Christ.

It should also be noted that he says in the singular, “They lifted up a horn,” although he had spoken of four horns. For although the kings of the four kingdoms did not reign at the same time but succeeded one another in turn, they nevertheless lifted up one horn against the people of God.

Indeed, the fact that the prophet had said above that he lifted his eyes in order to see what was being shown to him indicates that the things spoken of are to be understood spiritually, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Lift up your eyes,” and see who created these things. The four horns are spiritual wickednesses and hostile powers that raise a most grievous horn of persecution against the Church. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age,” and so forth.

The Psalmist describes these four horns under the names of beasts, addressing the holy man in this way: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” For when the devil rages against the elect, he is an asp because he strikes secretly; a basilisk because at times he openly pours out the poisons of envy; a lion because he persecutes the innocent; and a dragon because he swallows those whom he can with impious voracity.

The four horns may also be understood as the four disturbances of the soul, two arising from supposed goods and two from supposed evils: namely, joy and hope, fear and grief. Against these passions stand the four virtues of the good craftsmen: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. These good craftsmen rebuild whatever those horns destroy. The saints who possess these virtues are also spiritual craftsmen. For the Apostle says of himself: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation”; and the Lord himself, the Creator of all things, was called the son of a craftsman.

## CHAPTER II

“And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring cord. And I said, ‘Where are you going?’ And he said to me, ‘To measure Jerusalem, and to see how great is its breadth and how great its length.’”

Prophetic Scripture always follows sad things with joyful ones. The one who previously lifted his eyes to see the sadness in the horns now lifts them again to see a man measuring Jerusalem. This is the man of whom it is written: “Behold, a man whose name is Rising”; and he is described in the book of Ezekiel. He has a cord and a measuring reed in his hand, to measure the city of God, Jerusalem, whose architect and founder is God. This [Col. 0227B] is the holy Church, mother of the saints, which began to be built in the Passion and resurrection of the Lord and is built every day so that it may grow in the increase of faith. He possesses the cord and measuring reed because he himself distributes the measures and merits of individuals. He also sees how great is the breadth of charity in each person, and how great the length of hope and long-suffering.

“And behold, the angel who spoke within me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him: ‘Run, speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall, because of the multitude of people and animals within her.’”

The angel who spoke in the prophet is understood literally by the Hebrews to be Michael, as was said above; the angel who came to meet him they believe to be Gabriel, [Col. 0227C] who joyfully tells him to run and speak to the prophet about the abundance of all things that Jerusalem will possess, although at that time it appeared to have been destroyed down to its ashes. He also tells him that it will be without a wall because of the multitude of people and animals and the abundance of peace. Why it will be without a wall he shows shortly afterward, saying:

“And I will be to them,” says the Lord, “a wall of fire all around, and I will be glory in her midst.”

These words can also be said spiritually of the Church, which is the city of God, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.” It is inhabited without a wall, needing no mortal defense, because the Lord is a wall of fire around it, and he himself is in its midst in glory.

This city has people and animals—that is, both peoples. For by the people the Jewish multitude is signified, those who lived according to the Law and used reason, possessing knowledge of God. The Gentiles, however, who did not know God, are rightly called animals. Some understand “people” to mean the wise and learned, and “animals” the simple who are in the Church, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “You will save people and animals, Lord.”

The Lord, therefore, is a wall of fire around the Church, so that he may warm it with the fire of charity and make it fervent in the Spirit; and he himself is its glory in the midst, glorifying it by his presence. Around it he defends it from adversaries like a wall of fire.

“Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I have scattered you among the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. Ho, Zion! Flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.”

The Assyrians and Chaldeans who had taken the people of God captive are in the northern region. When the prophet Jeremiah described a boiling pot facing the north, he immediately added: “From the north evil shall be opened upon the whole face of the land.” The prophet therefore urges—and not once only, but repeatedly admonishes—those who still remained in large part in the land of the north to flee from it and return to their own dwellings.

Spiritually, we are commanded that those of us who have dwelt in the north, in the coldest wind—that is, those who were in the time of unbelief, without the warmth of divine heat, and who lived amid the confusion of vices—should flee to Zion, that is, to the Church of the Lord. We must leave earthly and lowly things behind, ascend to the height of contemplation, and stand upon the summit of spiritual doctrines.

“For thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘After glory he sent me to the nations that plundered you.’”

This is the voice of the Lord the Savior, who says that he was sent by God the Father—not insofar as he is omnipotent and equal to the Father, but insofar as he is human and lesser than the Father. Hence he says that he was sent “after glory,” which he had when he was with the Father, although he never abandoned the Father. For this reason he himself says to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” And the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped.”

The Son of God was therefore sent, after the glory of divine majesty, [Col. 0228C] to the nations that had stripped the people of God, so that they might become spoils for those whom they had previously plundered.

“For whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye.” “Touching” should be understood as vexation and injury, in accordance with: “Do not touch my anointed ones.” For the saints are, as it were, the eyes of God, to whom it is said: “You are the light of the world.” Whoever harms them is as though he touched the apple of God’s eye and wished to deprive him of clear light.

“For behold, I lift up my hand over them, and they shall be spoils for those who served them; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me.”

The Lord then lifted his hand to strike the nations and to bring his people back to Zion. He lifts his power daily to recall his people—that is, the Christian people—through repentance into the Church, once the adversaries have been struck down, namely the spiritual enemies who do not cease to attack them.

“Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall join themselves to the Lord on that day, and they shall be my people; and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you. And the Lord shall possess Judah as his portion in the sanctified land, and he shall again choose Jerusalem.”

The Lord himself continues to speak and urges the people freed from captivity to rejoice and exult. But this is also commanded to the Church, which is the daughter of Zion—that is, of that heavenly city consisting of angels and holy human beings—that those who have been freed from the slavery of the devil should rejoice, [Col. 0229A] while their Lord dwells in their midst and many nations come to believe in him. Thus, when he was about to leave the apostles bodily, he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

He also promises that he himself will possess Judah—that is, the people who confess him—and that he himself will be its portion in the sanctified land, that is, in the Church; and that he will again choose Jerusalem, which he seemed to have cast aside amid the persecutions.

“Let all flesh be silent before the face of the Lord, for he has risen from his holy dwelling.”

Therefore, because the Lord is to possess Judah as his portion and choose Jerusalem, let all flesh—that is, the whole human race—be silent, fear, and fall quiet from dread before his coming, because he has risen for vengeance, [Col. 0229B] to repay each person according to his merits. God is said to rise when he is stirred to vengeance. “All flesh” means every human being, not dumb animals, in accordance with: “All flesh shall come to you,” that is, every human being.

## CHAPTER III

“And the Lord showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan was standing at his right hand to oppose him.”

The Hebrews understand this passage literally as referring to Jesus the high priest, son of Jehozadak. At his right hand stood Satan—that is, his adversary, the devil. “Satan” is the Hebrew word for “adversary.” He stood at his right hand to oppose him, that is, to accuse him. He stood at his right hand because he had a just accusation, since Jesus, like the others, had taken a foreign wife.

“And the Lord said to Satan: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord rebuke you, he who chose Jerusalem.’”

The Lord is mentioned twice in order to indicate the Father and the Son, as elsewhere: “The Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon Sodom”; and: “Is this not a brand plucked from the fire?”

The meaning is this: Since the Lord chose Jerusalem from all the cities of Judah, let him not charge against him the sins that he committed. Why do you attempt to overwhelm Jesus by accusing him, when he escaped from the Babylonian captivity like a half-burned brand? A “brand” is half-burned wood, which in common speech is called a firebrand.

“And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the face of the angel.”

He is said to have been clothed in filthy garments for three reasons: either because he had taken a foreign wife, or because of the sins of the people over whom he presided as priest, or because of the squalor of the captivity.

“And he answered and said to those who stood before him.” The angel before whom Jesus stood commanded the other angels in the person of the Lord, saying: “Take the filthy garments away from him.” When they had completed in action what had been commanded, “the angel said to him: ‘Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you.’” Here he shows what the filthy garments were: “And I clothed you in changes of garments,” that is, I joined an Israelite wife to you. The Septuagint translated “changes of garments” as *poderēs*, that is, “a robe reaching to the feet.”

[Col. 0230A] “And he said”—that is, the angel said—“‘Put a clean turban, or mitre, upon his head.’ And they placed a clean turban upon his head and clothed him with garments.”

By the turban—that is, the priestly cap—the dignity of the priesthood is understood, so that, once the stains of sins had been removed, he might have a clean priesthood.

Mystically, Jesus the high priest is the one to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever.” The Lord showed him to the prophet because he cannot be seen by himself. He stood before the angel of the Lord—that is, Christ, God and man, the mediator of God and human beings. He himself stands before the angel, and he himself stood before himself. In Christ the substances of God and of the human being are distinct within one person.

He was clothed in filthy garments because he bore our sins. Satan stood at his right hand because [Col. 0230B] he willingly submitted to temptation by the devil, who wished to test whether he was the Son of God, seeing him hungry after the fast.

As for what follows—“May the Lord rebuke you, Satan”—the Son, the Lord, speaks of the Lord the Father. This is not because he himself could not rebuke him, since he works all things just as the Father does, but because of the unity of nature: when one rebukes, the other is understood to rebuke. For God the Father and the Son are one in substance, yet the Father is one person and the Son another.

He himself chose Jerusalem, that is, the Church. The brand plucked from the fire is Christ himself according to his humanity, who in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of the world—was not burned by the flame of any sin, because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth, just as once the bush in the midst of the flames was not consumed.

Jesus was clothed in filthy garments because, although he committed no sin, he was made sin for us—that is, a sacrifice for sin—and he himself bore our weaknesses. These filthy garments were taken away from him when he removed our sins. For this reason he was clothed in filthy garments, so that we might receive clean silk in baptism, and that, once cleansed, it might be said to us: “At all times let your garments be white.”

The clean turban upon his head signifies the splendor of his divine majesty. “For the head of Christ is God.” He himself is God, and he is also human, so that in the garment the humanity, and in the turban the brightness of the divine majesty, may be understood.

“And the angel of the Lord stood and testified to Jesus, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord of hosts: If you walk in my ways and keep my charge, you also shall judge my house and shall guard my courts.’”

According to the literal tradition of the Hebrews, the angel before whom Jesus stood speaks to him after he has been stripped of the filthy garments and clothed in changes of garments. These words are sufficiently clear in themselves and need no explanation.

According to the spiritual meaning, however, the interpretation is difficult if what is said to Jesus the son of Jehozadak—“If you walk in my ways and keep my charge,” and so forth—is taken literally. It is known, however, that Christ and the Church are head and members. Therefore let us understand this as referring to the members, for what is said to him is certainly said to his members.

Thus it is promised to his members that, if they walk in the ways of the Lord and keep his charges—that is, his commandments—they will judge his house, which is the Church. Concerning it the Apostle says: “Christ, however, is the Son over his own house, and we are that house.” He says the same to Timothy: “So that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.”

Jesus therefore judges the house of God according to the merits and words of individuals, appointing one over ten cities and another over five, making some teachers and others shepherds; giving some the power to perform signs; and making some eyes in his body, others hands, and others feet.

“And I will give you those who walk among those who now stand here.”

The Lord gave God’s Son ministers from the number of the angels, since he made his saints, while they were still in the flesh, like angels. Hence the Apostle said: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” For the companionship of angels is promised to virgins, the Lord saying: “They shall neither marry nor be given in marriage, but they shall be like the angels of God in heaven.”

He says that he will give him those who stand in attendance because those who do not waver but are stable and constant in the Church of God—such as the apostles, who persevered with the Lord while he stood—deserve to become companions of angelic dignity.

“Hear, Jesus the high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are men who are signs. For behold, I will bring my servant, the Rising One.”

Here we understand Jesus literally only as the one who was the son of Jehozadak, to whom the coming of the Son of God is promised. Since above we said that this Jesus the priest bears the type of Christ, we now understand him only literally. Let us see, then, what the angel, speaking in the person of God, says to this Jesus: “Hear, Jesus the high priest, you and your friends”—that is, the other prophets.

For Jesus too was a prophet, because he prefigured Christ not in words but in his name and actions. A prophet is not only one who foretells Christ in words, but also one who designates him through figures and symbols. Jesus is therefore commanded to hear, and his friends, that is, the other prophets, are also commanded to hear what is said: “Behold, I will bring my servant, the Rising One.”

“For behold, the stone that I have set before Jesus; upon one stone are seven eyes.”

They are commanded to hear this because they are men who are signs, that is, appointed as signs of future things. Those are called “signs” who announce future events, proclaiming them far in advance.

“Behold,” he says, “I will bring my servant, the Rising One”—that is, the one of whom it is said: “Behold, a man whose name is Rising”; and elsewhere: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise.” In the Gospel also: “The Rising One from on high has visited us, to illuminate those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.”

He calls him “my servant” because he assumed the form of a servant, as in: “Behold my servant; I will receive him.” He is also the stone set before Jesus—that is, announced and promised to the prophets. This is the cornerstone, which joined together in itself two walls coming from opposite directions, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God.

Upon this stone are seven eyes, because upon Christ rest the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The prophet Isaiah enumerates them: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him.”

“Behold, I will engrave its engraving,” says the Lord of hosts, “and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.”

Because he had spoken above of a stone, he preserves the metaphor and says: “Behold, I will engrave its engraving”—that is, the engraving of the stone. It is clear that this prophesies the Passion of the Lord. He calls the wounds that he received on the cross the engraving of the stone: “I will engrave its engraving,” that is, I will cause him to be wounded by nails and a lance. [Col. 0232B] This was done by God the Father, who handed him over to death for us all.

Then the iniquity of that land will be forgiven. For in the Passion iniquity was forgiven and righteousness restored in one day, concerning which the Psalmist says: “This is the day that the Lord has made.”

“On that day, says the Lord of hosts, each man will call his friend under the vine and under the fig tree.”

From the time of Christ’s Passion the Gospel began to be announced. The apostolic and perfect man, who is now able to climb to higher things, calls his friend—that is, believers, or certainly the Gentile people—under the vine, that is, Christ, who says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine,” whose fruit gladdens the human heart.

And he calls him under the fig tree, that is, to the glory of the Holy Spirit, whose fruits are exceedingly sweet, so that under such a [Col. 0232C] shelter they may rest in eternal peace. The prophet Micah also foretold this in nearly the same words: “On that day,” he says, “each man will call his neighbor and brother under the fig tree and the vine, and there will be no one to terrify him.”

## CHAPTER IV

“And the angel who spoke with me returned and awakened me, like a man who is awakened from his sleep.”

What does he mean by saying, “The angel returned”? Where had the one who spoke in the prophet gone? We should understand that whenever human frailty is left to its own weakness, God is absent from a person’s experience of the angels’ help. The prophet, therefore, stunned by the amazement of the great vision, was languid and, as though asleep in mind, unable to see the true light. Therefore the angel who had left him to himself for a short while and had, as it were, withdrawn from him returned and awakened him, so that he might see what previously he could not see with the eyes of his heart closed.

We may also understand the prophet’s sleep in a positive sense, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “If you sleep, you will not fear; you will rest, and your sleep will be sweet.” Whoever therefore sleeps away from the cares and disturbances of the world, and can say with the bridegroom, “I sleep, but my heart is awake,” deserves to be awakened by the angel and to enjoy angelic vision and conversation.

“And he said to me: ‘What do you see?’ And I said: ‘I saw, and behold, a lampstand entirely of gold, and its lamp upon its top, and its seven lamps upon it, and seven vessels for the lamps that were upon its top, and two olive trees above it, one at the right of the lamp and one at its left.’ And I answered and said to the angel who spoke within me: ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the angel who spoke within me answered and said to me: ‘Do you not know what these are?’ And I said: ‘No, my lord.’ And he answered and said to me:”

The Hebrew tradition concerning this passage is as follows. The lampstand, entirely solid gold, they say is the Law. The lamp—that is, the flame shining at the top of the lampstand—they say is Christ, who is the head of the Law and illuminates the whole world. The seven lamps upon the lampstand are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit enumerated above. These lamps are upon the lampstand because the Law was written under the direction of the Holy Spirit.

The seven vessels—that is, the containers in which the oil is held and poured into the lamps that shine upon the lampstand—they say signify that these seven graces descend from heaven to human beings through the Law. The two olive trees that were above the lampstand, at its right and left, between which the central lamp shone, they understand as the Law and prophecy.

When the prophet had told the angel who asked him what he saw, he asks the angel again what the vision itself signified. The angel in turn asks him: “Do you not know what these are?” When he answers, “I do not know,” the angel then replies, explaining the vision:

“This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: ‘Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my Spirit,’ says the Lord of hosts”—that the people had been brought back from captivity, would be brought back more fully, and that their adversaries would be destroyed.

“Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel, [Col. 0233C] becoming a plain?”—and before the people of the Jews, unwilling that they should prosper and that the temple should be rebuilt. It means: to spread you flat, to cast you down from your pride, humbled beneath the feet of Israel.

“And he shall bring out the chief stone”—that is, Christ, who has always been the help of the people of Israel throughout the ages.

“And he shall equal its grace with grace”—that is, the grace of the stone. To state the meaning plainly: He brought forth his grace from captivity and will make this grace equal to the grace that he exercised toward their fathers, showing them similar mercy. This is the Hebrew tradition.

The ecclesiastical teachers, however, explain the passage in this way: The lampstand, entirely golden, is the holy Church, which in the divine Scriptures seeks the meaning more than the words. The lamp above the lampstand designates the Lord Christ, who illuminates the Church and who says of himself: “No one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel”—that is, under the measure of the Law—“but upon a lampstand,” that is, in the freedom of the Gospel, by which the Church is illumined.

The seven lamps and their vessels are the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which the Church receives the oil of divine mercy and of all the virtues. The two olive trees are Moses and Elijah, who appeared on the mountain with the transfigured Lord and spoke of what he was about to suffer in Jerusalem.

Some understand the two olive trees, at the right and left, as the Gospel and the Law, so that the Gospel is understood in the olive tree on the right and the Law in the olive tree on the left.

The great mountain before Zerubbabel is the devil or Antichrist, who raised himself against Zerubbabel, from whom Christ was to be born. When the kingdoms and honors of the world were shown to Christ in the Gospel, the devil dared to say to him: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.” The Lord himself also calls the devil a mountain in the Gospel, saying: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move.”

But this pride had to be leveled and humbled down to the dust. The chief stone is the one of whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word.” What follows—“he shall equal its grace with grace”—means what the Apostle says: “We have all received from his fullness, grace for grace”: the grace of the Gospel in place of the grace of the Law, so that both believers from Israel and those coming to faith from the Gentiles may receive equal and equivalent glory. Hence John says: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundations of this house, and his hands shall complete it; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you.’”

Anyone who has read the prophet Ezra will find that the temple was founded by Zerubbabel and brought up to its highest summits.

“Who indeed has despised the day of small things?” Here, “who” is taken to mean “the rare one,” or “the few.” This must be referred to the royal authority which at that time the adversaries despised in Zerubbabel [Col. 0234C] and regarded as worthless. He therefore admonishes Zerubbabel and Joshua, and the whole people who were building, not to fear the adversaries who were preventing them from building, but rather to listen to the Lord exhorting them and promising them his help. For it follows: “And they shall rejoice”—that is, after despising the few days, they shall be filled with greater joy.

It may also be understood in this way: Rare is the person who despises the small days of this age, since there are many who take delight in this world to such an extent that, if they could, they would always wish to live here. Therefore, when we see the lovers of this age shining with gold, glowing with purple and sparkling jewels, surrounded by the services of attendants, we can take up this saying and declare: “Who indeed has despised the day of small things?” For all the days of the present life are small, however long they may be stretched out over the course of time. Hence Jacob also said: “My days are small and evil.”

“And they shall see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel. These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which range throughout the whole earth”—that is, the help of the Savior, who is born from the stock of Zerubbabel. He is called a stone because of his unconquerable strength. But why a tin stone? They say that tin has the property of protecting other metals from fire. Although bronze, iron, and the other metals are naturally harder, if they are committed to the furnace without tin, they are burned. So too the strength of angels and human beings, if it does not possess divine assistance, is fragile and feeble. Christ, therefore, is called a tin stone because, just as tin separates metals that have been mixed and adulterated, [Col. 0235A] so the Lord and Savior—of whom the prophet says, “He will sit refining and purifying silver”—separates the silver and gold of good works from the bronze and lead of vices, so that pure gold and silver may remain.

“And I answered and said to him: What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on its left? And I answered a second time and said to him: What are the two ears of olives that are beside the two golden beaks, in which there are channels made of gold? And he said to me: Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, my lord. And he said” to me: “These are the two sons of oil”—that is, of splendor—“who stand beside the ruler of the whole earth.”

The prophet asks what the two olive trees on the right and left of the lampstand signify. [Col. 0235B] But the angel who was speaking in the person of the Lord did not wish to answer him—either because he had previously heard about the two olive trees and therefore was not now worthy to hear the angel’s answer, since he did not retain what he had heard before; or because, wishing to show that he knew greater things, he is rebuked by the angel’s silence; or, as the Hebrews say, the angel did not answer him because he had not asked properly and had not inquired about everything he ought to have known. For, while asking about the olive trees, he had asked nothing about the ears of olives, the golden beaks, or the receptacles.

By “ears of olives” he means the trees themselves, using a transferred expression, because they stand straight in the manner of ears of grain, and just as ears of grain are enclosed by awns, so these trees rise straight up into the height as though enclosed by a kind of barrier of branches and leaves. Some understand the two ears of olives as the two Testaments, the Gospel and the Law, and as the sons of splendor who stand beside the ruler of all flesh. Others understand them as the priesthood and the Law; some as Elijah and Enoch, one of whom pleased God in uncircumcision and the other in circumcision.

## CHAPTER V

“And I turned and lifted my eyes, and I saw, and behold, a flying scroll. And he said to me: What do you see? And I said: Behold, I see a flying scroll. Its length is twenty cubits and its width ten cubits. And he said to me: This is the curse that goes forth over the face of the whole earth.”

The prophet turned from one vision to another and lifted the eyes of his mind from joyful and prosperous things to those that were sad. Lest his heart become exalted, since he was announcing everything happy [Col. 0235D] and full of joy, he sees also the things that are grievous. He therefore sees a flying scroll on which the deeds of all had been written. This scroll signifies the nature of both Testaments. By its length of twenty cubits, the Gospel is understood; by its width of ten cubits, the Decalogue of the Law. Twenty in relation to ten is double in relation to single, because in the Decalogue sins of action are prohibited, whereas in the Gospel sins of thought are cut away. For example, the Law prohibits murder, while the Gospel prohibits anger; adultery is condemned in the Law, while in the Gospel desire is punished, since “whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,” and so forth. In the Law robbery makes a person guilty; in the Gospel greed is subjected to the flames of Gehenna.

The Seventy translators rendered “scroll” as “sickle,” having the same measurement in length and width. This sickle signifies the severity of divine judgment: just as a sickle encompasses everything externally in its circuit and cuts internally, so the power of divine punishment embraces all things outwardly, divides and distinguishes them inwardly, judging deeds and thoughts.

“For every thief, as it is written there, shall be judged, and every person who swears shall likewise be judged on this account. I will bring it forth, says the Lord of hosts, and it shall enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely by my name; it shall remain in the midst of his house and consume it, its wood and its stones.”

There are many who think theft and perjury either minor or no crimes at all, and who do not consider that the curse of this scroll [Col. 0236B] is said to come upon the house of the thief and of the one who swears falsely by the name of the Lord, consuming both its wood and its stones—that is, his hard and serious sins. What, then, will become of the graver sins, such as murders, adulteries, and the other works of the flesh, if theft and perjury are punished with such a penalty?

“And the angel who spoke in me went out and said to me: Lift your eyes and see what this is that is going forth. And I said: What is it? And he said: This is a measure going forth; and he said.”

The angel who was speaking in the prophet went out in order to show him another vision. He therefore commanded him to lift his eyes to contemplate great things and to see a measure—that is, the measure of the sins of the people of Israel, completed and full. For the measure called in Hebrew *ephah* or *ephi* signifies the fullness of sins. The angel also gives the measure its name, saying: “This is their eye throughout the whole earth”—that is, the manifestation of all their sins. Once the measure of sins had been filled, in accordance with what the Lord says to the Jews, “Fill up the measure of your fathers,” and with what is said in Genesis, “The sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed,” it remained that there should be an “eye,” that is, a manifestation and vengeance when the just anger of God came upon them. Thus the offenses of that people had remained hidden while they were not yet complete. But once they had been completed, they were laid open to all and displayed before all the nations, showing what they had been in their own land.

“And behold, a talent of lead was being carried, and behold, a woman sitting in the middle of the measure. And he said: [Col. 0236D] This is impiety. And he threw her into the middle of the measure and put the mass of lead into its opening.”

As the angel himself explains, she was called “impiety,” that is, idolatry and denial of God. He calls the talent a mass of lead. It was being carried either through the air by its own force or by God’s command. That talent, or mass of lead, signifies the exceedingly heavy weight of sins by which that people was oppressed. The angel of the Lord therefore seized the woman and threw her into the middle of the measure, so that, in the fullness of sins, she might be carried to Babylon, where, as is read in what follows, she was transported and weighed down by the burden of captivity. And because she gloried in her crime, the angel put the talent, or mass, of lead into her mouth—that is, into the mouth of the measure—so that he might shut up impiety [Col. 0237A] and, with its mouth stopped, prevent it from boasting any longer in its crime, but make it fall silent in eternal silence.

“And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, two women coming forth, and a spirit was in their wings.”

The two women are the ten tribes called Israel and the two called Judah. The ten tribes were captured by the Assyrians, and the two by the Chaldeans. “The spirit in their wings” may mean the powers of the devil, who is called in the Gospel the unclean spirit, and of whom Solomon says: “If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you, do not leave your place.” Seized, then, by this spirit as by a blast of wind, these women were carried with swift flight toward every form of wickedness.

“And they had wings like the wings of a kite,” which is an extremely rapacious bird and constantly lies in wait for domestic birds. [Col. 0237B] This bird therefore aptly suits these women, Judah and Israel, who, because of their excessive sins, were handed over to the power of demons and led by them into captivity.

“And they lifted up the measure,” in which were the impiety and the enclosed mass of lead, “between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who spoke in me…”

The prophet no longer asks who the women were, for he knew this through the prophetic spirit; nor does he ask what they were carrying, because he had learned that from the angel’s instruction. Instead he asks where they were carrying it, saying: “Where are they carrying the measure?” And he said to me…”

The angel answered: “To build a house for it in the land of Shinar, and to establish it there and set it there upon its base.”

Shinar is the plain of the Chaldeans, where, after the Flood, the sons of Adam attempted to build a tower of pride, but the Lord confused the language that had previously been one for all. Hence the city itself was called Babylon, that is, “confusion.” The measure, therefore, was carried with its impiety into Babylon, so that it might be placed there upon its base—that is, upon a stable seat—and remain there in an eternal dwelling.

Shinar is interpreted as “the shaking out of teeth,” or “their stench.” Thus the measure with its impiety is carried to the land of Shinar, and a place of dwelling is prepared for it there, because the devil, the author of impiety, rests in the hearts of the reprobate, whom impiety or the stench of lust possesses. The fact that Shinar is called “the shaking out of teeth” signifies that the reprobate have teeth shaken out and ruined—teeth with which they ought to have ground, that is, meditated upon, the words of God. They therefore perish because they do not transmit the food of divine speech into the stomach of memory.

According to the spiritual meaning, these two women signify heretics and Jews, who go forth from the presence of the Lord and are carried along by the uncertain spirit of error, delighting in quarrels and disputes. They also lift upon themselves the weight of impiety and build themselves a house in Babylon—that is, in confusion.

## CHAPTER VI

“And I turned and lifted my eyes, and I saw, and behold, four chariots coming forth from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, in the second chariot black horses, in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot mottled, strong horses. And I answered and said to the angel [Col. 0238A] who spoke in me: What are these, my lord? And the angel answered and said to me…”

The prophet passes to another vision and extends the eyes of his heart higher. He sees four chariots coming forth from between two mountains, which were of bronze and exceedingly strong and which no age could wear away.

“In the second chariot were black horses”: the kings of the Persians and Medes, deadly because of Ahasuerus, under whose reign that king, at the request of Haman, the enemy of the Jews, condemned the entire Jewish people to death by public decree.

“In the third chariot were white horses”: the Macedonians, under whose king Antiochus the victory of the Maccabees is described.

“In the fourth chariot were strong, mottled horses”: mottled because some Roman kings were merciful toward the Jews, such as Gaius Claudius, while others were their persecutors, such as Gaius Caligula, Nero, and Vespasian.

When the prophet asked what the things he saw signified, the angel answered: “These are the four winds of heaven”—that is, regions or quarters—“which go forth to stand before the ruler of the whole earth.” For the kingdoms of the earth can do nothing without God’s permission and will.

“In the chariot” in which “were the black horses, they went forth to the land of the north, and the white ones went forth after them, and the mottled ones went forth toward the land of the south. But the strongest ones went out and sought to go and range throughout the whole earth. And he said: Go, traverse the earth. And they traversed the earth. And he called me and spoke to me, saying…”

The prophet therefore passes over the first chariot, in which were the red horses, since the whole Babylonian kingdom had already come to an end, and the Medes and Persians held all Asia. It was under their king Darius that Zachariah contemplated all these things. The chariot in which were the black horses therefore went out toward the north, so that, at the Lord’s command, the empire of the Chaldeans might there be destroyed. The white horses also went out after them—that is, the Macedonians followed in the footsteps of the Medes, so that they might subject the kingdoms of the Chaldeans to their own empire.

The fourth, that is, the mottled and strong Roman horses, went out toward the land of the south, and they were commanded to go and traverse the whole earth. For the power of the Romans extended their empire throughout the four regions of the world.

Then the angel turned to the prophet and said: “Behold, those who go forth to the land of the north have caused my spirit to rest in the land of the north.” [Col. 0238D]

He speaks of the third chariot, in which were the white horses, by which the Macedonians were represented; they too went out after the black horses toward the land of the north. These, therefore, caused the Lord’s spirit to rest in the land of the north because they fulfilled God’s vengeance by overthrowing the empire of the Medes. For Alexander, king of the Macedonians, killed Darius, king of the Persians and Medes, and transferred his kingdom to the Macedonians. They therefore caused the prophetic spirit, the Spirit of God, to rest in the land of the north because they carried out vengeance on behalf of God’s people and fulfilled his will in the destruction of those people. For great is the consolation of the oppressed if they quickly learn that their enemies are destined to perish.

Some understand spiritually by the four chariots the four [Col. 0239A] Gospels, and by the horses God’s elect, possessing different graces in accordance with the diversity of their colors. Some are red through martyrdom; others are black, darkened by the squalor of repentance, or they are those who penetrate the obscure mysteries of Christ. For it is written: “He made darkness his hiding place.” Others are white, shining with the radiance of virginity, or cleansed in baptism. Some are strong and mottled, possessing the grace of diverse healings and powers.

The statement, “Those who go forth to the land of the north have caused my spirit to rest in the land of the north,” signifies that, through evangelical preaching, the nations that were in the north—that is, in the cold of unbelief and under the power of the devil, who said, “I will set my throne in the north”—believed, and the Spirit of the Lord rested in them.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Take from the exiles—from Heldai, from Tobiah, and from Jedaiah—and you shall come on that day and enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who came from Babylon. You shall take gold and silver and make crowns, and place them on the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and you shall speak to him, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, a man whose name is Branch; he shall branch out beneath him, and he shall build the temple of the Lord.”

The order of the words is confused. The connection is as follows: Take for yourself something from Heldai, Tobiah, and Jedaiah, who came from Babylon; from them, you are to understand, take the gifts that are being brought—gold and silver. Enter the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, and there make crowns [Col. 0239C] adorned with gold and silver. Place one of them upon Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and speak to him: “Behold, a man whose name is Branch; he shall branch out beneath him”—that is, he will suddenly grow up from his root and sprout like a shoot.

This signifies Zerubbabel, who rose from a humble and captive condition to become leader of the people and built the temple of the Lord. For this is what the statement means: “And he shall build the temple of the Lord.”

“And he himself shall build the temple of the Lord, and he himself shall bear glory”—that is, another crown. “And he shall sit and rule upon his throne. And he shall be a priest upon his throne, and there shall be a counsel of peace between the two of them. And the crowns shall belong to Helen and Tobiah and Jedaiah and Hen.”

Up to this point he has been speaking about Zerubbabel; now he again speaks about the priest Joshua, whom he had mentioned earlier. “And the high priest,” he says, “Joshua shall sit upon his throne”—that is, upon the priestly throne—and there shall be peace between those two, namely between Zerubbabel, who was descended from the royal stock, and Joshua, who descended from the tribe of Levi, so that priesthood and kingdom may together govern God’s people. After the crowns have been placed upon the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak and upon the head of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, you shall consecrate them in the temple under the names of those by whom they were offered, namely Helem, Tobiah, Jedaiah, and Hen.

“A memorial for the son of Zephaniah in the temple of the Lord. And those who are far away shall come and build in the temple of the Lord, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. And this shall happen if you diligently listen to the voice of the Lord your God.”

After the crowns have been restored to the temple of the Lord and consecrated as an eternal memorial, nations will come from the whole earth and build in the temple, and you shall know that the Lord sent me to you.

It should be noted that above he named three men, Heldai, Tobiah, and Jedaiah, but now the first name is changed: instead of Heldai, Helem is given. A fourth is added that had not previously been mentioned, namely Hen. Heldai is interpreted as “the Lord’s supplication,” Tobiah as “the goodness of the Lord,” Jedaiah as “known by the Lord,” and Hen as “grace.” Helem, which is given in place of Heldai, is interpreted as “dream.”

The Hebrews relate that these three—Heldai, Tobiah, and Jedaiah—are the three young men, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, who came from captivity and offered these gifts, gold and silver, in the temple of the Lord. They say that the fourth, who is not mentioned above, namely Hen, is Daniel, and that he too came with a gift. Helem was therefore placed in place of Heldai because Helem is interpreted as “dream,” so that through the interpretation the reference to Daniel and the three young men who in Babylon understood the mysteries of the king’s dream might be shown.

This Josiah, whom the prophet is commanded to enter and in whose honor the crowns are said by the translators of the Seventy to have been made, because they were kept with him, was a temple official, that is, a guardian of the Lord’s temple. This is the literal interpretation, in accordance with the tradition of the Hebrews.

Spiritually, the prophet is commanded to take gold and silver from the exile. The exile of the Jewish people—that is, of the people who confess God—consists of vices and sins. When a person begins to abandon these, practice repentance, and long for his homeland, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, he offers gold and silver in the temple of the Lord by confessing the Lord in understanding and speech.

From this gold and silver crowns are made in the house of Josiah, whose name is interpreted as “saved,” and who is the son of the Lord’s salvation. The house is the Church, in which there is a people saved by the Lord, who is the son of the Lord’s visitation. For the Lord visited those who were seriously ill, lying sick with the disease of sins.

These crowns are placed upon Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. This means that, after we have been freed from the captivity of the devil and have advanced through our individual virtues, the Lord is crowned—or rather, he himself receives crowns in us. He is rightly called the son of Jehozadak, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord of righteousness,” because God the Father of the Lord Savior will justly restore to each person according to his merits. Hence the Apostle confidently said: “The crown of righteousness has been reserved for me,” and so forth.

The prophet is therefore commanded, after placing the crowns upon the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, to say to him: “Behold, a man whose name is Branch.” Christ, who is called Jesus because he saved the world, is now called Branch because in his days righteousness arose. “And he shall branch out beneath him”—understand, a multitude of believers. “And he shall build the temple of the Lord”—that is, the Church. “And he shall rule upon his throne,” because when he comes for judgment, he will sit upon the seat of his majesty. “And he shall be a priest upon his throne,” because he himself is king, he himself is high priest, and he himself will sit both upon the royal and upon the priestly throne. [Col. 0241A] “And there shall be a counsel of peace between those two,” so that neither royal majesty may diminish priestly dignity nor priestly dignity royal majesty, but that both may agree in the glory of the one Lord Jesus.

## CHAPTER VII

“And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Darius that the word of the Lord came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Kislev. And Sarasar and Regemmelech and the men who were with him sent to the house of God to entreat the face of the Lord, saying to the priests of the house of the Lord of hosts and to the prophets who spoke…”

The ninth month, which among the Hebrews is called Kislev, is called December among us. On the fourth day of that month they sent to the temple of the Lord, which had already [Col. 0241B] been restored, to Zerubbabel and Joshua, Sarasar and Regemmelech. According to the opinion of the Hebrews, these were Persian princes who feared the Lord. Since they had heard that the temple had been restored, they asked the priests and prophets whether, according to the former custom, they ought still to weep and fast, or whether they should turn mourning into gladness and joy.

“Must I weep in the fifth month?” In the fifth month, which among the Romans is called August, Jerusalem was overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar. For this reason they had fasted up to that time, consoling the temple’s desolation with mourning and sorrow. But now, since they saw that the temple had been rebuilt and that there was no longer any reason for sadness, they ask whether they should now do this.

This is what the statement means: “Must I sanctify myself, as I have done for so many years?” They call fasting “sanctification,” because during the fast they abstained from all pleasures and devoted themselves to good works and almsgiving. Hence the prophet also says: “Sanctify a fast.” To sanctify a fast is, together with other good works, to abstain from vices.

After the Persian princes had asked this through the messengers whom they had sent, the word of the Lord comes to the prophet, commanding him to speak to the whole people. He also addressed the priests concerning what they ought to answer.

“And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Speak to all the people of the land and to the priests, saying: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months during these seventy years, did you fast for me?”

They fasted in the fifth month because Jerusalem was overthrown by the Chaldeans in that month; in the seventh month because then Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land, was killed and the remnant of the people was scattered. The Lord therefore says: What benefit was there for me in your fasting and mourning during the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation, since you fasted not for me but for yourselves?

And conversely: “When you ate and drank” at your festivals, “did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” God is not appeased by such things, but by good works, judgment, justice, and truth. Food does not commend us to God.

“Are these not the words that the Lord spoke through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was still inhabited and prosperous, both it and the cities surrounding it, and when the south and the lowlands were inhabited?”

When Jerusalem still stood, he says, and abounded everywhere in every good thing and enjoyed the greatest peace, the earlier prophets were speaking to you precisely what I am now saying. What those words were is made clear in what follows.

“And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Judge with true judgment, and practice mercy and compassion, each one toward his brother. Do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, or the poor, and let no man devise evil against his brother in his heart.

“But they refused to pay attention, turned their shoulder as they withdrew, and made their ears heavy so that they would not hear. They made their heart like adamant, so that they would not hear the law and the words that the Lord of hosts sent by his spirit through the hand of the earlier prophets. And great indignation arose from the Lord of hosts.

“And it came to pass: just as he had spoken and they had not listened, so they shall cry out and I will not hear, says the Lord of hosts. And I scattered them among all the kingdoms that they did not know, and the land was desolated by them, because there was neither one passing through nor one returning, and they made the desirable land a wilderness.”

These are the things, he says, that please me more than the fast of the fifth and seventh months. Because you did not do them, you were handed over to captivity and disgrace.

“Practice mercy and compassion.” To practice mercy is to give alms to the poor; compassion means forgiving debtors. These two things are expressed in the prophet Isaiah as follows: “Break your bread for the hungry”—this is mercy. And shortly above: “Undo the bonds of wickedness; loosen the bundles that oppress”—this is compassion.

The proper order is that mercy should follow judgment, especially toward brothers whom either blood or the fellowship of the same faith joins to us. For when the Law says, “You shall not show mercy in judgment,” mercy is not to be shown during the judgment itself; but once a person has been convicted and confessed his guilt, mercy is to be extended to him.

Concerning widows and orphans also the Lord commanded: “Be a father to orphans and a mother in place of a husband to them.” He also commands that no oppression be inflicted upon the foreigner or the poor, because exile humbles one and poverty the other.

Although the Lord had commanded these and other things, they acted in the opposite way: they turned their backs on him, withdrawing—that is, turning their shoulder away—and made their ears heavy, like deaf asps. Therefore, because of their great sins, great indignation arose from God, and they were scattered among kingdoms they had previously not known—the kingdoms of the Assyrians, Medes, and Persians. The land that had flowed with milk and honey was turned into a wilderness.

These things may also be referred to those who, placed in the Church, grow proud of an abundance of virtues and do not give thanks to God their teacher. For this reason, by God’s just judgment, they are permitted to be tested by the devil, are taken captive under the law of sin, and their land—that is, the soul that was once a dwelling place of the Trinity—is desolated and turned into a wilderness, abandoned by God its inhabitant.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0243A]

“And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts…”

Speak about Jerusalem as a man speaks about an adulterous wife. For God loved the Israelite people and joined it to himself in chaste love through the dowry of faith, as the prophet Ezekiel describes in full. Later, having abandoned God, it fornicated with the idols of various nations. Handed over to captivity for this reason, it practiced repentance, saying: “I will return to my former husband, because it was better for me then than now.”

The merciful God received her and did not reckon her sins against her, saying: “I have been jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I have been jealous for her with great indignation. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have returned to Zion, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the city of truth, and the mountain of the Lord of hosts, the holy mountain.”

Because Zion, which is Jerusalem, abandoned me, he says, and followed many lovers and was defiled by them, I was jealous with great jealousy, in proportion to the magnitude of her crimes. Because she has returned to me in repentance, I have returned to her with greater mercy. Build a temple for me, and I will dwell in your midst. You shall be called the city of truth, though once you were called the city of falsehood. You shall also be called the holy mountain and the mountain of the Lord.

Spiritually, these things may be referred to the soul that ought to have been Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace—and Zion—that is, a watchtower contemplating God. When it sins, it is handed over to the power of the devil and subjected to the captivity of vices. But if it repents and strives to reconcile the offended God to itself, God will return to it, and it will be a holy mountain and the city of God. He will dwell in its midst, and it will be said to it: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised,” and so forth.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Old men and old women shall still sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each man with his staff in his hand because of the multitude of his days. And the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets.”

With me dwelling in Jerusalem, he says, such will be the prosperity and abundance of peace that, with no enemy remaining, men and women will live to the utmost old age. Their limbs will tremble and be supported by a staff because of the multitude of their days, and its streets will also be filled with boys and girls at play.

Spiritually, the streets, which are so called from breadth, are the virtues in which the saints walk freely and act with confidence. For the Psalmist calls God’s commandment broad. In these streets old men and old women sit—that is, all those perfected and experienced in virtues. “Old age is venerable,” and so forth. They will be filled with boys and girls—that is, with those who receive the rudiments of the word of God. To such John says: “I write to you, children, because your sins are forgiven you through his name.” Thus what the Psalmist says will be fulfilled: “Young men and virgins,” and so forth.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: If it seems difficult in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, will it also be difficult in my eyes, says the Lord of hosts?”

Because great and almost unbelievable things were being promised to Israel, they might perhaps doubt because of the magnitude of what was involved. Therefore the prophet now speaks in the person of the Lord: If what I promise seems difficult to you, O remnant of my people, will it be difficult for me, who am almighty?

In the same way it seemed impossible to the saints, when during various periods of persecution the Church was afflicted in different ways, that peace would ever be given to them. But now the kings and rulers of the world have bowed their necks to Christ, and the emperor’s knees bend at the tomb of a fisherman.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will save my people from the land of the rising and from the land of the setting sun, and I will bring them here, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. They shall be my people, and I will be their God in truth and in justice.”

These things were fulfilled in part under Zerubbabel and Joshua, when God’s people returned from captivity, dwelt in Jerusalem, and called the Lord their God. Now they are fulfilled more fully under the Lord Savior in the Church, which is the true Jerusalem, when people come to the faith from every part of the world, just as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “For many will come from the east and the west,” and so forth.

The statement “in truth and in justice” signifies that, as the shadow and figure of the Law pass away, the truth of the Gospel succeeds them.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Let your hands be strengthened, you who hear these words in these days through the mouth of the prophets, on the day when the house of the Lord of hosts was founded, so that the temple might be built.”

Because they already saw the temple constructed according to what the prophets—that is, Haggai and Zechariah—had foretold, the Lord now exhorts the people, on the basis of the truth of the earlier promises, to place faith in what is promised for the future and to strengthen their hands, fearing none of those who wished to prevent them from building.

“For before those days there was no wage for human beings, nor any wage for animals; there was no peace for the one entering or the one going out because of the tribulation, and I set every person against his neighbor.”

Before the temple of the Lord was founded and built, all their labor was fruitless. Both human beings and animals, in agriculture and in various tasks, were frustrated by their useless efforts. There was no peace for the one entering or going out, since internal sedition and external adversaries disturbed them.

The same thing happened in the Church, because before the temple of the Lord was spiritually founded in human beings, and before it was said to them, “You are the temple of the living God,” there was no wage with God for human beings—that is, rational creatures—or for animals, the irrational creatures. But after they were converted and God began to dwell in them, they heard from the Apostle: “Each one will receive his own wage according to his labor.”

“But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in former days, says the Lord of hosts, but there shall be a seed of peace. The vine shall give its fruit, and the earth shall give its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew, and I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things.”

Since the temple has been founded, I will no longer deal with this people as I did before by afflicting them. Instead, I will give them peace, and I will compensate for the former famine with future abundance.

So also now the virgins of the heretics, the abstinence of the philosophers, and the observance of the Jews have no reward, because whatever good they do, they do not do it in the name of the Lord, nor do they build the Lord’s house within themselves. But after they have been converted to God and, freed from the captivity of the devil, have begun to build the Lord’s temple within themselves, an abundance of peace will arise in them. The vine of which the Gospel speaks—“I am the true vine”—will give its fruit. The good earth also will give its fruit, a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. The heavens too will give the dew of preaching, of which it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

“‘And it shall be: just as you were a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I shall save you, and you shall be a blessing. Do not fear. Let your hands be strengthened, for thus says the Lord of hosts: Just as I determined to afflict you when your fathers provoked me to anger, and I did not show mercy, so now, having turned again, I have determined in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.’”

These are open promises and consolations of the Lord, strengthening his people. By the house of Judah he means the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin; by the house of Israel, the other ten tribes. To all of them he promises that he will show mercy. This consolation may be applied to the Church afflicted by persecutions: whoever, on account of his sins, is expelled from the Church and delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and is taken captive by the devil—if he performs repentance, he returns to his former state, sees the peace of the Lord, and possesses the glory of his confession.

“‘Do not fear. These, therefore, are the words that you shall do: Speak truth, each one with his neighbor. Judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates, and let none of you devise evil against his friend in your hearts.’”

Because, he says, I have promised you good things, so that my promise may remain in force, do what I command: speak truth with your neighbor. Let us understand “neighbor” to mean every human being, since we have all been generated from one parent. For if we are commanded to speak truth only to those who are neighbors according to the flesh, is it then permissible to lie to foreigners and outsiders?

“Judge truth and judgment in your gates,” so that truth and justice may come first in judgment, and mercy follow afterward. The judgment of peace is that the judge should have as his purpose the reconciliation of discord. As for what follows, “in the gates,” it was their custom for judges to sit at the gates of the city and determine the cases of individuals. Hence the Psalmist says of the holy man: “He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate”; and the prophet says: “They hate him who rebukes in the gate.”

They did this in the gate so that farmers would not be forced to enter the city and thereby suffer some loss, and so that both townspeople and country people could hear the judges’ decisions at the entrance to the city and then return to their own homes.

When he says, “Let none of you devise evil,” “evil” can here be understood in two ways: as affliction and as sin. Therefore the holy man should neither devise how to afflict anyone nor how to make anyone sin.

“‘And do not love a lying oath.’”

When he says “a lying oath,” he does not forbid swearing a true oath. In the Gospel, however, an oath is altogether abolished, when the Lord says: “I say to you, do not swear at all.” For whoever does not swear never commits perjury.

“‘For all these are the things that I hate,’ says the Lord. And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid festivals. Only love truth and peace.’”

In response to what the princes of Persia had earlier asked through their envoys—whether they ought to fast in the fifth and seventh months, or whether, after the Temple had been rebuilt, they should end the fast and lay aside their mourning—the prophet, inserting many intervening matters that they ought to pursue and that should prosper, answers in the person of Christ.

“The fast of the fourth”—with “month” understood—and “of the fifth” and “of the seventh,” with the expression understood by *a common construction* (*ἀπὸ κοινοῦ*, that is, “from a common [word]”: “month”).

The fourth month among the Hebrews is called July among us. In that month Moses descended from the mountain and, when he saw the people dancing before the golden calf they had made, threw down the tablets of the covenant that he had received from God and broke them at the foot of the mountain; and twenty-three thousand idolaters were struck down. In this same month, as we read in Jeremiah, the walls of the city of Jerusalem were breached by the Chaldeans. For this reason the Jews have always fasted in the fourth month.

Their fifth month is called August among us. In this month the Jews suffered many adversities. For when they were in the desert, a rebellion arose in this month on account of the spies, who, after returning, caused the people to murmur. Therefore the Lord became angry and forbade them to enter the promised land immediately; instead, they were to wander in the desert for forty years, until all who were twenty years old and above and had gone out from Egypt died, except Caleb and Joshua.

In this same month the Temple was destroyed and burned, first by Nebuchadnezzar and, many centuries later, by the Romans. For these reasons they imposed upon themselves each year an extremely severe fast.

The seventh month of the Hebrews is called October by us. In that month Gedaliah was killed by Ishmael, as was mentioned above, and the remnant of the Jews was scattered. This is the reason for the fast of the seventh month.

Their tenth month is called January among the Romans. In that month the prophet Ezekiel and all the captive people who were in Babylon heard, in the fifth month, that the Temple had been overthrown. For this reason they fasted every year in that month.

The meaning, therefore, is this: The days of fasting that you have until now observed in mourning—know that in these times they are to be changed for you into joy, if I grant you prosperity, but only on this condition: that you love truth and peace.

“‘Thus says the Lord of hosts: Until peoples come and dwell in many cities, and the inhabitants go from one to another, saying, “Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord, and seek the Lord of hosts.”’”

The fasts, he says, of the fourth and fifth months mentioned above will be changed into splendid festivals, to such an extent that the cities of Judea, which had previously been deserted, will be filled with a multitude of inhabitants, and one city will go to another.
