They will encourage one another, because during these seventy years there was no one who came to the Temple of the Lord, since the roads of Zion were in mourning and solitude. Now that peace has been restored, let us go to Jerusalem to celebrate the festivals that the Law commands to be held each year. When one city says this, another will answer: “I too shall go.” At that time:

“‘Many peoples and powerful nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the face of the Lord,’”

and to offer sacrifices to the Lord God and entreat his face. In the deeper sense, however, the face of the Lord is the Son of God the Father; through him, as through a face, God the Father is recognized, just as the Son himself says: “I have manifested your name to human beings.” Therefore all the peoples of believers stream together to the Church, and there they entreat the Son of God and offer sacrifices of praise to God.

“‘Thus says the Lord of hosts: In those days, ten men from every language of the nations shall take hold—yes, they shall take hold of the hem of a Jewish man, saying, “We shall go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”’”

Although the Jews refer this to the final times of the Antichrist, we say that it took place at the coming of the Lord, when he was born from the Virgin Mary.

These ten men are the Church spread throughout the world. For ten is a perfect number, the completion of the sequence of numbers. The letter iota also, among the Greeks, from which the name Jesus begins, expresses the number ten.

The Lord sought these ten men from Abraham: “If I find ten there, I will not destroy the city because of the ten.” These Churches, which are represented here by the number ten, John displays in the Apocalypse under the number seven, saying that he saw the Son of Man in the midst of lampstands—that is, Churches—which he mystically describes under the names of cities.

Isaiah also says: “Seven women shall take hold of one man on that day.” The apostle Paul likewise writes to only seven Churches: to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, and to the Thessalonians.

The Churches, therefore, which they marked by the number seven because of the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit, the prophet Zechariah here expresses by the number ten because of the perfection represented by ten.

“And ten men shall take hold”—that is, the Churches, advanced to the stature of the perfect man and possessing the rational understanding of spiritual things, shall take hold of the hem of the Jewish man, that is, of the Lord and Savior, concerning whom it is written: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you”; and in the Psalm: “Judah is my king.”

The Churches shall take hold of this Jewish man’s hem—that is, they shall believe the mystery of his incarnation. Through the hem, which is the smallest part of a garment, the humility of his incarnation is indicated. The woman with the hemorrhage touched it and was healed. They shall therefore take hold of him, desiring to cling to his footsteps.

All who are reckoned by the Christian name and have come, as has been said, to the measure of the perfect man are included in the ten men. These shall take hold of the hem of the Jewish man, that is, they shall strive to be imitators of Christ by faithfully believing his incarnation.

We may also understand the apostle Paul specifically as the hem of the Jewish man. For the hem is the smallest part of a garment, and he says of himself: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle.” The hem of the Jewish man, therefore, is Paul, the apostle of our Lord. Ten men take hold of this hem—that is, all who believe in Christ follow his teaching, in accordance with what he himself says: “Be imitators of me.”

## CHAPTER IX

“‘The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach and Damascus is its resting place.’”

This prophecy concerns the building of the holy Church, which consists of both Jews and Gentiles.

The order of the words is as follows: “burden” means the weight of the word of the Lord—sharp and gentle, sharp, that is, toward sinners and gentle toward the righteous. In Hebrew, *had* means “sharp” and *rach* means “gentle.” Therefore the weight of the word of the Lord is most heavy for sinners and gentle for the righteous.

By the land of Hadrach let us understand the Jews; by Damascus, the Gentiles. Thus the burden of the word of the Lord comes upon the land of Hadrach, that is, upon the Jewish people, toward whom the Lord exercised both severity and mercy: severity toward those who refused to believe, but mercy toward those who turned from unbelief to faith.

Damascus is called the resting place of the Lord because the Lord rested in the faith and devotion of the Gentiles, in accordance with what had been foretold through Isaiah concerning Christ: “Before the child knows how to call his father or his mother, he shall receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria.”

Damascus is rightly interpreted as “drinking blood” or “the blood of sackcloth,” because the Gentile world, first bloodied through idolatry, was wounded by the blood of sinners; afterward it strove to wipe away the blood of wickedness with the sackcloth of repentance.

“‘For the Lord is the eye of humanity and of all the tribes of Israel.’”

Therefore, he says, the house of the Lord—that is, the Church—is built from both peoples, from the land of Hadrach and from Damascus, because whoever looks toward the Lord, whether from the Gentiles or from the Jews, belongs to the Lord by believing in and hoping in him. For the eye is the gaze of contemplation.

“‘Hamath also shall be within its borders, and Tyre and Sidon, for they have acquired wisdom for themselves—very great wisdom. Tyre built its fortress and heaped up silver like dust, and gold like the mud of the streets. Behold, the Lord shall possess her, and he shall strike her strength in the sea, and she shall be devoured by fire.’”

Hamath is a city of Coele-Syria. Because it was rebuilt by Antiochus Epiphanes, it is now called Epiphania. For Hamath is interpreted as “indignation.”

This city, and Tyre and Sidon, will therefore be within its borders—that is, the borders of Damascus, or within the borders of the land of Hadrach—so that they too may believe with them in the Lord the Savior, to whom the prophet says in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” and so forth.

Hamath, which means “indignation”; Tyre, which means “distress”; and Sidon, which means “useless hunting,” signify the peoples of the nations. At first they were indignant at the preaching of Christ’s name, were in distress because of their sins, and were hunted by the devil, whose type had gone before in Nimrod, “a mighty hunter before the Lord.”

That these cities—or rather the nations signified by them—would be most ready to believe, the Lord shows in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented.”

They therefore acquired wisdom—very great wisdom—that is, the sophistries and cunning devices of the art of dialectic. Tyre also built its fortifications, that is, strong arguments by which the Gentile world, once fortified as though by a wall, could be overcome by no teacher of the truth.

It heaped up silver, that is, rhetorical eloquence, and gold, that is, moral meanings and allegories. But how worthless and contemptible these things are, he shows by comparing this silver and gold with the mud of the streets.

They gathered these things in order to fortify the kingdom of idolatry and make it impregnable. The Lord therefore possessed Tyre and Sidon when he struck their strength—which they possessed in the stormy sea of this age—and destroyed all secular wisdom, refining and purifying their gold and silver by that fire of which he himself says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth,” and so forth.

“‘Ashkelon shall see and fear, and Gaza shall grieve exceedingly, and Ekron, because her hope has been confounded. The king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited. The divider shall sit in Ashdod.’”

When Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ekron—which are cities of the Philistines—see that Hamath is within the borders of Damascus, and that Tyre and Sidon have passed over to it and see them possessed by the Lord, they will grieve and be filled with fear, because they will see that the hope they had placed in idols has been confounded.

Ashkelon is interpreted as “ignoble fire” or “weighed”; Gaza as “strong” or “rule”; Ekron as “sterile” or “uprooted”; and Ashdod as “fire producing,” “fire of an uncle,” or “fire of the breast.”

“Jebusite,” meaning “trampled,” signifies souls deceived in this manner by the devil. Ashkelon, in which the devil had previously been—he who is “ignoble fire”—and which had reached the measure or weight of sins, namely, the people of the nations, feared, terrified by such dread.

Gaza, which had been strong and had promised itself the rule of idolatry, grieved exceedingly, performing repentance for its former crimes. Ekron also, sterile and without knowledge of God, having no spiritual children, was uprooted from the error by which it had been held as though by a firm root.

When these cities, which we have said represent the nations, had been terrified and had grieved because their hope had been frustrated, then the divider would sit in Ashdod—that is, the Lord and Savior, who separates the wheat from the chaff, the bad fish from the good, and who at the judgment will separate the sheep from the goats.

He will sit in Ashdod, where the fire of God’s Spirit produces children of adoption; where there is the fire of the uncle—that is, of our same Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to assume flesh from us, and concerning whom Isaiah says: “I will sing, he says, to my beloved the song of my uncle, my vineyard.”

There also is the fire of the breast, that is, the desire and ardor to suck the milk of spiritual teaching. For the two breasts of the Church are the two Testaments, as the bride indicates in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is a cluster of henna to me; he shall dwell between my breasts.”

“‘I shall destroy the pride of the Philistines, and I shall remove his blood from his mouth and his abominations from between his teeth. He too shall be left for our God, and he shall be like a leader in Judah.’”

The Philistines—whose name is interpreted as “those falling by the cup,” because they fell after being intoxicated from the cup of demons—signify the summons of the nations, that is, blasphemies and the eating of things sacrificed to idols.

When these things have been removed, the people themselves will be left for our God. Rejecting the worship of many, they will begin to adore one God alone, and will be a leader in Judah, so that the former people, signified here by Judah, will become the tail, while the one that had been the tail will pass into the head.

“And Ekron,” once sterile and uprooted—that is, the Gentile world—shall be “like a Jebusite,” that is, like Jerusalem, which at different times was called by three different names.

It was first called Salem. Then, when it was possessed by the Jebusites, it was called Jebus. Thus, when the two names Jebus and Salem were joined, it was called Jerusalem.

Ekron will be like a Jebusite because the nations will receive the grace that the inhabitants of Jerusalem once had when they believed in God.

“‘And I shall surround my house’”—that is, the Church—“‘with those who serve me, going and returning,’” that is, with the angels who minister to me in various services, for the sake of those who inherit salvation. The Church is fortified by their protection, as the Psalmist says: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him.”

“‘And no oppressor shall pass over them again,’” that is, the devil, concerning whom Isaiah says: “How the oppressor has come to rest; the tribute has ceased!”

“‘For now I have seen with my eyes,’” that is, I have caused my prophets to see. For they are the eyes of the Lord, through whom he saw—that is, announced—the calling of the nations and the security of the Church.

“‘Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king shall come to you, righteous and saving, he himself poor and riding upon a donkey and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.’”

This prophecy, as the evangelist Matthew explains, was fulfilled in the Savior when he came to Jerusalem, sitting upon the foal of a donkey, and was received by the crowds with palm branches, who acclaimed divine praises to him.

It therefore says: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem”—which is one city. “Behold, your king,” promised by the voices of all the prophets, “shall come to you,” that is, for your sake, to free you, “righteous and saving.” In Hebrew he is called Jesus, because he himself will save his people from their sins.

He himself is poor: although he was rich, he deigned to become poor for our sake. “He rode upon a donkey and a colt, the foal of a donkey,” that is, upon both peoples.

For by the donkey the synagogue is understood, which had borne the most burdensome yoke of the Law. The colt, however, being wanton and free, signifies the people of the nations, who had no ruling lord or bridle of the Law.

The Lord, sitting upon both peoples, enters Jerusalem and governs them from the present Church toward the vision of true peace.

“‘And I shall destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem; the bow of war shall be destroyed, and he shall speak peace to the nations; his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.’”

The voice of God the Father, who had commanded the daughter of Zion to rejoice and the daughter of Jerusalem to shout aloud, continues to speak, saying what he will do.

“I shall destroy the chariot,” he says—that is, there will be no more battles throughout the world, once the whole world has been made peaceful by the coming of Christ.

Allegorically, Ephraim, which is interpreted as “fruitfulness,” signifies heretics, who gloried in chariots—that is, in the pride of their knowledge. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses,” and so forth. Elsewhere he says: “The sons of Ephraim, armed and shooting the bow.”

He will also destroy the horse from Jerusalem—that is, all pride and pleasure of the flesh, which is signified by the horse. Hence the Psalmist says: “Do not become like the horse and the mule.”

Then the bow of war will also be destroyed: all instruments of battle will cease, while peace flourishes throughout the world. Or the bow of war will be destroyed so that the fiery arrows that could wound the hearts of the fleshly will no longer be shot.

“He shall speak peace to the nations,” concerning whom it was said: “He shall be the expectation of the nations.” To these nations he will speak of the peace made between God and human beings through his blood.

“And his dominion shall be from sea to sea.” His dominion is throughout the whole world, and everywhere Christ is adored and worshiped. Hence the Psalmist says: “He shall rule from sea”—understand, the Indian Ocean—“to sea”—understand, the Ocean—“and from the river”—the Jordan, in which he was baptized—he began to preach “to the ends of the earth.”

“‘You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.’”

Now the prophet makes an apostrophe—or rather, God himself speaks to Christ his Son—and says: You too have led out your prisoners, that is, the saints who were held in bonds, from the pit in which there is no water. This means that you freed them from hell, in which there is no mercy.

Finally, at the Lord’s resurrection, many of the saints who were held in hell by the bonds of original sin rose with him, came into the holy city, and appeared to many.

Concerning this blood of the covenant, he himself said to the apostles at supper: “This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which shall be poured out for you.”

“‘Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope. Today also, announcing this, I shall repay you double.’”

Again the speech turns toward us, who were prisoners and are to be freed by God’s mercy.

You, he says, who are now bound in the terrible prison of hell and hope for release from hell at the coming of Christ, return to the stronghold—that is, to confidence in divine protection—and say with the Psalmist: “Be for me a protecting God.”

Or, “return to the stronghold” means: remember the paradise that you now possess in hope, but from this time onward will possess in reality. There your stronghold and secure tranquility will be, when you will no longer fear the rule of any enemy.

“Today also, announcing this, I shall repay you double”: from this time onward, when I announce these things, I shall repay you double, so that in place of brief tribulation you may receive eternal rewards.

For, as the Apostle says: “Everything that is in the world is momentary and brief in tribulation, and it works in us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory, while we look not at the things that are seen but at those that are unseen. The things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal.”

“‘For I have stretched Judah for myself like a bow; I have filled Ephraim.’”

Judah is Christ the Lord, who was born from the royal tribe. God the Father stretched him for himself like a bow when he willed him to assume flesh from a virgin.

He himself is the bow, he himself the arrow, and he himself the *τοξότης*, that is, the archer.

He is the bow, as here: “I have stretched Judah for myself like a bow.” He is the arrow, as he himself says through Jeremiah concerning God the Father: “He made me like a chosen arrow; in his quiver he hid me.” He is the archer, as David says to him in the Psalm: “Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you.”

Ephraim—that is, the assembly of heretics, armed against the Lord and prepared for battle—has been filled by this arrow, so that it too may be wounded by the Lord’s arrows unto salvation and say with the Church: “I am wounded by love.”

“‘And I shall raise up your sons, Zion, over your sons, Greece, and I shall set you like the sword of the mighty.’”

If heretics are understood by Ephraim, then rightly the teachers of worldly philosophy are understood by the sons of Greece.

The Lord therefore filled Ephraim with arrows and raised up the sons of Zion—that is, the sons of the Church—over the sons of the Greeks, that is, the philosophers. For when the apostles preached, every leader of perverse doctrine and every philosophical assertion, which flourished especially at Athens, was destroyed by the sword of God’s word—or rather, by Christ himself, who is the sword of the mighty.

Concerning him the Psalmist says: “Gird your sword upon your thigh”; another prophet says: “You Ethiopians also shall be slain by my sword”; and the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword.”

“‘And the Lord God shall be seen over them, and his arrow shall go forth like lightning. And the Lord God shall sound the trumpet, and he shall go in the whirlwind of the south.’”

When, he says, the heretics and the wise men of the nations have been slain by the Lord’s bow and sword through the sons of Zion, the glory of the Lord will appear over them.

This is what he means by saying: “The Lord God shall be seen over them, and his arrow of preaching shall go forth like lightning,” flashing with the splendor of miracles.

Hence another prophet says: “They shall go in the light of your arrows, in the brilliance of the flashing spear.”

That splendor and those flashes are called the trumpet or blast, so that those whom the splendor has illuminated may be awakened by the trumpet’s blast to hear and may be able to say with the prophet: “The Lord God has opened my ear.”

“Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear for me,” so that I may hear like a teacher.

The Lord also sees in the whirlwind of the south—that is, in the movement of threat—which is called punishment for this reason: so that he may show mercy. Hence it follows:

“‘The Lord of hosts shall protect them,’”

those whom he had terrified by his threat.

“‘And they shall devour and shall subject them with the stones of the sling.’”

The sons of Zion, protected by the Lord—that is, ecclesiastical men—shall devour, with “their adversaries” understood, who are signified by the sons of Greece.

“And they shall subject them with the stones of the sling,” subjecting them by the threats of the Scriptures, and by the rotation of the sling—that is, by the testimonies and examples of the divine utterances.

They shall become intoxicated as though with wine, filled with the knowledge of the Scriptures, to which intoxication Wisdom invites us: “Eat, friends; drink and become intoxicated, beloved.”

Their intoxication will therefore please God like a libation offered in sacrifice, and like the horns of the altar—that is, its four corners, which once a year the high priest entered the Holy of Holies and touched with a finger dipped in blood.

“‘And drinking, they shall become intoxicated as though with wine; they shall be filled like bowls and like the horns of the altar. And the Lord their God shall save them on that day like the flock of his people, because holy stones are raised up over his land.’”

Because the holy stones—that is, the chosen also—will be raised up over his land, light and entirely free from any burden of sin, they will not wait to be lifted up by the builders. They themselves will be raised up and will hasten to be placed upon the foundation of Christ and held together by the cornerstone.

Peter speaks of these stones: “Coming to him, a living stone, you yourselves also, as living stones, are being built up upon him.”

“‘For what is his good and what is his beauty, except the grain of the chosen and the wine that produces virgins?’”

According to the deeper sense, the grain of the chosen and the wine that produces virgins are the Lord and Savior, who says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone.”

From this grain, crushed by the millstone of his Passion and cooked by the fire of death, bread was made for us—the bread that descended from heaven and gives life to the world.

He who is bread is also wine, which makes the human heart glad. This wine is drunk by those virgins who, according to the Apostle, are holy in body and spirit, and who, intoxicated, say with the bride: “The king brought me into the wine cellar and ordered love within me.”

This wine produces virgins because those whom the love of Christ intoxicates despise all the delights of the world, become as though drunk and insensible to the world, love Christ alone, and say with the Apostle: “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh.”

## CHAPTER X

“‘Ask the Lord for rain in the latter season, and the Lord will make snow and showers of rain. He will give each person vegetation in the field.’”

The Lord urges those who believe in Christ to ask for the latter rain—that is, the fullness of spiritual grace at the consummation of the age.

Then the Lord will give snow and showers of rain, because the more the Church is afflicted, the more it is strengthened by greater hope and steadfastness. Then, in each person, green vegetation of virtues will grow in the field of the heart, so that they may be able to say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is my shepherd,” and so forth.

“‘For the idols have spoken uselessly, and the diviners have seen falsehood; the dreamers have spoken in vain; they offered empty consolation. Therefore they were led away like a flock; they shall be afflicted, because there is no shepherd for them.’”

This is said about heretics, who will abound especially at the end of the world. Under the Christian name they deceive people, attending to spirits of error and to demons that speak lies in hypocrisy. They offer empty consolation because the things they promise to themselves and their followers are false.

Because they do these things, they have been led away and taken captive by the devil, delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. They are afflicted because they do not have Christ as their shepherd—the Christ whom they falsely profess to possess and promise.

Except for the passage that says, “I have stretched Judah for myself like a bow; I have filled Ephraim,” the Hebrews refer all these matters to the time of the leaders of the Maccabees, who defeated the Macedonians and, after a period of three and a half years, cleansed the Temple that had been defiled by the Gentiles.

As for what is said, “They shall become intoxicated as though with wine, and they shall be filled like bowls,” they explain it as follows: Those who were with Judas Maccabee fought with such desperation that they were like drunk men who had forgotten their own safety and had no concern for life, but only for victory.

They also understand what is said, “What is good, what is beautiful, except the grain of the chosen and the wine producing virgins?” in this way: The Maccabees did such great things and accepted death most willingly so that, after their enemies had been overcome, the Temple might be cleansed, the precepts of the Law observed again, and the instruction of the Scriptures produce virgins—that is, peoples believing in one God.

They would again have learned men who ought to eat the grain of the divine Law. For this reason they would ask the Lord for the latter rain: because the prophets had already failed and the world was moving toward its end, Christ, who had been sent, would finally come and grant them snow and showers of rain—that is, he would openly fulfill what had been foretold by the prophets.

“‘My fury is angry against the shepherds, and I shall visit the goats, because the Lord of hosts has visited his flock, the house of Judah, and has set them like his glorious horse in battle.’”

It often happens that on account of the sins of shepherds the people are afflicted and handed over to their adversaries. When David sinned, many thousands of the Jewish people were destroyed by plague.

Therefore the prophet says that the Lord is angry against the shepherds. But, being angry with the shepherds, he visits the goats—that is, the people—because they follow their teachers in guilt.

Afterward, when he has exacted punishment for their sins, he will visit his flock for good, the house of Judah—that is, those who confess God in word and conduct. He will set them like a glorious horse because he will preside over them and govern them, and he will appear wondrous in them.

Concerning these horses the prophet says: “He who rides upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.”

“‘From him’”—that is, from the one who will set them like his glorious horse—“‘shall come the corner,’” that is, some perfect person who, like a cornerstone, will hold together and strengthen those engaged in the contest.

“And ‘from him’ shall come ‘the peg,’” some humble person in the Church who nevertheless, through his patience, supports the others like a stretched-out tent.

“And ‘from him the bow of battle,’” that is, a preacher shooting arrows of threat at sinners.

“And from him shall go forth every oppressor together,” one who, as though compelling the unwilling, demands that they submit to Christ, terrified by fear of judgment when they hear how great are the punishments prepared for unbelievers.

“‘And they shall be like mighty men, trampling the mud of the roads in battle, and they shall fight, because the Lord is with them.’”

This will occur when they have been crowned with martyrdom for Christ and have said with the Psalmist: “Though an army encamp against me,” and so forth.

But here the Hebrews explain that the persecution which occurred to the Jews under Antiochus came about through the fault of the teachers. Therefore he visited the goats—that is, the people—and handed them over to the nations. Afterwards he visited his flock, the house of Judah, raising up for them Judas Maccabee and the others, who were like a glorious horse.

As for what is said, “From him the corner and from him the peg,” they interpret the corner as royal power, because it holds together two walls; the peg, however, as the priesthood.

“From him the oppressor” means all the other lesser dignities, so that the meaning is: There will be no dignity that is not arranged according to the will of that man, namely Judas Maccabee.

“‘And the riders of horses shall be confounded, and I shall strengthen the house of Judah, and I shall save the house of Joseph. And I shall turn them back, because I shall have mercy on them, and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them away. For I am the Lord their God, and I shall hear them.’”

This too should be understood according to the preceding interpretation. When the Lord strengthens his martyrs amid persecutions and grants help to the desperate, then the riders of horses—that is, the proud persecutors—will be confounded.

Then he will strengthen the house of Judah—that is, those who confess the Lord—and save the house of Joseph, whose name is interpreted as “increased” or “blessed.”

“‘And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim, and their heart shall rejoice as though from wine; their sons shall see and rejoice, and their heart shall exult in the Lord.’”

Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness,” so that they may be worthy of this name. They will rejoice when they have drunk the wine of the true vine—that is, when they have become companions in Christ’s sufferings.

Their sons also are those to whom the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor,” and to whom the Psalmist says: “Come, children, listen to me.”

They will rejoice, and their heart will be glad in the Lord, saying with the Apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, the Hebrews also refer these matters to the Maccabees: after their enemies had been defeated, the house of Judah—that is, the two tribes—and the house of Joseph—that is, the ten tribes—would be saved, and they would rejoice as though intoxicated with wine.

Then the two tribes and the ten tribes, which had been separated from one another under Jeroboam, would also be joined together. At that time they would be as they had been before the Lord had cast them away. Their sons too, seeing the triumphs of their parents, would rejoice in the Lord.

“I will whistle for them, and gather them, because I have redeemed them; I will multiply them as they had formerly been multiplied, and I will sow them among the peoples.”

In the more sacred sense, the Lord will whistle—that is, he will give a sign—to those who had been scattered by sins, so that they may return to him. And in the Gospel he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” [Col. 0256B]. They are gathered because the Lord redeemed them with his precious blood. They are multiplied because they are multiplied as they had formerly been multiplied—that is, according to what was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed.” And the Apostle says: “Those who are of faith are sons of Abraham.” They are also sown among the peoples so that they may proclaim Christ among all nations, just as he himself commanded: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

“And from afar they will remember me.”

By these words the nations are indicated, which, on account of unbelief, were far from God. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “They will remember and turn to the Lord”; they were dead in sins.

“And they will live with their sons,” namely, with those whom [Col. 0256C] they brought forth for Christ by preaching. To such people the Apostle says: “As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

“And they will return, and I will bring them back from the land of Egypt,” that is, from the darkness of ignorance, in which the devil reigns.

“And from Assyria I will gather them,” from the proud understanding of the heretics’ false doctrine.

“And I will bring them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, and no place will be found for them.”

Gilead is interpreted as “testimony of migration,” and Lebanon as “whitening.” They are therefore brought back to the land of Gilead who pass from carnal things to spiritual things and from earthly things to heavenly things. They are brought to the land of Lebanon who, having laid aside the blackness of sins, are whitened in baptism; afterward, when brought forth from the body, they will be whitened, receiving the shining white robe of immortality [Col. 0256D].

“And they will pass through the strait of the sea, and he will strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the river will be confounded. And the pride of Assyria will be humbled, and the scepter of Egypt will depart. I will strengthen them in the Lord, and they will walk in his name, says the Lord.”

According to the literal sense, it is the tradition of the Hebrews that the Jewish people, having been captured by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, was delivered not only to the Medes and Persians, or to Babylon, but also to the northern region and to the Bosporus; afterward, part of it was summoned from there when God in his mercy looked upon them. This is what is said here: “They will pass through the strait of the sea,” that is, through the narrow sea of the Propontis, where the extremely narrow strait divides Chalcedon and Byzantium [Col. 0257A]. The Lord will strike the waves in the sea, going before his people, and the depths of the rivers will be confounded, as once happened when the Red Sea was divided and the Jordan was dried up. Then the pride of the Assyrians will be humbled, and the scepter of Egypt will be taken away from them when God’s people have been liberated. They will be strengthened in the Lord and will walk in his name, returning to their land.

Let this be said according to the tradition of the Hebrews. According to the mystical sense, we too pass through the narrow sea of this age, which is extremely narrow and full of dangers for the saints; but for lovers of this age it is broad, because broad is the way that leads to death, while narrow is the way that leads to life. In this narrow and turbulent sea of the present age, our Redeemer passed first [Col. 0257B]; afterward the apostles followed him, concerning whom it is said: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, they have seen the works of the Lord.” Then the pride of Assyria—that is, of the devil—will be humbled, and the rule of Egypt, that is, of darkness and the powers of the air, will depart when the final death is destroyed and he who held the power of death is shut up in the prison of Gehenna. But the saints will be strengthened in the Lord and will say: “My strength and my praise.” And they will walk in his name, that is, in the name of Christ, from whom Christians are called; under the dignity of this title they will go from strength to strength until the God of gods is seen in Zion.

## CHAPTER XI

“Open, Lebanon, your gates, and let fire consume your cedars” [Col. 0257C].

Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, where the boundary of Judaea lies toward the north. But in this passage he calls the temple Lebanon, because it had been constructed from the woods of Lebanon. The prophet therefore foretold that the temple, which had recently been built by Zerubbabel and Jeshua, would be destroyed by Vespasian and Titus, the Roman rulers.

“Open,” he says, “Lebanon, your gates,” so that you may receive those who enter—the enemies. And having called it Lebanon, he preserves the metaphor by adding: “Let fire devour your cedars.” By the cedars, firs, oaks of Bashan, and wooded forest, he signifies the rulers, priests, and people of the Jews. “Let fire consume your cedars,” he says, so that everything may be devastated either by fire or by hostile power, and both leaders and peoples may be destroyed.

“Howl, fir, because the cedar has fallen, because the mighty have been devastated; howl, oaks of Bashan, because the fortified forest has been cut down” [Col. 0257D].

With mutual lamentation, he says, priests, rulers, and people, mourn your destruction. And as though one might ask what the cedars, firs, and oaks signify, he replies, showing that he is speaking about human beings: “Because the mighty have been devastated.” Bashan is called “confusion”; by the oaks of Bashan he means people of confusion and disgrace, because the fortified forest has been cut down. By the fortified or wooded forest he means the temple itself, which had been built with impregnable strength by various kings, and finally by Herod. He says metaphorically that it is to be cut down [Col. 0258A], that is, devastated by the Romans in battle.

“The sound of the howling of the shepherds, because their magnificence has been devastated.”

Those whom above he had called cedars, firs, or oaks, he now explains by another metaphor, calling them shepherds—that is, their priests and rulers. He now says that the howling is heard because their magnificence and splendor, namely the temple in which they chiefly gloried, has been burned and destroyed.

“The sound of the roaring of lions, because the pride of the Jordan has been devastated.”

Those whom above he had called trees or shepherds, he now calls lions. And just as above he compared the height of the temple with the height of Mount Lebanon—than which nothing in the land of promise is higher or denser—so now he joins the roaring of lions with the pride of the Jordan, because in that region the Jordan is the greatest of all rivers. Lions dwell beside it either to relieve the heat of thirst with the river’s water or because the desert and vast wilderness are nearby.

The prophet therefore says: “The sound of the roaring of lions”—that is, the sound of the nobles and rulers, as is understood, has been heard—“because the pride of the Jordan has been devastated”; that is, the dignity of the temple has been destroyed, from which help was hoped [Col. 0258B].

“Thus says the Lord my God: Feed the flock for slaughter, which those who possessed them were slaughtering, and did not grieve, and were selling them.”

The Lord speaks to the prophet. “Now,” he says, “let the flock be fed and increase, the flock that afterward is to be captured by enemies.” The Romans [Col. 0258C], who possessed these sheep by the right of conquerors, slaughtered them without grieving or pitying them; those whom they had preserved for life they sold, and they rejoiced, saying: “Blessed is the Lord, we have become rich.” Whoever reads the history will find that these things happened in this way.

In the tropological sense, these things can be referred to the bishops and presbyters of Christians. Evil shepherds feed the flock for slaughter, for through their negligence the Lord’s flock perishes: they see those under their authority going over the precipices of vices, yet neither correct nor reform them. Fearing to lose the temporal advantages they love, they feed them not for life but for slaughter, and they cannot say with the Apostle: “Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” They also sell the peoples placed under them when they prepare riches for themselves from their destruction [Col. 0258D]. They favor sinners, praising those who make plunder from the wretched, and blessing the unjust.

“And their shepherds did not spare them, and I will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord.”

“Because,” he says, “the shepherds did not spare the flock, but themselves were the first to devour my people, therefore I too will no longer spare the inhabitants of the land”—that is, Judaea, as is understood. For, according to the literal sense, this is said about the land of the Jews, not about the whole world. “I will no longer spare,” he says, “but will immediately take vengeance and deliver them to their enemies.” This was fulfilled in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion, the period that had been granted to them for repentance.

“Behold, I will deliver human beings, each one into the hand of his neighbor and into the hand of his king; and they will cut down the land, and I will not rescue it from their hand. And I will feed the flock for slaughter, for this reason, O poor of the flock” [Col. 0259A].

“I will abandon human beings,” he says, “so that they may kill one another in mutual slaughter.” Let us read Josephus, and we shall find that during the very siege of Jerusalem there was such discord and sedition among the Jews that the people were divided into three factions and fought against one another. “And they will cut down the land,” he says—the Romans will do this.

When he says “his king,” the Jews at that time did not have a king, but he used “king” for protector and ruler. He shows what that eternal desolation is when he says: “I will not rescue them from their hands,” that is, from the hands of the Romans, because it is God’s sentence that this should happen. “O poor of the flock”—you righteous of Israel who believed in the Lord God; as is understood, hear and understand what is being said [Col. 0259B].

“And I took for myself two staffs; I called one ‘Beauty,’ and I called the other ‘Cord,’ and I fed the flock.”

The Lord God, Creator and Shepherd, took for himself two staffs, that is, two peoples. He first had as a staff the whole human race under Noah, which he called “Beauty,” because, after the world had recently been restored following the Flood, human beings had not yet been stained by crimes. Nothing was more just than for all alike to call the Creator of the universe their God, since he had created them under equal conditions. He called the other “Cord,” choosing the Israelite people under Abraham. “For when the Most High divided the nations,” and so forth. “And I fed the flock,” he says, whether Israel or the whole human race.

“And I cut off three shepherds in one month, and my soul grew weary of them, for their soul also turned against me, and I said” [Col. 0259C].

We must understand the three shepherds as Moses, Aaron, and their sister Miriam. Miriam died in the first month, which among them is called Nisan and among the Romans April, in the wilderness of Zin. In the same month and in the same place, Moses and Aaron were condemned not to enter the promised land, because they had not sanctified the Lord at the Waters of Contradiction. Thus three shepherds were cut off in one month: Miriam by present death, Moses and Aaron by the sentence of future death.

“And my soul grew weary of them”—that is, through a certain indignation my soul became wearied with those three shepherds whom I had appointed over my flock. “For their soul turned against me” [Col. 0259D] by doubting, because they did not glorify me before the children of Israel at the Waters of Contradiction.

But if we wish to refer this to the people, the meaning will be: I was indignant for this reason, because their soul—that is, the soul of the people—turned against me, wavering between me and idols and fighting against me in various ways. Therefore, in my indignation, I said: “I will not feed you”; and to Moses he said: “Let me alone, that I may destroy them.” He was indeed angry, but he was still waiting; for when he says “Let me alone,” he prompts him to beg him and shows that he can be restrained.

“Let what is dying die; and let what is being cut off be cut off by death; and let the rest devour, each one the flesh of his neighbor.”

“Let all their bodies,” he says, “be laid low in the wilderness, and let the survivors devour, each one, the flesh of his neighbor.” “Let them,” he says, “be turned to sedition, and like beasts they will be torn apart by mutual bites; and let no one enter their promised land” [Col. 0260A].

“And I took my staff called Beauty, and I cut it off.”

After Israel had been taken up—for this is the second staff, which was called Cord—the Lord took the first staff called Beauty, namely the nations of the whole world, because, having abandoned God, they followed idols. As the Psalmist says: “They have all turned aside.” And as though explaining what this staff was, he added: “So that I might annul my covenant which I made with all the peoples.” It was annulled on that day, and the poor of the flock who keep watch for me understood that it is the word of the Lord [Col. 0260B].

For as soon as Israel had been taken up, the multitude of the nations was cast away, and the covenant that I had made with all the nations was annulled. Thus the poor of the flock, that is, the faithful from Israel who keep my commands, understood. “Because it is the word of the Lord”—that is, it is his will that the nations be rejected and Israel be chosen in Abraham.

“And I said to them: If it is good in your eyes, bring me my wage; and if not, cease.”

“I said,” he says, “to them”—that is, to the poor of the Israelite flock—after they had understood that it was the word of the Lord, namely that it was the Lord’s will that, after all the nations had been rejected, the nation of Israel should be chosen, amid its errors [the Latin is uncertain: *et suis promissis erroribus*].

“If it is good in your eyes,” that is, if [Col. 0260C] it pleases you—for you have free choice to choose what you wish—then, for this elevation by which all the nations have been rejected and I have chosen you for myself as a special people, give me my wage, that is, keep my commandments. But if you do not wish to be reckoned by my name or to do what I have commanded, openly do what you wish.

At that time, when these things were said to them, they answered Moses: “Everything that the Lord our God has commanded us, we will do.” But at the end of the ages, in return for all that I had done for them—freeing them from Egyptian slavery and taking them for myself as a special people—

“And they weighed out my wage,” giving thirty pieces of silver for my blood to Judas the betrayer. “And the Lord said to me”—the Savior [Col. 0260D], whose words the preceding passage contains—“Throw it to the statuary,” that is, the maker or potter, whom we understand to be God, the maker and molder of all things, so that by the judgment of this maker the returned wage might be weighed out.

Then, seeing the Creator and Lord of the world valued at so low a price as thirty pieces of silver, he said ironically: “A fine price at which I was valued by them.” As though with indignant mockery he were saying: Behold at what price the people specially loved by me, whom I had adopted as sons, judged that I should be sold.

“And I took,” the prophet says, “the thirty pieces of silver,” and I did not set them down, “but threw them into the house of the Lord to the statuary.” That is, I caused that price to be carried by the betrayer into the house of the Lord and returned to the priests [Col. 0261A], while he himself confessed: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” But they did not wish to put it into the *corban*, that is, into the treasury; instead, they bought with it a potter’s field for the burial of foreigners.

For we were represented by this deed: we were foreigners from God’s covenant, but, having been redeemed by the precious blood of his Son, we rest in the potter’s house—the Creator and maker of all things—at the price of Christ’s blood.

“And I cut off my second staff, which was called Cord, so that I might dissolve the kinship between Judah and Israel.”

After the Lord had been valued at thirty pieces of silver, and the price had been used for the burial of foreigners—that is, of the nations that were alien to God—“I cut off,” says the Lord, “the second staff,” that is, I rejected that people whom I had loved [Col. 0261B], so that I might dissolve the kinship between Judah and Israel. That is, from that people I separated believers from unbelievers: namely, the apostles and those who had done penance, whom they call Judah, separating them from those who cried, “Crucify him,” and “We have no king but Caesar,” and who chose to remain in their unbelief.

This is what he says: “Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth,” and so forth.

“And the Lord said to me: Still take for yourself the implements of a foolish shepherd, for behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will not visit what has been abandoned, will not seek what has been scattered, will not heal what has been broken, will not nourish what stands, but will eat the flesh of the fat sheep and tear off their hooves.”

The foolish and ignorant shepherd is the Antichrist, who is said to come at the consummation of the age [Col. 0261C]. By the implements of the foolish shepherd he means his appearance and the rest of his insignia: his bag, staff, pipe, and whistle. Just as Isaiah, to show the future captivity by his clothing, walked naked and barefoot, so Zechariah is commanded to assume the clothing of a foolish shepherd, so that he might show as though already present the one whose coming he announced.

For because earlier the good shepherd, in anger, had said, “I will not feed you,” the foolish shepherd is foretold as coming—one so foolish that he will sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God, and will come not to heal but to destroy the flock of Israel. The Jews will receive this foolish shepherd by the just judgment of God, so that, because they did not wish to believe the truth, they may believe the lie. The prophet describes most clearly what he will be like [Col. 0261D], showing that he will act in every respect contrary to Christ.

“O shepherd and idol who abandons the flock! A sword upon his arm and upon his right eye. His arm will be utterly dried up by withering, and his right eye will become dark and be completely obscured.”

After describing the foolish and most wicked shepherd, he turns to him and says: “O shepherd and idol.” He shows him to be so criminal that he calls him not a worshiper of idols but the idol itself, since he wants all to worship him as God. Yet he abandons the flock to be devoured by beasts, the flock that the Lord had guarded for so long.

“A sword upon his arm”—that is, manifest vengeance, so that all his strength and power may wither—“and upon his right eye,” so that all his knowledge and understanding, of which he boasted, may be obscured by eternal darkness [Col. 0262A].

That sword can also be understood as the one of which it is said elsewhere: “My sword has become drunk in heaven.” This sword, namely the word of God, penetrating all things, will cause the strength of the Antichrist to wither and will condemn his eye—that is, the sharpness of his mind, by which he thought that he saw the mysteries of God with the utmost clarity—to perpetual blindness.

## CHAPTER XII

“An oracle of the word of the Lord concerning Israel. The Lord says, stretching out the heavens, founding the earth, and forming the spirit of man within it. Behold, I will make Jerusalem a threshold of drunkenness for all the peoples round about [Col. 0262B]; but Judah also will be in the siege against Jerusalem. And on that day I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all the peoples; all who lift it will be torn apart by laceration, and all the kingdoms of the earth will gather against it.”

The Lord stretched out the heavens like a tabernacle, and, according to the Psalmist, like a skin. Just as a skin surrounds the body of an animal on every side, so the heavens contain everything within their circumference. He founded the earth, which is central and lowest among all the elements, because he established it immovable and standing upon its own mass. He formed the spirit of man within it—that is, he placed the soul in the human body and joined one living being from the two substances, soul and body. Here “spirit” is used for “soul.”

This Creator and Lord of the universe therefore says [Col. 0262C], according to the literal sense, that he will make Jerusalem a threshold of drunkenness for all the peoples round about, so that whoever touches its threshold will become drunk and fall, or so that the threshold itself will fall upon whoever touches it. But Judah too, captured by the enemies and joining their company, when its own city Jerusalem has been besieged, will be forced to besiege its own city.

The Lord will also make Jerusalem itself a burdensome stone for all the peoples. Whoever wishes to lift it will be torn apart by laceration. It is the custom of the cities of Palestine, as blessed Jerome says, for very heavy round stones to be placed in citadels and villages. Young men train with them, lifting them according to the measure of their strength: some to the knees, others to the navel, some to the shoulders and head, and some raising them above the crown of the head with their hands extended and joined [Col. 0262D]. In this way they test the magnitude of their strength.

The meaning is therefore: I will place Jerusalem like an extremely heavy stone before all the nations, so that they will gather to capture it as though to lift a stone in a game and display their strength. But it will be necessary that, while the stone is being lifted—that is, while Jerusalem is being attacked—the effort and lifting leave some tearing or scraping upon the bodies of those who lift it.

“On that day, says the Lord, I will strike every horse with bewilderment, and its rider with madness; and I will open my eyes over the house of Judah, and I will strike every horse of the peoples with blindness.”

On that day—that is, at the time when Jerusalem has been besieged [Col. 0263A], so that Judah too is forced to besiege it—the Lord will strike all the horses of the adversaries. “With bewilderment,” that is, so that all who see them struck will be astonished; or, “he will strike them into bewilderment,” so that they become like stupid creatures without sense. Their riders he will strike with madness—that is, they will be oppressed by such great fear that they will be driven into madness.

Over the house of Judah, which the enemies had compelled to act against its own city, the Lord will open his eyes—that is, the gaze of his mercy—so that he may make them worthy of his sight and illuminate them with the light of his eyes.

Spiritually, horses, when understood in a negative sense, signify the lustful and the proud. Their riders are demons or teachers of false doctrines. All of these will be turned to bewilderment and madness [Col. 0263B], so that they may be convicted of having possessed no knowledge, and palpable darkness will oppress them, as once it oppressed Egypt. But over the house of Judah—that is, those who confess the Lord—the Lord will open his eyes, that is, he will have mercy on the one who cries to him: “Look upon me and have mercy on me.”

“And the leaders of Judah will say in their hearts: May the inhabitants of Jerusalem be strengthened for me in the Lord of hosts, their God.”

“When,” he says, “the Lord has opened his eyes over Judah and had mercy on them, then the leaders of Judah, who were in the siege against Jerusalem, compelled by the enemies, will make vows in their hearts, since they will not dare to speak freely, so that Jerusalem, which they are besieging, and Judah itself may prevail together with its citizens.”

In the tropological sense, the leaders of Judah are the apostles, apostolic men, and the other teachers who preside over Christ’s armies [Col. 0263C]. They do not wish to have any other helpers than the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, orthodox and catholic men—and they desire that these be strengthened in the Lord their God. One of these leaders was Peter, who found Mark, an inhabitant of Jerusalem. Paul too, that outstanding leader, had Timothy, Titus, and Luke, true Jerusalemites; with them he subjected the whole world to Christ.

“On that day I will make the leaders of Judah like a furnace of fire among the wood and like a torch of fire among the hay; and they will devour all the peoples round about, on the right and on the left. And Jerusalem will again be inhabited in its own place, in Jerusalem, and the Lord will save the tents [Col. 0263D] of Judah as in the beginning, so that the house of David may not boast arrogantly, nor the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem against Judah.”

“When,” he says, “the leaders of Judah, who by necessity were with the enemies against Jerusalem, have made these vows, then I, the Lord, will give them such great strength that, like fire consuming wood and a torch consuming hay, they will devour all the adversaries round about. After the victory has been completed, Jerusalem will again be inhabited, and the tents of Judah—that is, the citadels, villages, and towns that had been devastated—will be restored. Thus the house of Judah—that is, the royal family descended from David—and the illustrious and powerful men of Jerusalem will not boast against Judah as though it were governed by their authority and counsels; instead, they will know that the Lord is their king and their victory.”

According to the allegory, when the Lord has given peace to the Church [Col. 0264A] and turned her enemies to bewilderment and madness, the leaders of the Church will be like fire among wood and like torches among hay, burning away every vice. The unfruitful wood—that is, all perverse doctrines—will be consumed, and they will devour on the right and on the left those who refused to hold to the middle path of virtue. For every virtue lies in the middle. On the right and on the left are those who know either more or less than they ought.

Then the Church will recover her former glory, and the tents—that is, the assemblies of the faithful—will be restored throughout the whole world. The teachers will not claim this glory for themselves, as though this peace had come to the Church through them; all joy and prosperity of the faithful will instead be attributed to the Lord.

“On that day the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem [Col. 0264B], and the one who among them stumbles on that day will be like David, and the house of David will be like God, like the angel of the Lord in his [their] sight.”

“At that time,” he says, “when, with the Lord’s help, Judah has obtained victory, the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem who were being besieged. Everything will then be changed for the better, so that the one among them who has offended God and is considered most insignificant will be like David—that is, like the royal family—and the one who belongs to the royal house will be like one belonging to the house of God, like the messenger of the Lord in the sight of those who see them at that time.”

In a higher sense, when the Lord has liberated his Church from the hands of persecutors, those who remained steadfast during the persecution will be so glorious among all that the one who was least—even one who by word or deed offended God [Col. 0264C]—will be placed among the teachers; and the teachers will be like the house of God, and like an angel transformed into evangelical dignity.

“And on that day I will seek to crush all the nations that come against Jerusalem.”

What he says—that he will seek to crush all the nations—is to be understood in a good sense. For the Lord crushes them not for destruction but for correction, so that they may cease persecuting Jerusalem and become sheep from enemies.

“And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication.”

By the abundance of the outpouring he shows the generosity of the giver: God grants the grace of the Holy Spirit, of which Paul says [Col. 0264D]: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts.” And through another prophet it is said: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.” Appropriately, after saying “a spirit of grace,” he added “and supplication,” because those whom the Holy Spirit has filled he immediately kindles to worship.

These things were fulfilled in the resurrection of Christ and are fulfilled daily in the Church.

“And they will look upon me whom they pierced, and they will mourn for him with mourning as for an only son, and they will grieve over him as one grieves at the death of a firstborn.”

The prophet introduces the Son of God himself speaking most plainly about himself: “They will look upon me whom they pierced.” This may refer both to the time of the Lord’s Passion and to the day of the final judgment. While the Lord was placed upon the cross, there is no doubt [Col. 0265A] that the devout and faithful also looked upon him and were moved with the deepest inward grief over him. But at the judgment they will look upon him coming in the glory of his majesty, whom they pierced with nails on the cross, and they will mourn and grieve with the greatest lamentation and sorrow, as at the death of an only son, whose bitter funeral calls forth immense mourning from his parents.

The Jews will therefore mourn as for an only son—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “a firstborn.” Christ is an only son according to the property of his nature: through divinity, the Father’s only one; through humanity, the mother’s only one. He is also the firstborn, because, as John says: “He is the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.”

“On that day there will be great mourning in Jerusalem [Col. 0265B], like the mourning of Hadremmon in the plain of Megiddo, and the families of the land will mourn, each family separately: the family of the house of David separately, and their wives separately; the family of the house of Nathan separately, and their wives separately; the family of the house of Levi separately, and their wives separately; the family of Shimei separately, and their wives separately.”

Hadremmon is a city near Jezreel, now called Maximianopolis, situated in the plain of Megiddo, where Josiah, the most righteous king, was killed by Pharaoh Neco. Jeremiah made great mourning over him and also remembers him in the book of Lamentations, saying: “The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, was captured in our sins; to him we said: Under your shadow we shall live among the nations.” Although, according to the spiritual sense, this refers to the Lord Savior [Col. 0265C].

Therefore, just as there was then great mourning in the city of Hadremmon, so great mourning will be recalled in Jerusalem when the Savior has been killed. What follows—“the families will mourn, each separately”—indicates that in a time of tribulation those who have wives ought not to devote themselves to marital activity. For in Genesis too we read that, when the Flood was impending, it was said to Noah: “Enter the ark, you and your sons, your wife and the wives of your sons,” placing first the father with his sons and then separately the father’s wife and the wives of his sons.

Thus now also the family of David, the family of the house of Nathan, the family of the house of Levi, and the family of the house of Shimei are separated from their wives, so that they may mourn the only-begotten Christ, against whom they cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” [Col. 0265D].

By David the royal house is understood, that is, the tribe of Judah; by Nathan, prophecy; by Levi, the priestly order, because their priesthood arose from the tribe of Levi; by Shimei, the teachers, because the tribe from which Shimei came possessed the privilege of teaching and instruction.

What follows—

“All the families, the remaining families, each family separately, and their wives separately”—

comprehends all the remaining families *synonymically* (*συνωνύμως*), that is, under a common designation, since they possess no privilege of rank.

These things have been said according to the way they are expounded by the Hebrews. We must now explain how the teachers of the Church refer them to the day of judgment.

“On that day,” he says—that is, at the time of judgment, when Jesus Christ comes in his majesty [Col. 0266A] and displays the marks of his Passion in his body before all, and causes the cross itself, borne by angelic hands, to be seen by the whole world—there will be incomparable mourning. All will mourn because their Lord and Creator endured such great and such unworthy things for the unworthy and sinful.

There will therefore be four orders of mourners. By the family of the house of David is signified the royal order and all the dignities of the age. In this order there will be some who are righteous and elect, who diligently ruled the people entrusted to them according to God’s will; these are signified by the men.

By the family of the house of Nathan is indicated the order of the teachers of the Church. Nathan was a prophet in the time of David, and therefore by him the teachers are understood [Col. 0266B], whom the Apostle Paul calls prophets. In this order also there are some who are like men, preaching the word of God sincerely; these are understood by the men. Others seek praise or payment for their preaching from human beings, not from God; these are marked by the women.

By the family of the house of Levi the priestly order and the dignity of all ecclesiastical ranks are indicated. Among these likewise some please God and labor manfully to win souls; others live feebly like women and care very little for the destruction of souls.

By the family of the house of Shimei the lay order is signified. Shimei lived among the people, yet also took care of his own household; therefore those who live in a secular manner are signified by him. But in this order [Col. 0266C] there are good people, who are called men, and reprobates, who are called women.

Thus at the judgment each will be distinguished according to the quality of his merits and placed in separate stations: some will be set at the right hand to be crowned, others at the left to be condemned. All will mourn, but the mourning of the righteous will be changed into eternal rejoicing, while that of the reprobate will become weeping that never ends.

## CHAPTER XIII

“On that day a fountain will be opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman.”

According to blessed Jerome, this open fountain for the house of David is the knowledge of the Scriptures. The fountain is open to the house of David, that is, to the whole Church [Col. 0266D]. For the Church itself is the house of David, because in it dwells the strong-handed and desirable-to-behold one.

This is the fountain that the prophet Ezekiel says he saw flowing out from the temple. It grew into a great river and proceeded to the wilderness of the nations to irrigate it with the streams of divine knowledge. This fountain is open for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman, so that, having received faith, we may be reborn in Christ and our sins may be washed away in the water of baptism.

According to blessed Gregory, this fountain is the exceedingly abundant mercy of God, open to the house of David, that is, to the whole Church. It is for the cleansing of the menstruating woman and of the one who has already committed in deed the wickedness he conceived; he calls the latter “the sinner,” and the one who conceived an evil deed deliberately in his mind but has not yet carried it into effect he calls “the menstruating woman” [Col. 0267A].

For a menstruating woman is neither touched by another’s flesh nor herself defiled in her own flesh. Such is the soul stained by the passions of vices and the filth of an evil will. The mercy of God is therefore open to all.

“And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord of hosts: I will destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and they shall no longer be remembered; and I will remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the earth.”

On that day, when Christ has saved his Church, he will destroy the names of the idols from the earth—whether those carved by the hand of an artisan, or the idols of perverse doctrines fabricated by heretics. For just as idols are made by the hand of an artisan, so the perverse teaching of heretics is turned into an idol: they worship Antichrist in place of Christ. He will also remove the false prophets, that is, the priests of idols, whom the pagans call prophets or seers. He will likewise remove the unclean spirit that rests in the hearts of the unclean, so that they may no longer be able to deceive anyone through fanatics and diviners.

“And it shall be, when anyone prophesies thereafter, that his father and his mother who begot him shall say to him: ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken falsehood in the name of the Lord’; and his father and mother, his parents, shall pierce him when he prophesies.”

When the things mentioned above have been fulfilled, and their names dispersed, and the false prophets and the unclean spirits that spoke through them have been removed, if anyone thereafter attempts to prophesy in the name of the Lord, his father and mother will immediately forget paternal and maternal affection [Col. 0267B] in order to fulfill God’s will. They will pronounce a sentence of death against their son, and no public judgment will be awaited; rather, he who has dared to prophesy will be condemned by the judgment of his own relatives.

“And it shall be: on that day the prophets shall be ashamed, each one because of his vision when he prophesies; nor shall they cover themselves with a hairy cloak in order to lie.”

When, he says, such a prophet has been convicted of having spoken falsely in the name of the Lord, he will be put to shame by the contrary outcome of events and will not cover himself with a hairy cloak. This was the customary dress of the prophets: they wore sackcloth when they announced repentance to the people, as we read that the prophet Isaiah did. Therefore the false prophet will not dare to assume this garment and pretend to be a prophet.

[Col. 0267D] “But he shall say,” as what follows: “I am no prophet; I am a farmer, for Adam has been my example from my youth. And it shall be said to him.”

“I am a farmer,” he says, “a man cleaving the earth with the plow, and subject to the sentence pronounced against the sinful Adam, when the Lord said to him, ‘In the sweat of your face,’” and so forth. When he has professed that he is not a prophet but a farmer, someone will question him and say: “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?”

Why, he says, have you been pierced with nails? For it was said above that his parents had pierced him when he prophesied. If, therefore, he says, you are not a prophet, what sin did you commit that you should be subjected to this punishment? Perhaps for this reason the Jews condemned the Lord Christ [Col. 0268A] to the cross, as though he were a false prophet; and this is what they said: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die.” For not only those five books of Moses are called the law, but also the Prophets and the Psalms. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, You are gods,’” although this is written in the Psalms?

He will answer: “And he shall say: ‘With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.’” By this answer he shows that at that time such great safeguarding of the truth would prevail that even he who had been condemned through his own fault would not dare to lie, but would rightly confess that he had suffered everything. “I received these wounds or scars in the house of my parents, who loved me; I was condemned not by the judgment of those who hated me, but of those who loved me.”

[Col. 0268B] “Sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man who is joined to me, says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered; and I will turn my hand toward the little ones.”

The *framea*, or *rhomphaea*, that is, a double-edged sword, although some wish to understand it as a spear. The Lord therefore commands the sword to arise against the shepherd, whom no one doubts to be Christ. For God the Father, because of the immense love with which he loved the human race, ordained before the ages to redeem the world through the death of his Son; and, when the fullness of time had come, he hastened to complete the work of his mercy.

He therefore commands the sword—or the *framea*—which we may understand either as the pain of the Passion, or death, or certainly the malice of the Jews themselves. Concerning this he speaks to the Father: “Deliver my soul from the sword.” This sword is raised against Christ the shepherd by the Father’s command, of whom it is said: “The one whom you struck, they pursued.” It is also raised against the man joined to him, that is, to God the Father. For the Son is always joined to the Father, as he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” He is joined to him not by conjunction, but by unity of substance.

It should be noted that here the Father is introduced as issuing the command, whereas in the Gospel the Lord himself is presented as speaking: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.” After the good shepherd had been struck, and the man joined to God had been suspended on the cross, the sheep—that is, the apostles—were scattered, together with whatever believers there were. Then he turned his hand toward the little ones, to whom he had said: “Do not be afraid, little flock,” and so forth.

[Col. 0268D] The apostles and the other followers of the Lord were the little ones: they were simple and innocent, little in malice; or they were called little because, in comparison with the unbelievers, who were innumerable, they appeared very few. He turned his hand toward them—that is, his action—in order to save them and to bring to completion in them the benefit and fruit of his Passion. Hence it follows:

“And it shall be in all the earth, says the Lord: two parts in it shall be destroyed and perish, and the third part shall be left in it.”

The two parts are the Jews and the Gentiles, both of whom perished and failed; and what was said in the Psalms was fulfilled: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed.” The third part is this remnant of believers, from both the Jewish [Col. 0269A] and the Gentile peoples, preserved for life and salvation.

“And I will lead the third part through the fire, and I will burn them as silver is burned; and I will test them as gold is tested.”

This third part, he says, which will be left in the earth, will be led through the fire of tribulation, tested and afflicted—not so that it may be consumed, but so that it may be proved like gold and silver, and may be able to say with the Psalmist: “You have tested us, God,” and so forth.

Or they will be led through that fire which the Lord sent upon the earth, concerning which it is said: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” They will therefore be led through the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that whatever in them is fragile and fluid may dry out and become firm, and so that they may not be overcome by any adversities.

“He shall call upon my name, and I will answer him. I shall say: ‘You are my people’; and he shall say: ‘The Lord is my God.’”

When the little ones, toward whom the Lord turned his hand, have been tested, and through them the whole multitude of the nations has believed, then the people of believers will call upon Christ by his name, which is Jesus, that is, Savior—the holy name Jesus, Savior of all ages. God himself, showing that their faith and devotion are pleasing to him, will say: “You are my people, whom I know by name”; and the people will answer: “The Lord is my God.”

## CHAPTER XIV

“Behold, the days of the Lord are coming, and your spoils shall be divided in your midst; and I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for battle, and the city shall be captured, and the houses shall be laid waste [Col. 0269C], and the women shall be violated; and half of the city shall go out into captivity, but the remainder of the people shall not be taken away from the city.”

After the prophet has introduced God the Father as speaking about the Lord’s Passion, he consequently begins to speak, from the voice of that same Lord, about the destruction of Jerusalem, in order to show that this overthrow occurred because of the Lord’s death.

The days whose coming he threatens are that time of which Isaiah says: “The day of the Lord is full of indignation and wrath and fury, to make the nations desolate”—plainly identifying it as the time of the final captivity. When he says, “The spoils shall be divided in the midst of the captured city,” he means that not only will Jerusalem be captured, but every kind of outrage will be perpetrated in it. The houses of the inhabitants will be plundered, and the women violated, to increase the grief of their husbands [Col. 0269D], who were unable to help their wives—nothing more cruel can be done by the savagery of an enemy.

“And the Lord shall go out and fight against those nations, as he fought on the day of battle; and his feet shall stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem toward the east.”

When we hear that God goes out or stands, or anything of this kind, we must not imagine in him a body or any bodily movement. God is incorporeal; concerning him the Apostle says: “To the King of the ages,” and so forth. In the Gospel the Lord says: “God is spirit.”

When the Lord is described in Scripture as standing or walking, or as possessing human limbs, this must be understood according to the variety of circumstances. He is said to go out or rise either when he liberates the saints placed in tribulation, or when he condemns their persecutors with a just vengeance. Thus the prophet says, “The Lord shall go out,” that is, he will manifest his clemency and gentleness, which he possesses by nature, by forgiving sins.

Although the Lord is naturally sweet, he becomes bitter through our fault, because to us, suffering evils on account of our sins, he seems bitter. The Lord, who is always the same and who speaks through the prophet, “I am God, and I do not change,” is now said to go out and fight as on the day of battle, when he fought for the people of Israel and drowned Pharaoh.

“And his feet shall stand.” Standing belongs to one who fights and assists. The Lord’s feet will therefore stand with and for those for whom he fought. He also walks and moves among those with whom he is angry, as we read concerning Adam, after whose sin the Lord walked about in the breeze of the afternoon.

He stood not in a valley but upon the Mount of Olives, which is the place of light, peace, and mercy, and from which it also received its name through mercy. This mountain too is opposite Jerusalem toward the east, from which the sun of righteousness rises for us. Hence the prophet says: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings.”

This Mount of Olives is Christ, planted with those olives of which it is said in the Psalm:

“Your children are like young olive trees.”

He is himself the rising, the splendor of the Father. For just as he is the door, and he himself the doorkeeper, and he himself the way by which we come to him, so he himself is the one who stands, and he himself is the mountain upon which he stands.
