“And the Mount of Olives shall be split from its middle toward the east and toward the west, with a very great precipice, and half of the mountain shall be separated toward the north, and half of it toward the south.”

The Mount of Olives, which we have said signifies Christ, although he is always one and the same, will be split—that is, he will divide the two peoples through the middle. The part split toward the east signifies the Church, in which olives from the Gentiles have been planted, one of whom says: “But I, like an olive tree,” and so forth. The other middle part, which is split toward the west by a great precipice, is the people of the circumcision, following the west—that is, the letter.

He does not simply say, “It shall be split,” but adds, “with a great precipice,” that is, a great chasm of perdition. Concerning this the prophet Micah says: “I will cast down its stones into the valley,” meaning Jerusalem, “and I will uncover its foundations.”

“And half of the mountain shall be separated toward the north, and half of it toward the south.” When the Mount of Olives has been split by a great chasm, so that one side of the chasm faces north and the other south, suddenly within that chasm and precipice another chasm will break open, separating one part toward the north and the other toward the south. A quadrangular precipice will result, so that the chasm will extend in four directions toward the four regions of the world.

“And you shall flee to the valley of their mountains, because the valley of the mountains shall be joined as far as the nearest place.”

There were two mountains, namely the Temple Mount and Mount Zion, which were called the mountains of God. This is what he says: “You shall flee to the valley of their mountains.” What follows—“because the valley of the mountains shall be joined as far as the nearest place”—shows how the valley, split by mountains on either side, will draw its chasm as far as the Temple Mount, which is holy.

“And you shall flee as you fled from the face of the earthquake in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah.”

He touches upon the history of that time when Uzziah, king of Judah, otherwise called Azariah, attempted to usurp the priesthood unlawfully. For this reason he was struck with leprosy and expelled from the Temple by the priests; and because of this impiety an earthquake occurred.

The prophet Amos recalls this earthquake at the beginning of his book, saying: “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, two years before the earthquake.”

This is the literal interpretation according to Hebrew tradition [Col. 0271B]; the Jews believe that all these things are to be fulfilled at the coming of Christ. We must now see what the spiritual understanding of the teachers of the Church contains.

We have said that the Mount of Olives signifies the Lord Christ. When this mountain has therefore been divided toward the east and the west—that is, when the Gentiles, signified by the east, have been chosen, and the Jews, understood by the west, have been rejected—there will again be another division of the northern and southern parts. The north will be joined to the west, and the south will be associated with the eastern region. The circumcision will stand on the left, and the Christian people on the right.

For by the left, the north, a most cold and icy wind, the devil is understood, the head of all the reprobate, who are to be placed on the left at the judgment. By the south, however, the right side, always illuminated by the light and warmth of the sun, the saints are represented: they burn with charity and shine with the grace of the true sun, and are to be placed at the judge’s right hand.

Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Rise, O north wind, and come, O south wind,” desiring the cold north wind—that is, the devil—to depart, and the south wind—that is, the fervor of love—to come. Through Habakkuk it is said: “God shall come from the south.”

When the division of the two peoples has thus become so great, and some have been separated toward the east and south, others toward the north and west, we are commanded to flee to the valley of the mountains of God—that is, to the two Testaments—because the valley, that is, the chasm first formed between the two mountains, will be joined to the nearest place, or, as the Septuagint translated it, to the house of God, namely paradise [Col. 0271D] and the heavenly Jerusalem.

What is stated above—“as far as the nearest place”—signifies that the two Testaments are joined to one another, but not in such a way that they are identical in every respect; rather, they are adjacent. For we have lost much from the ancient law and do not observe it in the New.

And just as the earthquake under King Uzziah terrified the hearts of mortals, so the separation of the two peoples—the eastern and western, Gentiles and Jews—and again the association of believers in a vain faith, signified by the joining of the eastern and southern divisions, will turn minds toward astonishment and fear as they marvel at the inscrutable abyss of God’s judgments.

When this has happened, and Jews and Gentiles have been joined into one, then “the Lord my God shall come” for judgment, “and all the saints with him.” And it shall be on that day: there shall be no light, but cold and frost; and there shall be one day known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and at evening time there shall be light.”

When the Lord comes for judgment, as John says in the Apocalypse, “Behold, he shall come with clouds,” that is, with his ministering angels, and with the apostles and prophets, on that day of his coming there will be no light, but cold and frost: charity will grow cold in everyone, and the warmth of faith will become tepid.

After all the reprobate have carried their cold and frost into hell, there will be one perpetual day for the saints, neither day nor night, with night and day no longer succeeding one another in turn. This day is known to the Lord because the Lord is the day of all the elect. Concerning it Isaiah says: “The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you, but your God shall be your everlasting light.” And the Psalmist says: “One day is better,” and so forth.

“And at evening time there shall be light.” When evening and darkness have obscured all the reprobate, there will be light for the holy elect of God. That day is therefore known to the Lord; he cannot be ignorant of what he himself created. When it says, “It is known to the Lord,” it shows that it is unknown to human beings and even to the angels, as the Lord says: “No one knows that day, not even the angels.”

“And it shall be on that day: living waters shall go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and half of them toward the western sea; in summer and in winter they shall be. And the Lord shall be king over all the earth.”

The eastern sea, literally, means the Dead Sea, which in Greek is called *λίμνη ἀσφάλτου* (*limnē asphaltou*), that is, “lake of bitumen”; we call it the Dead Sea because nothing can live in it. The western sea is the Tyrrhenian Sea, which leads toward Egypt and forms the coast of Palestine.

This is what he says: the waters that go out alive from Jerusalem will have one half flowing toward the east and falling into the Dead Sea, into which the Jordan flows; the other half will run into the western sea, which he calls the westernmost because there is the end of Judea. They will exist in summer and winter, so that they will neither be frozen by the cold of winter nor dried up by the excessive heat of summer, but will always flow in a full channel.

When this has happened, the Lord will be king over all the earth.

According to the mystical sense, the waters that go out from Jerusalem—that is, from the Church—are the teaching of the Savior. The prophet says: “The law shall go forth from Zion,” and so forth. One half of these waters will go toward the eastern sea, that is, toward the Jewish people, who first received the light of divine knowledge, as it were, at its rising in the apostles, and through them were led to the faith. The other half will go toward the westernmost sea, that is, toward the nations of the Gentiles.

By these eastern and western regions we must understand all the parts of the world into which the waters of divine knowledge have been channeled. Hence the Lord says: “Many shall come from the east and from the west, and shall recline with Abraham,” and so forth.

We may also understand by the eastern sea and the westernmost sea the two Testaments, the Law and the Gospel. It is necessary that they be sweetened by the Savior’s stream—that is, by spiritual understanding—and that the bitterness of the western letter be removed.

These waters will exist in summer and winter because heavenly teaching does not cease to flow either in prosperity, signified by summer, or in the adversity of persecution, signified by winter.

It should be noted that the Septuagint does not have “in winter,” but “in spring and in summer they shall be.” For this reason some refer the living waters to baptism, since throughout the Church it is generally celebrated in spring and summer, that is, at Easter and Pentecost.

“On that day there shall be one Lord, and his name shall be one. And the whole land shall return as far as the wilderness, from the hill of Rimmon toward the south of Jerusalem; and it shall be exalted, and shall dwell in its place, from the gate of Benjamin to the place of the former gate, and as far as the Corner Gate; and from the tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses. And they shall dwell in it, and there shall no longer be an anathema, but Jerusalem shall sit securely.”

All these statements concerning the construction of an earthly Jerusalem and the outflow of waters that run to both seas are understood literally by the Jews and by the Judaizing heretics whom they call Chiliasts, from the number of the thousand years during which they promise themselves that they will happily reign with their Christ at the end of the age.

For he says that once they have reigned with Christ in a golden and jeweled Jerusalem, there will no longer be idols or diverse forms of worship, but there will be one Lord, and he alone will be named; and the whole earth will return to its former condition, when the whole earth will be uncultivated and deserted.

The names of places are given to indicate from what place to what place Jerusalem is to be built: from the hill of Rimmon to the south of Jerusalem; and it will be exalted in its former state, from the gate of Benjamin to the Corner Gate, and from the tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses.

“And there shall be no anathema,” that is, no fear and no attack by enemies; rather, Jerusalem will sit secure and at leisure in peace. *Anathema* is a Greek word that may be rendered in Latin as “alienation.” The expression was derived from objects that people, when making vows, attached to temples and alienated from themselves—that is, from *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνατιθέναι*, “from placing on high” or “hanging up.”

They suppose that these things will occur literally. Let us examine the mystical sense and interpret what they fabricate about the earthly Jerusalem as referring to the heavenly and celestial Jerusalem.

When the Lord Jesus has become king over all the earth and his name is one, so that he alone is invoked and worshiped as God, with every false religion removed, and what the Psalmist says to the Lord has been fulfilled—“Lord, our Lord,” and so forth—then the whole earth will return to the wilderness. That is, the unbelieving Jewish nation will be as the nations once were, nations called a wilderness because they did not possess knowledge of God.

The Gentiles who believe in Christ will possess before God the place that the Jews once possessed. Hence through Isaiah it is said: “Lebanon shall be turned into Carmel, and Carmel shall be reckoned as a forest.”

“And it shall return from the hill of Rimmon toward the south of Jerusalem.” Rimmon is interpreted as “exalted” or “pomegranate.” This signifies that the Church, [Col. 0274A] which is Jerusalem, will rise from the wilderness toward the hills, and from the hills advance toward the heights, progressing from virtue to virtue; and, not content with this end, will reach the southern region, where there is the fervor of love and the splendor of eternal brightness, namely the fellowship of the divine vision, concerning which the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed.”

Rimmon is also interpreted as “pomegranate,” which is a tree whose fruit is very beautiful and full of seeds contained in various chambers by little membranes beneath a crimson rind. It is said to cure burning of the stomach, cleanse a diseased belly, and benefit all the internal organs.

The beauty of this fruit suits the Church: its red color signifies the modesty of chastity; the arrangement of its seeds signifies the grades and members of the whole ecclesiastical body, distributed among their several offices.

The boundaries of the Church begin from the hill of Rimmon because it begins from humility and from lesser things, so that the ecclesiastical order may be built through successive advances. It will then be exalted, beginning from the hills, and will dwell in its own place in the station of perfection.

Concerning this place the Psalmist says: “He placed me there in a place of pasture.” It follows: “from the gate of Benjamin to the place of the former gate.”

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand,” because the holy Church begins from virtue, which is signified by the right hand, and reaches the former gate, that is, faith, through which we enter into the remaining virtues.

Immediately the Corner Gate presents itself, that is, Christ, the cornerstone, containing and joining together two walls. Upon this stone other cornerstones are built, namely the apostles and apostolic men, who contain the remaining corners of the Church. To them Paul says: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God,” and so forth.

The Church is also built from the tower of Hananel, which is interpreted as “most gracious to God”—that is, the stronghold of faith, hope, and charity. The Psalmist rejoiced that he had reached this, saying: “You led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy.” Nothing is more pleasing to God than this tower.

From there the building reaches the king’s winepresses, in which Christ’s vintage is pressed, which he himself first trod. Hence through Isaiah it is said: “I alone have trodden the winepress,” and so forth.

In these winepresses the clusters of the martyrs are trodden: they follow the footsteps of Christ’s Passion. And just as he laid down his life for them, so they do not fear to undergo death for love of him.

When the city of God, having been built, reaches the winepresses of Christ the King, there will no longer be an anathema, that is, a curse or alienation; rather, Jerusalem will be secure and confident: “For blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord.”

“And this shall be the plague with which the Lord will strike all the nations that fought against Jerusalem: the flesh of each one who stands upon his feet shall waste away, and his eyes shall waste away in their sockets, and their tongues shall waste away in their mouths.”

Here it is clearly shown that everything the Jews believe about an earthly Jerusalem is vain. For the Romans were the last to fight against Jerusalem and utterly destroyed it, yet they suffered nothing of this kind [Col. 0275A].

We may, however, say concerning the persecutors of the Church, who fought against her with every effort, that these things were also very often fulfilled in them bodily. To say nothing of the torments they endured in hell after death, even in this life the flesh of many rotted, their eyes wasted away in their sockets, and their tongues dissolved into corruption and foul matter.

Spiritually, in the one who stands upon his feet and says with the Psalmist, “The Lord set my feet upon a rock,” carnal vices flow away so that spiritual virtues may arise. The eyes that previously turned wickedly toward lust fall away, so that better eyes may be put in their place, and he may say: “I lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in the heavens.” The tongue that blasphemed God will fail, so that one may be born anew that glorifies God.

Thus God’s scourges are shown not to be acts of cruelty but of mercy: when evils are uprooted, good things grow in their place.

“On that day there shall be a great tumult from the Lord among them; and each man shall seize the hand of his neighbor, and his hand shall be joined to the hand of his neighbor.”

Let us refer spiritually to the happiness of the Church what the Jews and Judaizing heretics understand literally: when those enemies have been subjected and have received the faith of Christ, there will be tumult and astonishment among all at so sudden a change of circumstances.

Then each man will seize the hand of his neighbor, and hand will be joined to hand, so that they may give one another the right hands of mutual fellowship in the faith of Christ and, like recruits, swear that they will remain in his worship and religion.

What follows—

[Col. 0275C] “But Judah also shall fight against Jerusalem”—

signifies that many who previously confessed the name of Christ, compelled by the necessity of persecution, will act against the Church. Yet the Septuagint translators do not have “shall fight against Jerusalem,” but “shall be prepared in Jerusalem,” so that the sense is: those who confess the Lord will be prepared in the Church to fight against its adversaries.

Then “the wealth of all the nations round about shall be gathered,” implicitly, in the Church: “gold,” that is, understanding; “silver,” that is, speech; and “very many garments,” the diversity of virtues with which the Church is adorned.

“And so there shall be the ruin of the horse, the mule, the camel, the donkey, and all the beasts that were in those camps, like this ruin.”

All the evils that previously fought against the Church are foretold to collapse, so that good things may suddenly arise.

The one who was previously a horse impatient for lust will see luxury collapse within him; chastity will arise in him, and he will begin to have the Lord as his rider. Those who were previously sterile mules, having no children of good works, will be overturned and will produce spiritual offspring; and it will be said to them: “Your children are like young olive trees.”

Camels, weighed down by a heavy hump, ruminate but do not divide the hoof; they signify those whom grave sins oppress. They read the Scriptures but neglect what is written there. They also signify the Jews, who ruminate upon God’s law—that is, meditate upon it—but do not divide the hoof, because they do not believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Donkeys are unclean and do not resist the passions of their flesh. It is beneficial for all these that what stood wrongly in them should fall, so that, rising again, they may receive within themselves the gentle God, by whom they may be led into the heavenly Jerusalem.

“And all who remain of all the nations that came against Jerusalem shall go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.”

The feast of Tabernacles, called in Greek *skenopegia*—that is, “the setting up of tents”—was celebrated in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, in memory of the time when, in the wilderness where there were no houses, they lived in tents for forty years.

And we, mystically: as long as we are engaged in the struggle and know that we are pilgrims and guests upon the earth, we dwell in tents, confessing that “we have no abiding city here, but we seek the one that is to come,” and we yearn for it with all our heart, saying with the Psalmist: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged.”

But when we have reached our homeland and can say, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house,” and, “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek,” and so forth, then it will be fitting to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles: that is, always to keep in memory the time of our deliverance and that eternal rest which, after the ages of the world, is promised to us as the seventh age, like one Sabbath.

We shall take for ourselves branches of the most beautiful tree, that is, wisdom, for unfading verdure, in whose praise it is said: “It is a tree of life to those who grasp it.” Also branches of palms, in which the sign of victory and its reward are contained. Also branches of a tree with dense foliage, which the Jews think is the myrtle, so that we may mortify in ourselves the incitements of vices. This is also signified by the willows of the torrent, which we are likewise commanded to take.

For physicians report that if someone drinks a willow blossom mixed with water, every natural heat in him will be cooled and the poisons of lust dried up, so that he will no longer generate them. Whoever wishes to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles should make shelters for himself from such trees.

“And it shall be: whoever does not go up from the families of the earth to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, there shall be no rain upon them.”

The heavenly Jerusalem is the city of our King, the Lord Jesus Christ. Concerning it the Apostle says: “The Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother.” Whoever wishes to come to it must ascend. For it is situated not in a low place but upon a high mountain. Concerning it the Lord says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

The citizens of Jerusalem therefore ascend to worship the King, the Lord of hosts. Those who are not citizens but belong to families and tribes—such as the Jews and heretics—have not ascended; therefore the rain of apostolic preaching has not come upon them. Concerning them it was said: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.”

“But if the family of Egypt does not go up and does not come, nor shall it be upon them; but there shall be the ruin with which the Lord will strike all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.”

Egypt is interpreted as “darkness” or “grief.” Whoever is Egypt—that is, whoever is established in the darkness of ignorance of God or of crimes—cannot ascend to Jerusalem, since he lacks the light that goes before him, concerning which it is said: “Walk while you have the light.” He cannot possess joy in the hope of future things. Therefore the heavenly rain of blessing will not come upon him.

“This shall be the sin of Egypt, and this shall be the sin of all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles.”

That is, of the Ammonites, Moabites, Assyrians, Chaldeans, and the remaining nations, by whom those are signified who choose to remain in their errors and do not wish to leave their own land in order to come into fellowship with the Church, become Israelites, and become citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

“On that day what is upon the horse’s bridle shall be holy to the Lord.”

The Hebrews, according to their customary literal interpretation, say that after their king has come with equity and reigned in the golden Jerusalem, when peace has been established everywhere, there will be no need for horses or cavalry. Rather, the bridles and ornaments of the harness will be transferred to the worship of the Lord; and when it says, “what is upon the horse’s bridle,” we should understand every military ornament.

According to the mystical sense, the bridle is the discipline of heavenly instruction, by which raging lust and wanton licentiousness are restrained. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle.” This bridle is placed in the horse’s mouth so that, abandoning the winding paths of error, it may proceed along the straight way and offer its gentle back to the Savior for riding.

Such ornaments, and such a bridle, adorned with gold and silver—that is, with understanding and eloquence—are holy to the Lord and specially consecrated to his worship.

It is worth noting that the account found in the little book concerning the discovery of the holy cross—that this was fulfilled when Helena Augusta, the mother of the emperor Constantine, ordered the nails of the Lord’s cross to be made into bits for the king’s horse—was, according to blessed Jerome, fabricated with pious intent but is ridiculous.

And there shall be cauldrons in the house of the Lord, like bowls [Col. 0278A] before the altar. “And every cauldron in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be sanctified to the Lord of hosts.” The cauldrons—that is, the bronze pots in which the flesh of the sacrificial victims was boiled—shall be as holy and worthy of veneration as the golden bowls in which libations and aromatics were offered to the Lord. This shows that every carnal tradition and observance of the Jews must be converted into something spiritual, and that the virulence of flesh must give way to the fragrances of spiritual understanding. Concerning these bowls John says that he saw twenty-four elders holding harps and bowls full of incense, which, he says, are the prayers of the saints; and in the Song of Songs, according to the Septuagint: “My beloved went down to his garden, to the bowls of aromatics, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.” [Col. 0278B] For the bowls of aromatics are receptacles of holy souls, full of the fragrances of virtues and pure prayers, from which a good odor is daily diffused before the Lord. When, therefore, the cauldrons have been changed into bowls, and carnal things exchanged for spiritual ones, then every cauldron will be consecrated to the Lord in Jerusalem and in Judah—that is, in the Church, which is the vision of peace and where there are those who confess, that is, praise, the Lord.

“And all who sacrifice shall come and take from them and cook in them; and there shall no longer be a merchant in the house of the Lord of hosts on that day.” When, he says, the cauldrons have been changed into bowls, and carnal understanding has passed over into the subtlety of spiritual understanding, then all who sacrifice to the Lord will come—that is, those who make themselves an acceptable whole burnt offering. And they will take and cook the flesh of the victims in them, so that whatever is carnal and perishable in them may be boiled away in the fire of the Holy Spirit. For in the Law we are also said to eat the flesh of the paschal lamb raw—that is, to celebrate Passover carnally with the Jews. Then such a fragrance of good odor will be offered from the bowls that no one will dare conduct trade in the house of the Lord or sell oxen, sheep, and doves there. For they will fear that, just as he then made a scourge from cords and drove everyone out of the temple, so now, coming spiritually, he might exclude the wicked merchants from the temple of the heavenly Jerusalem.

## ON THE PROPHET MALACHI

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277D] The Hebrews think that Malachi, the last of the twelve prophets, was Ezra the prophet and priest. He prophesied at the same time as Haggai and Zechariah. Hence no date is given in the heading. His name is interpreted as “angel of the Lord,” or “my angel,” because he possessed such authority that whatever he said was believed as though it had been spoken by an angel of the Lord. For this reason some thought that he had been an angel by nature, descended from heaven clothed in flesh to admonish the people who had recently returned from captivity.

## CHAPTER ONE

“The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by the hand of Malachi” [Col. 0278D] the prophet. As has already been said in the preceding books, wherever “burden” is used among the prophets, it announces the weight of a threat or of some adversity imposed upon sinners. Here too, therefore, the word of the Lord is called a burden, since it is indeed heavy for those to whom it is addressed. Yet it contains something consoling, because it is not said against Israel but “to Israel”: the things that follow are not said as destined to come against the people of Israel, but to that people, so that it might know beforehand what was being announced as destined to occur. Here, however, we must understand Israel as the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin. Once the ten tribes that had been called Israel had been led into captivity, the remaining two tribes likewise began indiscriminately to be called Israel. As for the phrase “by the hand of Malachi,” he says “hand” because through good works he earned the gift of prophecy. Whoever washes among the innocent and shakes his hands free from every gift deserves to receive the spirit of prophecy. But to those of whom it is said, “Your hands are full of blood,” the word of the Lord is not addressed, either in them or to them.

“I have loved you, says the Lord, and you said: ‘In what way have you loved us?’ Was not Esau Jacob’s brother, says the Lord, and yet I loved Jacob, while I hated Esau? And I made his mountains, the mountains of Seir, a desolation, and his inheritance to the dragons of the desert. But if Edom should say: ‘We have been destroyed, but we shall return and rebuild what has been destroyed,’ thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘They shall build, and I shall destroy, and they shall be called the boundaries of wickedness, and the people with whom the Lord is angry forever.’ And your eyes shall see, and you shall say: ‘May the Lord be magnified over the territory of Israel.’”

Because he had first mentioned the burden of punishments that they were compelled to bear, he adds why they did not deserve these punishments: “I loved you,” he says, with the unstated implication, “but you in no way returned a mutual love to me.” For, as the proverb says, not to love in return one who loves is to waste the expense of love. Because they had not loved the Lord who loved them, he threatens them with punishment, so that through torments they may feel what they refused to feel through benefits.

Certainly, when he says in the past tense, “I loved,” he denies that he loves in the present, while confessing a former love. When the Lord had therefore said, “I loved you,” they, with the same recklessness with which they sinned, replied, “In what way have you loved us?”—as though they had forgotten the countless benefits he had bestowed upon them. The Lord answered them: “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother?” “To say nothing,” he says, “of the other things—how I recently freed you from the captivity of Babylon, and to pass over these and many other matters—let me go back further and show from your very conception how I loved you. Before Rebecca gave birth to Jacob and Esau, I loved you in Jacob, but in Esau I hated the Edomites. And I made his mountains,” he says—that is, the region of Seir—“a desolation,” and I caused his cities, deserted by human beings, to be possessed by dragons and wild beasts.

“But if Edom, who is Esau, should say: ‘We have been destroyed, but, returning again, we shall rebuild our cities,’ they will indeed build, but I shall destroy.” God’s hatred and love must not be conceived carnally in the human manner. For just as God created everyone, so he also loves everyone: he has mercy on human beings and hates none of the things he has made. Therefore God’s hatred arises either from his foreknowledge of future things or from deeds. God loves those whom he sees resisting vices and obeying the divine commandments. But he is said to hate those whom he sees serving sins and wishing to rebuild vices that have already been destroyed.

This is how the Hebrews explain the passage historically. They also wish the Romans to be understood through the Edomites: cruel and bloodthirsty, because Edom is interpreted as “red” or “bloody.” Their empire, they say, is destined to be destroyed at the end of the world, and sovereignty over the whole earth will pass away from them.

In the allegorical sense, Esau and Jacob, brothers born from one stock, represent the figure of vices and virtues. Although these two are opposed, they proceed from one source, the heart. For since we possess free choice, according to our will we either turn toward vices or toward virtues. Esau was born first, because vices come first through infancy, adolescence, and youth. Jacob was born afterward; his name is interpreted as “supplanter,” because a more mature age follows and corrects and supplants the errors of a more fragile age. Hence it is appropriately said that the elder brother was hairy and uncultivated, accustomed to hunting and the forests, while the younger, gentle and simple, is said to have lived at home.

Thus, under the name of Esau, God asserts that he hates vices, not the nature he made good. For this reason he sets his boundaries in a desolation, so that every evil may be uprooted and vices may not grow up again. But if shameless wickedness should attempt to rebuild what has been destroyed, the Lord declares that he will destroy it again. This happens in two ways: either when sinners are corrected, or when those who persist in sin are condemned by just retribution.

“A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a Father, where is my honor? And if I am a Lord, where is my fear? says the Lord of hosts.” It is as though he were saying: “Although, before you were reborn, I loved you in Jacob as sons, nevertheless choose by which name you wish to call me—as Father or as Lord. If I am Father, why do you not give the honor owed to a father? If I am Lord, why do you despise me? Why do you not fear me as Lord?”

He says this to those who had recently returned from captivity and, although neither the temple nor the city had yet been rebuilt, nevertheless remained in their former sins, revering God neither with fear nor with love. Spiritually, God first wishes us to be his sons, obeying him voluntarily and serving him not through fear but through love. If we do not wish to be this, he at least wishes us to be servants, withdrawing from evil through fear of punishments and doing good. Thus the Lord seeks honor from sons, but fear from servants. “For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,” so that, beginning with fear, we may pass over to the love of sons.

“To you, O priests, who despise my name, and you have said: ‘In what way have we despised your name?’ You offer polluted bread upon my altar, and you say: ‘In what way have we polluted you?’ In that you say: ‘The table of the Lord is despised.’”

“To you,” he says, “O priests, my speech is directed especially: you despise my name by disparaging my sacrifices. After returning from Babylon, you ought to have turned with your whole mind away from your former crimes, yet you join contempt for my sacrifices to them.” But, as though ignorant of these things, they continue to ask him who knows all things, “In what way do we despise you?”

The Lord answered: “You offer polluted bread upon my altar”—namely, the bread of the Presence, which, according to the traditions of the Hebrews, the priests themselves ought to sow, reap, grind, and bake. Disdaining to do this, they took whatever sort of bread they could find and placed it upon the Lord’s table on the Sabbath. It was kept there until the following Sabbath, and it was called holy bread, which no one except the priests was permitted to eat. He therefore says: “You offer polluted bread upon my altar”; and, while you treat my sacrifices badly, you violate me, whose sacraments they are.

What follows—“In that you say: ‘The table of the Lord is despised’”—may be explained in this way: the altar they had made after returning from captivity did not possess the glory of the ancient altar. Therefore they said that the table of the Lord was despised, as though the religion lacked holiness because it lacked magnificence. Yet, on the contrary, God seeks not the adornment of the altar but the devotion of the one who offers.

In a deeper sense, the divine word reproves priests and ministers of the Church because they handle the divine mysteries negligently and offer polluted bread upon the Lord’s altar: namely, when they approach the altar unworthily, drink pure blood with a polluted conscience, and receive the most holy bread with an unclean mouth. Thus the Lord’s table, holy in itself, comes to be despised because of the baseness of its ministers.

According to another interpretation, when a preacher, who ought to distribute spiritual bread—that is, teaching—to the people, flatters the powerful and wealthy of this world and says what pleases them, failing to rebuke sinners with appropriate severity, he pollutes the bread of doctrine and insults the Lord himself, since he considers the table of the Scriptures, which is the table of idols, to be like secular teaching.

“If you offer a blind animal for sacrifice, is that not evil? And if you offer a lame and sick animal, is that not evil? Offer it to your governor: will he be pleased with it, or will he accept you? says the Lord of hosts. And now entreat the face of God, so that he may have mercy on you. This has come from your hand: will he accept you in any way? says the Lord of hosts.”

After returning from Babylon, the priests and the other ministers of the Lord’s temple offered unlawful victims in the Lord’s sacrifice—blind animals, as well as lame animals and those afflicted with various disabilities—complaining that poverty and necessity forced them to offer such things. He therefore says: “If you were to offer such gifts to your governor, would he not reject them? He would certainly say that an injury had been done to him. By what reasoning, then, do you offer to the Lord what you would not dare give to human beings?”

Allegorically, God’s victim is some good work, prayer, almsgiving, and other sacrifices pleasing to God. But if the victim is blind—if the mind of the one offering is not illuminated by the light of truth, that is, if the intention of the one who offers is not simple—then the victim of prayer is lame, since it approaches God in prayer with a divided mind. It is also weak because it does not have Christ, who is power and wisdom. Such victims, if offered, can in no way please God; rather, they make the one who offers them guilty.

“And now entreat the face of the Lord, so that he may have mercy on you,” as above.

“Who is there among you who would shut the doors and kindle my altar for nothing?” The meaning is this: there is no one among you who serves me for nothing—that is, without payment—not the high priest, not the priest, not even the doorkeeper or the one who places the fire beneath the altar to burn the whole burnt offerings. For you receive from the people tithes of all crops and the other things that the law has decreed for you from the sacrifices of victims.

Therefore, because you offend God in your sacrifices by offering the weakest things, repent and entreat the face of the Lord, to see whether he might have mercy on you. From this passage we gather that the service God finds more pleasing is that which does not receive payment in the present. Hence the Apostle preached the Gospel freely, laboring night and day and working with his hands for his food, so as not to burden anyone.

“I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand.” The prophecy is perfectly clear and requires no deeper exposition. It speaks specifically to the priests who were offering unlawful victims, and therefore the pleasure of God, whom they were provoking, was not in them. At the same time it teaches that spiritual victims would succeed their carnal sacrifices—not merely in one province of the Jews, but that in every place a pure offering would be offered to God, namely, the sacrifice that the Church now frequently offers.

“For from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place an offering is sacrificed and presented to my name, a pure offering, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts. But you have polluted it in saying: ‘The table of the Lord is contaminated, and what is placed upon it is contemptible, together with the fire that devours it.’”

As was briefly stated above, the people who had returned from captivity had built only an altar from rough and unworked stones. Because the ornaments of the temple were lacking, however, they thought that the worship of religion was diminished in it. The Lord therefore speaks to them through the prophet: “You think the altar is polluted, as well as the whole burnt offerings and victims placed upon it, and you do not understand that the Lord does not seek adornment of gold or silver, nor a multitude of victims, but the pure will of those who offer.”

Here we must not think that “table” means the table upon which the bread of the Presence was placed, but the altar on which sacrifices were burned. This is clearly indicated by the words “together with the fire that devours it.” For fire did not consume those loaves; they were eaten by the priests.

Or the words “The table of the Lord is contaminated, and what is placed upon it is contemptible, together with the fire that devours it” may be understood in this way: “What does it matter if we offer the best things? Whatever they may be, they must be consumed by fire.”

“And you said: ‘Behold, it is from labor,’ and you blew upon it, says the Lord of hosts. And you brought the lame and the sick from what had been stolen, and you brought an offering. Shall I accept it from your hand? says the Lord of hosts.”

When the people who had returned from Babylon offered victims to the Lord, they said reluctantly and sadly: “Behold, we offer this from our labor. We are the prey of our enemies, and whatever we were able to possess we consumed during the long journey. Whatever we have, we offer.” As they said these things, they blew scornfully upon their sacrifices—that is, they treated them as contemptible.

Some manuscripts read, “You blew upon me,” so that the meaning is: “You did not wrong the sacrifice, but me, to whom you were sacrificing.” Therefore I will not accept it.

“Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male animal in his flock and, when making a vow, sacrifices to the Lord what is weak, because I am a great King, says the Lord of hosts, and my name is terrible among the nations.”

He openly rebukes those who said, “Behold, it is from labor,” and shows that they deceitfully pleaded poverty although they possessed the best animals, and that, when making vows, they offered inferior ones. These too were not from their own flock but from the plunder and tears of the wretched.

## CHAPTER TWO

“And now this commandment is for you, O priests. If you will not listen, and if you will not take it to heart, to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send poverty upon you.” You have done, he says, what is impious. But because I prefer the sinner’s repentance to his death, if you will not listen to me and give glory to my name—which is terrible and awe-inspiring among the nations—namely, if you will not repent of having done such things, I will send true poverty upon you, so that you will no longer say, “Behold, it is from labor,” as a lie, but will say it because necessity has compelled you.

“And I will curse your blessings, and I will curse them, because you have not taken it to heart.” He means the goods that you now possess through my blessing, because you have not taken it to heart—that is, you have not wished to hear and do what was said to you.

Tropologically, we can interpret the “deceitful man” who is cursed as the Jewish people. Although they possessed an excellent and spotless male animal, the Lord Savior, and had been warned by the voices of all the prophets to receive him and sacrifice him, believing that the Son of God had come for the salvation of all, they did not wish to do this. Instead, rejecting Christ, they chose the weak and diseased animal, Barabbas, who prefigured the type of Antichrist. Yet although they did this, the name of Christ is nevertheless terrible and venerable among the nations.

“Behold, I will cast the arm away from you, and I will scatter the dung of your festivals upon your faces, and it will carry you away with it.”

This threat is directed against the priests who misused the legal ceremonies. He contemptuously calls the holier things they received as offerings according to the law the “dung of festivals”: namely, the right shoulder and breast, the tongue and stomach, and the other things that Leviticus commands the priests to receive from the people’s victims. He declares that he will now cast these things away and throw them upon their faces, to show that they are of the same kind as the things they offer. “And it will carry you away with it”—with the implied subject, the dung of your festivals—so that your faces will be disfigured by the foul mixture of dung.

“And you shall know that I sent this commandment to you, so that it might be my covenant with Levi, says the Lord of hosts. My covenant with him was one of life and peace.”

For this reason, he says, I will do these things to you, so that you may know that I am the one who once chose Levi, your father, and in Levi, Aaron, so that my covenant might be with Levi and his descendants, that they might minister to me in an everlasting priesthood.

Tropologically, God wished all human beings, but especially priests, to be holy and without any stain. He commanded them to possess an arm, or right shoulder—that is, the adornment of good works. He commanded them to receive a breast, signifying a good and innocent conscience; a tongue, signifying holy confession; and a stomach, so that they might contain within themselves nothing deadly or poisonous. For food is digested in the stomach, and the body is irrigated by its juices. Therefore the stomach signifies the bond of charity, by which all the members cherish one another, seeking not what is their own but what belongs to others.

If priests act contrary to this, God threatens that all these things will be turned into dung, that the dung will carry them away, and that it will disfigure the face of the soul, so that its face cannot lift itself up and say: “Your face, O Lord, I will seek,” and so forth.

“And I gave him fear, and he feared me, and he was afraid before the face of my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found upon his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many away from iniquity.”

In these divine words of praise spoken concerning Levi, the office of the priest and the kind of person he ought to be are described. God’s covenant was with Levi the patriarch; through Levi it came to Aaron and his descendants. The covenant of life is not the ordinary right of life that you share with all living creatures, but the life of the one who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life,” and of which the Apostle says, “Our life is hidden with Christ in God.” He is also our peace, according to the Apostle, “who made both one.”

“I gave him fear,” he says—that fear which is the beginning of wisdom. “And he was afraid before the face of my name,” showing the disposition of his mind by the trembling of his agitated body, in accordance with what is written: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?”

“The law of truth was in his mouth”—that is, simple teaching, darkened by no stain of falsehood. “And iniquity was not found in him,” because he imitated that one High Priest of whom it is truly said: “He committed no sin,” and so forth.

“He walked with me in peace and uprightness,” so that he himself might have peace, make peace for others, and show partiality toward no one in judgment. “And he turned many away from iniquity.” For whoever is a priest and does not rebuke those who sin destroys the office of the priest.

“For the lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” He did not say “they will bring forth” or “they will speak,” but “they will guard,” so that they may fulfill it in their actions and thus set before the others, by word and example, the things they ought to do. “And they will seek the law from his mouth”—that is, from the priest’s mouth. We read the same thing in Haggai: “Ask the priests about the law.” It belongs to the discipline of priests to answer when questioned about the law.

For this reason Paul, describing the form of a priest to Titus, says that he must be “able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it.” Malachi is interpreted as “angel of the Lord,” and every priest is an angel of the Lord, a mediator between God and human beings who announces God’s will to the people.

“But you have departed from the way and have caused many to stumble in the law. You have annulled the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts. Therefore I too have made you contemptible and lowly among all the peoples, because you have not kept my ways and have shown partiality in the law.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “I wished you to be such as I described your ancestor Levi to have been. But you, on the contrary, have departed or turned aside from the way I showed you, concerning which it is said elsewhere: ‘This is the way; walk in it, turning neither to the right nor to the left.’”

They cause many to stumble in the law when they make those whom they instruct by word go astray through the example of their evil conduct. “You have annulled my covenant with Levi” by acting negligently in the matters belonging to the priestly office. Therefore “I too have made you contemptible,” so that, instead of the honor and reverence owed to you, people would trample upon you as despised and rejected.

As blessed Gregory says, when a person’s life is despised, it remains only for his preaching also to be despised. He places last what he regards as most serious: they show partiality, despising righteous poor people while welcoming proud rich people.

“Is there not one father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why, then, does each of you despise his brother, violating the covenant of your fathers?”

As we read in the book of Ezra, after returning from Babylonian captivity, both the leaders and many of the priests and Levites cast away wives of Israelite origin. These women had been worn out by age, poverty, the labor of the long journey, and the fragility of their sex, and had acquired weakness and deformity. The men joined themselves instead to young women flourishing in bodily beauty or distinguished by nobility and wealth. The prophet rebukes them and urges them, after dismissing the women whom they had illicitly married, to take back those whom they had wrongly cast away. He therefore says: “Is there not one father of us all?”

“Judah has transgressed, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has profaned the sanctuary of the Lord, which he loved, and has taken the daughter of a foreign god.”

Here we must understand Judah and Israel, or Jerusalem, as only the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, together with the priestly—that is, Levitical—tribe. Only these had returned from captivity. For the ten tribes were still being held in captivity by the Assyrians.

“Judah, therefore, has profaned the sanctuary”: the seed chosen by God, by mingling with foreigners and taking the daughters of the wicked in marriage. What follows—“And he has taken the daughter of a foreign god”—means that he took as a wife a woman who worshiped idols, contrary to God’s command: “You shall not take a daughter from the stock of Canaan as a wife for your son.”

“The Lord will destroy the man who does this, both teacher and disciple, from the tents of Jacob, and the one who offers an offering to the Lord of hosts.”

Notice that he does not say, “The one who has done this,” but uses the future tense: “The one who does this.” He does not remove forgiveness for a crime that has been committed, but threatens future punishment. He calls those who had fallen into sin to repentance and makes no exception: whether teacher, disciple, common person, or one who offers an offering—that is, a priest—all are struck by one sentence of condemnation, so that there is no distinction among those whose guilt is equal.

“And this you have done again: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and groaning, so that I will no longer look upon the sacrifice or accept anything appeasing from your hand. And you said:”

The Israelite wives abandoned by their husbands, seeing foreign wives in the beds of their husbands, fled to the help of God alone. Prostrate with tears and groaning before his altar, they complained that God permitted such things to occur, since everything is governed by his providence. He therefore says that he could not look upon the sacrifice of the priests who had committed these acts or accept anything from their hands, being obstructed and, as it were, overwhelmed by the tears of the afflicted.

But they, proudly and as though unaware that they had done anything wrong, ask “for what reason” he could not accept a sacrifice from their hands. They are answered:

“Because the Lord has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised, although she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make one, and is not the residue of his spirit his? And what does that one seek, if not the seed of God?”

He says: “For this reason a man will leave his father or mother and cling to his wife.” She who was formed from the man’s rib is thus your companion and the wife of your covenant, and she is “the residue of his spirit”—that is, of the man’s spirit—because the union between husband and wife is so great that one soul appears to exist in two bodies.

“And what does the one seek”—with “God” understood—“if not the seed of God?” God, he says, who joined them with such a bond of affection, seeks the seed of God, so that children of Israelite descent may be born from them. Since marriage was instituted for the procreation of children, and since you have fertile wives from whom you can receive the joy of children, why do you seek beautiful wives and cast away your lawful wives?

He therefore exhorts us to repentance, saying: “Guard your spirit, therefore, and do not despise the wife of your youth”—the woman first joined to you in virgin marriage, who should remain with you into old age.

“When you hate her, dismiss her, says the Lord, the God of Israel. But iniquity will cover his garment, says the Lord of hosts.”

This must be understood as spoken from the perspective of the priests, Levites, and others who did not wish to dissolve illicit marriages. When the prophet rebuked them for having done this, they replied: “God commanded it in the law: ‘If you hate your wife, dismiss her.’”

The Savior explains in the Gospel why the Lord permitted this, when the apostles asked: “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife?” When the good Teacher had clearly shown that she ought not to be dismissed, they asked again: “Why, then,” they said, “did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given?” The Lord answered: “Because of the hardness of your heart this commandment was given,” or rather, this lesser evil was permitted, so that a greater sin—that is, homicide—might not occur.

“If anyone,” he says, “dismisses his lawful wife and marries another, except in the case of fornication, he commits adultery.” “And iniquity will cover his garment”—that is, his flesh, with which the soul is clothed as the body is clothed with a garment—so that he may be punished in the very thing through which he sinned.

“Guard your spirit, and do not despise her.” Since, he says, you cannot dismiss your wives without great sin, guard your souls and do not despise your wives, whether they are poor or disfigured by some bodily defect.

“You have wearied the Lord with your words, and you have said: ‘In what way have we wearied him?’ In this, when you said: ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him.’ Or certainly: ‘Where is the God of judgment?’”

When the people returned from captivity and saw that all the surrounding nations that served idols, as well as their own Chaldean enemies and plunderers, rejoiced in wealth and prosperous success and possessed everything considered good in this world, while they themselves, worshipers of the true God, were oppressed by poverty and servitude, they were scandalized. They said that there was no providence of God, but that everything happened by chance. Worse still, they said that the wicked pleased God and the good displeased him.

The prophet David develops this more fully, saying that he almost doubted and fell when he saw the peace of sinners. At last he added: “Therefore I have cleansed my heart without cause and washed my hands among the innocent.” The human race suffers from this disease and laments such a complaint.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0287C]

“Behold, I am sending my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face.”

The Lord himself explains in the Gospel that this prophecy was spoken beforehand concerning John the Baptist, saying: “This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, and he will prepare your way before you.’” But in the Gospel it is the voice of God the Father speaking to the Son; here, however, Christ speaks about John: “Behold,” he says, “I will send my angel, who will prepare the way before my face.” For the Savior sent John ahead of him in the desert to preach a baptism of repentance.

What follows—“And suddenly the ruler whom you seek and the angel of the covenant whom you desire will come to his temple”—Christ the Lord begins to speak about himself as though about another, in the customary manner of the Scriptures. For he himself is the ruler who rules every creature; he himself is the angel of the New Covenant; he himself is the one whom all should seek and desire, the one whom the ancient fathers always awaited.

When John was preparing the way of the Lord in the hearts of human beings, the Lord the ruler therefore came suddenly to his temple—that is, to his Church—or to the hearts of individual believers, concerning whom the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.”

The Hebrews refer the words “I am sending my angel” to Elijah. What follows—“Suddenly the ruler will come to his temple”—they apply to the Antichrist, whom they will receive in place of Christ at the end of the world.

“Behold, he is coming, says the Lord of hosts, and who will be able to consider the day of his coming? And who will stand to see him?”

He is the one of whom he said above: “Suddenly the ruler and the angel of the covenant will come to his temple.” “Behold, he is coming,” and he will make no delay. Who will be able to consider with how much glory and majesty he will come? If no one can consider it, who will be able to endure it?

“For he himself is like a refiner’s fire,” burning sinners. “For a fire will burn before his face,” and so forth. By this fire wood, hay, and straw will be consumed. He will not only be like a fire, but also “like fuller’s herb,” which in Hebrew is called *borith*, by which garments heavily stained with dirt are washed.

For those who have committed grave sins he will be a refining and burning fire; for those who have committed lesser sins he will be fuller’s herb. Hence Isaiah says: “If the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleanses the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.” Those who have the filth of lesser sins will be purified by the spirit of judgment; those who are stained with blood—that is, with grave crimes—will be burned by the spirit of burning so that they may be purified.

“And he will sit as one who refines and purifies silver”—that is, understanding and eloquence—so that whatever has been mixed with tin or lead may be burned away in the Lord’s furnace, and pure gold and silver may remain.

“And he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and like silver, and they will offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness.”

In the sons of Levi we understand the entire priestly order, from which judgment will begin, because it is written: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord”; and elsewhere: “Begin from my sanctuary.” If the sacred order must be purified and refined by flames, what must be said of the others, whom no privilege of holiness commends?

“Then the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please the Lord, as in the days of old and as in ancient years.” When (he says) the sons of Levi have been purified, then the sacrifice offered for Judah and Jerusalem will please the Lord—that is, for those who confess the Lord in deeds and words and contemplate his peace in their minds. What follows—“as in the days of old and as in ancient years”—means that just as they pleased the Lord in the beginning, so after sin they will begin to please him again once purified through repentance.

[Col. 0288D] “And I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers, and against those who defraud the hired laborer of his wages, widows and orphans, and oppress the foreigner, and do not fear me, says the Lord of hosts.” It is exceedingly terrifying: “I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness.” He himself who is judge will also be witness, because he will judge the deeds of actions outwardly; he himself will be witness to the hidden conscience of sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers. These crimes, committed secretly, will be brought into the open.

There follow also those things that are manifest: those who defraud the hired laborer, although the Lord says, “The wage of a hired laborer must certainly not remain with you”; those who defraud widows and orphans, although the prophet says, “The Lord will not despise the cry of the orphan and the widow when she pours out the speech of her lament”; and those who oppress the foreigner, although the Lord expressly commands, “You shall not grieve the foreigner and resident alien.” In a deeper sense, he calls a catechumen a foreigner—one who has not yet become a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem through baptism. Let no one, therefore, think that perjury or fraud, defrauding a widow and an orphan, and oppressing a foreigner are minor sins, since the Lord joins these with sorcery and adultery and declares that he will judge them alike.

[Col. 0289A] “For I am the Lord, and I do not change.” So that we would not think that his nature changes when he judges, or that he assumes within himself some passion of anger or fury, after saying, “I will draw near in judgment,” he consequently added, “and I do not change.” Of him it is most truly said: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility.”

“And you, sons of Jacob, have not been consumed. For from the days of your fathers you have withdrawn from my statutes and have not kept them.” You (the Lord says), O sons of Levi, are often changed by sorceries, adulteries, and other evils; but I, who am a just judge and judge everything with tranquility, am not changed by any alteration of persons. Therefore, although I confess myself to be a severe and just judge, you nevertheless, O sons of Levi, have not been consumed, even though you have been melted in the fire of tribulations and not cleansed from your evils by punishments. Such also is what is said through Jeremiah: “In vain I struck your sons; they did not accept correction.”

[Col. 0289B] Nor is this new, nor was it committed by you only once, so that you might deserve some pardon. You possess an inherited impiety from the days of your fathers, by withdrawing from my statutes and not keeping what I commanded. This can also be said of those who have been established in the Church. They are sons of Jacob—the one who supplants vices—that is, disciples of the Church’s teachers and masters. Though they bear the name of the Church, they do not withdraw from vices or keep God’s commandments; they falsely assume for themselves the name of the Christian religion.

“Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord of hosts.” God’s mercy is great: he exhorts the contemptuous to return to him and promises that he will return to them. But they do not understand that they have withdrawn from the Lord by sinning, and shamelessly ask, “In what way shall we return?”—we who have never withdrawn from you. To them the Lord replied:

[Col. 0289C] “Can a man afflict God? Yet you pierce me, and you have said, ‘In what do we pierce you?’ In tithes, firstfruits, and scarcity. You are cursed, and you, the whole nation, pierce me.’ Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me concerning this, says the Lord, whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out for you a blessing in abundance. I will rebuke the devourer for your sake, and he will not destroy the fruit of your land; nor will the vine in the field be barren, says the Lord of hosts. And all nations will call you blessed. For you will be a desirable land, says the Lord of hosts.”

In the time of Malachi—who is also believed to have been Ezra—and of Nehemiah, there was an extremely severe famine. Because of it, the poor among the people were compelled to sell their sons and daughters, as well as their possessions and all their property. Finally, they said, as is read in the Book of Ezra: “We have very many sons and daughters; let us receive grain in exchange for them, so that we may eat and live.” Others said: “Let us pledge our fields, vineyards, and houses, and receive grain during the famine.”

[Col. 0290A] But those who had grain in their storehouses were unwilling to return tithes to the Levites, who possessed no inheritances, since the firstfruits and tithes were their inheritance. If (he says) a man fastens God—that is, defrauds or supplants him—you have defrauded me, because you do not return tithes and firstfruits to my ministers. I endure the fraud, while my ministers, the Levites, compelled by scarcity, have abandoned the Temple.

Thus he says that he is defrauded in those who serve him, just as he says that he is visited in those who are in prison, receives food and drink in the hungry, and so forth among the things mentioned in the six works of mercy. As for what is said, “If a man defrauds his God,” although it can simply be understood as “cheats” or “supplants,” in a more hidden interpretation it may be referred to the Lord’s Passion, so that the meaning is: It is no wonder that you now fasten me in my ministers and, insofar as it lies with you, suspend me, since one day you will fasten me to the cross with nails in my own person.

[Col. 0290B] Since, therefore, you do not return the tithes that I commanded through Moses to be given to the priests and Levites, you are cursed in famine and scarcity, and for this reason this famine has been brought upon you. For you, the whole nation, pierce me—not my ministers. And so that you may know that this has happened because I am angry with you, I exhort and admonish you to bring tithes into the storehouses of my Temple, so that my ministers may have food there.

“And test me concerning this, whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven”—that is, whether I will not pour out such an abundance of rain upon you that the windows of heaven will be thought to have been opened—and pour out upon you blessing in abundance. By the word “pouring out” he shows extreme generosity. “And I will rebuke the devourer for your sake”—that is, the locust, the caterpillar, the rust, and other things harmful to human labor. By rebuking them, that is, by the command of my majesty, I will keep them from you, and he will not destroy the fruits of your land.

[Col. 0290C] Your happiness will be so great that all the surrounding nations will marvel at the fertility of your land, and you will be a desirable land, because everyone will desire to dwell in it. What is said about their tithes we can also say about the peoples of the Church, who are commanded not only to give tithes but also to distribute all their possessions to the poor and the ministers of the Church. But if they are unwilling to do this, let them at least, like the Jews, give some portion to priests and the poor, so that they may not experience God’s anger but rather prove his most gracious generosity.

[Col. 0290D] “Your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord, and you have said: What have we spoken against you? You have said: He who serves God serves in vain; and what profit is there in our keeping his commandments?”

As was already briefly indicated above, the people who had returned from captivity, who knew God’s law, appeared to observe the law, to pay tithes, and to fulfill the other things commanded in the law. But when they saw all the surrounding nations abounding in every good, while they themselves wasted away in scarcity and poverty, they said: What benefit is it to me that I worship the true God and keep his commandments? Therefore the Lord says through the prophet: “Your words have prevailed”—that is, “your words have become burdensome”—“against me.”

But they, not understanding that they were committing an extremely grave sin in the blasphemous words they uttered against the Lord, ask: “What have we spoken against you?” The Lord answers them: “You have said: He who serves God serves in vain; and what profit is there”—that is, what advantage, what fruit, what reward—“in our keeping his commandments?”

[Col. 0291A] They spoke this way because they wanted a reward for serving God only in the present life. For this reason they neither deserved to find it in the future nor said what the holy Tobias says: “We are children of the saints, and we await another life.”

They add further: “And what profit is there in our walking mournfully before the Lord of hosts?” There is, in fact, a religious sadness, when someone proceeds simply and humbly, just as there is a praiseworthy shame, of which it is said: “There is a shame that brings glory.” Of such sadness the Psalmist says: “All day long I walked in sorrow.”

“Therefore we now call the arrogant blessed”—that is, the proud, who are not afraid to hurl such blasphemies against God. Why he called them blessed he shows by adding: “Indeed, those who practice wickedness are built up”—that is, they prosper in the glory of the world, and after their crimes they enjoy every prosperity. “And they tested God”—or, “resisted God”—by doing things contrary to his commandments. “And they were saved,” while they think that their only salvation is the prosperity of the present age.

[Col. 0291B] These things, which are said literally about the Jews, can suitably also be understood of heretics and of all who grow proud over the prosperity of the present life: they advance in their wickedness and gather many people to share in their crimes.

“Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another.” The meaning is this: while those who blasphemed and criticized God’s judgments—which are sometimes hidden but always just—were speaking, those who feared God spoke to one another. It should be understood that the recompense of good and evil does not always take place in the present age but is reserved for the future; that human beings cannot know God’s inscrutable judgments; and that they ought not to dispute his equity and justice. It is fitting for the saints to speak these and similar things.

[Col. 0291C] Therefore he did not say what those who feared God spoke, so that we might understand that they spoke the things contained in the words of the Scriptures. But if we read according to the Septuagint translators, “These things those who fear spoke,” it should be understood ironically—*ironikōs*—and announced in a compressed tone: “Those who fear spoke these things that we have mentioned,” that is, those who do not fear God, who ought not even to have thought such things, much less spoken them.

“And the Lord attended and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who feared the Lord and considered his name.” When the just and those who feared the Lord were discussing these things among themselves, the Lord attended and heard. His hearing is eternal knowledge, for to him hearing is no different from seeing. He is wholly ear and wholly eye; entirely he sees, and entirely he hears. Therefore he heard—that is, he foreknew—and ordained it before all ages.

[Col. 0291D] “And a book of remembrance was written”—that is, of memory—“before him.” This book is eternal memory, in which all the saints have been inscribed and predestined before God. Concerning this book it is said in the Apocalypse: “The books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life.” The books that were opened are the two Testaments, by which each person will be judged. The book that was opened is the record of the things each person has done. Hence some manuscripts rightly read: “which is the book of the life of each individual.”

[Col. 0292A] This book of remembrance, then, was written for those who feared God, so that they might know that when the day of judgment comes, punishments are to be repaid to blasphemers and wicked people, and rewards to those who fear God. Of this book the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.” The Psalmist says something almost explanatory of this: “The righteous will be in eternal remembrance.”

“And they will be mine, says the Lord of hosts, on the day when I make them my treasured possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. And you will return, and you will see what difference there is between the righteous and the wicked, and between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.”

[Col. 0292B] “They will be mine as a treasured possession,” he says, because I will choose them not only by the general calling by which all Christians are called, but also by the particular and individual calling by which only the elect are called. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Those whom he called, he also justified.” He also asserts that he himself was called, saying: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle.”

And I will spare them as a human father spares a son who serves him; in this there is a twofold affection: affection toward the son and the service owed by a servant. Then you who now blaspheme and say, “What profit is there in our keeping his commandments?” will learn, through their election and your rejection, what difference there is between the righteous and the wicked, and between one who serves God and one who does not serve him.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0292D]

“For behold, the day will come, burning like a furnace, and all the proud and all who practice wickedness will be straw; and the coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts.” This day is the time of universal judgment. For the saints it will be light, but for sinners darkness. It will be a day burning like a furnace, so that all the wicked will be changed into straw and consumed by the eternal fires of that day. When it has set them ablaze and burned them, it “will leave them neither shoot nor root.” This is said about the wicked, what they will suffer on the day of judgment.

[Col. 0293A] He next says what, by contrast, will come to those who fear the Lord’s name:

“And for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings; and you will go forth and leap like calves from the herd. And you will trample the wicked, when they have become ashes beneath the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the Lord of hosts.”

Christ is the sun of righteousness. God the Father has given him judgment, and he will judge all things justly, permitting neither vices nor virtues to remain hidden. He will rise for those who fear God, but he will set and grow dark for those who despise and blaspheme him. Hence the condemned will say what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “The light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us.”

[Col. 0293B] In the wings of this sun there is healing, so that he may protect those healed through repentance and carry them back to the folds of his flock, according to what is written in Deuteronomy: “He spread out his wings,” and so forth.

Then those who were held shut in the prison of this world will go forth and leap like calves from the herd—victims pleasing to God, renewed and shining, having cast off the squalor of mortality. Or, as another edition says, like calves released from bonds—the bonds from which the Apostle desired to be freed when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”

[Col. 0293C] Nor content with such joy, they will trample the wicked when they have become ashes beneath their feet, according to the Apostle’s prayer: “God will soon crush Satan beneath your feet.” They will trample them not by mocking their destruction but by agreeing with God’s just judgment and allowing their hearts to be moved by no compassion toward them.

For the saints, in comparison with the divine majesty, recognize themselves as ashes. Hence Abraham says: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes.” But the proud, whose leader said, “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High,” will be dragged down into the pit of hell and will truly be ashes beneath the feet of the saints.

“Remember the law of Moses my servant, because I commanded him at Horeb concerning all Israel, statutes and judgments.” Horeb is a mountain in Sinai, where Moses received the law written by the finger of God on stone tablets. When (he says) you know for certain that the day of judgment will come, when the flame will consume the root and branch of the proud, while the sun of righteousness will rise for those who fear him, you must remember the law that I gave you through Moses and fulfill in action what is commanded there.

[Col. 0293D] We too are commanded to remember the spiritual and divine law and to fulfill it not carnally but spiritually. For the Apostle says that the law is spiritual. The Psalmist likewise shows that the law is spiritual when he says: “Reveal my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law.”

[Col. 0294A] The Lord gave this spiritual law at Horeb. The name of the mountain is interpreted as “dryness,” because the law understood spiritually dries out all the moisture of vices. He spoke to Israel statutes and judgments because the mysteries of the Scriptures are to be entrusted to those who deserve to see God with pure eyes of heart.

“Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And he will turn the heart of the fathers toward the sons and the heart of the sons toward their fathers, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

After warning them to remember the law of Moses, he says that he will send Elijah, because the law is signified in Moses and prophecy in Elijah.
