Hence, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, Moses and Elijah appeared with him, speaking with him, because both the law and the entire chorus of the prophets foretold Christ’s coming.

[Col. 0294B] Therefore, before the day of judgment comes, the Lord will send Elijah, whose name is interpreted “My God is the Lord.” He is the Tishbite from the town of Tishbe, whose name is interpreted as “conversion.” Whose conversion? Clearly, that of the prophets, who daily exhort us to conversion and repentance, so that the heart of the fathers may be turned toward the sons—that is, so that they may inspire and communicate to their prophetic sons the faith held by Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other patriarchs, so that what they believed about Christ as future, these may believe as fulfilled.

Or by “the heart of the fathers” he means the mind of God, which was in the fathers, transferring it into the sons of adoption, and turning the heart of the sons toward the fathers, so that believers from the Gentiles and the Jews may agree with the Father in Christ through faith and religion.

[Col. 0294C] Unless the spiritual understanding of prophecy turns the heart of the fathers toward the sons and the heart of the sons toward their fathers in this way, the Lord, when he comes, will strike the earth with a curse—that is, with exclusion from eternal blessing. Then he will say to those who are on the left: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire.”

He says that he will strike not only heaven with a curse—that is, those whose way of life is heavenly—but also the earth, that is, those who think earthly thoughts and yearn for earthly works.

We have said these things about Elijah in accordance with the teachers, although many among our own people also believe that he will come literally, restore all things, and pay the debt of death. But when the apostles questioned the Lord about Elijah’s coming, he answered: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished,” intending John to be understood in Elijah. Therefore he added immediately afterward: “If you are willing to receive it, he himself is Elijah who is to come.”

[Col. 0295]

# COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS BY HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT

*(From the Cologne edition of the year 1529.) (C, G)*

[Col. 0295A] Solomon, inspired by the divine Spirit, composed this little book concerning the marriage of Christ and the Church and, in a certain way, made it a nuptial song of Christ and the Church—that is, a song about the bridal chambers. Hence he called this little book the Song of Songs, because it surpasses all songs. For just as one says “King of kings,” “Lord of lords,” and “solemnity of solemnities,” so it is called the Song of Songs because of its excellence and dignity. This book is exceedingly obscure, because no persons are identified in it, and it is composed, as it were, in comic style.

## CHAPTER I

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” This is the voice of the Synagogue desiring Christ’s coming. It is as though she were saying: He has so often promised me his coming through the prophets; let him come now and kiss me with the kiss of his mouth—that is, let him speak to me through himself.

[Col. 0295B] “For your breasts are better than wine.” Suddenly turning her words toward him whose coming she ardently desired, she adds: “For your breasts are better,” and so forth. By Christ’s breasts the sweetness of the Gospel is understood, because the infancy of believers is nourished by it as by milk. Wine signifies the austerity of the law. But Christ’s breasts are better than wine, because the sweetness of the Gospel is better than the austerity of the law. In the law no repentance is reserved; rather, it is commanded that whoever sins be put to death. But the Gospel says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner,” and so forth.

“Fragrant with the finest ointments.” The ointments are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or also the reputation of virtues, concerning which the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ.”

[Col. 0295C] “Your name is poured-out oil.” Your name, O Christ, is poured out. *Chrisma* in Greek, *unctio* in Latin, means “anointing”; hence Christ’s name is derived from anointing. The Holy Spirit is commonly called by the name of oil, according to what the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with oil”—that is, with the Holy Spirit.

This oil was poured out when the grace that Christ possessed uniquely was given to all the elect. Hence Christians are called from Christ, sharing in Christ’s name. And rightly the oil is said not to have been dripped but poured out, because this grace was given abundantly to all who remember Christ’s faith.

“Therefore the maidens loved you.” The maidens are called the souls of the elect, because in baptism they left behind the filth of the old person and were renewed in Christ. They are rightly called by the feminine gender, because the more conscious the souls of the saints are of their own weakness, the more ardently they love Christ.

The voice of the Church:

“Draw me after you; we will run.” Here the speaker changes. Until now the Synagogue has spoken; here the Church from the Gentiles begins to speak: “Draw me after you; we will run.” Because (she says) I recognize my weakness and see that I can accomplish nothing good by my own powers, draw me by your grace to imitate you—or, when you have ascended into heaven, draw me after you.

[Col. 0295D] “The king brought me into his chambers.” Here she speaks of Christ her bridegroom to the faithful souls. God’s chambers are eternal blessedness and the joys of the heavenly homeland. The Church has already been brought into them through faith and hope and will one day be brought into them in reality.

[Col. 0296A] “We will exult and rejoice in you.” We will exult and rejoice (she says) in your gifts. But because we know that this is not due to our merit, we will exult in you, not in ourselves. This is what the Apostle says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

“Remembering your breasts more than wine”—that is, remembering your grace and mercy by which we have been saved. The breasts are the grace itself by which we have been saved. We also remember that you deigned to temper the austerity of the law with the breasts of evangelical teaching.

“Those who are upright love you.” Those who are upright of heart (she says) love you—that is, those who attribute nothing to their own merits but assign everything to your grace. No one loves you except the upright, and no one is upright except the one who loves you.

The Church concerning her afflictions:

“I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” Here the Church again speaks to the holy souls: I am black because I suffer persecutions, but I am beautiful in virtues, O daughters of Jerusalem—that is, faithful souls. I am black, disfigured by the persecutions and hardships I endure, but I am beautiful in the splendor of virtues.

[Col. 0296C] She shows how she is both black and beautiful when she adds: “Like the tents of Cedar, like the curtains of Solomon.” The distinction is this: I am black like the tents of Cedar and beautiful like the curtains of Solomon.

Cedar was the son of Ishmael, whose name is interpreted as “darkness.” The Ishmaelites were accustomed always to live in tents and had no houses. The Church therefore says that she is black like the tents of Cedar because of the persecutions she suffered from the sons of darkness, which is what Cedar signifies.

[Col. 0296D] Hence the Psalmist says: “I dwelt with those who dwell in Cedar”—that is, I lived among persecutors and sinners blackened by unbelief.

[Col. 0297A] But she says that she is beautiful like the curtains—that is, the tents—of Solomon, whose name is interpreted as “peaceful,” because amid her hardships she was worthy of the visitation and consolation of her bridegroom Christ. And just as tents are made from the skins of dead animals, so the Church, the tent of God, is built from those who mortify themselves with their vices and desires.

“Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.” O faithful souls devoted to God, “do not look at me because I am dark”—that is, because I am afflicted by tribulations and oppressed by persecutions—“because the sun has discolored me”—that is, the heat of persecution has in some way obscured my brightness.

[Col. 0297B] It is as though she were saying: Consider my inner beauty and pay attention to it, not to what I appear outwardly to be suffering. The Apostle says something similar: “Do not lose heart over my tribulations for you, which are your glory. For the sufferings are not worthy,” and so forth.

The sun has many meanings in Scripture. At times it signifies Christ himself, the mediator between God and human beings. Hence it is written: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise”—that is, Christ. It signifies the Church, as David said: “The righteous will shine like the sun.” At times it signifies the heat of persecution, as here and in the Gospel, where it is said of the seed that fell upon the rock and, when the sun rose, was scorched. The Lord himself explains this: “When persecution occurs because of the word, they fall away.”

“The sons of my mother fought against me,” and so forth, up to “I did not guard it.” He shows the origin of this persecution when he adds: “The sons of my mother fought,” and so forth.

[Col. 0297C] This is the voice of the primitive Church. The Synagogue is the mother, to whom it is said through the Prophet: “You will be called a faithful city and a mother of cities, daughter of Zion.” Her sons are the Jews, who fought against the primitive Church when they stirred up persecution against the believers, and all of them were scattered throughout the regions of Samaria.

“They set me as a guard over the vineyards.” At first there was one vineyard, the Church in Jerusalem. But because of the Jewish persecution, when all the believers had been scattered, many vineyards came into being—that is, many Churches were established throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0297D] The primitive Church therefore says: “They set me”—namely, the apostles and teachers—“as a guard,” that is, so that I might be the guardian of the Churches. Hence the Greek rightly says, “They were disseminated,” where we read, “They were scattered.” For they were divinely scattered for this purpose: so that more Churches might be established throughout the whole world.

“My vineyard”—that is, the one Church that had been in Jerusalem—“I did not guard.” This is not to be understood as a matter of intention or desire, but of place. “I did not guard it,” meaning that it should remain in the place where it began.

“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at midday.” This is the Church’s voice to her bridegroom Christ: O bridegroom, whom my soul loves—that is, whom I love with the whole intention of my mind—tell me where you pasture, that is, where you cause your sheep to feed. For he is the good shepherd, as he himself says in the Gospel.

[Col. 0298A] “Tell me where you pasture and where you lie down”—that is, rest—and do so at midday, that is, amid the heat of persecution or temptation. The Church, laboring in persecutions, beseeches her bridegroom to tell her in whose minds he rests. For the bridegroom’s lying down is resting, as he himself says: “Upon whom my spirit rests,” and so forth.

So that the saints do not wither in the heat of temptation, he lies down and rests in their hearts and protects them from every heat of temptations and persecutions. Why does she ask this? “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” By the flocks of his companions she means the gatherings of heretics, who are Christ’s companions in the sense that they too feed their own flocks.

[Col. 0298B] The meaning is: O bridegroom, show me your saints and elect, lest I stumble and fall among heretics, thinking that I can find you there. Heretics wrongly divided this verse, as though the bride asked, “Where do you pasture? Where do you lie down?” and he answered, “I lie down at midday and in the southern region.”

“If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks.” This is the bridegroom’s voice to his bride, the Church. It is as though he were saying: You complain that you have been abandoned by me and blackened by the heat of persecutions, yet you do not consider that you are beautiful among women. You do not attend to the beauty of spiritual virtues with which you are adorned above others, although you are darkened by temptations.

[Col. 0298C] Therefore, if you do not know yourself—that is, if you do not recognize this dignity and beauty of yours—go out from my fellowship and follow the tracks of the flocks. That is, follow and imitate the teaching of erring heretics, who, having rejected the true shepherd of the one flock, have amassed many flocks for themselves.

“And pasture your young goats”—that is, sinful and erring hearers—“beside the tents of the shepherds,” that is, according to the doctrines of the heretics. There is one shepherd, Christ, who has one flock—that is, the unity of the Catholic Church. But there are many shepherds, the heretics, who gather to themselves a flock of deceived people and feed them to the devil. Of them the Psalmist says: “Like sheep they have been placed in hell.”

They are called sheep here not because of simplicity or innocence but because of dullness: they do not know how to resist perverse teaching but endure everything imposed upon them by wicked teachers, without the good patience that would be appropriate.

“I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.” He calls his cavalry the army of the children of Israel—namely, the six hundred thousand who came out of Egypt and crossed the Red Sea.

[Col. 0298D] He calls that multitude his cavalry because, just as a charioteer rules a chariot, so God ruled over the people, protecting and defending them and bringing them into the promised land.

He compared his beloved to this great cavalry because, just as that people was saved through the Red Sea when Pharaoh was drowned, so the Church of the Gentiles was freed through baptism from the service of the devil and brought into the true promised land and evangelical freedom. Thus she who had been a slave of vices became Christ’s beloved, cleansed and washed through baptism from the filth of sins.

“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” It is the nature of the turtledove that, if by chance it loses its mate, it does not seek another thereafter. The Church is therefore compared to a turtledove because, ever since Christ departed from the world in bodily presence and went to heaven, the Church has persevered most firmly in his love and accepts no adulterous lover. She despises the world and contemplates in her mind the beauty of her one bridegroom.

[Col. 0299A] He compares the cheeks of the Church to the cheeks of the turtledove because modesty appears in the cheeks and jaw. Through this he shows the Church’s modesty and shame, since she is ashamed to commit anything foul or displeasing to her bridegroom.

The meaning is: Do not fear that you will wander among the flocks of my companions, because I have given you such modesty in your love for me and such shame that I am certain you cannot abandon me or turn aside to strangers.

“Your neck is like necklaces.” The holy teachers are signified by the neck of the Church, since through the neck food is supplied to refresh the body. Speech also, by which the secrets of minds are revealed, emerges through the throat’s passage.

[Col. 0299B] Thus the holy teachers supply us with the food of saving doctrine and also make known to us the secrets of the Scriptures. This neck of the Church is therefore like a necklace, because the holy teachers adorn it with the jewels of chaste doctrine and the ornaments of virtues. A necklace is an ornament of virgins or married women.

“We will make for you golden necklaces, variegated with silver.” Literally, necklaces are ornaments of a virgin’s or young woman’s neck: rods of gold woven together, sometimes interwoven with a beautiful variety of the finest threads of silver. This is what he means by “variegated with silver”—that is, marked out in the form of earthly worms, which are called *lumbrici*.

[Col. 0299C] The necklaces are called *murenulae* because of their resemblance to the marine fish called the moray eel.

Mystically, the necklaces are the intricate doctrines of the Scriptures, joined together by the differing opinions of the holy Fathers. Gold signifies the brightness of spiritual meaning, while silver signifies the brilliance of eloquence.

The bridegroom makes golden necklaces for his bride when Christ instructs his Church with the doctrines of the holy Fathers, radiant in meaning and expression, and kindles her to imitate their faith and virtue. It should be noted that he says in the plural, “We will make for you,” as though Christ joins himself to the persons of the teachers, through whom the necklaces themselves are linked together so that his Church may be adorned.

[Col. 0299D] “While the king was at his table.” The bride’s voice calls her bridegroom, Christ, king: through his divinity he rules all things, and according to his humanity he was also born from David’s royal stock. The king’s table was his incarnation. To recline means to lie down or recline again. Christ reclined then, when for our redemption he humbled himself so far as to assume our nature. And then “my nard gave forth its fragrance,” because the virtue of the Church shone forth more brightly. For when she considers that God became human for her sake, she is kindled more ardently toward the pursuit of spiritual virtues and the love of her Creator. Nard signifies the fragrance of spiritual virtues. There were certain holy men of God before the incarnation [Col. 0300A]. But, as has been said, holiness increased more greatly from the time of Christ’s incarnation; and then, in a certain sense, the nard of the Church—that is, the fragrance of her virtues—gave forth its scent more powerfully. Literally, nard is an aromatic plant with a thick, fragile root and a small, dense leaf; its tops spread out into spikes. The Gospel records that Mary Magdalene anointed the Lord’s feet and head with this ointment in Simon’s house.

“My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me.” Myrrh is an aromatic substance with which the bodies of the dead are embalmed. Here Christ’s passion and burial are signified: for the Lord’s body, taken down from the cross by Nicodemus and Joseph, was embalmed with myrrh and aloe, wrapped in linen cloths with spices, and [Col. 0300B] committed to burial. Therefore the Church, his bride, says: “My beloved has become a bundle of myrrh to me,” because he died and was buried for my sake. “He will remain between my breasts.” No one doubts that the place of the heart is between the breasts. Therefore she says: “He will remain between my breasts”—that is, the memory of him will be held eternally in my heart, and I shall never forget such great benefits of his; but whether in prosperity or adversity, I shall remember him who loved me and died.

“My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me in the vineyards of Engaddi.” Cyprus is an island where, it is said, excellent vines grow and produce very large clusters. Engaddi is likewise said to be a place with little trees exuding balsam. The bride therefore speaks of the resurrection of her bridegroom Christ: “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me [Col. 0300C].” It is as though she were saying: My bridegroom, who tasted the bitterness of death for me and was like a bundle of myrrh to me, became for me, in his resurrection, a cluster of Cyprus, when he gladdened me with the joy of his resurrection. For wine gladdens the human heart; and this occurred in the vineyards of Engaddi, because through his resurrection he spread throughout the whole world like the sweetest fragrance of balsam and dispersed widely the fragrance of his faith. Engaddi is interpreted as “the spring of the kid,” by which baptism and the sacrifice in which all sins are washed away are signified; for the kid signifies sinners. Baptism, then, is the spring of the kid, because it receives sinners but renders them immaculate and cleansed from all sins.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.” This is Christ the bridegroom’s voice to his bride, the Church. “Behold, you are beautiful”: he repeats twice that she is beautiful because of the perfection of her works and the purity of her mind. “Behold, you are beautiful”—that is, you are perfect in good works, living holily, piously, and justly, according to the Apostle. “Behold, you are beautiful”: you possess a pure and simple intention of heart, because you do good works not for the sake of earthly advantages or the glory of the world, but solely to please God. “Your eyes are like those of doves.” The dove is a most simple bird, and through it the simplicity and innocence of the Church are represented. She has, as it were, the eyes of doves because she guards herself from every kind of deceit and pretence. Or she has the eyes of doves because she understands the knowledge of the divine [Col. 0301A] Scriptures with a chaste and simple gaze, seeking spiritual and divine meanings in them; for since the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, heavenly doctrine is rightly understood in the eyes of a dove.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely.” It is as though she were saying: You indeed say that I am beautiful in work and thought, but I believe and recognize that I have all this beauty from you. For you are beautiful and comely; you are the source of all good, and whatever good I possess, I possess by your grace. He is called beautiful and comely because he is wondrous both in the eternity of his divinity and in the dignity of the humanity he assumed. “Our couch is verdant.” The couch is any kind of tranquility or rest in the present [Col. 0301B] life. For the Church is, as it were, in battle while she endures various struggles for Christ; but she rests, as it were, on a couch when she enjoys the small measure of peace granted to her. Yet this couch is verdant: that is, the Church’s rest is marked by a variety of virtues, like spring flowers. For then she applies herself more freely to divine contemplation; then she carries out fasts, vigils, and other good works more freely.

“The beams of our houses are cedars; our rafters are cypresses.” The houses of the Church are the assemblies spread throughout the whole world. The beams and rafters are the persons of the faithful themselves, from whom the Church is constituted. But one must observe that beams are for the reinforcement of a house, while rafters are for its adornment. Therefore the beams signify teachers, whose doctrine supports and sustains the Church [Col. 0301C]; the rafters, however, signify the saints who rejoice in simplicity and adorn the Church by their virtues, though they do not fortify it by doctrine. It should also be observed that the rafters are attached to the beams; so the life of the faithful in the Church depends upon the teachers, because it is instructed and strengthened by their doctrine. It is fitting that the beams are called cedars and the rafters cypresses. For both trees are of an incorruptible nature, signifying the saints, who burn with an unfading desire in love for their Creator and, despising transitory things, hasten toward eternal realities. The cedar also drives away serpents by its fragrance; so holy teachers repel demons or heretics by the fragrance of their doctrine.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0301D] “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” After the bride has shown what kind of house she and her bridegroom possess, the bridegroom himself also shows what he is like, saying: “I am the flower of the field,” and so forth, because I spread the fragrance of my virtue throughout the breadth of the whole world. I am a flower—that is, the God of the world. For just as a field is adorned and made verdant by flowers, so the whole world is beautified by the faith and knowledge of Christ. I am also the lily of the valleys, because I grant my grace especially to those minds that, possessing no hope in themselves, submit themselves to me with humble devotion. The valleys signify humble minds, whose lily is Christ, because he himself is the beauty of humble minds, who said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart.” What he says, “I am the flower of the field,” can also be referred to the incarnation. For a field is not plowed, cut, or furrowed by any plowshare. Therefore he says: “I am the flower of the field”—that is, the son of a virgin. He does not call himself the flower of the countryside but of the field, because he is the fruit of virginal flesh, according to Isaiah’s prophecy: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse.” Christ himself is the lily of the valleys—that is, the son of humble parents. For the valleys signify humble persons, as do his parents. For when the Son of God came into the world, he not only deigned to become human, but also became a poor human being for our sake; and he chose not the rich but the poor as his parents, so that, having become a sharer in our poverty, he might make us sharers in his riches and glory [Col. 0302B].

“As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” Seeing his bride hasten toward rest and flee from labors, and recognizing that through the repose of the present time she must advance toward eternal blessedness through the pressures and labors of this age, he says: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” The thorns, which prick and tear, signify all the perverse, whether within the Church or outside the Church. The meaning is this: You must live in this way, and you must be prepared in this way for every adversity, just as the lily is among thorns and yet does not cease to flower and emit its pleasant fragrance; so is my beloved among the daughters. For you suffer evil not only from those who are outside the Church, but also from those who [Col. 0302C] appear to have been regenerated through baptism and to have entered into the adoption of God’s children. And observe that above the bridegroom called himself the lily of the valleys, while now he calls his bride, as it were, a lily among thorns, because he who is truly the lily makes his Church a lily by grace—white, that is, with virtues, or free from every stain of vices.

“As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” Now the bride, praised by the bridegroom, returns the favor and says what he is like. “As an apple tree,” she says, and so forth. Just as an apple tree possesses the beauty of its fruit and a pleasant fragrance among the wild trees of the forest, so Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, shines with a special grace among the sons—that is, among the elect. For he alone is Son of God [Col. 0302D] by nature; the other elect are sons of God by grace, through the power of the one Son of God. Hence John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father.” Not just any glory, but glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father. “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat,” because I trust in his protection and hope to be governed by him amid adversities. The shadow of Christ is the protection of his divinity, because he guards and defends the elect. “And his fruit is sweet to my throat”—that is, the contemplation of his divinity, with which I trust I shall be satisfied. For this is the expectation of the saints, this is their reward and satiety: the vision of their Creator. The Church therefore desires the shadow of her Creator, because she longs for his protection amid the adversities of the present life. “His fruit is sweet to my throat” [Col. 0303A], because I await the enjoyment of the sight of him and satisfaction in the sweetness of his love.

“The king brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered love in me.” The wine cellar is the Church, in which there is the wine of evangelical doctrine. The bride, the beloved of the bridegroom, is brought into this cellar when the faithful from all nations are united into one Church. “He ordered,” she says, “love in me.” Love holds the first place among all things, because the Church subsists in love. Love is therefore ordered in the Church, because it must be maintained neither rashly nor confusedly, but in due order. God must be loved above all things with the whole heart, the whole soul, all one’s strength, and the whole mind. Finally, one’s neighbor must be loved as each person loves himself. For the person who places love of neighbor before love of God wants to confuse love. Concerning such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” Or “he ordered love in me” may mean that he first loved me and then taught me how I ought to love him. Hence he himself says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” And John says: “Let us love God, because he first loved us.”

“Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, because I am sick with love.” After the Church, or the soul beloved by God, has said that she orders love within herself, she shows how she wishes to rest, or on what couch she wishes to repose with her beloved bridegroom, saying: “Strengthen me with flowers,” and so forth. She addresses souls already clinging perfectly to divine love. By flowers are understood the beginnings of holy conduct [Col. 0303C]; by apples, the perfected examples of good works. The meaning is this: O holy souls who cling to the love of your Creator, strengthen me with examples of good works, and show how you have lived at the beginning of virtue, in progress, and in the perfection of good works, because I am sick with love. The soul is then sick with love of God when she places nothing before his love; indeed, she becomes weak and powerless with respect to worldly works, and nothing delights her except meditation on heavenly things and contemplation of her Creator.

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” “When,” she says, “I have lain on such a couch, his left hand”—that is, the bridegroom’s—“will be under my head.” By the left hand are understood the prosperity of the present time and also the gifts of God bestowed upon the saints in the present; by the right hand, the blessedness of the heavenly homeland is understood. The bridegroom’s left hand is therefore under the bride’s head because the Church receives all these gifts for the purpose of learning through them to sigh for eternal realities. The bridegroom’s right hand embraces her because the whole intention of the Church, or of the faithful soul, is that she may eventually arrive at eternal blessedness and rejoice in the hope of her Creator. It is fitting that the left hand is first under the head and afterward the bridegroom’s right hand embraces her, because she cannot reach the embraces of eternal blessedness unless here she strives to share in heavenly mysteries and divine gifts.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the hinds of the fields [Col. 0304A], do not arouse or awaken my beloved until she herself desires it.” This is the bridegroom’s voice adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, those friends intent upon eternal desires and seeking the vision of peace—not to arouse or disturb his resting soul. “I adjure you,” and so forth: that is, do not wish to disturb the soul devoted to divine contemplation and occupied with prayer or sacred reading, or awaken her to external works; “until she herself desires it”—that is, until, when the time of contemplation has been completed and the frailty of the body gives warning, she herself wishes to be awakened from the sleep of inward rest and to proceed to temporal activities. Let us see, however, by what means he adjures the daughters of Jerusalem: by the does and the hinds of the fields. Does and hinds are clean animals, hostile to serpents and poisons [Col. 0304B]. They signify the virtues of the saints, which shine with spiritual purity and not only avoid the poisons of diabolical deceit but also pursue them and reduce them to nothing. The meaning is this: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by your virtues, which you rejoice to have received from divine grace, not to disturb the soul devoted to my contemplation until, when the hour of contemplation has ended, she herself wishes to do something else.

“The voice of my beloved”—the Church’s voice. “The voice of my beloved,” with the following words understood: this is it. The Church, rejoicing that she is so greatly loved by the bridegroom that he even adjures the daughters of Jerusalem on her behalf not to disturb her as she rests, says: This is the voice of my beloved speaking for me. Desiring to see her beloved but unable to do so, she adds: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains [Col. 0304C], bounding over the hills.” The mountains and hills are understood as all those perfect in holy conduct, lifted sublimely above earthly things and surpassing, as it were, the level ground of the fields through the merits of a better life. Isaiah speaks of these mountains: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills.” The bride therefore speaks of her beloved: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills”—that is, even according to his humanity he surpasses the excellence of all the saints and all purity of divine contemplation. He is said not to stand on the mountains but to bound over them, because although he visits the hearts of the saints for a time through inward inspiration, he nevertheless suddenly withdraws, in order to kindle them to love him. This may also be referred to Christ’s incarnation, in which he made certain leaps [Col. 0304D]: from heaven he came into the Virgin’s womb, from the Virgin’s womb into the manger, from the manger into baptism, from baptism to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb to heaven. Hence the Psalmist says: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course,” and so forth.

“My beloved is like a doe or a fawn of the hinds.” Although does and hinds possess many features in their nature that suit allegorical meanings, they have this particular characteristic: they do not remain in level places but are accustomed to make leaps in lofty and elevated places. Christ is therefore rightly likened to them because of the subtlety of contemplation and because his majesty cannot be comprehended by any understanding of his divinity. He is likened not to full-grown stags but to does [Col. 0305A], that is, to smaller animals, on account of the humility of his incarnation, because he deigned not only to become human but to become a humble human being. He is called like a fawn of the hinds because according to his humanity he derived his origin from the hinds—that is, from the patriarchs; or he is compared to a fawn of the hinds because of the variety of his virtues and his innocence. “Behold, he stands behind our wall.” The wall is called our mortal condition, because a kind of thick wall has, as it were, been established between us and God and does not permit us to enjoy his contemplation. For the first human being was so created as to enjoy the vision and conversation of God; but after he sinned, a wall was set up, namely mortality itself, by which we are weighed down. For, as the Wise Man says, “the corruptible body weighs down the soul [Col. 0305B], and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things.”

The bride therefore says that her bridegroom, whom above she compared to does or fawns of hinds, now stands behind her wall, because Christ sometimes becomes near when he permits himself to be contemplated as far as the human mind can grasp; at other times he withdraws and, like a doe or a hind, escapes by certain leaps. Since a wall had been placed between us and him, and we could not see him, he deigned to make windows and lattices in that very wall, through which he might in some measure be sensed and in some measure perceived. Hence it follows: “looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.” Windows and lattices are made in the wall, as it were, when by his grace he permits himself to be contemplated, although in a mirror and [Col. 0305C] in an enigma. What he says, “He himself stands behind our wall,” may also be referred to his humanity: he stood, as it were, behind our wall when he joined our flesh to himself, in which his divinity lay hidden. But what follows—“looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices”—refers to his divinity. For the one who looks through windows or lattices sees everything that happens outside, while he himself is seen by no one; he searches out all things, yet no one can investigate or comprehend him.

“And my beloved speaks to me,” urging me to preach, saying: “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.” This is the bridegroom’s voice calling her to the zeal of public activity. “Arise, hasten, my beloved,” through faith and love; “my dove,” through innocence and simplicity; “my beautiful one,” through the beauty of virtues; hasten “and come.” It is as though he were saying: Arise from that sweetest bed of yours—that is, from the rest in which you desire to please me alone through psalms, hymns, and prayers—and hasten “and come,” that is, hasten toward the benefit of your neighbors, so that through the ministry of preaching and the example of good works you may make them imitators of you and lead them to salvation. It should be noted that above he adjured the daughters of Jerusalem not to arouse or awaken his beloved; here, however, he himself awakens her and urges her to rise for labor, because everything has its time, and there is a time for every matter under heaven: a time for contemplation and also a time for action. At one time holy preachers must devote themselves to divine contemplation and delight their minds in heavenly rest; at another time they must, through love, care for their neighbors, offer them examples of good works, and provide them with the teaching of divine contemplation.

“For winter has now passed; the rain has gone away and departed.” By the names of winter and rain the harshness of unbelief is expressed, which held the whole world until the coming of Christ. The bridegroom therefore says: “Arise, my beloved, and come, because winter has passed,” with the Sun of Justice appearing, and the rain of unbelief withdrawing, while the serenity of true faith shone upon the world. The Apostle says something similar: “The night has advanced; the day has drawn near.”

[Col. 0306B] “Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come.” When winter and rain had ended, flowers appeared—that is, the beauty of virtues and chastity—and, as the harshness of unbelief passed away, the springtime mildness of faith succeeded it. “The time of pruning has come”—that is, the purification of the saints. The pruning of vineyards signifies the purification that is in Christ and through Christ, concerning which he himself says: “I am the vine, you are the branches.” “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” This is the voice of the apostles preaching. The turtledove is a bird; and because it is accustomed always to dwell and build its nest in lofty trees, it signifies the apostles and the other teachers, who can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Its having a moan instead of a song signifies the weeping of the saints, who urge their own people to tears and lamentation, saying: “Be sorrowful and mourn,” or, “your mourning will be turned into joy.” “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land”—that is, the voice of the apostles preaching in our land, which is the Church. Of this the Psalmist says: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.”

“The fig tree has produced its unripe figs.” The fig tree signifies the Synagogue; the unripe figs are so called because they are the first and immature figs, unfit for eating, which easily fall at the shaking of the wind. When the voice of the turtledove sounded, the fig tree produced its unripe figs, because, while the apostles preached, many emerged from the Jewish Synagogue who believed in Christ yet wished to observe the law carnally, taking greater pleasure in the authority of the law than in the sweetness of the Gospel, and wishing to observe circumcision, the Sabbath, and the other precepts of the law literally. Concerning them the Apostle says: “They are zealous for you, but not rightly; they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.” “The flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.” After the voice of the turtledove was heard, after the fig tree produced its unripe figs, the flowering vines gave forth their fragrance, because a multitude of Churches was spread throughout the breadth of the world, sending forth everywhere the flowers of virtues and the fragrance of a good reputation. “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come.” Do not, he says, my bride, whom I have made my beloved through faith and love, grow sluggish in idle time; rise and come, and show the examples of virtues publicly to your neighbors.

[Col. 0307A] “My dove, in the clefts of the rock.” If the rock is Christ, according to the Apostle’s statement, “the rock was Christ,” the clefts of the rock are the wounds that he received on the cross for our salvation, namely the piercings of the nails and the thrust of the lance. The dove, therefore—that is, the Church—dwells in these clefts because she places all her hope of salvation in the passion of her Redeemer. There she hides securely from the snares of evil spirits, as from the attack of a hawk; there she builds her nest, that is, she gathers the offspring of good works. “In the hiding place of the wall.” Walls of dry stones are usually built to protect vineyards, to drive away foxes and other harmful little animals. The wall therefore signifies the guardianship of heavenly virtues, namely angelic protection, as Isaiah says of the Lord’s vineyard [Col. 0307B]: “He surrounded it with a wall and dug around the vineyard.” She dwells in the hiding place of the wall because she is surrounded on every side by the protection of angels and guarded from the temptations of the devil.

“Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.” You, he says, my beloved, who rest most sweetly on the couch of contemplation, come and show me your face—that is, emerge from the secret place of rest into public action and display the beauty of your good works to others as an example. “Show me,” he says; for the Church shows her face to God, as it were, when through works of virtue she demonstrates to her neighbors, for their benefit and progress, how much beauty she possesses inwardly. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let them see your good works [Col. 0307C], and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” “Let your voice sound in my ears”—the voice, namely, of preaching or divine praise, by which you may make others progress. The voice of the Church sounds in the Lord’s ears when God delights in the conversion of many through preaching. He rightly says: “Show me your face,” and your voice—not another’s. Show me your own face, which I gave you in baptism when I cleansed you from every sin. “Let your voice,” he says, “sound in my ears,” so that it may proceed from a sincere intention of love for me, and so that you may preach for no other reason than for my sake.

“Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has flowered.” This is the bridegroom’s voice commanding his bride and the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the holy teachers or faithful souls [Col. 0307D]. “Catch,” he says, “the little foxes.” The fox is a deceitful and fraudulent animal, living in caves and dens and proceeding not along a straight but a winding path; therefore it signifies heretics or schismatics, who destroy the vineyards—that is, the Church of God, the people of the faithful—and never cease to tear them apart and deceive them. He therefore commands that the little foxes be caught, that is, that they should not cease to combat and destroy heretical perversity at its very beginning, lest, once it has grown strong, it attack more vigorously. “For our vineyard has flowered”—that is, the Church has sent forth flowers of virtue throughout the whole world. Observe that although above he spoke of vineyards in the plural, now he says in the singular, “our vineyard has flowered,” because from the many Churches there is one chosen Church.

“My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” The bride’s voice: “My beloved is mine,” with the following understood: he is joined to me by the bond of love and charity, and I am joined and united to him in mutual love. And “my beloved” is understood to mean that he speaks words of exhortation and divine promise, “and I,” it is understood, shall show him my face. Or, my beloved may deign to join himself to me with the bond of love, and I shall be joined to him by the bond of worthy obedience, obeying the commands of him who feeds among the lilies—that is, who delights and rejoices among the pure and fragrant virtues of the saints. It should be noted that above “lily” is said in the singular [Col. 0308B], but here “lilies” is plural, because the virtues of the saints are many, while there is one faith and one love, in which God especially delights. Or “he feeds among the lilies” may mean that he takes the greatest delight among the choirs of virgins. For the whiteness of lilies is rightly compared with virginal purity. “Until the day breathes”—that is, until the clouds of the present life pass away and the day appears, namely, until the brightness of eternal blessedness comes. The meaning is this: My beloved grants me assistance, and I offer him worthy obedience; he delights in the virtues of the saints until, when the night of the present life has passed—the night in which he is seen through a mirror and in an enigma—the day of heavenly brightness appears, so that he may be seen face to face.

“Return; be like, my beloved, a doe or a fawn of the hinds upon the mountains of Bethel.” This is the Church’s voice, desiring the appearance of her bridegroom. O my beloved, who command me to rise from my couch and urge me to show you my face, return—that is, permit me to contemplate the brightness of your divinity, and grant that in this pilgrimage I may at least possess in figure and in an enigma what you perfectly promise me in the other life, namely your blessedness. “Be like a doe or a fawn of the hinds upon the mountains of Bethel.” It has already been said above that does disdain the fields and strive toward the heights of the mountains. Christ is therefore compared to does because, having risen from the dead according to the flesh, he sought the heights of heaven; and he is called a fawn of the hinds, that is, the son of the ancient fathers. For the hinds are the patriarchs and prophets [Col. 0308D], from whom Christ derived the origin of his flesh. It is said that a fawn has this nature: when the sun burns hot, it seeks shady and shadowed places in which it may be protected from the heat. So Christ also rests in the minds of those who are tempered by the dew of the Holy Spirit against the heat of carnal desires. It is as though he were saying: O beloved, return—that is, gladden me by illuminating me more often with your visitation—you who, through the flesh you assumed, have already penetrated the heights of heaven.

The mountains of Bethel signify the minds of the saints, lifted above earthly things by heavenly desires. For Bethel means “rising house” or “house of vigils,” and signifies the watchful minds of the saints, which rise to desire heavenly things and keep vigil in order to receive them. [Col. 0309A] They have within themselves God as an inhabitant, who says through the Prophet: “I shall dwell in them and walk among them.” Therefore, upon the mountains of Bethel, the beloved is like a doe or a fawn of the hinds, because he deigns to visit those who strive to be the house of God.

## CHAPTER III

“In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.” This is the voice of the Church gathered from the nations. “In my bed,” she says, “while I was still placed in the darkness of unbelief and ignorance, I sought him whom my soul loves.” For many philosophers, although ignorant of God, nevertheless sought him with the greatest zeal, wishing to know the Creator through the creature—such as Plato, who discussed the soul at length in the *Timaeus*, and Aristotle, Socrates [Col. 0309B], and the others, who spent the whole time of their lives in the pursuit of truth through study. “I sought him and did not find him.” For God could not be known through worldly wisdom.

“I shall rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I shall seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.” I shall rise from there, from the bed of the body and carnal pleasure, and I shall go around the city of this world, traversing seas and lands. “Through the streets and squares I shall seek him whom my soul loves”—that is, I shall look upon those who walk along the broad paths of this age and are devoted to its pleasures, to see whether I might find in them some trace of my beloved. Although this may be said of many, it was fulfilled especially in that eunuch who came from the ends of the earth to worship the God of heaven in Jerusalem, whom Philip found and to whom he revealed Christ in Isaiah’s prophecy. It was also fulfilled in Cornelius, who, while still a pagan and ignorant of God, gave alms and devoted himself to prayers; Peter baptized him and his household. Yet the difficulty of finding him still remained, and she says: “I sought, and did not find him.”

“The watchmen who guard the city found me.” The watchmen are the saints and the other teachers of the Church, who guard the city—that is, the holy Church—and defend it from the snares of unbelieving enemies. She asks them: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” The Church questions the watchmen, as it were, when she receives their preaching with attentive ear.

[Col. 0309D] “A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.” To pass by the watchmen means to examine their words and doctrine carefully. We customarily say, “I ran through a book while reading,” or “I passed through it.” “When,” she says, “I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.” For when with attentive meditation we seek the words or writings of the saints, we immediately find the beloved, because we discover the Lord in their teaching. It may also be understood in this way: “When I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves”—that is, when I understood that Christ surpasses every sublimity and every grace, then I found him whom my soul loves; that is, then I truly understood how far he stands above the merits of all the other saints.

“I took hold of him [Col. 0310A] and will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” That is, I clung to him with the most ardent faith and devotion. “I will not let him go,” but I shall persevere in his love and faith, “until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me”—that is, until I preach him to the Synagogue, which is spiritually my mother, and lead her also to faith in him. This will happen on the day of judgment, when, as the Apostle says, “the fullness of the nations has entered; then all Israel will be saved.” The Church therefore promises herself so much from the love of her bridegroom that she believes she will even be able to convert the Synagogue.

When she says, “Until I bring him in,” it should not be thought that she will abandon him once she has brought him into her mother’s chamber [Col. 0310B]. Rather, “until” is used of what is everlasting: that is, I shall always cling to him, and shall always persevere in his faith and love. The same occurs in the Psalm: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God until he has mercy upon us.” Surely, once he has had mercy upon us, our eyes will not cease to be directed toward him? Indeed, they will.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the fields: do not rouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wills it.” This little verse is repeated twice: it has already been spoken above, but there it pertains to the primitive Church gathered from the Jews, whereas here it pertains to the Church assembled from the Gentiles and joined to Christ by the bond of love. For God has one and the same care for the saints who pleased him either in circumcision or, in the time of baptism, when the grace of the Gospel shone forth [Col. 0310C]. Since this little verse has been expounded above, we must now consider why he presents the Church as though sleeping, and therefore adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken her, when a little earlier he introduced her not as sleeping or resting, but as intent upon the most laborious pursuit by which she sought her bridegroom. If, then, she sought the bridegroom, how did she rest? Yet to seek Christ is a most sweet and delightful sleep. The Church therefore sleeps and seeks Christ: she sleeps, that is, to earthly desires and worldly acts; but she watches and seeks the bridegroom, because she clings to his contemplation, desires him alone, and strives to attain him. The bridegroom therefore adjures the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls clinging to desires for the heavenly homeland—not to rouse her from this sleep of sweetest rest and contemplation until she herself wills it. Sleep is rightly called death, because, just as one asleep closes the eyes to visible things and contemplates invisible things, so one intent on divine contemplation is, as it were, estranged from and asleep to outward things, seeing spiritual and heavenly things alone. Nor is it surprising that love is called sleep, since in what follows love is called death: “Love is strong as death.” But when he says, “Until she herself wills it,” he shows that the Church from the Gentiles will voluntarily prepare herself both for labors and for persecutions to be endured for Christ.

“Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every [Col. 0311A] powder of the perfumer?” This is the voice of the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, of the saints of the primitive Church, admiring the beauty of the Church gathered from the Gentiles. “Who,” they say, “is this?” That is, what kind of woman is she? How worthy of praise and admiration she is, who, though not cleansed by circumcision and not yet sanctified by baptism, already runs to God! “She comes up,” he says, “through the wilderness.” This is said in imitation of the ancient Jewish people, which, delivered from Egyptian bondage, crossed the Red Sea through the wilderness and came to the promised land. So too the Church came up through the wilderness of the nations, already delivered from Egypt—that is, from the confusion of idolatry—with Pharaoh, that is, the devil, submerged, so that she might be fed with heavenly manna and enter the true promised land. “She comes up,” he says, “to the mountains [Col. 0311B] of virtues,” or rather, raised up by virtues, to him himself who says in the psalm, “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains,” etc., and elsewhere, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in the heavens.” These mountains are the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and other saints of God, who are rightly called mountains because of their virtues. For first the Church or faithful soul lifts its eyes to the mountains—that is, to the saints—because it considers their teaching and deeds and delights to be strengthened by their example and intercession. Then, making progress, it also dares to direct the gaze of its heart toward him who made the mountains, saying, “I have lifted up my eyes to you, who dwell in the heavens,” that is, who graciously rest in the saints. “Like,” he says, “a slender column of smoke from spices of myrrh and frankincense.” Smoke is born from fire and immediately seeks the higher regions of the air, until [Col. 0311C] it is withdrawn from the sight of those looking upon it. Smoke, then, signifies holy desire infused with the fire of divine love. Nor without reason is the Church, or a soul loving God, compared to a slender column of smoke: it is slender and delicate, made fine by the disciplines of the Holy Spirit, having none of the grossness of carnal desires. Or the slender column of smoke is contrasted with smoke dispersed abroad because of the Church’s unity, which is one in Christ. He shows whence that smoke comes when he adds: “Of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.” Myrrh is used to preserve dead bodies, while frankincense is burned in sacrifice to God; thus myrrh signifies the mortification of the flesh, and frankincense expresses the purity of prayers. The Church is therefore likened to a slender column of smoke of myrrh and frankincense, because the saints strive to please God through mortification of their flesh [Col. 0311D] and prayers poured forth from a pure and simple heart. “And every,” he says, “powder of the perfumer,” that is, a collection of every virtue. The spices are said not to have remained whole but to have been reduced to powder, because the actions of the saints must be considered with great discernment and, as it were, sifted through the finest sieve of reflection, lest perhaps anything unsuitable be found in them, or lest the adversary of a thousand forms steal in through the virtues themselves; for in his cunning he is accustomed to harm even through good things.

“Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty mighty men surround it, of the mightiest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilled in war. Each man has his sword upon his thigh.” The place to which this beloved has ascended is shown [Col. 0312A] when it is added: “Behold Solomon’s bed,” etc. Although Solomon’s bed may be understood as that rest of heavenly blessedness above, in which God rests with his saints, it is more plausibly understood as the present Church, in which God’s saints, having stilled the tumults of vices, delight in the embrace of Solomon—that is, of the true Peacemaker. Hence the Psalmist says of Christ: “His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.” Solomon’s bed, then—that is, Christ’s Church—is surrounded by sixty mighty men, drawn from the mightiest of Israel. By the sixty mighty men is understood the order of the elect, who either strengthen the Church by preaching or desire, through contemplation, to attain that heavenly blessedness. The number sixty consists of six and ten. For six times ten, or ten times six, [Col. 0312B] makes sixty. Six signifies the perfection of work, because God completed his works in six days; ten signifies the recompense and reward that will be given to the elect at the end. Hence those who came into the vineyard are said to have received a denarius. The sixty mighty men therefore signify, as has been said, holy teachers, strong and steadfast in spirit. It is added: “Of the mightiest of Israel.” All who believe in Christ and love Christ are called Israel—that is, “a man seeing God.” But the mightiest of Israel are those who know how to protect the Church by preaching and defend it from the assaults of demons and the attacks of heretics. They surround Solomon’s bed because the Church has been entrusted to them and must be guarded by their watchful care. “All holding swords, and [Col. 0312C] most skilled in war”; for they hold the spiritual sword of God’s word, concerning which the Apostle says: “Take,” he says, “the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” They are most skilled in war because those who wage war against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens, must be trained in the art of spiritual battle. For that enemy against whom the saints undertake war is most crafty, of such subtlety as belongs to a spiritual nature, and, through great age, most experienced. “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of fears by night.” By the thigh is understood the propagation of offspring. They have swords upon their thighs because all are restrained and check the impulses of carnal pleasure by fear of God. And this is “because of [Col. 0312D] fears by night,” that is, because of the hidden snares of the malicious enemy, who in the night of this age especially lies in wait for the saints who hold preeminence in the Church, so that, if they are deceived, he may defile Solomon’s bed—that is, the rest of the saints. It should be noted that above they are said to hold swords, but here to have a sword upon the thigh. They hold swords in order to resist adversaries and pierce heretics and all who contradict the sound faith. They have swords upon their thighs in order to care for themselves and restrain the flow of carnal pleasures, lest, while preaching to others, they themselves become reprobate.

“King Solomon made himself a litter of the wood of Lebanon.” What was represented above by Solomon’s bed is [Col. 0313A] now signified by the litter: namely, the holy Church, in which the saints of God rest as on a bed and recline as at a banquet for the feasts of eternal satisfaction. Solomon made the litter from the wood of Lebanon. Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, whose trees surpass others in height, beauty, and durability; they therefore signify saints radiant with hope of virtues and hastening toward eternal things. For Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening,” or “making white.” Thus the woods of Lebanon are saints made white and cleansed in baptism and adorned with every beauty of virtue.

“He made its columns of silver.” By the columns are signified the teachers of the same Church, who sustain and strengthen it by word and example. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “James, John, and Cephas, [Col. 0313B] who seemed to be pillars.” These columns are silver because they shine with the brightness of heavenly speech. “For the words of the Lord are pure,” etc. “Its support of gold, its ascent of purple.” By the support of gold is understood eternal rest, which is promised to the saints in the Church; yet the ascent thereto is purple. The purple ascent is Christ’s passion, because purple imitates the color of blood. By the purple ascent, therefore, one comes to the support, because those come to the reclining at the eternal feast and to the rest of heavenly quiet who strive in the present worthily to venerate and imitate the passion of their Redeemer. “He paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.” He paved the midst with love because Christ commended his love to all believers [Col. 0313C] by suffering for us and preparing rest for us, as the Apostle says: “But God commends his love toward us, in that, while we were still sinners, he delivered his Son to death for us.” Alternatively, the silver columns signify the apostles and apostolic men; the support of gold, the order of teachers, who, by promising the ineffable things of eternal life, surely make us rest sweetly. This support is rightly called golden, because the reward for which the saints wait is ineffable. For among perishable things nothing is more precious than gold. The purple ascent signifies the order of martyrs, who, imitating Christ’s passion, shed their own blood for him. But what shall we do, says blessed Gregory, who are of no merit? We seem to have no place [Col. 0313D] among teachers or martyrs. It follows: “He paved its midst with love.” Let us therefore have love, with which the midst of this litter is paved, and which is for that reason called the broad commandment, because it prepares eternal salvation for all who keep it. Let us hold it effectively, and through it we shall be saved. And this is for the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, for simple souls conscious of no virtue in themselves, who, the more they are conscious of their own frailty, strive all the more to love their Savior and Redeemer.

“Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s joy.” [Col. 0314A] This is the voice of the Church inviting the souls of the faithful to behold how wonderful and beautiful her bridegroom is. For the daughters of Zion are Churches, and also daughters of Jerusalem: namely, holy souls who are citizens of that heavenly city, who enjoy perpetual peace with the angels and, through contemplation, behold the Lord’s glory. “Go forth,” he says, “O daughters of Zion,” that is, go out from the turbulent manner of life of this age, so that with an unencumbered mind you may contemplate him whom you love. “And see,” he says, “King Solomon,” that is, Christ the true Peacemaker, “in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” As though he said: Consider Christ clothed in flesh for your sake, the flesh which he took from the flesh of his virgin mother. He calls that flesh a diadem, which Christ took [Col. 0314B] for us, in which by dying he destroyed the dominion of death and in which he also gave us the hope of resurrection. Of this diadem the Apostle says: “We see Jesus crowned with glory and honor through suffering.” His mother is said to have crowned him because the Virgin Mary supplied him from her own flesh with the material of his flesh. “On the day of his betrothal,” that is, at the time of the incarnation, when he joined to himself the Church having neither spot nor wrinkle, or when God was joined to man. “And on the day of his heart’s joy.” For Christ’s gladness and joy are the salvation and redemption of humankind. Thus, when he saw many flocking to faith in him, “in that hour,” says the Evangelist, “he rejoiced and said: ‘I confess to you, Father of heaven and [Col. 0314C] earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.’” And in the Gospel parable, after finding the sheep, he called together his friends, saying: “Rejoice with me.” This may also all be referred simply, according to the letter, to Christ’s passion. Foreseeing Christ’s passion in the spirit, Solomon long beforehand warned the daughter of Zion—that is, the Israelite people—saying: “Go forth and see King Solomon,” that is, Christ, “in the diadem,” that is, in the crown of thorns, “with which his mother,” the Synagogue, “crowned him, on the day of his betrothal,” when he joined the Church to himself, “and on the day of his heart’s joy,” when he rejoiced that through his passion the world was redeemed from the devil’s power. Go forth, then: that is, leave the darkness of unbelief, and see—that is, [Col. 0314D] understand in your mind—that he who suffers as a man is true God; or rather, go forth beyond the gate of your city in order to see him crucified on Mount Golgotha.

CHAPTER IV.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful and comely.” The voice of Christ. He repeats, “How beautiful you are,” referring namely to her works and preaching. In her works, because she do nothing vile or unworthy of my eyes; in her preaching, because you do not cease inviting even your companions, the daughters of Jerusalem, to contemplate the mystery of my incarnation.

“Your eyes are like those of doves.” By the eyes is understood the keenness of the spiritual senses by which the Church contemplates divine and everlasting things. The Church’s eyes are compared with those of doves because of spiritual grace, since the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. It follows: “Apart from what lies hidden within”—that is, apart from the glory of that heavenly reward which you are to receive at the end of the age. Although in the present you contemplate it through faith, it nevertheless remains hidden within; for it cannot be seen in the present, but will be perfected in the future.

“Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead.” By the hair of the Church are understood the Church’s subtle thoughts, by which temporal matters are for the most part ordered. They are compared with flocks of goats because these animals are clean and feed lying back on rocks or in elevated places; so the thoughts of the saints, although they concern temporal things for the sake of bodily necessity, nevertheless do not depart from the intention of eternal things. Even in the care they devote to bodily necessity, they are as though always gazing toward heaven.

We may also understand by the eyes the teachers and preachers of the Church, who occupy the highest place in the body whose head is Christ, and who see heavenly and spiritual things more than the other members. By the hair, however, we may understand the innumerable multitude of ordinary believers belonging to the lay order. Although they see spiritual things less clearly, they provide great adornment to the Church by their multitude and number.

And rightly are they compared with flocks of goats. The goat is suitable for sinners; by it are understood the peoples of the faithful devoted to worldly activities, which cannot be performed without sin. Rightly, however, it follows: “That have come up from Mount Gilead.” Literally, Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” because when Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia, Laban pursued him and found him on the third day; there they raised a heap of stones as a testimony to their mutual covenant.

Mystically, the “heap of testimony” is Christ, in whom the multitude of all the saints is established. They are living stones adhering to that true stone of which Peter says: “Approaching him, a living stone, you yourselves also are built up as living stones.” Thus the flocks of goats have come up from Mount Gilead, because multitudes of saints ascend to the heights of virtue and strive in all things to follow Christ’s teaching and commandments.

“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.” Just as by the hair of the Church the innumerable multitude of ordinary believers is understood, so by the teeth of the Church are understood its teachers; for with our teeth we grind food. The holy teachers are appropriately compared with teeth because they in a certain way break up by explanation the spiritual food that ordinary people cannot grasp.

Peter was especially the tooth of the Church; in a vision it was said to him: “Rise, kill, and eat.” As though it were said: Kill those whom you convert to the faith with respect to what they are, so that they cease to be sinners; and eat—that is, transform them into the body of the Church.

These teeth are rightly compared with sheep that have been shorn and washed. Sheep are customarily washed in running water after shearing, so that unwashed sweat may not cling to the body and produce mange. The holy teachers and masters of the Church have been shorn and washed in the bath of baptism; they have lost their fleeces—that is, their possessions and resources—for Christ.

What is said, “that have come up from the washing,” applies to all the faithful, for no one can be faithful without the washing of baptism. Shearing, however, does not apply to everyone, since not all are so perfect that they can give up their possessions for Christ. It applies especially to those who, according to the Lord’s word, sell all they possess, give to the poor, and follow Christ naked and unencumbered.

Such, then, are the teeth of the holy Church: its preachers and teachers, sheep washed in baptism in innocence, rejoicing in voluntary poverty and the surrender of their possessions. It follows: “All bearing twin young, and none is barren among them.” For they excel in the twofold charity of love for God and neighbor, and teach this to be observed; or because they preach faith and works. None among them is barren—that is, no one is alien to good works.

“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.” By the lips of the Church are understood its holy preachers, who are also represented by the teeth. Scarlet has the appearance of blood or fire. Thus the lips of the Church—that is, its holy preachers—are compared with a scarlet ribbon because they constantly proclaim the passion of Christ, who poured out his blood for our redemption. Or they are likened to a scarlet ribbon because the preachers burn with love: they love those to whom they devote their words, even those from whom they suffer evil.

This also pertains to the fact that the Holy Spirit appeared in tongues of fire, because he made the apostles both speaking and burning: burning with love and speaking in preaching.

And rightly is it called a scarlet ribbon. A ribbon binds and constrains the hair, and by their preaching the holy teachers bind the multitude of the faithful in the Church into the unity of faith and love and bring them together into a single adornment.

The hair may also be understood as the subtle thoughts of the mind. We bind our locks with a scarlet ribbon when we constrain and restrain our thoughts by the discipline of the fear of God.

“And your speech is sweet.” The speech of the Church is sweet when the holy teachers recall and proclaim the passion of their Redeemer, how greatly God loved humanity, or when they announce the heavenly rewards to their hearers.

“Your cheeks are like a section of a pomegranate, apart from what lies hidden within.” Above, we said that by the cheeks the Church is represented. When we blush, the redness of blood spreads across the cheeks. A pomegranate has a red outer rind and is filled within by a multitude of seeds; hence it is also called a “seeded apple” (*malum granatum*).

By a section of a pomegranate, therefore, is understood the memory of the Lord’s passion, which was also represented above by scarlet. One and the same reality is often expressed through different figures.

The cheeks of the Church are therefore compared with a section of a pomegranate because the holy teachers reverently keep alive the memory of the passion of their Redeemer and are not ashamed of his cross; rather, they glory in it, saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” And elsewhere the Apostle writes to his disciple: “Do not be ashamed of the cross of Christ, nor of me, his prisoner.”

The cheeks are rightly compared not with a whole pomegranate but with a section. When a pomegranate is broken, redness appears on the outside and whiteness within. So also, when the holy preachers announce Christ’s passion, there is, as it were, redness on the outside. But when they demonstrate the great benefit that came from our redemption, and that through Christ’s passion human beings are not only justified from sins but also deemed worthy of divine fellowship, then what is hidden within is, as it were, white.

The cheeks of the Church may also represent the martyrs, who are red with the outpouring of their blood like a pomegranate. But when the pomegranate is broken, whiteness appears within, because after death they shine through miracles.

“Your neck is like David’s tower, built with battlements.” The holy preachers and teachers of the Church are the neck of the holy Church. Those same persons are represented here by the neck who were represented above by the eyes or by the teeth—namely, the holy preachers. Like necks, they pass on the food of the word they have received by nourishing the body, and they bring forth the voice of divine preaching to their hearers.

Or the holy teachers are represented by the neck because, just as through the neck the head and the other members are joined to the body, so the holy teachers are mediators between Christ and the other faithful whom they instruct; as it were, they join Christ to his body, the Church.

This neck is compared with David’s tower. David, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance,” signifies Christ. Indeed, the whole Church is the city of David, that is, of Christ the great king, who is strong of hand because he conquered the devil, according to the Psalmist: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” He is also desirable in appearance because, as the Apostle says, the angels desire to gaze upon him.

The tower of this city consists of those who excel the others either in knowledge or in the perfection of their conduct. “Which is built with battlements.” The battlements are the divine mysteries of the holy Scriptures, from which, as though from a fortress, arrows proceed by which hostile powers are driven back.

“A thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty.” The thousand shields signify the innumerable defenses of divine protection by which the holy Church is surrounded and defended. “All the armor of the mighty” means the equipment either of holy conduct or of divine preaching.

And rightly is the neck of the Church—that is, its preachers and teachers—compared with David’s tower, because they are always, as it were, in battle, fighting for the defense of the holy Church.

“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.” The two breasts of the Church signify the same holy teachers. It is not surprising that one and the same reality is represented in different ways.

The holy teachers are eyes because they show their subjects the paths of life they ought to enter. They are teeth because they grind and break up the food of the divine Scriptures so that it may be eaten. They are the neck because they join the head and the members—that is, Christ and the Church.

Those same teachers, then, are also the breasts of the Church, because they nourish the little ones and simple believers with the milk of God’s word. Thus the Apostle, speaking to the less advanced, says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.”

He rightly says not simply “breasts,” but “two breasts,” since a woman has neither more nor fewer than two breasts. For the holy teachers nourish the little ones from both peoples—namely, the Jewish people and the Gentiles—with the milk of God’s word. Paul also says of himself: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised also worked through me among the Gentiles.”

The two breasts are appropriately said to be like two twin fawns of a gazelle, because they are offspring and children of our Savior Jesus Christ, who was represented above by the gazelles. These animals see with exceptional sharpness and climb to elevated places with great speed. So Christ’s teachers themselves see what must be done, show it to others, and, despising earthly things, strive toward what is above.

“Which feed among the lilies”—that is, they delight in the purest and clearest meanings of the Scriptures.
