“Until the day breathes,” that is, until that eternal day comes, which the Psalmist desired, saying: “One day in your courts is better than thousands.” “And the shadows incline,” that is, let the sorrows and disturbances of this age pass away.

“Until the day breathes”—that is, until the day rises. The day will appear, that is, it will rise, when that true sun of righteousness, Christ, appears. Then the shadows will incline: all the clouds of sorrow and darkness of the present age will pass away.

But even if we consider the literal sense itself, he has beautifully expressed the rising of day and the passing of night. For night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth, which rises as the sun descends. When the sun again ascends above the earth, the shadows incline—that is, night falls.

Thus they feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline, because the preaching and teaching of the holy teachers are necessary only in the present life. In the other life, after the eternal day has appeared and the night of the present age has ended, no one will need to be taught, because all, with unveiled face, will contemplate the glory of the Lord.

Hence the Lord also says through the Prophet: “A man will no longer teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all will know me, from the least to the greatest.”

“I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” In myrrh is understood the mortification of the flesh or endurance of sufferings for Christ; in frankincense, the devotion of holy prayers. The mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense are therefore the minds of the saints, raised up through contemplation.

The bridegroom promises that he will come to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense because he deigns to visit those minds with his presence which mortify their members, together with their vices and desires, and which also make themselves a sacrifice pleasing to God through devotion to holy prayers.

“You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” The voice of the bridegroom to his beloved bride.

“You are wholly beautiful.” “In every respect,” he says, “you admit no blemish or wrinkle.” For it is not only the teachers or those who are altogether perfect who are beautiful in God’s sight—those who excel in supreme knowledge and contemplation—but also all the simple faithful who are adorned with right faith and good works. They are beautiful in the eyes of the bridegroom.

As the Psalmist says, “He has blessed all who fear the Lord, the small together with the great.” Therefore he says, “You are wholly beautiful,” not merely a part of you.

We say this not because anyone in the present life can be without sin, since it is written: “No one is upon the earth without sin, not even an infant of one day,” but because perfect faith and heavenly desire wipe away every blemish of lesser sin.

For the present discussion does not concern grave sins. Those who commit them are no longer the bride of Christ, nor do they possess any share in this holy beauty. Hence John says: “Whoever is born of God does not sin”—understand, with a sin unto death—not that anyone is free from lesser sin, without which this life cannot be lived.

The Church, then, is wholly beautiful insofar as she guards herself chaste and free from every sin. If at some time she is darkened by a lesser sin, her former beauty is restored in her through swift repentance and right faith directed toward heavenly desire.

“Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come.” Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia. In Hebrew, *Lebanon* is interpreted as “whitening” or “making white”; in Greek, it is interpreted as “frankincense.” Hence above, where he says, “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hills of frankincense,” the hill is understood to be Lebanon.

The bridegroom therefore calls his bride one made white by baptism, whitened by the radiance of every virtue, and fragrant with devotion to holy prayers. He calls her to come—that is, to advance in virtue.

God does not call the soul only when he leads it, stripped of the bonds of the flesh, to heavenly rewards; he also urges it through inward inspiration to advance in virtue. For as many virtues as the saints advance in, so many steps do they, as it were, take toward God.

He says “Come” three times because he wishes her to be perfect in thought, word, and deed. Or he calls her first to come to him through faith; he calls her a second time to receive the worthy repayment of heavenly rewards, once freed from the body; and he calls her a third time to rejoice on the day of the general resurrection, after receiving the body and being adorned forever with a double garment.

“You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens and the mountains of leopards.” Amana, they say, is the Cilician mountain Amanus, which is also called Taurus. Sanir and Hermon are mountains of Judea, where lions and leopards are said to dwell.

By these mountains are understood the powers of the world—kings and princes—who are raised up like mountains in pride and provide dwelling places to wicked spirits, as to lions and leopards.

Wicked spirits are called lions because of their pride, and leopards because of their ferocity, or also because of their thousand arts of doing harm, since the leopard is a variegated animal.

The Church is crowned from these mountains when the princes of the world are converted to the faith of Christ, and the Church is rewarded not only for her own virtues but also for the conversion and salvation of such people.

This may also be understood in the present age. The Church is crowned from the summit of these mountains when, after the rulers have been subjected to the Catholic faith, the Church, which was previously oppressed, is crowned and glories in Christ. This happened in the time of Constantine, when, after his conversion, the Church was wonderfully glorified.

She is also crowned from the lions’ dens and the mountains of leopards when she converts the proud and all who are savage and deceitful, and receives eternal rewards for their conversion as well.

“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.” He calls the holy Church his bride and sister. She is his bride because Christ, having become incarnate, espoused her to himself and, cleansed from the filth of sins, joined her to himself as his dowry through the Holy Spirit.

She is his sister because he became incarnate for her sake and deigned to become her brother, as he said to the women after rising from the dead: “Go, tell my brothers.”

When he says that his heart has been wounded, he expresses the greatness of the love with which he loves his holy Church. He confirms this by repeating and emphasizing it: “You have wounded my heart,” so that through such repetition he might show how greatly he loves his Church.

He then demonstrates by what she has wounded him, adding: “With one of your eyes and with one lock of the hair of your neck.”

Above, we said that by the eyes of the Church are understood the spiritual senses or the holy teachers. By the hair are understood the multitudes of the peoples subject to her, by whom the holy Church is adorned.

The meaning is this: Although you are wholly beautiful, O Church, and although I love you for many reasons, nevertheless the radiance of your spiritual senses and the sincerity of your teachers especially delight me; so too does the simplicity of the peoples subject to you, who piously and faithfully obey the words of the teachers.

Although above he spoke of eyes and hair in the plural, here he speaks in the singular of one eye and one lock, so that by this the unity of the holy teachers may be expressed. The heavenly teaching which they impart to their subjects is one. “There is one Lord,” as the Apostle says, “one faith, one baptism,” and likewise one devotion among the faithful who are subject to them.

What he says, “You have wounded my heart,” may also be understood of Christ’s passion: “You have wounded my heart”—that is, by your love you caused me to be wounded on the cross.

It should be noted that he says, “with one lock of the hair of your neck.” For by the neck we said that the teachers are signified, and the hair of the Church clings to the neck. Through it the subject peoples are nourished by the holy teachers, adhere to their sound teaching, and strive to live according to their commandments.

“How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride.” Above, we said that the same teachers are represented by the breasts as are designated by the eyes; for the holy teachers are breasts—that is, they nourish the humble with simple teaching—and they are eyes when they proclaim the highest and heavenly things. He therefore says: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride”—that is, how beautiful are your teachers, since their speech excels in expression, and is precious in the weight of its meanings. “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine.” This verse has already been explained above, where it says: “Your breasts are better than wine.” It should also be noted that above the Church praised the breasts of her bridegroom, saying: “Your breasts are better than wine,” but now, in turn, the bridegroom extols the breasts of his bride, so that by this the unity of Christ and the Church may be commended. For Christ is the head, and the Church is his body; the beginning of evangelical preaching excels the legal injunction.

“And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices” [Col. 0321B]. The ointments of the Church are the gifts of heavenly teaching, or also the reputation for virtues that spreads fragrance from the Church; by spices, however, legal observances are understood. The fragrance of the Church’s ointments therefore surpasses the spices, because the renown of evangelical perfection transcends all praise of legal observance.

“Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb.” A honeycomb is honey in wax. Honey in wax is spiritual understanding within the letter. The lips of the Church are therefore called a dripping honeycomb, because the holy teachers, who are signified by the lips, bring forth spiritual instruction for the formation of the faithful. The lips of the Church are called not merely a honeycomb but a dripping one. A honeycomb drips when, overflowing with an abundance of honey, it can no longer be contained in its waxen cells. Holy Scripture is rightly called a dripping honeycomb, because it is understood in many ways and expounded according to various senses: sometimes according to the letter, sometimes according to allegory, sometimes according to morality, and sometimes according to anagoge—that is, the higher sense.

“Honey and milk are under your tongue.” Milk suits little children, and therefore milk signifies simple teaching by which the beginnings of believers are nourished; honey, however, which is believed to be made from the dew of heaven, signifies heavenly and spiritual teaching, which suits the mature and instructed. Under the tongue of the Church, therefore, there are honey and milk, because sometimes she announces heavenly mysteries to the mature, and sometimes plain and simple things to the inexperienced.

“And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” The garments of the Church are the adornments of good works, in accordance with what John says in the Apocalypse: “For the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.” And in Job it is said: “I clothed myself with righteousness, and I adorned myself with it as with an ornament and a diadem, with my judgment.” By incense, we said, the purity of holy prayers is signified. The garments of the Church are therefore compared with incense, because all the works of the Church are, as it were, prayers. In everything she does, she continually entreats the Lord, and in this way what the Lord says is fulfilled: “It is necessary always to pray.” This cannot always be fulfilled before the Lord in any other way than if our entire life and conduct are such that they are reckoned as prayer in the sight of God.

Frankincense is a tree of Arabia, similar in bark and leaf to the laurel, emitting sap in the manner of an almond tree, which is collected twice a year, in autumn and spring. For the autumn harvest, the trees are prepared by cutting their bark in the fiercest heat of summer; thus a rich foam bursts forth, which thickens as it congeals, being received, wherever the nature of the place requires, on a palm-leaf covering. What remains stuck to the tree is scraped off with iron, and therefore appears to be bark-like; this is the purest, that is, the whitest, frankincense. The second harvest is in spring. For this, the bark is cut during winter; from it a red substance emerges, inferior to the former. The product of a young tree is also believed to be whiter, but that of an old tree more fragrant. What hangs from it in the roundness of a drop we call “male” frankincense; the drop expelled by shaking we call manna.

“A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed spring” [Col. 0322B]. He calls the Church his sister and bride: from a handmaid he made her his sister, and, pledged to him by the dowry of the Holy Spirit, he made her his bride. This Church is therefore a garden, because she produces the shoots of spiritual virtues, which are designated in what follows by the names of spices. This garden is enclosed because the holy Church is fortified by the help of the Lord her Redeemer and surrounded by the protection of angelic powers; she is open to none of the snares of evil spirits. This same Church is a sealed spring. A spring, because she pours forth the streams of heavenly teaching, by which she washes all who believe in Christ from sins and gives them drink from the knowledge of truth. It is a sealed spring because it is fortified by the seal of evangelical truth, so that neither heretics nor evil spirits can violate or break into the Catholic faith.

This garden, or this spring—that is, the Church—was first planted or arose in a small corner of Judea; then, through preaching disseminated throughout the whole world, it sent out its garden plots or its streams. Hence it follows:

“Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranate trees with the fruits of fruit trees.” The shoots of the Church, as has been said, are the growth of faith and the dissemination of preaching. These shoots are a paradise. *Paradise* is Greek, while *garden* is Latin, because that primitive Church which was like a garden in Judea sent out throughout the whole world many gardens—that is, Churches.

Pomegranates, which have a red rind, signify those who have been sanctified not only by general baptism [Col. 0322D] but also baptized in their own blood through suffering, becoming martyrs. The fruits of fruit trees signify works of virtue, or those who practice these virtues in their actions. The shoots of the Church were therefore a paradise of pomegranate trees, because after the apostles the martyrs held the first place in the Church: they strove to imitate the Lord’s Passion by undergoing suffering. Yet the whole multitude may generally be understood as a paradise of pomegranate trees, since they are pomegranates because they always retain the Passion of their Redeemer in memory. And just as a pomegranate contains a multitude of seeds within one rind, so in the Church a multitude of the faithful is contained within faith in the Lord’s Passion. Hence the Apostle says: “All who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.”

“Cyprus with nard, nard and saffron, reed and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon.” Cyprus is an aromatic tree bearing a seed like coriander, that is, white and somewhat shining. This seed is boiled in oil and then pressed; the resulting substance is called *cyprus*, from which royal ointment is prepared. We read in Exodus that the manna was like coriander seed. Cyprus and manna therefore have one meaning. They signify heavenly grace, as though manna comes from the heavens. Cyprus is therefore born in the garden of the Church when all the faithful are taught to prefer heavenly grace to everything else and to hope for salvation through it. For no one can be saved by his own virtues, but only by the grace of God [Col. 0323B].

Nard is a type of the Lord’s Passion. Hence Mary anointed the head and feet of Jesus with genuine nard. Nard is therefore in the garden of the Church when all the saints honor the memory of the Lord’s Passion and give him thanks because he loved them so greatly that he accepted death for their salvation and deliverance.

“Nard and saffron.” Saffron has a flower of golden color, and therefore signifies love. For just as gold is more precious than all metals, so love holds first place among all virtues, as the Apostle says: “But now faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love.” Saffron therefore grows with nard in the garden of the Church when the members of Christ, that is, all the faithful, strive effectively to maintain love of God and neighbor. Saffron is said to cool burning fevers; likewise true love cools the heat of worldly desire and kindles in the mind love of God and neighbor.

“Reed and cinnamon.” Reed is a short tree, also called cassia, with purple bark. It signifies the saints in the Church who are distinguished by humility and patience: the poor in spirit, whose is the kingdom of heaven. The purple bark signifies the likeness of Christ’s Passion, which those grounded in true humility always retain in their hearts and strive to imitate.

Cinnamon is also a short tree, but of extraordinary virtue and fragrance; therefore it signifies the progress of humility, which is also signified by the reed. Reed and cinnamon are therefore in the Church when the saints of God truly retain humility and patience in their hearts and display them outwardly to others.

The reed’s reddish bark and cinnamon’s gray color signify that the more the saints of God remember the Passion of their Redeemer, the more despicable and contemptible they are in their own eyes, saying with Abraham: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am ashes and dust”; and with Job: “Therefore I condemn myself and repent in dust and ashes.”

“With all the trees of Lebanon.” The trees of Lebanon excel in beauty, height, and strength, and therefore signify the teachers and all the mature members of the Church. Of them the Church is read above as having been built, when the same Church says: “The beams of our houses are cedars; our ceiling panels are cypresses,” because the holy teachers fortify the Church by their preaching [Col. 0324A]. Reed and cinnamon are therefore mentioned together with all the trees of Lebanon in the garden of the Church, because whether humble and patient or perfect teachers, they have the same faith in the Church and await the same blessedness.

“Myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments.” Myrrh is a tree whose sap is called *stacte*, possessing such power that whatever is touched by it is preserved unharmed from all decay and worms. Aloe is a tree of such sweet fragrance that it is burned on altars in place of incense. Its sap, however, is extremely bitter and resists decay and worms. Hence in the Lord’s Passion Nicodemus is said to have brought a mixture of myrrh and aloe, about one hundred pounds [Col. 0324B].

These trees therefore signify restraint of the flesh and chastity. Decay usually signifies sexual vice, as the Prophet says of certain people: “The beasts have rotted in their dung.” In the garden of the Church there are therefore myrrh and aloe—that is, heavenly minds, free from every corruption—hearing the Apostle say: “Pursue peace with everyone and chastity, without which no one will see God.”

“With all the finest ointments.” What is more appropriately understood by the finest ointments than love, of which the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way,” and then: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels but do not have love, it profits me nothing.” The finest ointments are fittingly placed after myrrh and aloe, because after restraint of the flesh true love follows, which is God, since God is loved above all. For those who are held by worldly love—that is, who still take pleasure in pleasures and enticements—cannot share in this love [Col. 0324C].

“A spring of gardens, a well of living waters that flow forcefully from Lebanon.” The spring of gardens is the primitive Church herself, who irrigates gardens—that is, Churches disseminated throughout the whole world—with the knowledge of truth. She is also a well of living waters, because the knowledge of truth, which is the Church, is like a spring in some people, where it lies open, and like a well in others, where it lies hidden and cannot be perceived clearly.

For this is the difference between a spring and a well: a spring is said to be both at the bottom and on the surface of the earth, whereas a well is always below. The Church is therefore both a spring and a well, because in some people the mysteries of God are easily grasped like a spring, while in others they are drawn out with difficulty, like water from a well. The living waters signify the mysteries of Scripture, because they possess heavenly power within themselves.

By contrast, the documents of heretics are called cisterns—that is, collections of water—concerning which the Lord says through the Prophet: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water.”

These flowing waters flow forcefully from Lebanon—that is, they stream from the Church, which has been washed and made white by baptism and good works, as *Lebanon* is interpreted. From this Lebanon, that is, from the Church, waters of heavenly teachings flow—that is, they emanate—and they do so forcefully, with a certain power by which all the fabrications of heretics are destroyed and overthrown. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The force of the river makes glad the city of God,” that is, the power of divine utterances [Col. 0325A].

“Rise, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.” Having enumerated the virtues of the Church under the name of spices, the Lord, who is the bridegroom and Redeemer of the Church, knowing that the Church would be multiplied through persecutions, next commands persecution, as it were, to come—not by ordering it, but by permitting it. “Rise,” he says, “North Wind, and come, South Wind.”

By the North Wind and the South Wind are understood the blasts of persecutions and disturbances raging against the Church [Col. 0325B]. The North Wind is extremely cold, while the South Wind is hot. Therefore the North Wind signifies terrors and threats, and the South Wind the snares of flattering persuasion. By these two means the Church is tested: by terrors and by flatteries.

When he says, “Rise, North Wind, and come, South Wind,” he does not command evil powers, nor compel them to do evil, but permits the wicked and gives them the opportunity to rage against the Church, so that through their wickedness the Church may be tested and they may be punished more severely. For the Lord knows how to bring certain good from human evils, but he keeps persecution itself under his control, so that they do not rage as much as they wish. Hence it is written: “He who gives weight to the winds,” because he imposes a certain limit on the blasts of persecution, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “With the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure.”

“Blow through,” he says, “my garden,” that is, my Church, “and let its spices flow,” that is, let the fragrance of virtues and the odor of good works proceed from it. For the more harshly the Church is shaken, the greater the fragrance of virtues she emits.

## CHAPTER V

“Let my beloved come into his garden, to eat the fruit of his fruit trees.” Hearing persecution called forth, the Church, as though preparing herself for adversity, says: “Let my beloved come into his garden”—that is, let Christ, my bridegroom, whom I love with my whole heart, come to his Church, “to eat the fruit of his apple trees,” that is, to delight in and be nourished by the good works of his faithful. For our good works are the Lord’s food, just as, seeing the faith of the Samaritans or of the Gentiles, he said to his disciples: “I have food to eat of which you do not know.”

“I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” To the Church’s desire that the bridegroom come to her, he responds that he has already done so. “I have already come,” he says, for *veni*—“I have come”—is not an imperative but an indicative of past time. “O my sister, my bride, I have already come into my garden; I have already visited my Church, and I visit it daily. I feed on the fruits of its virtues and enjoy its fragrance. I come to it to correct those who wander, strengthen the weak, confirm the doubtful, and also reward the mature with heavenly gifts.”

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.” Myrrh signifies those who ended their lives in martyrdom, or those who crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. The spices are works of holy virtues, fragrant with the odors of a good reputation. The Lord therefore gathers myrrh with his spices when he cuts off holy martyrs, or other elect persons distinguished by good works, from this life with the sickle of death, and, having brought them to the maturity of good works, stores them in the granaries of the heavenly homeland [Col. 0326A].

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” The holy preachers are represented by the honeycomb and the wine; good hearers by the honey and the milk. The honeycomb signifies preachers who draw forth the hidden and innermost mysteries of Scripture like honey from honeycombs and make them known to others through preaching. Honey signifies good hearers because they strive attentively to receive the sweetness of God’s word and to be nourished by it with delight.

Wine signifies the same preachers as does the honeycomb, because they proclaim the powerful mysteries of Scripture. Milk signifies the weaker hearers, for whom open mysteries are suitable, like milk. When the Redeemer is nourished and delighted by the good intention of all these, he eats, as it were, the honeycomb with the honey and drinks the wine with the milk.

We can also refer this to the death of the elect, whom the Lord “eats” when he calls them through death to eternal life and joins them to his body—that is, to the company of the elect already rejoicing in heavenly blessedness. If we understand this of the death of the saints, we should take them as wine whose souls already rejoice in heavenly blessedness, but as the honeycomb those who already rejoice in that blessedness in body and soul, such as those who rose with the Lord [Col. 0326C].

“Eat, friends, and drink; become drunk, beloved.” The Lord not only rejoices in the progress of the saints, but also urges us to rejoice in their virtues and imitate them: “Eat,” he says, “friends”—that is, my faithful, who are my friends because you do what I command, and my beloved because you love me with perfect devotion. “Eat,” therefore, he says, “and drink”—that is, rejoice with the good deeds of the saints and set them before yourselves for imitation.

It should be noted that he says, “Drink and become drunk.” In Scripture, drunkenness is sometimes used for satiety, as it is said of Joseph’s brothers: “They drank and became drunk before him,” and the Psalmist says: “You visited the earth and made it drunk”—that is, you satisfied and filled it. He urges us, therefore, not only to eat and drink but also to be filled, because there are some who eat and are not satisfied: they listen to divine preaching with delight but carelessly forget it and do not bring what they have heard to the fulfillment of good works.

Those eat and are satisfied who store within their inner senses the words of life that they hear and strive to fulfill them in action. Of them the Psalmist says: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied.”

But if, as was said above, we understand this of the death of the saints, the “friends” and “beloved” are the angelic spirits, whom the Lord commands to rejoice with his elect when they are transferred from this life to the rest of eternal blessedness, in accordance with what is read in the Gospel parable: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” [Col. 0327A].

“I sleep, but my heart is awake.” The voice of the Church: “I sleep,” because, as my bridegroom grants me some peace, I rest and do not suffer such pressures as the primitive Church. “And my heart is awake,” because, with the peace granted to me, I cleave more securely to the love of my bridegroom and direct toward him the eyes of my heart.

But since this time is not one of rest but rather of labor and struggle, the bridegroom again rouses the Church to labor and urges her to the contest of preaching.

“The voice of my beloved, knocking.” The beloved knocks when Christ urges his faithful toward growth in virtue; or he knocks when he admonishes them to win their neighbors by preaching. There is also a third knocking by which the Lord knocks on his elect when, through the distress of illness, he indicates that death is near. Concerning this knocking the Gospel says: “When he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.”

But in this passage he is said to knock in the sense that he stirs the Church to the work of preaching.

“Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one.” “Open to me, my sister,” because you have been made a co-heir of my kingdom; “my friend,” because, freed from the yoke of slavery, you have come to know the secrets of my truth; “my dove,” because you have been sanctified by the gift of my Spirit; “my undefiled one,” because by the outpouring of my blood you have been cleansed from every stain of sin [Col. 0327C].

“Open to me”—that is, leave the repose and leisure of the contemplation you love and go forth to the work of preaching.

“For my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights.” The head of the Church, as the Apostle says, is Christ. The locks are the innermost thoughts of the saints, which do not flow loosely and disorderedly but are bound by the bond of fear and love of God.

The dew and drops of the nights here signify minds that are dark, full of unbelief, and cold. The bridegroom’s head is therefore full of dew when worldly people grow sluggish in the love of God, and, as the Lord says, love grows cold because sin abounds. And when such people persecute and hate the saints of God as they meditate on heavenly things, the bridegroom’s locks are, as it were, full of the drops of the nights.

When such people multiply and burden the Church, the bridegroom admonishes his bride to rise and devote herself to the work of preaching.

“I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” Challenged by her bridegroom to undertake the ministry of preaching, the Church replies: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” I have stripped myself of the cares and occupations of this world, without which the ministry of preaching is scarcely, or not at all, carried out; so how can I return again to what I abandoned?

For one who prepares to undertake the ministry of preaching must also provide temporal necessities for those subject to him, and these cannot be managed without great anxiety. That the tunic signifies anxieties and cares, the Lord shows in the Gospel: “The one who is on the roof must not come down to take his tunic.” This plainly means: Let the one who stands upon the lofty citadel of contemplation not come down to take his tunic—that is, to become entangled again in the occupations of the world [Col. 0328A].

The Church, or any holy soul, therefore fears being stripped of this tunic and, while resting in contemplation of her Creator, being clothed in it again and occupied with worldly affairs.

“I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” I have washed my feet—that is, I have washed with the worthy tears of repentance the actions by which I was accustomed never to touch dust, that is, to engage in earthly affairs—so thoroughly that now I desire to think of nothing except divine things. “How shall I soil them?” That is, how can I return again to thinking about transitory and earthly things, when now, with my heart freed from occupations, I enjoy the divine vision? [Col. 0328B]

“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.” The beloved puts his hand through the opening and touches the belly when the Creator visits the heart through an inner inspiration and kindles it toward growth in virtue. This also occurs when he recalls us to the memory of his works, so that we may consider that, although he was God, he graciously became human for us, assuming our earthly nature in order to make us heavenly, and by dying for us granting us eternal life.

When this happens, the belly trembles, because when we begin to think about such things, the secrets of our heart are shaken as we begin to be astonished at the great condescension with which the Creator graciously undertook these things for us.

That the belly signifies the heart is shown by the Prophet, who says: “My belly, my belly, I suffer.” He explains what this means by adding: “The thoughts of my heart are scattered.”

“I arose to open to my beloved.” We open to the beloved not only when we receive his coming, but also when we preach to others and, through our preaching, make those who had closed their breast through wickedness turn and open the door of their heart to Christ.

It is rightly said first, “I arose,” and then, “to open to my beloved.” For whoever wishes to open the hearts of others to Christ by preaching must first rise—that is, be lifted up toward the pursuit of good works—and fulfill in action what he preaches, lest, while preaching to others, he himself become rejected.

Hence Luke also says of the Lord: “Jesus began to do and teach.” He says “to do” first, and then “to teach” [Col. 0328D].

“My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of choice myrrh.” The hands by which we work signify action itself; the fingers signify discernment in action, because no member has as many distinctions of joints as the fingers.

The hands of the Church drip with myrrh when her preachers devote themselves to restraint and mortification of the flesh, saying with the Apostle: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection.” Or when they are prepared to die for Christ, as John says: “If Christ laid down his life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” [Col. 0329A].

The fingers are full of choice myrrh when we carefully discern the very work of mortification, whether it is done with a view to the heavenly reward or for the praises of the world. Whoever fasts for human approval, or devotes himself to works of abstinence or restraint, has myrrh in his hands but not in his fingers, because he does not discern why he does it. Of such people the Lord says: “They have received their reward.”

Or the bride’s hands drip with myrrh when, through the works of the holy Church, they apply themselves to chastity and holy restraint.

“I opened the latch of my door to my beloved, but he had turned aside and passed by.” The latch of the door is opened when the Church, or any faithful soul, lays open its heart to the Creator who is coming.

“But he had turned aside and passed by.” Often, when we wish to consider spiritual matters, the more attentively we concentrate, the more the sharpness of the heart’s vision is thrown back. Hence Solomon says: “I said, ‘I will become wise,’ but it withdrew farther from me.” The Psalmist also says: “A person will approach the deep heart, and God will be exalted.”

For the more each person, through purification of the flesh, raises his heart toward divine contemplation, the more deeply he discovers that what he sought exists. He therefore says: “He had turned aside and passed by,” because no one in the present life can comprehend him as he is.

“My soul melted when my beloved spoke.” The closer, he says, I sensed the coming of my bridegroom through the touch of his secret inspiration, the more everything cold within me grew warm, so that now I desire nothing except to dissolve into tears.

The bridegroom speaks when Christ inspires a holy soul through an inner inspiration, suggesting heavenly desire to it. As he speaks, it melts, because the more it is breathed upon by heavenly desires, the more it dies to earthly things, becoming, as it were, insensible to the world and living only for heavenly desire.

This is also what is said through the Prophet: “Who is blind except my servant? Who is deaf except the one to whom I sent my messengers?”

“I sought him, but I did not find him. I called him, but he did not answer me.” She repeats the cause of her grief. The Lord is always present to all who seek him faithfully, and he answers those who call upon him—that is, he hears them for salvation. Yet often he does not answer a faithful soul that desires him and longs to come to him, so that he may not show himself to it in the present as he promises to show himself in the future.

Or he does not answer—that is, he does not hear—in order that each saint may be released from the bonds of the body at his appointed time and be caressed in the embraces of his bridegroom. For when the Apostle said, “I desire to depart and be with Christ,” he was, as it were, seeking to cleave to his bridegroom and calling him with the desire of his mind. Yet he did not answer him, because he did not immediately free him from the body; rather, he allowed him to be exercised by labors and to labor for the benefit of the Church [Col. 0329D].

“The watchmen who go around the city found me; they struck me and wounded me.” The watchmen who guard the city are the holy teachers, who go around the city of God—that is, the Church—keeping vigilant watch over it, so that they may both protect it from adversaries and kindle it toward heavenly desires by their word and example.

They find the bride seeking her beloved when the holy teachers instruct and form a soul intent on heavenly desires, either by their present word or, when absent, through their writings.

“They struck me,” she says, “and wounded me.” The word of God is a sword, as the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.” The bride is struck and wounded by this sword when the preacher’s word speaks of God and pierces the hearers as if with a dart of compunction and love.

“They took my mantle from me.” Here the mantle is understood as the tunic mentioned above, where it says: “I have taken off my tunic”—the covering, that is, of worldly desires. The watchmen take it away because the holy teachers remove everything that remains in anyone’s mind of love for the present world and make that person love Christ the bridegroom alone. Such people can say with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

“The watchmen of the walls.” The walls of the city are the holy teachers of the Church. The watchmen of the walls are those who also instruct people capable of preaching to others, such as Paul, who instructed and guarded Timothy and Titus—the walls, as it were, of this city—that is, exhorted them toward perfection in good works.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love” [Col. 0330C]. The daughters of Jerusalem are faithful souls, whether they are still pilgrims in the present life or already enjoying Christ: daughters of Jerusalem, that is, daughters of that heavenly city in which there is perfect peace and the happiness of divine contemplation.

But here we should understand the daughters of Jerusalem as souls who desire God but still remain in this pilgrimage. The bride therefore adjures the daughters of Jerusalem to tell the bridegroom that she is sick with love when a faithful soul adjures other faithful people who desire God to make known to Christ that she is held by his love.

She rightly says that she is sick with love. For the more she begins to desire heavenly things, the more she grows weak with regard to the things of the world. Nor is it surprising that such people are called sick, since the Apostle calls them dead: “You have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ.”

Thus the daughters of Jerusalem answer the bride who is adjuring them.

“What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?” This occurs when one faithful person addresses another faithful person, and they mutually offer one another words of heavenly desire by which they kindle each other toward love of what is above.

“Tell me,” she says, “now that I am already desiring, now that I long to reach the vision of my Creator, what your beloved is”—that is, how Christ ought to be loved. “For some time now,” she says, “I began to fear him; but now, with love driving out fear, I long to hear words by which I may be kindled toward love of him. You, then, who already seek him in love and languish with love for him, tell me what your beloved is more than another beloved.”

“Beloved from beloved” is the Son from the Father, just as God is from God and light from light. Or “your beloved more than another beloved” means that Christ is to be understood from the aspect in which he is to be loved, not from that in which he is to be feared. For fear is more characteristic of the imperfect, whom fear holds back from sins, whereas love is characteristic of the perfect.

She therefore asks what the beloved is more than another beloved—that is, how Christ ought to be loved, or what he is like toward those who know only how to love him [Col. 0331A].

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from thousands.” The voice of the Church answering: “My beloved is white and ruddy”: white in virginity, ruddy in Passion. White because he is without sin, for he lived without sin: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.” Ruddy because “he washed us from our sins in his blood.”

“Chosen from thousands.” Christ the human being shone forth by singular grace amid the whole mass of the human race, because through him God purposed to save the human race; and he is the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “There is no one who does good, not even one.” And Solomon says: “I found one man among a thousand”—that is, Christ. And he himself says in the Psalm: “I am set apart until I pass over.”

He is therefore “chosen from thousands,” because from the whole multitude of the saints he alone was worthy to hear: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

“His head is finest gold.” The head of the bridegroom is God, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God.” It is compared with finest gold because, just as gold is more precious than all metals, so almighty God excels and surpasses the good things made by him. Hence the Lord says: “No one is good except God alone.” The bridegroom’s head, then, is finest gold because God’s goodness is ineffable, surpassing the goodness of all things, since nothing is good except by participation in this supreme Good.

“His locks are like the raised branches of palm trees.” The bridegroom’s locks are the multitudes of the faithful, clinging to God through faith and love; they are compared with the raised branches of palm trees. The raised branches of palms are their longer and more excellent branches, sometimes golden and gleaming, curling, always reaching upward, and never losing their greenness. Thus the Church calls the locks of her bridegroom curled and shining.

Some say that “the raised branches of palm trees” refers to a kind of aromatic tree which in Latin they call *abies* or *spata*. For in Greek, fir is called ἐλάτη (*elatē*). This is a kind of tree suitable for the preparation of perfumes. Here, however, we must understand not the large fir tree suitable for ships and houses, but—as we have said—a species of aromatic tree. This, according to the literal sense, concerns the raised branches of palms.

The bridegroom’s locks, then, are compared with the raised branches of palms because the multitudes of the faithful rejoice in the greenness of faith, are lifted up toward the desire for eternal things, and taste the sweetness of heavenly delight. The more they perceive it, the more they see themselves as sinners and contemptible in their own eyes. Hence it follows:

“Black as a raven.” The bridegroom’s locks are black as a raven because the multitudes of the faithful are conscious of their own frailty and know that they possess no good of themselves. Or again, they are “raised branches of palms” in hope and victory, but “black as a raven” as those who are despised and contemptible amid the pressures of this age. The saints are raised branches of palms because, by God’s grace, they strive toward the palm of heavenly victory; but they are black as a raven because they recognize themselves as weak and sinful in themselves.

The bridegroom’s locks may also be understood as the angelic powers, which cling especially to God, like hair to the head, and contemplate him from near at hand. They are rightly compared with raised branches because they never bend away from the uprightness of their state, but remain undefiled in the dignity of their office. The more they contemplate the radiance of their Creator, the more they perceive how worthless every created thing is in comparison with him; and therefore they are said to be black as a raven.

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk.” His eyes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. John shows this in the Apocalypse when he says: “I saw a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.” Thus they are rightly compared with doves beside streams of water, because the Holy Spirit delights in pure and sincere minds. Doves do not settle beside stagnant pools or marshes, but beside streams of water, because—as has been said—the Holy Spirit makes chaste and clean minds his dwelling place.

“Washed with milk,” because—as has been said—the Holy Spirit is understood under the name of milk, that is, the grace of God, which is granted to the Church through the Holy Spirit and by which the Church is nourished, like infants with milk.

By the bridegroom’s eyes we may also understand teachers, who are compared with doves because of their innocence and simplicity. These doves dwell beside streams so that they may see the hawk’s approach from afar and take precautions against it. So too the holy teachers, washed in the water of baptism and whitened by the brightness of chastity and holiness, “sit beside abundant streams,” that is, beside the overflowing knowledge of the Scriptures.

If we think there is some difference between “streams” and “abundant waters,” it must be said that the streams signify the Scriptures of the Old Testament, while the abundant waters signify the plentiful Scripture of the holy Gospel. These doves, then, are both beside streams of water and seated beside abundant waters, because the holy teachers continually search out the mysteries of both the Old and the New Testaments.

“His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers.” The bridegroom’s cheeks signify Christ’s modest compassion, or his severity, or the expression of his face. His cheeks were seen when, as the Gospel says, he rejoiced in spirit, or when he wept over the dead Lazarus, or when he grieved over Jerusalem destined to perish, and in many other such instances.

These cheeks of the bridegroom are compared with beds of spices. For just as beds of spices, beautifully arranged and ordered, delight the eyes of those who look upon them and offer them the sweetness of their fragrance, so Christ’s gentleness delighted those who were absent through its reputation and those who were present through the reality itself, and summoned them to love him.

These beds are planted by perfumers. The perfumers are the prophets or the apostles: the former described all these things as future, the latter as already accomplished.

“His lips are lilies, distilling prime myrrh.” By the bridegroom’s lips are understood the words of our Lord, which are compared with lilies because they announce the rewards of eternal brightness. They distill prime myrrh because they teach that these rewards are attained through the mortification of the flesh.

Or again, the Lord’s lips are compared with lilies because they teach works of chastity and purity. They distill prime myrrh because they suggest that every adversity must be endured patiently. The Lord’s lips were lilies when, teaching on the mountain, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the pure in heart.” They distilled prime myrrh when, after these words, he added: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

“His hands are turned work, made of gold.” In the bridegroom’s hands the saving work of the Savior is rightly understood. For just as one works easily on a lathe, without needing any rule, so the Savior’s work was easy: whatever he wished, he immediately accomplished, because “he spoke, and they were made”; and, as the Evangelist says, “he was as one having authority in his word.”

They were golden because his work was carried out by the power of his divinity. For divinity is signified by gold: just as gold surpasses all other metals and is more precious, so divinity surpasses all its works in an ineffable manner.

“Full of hyacinths.” Hyacinth is a stone of the color of the sky. What, then, is understood by hyacinths except heavenly hope and desire? The Lord’s hands are full of hyacinths because all his work arouses in us hope and desire for heavenly things.

Hyacinth is also an aromatic flower, purple in color and of pleasant fragrance. The Lord’s hands are full of hyacinths because they were pierced by nails on the cross and sprinkled with the redness of his blood, as though with a purple color. But the earlier explanation, concerning the stone hyacinth, is more suitable here. In another translation, “stone” is found. For his hands are said to be turned work, full of *tharsis*. *Tharsis* is a stone which we call chalcedony.

“His belly is ivory.” Among the members of the human body nothing is more fragile or more tender than the belly; therefore the frailty of Christ’s assumed humanity is understood by the belly. Ivory is the bone of an elephant, an animal which they say is most chaste and of an exceedingly cold nature; hence it is intensely desired by the dragon, which has a hot nature.

The bridegroom’s belly, then, is ivory because the assumed humanity of the Redeemer admitted no corruption and no stain. “He committed no sin, nor was any deceit found in him.” He assumed the frailty of the flesh, yet remained entirely free from sin, just as the bronze serpent lifted up by Moses in the desert had the form of a serpent but lacked the serpent’s poisonous malice.

“Marked with sapphires.” Sapphire is a stone having the color of a clear sky. Hence, in the vision of the Lord, it is said: “They saw the God of Israel, and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear.” Sapphires, therefore, signify the works of divine majesty accomplished in the flesh.

The bridegroom’s belly, then, was marked with sapphires because Christ’s humanity shone with heavenly virtues. It is not said to be full of sapphires, but “marked” with them, so that the whiteness of the ivory appeared among the sapphires. Thus the Lord performed what belonged to divinity while nevertheless accomplishing what belonged to humanity, and he did not abandon what belonged to divinity. In Christ the operation of divinity and humanity is distinct.

For his hunger, thirst, weeping, weariness, and ultimate capacity to be crucified and to die were works of humanity. But his raising the dead, aiding all who were sick, and raising himself from the dead were unmistakable works of divinity.

“His legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases.” The bridegroom’s legs are the journeys of the Savior, by which he deigned to become human and come to us. They are rightly compared with marble columns, because nothing is stronger than marble and nothing is straighter than a column.

The bridegroom’s legs are marble columns because all the Lord’s journeys are both strong and straight. The Psalmist speaks of his strength: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven.” Elsewhere he speaks of his uprightness: “The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity”; and, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.”

These legs are founded upon golden bases because everything that was to be accomplished through Christ or in Christ was preordained and determined by the divine plan before the foundation of the world. Gold, which—as has often been said—is brighter and more precious than the other metals, signifies the purest secret of the divine plan.

Marble columns proceed from golden bases because from the beginning of the age the incarnation, birth, passion, and resurrection of the Savior, together with the other mysteries by which the human race would be redeemed, were preordained. Hence the Prophet, praising God, said: “Lord my God, I will honor you; I will sing praises to your name, who do wonderful things: may your ancient plan come true.”

“His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars.” Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, the boundary of Judea toward the north, and it is higher than the other mountains. The trees of that mountain surpass the timber of other forests in height, appearance, and strength.

Just as Lebanon is higher than the other mountains of the land of Judea, so our Redeemer is more beautiful than all the elect, because “he is beautiful in appearance beyond the sons of men.” And just as he is more beautiful and taller than the other trees, so he surpasses all the saints from the beginning of the age by the grace of his divinity.

“His throat is most sweet.” Earlier, the bridegroom’s lips signified his words; now, by his throat, the inward sweetness of those words is signified, by which our understanding is refreshed. Hence the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.”

Many can easily understand the Lord’s words, but few are able to penetrate their sweetness—that is, few strive to fulfill God’s commandments out of love and desire. “And altogether desirable.” It is as though he were saying: Why do I linger in describing him limb by limb? My bridegroom is altogether desirable.

“Altogether,” he says, because he is perfect God and perfect man. He is altogether desirable because he kindles the angels and all the elect with desire for him, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Into whom the angels desire to look.” The more closely he is perceived, the greater the desire with which he summons those who behold him to gaze upon him.

“Such is my beloved, and such is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.” He is beloved because I cling to him through faith and love; he is a friend because, having redeemed me from the bondage of sin, he has deigned to make me his friend and one who knows his secrets. The more deeply anyone loves him, the more worthy that person becomes of his friendship.

“Where has your beloved gone, O fairest among women?” This is the voice of the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, of the Churches, or also of holy souls. For the bride of Christ is the Church, and the daughters of Jerusalem are that same Church, which consists of the individual souls of the faithful.

They say: “Where has your beloved gone, O fairest among women? Where has your beloved turned aside? We will seek him with you.” Earlier the bride herself had adjured the daughters of Jerusalem to tell the bridegroom that she was languishing with love for him. Those same daughters of Jerusalem had asked what the bridegroom was like, and she had consequently described his form. Now the daughters of Jerusalem themselves ask where that bridegroom has gone, so that they may seek him with her.

Holy souls do this when, aflame with love for Christ and desiring to behold him, they converse with one another about eternal salvation; or when they diligently investigate in whose hearts Christ most especially dwells, so that they may be edified by their example and way of life.

It should be noted that it says, “Where has he gone?” or, “Where has your beloved turned aside?” He seems to turn aside for a time while he is being sought, in order to arouse a greater desire to seek him. For this reason he often delays the prayers and petitions of the saints, so that they may begin to desire him more ardently. Thus, when Mary once sought him, he did not immediately reveal himself to her, but appeared in the form of a gardener and finally showed that he himself was the one being sought.

Christ always hears his elect, but he seems always to turn aside when he does not immediately grant what they ask. It is rightly said, “We will seek him with you,” for one who seeks Christ without the Church may wander and grow weary, but cannot make progress.

## Chapter VI

**[Col. 0336A]**

“My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the bed of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.”

We have already learned what Christ’s garden is: namely, the holy Church, of which it was said above, “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride.” Christ has gone down, he says, to his garden, to the bed which he himself prepared and cultivated, which he sowed with the shoots of virtues, which he illumined by his grace, and which he protected from the attacks of evil spirits by the wall of his guardianship.

He is rightly said to have gone down into his garden, for he wished to be buried in a garden, and he first appeared to Mary Magdalene in a garden, consecrating there, in a certain sense, the firstfruits of the Church.

He is said to have gone down when he descended from the heavenly and exalted dwelling places into the garden which he planted in a lowly place. But he descended for this purpose: that the garden—that is, the Church—might ascend to him. Hence, in what follows, he says of the garden, that is, of his Church: “Who is this who comes up through the desert?”

“To the bed of spices,” he says. By the bed is understood the soul of each believer, cultivated by heavenly discipline, carefully ordered, and squared with the evenness of its sides.

“To pasture in the gardens,” he says, that is, to delight in the pious labors of the saints. For he himself is nourished by our good works, to such an extent that in the poor he himself is refreshed.

“And gather lilies,” he says—that is, gather holy souls who have been brought by the maturity of virtue to perfect brightness from this world to himself, and make them rejoice with him in eternal blessedness. For the lilies are holy souls, whitened by the pursuit of virtue and good works.

“I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, who pastures among the lilies.” “I am my beloved’s”: this implies, I prepare the grace of nourishment. “And my beloved is mine”: he will grant me the grace of perfection, or the reward of eternal recompense.

Or, “I am my beloved’s”: I prepare a dwelling for my beloved in myself; “and my beloved is mine,” because he himself dwells in me and makes me dwell in him, as he says in the Gospel: “I in you, and you in me.”

“Fair are you, my friend, sweet and comely as Jerusalem.” The Church sought her bridegroom as though he were absent; but he, in order to show that he is always present, and to demonstrate that he is ever near her when she speaks of him and desires him, promptly replies: “Fair are you, my friend, sweet and comely as Jerusalem.” [Col. 0336D] You are fair because you have neither spot nor wrinkle of sin, but flourish with every brightness of virtues. “My friend”: the Church, or every faithful soul. “Sweet and comely as Jerusalem.” Jerusalem, interpreted “vision of peace,” signifies that heavenly city in which true peace and happiness are found; for there the saints so rejoice in their gift that there is nothing for them to grieve over through corruption. Therefore the Church which is still on earth, or every faithful soul, is sweet and comely in likeness to that Jerusalem, because it imitates that peace insofar as it can.

It follows: “Terrible as an army set in array.” The Church is terrible to evil spirits, and is ordered as an army set in array when each believer rightly preserves his own rank and calling. For there are three orders in the Church: teachers, the continent, and the married; these kinds are represented in those three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job. Noah, who guided the ark amid the waves, signifies holy teachers; Daniel, unmarried and chaste, signifies the order of the continent; Job, who had a wife and children, represents the order of the married. Therefore the Church is ordered like an army in battle array, because every order in the Church stands as though in battle against the hostile evil spirits: holy teachers devote themselves to preaching and instruction; the continent, despising the things of the world, think only upon the things of God and, with minds free from earthly occupations, devote themselves to God alone; the married apply themselves to almsgiving and the other good works of the active life, and thus use the world without abandoning the things of God. [Col. 0337A] This most orderly disposition of the Church is terrible to unclean spirits, like an army set in array for battle.

Or, the Church is fair and comely as Jerusalem in virtues, but terrible as an army set in array because it does not cease to extend its rule and authority to the ends of the whole world. Or, it is terrible as an army set in array because it is so bound and united by the unity of charity that no force of the malignant enemy and no pest of discord can penetrate it; for nothing so terrifies evil spirits as charity.

“Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me fly away.” It is as though he said: I indeed gave you dove-like eyes, by which you might behold me and most keenly penetrate the hidden things of Scripture; but take care not now to desire to fix them upon seeing me, because while you live in the present life you cannot do so: “For no man shall see me and live.” But when, released from the bonds of the flesh, you come to me, then you shall see me in open vision, and what is promised in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

But when it is said, “Because they have made me fly away,” we must not suppose that God abandons those who seek him and withdraws from them, since he himself commands, “Seek and you shall find.” Rather, it must be understood thus: the more anyone wishes to search out the divinity of God’s majesty, the more he understands how unsearchable and incomprehensible it is. This is what the Psalmist says: “Man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted.” It is as though he said: although a person raises his heart in order to see God, God will be exalted, because his greatness cannot be comprehended. [Col. 0337C]

“Your hair is like a flock of goats that appeared from Gilead.” These verses have been explained above; yet let us not be reluctant to explain again what the Holy Spirit was not reluctant to repeat. For this reason he set down these verses twice: that we might hold as most certain and firm what we hear confirmed by repetition. The hairs of the holy Church are the manifold varieties of subtle thoughts. They are rightly compared with a flock of goats, for the goat is a figure of the sinner. Hence the Law commands that whoever sins through ignorance and recognizes his guilt shall offer a goat as a burnt offering for that fault. Therefore the Church’s hairs are compared with a flock of goats because the saints, who are members of the Church, strive to blot out every guilt of their thoughts by worthy repentance and the tears of just compunction.

They are rightly said to have appeared from Mount Gilead. Gilead is interpreted “heap of testimony.” Therefore Gilead signifies the mind of the saints, who are a heap of testimony because they attest by the clearest signs that they disregard all things of the world and desire God alone. Gilead may also signify the Lord himself and our Redeemer. For Gilead is the name both of a mountain and of a city. Thus a flock of goats appeared from Mount Gilead because the Church is founded upon Christ, as he himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” He is the heap of testimony because the multitude of prophets and patriarchs bear testimony to him in deeds and writings. [Col. 0338B]

“Your teeth are like flocks of sheep which have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none among them is barren.” By the teeth of the Church is understood the firm stability of her utterances. They are rightly compared with a flock of sheep which has come up from the washing, because the Church’s words sound nothing but innocence and meekness; they retain in themselves nothing foul, nothing shameful or unclean, but are washed in the washing of sincerity and purity, heeding the Apostle’s words: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth.” They are rightly said all to bear twins because the speech of the saints neither sounds nor speaks anything except what pertains to the love of God and neighbour. For the saints ought to speak only those things which concern the everlasting health of bodies and souls. [Col. 0338C]

“As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from your hidden parts.” Above we said that the cheeks signify the chaste modesty of the saints; the rind of the pomegranate signifies the mystery of Christ’s passion, as we hear from the Apostle Paul: “Do not be ashamed of the cross of Christ, nor of me his prisoner.” Great indeed are the things which are in the open; but far greater are those which are within, that is, those reserved for the saints in the life to come.

“There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number.” The queens are the teachers of the holy Church, who by the merit of faith and knowledge draw near to the bed of the eternal King and bear spiritual children to God. The number sixty is made up of ten and six: ten multiplied by six rises to sixty. Ten signifies the divine commandments, because of the Decalogue of the Law; six signifies perfection, because God completed his works in six days. Thus the queens are said to be sixty because they signify, as we have said, those who excel in perfection of knowledge and work, and who preach solely for love of their Creator and with a view to heavenly recompense.

This number, sixty, is also made up of twelve taken five times: for five times twelve, or twelve times five, makes sixty. The queens are said to be sixty because they signify those who, established in the Church, know how chastely to order the five senses of their body according to the teaching of the twelve apostles. The concubines signify those who do not preach Christ sincerely, but for temporal gain or popular praise. For they too are queens, draw near to the King’s bed through knowledge, and bear spiritual children; yet they remain excluded from the crown of the eternal kingdom. They are rightly comprehended by the number eighty, for this number is made up of ten and eight. Eighty is sometimes taken in an evil sense because it is constituted by the multiplication of four. Four signifies all temporal and present things, because of the four quarters of the world or the four seasons of the year. Therefore these concubines are rightly said to be eighty because, as has been said, they preach only for temporal and visible things and care less for spiritual things. Of such people the Apostle said: “There are some who proclaim Christ insincerely,” and so on, until he says: “In this I rejoice, and I shall rejoice.” [Col. 0339B]

“The maidens are without number.” The maidens are souls already regenerated in Christ, which, having laid aside the old age of the first man, have been renewed in Christ; yet they are not noble, nor yet fit for the King’s bed, because they have not yet attained the perfection of preaching Christ. They are without number because the number of souls believing in Christ is infinite and cannot be comprehended by any human being. Yet all the elect are numbered by God; for with him, who has even comprehended the number of the stars, the number of the elect cannot be unknown.

“My dove, my perfect one, is one”: that is, the one catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, which, consisting of queens and maidens, also has concubines—that is, some who are called Christians or teachers only in name. The Church is one because it admits no division or schisms; but as there is one God, one faith, and one baptism, so there is one universal Church. It is rightly called a dove because it has been espoused to Christ and sanctified by the gift of the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove.

“She is one to her mother, chosen by her who bore her.” Our mother is that heavenly Jerusalem, of which the Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother.” Thus this Church is one with her mother because, after the example of that Church which already enjoys Christ, it is instructed and formed during this pilgrimage, and strives to attain that blessedness in which it reigns with Christ.

“The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.” Those whom he above called maidens, he here calls daughters. Let us understand queens and concubines here as above. Thus daughters, queens, and concubines proclaim and praise the Church because the whole body of the faithful admires the catholic Church. For this Church, which consists of many persons among the faithful, makes up the catholic—that is, universal—Church. [Col. 0340A]

“Who is she that goes forth like the dawn rising?” This is the voice of the Synagogue. At the end of the age, when the Jewish people have been converted to Christ through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, it too will marvel, saying: Who is she? That is, how great and what manner of Church is this which goes forth—that is, which advances from virtue to virtue? The Church is said not to stand still but to advance because, not content with one place, it has occupied the whole world by heavenly preaching. It goes forth like the dawn because, the darkness of unbelief having passed away, it shows that it possesses the light of truth.

“Fair as the moon.” Natural philosophers say that the moon is illuminated by the sun. The Church is fair as the moon because it is illuminated by the charity of its bridegroom Christ and shines by his grace. Or, it is fair as the moon in the present life, in which at times it increases when peace and security are granted to it, and at times it diminishes when worn down by adversities. “Chosen as the sun” in the other life, where it will shine perpetually with joy at the vision of its Creator. Or, it is chosen as the sun because it strives to imitate him of whom it is written: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall arise.” It imitates this sun by living in humility, righteousness, and godliness. “Terrible as an army set in array”: terrible to storms of the air, and ordered as an army set in array—that is, united in the unity of charity—so that it may be penetrated by no temptations. [Col. 0340B]

“I went down to the garden of nuts.” The Church, praised by the Synagogue, replies: “I went down to the garden of nuts.” The garden of nuts is the present life. For just as in a nut the shell seems very hard, but the kernel lies hidden, so in the present life our consciences are closed and do not appear until they are made manifest when the shell of the body is broken. Thus the Church goes down to the garden of nuts when, through its teachers, it considers the life of individuals. Hence follows: “that I might see the fruits of the valleys.” The fruits of the valleys are virtues seasoned with humility. “I went down,” he says, “to the garden, that I might see the fruits of the valleys”: that is, that I might consider the saints, endowed indeed with excellence of virtues but lowly in humility.

“And that I might see whether the vine had flowered”: that is, that I might consider who were making progress in the pursuit of holy virtues. “And whether the pomegranates had budded”: that is, that I might also seek out those who are already fitted to imitate Christ’s passion. For pomegranates, as has often been said, signify the mystery of Christ’s passion. Therefore the Church considers through its prelates who are advancing in virtues, and who are already perfect enough, by imitating Christ’s passion, to be fit to shed their blood for him also—such as those to whom the Apostle said: “To you it has been given, not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for him.” [Col. 0340D]

“I did not know.” This is the voice of the Synagogue. Seeing the Church’s so great grace upon beholding the truth of the Gospel, it grieves that it had not previously known the faith of Christ; and, as though excusing itself for having been converted late, it says: I did not know, O Church, bride of Christ. I did not know—that is, I did not recognize such great grace and such great gifts of spiritual virtues bestowed upon you by your bridegroom.

“My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.” “I was troubled,” it says, “by excessive anxiety of mind because of the Gospel’s so sudden preaching. For I knew that the Law and the prophets had been given by God, and therefore, when I suddenly saw the Gospel being preached, I was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab.” Aminadab was Judah’s great-grandson, through whom Christ’s genealogy is traced. Aminadab is interpreted “the willing one of my people,” because, though he was God, he willingly became man; though he was maker and creator, by his goodness alone he became a portion of his people. And the sense is: “I was troubled because of the sudden preaching of the Gospel, which, like the swiftest chariots, suddenly sped through the whole world.” It rightly calls this preaching not a chariot but chariots, because the preaching of the Gospel rests upon the authority of the four evangelists, and the four Gospels are as the chariots of the New Testament; Christ himself presides as their charioteer, directing and ordering the course of the Gospels. [Col. 0341B]

“Return, return, Shulamite.” This is the voice of the Church inviting the Synagogue to faith: “Return, return, Shulamite.” Return, O Synagogue, from unbelief to faith; return from hatred to love. Shulamite is interpreted “captive” or “despised.” Such was the Synagogue before Christ’s coming: captive in the bond of the devil, and despised by God because it did not recognize Christ, sent for its salvation. “Return, return, that we may look upon you”: that is, that we may behold the beauty of your chastity. [Col. 0341C]

## Chapter VII
“What will you see in the Shulammite except the choirs of camps?” This is the voice of the bridegroom. Hearing that the Synagogue is being invited to the faith by his bride, the Church, he says: “What will you see in the Shulammite except the choirs of camps?” As though he were saying: You, my bride, grieve over the ruin of the Synagogue and because it is coming late to the faith; but the time is at hand when it will be converted, and then you will see in it nothing but the choirs of camps—that is, nothing but harmony in charity and the steadfast strength of faith, with which it will fight in defense of my faith. For choirs are groups of singers, whereas camps are groups of fighting soldiers. Thus the choirs of camps will be seen in the Shulammite, because the converted Synagogue will preach Christ harmoniously with the Church and will fight for the faith of Christ even unto death.

“How beautiful are your steps!” From this point the bridegroom begins to expound the praises of his bride. It should be noted that he begins to weave her beauty from her steps and ends her praises at her mouth, just as above he had begun with her eyes. He did this either to vary the beauty of the poem, or also because this is most suitable to its mysteries.

“How beautiful,” he says, “are your steps!” He saw that the Church was not standing idly in one place, but traversing the whole world through swift preaching; therefore he began to praise her from her steps. The steps of the Church are the swift preaching of the apostles, through whom the Gospel resounded throughout the whole earth.

“In sandals”—that is, in the examples of the preceding fathers. For sandals are made from dead animals. The sandals of the Church are therefore the examples of the preceding fathers, by which its steps are protected, so that it may walk more securely and without stumbling by imitating them.

“Daughter of a prince.” Another translation says, “daughter of Aminadab.” As stated above, Aminadab means “my people’s spontaneous one,” and he rightly represents Christ. For the Church is both daughter and bride: daughter because she was redeemed by his blood and regenerated by his baptism; bride because she has been joined to him by the dowry of the Holy Spirit.

“The joints of your thighs are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan.” In the thighs or loins, sacred Scripture usually signifies the descent of a generation. Thus we read concerning Jacob: “All the persons who came forth from the thigh of Jacob.” The thighs of the Church, therefore, are the spiritual generation of the believing people through the word of preaching and the bath of regeneration. The joining of the thighs is the union of two peoples in one faith, the Jewish and the Gentile. These joints are aptly compared with necklaces, because the faith of both peoples is manifested especially in works. For “faith without works is dead.” They are fashioned by the hand of an artisan—that is, of almighty God, by whose gift the power to perform good works is granted to believers. This is the artisan of whom Paul spoke when he recalled the patriarch Abraham: “For he was awaiting the city that has permanence, whose founder and artisan is God.”

“Your navel is a turned-work cup, never lacking cups.” The navel is the coldest part of the body, and therefore through the navel we should understand the frailty of our mortality. A cup, however, is a larger vessel, with handles on either side. The navel of the Church is therefore a turned-work cup, because the more the teachers of the Church remember their own frailty, the more earnestly they devote themselves to the word of preaching, so that by offering the alms of God’s word they themselves may obtain mercy from God.

It is rightly called a turned-work cup. For we work more easily on a lathe; by this is signified the ease with which the word is distributed or alms are given.
