Alms should not be given slowly or hesitantly, in accordance with what Solomon says: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back; tomorrow I will give to you,’ when you are able to give immediately.” What is made on a lathe does not require an external rule or line to be applied, but is completed accurately from within itself. The navel of the Church is therefore a turned-work cup, because whoever preaches or gives alms ought to do so solely out of love and in expectation of the heavenly reward. Whoever preaches or shows mercy to his neighbors for temporal recompense or praise is a cup, but not a turned-work one.

And this cup never lacks drink, because preaching the word of God is never lacking for preachers: the one whom they preach supplies them with the cups of knowledge and the strength of perseverance. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power.”

“Your belly is like a heap of wheat, enclosed with lilies.” The same frailty that was signified by the navel is displayed here through the belly, because the belly is not supported by the firmness of any bones. The belly of the Church is therefore aptly compared with a heap of wheat, because the more the saints remember their frailty, the more diligently they devote themselves to bringing forth the fruits of good works.

He rightly says not “an abundance of wheat” but “a heap of wheat,” so that by this he may signify the growth of virtues, which, like a heap, rise by increasing from lower things to higher. For just as a heap spreads out broadly at the bottom but is contracted and pointed toward the top, so in the Church there are many who live with greater indulgence, but few who devote themselves to the highest perfection. More are found who give alms from their possessions than those who abandon their possessions for God.

This heap is said to be enclosed with lilies because the saints perform the good things they do out of desire for heavenly brightness and radiance. For by lilies that heavenly splendor is signified. The belly of the Church may also be understood as the divinely given fountain of baptism, by which the faithful are regenerated as a new creation. This belly is therefore compared with a heap of wheat enclosed with lilies, because those regenerated in the fountain of baptism are taught to labor at good works and continually yearn to behold the glory of heavenly splendor.

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.” The breasts of the Church, as was already said above, signify the holy teachers, who instruct the little ones—that is, those recently regenerated in Christ—with the milk of clearer and simpler teaching. They are rightly called two breasts because the faithful are gathered from two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, and are nourished with the milk of spiritual teaching.

These two breasts are said to be like two twin fawns of a gazelle. The two fawns are the two Testaments, upon which all the preaching of those teachers rests. Christ is the one author and promulgator of both Testaments, in accordance with what Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply; they were given by one shepherd,” namely Christ.

The gazelle rightly signifies Christ, because it surpasses other animals both in sight and in speed, and because it is a clean animal that divides the hoof and chews the cud. Such are the members of Christ—namely, the teachers—distinguished by the insight of knowledge, and abandoning earthly things with that speed, hastening toward heavenly things; dividing the hoof, that is, possessing discernment between good and evil; and chewing the cud, that is, meditating on God’s commandments with diligent remembrance.

“Your neck is like an ivory tower.” The holy teachers, who are signified by the breasts, are also signified by the neck. For through the arteries of the neck the voice proceeds, and through the service of the neck vital nourishment is supplied to the other members. Thus the holy teachers proclaim the words of life to the peoples and nourish them with the food of heavenly doctrine.

The neck of the Church is therefore compared with an ivory tower, because its holy teachers provide that Church with both beauty and strength. They provide beauty, signified by the whiteness of ivory, by living chastely and sincerely. They provide strength, signified by the tower, when they fortify that same Church against the temptations of the devil and the attacks of heretics.

“Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude.” That is, the very teachers who were signified by the neck are also signified by the eyes. For they watch over the entire body of the Church and show it the path it ought to enter.

These eyes are compared with the pools of Heshbon at the gate of the city, because the holy teachers wash the peoples who believe in Christ with the life-giving bath and refresh them with the drink of saving doctrine. Heshbon is called “daughter of the multitude” according to the literal sense because of the multitude of peoples who flock there. Likewise the holy Church is rightly called “daughter of the multitude,” because it daily gathers a multitude of nations.

Heshbon, however, is interpreted as “a belt of mourning.” The eyes of the Church are therefore compared with the pools of Heshbon because the holy teachers, disregarding the fleeting joys of the world, bind themselves with a belt of mourning. Living chastely and soberly in this world, they grieve for their own errors, so that by mourning in the present they may attain true and eternal joys.

These pools are said to be at the gate of Heshbon because no one can enter the Church unless first washed with the water of baptism and unless he drinks from the fountain of saving doctrine. This was also signified by the bronze basin that Solomon had placed in the portico of the temple, so that the priests, when they were about to enter the temple and sacrifice victims, might wash their bodies there.

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.” Since by the nose we distinguish foul odors from good ones, the same holy teachers are rightly understood through the nose of the Church. They know how to discern astutely between the fragrant doctrine of the Catholic faith and the deadly stench of the heretical body. For among the divine gifts distributed through the Holy Spirit it is said: “To another, through the Spirit, the discernment of spirits.”

The nose of the Church is therefore compared with the tower of Lebanon, because the holy teachers hold the highest place in the Church and stand, as it were, on Mount Lebanon, defending the Church against the attacks of wicked spirits. This tower is said to face Damascus. Damascus is the metropolitan city of Syria, which once fought against the children of Israel, since it had kings who were exceedingly strong and cruel.

Damascus is interpreted as “drink of blood” or “eye of blood.” They say that Abel was killed there, and therefore it signifies the powers of this age, which thirst for the drinking of blood because they delight in the pleasures and allurements of flesh and blood. It also signifies the aerial powers, which thirst for the blood of our souls. This tower is therefore against Damascus, because this Church, fortified by Christ’s help, always resists the devil and his members.

“Your head is like Carmel.” The head of the Church is therefore understood as the primacy of the minds of the faithful. For just as the other members are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. The head of the Church is aptly compared with Carmel. Carmel, which is also called Carmelus, is interpreted as “knowledge” or “the knowledge of circumcision.”

The head of the Church is therefore likened to Carmel because it knows that circumcision, once observed bodily, must now be observed spiritually, in accordance with what the Prophet says: “Be circumcised for the Lord in your hearts.” The Jews did not possess this understanding of circumcision, and therefore they are reproved by blessed Stephen, the first martyr, who says: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit.”

It is also read in the Book of Kings that Elijah ascended Mount Carmel and there, by praying, watered the dry earth with heavenly rains after a long drought of three and a half years. This narrative conveys a beautiful allegory. For Elijah, whose name is interpreted as “My God is the Lord,” signifies Christ. Although he is God and Lord of all and of the whole creation, he is specially his own—that is, the proper God and Lord of the Church.

He ascends Carmel when, by his grace, he ascends into the minds of his faithful and through them grants the rains of his gifts to the parched world. Therefore, as has been said, the head of the Church is rightly compared with Mount Carmel, because the mind of the saints is exalted by its way of life and provides Christ with an ascent into itself through the progress of virtues.

“And the hair of your head is like royal purple bound in channels.” If the head of the Church is understood as the mind, then by the hair of the head we must understand the thoughts of the mind, which continually proceed from it. The purple color, which resembles blood, signifies the mystery of the Lord’s passion.

According to the literal sense, what he says—“royal purple bound in channels”—signifies wool already treated with purple dye, but not yet drawn out into threads; it is still in the channels that the Greeks call *batia* (βάτια), in which the blood of shellfish ordinarily flows and turns the wool purple.

Mystically, these channels signify the humility of the saints, in which the purple of the eternal King is dyed when the saints, imitating the humility of their Redeemer, strive to become conformed to his sufferings, so that they may be transformed into the dignity of purple—that is, by laboring for Christ, may deserve to reign with Christ. This purple is said to be bound because the inmost hearts of the saints are fixed and established in fear and love of their Redeemer, and can never be separated from his charity.

“How beautiful and how lovely you are, most beloved, in delights.” How beautiful you are, namely in faith, and lovely in action, most beloved in delights. Above it was said of the Church: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle order.” Here, however, it says: “Beautiful and lovely, most beloved in delights,” which seem almost contradictory. To be ordered like an army drawn up in battle array and to be in delights appear incompatible, because delights usually enervate the strength of soldiers.

But the holy Church does both. She is ordered like an army drawn up in battle array because she resists unbelieving heretics and terrifies wicked spirits by her holiness and perfection. She is also in delights because she continually tastes the sweetness of heavenly delight on the palate of her mind, and amid the pressures of this age desires to attain them and to be continually satisfied with them. Hence she who is such is rightly called most beloved by her bridegroom Christ.

“Your stature is like a palm tree.” The stature of the Church is her perfect uprightness. For she is not bent toward vices but remains upright and immovable. Thus the Psalmist spoke in the voice of those who await: “I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly.” And the prophet, speaking under the figure of Jerusalem to the sinful soul concerning wicked spirits, says: “For they have humbled you and said to your soul, ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over you.’”

But the holy Church stands upright and never consents to be bent, hearing the Apostle say: “Watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully and be strengthened, and let all your affairs be done in charity.” And the Lord says to the children of Israel: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the prison of the Egyptians, so that you might walk upright.”

The stature of the Church is therefore likened to a palm tree, which in everything it does always keeps the heavenly reward in mind. For the palm adorns the victorious hand, and therefore signifies that prize which is to be given in heaven to the victorious saints.

“And your breasts are like clusters of grapes.” The breasts of the Church, as was said above, are the holy teachers, who nourish those regenerated in Christ with the milk of simple doctrine. But these breasts become like clusters of grapes when the same teachers proclaim more perfect things to the perfect, just as the Apostle, speaking to the simpler, said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food.” Behold, breasts full of milk.

These breasts were changed into clusters of grapes when he said: “We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, and we speak wisdom among the perfect.”

“I said, ‘I will ascend into the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruits.’” To show that all this excellence and greatness of the Church’s gifts comes from God’s grace, the same bridegroom is introduced as saying: “I will ascend into the palm tree.” It is as though he were saying: You have breasts with which to nourish the little ones, and from them you have clusters of grapes with which to offer perfection as doctrine to those who are more perfect, because by my grace I have ascended into you and granted you this perfection.

“I will ascend,” he says, “into the palm tree.” The palm signifies the Church, or also the soul of any believer who remembers the Lord his God, who says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world.” She herself also strives to be victorious over every vice and iniquity.

It is appropriate that he is here said to have ascended into the palm tree, whereas above he is read to have descended into the garden. For the Church said: “My beloved descended into his garden.” The garden and the palm tree are the same thing, namely one and the same Church. But the Lord descends into her and ascends to her. He descends into her by sending her an abundance of his grace from heaven; he ascends to her by increasing his gifts within her and raising her through certain advances, as though through certain steps, to higher things.

It should also be known from the nature of the palm tree that below it is rough, while above it is exceedingly beautiful in the splendor of its leaves and the beauty of its fruits. So also the holy Church in the lower things—that is, in this world—endures the roughness of labors and sufferings for Christ; but in the higher things, that is, in heaven, she awaits the beauty and sweetness of rewards.

The palm tree may also express the tree of the Lord’s cross, upon which our Redeemer ascended for the redemption of the human race and on which he conquered the enemy of the human race. Therefore he says: “I said, ‘I will ascend into the palm tree,’” that is, I spoke through my prophets and promised that I would come to my passion and redeem my Church.

“I will take hold,” he says, “of its fruits,” that is, I will reward the fruits of good works and labors with which the Church toils; or, according to my understanding, in which the palm signifies the cross: “I will take hold of its fruits,” that is, when the triumph of the passion has been completed, I will come to the glory of the resurrection and grant spiritual gifts to my apostles.

“And your breasts will be like clusters of the vine.” This has already been explained above. The breasts of the Church are the teachers when they nourish the little ones with simple doctrine; but they become clusters of the vine when they announce exalted things to those who are more perfect.

For blessed Paul possessed breasts and clusters of grapes at one and the same time when, speaking of Christ, he said: “Whose fathers are, and from whom is Christ.” Behold the breasts, namely the simple preaching about Christ. But these breasts were changed into the sweetest and strongest wine when he added: “Who is God, blessed forever.”

“And the fragrance of your mouth is like apples. Your throat is like the finest wine.” The mouth and fragrance of the Church are her present preaching, which reaches those absent from her either by reputation or by writing. The throat, however, is the preacher’s very voice, which is heard in the present.

The fragrance of the Church’s mouth is therefore compared with the fragrance of apples, because the reputation of her preaching is full of sweetness and grace. Her throat is likened to the finest wine because the very voice of the preachers displayed great power in its hearers. The fact that the fragrance of apples belongs to what is new, while wine belongs to what is old, signifies that the Church’s preaching possesses all sweetness and grace both in its newness and in its perfection.

“Worthy for my beloved to drink, and to be chewed by his lips and teeth.” This is the voice of the Church. Hearing herself praised by the bridegroom, she responds joyfully: “Worthy for my beloved to drink.” As though she were saying: My bridegroom compared my throat with the finest wine, and that wine is worthy to be drunk by my beloved himself—that is, the evangelical preaching that he placed in my mouth ought to be proclaimed in the world through him and through no other.

For it was not fitting that the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven should be preached in the world through anyone other than the mediator between God and human beings.

“And,” he says, “to be chewed by his lips and teeth.” The lips and teeth of the bridegroom, as was said above, are the holy teachers. That finest wine must therefore be chewed by the lips and teeth of the bridegroom, because the evangelical preaching must be handled and expounded by the teachers.

Nor is it absurd that, although wine is drunk and not chewed, it is nevertheless here said to be savored by lips and teeth, since this expression belongs more properly to food than to drink. For the holy teachers chew spiritual wine when they diligently investigate the evangelical commandments, examine them through repeated meditation, and discuss them with one another.

“I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me.” “I am my beloved’s”—understand, I offer him the service of justice and devotion; to him, and to no other, I promise my faith and servitude. “And his turning is toward me,” so that he may protect me in the present amid the labors and hardships of this life and in the future lead me into the joys of heavenly life.

This may also be the voice of the Synagogue, spoken through the person of the holy fathers who desired the coming of Christ. As though it were saying: I know, he says, that he is always present to me by his spiritual presence, and therefore I desire to serve my beloved with complete devotion. But “his turning is toward me” because I desire that at last, as he promised, he may appear to me in my substance.

For above the bridegroom had said: “I will ascend into the palm tree,” that is, he had promised that he would come in the flesh and suffer for the human race. Therefore she joyfully said: “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me,” that is, I believe that he will come as a human being and be manifested to the world as a human being in my substance.

“Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us dwell in the villages.” This is the voice of the same Synagogue: “Come, my beloved,” that is, appear through the human being you have assumed. The same is expressed in the Psalmist’s words: “Stir up your power and come,” and in Isaiah’s: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come.”

“Let us go out into the field.” The field is this world. “Let us go out,” she says, “into the field,” that is, let us preach to the world.

“Let us dwell in the villages,” that is, let us announce your faith also to the pagans. No one is unaware that pagans are called from *villa*, because *pagos* in Greek means “village” in Latin. Hence they are called pagans because they are far from the city of God.

The voice may also be that of the Church: “Come, my beloved.” As though she were saying: You have already raised the human being you assumed to heaven through the mystery of the Ascension, but come, visiting me more often by the presence of your divine majesty.

“Let us go out into the field,” in the same sense as above: let us preach the faith of your incarnation to the world. “Let us dwell in the villages,” that is, let us announce your faith even to the pagans who do not know you; and let us not remain there merely in passing, but let us dwell there until we make them, from pagans, Catholics, and from strangers, your own people.

“Let us rise early to the vineyards.” Morning arose with the new grace, when, as the darkness of unbelief passed away, the Gospel began to be preached to the world.

“Let us see whether the vineyard has flowered.” That is, let us inspect the Church to see whether it has already received the first beginnings of faith.

“Whether the flowers are bringing forth fruit.” Let us also inspect whether the flowers are bringing forth fruit—that is, whether those who have already believed in Christ are capable of doing good. The Church sends forth flowers when the faithful first come to the faith. The flowers bring forth fruit when, through that faith and love, she already acts well, lest faith itself be idle or dead without works; for, as James says, “faith without works is dead.”

“Whether the pomegranate trees have blossomed.” Pomegranates, as was said above, have a red or blood-colored rind, and therefore signify the passion of the Lord or of his members. He therefore says: “Whether the pomegranate trees have blossomed,” that is, whether the saints who are already perfect in faith and action are also capable of imitating Christ’s passion and suffering for him.

Those pomegranate trees were the people to whom the Apostle said: “It has been granted to you not only to know, but also to suffer for him.”

“There I will give you my breasts.” The breasts of the Church are the teachers, who first instruct the faithful in the faith. “When we have gone out,” he says, “to the vineyards, there I will give you, O bridegroom, my breasts,” that is, I will beget children for you. Hence he adds:

“The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates.” The mandrake is an aromatic herb whose root resembles the human body. Its fruits have an excellent fragrance, resembling the *malum Matianum* [Matian apple], which our people call the “apple of the earth.”

**[Note: Matian apples were held in the highest esteem at Rome and were brought from a certain village situated in the Alps near Aquileia, as Athenaeus testifies in Book III, chapter 7. They are therefore mentioned more than once by ancient authors, as in Columella, Book V, chapters 10 and 19, and Macrobius, Book II, chapter 15, where he discusses the various kinds of apples and pears and indicates that they received their name from Gaius or Gnaeus Matius. Pliny, Book XV, chapter 14, says that Matius belonged to the equestrian order, was a friend of Augustus, and was exceedingly devoted to planting trees; see also Book XII, chapter 2. EDITOR.]**

This herb is especially suitable for medicinal purposes. For they say that those who suffer from the affliction of sleeplessness are relieved by drinking this fruit and are able to sleep. They also say that those who are about to undergo surgery, if they drink the outer rind of this fruit, do not feel cutting or cauterization.

**[Note: From this it is clear, as other writers also report, that already in the Middle Ages surgeons used to lull patients into insensibility with the soporific juices of plants when excising limbs or cauterizing wounds, so that they did not feel the pain. EDITOR.]**

If anyone wishes to investigate all these matters mystically, he will find there spiritual meanings suited to the Church. He therefore says: “The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates.”

The gates of the Church are the apostles and their successors, because no one enters the city of God—that is, the Church—unless he has been regenerated through the holy teachers by the water of baptism and instructed in life-giving doctrine. Concerning these gates the Psalmist said: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.”

The mandrakes signify the fragrance of virtues. The mandrakes therefore gave forth their fragrance at the gates of the Church when the apostles or their successors spread far and wide the reputation of the sweetest good name and the fragrance of virtues. Therefore she invites her bridegroom to come, because his name is already being announced far and wide through the apostles, and the fragrance of Christ’s preaching is being dispersed throughout the world.

“All new and old fruits, my beloved, I have kept for you.” That is, I have kept for you, my beloved, the commandments or promises of both the Old and the New Testament. For she knew that everything announced in the Old Testament could be fulfilled only through Christ and in Christ.

Therefore she said: “I have kept new and old fruits for you,” that is, I await you, so that through you the things foretold in the Old Testament may be fulfilled in the New Testament. Hence, while already hanging on the cross in his passion, when he had tasted vinegar, he said: “It is finished.” And after the resurrection he said to the apostles: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled.”

The new and old fruits may also be understood as the persons of the righteous who lived either in the Old or in the New Testament. The Church therefore says: “I have kept new and old fruits for you,” that is, I have kept for you the righteous who preceded in the Old Testament and those who followed in the New, so that through you they might receive the rewards of their labors. For none of the righteous was able to enter the kingdom of heaven except through Christ, because he was the first to ascend and opened heaven to his members who would follow.

## CHAPTER VIII

“Who will grant me that you might become my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother?” From these words it is understood that this entire song is divine and spiritual, and that it contains nothing that can be understood according to the literal sense. For what lover ever desired that the one whom she loves should become a little child, become her brother, and, transformed into an infant, suck the breasts of her mother?

It is therefore the voice of that Church which preceded Christ’s coming, whom we call the Synagogue—that is, the assembly.

“Who,” she says, “will grant me that you might become my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother?” The meaning is: You who are now in the bosom of the Father, who will grant that you might become human and, being made a participant and sharer in my nature, be called my brother?

For he himself deigned to call the apostles his brothers, saying through the Psalmist: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.” And after the resurrection he said to the women: “Go and announce to my brothers.”

“Nursing at the breasts of my mother,” she says—that is, fulfilling everything proper to human nature except sin. For in this passage the mother of the Synagogue is understood as human nature itself, from which the Synagogue arose.

“Nursing at the breasts of my mother,” she says, that is, enduring everything appropriate to human frailty.

“So that I might find you outside.” This means: so that I might see you openly after you have become human. He was, as it were, within, since he was already hidden in the bosom of the Father’s majesty; but he was found outside when, having become human, he presented himself to human beings in a lowly condition and wished the incomprehensible to become comprehensible.

“And kiss you.” “And kiss you,” she says—that is, let me behold you in a manifest vision, you whom I now possess only in the kiss of faith, which she desired at the beginning of this song when she said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” that is, let him now come through himself and appear to me.

For the beloved used to kiss the Church through the prophets when he promised his coming through them. She therefore desires that, coming through himself, he might kiss her—that is, that he might display his presence in his flesh.

“And then no one would despise me.” Before Christ came, the Synagogue was, as it were, despised, because, being devoted to legal observances, it proclaimed Christ’s coming under type and figure, and not in truth. But after Jesus appeared and illuminated the world by the grace of his coming, no one despised her any longer. Rather, she became terrible to her enemies like an army drawn up in battle array, because she preached Christ throughout the world and subjected worldly power to herself.

Nor should it seem strange if we now call the Church the Synagogue. For there is one Church in the fathers who preceded and in those who followed.

“I will take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother.” O beloved, by clinging to you through faith and charity, I will lead you into the house of my mother. The mother of the Church is understood here as the heavenly Jerusalem, of which Paul says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.”

“I will lead you,” she says, “into the house of my mother,” that is, I will accompany you as you return to heaven after the accomplishment of your incarnation and the mystery of your passion. “I will lead you” means “I will escort and accompany you,” because the apostles escorted the Lord ascending into heaven with their eyes and followed him with devoted attention until the cloud received him, until the attending angels said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

“There you will teach me.” This refers back to what was said above: “I will find you outside.” “When,” she says, “I find you outside—that is, when I behold you in the flesh you have assumed—there you will teach me, because you will answer everything I wish to ask.”

For the Lord often anticipated the apostles even when they wished to ask questions, and instructed them.

This may also be joined to the passage where she says: “I will lead you into the house of my mother; there you will teach me.” “When,” she says, “you have been received into heaven and have taken me with you into heaven, there you will teach me and lead me into all truth,” something that it is impossible for a human being to attain in the present life. Hence the Lord promises the apostles, saying: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly.”

Therefore, “there you will teach me” means: you will reveal yourself and the Father to me in an open vision; that is, you will show me your divinity face to face.

“And I will give you a cup of spiced wine.” By wine, the ardor of charity and love is understood. “I will give you,” she says, “wine,” that is, I will show how ardently I love you. This wine will not be plain, but spiced—that is, adorned with good works and virtues.

For the love of God, as blessed Gregory says, is never idle: if it exists, it accomplishes great things. If it refuses to act, it is not love. Spiced wine is therefore love joined with action. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.” The proof of love is the display of a deed.

“And the juice of my pomegranates.” A pomegranate is the same as a Punic apple. It is called a pomegranate because it is full of a multitude of seeds. It is called a Punic apple because it abounds especially in Africa; for Punic means African.

Its rind is blood-colored, and therefore, as has often been said, it represents the Lord’s passion. The juice of the pomegranates is therefore the love of the holy martyrs, who loved God so greatly that they did not hesitate to die for him.

It is rightly called juice, rather than some other kind of drink, because juice is exceedingly fervent, so that in its great heat it boils out and purifies every impurity from itself. The Church will therefore give her beloved the juice of her pomegranates—that is, in the sufferings of the holy martyrs she will show with what great love Christ is loved.

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”

By the left hand, as blessed Gregory says, all the prosperous circumstances of the present life are understood; by the right hand, the blessed future life in heaven. The Church therefore has the Bridegroom’s left hand beneath her head, and his right hand embraces her, because she counts as nothing whatever prosperity in the present age may flatter her with, despises all things that smile upon her temporarily, and, while striving toward the vision of heavenly blessedness alone, desires to be embraced by that alone.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not arouse or awaken the beloved one until she herself wishes it.”

The Church contains certain people who have been reborn through Christ’s baptism and marked with the title of Christianity, yet in their morals and manner of life serve the world. They strive to disturb the Church, lulled into the gentlest rest, and to rouse her to endure worldly upheavals. Because of the grace of Christ’s mysteries that they have received, these people are here called “daughters of Jerusalem,” although in their conduct they act contrary to them. The Bridegroom therefore adjures them not to arouse or awaken the beloved one—that is, not to disturb her while she lies in the sleep of the sweetest repose, namely, in contemplation of her Creator, nor by their restlessness compel her to awaken to the anxieties and cares of the world. “Until she herself wishes it”: that is, until, when the duty of her appointed service has been completed—the service by which she ministers to God in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs—she is again reminded by concern for bodily frailty to return to the use of the world.

“Who is this who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights, leaning upon my beloved?”

This is the voice of the Synagogue, wondering at the Church gathered from the nations. “Who is this,” it says—that is, what sort of person is she, and of what merit—“who comes up from the desert?” She had been abandoned by God through idolatry and ignorance of the truth. She therefore ascended by the steps of the virtues from the desert, that is, from the error of unbelief in which she had for a time been abandoned. “Overflowing with delights,” that is, abounding in virtues. “Leaning,” it says, “upon my beloved”: that is, acting confidently in Christ and referring all her virtues and every good thing to his grace. She knew that she could accomplish nothing good by her own strength, and therefore said with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

It should also be noted that it says, “upon my beloved.” For the Synagogue thought that it alone possessed knowledge of God, while the other nations were left in ignorance. “For God is known,” as the Psalmist says, “in Judea; his name is great in Israel.” But the Bridegroom and beloved of that very Synagogue answers her in her wonder with what follows.

“Under the apple tree I awakened you.”

We should understand the apple tree as the Lord’s cross. The Synagogue was awakened beneath that tree, because by Christ’s cross it was redeemed from the transgression of original sin and from the power of the devil; there she was awakened, having been dead in sins. And rightly does he call it the apple tree. For, as was said above, he compared Christ to this tree when he said: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.”

“There your mother was corrupted; there your mother was violated.”

By the mother and parent of the Synagogue he means the father who was greatest and most prominent among the Jewish people, such as the scribes and Pharisees who handed Christ over to Pilate. They ought, like a mother and parent, to have governed and instructed the rest of the people. Such also were those who, at the urging of those leaders, shouted shamelessly: “Crucify him, crucify him.” This mother of the Synagogue was therefore corrupted and violated beneath the apple tree when she bound herself and her descendants by a cruel curse, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” For these people too were beneath Christ’s cross, not indeed in faith and devotion, but through an imprecation of cruel vengeance upon themselves and their descendants.

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.”

“Because,” he says, “I awakened you beneath the apple tree”—that is, because by my passion on the cross I redeemed you—“set me as a seal upon your heart”: keep me always in memory and do not forget how much I endured for your salvation. “Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart through faith; set me as a seal upon your heart through worthy action.” For when we wish to retain something in our memory, we commonly place a mark upon a finger or arm, so that, reminded by it, we may remember the matter for which we are concerned. We too ought to place Christ as a seal upon our heart and arm, so that we may always remember him and, believing rightly in him, adorn that faith with good works.

If we do this, he too will take us as a seal and remember us, in accordance with what he promises Zerubbabel, ruler of Judea: “And I will set you as a seal in my presence.” But if we forget his benefits and do not return worthy thanks to him, he too will forget us, as is said of the wicked king Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim: “If he were a signet ring on my right hand, I would tear him away from there.”

“For love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as the underworld.”

The love of Christ is strong as death. Just as death separates the soul from the body, and a person is then permitted neither to desire anything nor to pursue anything in the present life, so the love of Christ, when it has truly penetrated someone, makes that person wholly dead to this age and, as it were, insensible to it. Living only for Christ, he is dead to the world.

The same meaning applies when he says: “Jealousy is hard as the underworld.” Just as the underworld never restores those whom it has once received, but always retains them, so true love of Christ never releases the one whom it has once taken hold of. Hence the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?”

Yet in this passage “the love of Christ” may also be understood as the love by which he loved us, which was strong as death because he loved us so greatly that, though immortal, he accepted death for us. His jealousy was hard as the underworld because the underworld does not know how to show mercy or to moderate the punishments of the wretched; likewise, Christ’s love could not cease from mercy or be removed from its love of the human race by any wickedness of persecutors.

Some refer the statement “Jealousy is hard as the underworld” specifically to the Synagogue, which was jealous of the nations and begrudged them salvation. By saying this, Christ therefore warns it to cease from envy and to rejoice with the Church in its salvation.

“Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame.”

That is, the lamps of love are lamps of fire and flame. The lamps of love are the inmost hearts of the saints, in which love dwells as in vessels. These lamps are lamps of fire because they burn in the heart through love; they are lamps of flame because they shine outwardly through action.

“Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.”

The waters and rivers are the violent threats of persecutors, or even their flatteries, by which they strive to separate the saints from the love of God. Concerning these the Lord says in the Gospel, speaking of the man who built his house upon a rock: “The rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon a rock.”

“Many waters therefore cannot extinguish love,” because no tribulation and no distress will be able to separate the saints from the love of God.

“If a man were to give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as nothing.”

This verse requires no exposition. No substance of the world and no wealth amounts to anything in comparison with love. We read that the saints abandoned their possessions for the love of Christ; yet, in comparison with Christ’s love, whom they loved, they seemed to themselves to be giving up nothing. Thus, when the Apostle abandoned not only earthly possessions but also his ancestral traditions for Christ, he said: “I consider all these things worthless, and regard them as refuse, that I may gain Christ”—that is, that I may acquire his love.

“Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?”

This is the voice of the beloved addressing the Synagogue concerning the Church of the nations. “Our sister,” he says—that is, the Church of the nations—“is little, and she has no breasts.” With great condescension, sharing the name with the Synagogue, he says, “Our sister.” Because he assumed flesh from the Jews, he therefore accommodates and likens himself to the Synagogue.

“Our sister is little.” Just as a person’s age is described, so the age of the Church is described. The Church, still being gathered from the nations, was little in the time of the Lord and the apostles, because it was small in the number of believers; and it did not yet have breasts, that is, it was not yet able through preaching to give birth to spiritual children for God.

He therefore speaks as though asking the Synagogue’s advice: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” God’s address to the Church occurs when, either through hidden inspiration within or through open preaching without, he admonishes the soul of each believer. The meaning is: When through my apostles I address the Church gathered from the nations, what shall we do? How shall we entrust heavenly commands to her? Shall we entrust to her the smallest commands, or, so that she may become greater, shall we hand over to her the more perfect mysteries of heavenly secrets?

For almighty God adjusts the word of preaching according to the measure and capacity of the human mind, considering the strength and capacity of the hearer. But while the Synagogue remains silent, the Bridegroom himself answers on its behalf:

“If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her; if she is a door, let us join it with cedar panels.”

“If,” he says, “our sister is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her.” It is as though he said: When my apostles begin to preach to the Church gathered from the nations, if there are hearers of such perfection that they may deservedly be called a wall—whether because they are endowed with natural ability or excel in philosophical learning, so that, like a wall, they can defend and fortify others—let us build silver battlements upon such a wall, that is, let us add to them the utterances of the divine Scriptures. For, as the Psalmist says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested in the fire.”

But if there are hearers who cannot resist enemies or repel the weapons coming against them, but are a door because, announcing simple things, they can bring some people into the Church and to the faith—such as priests of a lower rank, who introduce people into the Church by baptizing them and initiating them into the divine mysteries—then let us join that door with cedar panels. That is, let us set before them the examples of the fathers who, like cedars—namely, imperishable wood—possess unfading works and, like panels, are spread broad in knowledge and charity.

For the breadth of the panels signifies breadth of heart or knowledge, as the Psalmist says: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.” With these cedar panels—that is, with the examples of the saints—let us join that door, so that their examples, worthy of imitation, may open to others, like a door, the entrance into the Church.

“I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.”

This is the voice of the Church. When she heard her beloved consulting for her salvation, she joyfully replied: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.” “I am,” she says, “a wall; I am founded upon a firm rock and strengthened by the bond of divine love.”

Or I am a wall because I have been built from living and chosen stones—that is, from the saints—“and my breasts are like a tower,” because I contain within me people who can nourish others with spiritual teaching in the place of breasts, and can defend and fortify others in the place of a tower. Just as towers rise above the other parts of a wall, so these members of mine surpass the rest in merit of doctrine and conduct.

I possess this, however, not through my own merits or through the freedom of my will, but through the gift and grace of my Bridegroom.

“From the time I became in his presence as one who has found peace.”

That is, from the time when he poured out his blood for me and, making God the Father propitious toward me, dissolved the enmity that existed between God and humanity and made heavenly things peaceful for me. From the time when I found this peace, I have deserved to be a wall and breasts in the place of towers.

“A vineyard belonged to the peaceful one,” that is, to my beloved, who is truly the peacemaker, because through him all things in heaven and on earth have been made peaceful. Hence he is also called by the Prophet “Father of the future age” and “Prince of peace.” In the type of this true peacemaker, Solomon, the peaceful one and author of this song, came before him.

This vineyard therefore belonged to him, namely, the holy Church.

“In her that has peoples.”

He says this to show that he is singing of the Church of the nations, not of the Synagogue. The Synagogue belonged to one nation alone. The Church, however, has peoples, because she receives and contains all nations within her exceedingly capacious womb.

“He entrusted it to keepers.”

The keepers of this vineyard—that is, of the holy Church—are the prophets, the apostles, and the successors of the apostles. Or the keepers of this age are the angelic powers, which guard the Church from the attacks of temptations and demons.

“A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.”

By “men” he means the strong and perfect, for “man” derives from virtue. The fruit of the Church is the reward of heavenly life, for which the holy Church does not cease laboring in the present. The thousand silver pieces that the man brings for its fruit signify everything that can be possessed in this world. The number one thousand signifies complete perfection and fullness.

The man therefore brings a thousand silver pieces for the fruit of this vineyard because the saints abandon everything of their own and distribute it to the poor in order to obtain the fruit of this vineyard—that is, the heavenly reward. It is like what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.”

“My vineyard is before me.”

This is the voice of the Bridegroom. “You say,” he says, “that I entrusted my vineyard to keepers; yet the vineyard is always before me. Although I have committed it to my keepers, I nevertheless always care for it, nor do I cease to be concerned for it; I am with it until the end of the age.”

“Your thousand, O peaceful one, and two hundred for those who keep its fruit.”

“Your thousand”—with “silver pieces” understood—those that you gave for the fruit of the vineyard, are secure for you, O peaceful one. It is as though he said: O faithful soul, do not doubt the eternal reward for which you gave up everything, because the thousand silver pieces are secure for you. That is, that certain reward remains for you, and you will obtain its true fruit.

“And two hundred”—with “silver pieces” understood—“are for those who keep my fruits.” Just as the number one thousand signifies the fullness of perfection, so the number one hundred signifies the highest perfection, because one hundred is transferred from the left to the right. The two hundred silver pieces, therefore, which are a doubled hundred, signify those who are perfect in doctrine and holy action, who by living justly and piously guard themselves and also convert others through preaching.

For such people the two hundred silver pieces are peaceful, because a doubled reward remains for them in heaven. Of such people Daniel says: “Those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like stars for endless ages.” The Apostle commands that such people be honored doubly, saying: “Let the presbyters among us be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who preside over you and labor in the word.”

“You who dwell in the gardens, the friends listen; make me hear your voice.”

This is the voice of the beloved addressing the bride: O Church, “you who dwell in the gardens,” that is, who devote yourself to cultivating the shoots of the virtues. The garden is the Church herself, which, as was said above, he repeatedly promises to visit. The Church therefore dwells in gardens because she continually nourishes plantings of the virtues; she does not set up a temporary hut there, intending to withdraw after a short stay, but dwells there in a fixed station.

“Make me,” he says, “hear your voice”: preach the Gospel to those whom you can; proclaim both the commandments of my law and the promise of heavenly rewards. For this is pleasing and delightful to me, that I may hear your voice—that is, that I may hear you proclaiming words of eternal salvation.

“But the friends listen,” that is, the angelic spirits delight in hearing your voice. I made them your friends by the outpouring of my blood, and appointed them as helpers and protectors against evil spirits. Or “friends” means the spirits of the righteous whom I have taken from your company to myself in heaven. They rejoice in your preaching and in the salvation of your brothers.

Immediately the bride herself answers her beloved:

“Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.”

A remarkable answer. She is invited to preach, and the Bridegroom wishes to hear her voice, yet she urges her Bridegroom to flee. But the sequence of the mystery is profound. For Christ’s birth had been foretold above, when he said: “Who would give you to me as my brother, nursing at the breasts?” His passion had also been foretold, where it was said: “Under the apple tree I awakened you.” Now, consequently, she urges the Bridegroom to flee—that is, to return most swiftly to the Father through his ascension.

The meaning is: You command me to preach? Do you wish to hear my voice? Flee, my beloved—that is, having fulfilled the mystery of your incarnation and passion, return to heaven, so that I may begin to contemplate you not as a human being but as God above all things. Then you will hear my voice, because then I shall preach you more freely to the whole world.

This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “I tell you the truth: it is advantageous for you that I go away.” It was advantageous for the apostles and for the whole Church that Christ return and withdraw his bodily presence. While he was bodily present, they could not love him otherwise in spirit; they could not contemplate as the invisible and omnipresent God the one whom they saw as a human being. But after he ascended into heaven, the Church began to love him spiritually, and thus to contemplate and preach him as God.

This is what the Apostle says: “And although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way.” Therefore, my beloved, if you wish me to preach you in this manner, flee—that is, withdraw—to heavenly things. You who were comprehensible through your humanity, become incomprehensible through your divinity. Nevertheless, do not abandon me in the present without your visitation; deign to seek me through your frequent visitation and to make yourself visible to me more often.

This is what she says: “Be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” Just as gazelles and young stags, untamed animals, avoid human company and yet are frequently seen in the mountains, so you too, after your ascension, though invisible, deign nevertheless to appear to me more often through the gift of your grace—and this upon the mountains of spices.

The mountains of spices are the saints of God: they are close to heaven through the excellence of their holy conduct and spread far and wide the fragrance of their virtues and reputation. Hence the Apostle says of himself and those like him: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” And elsewhere: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place.”

# Exposition of Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, on the Epistles of Saint Paul

*(According to the editio princeps, published at Strasbourg in 1519.*

*[Note: The title reads as follows: “The Very Learned Haymo the Saxon, Bishop of Halberstadt, on the Epistles of Saint Paul: both a brief and a very clear Exposition, recently printed for the first time at Strasbourg with tin type.” It is followed by a quatrain by M. Hieronymus Gebwiler addressed to the reader:*

*Whoever desires to understand thoroughly the mystical doctrines of the divine Paul,*

*Let him purchase and read this book.*

*Here the obscure meanings and every riddle,*

*Now resolved, appear in a clearer light.*

*At the end of the book: “Printed at Strasbourg by Renatus Bect, citizen of Strasbourg, in the year 1519.” On the front of the work there is a note written in a later hand: “A rare work, according to Th. Bartholinus, On Biblical Diseases, chapter 24, p. 84; Th. Honertus, in the Prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans, p. 21; and Daniel Gerdesius, in Florilegium of Rare Books, p. 161 and following pages.” This edition is especially noteworthy because of the letter of Ottomar Luscinius, doctor of pontifical law, in which he replies to the editor Sixtus Hermann’s dedicatory letter and offers a living testimony to Christian truth.)*

## Ottomar Luscinius, Doctor of Pontifical Law, to Sixtus Hermann, Parish Priest of Saint Thomas in Strasbourg, greetings

If we advanced by our wishes, and if each person were promoted above all to whatever he most desired, could anything else be seen to take precedence in the desires of mortals, Sixtus—distinguished in letters and integrity—over what you repeatedly propose, repeat, and impress upon the Christian people as their single aim: namely, an abundance of every good and a certain complete happiness?

This is precisely what the various schools of philosophers have long sought, although somewhat less earnestly; that is, what no one at all fails to desire with the greatest intensity, what everyone wishes to possess as immediately as possible. Yet the outcome is far different from what we imagine. The way to this supreme goal is difficult; it is offered freely and without merit to no one, since God has appointed even sweat for virtue, though some pagan may also attain it.

We therefore cannot climb to that highest place unless we hold fast to the one who is himself supreme. He is the one who openly promises that he will assist those striving toward the heights, so that we may know which way must be taken. He is the one who showed himself to be the truth, lest through some error we turn aside from the straight path by wandering. Finally, he is the one who offered himself as life, lest we be uncertain toward what we should strive.

We must therefore follow the trustworthy guarantor—and indeed Truth itself—to whom alone everything is joined. Yet I hesitate above all to ask whether a living image, so closely resembling this blessedness, breathes anywhere more strongly than in the sacred writings, which were conceived by the Spirit of God and are truly animated by him, in which God continually addresses, teaches, and consoles us.

For, unless I am mistaken, it was long ago proclaimed even by Aristotelian decrees that a person is such as his own words and deeds reveal him to be. And unless we were permitted to learn from the sacred books what our Savior Christ—the herald of supreme happiness, or rather happiness itself in its perfection—did and what doctrines he established for posterity, may I perish if we would not long ago have fallen into a chaos of error.

Yet even then the danger of falling would not altogether be absent, when one sees the common people—both those entirely without learning and even those who boast of the empty title of teacher—scattering, astonishingly, such a quantity of weeds among Christ’s seed. I am mistaken if you do not find a thousand superstitions, a thousand impostures, and just as many delirious fantasies of old women that have gradually crept into the Christian religion, for no other reason than that we either do not approach those divine writings at all, or approach them more coldly and with less diligence, zeal, and care than was fitting.

In our age all things everywhere teem with an inexhaustible mire of questions. Factions of sophistical subtleties have burst forth in so immense and varied an examination that even those endowed with the greatest intellect seem satisfied if, after countless labors, they are at last, and often only late in life, able to claim for themselves the name of Thomist, Scotist, or Ockhamist.

Meanwhile, who is there who meditates day and night upon the law of the Lord? Yet nothing else can be said to lead more directly to the attainment of blessedness or more efficiently to the discovery of true wisdom.

With excellent reason, therefore, unless we wish to linger longer over our miseries, we are compelled, dearest Sixtus, at last to come to our senses and, abandoning streams that are not very pure—or rather, turbid in every respect—to approach as nearly as possible the purity of the spring. I mean those ancient, grave, and solid writers who have drawn out for us, from the hidden inner chambers of Scripture, the profound meanings of eternal wisdom through an open channel.

Would that everyone were devoted to them with equal zeal! You would see them agreeing with Christ not so much in name as in desire, word, and deed. For, in a certain way, disciplines of this sort are bound together with one another, so that through their contagion they have considerable effect upon morals.

In any case, while we examine all the teachers, as the saying goes, of this sort, through your efforts you have conveniently supplied us with Haymo, who weighs the words of the Apostle Paul—or, if you prefer to say so with Saint Jerome, his thunder—with such diligence, considers them on such a scale, and opens them with such ease that, even if he seems to have fallen short in some respects—for who is there who does not falter somewhere in so immense a task?—you could never say that he lacked diligence and the utmost care.

Let our Haymo therefore come into the light under your auspices, and, together with the other teachers of antiquity, be reborn in this age. Let the still-sharp thorns of sophistry withdraw; let the never-ending battles over words remain with their defenders, since every quarrel, insofar as it is farther from charity, will assuredly be that much farther from Christ.

Let ancient studies flourish again together with morals. Let whatever cannot make its teachers pious and holy be regarded as profane. We shall frequently taste this heavenly nourishment, suited to invigorating souls, and, like clean animals, chew it again, so that, with God as author, whoever lives with us may judge us true theologians by our way of life. We shall leave to those who glory only in a shadow their empty titles, like the masked kings of tragedies.

Farewell, excellent Sixtus, and love your Ottomar—as you do. Strasbourg, on the Kalends of December, in the year 1518 from the restoration of salvation.

## Sixtus Hermann, Master of Arts, to the Most Learned Ottomar Luscinius, Doctor of Pontifical Law, greetings

I carefully read, not without the greatest refreshment of spirit, the letter that you, distinguished doctor, sent me concerning the praise of Haymo, that most faithful expositor of the Pauline Epistles. You have learnedly and eruditely proposed a path—and indeed a shortened one—for those seeking to enter the inner chambers of Christian theology, rightly censuring those who, after setting aside the more ancient doctors of the Church, take excessive pleasure in quibbling questions, over which they fight among themselves with a Stentorian voice, as they say, almost into decrepit old age.

I do not deny that scholastic theology is necessary in the great schools of letters as an exercise for the intellect. But I judge it deserving of condemnation by anyone possessing a nose—that is, any sound judgment—to have devoted the entire course of one’s life to that same quarrel while despising the classical and ancestral writers of sacred literature.

As you know, both excess and deficiency must be avoided in every action. For this reason, I do not think that the more recent theosophers who labor over questions should be entirely eliminated and, as it were, thrown from the bridge. But anyone would judge it more foolish than folly itself to stretch every sinew of the intellect to the utmost in that direction alone, while passing over the ancient doctors.

Therefore, in this theological study we must take care that nothing is done to excess and nothing omitted. Let our Haymo therefore come into the light, adorned by your most auspicious letter, and we have no doubt that, with you as his patron, he will be safe from every biting attack of envy.

Moreover, proceed, excellent man, by your more refined studies and polished learning to make good and learned men immortal, and fix me, as they say, with a massive nail in the reckoning of your friends; in return, you will always find me entirely ready to serve your wishes.

Farewell. Strasbourg, on the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord 1519.

# Exposition on the Epistles of Saint Paul (G)*

## On the Epistle to the Romans

### Argument

The Apostle Paul wrote this Epistle to the Romans from Corinth, the metropolitan city of the region of Achaia. They had not first been instructed by Paul himself, nor by Peter, nor by any one of the twelve apostles, but by certain Jewish believers who came from Jerusalem to Rome, where the ruler of the world resided and to whom they themselves were subject. They evangelized the Romans with the faith they had learned at Jerusalem.

The reason for writing this Epistle is shown to have been the following. A dispute arose between Jewish believers and Gentiles who were likewise coming to the faith. The Jewish believers, because of the holy fathers from whom they derived their origin and because of the law, which they alone among all the nations had received, despised the Gentiles who were coming to the faith, since they had until then been devoted to the superstition of idolatry. They said that, because of their observance of the law to which they had been subject, they had deserved the grace of Christ and faith in the Gospel.

The Gentiles, on the other hand, preferred themselves no less to the Jews, reproaching them for the death of the Son of God. At the same time they protested that they would not have rendered obedient veneration to idols if they had possessed the commandments of the law or the oracles of the prophets.

The Apostle Paul therefore placed himself between all these parties, destroying all their disputes, which are related in the prologue of this Epistle. Like a good preacher addressing them with outstretched hand, he brought them all to one harmony, showing that none of them had been saved by his own merits but through the grace of Jesus Christ, because both Jews and Gentiles were held under sin.

### Prologue
The Epistle, a Greek term, is called in Latin *supermissa* or “sent over” [Col. 0362D], just as *epigramma* means “superscription,” and *epitaphium*, something placed over a tomb. For *epi* indeed means “over,” while *stola* means “sent.” These Epistles are called “sent over” or “added” because they were sent by the apostle to believers after the Old Testament and the grace of the Gospel, in which perfect salvation consists, in order to cut away present and emerging vices; and so that if anyone should transgress the Gospel, he might find in it the medicine of salvation, insofar as forgiveness is granted to him through worthy repentance, enabling him to escape the vengeance of the Gospel. They are “sent over” not because of their dignity, as though they surpassed the others, but because they were written afterward for their completion.

This Epistle does not occupy in the body of the Epistles the order in which it was written, but because of the dignity of the Romans, who at that time ruled all nations, it obtained the first place. This, however, was done not by the Apostle, but rather by the person who took care to gather all his Epistles into a single body [Col. 0363B].

It should be noted that, just as Moses the lawgiver gave the ten commandments of the law to the Israelite people after they had been liberated from Pharaoh (Exod. XXIX), so the apostle Paul wrote ten Epistles to those who believed in Christ and had been delivered from the spiritual Pharaoh. For he sent the remaining four to disciples: two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon.

*Paul.* As Jerome says, Paul adopted this name from the first spoil that he brought to the holy Church, namely Sergius Paulus the proconsul, whom he converted in Cyprus (Acts XIII). Thus, just as any Roman commander was called Parthicus after conquering the Parthians, or Germanicus after conquering Germany, so he was called Paul after the ruler whom he first conquered.

Blessed Augustine, however, says that *Paul* is interpreted as “small,” that is, “humble.” Hence he himself says: “I am the least of all the apostles” (I Cor. XV). According to some, he is also called *apotyspaulys* [ἀπὸ τῆς παῦλης], that is, “from the cessation of persecution.” Or certainly, as some say, he is understood to have had two names, as many people are found bearing two names: for example, Uzziah, who is also called Azariah, in the Old Testament; and Matthew, who is also called Levi, in the New. Thus in the Acts of the Apostles we read: “Saul, who is also Paul, grew strong and confounded the Jews.”

Or again, following the custom of the saints, he received a share in the name, as Abraham and Jacob did, and Simon, who was called Peter by the Lord. Thus the man who had been called Saul, that is, “infernal,” because he was a persecutor, afterward became Paul, that is, the humble disciple of Christ [Col. 0363D].

*Apostle.* In Greek, *apostle* is rendered in Latin as “sent.” And this man heard from the Lord: “I will send you far away to the Gentiles” (Acts XXII).

There are four kinds of apostles. The first is that which comes neither from human beings nor through a human being, but from God alone. Moses, Isaiah, and very many other prophets belonged to this number, as did the twelve apostles. Although they were sent by the man Christ, he was nevertheless both man and true God. Thus Moses was told: “I will send you to Pharaoh” (Exod. III). Isaiah was likewise asked: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And he replied: “Here am I; send me.” The Lord then said: “Go to this people” (Isa. VI).

The second kind is from God, but through a human being. Joshua belonged to this number: at God’s command and according to his will, he was sent through Moses [Col. 0364A]. Many others likewise were chosen by the choice of the people, on account of the merits of their lives, with God’s approval. For the will of the people is often the will of God.

The third is from a human being alone and not from God, when someone is chosen through human favor, not for a good way of life or on account of religion, but because of noble family connections; or when someone is appointed to priestly dignity for money. To this number, blessed Bishop Ambrose says to one man: “If you had not given a hundred solidi, you would not be a bishop today.” To this number also belonged those of whom it is said in the Book of Kings (I Reg. XII), who in the days of Jeroboam filled their hands and became priests of idols. Of such men the Lord says through the prophet: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. VIII).

The fourth kind of apostles is that which comes neither from God nor through a human being, but exists from the person himself alone. Such are false prophets and false apostles, who say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them.

It should be known, however, that among all these there are some of such great dignity that they are raised to the honor both of apostle and of prophecy. Such was Moses, Isaiah, and John the Baptist, of whom it is said: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Mark I). Among them were also the apostles who foretold to their hearers the rewards of the elect and the punishments of the reprobate, distinguished by a certain honor of prophecy.

*To the Romans.* The Apostle here calls “Romans” those believers from Jews and Gentiles who lived in the regions of Italy. “Romans” is interpreted as “exalted” or “thunderers,” because at the time when the Apostle sent this Epistle to them, they ruled all nations. Therefore they were more exalted than all peoples, and they thundered forth public and private commands; their reputation resounded in the mouths of all people.

## CHAPTER ONE

*Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ.*

The name “Apostle” has already been discussed above. But one must ask: since the Lord says, “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John XV), why does the Apostle call himself a servant?

The answer is that there are two kinds of servitude: one of fear and the other of love. Servitude of fear is that by which a servant fears his master, fearing that he will be scourged by him if he does not obey his will in everything. There is also the servitude of love and sonship, by which a good son serves his father, fearing to offend him. It is in this latter kind of servitude that the Apostle calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ.

The Lord himself speaks of this when he says: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke XVII). This means not a servant of fear and punishment, but a servant of love and sonship, who, after the manner of a son, does not wish to offend Christ Jesus.

This name was given to the humanity by the angel, who said to Mary: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Luke I; Isa. VII; Matt. I). For *Jesus* is interpreted in Latin as “savior” or “salutary.” Explaining the etymology of this name, the angel said: “For he will save his people from their sins.”

If you seek the name of his divinity, he is called the Word of the Father. *Christ*, in Greek, is rendered in Latin as “anointed,” and in Hebrew as *Messiah*. For he was anointed not with visible oil, but with invisible oil, namely, with the fullness of the Holy Spirit. Concerning this anointing the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Ps. XLIV).

In former times this name was also an adjective applied to priests, kings, and prophets, but it became proper to Jesus.

*Called an apostle.* There is a general calling, of which it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). There is also a special calling, concerning which the Apostle says elsewhere: “Those whom he called, he also justified” [Col. 0365B] (Rom. VIII). According to this calling Paul was called an apostle, that is, one who was sent.

It should be noted that the Apostle placed the name “apostolate” in all his Epistles for this reason: so that his Epistles might possess greater honor and dignity among his hearers.

*Set apart*, that is, chosen to preach the Gospel. Or, *set apart*, that is, separated from the flock, namely from the other disciples—not in mind but in body, because he had one heart and one soul with the others. He was separated bodily from the others at the command of the Holy Spirit: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul” (Acts XIII), and he was appointed preacher to the Gentiles throughout the whole world.

For example, just as a person extends his arm for work and yet is not thereby cut off from the rest of the body, so the apostle Paul was appointed to preach to the Gentiles, but was not for that reason separated from the other apostles in mind or desire. And while the other apostles preached in particular places and held particular kingdoms—for example, Andrew Achaia, Thomas India, and Matthew Ethiopia—Paul became preacher to all nations and all kingdoms. Hence he himself says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked through me also among the Gentiles” (Gal. II).

This is as though he had said in other words: “He who appointed Peter teacher of the Jews also wished to appoint me teacher of all the Gentiles.”

*For the Gospel of God.*

Mark says: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.” This writer, on the other hand, affirms that it is the Gospel of God the Father. Why is there this difference? Because, as the Son says, all things belonging to the Father are his, and those belonging to him are the Father’s. Therefore they possess one Gospel in common, that is, good news.

For just as the Father and Son have one substance, one power, and one divinity, so they have one Gospel. What, then, is the Gospel? As we have said, good news. And what news is better than to announce that the almighty God is Trinity in persons and unity in substance; that the Father is unbegotten, the Son only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both; and also to announce Christ’s birth according to his divinity before the ages and according to his humanity at the end of time; his miracles, passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, coming to judgment, the general resurrection, the glory of the elect, and the condemnation of the reprobate? The Apostle was set apart to preach all these things.

It follows:

*Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets.*

Just as God the Father promised through the prophets that he would send his Son into the world for the salvation of the human race, so he also promised the holy Gospel.

It should be noted that, after saying “through the prophets,” he immediately added “his.” For the term “prophet” is common and is sometimes understood in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one. Just as there were good prophets in the Old Testament, inspired by the Holy Spirit, who foretold many mysteries divinely revealed to them, so there were also false prophets saying, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord had not sent them. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “The prophet who speaks falsehood, he is the tail” (Isa. IX).

The Gospel was not therefore promised through the mouths of those men, but rather through the mouths of those whom he himself truly sent. Hence through Jeremiah he says: “I will establish,” he says, “a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jer. XXXI), that is, the Gospel. And again: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant” (ibid.).

The Psalmist also, who possessed the Mosaic law, prayed, saying: “Establish for me the law of the Gospel” (Ps. CXVIII).

*In the holy Scriptures concerning his Son.*

There are non-holy writings, such as the sayings of philosophers—Plato or Aristotle—the poems of poets, Homer or Virgil, and those of other pagan poets. The holy Scriptures, however, are called the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, because they sanctify those who observe them by forbidding vices and commending virtues.

These holy Scriptures, or the Gospel, are about the Father’s Son, that is, about Christ, because they announce him. There are indeed many sons of God by adoption, concerning whom John says: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John I). But there is one proper and natural Lord, Jesus Christ, concerning whom the Father himself says: “This is my most beloved Son” (Matt. III).

And concerning him the Apostle says that he was made—or constituted by God the Father—the Son from the seed of David according to the flesh. The Lord Jesus, subsisting from two substances, divine and human, in the unity of one person, is true God and true man. According to his divinity he was not made but begotten, because he is not a creature. According to the flesh, however, he was made from the seed of David, who belonged to the tribe of Judah.

From David’s lineage descended the most blessed virgin Mary, from whose seed the Lord’s flesh was formed in the virgin’s womb through the work of the Holy Spirit. Thus the Apostle very appropriately says that he was made for God the Father from the seed of David according to the flesh, although according to his divinity he was Lord and creator of David.

*Who was predestined*, that is, preordained and predetermined, to be the Son of God in power—“in power” meaning in the power of divinity and of the Word, by whom the man himself was assumed in the unity of the person.

Origen says: “Who was appointed as the Son of God,” maintaining that one who exists can be appointed, whereas one who does not exist can be predestined. But according to blessed Augustine, it is better to say: “Who was predestined to be the Son of God,” because here the Apostle is not speaking about the Word but about the man, who did not exist before he was made [Col. 0367A].

The humanity, which did not previously exist, was predestined, predetermined, or preordained—without any preceding merits—to be the Son of God. It was assumed by the Word in the power of divinity, in the power of the Word, and united to him in the unity of the person, according to the Spirit of sanctification.

Here “Spirit of sanctification” means the Holy Spirit, because he grants holiness to angels and righteous human beings. He also formed, enlivened, and sanctified that man in the virgin’s womb, from the virgin’s seed and without the seed of a man.

It must be considered, however, that the Holy Spirit did not serve as seed for him, nor do we say that the Spirit was the father of his humanity, lest there be said to be two fathers, which it is wholly impious to assert. For not everything that is born from us is necessarily our son. For example, a hair grows from the head, yet it is not rightly called the son of the head. Lice also arise from us, yet they are by no means called our children.

Thus that man, assumed by the Word and conceived from the Holy Spirit—that is, formed through the work of the Holy Spirit—was nevertheless not the son of the Holy Spirit.

Let it therefore be joined together as blessed Augustine teaches:

*Who was predestined to be the Son of God in the power of divinity and of the Word, through the resurrection of the dead*—the first to rise and the first to penetrate the heavens.
