For after the dominion of death had been destroyed, he was the first of all the elect dead to rise, according to what John says about him: “Who is the firstborn of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth, and Christ the firstfruits of those who sleep” (Rev. I). And just as he was the first to rise, so also he was the first to penetrate the heavens, giving his faithful access to enter after him.

Alternatively, according to blessed Ambrose, he is rightly said to have been predestined to be the Son of God through the resurrection, or after the resurrection, because it was then made evident that he was truly the Son of God, when the many miracles occurring at his death compelled people to say: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII).

Before he was hung upon the cross for the salvation of the human race and died, and before the many miracles occurred during his passion that the Gospel recounts, only a few knew that he was the Son of God. Indeed, even the apostles, when he was seized, abandoned him and fled.

But after the sun was darkened at his death, the earth quaked, the tombs were opened, the veil of the temple was torn, and he rose again, it became known that he was the true Son of God. This was also the case when, after his resurrection and ascension, he sent the Holy Spirit to the apostles. Inflamed by the Spirit, they began to speak in the languages of all nations the mighty works of God. Then, rather, he was recognized as the true Son of God by those concerning whom Luke says that three thousand believed on one day and five thousand on the next (Acts II).

It is worthy of careful consideration that the Apostle did not say simply: “Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power through the resurrection of the dead,” but added something further, saying: “Through the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ.” This means only the elect who belong to him. At the same time, it is shown to us that, just as he brought about his own resurrection, so he also raised with himself the bodies and souls of many of the dead—both those of whom it is said, “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose” (Matt. XXVII), and all the elect.

Through the resurrection, then, of these dead—of Jesus Christ, that is, of those who belonged to him, whom he raises to life—Christ appeared to be the true Son of God. Concerning them the same Apostle says that he might be “the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII). Nothing is said here about the resurrection of the reprobate.

It may also be joined in this way: *Paul, a servant, called as an apostle through the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ.* All the apostles were indeed called by him before the Lord’s passion, but Paul was called after his resurrection [Col. 0368B].

*Through whom we received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all the Gentiles for his name.*

“Grace” means something given freely. Here we should understand grace as faith, the remission of sins, or endurance of all labors, for which we shall be rewarded in the future. All these things were freely given to all the faithful without preceding merits, as that outstanding preacher himself says: “By grace you have been saved” (Eph. II).

By “apostleship” we should understand the embassy of preaching, which the apostles alone and their successors received—those who likewise held the office of preaching after them.

And lest anyone think that they had received the embassy of preaching only among one nation, the Israelite nation, he says: “among all the Gentiles for obedience to the faith.” They received apostleship so that all nations might obey the faith of the Gospel and of Christ, which is one and the same.

Faith is so called because what is promised is brought about. It is established between God and human beings. For example, at the time of baptism we profess that we believe in God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, and that we renounce the devil, all his pomp, and all his works. If we observe this, we obey the faith; but if not, we are convicted of unbelief.

Faith, then, as we have said, is confession of the holy Trinity and the solid foundation of religion, by which we truly believe what we cannot in any way see. But if we already see what we believe, faith is no longer required; there is knowledge instead.

It should also be noted that he says he received apostleship “for the name of Christ,” that is, in place of his name. For the Lord says to them: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John XX), that is, “As the Father sent me in his name, so I send you in place of my name to preach.”

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “We act as ambassadors in place of Christ.” And again: “We entreat you in place of Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. V).

*Among whom you also are*—that is, among the Gentiles, you who live in Rome, Jews and Gentiles—*called by Jesus Christ.* You have been called by him through us to believe in him; or you have been called his in this respect, because you have received from him the name of Christianity.

[Col. 0369A] *To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as saints.*

He says “beloved of God,” that is, chosen for faith and grace. But when he says “called as saints,” these words appear to mean that they were already holy when they were called; this is not appropriate. Those who were sinners and unrighteous were called saints—that is, they were chosen and called for the purpose of being sanctified through baptism.

The same is true of the passage in the song of Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist: “He visited,” he says, “and accomplished the redemption of his people” (Luke I). He did not find them already to be his people; rather, by visiting and redeeming them, he made them his own.

It should be noted that the beginning of this Epistle is extended through a lengthy circuit of words, and for that reason its division must be considered carefully. It should likewise be considered that the salutations of Epistles are expressed in the third person.

It should therefore be read by clauses and with divisions as follows: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus,” and so on, up to “among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ.” There a medial division should be placed. Then let it continue: “To all who are in Rome, called as saints,” and there let a full division be made, with the third person understood: “he wishes you greetings.”

For what follows, “Grace to you,” lies outside the salutation, because it is in the second person, to whom he should speak after the first salutation.

*Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*—understand, “be given.”

“Grace to you,” that is, faith and salvation, by which sins are remitted at the time of baptism; and peace, by which we are reconciled to God the Father through the blood of his Son.

Some wish to understand the distinction in this way: “Grace to you from God the Father,” who freely sent the Son, “and peace from the Lord Jesus Christ,” through whose passion we are reconciled both to God and to the angels. But it is better to understand both as given by God the Father and both as given by the Son, because grace and peace are equally conferred by the Father and the Son.

He passed over the person of the Holy Spirit for this reason: he included the Spirit in his gifts, namely, in grace and peace. For Truth says to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God” (John IV)—that is, the Holy Spirit. Because the elect are divinely honored through him, he is therefore, as we have said, understood in the gifts.

Grace, that is, remission of sins, which believers receive in the laver of baptism, and peace, through which they merit reconciliation, are bestowed equally by the whole Trinity.

*First, I give thanks to my God for all of you* [Col. 0369D].

Up to this point there is the salutation; after the salutation the text of the Epistle immediately follows.

The blessed Apostle began his Epistle with thanksgiving, thereby fulfilling his own command, which he gave elsewhere: “Give thanks in all things” (I Thess. V). “I give thanks,” he says, that is, “I render praise to God for you.”

He rightly adds “my,” because although there is one God of all things by nature, since he is the creator of all, he is nevertheless properly called God of those who, by the merit of faith and righteousness, are shown to be his worshipers, as in the case of blessed Paul and the other faithful of Christ.

Hence it is said: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. II)—by grace and by the merit of their lives.

*Because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.*

Take a part for the whole. The whole world did not proclaim their faith; rather, it was spread through many parts of the world that they had received the new faith of the Gospel, since at that time they ruled almost all nations. Their faith was proclaimed to many nations by those who came to Rome and then returned to their own regions.

Faith is so called because what is promised is brought about, so that what is promised ought to be fulfilled. If it is not fulfilled, it is no longer faith.

*For God is my witness.*

The Apostle appears to swear contrary to the Lord’s command, which says: “Do not swear at all.” But since swearing to the truth when necessity compels one to do so is not sin—as Augustine says—the Apostle, compelled to make his hearers believe him, does not sin when he swears. Nevertheless, it is safer not to swear, because one who never swears never commits perjury.

*Whom I serve in my spirit.*

He does not say “whom I worship,” but “whom I serve.” There are some who falsely worship God or human beings with body and voice, but not with the spirit, that is, with the affection of the mind. It is therefore more to say “whom I serve in my spirit” than “whom I worship,” because here the service of love and complete devotion is understood.

*In the Gospel of his Son,* that is, in the preaching of Christ. As we have said, “Gospel” means good news. For he says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III). To preach Christ’s conception and birth and the other mysteries of his dispensation is also to evangelize.

*That without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers.*

He says “without ceasing” because, applying himself to prayer every day and every night, he made mention of them. Otherwise these words could not stand, since he ate and slept. The Apostle was still a mortal human being and therefore, as a mortal, needed to work, eat, and sleep. A human being clothed in mortal covering needs all these things.

But in this respect—that he persisted in prayer—he first demonstrated in himself by his actions what he had elsewhere commanded his hearers by exhortation: “Pray without ceasing.”

*Requesting, if somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you* (I Thess. V).

“If somehow” means “in some way”; “at last” means “finally” or “with difficulty.” He rightly says, “Requesting, if in some way I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you,” because there are some who, by God’s permission but not by his will, appear to have a prosperous journey toward evil—for example, when they hasten to commit murder or some other crime.

But the Apostle considers all prosperity that comes without God’s will worthless and counts it as nothing. For he did not think he could have a prosperous journey in any other way than if the will of God—which knows all things, goes before us in all good things, precedes us, and supports us—led him to a place where he might bear some fruit.

*For I desire to see you.*

He says that he desires to come to them in order to stir them to love him, so that they too might desire him. He desired to see them in order to bestow on them something of the grace of preaching and miracles, as the following words make clear.

“I desire,” he says, “to see you, so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift for your strengthening,” so that I may confirm your faith by teaching, preaching, and the power of miracles; and so that by my arrival I may make up whatever you lack in faith. Or even so that I may teach you to possess perfect charity, lest you disagree among yourselves and fall into discord, as I now hear.

*That is, to be mutually consoled among you by the faith that is mutually yours and mine.*

Teachers are consoled by the progress of their disciples when they find in them stability of faith. Conversely, disciples are consoled when the grace of the Holy Spirit is increased in them through the arrival of their teachers, or when they understand that their own knowledge and faith correspond and participate in the knowledge or faith of their teachers.

[Col. 0371B] *I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often planned to come to you*—that is, I both wished and planned to come, but have been prevented until now.

Paul was prevented by God from coming to Rome earlier, before he had administered the sacred Gospel to the Gentiles living around Jerusalem. Then, preaching through Macedonia and Asia Minor, he came to Illyricum, which is the first region of Europe, and at last reached Rome according to the desire of his heart.

When the Apostle said that he had often planned to come to them, one of them might have objected by asking: “O blessed Apostle, why did you plan to come to us sinners?”

To this he replied: *So that I might have some fruit among you, as also among the other Gentiles*—that is, so that through my labor I might have an eternal reward of spiritual grace among you, as also among the other Gentiles.

*I am a debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish.*

He calls the Jews and Greeks “wise,” because all divine wisdom and all worldly philosophy took their origin from them; the other nations he calls “foolish” and “barbarian,” such as the Teutons, Britons, and others who, in comparison with them, were unlearned and almost without letters.

For just as the Latins received all divine Scripture from the Hebrews, so they received all secular philosophy from the Greeks. And because the Greeks flourished in wisdom, they called themselves wise and all the remaining nations barbarians.

The Apostle confounds their pride when, in what follows, he places the Jews above them.

But it must be considered what the Apostle had received that made him a debtor to these people, that is, to the wise and the foolish. He had received nothing from them. Rather, he had received this gift so that he might speak in the languages of all nations and, as their debtor, preach the faith of Christ to those same nations.

Or certainly he was a debtor to all nations because, as blessed Augustine says in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, he received divine wisdom above all the apostles. And why did he receive it, unless so that by the wisdom given to him he might resist all rulers and all philosophers?

Hence the Lord says of him to Ananias: “He is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name before kings and nations” (Acts IX).

He was a debtor to the wise so that he might disclose profound and lofty mysteries to them, as he says elsewhere: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” [Col. 0372A] (I Cor. II). He was a debtor to the foolish so that he might entrust the word of the mysteries to them according to their capacity, for he himself says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (I Cor. III). He was also a debtor to the foolish in this respect: that he patiently endured their foolishness.

*Thus, as far as I am concerned, I am ready*—that is, it is evident and manifest—*to evangelize you also who are in Rome.*

The order of the words and the meaning are as follows: “Because I am a debtor to the wise and the foolish, I am also a debtor to you who are in Rome. My will is all the more ready to evangelize, and just as I desire to shine greatly and sublimely through the faith of all nations, so I desire to shine through the progress of your faith.”

[Col. 0372B] *For I am not ashamed of the Gospel*—understand, “to preach it.”

Some believed in the Son of God yet were ashamed to preach that he had been born from a woman and crucified, as though they were unwilling to inflict an insult upon the Son of God. But Paul was not ashamed. He said: “I am not ashamed to preach the Gospel,” as though he were saying in other words: “I am not ashamed to preach the Son of God, born at the end of time, whom I know to have been begotten equal to the Father before the ages. I am not ashamed to preach him dead, whom I know to have risen on the third day after overcoming death, and afterward to have penetrated the heavens.”

And as though someone might ask, “Why are you not ashamed of the Gospel?” he says:

*For it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek.*

For the Gospel is the power of God for the salvation of every believing person, because through the faith and work that the Gospel announces he decreed to save the human race.

The Jews are now placed before the Greeks either because they possessed divine and human laws before them, or because, nourished in the law, they came through knowledge of the law to faith in the Gospel before the Greeks did—namely, when after the Lord’s ascension, through the preaching of the apostles, three thousand of them believed on one day, five thousand on the next, and many thousands thereafter.

Or the Jews are placed before the Greeks for this reason: the apostles themselves, from whom the Greeks received the teaching and faith of the Gospel as from teachers, were by nature Jews.

It should be noted that by the term “Jews” all believing Jews are to be understood, and by “Greeks” all Gentiles are to be included.

*For the righteousness of God is revealed in it,* that is, in the Gospel, *from faith to faith.*

The righteousness of God, that is, the justification by which he justifies those who believe in him, is manifested in the Gospel when it says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” that is, “will be justified” (Matt. XVI).

This is the righteousness by which all believers are justified through the gift of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It is called the righteousness of God because, imparting it to the faithful, he makes them righteous.

If the passage is referred to the Jews, this is “from faith”—understand, from the faith of the law—“to the faith of the holy Gospel.” For because in the law they possessed knowledge and faith in the one God, as it is said in Exodus that “they believed in the Lord and in Moses his servant” (Exod. XIV), they passed more easily from faith in and knowledge of the one God to the Gospel and received faith in the holy Trinity.

In general, all believers will eventually pass from faith in words to faith in realities. For what the Gospel promises is faithfully given to hope of rewards: what we now hold in faith and hope, we shall then possess in reality, according to what blessed John says: “Beloved, we are children of God in hope, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be in reality. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

*As it is written: “But the righteous person lives by faith.”*

This example is contained in the oracle of the prophet Habakkuk. The righteous person therefore lives by the faith that is conceived in the heart, expressed by the mouth, and adorned with good works—the eternal life.

“Faith without works is dead” (James II).

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and unrighteousness of human beings. The wrath of God is called in this passage the vengeance of the day of judgment, and the divine retribution which the Lord will inflict upon all the reprobate on that day, saying to them: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25). This divine retribution will be manifested from heaven, because the Lord will come from there for judgment, as he himself says: “The Son of Man will come to repay each according to his works” (Matt. 16). Or certainly the divine retribution is manifested from heaven, that is, from the Church, through the trumpet of the Gospel, because the things we have said about the day of judgment and the Lord’s coming are contained there. For the Church is designated by the name “heaven.” As the Truth himself says: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins” (Matt. 25). In John’s Apocalypse also, heaven is designated by this name in many passages.

It can also be understood absolutely that divine retribution is said to be manifested from heaven, that is, from the Gospel, of which the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Matt. 13). He says, “Divine retribution will be revealed against all impiety and unrighteousness.” “Impiety” signifies idolatry, as it is written in Zechariah: “Impiety will sit upon the talent of lead.” Unrighteousness is what occurs when someone acts unjustly against the Lord and his neighbor. The meaning is: The vengeance which the Lord threatens in the Gospel comes upon all idolaters and sinners.

It continues: “Of those who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness.” The simple truth is that God is invisible and unchangeable. Those who judged that worship due to God alone should be offered to corruptible creatures suppressed his religion in unrighteousness. They were suppressing the truth of God in unrighteousness when, insofar as it lay within them, they unjustly attributed the religion and honor of the true God to a creature, saying to a stone, “You are my god,” and to wood, “You gave birth to me.”

For what can be known of God is manifest among them. From this point the Apostle speaks, for the most part, against the philosophers of this age. The meaning is: Therefore the wrath of almighty God will come upon the reprobate, and especially upon the philosophers, because what is properly God’s—that is, being—has been made manifest to them: namely, that he alone is truly the true Creator of all things. For from the beauty of visible works the knowledge and majesty of their Maker became known to the philosophers, since creatures so beautiful must have had an even more beautiful Creator. Thus it is related by the Hebrews concerning Melchizedek: having considered the structure of the world, he declared that there is one God superior to creatures; and therefore he offered to the true God things superior to others, namely bread and wine. For God revealed this to them.

Whether God revealed it through natural intelligence, the gift of reason, and the sharpness of study, or through hidden inspiration, he revealed that the Creator is not the same as the creature: the Creator is God, whereas the creature is God’s handiwork.

For his invisible things, understood through the things that have been made, are seen from the creation of the world. This means: The invisible mysteries of almighty God are seen, understood, or perceived and known from the creation of the world—that is, chiefly by human beings and by the philosophers of the nations—through the visible things that have been made. They are understood not by bodily eyes but by the eyes of the mind.

For through the things that have been made, his sacred invisible realities—his eternal power also and divinity—are perceived. The implied meaning is: Through the visible things that have been made, these realities are seen by the mind of those philosophers. Thus they are without excuse. The power of God is that which governs all created things; his divinity, that which fills the universe. Therefore almighty God, through natural intelligence and through the visible things that have been made, granted philosophers knowledge of many things concerning his divinity, so that, worshiping idols—that is, the creature instead of the Creator—they might be without excuse and unable to say that they had been ignorant of God. For the power of God, which is eternal, and his divinity, which is likewise eternal, are shown by inferences drawn from creation.

For although they knew God through natural intelligence [Col. 0374C] or through the invisible creation, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; rather, they became futile in their thoughts—that is, through their pride they became vain because of their wisdom—and they returned to their former errors, attributing to themselves the ability to possess the wisdom given by God. Their foolish heart was darkened. They did not glorify God, or did not honor him, because they did not publicly proclaim his majesty or teach that he alone should be worshiped, with idols cast aside. They did not give thanks, that is, they did not offer him praises for the manifestation of the highest and invisible good.

Their heart, which had been enlightened through natural intelligence and through God’s grace, became darkened through ignorance after they began to worship idols and the creature instead of the Creator. For what is worse or more obscure than to worship serpents instead of the true God?

For while claiming to be wise, they became fools through themselves: although wisdom was not from them, they supposed that they possessed it from themselves. What divine grace had freely bestowed upon them, it took away because they were ungrateful.

And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, and of birds, and of four-footed animals, and of serpents. Every creature that can be changed for better or worse is corruptible. For example, a human being is corruptible because he is corrupted by old age and illness, and finally when, through death, he is reduced to dust. Almighty God, however, who cannot be changed either for better or for worse but always remains the same and equal, alone exists incorruptibly.

Human beings exchanged his glory and worship—which belong solely to the one who is God—for the likeness of other human beings: for example, the Assyrians, who worshiped the image of Bel, the father of King Ninus, as a god; the Babylonians, likewise, whom they called Bel; the Sidonians, Baal; the Jews, Beelzebub; and the Philistines, Zebet. They did so not only in the likeness of a dead and corruptible human being, but also in the likeness of birds, as the Romans did when they worshiped a goose, and the Egyptians when they worshiped a hawk.

They also did so in the likeness of four-footed animals, as the Egyptians did when they worshiped Apis, that is, a white cow. They did so also in the likeness of serpents, as the Babylonians did when they worshiped a dragon, and the Egyptians when they worshiped the crocodile, which is a water serpent, swimming in water like a fish and feeding on land like an ox.

Therefore—that is, because they handed over the worship and religion of God to false images and were unwilling to give him thanks for the gifts divinely bestowed upon them—God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity. That is, he permitted them to be handed over by themselves, or to go according to the desires of their hearts into impurity, so that they might dishonor—that is, defile with the shamefulness of lust—or disgrace their own bodies among themselves. He permitted them to go into the desires of their hearts so that they might be punished more severely. How God permitted them to follow the desires of their pleasures is reported more fully in what follows.

Who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, that is, the worship and religion of the true God for idolatry. For God is the truth, whereas an idol is a lie.

Alternatively: The truth was created by God; therefore the creature itself is not the truth, although they converted it into a lie by saying that the sun, moon, and other creatures were gods, reckoning God, who is blessed forever, as nothing. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie when, through a lie, they said that the true creature made by God was what it was not. For they falsely said that the sun and moon were gods, denying what they were, since in truth they are not gods but merely creatures.

A creature made by God is truly a creature, but it is not that Truth who is God, because it is not God—who is blessed forever. If, then, that one is the God blessed forever, those who offered his worship and religion to idols were certainly accursed forever and subject to decay—that is, suffering decline and corruption—according to what the psalm says about them: “Their time will be forever” (Ps. 80). This means: Their decline will remain forever, because they will always be corrupted by fire and worms. It continues:

Therefore God handed them over to dishonorable passions. “Therefore,” he says, because they exchanged the religion of the true God for a lie, God handed them over—that is, permitted them to be handed over, or to go into dishonorable passions and crimes. “Dishonor” is so called as though it were the condition of one without the name of dignity. Hence “dishonorable” is one who ceases to possess the name of dignity when he is discovered in some crime, just as “ignoble” means without a good name, and “infamous” means without a good reputation. Such were those of whom he continues:

For their females exchanged natural use for that use which is against nature. Likewise, the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned with desire for one another, males committing shameful acts with males. That is, natural use is for a man and a woman to come together in one intercourse; against nature, however, is for a male to defile a male and a woman a woman.

If someone, having abandoned his wife, has intercourse with another woman, he indeed commits a shameful act and sins, but not against nature. But if he has intercourse with his own wife in a way other than he ought—that is, with a member other than is proper—he commits a shameful act against nature and perpetrates a very grave crime.

And receiving in themselves the recompense which was due—that is, because, having first known God, they did not honor him, by the just judgment of God they received a reciprocal recompense for their error, so that they did not preserve honor for themselves, having been handed over to the most shameful passions. Or they received the recompense of eternal condemnation, which they deserved for such acts. Concerning this the same outstanding preacher says elsewhere: “The wages of sin,” he says, “is death” (Rom. 6).

[Col. 0376C] And just as they did not approve—that is, did not choose or love—to retain God in knowledge, God handed them over—that is, permitted them to go—into a depraved mind, to do what is not fitting, namely, what both divine and human laws prohibit.

Those are said to retain God in knowledge who always fear him as present; and while they consider that he is present everywhere, they do not dare to sin. Those, however, are said not to retain him in knowledge who are unwilling to consider that he is present everywhere, so that they may sin more freely without fear.

Filled with all unrighteousness. Unrighteousness, also called *anomia* (“lawlessness”), is whatever is done against the law of God. For *nomos* means “law,” whereas *anomia* means, as it were, “without law.” Unrighteousness is also called the bitterness of the mind, when evil is conceived in the heart.

Sin is the perpetration of evil. Unrighteousness and sin are distinguished in this way: unrighteousness refers to the bitterness or hardness of the mind, as we have said, whereas sin refers to the body’s falling into evil. Malice is deceit or cunning, namely, when one thing is held in the heart and another is brought forth by the mouth; a thought is brought forth. The thought of a depraved mind is called malice. The intention or work of malice is called malignity.

Fornication. Fornication is so called from *fornices*, that is, vaulted buildings, which were called *fornices*, where public prostitutes were made to lie down. A fornicator is one whose body is public and common.

Greed. Greed is an insatiable desire for possessions, or adultery; and in this passage it is to be referred not only to money but also to sexual intercourse.

Wickedness. Wickedness is pride or boldness in sin. Hence it is said: “I know their wickedness.”

Full of envy. One is called envious, full of envy, when he is tormented by another’s prosperity. Envy is divided into two kinds of suffering: either one does not want another to be what he himself is, or, seeing another to be better, he grieves that he is not like him.

The distinction between envy and zeal is this: zeal or emulation—terms which are equivalent—is sometimes used in a good sense, as in: “The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this” (2 Kings 19). It is also used in a bad sense, as when it is read concerning Joseph that his brothers, emulating or envying him, sold him (Gen. 37). Envy, however, is always used in a bad sense.

Murder. “Murder” is derived from *homo* (“human being”) and the verb *caedo* (“I strike or kill”); hence a murderer is one who kills a human being. It rightly follows envy immediately, because murder proceeds from envy. For example, the Devil, seeing that the human being had been made to receive the place of glory which he had lost through pride, driven by envy, killed him in soul (Gen. 3). Likewise Cain, moved by envy against his brother Abel because the Lord had looked upon him and kindled approval toward his offerings, but had not looked upon Cain or kindled approval toward his offerings, killed him (ibid.).

Strife. Strife exists where something is defended not by reason but by obstinacy of spirit, or where truth is not sought but animosity—that is, pride—is exhausted. To speak against another without any usefulness can rightly be called the greatest strife.

Deceit. The distinction between *dolor* (“pain”) and *dolus* (“deceit”) is that pain belongs to bodily weakness, whereas deceit is the cunning of the mind. It is so called because it deceives through fabricated words. The distinction among deceit, ambush, and fraud is that deceit is carried out in the mind, ambush in a place or through zeal, whereas fraud concerns mutual trust.

Malignity. Malignity is the work of malice, which can also be called ill will.

Slanderers. “Slanderer” takes its name from the sound of speech, because he does not speak to someone’s face but into his ear, defaming him. It is an onomatopoeia, a name formed from a sound.

Detractors. Some manuscripts have *detractatores*, but this is falsely written. Detraction is maliciously changing another’s good works into evil, or diminishing them through deceitful fraud out of envy: saying that what is good is evil, or that great goods are small. For one is said to detract when he is shown to take something away from someone and diminish it.

Hateful to God, that is, those who incur God’s hatred.

Insulting. Those who are swift to inflict verbal injuries are called insulting; they injure others either by words or by deeds—by words, namely, through abuse or reproach; by deeds, through scourging. Hence we read concerning the apostles that, after being scourged in the council, they went away rejoicing because they had been considered worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus (Acts 5), that is, scourging, insult, and disgrace.

Proud. The proud person is one who seeks perverse elevation and wishes to surpass others. Hence, in the Greek expression, he is called *hyperephanos*, that is, “appearing above” or “exalted above.”

Arrogant. An arrogant person is one who is lifted above his proper measure, or who does not submit to the institutions of his elders.

Inventors of evils, who devise many evils, as were those about whom we have spoken up to this point.

Disobedient to parents. They do not obey earthly parents; but those who are disobedient to God the Father likewise belong here.

Foolish. The foolish are stupid and senseless, deprived of the salt of wisdom.

Disorderly, that is, unregulated and wanton: those who conduct all their affairs disorderly and wantonly. For every foolish person is disorderly and unregulated.

Without affection, that is, without love of God and neighbor. “Affection” is also used for affliction, as in the Gospel, where it says that they killed servants who had been treated with insults—that is, afflicted (Matt. 22). But affection is used in the present passage for love.

Without a covenant, that is, without friendship and peace.

Without mercy. There are those who have mercy neither on themselves nor on others. For it is necessary first that we show mercy to ourselves, and then to others. Hence Solomon says: “My son, have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Eccl. 30).

Although they knew God’s justice, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death. Everything shameful is displeasing to God. Although the philosophers practiced evil, they nevertheless agreed with God’s justice in this respect, because they censured those same vices in others. For God’s justice hates and detests vices and teaches virtues.

They knew this justice because they understood that vices were displeasing to God. Yet they are said to have been ignorant in this respect: they did not understand that those who do things such as they themselves did are worthy of death—that is, of eternal condemnation. They were as though without understanding when they sinned without fear.

Not only those who do such things are worthy of death—that is implied—but also those who consent to those who do them. One who commits sin and does not consent to it is worthy of death. One who does not commit it but consents to it among his subjects by failing to punish it is worthy of death. Those who both commit and approve such things are worthy of a double death.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, because not only the one who commits sin but also the one who consents to it is worthy of death, you are without excuse, every human being who judges. Here he addresses not only any Gentile but also the Jew and all rulers generally.

He addresses the Jews because they reproved and condemned the Gentiles as idolaters and sinners, boasting that through observance of the law they had deserved to attain the grace of the Gospel. He addresses rulers because they judge and censure sin in others, understanding that it is sin, but do not condemn it in themselves when they do the same thing.

The same must be understood of all who censure the vices of others but do not correct those same vices in themselves. For in whatever you judge another, you condemn yourself. This is to be understood as follows: If you reprove and judge another, and you yourself avoid the vices for which you reprove him and free yourself from others, then you judge rightly. But if you perform the same deeds—or worse deeds—than those for which you reprove your brother, then, in judging him, you condemn yourself, because you who judge another will someday be judged, and rightly, since you do the things you judge.

For we know that God’s judgment is according to truth, that is, without partiality, against those who do such things—that is, who do things like those they censure in others. In the present age people take account of the persons of the powerful, the wealthy, and their relatives in judgment. But God’s judgment is true in this respect: he who is king does not consider persons but the merit of a life.

But do you suppose this, every human being who judges those who do such things and does them yourself—that you will escape God’s judgment? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that God’s kindness—that is, God’s exceedingly good mercy—leads you to repentance?

He speaks specifically to the Jews, who reproved and condemned the Gentiles as idolaters, as we have already said, while claiming that they themselves had deserved to come to the faith of Christ. But in general he addresses everyone, both Jews and Gentiles.

The meaning is: If your servant or subordinate cannot escape your judgment, O human being, who possess only human understanding, how will you be able to escape the judgment of almighty God? The riches of God’s goodness are those by which he does not immediately punish the whole world, which sins daily, but waits for it to repent. Moreover, in his kindly generosity he grants it the sun and rain, which people often despise because they do not give him thanks.

Patience is that by which he does not immediately punish those who sin through pride and insolence. Long-suffering is what elsewhere is called support or endurance: through it he bears patiently for a long time those who sin through weakness and frailty, and not with deliberate intent, awaiting their repentance.

But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up—that is, reserve and accumulate for yourself—wrath on the day of wrath: that is, vengeance on the day of judgment and the revelation of God’s just judgment, when he will repay each according to his works, good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

The day of wrath and of the revelation or manifestation of judgment is understood as the judgment itself and the manifestation of almighty God the Judge. In the divine Scriptures, a hard and unrepentant heart is spoken of when the human mind, bound as wax is bound by the cold of iniquity, does not receive the seal of divine majesty—namely, what the Lord teaches us to have in our soul when he says: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Lev. 19). Concerning this the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4).

To those who, according to perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption, he will give eternal life. The order of the words, with the implied meaning, is this: To those who now labor or live according to perseverance in good work, seeking eternal life—that is, awaiting God’s judgment, since they seek the reward of their goodness not only in the present but also in the future—he will give glory and incorruption on the day of judgment.

He will give them the glory of brightness, by which they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He will also give them honor, by which they will be sons of God, as blessed John says: “Beloved, we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). He will also give them incorruption, that is, immortality, because all the elect will be unchangeable in soul and incorruptible in body.

But upon those who are of contention—that is implied, those who criticize God’s judgment—and who assent to the truth, that is, the Gospel or Christ, but believe in unrighteousness, that is, in falsehood and every evil, or even in the devil by fulfilling his will, wrath—that is, God’s judgment—will come, and indignation, that is, vengeance or the severity of condemnation.

Tribulation also comes upon them from the guilt of conscience and the consideration of sin, and anguish from delayed repentance. All these things will come upon every soul of a human being who works evil, the Jew first and the Greek.

He says “upon every soul,” meaning upon the whole human being, understanding the whole from a part. For this is a frequent expression of the Apostle, as in: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Gen. 46; Deut. 10). Or he says “upon the soul” because sin is first conceived in the mind through thought and afterward perpetrated in action.

It is therefore to be feared, and greatly feared, that he says these things will come upon every soul of a human being who works evil. For God spares no one—not an angel, not a friend. An angel sinned and was cast from his heavenly seat. A human being also sinned and was expelled from the joys of paradise. Moses sinned at the waters of contradiction, and therefore did not enter the promised land.

The Jew is placed before the Gentile in guilt because those who had the law before Moses sinned more gravely by transgressing both the natural law and the written law. In glory, however, the Jew is not placed before the Gentile on account of honor but on account of the time of belief.

Glory, by which the righteous will shine in the kingdom of God like the sun; honor, by which they will be sons of God; and peace, that is, the remission of sins, or the reconciliation by which we are reconciled to God the Father, comes to everyone who does good—that is implied. To the Jew first and to the Greek, because the first fruits of the Church were from the Jews.

For there is no partiality with God. There would be partiality or distinction with God if, on account of Abraham, he chose the Jews and rejected the Gentiles who had long worshiped idols, or if he rewarded a Jew who lived well while neglecting a Gentile who believed and acted rightly.

For all who sinned without the law, whether the law of Moses or the Gospel, as the pagans did, will also perish without the law, because the law will not be required of them. Nevertheless, they will perish because they despised the natural law and refused to receive the Gospel. And all who sinned while placed under the law of Moses will be judged by the law, because they transgressed it.

For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified. That is, they will be regarded as righteous and will appear righteous, as was intended of the one about whom it is said: “Desiring to justify himself” (Luke 10), that is, desiring to appear righteous. One who hears the law and does not fulfill its commandments will not be justified merely because he has heard it. But the one who is both a hearer and a doer of the law will certainly be justified through the law.

For when Gentiles who do not have the law naturally do the things of the law, although they do not have the law, they are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts.

This can be understood in two ways. When Gentiles who do not have the written law do the things which the written law commands those to whom it was given, they show that they have the natural law written in their hearts, and they are a law to themselves, because they do what the law teaches although it was not given to them.

For example, the Saracens, who have neither the law of Moses nor the Gospel, while naturally observing the law by refraining from murder, adultery, and the other things contained in the written law, are a law to themselves, since through the works they perform they show the written law in their hearts. The law says: “You shall not kill.” One who has not received the law, if he does not kill, is a law to himself.

Alternatively: When Gentiles who do not have the law of Moses, having been instructed by the teaching of the Gospel, naturally do the things which the law of Moses commanded, they are a law to themselves because they have that same law of Moses written in their hearts through the inspiration of almighty God.

Their conscience bears witness to them, and their thoughts accuse or even defend them among themselves. And when does this happen? On the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings according to my Gospel, that is, according to what I proclaim to you “through Jesus Christ.” Through him God the Father will judge the world, as he himself said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

Just as a mark is impressed in wax by a stylus, so certain marks of evil or good thoughts are fixed in our mind and conscience. These will either accuse or defend us on the day of judgment, when not only things that are open but also those now hidden from us will be judged. Our conscience will therefore bear witness to us by making clear whether our sins or good works are more numerous, whether they are old or recent, and whether they have been erased through repentance or accumulated through new crimes.

But if you are called a Jew—that is implied, from the patriarch Judah—and rest in the law, reading, meditating upon, and understanding it according to your false doctrine, and boast in God, that is, in knowledge of the one God,

and know his will through that law, and, instructed by the law, approve the more useful things, and so forth, up to the point where I say: “Having a form of knowledge and truth in the law,” that is, possessing indeed a likeness of knowledge but not the truth of wisdom, because you do not believe in Christ.

He speaks to the unbelieving Jew who boasts as though in the knowledge of the one God and in circumcision, and who approves what is more useful in the law of Moses.

And you suppose yourself to be a guide of the blind—that is, of the nations which were blind in the unbelief of ignorance and in sins—just as those to whom the same Apostle once spoke had been: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.” He rightly says that you approve what is more useful in the law of Moses.

In the natural law, the useful things are what it says:

“What you do not want to be done to you, do not do to another.”

But in the written law there were more useful things, because there is knowledge of God there; in the Gospel there are the most useful things.

For the Gentiles in a certain sense knew useful things through the natural law. The Jews knew more useful things through both the natural law and the written law of Moses. The faithful in the New Testament know the most useful things, because they possess faith in the holy Trinity.

You, then, who teach another, why do you not teach yourself? This must be read as a rebuke, with an implication of this kind: O Jew, you who teach another, why do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, why do you steal another’s goods? Or, you who preach the law, why do you steal spiritual understanding from the law?

You who say that one must not commit adultery, why do you commit adultery? An adulterer is one who violates another’s wife. But not only is the one who violates another’s wife called an adulterer; the one who, insofar as it lies within him, attributes through false superstitions the worship and religion belonging solely to God to other things is also called an adulterer.

The meaning is: You who say that another’s wife ought not to be violated, why do you commit adultery? Or, since you say that one ought to serve God, why do you serve vices?

You who abhor—that is, reject or hate—idols, why do you commit sacrilege? To read or read away secretly is to steal. Hence sacrilege is so called because it is the theft of sacred things. For example, whoever secretly takes something from the treasury of the Church or from the property of those who serve God commits sacrilege. Spiritually, however, sacrilege is the transgression of sacred words.

You who boast in the law, why do you dishonor God through transgression of the law? God is dishonored when his will and command are trampled underfoot and treated as nothing. In the same way a king or any authority is said to be dishonored when his letter is not observed and his command is not kept.

For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written in Isaiah. The people of Israel were taken captive among the Assyrians, in Babylon, and among the other nations. The name of God was blasphemed by them when their enemies said mockingly: “Look at the God whom you worshiped, who was unable to free you from our hands. Truly our idols have proved victorious over your God.”

Likewise, when the holy Church is plundered by enemies, and when those who ought to bear the name of holiness live badly, the name of God is blasphemed, because Jews and pagans say: “Look at the people of the Lord; see what sort of servants your Jesus has.”

[Col. 0383A] Circumcision is indeed beneficial if you observe the law. In this passage Claudius should not be followed, but Ambrose should rather be followed. Understand this circumcision here as referring to the very origin of the race, that is, to the lineage of Abraham from which that people derives its bodily origin, and from which circumcision itself also took its beginning.

For the Apostle has the custom of calling the Jews “circumcision” and the Gentiles “foreskin.” The meaning is: O Jew, what benefits you is that you are of the lineage of Abraham and of the lineage from which circumcision itself took its beginning, if, understanding the law spiritually, you believe in Christ, to whom the law bears witness, and if you observe circumcision not carnally but spiritually. Otherwise, being of Abraham’s lineage does not benefit you but rather harms you.

For, promising Christ, the law says through Jacob: “The ruler will not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49). And through the lawgiver the prophet: “The Lord will raise up for you from among your brothers a prophet like me; you shall hear him according to everything he will say to you.” Concerning spiritual circumcision also, he says: “In the last days the Lord will circumcise your heart, and not your flesh.”

But if you are a transgressor of the law—that is, if you do not believe in Christ whom the law promises, and if you do not observe circumcision spiritually—

your circumcision has become foreskin. That is, you are such as the Gentile who does not have the law, because although you ought to have been a Jew by believing in Christ and fulfilling the law spiritually, you have become like a Gentile. Therefore you will be reckoned among the Gentiles.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Carmel will be reckoned as a forest” (Isa. 32), that is, circumcision will be reckoned as Gentileness.

Therefore, if the foreskin keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his foreskin be reckoned as circumcision? The meaning is: If any Gentile keeps the law by believing in Christ, observing circumcision spiritually, and preserving the other things commanded by the law through spiritual understanding, will his Gentileness not be reckoned as circumcision? Certainly it will, because he will be that true Jew, namely, one who confesses Christ.

Hence the prophet says: “Lebanon will be turned into Carmel” (Isa. 29), that is, Gentileness into true circumcision. For Lebanon means “whiteness,” whereas Carmel means knowledge of true circumcision. Lebanon was therefore turned into Carmel when the Gentiles, whitened in baptism, took the place of the Jews while possessing knowledge of true circumcision.

And that which is foreskin by nature, fulfilling the law—that is, perfecting it—will judge you, who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law. A transgressor of the law is one who does not believe in Christ.

These words depend upon what came before, and the meaning is: Will the one who is naturally a Gentile and brings the law to completion, or perfects and observes it, not judge you by comparison, because he has become better, since you transgress the law through literal understanding and bodily circumcision? Certainly he will condemn you, as we have said, because he searches out spiritual understanding in the law, whereas you always seek a carnal understanding, reading only the surface.

For it is not the one who is outwardly a Jew who is pleasing to God; nor is circumcision which is outward and in the flesh pleasing to God.

But the one who is a Jew inwardly, that is, who is a Jew in his heart, is pleasing to God. And circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter—understand, it is pleasing to God—whose praise, that is, the Jew’s praise, comes not from human beings but from God. Carnal circumcision, which is outward and is an explanation according to the letter, or a stripping away of the flesh, is praised by all Jews. Circumcision of the heart, however, which takes place in the spirit, is the removal of unbelief and the reception of faith in Christ, as well as the stripping away of vices. The meaning is this: the one who is a Jew merely by race and name, and observes circumcision in a carnal manner, is not pleasing to God and does not deserve praise from him, although he may be praised by human beings. But the one who is inwardly a Jew, in his heart—that is, confessing Christ—and who in his heart has been circumcised of all unbelief and every evil will and thought, is pleasing to God and deserves to be praised by God, hearing from him: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER III

“What, then, is the Jew’s advantage?” Understand: greater than the gentile’s, on account of circumcision. “Or what is the benefit of circumcision?” Much, in every respect—that is, for many reasons. “First, indeed”: understand, it benefited them in this respect, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them. There were Jews and gentiles believing in Christ among the Romans, but before the Lord’s coming the Jews had more than the gentiles, because the utterances of God had been entrusted to them. The meaning is this: what good did the Jew receive on account of circumcision, more than the gentile, or what greater benefit did the circumcised Jew have than the uncircumcised gentile? It benefited him greatly in every respect, because he deserved to receive the law, to receive manna from heaven, to enter a land superior to all others, and to possess kingship and priesthood. Hence the Apostle says: What benefit did they first receive, since they deserved to receive the law and the prophecy?

“What, then, did it harm”—understand, what harm was done—“if some of them did not believe? Did their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God? Certainly not.” This can be understood in three ways. What harm, he says, did it do Joshua and Caleb and the others who deserved to receive the promised land, if six hundred thousand did not believe but perished because of their unbelief? Did their unbelief and destruction nullify the faithfulness of God—that is, God’s promise—or make void what he said to Abraham: “I will give this land to you and to your offspring”? It harmed them not at all, because they themselves were not frustrated of God’s promise.

Alternatively: if some of them did not believe but died in the wilderness, did their death make void God’s promise, which he made to Abraham, saying concerning Christ: “In your offspring all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. 26)? Surely not, because some of them remained, from whose descendants Christ was afterward born.

Alternatively: although the multitude of the Jews did not believe at Christ’s coming, what had been promised to David was nevertheless not nullified: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. 131), because Christ received the seat of princely rule over those among the Jews who believed. Nor was this promise, made through the prophets, nullified: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

“But God is truthful, and every human being is a liar.” God is truthful because he fulfilled in deed what he promised them: to give them the promised land. Likewise, he completely fulfilled what he promised Abraham concerning Christ, that all the nations would be blessed in his offspring; what he promised David, that a king from the fruit of his loins would sit upon the throne of his kingdom; and what he promised through another prophet concerning the salvation of the remnant. Every human being who contradicts God’s promises is a liar; or every human being, insofar as he is from himself, is a liar, but insofar as he is truthful, he is so from God.

“As it is written: ‘So that you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.’” “May you be justified,” that is, may you be declared just and truthful in your promises and truthful in fulfilling them, while you are judged by the peoples. After David became an adulterer and a murderer by taking Uriah’s wife and having him killed by the sword of the children of Ammon, many were saying: The promise of almighty God made to David—that Christ would be born from his offspring—will be made void, because it is not fitting that Christ should be born from a murderer and adulterer; what he claimed had been promised to him will prove false. And even if Christ were born from his offspring, it would be unjust and unworthy for him to derive his origin from an evil and sinful man.

But David, on the contrary, confesses his sin, saying humbly: “Against you alone have I sinned, because I am king, and I have done evil before you” (Ps. 50), and he begs that God fulfill in deed what he promised and show those who contradict him to be liars.

Alternatively: “May you be justified” by granting pardon for sin to those who turn to you, as you promise, and “prevail” by forgiving sins when you are judged unable to forgive them.

“But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say?” There were certain less perfect people who said that God therefore wanted us to sin, so that he alone might appear just in comparison with us when he forgave our sin, and so that he might reveal himself to be merciful. For this reason, they also said that he wanted us to lie, so that he alone might be found truthful. If this were so, we would be unjustly condemned by the one who would become greater and more exalted through our evil.

The Apostle speaks against such people by assuming the role both of a foolish person and of a wise one, and he destroys their perverse opinion. If, he says, our iniquity and falsehood commend God’s justice, holiness, and truth—that is, make them praiseworthy—what shall we say? “Commendation” is sometimes used in the sense of praise, as here. Elsewhere the same Apostle says: “I ought to have been commended by you,” that is, praised.

He therefore adds: “Is God unrighteous, who inflicts wrath,” that is, punishment? The meaning is this: if our iniquity and falsehood make God praiseworthy, and if the more we sin, the more pleasing we are to him, so that he alone appears just and truthful, is God unjust in inflicting punishment for the evils that he supposedly wants us to commit? This is what the most foolish people say: If he wants us to sin, as some fools claim—a thing that it is impious even to think when they condemn the sinful person—then he is unjust, because he judges unjustly. Rather, he ought to honor the person whose iniquity makes him praiseworthy. But because this is not true, the Apostle adds:

“I speak according to human understanding,” that is, according to the understanding of the carnal human being, who is capable of thinking nothing good. He adds further: “Certainly not.” This must be joined to what came before, where he said: “Is God unrighteous, who inflicts punishment?” Certainly not—understand, no believer should think that God is unrighteous or that our iniquity makes him praiseworthy.

“Otherwise, how will God judge the world?” That is, if God wants us to be unjust, why will he judge people who, when they sin, fulfill his will, and whose iniquity makes him praiseworthy?

“For if the truth of God has abounded, through my falsehood, to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?” The meaning is this: if God appears truthful through my falsehood, and while I lie he alone is proclaimed truthful, why does he condemn and judge me as a sinner? These words are not spoken as an affirmation but rather as a denial. No one should accept as true the claim that God, who is naturally and essentially just, merciful, and truthful, is increased in praise and justice by our sin and falsehood, since he is never pleased when we sin and lie.

“And why should we not say—as we are slandered and as some unbelievers claim that we say—‘Let us do evil so that good may come’?” Their condemnation is just. Some simple and less perfect people, hearing the preaching of Paul and the other apostles, who said: “Where iniquity abounded, grace abounded all the more” (a brief statement to be explained below), received condemnation where they ought to have received salvation and life. Not understanding it correctly, they said: Let us do evil, as our apostles preach, because the greater the crimes we commit, the greater the good things we will receive and the greater our glory will be. God wants us to sin, they said, so that he may have something to forgive and thus appear just and merciful.

Against such people the Apostle brought forward this statement: Some people say that we teach these things, but we are not what we are said and slandered to be, nor do we teach what they claim we teach. Their condemnation is just if they persist in such things, hoping to receive good through evil, and especially because they form such a false opinion of us. We, however, must not say, “Let us do evil so that good may come”; rather, “We did evil, and good came to us through the grace of God; now let us do good so that better things may come.”

“What then? Are we superior to them?” Not at all. He returns again to what came before, where he says that the Jew has an advantage over the Greek. What then? Are we superior to them? That is, are we Jews ever superior to the gentiles? Not at all, because God shows no partiality; rather, in every nation whoever fears God is acceptable to him (Acts 10).

“For we have already charged both Jews and Greeks,” that is, we have shown them the case and declared that all Jews and gentiles are under sin, because the Jews were found to be sinners by transgressing the natural and written law, and the gentiles by transgressing the natural law.

“As it is written: ‘There is no one who is righteous’”—understand, righteous from himself, or among all wicked people. Among Jews and gentiles there is no one who is righteous. The same applies to the statement: “No one accepted his testimony,” although many of the elect did accept it; no one among the rejected accepted it.

“There is no one who understands God; there is no one who seeks him.” The person who understands and seeks God is the one who, knowing his will, strives to please God.

“All have turned aside,” Jews and gentiles—that is, they have withdrawn from God by not doing his will. “Together they have become worthless,” that is, they have become nothing, worshiping the creature instead of the Creator. “There is no one who does good, not even one,” that is, apart from Christ, or up to Christ. For we are accustomed to say: That field extends as far as the sea. In saying this, we do not include the sea, because the field does not enter into the sea; rather, we mean the place extending as far as the sea. Thus there is no one who does good up to Christ, that is, until he comes to him by believing, through whom faith and the ability to do good are given. Unless he comes to Christ by believing in him, he cannot otherwise accomplish a good work, as will be explained.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” This is understood particularly of the Jews, although it can also be applied to philosophers. A tomb is open for the purpose of receiving the bodies of the dead. Such are those who deceive others by their errors and persuasions and swallow others into evil, killing them in soul, like the scribes and Pharisees and the philosophers of the gentiles, whose mouths and throats were open for the purpose of killing the simpler people through their wicked teaching.

Alternatively: anyone is an open tomb who conceives and meditates upon evil with clear indications and then carries it out publicly, without any fear or shame.

“With their tongues they acted deceitfully.” The Jews acted deceitfully when they sought cunningly to deceive the Lord with their words, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Matt. 22), and so forth.

“The poison of asps is under their lips.” By biting, the asp pours out poison, which is harsher than almost all poisons. In the same way, by biting, the Jews in a certain sense poured out the poison of error and persuasion, killing their hearers in soul through speaking and flattering. Their malice was directed not only against others but also most cruelly against Christ.

He says “under their lips,” that is, in their hearts, where the seeds of malice and blasphemies are conceived and afterward brought forth by the mouth, in accordance with what the Truth says: “From the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts” (Matt. 15), and so forth.

“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.” The mouths of the Jews were full of cursing, unbelief, and perverse teaching when they said of Christ: “He has a demon” (Matt. 11), and when they cursed the blind man, saying: “You are his disciple” (John 9), and: “He is also the son of a craftsman and a Samaritan” (Matt. 13; John 11), and so forth. With such words they provoked God to bitterness.

Or, if we apply “bitterness” to the Lord’s passion, the mouths of the Jews were filled with bitterness when they cried out: “Crucify him, crucify him; he is guilty of death” (John 19; Matt. 26).

“Their feet were swift to shed blood,” because they were always ready to shed the blood of prophets and righteous people. They killed not only servants, such as Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Zechariah, but also the Lord of the prophets. Therefore, because they did this, there came upon them:

“Destruction,” that is, affliction from the Romans, which they endured in their bodies, “and misery in their ways,” that is, the wretchedness they suffered in body and soul on account of their ways, meaning their evil actions.

“And they did not know the way of peace,” that is, the mediator between God and human beings, who brought peace to the world and said, “I am the way” (John 14). They did not recognize him in order to believe in him, ignorant that he had come so that through his passion he might reconcile them to God the Father.

Or he calls the way of peace an action of justice: they did not choose to act justly, so as to perform fitting repentance, through which we are reconciled to God the Father, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Repent; the kingdom of heaven will draw near to you” (Matt. 3).

“There is no fear of God before their eyes.” The person who always keeps the fear of God before the eyes of his mind considers God and his Lord to be present and everywhere. Recalling his presence, he fears to sin and therefore never offends him. But because the Jews did not keep this fear before their eyes, they offended him.

“Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law.” The law is generally called the Old Testament. At times, however, it is divided into three, as in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24). At other times it is divided into two, as in the statement: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16), that is, until Christ, to whom John bears witness.

Sometimes the Psalms are called the law. Thus the Lord said: “Is it not written in your law: ‘I said, You are gods’?” (John 10). And elsewhere: “So that the word written in their law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause’” (John 15). In the same way, here the Apostle calls the Psalms the law, in which it had been foretold concerning the Jews: “The fool said”—that is, the Jewish people, seeing Christ present in the flesh—“There is no God” (Ps. 52).

Therefore, to show that what he said above from the Psalm properly concerns the Jews, who boasted of the nobility of their race and the merits of their life, as though they themselves had neither killed nor condemned Christ but were observers of the commandments of the law, on account of which they wished to place themselves above the gentiles, the Apostle said: “We know that whatever the law”—that is, the Psalms in this passage—“speaks, it speaks to those who are under the law,” that is, to the Jews who possess the law. Therefore the Jews should not glory in their own righteousness or place themselves above the gentiles; rather, recognizing themselves to be guilty, they should subject themselves to God, by whose grace they were called, just as the gentiles, who truly are transgressors of the written and natural law.

It is as though the Apostle said: O Jews, do not glory; do not exalt yourselves against the gentiles, because what I have said from the Psalm applies especially to you. For the law speaks to you, to whom it was specifically given.

“So that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God.” In other words, the law of the Psalms said, “There is no one who is righteous; there is no one who does good,” so that the mouths of Jews and gentiles alike might be closed, so that no one could boast that he had been saved by his own merits and not by the grace of God, since all were found to be sinners and were saved by God’s grace, not by their own merits.

The whole world ought to be subject to God by acknowledging its guilt and seeking the medicine of salvation. Thus the law properly belongs to the Jews, but it also extends to the gentiles as to outsiders, because they said, while worshiping idols: “There is no God,” meaning no god except those whom they worshiped and revered.

“For no flesh will be justified before him by works of the law.” The law of Moses is divided in two, because it consists of mysteries and commandments. According to its mysteries and sacraments, it ceased with the coming of Christ, because Christ is the end or completion of the law. According to its commandments, however, it still remains, because they must be observed: “You shall not worship foreign gods”; “Honor your father and your mother”; and the other commandments.

Therefore, by the works of the law—that is, by carnal circumcision, observance of the Sabbath, and the legal sacrifices—after the Lord’s coming no flesh, meaning any human being or anyone living and observing these things carnally, will be justified, because all these things ceased with Christ’s coming, like a shadow.

“For the law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16). Alternatively, a work of the law is: “Honor your father and your mother.” Elsewhere it is said: “Whoever curses father or mother shall die the death.” If someone honors his parents, or does not kill, because of the punishment and vengeance threatened, and not rather because of love of God and justice, he appears righteous to human beings, since he does not commit anything deserving death. Nevertheless, before God he is not sufficiently righteous, since he is shown to fulfill God’s good command out of necessity and not out of love. Thus, although he is not justified before God, even if he appears righteous to human eyes, in the sight of the divine majesty he is considered less righteous.

Here, however, the question arises: Were Moses, Joshua, David, and many others not justified by the law? They were indeed righteous, but not by works of the law. Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the believing brothers, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they were” (Acts 15).

Therefore, just as we are now saved by the grace of God through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, so they too were saved by the same grace and through the same faith, because they believed in the Son of God whom they awaited as Savior, whom we have now received as the one who makes atonement for us.

And why were they not justified by works of the law? Because it was impossible for sin to be taken away by the blood of goats, and whoever performs righteousness and trusts in it grows proud against God. For the law did not come to remove sin but to reveal and punish it.

“For through the law comes knowledge of sin.” Was sin known before the law? And if sin was not known, why was Joseph, although unjustly, sent to prison? Was he not accused of a crime? And did his brothers not know sin when they said: “We rightly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother” (Gen. 42)?

Sin was therefore known, but it was not known how great an evil it was or what punishment it justly deserved. Thus through the law there is a greater knowledge of sin than before the law, because the law says: “You shall not kill”; “You shall not commit adultery.” Through the law the punishment for sin itself is also made known, since it shows how sin ought to be punished, saying: If someone does this or that, let him be killed.

It can also be understood in this way: there were certain evils that were not recognized as sin, such as desire, concerning which the same Apostle says: “I would not have known desire to be sin unless the law said: ‘You shall not desire.’”

But now—that is, at the Lord’s coming and in the present time—“the justice of God has been manifested apart from the law.” The justice of God has been manifested in the present time apart from the law—not only that by which God himself is just, or by which the one who is essentially justice is justified, but that with which he clothes the ungodly when, in his mercy, he makes the unbeliever faithful, the adulterer and fornicator chaste and continent, and the unjust and sinner just and a lover of virtues.

This justice has been revealed in Christ and given apart from the law, that is, apart from legal observance, because no law is now handed down for observance according to its mysteries and sacrifices. Rather, it says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16). This means: he will be righteous.

We can also understand the justice of God the Father himself, that is, the Son, by whom and through whom we are justified, because, apart from observance of the law, the Son was manifested through the works of his divinity.

“Witnessed by the law and the prophets.” The justice of baptism, by which we are justified, is witnessed by the law when it says: “In the last days the Lord will circumcise your heart,” that is, he will remove your sins and justify you through baptism (Deut. 30). It is also witnessed by the prophets when it says: “He himself will bear our iniquities, and he himself will take away our sins” (Isa. 53). And elsewhere: “I will pour clean water over you, and you will be cleansed from all your impurities” (Ezek. 36). Christ himself, who is our justice, also has testimony from the law and the prophets.

“But the justice of God,” that is, the justification by which we are justified by God, has come upon all Jews and gentiles who believe, “through faith in Jesus Christ,” by which we believe that he is the Son of God the Father. He then returns to the reason why he said that the justice of God would come upon all who believe, immediately adding:

“For there is no distinction,” that is, there is no difference between Jews and gentiles, because just as the Jews were found to be sinners, so also were the gentiles. Hence it follows:

“For all have sinned and lack the glory of God,” that is, all, Jews and gentiles alike, need forgiveness and pardon of sins, for which God must be glorified.

“Justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” He says “freely,” that is, without any preceding merits. For example, someone who comes to baptism and has never done anything good is baptized and immediately justified.
