Behold, he is justified freely by grace—that is, through the house of God—and this occurs through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, not through works of the law.

Our redemption, by which we have been redeemed and through which we are justified, is Christ’s passion. Joined to baptism, it justifies a person through faith, and afterward through repentance. These two are joined together so closely that one without the other cannot justify a person. For neither faith in the Lord’s passion cleanses a person without the water of baptism, except perhaps in martyrdom, which is accepted in place of baptism; nor can the water of baptism purify a person without faith in the Lord’s passion. Let them therefore be joined together, and thus they will provide complete redemption and complete cleansing.

Thus neither the Jew nor the gentile is justified by his own works, since each is a transgressor of his own law: the Jew of the natural and written law, and the gentile of the natural law. Rather, justification comes through the redemption by which Christ redeemed us with his blood and through faith, and through the water of baptism, by which whoever is reborn will be saved in life if he dies immediately. If he lives, however, he must adorn his faith with works, because faith without works is dead.

It should be noted that he says “through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” Through redemption, captives are ransomed who have been taken captive by enemies. How, then, could a human being be taken captive, since God is everywhere? He was taken captive in his mind by the devil when he subjected himself to the devil by transgressing God’s law and began to serve vices and idols. This captivity was dissolved when the mind returned to God and recognized itself as weak and him as physician; and complete redemption became evident in the shedding of Christ’s blood.

“Whom God the Father set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood.” God the Father set forth his Son—that is, decreed and appointed him—as propitiator and reconciler, so that he might make God the Father favorable and open to appeasement toward us through faith in his passion. Or he placed him openly before the eyes of all, so that he might save all who believe in him, because when we believe in him and confess that his blood was shed for us, without which we cannot be justified, we are justified completely.

“For the demonstration of his justice”—understand, before those below. “At this time,” that is, in the final age. Justice in this passage can be understood in two ways: either as Christ himself, who justifies us, or as the justice by which God the Father justifies those who believe in his Son.

God the Father therefore openly demonstrated his justice—that is, his Son—or demonstrated it because he justifies us through the shedding of his Son’s blood at this time, that is, from his coming until the end of the world. For unless he had wished to justify us, he would not have handed over his Son to death for us, although he had committed no sin.

He also appointed him to come and suffer for the remission of previous offenses, that is, original sins which we draw from our parents before we are born, or all the sins we commit before baptism.

“In the forbearance of God,” that is, to demonstrate God’s patience, because when we sin we are not immediately punished; rather, in his patience and endurance, we are awaited for repentance. If this forbearance did not come from God, the human race would have ended in the first human being through judgment.

“For the demonstration of his justice at this time”—understand, at the final time—that is, for this purpose he appointed his Son to become our propitiator, so that through him he might demonstrate his justice and the mercy by which he awaits us for repentance.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] These words appear to be redundant.]

“So that he himself may be just.” The person who grants what he promises is just. Thus God the Father promised us his Son and justification in him, and he certainly fulfilled this by sending him into the world through the mystery of the Incarnation. We are justified by faith in his passion, having been washed by the water of baptism. Hence it follows:

“And justifying the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ,” that is, any human being who has faith in Jesus Christ. He does not, however, justify that person through works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, because without faith in him we cannot be justified.

“Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded.” He addresses the Jew and confirms that no one can be justified through works of the law. It is as though he said: O Jew, who glory in your works, see that justification is impossible without faith in God. Why? Because the law of justification through sacrifices, in which you gloried, has been excluded and cast far away.

Through what law has it been excluded? He again questions the Jew, so that he may consider through what law the law in which he gloried has been excluded. He continues to ask: “By a law of works?” That is, was it excluded by a law of works, so that another law was given in its place, likewise consisting in carnal practices? No, but by the law of faith. That is, it was not excluded by a law of works but by the law of faith and the New Testament.

At the same time, it must be noted that God does not command us to be circumcised carnally but to be baptized in true faith, where all sins are freely forgiven. For when he said: “Repent; the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. 3), he did not say: Observe the law carnally.

“We conclude”—that is, we judge, define, or testify—“that a person is justified by faith in Christ, in baptism, without works of the law,” that is, without carnal observances. To conclude is properly to judge or testify; hence judges and witnesses are called arbiters.

A person is justified by faith in Christ in two ways. For example, if someone has no good works before baptism, he is justified in baptism itself. Or even afterward, apart from the works of the law—which are no longer to be observed—he is considered righteous, provided that he keeps the divine commandments.

To the Jews who boasted and said, “The true and one God is God only of the Jews, to whom he gave the law, and of whom it is said, ‘God is known in Judah,’” the Apostle says:

“Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also the God of the gentiles?” That is, did he create only the Jews, so that he might care only for them? Indeed, he is also the God of the gentiles, and much more so the God of the gentiles, since many gentiles believed in God and pleased him before the Jews were chosen in Abraham and taken into God’s portion, such as Abel, Noah, Shem, Job and his friends, and many others whom Scripture mentions or even passes over in silence.

Or he says that God is much more the God of the gentiles because far more gentiles than Jews believe in him. Jeremiah makes clear that he is the God of the gentiles when he says: “Who will not fear you, O King of the nations?” (Jer. 10).

“For there is one God who will justify the circumcised by faith”—and not by works—those called from the Jews, namely, those who are called circumcised because of Abraham, who first received circumcision and from whose stock they descended.

“And the uncircumcised through faith,” that is, the believers from the gentiles, whom the Jews called uncircumcised. What he says “from faith” means the same as “through faith,” because the Apostle often changes the prepositions while retaining one meaning.

Therefore, “Do we overthrow the law of the commandments”—understand, the law that says, “You shall love the Lord your God,” and, “Hear, Israel: the Lord is one”—through faith and through the New Testament? Certainly not. Here the Apostle guards against the Jews’ interpretation.

Rather, “we establish the law”—understand, the law of the commandments—that is, we confirm it, praise it, and declare that it was given by God. Or we establish the whole law in general as holy, because it was given by God and was to be observed in its own times, although it has now ceased in its mysteries and remains in its commandments.

Or we establish it through faith because whatever it promised concerning Christ, we confirm as true and fulfilled, and we believe in the one whom it promised. Such is the statement: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. 18). And again: “A ruler will not fail from Judah until the one who is to be sent comes, and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49), in whom the gentiles now believe.

## CHAPTER IV

“What shall we say, then? What did Abraham our father find according to the flesh?” That is, what good did Abraham gain on account of carnal circumcision? Nothing. For he was not yet circumcised when he pleased God and deserved to hear: “Go out from your land, and I will make you into a great nation” (Gen. 12), and, what was greater, concerning Christ: “In your offspring all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22).

“For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God.” Some manuscripts read “by works of the law,” but this is written falsely. For the law had not yet been given, unless perhaps it is to be understood as referring to works of the law given later.

The meaning is this: if Abraham was justified by his own works, without faith and without the preceding grace of God, he would indeed have glory and praise before himself in the present age and before human beings, because he himself had been righteous; but before God he is not and will not be praiseworthy.

Why? Because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Abraham would therefore have had glory and praise in himself and before human beings on account of his works if he had been justified by his works without faith, like that Pharisee who went up into the temple with the tax collector and boasted.

Abraham’s work was circumcision. Certainly, it was given as a sign of his great faith. Yet before he was circumcised, he had already been chosen by God. Therefore he was not justified by works but through faith. Hence Scripture does not recount his works but his faith. It continues:

“What does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God,’” obeying his commands, because he went out from his land; and he believed God’s promise concerning Isaac and Christ, when God said to him: “In your offspring all the nations will be blessed.”

“And because he believed God, it was reckoned to him as righteousness,” that is, as the remission of sins, because through the very faith by which he believed he became righteous, and afterward received circumcision as a sign of the righteousness by which he had been justified through faith.

But to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to what is owed. He takes an example from human custom: when we give payment to those who have worked, according to their merit, they show us no gratitude; but if we give some benefit to those who have not worked, it is not payment but grace, and therefore we receive their thanks. The meaning is this: if Abraham could have been justified on account of his works without the preceding grace of God and without faith—which too was freely bestowed [Col. 0395A]—the reward of his justification would not have been freely given to him but would have been owed to him. Or, if the other Jews had been justified by their works, they would have had no reason to give thanks to God; and therefore Christ’s passion would have been superfluous, that is, without cause.

But to the one who does not perform the works of the Law—understand, the Gentile—but believes in him, that is, in God, who justifies the ungodly not through works but through faith, and who, without preceding merits, makes a godly and righteous person out of one who was ungodly and sinful—to such a person faith is reckoned as righteousness, that is, as remission, according to the purpose of God’s grace; that is, according to the decree of God’s justice and mercy, by which he decreed freely to forgive sins.

This is to be understood of the Gentiles who, before faith, possessed none of the works of the Law, and yet, like the Jews who were converted [Col. 0395B], are justified through faith in Christ without the works of the Law. And he rightly says “according to the purpose,” or decree, “of God’s grace,” because before the foundation of the world, when humanity did not yet exist, God the Father, together with his Son, decreed to save the human race without any preceding merits. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians I).

Therefore, wishing to demonstrate the righteousness—that is, the justification—by which people are justified without the works of the Law and their own merits, the Apostle adduces the testimony of the Psalm, in which it was proclaimed that at Christ’s coming the Gentiles too would be saved through faith. For he says: “As David also speaks of the blessedness of the person,” implicitly describing the person to whom God willingly grants righteousness, or justification, without the works of the Law. When he says “willingly grants,” he uses the expression adverbially: “willingly grants,” that is, freely bestows. Or it may be joined with the implied wording in this way: to the one whom he regards as acceptable to himself—that is, whom he has chosen and loves—he grants righteousness.

We may also understand it in a third way. For “to whom God willingly grants righteousness” is an unusual mode of expression, meaning: to whom God gives righteousness as acceptable, or whom he regards as acceptable without the works of the Law.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven”—that is, all their sins in baptism—and whose sins have been covered through repentance after baptism. A covered and concealed thing is not seen; and we cover sins when we place good works of righteousness over evil ones, namely, when we perform worthy repentance for past deeds and do not commit other such deeds. According to certain authorities, this is the distinction between iniquity and sin: iniquity belongs to the time before the Law, whereas sin belongs to the time after the Law; or iniquity belongs to thoughts, whereas sin is a deed. Some also say that iniquity is what is committed against the Law, while sin is what is committed against nature and conscience. But the one term is often used indiscriminately for the other.

“Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin.” In his mercy, God will not reckon against him sins erased in baptism, nor sins removed through repentance, provided he remains steadfast in faith. Or this may be understood of martyrs who were baptized in their own blood, for all their sins were forgiven in martyrdom itself. Certainly it may also be understood of those who committed many sins after baptism but, when the opportunity came and they endured martyrdom for Christ’s name, had their sins forgiven in that very martyrdom [Col. 0396A], since they underwent bodily repentance.

Does this blessedness, then, of which the Psalmist speaks, remain only in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision? That is, does it pertain only to the Jews, represented by circumcision, or also to the Gentiles, represented by uncircumcision? That blessedness by which sins are freely forgiven without the works of the Law—in baptism, through repentance, and through martyrdom—pertains both to Jews who come to faith and to Gentiles. By this grace Abraham, although he had not been baptized, was nevertheless justified through faith while he was still in uncircumcision. Hence the Apostle adds: “We say, then, that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness,” not circumcision. That is, we apostles affirm that he deserved to be justified not on account of bodily circumcision [Col. 0396B], but on account of the faith he possessed, by which he believed God.

How, then, was it reckoned to Abraham? Was faith reckoned as righteousness in circumcision or in uncircumcision? That is: was faith reckoned to him as righteousness after he had been circumcised, or while he was still an uncircumcised Gentile? The Apostle answers himself: “Not in circumcision but in uncircumcision.” That is, faith was reckoned to him as righteousness not after he had received circumcision but while he was still in uncircumcision, that is, among the Gentiles, because he had not yet been circumcised. Therefore he was justified through faith before he was circumcised.

“And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith that he had in uncircumcision.” Lest the Jews say that Abraham had been circumcised uselessly if he had not been justified through circumcision, he shows that circumcision was a sign of righteousness, not an increase of it, and that it signified the righteousness of Christ, which comes from faith. A sign exists when one thing is understood through what is seen, as the Lord makes clear when he says: “This generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matthew XII): “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth.”

Here it is clear that Jonah, having been swallowed, was a sign. In the same way, Abraham’s circumcision signified the faith he held in his heart and through which he deserved to be justified. This circumcision is the stripping away of unbelief and the abolition of vices.

There is, however, a difference between a sign and a seal. A sign is one thing that signifies another; a seal, on the other hand, is impressed upon something so that it remains concealed until it is opened by the one who impressed it [Col. 0396D]. Thus that circumcision signified the righteousness of faith that was in Abraham; and concealed within that seal was the true circumcision by which Christ—who was to be born from Abraham’s line—would circumcise his faithful from all the filth of sins through the grace of baptism, and on the day of judgment would cleanse them from all the frailty of mortality and the dregs of corruption.

Because it was performed on the eighth day, it also signified the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the eighth day. Christ himself was also signified by the stone knife with which circumcision was performed.

Moreover, circumcision was given as a sign to the Jews so that their lineage might be recognized and not confused through intermarriage while they lived among many nations, or when they were led captive among many peoples and it might otherwise be unknown that Christ would descend from Abraham’s line. It remained in type and figure until it was truly fulfilled at Christ’s coming, when the seal under which it had been hidden—that is, the same bodily circumcision—was completely removed.

Circumcision was also a sign for those same Jews so that, when they were defeated in battles with others and left naked, they could be recognized by the sign of circumcision and committed to burial.

Thus he received the sign of circumcision for the reasons we have mentioned. Circumcision was the seal of the righteousness of faith that is in uncircumcision, because he was justified through faith before he was circumcised. It is also called the righteousness of faith because he first possessed faith and through it obtained righteousness, since he was justified and cleansed from all sins. For while he was among the Gentiles, that is, while he was in uncircumcision, he was justified through faith.

And he gives the reason for this: so that he might be the father of all who believe while in uncircumcision. Through the faith he possessed in uncircumcision, he is the father of all believers, both Jews and Gentiles. By the flesh he is the father of unbelieving Jews, but by faith he is the father of all believing Jews and Gentiles, because believers retain, as if by paternal inheritance, the faith by which Abraham believed that God was almighty, that he possessed distinction of persons in the Trinity, and unity in substance.

And why are all believers sons of Abraham through faith? So that the same faith might be reckoned to them as righteousness, or justification, just as it was reckoned to Abraham while he was still among the Gentiles [Col. 0397C]. For just as Abraham possessed faith before he was circumcised, through which he became the father of believers, and afterward begot Isaac, through whom he became the father of the Jews, so he is rather the father of spiritual than of carnal descendants; and thus it came about that he became the father of the Gentiles through faith.

“And the father of circumcision,” that is, of believing and unbelieving Jews according to the flesh—not only of those who are from circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had in uncircumcision.

It is as though he said in other words: Abraham is not only the father of those Jews, or is faith not only reckoned to their justification, who descended from his offspring after he received circumcision; he is also the father of those Gentiles who imitate the examples of the faith that our father Abraham had in uncircumcision. Abraham is their father, and his faith is reckoned to the justification of those who imitate the example of his faith, which was given to him while he was still among the Gentiles, a state called uncircumcision.

“For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring”—that is, to Christ—“that he would be heir of the world” was not given through the Law, but through the righteousness of faith that he possessed before he was circumcised and before he received that promise.

The promise to Abraham was not made or given through the Law—the promise in which it was said to him, “I have appointed you the father of many nations,” and “In your offspring all nations will be blessed” (Genesis XXII)—because the Law did not yet exist; it was given four hundred and thirty years later. Abraham, therefore, is heir of the world in Christ, because all believers are sons of Abraham through faith; and in Christ he possesses all things, to whom the Father said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm II).

“For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished,” that is: if only those Jews who are of circumcision and possess the Law are heirs of the promise made to Abraham concerning Christ, and not the Gentiles as well, then the faith by which Abraham himself believed God has been nullified, and the promise concerning Christ has been abolished and erased.

The meaning is this: if you Jews alone, as circumcised people, are heirs of God’s promise, as you wish, then God has not fulfilled the promise he gave to Abraham, that he would be the father of many nations. And if that is so, it will now appear that he believed God in vain. The promise, therefore, was not given to Abraham through the Law but through faith. Why?

“For the Law produces wrath,” that is, God’s vengeance. The Law did not give that promise to Abraham; rather, it produces vengeance when it says: “A tooth for a tooth,” and “Whoever kills shall be killed.”

“But where there is no Law, there is no transgression”—understand, no transgression of such magnitude, or it is not reckoned in the same way. This may be understood in two ways.

First, where there is no natural law, there is not so great a transgression of that law. For example, as long as understanding, or the natural law’s capacity to distinguish between good and evil, is not active in infants, even if they strike their father, beat their mother, or curse their parents, their transgression is not so great, nor is it reckoned against them in the same way as it is afterward, when they have reached the lawful age and natural understanding has begun to operate in them.

Alternatively, where there is no Law of Moses, even if someone sins, the transgression is not so great [Col. 0398C], nor is it reckoned against the person who does not possess that Law in the same way if he sins, because he is not its transgressor as is the one to whom it was given for observance. Therefore, where the precepts of the Law exist, there is an occasion for transgression; where there is transgression, there is greater wrath and vengeance from God against the transgressor.

It may also be understood in a third way: where there is no Law of the Gospel, as among pagans, the transgression is not so great. Yet they were not thereby immune from God’s vengeance, because through creation they could have recognized the Creator.

“Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all Abraham’s offspring.” The meaning, then, is this: because transgression is not as great among the Gentiles, where there is no Law of Moses, as among the Jews, therefore all believing Jews and Gentiles are justified from faith and through faith [Col. 0398D], and through faith they are heirs, not through the Law, so that the promise God freely made according to grace—not according to merit and not according to the Law—might remain firm for all Abraham’s offspring, not only those from the Jews but also those from the Gentiles.

What promise is this? “All nations will be blessed in you” (Genesis XXII), he says, and “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Genesis XVII). Hence he continues: “Not only for the one who is of the Law, but also for the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all.”

The meaning is this: the promise made to Abraham concerning Christ—that all nations would be blessed in his offspring—was not confirmed only to that Jew who descended from the Law of circumcision, but was also confirmed to the Gentile who, through faith, is a son of Abraham, who is the father of all believers.

“As it is written in the Law of Moses: ‘I have appointed you the father of many nations,’ before the God in whom you believed” (Genesis XVII).

Here the pride of the Jews is struck down, for they glory in having descended from Abraham’s offspring. He does not say, “I have appointed you the father of the one Israelite nation,” but “I have appointed you the father of all nations through faith.” For by the flesh he is the father of the Jews, but by faith he is the father of all nations.

The Apostle rightly adds, in his own interpretation, “before the God in whom you believed,” that is, before the God in whom you believed in your heart. For many appear to believe in God but do not believe before God. Those do not believe before God who confess in words that they believe in God but hold something else in their hearts. Those truly believe before God who love him with their whole soul, their whole heart, and their whole strength, like Abraham, and who preserve faith in the inner person before God’s sight rather than in the display of human beings, as is the case with bodily circumcision.

“He who gives life to the dead” through his faith and grace—that is, to the Gentiles and to all who are dead through unbelief in sins. For the righteous lives through faith, while the sinner dies through unbelief. Or perhaps he says “gives life” in the present tense in place of the future: “he will give life.” For he will raise, or give life to, the dead on the day of judgment, as he says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth, those who have done good to the resurrection of life” (John V).

“And he calls into existence the things that do not exist as though they did.” God almighty alone possesses being essentially; those who cling to him through faith and love possess being from him, and they exist, as he himself said: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus III). By contrast, those who do not cling to him, in comparison with him, are as though they did not exist. Hence the prophet Isaiah said: “All nations are as nothing before him; they are regarded by him as nothing and vanity” (Isaiah XL).

According to this meaning, the Apostle says here: just as he called Abraham, who existed because he clung to God through faith, saying, “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Genesis XII), so he calls those things that do not exist; that is, he calls unbelieving Gentiles to faith so that they may have being by clinging to him—those who previously did not exist because they did not cling to him.

“He believed in hope against hope, so that he might become the father of many nations through faith.” Against the hope of offspring, which had been despaired of, he believed in the hope of offspring that was to be hoped for. Or certainly, against the hope of nature he believed in the hope of God’s grace and power. For it was against the hope of nature that an old woman should give birth, she who had remained sterile even when she was young and in the prime of life.

Nature dictates that a young man joined to a young woman should beget children. Similarly, it is natural that an old man joined to a young woman should beget children, as with Abraham, the old man, and Hagar, the young woman, from whom Ishmael was born. But it is against the hope of nature that an old man united with an old woman should beget a child.

Abraham, however, did not attend to the ordinary course of nature, namely, that a son could not be begotten from himself and Sarah, who were already old. Instead, he believed in the hope of God’s power, because he knew that the one who had promised was almighty.

It should be considered that, as blessed Ambrose says, there are four causes that make women sterile: either the male seed does not reach the place of conception; or the woman is unable to retain it; or she lacks the power to prepare it; or the two partners are both old and are burdened by old age. Accordingly it was said to him: “So shall your offspring be, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.”

In this passage Abraham’s offspring is understood to mean both the multitude of the Jews, whose father he is by flesh and by faith, and the multitude of all nations, whose father he is solely by faith. This was said hyperbolically, that is, through a trope exceeding belief. For although Abraham’s offspring cannot be numbered by human beings because of its multitude, it can nevertheless be numbered by God.

It should also be noted that, according to one teacher, the stars and the sand are to be understood generally as all Abraham’s offspring: namely, believers from the Gentiles and from the Jews, and the whole of Israel. According to another, the stars signify only the elect from both peoples, while the sand signifies all unbelieving and faithless Jews, weighed down by the burden of their sins.

Nor is it inappropriate that the elect are represented by the stars, which cling to heaven and illuminate the world with their brightness: they always desire heavenly things, saying with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III), and they mock the world by their words and examples. The reprobate, however, are represented by the sand, which is heavy and barren, because weighed down by the burden of sins they are barren of good works.

[Col. 0400C] “And he did not grow weak in faith.” The person who doubts and does not believe God’s promises grows weak in faith. But Abraham, hearing God say, “I have appointed you the father of many nations,” and, “At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son” (Romans IX), did not grow weak in faith. Although what was promised appeared contrary to the course of nature, he did not doubt the promise.

Faith considers nothing belonging to nature, because in what God promises, nature readily serves its author. Nor did Abraham consider his own body, which was dead with respect to begetting children, since he was already almost a hundred years old—for he was a centenarian—nor did he consider Sarah’s dead womb.

Abraham and Sarah are called “dead” with respect to begetting children because of the great number of their years, and because all hope had already been abandoned. Abraham was a hundred years old and Sarah ninety when God promised, saying through the Gospel: “At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.”

Sarah’s womb was dead because the time for bearing had already passed and her womanly functions had ceased—that is, she had ceased to menstruate. The power of conception resides especially in this; when it ceases in women, the time for bearing children has passed. Abraham, however, did not attend to the course of nature but to God’s power, believing his promises. Hence it follows:

“He did not waver through unbelief at the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God.” At God’s promise, of which we spoke above—whether concerning Isaac or concerning Christ—he did not waver through unbelief, that is, he did not doubt through lack of faith. Rather, he was strengthened in faith concerning the promises, giving glory to God by offering thanks for his promises as though for benefits already received. He understood that the gift and grace belonged to God alone, since the ordinary operation of human fertility and nature had ceased.

“Fully, or most certainly, convinced that whatever God has promised, he is able to accomplish.” Therefore, understand: because he believed God concerning the promises, his faith was reckoned to him as righteousness.

Now it was not written only for his sake, that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, but also for our sake, to whom it will be reckoned if we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead. It was not written, he says, merely for this reason: that Abraham’s faith might be read by Abraham himself, who had long since died when Moses wrote these things. It was written for us and for our benefit, so that we might imitate his faith. His faith is reckoned as righteousness to us who believe in him—that is, in God the Father—who raised Jesus Christ from the dead, that is, from the tomb, which is the proper place of the dead, or certainly from the underworld.

If we believe with equal completeness that Christ rose from the dead, just as Abraham believed that Sarah’s dead body could be given life for conception, and if we believe in God the Father who raised Christ from the dead, our faith will be reckoned as justification, because we will receive forgiveness of all sins.

God the Father raised his Son from the dead, and the Son himself also raised himself. To speak more profoundly, the whole Trinity raised that man whom the Word of God had assumed from the dead.

“Who was delivered up for our trespasses and rose for our justification.”

The Lord Jesus Christ is read as having been delivered up in many ways. God the Father delivered him up, as the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans VIII). The Son himself delivered himself up, as the outstanding preacher says in the present passage, and elsewhere: “He loved me and delivered himself up for me” (Galatians II).

The demons delivered him up: they persuaded Judas to hand him over. Hence the Evangelist says that Satan entered Judas’s heart so that he might hand him over (John XIII). The Apostle makes this clear when speaking of the demons: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians II).

Judas delivered him up for thirty pieces of silver. The Jews delivered him up to Pilate. Pilate in turn delivered him up to the soldiers, who crucified him [Col. 0401D]. Amid all these events, however, we must carefully consider that what God the Father and the Son did out of love and mercy, Judas did out of greed, while the demons, the Jews, and Pilate did it out of envy.

“He was delivered up for our trespasses and rose for our justification,” so that, by believing that he suffered for our salvation and truly rose from the dead, we might through this faith deserve to be justified. In Christ’s being delivered up, ineffable mercy was manifested; in his resurrection, the incomprehensible power of the divinity was also demonstrated, and so forth.

## CHAPTER V

“Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God” [Col. 0402A] “through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

While Jews and Gentiles were disputing among themselves—the former presumptuously boasting of the works of the ancient Law, the latter of the new calling of Christ—the matter had been examined and clarified: none of them had been justified by his own merit, but all had been justified by grace, which infuses faith and reveals the truth. Moreover, neither ancestry nor circumcision makes people sons of Abraham, but the right faith by which Abraham shone, illuminated and preceded by God.

The Apostle therefore immediately adds: “Having been justified by faith”—and not by the works of the Law, nor by any merit of ours that preceded faith—“let us have peace with God the Father through our mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ.” Through his passion we have been reconciled to God the Father, just as the angels sang at his birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

We have peace with God if we maintain peace and fraternal concord among ourselves. It is as though he said: Since we have been reconciled through the blood of the Son of God and have peace with God the Father, let us also have peace among ourselves, presuming on nothing in ourselves, since we possess everything through the faith of God:

“Through whom we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand.” Through Christ, he says, he reconciled us to God the Father. Through him we have access and entrance, through his faith, into this grace in which we stand by believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

In this passage he calls faith “grace,” through which we freely received from God the fullness of justification at the time of baptism. In addition, whatever spiritual gifts we possess are included here under the name of grace. Into this grace, or toward this grace, we have entrance and access through him, although previously we were far away. For he is the door, as he said: “I am the door” (John X), and “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV).

In this grace—that is, in the faith of justification and the forgiveness of sins—we must stand, laboring courageously in good works. Previously we lay in the mud and stench of vices; now we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. In the present age we are children of God in hope; in the other life we shall be so in reality, if death finds us engaged in good works. Hence John says: “Beloved, we are children of God in hope, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be in reality” (1 John III).

[Col. 0402D] “And not only this”—understand, not only do we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God—“but we also glory in tribulations,” that is, in the distresses and adversities of persecutions endured for Christ. We know that tribulation and affliction produce patience in the elect, who patiently bear the adversities of this age.

The word “patience” comes from *pati*, “to suffer,” that is, “to be struck.” Patience exists when body and spirit are struck by fear and the affliction of torments, but vengeance is not sought. Through this the holy martyrs overcame persecution and the savagery of tyrants, not returning injury for injury but preserving patience, or endurance.

“Patience produces testing”—of merits and of faith—as the holy martyrs were tested, and as Job was tested, not failing in tribulation. Testing also consists in honorable conduct and praiseworthy actions; hence *probus* means one worthy of praise. Testing produces the hope of eternal life. Hope is the expectation of future goods. Those who, amid tribulations and adversities, prove worthy through patience in faith therefore await future blessedness, secure of their rewards.

“Hope does not disappoint.” Hope, or expectation of future goods, drives away all confusion and shame belonging to this age. Hope therefore does not disappoint: the person who has been tested in faith and good works and possesses hope of eternal rewards does not blush at whatever adversity he has endured in this age, being secure of his reward.

And why is this so? Because the charity of God—by which God loves us, or by which we love God—has been poured into our hearts at the time of baptism and at the time of the laying on of hands, through the Holy Spirit who was given to us not on account of our merit.

The word “pouring” or “diffusion” signifies the abundance of gifts, as it is written in Joel: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II). Thus it may mean the charity by which we love God, which is in us and for whose sake we patiently endure every adversity; or it may mean the charity by which we love our neighbor; or whatever good exists in us. None of these is granted to us on account of our merit, but through the grace of God, with the Holy Spirit cooperating.

Therefore, having received these gifts, we ought to obey his will and have among ourselves the peace that he commended to his disciples, saying: “I leave you peace” (John XIV). Hope itself is also given to us through the Holy Spirit, who makes us believe what God promises. Hope does not disappoint us because he will give us more than we hope for: namely, the joys of the heavenly homeland.

“For why, when we were still weak, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time?” Why did Christ, when we were still weak—that is, sinners—die at the appointed time for the ungodly, that is, for the irreligious, unless it was to commend to us the abundance and fullness of his charity, as the following words make clear?

Every sinner and every unbeliever is weak; the righteous, the faithful, and the person who knows God are strong. Piety is the worship and religion of God, from which comes *pius*, “pious,” that is, religious. In contrast, impiety is irreligion, from which comes *impius*, “ungodly,” that is, irreligious.

Christ’s charity was so great that he died not only for those who, in comparison with the reprobate, were religious, but also for the ungodly, whom he afterward made righteous through his faith. He commended this charity to us so that we might imitate it, as he said to his disciples when he washed their feet: “I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also should do” (John XIII). That is: just as I have washed your feet, so should you wash one another’s; and just as I do not hesitate to lay down my life for you, so you too should not hesitate, whether for me or for your brothers, to lay down your lives if necessity arises for the sake of my love.

When the Apostle says that Christ died “at the appointed time,” this may be understood in three ways. Blessed Ambrose explains it as follows: he died “at the appointed time” because he could be held by death only for a short and brief period, since he rose on the third day.

Alternatively, he died “at the appointed time,” that is, at the time when the whole world was held under sin. Concerning that time the Apostle says elsewhere: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law” (Galatians IV). And God the Father says to the Son through the prophet: “At an acceptable time I heard you” (Isaiah XLIX).

It may also be understood in a third way: he died “at the appointed time,” that is, bodily and in the body, not in the soul, because he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth. Time is said to exist wherever there is some change. For example, where the sun rises and sets, where the moon waxes and wanes, time is said to exist; likewise where spring passes into summer, summer changes into autumn, and autumn in turn into winter.

Christ died “at the appointed time,” that is, according to the flesh, which is changeable and subject to variation; he died temporally. For where eternity is, time cannot exist.

“For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might even dare to die for a good person.” The implied meaning is either “no one” or “only rarely.” The word “who” is often used in place of “no one” or “rarely.” It means “no one” in the Psalms: “O God, who will be like you?” (Psalm LXXXII), that is, no one. It means “rarely” here and elsewhere, where it says: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Psalm CVI), because such a person is rarely found.

The meaning is this: scarcely can anyone be found who would dare to die not only for the ungodly, but even, in word, for the righteous and good. And although someone who would dare to die for the righteous and good is rarely found, Christ died for the ungodly.

There is this difference between the righteous and the good: the righteous person is so through zeal and the practice of the virtues, as are the holy martyrs; the good person is so through innocence, as are infants who are washed in baptism. It is also possible to understand “righteous and good” as referring to one person.

God commends his love in us, because, while we were still sinners—that is, before we were justified by faith—Christ died for us at the appointed time. Why does God commend his love in us? So that we may imitate it in the manner explained above. Much more, therefore, now justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath [Col. 0404D]. If, while we were sinners, Christ deigned to die for us, much more, now that we have received the forgiveness of sins through the blood of his passion and have been justified by faith, shall we be saved through Christ from wrath—that is, from the vengeance of the day of judgment which is to come upon the reprobate. Although we read in many places that almighty God has wrath, we must not suppose that any disturbance falls upon him, because he always remains the same, as the Psalmist says: “You are always the same” (Ps. 101). His wrath, rather, is called his vengeance and retribution, which he exercises without any change in himself, in accordance with what the most wise speaker says to him: “But you, Lord Sabaoth, judge with [Col. 0405A] tranquillity” (Wis. 12).

At this point blessed Augustine raises the following question: “If,” he says, “we received the forgiveness of sins in the blood of the passion of the Son of God, it is not necessary that we be baptized; and if we received forgiveness in baptism and are cleansed from every stain of vice, why was it necessary for Christ to suffer?” He resolves the question in this way: These two things—namely, Christ’s passion and baptism—are so joined together that baptism cannot wash away sins or make a person perfect without faith in Christ’s passion, since “without faith it is impossible to please God”; nor can faith in Christ’s passion grant forgiveness of sins without the grace of baptism, unless a person has been baptized in the blood of his martyrdom, because the Lord said: “Unless someone has been born again of water [Col. 0405B] and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. He says: If, while we were enemies—that is, sinners—we were reconciled to God the Father through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled as we deserved and restored to friendship, shall we be saved in his life—that is, in the life of Christ, who is life and in whom we shall possess eternal life. Those who are enemies of one another are reconciled to one another. How, then, did almighty God become angry with us and our enemy, when it is said of him that he hates nothing that he has made? We must understand that he did not hate our nature, which he himself made holy and good, but the vices and sins that we ourselves [Col. 0405C] drew upon us. Therefore, by a certain justice of God, we were handed over to the devil as long as we remained under sin.

Thus, after humanity deserved to hear, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go”—that is, “You have become wholly earthly, and therefore you shall die”—it is read that God also said to the devil in the serpent: “You shall eat earth,” that is, “You shall devour sinners.” When the vices and sins had been taken away, through the passion of his Son we were reconciled to what we had been before. Hence the Apostle says: “If,” he says, “while we were enemies of God in our actions, though not by nature, we were saved through the death of Christ, how much more shall we be glorified in his life [Col. 0405D], if we imitate it.”

Not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. He says: We shall not only be saved and be given eternal life, but we also glory in God the Father—or in the knowledge of God, which we possess through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whose passion we have now received reconciliation. “Now,” he says, “we have been reconciled to God the Father,” that is, at the time of Christ’s coming. For just as we were created by the Word of the Father, according to what John says, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1), so also we were redeemed by him and reconciled to God the Father.

Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned. The defective wording at this point is of the following kind [Col. 0406A]: “Just as through Adam sin and death entered, so through Christ justification and eternal life came.” Therefore, the Apostle says, we have been reconciled to God, because just as through one man, Adam, sin entered this world—that is, the whole human race, except Christ, who is from above—and through sin death came, so also bodily and spiritual death passed to all human beings, just as it did to that first man, in whom all sinned. In the same way, through our Lord Jesus Christ justification entered, and through justification the life to come.

The meaning is this: Just as through Adam sin and death entered the human race and passed through all, so through Christ justification and life came. All also sinned in Adam, who were in his loins, just as Levi was in the loins [Col. 0406B] of his father when he was tithed (Heb. 7). He appropriately says that sin entered first and that death then entered through sin, because as soon as Adam sinned he became mortal, just as God had foretold to him: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.” He sinned by desiring and eating, and he became mortal through sinning.

For until the law, sin was in the world. He does not say “until the time when the law was given,” but “until the end of the law that was to be completed.” For this is how we are accustomed to speak: “The Huns ruled until King Attalus [F. Attila],” that is, until the death of King Attalus. Until that time—that is, until the end of the law and the beginning of grace—original and actual sin was in the world. Through the grace of Jesus Christ, however, not only original sins [Col. 0406C] but also actual sins were removed.

But sin was not reckoned when there was no law. This can be understood in three ways. As long as the natural law is not present in a person, as in infants, whatever an infant does is not reckoned as sin, because the infant does not know what is good or evil. Alternatively: Before the law was given, sin was not recognized as such a grave evil as it was shown to be through the law. Or otherwise: When the law was absent, sin was not reckoned—that is, it was not known what punishment sin deserved—until the law itself said: “Whoever does this or that shall die.”

But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression. That is, death is the same as sin; therefore he says that death reigned, because death held the whole world, both the death of sin and [Col. 0406D] bodily death. What he says about “until Moses” must be understood as we have already explained: until the end of the law and the beginning of grace. For Moses signifies the law, as it is said in the Gospel to the rich man: “They have Moses,” that is, the law. And elsewhere: “Beginning from Moses” (Luke 27), that is, from the law.

Death of the soul, he says, reigned throughout the world from the time when the first man sinned until the end of the law of Moses and the beginning of the Gospel—not only over others, but also over those who sinned neither willingly nor knowingly, such as infants, who were held liable for original sins. Those sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression who sin knowingly and willingly, like the one to whom God said: “Eat from every tree of paradise, but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge [Col. 0407A] of good and evil,” and so forth (Gen. 2). But the one who possesses neither the natural law nor sins deliberately does not sin in Adam’s likeness.

Who is the form of the one to come. This can be understood in three ways. Adam, who brought sin into the world, is an exemplar or form of the Adam who was to come, that is, of Christ, because just as the former was made from virgin earth, so Christ was born from the Virgin Mary. Or, from the opposite perspective, it is understood otherwise: Adam is the head of sin, while Christ is the head of righteousness; for just as Adam brought sin and death, so Christ brought justification and life.

Or otherwise: If we read it as some manuscripts have it, “who is a form for those to come,” the meaning will be: He is an example to his descendants in sin, because just as he became sinful and mortal, so all his descendants were and are born sinful and mortal [Col. 0407B], original sin having been transmitted to his descendants, as blessed Augustine says, through sexual desire in intercourse. Yet through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ they are freed from sin and eternal death. For just as no human being exists outside Adam—that is, outside his lineage—so no human being exists apart from his sin, except Christ.

But not as the trespass of Adam, so also the gift of justification. That is, Christ’s gift, through which the forgiveness of sins came to us, was greater than Adam’s sin, through which death came. The righteousness of Christ was more powerful in justifying than Adam’s sin was in killing, because in those who are redeemed through Christ the pattern of death from Adam has effect for a time, whereas the pattern of life through Christ will endure forever.

For if, through the trespass of one man, Adam, many [Col. 0407C]—that is, the elect—died temporarily, much more did the grace of God, through which our sins are forgiven, and the gift, in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, abound for the many. “Many” and “the more numerous” refer to the elect. Nor is there a comparison implied by his saying “the more numerous,” as though there were more reprobate who will be condemned than righteous who will be saved; the expression is simply used absolutely.

This may also be joined in the following way: If, because of the trespass of one man, Adam, not only the reprobate and exceedingly sinful but also the elect died temporarily in the body, though not in the soul, much more did the grace of God abound and increase, and the gift through the grace of Jesus Christ abound for the more numerous—that is, for the elect. In this respect grace abounded much more: the forgiveness of sins among the elect was greater than sin, because it removed not [Col. 0407D] only that original sin through which we fell into the death of soul and body, but also all actual sins among the elect, and moreover granted life that will endure without end.

And not as through one sin—understand, original sin—death came, so also the gift—understand, of grace—came. This means that Adam’s sin came in one manner and for one purpose, while Christ’s gift came in another manner and for another purpose. Adam’s sin came through disobedience in order to bring death; Christ’s gift of grace came through obedience, by which he was obedient to God the Father so as to remove not only original sin but also all actual sins.

What the trespass through the one who sinned means must be understood as follows. “And not as through one [Col. 0408A] who sinned”—that is, through Adam—“death came, so also the gift of grace came through Christ.” For judgment indeed came from one trespass to condemnation, but grace came from many trespasses to justification.

Judgment, or condemnation, came from one man, Adam, or from the one original sin, to the condemnation of all human beings. But the grace of Christ, through which our sins are freely forgiven, came to the justification of the faithful from the many trespasses that were added after original sin. The meaning is this: Condemnation came from one man, or from one original sin, for the condemnation of the human race; but the grace of Christ came to the justification of the elect from many trespasses—that is, it came for the purpose of justifying us not only from that one original sin but also from all actual sins. Therefore sin came in one way and grace in another [Col. 0408B].

It must be considered that when he says judgment came from one man to condemnation, he speaks against the Pelagians, who deny that original sin is transmitted to infants when they are born, saying that sin is not transmitted by origin but by imitation. This is altogether false. For if it were as they foolishly claim, the Lord would by no means have said explicitly in the Gospel: “If anyone is not born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). Nor would he have said in the Old Testament: “The male whose flesh has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. 17)—not on his own account, but in his father Adam in paradise.

For if, because of the trespass of one man, death reigned through that one man, much more shall those who receive the abundance of the gift of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ [Col. 0408C]. The meaning is this: If, because of the trespass of one man, Adam—which came through that one man—bodily and spiritual death reigned temporarily, and for a time even over the elect, much more shall they reign in eternal life, receiving through Jesus Christ an abundance—that is, the fullness—of grace, by which sins are forgiven, and the fullness of dominion, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit bestowed upon the elect when the word of wisdom is given to them through the Spirit and the other gifts are distributed to each individually. They also receive the fullness of righteousness, that is, all virtues, so that after the grace of baptism we may live justly and holily.

For if the elect die temporarily because of original sin, nevertheless through the grace of Christ they receive everlasting life, where they will reign with him [Col. 0408D].

Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation to death came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification to life came upon all human beings. That is, just as through the trespass of one man death and sin came generally upon all human beings for condemnation, so through the righteousness of one man, Christ, grace came upon all human beings—the elect and those predestined to eternal life—for the justification of life.

For just as through the disobedience of one man, Adam, the many—that is, the whole human race, which was in Adam’s loins—were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man, Christ, by which he was obedient to the Father [Col. 0409A] even unto death, the many will be made righteous, though not all.

But the law entered in addition so that the trespass might abound. The Jews did not understand why they had received the law, and they thought that they could be saved through circumcision and carnal observances without the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore the Apostle, wishing to show them that the law was not given to remove sins but to reveal them, said: “But the law entered in addition,” that is, it entered suddenly, “so that the trespass might abound.”

How does the trespass abound through the law? In two ways. Either because, when it commands, saying, “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20), the mind is inflamed toward lust and covetousness, whereas previously it did not know that such coveting was sin—or [Col. 0409B] in some other such way. Or because a person becomes a transgressor of the law, and the trespass increases toward punishment, since one who knowingly sins against the precepts of the law is deserving of a greater penalty and vengeance than one who, having no law, commits an offense in ignorance.

But where sin abounded, grace abounded even more. To original sin, which reached everyone, actual sins were added, and the trespass abounded or increased. But where the trespass abounded and increased through actual sins and contempt of the law, the grace of Christ abounded even more. It removed not only original sin but also actual sin, and, in its holy goodness, additionally bestowed life that will endure without end.

So that, just as sin reigned in death, so grace also might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord. It is as though he said: Just as [Col. 0409C] original sin reigned and held dominion, and actual sin was added among the elect so as to draw them into death for a time, so grace, through which sins are forgiven, may reign among the elect through their righteousness, bringing them into eternal life by the help of Jesus Christ.

In this respect the grace of Christ given to us is greater than Adam’s sin, and it benefited us more than that sin harmed us. Adam’s sin causes us to die for a time, but Christ’s grace forgives us not only original but also actual sin, and moreover makes us live unto eternal life, and so forth.

## CHAPTER VI

What shall we say, then? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means. This relates to what came before [Col. 0409D], where the Apostle says: “And let us not do evil, as some claim that we say, so that good may come”; and also: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded even more.”

Some of the Gentiles, when they heard the preaching of Paul and the other apostles, received death where they ought to have received life, because they did not understand the meaning of their preaching. Therefore they said that the apostles preached that the more a person sinned, the more he pleased God; and that where guilt was greater, there the grace of God was greater, so that, while everyone was exceedingly sinful, God alone would appear righteous; and the more serious and numerous the sins he forgave, the more he would be praised as merciful.

Therefore they said: “Let us do evil so that good may come,” because the more we sin, the greater grace we have with God [Col. 0410A]. But we ought to speak otherwise: “We did evil, and good came without any merit of ours through the grace of Christ. Let us now do good, so that good may come to us,” bearing in mind what the Apostle says while speaking in the person of the faithful, who preserve themselves from sins: “Shall we remain in sin?” That is: Shall we always sin, so that the grace of God may abound in this respect—that it may have more to forgive us and increase for us by forgiving us, as some carnal people say? By no means. Let it not happen that we remain forever in sins.

This must be weighed with careful consideration, because the Apostle contradicts these ideas for this reason: so that no unbeliever might be able to say that he himself asserts that one must sin so that the grace [Col. 0410B] of God may abound. For “we who died to sin at the time of baptism”—how shall we still live in it? That is: If all sins were forgiven us in baptism, why do we obey vices and the suggestions of the flesh? The person who has no sin is dead to sin, because all his sins have been erased in baptism. Conversely, the person who obeys the pleasures of sin and the suggestions of an evil will lives in sin.

The Apostle teaches that after we have received the forgiveness of sins in baptism, we should abstain from carnal sins and, insofar as human frailty permits, restrain ourselves by the grace of God from the pleasures of the flesh and evil thoughts.

Or do you not know, brothers, that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? [Col. 0410C] Blessed Paul speaks mystically and most subtly at this point. He wishes to show how the mystery of Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection relates to our baptism, and he says: Do you not know, O Romans, how the mystery of Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection corresponds to the mystery of baptism? Surely, I think, you do not know; and if you do not know, I shall disclose it to you.

But a question arises here. Since the Lord commands the apostles in the Gospel to baptize believers in the name of the Holy Trinity, why does the Apostle at this point assume only the person of Christ, saying: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death”? This is resolved as follows: At this point the Apostle did not intend so much to describe the rationale and institution [Col. 0410D] of baptism as the mystery of Christ’s death. Since he was about to speak of death, he considered it unfitting to introduce the person of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, who did not assume flesh or undergo death, but only the person of the Son, who assumed flesh and died for us. For it would not have been fitting for him to say: “All of us who were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit were baptized into his death.”

Again, it must be asked how we were baptized into Christ’s death. When Christ died on the cross for our sins, he was the head of all the elect; all the elect, who are his members, died together with their head, Christ, to sin. For example, just as, when the head of any living creature is removed and cut off, all its members die with it, so when Christ died, all the elect died with him [Col. 0411A], being baptized into his passion.

For his passion was our baptism. He died in the body, while we died to sin, because he died for sinners and killed our sin in his death. Alternatively: “We were baptized into his death” means into faith in his passion and death, because through faith in Christ’s passion and through the grace of baptism we are washed from sins. These two things are so joined together that neither Christ’s passion without baptism nor baptism without faith in Christ’s passion can save us.

Let us give another interpretation: “We were baptized into his death” means according to the example and pattern of his death, so that we might die with him to sin, just as he died in the body; or according to the example of his death, in the manner that will be explained below.

Meanwhile, it must be considered that there are four kinds of baptism. The first is solely in water, such as John’s baptism, which did not grant forgiveness of sins. The second is in fire or the [Col. 0411B] Spirit, with which the apostles were baptized on the day of Pentecost, and of which the Lord said: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1), because on that day he appeared in fire over the apostles. The third is in water and the Spirit, in which the holy apostles baptized at the Lord’s command; the holy Church retains this kind of baptism to the present day. The fourth is in the shedding of blood, with which the Lord himself and all the holy martyrs were baptized. Of this the Lord also said to the sons of Zebedee: “Are you able to be baptized with the baptism with which I am to be baptized?” (Mark 10)—that is [Col. 0411C], “Are you able to endure the shedding of your blood?” One of them, namely James, was baptized with that baptism, having been beheaded by Herod.

This also must be noted: in baptism there are three bodily and visible things and three incorporeal and invisible things. The three visible things are the priest, the body to be baptized, and the water. The three invisible things are faith, the soul that is washed from sins, and the Spirit, through whose cooperation the forgiveness of sins is granted.

Perhaps someone may also ask why baptism is consecrated only in water and not sometimes in wine. Blessed Ambrose answers that this is done uniformly in water so that it may be understood that just as water washes the dirt from the body or garment, so baptism washes away the stains of the soul and the filth of vices by cleansing them.

[Col. 0411D] For we were buried with him through baptism into death—understand, the death of sin and vices. How can we, while living in the flesh, be buried with Christ? If we die to sin, just as he died on the cross, and are baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, we are buried with him. But if we live in sin, we can in no way be buried with him.

Let us therefore consider how we die to sin, are buried with Christ, and rise again with him, and how the mystery of his death, burial, and resurrection corresponds to our baptism. After Christ died on the cross, he was taken down from the cross and placed in a tomb; on the third day he rose victorious from the tomb.

Similarly, when we come to the baptismal font, as we renounce the devil, all his pomp, and all his works, we die to sin, just as Christ died on the cross. Christ was taken down from the cross and placed in the tomb, while we, after confessing the Holy Trinity, are buried with him in what is related to birth—that is, in the element born together with the earth, namely, in water [Col. 0412A].

He rose alive on the third day, and we, after the threefold immersion, shall rise from the death of sins to life, so that we may live for God in holiness, goodness, and the other virtues. He ascended into heaven, and we shall ascend after him if we walk in newness of life.

And as though someone might ask the Apostle, “For what purpose were we buried with Christ?” he added: “So that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.” Christ rose from the dead—that is, from the tomb, which is properly [Col. 0412B] the place of the dead, or from the underworld.

He says that Christ rose through the glory of God the Father—that is, through the power of his divinity—so that God the Father might be glorified in Christ’s raising, just as Christ himself, speaking to the Father, said: “Father, glorify your name” (John 12), that is, “Raise your Son, so that you may be glorified through my raising.”

It may also be understood that the Son himself raised himself by the power of his divinity, for he is the glory of the Father, as the Psalm says to him: “Rise up, my glory; rise up, psaltery” (Ps. 56)—that is, the choir of all virtues. To him the Son says: “I shall rise at dawn” (ibid.).

The Son himself also speaks of his raising when he says to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I shall raise it.” This must be understood in such a way that just as the whole Trinity created that human being, so the whole Trinity raised him, because the works of the entire Trinity are inseparable [Col. 0412C].

Therefore the Apostle commands that, just as Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, so we too should walk in newness of life. That is, just as we have been made new in baptism, so we should always live as new and undefiled people, going from virtue to virtue.

For the newness of life consists in not committing grave sins after baptism and, insofar as possible, abstaining from lesser sins. Through this newness the elect are renewed daily as they advance in virtue, and almighty God is praised in their works, as God says: “Let your good works be seen, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death—that is, of Christ’s death—we shall also be so in his resurrection [Col. 0412D]. Understand “planted together” as joined and conformed. Some manuscripts have the genitive case, “of the resurrection,” but it is better, as the teachers say, to use the dative, “to the resurrection,” because the verb “planted together with him” is joined to what precedes. A tree is planted with another tree when it is grafted, and Christ is a tree by analogy, of whom Solomon speaks in the person of the wise man, who is Christ: “She is the tree of life to those who grasp her” (Prov. 3).

He is also the tree of life planted in the middle of paradise, that is, in the middle of the Church. He is compared to a tree because, just as a tree feeds and provides shade, so Christ feeds angels with spiritual food, namely, contemplation of him, and human beings with knowledge of him, protecting [Col. 0413A] both from every adversity. In general, he also feeds and refreshes the whole world with bodily food.

His death may also be understood as a tree, because just as a tree is planted in order to bear fruit for the one who planted it, so Christ’s death was accomplished on the cross in order to bring the fruit of salvation and redemption to the world.

It is asked why the Apostle said, “We have been planted together in the likeness of his death,” that is, of Christ’s death, and did not simply say, “We have been planted together in his death.” Christ’s death can be understood here in two ways, namely, spiritually and bodily.

We are planted together in the likeness [Col. 0413B] of his bodily death when, just as he died in the body for sinners, we die to sin. The likeness consists in this: he died in the body, while we die to vices.

Alternatively, we are planted together in the likeness of his spiritual death when we die to grave sins. He truly died to sin, though he never sinned. We cannot be planted together with and joined to this truth, because as long as we are in this mortal body we cannot be entirely free from lesser sins, as John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (John 1).

We assume the likeness of his spiritual death when, relying on his help, we do not commit grave sins. Thus in the present world we are planted together in the likeness of his death, both bodily and spiritual: just as he died in the body and died to all sins, because he never sinned, so we too should die to all [Col. 0413C] grave sins. We shall certainly be planted together with and joined to his resurrection in glory, and when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (John 3).

Knowing this, that our old self was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin. As blessed Augustine says, some wished to understand the old self as the body and the new self as the soul. But this does not fit, because the outer human being is called the body by many, while the inner human being is the soul.

Here, however, he calls the old self the life and conduct of the old man Adam, which was crucified—that is, killed and put to death—once in baptism. Whoever is still held liable for the original and [Col. 0413D] actual sins committed by Adam, or for even more sins, is the old self and a follower of Adam, because he imitates Adam’s life and conduct.

Why, then, was that conduct, which is called the old self, killed and destroyed? So that the body of sin might be destroyed. Our body is the body of sin because it draws us toward sin through the suggestion of the flesh and evil desire. The Apostle does not command that this body be destroyed in the sense of being annihilated, but that it cease from the work of sin. It is then, as it were, destroyed when it is restrained and drawn back from sin and from the evil will that it desires to fulfill, and is not permitted to serve sin.

Alternatively, we can understand “sin” here as the devil, who is the author of sin, and his body as the totality of vices. Just as Christ is the head [Col. 0414A] of all the elect and of all virtues, and all the elect and all virtues are his body, so the devil is the head of all the reprobate and of all vices, and all the reprobate and all vices are his body.

For this reason the life and conduct of the old man Adam were put to death once in baptism: so that the totality of vices, which is the devil’s body, might be destroyed, and so that we might no longer serve the devil.

Alternatively, according to Origen, the body of sin can be called the totality of vices, which in some manner make up one body of sin; the individual vices are members of that totality. The Apostle commands that this body be destroyed through abolition—that is, through the removal brought about by cessation.

The Apostle rightly says that the old self died once, so as to admonish us to avoid grave sins. For just as Christ died once and no longer dies, so, if we have once died to sin in baptism, we cannot be baptized again [Col. 0414B].

For whoever has died—understand, to sin in baptism—has been justified from sin, that is, has been made alien to all sins. Therefore he ought to guard himself, lest he again defile himself with grave sins, because he will not be able to be justified again through baptism.

But if we have died with Christ to sin at the time of baptism, in the manner explained by the preceding discussion, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ in heaven after the general resurrection.

Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead—that is, from the tomb, which is properly the place of the dead, or from the underworld—no longer dies, death shall no longer rule over him.

The Apostle’s concern [Col. 0414C] at this point is to show believers that, once they have received the forgiveness of sins, they cannot be baptized again, just as Christ could die only once. And just as Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, so we too must always live in the virtues, because the soul that sins will die through grave sin.

When he says that death shall no longer rule over him, we can understand “death” in two ways: either bodily and temporal death, which ruled over him for a time with his permission, or the devil, who in a certain manner was also permitted to rule over him through his ministers, with his permission. The devil entered the heart of Judas so that he might betray Christ (Luke 22). He also persuaded the Jews and Pilate to crucify him. That the devil is called death because he brought death into the world is shown by John, who says: “And his name was Death” (Rev. 6) [Col. 0414D].

For in that he died—understand, Christ—he died to sin once. This verse must be punctuated so that it first says, “For in that he died,” and then continues, “he died to sin once,” that is, he was always dead to sin, because he never sinned. Christ alone died to sin once—that is, always—because he never sinned.

Alternatively: Christ died bodily; he died once for our sin, and no more. So also we die once in baptism. Nevertheless, after baptism, if we have sinned, we can die to sin and rise again through worthy repentance.

But as for what lives, it lives to God. [Col. 0415A] Christ, while he was dead on the cross and buried in the tomb, seemed not to be alive. But what did he do? He entered the house of the strong man—that is, he descended into the underworld—and took from the devil those elect whom he held captive. He also took away from him the power that he possessed in this world.
