Thus, ascending into heaven on the fortieth day after his resurrection, he lives eternally to God—that is, in the glory of the Father’s majesty.

Thus you also should consider yourselves dead to sin at the time of baptism, but alive to God. The Greek, as Origen reads it, is better: “Consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God.” The meaning is this: Just as one who has been crucified thinks of nothing else except begging God’s mercy, so that He may deign to receive his spirit, just as the Lord said to the Father, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23), so you too, whenever evil desire comes and perverse pleasure inflames you to lust and to commit other evils, should think and recall that in baptism you died to all sins, where you received forgiveness of sins. Living with such thoughts, live for God—that is, for wisdom, prudence, chastity, and the other virtues. For whoever lives for God lives for all the virtues that are in God.

Do not, therefore, let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. Since you have died to sin in baptism and live for God, take care that sin does not reign in your mortal body—that is, as long as you are in the present age. The Apostle does not say, “Let there be no sin in your mortal body,” but “Let it not reign.” As long as we are in this mortal body, we cannot be entirely without sins. Of what sins, then, does he speak? Of murder, adultery, and the other criminal vices that separate us from the kingdom of God—not of lesser sins, such as sins of thought and desire. And how does sin not reign in our mortal body if, as soon as it knocks, we consent and obey its pleasure, because we submit to it?

Nor should you present—that is, prepare—your members as weapons of iniquity for sin. Iniquity is whatever is done against the law, and therefore by “iniquity” we must understand all vices. The members of our body were made for this purpose, and the senses of our body were given to us for this purpose: to provide what we need and to serve God. But if we incline our ears to hear slander about our neighbor, to delight in idle words and in the songs of prostitutes; if we open our eyes to desire a woman; if we spread an evil odor—that is, an evil reputation—from ourselves; if we delight in the perfumes of prostitutes; if we open our mouths to speak blasphemy against God or our neighbor; if we extend our hands to robbery; if we direct the steps of our feet to shed blood—then we present our members for this purpose: that they may be weapons serving sin and the devil, who is the author of death and of all vices. That is, we prepare them to serve sin and the devil.

But present—that is, prepare—yourselves to God as those living from the dead, and present your members as weapons of righteousness to God. That is, let them be weapons of every virtue for God, serving Him. If we set aside all the things we mentioned above concerning our members and employ them in God’s service—if we incline our ears to hear the words of God, open our eyes to examine the divine utterances and to look upon the poor, open our mouths to recount God’s mighty works, extend our hands for almsgiving, direct our feet toward peace, and give off a good odor from all these things—then our members will be weapons of every virtue and will serve God.

When he says “as those living from the dead,” the meaning is this: Just as those who rose when the Lord rose—of whom the Evangelist says, “Many bodies of the saints arose” (Matthew 27)—live, but neither desire nor seek to sin, so you too should consider yourselves dead to sin and live for God, turning away from criminal sins.

For sin will not rule over you—that is understood, if you do these things. But would that sin did not rule over you: where sin rules, there it is brought to completion. It rules a person when he obeys its desires. For you are not under the law but under grace. “You are not,” he says, “under the law of Moses, which punishes and condemns sinners, but under the grace of Christ,” that is, under the forgiveness of sins. And because you have already received forgiveness of sins, you ought not to sin.

What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law of Moses, which punishes sinners, but under grace, which forgives sin? Someone might say: Since we are no longer under the law, which imposes punishment on those who sin, we may sin freely, because whatever we commit will be forgiven us through the abundant mercy of Christ’s grace. To this the Apostle responds, not by affirming but by denying: “Shall we therefore always sin, because the law whose punishment would restrain us is absent?” Far be it from us always to sin, because grace wishes us to live in such a way that we do not commit criminal sins.

Or do you not know—that is, do you not realize—that to whomsoever you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey, whether you are servants of sin leading to eternal death, or of obedience to Christ leading to righteousness? If we serve the virtues and God, we are servants of the virtues and of God. But if we serve vices and the devil, we are servants of vices and of the devil.

But thanks be to God that you were servants of sin. You were indeed, but you are no longer. In giving thanks to God for their faith and good works, the Apostle praises them, just as he praises those of whom he said, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). But you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over. “You obeyed,” he says, “God in that pattern of teaching”—that is, in Christian teaching, in ecclesiastical teaching—in which you were taught, or called and assigned, to God.

But having been freed from sin—that is, from all vices and all sins in baptism—you were made servants of righteousness, that is, of all the virtues. Just as the word “sin” signifies all vices, so the word “righteousness” signifies all virtues.

I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. What does the Apostle mean by saying, “I speak in human terms”? He means: this is easy and simple to fulfill—as though he were saying in other words: Since you are still carnal and, because of the frailty of the flesh, cannot bear and fulfill greater commandments, I will entrust you with easy commandments. For what is so easy, as Origen says, and what is so simple as for a person to be as ready to fulfill righteousness and the will of God as he is habitually ready everywhere to do evil? Indeed, it is much easier to serve the virtues than the vices, and to fulfill God’s will than the devil’s.

Let us see how this is so, and say a few things from among many. There is a robber, and there is another man living by his own righteousness, not by robbery. While the robber is tortured by frost and cold and tormented day and night by excessive anxiety, turning the matter over in his mind and waiting in the field for an opportunity to complete his theft, the righteous man safely feasts by day on the fruits of his labor and enjoys the quiet of night in security. While he sleeps this most pleasant sleep, the one who is tortured by the frost of cold and the emptiness of hunger is often killed by those whom he was attempting to assault.

Similarly, the man who commits adultery fears that the husband may arrive and kill him; he also fears his neighbors because of the rumor spreading abroad. In contrast, the chaste man and lover of his own marriage securely preserves his chastity, or even embraces his own wife in safety and desired repose.

Therefore the Apostle adds: “For just as you presented”—that is, prepared—“your members to serve impurity,” that is, lust, fornication, and shamelessness, “and iniquity for iniquity,” with “for its commission” understood, “so now present your members to serve righteousness and all the virtues for sanctification”—that is, so that you may be holy, according to what God commands: “Be holy, because I too am holy” (Leviticus 11).

By “iniquity” we must understand all sins, because whatever is done against the law of God is called iniquity. By “righteousness,” however, we must understand all virtues. The meaning is: Just as, before you were called to the faith, you prepared yourselves to serve every impurity and every vice, so now, established in the faith, prepare your members and all the senses of your body to serve every virtue.

[Col. 0417D]

For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness—that is, you were alienated from righteousness. Just as one who serves sin and the devil is the servant of the one whose will he fulfills, so one who serves righteousness is the servant of righteousness and of God. For one who serves theft and adultery is the servant of theft and adultery.

This also must be understood: Just as being a servant of righteousness is praiseworthy, whereas being free from righteousness is not praiseworthy, so being a servant of sin is detestable, while being free from sin is praiseworthy.

What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things—that is, in the impurities of sins—of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death. Before coming to faith in the Lord, the Romans served every vice and every disgrace—things which, as the Apostle has already mentioned earlier in this Epistle, are shameful even to speak of. But when they came to the faith, they were ashamed and embarrassed, not only because of what they had done but even at the recollection of it. Therefore, wishing to strengthen them so that they would not return to those things, he said: Tell me what fruit—that is, what good or what beneficial reward—did you obtain from those impurities that you committed before coming to the faith, whose recollection and memory now cause you shame and embarrassment? For their end—that is, the completion of those sins—is eternal death.

When a person dies in criminal sins and brings his life to an end, the end of sins is death for him, because from them he receives eternal death. Of such people the Prophet says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1). “Beasts” are called people who live irrationally, without uprightness of conduct and way of life. For beasts to rot in dung means to end their life in the filth, in the stench of luxury and in the disgrace of vices.

Now, however, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life. “Now,” he says, “having been freed from sin through Christ’s Passion and through the water of baptism, and having been made servants of God, whereas previously you were servants of the devil, you have the fruit of your works for sanctification, because your holy work procures sanctification for you. But the end is eternal life”—that is, because of the completion of your works you will have eternal life, which will be given to you for your perseverance.

For the wages of sin—that is, the reward of sins—is eternal death. This should not, however, be understood of all sins, but of criminal sins, concerning which John says: “There is sin leading to death; I do not say that anyone should pray for that” (1 John 5).

“Wages” is said from *stipite pendenda*, “to be weighed from a stock,” because in ancient times money was weighed rather than counted. Hence a wage, that is, substance and remuneration, was given from the public treasury to soldiers serving for the king’s life and the freedom of their country. And just as wages were given to them as a reward, so death—that is, eternal condemnation—will be given as a reward to those serving the devil.

But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus. Why, when speaking of the reward of sin, did he call that reward “wages,” while in speaking of the reward of the elect he spoke of the grace of God? Because those who serve receive their own reward; but whatever the elect possess, they receive entirely from God’s grace—whether faith, charity, or some good work. Moreover, for this grace of faith and good works, they will freely receive eternal life from God through the assistance of Jesus Christ, without whom we can possess no good thing.

## CHAPTER 7

[Col. 0419A]

Do you not know, brothers—that is, do you not know what I am going to say? For I am speaking to those who know the law, because the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives. There is a comparison here, and in what follows, extending from human law to divine law, or from the law of Moses to the law of the Gospel. The Apostle was speaking to Gentiles and Jews living in Rome. The Jews knew the divine law; the Romans too had adopted laws from the Athenians, whose king Phoroneus had composed human laws. Therefore he said, “to those who know the law.” I am speaking of a law that has this custom: it rules over each person for as long as that person lives.

For the woman who is under a husband, while her husband lives, is bound to the law—that is, to the husband’s authority. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. According to the law of Moses and the Gospel, and likewise according to human laws, this is the custom: while the husband lives, the woman is under his authority; when he dies, she is released from his authority and may marry whomever she wishes.

Or otherwise: If a Gallic man takes a Roman woman as his wife, then as long as her husband lives she will live under the law under which her husband lives, and through him she will answer when questioned in public. But when her husband dies, she will return to her own law and thereafter will not live under her husband’s law.

Moreover, it must be carefully considered that the Apostle introduces two husbands spiritually in this passage, and one woman. One husband is understood as the law of Moses, which, like a husband over a wife, held dominion over the Israelite people. The other husband is understood as sin, which often rules the soul. By the name “woman” he wishes to signify either each individual soul in particular or the whole Israelite people in general. This will be made clear in the individual passages that follow.

When the Apostle says, “The woman who is under a husband,” by “husband” he wishes the law of Moses to be understood, and by “woman” either any soul in particular or, as we have said, the Israelite people in general, which existed under the law of Moses. But when he adds, “while the husband lives, she is bound to the law,” he wishes “husband” here to signify the passions of the flesh, that is, vices. As long as they live in a person, he is bound to the law of Moses, which says: “If anyone does this or that, he shall surely die.”

The meaning is: The soul or people who are under a husband—that is, under the law of Moses—while the husband lives, that is, while the passions, pleasures, and vices of the flesh reign in them, are subject to the vengeance of the law of Moses, which was given against the wicked and sinners. But if her husband dies—that is, if sins and the vices of the flesh die in the soul—she is released from the law of her husband, that is, she is no longer subject to the Mosaic law, because she has nothing for which she owes it anything. For the law is not imposed on the righteous but on sinners and the wicked.

Sin lives and reigns in the soul when, as soon as it knocks against a person, it is brought to completion. It dies, however, when the mind does not obey its suggestion and pleasure.

Therefore, while the husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another husband. This is to be understood simply and in the same way as that saying in the Gospel: “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, except on account of fornication; and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery” (Matthew 5). Both the man who dismisses his wife and takes another, and the man who joins himself to a dismissed woman, commit adultery.

This can also, though less appropriately, be referred to the Israelite people, as can the preceding passages. As long as the law lived—that is, as long as it was required to be observed by the Jews—if any Jew abandoned it and the worship of the true God and joined himself to the error of the Gentiles by worshiping idols, he was an adulterer. Hence that people itself is also called a prostitute, as Ezekiel says: “Therefore, prostitute, hear the word of the Lord” (Ezekiel 16).

But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another husband. The literal meaning is sufficiently clear: If her husband dies—that is, if the sins and vices of the flesh, which usually rule the soul, die—she is freed from the law of her husband, that is, from Moses’ law, which ruled over a person as long as he sinned. And she will not be an adulteress if she is with another husband—that is, with Christ and under the Gospel. For the soul that has been freed from sins ought to cling to Christ.

Therefore, my brothers, you also have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ. He ought to have said, “The law has died for you,” but, so as not to scandalize the Jews to whom he was writing, he preferred to say, “You have been put to death to the law,” because it has nothing in you that it can punish. For those have been put to death to the law in whom it has nothing to punish. When he says, “You have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ,” of which body does he speak?

The body of Christ is that which he assumed in the Virgin’s womb. The body of Christ is the whole Church of the faithful. The body of Christ is that which is consecrated daily in the Church. It is evident, therefore, that the Apostle spoke of the body which Christ assumed in the Virgin’s womb. Through his body, therefore, Christ freed us from the law; that is, through the Passion of his body he gave us forgiveness of sins, so that we are no longer subject to the law if we cease to sin.

So that you may belong to another—that is, to Christ—who rose from the dead, so that you may bear fruit for God. “For this reason,” he says, “you were redeemed through Christ’s Passion; for this reason you received forgiveness of sins, so that you may no longer be subject to the law but to Christ, and may bear fruit for God.” The person bears fruit for God who multiplies souls for Him and acquires them by word, example, and every possible means.

For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which existed through the law, were at work in our members so that they might bear fruit for death. “When we were,” he says, “in the flesh”—that is, placed in the hope of carnal things and in carnal desires—the passions of sins, namely adultery, robbery, and murder, which were made known to people through the law, and which were recognized through the law as sins, produced vices and sins in our members so that they might bear fruit for death—that is, so that they might acquire eternal death for us.

For just as one who serves the virtues bears fruit for eternal life, because he acquires eternal life, so one who serves vices acquires eternal death for himself. “For the wages and reward of sin is eternal death” (Romans 6).

[Col. 0421A]

But now we have been released, through Christ’s Passion and through baptism, from the law of death—that is, from the law of Moses, which brought death upon sinners—in which we had been confined, as is understood, before we were released through Christ. Thus we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

He serves in the oldness of the letter who observes circumcision and the Sabbath carnally, and who thinks that he can be saved through carnal observance of the law. But he serves in the newness of the spirit who observes circumcision spiritually, circumcises his heart from all vices, rests from evil works, and understands spiritually and fulfills the other things taught by the law.

What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Far be it from us to say that the law, which forbids sins, was given to us as the cause of sin. It is indeed the judge of sins, and teaches what ought to be desired and what ought to be avoided; yet it is not the producer of sin, nor is it the cause of death for those who sin.

For example: A physician warns a person to abstain from deadly foods and from the juice of a poisonous plant. If that person eats or drinks against the physician’s command and dies, the physician is not thereby the cause of death for the one whom he warned. Rather, the person who ate what was forbidden is himself the cause of his own death. In the same way, the law, which forbade sins by saying, “If anyone does this or that, he shall surely die,” was not the cause of death for those who sinned and did what it itself forbade. Rather, those who became transgressors were themselves the cause of their own condemnation.

But I did not know sin except through the law. That is, I did not know the punishment and vengeance of sin except through the law, which punishes sins. Or, alternatively, I did not know that certain evil works were sins until the law came. There were certain sins that were not thought to be sins before the law, such as the sin of desire, concerning which he adds: I did not know that lustful desire, or desire for other evil things, was sin, as is understood, unless the law said, “You shall not covet.”

By “desire” many other sins are also understood, sins whose sinful character was unknown before the law, or whose deserving punishment was unknown.

But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every desire. The Apostle speaks in the person of the Jews doing penance, or in the person of every individual person doing penance. For when he said these things, he had been justified by the grace of baptism.

In this passage, blessed Ambrose wishes the name “sin” to be understood as the devil, who is the author of sin. When the devil saw that through observance of the law a person would be restored to forgiveness, he again became envious of him, as he had been of the first man. Considering the law, he found a way, through its transgression, to condemn the one whom he had previously condemned through original sin. Seizing the opportunity, he inflamed him through transgression of the law not only to lustful desire but to every vice, so that through desire he might become a transgressor of the law.

For human weakness has this characteristic in transgressing: things that are forbidden are more difficult to observe. Without the natural law or the law of Moses, sin was dead—that is, it was hidden, unknown, and not apparent. Before the natural law and understanding begin to be active in children and in other people, they do not sin even if they strike their father and mother or curse their parents. But after they have reached the proper years of understanding, if they do anything of that kind, they sin and receive punishment.

Similarly, before the law of Moses was given, there were certain sins whose character as sins was unknown, and whose commission was not considered so serious. Or even if they were recognized as sins, it was unknown what punishment they deserved.

I was once alive without the law. He places himself in the position of everyone, and the meaning is: Once—that is, before I knew the law—I thought I was living rightly, although I was serving almost every vice. But when the commandment of the law of Moses came, saying, “If anyone does this or that, he shall surely die,” sin revived.

That which has already lived is said to revive. Sin first lived in the man who sinned knowingly, and in Cain, who said, “My iniquity is greater than that I can deserve forgiveness” (Genesis 4). But in his descendants it was dead, for they had reached such an error that they did not think what was sin to be sin. When the law of Moses arrived, what had begun not to live revived, because it had previously been hidden.

But I died—that is, I understood myself to be deserving of death—after I received the law and transgressed it. And the commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death. The meaning is this: The commandment was given to me so that, when observed and kept, it might advance me toward eternal life; but when neglected, it led me to eternal death. Thus what was given to me for my good was changed into evil through my fault.

For sin—that is, the devil, the author of sin—seizing the opportunity through the commandment of the law, in the manner we described above, deceived me and misled me by the sweetness of sin and desire, so that I might fulfill the things forbidden by the law. Through that commandment—that is, through transgressing the commandment—it killed me in my soul.

Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good. Take one commandment as standing for all the commandments. The law is holy, righteous, and good because it proclaims holiness, righteousness, and goodness, and makes those who observe it holy, righteous, and good.

Did then what is good become death for me? That is, did the commandment of the law, which is good in itself if observed, become death for me? Far be it from us to say that it was the cause of death for me. For the commandment of the law, which is good in itself, did not kill me; rather, I killed myself and became the cause of my own death by transgressing it.

But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, produced death for me through the good commandment. In this passage, according to blessed Ambrose, “sin” is understood as the devil, as in the preceding passages. The law therefore did not produce death for me; rather, the devil, so that sin might appear—that is, so that the enemy of the human race might be revealed—produced death for me through the transgression of the good commandment, because he dragged me to death.

Alternatively, according to blessed Augustine: Sin, which before the law was hidden and was not recognized as sin, so that its nature might become apparent, led me to death through transgression of the law. I deserved a greater punishment if I sinned after I had come to know the law, because I sinned knowingly. Thus, through the commandment of the law, sin became sin beyond measure.

Before the law of Moses was given, there was the great sin of original and actual sin, by which the transgression of the natural law was recognized. But that sin increased through the transgression of the written law, which says, “You shall not kill; you shall not covet,” and so forth (Exodus 20). When he says, “so that it might become beyond measure,” he shows that sin has a certain measure and limit.

Hence the Lord says to Abraham, “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Genesis 15), and to the Jews, “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matthew 23). The transgression of the commandment of the law therefore exceeded the whole measure of sin that existed before the law. It is as though he said: For this reason the devil deceived the human being through the sweetness of sin, so that through transgression of the commandment he might become a sinner beyond measure—sin itself becoming worse and exceedingly great—as blessed Jerome says: “a more sinful sin.”

For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. Here and in what follows the Apostle speaks in the person of the human race, or in the person of any individual doing penance and turning to the Lord with all his heart.

The law of Moses is spiritual because, through the spirit, it contains commandments teaching what pertains to the salvation of the soul. Or it is called spiritual because it wishes to be understood by us spiritually.

But I am carnal—that is, I am still mortal—and therefore I place my hope in carnal desires and lusts, sold under sin. The first man, having tasted the sweetness of the forbidden fruit, sold himself as a slave to the devil, although he was free. And everyone who delights in carnal desire and enjoys the sweetness of sin sells himself to the devil and to sin, to which he subjects himself.

For I do not understand what I do. In these words the Apostle assumes the person of two human beings: the inner person, that is, the mind, and the outer person, that is, the flesh. What was the Apostle doing? He was desiring against the commandment of the law. He did not understand this desire—that is, he did not approve it, choose it, or wish to bring it to completion.

It should be noted that here the Apostle speaks much in the person of the human race about desire. By desire we must understand the totality of vices, all of which are fulfilled through desire. For no sin is brought to completion without desire. For example, one who commits murder desires to kill the person against whom he uses violence. The same must be understood of the other vices.

For I do not do what I want, but I do the evil that I hate. What did the Apostle want? He wanted not to desire, and yet he desired.

But if I do what I do not want—that is, if I desire—it follows that I agree with the law, because it is good. Although he desired through the weakness of the flesh, nevertheless, because in his mind he did not want to desire, he agreed with the law that says, “You shall not covet.”

But now—strengthened, as is understood, by the grace of God—it is no longer I who produce that desire for sin. I do not desire it with the inclination of my mind; rather, sin that dwells in me—that is, the evil habit of sinning that I have inherited from Adam—produces desire in me.

For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. When he says, “It does not dwell in me,” he uses the whole for a part, just as Mary says in the Gospel, “They have taken away my Lord” (John 20), meaning the body of her Lord. But by adding “that is, in my flesh,” he himself explains what he means when he says, “No good dwells in me,” and separates the inclination of the mind from the desires of the flesh, in which there is nothing good, because it is always delighted to bring carnal works to completion.

For the will is present with me—that is, I possess the will, and the will belongs to the mind—not to desire the evil that I do not want. But I do not find the ability to bring the good to completion, because I cannot refrain from desiring. Perfect goodness consists not only in failing to commit an act but also in not desiring it.

For I do not do the good that I want, because I would not want to desire, yet I desire. Rather, I do the evil that I do not want, because I desire it.

But if I do what I do not want—that is, if I desire and delight in carnal desires—then it is no longer I who produce that desire through the rationality and intention of my mind. Rather, sin that dwells in me—that is, the evil habit of sinning—produces it.

I therefore discover this law when I want to do good: that I should not desire, because evil is present with me—namely, the evil habit and desire of sin. The order of the words is: “When I want to do good, I find a good and useful law.” It is as though he were saying in other words: Because the pleasure of the flesh and the devil’s suggestion drive me toward evil, when I want to do good I find the law of Moses, which commands me to turn away from evil and do good.

For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person—that is, according to the rationality of the mind. The law says, “You shall not covet,” and I delight in it because I do not want to covet. Therefore what delights the law delights me also.

But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind—that is, against the rationality and intention of my mind—and taking me captive in the law of sin, that is, wishing to take me captive in the law of an evil habit, which is in my members.

By “the law of the members” he calls the burden and weight of mortality, because our still-mortal body draws us daily toward evil desire and perverse habit. The law of the members of the body is to desire, just as the law of the mind is not to desire.

Alternatively, according to blessed Gregory: The other law that is in the members, warring against the law of the mind, is understood as the stimulation of the flesh—that is, the impulse toward lust—or, certainly, every evil desire.

Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. He speaks in the person of the human race, as above, or in the person of those who turn away from sins and desire with all their heart to serve God but are attacked by the desires of the flesh and the pleasures of the body. Therefore they desire to be freed from the mortal and corruptible body through which they are drawn toward desire.

But not all people will be freed from this body of corruption. Although the reprobate will receive immortal bodies, they will not thereby be freed from corruption, because those bodies will be corruptible and will be able to be corrupted by worms and fire. Just as they served their own pleasures and delights in body and soul, so in body and soul they will suffer eternal punishments.

The elect, however, will be freed on the day of judgment from every dreg of sin, mortality, and corruption, because they will receive immortal and incorruptible bodies, and in the soul they will receive unchangeability. They will no longer be able to desire or think anything evil, but will be intent upon the contemplation of almighty God. This will occur through the grace of God the Father and the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we possess every good thing.

Alternatively, we may understand “the body of death” as the totality of vices, as has already been said above. Each sin individually is a member, while the totality of sins is called a body. It is called the body of death because it inflicts eternal death. The Apostle prayed to be freed from this body of death—that is, from the totality of all sins.

Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin. With the rationality and intention of my mind I serve the law of God, agreeing with it, since I want not to be subject to carnal desire; but with my flesh I serve the law of sin—that is, the evil habit—because I desire. To the extent that the evil spirit suggests and the flesh takes delight, a person serves the law of sin; but to the extent that the mind resists these things, it strives to serve the law of God.

## CHAPTER 8

There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. From this we are given to understand that he places himself in the position of all believers. Those who serve the law of God with their minds, although they desire with the flesh, have no condemnation, because they do not walk according to the flesh—that is, they do not live according to carnal desires.

Or, certainly, this may refer to those who have already been freed from the body of death—that is, who have been stripped, by God’s grace at the time of baptism, of the totality of all sins and remain in that same holiness. There is no condemnation in them by which they would be subjected to eternal death.

For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death. He calls the grace of the Holy Spirit “the law,” and this Spirit is called the Spirit of life because, whoever it fills, it makes live in the virtues and, by forgiving sins, leads that person to eternal life. “For the law of the Spirit of life,” that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which gives life to us in the soul at the time of baptism, has freed me from the habit of sin, through which one reaches the condemnation of eternal death. Alternatively, in this passage we may understand “law” as the grace of the holy Gospel, which we have learned through the Holy Spirit, in which eternal life is promised to us; or “the law of the Spirit” is understood as faith, which is said to belong to the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0426B] because it is granted by him and through him. For no one says, “The Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit (I Cor. XII), and faith is life, because it leads us to eternal life.

For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh: God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. It was impossible for the law to justify a human being, cleanse him from sins, and open the door of the heavenly homeland; the grace of the Gospel grants these things to believers through the passion of the Lord and Savior and through the water of baptism. It was impossible for it to do this because it was weakened through the flesh, that is, through carnal observances and through the carnal observance of those who understood them carnally and lived carnally. For it was impossible for sins to be cleansed by the blood of goats, because the law did not come to remove sins but to reveal them. It was weak in this respect because it could justify neither the person who observed it carnally nor the person who destroyed the things it itself prescribed; and therefore it was weakened through the flesh, because none of mortal humanity could fulfill it according to the flesh. Hence blessed Peter says: “Why do you put God to the test by placing upon the necks of the brothers a yoke of the law which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts XV).

Or it was weakened through the flesh because, on account of the desires of the flesh, it justified no one. For just as a physician is weak in that respect in which he cannot restore sight to a blind person or give health to other sick people, so the law was weak in that respect in which it could not cleanse a human being from criminal [Col. 0426D] sins. But God the Father, sending his Son to save the human race—a sending which is nothing other than his incarnation—conferred what the law could not confer.

Why, then, does he say that he was sent “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” when we must believe that he truly assumed a real body of flesh and bones? Our body and our flesh are sinful flesh because they are procreated through the lustful union of man and woman; and therefore it is conceived with sin, born with original sin, and cannot live in this world without sin. Christ’s body, however, was not procreated through a lustful union of male and female, but by the work of the Holy Spirit from the woman’s seed, without male seed. Therefore he was conceived without sin, born without sin, [Col. 0427A] and passed from this world without sin. In this respect his flesh was in the likeness of sinful flesh: he had true flesh, but without sin, which we do not have.

And by sin he condemned sin in the flesh. Although this verse may seem difficult, its meaning is nevertheless this: in this passage the Apostle calls Christ’s flesh “sin,” not because it bore the stain of sin, but because it was offered for sinners, just as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “God the Father made him, that is, Christ, sin for us” (II Cor. V), that is, a sacrifice for sins. In the Old Testament a sacrifice offered for sin was indeed called “sin,” especially in the Septuagint interpreters, where it says: “He placed his hand upon the head of the sin,” that is, upon the head of the sacrifice that was offered [Col. 0427B] for sin (Lev. I).

“By sin he condemned sin in his flesh,” that is, from his flesh, which was a sacrifice for sin, he condemned the sin of the human race, without sinning through the flesh. For he condemned—or killed and put to death—sin in two ways: either because he did not sin in his flesh, or because he put it to death on the cross. This is like someone from among barbarians winning a victory over barbarians, and a Goth defeating Goths.

So that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us. That is, so that, redeemed through his passion, freed from all sins through baptism, and strengthened also by the Spirit, we might be able to fulfill the works of the law spiritually; through fulfilling them, we can be justified. We are those who do not walk according to the flesh, that is, who do not live according to carnal desires, but according to the Holy Spirit, that is, according to what the Holy Spirit teaches and commands.

Or certainly God condemned sin—that is, the sin of the human race, or the devil who is the author of sin—by becoming a sacrifice for sin, so that the righteousness prefigured by the law in its sacrifices, namely in the lamb, ram, dove, and turtledove, might be fulfilled in us through Christ in his passion, for these sacrifices signified him.

For those who are according to the flesh—that is, those who live carnally and delight in carnal pleasures—set their minds on the things of the flesh; that is, they seek only carnal and temporal things, caring nothing for spiritual matters. But those who live according to the Spirit live according to what the Spirit himself teaches and wills: they set their minds on the things of the Spirit, that is, they pursue spiritual things, seeking the joys of the heavenly homeland.

Alternatively: the human being consists of two substances, namely flesh and soul. If the activities of the flesh prevail over the mind’s inclination, then the person seeks carnal and temporal things; but if the inclination of the spirit or mind prevails over the activities of the flesh, then the person pursues spiritual things.

For the mind of the flesh is death. The mind of the flesh—or carnal mindedness—is to repay evil with evil and to pursue carnal desires. Whoever fulfills these desires acquires eternal death for himself. Philosophers defined prudence as desiring temporal goods and avoiding temporal evils. Since this prudence is carnal, it therefore produces eternal death, because while the goods of the present life are desired with complete avidity and its adversities are desired for Christ’s name, the goods of eternal life are regarded as nothing. [Col. 0428A]

But the mind of the Spirit is life and peace. The mind of the Spirit, that is, the rationality of the mind, is not repaying evil with evil; loving friends in God and enemies for God’s sake; praying for persecutors and slanderers, as the Gospel commands; despising all temporal and passing things; and desiring with the whole effort of the mind the joys of the heavenly homeland. The mind’s rationality has peace in the present, because it does not repay evil with evil, and in the future it earns eternal life.

For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. What he earlier called “the mind of the flesh” he now calls “the wisdom of the flesh.” The carnal and worldly wisdom of a human being is to place one’s hope in perishable things and to do what we mentioned above. Carnal wisdom is not subject to the law of God, that is, to the law of the Gospel, which says: “Do not repay evil with evil.” Why is it not subject? Because it cannot be; and why can it not? Because it does not wish to, fearing the loss of temporal goods. While they repay evil with evil and hate one another, they are opposed to the Gospel, which commands that enemies be loved.

Those who are in the flesh—that is, those who live according to carnal desires and have placed their hope in carnal goods—cannot please God, that is, so long as they remain in such things.

But you, O Romans, are not in the flesh, that is, in carnal desires, because you have already put your members to death together with vices and desires; rather, you are in the Spirit, [Col. 0428C] that is, in spiritual things, and you seek spiritual things—if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. That is, if the Holy Spirit dwells in you, then you certainly live spiritually.

But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him. The Holy Spirit is the common Spirit of the Father and the Son. How can it be known whether the Holy Spirit dwells in us? Through good and true conduct, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit.” Whoever imitates Christ’s deeds—praying for persecutors and slanderers, for example—certainly has his Spirit dwelling within, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is the mark of his possession, because whoever he fills he makes belong to Christ’s body. But whoever does not imitate Christ and does not have his Spirit does not belong to Christ’s Father.

[Col. 0428D] But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead, that is, mortal and destined to die, because of Adam’s sin and because of the actual sins subsequently committed; but the spirit, that is, the soul, lives with God through faith, because of the justification of faith and baptism. He says in anticipation that the body is dead, instead of saying that it is mortal and corruptible. We should know, however, that our body is mortal not because of earthly frailty but because of sin.

But if the Spirit of him—that is, of the Father—who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you through faith, love, and hope, as it is said through the Prophet, “I will dwell in them,” then he who raised Jesus [Col. 0429A] Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies on the day of judgment, so that thereafter they will no longer be mortal, because of his Spirit dwelling in you. Whomever God the Father finds the Holy Spirit dwelling in during the present age, he will surely raise to glory on the day of judgment by the power of his divinity, by which he raised Christ, giving the body immortality and incorruptibility, and the soul immutability. For Christ’s passion freed us from the death of the soul in the present age, but bodily death will come equally upon all until the general resurrection.

Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. A debtor is someone who owes something to another. We were not created by almighty God for this purpose: to live according to the flesh, that is, according to the desires of the flesh. We are not debtors to the flesh but to God, so that we may live spiritually, regarding all passing and perishable things as nothing and repaying our debt to God. What, then, have we received from him that would make us his debtors? Whatever good we possess. When we did not exist, we were created by him from nothing; and when we were lost through our own fault, we were redeemed by him, while he also granted us temporal goods and promised us eternal ones. How can we repay our debt to him? By serving his will, obeying his commands, and attributing whatever good we possess not to our own merits but to his grace.

For if you live according to the flesh—that is, if you fulfill in practice carnal desires and pleasures according to the appetite of carnal desires—you will die by eternal death. What does it mean to live according to the flesh? To practice the works of the flesh, namely adultery, murder, theft, and other such things. But if by the Spirit, that is, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live with eternal life.

Let us first see what the works or deeds of the flesh are, from the Apostle’s other words: “The works of the flesh are obvious: fornication, impurity, licentiousness,” and the other things that follow. And what does he say about the fruit and works of the Holy Spirit? “The fruit of the Spirit,” he says, “is love, joy, peace” (Gal. V), and other such things.

How, then, can we put to death the works of the flesh through the grace of the Holy Spirit? In this way. For example, pride lives and reigns in us: receiving humility from the Holy Spirit, let us be humble, and thus we shall put pride to death. Lust lives in us: receiving chastity from the Holy Spirit, let us be chaste, and thus we shall be able to put lust to death. “If,” he says, “by living according to God you extinguish the pleasures of the flesh and carnal desires, you will be blessed in eternal life.”

For whoever is led by the Spirit of God—that is, ruled and guided toward the gift—these are the children of God, not by nature but by adoption.

For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as children of God, in whom we cry, “Abba (Father).” The Jews to whom the Apostle was writing had received from their fathers the spirit of slavery in fear, that is, the law dictated and written by the Holy Spirit, which compelled them through fear to observe it, threatening and saying: “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death.” The same Holy Spirit, whom they received when the law was given, compelled them to observe the law.

And because these people had then received the Holy Spirit and the law from their fathers, the Apostle says: “You did not again receive the spirit of slavery,” which compels you through fear to serve almighty God. Rather, you received the grace of the Gospel, in which no one is compelled to come to faith in Christ through fear. You also received the Spirit of adoption, or of election, as children of God. He called you into God’s portion, into freedom, so that you are no longer servants of God through servile fear, but through love and filial fear—the fear by which a good son serves his father, fearing to offend him.

[Col. 0430B] When he adds, “in whom we cry, ‘Abba (Father),’” the meaning is as though he said: “Taught and enlightened by this Holy Spirit, we cry, ‘Abba (Father).’” For unless we had received the Holy Spirit at the time of baptism, we would certainly not dare to call almighty God, our Creator, “Father,” saying in the Lord’s Prayer: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. VI). No pagan dares to say this.

“Abba” is Syriac and Hebrew; “Father” is Greek and Latin. Therefore, foreseeing that both peoples were to be gathered into the faith, the Apostle placed two names with one meaning, so that those who believe from among the Hebrews and Syrians may say, “Abba, have mercy on us,” while those who believe from among the Greeks and all the other nations may say, “Father.” Something similar is found in the Gospel of Mark, where he says to the Lord: “Abba (Father), if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI).

For the Holy Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. Whenever we do good works in serving God, the Holy Spirit, who dwells in us, bears witness to us in our hearts through hidden inspiration, without the sound of a voice, that we have become children of God in baptism—not by nature but by adoption—and that, by doing such things, we shall persevere in his sonship.

But if children, then heirs. A servant does not deserve to receive an inheritance; a son receives one. If we are children of God, we shall deserve to receive an inheritance. We must also consider that, according to human laws, an inheritance is confirmed at the death of the father. What inheritance, then, can God the Father give us, since he cannot die? He will certainly give us himself, so that, just as he is immortal and incorruptible, we too may be immortal, incorruptible, and unchangeable, and may possess the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of his divinity.

Heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ. We shall be heirs of God the Father, as we have said; but let us consider how we are heirs of Christ. We are already heirs of Christ in part, because, when he went to his passion, he left us the possession of ecclesiastical peace, saying: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John XIV). What more should I say? Everything that he himself did in the present age, whether in preaching or in miracles, he left to us to believe [Col. 0431A] and hold fast; he also left us the Testament of the Gospel, and confirmed all these things in his death.

We shall also be his fellow heirs after the general resurrection, when we shall be immortal and incorruptible in body and unchangeable in soul, as he is. We shall also be like him in glory, because we shall see him as he is, as John says: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (I John III). And the Lord himself said to the Father (John XII): “Father, I desire that where I am, my minister may also be there.”

For just as Christ dwells at the right hand of the Father, that is, in the greatness of the Father’s majesty, so we too shall be his fellow heirs, because we shall shine as he shone on the mountain. And we shall be his fellow heirs not only in glory [Col. 0431B] but also in power, just as he said to the apostles: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

What more should I say? Whoever becomes a son and heir of God will certainly deserve to receive whatever belongs to God. We can await all these things with confidence if we do what follows: “if indeed we suffer with him,” with Christ, that is, “so that we may also be glorified with him.” The meaning is this: we shall then deserve to be Christ’s fellow heirs in glory if, compelled by necessity, we suffer for love of his name the kinds of things that he himself endured for us, imitating his passion and love, in accordance with what Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). [Col. 0431C]

For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us. If any human being could fulfill all the commands of the Old and New Testament and despise every kind of torment—prisons, goads, flesh-hooks, burnings, stonings, crucifixions, and frying in a pan over many successive periods of time—he would nevertheless not be worthy of the future glory that the elect will receive.

Someone may ask, “Why?” Certainly because these things are temporal, while those are eternal. What will that glory be? The elect will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father and will be like the angels of God, beholding the immediate presence of God, as John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III). [Col. 0431D]

For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God. In this passage he calls the human being “creation,” and rightly so, because through his fault he lost the image and likeness of almighty God, which he had in his soul. This creation, then—that is, every faithful human being—awaits the manifestation of the children of God, so that what has been promised may appear, when it will be manifested in reality who the children of God are, whereas now we possess this only in hope.

For at present the Church is mixed with the good and the wicked; all cry out to Christ, but it is not apparent who will in reality be the children of God. But when Christ comes for judgment and separates the sheep from the goats, saying to the righteous, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV), then it will be revealed who in reality are the children of God.

When he says, “The expectation of creation,” or “Our expectation awaits the revelation of the children of God,” these words seem to sound as though creation were one thing and the Son of God another, although they are one. Thus people are accustomed to speak when, in their presence, they see many colors arranged in different vessels: “The expectation,” or “expression,” of these colors awaits the manifestation of the image, although the image is not one thing and the colors another.

For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it, in hope. In this passage and also in what follows, where the Apostle says that all creation groans, blessed Augustine very incisively criticizes Origen for including under the name “creation” not only beasts but also the sun, the other stars, and the angels together with humanity, saying that all things were subjected to vanity and, what is more, that they groan in their course and activity.

Yet although every creature that can be changed for better or worse—just as the holy angels once could be changed, although now those who cling to God cannot—or that can be converted from joy to sorrow, such as the human being and all the other creatures of the world, is vanity in comparison with almighty God, who is always the same, as Ecclesiastes says, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I), nevertheless not everything groans.

The angels who cling to God do not groan, because they have already become unchangeable, as was shown to Ezekiel (Ezek. I) in the crystal that was above the heads of the living creatures. Nor does that which is irrational or lacks a soul groan. Therefore, by the name “creation” we should understand the human being, who has a certain communion with all creatures.

For every creature is divided into three classes: it is either bodily, able to be moved and carried through places; animal, vivified by a soul; or spiritual, like the angels, who use reason. Thus, insofar as he possesses a body, the human being is joined to bodily creatures; through the soul, to living things; and through reason, by which he distinguishes between good and evil, to spiritual beings.

Blessed Gregory explains this in different words but with the same meaning, saying: “The human being has being with stones, life with trees, sensation and life with animals, and understanding—that is, rationality—with angels.”

Creation, that is, every human being living in the flesh, is subject to vanity, that is, mutability, mortality, and corruption, not willingly. He did indeed sin voluntarily in paradise, but he was not voluntarily or willingly subjected to mortality and punishment. For example, a thief voluntarily commits theft, but he is not voluntarily hanged; and although he does not wish it, he is nevertheless subjected to vanity because of him—that is, because of the just judgment of almighty God, who subjected him in the hope of liberation and forgiveness.

In this God is shown to be almighty and just: he did not leave the thief’s sin unpunished. And in this he is proclaimed merciful: he did not immediately condemn and destroy him utterly, but preserved him for repentance, giving him hope of forgiveness, liberation, and return to his former state, so that he might await what is said in what follows.

For creation itself—that is, every elect human being—will be freed on the day of judgment from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. In the present age the human being has been placed under the slavery of corruption and mortality, because he is subject to mutability and vices. But on the day of judgment he will be freed from every dreg of mortality and sin, when this mortal body receives immortality and this corruptible body receives incorruption. He will pass into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, because he will be like Christ in glory, and into the freedom of adoptive sonship, of which the Lord said to the Jews: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John VIII).

There may also be a distinction in this passage between the Creator and creation. For a little earlier, where he said, “The expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God,” only the faithful may be understood, those who already believed. Here, however, where he says, “Creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption,” unbelievers may be understood, those who had not yet believed in the time of the apostles, although they had been predestined to life; hence they believed afterward.

For we know that all creation—that is, every human being—groans and is in labor until now. In this passage, as blessed Augustine says, we should not follow Origen or his followers, who include every rational and irrational, corporeal and incorporeal creature. Not every creature groans, as they wish; rather, the human being does, for he has a certain communion with every creature.

In the manner in which he said a little earlier, “All creation”—that is, every human being—“groans,” is afflicted, and is sorrowful in pain, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, prisons, and labor. Or, as it is better expressed in Greek, “he suffers in many distresses until now,” that is, until the day of judgment. And as long as “until now,” or “today,” is said, human creation will always remain subject to distresses and pains. But those who already reign with God and daily pass into everlasting rest do not groan once they have been freed from the hardships of this age.

Not only that creation—which means not only believers and unbelievers—groans and suffers in the present life, but we ourselves also, that is, the apostles, who are perfected in faith and possess the first fruits of the Spirit, suffer; and we ourselves groan inwardly in heart and mind, enduring prisons, scarcity, poverty, and many distresses and afflictions.

He rightly and appropriately says, “Not only do others groan, but we apostles ourselves, who possess the first fruits of the Holy Spirit,” because just as God chose them first, so they deserved to receive the Holy Spirit first on the day of the resurrection, when he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). This also occurred on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came upon them in tongues of fire.

Or he called them “the first fruits of the Spirit” because they received the greater gifts of the Holy Spirit in preaching, so that they spoke in the languages of all nations, and in miracles, by which they became glorious, surpassing all mortals. For it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that they placed the sick and the dead in the streets so that, when Peter came, at least his shadow might fall upon them and they might be healed. We also read that blessed Andrew raised thirty or more dead people in one day.

The first fruits are called the best and most precious things, as it is written in the law: “You shall offer the first fruits of your gold and silver to the Lord,” that is, the best and most precious things. Truly, then, it was fitting that those through whose ministry the evangelical teaching and the faith of the Lord were to be spread throughout the fourfold world should receive the greater gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Alternatively: “Not only,” he says, “do others groan, but we also, who already have offered the first fruits of our spirit—that is, the rationality and devotion of our mind—to God as a burnt offering.” This offering burns with the fire of love for God and neighbor, concerning which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

Did the same Apostle not have the first fruits of his mind offered to God, when he said: “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. VII)? For the Apostle served the law of God through the rationality and intention of his mind, consenting to it in this respect: he did not wish to be subject to carnal desire. But with the flesh he served the law of sin, that is, the evil habit by which he desired.

Awaiting the adoption of the children of God, the redemption of our body. A question arises here. In earlier passages of this Epistle the Apostle says, “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God”; and elsewhere, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law” (Gal. III). Why, then, does he now say that we await the adoption, or election, of the children of God, and the redemption of our body, that is, of the whole Church, which is Christ’s body? This question is resolved in what follows, where the Apostle says:

For by hope we were saved. In hope, indeed, all believers are already children of God and redeemed through Christ’s passion; but we still await the time when what we now are and possess in hope we may finally be and possess in reality. All believers have faith that we are children of God and redeemed by the blood of his passion. But his passion will not benefit others except the elect, who will be children of God, as John says: “Beloved, we are now children of God in hope, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be in reality” (I John III). “But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (ibid.).

“For by hope we were saved.” Just as faith is believing what we do not see, so hope is expectation of future goods. Through Christ’s passion we were redeemed in hope; through baptism we receive forgiveness of sins, and we are children of God in hope, not in reality, because it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

But hope that is seen is not hope, as though he were saying: “The thing that is seen is not hope. For what does one hope for if one sees it?” We do not hope for what we see. For example, I see you standing in my presence; I do not hope that you will come.

But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience, that is, we do not give up. Between hope and reality stands patience, because through the patience by which the saints endure the adversities of this age, without seeking their reward in the present, they hope to attain eternal glory.

Likewise, the Spirit also helps our weakness. That is, just as hope and patience help and sustain the weakness of our mind, so too does the Holy Spirit. The weakness of the soul is often that it asks for things which are not suitable for us, as what follows makes clear: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for.”

Often, while we wish to ask good things for ourselves, we ask for things contrary and harmful to us. If these were granted to us, we would be like blessed Paul, who asked for things contrary to himself when he asked that the spirit of temptation and weakness be taken away from him. If he had been heard, perhaps he would have been lifted up by the greatness of his revelations and fallen into ruin.

Similarly, when placed in prosperity, we often ask that it be preserved for us; if it remained with us always, perhaps our soul would become entangled in love for it. Likewise, when we are placed in weakness, we implore deliverance for the sake of testing or correction. If it were taken away from us, perhaps we would return to our former sins or labor less earnestly in good works.

Therefore, we do not know how to pray as we ought unless the Holy Spirit teaches us. But the Holy Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings. Blessed Ambrose says that whenever the faithful ask for something contrary to their salvation through ignorance, not through presumption, the Holy Spirit—who is of one substance with the Father and the Son—places himself between us and God the Father and asks for what is useful for us.

He does so neither with the movement of the air nor with sound or the noise of a voice, but inexpressibly, as befits his divinity, which is equal and consubstantial with God the Father. Often he changes into something better the things we ask for that are contrary to us, not giving us what we ask.

According to other teachers, he is also said to plead and groan for us because, whoever he fills with his grace, he makes them both ask and groan over their own sins and those of others; or because they are delayed from the kingdom. These groanings are rightly called inexpressible, because no one can express how great the compunctions in the hearts of the faithful are or how great a reward they deserve before God. [Col. 0435D]

But he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God. God the Father, together with his Son, who penetrates all the hidden things of hearts and secrets—not only of human beings but also of angels—knows what the Holy Spirit desires as he dwells in the hearts of his faithful, because they possess one knowledge; or he knows what the Spirit causes us to desire.

He also pleads for the saints according to God, because he makes us ask for those things that both please God and are useful to us, so that in prayer we may say: “Eternal God, who knows hidden things and future things, have mercy on us, as you know is necessary for us and as pleases you.” Thus he speaks to God without the sound of a voice, when he seems to us to be silent, because he sees even when he is not seen, and asks for those things that he knows please God the Father and benefit us, for he and the Father have one will.

Now we know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called as saints according to his purpose. Those who love God, who keep and observe his commandments, as the Lord says, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV)—this is what he means: those who love God and keep his commandments, and who have been called according to the purpose, or predestination, of almighty God for this purpose, that by living holy lives they may be holy.

If at any time they ask foolishly and ignorantly for something contrary to their own benefit, as Paul and the sons of Zebedee did, almighty God works together with them for good, either by not giving what they ask or by changing it into something else in place of what they requested. He does not charge this to them as sin, but grants them the things that should be given to those who love God.

He rightly says “work together,” because those who ask are at work, while almighty God works together with them by fulfilling what pertains to their salvation.

For those whom he foreknew—that is, whom he understood beforehand to be believers and to remain in their faith—he also predestined, or predetermined and appointed, to be conformed to the image of his Son; that is, to become like the Son in the glory of his humanity, who “transformed the body of our lowliness,” as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3). Although in the power of his divinity we are not equal to him, nevertheless in glory, immortality, and incorruption we shall be like him, because “we shall see him just as he is” (1 John 3). Or certainly he predestined them to be conformed to the image of his Son so that, just as Christ committed no sin and “no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2), so those who wish to become brothers of the Lord Jesus Christ may have no desire to sin.

“So that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers.” Every only-begotten son can be called firstborn, but not every firstborn can be called only-begotten. Whoever first opens his mother’s womb by being born, and has no other brothers following him, is both firstborn and only-begotten. But whoever first emerges from his mother’s womb and afterward has brothers following him is only firstborn. The Son of God, however—the Redeemer of the human race—if we weigh the matter with careful consideration, must be proclaimed both only-begotten and firstborn, according to both his divinity and his humanity. He is only-begotten according to his divinity, because in the nature of divinity he has no other brothers; but he is firstborn because, before every creature, he was not made but begotten, as he says through Solomon: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

According to his humanity, he may indeed be called the only-begotten of blessed Mary, and firstborn among many adoptive brothers, because he was the first to rise from the dead and the first to ascend into heaven. These are the brothers of whom he himself said to Mary: “Go to my brothers and say to them” (John 20). All the faithful are called his brothers because he deigned to become human. Yet he who is our brother according to the flesh is himself our Lord and God according to his divinity.

Those whom he predestined, or predetermined, to reign with him in eternal blessedness, he also called through himself and through his apostles. He continues to call them until the end of judgment. Those whom he called by his grace to remain with him in glory, he also justified through his Passion, adorning them through baptism and faith accompanied by good works; and he will justify them until the end of the age. Those whom he justified, he also glorified.

He uses the past tense. In this passage the Apostle uses it for the future when he says “he glorified,” following the manner of sacred Scripture, which commonly narrates future events as though they had already happened. Those whom he called and justified in the present age, he glorified on the day of judgment, just as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “When Christ appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3).

“What, then, shall we say about these things?”—that is, about what we have just said concerning calling, justification, and glorification. What thanksgiving shall we render to him who, freely and without any preceding merits, predestined us, before we existed, to reign with him, and afterward called and justified us, and at last will also glorify us? The same thought is found in the Psalmist: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Psalm 115).

It may also be understood thus: What can we say against God’s predestination, if not all of us are yet predestined to reign with him? “If God is for us”—that is, if he fights for us, since he predestines, justifies, and glorifies—who can fight against us? No one: neither the devil, nor Nero, nor any persecutor.

“He who did not spare his own Son,” that is, did not preserve him from death, but handed him over for all of us who were predestined to eternal life. The Father himself handed over the Son because he permitted him to be handed over, and the Son himself was handed over in many ways. The word *parcere*—“to spare”—sometimes means “to release,” as in Virgil: “Spare your fear, Cytherea,” that is, “release yourself from fear.” Sometimes it means “to preserve,” as here: “He did not spare his own Son.” Hence bees are called *parcae*, that is, preservers, because they preserve their honey.

“How will he not also give us all things with him?” This refers especially to the apostles, to whom the Truth said: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones” (Matthew 19). It may also refer to all the predestined, who possess in their Head, Christ, everything that he himself possesses. Since every creature is incomparably far below the Son of God, through whom all things were made (John 1), if God the Father loved us so greatly that he handed him over for us, he will certainly be able to accomplish these things in us.

“Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” That is: Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? The devil accuses God’s elect, as he accused blessed Job, but he increased rather than diminished his merit, because that righteous man patiently endured his adversities.

It should be noted that, according to blessed Augustine, this sentence must be read as a question and interrogation. As he himself says, many answers can be given to an inquiry, whereas a question must be answered either affirmatively or negatively. Therefore it should not be pronounced in such a way that, after the emphatic question “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?”, the words that follow—“God, who justifies”—are spoken in the tone of someone asking a question, so that the unspoken answer may be “No.” Likewise, the following words, “Who is the one who condemns?”, should be read interrogatively, so that the words “Christ Jesus, who died, indeed who also rose again” may be understood as the answer, with “No” silently supplied.

The sense is: Will Christ, who died for us and rose again in order to give us life, condemn us? Certainly not; rather, he will save us. But the words that follow—“who is at the right hand of the Father, who also intercedes for us”—should no longer be pronounced as a question, but rather as an affirmation. Who is at the right hand of God—that is, in the fullness and greatness of the Father’s majesty—and who also intercedes for us with God the Father, not by voice but by compassion? Each day he presents before the Father’s countenance the human being whom he assumed and the most grievous kind of death that he endured for us, so that the Father may have mercy on us.

“Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ?” This belongs with what was said above, where he states: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory,” because everything in the present is momentary in comparison with future glory. Therefore he addresses the Romans so that they would not fail in tribulations: Look at Peter; consider Paul. Nero was able to kill them before he could separate them from the love of Christ. Stephen, buried under stones, and Laurence, burned alive, could not be separated from Christ, because their minds were so joined to God that they were insensible to every torment they had to endure.

“Will tribulation separate us, or distress?” Distress means every necessity and every deprivation. Persecution, however, is the force of evil, for to persecute is openly to inflict violence. “Danger?” Danger is understood in many matters and in ambushes. “The sword?” The sword can signify every kind of punishment. “Hunger and nakedness?” These could not separate them, because they possessed the true bread, Christ, who spiritually fed and clothed them, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3).

“Because for your sake we are put to death all day long.” This is the voice of the martyrs addressing Christ. “All day long” means at all times, for as long as we live, since “the one who perseveres to the end will be crowned” (Matthew 10). It is not enough to suffer tribulation for Christ for one day; it must be endured at all times, if necessary. “We have been regarded as sheep for slaughter,” which are killed without resistance. Just as sheep do not resist when they are led to death, so we should not resist when we are prepared for execution.

“But in all these tribulations and torments we overcome and conquer because of him who loved us,” that is, because of Christ, who loved us unto death, since he died for us and said to us: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

“For I am certain that neither death,” which is inflicted upon the body, “will be able to separate us from the love of Christ.” He did not say “I suppose,” but “I am certain.” Nor will life—that is, the present life, which is prolonged through the denials of Christ—be able to do so. The sense is: If Nero were to threaten me with a death more cruel than all others, or with a life in the present age more prosperous than all others, he would not be able to separate me from the faith of Christ, nor my fellow apostles from it.

“Nor angels”—that is, evil angels, who transform themselves into angels of light—or according to the statement: “If an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what we preached, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1). The sense is: Even if an angel from heaven wished to separate me from the love of Christ—which cannot happen—he would not be able to separate me.

“Nor principalities,” that is, the opposing powers of demons, who exercise authority over others, concerning whom he himself says in the Letter to the Ephesians: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age” (Ephesians 6). “Nor powers,” meaning the opposing demons who stand under those principalities. “Nor things present,” that is, present good things promised to believers, or evils that are threatened. “Nor things future,” that is, the good or evil things of this age.
