“Nor strength,” that is, the devil, the prince of demons, of whom it is said: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard” (Luke 11). “Nor height,” that is, astrology. “Nor depth,” that is, necromancy, which searches out the lower regions of hell. Through these two practices many were turned away from the faith.

The sense is: Even if all astrologers and mathematicians—that is, observers of the stars, who profess to penetrate the order and courses of the heavenly bodies—should come against us, or even those who through necromancy, that is, the raising of the dead, summon souls back from the underworld, as that pythoness summoned back the soul of Samuel, they will in no way be able to separate us from the love of Christ.

“Nor any other creature,” that is, if there is any creature above or below, besides those I have mentioned, it too will not be able to separate us and turn us in another direction. Or, according to Gregory, “another creature” here means a human being, who can separate himself from the love of God by living wickedly. The sense is: No other creature except ourselves can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus; yet we ourselves can separate ourselves from it by living wickedly.

For the minds of the saints are joined to God, who is supreme Spirit, by such love that no creature stands between them and God. “For the one who clings to God is one spirit.”

## Chapter 9

“I speak the truth in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ; “I do not lie.” Under the compulsion of necessity the Apostle often swore an oath, without acting against the Lord’s command. Because he was about to state something almost unbelievable, he therefore swore under the compulsion of necessity.

Among the Romans who had believed were believing Jews, to whom he was writing these things. Since there were people who said that Paul did not love his own nation because he was preaching to the Gentiles, he binds himself by an oath, asserting that he loved and cherished his nation. Therefore he adds: “My conscience bears witness to me in the Holy Spirit that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart.”

He does not say, “I have a slight and small sorrow,” or “a temporary pain that suddenly arises and suddenly departs.” Rather, he testifies that great sorrow and continuous pain were present in him on behalf of his brothers, who not only refused to receive the Son of God sent to them, but even proclaimed him worthy of death, saying to Pilate: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23); “He is guilty of death.”

When he says “in the Holy Spirit,” or “through the Holy Spirit,” he swears by Christ—that is, he calls upon the Holy Spirit, who was in his mind, as a witness to his conscience. His own conscience bears witness on his behalf that he grieved exceedingly over the destruction of his brothers.

“For I could wish”—that is, “I wish”—“that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who are my relatives according to the flesh, who are Israelites,” that is, descended from Israel.

What caused such a sudden change in the Apostle’s mind that he wished to be accursed from Christ, when in many passages this is understood as separation, although shortly before he had said that he could in no way be separated from the love of Christ?

It must be considered that *anathema* has several meanings. It is used for separation, as in the edict of the emperor Justinian, and where the same Apostle says: “If an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what we preach to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1), that is, separated from God. It is also used for a curse, as is very frequently found in the Canons: “If anyone does this or that, let him be accursed,” that is, cursed. It is used for bodily death, as here, where the meaning is as if he said: “I wished to be killed by Christ in the body.” This is what he means by “according to the flesh.”

Someone might say: “Blessed Apostle, why did you wish to be killed according to the flesh?” He himself supplies the answer: “So that my brothers, who are my relatives according to the flesh, might be saved and live in their minds for God.” By saying “who are my relatives according to the flesh,” he shows that they are not his relatives in the integrity of faith and devotion of mind.

In this passage the Apostle imitated the love and deed of Moses the lawgiver. When the Lord said to him, “Go down, for your people have sinned; let me destroy them and make you into a great nation” (Exodus 32), Moses, moved by exceedingly great love, said: “Either forgive them this offense, or erase me from your book” (ibid.). When the Lord saw his love for the people, he said: “I will not erase you from my book, but I have forgiven them according to your word” (Numbers 14).

So also the Apostle, wishing rather to please Christ, spoke these words about the killing of his body under the compulsion of love, although in the affection of his mind he in no way wished to be separated from Christ.

“Their adoption and sonship,” that is, their election. They possess the election of sons because sons were adopted from them, and that people itself was called the Son of God. Hence it is said to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4), and through Isaiah: “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Isaiah 1). It was their glory that, from all the nations, they were chosen as God’s special people.

To them also the Old Testament was given—or, as some copies read, “the Testaments,” namely the Old and the New, if they are willing to believe. The New Testament was given to them so that they might pass from the slavery of the law into the freedom of Christ’s grace.

“To them belong also the legislation,” that is, the giving of the law, because the law was given to them through Moses; “and the worship,” namely the practice of divine religion, which was handed down to them; and “the promises,” both concerning Christ and concerning their redemption. Eternal life was also given to them, so that whatever had been promised to the fathers might be fulfilled in their sons.

“Their fathers”—that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—from whom, according to the flesh, Christ was born, not according to his divinity. He is “God over all, blessed forever.” Christ is God and man. According to his humanity, he assumed flesh from them and was among all things; according to his divinity, begotten from God the Father before the ages, he is above all in the power of divinity.

It should be noted that, although he had spoken of the rejection of his ancestors, he did not proceed by murmuring or reproving God’s judgment. Rather, he blessed him, knowing with certainty that all things are governed and ordered by him according to a just judgment. Therefore he adds:

“But it is not as though the word of God has failed.” The sense is: Although the multitude of the Jews, my ancestors, remained in the error of unbelief, unwilling to believe in Christ, I do not therefore say that God’s promise has vanished or been annulled—the promise made to Abraham that “in his seed all the nations will be blessed” (Genesis 12). It has been fulfilled in those who have believed, both Jews and Gentiles, and in those who will yet believe.

“For not all who are from Israel are Israelites.” Jacob and Israel were names belonging to one man. But not all who descended from his stock are Israelites—that is, people who see God with the mind—because they do not behold God with mind and faith. Israel is therefore divided into a spiritual and a carnal Israel.

Believing Jews are sons of Israel and of Abraham according to the flesh and according to faith. Those who do not believe, although they are sons of Israel according to the flesh, are not so according to the Spirit. The Gentiles, although they are not sons of Israel according to the flesh, are nevertheless sons of Israel and Abraham according to faith and mind, because they contemplate God with the mind.

“Nor because they are Abraham’s seed are they all sons.” It was said only of Isaac: “In Isaac your seed will be called.” Ishmael indeed came from Abraham’s seed, yet he is not counted as his son. Just as not all Abraham’s sons according to the flesh are called his sons, but his seed is established in Isaac, so now not all who descended from his stock through Isaac are regarded as his sons, but those who possess his faith and believe in Christ, concerning whom it was foretold: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.”

That is, not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed. Although the Jews who remain in unbelief are sons of Abraham by the nature of the flesh, because they descended from his lineage, they are not therefore sons of God, since they have degenerated from Abraham’s faith and works. Nor does anything belonging to the gift of spiritual blessing made to Abraham concerning Christ and the multitude of believers pertain to them.

The Gentiles, however, who are children of the promise, are counted as Abraham’s seed—that is, in Christ—because they imitate Abraham’s faith and works. The Gentiles are called children of the promise because of the promise made concerning them to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.”

In this way Isaac preceded as a figure of the Gentile people. Therefore, although not all the Jews believe, what was promised to Abraham remains true: “In Isaac your seed will be called,” that is, in those who are promised to you as future sons. He gives an example:

“This is the word of the promise: ‘At this time I will come,’” namely through an angel; that is, “I will appear.” “And Sarah will have a son.” Therefore, just as Isaac came through the promise expressed in the words “In Isaac your seed will be called,” so the Gentile people, by following Abraham’s faith and footsteps, are deemed worthy to obtain the grace of blessing through the promise made to him.

“Not only those [two], but also Rebecca, having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father.” The order of the words and of the meaning is as follows: Not only those two sons of Abraham, Isaac and Ishmael, represented the two peoples, the faithful and the unbelieving, but Rebecca too bore a figure of believers and reprobates in her two sons, Jacob and Esau, whom she conceived from one act of intercourse with our father Isaac.

It is not without significance that he says “from one act of intercourse.” For perhaps Jacob might have said: “When my father begot me, he was of a good mind and good will; but when he begot my brother Esau, he was of an evil will. Therefore his goodness was diffused through his seed into me, while his wickedness passed into my brother.” Or, so that no human being might make such a claim, the Apostle says that those two were born from one act of intercourse, showing that one was loved through the gift of the One who calls, while the other was hated according to a just judgment.

For all who descend from Adam’s lineage are born as children of sin and are therefore worthy of condemnation. If any are delivered, this is the goodness and grace of God, not a repayment of their merits.

“When they had not yet been born, and had done nothing either good or evil, so that God’s purpose, or preordination, might remain according to election—not from their works, which did not yet exist, but from the one who calls—it was said to her: ‘The elder will serve the younger.’”

“From the one who calls” means: From the gift of almighty God, who called them, it was said to Rebecca that Esau, the elder by birth, would render the service of servitude to the younger (Genesis 25), namely Jacob.

And so it happened. For, as we read in the Books of Kings, in the times of David, Solomon, and the other kings, Edom served Israel until the time when, as the same volume records, Edom prepared itself not to remain under Judah. This had certainly been foretold to him by his father Isaac: “The time will come when you will cast his yoke from your neck” (Genesis 27).

Who among human beings can explain why almighty God chose Jacob before he was born and rejected Esau, when neither one nor the other could yet accomplish anything good or evil, except that in Jacob he displayed his grace and mercy, while in Esau he fulfilled his just judgment? For when Rebecca had already conceived in her womb and went to consult the Lord—whether through Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, or through someone else by whom God at that time gave responses—it was said to her by the God who calls: “Two sons are in your womb, and two peoples; and the elder will serve the younger.”

Therefore, just as God’s purpose and predestination were not according to Jacob’s election on the basis of good merit, so the election of the Gentiles was not according to an election based on merits, but according to God’s grace and predestination.

Why Jacob was chosen without good works, while Esau was hated without evil works, is known to God alone, who knows all things before they happen; his judgments are always just.

As it is written in the prophet Malachi: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau.” When Scripture says, “You hate nothing that you have made,” and since God saw all that he had made and it was very good, the question arises why Esau is said to have been hated.

The answer is that God did not hate the nature he had made, but the sin and vice that he had not made. He loved Jacob by his freely given mercy. He hated Esau by a just judgment. Since both were stained by original sin, his loving one was an act of mercy, while his rejecting the other was the expression of his just judgment.

“What, then, shall we say? Is there injustice with God?” The implied meaning is: Since he loved Jacob by his mercy and rejected Esau by his just judgment, loving one and hating the other, must he be called unjust? Certainly not.

“For he says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’” The order is this: “I will have mercy on the one upon whom I have mercy,” by calling him to my faith and giving him my faith so that he may believe in me; and “I will show compassion to the one upon whom I show compassion,” by enabling him to live justly, to be merciful, and to persevere in good works, for which he may receive a reward.

“Therefore it depends not on the one who wills”—that is, it is not the human will—“nor on the one who runs,” that is, human exertion, “but on God who has mercy”: his mercy gives a person the will to do good, the ability to act, and perseverance.

A good human will alone is not sufficient unless, through God’s mercy, it also reaches the point at which God gives the person the will to do good and to accomplish that good, according to what the Psalmist says: “His mercy will come before me, and his mercy will follow me” (Psalm 63).

But someone may perhaps ask: How are the elect rewarded, or what reward do they deserve, if both good will and the completion of the work are given to them by God? The answer is that the elect are worthy of reward because, as soon as they perceive that they are being preceded by God’s grace, they labor with all their strength to obey by submitting themselves to his will.

For Scripture says to Pharaoh—not that Scripture speaks by itself, but another speaks through it, just as God speaks here: “For this very purpose I raised you up,” that is, “I made the hardness of your heart known to others for this purpose, so that I might show my power in you, or my might, and so that my name,” that is, my divinity, “might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”

So it is now. Throughout the whole earth, and across the fourfold world, the name of his divinity is proclaimed, because the Book of Exodus is read almost everywhere.

Before Pharaoh was raised up through the ten plagues by God, he was, as it were, asleep. When he was raised up, the kind of heart he possessed was made manifest to people who had not known it. Therefore the Lord says: “I raised you up by striking you with ten plagues,” that is, “I revealed the wickedness of your heart, which was not hidden from me.” Thus, when he was raised up, he said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exodus 5).

And because he ignored God on account of his own wickedness, God hardened his heart (Exodus 14), that is, he did not soften it, since Pharaoh’s merits demanded this. But someone asks why God destroyed either Pharaoh with his army, or the Sodomites, or those who perished in the flood.

The answer is that their wickedness had already reached completion and exceeded the measure of sinning; therefore, by God’s just judgment, it had to be punished. Thus every sinner is divinely punished when the course of his sins has been completed. Concerning this the Lord says to Abraham: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Genesis 15), and to the Jews: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matthew 23).

Yet because God revealed Pharaoh’s wickedness by not softening his heart, the blame does not fall upon God, who does not perform evil. Rather, Pharaoh’s evil, which he himself committed, is properly attributed to him.

For example, if there were two vessels, one full of balsam and the other of dung, and someone shook or fanned them, he would not be the author of the fragrance or the stench. Likewise, God, who touched Pharaoh with his plagues, is not the author of Pharaoh’s wickedness.

Pharaoh was struck, together with his army, and drowned in the sea for two reasons: first, so that their multiplied wickedness might be punished; and second, so that terror might be instilled in the Israelites, so that they would fear to sin lest they suffer similar things, knowing that God condemns iniquity.

For he says: “So that I may show my power in you,” namely through signs and punishments, “and so that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” Everywhere the great God is proclaimed, who drowned Pharaoh with his chariots and horsemen in the sea.

Therefore, the implied meaning is this: If the will does not depend on the one who wills, nor the course on the one who runs, but mercy belongs to God who has mercy, then “he has mercy on whom he wills,” as with the Israelites, whom he rescued not because of their merits but because he regarded them with his own compassion.

For the Israelites had done no good in Egypt by which they deserved to be delivered. And “he hardens whom he wills,” that is, he permits a person to be hardened and abandons him in his hardness, as he did Pharaoh and his army. By his mercy God suspended the plagues against Pharaoh, and this hardened his heart.

“You will say to me, then: ‘Why does he still find fault?’” That is, why does human frailty still bring a charge against God because he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills? “For who can resist his will?”

That he has mercy on some is the effect of his goodness and grace; that he condemns others demonstrates his just judgment, because before we are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit (John 3), we are all children of wrath.

“O man, who are you to answer back to God?” He calls “man” one who is merely humanly wise and attempts to criticize God’s judgment.

“Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” That is, “Why did you make me into such smallness, or for such a lowly service?”

“Does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor”—to be used for serving food or drink that passes into the service of a king—“and another for dishonor,” that is, for a lowly task, namely kitchen work, where meat is cooked?

So almighty God, the potter of the human race, has authority from the mass of sin and perdition—that is, from the mass of the human race—to make one vessel for honor: to create one person for the purpose that God himself may be honored in him, honoring him by calling him to his faith and saving him for life; and another for dishonor, that is, to destroy the reprobate by a just judgment because of their wickedness.

For all vessels are corrupt when they come from a corrupt mass. But if, by the skill of his craft, the potter purifies some of them from the defect of the mass by firing them in the furnace, can he not be glorified in them? If he leaves some unpurified, he is not to be reproved, because he remains within his own authority. The mass is his.

“But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with great patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction”—the implied question is, “Who are you to answer back to God?”—God wished to show his wrath, that is, his vengeance, against Pharaoh and the Egyptians, against the Sodomites and those destroyed in the flood; and to make known his power by delivering the Hebrews.

He endured with great patience the vessels of wrath—that is, he waited for the Egyptians, through the plagues, to come to repentance, not pouring them all out at once. He calls them “prepared for destruction” because by living wickedly they had prepared and fitted themselves for eternal destruction.

To this someone might object to the Apostle: “Why did he destroy them and save the Jews?” He answers the objection by saying:

“In order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy,” that is, in the Hebrews, “whom he prepared for glory,” so that he might be glorified and praised in them. He rescued them from Egypt, killed their enemies, led them across the Red Sea, and gave them the land of promise.

“Whom he also called,” that is, those whom he called to his faith, as he also called us—the apostles and other believers—from the same people. He called them from Egypt by the grace of his mercy, and he called us from the evil age: we are vessels of his mercy.

All human beings are born sinners after Adam’s transgression and are worthy of condemnation. According to their merits, they ought all to perish. But the fact that a few are counted worthy to be saved, being transferred from vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy, occurs so that the mercy of the Author may be revealed in those who are freed from eternal death. The fact that more perish by remaining in vessels of wrath, hindered by their sins, shows that all deserved to perish and that, accordingly, a just judgment according to their merits remains in them.

But because the Jews excluded the Gentiles from the faith of Christ, saying that they could not be saved, the Apostle adds: He called to his faith not only people from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles.

As he says in Hosea: “I will call the one who was not my people, ‘My people,’” that is, the Gentiles, so that they might be his people. This is understood according to blessed Jerome. According to blessed Augustine, however, it may also be understood of the Jews, who became “not God’s people” when they withdrew from God and rejected Christ, saying: “We do not know where he is from” (John 9). As we have in the Psalm: “The sons of strangers lied to me” (Psalm 17).

Later they became Christ’s people when, on one day, three thousand believed, on the next day five thousand, and afterward many thousands (Acts 2). Thus they who had not obtained mercy by remaining in unbelief obtained mercy by becoming faithful.

“And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God.”

When the Gentiles were oppressed by unbelief, God said to them through the prophets that they were not his people. Although by the condition of creation they were God’s creatures, they were not his people through grace. After they came to the faith, in the place—that is, throughout the whole world—where it had previously been said to them, before they believed in God, “You are not my people,” there they are now called sons of the living God, not by nature but by adoption.

As the Evangelist says: “To all who believed in him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1). He rightly says “of the living God,” in distinction from the dead gods whom they had formerly worshiped. The passage may likewise be understood of the Jews, as is evident.

“Isaiah cries out concerning Israel,” that is, on Israel’s behalf: “If the number of the sons of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

Just as the number of the sand of the sea is unknown to human beings, so the Israelite people became innumerable through its own multitude. Although they multiplied in this way and were weighed down by the burden of their sins, only a remnant was saved—that is, the apostles and the others who believed from among them.

“For he will bring a word to completion,” that is, perfect it, “and shorten it in righteousness, because the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.”

The word that perfects all things and is shortened in truth is understood in three ways. The shortened word is the one concerning which the Lord says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deuteronomy 6). Upon these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend.

The shortened word may also be understood as the Apostles’ Creed, in which the faith is contained, although it is proclaimed through many different books; or as the four books of the Gospel in comparison with the law and the prophets. The shortened word may also be called that which contains perfection.

And as Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed”—namely, the apostles, who were sown throughout the whole world, sent by Christ, and multiplied the fruit of believing souls—“we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.” Unless the apostles, who emerged as the seed of the entire harvest of believers, had been sown by the Lord throughout the whole world and had believed in him, all the Jews would have perished at one time through the sin of unbelief, just as the Sodomites and Gomorrhites perished in a single destruction and moment [Col. 0447B] (Gen. XIV). For many of the Jews who would have perished afterward believed the apostles’ teaching, since the apostolic seed had remained. Ambrose understands this seed differently: as Christ, without whom, unless he had been preserved by the Father, the Jews would have perished; the apostles who fled after abandoning him would have perished, and we also would have perished.

What then shall we say? We shall say this: the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness—namely, the circumcision of the Law, the Sabbath rest, and the legally prescribed sacrifices—apprehended righteousness, that of evangelical faith. Hence he adds: “But righteousness”—I mean, the righteousness that the Gentiles apprehended—“which is from faith,” because Christ’s faith justifies those who believe: when they are baptized in it and produce the fruits of righteousness and faith [Col. 0447C]. Or certainly, we can understand “righteousness” here in another way as Christ, who was made for us “righteousness and redemption” by God the Father, as the Apostle says elsewhere (Eph. I), because through him God the almighty Father justifies all who believe in him. The Gentiles apprehended this righteousness—not by drawing near to it spatially, but by believing through faith, since one approaches it by faith. Hence it is also called “righteousness from faith.”

Israel, however, by pursuing the law of righteousness—that is, the legal observance through which it thought it could be justified without the faith of Christ—did not attain the law of righteousness, that is, the law of the Gospel, where a person is justified through the faith of Christ and not through the works of the Law. We rightly understand “the law of righteousness” also to designate observance of the Law of Moses, because those who kept it in its own time were considered righteous [Col. 0447D], just as, conversely, those who did not keep it were condemned as unrighteous.

Why? The implied answer is: Why did Israel not attain the law of righteousness? Because it did not wish to be saved through the faith of Christ, but as though through works of the Law. For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling—that is, over Christ, refusing to believe in him; instead they said: “We have no king but Caesar; crucify this man” (John XIX). This stone is rightly so called on account of the firmness of faith. And just as he is the stone of salvation and firmness for those who believed in him, so he is the stone of stumbling for those who reject him.

As it is written in Isaiah: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal.” This is as though he were saying: “Behold, I shall send Christ among the Jewish people” [Col. 0448A]. He is called the stone of stumbling because, as soon as he was born, Herod and the Jews stumbled over him, killing the infants on his account (Matt. XIV). Then, as the Gospel relates, they were scandalized by him; and many of his disciples, hearing his word, were scandalized, and from that time no longer walked with him. Moreover, during his Passion his disciples abandoned him and fled (Matt. XXVI). Everyone who believes in him—that is, in Christ, who is of one essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit—and keeps his commandments will not be put to shame. That is, he will not blush at the sentence by which the rejected and unbelieving will be condemned when they hear him say: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” Rather, he will rejoice when he hears him say, together with the other elect: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Col. 0448B] (Matt. XXV). And because someone might object to the Apostle, “Why do you not pray for the unbelievers of your own nation?”—or lest the Gentiles become proud and despise the Jews—the Apostle adds:

## CHAPTER X

Brothers, who believe with me in Christ, the desire of my heart and my supplication to God are made for them, namely, for the unbelieving Jews, for their salvation. Here he shows that if someone could have been justified by works of the Law and could have earned the ability to attain the faith of Christ for them, all of them would have been called and saved, while the Gentiles, who were ignorant of the Law, would have been excluded from salvation. Salvation, therefore, is given freely by God and is not earned by a human being: namely, the faith of Christ [Col. 0448C] by which we are saved.

For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God—that is, the ardor of love for God—as I also had before my conversion, but not according to the knowledge of God. For it is foolish to venerate the Law given through a servant and persecute the Gospel given through the Lord. It is also foolish to confess the Father and deny the Son. In this respect the Jews did not possess the knowledge of God: they wished to cling to the Law given through a servant in such a way that they rejected the grace of the Gospel given through the Lord; and by persecuting the Son, they thought they were pleasing God the Father.

This is said of those who were held in ignorance, concerning whom the Truth says: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John XVI). Peter likewise says: “I know, brothers, that you did this evil through ignorance” (Acts III). For while many of the Jews were persecuting Christ’s apostles, they thought that by doing so they were pleasing God. On the other hand, many who knew the truth denied Christ, such as the scribes and Pharisees.

For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness—not that by which he is essentially righteous, but of Christ, through whose faith we are justified together with good works—and wishing to establish their own righteousness, namely, the Law, through which they thought they could be justified without Christ’s grace, they were not subject to the righteousness of God. They did not wish to submit themselves to the faith of Christ and to his Gospel. For since no one was perfectly justified by works of the Law, God sent his Son, who handed down to us the commandments of righteousness, which are called the Gospels [Col. 0449A], and in himself displayed for us the perfection of righteousness, so that by the grace of faith in him we might merit to attain perfection. And because the Jews sought to establish their own righteousness—that is, because they thought the righteousness of the Law sufficient for themselves—they did not wish to bend their necks to the righteousness of God, that is, to Christ, to faith in him, and to evangelical teaching.

For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes. “End” is understood as consumption, as when we say, “The dinner is finished,” that is, consumed. It can also mean consummation and perfection, as when we say, “The fabric is finished,” that is, perfected and completed. In this sense Christ is said to be the end of the Law: not its consumption, but its completion and consummation, for righteousness to everyone who believes. He himself is the completion [Col. 0449B] of the Law and the prophets, because he fulfilled through himself everything that the Law and the prophets had foretold about him in words and mysteries. Hence, hanging on the cross, he said: “It is completed” (John XIX). Whoever believes and confesses this is justified, provided that he performs works worthy of faith.

There is, however, a distinction between a task and an end. The task is the thing being done; the end is that for the sake of which it is done. The task is the Law and the prophets; the end is Christ, for whose sake all those things came beforehand.

For Moses wrote that the person who performs the righteousness that is from the Law will live in it—the implied noun being “righteousness.” Or, as some manuscripts have it, “he will live in them,” with “commandments and precepts” understood. He put “Law” for the works of the Law, namely circumcision, Sabbath rest [Col. 0449C], and the other legal works. The righteousness that is from the Law caused a person to live in it, because he was not killed. The reward of that righteousness, therefore, was nothing other than the present life, which was not taken away. “He will live in it” means that he will escape present death. But if someone fulfills spiritually the things prescribed by the Law, although he is not rewarded in the present age, nevertheless in the future he will receive eternal life as the reward for his labor—that is, the most immediate vision of the almighty God.

But concerning the righteousness that is from faith, he says the following. Here he calls Christ “righteousness,” for through his Passion and faith he justifies those who believe in him. This righteousness, Christ, who is the Word of God the Father, speaks in Deuteronomy through Moses, because he himself was speaking through the mouths of the prophets: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’”—that is, to bring Christ down—“or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead.

These words belong partly to Moses and partly to the Apostle. When Moses gave the Law to the Jews, he said to them: “Do not say in your heart”—that is, do not imagine in your mind—“Who will go up into heaven to bring me God’s command from there? Or who will descend into the abyss to bring me that command from there?” You do not need to seek it in this way, because:

“The word is near”—that is, the commandment of the Law—“in your mouth and in your heart,” and written in your presence. Or even God himself, in your heart and in your mouth, will teach you. But because Moses was a prophet and foretold many things about the future [Col. 0450A], the Apostle Paul referred his words to Christ, asserting that Moses spoke this through him who is true righteousness.

Through these words he instructs us not to say in our heart or suppose that Christ is local, as though he were contained in some particular place. Rather, we should believe that, according to the fullness of his divinity, he is everywhere and spread throughout all things with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what God the Father says through the prophet Jeremiah: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). Therefore he is not confined by a place, because every place exists in him. By presiding, he sustains all things; by sustaining, he presides; by filling, he surrounds; by surrounding, he fills.

The sense, therefore, of the Apostle’s words is this: “Do not say in your heart, whoever you are, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’”—that is, do not believe Christ to be local, so that you think that after his Ascension he is in heaven in such a way that he is not on earth, or that he is below in the abyss among the dead in such a way that, while you are placed above, he is unaware of you. Rather, believe him to be present everywhere according to his divinity, as it is said of him: “Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII).

Do not say, therefore, O man, “Who will ascend into heaven to bring Christ down to me from there, so that he may teach me?” At least do not say this in your heart, because Christ is here and everywhere. For he was on earth and said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III). How much more, then, since he is in heaven, is he also on earth?

“Or who will descend into the abyss?” The Apostle adds this from his own exposition: “That is, to bring Christ back from the dead” [Col. 0450C]. Likewise above: “That is, to bring Christ down.” You do not need to call Christ from the underworld, since you ought to acknowledge him as present everywhere. Hence Scripture itself says in Deuteronomy: “The word is near, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. XXX).

If we wish, we can understand “word” here simply as the word of the Law, which they continually had in their mouth by reading it, and likewise in their heart by constantly meditating on it and committing it to memory. In a higher sense, however, this Word is the one of whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I). Since the Word was God, he was near in their mouth and heart, as the one who fills all things.

For blessed Jerome says: “Just as a garment surrounds the whole body on every side, so Christ embraces his elect by surrounding them everywhere—and even more so, because a garment surrounds the body only externally by adhering to it, whereas Christ is externally in the mouth through confession and internally in the heart through belief,” as it is said here and elsewhere, where the same Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person” (Eph. III).

This is the Word of faith that we apostles preach. “This is the Word,” he says, namely the Son of God the Father, in whom it is necessary to believe according to our preaching.

For if you confess in your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved—that is, you will attain eternal salvation [Col. 0451A]. This is so, however, provided that you pursue works of righteousness, because it is not fitting for a servant of God to remain idle.

For one believes with the heart for righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth for salvation. He develops more carefully what he touched on above concerning faith. Faith must be placed in the heart, believing that God is a Trinity in persons and one in the omnipotence of his majesty, and that the Son became human. According to the Gospel, it must firmly hold that the human race was redeemed by his blood, and must not doubt that the things done concerning his humanity were displayed in a divine manner.

There must also be confession in the mouth, because the faith of the heart must be brought forth through the service of the mouth. This confession leads to salvation, provided that it is adorned with good works throughout the span of life. Otherwise faith without works is dead (James II). He is not speaking of bodily salvation, which even those who do not confess God possess, but of the salvation of the inner person, that is, the soul, which is saved by confession of true faith—not temporarily but eternally, because the salvation brought by this confession is everlasting.

For the Scripture of the prophet Isaiah says: “Everyone who believes in him”—that is, in Christ, with the faith that works through love—“will not be put to shame.” Whoever believes in Christ as one ought to believe will not be ashamed with the unbelievers on the day of judgment, when the Judge himself will say to them: “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. XXX). Rather, he will rejoice when he is rewarded by the one in whom he believed, gathered into the number and fellowship of the elect who confess God.

This example is directed against the Jews, who thought that the Gentiles ought to be separated from the faith of Christ. Hence he adds:

There is no distinction—that is, in the example I have given. Between whom is there no distinction or separation? Between Jews and Greeks, because it is said of both: “Everyone who believes in him,” whether Jew or Gentile, “will not be put to shame.”

For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who invoke him. That is, the Lord who is the Creator and Lord of the Jews is himself the Creator and Lord of the Gentiles, that is, of all human beings. He is called “rich toward all who invoke him” because he is able to rescue all who believe in him from present tribulations and lead them to eternal life, granting them the reward promised by him.

Or he is called rich for this reason: he is powerful enough to hear and save the Gentiles as well as the Jews, because there is no partiality with him; he does not attend to one in such a way as to deny himself to another [Col. 0451D]. If our voice reaches all who hear equally and yet remains one voice, how much more can the almighty God mercifully hear everyone, without, while hearing one person, forgetting the prayer of another? Therefore he adds:

“For everyone who invokes the name of the Lord will be saved.” Whoever invokes the name of the Lord as it ought to be invoked—namely, with faith, mouth, and deed—will be saved.

How, then, will they invoke him—namely, the Jews—whom they have not believed? And for this reason they are not saved, because they do not invoke him. Or how will they believe in him whom they have not heard?

Therefore the Jews heard Christ [Col. 0452A] and did not hear him. They heard with the bodily ear, but not with the ear of the mind, which the Lord required when he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII). Moreover, they turned away their ears so that they would not hear his words. When he cried out in the temple and said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII), they refused to come to him by believing. Therefore they did not hear because they were not obedient.

But how will they hear without a preacher? Here he shows that he and his fellow apostles and preachers were sent by Christ to preach to the Jews, so that they might be instructed through their ministry. But the Jews persecuted them and drove them away, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is also recounted how Paul said to them: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but because you reject it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII). Hence he adds:

And how will preachers preach the word of life to them unless they are sent? They killed some preachers sent to them, such as James the brother of John and Stephen; they scourged the rest and drove them away. The sense is this: We apostles could never have undertaken the office of preaching unless, admonished and directed by the grace of God—which protects us—we had been sent first to announce the word of life to the Jews and then to the Gentiles. Therefore the Jews will not be excusable concerning the coming of the Son of God, because they drove from their territory the apostles sent for their salvation.

This may also suitably be understood in another way: “How,” he says, “will those preachers preach the word of life to them who have been expelled by them, unless they are sent again?” He also confirms by a prophetic example how the preachers wished to evangelize good things to them, but they refused to believe them, except for a few, as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things!”

The apostles’ feet were beautiful because they had been washed by the Lord. In sacred Scripture, feet sometimes signify good actions, as Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, shows when he says: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us, to illuminate those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to direct our feet”—that is, our actions—“into the way of peace” (Luke II).

At other times, feet signify the word of preaching, as in: “He subjected peoples to us, and nations under our feet” (Ps. XLVI). The apostles preached peace according to the Lord’s instructions, saying: “Into whatever house you enter, first offer peace, saying: ‘Peace to this house’” (Matt. X).

They evangelized good things, namely the rewards of the future kingdom, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man.” And concerning these the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. LVI). They also announced good things: faith in the Holy Trinity, the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, his Passion, resurrection, and Ascension, his coming for judgment, the glory of the elect, and the condemnation of the rejected.

But not everyone obeys the Gospel. Although the apostles had evangelized the good things of the heavenly homeland [Col. 0453A], not all the Jews, nor all the Gentiles, were obedient at that time to the preaching of the Gospel; nor do all obey even now.

For Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report?” Here Isaiah speaks in the person of the apostles, for he was filled with the same Spirit with which the apostles were filled. It must be observed, however, that in sacred Scripture “who” is sometimes used for “no one” and sometimes for “few.”

It is used for “no one,” as in: “Who among the clouds can be compared to the Lord?” (Ps. LXXXVIII)—that is, no one. It is used for “few” here: for only a few of the Jews were found who believed the apostles’ report. Their report is so called because inwardly, in their minds, under the Lord’s inspiration, they heard with spiritual hearing what they ought to bring forth externally, in bodily speech, for the salvation of their hearers [Col. 0453B].

Hence Paul also says elsewhere: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (1 Cor. XIII). David likewise says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. LXXXIV). The Jews withdrew from this hearing of the apostles—that is, from their preaching—refusing to believe in Christ.

Therefore faith comes from hearing. First a person hears a preacher explain how one ought to believe; afterward he receives faith. The hearing is through the word of Christ. The word of Christ that is preached by the apostles and teachers is the word of Christ because they preach nothing other than what is contained in the Gospel, which was spoken from Christ’s mouth—or what Christ himself reveals to them in their hearts and speaks through their mouths.

To this the Jews could have replied, although falsely: “We did not hear the word of Christ through the mouths of the apostles.” Against them the Apostle continues:

But I say: “Have they not heard?” The implied object is the Jews’ hearing of the apostles’ word of preaching. The Apostle answers himself and affirms that they did hear. Indeed, behold the affirmation—and here a distinction must be made. The sense is this: “Have the Jews not heard the word of Christ?” Indeed, that is, most certainly, I say in truth that they heard, but they disdained to believe.

Someone might have said in response: “The apostles departed from them; how, then, could they have heard?” The Apostle also asserts this by a prophetic example and says: “How could it have happened that they did not hear? Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

The same Psalmist had said above: “There are neither speech nor language whose voices are not heard” (Ps. XVIII). If the apostles’ voices were heard among the nations in the languages and speech of all peoples, how much more were they heard among the Jews in their own Hebrew language?

For if the Gospel was spread from Jerusalem to the four regions of the world, how was it not preached to the Jews themselves, from whom the preaching of that same Gospel began—especially since they too are situated in the interior of the world? That Jerusalem lies in the middle of the earth, like the navel of the belly, the Psalmist testifies when he says: “But God, our king before the ages, has worked salvation in the middle of the earth” (Ps. LXXII)—that is, in Jerusalem. And through Ezekiel the Lord says: “This is Jerusalem: I have placed her in the middle of the nations” (Ezek. V).

But perhaps someone asks why the almighty God determined to place that people in the middle of all the nations. The answer should be that this was done because, since that people alone among all the nations possessed knowledge of the true God, it might invite the others to the worship of the almighty God through the written Law, its worship, and its religion, just as we read that many Gentiles converted to Judaism.

Or it was done so that, if that people kept God’s Law, it would be honored and feared by all those around it, as happened in the days of David and Solomon, when all the kings situated around it sent it gifts. Or, if it withdrew from the Law and worship of God, it would be afflicted and devastated by its enemies, which happened very often [Col. 0454B] (1 Kings XIV).

There was also a fourth reason: because Christ was to be born from that same people, redeem the human race, and perform many miracles in the world while dwelling there, so that his fame could more quickly fly out from there to all the nations.

Let us return again to what came before. Therefore the sound of the apostles’ preaching went out into the whole earth, and their words to the ends of the world, because the earth almost failed them before their language did. In this example, by “earth” we can understand earthly people, who received only the sound—that is, the fame of the preaching and its simple instructions. By “the ends of the earth” we can understand philosophers and those educated in the liberal arts, who examined the words of evangelical preaching, as Augustine and Cyprian did.

[Col. 0454C] But I say: “Did Israel not know?” That is, if the apostles’ preaching reached all the nations, how much more did it reach the Jews, among whom it began to be sown, especially since they themselves are situated in the interior of all the nations.

Or alternatively: “Did Israel not know first?” It certainly knew, through the apostles and apostolic men. First Moses says: “I will bring you to jealousy against a non-nation.” “Jealousy,” which in Greek is called *zelos*, is not always understood uniformly or in one sense. For it is used for imitation, zeal, love, and envy, as here.

Moses speaks this against the Jews in the person of the almighty God. They were led to jealousy and envy against a non-nation—that is, against a people believing from among the nations—because they are always envious when they see it believing in the one whom they themselves killed, as is reported in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Jews saw the crowds of Gentiles believing, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what Paul was saying” (Acts XIII).

Before the Lord’s coming, the human race was divided into Jews and Gentiles. But through the enormity of their evils, the Gentiles had so exceeded the condition of their nature that they did not deserve even to be called a nation; rather, they were called dogs, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matt. XV).

Hence they were called a non-nation, because, having lost reason, they pursued irrationality. But afterward, when they believed both the apostles who preached and their successors, the Jews were stirred up and inflamed against them by the torches of envy.

Thus, explaining what he had said—“a non-nation”—the Apostle adds: “Against a foolish nation”—that is, one that worshiped idols instead of the true God—“I will provoke you to anger,” with “against this foolish nation” understood. Although it had been foolish until Christ’s coming, once it had obtained his faith it became wise. Against it, now believing, the Jews are provoked to anger—not because God produces jealousy and anger in them, but because he bestows upon the converted Gentiles the benefits that displeased the Jews.

The phrase “a non-nation” can also be understood in another way. Before receiving the faith, unbelieving Gentiles were called a nation. After receiving the grace of faith, however, they are no longer called a nation, but are called the people and nation of God, as the Lord says through the Psalmist: “The people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. XVII).

Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to mute idols, being carried along” (1 Cor. XII). This is as though he were saying: “Once you were Gentiles, but now you are no longer Gentiles.” Against this non-nation, therefore, the Jews, driven by envy, are angered.

Isaiah also says: “Not without reason did the Apostle use this word, ‘dares.’” Isaiah, filled with the prophetic Spirit, knew that the Jews would despise him and even cut him apart with a wooden saw; nevertheless, he “dares”—that is, he speaks boldly in the person of Christ, without fearing the rebellious Jews: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who were not asking about me.”

Christ himself appeared to the Gentiles, who were not seeking him and possessed no instruction or promise concerning him from either the Law or the prophets [Col. 0455C]. Someone is said to appear when he is not separated but comes suddenly and unexpectedly, as the Lord appeared to Abraham when he was not expected, and as the angel appeared to Zechariah. So the Lord Jesus appeared to the Gentiles through the preaching of the apostles and the flashing forth of miracles, when they were not expecting him.

That he himself appeared to the Gentiles in the apostles is testified by his own words: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXIX). Through heavenly teaching and the signs of miracles performed by the apostles, Christ appeared to the Gentiles, because he himself cooperated with them and spoke through their mouths.

For the Gospel says that, after setting out, they preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the accompanying signs.

It continues: “And to those who were not asking me.” The almighty God is often read as having been questioned by the saints, such as Moses, Abraham, Samuel, and others. The Gentiles, however, did not question God; they consulted idols and demons.

But to Israel the same Isaiah says in the person of Christ: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe but contradicted me.” He calls the entire time of the Lord’s preaching, up to his Passion, the whole day. He stretched out his hands to that same people because he displayed the most generous gifts of his benefits through abundant goodness. The stretching out of hands signifies the giving of gifts; and the one who grants benefits most generously to those who ask is said to stretch out his hands.

For he raised their dead, cured various bodily illnesses, fed the hungry and famished with his own bread, and bestowed upon them many countless blessings. Yet they continually contradicted him, saying about him: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. XII), and: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX).

Or he stretched out his hands when he allowed them to be fastened to the cross. It is also the custom of parents to stretch out their arms so that they may embrace their dearest children and place them in their lap. Thus the Lord wished to embrace the Jews and draw them into the bosom of his love, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. IV). But they always strove to contradict him, saying: “We do not know where this man is from” (John IX).

A nurse also ordinarily stretches out her hands so that the one being nurtured, encouraged by coming to her, may learn to walk. The Israelite people likewise were exceedingly lame, because they no longer possessed the steps of good action. The Lord, in a certain sense, stretched out his hands toward them so that they might come to him, when he said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). But, neglecting the benefits of his gifts, they drew their steps backward into unbelief.

## CHAPTER XI

I ask, then: Has God rejected his people? The implied qualification is: “Entirely.” Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. I was not rejected, but was saved with the others through the faith of Christ. For if he had entirely rejected his people Israel, he would not have saved me, since I derive my origin from their lineage [Col. 0456C].

God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Foreknowledge precedes predestination, and not everything that is foreknown is predestined; nevertheless, everything that is predestined is foreknown. In this passage, however, “foreknowledge” is understood as predestination, by which he shows that no one predestined—whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles—has been rejected.

For God foreknows good and evil, but he predestines only good. There is also a distinction between predestination and grace: predestination is the preparation of grace, while grace is the actual free bestowal of gifts.

Or do you not know—that is, are you unaware of—what Scripture says in the passage about Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? That is, against those who, from the ten tribes, killed the worshipers of the one true God because of idolatry.

“Lord, they have killed your prophets.” This is narrated more fully in the Books of Kings (3 Kings XVII; 2 Chronicles XVII): how Ahab and Jezebel, together with those who supported them, killed the Lord’s prophets. They destroyed your altars. This occurred among the ten tribes, which had received golden calves from Jeroboam at Dan and Bethel to worship. They had not destroyed the altars of the temple at Jerusalem, and therefore we understand that this refers to those ten tribes.

Although some built altars to the gods of the nations, there were nevertheless others who built them to God and sacrificed there, not daring to go to Jerusalem because the idolatrous kings of Israel barred them from God’s temple. The altars of these worshipers of God are understood to have been destroyed and utterly overthrown by those who worshiped idols [Col. 0457A].

“And I alone am left.” For, because of the magnitude of the slaughter and killing by which the worshipers of God were being savagely attacked, it seemed to him that he alone had remained out of all the Lord’s prophets. “And they seek my life.” For the most impious Jezebel had threatened him in this way: “May the gods do these things to me, and add these things, if by tomorrow I do not make Elijah’s life like the life of one of them” (3 Kings XIX).

But what divine answer was given to him? “I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent the knee before Baal.” While he was in the cave on Mount Horeb, he received this divine answer. It did not say, “Seven thousand men have been left for me,” but, “I have left and reserved for myself seven thousand men who, while others were turning to idolatry, did not bend their knees before Baal,” who was the god of Ahab and Jezebel.

They are rightly called men because they rejected idols manfully. Those seven thousand signify many thousands of those whom God preserved by the gift of his grace, so that they would not bend their knees before Baal at Dan and Bethel or in any shrine of idols.

Thus the five wise virgins signify all the righteous who possess integrity of faith, and the foolish virgins signify the unrighteous. The five brothers of the rich man who was tormented in the underworld signify all unbelieving Jews. In the same way, those seven thousand signify all who did not worship idols.

For the number seven is sacred in many places and very often stands for totality. Thus in the Psalm the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Seven times a day I shall praise you” (Ps. CXVIII). He explained what “seven times a day I shall praise you” means when he said: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. XXXV). John also writes in his Apocalypse (Rev. I) to seven churches, which generally signify all the churches.

Therefore, in this present time also—that is, at the coming of the Lord and the preaching of the apostles—the remnant has been saved, concerning which it was said above: “If the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved.” Just as, in the days of Elijah, many were reserved by the gift of God’s grace so that they would not worship idols, so also in the time of the apostles many from the Jews were saved according to the election of God’s grace by coming to faith; [Col. 0457D] they are also called the remnant. It must be considered that they were saved according to the election of God’s grace—that is, according to the gift of predestination—not according to the merits of their works. Hence he says in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “He chose us,” he says, “before the foundation of the world in him,” that is, in Christ, “so that we might be holy and blameless” (Ephesians 1).

But if those from the Jews who believed were saved by grace, then it was not from the works of the Law, by which those who remained in unbelief thought that they could be justified; otherwise grace is no longer grace. This means: if they were saved in any other way—which cannot happen except by the grace of God—then that grace would no longer be grace, but merit.

[Col. 0458A] “What then?”—the words “must be said” are understood. This, without doubt, which Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it. What was Israel seeking? To fulfill the works of the Law without the grace of Christ, and to be justified by those works themselves without the grace of Christ and without faith in the Gospel. It did not obtain this because it was neither able to fulfill the works of the Law without the grace of Christ nor to be justified without faith in him. This, however, must be understood of those who were unwilling to pass over to faith in Christ. Concerning those who did pass over to Christ, he adds: “But the election obtained it,” that is, those who were chosen from the same people. What above he called the remnant, he now calls the election. And just as in the preceding passage circumcision was used for the Jews, so here election is used for the elect, who obtained justification [Col. 0458B] through the faith by which they believed in Christ. Yet “election” can also be referred to believing Gentiles, who became one with the faithful Jews.

The same is true of the Psalmist’s statement: “The Lord is just and has loved justice” (Psalm 10), that is, the just, who love justice. The rest, however, were blinded by the darkness of unbelief. For just as one who has faith is said to stand in the light, so the unbeliever remains in the darkness of ignorance. Hence that distinguished preacher likewise says to believers: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

As it is written: “God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear, unto this present day.” These words are partly those of the Apostle and partly those of the prophet Isaiah. What he says—“God gave them a spirit of compunction” [Col. 0458C]—is the Apostle’s wording; what follows belongs to the prophet Isaiah.

“Spirit of compunction” is sometimes understood in a good sense and sometimes in the opposite sense. It is understood positively, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: when the Jews heard the apostles’ preaching, they were pierced in heart and said to the apostles, “What shall we do, men and brothers?” (Acts 2). It is understood in the opposite sense here: “God gave them”—that is, he permitted them to have it—just as “he handed over” and “he hardened” are used for “he permitted them to be handed over” and “he permitted them to be hardened.”

By “a spirit of compunction” he means a mind of envy, by which they envied—and still envy—the salvation of the Gentiles. Sometimes “spirit” is used for “soul,” as in the Gospel, where it is said of the Lord that, bowing his head, he gave up [Col. 0458D] his spirit (John 19). Sometimes it is used for “mind,” as here. The soul is that by which the body is given life; the spirit, however, is reason itself, by which we distinguish between good and evil, and between truth and falsehood. Mind and reason are not two different things.

It is called a spirit of compunction because a mind of envy often torments and afflicts people when they see another’s happiness, to such an extent that they even break into tears through envy. Thus, to intensify the envy with which the Jews are tormented on account of the salvation of the Gentiles, he said that they have a spirit of compunction.

Alternatively, we may understand “a spirit of compunction” as an evil spirit, which is the spirit of destruction and which takes contemptuous people into its power. Thus the good God, in response to the sins of the Jews, permitted them to have a spirit of destruction, which kills them in soul, just as it is also said of the philosophers of the Gentiles that God handed them over to a depraved mind: “eyes so that they would not see.”

With the eyes of the body the Jews did see the Lord and saw many miracles performed by him; but because they devoted themselves excessively to earthly affairs, they did not deserve to behold him with the eyes of faith and love. “And ears so that they would not hear”—the words “he permitted them to have” are understood. They heard Christ with the ears of the flesh, but they did not hear with the ears of the heart, which the Lord required when he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8). Thus blindness, deafness, and a mind of envy remain among the Jews to this present day, because, while they refuse to obey the Gospel and thereby believe in Christ, inflamed by the jealousy of envy they continually envy the salvation of the Gentiles.

“Let their table become a snare.” The wicked are accustomed to deliberate over the killing of the innocent at a table, as Herod did concerning the beheading of the blessed John, and the most filthy Holofernes concerning the violation of Judith (Judith 12, 15). They also customarily invite people to a table in order to kill them by deceit, as Absalom killed his brother Amnon (2 Samuel 13).

Thus the Jews are understood to have deliberated at their tables concerning the death of the innocent Christ. Therefore, by “table” we should understand the exchange of their words, which they conducted over the table concerning Christ. Hence the Prophet says: “Let their table”—that is, the Jews’ exchange of words—“become a snare,” so that they may be ensnared and entangled; or “a trap,” so that they themselves may be captured by the retribution for the wickedness of their table; let it also become a stumbling block, that is, a ruin or offense, or a quarrel, so that, having incurred the offense of almighty God, they may suffer the ruin of condemnation and may quarrel and contend among themselves.

“Stumbling block” is Greek and is rendered in Latin as “offense,” “ruin,” or “quarrel.” It is used in the sense of offense and ruin where the Lord says: “Woe to the one who causes one of these little ones to stumble” (Matthew 18), that is, who offends or causes to fall. It is used in the sense of quarrel where the Evangelist says: “When the Pharisees heard the word, they were scandalized” (Matthew 15), that is, they quarreled. Here it can be understood in both senses.

“And as a recompense,” he says: just as they did to Christ, so let it be repaid to them—and this happened to both. For example, they wanted to erase Christ’s name from the earth; their own name has been erased, so that they are no longer called the Lord’s people. They killed Christ; they themselves were also killed by the sword of the Romans.

Sacred Scripture is also signified by the table that was given to the Jews in the Law and the Prophets, as the Psalmist shows when he says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Psalm 11). Since the Jews did not rightly investigate its meaning, that very table became for them a snare and the other things mentioned above, because they were unwilling to believe in Christ, to whom all that Scripture bore witness. And because they handed Christ over to death against the authority of that Scripture, retribution was brought upon them according to their deserts.

[Col. 0460A] “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see; and always bend their back.” These words are spoken not as the wish of one praying, but as the duty of one prophesying. Let the eyes of their heart—that is, their understanding—be darkened, so that they may not understand that Christ is the Son of God. And “always bend their back”: just as one who carries a heavy burden is bent toward the ground, so in a certain way the sinner who is weighed down by the burden of sins is bent over, as the Psalmist laments: “My iniquities have risen above my head” (Psalm 37).

I say, therefore: Did the Jews stumble in such a way that they should fall? The words “only, so that their fall might benefit no one” are understood. By no means. The meaning is this: the Jews did not offend God only so that they themselves might fall, but so that the multitude of the Gentiles might rise in their place, [Col. 0460B] and their fall might provide us with great benefit. Hence he continues: “But through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to provoke them to emulation.”

It is as though he were saying in other words: Through their transgression salvation was secured for the Gentiles, because if the Jews had not perished, the Gentiles would by no means have been saved. “Transgression” is so called as though from “that which has been left behind”; transgression occurs in thought, whereas sin occurs in action. It is also called transgression when God’s command is not fulfilled, whereas sin occurs when what has been forbidden is done. But the Apostle uses “transgression” indifferently for sin.

The transgression of the Jews, therefore, was the death of Christ, together with an unrepentant heart and unbelief. Through that death the Gentiles were redeemed and washed in sacred baptism. The Jews ought to emulate them—that is, imitate them in faith—so that, believing as they believe, they may be saved.

[Col. 0460C] “But if their transgression is the wealth of the world.” Because of the transgression that the Jews committed against the Son of God, and because of their unbelief, the multitude of the Gentiles was enriched with the riches of the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the grace of faith. For the Lord took all these things away from them and handed them over to the Gentiles who believed in him, just as he threatened them in the Gospel, saying: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21).

Great and immeasurable were the riches of the Jews, which enriched the entire world. “And if their diminution is the wealth of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness?” Here “diminution” is understood as smallness and a reduced number. The diminution of the unbelieving Jews consisted in the apostles and the other believers from the same people. The meaning is: if the small number who believed from among the Jews brought such salvation to the Gentiles that through them the Gospel was preached to nearly all the nations, how much more benefit would there have been if they had all believed? It would have been much more beneficial, because by them the Gospel would already have been preached throughout all the nations.

The apostles and the other believers from the Jews are the wealth of the Gentiles, because through their ministry the Gentiles received faith and knowledge of the divine Scriptures, in which the knowledge of God is found. They also appointed bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the other ecclesiastical orders for the Gentiles. And, to say even more, whatever good we have—God’s grace cooperating and bestowing it—we received through their ministry.

[Col. 0461A] “For I say to you Gentiles: Inasmuch as I am indeed the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry.” While the other apostles preached in the individual places assigned to them, the Apostle Paul preached to nearly all the Gentiles, because he heard from the Lord: “I will send you far away to the Gentiles” (Acts 22). For this reason he was especially the Apostle of the Gentiles, as he testifies elsewhere, saying: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Galatians 2). This means: the one who appointed Peter as leader of the Jews also appointed me to be leader and apostle of all the Gentiles.

He rightly says, “I will honor my ministry,” that is, I will turn preaching into action. A preacher honors his ministry when he strives to live according to what he preaches, so that what he preaches with his mouth he may honor and confirm by good example [Col. 0461B] and good works.

Alternatively: “I will honor my ministry” means that I will not preach the grace of the Gospel only to the Gentiles, to whom I have been appointed as apostle, but will also take care to impart it to the Jews. The honor of teachers is the multitude of their hearers.

“If somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation and save some of them.” “If somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation” means: for this reason I will honor my ministry, so that in some way I may provoke the Jews, from whom I took my flesh, to imitate me, and so that by imitating me they may be saved, just as I too have been saved—even if I cannot save all of them, at least some or a few of them.

For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be—unless life from the dead? The sense [Col. 0461C] is as follows: if the loss of the Jews, by which they were abandoned by God on account of their unbelief, was the reconciliation of the Gentiles, with whom God had been in a certain sense angry before the coming of his Son, how much more will their acceptance, by which they are accepted into faith, provide the elect with life from the dead?

For as soon as they begin to live for God through faith—those who were previously dead in unbelief—the day of judgment will arrive, and all will rise from the dust of the earth, and all the elect will live forever with Christ in eternal life. Their loss benefited the Gentiles in bringing them to faith, and their acceptance will also benefit them, because eternal life will be given to the elect from the dead.

In another way, by “acceptance” the apostles may be understood, for they became life to the believing Gentiles. “What,” he says, “will their acceptance be except life from the dead?” That is: what else are those who have been accepted and chosen by God from the same people—such as I, Peter, and the other believers—except those who have also brought you into the faith of Christ, living through Christ’s life after being saved from the dead unbelieving Jews?

For if those Jews, through their death in unbelief, provided reconciliation to the world, we who did not die in unbelief were preserved for the life of others, as living people from the dead.

“But if the first portion is holy, so is the lump.” The first portion is a kind of tasting, or the first fruits, of something. For example, when a portion is taken from a mass of kneaded flour and tasted to determine what flavor the remainder has. It is natural that everything which is of one substance, when divided into parts, should remain of the same nature and have one flavor and quality, as the quality of flour is discerned from the leaven.

Here the first portion signifies the holy apostles, while the lump signifies the holy fathers—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Isaiah, and the others—from whose lineage the apostles descended. Therefore, if the apostles were holy, and the fathers whose faith the apostles attained and imitated were holy, it may also, in the reverse order and with no less appropriateness, be said: if the lump is holy in the fathers, then the first portion is likewise holy in the apostles and the other believers who truly possessed the faith of the fathers.

“And if the root is holy, so are the branches.” He now calls the same thing the root that he called the lump above; and the branches signify the same thing as the first portion. The fathers of the Old Testament are the lump and the root, because from their lineage the first portion was taken and the branches—that is, the apostles—sprang forth.

Therefore, just as a good root diffuses good sap through its branches, where there are fruits of good flavor, so the apostles, who derived their origin from the holy fathers and imitated their faith, were holy and good.

Earlier in this Epistle he had introduced another lump, signifying the mortality and sin of Adam, from which some vessels are made for honor through the mercy of God’s grace, while others are made for dishonor by God’s just judgment. Here, however, “lump” is understood positively.

The root may also be understood as Christ, and the branches as the apostles and the other believers, because just as sap is sent from the root into the branches so that they may live, so all believers live in Christ, receiving every good thing from him, of whose body they are also members.

[Col. 0462C] “But if some of the branches were broken off by remaining in unbelief, while you, though you were a wild olive”—that is, entirely pagan—“were grafted in among them,” that is, succeeded to their place, “and became a partaker of the root,” that is, of the faith of the holy fathers, “and of the richness of the olive tree,” namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit, “do not boast or exalt yourself against the branches that remain in unbelief.”

Those holy fathers had the Holy Spirit; hence they were also called the anointed of God, as in the statement: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 104), which is to be understood of Abraham, Isaac, and the others.

Alternatively, we may again understand “root” in another way as Christ, so that the meaning is: you have become a partaker of the root—that is, of Christ—and of the richness of the olive tree, namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore do not exalt yourself in pride, lest you lose the grace that has been given to you.

The Apostle addresses the Gentiles and speaks to all as though to one.
