As we have said, he calls the broken branches the Jews who remain in unbelief, who have departed from the root—that is, from the faith of the patriarchs—or from Christ. He calls the Gentiles a wild olive because before the coming of the Lord they were fruitless, leading a wild life.

The meaning is: O Gentile, if you see some Jews alienated from the grace of Christ and from the faith of the patriarchs, and if you see yourself placed in their place, made a partaker of the faith of the fathers, of Christ, and of the grace of the Holy Spirit, do not despise them and do not exalt yourself, lest perhaps you lose the grace that was freely given to you.

“But if you boast against them who have fallen, remember that you do not bear the root, but the root bears you.” It is as though he were saying: if you wish to exalt yourself, listen to the reason why you should humble yourself. You do not bear the root [Col. 0463A]—that is, you contribute nothing to the holy fathers who preceded you—but the root bears you, because you are saved by their faith. You received from them; they did not receive from you.

Alternatively: “You do not bear the root” means Christ, to whom you contribute nothing of your own; rather, he bears you, and from him you have whatever good you possess—and, in addition, from him you have your very existence.

Therefore you will say to me, O Gentile: “The branches were broken off,” that is, the unbelieving Jews were rejected, “so that I might be grafted in among them.” “You speak well”—the words “you say this because it is so” are understood—but consider what follows: “The branches were broken off because of unbelief.” Because the Jews were unwilling to believe in Christ, they fell into the death of condemnation, being broken off from the grace of God. “But you stand by faith, not by your own merits.”

Therefore do not boast; do not “think highly”—that is, do not be proud—but fear falling. It is God’s gift that you were called, not your own merit. Accordingly, that distinguished preacher says elsewhere: “By grace you have been saved, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2).

For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either. He calls the Jews natural branches because they derived their origin from holy fathers beloved by God. The meaning is: O Gentile, consider that if God did not spare the Jews, who derived their origin from holy fathers and from whose people he himself assumed flesh, much less will he spare you if you depart from the faith of God—you who were a wild olive—or if, in the arrogance of pride, you exalt yourself by despising the Jew.

[Col. 0463C] See, therefore, the kindness and severity of God. A judge is called severe when he bends his judgment in no direction but proceeds with uprightness. Severity is the judgment that flatters no one but judges everything justly.

Toward those Jews who fell, he exercised severity—that is, the most just judgment; but toward you he will display God’s kindness—that is, the grace of his mercy—if you remain in his kindness, that is, in right faith. Otherwise you too will be cut off: if you depart from the faith, you will perish completely.

There is a difference between being broken and being cut off: a broken branch may in some way be reattached to its tree, but one that has been cut off cannot be restored. It should also be noted that he called the Jews “broken,” because when Elijah and Enoch preach they will be strengthened in the faith of Christ. The Gentiles, however, if they depart from the faith of Christ, are to be completely cut off from the grace of God and thereafter destroyed. Hence he continues:

“But they also”—that is, the Jews—“if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in,” into the faith of Christ and the faith of the patriarchs. “For God is able to graft them in again into the faith of Christ.”

For if you were cut from a natural wild olive and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree. He addresses the Gentile who is boasting against the branches that were broken off and who boasts as though he had deserved to be saved by his own merits. He says: if you, O Gentile, through the grace of God, were separated from paganism and from those who from their beginning were separated from God by various errors, and if you were grafted contrary to custom into a good olive tree—that is, into the faith of the preceding fathers, who possessed the richness of the Holy Spirit—how much more will the Jews, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree, namely, the faith of their fathers?

When he says that a branch of a wild olive was grafted into an olive tree “contrary to nature,” he speaks according to human custom. It is natural for us to graft a shoot of a good tree into the trunk of a bad one, not a shoot of a bad tree into a good trunk; this is called grafting. But God, the author and creator of all things and of all natures, does nothing contrary to nature.

[Col. 0464A] “For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery.” A mystery is a hidden matter containing some secret within itself. He therefore addresses believing Gentiles so that they might understand the reason for which they were saved—whether by their own merits or by the grace of God—and why the Jews were rejected. He says: I do not want God’s hidden and secret judgment, insofar as a human being can penetrate it, to remain concealed from you: why he once rejected the Jews as his special people, joined sinful Gentiles to himself through faith, and for what reason he gave this warning.

He adds and says: “so that you may not be wise in your own eyes,” that is, so that you may not become proud, saying that you were saved by your own merits and consequently despising others. One is said to be wise in one’s own eyes when one attributes the gift one possesses not to God’s grace but to one’s own merits and effort. But the one who is wise according to God does not insult those who have been rejected because of God’s benefits; rather, with fear, he gives thanks for the mercy of the giver.

Alternatively, one becomes wise in one’s own eyes when one despises any sinner, although one ought rather to be humbled by consideration of the sinner, because we are all of one nature, even though we do not all have the same grace.

The Apostle himself will show what mystery he is speaking about: “because blindness has happened in part to Israel.” He rightly says that blindness happened “in part,” and not entirely, because the remnant fell. The blindness that happened in Israel was not bodily blindness, which occurs when the light of the eyes is lost, but blindness of the heart, which occurs through the darkness of unbelief.

In these statements of the Apostle, therefore, we say that there is a mystery in the fall of the Jews, but we do not know from what depth of counsel it comes, together with Paul himself. Even if he knew, he did not disclose it.

He says: “because blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters; and thus all Israel will be saved.” We do not understand “the fullness of the Gentiles” as the conversion of all of them, but as the multitude that has already been gathered by divine predestination or will be gathered in the future. This fullness does not pertain to the number of everyone, but to the number predetermined by God.

The Jews therefore fell so that the Gentiles might rise. Who can penetrate this mystery? Why did God reject the multitude of the Gentiles almost from the beginning of the world—that is, from the time when the language of the whole earth was confused—and make only the Jews, who descended through the line of Heber, his special people, and then, at his coming, gather the Gentiles while rejecting the Jews, who are to be received at the end of the world? Who, I ask, [Col. 0465A] is sufficient to investigate so subtle a divine arrangement?

“There will come from Zion the one who will rescue and turn impiety away from Jacob.” Zion itself is Jerusalem, concerning which Micah says: “From Zion the Law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Micah 4).

For the Savior, by being born from the Israelite people, according to what the prophet Isaiah once foretold when he said, “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7), will come from Zion, or from Jerusalem. By placing his members upon the cross, shedding his own blood, and giving the washing of baptism, he rescued both the Gentiles and those remnants who believed from Israel—something no one previously had the power to do. He likewise turned impieties away from Jacob, that is, from those who believed among the Jews at his first coming.

He will also turn them away fully from those who, after the multitude of the Gentiles has been received, will be converted and saved, as it is written: “He himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities” (Psalm 129). And when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

“And this will be the covenant from me with them”—the words “it will be given” or “it will be fulfilled” are understood. The word “covenant” sometimes signifies a promise and the Gospel. Here both may be understood: namely, the promise of the kingdom of heaven and the Gospel in which that promise is contained, as the Lord says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 4).

The prophet spoke of this covenant: “I will make,” he says, “a new covenant with them, and I will write a new testament in their hearts.” He continues: “When I take away their sins.” By these words he shows that, although the sins of some believers from among them have been taken away, at the end of the age they will be removed more fully through the grace of baptism.

[Col. 0465C] “According to the Gospel, they are indeed enemies of God for your sake.” He does not say “according to the Law,” which the Jews zealously pursued according to their strength, but “according to the Gospel,” which they themselves despised, where it is related how they handed the Lord over to death. Therefore, insofar as the Gospel is concerned—which the Jews do not receive—they are enemies of Christ and of that same Gospel.

The Jews incurred this enmity so that the Gentiles might believe; and this is what he says: “for your sake,” O Gentiles, so that you might believe, the Jews became enemies of God according to the Gospel—that is, according to what the Gospel says. For the Gospel relates how the impious Jews carried out the killing of Christ, on account of which they incurred the enmity of God, because they remained in unbelief.

“But according to the election, they are beloved, for the sake of the fathers.” This must not be understood to mean that those who are called enemies of God are themselves also beloved, especially since the Jews are one people divided into believers and unbelievers. Thus the Jews alienated from faith in Christ are enemies of God; but those who have been justified through the election, or predestination, of God are beloved.

Concerning this election it is said: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless” (Ephesians 1). They are called beloved for the sake of the fathers—that is, Abraham and the others—because those who believe truly hold to the model of the justice and faith of the preceding fathers.

[Col. 0466A] “For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance.” In sacred Scripture, “repentance” is sometimes understood as change, as when the Lord says to Samuel: “I repent that I made Saul king over Israel; anoint the son of Jesse” (1 Samuel 14, 16). By commanding the son of Jesse to be anointed, he shows that he is changing the disposition of what he had done, and therefore says: “I repent.”

And elsewhere: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent” (Psalm 106), that is, his will will not change.

But when he says “the gifts and calling of God,” the order is understood in reverse. First God calls people to his faith according to the election of grace; afterward he bestows the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the rewards of life. Therefore the gifts and calling of God are without change in those of whom it was read above: “Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Romans 8), not in those concerning whom it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22).

Alternatively: the gifts and calling of God are without repentance in those who come to the faith of God. For example, someone is called from paganism, is baptized, and is absolved from every guilt. What good has he done that he should be called and obtain the gift of remission of all his faults? He has not fasted; he has not wiped away his faults through almsgiving or through years of reckoning in penitence.

Let us state it more clearly: someone is born with original sin and afterward adds many actual sins. If he believes, he has been called; if, after being baptized, he is immediately taken from this life, he receives the gifts of eternal life. Behold: the gifts [Col. 0466C] and calling of God are without repentance.

“For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they too now have not believed in your mercy, so that they themselves also may obtain mercy.”

Here the Apostle calls “mercy” faith, the grace of baptism, the remission of sins, and the gift of the Holy Spirit, as well as the reconciliation by which the Gentiles were reconciled to God. He also includes whatever good they received freely from God after the Lord’s coming. He shows that just as the Gentiles obtained God’s mercy at the Lord’s first coming, so the Jews will obtain it as the second coming approaches, through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, according to what the same distinguished preacher says elsewhere: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

“Just as you,” he says, “O Gentiles, once did not believe God, but now, at the Lord’s coming through the preaching of the apostles, you have obtained the mercy of almighty God because of the unbelief of the Jews, entering by faith into their place, so those Jews have not now believed in your mercy—that is, in what God has given you—at this time when you obtained mercy. Or by ‘your mercy’ he means that you might be able to obtain mercy. For their fall was the salvation of the Gentiles.”

Someone might have said: Why did the Jews not believe at the Lord’s first coming? [Col. 0467A] The Apostle answers: “So that the Gentiles,” he says, “might obtain mercy, and so that they themselves might afterward obtain it at the end of the age.” For if they had believed at the Lord’s first coming, they would have thought that they had been justified by the works of the Law; but when they believe at the end of the age, they will not doubt that they have obtained mercy. Hence he adds:

“God has shut up all things”—that is, every kind of human being—“in unbelief,” that is, he permitted them to be shut up within unbelief, “so that he might have mercy on all.”

He shows that both Jews and Gentiles were shut up under the sin of unbelief: the Jews by destroying the natural and written Law, and the Gentiles by trampling upon the natural Law. But so that his grace, by which sins are forgiven to those thus shut up, might become clearer, it pleased him to bring the sacrament of the remission of human sins when no one could boast of his own merits.

The Gentiles were indeed unbelievers, but, called by him, they obtained God’s mercy. The Jews are now also unbelievers, but he will have mercy on them. Yet why God rejected the multitude of the Gentiles for so long, loved the Jews, and afterward, at his coming, rejected the Jews after gathering the Gentiles to himself—this is known only by him who sees all things.

The Apostle, considering the immense riches of God’s goodness and the greatness of the work of divine wisdom, and unable to comprehend it, was suddenly struck in the inner eyes of his heart by astonishment and fear at once, and exclaimed:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” [Col. 0467C] “Depth” signifies sublimity and profundity. Wisdom is understood in relation to divine matters, and knowledge in relation to human matters. Thus the abundance of wisdom concerning divine and human affairs in God is sublime and profound. He alone sees all things as they are, and all our understanding is blunted before his knowledge.

“How incomprehensible are his judgments!” By them he judges angels and human beings, Jews and Gentiles, from whom he now chose some and rejected others. “And how unsearchable his ways!” By them he passed from the Gentiles to the Jews, and from the Jews to the Gentiles, and by them he will again pass from the Gentiles to the Jews. Or by “ways” we may understand God’s actions, by which he accomplished all things; these are certainly unsearchable.

[Col. 0467D] For who has known the mind of the Lord—that is, who has penetrated the depth of his understanding? Or who has been his counselor? The only counselor of the Father is his only-begotten Son, who is also called the Angel of the Great Counsel; but among human beings and angels no one has been his counselor. Or who first gave to him—understand: his faith or some good work—before being preceded by his grace, so that he might receive a recompense from him, a reward from the Lord, because he first gave him his faith?

Some have wished to understand this in opposition to the case of the centurion Cornelius, as though he had received faith from God because his good merits demanded it, as a kind of recompense for the almsgiving and prayers to which he devoted himself. They spoke ignorantly for this reason: [Col. 0468A] one proceeds from faith to the performance of good works, not from works to faith. For unless Cornelius had first possessed faith, having been preceded by divine inspiration, he would certainly not have possessed good works. But, as blessed Gregory says, he was preceded by God so that he might have faith in the one Deity; nevertheless, he did not know that there were persons in the Trinity until Peter was sent to him.

Each person gives his faith and works to God when, preceded by his grace, he believes in him and, by practicing good works, strives to please his will. For from him—that is, from the Father—are all things, because they took their origin from him; and through him—that is, through the Son—are all things, because through him all things were made; and in him—that is, in the Holy Spirit—are all things, because in him they subsist. Behold the Trinity of persons.

[Col. 0468B] But when he adds, “To him be glory,” the one and singular substance of the three persons is declared, just as Isaiah also says that he heard the Seraphim say: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI). He says “holy” three times with respect to the persons, but “Lord” only once with respect to the majesty. Likewise the Psalmist says: “May God the Father bless us; may God the Son bless us; may God the Holy Spirit bless us; and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. LXVI).

As for the statement that all things are “from God the Father,” it must be observed that he did not say “of him.” For “from him” is one thing, and “of him” another. Everything that is “from him” is not necessarily “of him”; but whatever is “of him” is certainly also “from him.” For example, the Son is from the Father, because he received his origin from him, and he is of him because he is of his substance. A house, however, which is built from wood or stones, is from the man by whom it is made and from whom it receives its origin; but it is not of him, that is, of his substance.

[Col. 0468C] God, therefore, the creator of all things, is an invisible and immutable spirit, whereas every creature is mutable. Thus all things were not created from his immutable substance, but everything was made from nothing by the immutable Deity. Consequently, all things are from the Father, since they derive their origin from him.

## CHAPTER XII

Therefore I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service.

[Col. 0468D] Since the Apostle had said above that God had shut up all things in unbelief so that he might have mercy on all, showing that both believing Jews and Gentiles were saved not by their own merits but by the mercy and grace of God, he now appeals to them—and to all believers—by that same mercy by which they were redeemed through the blood of Christ and washed from all defilement at the time of baptism, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. He says: “I appeal to you by the mercy of God,” as though he were saying: “I do not command you by the authority of a master, by which I am your teacher and apostle; rather, I appeal and plead as a companion.” For this reason he calls them “brothers,” not according to the flesh but according to faith, recalling what the Savior said to the faithful: “You are all brothers, because you have one Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. [Col. 0469A] XXIII).

He says: “I appeal by the mercy of God by which you have been saved, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice.” The believing Jews at Rome had formerly offered victims and legal sacrifices to God in the temple at Jerusalem. He urges them now to sacrifice to God as spiritual offerings not cattle, goats, or rams, but themselves. When the Apostle wrote these things, the temple at Jerusalem was still standing and had not yet been overthrown by the Romans.

A sacrifice, therefore, is both slain and living when a person does not perish from this life but kills his carnal vices by putting to death his members together with sins and desires. For example, one who was proud becomes humble; one who was lustful becomes chaste; one who was gluttonous becomes temperate and develops a desire for frugality [Col. 0469B] and every kind of moderation. Thus a person lives by virtues and dies to vices.

In the Old Testament, the animals brought to the entrance of the house of the Lord and handed over there to the priests were called *hostiae* (“sacrifices”); they were called *victimae* (“victims”) from *vincire* (“to bind”), because bound animals were brought to the sacrifice with ropes and cords. With respect to pagan ritual, a *hostia* was the sacrifice offered to idols when battle was to be waged against enemies; a *victima* was the sacrifice offered to the gods in thanksgiving after victory had been won.

“Holy”: our bodies must become a holy sacrifice because they are the temple of the Holy Spirit, as it is said elsewhere: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (I Cor. III). And again: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (I Cor. VI). [Col. 0469C] Therefore the bodies that are dwelling places of God must be holy.

“Pleasing to God,” that is, separated from vices and sins; for whoever withdraws from vices and is filled with virtues certainly pleases God.

“Let your service be reasonable.” Service (*obsequium*) properly means obedience, from the verb *obsequor* (“I obey”), but here the Apostle uses it for the worship of divine religion. Formerly this worship was in a certain sense unreasonable among the Jews, when they thought that they could please the invisible and incorporeal God and be cleansed from sins by means of bodily and bloody sacrifices. For it is not consistent with reason that a rational creature, the human being, should offer irrational creatures on his own behalf. Therefore reasonable worship consists in offering to God, who is spirit, the human mind, made dead [Col. 0469D] to vices. Whenever we put to death the vices of the flesh and recurring sins within us and grow strong in virtues, we become a living and reasonable sacrifice.

But perhaps someone asks why almighty God commanded legal sacrifices and victims to be offered to him if he was not made propitious to those who offered them through these sacrifices, so as to forgive their sins. The answer is that God commanded this chiefly for two reasons: either because the minds of the Jews were inclined to worship idols, and therefore it was more tolerable for God that things created by him should be offered to him rather than to demons; or because the true sacrifice that was to come into the world was the Lord Jesus Christ, who by his immolation took away the sin of the world. It was entirely fitting that this sacrifice should [Col. 0470A] have figurative sacrifices long before his coming, so that through those types people might more easily arrive at the true sacrifice.

Or there was also a third, mysterious reason: these typical sacrifices were offered so that the sacrifice might be prefigured which is offered daily in the Church for the salvation of the faithful.

And do not be conformed to this age.

By “age” here we should not understand the present life, which continually turns through years, seasons, days, nights, hours, and moments, but people devoted to the age through carnal conduct—namely, pagans, Jews, heretics, and false Christians. We must not become like them or associate with them, lest we be defiled by their vices and our own.

“Do not,” he says, “be conformed to this age,” that is, do not become like the lovers of this age, who despise virtues and pursue vices; [Col. 0470B] “but be transformed by the renewal of your mind,” through the study and meditation of the Old and New Testaments. Every day our mind and understanding are renewed and transformed as we make progress and grow more and more in wisdom, understanding concerning God what we previously did not know. Our mind is also renewed in its transformation as good work progresses within us; for the more understanding is turned into effective action, the more it is renewed.

Let us put it more plainly. Someone was situated in the letter of the law and did not penetrate its interior meaning; he passed over to the Gospel and learned that the law must be understood spiritually. Thus he was transformed by the renewal of his mind: having lost the darkness of carnal understanding, he passed over to the fruit of spiritual allegory. [Col. 0470C] The same should be understood of those who, rejecting vices, pass over to virtues and, as they advance from virtue to virtue, are renewed each day.

“So that you may prove what the will of God is”: whoever reads the sacred Scriptures for the sake of this age discovers what the will of God is—that is, what pleases God, what displeases him, and how his will can be fulfilled. In all our actions we must weigh whether the works we perform are acceptable to God: good, pleasing, and perfect.

The will of God is good because it always desires good things; pleasing because all good things are pleasing to him; perfect because nothing duplicitous pleases him, but only what is done with a sincere heart.

[Col. 0470D] Alternatively: it is good in faith, pleasing in hope of future goods, and perfect in charity, that is, in love of God and neighbor. For these three perfect the will of God.

Or alternatively: the will of God is good in married people, pleasing in widows, and perfect in virgins. If these three orders proceed according to the will of God and the path of the virtues, they will be rewarded with the rewards of God’s will.

I say, by the grace that has been given to me, to everyone among you: not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment.

According to blessed Ambrose, “grace” in this passage should be understood as wisdom, which was freely given to Paul without his merits, in knowledge of the Old and New Testaments and in the languages of all nations. Blessed Augustine says in one of his sermons that divine providence arranged matters so that, because the Apostle was going to preach to [Col. 0471A] all nations, he possessed greater wisdom than all the apostles, sufficient both for all the philosophers of the nations and for simple people.

For this reason Peter also praises him in his Epistle, saying: “As our brother Paul writes in all the churches according to the wisdom given to him by God” (II Pet. III).

What he says, “to everyone among you,” may be understood simply, as though he were saying: “I speak to everyone who is among you”; or it may be understood in a higher sense, as addressing those who adhered through faith to God, who always is. For God alone is, because he possesses being substantially, as he says to Moses: “I am who I am,” and “I am the God of Abraham,” and so forth (Exod. III). Therefore all who adhere to him are; just as those who do not adhere to him are not. Thus when he says “those who are,” he means those who are joined to God through faith that works through [Col. 0471B] love.

And what do I mean? This is what I mean and command: “not to think more highly than one ought to think,” that is, not to be proud. He says this against the swelling Gentiles who insulted the Jews as though they were broken branches. For one thinks more highly than one ought when he exalts himself because of another’s misery, although he ought rather to humble himself lest he too fall.

This must also be said against those who, not following sound doctrine, devise certain false teachings by which they corrupt the minds of simple people: they must not think more highly than they ought to think. Finally, one ought to imitate the way of the earlier teachers and the understanding of present masters, fulfilling what Wisdom says: “Do not move the boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. XXII).

“But to think with sober judgment,” that is, with moderation. [Col. 0471C] A person thinks soberly when he recognizes what he is and speaks as one who stands before God in Christ. All heretics have transgressed this command.

“And to each”—understand: I say that he ought to think in accordance with the measure of faith God has apportioned. In faith there is a measure, insofar as it concerns our capacity: one believes more, another less. The apostles had greater faith when they moved mountains than we possess.

Or this measure may be understood as the gifts of faith: to one who has faith is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge (I Cor. XII), and so forth. Such a measure is given according to the rule of faith, since it is granted only to those who hold the faith.

It may also be understood of faith in ecclesiastical ministries, which must be carried out according to their proper measure and not usurped beyond [Col. 0471D] what is permitted. For example: you are a presbyter; do not usurp the ministry of a bishop. You are a deacon; do not claim for yourself anything belonging to the office of a presbyter. The same should be understood of the other ministries and ranks.

For just as in one body we have many members, and all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ.

Just as many members in one body make one body, so the multitude of the faithful, joined through faith and love to its head, which is Christ, is one body with him. Yet the members of our body have their own proper functions: the eyes are for seeing, the ears for hearing, and the rest likewise. And just as one member does not usurp the function of another member, so none of us ought to invade another’s ministry. [Col. 0472A]

Nevertheless, just as the eyes see for the whole body, the ears hear, the mouth speaks, and the hands work for their body, so the spiritual members of the Church ought to act. The eyes are those who minister spiritual light to others, such as teachers. The ears are good hearers who humbly listen to the words of their teachers. The noses are those who possess the knowledge to distinguish between the stench of vices and the fragrances of virtues. The mouth consists of those who instruct others. The hands are those who minister necessities to others, such as good distributors of alms. The feet are those who run to free innocent blood and to visit the sick.

These members ought to care for and serve one another. Therefore the Apostle adds: “each one is a member of the other,” because each person ought, according to the grace divinely [Col. 0472B] bestowed upon him, to help others, so that they may be members of one another both in spiritual and in temporal matters.

But having gifts differing according to the grace that has been given to us—

In this passage there is an omission in the wording, and therefore something must be supplied to complete the sense. It should be expressed in this way: “We therefore have gifts according to the grace given to us by God, differing and distinct from one another, just as the members of the body do.”

For example, the eye is not the ear, nor the ear the eye. Thus in the Church there are eyes and not ears, ears and not eyes; there are teachers, hearers, distributors of alms, and the other orders in which grace has been divided. [Col. 0472C] Grace is so called because it is given freely, and whatever gifts and endowments the faithful possess are the grace of God, because they received them without their own merits.

“Whether prophecy”—understand: whether someone has prophecy; “according to the measure of faith”—he has it because faith earned this gift. For if we had not believed, we would never have received the spirit of prophecy. We read that Agabus prophesied after the Lord’s ascension, as did the four daughters of Philip (Acts XI). The apostles themselves were also prophets, because they proclaimed to their hearers the future rewards of the elect and the punishments of the reprobate.

Alternatively, “prophecy” here may be understood as “doctrine,” so that the sense is: “if someone has prophecy, that is, doctrine, according to the measure of faith, let him administer it and not think more highly than he ought to think.” [Col. 0472D] By “the measure of faith” he means the truth of the Catholic faith, according to which every teacher must administer his preaching, lest he deviate from the truth.

“Whether ministry”—understand: whether someone has a ministry; let him exercise it in ministering and not think more highly than he ought to think. In the ministry freely given to him by God, no one ought to be proud, that is, no one ought to think more highly than he ought to think. You have been given a ministry: you minister to the poor and orphans; do not be proud, because it was freely given to you by God.

This may also be understood of ecclesiastical ministry. No one ought to be proud of it, whether he is a bishop, a presbyter, or the head of a monastery; rather, he ought to humble himself, remembering what is said: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV), and “the greater you are, humble yourself in all things.”

[Col. 0473A] “Whether he who teaches, in teaching”—understand: the doctrine freely given to him by God—he ought not to think more highly than he ought to think. This doctrine is understood as the doctrine of the Old and New Testaments.

He who exhorts, in exhortation—understand: he ought not to think more highly than he ought to think, because he ought not to become proud on that account.

It must be noted that from this point onward the words “not to think more highly than one ought to think” must be supplied from the earlier part of this Epistle. Exhortation is a form of preaching and teaching, and it is directed especially toward one who is grieving or despairing.

For example, there are many teachers who, endowed with the wisdom of the divine Scriptures and flourishing equally in eloquence of speech, address the people all day long, disputing about the correctness of faith, the pursuit of virtues, [Col. 0473B] the hatred of vices, the happiness of the eternal kingdom, and the destruction of hell. Yet, after extending their speech almost until sunset, they offer no example of consolation to those who have fallen.

Meanwhile, someone among the hearers may hear the punishments of hell that they threaten against those held guilty of serious crimes and may remember that he has committed some most grievous offense—murder, adultery, or something of that kind. Because of the enormity of his crime, he is overwhelmed with the sorrow of despair, since he has heard no word of consolation from the preachers.

If some simple preacher encounters him, he immediately asks him why he is grieving and why he walks sorrowfully. Once he has learned the cause, he consoles him with the simple words he can [Col. 0473C] offer and at the same time urges him not to despair of the forgiveness that leads to salvation. He gives consoling examples, saying:

“Why do you fall into the evil of despair? Consider, if you prefer, how great the mercies of the Lord are, of which the Psalmist says: ‘The mercy of the Lord is over all his works.’ Was David not both king and prophet when he committed adultery together with murder? Yet he obtained forgiveness. Did Peter, after being chosen by the Lord, not deny him three times, saying, ‘I do not know him’ (Matt. XXVI)? Yet afterward the merciful Lord placed him over his Church. And did the thief not deserve to hear: ‘Today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke XXV)?””

Addressing in such words the man who had fallen into despair, the preacher restores him to the hope of forgiveness. [Col. 0473D] This shows how exhortation is a form of preaching.

“He who gives, in simplicity”—that is, he who generously distributes alms to the poor—should do so in order to please God and not human beings; this applies both to almsgiving to the poor and to teaching the ignorant.  The sense must be supplied as follows: “Let the one who gives give in simplicity.”

“He who presides, with diligence”—understand: he ought to preside diligently, so that he does not neglect those entrusted to him. This diligence—that is, great care—must be directed especially toward souls.

“He who shows mercy”—understand: to the poor, by giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the cold, and shelter to the wanderer—should do so with cheerfulness and gladness of heart, because God loves a cheerful giver. Alms should be given and mercy shown with joy of heart.

Let the person devoted to this work be confident of his reward, because [Col. 0474A] whoever gives small and temporal things will receive great and eternal rewards. For the alms given to the poor on earth are received from the Lord in heaven, as blessed Ambrose says. He himself will say to the elect on the day of judgment: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these who are mine, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV).

But whoever doubts the reward of eternal recompense does not give alms with gladness of heart. What he offers does not profit him, because here he loses what he gives, and in the future he will receive neither prize nor reward.

Let love be without pretense—understand: it must be fulfilled.

Every love that is not according to God and is not practiced for the love of God must be called pretense and hypocrisy. Therefore, whoever is said to love his brother, [Col. 0474B] if he does not correct him when he sees him going astray, is shown to possess feigned charity toward his neighbor.

Hating evil—that is, the devil and his members—and hating every sin. It must be noted that “hatred” here is understood in a good sense, since there is also an evil hatred by which we hate our brother.

Clinging to what is good—that is, to God, who is the supreme good, and to his members and righteousness and every virtue.

Loving one another with fraternal charity—that is, love one another with fraternal charity, because you have one Father who is in heaven. All who have one faith and have been washed in one baptism ought to love one another according to God, as brothers who have come forth from one mother’s womb.

[Col. 0474C] Outdoing one another in honor—that is, show honor to one another: those in authority to their subjects, and subjects to those in authority, because the virtue of humility is pleasing even to pagans.

Do not be sluggish in diligence—that is, do not be negligent or sluggish in caring for your subjects, lest you be condemned with the useless servant who, with hands and feet bound, was sent into darkness.

And not only the one who presides, but every subject as well, ought to be diligent and swift in every good work.

Be fervent in spirit—that is, possess the warmth and fervor of the Holy Spirit; or “in spirit,” that is, in mind, do not be lukewarm in love of God and neighbor, lest you hear: “Because you are neither cold nor hot, I will spit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III). Concerning the fervor of this fire, the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” [Col. 0474D] (Luke XII), and so forth.

Serve the Lord, not wealth, vices, or pleasures. Those serve the Lord who keep his commandments.

Rejoice in hope. Hope is the expectation of future good things. Therefore the Apostle now says: “Rejoice in the hope”—or expectation—of heavenly rewards, even amid hardships.

Be patient in tribulation, the tribulation inflicted upon you by persecutors; that is, do not resist in anger and do not seek a reward in the present.

Be constant in prayer, because what we cannot obtain or accomplish through human help or our own strength, we must obtain from God through prayers, as we read concerning Daniel and his companions.

Sharing in the needs of the saints.

[Col. 0475A] He did not say, “Give alms to the saints” or “provide for the saints,” but used a more honorable expression: “Share your goods with the saints.” At the time when the Apostle wrote these things, believers were being deprived of their possessions. Therefore, praising the believing Jews, he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “You joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions” (Heb. X).

For this reason the Apostle urged those who had not yet been deprived of their own possessions to administer temporal support to those stripped of theirs, regarding their need as their own and sharing temporal goods with them in common. For God’s gifts ought not to become private possessions.

Pursuing hospitality.

He did not say, “Be hospitable,” or “Follow hospitality,” but said: “Pursue hospitality.” [Col. 0475B] He said more in this way. Whoever follows hospitality receives those who ask; whoever pursues it even compels and seeks out those who do not ask, lest they remain without shelter in the alleys and streets. Hospitality is a great virtue, through which many have pleased God, receiving angels as guests, as Abraham and Lot did, along with many others.

Bless those who persecute you—that is, bless them and speak well with those who inflict violence upon you; bless them and do not curse them, that is, do not speak evil.

For example, to slander someone, blaspheme, or insult is to curse. It is as though he were saying: Although they speak evil about you, calling you magicians and disciples of a deceptive man, do not therefore curse them, but patiently endure their reproaches. [Col. 0475C]

What the Apostle fulfilled in himself, he commanded his hearers to fulfill. For elsewhere he says: “We are cursed, and we bless” (I Cor. IV).

Strive to rejoice with those who rejoice.

He does not command us to rejoice with those who rejoice in transitory and perishable things, but with those who rejoice that their names are written in heaven. For we must not share in just any joys of Christians, nor join our tears to just any of their weeping.

For example, if we see some people rejoicing over monetary profit or an increase in possessions, we ought not to congratulate them, because their joys are followed by mourning and tears. Therefore the Lord warned not only [Col. 0475D] concerning such things, but also the Apostle, that one should not rejoice because demons were subject to them, but rather because their names were written in heaven.

The sense is: if you see someone performing works worthy of being written in heaven, rejoice together in that person’s salvation.

Take care to weep with those who weep—not with those who mourn and lament the loss of temporal possessions, but rather with those who lament their own sins or those of their neighbors, as Samuel mourned Saul because the Lord had departed from him, and as Paul mourned many of the Corinthians who had not repented after fornication.

Or he also commands us to mourn with those who mourn because the coming of the heavenly kingdom is delayed, although they are already confident of the reward. [Col. 0476A] Concerning all such people the Lord says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V).

Having the same understanding toward one another.

This statement is expressed more clearly in Greek. Its sense is: think about another as you do about yourself; that is, just as you wish good things for yourselves, so wish them for others; and just as you love yourselves, so love others. Or: consider yourselves loved by your brother as though you were loved by yourselves.

Do not be high-minded—that is, proud—but associate with the humble, so that you too may show yourselves humble. “Learn from me,” says the Lord, “because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). He associates with the humble who humbles himself with the humble, not preferring himself to them but joining them, and awaiting what the Lord promised: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV). For all who possess true humility certainly [Col. 0476B] honor that same humility in others.

Do not be wise in your own eyes.

A person is wise in his own eyes and not before God when he attributes the wisdom he possesses not to the Author of all wisdom but to himself, his merits, his natural ability, or his own studies. The philosophers of the nations are found to have suffered from this fault. Concerning them the same Apostle says at the beginning of this Epistle: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. I); that is, they became vain because they did not give thanks to God for the gift bestowed upon them without their merits.

Alternatively, someone is wise or prudent in his own eyes when, although he is foolish, he thinks himself wise and takes pride in himself because he hopes that he knows what he does not know.

Or, in a third sense, a person is said to be prudent in his own eyes when, by seeking revenge, he [Col. 0476C] avenges his injuries. The following verse indicates this:

Repaying no one evil for evil.

Many think that it is not a sin for someone to avenge an injury received and exact retaliation. If that were so, the Apostle would never have given such commands. Therefore some say that it is often an even greater offense for someone to repay evil for evil, because it may happen that the person who first inflicted the evil did not know that it was a sin or evil, whereas the person who seeks revenge and returns the injury immediately shows that he knows it was evil.

Thus it may be understood that inflicting evil upon another is a fault, but returning evil for evil is a sin. When the Apostle says that evil must be repaid to no one, he addresses both the faithful and the [Col. 0476D] unbeliever: the faithful because he is a brother, and the unbeliever so that he may be won.

Providing what is good not only before God but also before all people.

A person provides what is good before God when he strives in the depths of his heart to please him who sees what is hidden and, as far as he is able, wishes neither to offend him in thought, word, or deed nor actually does so.

He also provides what is good before all people when, in word and conduct, and in every aspect of his life, he presents himself as irreproachable to the extent of his ability.

If it is possible, so far as it depends on you—that is, so far as is consistent with your religion—live at peace with all people. [Col. 0477A]

Before stating something difficult, he prefaced it by saying “if it is possible,” because it is scarcely, or perhaps not at all, possible for peace to be maintained with everyone. If you rebuke a pagan and he despises you, he does not wish to be at peace with you. The same should be understood of a Jew or a heretic.

Let us express it another way. Every person in authority rebukes subjects who are delinquent. When the rebuke of the one in authority displeases them, he cannot be at peace with them. Nevertheless, each person should keep his own spirit peaceful and calm, having peace within himself toward them by loving them, because the Lord is the author of all, even though they separate themselves from him through their vices.

Here and in what follows he forbids disputes and quarrels, by which peace is especially violated.

Do not defend yourselves, beloved.

This must be understood in two ways. First, with respect to our adversaries, namely heretics and false brothers, [Col. 0477B] who often rage against us. We must not defend ourselves against them by seeking revenge. Second, if one of the unbelievers rises up against us because of the name of Christ or because of some quarrel, we should answer sparingly with words of contradiction, as reason dictates, so that we may appear gentle and humble, imitating the Lord, who gave few answers before Pilate.

But give place to wrath.

We give place to wrath in two ways: either when we restrain our spirit so that we do not seek revenge, or when we flee from one place to another.

“Give place to wrath,” he says: allow those who rage angrily against you to harm you, because your patience will be rewarded and their savagery punished.

Or, “give place to wrath” means: do not avenge yourselves, but flee from place to place, according to what the Lord commands: “If they persecute you [Col. 0477C] in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X).

When he says, “Give place to wrath,” this wrath may be understood either as the wrath of the one who rages or as that of the future Judge, who speaks in what follows through a prophetic example. For it is written: “Vengeance is mine”—understand: reserve it for me—“and I will repay,” giving rewards and a crown to you who have endured patiently, and the vengeance of the punishments of Gehenna to those who have inflicted evil.

Because human beings exceed [Col. 0477D] the proper measure in taking revenge and cannot avenge themselves with a tranquil mind, almighty God commands that vengeance be reserved for him, so that he, who is immutable, may judge them, and he, who is not moved to anger, may judge them according to what the outstanding orator Solomon says to him: “But you, Lord, judge all things with tranquility” (Wis. XII). The judgment of this Judge is just because he exceeds no measure and is not disturbed in his judgment.

But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink.

If you do this, then you will repay evil with good and receive great rewards. For in doing this, you will heap burning coals upon his head.

By “burning coals” he means here the fervor of love of God and neighbor, concerning which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). If you do what we have said above—namely, provide food and drink for your enemy—you will place burning coals, that is, the ardor of charity, upon his head, that is, upon his mind. Delighted by your kindnesses, he will begin to love you, although previously he hated you, to the point of saying:

“What is this that I have been doing against [Col. 0478A] this man until now? Why have I inflicted so many evils upon him, when he has done so much good to me? I was hostile to him without cause. Therefore, since he acts toward me with such kindness and patience, I will begin to love him as a dearest brother, although until now I persecuted him as an enemy.”

If someone gives him food and drink for the purpose that some have wished to understand—that he might prepare burning coals, that is, the punishments of hell, for him, if he does not love the one who honored him through his kindnesses—then this is no longer charity. It is therefore better to understand the passage as we explained above, first, of the ardor of charity.

As for the phrase “upon his head,” the head is rightly understood as the mind, that is, the rational and ruling faculty of the soul. For just as all the members are governed by the head, so thoughts and desires are directed by the mind.

[Col. 0478B] Do not be overcome by evil. “Do not,” he says, “be overcome by evil,” that is, by any vice—not by anger, not by hatred, not by injustice. Or, “Do not be overcome by evil,” that is, by the devil, by whom you are overcome when you are inflamed with anger against your enemy, because he draws you to his own will. Alternatively: If you wish to avenge your injuries, you are overcome by evil, because you are made like the one who did evil to you; for whenever we obey the devil or some vice, we are overcome by it. When we return evil for evil, we are overcome by the one who inflicted the injury upon us and to whom we repay it, because he makes us like himself. But if we restrain our disturbed spirit so that we do not inflict vengeance upon our neighbor, then we prove victorious and triumph over our brother, winning him from sin for salvation.

But overcome evil with good. Overcome evil with good, that is, overcome the devil in God. Overcome evil with good: in patience conquer your enemy and adversary by providing him with food and drink, clothing and footwear; for when by your benefits you provoke him to begin loving you in the manner we explained above, you somehow overcome him. Or, “overcome evil with good,” that is, conquer and overcome vices and sins through the virtues, receiving from them the palm of victory.

## CHAPTER XIII

Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities. At the beginning of the holy Church, people from every condition came to the faith. Lest slaves, maidservants, or any other subjects say that, having obtained freedom from all sins and having become children of God, it was unworthy for them to serve the authorities of this world, the Apostle said: “Let every soul”—that is, every human being, free and slave, believer and unbeliever—“be subject to the higher authorities.”

He says “every soul” instead of “every human being.” For in Sacred Scripture, “soul” alone frequently signifies the whole human being, as here and in Genesis, where it is said: “The number of those who entered Egypt with Jacob was seventy souls” (Gen. 46); and in the Acts of the Apostles: “There were in the ship two hundred and seventy-six souls” (Acts 27).

By “higher authorities” he means kings and princes, tribunes, centurions, masters, and all who are set over others. Peter likewise commands this (1 Pet. 2): “Be subject,” he says, “to every human creature,” that is, to all human beings appointed over you, “for God’s sake,” or “because of love for the Lord.” Insofar as a person does not offend God, he ought to serve and obey those who are superior. For a human being consists of soul and body: in the soul, he ought to preserve inviolate faith in God; in the body, he ought to serve those who rule over him according to the servitude of the present life.

But if he sees that the princes, authorities, or masters of this age command something contrary to the profession of faith, then he must strive to labor for the faith even unto death, lest he lose what is greater—namely, his soul—for although that authority may kill the body with the sword, it cannot kill the soul.

For there is no authority except from God. Every authority, whether greater or lesser, that is granted to human beings has been established either by God’s will or by his permission, as is said through Solomon (Prov. 8): “Through me kings reign, and princes administer justice.” If we ask why these authorities were ordained, the answer is that the human race, having become beastlike, began to rage against itself in the manner of wild animals, so much so that the son of the first parent rose against his brother and killed him. For it is characteristic of beasts and of human beings to tear one another apart, lacerate one another, and devour one another. For example: a lion devours a human being and a bear; a bear and a wolf devour human beings, oxen, and sheep.

For this reason almighty God placed princes over beastlike human beings, so that by their terror the bitterness of their spirits might be restrained. There are also fish that swallow others; human beings imitated them when they raged against one another, and their recklessness was subdued by fear of the princes.

Whatever, then, these authorities are—understand: the authorities ordained by God over others—or whatever the rights of authorities are, they have been ordained by God. For the authorities, or the rights of authorities, that govern in the world have been established by God, as we have already said above. Hence the Lord said to Pilate: “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19). By these words it is indicated that whether the authority is good, as David’s was, or bad, as Nero’s was, it exists only either because God wills it or because he permits it.

The Apostle pursues this entire subject for the reason that people should be subject to the authorities. For some, as we have already said, coming to the faith did not wish, as though they had become free, to render their former obedience and service to their masters and princes, although the Lord Jesus did not come to change social conditions but to save souls destined to live eternally.

The Romans who believed were saying: “We who obey the divine laws and serve God ought not to serve Nero or render honor to the other earthly authorities.” Therefore the Apostle wrote such things to them. A scandal could arise among masters and princes if their slaves and subjects, having become Christians, were made strangers to their service. It would also harm the Church, since others would not be permitted to believe, whereas masters ought rather to receive their slaves as improved people, made faithful to Christ.

The Truth himself also commands this, saying: “Therefore give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matt. 22).

Therefore whoever resists the authority resists God’s ordinance. [Col. 0480A] Whether that authority is good or bad, whoever resists it by withdrawing service from it, refusing tribute, and failing to render the honor he ought to render, resists God’s ordinance and arrangement, by whose ordinance those authorities rule.

Some, thinking wrongly, have interpreted these authorities as demons, concerning whom it is said in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and authorities” (Eph. 6). But this interpretation is wholly superfluous, because we ought in no way to be subject to demons.

Those who resist the authorities—that is, their kings, princes, and masters—acquire condemnation for themselves. According to the character of their offense, they bring punishment upon themselves, because those authorities, angered when their subjects disdain obeying them, either kill them, send them to prison, or even dispatch them into exile. If someone asks why the Lord has condemned a slave, or why a prince has condemned a subject, answer: “He was resisting me, and therefore I took vengeance upon him.”

It must be considered, however, that the Apostle is not speaking of eternal condemnation but of bodily condemnation, in the manner we have indicated.

For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil: that is, they were not established to cause fear to those laboring well and persisting in good works, but to those doing evil and refusing to serve. They were established for this purpose: to praise and assist those who labor well, but to condemn those who do evil.

But if someone does good, he does not fear the authority; whoever does evil fears it and is condemned by it. Hence the Apostle adds: “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it.” He does not say, “That authority will praise you,” because there are many authorities that love evil rather than good in their subjects. Rather, “you will have praise from that authority,” that is, it will itself be an occasion for you to be worthy of praise. For if by your example it is led to faith or to works of justice, you will be praised both by it and by others, and you will also be worthy of praise before God.

Alternatively: if that authority afflicts you with punishments even unto death or proves hostile to you in some other way, so that in lawful struggle you patiently endure death or some injury, “you will have praise from it,” that is, it will provide the occasion for you to be praised. For through the persecutions inflicted upon you by it, you will receive everlasting blessedness, and you will be praised before God and human beings.

Let us consider Laurence, who was burned with the greatest severity for the name of Christ. He would not have been found perfectly worthy of praise had he not been burned by his persecutor; therefore that authority itself became the occasion of his praise. The same is to be understood of the other holy martyrs and of all who are unjustly condemned.

For he is God’s minister for your good. He is God’s minister—that is, he has been appointed by God for your good—so that by fear of him and by his assistance he may guard and protect you, lest you be killed by your enemy and lest others plunder your property.

Alternatively: There are many who do not wish to do evil but fear worldly authority, and because of this fear they do not obtain what they desire. Therefore those authorities have been placed over them for their good, so that they may not do evil, because the more a person does evil, the greater the punishments he will endure.

But if you do evil, be afraid; that is, do not take lightly the need to fear the authority, for it may condemn you when it finds an opportunity. For it does not carry the sword without reason. By “sword” vengeance is understood. “It does not carry the sword without reason,” that is, it does not possess the power of vengeance without reason.

There are certain outrageous crimes that are judged rather by the judges of the world than by the bishops and rulers of the churches—for example, when someone kills the apostolic pontiff, a bishop, presbyter, or deacon. The kings and princes of the world condemn those guilty of such offenses. Therefore he who judges such crimes does not carry the sword without reason.

They have also been established especially because of robbers, murderers, and plunderers, so that they may condemn them and compel others to restrain themselves through fear of them. Hence it follows: “For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath”—that is, for vengeance—“against the one who does evil.”

Therefore be subject of necessity. This means: Since they are God’s ministers for your good, obey them, so that you may be able to have peace with them. Or, “be subject of necessity,” because they will take vengeance upon you if you contradict their authority. For he has been placed over you by God for this purpose: to protect and defend those who do good and live justly, fortifying them with his protection, and to inflict vengeance upon sinners and those who resist him.

Therefore it follows: “not only because of wrath,” or the vengeance with which they will rise against you, “but also because of conscience”—that is, because of the disposition you ought to have, keeping your mind pure in love for the one to whom you are subject; especially for this reason, because he has been established by God, whose ordinance you ought not to resist.

For example: You are subject to him because you fear temporal harm, while you serve outwardly; be subject because of the conscience of your mind, so that within that conscience, which the Lord sees, you do not hate the one to whom you render service, but your mind bears witness to you that you love him from the heart.

For this reason you also pay taxes. Understand: because they have been placed over you by God, or because they defend you from enemies and by fear of themselves restrain your enemies, lest you be killed by them or your goods be plundered, or lest they exercise their vengeance against you if you have rebelled in some matter. You may suffer their anger, as the Jews suffered when they refused to pay tribute to the Romans.

Hence it also follows: “For they are God’s ministers, serving precisely for this purpose.” Understand: so that they may defend you, punish the guilty, and receive tribute from you.

So too John the Baptist replied to soldiers who asked what they ought to do: “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay” (Luke 3). It should be noted that he did not say, “Do not serve as soldiers,” because soldiers are appointed by God so that through them the countries entrusted to them may be protected.

Therefore give to everyone what is owed, that is, customary service, just as the Lord says: “Give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matt. 22). To the one to whom tribute is owed, you ought to pay tribute; give him tribute, just as the Creator himself paid the didrachma for himself and Peter (Matt. 17).

“Tribute” is named from tribunes, and tribunes from “three.” For Romulus, founder and author of Rome, divided the people subject to him into three parts by a rational distribution: namely, into senators, who were also called consuls, soldiers, and farmers. He appointed one leader over each part, who was called a tribune because he presided over one of the three parts.

“To the one to whom census is owed, census.” Since a census was exacted from subjects. “To the one to whom tax is owed, tax.” A *vectigal* is a fiscal tribute, and it is so called from *vehere*, “to carry,” because it was collected from transported goods, that is, from merchandise carried away.

“To the one to whom fear is owed, fear”: you owe it to him; render it to him as to a master. “To the one to whom honor is owed, honor”: you owe it to him; render it to him, not only by resting and humbling yourself, but also by giving gifts.

Owe nothing to anyone except mutual love. Thus render to all the services and debts of your subjection [Col. 0482B] so that you owe no one anything for which he may be angry with you, except that you love one another. Render the debt and service that you ought to pay to all authorities and princes: that is, you ought to love those who have been placed over us.

This debt of love is owed as long as one lives in the present age; in the future it will also be more fully and firmly established without burden. For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

This “neighbor” does not mean only a relative by blood or someone related by affinity, but every human being as well. By loving him, we fulfill the law of Moses, because if we have love for our neighbor, we do not do what Moses forbids through the law: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery,” and other such commandments.

For if you love your neighbor as yourself, you will not kill him, because you do not wish to be killed. You will not defile his wife, because you do not wish your own wife to be adulterated by him. The same is to be understood concerning the other commandments.

And in order that our righteousness may exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees and of the other Jews, we must also love our enemies for the love of God. Although we endure persecution from them, we must not love and cherish their vices in them, but their nature, fulfilling what the Truth commands: “Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5).

But it may be asked why the Lord says that the whole law consists in love of God and neighbor, while the Apostle says that the law is fulfilled in love of neighbor alone. This is resolved as follows: love of God also consists in love of neighbor. For neither can neighbor be loved without God, nor God without neighbor.

Or he says that the whole law is fulfilled in love of neighbor because we cannot so easily prove, in love of God, whether or not we love God, as we can in love of neighbor. For example: When I do not return evil for evil; when I forgive a brother who has sinned against me; when I gather a wanderer into lodging; when I strive to give alms with cheerful mind and face; when I pray for those who persecute me—it is evident in these and similar actions that I love my neighbor. And when I love my neighbor, I show that I also love God, whose commandments I obey.

For this commandment we have from God: that whoever loves God should love his neighbor, because through love of neighbor one reaches love of God, and through love of God one reaches love of neighbor. For although love of God is greater in dignity, love of neighbor comes first in action. For John says: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4).

Let us also understand by “neighbor” that Samaritan who showed mercy to the man wounded by robbers—that is, Christ, who became our neighbor by assuming flesh. Therefore whoever loves him fulfills the law of love and the law of Moses, because he does nothing against his will.

“And if there is any other commandment”—understand: besides those we have listed, concerning adultery, murder, fornication, false witness, and covetousness—it is restored, that is, renewed, or fulfilled in this word, namely, love of Christ: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Love of neighbor does no evil. It not only does no evil; it does not even think evil concerning one’s neighbor. Therefore the fullness of the law, both of Moses and of the Gospel, is love of God and neighbor.

Where love is, what can be lacking? And where love is absent, what can be of benefit? Therefore love of God and neighbor must be desired and held with all one’s strength. For love is so called because it binds two together: namely, because it joins God and the human being, or each neighbor to another.

Knowing this, that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep. It is the custom of Sacred Scripture very frequently to use “hour” for “time,” just as it uses “day.” What, then, is this hour of which the Apostle speaks? It is the time not of the law but of evangelical preaching; indeed, it is the age and the end of the world in which we have now been placed. Concerning this the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (2 Cor. 6).

The Apostle speaks to the Romans and to all believers, including those who do not yet believe. “Knowing this,” he says—that is, “knowing this, we know that it is already the hour, or time, for us to rise from the sleep of laziness and idleness,” and also from the sleep of unbelief, vices, and ignorance.

The Prophet also commands us to awaken from this sleep, saying: “Awake, you drunkards” (Joel 1). And why does he say that it is already time to rise? The one who was lying rises; and if we have until now lain in vices and in the torpor of vices, let us rise to perform good works and labor courageously and diligently.

Someone could object to Paul: “Why do you command us to rise now from sleep?” In response, he gives the reason: “For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed.” What salvation is this? Eternal life, joy that will endure without end, perpetual blessedness that the elect alone will possess with the angels. This blessedness and eternal salvation is now nearer to us than at the time when we believed, because, as the end of the world draws ever nearer, the future life and eternal salvation hasten ever closer.

The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. The night is the blindness of unbelief; the night is ignorance; the night is also a dark way of life in sins. This night passes daily in the elect, and the day draws near to those predestined for eternal life—namely, the illumination of faith, knowledge of the holy Trinity, and the splendor of the virtues—for as they pass daily through bodily death away from the sufferings of this age, they are gathered into the light of heavenly glory.

Or by “night” we may understand the entire span of the present life until the end of the world. By “day,” however, we may understand eternal life, in comparison with whose brightness the present life is not improperly called night, because the present life is always occupied with pain and sorrow and does not possess perpetuity. That life, however, will flourish with joys that endure without end, admitting no sadness. It will then be manifested in full when the Lord passes from judgment into the kingdom.

Therefore, because it is already drawing near, let us cast off the works of darkness—that is, adultery, murder, fornication, and other such things—which separate their practitioners from the kingdom of heaven and draw them into everlasting darkness. They are rightly called works of darkness because they are practiced especially in darkness, in accordance with what the Lord reveals when he says: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3).

And let us put on the weapons of light. The weapons of light are faith, hope, love, peace, patience, and the other virtues, which lead us to the light of eternal blessedness. They are rightly called weapons because they defend us from the wickedness of evil spirits.

We cast off the works of darkness, therefore, when we strip off vices and put on virtues. Let us therefore put on the weapons of light—that is, let us arm ourselves on every side with all the virtues, so that we may be protected and safe against the attacks of the devil. And how we ought to put on those weapons and adorn ourselves with these virtues, the Apostle declares, adding:

Thus—that is, in this manner—put on the weapons of light, so that we may walk honorably in the day, that is, in the brightness of the virtues. Whoever walks in the day walks honorably, because he does not strike his foot against a stone, does not fall, and does not stumble as one who walks in the night does.

According to this admonition of the Apostle, we too must walk honorably and without offense to faith, grace, or knowledge.

Not in revelries. A *comessatio* is so called from the sharing or alternation of a table. There are banquets celebrated in rotation and prepared by companions on successive days and turns. There are also other banquets prepared through common contribution, when one person brings bread, another meat, another wine, and another something else. For this reason they are called *comessationes*, that is, contributions to the table.

The same *comessationes* are also called disgraceful and dishonorable banquets, because, just as everyone uses both his own foods and those held in common, so each person speaks, according to his own pleasure, whatever buffoonery and idle talk he likes.

Not in drunkenness. In the masculine gender we call a *briam* a cup suitable for drinking; from it *ebrietas*, “drunkenness,” is derived, which is excessive drinking of wine.

Not in bedrooms. Properly speaking, *cubilia* are beds, or lairs of wild beasts; the term is derived from foul acts of lying down, to which the beds of those who have intercourse with prostitutes in brothels are compared.

And in impurities. Impudence is shamelessness and irreligion, or shameful and irrational intercourse. In general, every lust, lack of self-restraint, or impurity is called impudence. Those who practice it are called impudent, shameless, and irreligious.

Not in contention. Contention is quarrelsome disputation or controversy, which usually arises from questions concerning the Scriptures, so that someone may appear to possess wisdom when he has defeated another by his argumentative assault. It arises especially from matters of no usefulness. It must therefore be avoided because it produces strife, from which hatred proceeds, and from hatred an enormity of evil.

And not in rivalry. *Aemulatio* has various meanings: it signifies imitation, it signifies zeal, and it also signifies envy, by which someone is tormented by another’s happiness, as in this passage. Hence *aemulus* means an imitator, a zealous person, and an envious person.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. The sense depends on what precedes, where he commands us to put on the weapons of light in such a way that we may walk honorably in the day: “Do not,” he says, “walk”—that is, do not live—in revelries and the remaining vices, “but put on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

A question arises: How can we put on the Lord Jesus Christ, who on the fortieth day after his resurrection penetrated the heights of heaven, where he is now believed to sit in the fullness of the Father’s majesty?

Christ himself, therefore, is wisdom; he himself is diligence; he himself is peace; and the other virtues are in him. Thus the one who puts on Christ assumes, insofar as he is able with God’s help, all the virtues that he knows to be in him, in accordance with what the Apostle says elsewhere: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3)—that is, “you then put on all the virtues,” because you were cleansed from all sins.

The same is to be understood here: “Put on,” he says, “the Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, put on all the virtues that you know to be in him, so that he himself may be your beauty and adornment.

And do not make provision for the flesh in its desires. He does not say, “Do not make provision for the necessities of the flesh,” because it is necessary for us to eat, drink, sleep, and clothe ourselves. Since this is necessary, he did not forbid it. Rather, he says that we should not make provision for the flesh in its desires—that is, we should not fulfill what is evil, such as adultery, gluttony, drunkenness, excessive use of baths beyond what is expedient, and the other things desired by wretched flesh.

He does not say, “Do not think about them,” since it is impossible to cease entirely from thoughts of pleasures. But this should be considered: what he prohibited in desires he permitted in necessities. Care must indeed be taken for the flesh in necessities; in delights, luxury, and every form of lust, however, it must be wholly excluded.

## CHAPTER XIV

But receive the one who is weak in faith—understand: in the affection of love, not in disputes over thoughts; that is, not in judgments or contentions.

One who is weak in faith is someone who doubts in some part of the faith and does not believe perfectly as he ought to believe. Someone who is wholly unbelieving is one who possesses no faith at all. But one who is firm is someone who exists in faith and doubts nothing in it.

Thus the Jew is weak in faith when, newly coming to the faith, he does not consider all foods clean. The gentile, however, is firm in faith, preserving what the Gospel says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person” (Matt. 15); and what the Apostle says: “All things are clean to the clean” (Tit. 1); and what is said in Genesis: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1).

Those who are firm in faith in this way ought to receive into their affection and love the Jew who considers pork, hare, eel, and the other things prohibited by the law to be unclean—things which before the grace of faith he called common, that is, clean. Nevertheless, the Apostle commands that this person be received into love.
