“Receive,” he says, “such a Jew into the affection of love, and do not judge him in your thoughts, nor contend with him,” even though, considering certain things unclean, he refuses to eat them.

For one believes that he may eat everything. The other—that is, the gentile, firm in faith—believes that all things are clean for those who are clean.

But let the one who is weak eat vegetables. The Jew who is weak in faith, who detests certain meats and therefore does not wish to eat them, should eat vegetables—that is, herbs from the garden—and whatever else pleases his heart.

But do not judge him. By “vegetables” every kind of herb suitable for eating is designated.

Blessed Jerome says: “Let the one who is weak from the force of lust abstain from meat and wine, by which lust is aroused, and let him eat vegetables,” that is, let him learn to eat cheap and dry foods, by which the flow of lust is restrained and curbed. For the richness of meats and luxurious banquets provoke the flesh of the body to lust.

The one—that is, the gentile—who eats all foods without distinction should not despise the Jew who does not eat, considering him in his heart less righteous. And the one who does not eat everything, like the Jew, should not judge or reproach the one who eats everything, namely the gentile, as though he were guilty and a sinner. He instructs both Jews and gentiles in turn through these statements.

It may also be understood spiritually, according to blessed Gregory: “The one who eats,” he says—that is, the one who is able to penetrate Sacred Scripture by meditating and investigating—“should not despise or scorn the one who does not eat,” that is, the one who is unable to penetrate it.

Conversely, the one who does not eat—that is, the one who does not understand or is unable to penetrate the depths of the divine Scriptures—should not distress or despise the one who understands and is wise.

For God has received him—understand: the gentile who eats everything—into his faith, and has taught him perfectly, so that he considers nothing unclean for those who are clean.

Who are you to judge another’s servant? The sense is this: If God has received that gentile into his faith so that he may eat everything, who are you to reproach him for his food?

This statement may nevertheless also be referred to the Jew received into the faith, as the following makes clear, so that it may be said: God has received the Jew into his faith, even though he still considers certain things unclean and rejects them. Who are you, faithful gentile, to judge another’s servant—that is, the Jew, a servant of Christ through faith?

He stands or falls before his own master—understand: he stands if he is perfect in faith, or falls before his own master if he doubts in it. The Jew stands before his own master if he is perfect and believes that all things are clean, because he stands in the faith of his own master.

But if he falls by not believing that all things are clean, he does not fall before you, gentile, who cannot raise him up, but before his own master, whom he has offended and who is able to raise him up and establish him firmly in faith. For we can fall of our own accord, but unless God raises us up, we cannot rise.

He will stand—that is, he will be perfected and established in faith. Why? For God, before whom he has fallen, is able to establish him and make him firm in right faith.

For example: A Jew now comes to baptism and passes over into the grace of the Gospel. He has never eaten pork or eel, nor [OCR uncertain: *naupraedam*], and he still abstains from them as though from unclean meat; he is still a newly converted Christian.

When such a person is more perfectly instructed over the course of time, when he learns that nothing is unclean which the faithful receive with thanksgiving, behold, he is established by God, his own Lord, before whom he fell by considering something unclean; behold, he is made firm in faith.

For one judges one day in relation to another. He judges—that is, he distinguishes and makes a difference between one day and another—who abstains from meat or wine on alternate days and does not abstain on the others. For example, there are now many who abstain from meat and wine on the second, fourth, and sixth days of the week; on the third, fifth, and seventh they eat meat and require wine.

Another judges—that is, decides and chooses—every day for abstinence from meat or wine, as hermits and many monks do.

Alternatively: He judges one day in relation to another who understands certain statements of the Old and New Testaments but is unable to penetrate others. He judges every day who understands the Old and New Testament in their entirety.

Sacred Scripture is rightly understood by “day,” because just as ignorance is blindness, so knowledge of the holy Trinity contained in the Old and New Testament is light and illumination of the heart.

In a third sense, he judges one day in relation to another who examines and judges only the present. For example, someone sees a person doing good or evil. The one whom he sees intent upon good works he judges good because of his present righteousness; the one whom he sees devoted to evil works he judges evil because of his injustice.

But if the one who is good today does evil tomorrow, he judges the one whom he had previously praised to be evil. And if the one who is evil today turns away from evil and begins to serve God with a pure mind, he judges him righteous. Such a person judges one day in relation to another, because according to the variation of time and the change of life he changes the judgment of his opinion.

But the one who judges every day is understood to be almighty God, who knows what each person is in the present, in the past, and in the future, because everything is present to him. He can make the one who did evil today good tomorrow.

Let each person abound in his own understanding. He does not say, in the indicative mood, “he abounds,” but in the imperative, “let him abound.” The sense is this: According to what each person has been permitted to understand, let him abound in his judgment. The one who understands that he ought to abstain from meat should abstain; the one who does not understand—that is, who does not wish to abstain or is unable to do so—should eat.

Alternatively: “Let each person abound in his own understanding.” Let the one who understands great and sublime things observe them and abound in good works. Let the one who cannot grasp the sublime mysteries of the divine sacraments fulfill humbly and devoutly, by serving the Lord and abounding in good works, what he truly believes and understands.

Cyprian abounded in his own understanding when he immersed infants once in baptism, because he diligently fulfilled what he understood, abounding in good works, although in this action he sinned through ignorance. But because he abounded in good works, he was later corrected by the Lord and abounded in a higher understanding by immersing them three times.

This is therefore not to be understood of a heretic or of false doctrine, as though each person ought to abound more and more in his error.

The one who esteems the day—that is, the one who chooses to abstain throughout the whole period—esteems it for the Lord, that is, agrees with the Lord, because his abstinence pleases him.

Alternatively: The one who esteems the day—that is, the one who judges that a sinner can be saved through repentance and does not despair of his salvation—esteems it for the Lord, that is, agrees with the Lord in this matter. For the Lord does not immediately punish sinners when they sin but waits for repentance.

Therefore the one who does not judge and condemn the sinner, but believes that every day he can come to forgiveness through the Lord’s mercy, esteems the day for the Lord, because he agrees with the Lord who said: “On whatever day the sinner turns to me, he will be saved” (Ezek. 33).

Thus, when the sinner does not despair, he esteems the day with the Lord; he understands and agrees with the Lord, who waits for the sinner and does not despair that the one who appears unjust today can become just.

And the one who eats—understand: everything, like the gentile—eats for the Lord. For this reason it follows: “For he gives thanks to God,” namely because he believes that everything is clean and that he is permitted to eat everything.

He eats for the Lord who gives thanks for the benefits received from him. And the one who does not eat everything, like the Jew, who is still less perfect in faith, abstains for the Lord. That is, he abstains for love of almighty God from the foods from which God himself has commanded abstinence, and he gives thanks to God because he has granted him the virtue of abstinence and knowledge through the law of the things from which he ought to abstain.

It should be noted that both offer thanksgiving to almighty God. The gentile gives thanks to him for the freedom to eat everything; the Jew, however, gives thanks for the fruit of abstinence, although in this respect he is less perfect because he abstains.

No one among us lives for himself, and no one dies for himself. This is understood spiritually, although it can also be said literally: no one among us lives for himself, because he does not possess life from himself; and no one dies for himself, because it is not in his power to determine when he will live and when he will die. But when he said, “No one among us”—that is, no one among the perfected faithful—he raised our understanding to a higher level. Christ our Lord died once for sin, because he committed no sin; and we, following the example of his death, died once to sin, cleansed from all offenses in baptism and redeemed by Christ’s blood. Thus in baptism we do not die to sin for ourselves [Col. 0489A], but to Christ, since we do not obtain cleansing by our own power, but are cleansed through his passion and baptism, and through faith in him. And no one lives for himself—understand, by means of virtues—but for Christ, who, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him (Rom. VI). Following his example, after we rise from the baptismal font, we must in no way die by sinning. He said “to die” by sinning because “the soul that sins shall itself die.”

For whether we live—through virtues and spiritual life—we live for the Lord, because by abstaining from sins after baptism we attend to the pattern of his resurrection, since he no longer dies, so that we may likewise ascend to heaven with him; or whether we die [Col. 0489B]—understand, to sin in the time of baptism—we die for the Lord, because, in order to please him, in imitation of the one who never sinned, we are cleansed in baptism from original and actual sins through faith and the redemption of his blood. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we belong to the Lord—understand, as servants—because we remain in his power.

These words can also be understood as spoken concerning the martyrs and all the perfected, who do not live for themselves because they do not seek to fulfill their own will but the Lord’s, doing through love what is beneficial to others. That they do not die for themselves a temporal death, in which they are neither granted nor left to themselves but are taken up by God; or that they do not die for themselves a spiritual death—namely, through sins, to which they die when they are regenerated through the Holy Spirit and water—this is clearly indicated [Col. 0489C] by the fact that they must not grow sluggish in idleness, but must always burn with love of God and neighbor. The martyrs likewise did not die for themselves but for the Lord, because they were not killed on account of their own wickedness, but for the knowledge of God and the confession of faith, as the Lord himself says: “Blessed will you be when they cast out your name as evil on account of the Son of Man” (Luke VI).

For Christ died and rose again for this purpose, whether by the death of the flesh or by the death of sin—for he never sinned—so that he might rule over the living and the dead; that is, so that he might rule over those who now live by virtues, cleansed from sins by God’s grace, and over those who daily die to sin so that they may likewise live by virtues, walking in newness of life.

[Col. 0489D] But you, Jew, why do you judge your brother—the gentile who eats everything? Or you, gentile, why do you despise and look down upon your brother—the Jew who is still weak in faith and unwilling to eat everything—when Paul himself says elsewhere: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more worldly matters?” (I Cor. VI); and again, when he himself judges: “Those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V), why does he here forbid us to judge?

We must understand that we are freely granted the power to judge in the case of manifest crimes, such as public homicide, adultery, and theft. But concerning hidden matters, which can be done with either a good or a bad intention, we are forbidden to judge, because judgment concerning these must be reserved for God. For all of us—that is, the good and the wicked [Col. 0490A], the perfected and the imperfect, gentiles and Jews—shall stand before the tribunal of Christ. A tribunal is the seat of a judge, placed in a high position so that the judge may be seen by everyone and, from his elevated place, may himself observe both the accusers and the accused. In the same way, the Lord Jesus will sit as if on a tribunal, because he will be seen by all, and by him the consciences and cases of all will be most fittingly judged. The meaning is: You who judge one another, insofar as it lies with you, take away from God his authority.

For it is written: “As I live, says the Lord.” This is properly God’s oath in the Old Testament—if one may so speak—as “Amen” is in the New. For he alone properly lives and is life, because he cannot be changed; in comparison with him, whatever can be changed is dead [Col. 0490B], since no creature possesses life from itself. “For every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.” How, then, will the angels, who are spirits, bend the knee to God? By the bending of knees we must understand subjection, because at the judgment all things will be subjected to Christ. Every knee, therefore, will bend to God when every creature is subjected to him.

Every human tongue will likewise confess to God when it praises God the Father through the Son; this is understood of the elect alone. For concerning the impious it is said: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccles. XV). The angels, in the manner proper to their incorporeal nature, praise and will praise God. For the voice of the angels in praise of the Creator is itself the inward wonder of intimate contemplation.

Therefore each of us will give an account for himself [Col. 0490C] to God. The meaning is: O Jews and gentiles, who now judge one another, why do you anticipate God’s judgment by your own judgment and, insofar as it lies with you, rashly usurp his authority? Let this be sufficient for you: each person will have to give an account for himself—not only of deeds and words, but also of thoughts.

Therefore let us no longer judge one another—understand, since we are by no means ignorant of God’s future judgment. This is said concerning hidden matters, not manifest ones. Rather, judge this: that you should not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother; that is, take the greatest care and decide above all that no one be scandalized or offended by your evil word or perverse example. Or establish this: that you should not cause offense to your less-perfect brothers on account of bodily foods.

[Col. 0490D] I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing created through him is common. The Jews called only the foods permitted to them by the Law clean; foods that the nations commonly used they called “common,” that is, unclean, as Peter also says: “I have never eaten anything common” (Acts XIV)—that is, unclean. Hence the Apostle says: “I know,” he says, “and I believe in the Lord Jesus,” or “through the Lord Jesus,” who revealed this to me, “that nothing was created unclean through him, but all things were made clean by him,” as it is written: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. I). But if something is common—that is, unclean—to a Jew or to anyone else who thinks that a particular food is common, it is common for that person, because it appears unclean to him according to his own understanding, not according to God, who made everything clean. [Col. 0491A]

For if, on account of the food that he considers unclean, and you urge him to eat, your brother—the Jew, still weak and unbelieving—is saddened, you are no longer walking according to charity; that is, you do not possess charity, because you do not love your brother as yourself. Do not destroy him by your food, giving an occasion for offense and scandal, for whom Christ died. You destroy him when you scandalize his mind, because he offends God while becoming angry with you, who are his neighbor.

Therefore let our good not be blasphemed. Here “good” can be understood as charity, because we ought to love our neighbor; or as faith, by which we believe that all things are clean and by which we possess the freedom to eat everything [Col. 0491B]. Therefore let neither our charity be blasphemed or reproached, so that it is not displayed to our weak Jewish brother, nor let the faith and belief by which we have received the freedom to eat everything be blasphemed. Our freedom is blasphemed when we compel those who consider something unclean to eat with us what they abhor.

This freedom is good for us, because all things are clean for clean people. “And everything was very good”; to be in agreement with Scripture is good. Nevertheless, do not compel a Jew to eat what he rejects, nor eat it in his presence, lest your freedom be blasphemed by him.

For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. The meaning is: [Col. 0491C] It is exceedingly foolish for us to dispute about what must or must not be eaten—namely, about things that will not be necessary in the kingdom of heaven—when we ought rather to discuss righteousness, peace, and spiritual joy.

There will be righteousness in the kingdom of heaven, because those who now practice works of righteousness will enter the kingdom of heaven. Peace and joy in the Holy Spirit will be there; that is, those who are now enlightened through the Holy Spirit pursue peace and seek with the full effort of their minds the joys of the heavenly homeland, rejoicing in the present in spiritual joy and in the hope of the heavenly homeland.

Alternatively: There will be righteousness in that kingdom because no one there will harm another. There will be peace there—that is, complete harmony—which the elect will have with God and the angels. There will be ineffable joy from the vision of almighty God. In these matters, by whatever way we can, we ought to imitate and surpass others.

[Col. 0491D] For whoever serves Christ in this—that is, in righteousness, peace, and spiritual joy through the grace of the Holy Spirit, whom he has as an indwelling inhabitant through these virtues—pleases God and is approved by human beings, praiseworthy and worthy of praise, because he pleases not only God but also human beings.

Therefore let us pursue the things that belong to peace—that is, let us seek carefully and earnestly whatever preserves brotherly love—as was said above concerning hospitality: “Pursuing hospitality.” And let us mutually safeguard the things that belong to edification; that is, let us put aside every contention over a matter of no usefulness and preserve whatever pertains to the edification of ourselves and our brothers, so that by our word, example, and entire manner of life the temple of God may be built up in us, with the edification of faith preserved, and so that through us brothers who are still weak in faith may be built up.

[Col. 0492A] Do not destroy the work of God on account of food. The work of God is understood as the human being, made by God in body and soul. This work is destroyed when a person is scandalized, because he becomes angry, which is entirely displeasing to God. The work of God can also be understood as charity, which God works in us, or through which our work is offered to him; it is destroyed when a brother is scandalized by us.

Indeed, all foods created by God are clean in themselves and in their nature. But it is evil for the gentile who eats through causing offense. Whoever, however [Col. 0492B], eats everything indiscriminately for the purpose of scandalizing his brother, the Jew who is still weak in faith, draws upon himself the guilt of sin and offense.

It is good for you, O gentile, not to eat meat and not to drink wine, nor to do anything else by which your brother, the Jew, is scandalized or weakened in faith. He is weakened in faith when you urge him to eat foods that he considers unclean, or when you distress him by eating in his presence foods that he abhors.

To eat meat and drink wine is neither good nor evil, but morally indifferent. Similarly, not to eat meat and not to drink wine is morally indifferent, because there are many who eat meat and drink wine with sobriety. There are also many pagans and heretics, and especially hypocrites, who neither eat meat nor drink wine [Col. 0492C], and yet they are not thereby justified.

Nevertheless, it is better to abstain from meat and wine in the presence of a believing Jew than to scandalize him in any way. This can also be understood more generally of all who, on account of abstinence or fasts, scandalize many; or certainly of those who do so because of gluttony; or even of those who, with a simple intention, eat meat on ordinary days and thereby cause offense to many. It would be good for them not to eat, because they carry this out with insufficient caution.

Do you have faith? Keep it to yourself, and before God. Here he is not speaking of faith in the Holy Trinity, but of the faith by which we believe that all things are clean, as we said above [Col. 0492D]. He addresses the gentile: O gentile, do you have faith privately—that is, do you believe in your heart that all things are clean and lawful to eat? Keep it before God in your heart, not in a display of words and boastfulness, lest you scandalize another by saying that you have the power to eat everything.

Blessed is the gentile who does not judge or condemn himself—understand, because he has not scandalized his Jewish brother by proving that all things are clean. The gentile is called blessed in this respect when his conscience does not reproach him for having scandalized his Jewish brother by compelling him to eat meat that he detested, and when he has not eaten in that brother’s presence anything [Col. 0493A] that the brother abhorred, although he himself judged and knew that all things were clean.

But whoever distinguishes—that is, judges and makes distinctions between clean and unclean foods—after coming to faith, like a Jew, if he eats, is condemned, because he does not act from faith. That is, he acts unbelievingly, not believing that all things are clean.

He says this if some gentile, coming to faith, recognizes that all things are clean and afterward makes a distinction between one food and another, saying that some are clean and others unclean. If he then eats from the foods he had regarded as unclean, he acquires condemnation for himself, because he does not act faithfully, doubting in faith; he eats what he had declared unclean when others were eating it, and thereby denies that all things were made clean by God.

[Col. 0493B] But every thing—understand, everything pertaining to eating—which is not from faith—that is, which is not believed to have been made clean by God—if it is eaten, is sin, because he has eaten what he declared to be unclean.

## CHAPTER XV

We ought, however, we—namely, I, my fellow apostles, and the other believers who are stronger in faith because we believe that all things are clean—to bear the weaknesses of the weak; that is, to bear the weakness of faith of those who do not yet believe that all things are clean and lawful to eat. We should not please ourselves by urging them to eat common foods or by eating in their presence the foods that they themselves abhor.

[Col. 0493C] Let each of you please his neighbor for the good, for edification in faith, so that by your word and example and by your entire manner of life those who are still weak in faith may be built up.

For Christ did not please himself alone, but the Father, concerning whom he says: “I always do what pleases him” (John VIII), and good people as well, as it is written: “The reproaches”—that is, insults, curses, blasphemies, and slanders—“of those reproaching you, O Father, fell upon me.” This is Christ’s voice to the Father concerning the reproaches of the Jews. When they reproached his Son, saying (John VIII), “You are a Samaritan, and you have a demon,” and other such things, they reproached God the Father, who was in the Son; but those reproaches fell upon Christ because they persecuted him even unto death [Col. 0493D].

The Apostle therefore rightly says: “Christ did not please himself,” because he did not seek his own interests but those of the Father and of us, as he himself said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Likewise, we ought not to please ourselves or seek our own will, but the will of God and of our brothers.

For whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope. The Apostle joins himself to all believers and wishes to show that everything written in the divine Books was not written only for those whose deeds and actions are narrated there—for they would not read them, since they had long ago died and were at rest—but also for our salvation and that of those to come [Col. 0494A], so that we might have a place from which to take examples of faith and good works, and where we might learn by which works God is pleased and by which he is provoked to vengeance; namely, how virtues should be desired and vices rejected, and how we ought to be patient in faith and hope.

For what benefit was it to Abraham that Moses wrote that he had been obedient and praised him as pleasing to God? “Whatever,” he says, “was written in the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the other Scriptures was written for our instruction,” so that we who have come to faith might be taught from them.

How? So that, instructed by the patience of the fathers who came before us, we may patiently endure the adversities of this age, and through the consolation of the Scriptures have hope—that is, hold fast to the expectation of future goods.

Let us see how the things written in the divine Books pertain to our instruction. When we read that the people of Israel went out from Egypt, were led through the Red Sea, while Pharaoh and the Egyptians were drowned, received water from the rock, were granted manna from heaven, and, after many battles bravely fought against their enemies, entered the promised land, we ought both to be taught and to teach from these events.

Through Egypt we should understand this world; through the Red Sea, baptism, which is consecrated by the redness of Christ’s blood; through Pharaoh, the devil; through the Egyptians, original and actual sins, which perish in baptism; through the rock, Christ; through the water, his teaching, concerning which he himself says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink” (John VII), or the mystery of our redemption and cleansing [Col. 0494C]; through manna, his body, which is received daily by the faithful in the Church; through the battles that they endured, the struggles and wars that we have against demons. After conquering them, if we remain rightly in the faith, we will deserve to reach the heavenly homeland, which is signified by the promised land, concerning which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVII). The true Israelites alone receive this land—that is, the firmness of the eternal homeland.

Again, when we read of the faith, obedience, and patience of blessed Abraham—how he endured the adversities of this age when he dwelt as a stranger in a foreign land through the course of many years, and how he obeyed God’s words when he wished to sacrifice his only son, not doubting the promise, because God said to him, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI) [Col. 0494D]—we ought to imitate his faith. We are called his children through faith, patience, and obedience, not failing in tribulations.

Similarly, when we read that blessed Job was grievously struck and scourged, to such an extent that, deprived of his sons, daughters, and all his possessions, he sat on a dungheap scraping away the pus with a potsherd—although formerly he had been, as one of the most powerful of kings—and how he endured all adversities with the greatest patience, for which he again deserved to receive health, everything he had lost doubled, and, in addition, future rewards, we ought to receive great consolation from this.

And if such things should ever happen to us, we ought to recall these events and become imitators of his patience [Col. 0495A], saying with him: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job II). Turning such things and others like them over carefully in our minds, we ought to hold firm hope, awaiting the joys of future goods.

May the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same understanding toward one another according to Jesus Christ. The Apostle now gives a blessing to the Romans in the manner of the patriarchs. For example, Isaac blessed his sons Esau and Jacob, and afterward Jacob blessed the twelve patriarchs; and Moses blessed the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.

Just as God is called the God of righteousness because he grants righteousness to all who deserve to be justified and dwells in their hearts, so he is called the God of patience because he himself grants patience and dwells in the hearts [Col. 0495B] of those who preserve patience amid adversities. Likewise, he is called the God of consolation because he himself provides consolation to those who trust in him and deigns to dwell in the hearts of those who strive to offer consolation to others—or of those who, situated in adversities, receive consolation from the patience of others.

“May the God of patience and consolation,” he says, “grant you to have the same understanding toward one another”: that you may have one judgment concerning faith, hope, and charity; that what one person believes, he may hope another believes; and that the good which is in oneself may also be in another. Or may he grant you to have the same understanding, so that just as each person wishes for himself, so he may wish for his neighbor—that is, whatever he wishes to happen to himself, he may desire for his neighbor—and just as he loves the other, so he may believe himself to be loved by the other.

He rightly added, “according to Jesus Christ,” that is, according to [Col. 0495C] what the will of Jesus Christ is, because many have the same understanding and appear to love one another, but not according to Jesus Christ. For example, there are heretics who do not recognize in themselves the error that they perceive in other heretics; and there are those who love others not for the sake of God’s love, but because they seek temporal benefits from them or agree with them in wickedness.

So that with one mind—that is, with one understanding—and with one accord, or with one faith, and with one mouth—that is, with one confession—you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Almighty God the Father is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ both according to his divinity, in which he begot him coeternal and consubstantial with himself before all ages, and according to his humanity [Col. 0495D], in which he created him at the end of the ages in the virginal womb. God, however, is spoken of only in relation to the humanity assumed by the Word, that is, according to his humanity. Hence, after the glory of the resurrection, he himself said to Mary: “Go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX).

We glorify or praise him when, holding his most sincere faith in our hearts and with our whole understanding, we confess with our mouth that he is the true God, and adorn the faith we possess with good works, according to what Truth himself admonishes, saying: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Therefore—understand, for the honor of his glory—receive one another [Col. 0496A], just as Christ also received you for the honor of God. These words refer to what the Apostle said somewhat earlier, speaking about brothers still weak in faith and about the differences concerning foods, which he commanded to be received with the affection of charity and tranquility, saying: “Receive the one who is weak in faith.” The meaning is: I say these things for this reason, so that you may receive into the affection of charity brothers who are still weak in faith, and not scandalize them by urging them to eat foods that they detest as unclean. Receive them with charity, just as Christ also received you into his faith, for the honor of God the Father, so that God the Father may be praised through you.

If, then, Christ deigned to receive into his faith Jews who blasphemed and you gentiles who were idolaters, filled with every [Col. 0496B] uncleanness, and alienated from knowledge of God, how much more ought we not to despise our brother who is weak in faith, nor distress or scandalize him in anything, but rather gather him into the affection of charity.

For this reason he says that we have been received for the honor of God the Father: so that God the Father may be glorified and praised through us and through our good works, together with his Son, who said in the Gospel to his disciples and to all who would believe in him: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. The word “circumcision” in this passage can be understood in two ways, namely, both carnally [Col. 0496C] and spiritually, since the Lord was the minister of both by receiving them in himself and administering them to others.

He was the minister of carnal circumcision because, before he came into the world through the mystery of the Incarnation, he who is the Word of the Father administered it by giving it and commanding that it be observed. For he who spoke through the angel to the holy fathers—as is very often made clear in the prophetic books, where it says, “The mouth,” or “the word of the Lord, spoke”—when he came in the flesh also became the minister of circumcision, because he received it in himself, not in order to command that it be observed and maintained after his coming, but to show that the Law was holy, just, and good.

For when the Lord sent the apostles to preach, he did not say, “Go and preach that circumcision [Col. 0496D] must be observed by all the nations,” but: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI), and “baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” This has been said about carnal circumcision, but it is better—that is, in a higher sense—to understand it about spiritual circumcision, namely, the grace of baptism.

What is spiritual circumcision? Certainly, the stripping away of vices, which takes place through baptism. The Lord himself was its minister, receiving it in himself and giving it to others. For he received baptism when he was baptized by John the Baptist; afterward he administered it, because he baptized the apostles and others who approached him through faith, as the Gospel relates, saying: “Jesus was baptizing, and his disciples.”

When he also sent the apostles [Col. 0497A] to the office of preaching throughout the fourfold world, he charged them, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Holy Trinity” (Matt. XXVIII). Behold how the Lord Jesus was the minister of spiritual circumcision.

We can also truthfully say that he administers this same circumcision daily by forgiving sins in baptism. For he entrusted the ministry of immersing bodies to his faithful, but reserved for himself alone the power to forgive sins, as John his forerunner says concerning him to the crowds: “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III).

And again John says: “I did not know him,” he says, “that he would reserve for himself the power of baptizing and hand it over to no one; but the one who sent me to baptize said to me: Upon whomever you see the Spirit [Col. 0497B] descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes” (John I).

When the Apostle says that Christ Jesus was the minister of spiritual circumcision, someone might object: For what purpose did he himself become the minister of circumcision? The Apostle answers: “For the truth,” he says, “of God the Father, to confirm the promises made to the fathers”; that is, so that God the Father might confirm his promises, which he spoke to the holy fathers concerning the salvation of the nations, saying to Abraham: “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVI). Or, so that he might appear truthful by fulfilling the promises that the fathers had made concerning the salvation of the nations and that they had foretold concerning this same spiritual circumcision.

For unless the gentiles were cleansed through the grace of baptism and through faith in the Lord Savior, they would by no means pass into the sonship [Col. 0497C] of Abraham, nor would what Moses says be fulfilled (Deut. XXX): “In the last days the Lord will circumcise your heart,” and not your flesh—that is, he will cleanse it from unbelief and every sin through baptism. The same applies to what the prophet Ezekiel says: “I will pour clean water over you” (Ezek. XXXVI)—namely, the water of baptism.

The nations, however, ought to honor God on account of mercy—that is, concerning mercy—because they were called to faith freely, without any preceding merits, and freely received the forgiveness of all sins through spiritual circumcision, namely, through the grace of baptism and not through carnal circumcision [Col. 0497D]: “For to whom more is forgiven, he ought to love more” (Luke VII).

As it is written: “Therefore I will confess to you among the nations, O Lord, and I will sing to your name.” The Psalmist speaks in the person of the Son of God, giving thanks to God the Father for the obedience of the nations coming to faith.

How, then, does the Son glorify and praise God the Father, who is equal to him in all things? He praises him among the believing nations. Whenever the nations praise and glorify God the Father, the Son of God praises him through the mouths and works of the nations, who have been redeemed by his blood.

Therefore he says: “For this reason”—because you have subjected many peoples and nations to me through faith—“I will confess to you, Lord Father, and I will glorify you through those very nations, and I will sing to your name [Col. 0498A],” that is, I will praise the name of your divinity.

And again Scripture says in Deuteronomy: “Rejoice, nations, with his people.” Moses the lawgiver, extending the eye of prophecy to the time of the calling of the nations, addresses them and urges them to praise God the Father with the people of Israel, which once alone among all nations was called his people:

O believing nations, redeemed through the passion of the Son of God and cleansed and purified from all sins through his baptism, joining yourselves in the affection of charity to those who believe from Israel, rejoice with spiritual joy.

And again: “Praise the Lord, all nations, and magnify him, all peoples.” The chorus of the apostles [Col. 0498B] addresses the multitude of nations hastening to the faith of Christ and the grace of baptism, and commands them to offer praises of thanksgiving to the Lord in heart, mouth, and deed: to him by whose grace they have been redeemed and by whose mercy they have been purified from all guilt.

But in what follows, “Magnify him, all peoples,” he urges the Jews to rejoice in the salvation of the nations, saying: And you, all peoples—that is, all Jews—magnify God; that is, proclaim him great on account of the salvation of your gentile brothers and on account of the ineffable mighty works that he bestowed upon you from ancient days, telling the nations how many and how great were the gifts he most willingly granted you.

And again Isaiah says (Isa. XI): “There will be a root of Jesse, and the one who rises up to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope.”

[Col. 0498C] Jesse himself is Isai, the father of King David, from whose lineage Christ was born according to the flesh through the Virgin Mary. The statement “There will be a root of Jesse” can be understood in two ways, as follows. Jesse himself is the root, while David his son is the tree. The Virgin Mary is the branch of that same tree; the flower of this branch is Christ, who says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field” (Song II).

Therefore the root of this little flower—that is, of Christ—was Jesse, because just as a flower proceeds from the root of a tree, so Christ, according to the flesh, drew his origin from Jesse.

In a higher understanding, however, Christ is the root of Jesse: namely, the Word of God the Father, who, among the other things he created, was also the creator of Jesse. For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” [Col. 0498D] (John I). Thus the one who according to the flesh derived his origin from Jesse was also, according to his divinity, the root and creator of Jesse.

Jesse is interpreted as “It is for me” [Est mihi]. “Is” [est] is a substantive verb. The word “will be” [erit] in the statement “There will be a root” likewise comes from the same substantive verb and is used for the future tense. Therefore, whoever believes in the one who said to Moses, “The One who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III), can truly say: “It is for me”—that is, I believe in the one who always is; he is my God and will be so.

But one may ask why the Prophet said, “There will be a root of Jesse,” rather than “There will be a root of Boaz or Obed,” since they too were righteous and were the fathers of Isai. The answer is that the Prophet said “There will be a root of Jesse,” and not [Col. 0499A] “a root of Boaz or Obed,” in order to show that the Lord Christ Jesus descended according to the flesh from a royal lineage, though he was begotten before the ages by God the Father, King of kings and Lord of lords.

It must also be noted that by saying “There will be a root of Jesse,” speaking with a verb in the future tense, he looked toward Christ’s human birth, which was still future when this was foretold.

Let it therefore be expressed in this way: Jesse will be the root of Christ according to his humanity, and Christ himself, who will rise up to rule the nations by being born through a virgin—or by rising from the dead—is the one in whom the nations will hope. Christ therefore rules and governs the nations that believe in him, and he himself defends them from the snares and attacks of demons and all adversaries, because they hope in him.

[Col. 0499B] Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing. From what the prophet Isaiah said concerning Christ, “In him the nations will hope,” the Apostle took the occasion to give them this blessing: May the God of hope, who grants the hope of future goods to those who believe in him, fill you with every spiritual joy and peace—that is, harmony and brotherly love—in believing in him who reconciled you to God the Father through his blood.

May you also be harmonious and peaceful with one another, you who until now have been at odds with one another, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit; that is, so that through the power of the Holy Spirit you may possess the full hope of eternal reward, and, strengthened by his gift and assistance, may deserve to attain the power of complete goodness.

[Col. 0499C] I am confident, my brothers—and I myself am confident concerning you—that you are full of love of God and neighbor, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another; that is, to correct and rebuke one another. He addresses those who are perfected in faith with gentle words.

But I have written to you rather boldly, brothers, in part. Although “more boldly” is a comparative degree, here it is used in place of the positive, which is “boldly,” that is, with boldness and confidence. Therefore he added “in part,” because he himself knew many things in his heart that he did not bring forth with his mouth, and which they were unable to grasp; of these he was writing only a portion to them. Or he said “in part” for this reason also: they had already read his letters that he had sent to other churches, and what they had not read there in part he endeavored to include here. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0499D] As though reminding you, that is, reminding you that you had already read my statements in some of my letters. This is as though he were saying in other words: “Since I have recalled to your memory that you have already read my statements, I have written fewer things to you—and this because of the grace given to me by God, so that I might be a minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles.” Here he calls “grace” wisdom, which he deserved to receive above all the apostles, as blessed Augustine says. It may also be understood of the ministry of apostleship, which was freely bestowed upon him by God. “I have written to you,” he says, “a few things out of many, which are firmly held in my heart because of the grace of wisdom given to me by the Lord for this purpose: that I might expend it according to the capacity of my hearers; or also that I might fulfill the ministry of apostleship among the Gentiles.”

[Col. 0500A] Sanctifying the Gospel of God, that is, demonstrating it to be holy by preaching it without error or falsehood, by living holily, and by bearing witness through miracles of his powers; not seeking his own glory, nor doing these things or anything else for temporal gain, but acting for the reward of eternal life. He sanctifies the Gospel, or demonstrates it to be holy, who preaches it without error or falsehood, confirms by miracles what he preaches with his mouth, adorns it with holy conduct, and seeks not his own praise but God’s; so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, that is, so that the Gentiles may be offered to God through me in thanksgiving, and that this offering itself may be pleasing to him and sanctified through baptism, through the passion of Christ, and through faith in the Holy Spirit, that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0500B] It belongs to pontiffs to devote themselves to teaching and preaching, and it belongs to them to offer sacrifice to God. For just as in the Old Testament the high priest or priest carefully took care that the victim and offering he presented to God should be without blemish, so those who announce the Gospel must take care that no fault arise either in preaching, teaching, or instruction. Thus, just as those victims were acceptable to God, so their hearers, passing into God’s sacrifice, may be acceptable, imitating those preachers the outstanding teacher and master of the Gentiles, who desired that those whom he had offered to God in faith through his preaching and ministry should remain without the blemish of grave sin and thus be acceptable to God.

Therefore I have glory, prepared in Christ Jesus for God; as though he were saying: “Through the virtues that are in Christ Jesus, which I embrace, I have glory prepared for me and the greatest honor before God the Father.”

[Col. 0500C] For I would not dare to speak any of those things that Christ does not accomplish through me, in word and deed; that is, I do not dare to speak or preach anything other than what Christ inspires in my heart. Whatever he worked, whatever he spoke, Christ accomplished all of it through him, just as he says elsewhere: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII). For the obedience of the Gentiles in word and deed: that is, I devote myself to the word of preaching and to deeds of miracles so that the Gentiles may obey the Gospel.

[Col. 0500D] In the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit. “Signs” are so called in many places where, although something wonderful occurs, something also future is indicated through it, as in the healing of the royal official’s son, when the Lord said: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe” (John IV). For by the fact that, when the miracle of healing had been seen in his son, very few believed—namely, the father and his household—it was signified that only a small number of Jews would believe in God. Here is a sign that contains both elements in itself: something miraculous and something future. But “wonders” (*prodigia*) are so called as though they were *porodigia*, or *perrodicentia* (“foretellings”), because they indicate only something future, as though pointing it out with a finger. In this passage, however, “signs and wonders” are taken as one expression, namely, miracles worked through the power of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0501A] So that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum, which is a province at the beginning of Europe, I have filled the Gospel of Christ—understand: all the peoples and provinces. Illyricum is a province, as we have said. It is the end of Asia and the beginning of Europe.

Thus I preached this Gospel. How? Not where Christ had already been named by preachers, or where they already believed in him, lest I build upon another’s foundation. “I did not preach,” he says, “where Christ had already been preached and believed in, but where he was entirely unknown, lest I place my preaching and faith upon the preaching and faith of others.” Therefore the Apostle himself laid the foundations of faith, and he himself raised the walls.

[Col. 0501B] To those, certainly, of whom it had formerly been foretold: “Those to whom nothing has been announced by the prophets concerning him”—that is, concerning Christ—“will see” him through faith, “and those who have not heard him being preached will understand concerning him” through the preaching of the apostles.

For this reason—understand: because of the work of preaching—and I was greatly hindered from building up the word, from coming to you, O Romans, and I have been prevented until now. He was not hindered by Satan, but by the usefulness of preaching, so that he might first establish the churches of Asia and afterward proceed to foreign nations.

[Col. 0501C] But now, having no further place in these regions for preaching, and having had the desire to come to you for many preceding years, when I begin my journey to Spain, I hope that, as I pass through, I shall see you, and be sent on my way there by you, if I may first enjoy your company for a little while.

He appears to be saying this while situated in Achaia, at Corinth, a city of that province. Achaia is near and adjacent to Macedonia. After dwelling in these regions and traversing each of them, preaching the Gospel only within those boundaries in which Christ had not yet been preached, he had filled the whole area with the knowledge of God. He indicates that the time had now arrived when he ought to fulfill his desire, namely, by seeing those who lived in Rome. He appropriately promises his presence and his delay to people whom he had not yet seen according to the flesh and to whom he had not yet come bodily. We receive goods more eagerly when we have quickly earned them only to lose them, but we more securely neglect what we believe we shall possess for a longer time. To enjoy means to possess, embrace, or behold something with delight and joy.

Now, therefore—understand: before I come to you—I shall depart for Jerusalem to minister to the saints. He calls “saints” those who, for the love of Christ, had abandoned or sold all their possessions and brought their price to the feet of the apostles (Acts IV), or those who had been despoiled by unbelieving Jews, whom he praises when he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “You joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions” (Heb. X). Isaiah also speaks of these people: “He who departed from evil became exposed to their plunder” (Isa. LIX).

[Col. 0502A] All those who had abandoned their own possessions or had been stripped of them, and who did not possess the knowledge required for preaching, so that they could go out to preach to the Gentiles, remained in Jerusalem, continually occupied with prayers and fasts. The apostles endeavored to send them whatever money, gold, silver, or clothing they received from the various provinces and places where they preached, but Paul above all, since he preached to very many nations. Hence the teachers say that at times he sent them more than three or five *modii* of silver.

For Macedonia and Achaia approved—that is, it seemed holy and good to them—to make some contribution of gifts for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. Macedonia and Achaia, which is also called Achaea, from which its peoples are called Achaeans, are most renowned provinces of the Greeks, adjoining one another;

[Col. 0502B] the Apostle filled them with churches.

For they were pleased, and they are their debtors. What had the Macedonians and Achaeans—or Achaians—received from the saints who were in Jerusalem, so that they should be their debtors? They were their debtors in three ways: either because the saints had preceded them in faith, while they themselves were being instructed by the apostles and preachers; or because they were advancing through the saints’ example and teaching; or because they shared one faith and, having one God as Father, were brothers in faith. For all Christians who are brothers in faith are debtors to one another, so that each may bear the burdens of the other.

It may also be understood in a fourth way: they were their debtors because the saints devoted themselves day and night to prayers for their salvation, so that the faith of Christ might be strengthened in them.

[Col. 0502C] For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual goods, they ought also to minister to them in material things. They were partakers of their goods in the same ways in which they were debtors to them, and the meaning is this: since the saints supply them with what is lacking in spiritual matters, and since the Gentiles possess in the saints what they themselves do not possess, it is just that they should assist them with temporal benefits.

When, therefore, I have completed this work of ministry—that is, when I have finished it and delivered to them this fruit, namely, the contribution of gifts that the faithful are sending them through me—I shall depart by way of you to Spain. He appropriately says that he will go through Rome to Spain, because, for those traveling from Achaia to Spain, Rome lies midway along the route.

[Col. 0502D] I know, however, that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of the Gospel of Christ. Filled with the prophetic Spirit, he spoke such words confidently. What he says—“I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of the Gospel of Christ”—has the same meaning as what he said at the beginning of this Epistle: “I desire,” he says, “to come to you, so that I may impart some spiritual gift to you, to strengthen you” (Rom. I).

“I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of the Gospel,” that is, in a fullness of virtues, so that through my preaching you may receive in faith what you lack, through the power of the miracles that I shall work among you; you may be strengthened in that same faith, and may deserve to receive a greater grace of Christ at my coming. For this is what he did: when he came, he supplied by his arrival what they lacked [Col. 0503A] in faith, charity, and the other spiritual matters.

Therefore I appeal to you, Roman brothers, through the Lord Jesus and through the love of the Holy Spirit—that is, through the love that you ought to have toward God and neighbor, which is given to the faithful through the Holy Spirit—to assist me in your prayers to God, that is, before God, so that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judaea, and so that the offering of my service—that is, of my ministry or obedience—may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem; that I may come to you with joy through the will of God and be refreshed with you.

He seeks refreshment who is scorched by the heat of the sun, or who grows heated and weary by fighting and wrestling. The blessed Apostle fought vigorously against philosophers, Jews, and heretics, and therefore desired to rest for a time both in body and in spirit. Hence he says in one place: “If I fought with beasts at Ephesus” (I Cor. XV). He calls philosophers and heretics “beasts.”

He appealed for this reason: he feared that, while coming to Jerusalem, he might be seized by the unbelieving Jews, shut up in prison, or killed, and thus be unable either to carry his gifts and offering to the saints or afterward to come to Rome, as he desired. Here the pride of pontiffs, prelates, princes, and the powerful of this world is struck down: they disdain to entreat their subjects to pour forth prayers and supplications for them. If he who was both an apostle and the pontiff of all the Gentiles, and was filled with every grace of the Holy Spirit, did not disdain to seek the help of his subjects in prayers, how much more should those who are full of greed, pride, and every wicked act not disdain to do so? Therefore he is to be imitated with all one’s strength.

[Col. 0503B] May the God of peace be with you all. Amen. The God of peace is understood as the holy Trinity, by whose mercy the human race has been reconciled, and by whose gift peace and concord are given to all the faithful. It is very fitting that he ended in peace, with the two peoples recalled to concord, showing that the God of peace—who grants peace—can dwell only among those who are peaceful.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0503D] I commend to you our sister Phoebe—not according to the flesh, but as one common to us in faith—who is in the service of the Church at Cenchreae, so that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, that is, as is fitting for saints; or, as some manuscripts read, “in a sufficiently worthy manner,” that is, abundantly and humanely. And assist her—that is, help her and provide support for her—in whatever business or matter she may need your help.

Cenchreae is the port of Corinth, where there was a church of the faithful. Phoebe, a most noble matron and exceedingly faithful in the faith of Christ, ministered to it by supplying food and clothing. At that time, when the Apostle was writing this Epistle, the Romans ruled all nations. If one of the nobles had an important case arising from some matter, whether from the oppression of others or concerning estates or slaves, he hastened to Rome, where the emperor and the judges of cases were. It could therefore have happened that the matron Phoebe had then come to Rome for such a reason. Consequently Paul instructed the believers to assist her in every matter, whether with clothing, food, or some other temporal support. He also gives the reason why he issues this instruction: for she herself also stood by many—that is, ministered and offered assistance—and by me personally.

[Col. 0504A] Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, namely, in preaching and other works, who for my life—that is, to preserve it—laid down their own necks, exposing themselves to danger.

Prisca is the same woman who is also called Priscilla in the Acts of the Apostles. She was Jewish by birth, the wife of Aquila the Jew. At one time, when the Jews wished to kill the Apostle at Corinth, these two placed themselves between them and him and rescued him. Hence he adds: not I, Paul, alone give them thanks for this deed, but also all the churches of the Gentiles, over which I preside because they came to the faith through my preaching.

This, then, is Aquila and Priscilla his wife, with whom Paul stayed while he was at Corinth, because they practiced the same trade as Paul, namely, the making of tents, an occupation also called the craft of tentmaking. They were cobblers, sewing tents and pavilions from skins or linen materials, especially those in which the Saracens live; they sold what they made and lived from it.

Of these people it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “After this, Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth” (Acts XVIII). There he found a certain Jew named Aquila, of Pontic origin, who had recently come from Italy, together with his wife Priscilla, because the emperor Claudius had ordered all Jews to depart from the city of Rome, since they were seditious. Paul joined them, and because they practiced the same trade, they lived together and worked together. They were, as we have said, artisans who made tents—that is, leatherworkers who constructed tents from skins or linen curtains.

[Col. 0504C] But a question arises here. Since the Acts of the Apostles says, as was shown above concerning Paul, that Paul, Aquila, and Prisca were lodging together at Corinth, why does he write greetings to them in this Epistle from Corinth, as though they were living in Rome? The matter is resolved as follows: after the Jews had been expelled from the city by Claudius’s order, these two came to Corinth; when, after Caesar’s death, the freedom to return had again been granted, they returned to Rome, where the Apostle now greets them.

He also greets the members of their household and their servants, whom he calls a church, saying: “And the church in their house,” with “I greet” understood.

Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first-fruit of Asia. Epaenetus appears to have been the first person in Asia to believe; hence he calls him the first-fruit of Asia. Or he calls him this because he was the first of all to believe, or because he was a man of great rank and nobility. He mentioned him for this reason: to show that nobles, too, came to the faith, and thereby to invite the leading Romans to faith.

Greet Mary, who labored greatly in the Lord, namely, by performing the ministry of preaching among women of her own sex in their homes. For women did not teach in the church, but men did, because the Apostle himself had forbidden this, saying: “Let women keep silence in the churches” (I Cor. XIV).

Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are noble among the apostles and who were in Christ before me. It may be that these were the Apostle’s relatives according to the flesh, and that they likewise were Jews who became exiles from their native place for the sake of the faith, just as Paul did when he appealed to Caesar. They believed in Christ before him and were regarded as noble among the apostles—that is, among the twelve apostles. We may also understand of them that perhaps they themselves belonged to the seventy-two apostles and were among the noble ones.

[Col. 0505B] Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus. This Aristobulus is understood to have been a gatherer of brothers who believed in Christ. The Apostle confirms this by considering his disciples worthy of his greeting.

Greet Apelles, approved in Christ. Although some make two proper names from this, saying, “Greet Apelles and Probus,” that is not correct. It is one proper name with an adjective. “Greet,” he says, “Apelles, approved,” that is, approved in faith and worthy of praise; for we call a person *probus* when he is approved and praiseworthy.

Greet those who are of the household of Narcissus. This Narcissus, as is found in other manuscripts, was a presbyter at that time.

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, that is, advanced to the priesthood, and his mother, who is also mine through the adoption of love. This woman was distinguished by great religious devotion. She had earned from the Apostle the gift of being called his mother. We must not suppose that in these greetings the differences of praise and salutation are assigned to each person without reason. Whoever knows that Christ speaks in Paul is certain that each is named according to the merit of his life: one is called approved, another most beloved, another one who labors in the Lord, and another chosen—as Rufus here, the subject of the present passage, is greeted as chosen in the Lord. His mother is called the Apostle’s mother because of the highest affection.

[Col. 0505D] Greet one another with a holy kiss, that is, with a kiss that is not false or deceitful, such as the kiss with which Judas betrayed the Savior, or such as that with which the impure kiss others for the sake of uncleanness. That kiss is called not chaste, but dove-like [*columbinum*]. The meaning is: “Since I am not present, so that I can kiss you all, kiss one another for love of me when you have received this letter.”

From this passage and others like it, the Church received the custom that, when the faithful assemble in church to hear the divine word and celebrate the Mass, they receive one another after the prayers with a kiss of love.

[Col. 0506A] I appeal to you, brothers, to watch those who cause dissensions, that is, to avoid those who stir up discord and quarrels among you. Here he speaks against the false apostles and Jews who did not believe correctly.

For such people—understand: such men—who generate dissensions among you by going from house to house, flattering and praising some while disparaging others, and inciting one against another through their detraction, do not serve Christ but their own belly. They flatter some and disparage others in order to fill their own belly, and through sweet words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent.

[Col. 0506B] “For this purpose,” he says, “they preach and utter sweet words of flattery and blessing: so that they may deceive the hearts of simple brothers and take away their innocence.”

For your obedience, by which you obeyed the Gospel when you came to the faith, has been proclaimed in every place within your sphere of influence. This is what he said at the beginning of this Epistle: “I give thanks to my God, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. I).

Therefore I rejoice in you, O Romans, because you believed as I did. But I want you to be wise in what is good, so that whatever you know and understand, you may strive to fulfill entirely in your works; but innocent in what is evil, so that you may avoid and despise vices and everything that is evil.

This is like what he writes to the Corinthians, saying: “Be children in malice, but in understanding be mature” (I Cor. XIV); as though he were saying in other words: “Be wise in what is good by doing it; be ignorant of evil by avoiding it.” And thus what follows will be fulfilled in you:

[Col. 0506C] May the God of peace, because he loves peace and grants peace to his own, quickly crush Satan beneath your feet. “Satan” is interpreted in our language as “adversary,” and in this passage it may signify the devil and Nero, who opposed Christians. We may also understand by this name every adversity that resists and opposes the soul striving toward God, which the Apostle prays may be crushed and subjected to their power.

May the God of peace, to whom peace is pleasing, crush what is contrary to peace and produces dissensions. When he says “beneath your feet,” this may be understood simply as “under your power,” or as referring to a short time and rapid action.

[Col. 0506D] Timothy, my fellow worker in preaching, greets you, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen. He calls Timothy his fellow worker and calls all of them kinsmen together.

Concerning Timothy, it is stated at greatest length in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XVI) that he was from Derbe, the son of a faithful widow by a Gentile father. The Apostle himself also says that he asked him to remain at Ephesus in order to warn certain people not to teach differently or to give heed to endless myths and genealogies.

Some say that Lucius was Luke himself, who wrote the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. For the blessed Apostle is not concerned with the peculiarities of names, since names are sometimes pronounced according to the declension of their native language and sometimes according to Greek or Roman usage. Jason is the same person mentioned in the book of the Acts of the Apostles. Sosipater was the son of Pyrrhus of Beroea.

[Col. 0507A] Gaius, my host, greets you. This is Gaius, his fellow prisoner, who was baptized by the Apostle, as he says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “I give thanks to God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius” (I Cor. I).

I, Tertius, who wrote this Epistle in the Lord, greet you. Tertius is the proper name of the believing scribe who wrote this Epistle at the Apostle’s dictation. The Apostle allowed him to greet the Roman people in his own name. He is called Tertius as a name, not as a number.

[Col. 0507B] Erastus, the treasurer of the city, greets you. Erastus was the treasurer of the city of the Corinthians, that is, the chief official or administrator who presided over the treasury where the king’s taxes, tributes, and revenues were deposited. The addition, “and Quartus, the brother,” contains a proper name, just as does “Tertius.”

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen. Grace is called something freely given. By the name “grace” we ought to understand whatever good things the elect freely receive from God: faith, hope, charity, and the forgiveness of sins.

[Col. 0507C] To him be honor forever and ever, who is able to establish you in perfect faith and in every good thing, according to my Gospel—that is, so that you may be established as the Gospel that I preach admonishes, and so that nothing may be lacking to you from it.

When he adds “and the preaching of Jesus Christ,” this is the same as the Gospel, because Christ preached it, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent in eternal times, that is, hidden. By “eternal times,” understand the immeasurable ages that preceded the beginning of the world. From the beginning of the world, once man had been created, the mystery of the holy Trinity and the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and other such matters could be revealed; but the almighty Father did not wish so venerable a mystery to become known except to a few, especially since man, neglecting God, had surrendered himself entirely to the devil.

Therefore, from the eternal times that preceded the creation of the world—or, so to speak, from the time when the world began to exist—the mystery of the holy Trinity was silent and hidden. Now, at the advent of Christ, it has been disclosed by Christ himself through the writings of the prophets, who at times prophesied about that mystery in clear words and at times in obscure ones. For example, Moses said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (Gen. I).

[Col. 0508A] Behold the Trinity, though it was understood by only a few. What does Christ say? “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from my Father” (John XV); and elsewhere: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

The prophet Isaiah also spoke of his birth: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII). Christ was born of a virgin, and he disclosed the mystery contained in prophetic Scripture. The same prophet also speaks of his burial: “His tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. XI). Christ was buried, and the mystery that had been hidden was disclosed.

What more is there to say? Rising from the dead, he opened the understanding of the disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. Once these had been understood and recognized, they realized that the mystery had now been fulfilled and made manifest, whereas previously it had been hidden.

[Col. 0508B] For when the mysteries concerning Christ’s conception, birth, death, and ascension, together with the other prophetic announcements, agreed and were fulfilled in him, no doubt remained that the mystery hidden for ages and eternal times had been disclosed through the prophets.

According to the command of the eternal God—because the Son of God, who is of one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit, commanded, saying: “Go into the world; preach the Gospel to every creature, and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—for the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles, that is, so that all the Gentiles might obey his faith and his Gospel.

Therefore, when he said, “To him be honor and glory forever,” he wished to make this clear, adding:

To the only wise God, known through Jesus Christ, [Col. 0508C] that is, to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are of one substance and who in the Trinity are one God. He said “known through Jesus Christ” because through him God the Father and the Holy Spirit were known and manifested—namely, the mystery of the Trinity.

God is called wise not accidentally or by an accidental gift, as Solomon or some other human being is, but essentially he is called wise and is wise, because for him being is nothing other than being wise, nor is being wise anything other than being.

The end of this Epistle is clearer in the Greek, in which the Epistle was written. For when he says “to him be honor and glory,” and afterward adds “to whom,” although the preceding “to him be glory” would have been sufficient, he uses an unusual form of our speech. In saying “forever and ever,” he follows the usage of sacred Scripture and wishes thereby to designate the immeasurability of time. It is as though he were saying: “In all future ages, let honor and glory be given to almighty God.”

He added “Amen”—which is an oath or affirmation in the Hebrew language and means “true” in Latin—in order to confirm that everything written by him throughout the text of this Epistle is true.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0507]

## ARGUMENT

Admonished by the command of the Lord Savior, the Apostle Paul came to Corinth, the metropolitan city of Achaia, a province of the Greeks. He remained there for a full year and six months, and preached the Gospel there steadfastly, so much so that he converted almost all the inhabitants of that city to the faith of Christ.

But after he departed from them, many of them were led astray by Jews and false apostles. When the Apostle heard this, he wrote this Epistle to them from Ephesus and sent it through Timothy, wishing to recall them to the faith of Christ, from which they had withdrawn for a time, and to strengthen the rest.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God—understand: of the Father. Concerning the name Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans, insofar as we have been able to learn more accurately, we endeavored to speak with the authority of the teachers, and also concerning how he himself was called an apostle.

In saying “called an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God the Father,” he shows that the Father and the Son have one will. For just as the Father and the Son are of one substance, one majesty, and one power, so they exist with one will; and those who are called by the Son are called by the Father. Just as Paul was called through the Son, so he was made an apostle—that is, a messenger and ambassador—by God the Father, because he carried out the embassy of the Gospel.

By these words he strikes at the false apostles, as well as the Jews, who said that he had not been called an apostle by God.

[Col. 0509B] And Sosthenes, a brother in faith and in preaching, though not an apostle. Why did the Apostle insert the names of his disciples in his Epistles? For two reasons: either so that they might possess greater authority, in accordance with what the Lord said, “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII), lest anyone say that these things had been devised through the falsehood of one man; or so that he might fulfill what he himself taught, saying in one place: “If something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (I Cor. XIV).

For when he dictated his Epistles, his disciples were present; and if something else or something different had perhaps been revealed to one of them through the Holy Spirit than what he was saying—for the same Holy Spirit was in the disciples as in the teacher—he arranged it in the order given by that disciple, the good teacher not begrudging his disciples. Moreover, he placed that disciple’s name with his own at the beginning, because the disciple had some part in the matter.

[Col. 0509C] To the Church of God that is at Corinth. He writes generally to the whole Church, that is, to the multitude of the Corinthians, because they did not yet have a bishop to whom he might write in particular.

Sanctified in Christ Jesus, that is, through faith in Christ Jesus, through his passion, and through the water of baptism. Called saints. The Corinthians were not called to Christ through Paul because they were already holy, but so that they might be sanctified and live holy lives.

With all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. It belongs to priests to call upon the Lord for the salvation of the people, as is said of them in the Old Testament: “You shall invoke my name, and I will bless them” (Num. VI). And in the Psalm: “Moses and Aaron among his priests; Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

This may be understood in two ways: “with all,” understand, the priests who call upon the name of the Lord; or “with all believing Jews who live among them,” that is, with all those who live among them, in every place belonging to them and to us, understand, “we wish you salvation.” In every place belonging to them and to us, that is, wherever they may be, among them and among us, we wish them salvation.

Grace be with you—that is, faith, the forgiveness of sins, and peace, through which we are reconciled to God the Father through the passion of Christ—from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The person of the Holy Spirit is understood in his gifts, namely, in the forgiveness of sins and peace, because the Lord promised his disciples, saying: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Luke III).

I give thanks to my God—that is, I offer thanks or praise to my God—always for you. When the Apostle says, “I give thanks to God,” that is, “praise,” he did not add “my” without reason.
