Although by nature and power there is one God of all creatures, since he is the Creator of them all, nevertheless he is properly called the God of those who are proved to be his worshipers by the merit of their faith and righteousness, as were blessed Paul and the other apostles. Hence it is said: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus III), by grace and the merit of life.

But why does he say that he always gives thanks to God for their salvation, when no human being can always remain intent upon prayers or acts of thanksgiving? For, as we read in the writings of the Fathers, the Apostle devoted himself to manual labor from the first hour until the fifth; from the fifth hour until the tenth he devoted himself to preaching; after the tenth he again cared for the hospitality of the poor and strangers and for the needs of his own body; but during the night he applied himself most earnestly to prayer. Therefore, because of the great constancy with which, day and night, he offered thanks to God both for the Corinthians and for all those whom he had acquired for Christ, he said that he always gave thanks to God for them.

“In the grace of God”—understand, “of the Father”—that is, for the forgiveness of sins, which has been given to you—understand, freely by God the Father—in Christ Jesus, that is, through faith in Christ Jesus. For God the Father grants his grace, that is, the forgiveness of sins, only to those whom he truly knows to believe in his Son; it is called grace because it is freely given. Nor is it without reason that the forgiveness of sins and faith are called the grace of God, since whatever gifts we possess are God’s grace, because they are freely bestowed upon us without any preceding merits. [Col. 0510D]

For in all things you have been enriched in him, that is, in Christ. In what things had they become rich? In faith, in teaching, in diversity of languages, and in the effectiveness of miracles. These are the spiritual riches with which the elect are enriched.

“In every word,” that is, in the teaching of the New Testament; “and in all knowledge”—understand, of the Old and New Testaments—or, to put it another way, in all wisdom and knowledge, whether in the understanding of the Old and New Testaments.

Just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you. He calls the Gospel the “testimony of Christ,” because in it are related the testimonies of Christ’s birth, his miracles, his passion, resurrection, [Col. 0511A] ascension into heaven, and coming to judgment. Christ foretold these testimonies before his passion and confirmed them all in his death. Let us examine one testimony among many and consider how he foretold it and how he confirmed it. Long before his passion he said to the disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled,” and so forth, until he says, “and on the third day he will rise again” (Luke XVIII). Thus everything was fulfilled when he came to Jerusalem: he was handed over to the Gentiles, namely to Pilate, mocked by his soldiers, killed, and rose again on the third day.

Hence the Apostle says: “Just as the testimony of Christ”—that is, the Gospel—“was confirmed in you,” that is, was believed by you and confirmed in your hearts, because you believe all the things contained in it to be true. Thus you lack nothing in any grace, that is, neither in faith, nor in teaching, nor in diversity of languages, nor in the power of miracles.

A question arises here. If the Corinthians had been enriched in every word and in all knowledge, and if they had been so filled with grace that they lacked no grace, as is said below, why does the Apostle later in this letter say that they were contentious, and even add, “I say this to your shame”? The matter is resolved in this way. Just as in all churches there are two kinds of people, namely good and bad, so it was at that time among the Corinthians. The Apostle therefore began with praise and thanksgiving, addressing those who were perfect in faith [Col. 0511C] and good works and abounding in spiritual riches, so that they might always advance toward what was better. Afterwards he began forcefully to rebuke those who were erring in faith and sowing dissensions. He acted like a most skilled physician who, seeing that a wound must be cut but recognizing that the patient is fearful, spends a long time touching healthy limbs and then suddenly strikes; or like a ram, which first walks with its head lowered but afterwards strikes forcefully. First he praised the good, and then he struck the wicked.

For timid minds, unless they are reproved with a gentle touch, so that they hear from other matters something they can take as consolation, immediately fall into despair under harsh correction.

Awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Revelation means manifestation. Christ, therefore, is now hidden in a certain sense and does not appear, because he is seen by us only with the mind. But he will be seen on the day of judgment, when he manifests himself to all human beings, both elect and reprobate, as Scripture says—or rather, as the Prophet says through Scripture: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Then he will give the elect the glory he promised them and life that will endure without end. Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “You have died to sin, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III), because you will be like the angels of God in heaven. And what is greater: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III). [Col. 0512A]

He also will confirm you—that is, strengthen you in his faith and in good works—unto the end, that is, until the day of your death, or until the day of judgment, without accusation. He does not say “without sin,” but “without accusation,” that is, without mortal sin, which separates one from the kingdom of heaven. For there is no human being on earth who does good and does not sin, whether in word or in thought. Hence John also says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

When he says, “He will confirm you unto the end,” he explains this by adding: “On the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ,” when he will come to repay each according to his works. There are two callings. One takes place for individual human beings when, called by the Lord, they pass from this life through bodily death. The other will be general on the day of judgment, when all, both good and evil, will be called to judgment. Those whom almighty God finds laboring well in this first calling, he will certainly not call in the second in order to condemn them with the reprobate, who will hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire,” but rather in order to reward them with the elect, to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV). In all things he will appear truthful, as what follows will make clear.

God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son Jesus Christ. The Father is called faithful because he is truthful and fulfills his word. He promised Abraham that he would give him the land of his wandering, [Col. 0512C] and that all nations would be blessed in his seed, that is, in Christ; and he fulfilled this, as we now see. Through his Son he promised us the kingdom of heaven; he will certainly prove truthful, because he will give it to us if we remain in his faith.

Here, according to Ambrose, we should understand “fellowship” as brotherhood. “God the Father,” he says, “is faithful and truthful; he will give all the good things of the heavenly homeland. Through him you were called into fellowship, that is, into the brotherhood, of his Son Jesus Christ, so that we might be brothers of Jesus Christ and his sons—not by nature, but by adoption.” Through his Son he called us to his faith, so that he might be our Father and we might be brothers of his Son. Whoever truly believes in God and obeys his will is certainly a brother of our Lord Jesus Christ, not by nature but by the grace of adoption, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew VII); and to the women after the resurrection: “Go,” he says, “announce to my brothers” (Matthew XXVIII).

But I appeal to you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you. Until now he has praised those who have remained truly in the faith; from this point onward he begins to rebuke those who were sowing divisions—called schisms in Greek—saying that they were rather the sons of the human beings by whom they had been baptized, as what follows makes clear. Therefore the Apostle says to them: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of the Lord the Savior, through whom you have been saved, that you all say the same thing”—understand, the thing I said above: that you are sons of God—not calling yourselves the sons of some human being, but of God. Be perfect, however, in the same understanding and in the same knowledge, which are one thing; that is, remain in the same understanding that you received from me, and say that you are sons of God, as you used to say when I was departing from you in heart.

For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you. Chloe is a place, and the meaning is as though he were saying: “by those who are from Antioch,” or something similar.

I belong to Paul—understand, “I am his son,” or “I was baptized with his baptism.” After the Apostle’s departure, heretics arose among the Corinthians, especially those Jews who were believers from the circumcision. Whomever they baptized, they claimed as their own sons, baptizing them in their own name; and those who were baptized by them rejoiced to be called the sons of those by whom they had been baptized. The believers who held to the Apostle’s faith and teaching, however, said: “I belong to Christ,” which they rightly said, because this is how it should be said.

Something similar happened at a certain time when Donatus and Novatian arose, heretics who expelled from the Church all whom they could and baptized them again, claiming them as their sons. Those baptized by them rejoiced to be called Donatists and Novatians. When the Apostle learned that such things were taking place among the Corinthians, [Col. 0513C] he wrote to them what is said here, exposing their error but not disclosing the names of its authors. He preferred to transfer the matter to his own person and that of other faithful teachers rather than expose them, lest they become worse.

For if things were as they wished—so that everyone belonged as a son to the person by whom he was baptized, as though baptized with that person’s baptism—then there would be as many baptisms as there were baptizers, whereas there is one baptism of Christ, just as there is one God and one faith. The Lord Jesus gave his faithful ministers the ministry of immersing bodies, but he granted no one the grace of baptizing, that is, of forgiving sins; he retained this properly for himself, as John says of him to the crowds (John I): “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” And again: “I,” John says, “did not know him,” that is, “I did not know that he would reserve for himself the power of baptizing. But the one who sent me to baptize,” namely God the Father, “said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’”

Christ therefore retained the power of baptizing for himself to such an extent that, just as all sins are forgiven to the person who is immersed in water by a holy and innocent man, so also they are forgiven to the person for whom this is done in the name of the holy Trinity by a sinful and wicked man. The merit of the life of the baptizer or minister neither benefits nor harms the one who is baptized in this matter.

Is Christ divided? Understand: “if things are as you say.” This should not be read affirmatively or interrogatively, but with the voice left suspended. Christ is said in a certain sense to be divided when heretics among themselves permit the honor and glory that he himself properly retained to be divided, by dividing his baptism. Heretics likewise divided Christ when some said that he did not possess a true body, like the Manichaeans; some that he did not possess a soul, like the Apollinarists; and some that he was lesser than the Father, like Arius.

Was Paul crucified for you? Understand: “No.” The meaning is: you ought to be baptized in the name of the one who was crucified for you, and you ought to believe that you can be saved through the baptism of the one who was crucified for you.

Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? Here the Apostle puts himself forward on behalf of all those in whose name they claimed to have been baptized. He therefore began with himself, lest those heretics perhaps say: “Paul forbids such things for this reason: lest anyone say that he was baptized with our baptism and is our son; he is claiming all the honor for himself.”

I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, who were the firstfruits of Achaia. Paul baptized as a minister, not as the power itself. For this reason he rejoiced that he had not baptized many of them: since error had begun to arise over this matter, if he had baptized many, the error would have been increased all the more in his name, and they would have said: “I belong to Paul.”

I baptized also the household of Stephanas. Stephanas was a noble matron whose household the Apostle baptized. Whether he baptized her herself, however, or whether she remained in unbelief, is unknown.

For Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize. The Apostle was chosen more to evangelize than to baptize, because evangelizing is the greater task than baptizing. For everyone who evangelizes can also baptize, but not everyone who baptizes is qualified to evangelize. In a bishop there is the dignity of all the orders. For he is the head of the other members, and the Apostle, who was a pontiff, possessed all the ecclesiastical ranks. Therefore he could both baptize and evangelize, but he devoted himself especially to preaching, as did the other apostles.

His disciples, however, baptized, as we read (Acts X): when Peter came to the house of Cornelius, after the Holy Spirit fell upon his entire household, Peter instructed them to be baptized by his disciples. In the beginning of the faith everyone baptized, not only men but also women whenever necessity required it. But, so that such a great ministry would not be dishonored or improperly carried out by simpler people, as the number of believers increased throughout all the cities and villages, the holy Fathers decreed that only bishops and presbyters should baptize, and, in case of necessity, deacons.

Not in wisdom of speech—understand, “Christ sent me to evangelize”—so that the cross of Christ would not be emptied, that is, so that the passion of the crucified Christ would not be annihilated. Heretics and philosophers preached in the wisdom of speech, that is, in cultivated and polished language, so as to please their hearers and appear learned themselves. Or they preached in the wisdom of speech because they did not preach those things that the world—that is, lovers of this world—and the philosophers of human wisdom consider foolish.

For example, they did not preach Christ’s birth from a Virgin, his death, and his resurrection, all of which they denied, saying that nothing could be born except through the commingling of another seed; and that God, who is spirit, had not become man, nor could the Son of God have died, but that when he wished he appeared and when he did not wish it he withdrew, nor did he rise again because he had not died. Because philosophers and heretics could not penetrate all these things through human wisdom, they said that they were false and annihilated the passion of Christ.

But the Apostle preached in simple words that Christ had been born of a Virgin, had died, and had risen again, so that his hearers could understand what he was saying. For whoever wishes to adorn the faith of Christ with words seeks not the glory of God but his own. [Col. 0515B]

For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God. What does he mean by “the word of the cross”? Since the cross is an inanimate and insensible thing, how can it speak the word of God? By “the word of the cross” he means the Gospel and the preaching of Christ crucified. To those who remain in unbelief and do not understand the power and wisdom of God, it is foolishness to say that the Son of God was crucified. But to those who believe and hold the faith that they have been redeemed through his passion, that very passion is the power of God, because through it they deserve to be saved.

For it is written in Isaiah (Isaiah XXIX): “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.” Now he destroys or rejects the wisdom that God himself gives, but the human wisdom that people devise for themselves, namely dialectic and the other arts through which they hope to be wise, he reduces to nothing by God’s permission and shows to be foolish.

Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? This concerns the wise men of the Jews, namely the scribes and Pharisees. Where is the investigator or searcher of this world? This concerns the philosophers of the Gentiles, who searched into wisdom and other hidden and obscure matters, into the natures of creatures, and especially the astrologers, who said that everything done on earth depended upon the course and regulation of the twelve signs, as well as of the sun, moon, and five planets, and that God did not care about what happened on earth, whether concerning human beings or living creatures.

Of these, then, the Apostle says: “Where now are the wise men and scribes of the Jews? And where are the philosophers and astrologers of the Gentiles?” They have no place in the Church.

Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish? That is: has he not made it so, that is, demonstrated the wisdom of the lovers of the world and their philosophy to be foolish, by accomplishing in deed what they denied? They denied that anything could be born except through the commingling of male and female. Almighty God, however, showed their wisdom to be false by causing his Son to be born of a virgin. Likewise, he raised him from the dead, although they denied the resurrection.

For since the world—that is, the lovers of the world and the philosophers—did not know God the Father through its worldly wisdom, it pleased God—understand, the Father—through the foolishness of preaching, that is, through the preaching of the Gospel, which they called foolishness, to save those who believe.

The meaning is this: because the wise men of this age, trusting in their human wisdom, did not wish to believe in Christ, who is the wisdom of God, nor through him did they wish to know God the Father; or because they did not wish to believe that the things contained in the wisdom of God—that is, in the Gospel—were true, God permitted them to perish in their unbelief. It pleased him, through the preaching that they considered foolishness, to save those who wished to believe. [Col. 0516B]

For the Jews ask for signs. Because they believe that all things are possible for God, they always ask for signs, asking how the matter under discussion came about. Abraham did this when he said to God (Genesis XV): “By what shall I know that you will give me this land as a possession?” Gideon and many others did likewise. And the Greeks ask for wisdom—understand, human wisdom—which means philosophy. Since the seven liberal arts flourished especially among them, they regarded the simple teaching of the faithful as worthless.

But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, that is, a quarrel and contention; to the Gentiles foolishness. When the apostles preached the mysteries of the Son of God’s humanity—how he was [Col. 0516C] born of a Virgin, how he performed many miracles, how the Jews crucified Christ though he was innocent, and how, rising again, he ascended into heaven—the Jews were scandalized, that is, they quarreled and contended, saying that it could in no way be true that a virgin had given birth or that they had killed the Son of God. They said instead that he was some great man, and that the things reported in the Gospel concerning his resurrection and ascension had been invented by his disciples; they denied all of these things to be true.

Among other things they say: “Christ, whom you claim already to have come through a Virgin, has not yet come, because he was promised to us. Nor will he be born of a Virgin; rather, David will rise again, and he himself will be our Messiah.”

Likewise, it seemed foolish to the philosophers of the Gentiles that the Son of God, who is the author of life, should die for human beings. When they heard such things preached about Christ as worldly reason and philosophical wisdom could not penetrate, they were compelled to declare that it was foolishness. They said that a virgin could not give birth without a man’s seed and denied the resurrection.

But to those Jews who were called—understand, called to the faith of Christ—and to the Greeks, that is, to the Gentiles, who were likewise predestined to life and willing to believe, we preach Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Christ is the power of God the Father, because through him God the Father made all things. He is also his wisdom, which speaks through Solomon: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV). Concerning this wisdom the Psalmist says to God the Father: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm CIII), that is, through the Son.

He is rightly called the Wisdom and Word of the Father because through him God the Father manifested himself to human beings. For example, just as a human being manifests his will through his word, so the Son himself says in the Gospel: “Father, I have manifested your name to human beings” (John XVII).

For what is foolish of God—that is, what is thought foolish by human beings—is wiser than human beings; that is, it surpasses human wisdom. The meaning is this: what human beings consider foolish, namely that God the almighty Father should send his Son into the world to undergo suffering and endure death, surpasses all philosophical wisdom. Because they cannot penetrate it, they call it foolish and refuse to believe—not because it is truly foolish, but because it is wiser than all worldly wisdom.

And what is weak of God is stronger than human beings; that is, what they think and say is weak, namely that the Son of God could have died, is stronger than all human beings and than all the strength of giants. How so? Because the death that the giants could not escape was overcome by the weakness of Christ crucified. Therefore the weakness of God—which they call weakness—is not weakness, because the weakness of Christ is a great victory. For he overcame the devil; he overcame death.

Consider this, and test it among yourselves: your calling—understand, the calling by which you were called to the faith of Christ. For not many wise men were called by God to preach the faith and the Gospel, and so forth, up to what follows: “But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise.” That is, he chose fishermen, the poor, and the uneducated, whom the powerful of this age and the philosophers considered foolish and regarded as worthless.

And God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, that is, to show the philosophers and powerful of this age to be liars and make them ashamed. He calls the apostles the weak things of the world either because they appeared foolish to the wise men of this age and weak in worldly sense and understanding, or because of the weakness of the Son of God whom they preached.

Let us see how, through these weak things of the world, he showed the liars, the powerful, and the strong of this age to be false, and how he made them ashamed. While the apostles were preaching the mysteries of the humanity of the Son of God and the philosophers were contradicting everything as though it were false, the apostles ordered two dead men, or five, or even more, to be brought before them. When they raised them through invocation of the Son of God crucified, the philosophers and powerful of the world appeared to be liars and the apostles truthful.

And God chose the ignoble things of the world—that is, things without a name of dignity—and the contemptible things, that is, the despised things: namely, the apostles, who were held in contempt. And he chose the things that are not—understand, the same apostles, who seemed to the philosophers and powerful of this age to possess no dignity or usefulness—in order to destroy the things that are, that is, to empty the wisdom of those who seemed to themselves to be something.

And why he chose the weak things of the world rather than the strong, he partly makes clear when he adds: [Col. 0518A]

So that no flesh, that is, no human being, might glory in his presence. The wise and powerful cannot glory, because they were not called by him on account of their wisdom or riches; nor do they possess divine wisdom and spiritual riches. The apostles cannot glory because whatever they possess they received freely from God, without their own merits; nor can they glory that they were chosen on account of their wisdom and riches.

But from him you are in Christ Jesus. “From him”—that is, from God the Father—you are, because you were created by him. Or, “from him you are in Christ,” that is, it was brought about by God the Father that you should believe in Christ and be firm in the faith of Christ Jesus.

For the purpose and arrangement of God the Father was that through Christ we should know his truth and mercy. He—understand, Jesus Christ—was made for us wisdom by God the Father. We must not understand childishly that the Son of God, according to his divinity, was made, but that he was begotten by God the Father before all ages, although according to his humanity he was made in the Virgin’s womb through the work of the Holy Spirit.

Rather, it should be understood in this way: “He was made for us wisdom,” that is, he was made so that he might be wisdom for us and make us wise. Something similar is found in the Psalm: “The Lord was made for me a refuge” (Psalm XCIII), which means nothing other than: he was made so that we might have refuge in him.

And in the prophetic books: “The word of the Lord came to Joel and to Hosea,” that is, it came about that the Word of the Lord spoke to Joel. For the Word of the Lord was not made but begotten.

Let us put it another way: “He was made for us wisdom by God the Father,” that is, he who was begotten before all ages was made human, so that he might make us wise. In the same way he was made for us righteousness, because he justifies us; sanctification, because he makes us holy and sanctifies us through baptism; and redemption, because he redeemed us with his blood.

And why was this done?

So that, as it is written—understand, in Jeremiah—“Let the one who glories glory in the Lord.” He glories in the Lord, and not in himself, who acknowledges that every good thing he possesses has been produced by God, without his own merit. Therefore he does not seek his own glory and praise, but that of the one from whom he received whatever he possesses.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0518D]

And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not in loftiness of speech, that is, in eloquence of expression or worldly wisdom, because I preached nothing to you through human wisdom in polished language, but announcing to you the testimony of Christ. The testimony of Christ is the Gospel, because it contains the testimonies of his incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and coming to judgment.

For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. This means nothing other than: “I preached nothing else to you except Jesus Christ crucified.”

A question arises here. Since he says later: “For I delivered to you first what I also received: that Christ died for our sins, and that he rose on the third day,” speaking of the mysteries of his humanity, why does he now say that he preached nothing else except Jesus Christ crucified, that is, his passion?

The matter is resolved in this way: by saying “Christ Jesus crucified,” he includes all the mysteries pertaining to Christ’s humanity. For the one who is crucified is the one who was first born; the one who dies is the one who is crucified; the one who is buried is the one who dies; the one who rises is the one who had died. It is as though he were saying in other words: “Because you were not capable of grasping the higher mysteries of Christ’s divinity, although there was much wisdom in me, I judged, determined, and resolved in my mind to preach to you only those mysteries that pertain to the humanity of Jesus Christ and that you were able to penetrate.” [Col. 0519B]

And I was with you in weakness—understand, of body—and in fear of mind and much trembling of the limbs, O Corinthians! Perhaps, when the Apostle came to Corinth, he was weakened in body and feared greatly that, while in this state of weakness, he might be killed by the pseudo-apostles, to whom he preached contrary doctrines. He also feared that the Corinthians, deceived by those pseudo-apostles, might depart from the soundness of the faith they had received from him.

Or, alternatively, he was with them in weakness of understanding, because his wisdom appeared in a certain sense weak when, on account of the weakness and slowness of understanding of his hearers, it was not fully disclosed. He was also in fear and trembling, fearing that he might be killed—as we have said—by heretics and pseudo-apostles. [Col. 0519C]

My speech and my preaching—understand, “were”—not in persuasive words of human wisdom; that is, I did not preach Christ to you in philosophical or polished speech in order to deceive and mislead you through obscure language, as philosophers do. Rather, I preached in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that is, in the display of miracles. Through the power of the Holy Spirit I performed these miracles and confirmed my judgment or preaching, because I strengthened by miracles what I taught and preached in words and showed it to be true—something your philosophers and pseudo-apostles could not do.

I did this so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of human beings, that is, in merely human wisdom, but might be proved in the power of God, namely, in the power [Col. 0519D] of miracles.

We speak divine wisdom among those who are perfect in faith and understanding, who are able to receive it. Here he calls the apostles and other believers who had advanced so far in faith that they were companions and assistants in the ministry of preaching “perfect,” as were Timothy, Titus, Sosthenes, and many others at various times.

The meaning is this: “We do indeed possess divine wisdom, but you cannot receive it, nor could you at that time, because you are still shown to be infants in understanding.”

But we do not speak the wisdom of this age, that is, worldly wisdom, which the lovers of this age employ; nor do we speak the wisdom of the rulers of this age, that is, of the philosophers, who are being destroyed. [Col. 0520A]

How are the philosophers and powerful of this age destroyed? Through bodily death they are reduced to dust, and their wisdom is destroyed or annihilated. Plato and Aristotle were destroyed by death, and their wisdom is regarded as worthless in the Church. Or they and their wisdom were also being destroyed when God almighty, through the apostles, showed to be true what they, taught by human wisdom, said could in no way happen.

For example, they denied that the Son of God had been born of a virgin without a man’s seed, since human nature did not allow this. When the apostles raised the dead through invocation of that same Son of God, their wisdom was emptied and destroyed, and they themselves were considered foolish.

If, then, the apostles did not speak human wisdom, what did they preach? The Apostle explains this:

But we speak, he says, the wisdom of God, which is hidden in a mystery, that is, in obscurity of understanding. Here “wisdom” can be understood in two ways: namely, as the Gospel of Christ, in which ineffable wisdom lies hidden; or, what is better, as substantial Wisdom, which is the Word of God the Father and which speaks through Wisdom: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV).

The apostles therefore spoke this Wisdom, because it was she who spoke through their mouths, and it was she whom they preached. But if she was hidden, how did they speak her? She was hidden from the philosophers and powerful of this age, but she had been manifested to them through herself. Hence what follows:

This wisdom—that is, Christ—God the Father predestined according to his humanity before the ages for our glory, that is, for our glorification, since we who have believed have been redeemed and cleansed from sins through him, so that we might yet deserve to be glorified.

Therefore, before all ages, God the Father predestined the human being to be assumed by the Word, so that he might be the true Son of God and so that we might be glorified through him. Hence the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power” (Romans I). It follows:

This wisdom none of the rulers of this age knew. The rulers of this age are to be understood in this passage in two ways. First, the rulers of this age—that is, Octavian, Tiberius, Herod, Pilate, the scribes and Pharisees, and the priests of the Jews—did not recognize that Christ was the Son of God. For when they saw that he was human, saw him grow tired, thirst, and hunger, they did not suppose that he was God. Hence Peter says: “I know, brothers, that you did this through ignorance, as did your rulers” (Acts 3).

What then? If through ignorance servants killed the Son of God, are the apostles therefore free from guilt? Far be it that no sin should be attributed to them, since through the works of miracles they could recognize the one who performed them: for unless he were the Son of God, he could by no means have done such things, which no one else had ever done before him. Hence he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, and had not done among them works such as no one else has done, they would not have the sin of unbelief” (John 15). And what follows? “Now,” he says, “they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15). Although they did not know that he was God, nevertheless, because they were committing an impious and unjust act by condemning an innocent man, they were not ignorant of that fact, and therefore they are held guilty.

In another way, we can understand the rulers of this age as the aerial powers, namely demons who move about through this air. Concerning them he says in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers of these darknesses, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6). Concerning their ruler the Lord says: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out,” and, “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has found nothing in me” (John 12; 14).

Although the evangelist Mark says of the demons, “They knew that he was Christ” (Mark 1), and the demons themselves, as though supplying the words, say, “We know that you are the Son of God,” nevertheless they could not truly believe that he was the Son of God when they saw him again, after performing miracles, become hungry, thirsty, and weary. They did know that he was the one promised in the Law, but they did not know that through him they would lose the authority which they held in this world, nor that he would possess such great power. For this reason the Apostle goes on to speak of both orders of rulers.

For if they had known—that is, if the rulers of this age had known—that he was the Son of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. The Lord of glory is the Word of God the Father, through whom God the Father is glorified, because through him he made all things.

But we must inquire with the greatest care: if the Word is the glory of God the Father, how could the Lord of glory, who is spirit, be crucified? Christ the Son of God consists of two substances, namely the divine and the human, in the unity of one person. Therefore, the divinity of the Word, which was begotten by God the Father before all ages, remained fully in the same man from the time of the conception of the man whom he assumed in the Virgin’s womb. The same glory and power that was in the Word began to dwell in the man, and that man himself became the glory of God the Father, just as God the Father says to him: “Arise, my glory, from the grave” (Psalm 56).

The man himself is not only the glory of God the Father, but is also God. For if the Word became flesh—that is, if God became man—then certainly man also became God. Yet this must be considered most carefully: although the Jews and the rulers of this age were persecuting God, he himself was crucified in the form of a servant, because he was the Lord of glory, while the divinity remained incapable of suffering.

Let us see in this some likeness. When the sun is shining brightly and a clear lamp pours out its light, its ray and radiance illuminate and suffuse a tree. If people then approach that same tree with axes to cut it down, do they, by raising and lowering their axes, cut the rays of the sun, even though they cut the tree? Certainly not. Just as the sun’s ray remains incapable of suffering, although it is always seen and moreover strikes the tree which it illuminates, so his divinity, which fills all things, remained incapable of suffering, although the one whom it filled endured suffering on the cross.

Much could be said on this subject, but these few remarks should suffice for us, who hold most firmly that if the demons had recognized Christ as the Son of God, who is the Lord of the glory of majesty, through whom God the Father is glorified, they would never have compelled the Jews and the Roman soldiers to crucify him. Those who urged his crucifixion themselves crucified him; and the Jewish rulers and soldiers would by no means have obeyed their urging in order to crucify him if they had truly believed that he was the Son of God.

But, as it is written in Isaiah: “What the eye of the body has not seen,” because it is neither body nor color; “nor the ear of the body has heard,” because it is not sound; “nor has it entered into the human heart”—that is, the heart, or understanding, of a human being ought to ascend there—“what God has prepared for those who love him,” that is, for those who do not offend him in heart, word, or deed.

But to us—the apostles and those who believe in him—God has revealed it through his Spirit, that is, through the Holy Spirit. He did not reveal it to the demons, nor to those who possess human wisdom. For the Holy Spirit, who is in us, searches all things, that is, investigates all secrets, not only the secrets of hearts but also the depths—namely, the mysteries of God—and his foreknowledge, because he is of one substance with the Father and the Son.

For who among human beings knows what is in a human being’s heart, except the human spirit that is in him? The implied answer is: no one. The meaning is this: just as no one knows what is in a human being except the human spirit that is in him, so no one has known what belongs to God except the Spirit of God, and the one to whom that same Holy Spirit deigns to reveal it.

But we—the apostles and believers—have not received the spirit of this world, that is, the spirit of divination and the Pythonic spirit, but the Spirit who is from God, that is, the Holy Spirit. And in the teaching of the Spirit we speak, that is, in simple speech; and, as the Holy Spirit teaches us inwardly, with the power of miracles, we compare spiritual mysteries with spiritual people who are able to penetrate what we say. This happens when divine mysteries are entrusted to those who are more receptive.

But the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God—that is, what grace the cross of Christ bestows upon believers. The natural person is one who does not have the Spirit of God. Although such a person differs from an animal by reason, he nevertheless does not use reason well, because he does not believe that anything exists after death but conducts himself according to the practice of animals. Therefore he is called “natural” (*animalis*) from *anima*, “soul,” and “carnal” (*carnalis*) from *caro*, “flesh,” because he consists entirely of soul and flesh.

For what he hears concerning the mysteries of God is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand it because it is examined spiritually, that is, investigated and judged. And because a person cannot understand what he hears and is unwilling to believe, he is judged and condemned by spiritual people.

The philosophers who possessed worldly wisdom, and the heretics living at Corinth, so that they might more easily pervert the minds of their hearers and make them fall away from the state of uprightness, polished their perverse doctrines with respectable language. For this reason he said a little earlier: “We do not speak in words taught by human wisdom.” They said in refined language that human nature could not accept that the incomprehensible and incorporeal God could become man; that it was not credible that a virgin could conceive a man without male seed, or remain a virgin after childbirth; that it could not happen that a man should rise after death from the dust of the earth; and they presented other claims in the most brilliant language. They said that it was foolish to believe these things because they themselves were unable to penetrate them through human wisdom.

But the spiritual person judges all things, that is, distinguishes and tests everything that he hears, sees, and thinks: what is true and false, what is good and evil. He recognizes that what we preach is true, and he also distinguishes all the classes of carnal people. But he himself is judged by no one, that is, neither by spiritual people like himself nor by God is he condemned or reproved.

“For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has instructed him?” That is: which human being can understand and penetrate the Lord’s understanding and wisdom, by which he made all things? Who, the implied subject being a human being, could instruct, teach, or correct the Lord himself and say: “You did not do this or that well; you ought to correct this in such a way and improve that in such a way”? The implied answer is: no one.

Indeed, if he recognizes that all things were made by him, he will magnify and praise the Lord’s mind and understanding and power, saying that he made everything wisely. But we have the mind of Christ, that is, we have Christ’s understanding, and, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, who knows all things with the Father and the Son, we perceive true things concerning him. The meaning is this: because no one can penetrate the understanding and wisdom of God unless God himself grants it, no one ought to doubt that what we say concerning Christ’s birth and humanity is true, because we have the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER III

And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, because your understanding was hindered by its slowness, not by mine.

For you were not yet able—the implied object is, to grasp the mystery of Christ’s divinity. So that they would not say, “Now we can,” he added: “Indeed, even now you cannot.” In the future, however, by God’s gift, you will be able. Therefore, because you could not grasp it, I add: “I gave you milk to drink, not food,” that is, simple teaching about Christ’s humanity, not solid food about Christ’s divinity and the mystery of the Trinity.

For since there is jealousy and contention among you—jealousy, that is, envy, and contention concerning various baptisms—

When one says, “I have been baptized with the baptism of Paul, and I am his son,” while another says, “I belong to Apollos,” are you not human beings? That is: are you not carnal in your understanding? He uses the names of faithful apostles in place of false ones for the reason mentioned above.

What is Apollos? And what is Paul? The implied answer is: nothing in themselves in comparison with Christ. And he himself explains what they are:

“Ministers,” he says, “of the one in whom you have believed.” Therefore we cannot forgive sins in baptism, a power which Christ properly reserved for himself. He ministers who preaches rightly, and he ministers to each person as is fitting, just as the Lord gave him his ministry.

I planted, by preaching faith to you; Apollos watered, that is, baptized and immersed bodies; but God gave the growth—that is, the increase—to me who preached and to Apollos who watered. For I preached faith outwardly; God established it in the hearts of those who heard and multiplied the number of believers. Apollos immersed bodies, but God forgave sins. God has everything from himself and through himself; we, however, have everything both from him and through him.

Therefore neither the one who plants—that is, preaches—nor the one who waters—that is, baptizes—is anything in comparison with God, because he cannot infuse faith or forgive sins unless God gives his help.

But the one who plants and the one who waters are one, that is, they are ministers and servants of one God and are of one nature. This man and that man are two in person, but one in nature and in office. Each will receive his own reward according to his labor, that is, the one who preaches will receive the greater reward, and the one who baptizes the lesser. The same is understood of all human beings, because each will receive the measure of his gift according to the quality of his labor.

For we are God’s fellow workers. In Greek it is better expressed: “We are participants in God’s work.” God works faith through preaching and removes sins in baptism; those who preach and immerse the bodies of the baptized are participants in and helpers of this work.

You are God’s agriculture. The field here is the world, that is, its inhabitants, whose hearts he cultivates through his preachers. For just as a field is cultivated by its farmer with a plow and mattock, so the hearts of hearers are cultivated by the plow of preaching, so that they may receive the seed of faith and preaching and produce the fruit of good works.

You are God’s building, because he himself builds you in his faith through our preaching, so that you may retain him in your heart.

According to the grace of God, that is, according to the wisdom given to me above all the apostles, I laid a foundation as a wise architect. An architect is called the chief person in the construction of a house. A wise architect is one who imitates the will and authority of the one by whom he was instructed, as Paul did by imitating Christ’s teaching, preaching nothing other than what he received from him and saw in his mind.

Or, a wise architect is one who does not place his foundation upon sand, lest it be weak, nor upon empty ground. Similarly, Paul, as a wise architect, laid a foundation because he himself first preached to the Corinthians. No one before him had laid the foundation of faith in them. But let another—whether a good or bad builder or worker—take care and consider what he builds upon it, so that the walls, that is, good works, may proceed according to the strength of the faith or foundation.

For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. Here he calls the faith of Christ Jesus the foundation, and compares it to a good foundation. Just as the foundation is first laid in a house and afterward the walls are raised, so faith must first be established in the hearts of hearers, and afterward good works must appear as they rise.

And just as a house without a foundation, or with a weak and unsolid foundation, cannot stand without collapsing when struck by winds and rains, so works cannot be good or acceptable to God without perfect faith, because without faith it is impossible to please God. And just as a house with a firm foundation remains unmoved, so whoever possesses true and most sincere faith will remain firm amid the adversities and prosperities of this age, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Romans 1).

But just as a foundation without the structure of walls is of no use, so whoever appears to have faith without works will not therefore be considered perfect, because “faith without works is dead” (James 2). Therefore faith must be adorned with good works, so that what we believe in our hearts we may confess with our mouths, and by pursuing good works we may strive to embellish it.

Therefore no philosopher, no pseudo-apostle, and no heretic can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. For no one can preach another God than the one whom we preach, nor another faith than the one which we announce and which is in your hearts, namely, the faith of Christ Jesus.

He rightly says that Christ Jesus is the foundation, because whoever has his faith certainly has Christ himself dwelling in his heart. Therefore no one can lay another foundation in the hearts of the faithful than the foundation of the faith of Christ. For if someone begins to preach another faith, it will not be received by the faithful; and if anyone accepts that person’s teaching and error, it will no longer be a foundation but rather the destruction of the house.

But if anyone builds upon this foundation—that is, upon the faith of Christ—gold, that is, holy doctrine and right understanding; silver, that is, divine utterances, concerning which the Psalmist says, “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Psalm 11); and precious stones, that is, various kinds of virtues—for just as good stones are not dissolved by fire, so those virtues endure eternally and will not be consumed by the fire of the day of judgment—

But if anyone builds upon it wood, hay, and straw, that is, perverse doctrine and evil works, each person’s work will become manifest on the day of judgment.

Thus, just as by gold we understand perfect understanding, by silver incorrupt utterances, and by precious stones, which are not melted by fire, virtues, so by wood, hay, and straw we can understand perverse doctrine and evil action.

Alternatively, by gold, silver, and precious stones we can understand good works and distinguished virtues; by hay, wood, and straw, however, lesser sins, such as idle speech, disgraceful laughter, and other things of this kind. The holy teachers also add lead, iron, and tin: these signify grave and monstrous sins, which separate people from the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, just as gold, silver, and precious stones are tested by fire and yet are not consumed, so on the day of judgment those who have good works and good preaching, although they pass through fire, will suffer no punishment or injury. Those, however, who have lesser sins will be purified as they pass through fire, because there they will be consumed like hay or straw, or burned like wood by fire. Yet they themselves will not remain in the fire; once cleansed and tested, they will ascend to the Lord.

But those who have grave sins, which separate them from the kingdom of heaven and which the Apostle mentions elsewhere, saying “adultery, fornication, and murder,” and other things of this kind—just as iron, lead, or tin are melted but do not disappear in the fire—so those weighed down by the burden of sins will remain in the fire and suffer punishments that do not cease.

For the day of the Lord will make everything manifest, that is, the day of the Lord’s judgment and vengeance will reveal all human works, because the day itself will be revealed in fire, that is, it will be demonstrated together with fire.

The teachers transmit that as much space as the water occupied in the flood—which rose above all the mountains and, as the philosophers determine, reached as far as the circle of the moon—so much space the fire will occupy on the day of judgment. In it the elect will be tested like gold, while the lesser sins of some will be consumed and the impious will remain there.

Blessed Ephraem says that such terror will seize everyone on that day, both good and evil, when they see hell burning and the Lord Jesus coming in majesty and glory to judgment, that, if they had not already been made immortal, they would die again. By this fear even the lesser sins of the saints will be cleansed, as it is said: “When they see, the angels will be cleansed.” Here “angels” means the elect. And that fire will test each person’s work, whether it is good or evil.

If anyone’s work remains which he built upon the foundation of faith, he will receive the reward of eternal recompense. He is speaking here of those who build good works upon the foundation of faith, works signified by gold and stones, or silver. These will remain because they will not be consumed by fire but rather tested, just as gold is tested.

If anyone’s work burns in the fire—if he has lesser sins, which will be consumed like straw—he will suffer loss, that is, he will endure punishments while those sins begin to be tested and consumed. Although he himself will perish, as the following words show, “He himself will be saved”—yet as though passing through fire, the implied sense being that he passes through it and is purified and cleansed by the fire.

For in this life too the elect are tested by adversities and weaknesses like gold and silver by fire, as were the three youths, the holy martyrs, and also blessed Job. Those who draw lesser sins upon themselves are purified from them as they are burned by tribulations in this age, or after death in purgatorial fire, or by some other affliction, and are cleansed by the prayers of human beings. Nevertheless, what they have had only with unlawful love, they will certainly not lose without burning pain.

Those who heap up lead for themselves often begin to suffer torment in this age and to experience in part what they will suffer more fully in the future.

Do you not know that you are God’s temple? That is, the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. And that the Spirit of God dwells in you? From the time of baptism the Holy Spirit begins to dwell in us, and all angels and all the righteous are his temple.

But if anyone violates God’s temple—that is, if anyone harms himself by sinning, or others through perverse doctrine, like the pseudo-apostles, or anyone at all through his evil example—God will destroy him from the number of his faithful and from the assembly of the elect, just as a thief, murderer, or any guilty person is separated from the good by the judge’s sentence and the evil person is sent into the executioners’ prison.

For God’s temple, that is, the temple of the Holy Spirit, of the Father and the Son, is holy, and that temple is what you are. Therefore you must not violate it. He is addressing the faithful, in whom God dwells through faith and love.

Let no one deceive you, that is, let no false person mislead you by flattering you. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age—that is, in the eyes of worldly people—let him become foolish, considering temporal wisdom foolish and laying it aside, so that he may be wise before God in the future.

This can be understood and punctuated in two ways. First: if anyone wishes to have true wisdom, distinguish the words “in this age”; let him become foolish, that is, let him believe concerning Christ what appears foolish to the wise of this age.

Alternatively: if anyone seems to be wise in this age, the words “let him become foolish” are to be supplied, so that he may be wise before God, who was able to accomplish what human wisdom denied.

For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. The wisdom of this world is that by which it is denied that God begot a Son without a wife. For it is written in Job, chapter 5, in the words of Eliphaz: “I will seize”—that is, I will show to be liars—“the wise,” namely the philosophers, “in their craft,” when I cause my Son to be born from a virgin.

Therefore let none of you, O Corinthians, glory in human beings, wishing to be called by the name of the one by whom he was baptized, as the Donatists are named from Donatus, and the Apollinarists and Manichaeans from their founders.

For all things are yours, if you belong to God; all things belonging to God are yours. What things? Whether Paul—the implied sense being, “your minister”—or Cephas, he is your minister, not your Lord. Perhaps when Peter came to Rome he passed through Corinth.

Or the world—the implied sense being, “the world is yours,” because it was made for your sake, so that you may make proper use of the things found in the world and believe that it was made through the word of God.

Or life—the implied sense being, “the present life”—is yours, in which you ought to do good, if you live in such a way as to please God.

Or death is yours, so that, if you wish, you may die temporarily for God and live eternally.

Or the present things—the implied sense being, “the good and useful things of the present”—are yours, so that you may distribute them to the poor, from whom you may deserve to receive a return, and thereafter live and be clothed.

Or future joys are yours, so that by living well in this age you may eventually attain possession of them.

For all the things I have mentioned, and all that has been made, are yours, that is, they were created for your dignity and benefit.

But you must always be servants of Christ in two ways: either because through him, who is the Word of God the Father, you were created when you did not yet exist; or because, when you were lost, you were redeemed through him.

But Christ is God’s—the implied sense being, “Christ is God’s Son”—and he has his being from him both according to his divinity and according to his humanity. Before all ages he was begotten from him and has his origin from him; and at the end of time, according to his humanity, he was made by him.

## CHAPTER IV

Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.

After the Corinthians came to faith through the Apostle’s preaching, some of them, deceived by pseudo-apostles, did not think of him as highly as was fitting. They supposed that he did not possess such dignity and grace because he had not been called by the Lord through the presence of his flesh, as Peter and the other apostles had been, who followed the Lord and heard his preaching.

They also called him a deceiver and preacher of false doctrine, honoring their deceptive pseudo-apostles, who spoke to them flatteringly, more than they honored the one who, preaching the truth, rebuked their vices.

When this was made known to the Apostle, among other things he wrote the words stated here, showing that they ought to understand and believe this concerning himself: that God had chosen him for the dignity of the apostolate. He says: “Let a person”—a Corinthian or anyone else—“regard us,” namely myself, Barnabas, and Sosthenes, “as ministers of Christ.”

It is as though he were saying in other words: “Do not, O Corinthians, despise and reject us because we were not called by the Lord together with Peter and the other apostles. For I and Barnabas preach nothing other than what they preach; and the one who, while still mortal and placed on earth, called them and summoned them to the grace of the apostolate revealed to me from heaven the same things that he taught them on earth.”

Nor do I ask you to regard me and Barnabas as equal to Christ, but as ministers of Christ, who have ministered his Gospel to you. A minister of Christ is one who imitates him by keeping his command, just as he himself said: “Whoever ministers to me must follow me” (John 12).

He is also a minister of Christ who ministers to others by preaching his Gospel, as Paul did, who both kept the commandments—or preached—and ministered. Whoever distributes temporal goods to the poor out of love for Christ also ministers to Christ. The same Apostle fulfilled this duty, not by supporting the poor from what belonged to others, but from what he acquired through the labor of his hands.

As for what follows, “and stewards of the mysteries of God”—although some manuscripts have “of the ministries of God”—it is better to say “stewards of the mysteries of God.” For if we say “of the ministries,” the meaning will be that they were called only to establish and arrange ecclesiastical ranks, namely bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the other orders, which are also called ecclesiastical ministries.

But when we say “stewards of the mysteries,” we understand that they were chosen to distribute to their hearers the mysteries and sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, although they also established the orders of the Church, as did the other apostles.

They were therefore stewards because, just as a householder chooses a steward in his household to distribute his goods to his fellow servants according to his will—to some more, to others less, and to some in the third hour and to others in the ninth (Matthew 20)—so Christ chose Paul and the others to distribute the mysteries of his Gospel according to the capacity of their hearers.

To those who were perfect and of more receptive understanding and intellect they entrusted the lofty and profound mysteries of the divinity of almighty God; to the simpler they entrusted simpler things that they could grasp. The outstanding preacher did both, as he himself said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2). And what does he say to these same Corinthians in this Epistle? “As to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

He was a steward of these divine mysteries. Therefore he wanted his hearers to regard him as what he was: a minister of Christ and steward of his sacraments, in whom not merely words but power shone forth.

In this matter, it is now sought among stewards that someone be found faithful. Although some wish to read this verse as a question, according to blessed Augustine it should rather be read affirmatively, as the following meaning will show:

Here—that is, in the present age—God seeks and considers who may be found a faithful steward among the other stewards, as I and Barnabas are. Therefore the pseudo-apostles who deceive you are not faithful stewards, because they disagree with the faith and teaching of Christ. They were unfaithful stewards in this respect: they adulterated and falsified the word of God.

Paul, however, was a faithful steward because he spoke as one speaking from God, in the presence of God. For that person is a faithful steward of the Gospel who preaches nothing other than what is contained in the Gospel, without error or falsehood; who does not seek his own glory, so that he may be praised by his hearers, but seeks that God may be glorified through them; and who does not devote himself to preaching for temporal profit or to fill his belly, but so that he may receive from the Lord the reward for his labor.

Therefore, if the Gospel were not dispensed through the wicked, the Lord would certainly not say: “Do the good things that they say; do not wish to do the evil things that they do” (Matthew 23). Again, if it were not dispensed through the good, the Apostle would certainly not say elsewhere: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11).

There are therefore many stewards through whose ministry people attain eternal salvation. But in the present age God seeks among the stewards that someone be found faithful, namely one who adorns in his works what he preaches with his mouth.

But with me it is a very small thing to be judged by you or by a human day.

The pseudo-apostles, the philosophers, and some Corinthians deceived by them judged or mocked Paul because he did not differ in his preaching from Peter and the other apostles. They said that if Peter, Andrew, James, and John, who had been fishermen, preached in a rustic manner and not scholastically, it was not particularly surprising. But why should Paul, who had been a teacher of the Law, imitate them by arguing in a rustic rather than philosophical or dialectical fashion? This, they said, was surprising.

Therefore, they said, there is no other explanation than that he is a magician and a deceiver: since he had previously been unable to destroy Christians by persecuting them, he now deceives them by seducing them with his false preaching, pretending to be an associate of Peter and the other apostles. Outwardly he preaches one thing, they said, while inwardly and secretly he does another.

But the Apostle, unconcerned about their slanders and mockery, knowing for certain that another person’s words do no harm to someone whose own conscience does not accuse him, continued, saying:

“It is a very small thing to me”—that is, I consider it nothing—“that I should be judged,” that is, slandered and mocked by you, or condemned because you ought to be using divine laws, “or by a human day,” that is, by those who use human laws and delight in human praise and favor, speaking and preaching philosophically so that everyone may praise them.

For I commit nothing against either divine or human laws. He compares human laws or praises to a day because those who are educated in them and are exalted by human beings are regarded and seen as bright and pleasing.

But neither do I judge myself, that is, neither do I reproach myself for having done anything against divine or human laws, because I am subject to no fault. Why?

For I am conscious of nothing—that is, of no evil. I recognize in myself no evil of any crime, since I have been cleansed by Christ’s grace from all original and actual sins.

The meaning is this: if I find myself irreproachable—I who know myself better than you who judge and slander me—how can you judge my conscience? How can you examine with what disposition and intention I do whatever I do, especially since “no one among human beings knows what is in a human being except the human spirit that is in him”?

Happy is the conscience that dares to speak of itself so confidently. But lest the Apostle appear to confess such things presumptuously and proudly, he added:

“But I am not thereby justified,” the implied sense being, before myself or before God. It is as though he were saying in other words:

“Although I find nothing evil in myself and nothing worthy of reproach, so that some unjustly slander me while others exalt me with their favor, I am not thereby justified before myself, nor do I believe that I have thereby been justified before God. For I do not know whether what I do pleases him or how he receives it. He knows better what is in me than I do. Even if I have not fallen into the gravest works of sin, at least I have sinned and fallen short in my thoughts.”

I know myself better than you who judge and slander me, and God knows me better than I do. Hence what follows:

“But the one who judges me is the Lord.” My conscience is not good because someone praises it, nor is it bad because you judge it. For what do you judge or condemn that you do not see? The person who reproves another ought to see something blameworthy in him which offends his own eyes.

But you must not judge and slander me as though I were a deceiver and a rustic who displayed one thing outwardly while doing another inwardly. For the Lord judges me, that is, he distinguishes and tests my case and considers my actions. He knows how to judge not only deeds but also thoughts.

However much human beings may be able to judge another person, a human being can certainly judge himself more; but God can judge a human being more than that person can judge himself. Such depth exists in a human being that often the human being himself does not know what lies within him. Such was the depth of weakness hidden in Peter when he did not know what was taking place within him and rashly promised that he would die with the Lord or for the Lord. For Christ foretold to him what Peter himself did not know about himself.

Therefore—understand: “you who do not know what is in a person”—and since it is the Lord who discerns and judges me, do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes for judgment. Concerning manifest matters whose motivating intention can be known, we are permitted to judge—for example, murder, public adultery, fornication, and other such things. Yet, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, we are not permitted to condemn the perpetrator of a crime unless he has either confessed or been convicted by witnesses.

But concerning matters whose intention is doubtful and uncertain—such as abstinence and fasting, when many people say that they cannot abstain from wine and meat or that they cannot fast—it is not ours to judge, because such things may be done with either good or bad intention. The same applies to thoughts and to things done secretly: although they may be reported, they are not thereby demonstrated by proof. We must reserve them for the Lord’s judgment, because whoever judges matters regarded as uncertain is, insofar as he can, attempting to deprive almighty God of judgment.

Our credulity, however, is often deceived in such matters. It is our responsibility not to be misled by a harmful opinion. Since we cannot investigate people’s consciences, we should not rashly pronounce judgment on unknown matters. That is, if we do not know whether this or that person is unchaste or chaste, we should hate unchastity and love chastity, yet not presumptuously pronounce sentence, nor become narrators of other people’s crimes.

And if we do not know whether this or that person is unjust or just, let us love justice and detest injustice, but let us not pronounce judgment until the Lord comes for judgment. He will also illuminate—that is, make manifest, lay bare, and reveal—the hidden things, namely, the works of darkness that lead a person to everlasting darkness. Or by “the hidden works of darkness” he means those things done secretly by the good and the wicked alike. He will reveal not only their works but also the purposes of the hearts of the good and the wicked.

To whom, then, will he reveal the works, thoughts, or purposes of the hearts? As blessed Augustine says, he will make known to each of the elect the works and thoughts of all the elect. There will be nothing that he does not disclose to his friends and conceal from strangers, since there will be no stranger there. Likewise, we must believe that all the works and purposes of the reprobate will be exposed to their disgrace and shame. For now, so long as you do not see my heart and I do not see yours, it is night. Mortal people do not know the hearts of mortals. But the light by which all these things will be revealed is God himself, who is the true light.

Let us see what the Apostle adds: “And then,” he says, “when the Lord has revealed all the hidden works and the purposes of the hearts,” in accordance with what is said through the Prophet: “Behold, I have come for this purpose: to gather together the works and thoughts of each person”—then “each one will receive praise from God.” Not everyone will receive praise, but each person who possesses good works and purposes, or thoughts, will receive it. For then the righteous will be praised when he hears the Lord say: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 23), and: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matthew 25). The unjust person, however, will be reproved when he receives the sentence: “Cast him into the outer darkness,” and: “Depart, you accursed, into eternal fire” (ibid.). Those who are free from and excluded from that curse will reign happily with God.

## Chapter IV

“Now, brothers”—that is, the names of the false apostles—“I have transformed,” that is, transferred them to myself and Apollos, for your sake, namely so that I would not provoke you to envy and detraction, so that in us you may learn—understand, humility—not to be puffed up, contrary to what is written, one against another on behalf of another.

The connection of the passage is as follows: you are to learn humility from us, so that no one may be puffed up—that is, so that pride may not cause one person to rise against another on behalf of another, beyond what is written, that is, contrary to what has already been written and what you ought not to do. In other words, a Donatist should not be puffed up on behalf of another—that is, on behalf of Donatus, by whom he was baptized—against a Novatian, saying that he was baptized by a holier man and with a better baptism. Likewise, a Novatian should not rise against a Donatist on behalf of another, namely Novatus, by whom he was baptized, saying that Novatus’s baptism is holier, since he himself was baptized with Novatus’s baptism: “I have been baptized,” he says, “with a better baptism than you, because Novatus is better than Donatus.”

“For who makes you different?” Understand: who makes you faithful rather than unfaithful, learned rather than unlearned? That is, who made you better than the one to whom he did not give what he gave you? Or who made you, O Donatist, better than a Novatian by giving you virtues that he does not possess? Did Donatus give you this gift, or God? Certainly God does this through his gifts and grace, giving to one what another possesses. “What do you have that you did not receive?” Understand: from God.

“You are already full”—understand, with the divine mysteries—“you have already become rich in every word, in teaching, and in an abundance of good works; you reign without us,” secure in your reward. This should be read ironically and by way of contrast, because those who had been led astray by the false apostles were neither full of the divine mysteries, nor rich, nor reigning without them.

But what follows should be spoken optatively and affirmatively: “And would that you were reigning now, so that we too might reign with you.” Those reign with God in the present age who perform such works that they are already secure concerning the reward of eternal life, and who will reign with God, like the apostles and holy martyrs.

For I think that God has displayed us apostles—myself, Barnabas, Sosthenes, and the others who preached to you—as the last, as men condemned to death. That is, when he sent us to preach the Gospel to you, he condemned us to death, since your unbelief and savagery would not kill us. He called us “the last” because they were called and chosen after the calling of the twelve apostles and after the Lord’s ascension.

For we have become a spectacle—that is, a laughingstock, or an object of ridicule, or even a marvel—to the world, to angels, and to human beings: to pure spirits and evil spirits, and to people who rejoice in the evils and torments that we suffer for your sake. A spectacle is so called from “looking,” that is, seeing and contemplating. It may also be called a theater. For there was a place in cities where royal entertainments were performed, and where criminals—and often innocent people, such as the holy martyrs—were beheaded. The whole population flocked there to see what was being done.

We are fools for Christ, as you think, because we do not resist those who inflict evil and do not repay evil with evil. But you are wise in Christ, as it seems to you, because you want to be Christians without abandoning the wisdom of the world, and you want to have great thoughts about Christ while denying what is weak.

We are weak because we do not avenge our injuries; but you are strong, because you think that resistance must be made by your own strength. You are noble, boasting of the nobility of your lineage; we are ignoble, as you think.

All these statements must be understood by contrast and spoken ironically, because what he appears to deny he affirms, and what he appears to affirm he denies—as though he were saying: “We are wise, but you are fools; we are strong, because for Christ we endure the adversities of this world, but you are weak because you do not dare to endure such things; we are noble, descended from the race of the patriarchs, but you are ignoble, without a name of dignity, descended from Gentiles who worship idols.”

Until this present hour—that is, until the present time—we both hunger, enduring prolonged famine, and suffer nakedness and deprivation. Paul endured these things: called while still young, he persisted in them until old age. We are struck with blows—that is, with fists, by which he designates every kind of torment—and we are unsettled, being driven from place to place and expelled from city to city.

We labor, working with our own hands. Paul practiced the craft of tentmaking from the first hour until the fifth, and from the fifth hour until the tenth he devoted himself to preaching. He did not want to receive anything from the Corinthians or from his other hearers, so that he could freely rebuke and correct their vices, lest the vigor of evangelical truth grow dull for the sake of his belly, and lest he give the false apostles an opportunity to plunder households and make the Gospel a commodity.

We are cursed—that is, blasphemed by unbelievers as magicians, sorcerers, and sacrilegious men—and we bless, preaching Christ to them.

We are blasphemed as deceivers; we entreat them—understand, so that they may freely hear the Lord’s teaching, which they detest as blasphemy—and we ask them to give us an opportunity to offer a defense, so that we may plainly prove that we are not what we are accused of being.

We have become the refuse of everyone—that is, the most despised and worthless of all. *Peripsema* properly means the filings or scrapings of bronze or of some other metal, or the peelings of fruit, or household rubbish.

I am not writing these things to shame you—that is, not to make you embarrassed—but to admonish you as my most beloved children concerning what you ought to do as an example of your father; or I am showing you what I endure so that you too may not hesitate to endure similar things for Christ.

For even if you have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ—that is, in the teaching of Christ’s faith—you cannot have many fathers. Pedagogues are so called because they lead boys on foot; they are also called attendants. A father first begets a son and afterward entrusts him to a pedagogue for instruction. Although he may have many pedagogues, he has only one father.

So Paul had begotten the Corinthians for Christ through the faith of his preaching.
