But after his departure they acquired many pedagogues, not only good ones but also bad ones—namely, the false apostles. Therefore he says: Although they may have many teachers and instructors, they cannot have several fathers; they can have only the one who first preached the faith to them.

For this reason I sent Timothy to you, who is my most beloved and faithful son in the Lord. He strikes them indirectly and, in praising Timothy, censures them, as though he were saying: “You are not faithful.” He will remind you of my ways—that is, he will remind and inform you of what is happening around me, of what I preach and accomplish in my conduct, and of how I live. I preach the very same things in the Church, because I teach the same way everywhere.

As though I were not coming to you, you have become puffed up in your pride. For the Corinthians were saying: “Paul knows that, compared with us, he is an uncultured man, and for that reason he does not come to us. We do not care, since we have our own philosophers. He thinks that we are sinners, and therefore he disdains coming to us. We do not care, since we have our own apostles. Let him do what he wants.”

For this reason the Apostle adds:

I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills. But for the present I will not leave Ephesus to come to you, because here I am gaining greater profit for God than among you. When I come, I will know not merely their speech—understand, the speech of those who are puffed up—but their power. That is, when I come, I will not consider their pompous speech, with which they now show their pride, but their power: the merit of their life, the reasonableness of their truth, how they believe, and what miraculous powers they can perform, if they are so puffed up.

For the kingdom of God is not in pompous and polished speech. That is, the kingdom of heaven—which is so called because it leads those who observe it to the kingdom of God—does not consist in speech, in the language of preaching and the Gospel, but in the power of good works. For in the kingdom of heaven words do not reign, but deeds. Or it consists in the power of miracles, when what is preached in words is confirmed by miracles.

What do you want, O Corinthians? Do you want me to come to you with a rod—that is, with vengeance for your vices and with the severity of correction, as Moses came into Egypt, symbolized by the rod that he carried? Or do you want me to come in love, or affection, and in a spirit of gentleness—that is, with mildness of mind, humility, and tranquility?

The meaning is this: If you do not want me to come with a rod, you will remain uncorrected. But if you want me to come with a peaceful disposition and gentleness of mind, correct and amend yourselves by doing penance.

## Chapter V

Fornication of such a kind is heard to exist among you as is found not even among the Gentiles—that is, among the pagans—so that someone has his father’s wife, namely his stepmother.

And you are puffed up—that is, lifted up and made proud—and you have not rather mourned over this crime, as Samuel mourned over Saul. The meaning is this: although you ought to have mourned over his sin and separated such a person from your fellowship, you have instead been lifted up in pride because, by looking at that criminal, you think that you possess great merit and appear holier than he.

Although absent in body, I am present in spirit—understand, in the Holy Spirit, who fills all things, as blessed Ambrose says: Such grace was granted to Paul that, wherever he was, through the Holy Spirit he knew what was being done elsewhere by those to whom he had preached the Gospel.

I have already judged the one who has done this, as though I were present—that is, I have judged as though I were bodily present the man who took his father’s wife.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, in the place of the one whose ambassador I am—when you are assembled, and with my spirit—that is, with the Holy Spirit—with the power of the Lord Jesus—that is, with the sentence of the Lord Jesus which is in me.

Here are three persons: the Holy Spirit, the Lord Jesus, and those among whom every judgment is conducted and confirmed, in accordance with what the Lord says: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matthew 18).

By these three persons the Apostle had already judged that such a man should be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, or for affliction, so that he might be tormented by the devil in his body with a severe illness, yet not be made insane or delirious, so that his spirit—that is, his soul—might be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, on the day of judgment.

Blessed Augustine says that this power and grace were given to the Apostle so that he could hand sinners who refused to do penance over to the devil to be tormented in the body, as in the case of this man, and also of Hermogenes and Philetus, concerning whom he says: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1).

He expelled such a man from the Church and from every society. Thus the devil, by the Apostle’s command and permission, afflicted him with a very serious illness, thinking that through such means he could take away his soul. But the most devout preacher did not give him power over the man’s soul, so that he might make him insane or destroy him.

Your boasting is not good, O Corinthians, since you boast in his sin, thinking yourselves better by comparison with him. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?

Here we can understand “leaven” in two ways: as wicked teaching and as a sinful person. Just as a little leaven corrupts the whole mass of kneaded flour and draws it toward its own sourness, so evil teaching, or one sinful person, commonly corrupts the entire congregation of the Church through its—or his—evil example. And all who could correct him but do not correct him become like him in punishment. Whether it is wicked teaching or an evil and undisciplined sinner who refuses to amend himself, he must be expelled from the Church.

Purge out the old leaven. The distinguished preacher commands the Corinthians to expel from their assembly the fornicator who had taken his father’s wife. He had already handed the man over to the devil for purification, so that the one by whose persuasion he had sinned might purify him by tormenting him. When he saw himself expelled in the present age from the company of the faithful, he would be ashamed of his guilt, fearing that he might likewise be expelled in the future from the fellowship of the saints.

For this reason the Apostle gave this command: so that through present tribulation and misery he might escape the punishments of eternal fire and his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord.

“Purge out,” he says, “the old leaven,” that is, the fornicator who committed incest by taking his father’s wife. He calls him “old leaven” because he still remained in the conduct and sin of the old Adam, who sinned first. Every sin belongs to the old person.

“Leaven” is also used sometimes for good teaching and sometimes for bad teaching. It is used for good teaching when the Lord says in the Gospel according to Matthew: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened” (Matthew 13).

Here he calls leaven the fervor of love for God and neighbor and the knowledge of the Holy Trinity, which burns in the hearts of the faithful and is contained in evangelical teaching. The woman who received the leaven is the holy Church, which preached love of God and neighbor and knowledge of the Holy Trinity to Asia, Europe, and Africa, until the whole was leavened—that is, until it spread this preaching throughout the fourfold world and drew people from all nations to the faith of Christ.

Leaven is also used for bad teaching and bad conduct, as our same Redeemer says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matthew 16), that is, beware of their wicked teaching; and “beware of the leaven of Herod,” that is, of his murder and adultery.

So in this passage it is used with an added qualification for the preservation of the old person and for wicked teaching, because there were false apostles among the Corinthians who were sowing corrupt teaching among them, which the Apostle commanded them to reject.

So that you may be a new lump, just as you are unleavened. In Greek, leaven is called *zyma* (ζύμη); hence in Latin bread is called *azymus*, “unmixed,” without *zyma*, that is, without leaven.

The meaning is this: “For this reason,” he says, “I command you to purge out the old leaven from yourselves, so that you may remain in newness of life, just as you are unleavened.” That is, just as in baptism you have been made new, free from all original and actual sins, remaining without *zyma*, that is, without sin, insofar as human frailty is able, with God’s help, to do so.

For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Passover is the name of the festival that the Jews celebrated every year in memory of their departure from the land of Egypt. The lamb sacrificed at that festival was also called the Passover, as the disciples’ words show when they say to the Lord: “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Matthew 26)—that is, the lamb.

The Apostle speaks according to this custom here as well: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” as though he were saying: “Do you want to know what the Passover is? It is Christ sacrificed.”

It is not a legal or symbolic lamb that has been sacrificed for us, but the true Lamb, who takes away the sins of the world, has been sacrificed for us on the altar of the cross. John speaks of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

The flesh of this Lamb is sacrificed daily in the Church and eaten by the faithful. Those who ate the flesh of the symbolic lamb made the passage from Egypt into the promised land. We too must pass from the darkness of unbelief to virtues, from the slavery of the devil to the freedom of Christ, and from death to life.

They celebrated the paschal festival for seven days; we too now celebrate Passover for seven days if, throughout the entire period of our life—which revolves through seven days—we make the passage from vices to virtues.

Therefore let us celebrate the feast. Another edition reads: “Therefore let us celebrate the festival.” We, for whom the true Lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed, should celebrate the festival—that is, rejoice, exult, and delight in spiritual gladness.

Let us not feast—or let us not be—in the old leaven. We read in Exodus that when the children of Israel left Egypt, they did not take fermented dough from there, but only kneaded dough. For the Egyptians forced them to leave quickly and not delay, so they left the leaven there.

Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness,” signifies the darkness of unbelief; leaven signifies sin. We too leave Egypt and the leaven of sin when, through faith, we abandon unbelief and leave sin, passing through the water of baptism into the promised land.

Therefore he calls the old leaven the oldness of sin and the conduct of the old person.

Nor let us feast in the leaven of malice and wickedness. Malice and wickedness properly belong to the inner person, that is, to the mind. But the Apostle, without attending to the strict propriety of the words, applied one to the outer person and the other to the inner person. Malice is ill will or evil intention; here it is used for evil action. Wickedness is pride or boldness toward evil, or evil thought.

The meaning is this: Let us not feast or rejoice in the oldness of sin, in the conduct of the old person, in the perpetration of an evil deed, in evil intention, or in pride or boldness of mind toward evil, as lovers of this age commonly do—those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things.

But let us feast and rejoice in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Sincere matter is that which perfectly preserves its own nature, is not inwardly disguised or corrupted by any deterioration, and always advances toward what is better rather than what is worse.

We too are sincere when we do everything in simplicity and purity of mind, always advancing toward what is better, not returning evil for evil, and not causing others to stumble through an evil example.

We feast in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth when we do everything with integrity and purity of mind and without corruption, acting neither with duplicity nor with pretense, and not for human praise or temporal profits, but for the reward of the heavenly homeland and so that we may please God alone.

I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators—that is, not to become like them or to wish to participate in their society. The Apostle had sent them a short letter instructing them not to associate with fornicators such as the man who had his father’s wife.

But the Corinthians had misunderstood this, thinking that he was speaking about the unbelieving Gentiles and not about the faithful. Therefore he repeats the matter and corrects them, saying:

“Certainly not with the fornicators of this world”—that is, I did not say or write this about the fornicators of this world, namely the pagans, but about those who are among you. Otherwise, you would have had to leave this world—that is, if you were again to associate with pagans by passing over into paganism, it would be better for you to pass from this life than to associate with them.

Alternatively: “Otherwise, you would have had to leave this world” means that if you wish to remain in such sins, it would be better for you to die and depart from the body.

A person associates with a fornicator either by committing fornication, or by assisting him in some service involving food or drink, or by favoring him in conversation, or by failing to rebuke him. It is therefore better to leave this life than to remain in sins, because the longer someone lives in them, the greater punishment he acquires for himself.

If someone who is called a brother among you—that is, who is said to be a believer—is a fornicator, do not even eat with such a person.

For what is it my concern to judge those who are outside? That is, what does it have to do with me to judge those who are outside, namely the pagans who are outside the Church? Do you not judge those who are inside, in the Church? Or, do you not discern sufficiently with whom you ought to associate among those who are in the Church?

For those who are outside—that is, the pagans and unbelievers—the Lord will judge, since “whoever does not believe has already been judged.”

Remove the evil person from among yourselves—that is, expel from your fellowship the one who has committed the evil deed, lest his misery corrupt others. Or: Whatever evil is in you, remove it from yourselves, and so forth.

## Chapter VI

Does any one of you dare, O Corinthians, having a dispute (*negotium*, as it were, “not leisure”)—that is, a case and accusation against another faithful brother—to be judged before the unjust, that is, the pagans, and not before the saints, that is, the faithful?

Some of the Corinthians who believed but did not live rightly, having an accusation and a case against a faithful brother, went to pagan and unbelieving judges so that the man against whom they had a case, whether falsely or truthfully, might be condemned and judged according to their decision. They won those judges over with gifts so that they would judge him, whether falsely or truthfully, according to their wishes.

Those judges are called unjust either because they were alienated from God or because, frequently accepting bribes with flattery, they rejected the divine laws granted to human beings or, by false interpretation, attributed the authority of those laws to their idols, saying: “Such and such is what my god says in the law that he handed down to us, his worshipers.”

Because the Corinthians were doing this, the Apostle rebuked them, saying: “Does any one of you dare to do this?” There should certainly not have been such presumption among us that anyone would abandon the faithful and go to unbelievers for judgment, so that his brother might be judged by them.

Do you not know that the saints will judge this world? That is, do you not know that the saints will judge the lovers of this world by the example of their faith and by comparison with their better conduct, not by authority in the manner of worldly judges?

And if the world will be judged in you—that is, through you and by comparison with you, namely the lovers of the world—are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?

This should not be read affirmatively but rather as a rebuke and a question. Its meaning is as follows: If secular people and lovers of the world will be condemned by comparison with you, do you regard yourselves as unworthy to judge the smallest cases or disputes, such as the theft of a horse or some other theft? Understand instead: you are not unworthy to judge matters that belong to this world.

Do you not know that we shall judge angels? Namely, wicked spirits, in the same way that we shall judge the world. How much more, then, matters pertaining to this age—that is, the lovers of this age? Those who, relying on God’s help, have preserved obedience and humility will judge, by comparison with themselves, the wicked spirits who fell through pride.

Therefore, if you have worldly judgments—that is, matters pertaining to the body, such as a stolen garment, a horse, or something similar—appoint those who are contemptible in the Church to judge them.

This can be understood in two ways. According to Augustine, he calls “contemptible” the simple people who possessed neither knowledge of divine law nor human law, nor prudence in discerning business affairs, and whose persons were considered insignificant. The Corinthians had appointed such men as judges, and therefore Christians who had some case, compelled by necessity because they had no useful judges, went to pagan judges who were in their vicinity.

According to this interpretation, he does not say this affirmatively but commands ironically what they were doing, as the following words also make clear: “If you have worldly judgments, appoint those who can neither discern nor understand such matters to judge them.”

I say this to your shame, because you ought not to have acted in this way. As though he were saying: “I do not prescribe this imperatively, but ironically and by denial. Although you act in this manner, you ought not to have done so. You ought to have appointed people who knew how to discern and judge other people’s cases and whose persons were honorable, so that no one would need to go to a Gentile judge for this reason.”

Therefore, do not appoint contemptible people any longer.

According to Gregory, “contemptible” may be understood as worldly people who possess knowledge of human laws and are honorable in their persons, but who, compared with those who understand the divine laws and penetrate the mysteries of the Holy Trinity, are contemptible and simple, even if they themselves are faithful.

According to this interpretation, the passage should be read affirmatively: such people are to be appointed, and the sons of the Church are called by the canons. The Corinthians ought to have appointed such people. Hence he adds: “I say this to your shame,” because you ought to have done this even without my command.

He commands such people to be appointed because those who ought to serve at the altar, meditate on the divine utterances, and offer the word of preaching to the people must make themselves strangers to worldly affairs and judgments.

Is there not among you a wise person who can judge between his brother and his brother? But brother goes to law against brother—understand, certainly there is such a person. This too should be read as a question and a rebuke.

Earlier, according to Gregory, he called such a person “contemptible,” or simple, in divine laws, in comparison with teachers and preachers. Now he calls him wise in human laws and commands that he be appointed.

According to Augustine, however, since they had appointed insignificant people, he says: “Is there not someone wise among you who can be appointed, so that brothers do not go to law against one another?” And what is worse, they even do this before unbelievers, doubling their sin: both by engaging in litigation and by litigating in the presence of unbelievers, by whom the name of Christianity is blasphemed.

It is already altogether a fault—that is, an offense and a sin—in you that you have lawsuits among yourselves, because accusation produces litigation, litigation produces discord, and discord produces hatred.

Perhaps they might say: “It is not altogether a sin if I seek what belongs to me.” Therefore the Apostle says: In truth I tell you, there is a fault in you, because you act contrary to the Lord’s command, who said: “If someone takes away what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6), and who commended his peace to us.

Why do you not rather accept the wrong? That is, why do you not rather endure loss, so that you may keep the Lord’s command? Why do you not rather suffer fraud, instead of defrauding others or inflicting injuries upon them?

But you not only demand back what is yours; you also injure others by striking them and defraud them. And this you do, understand, to your brothers in the faith, with whom you ought to have peace.

Or do you not know that the unjust—that is, sinners—will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived, that is, do not deviate from the path of righteousness.

The Corinthians were mistaken because they did not believe that a person could be separated from the kingdom of God by one vice unless he had been involved in all of them. Therefore he adds, recalling the individual vices that exclude a person from the kingdom of God:

Nor will fornicators, understand, possess the kingdom of God, unless, while placed in this age, they have performed worthy penance according to the measure of their sin and redeemed it through almsgiving; or unless, while doing penance, death overtakes them, so that after death what is lacking in their penance may be removed in places of purification through the prayers of good people and the offering of sacrifices.

Blessed Gregory also says that they will not otherwise obtain the prayers and offerings of good works unless the person for whom they are offered earned them with good intention while still living in this age, and through almsgiving—as though, had time been granted him, he would have mourned those sins and, while mourning them, would not have committed others.

“All things are lawful for me,” that is, every kind of food is lawful for me to consume, because “whatever enters the mouth does not defile a person” (Matthew 15), and so forth. “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1). “To the pure all things are pure” (Titus 1).

But not all things are beneficial; that is, not all things are useful, because some are poisonous and dreadful in their use. Or they are not beneficial because of the scandal they may cause to brothers, since it is better not to eat than to scandalize a brother.

“All things are lawful for me”—understand, those things permitted to the apostles by the Lord Jesus, so that those who preach the Gospel may receive their support from the Gospel, from those to whom they preach.

But I will not be brought under anyone’s power; that is, I will not subject myself to anyone’s authority. The blessed Apostle did not want to make himself subject to the Corinthians by accepting any gift from them, so that he could freely rebuke every vice, lest the vigor of evangelical truth grow dull for the sake of his belly, and lest he provide the false apostles with an opportunity to plunder households and make the Gospel saleable.

Food is for the belly—understand, it serves the belly for a time—and the belly serves foods. But God will destroy both it—that is, the belly—through death, when the function of eating has ceased and it has been reduced to dust; and he will destroy food when human beings cease to be born.

But the human body ought not to serve fornication—understand—but the Lord; and the Lord serves the body—understand, he will grant it immortality.

God the Father raised up the Lord, and truly the Son raised himself; and God the Father, together with the Son, will also raise us by his power.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? In general, the whole Church is the body of Christ, because he is its head and ruler according to his humanity, since he became human for our sake. Individually, however, the elect are his members.

Therefore, if the Lord Jesus Christ had assumed only a soul, his members would be nothing but our souls. But since he also assumed a body—and through that body he is our head, because we consist of soul and body—our bodies too are certainly his members.

Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? By no means, because the members that cling and are joined to a prostitute cease to be members of Christ.

Do you not know that he who clings to a prostitute becomes one body in intercourse? They become one both by nature and through the stain of sin. By nature, male and female are one body, because the woman was taken from the man; through the stain of sin, by having intercourse together, they become one body in the very embrace of intercourse, just as does one who is joined to his lawful wife. Or alternatively, he who clings to a prostitute becomes one body because he is made like her through sin. “For,” he says, “the two shall be one flesh”: in persons—either because the woman was made from the man’s body, or because by having intercourse together they become one body.

But he who clings to the Lord is one spirit. The Holy Spirit is God in himself, and [this refers also to] the human mind: or, when the spirit lives spiritually and fulfills God’s will by clinging through faith and love to the highest Spirit, it becomes one spirit with him.

Flee fornication. He did not say, “Fight against fornication,” but “Flee.” Although there are many vices against which we must fight—for example, against drunkenness and gluttony, by abstaining from excessive drinking of wine and from taking food, and similarly against other vices—concerning fornication we are not commanded to fight but to flee, because it cannot be avoided more effectively in any other way. We ought to flee the places and avoid the persons by whom fornication is easily suggested, and seek the company of good people, whose reverence may make us fear committing fornication, even when desire suggests it to us.

“Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body.” A question arises here: Since the Lord says, “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, adultery, fornication, murder, theft,” and other such things, and since no sin is committed without the body taking pleasure and the soul consenting, why does the Apostle say that all sins are outside the body, while the sin of fornication alone consists in the body? The answer is that the Apostle said this merely to magnify so great an evil, since, by comparison with this sin, all other sins are as though outside the body. When someone commits theft, murder, or something similar, while doing it he may be thinking of something else. For example, he may wish to commit theft while considering that he will later do penance; or he may give false testimony while perhaps thinking about the penance he ought to perform. But when he commits fornication, his whole mind is so absorbed in intercourse above all other sins, and bodily pleasure makes the entire soul so captive and enslaved to itself, that the whole person becomes carnal and is unable to think of anything else, because he acts under the influence of bodily pleasure.

Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0543A] who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? Earlier he said, “the temple of God”; here, “of the Holy Spirit,” because in substance the Holy Spirit is the same as God. And wherever the Holy Spirit dwells, the Father also dwells, and the Son also, because just as they are of one substance and one Godhead, so they are inseparable.

Whenever the mind and pleasure draw us toward lust or toward some other vice, we ought to consider that we do not belong to ourselves and are not in our own power, but are servants of Christ. We must obey his will, and we have been redeemed by his blood, as what follows makes clear. The body is stirred by pleasure; the soul wishes to consent. The soul’s rational faculty ought to return to itself and say: “What are you thinking? Why are you burning? Where do you wish to go? You are not in your own power, but are Christ’s servant. He redeemed you from the devil’s captivity by his most precious blood. Why do you wish to be taken captive again by the devil and subjected to his power, when he robbed you of all glory in your first parent?” When it begins to consider such things, protected by the grace of almighty God it will escape the snares and incentives of pleasure.

For you were bought with a great price—not with gold or silver, but with the blood of Christ. Whoever is bought or redeemed is held captive and is the servant of the one by whom he is redeemed. Thus the human race was held captive by the devil and was the devil’s servant, because, by accepting the sweetness of the forbidden fruit, it sold itself to him. Once redeemed by Christ’s blood, however, it is his servant and must obey his will.

Glorify and carry God in your body. He glorifies God who, by keeping his commandments, arouses others to praise God, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father” (Matthew V). He also carries God who bears knowledge of him and his commandments in his mind, fulfills them in his works, and lives holily and justly, according to the Lord’s command: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Leviticus XI). Therefore, whoever is holy by living holily carries God in his mind, in whose image he was made in his soul.

## CHAPTER VII

“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me”—that is, in your letter—“it is good for a man not to touch a woman,” or, “not to take one.” The false apostles had said to the Corinthians: “You ought not to cling to women, you who serve the pure God; but you who believe in Christ ought to put away your wives.” The Corinthians therefore wrote to the Apostle on this matter, asking whether they ought to remain joined to their wives in intercourse or not. The Apostle answered them that it was indeed good to abstain from one’s wife, but that it was better to take a wife than to commit adultery with another’s wife or to commit fornication in some other way.

Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband—that is, let them not withdraw from one another in intercourse. When the husband wishes to have intercourse, the woman should grant him the opportunity and permission. Similarly, the husband should serve the woman by rendering her the debt of intercourse when she wishes it.

The woman has no authority over her own body—that is, over her sexual organ—so as to forbid intercourse to her husband; rather, it is in the husband’s power. Similarly, the man has no authority over his own body—that is, his private or sexual organ—so as to forbid intercourse to his wife; rather, it is in the wife’s power. Thus they are mutually indebted to one another, and, what is more, are servants, so that there ought to be one will between them according to the law of nature. The festival days, the days of purification, and the natural circumstances of conception and childbirth are shown to require abstinence from these relations according to the law.

Do not defraud one another—that is, do not withdraw from one another, lest separation produce fornication—unless perhaps by mutual agreement, that is, by common will and counsel, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer for a time. We ought indeed to pray at all times and must persist in prayer, but our prayer is more acceptable to God when it is offered with a pure heart and body. For when someone does not touch even what is permitted, he shows that he wishes to receive what he asks for.

And again return to the same thing—that is, to permitted intercourse. He advises married people to return to natural relations after the days of prayer, explaining why he gives this command: “Lest,” he says, “Satan”—or the devil—“tempt you because of your lack of self-control,” namely, lest, when one partner withdraws, the other commit fornication and Satan find an opportunity to tempt.

But I say this by way of indulgence, not by way of command, because I do not command but permit. For I wish all people to be as I myself am—that is, if it were possible, I would wish all people to be as I am and to love virginity as I love it. But because this cannot be done, I grant indulgence to the weak, who cannot remain continent; I do not, however, issue a command to the perfect, because I would wish all people to imitate me in everything and remain in bodily integrity, since I know how greatly chastity avails before God—one person in such a way as to remain a virgin, another in such a way as to live with a spouse.

For it is better to marry than to burn. He did not say “better to marry than to burn” in a comparative sense, as though burning were a good thing and therefore marrying were better, but he followed customary speech. We commonly say, for example: “It is better to make a profit than to suffer a loss.” “It is better to have one eye than none.” “It is better to stand on one foot and be supported on the other side by a staff than to crawl with broken legs.” Thus it is better to marry and take a wife than to burn—that is, properly speaking, to satisfy lust under the pressure of bodily heat and to commit wickedness in whatever way.

To those who are joined in marriage—that is, to a lawful wife, a union called marriage from *matrona*, because she is the mother of children—I give this command, not from my own judgment, but the Lord’s in the Gospel: that a wife should not depart from her husband, except on account of fornication.

But if she does depart, on account of fornication, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. For to the rest I say—not the Lord. Earlier he spoke with the unmarried, widows, and married believers; now he says “the rest,” that is, those in mixed marriages between unbelievers and believers. Why does he say, “I say,” and not “the Lord”? Was the Lord not speaking through him? Certainly he was. But he said that he himself spoke, and not the Lord, because this command is not contained in the Gospel as spoken by the Lord, as is the earlier command that a husband should not dismiss his wife except on account of fornication.

If any faithful brother has an unbelieving wife—that is, one who does not believe—and this wife consents to live with him—that is, if she does not revile the Christian name—he should not dismiss her. It used to happen that, when the husband believed, the woman remained an unbeliever; and often, when the wife believed, the husband remained an unbeliever. For this reason the Apostle gave such commands: if the unbelieving partner did not revile the Christian name, no one was to dismiss his or her companion.

For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife. This had already happened to many after the Lord’s ascension: through a believing woman, an unbelieving husband was sanctified by believing in Christ through her preaching and good example—she who had become humble and subject to her husband from being proud—and similarly, at some time, an unbelieving woman was saved through a believing husband.

Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy. That is, if you were both unbelievers, or if the one who had become a believer were to return to paganism because of the one who refused to believe, your children would certainly imitate you. Or again, if the believing partner dismissed the unbelieving companion and they were separated from one another, the children might be unclean, because they would serve idols, urged on by an unbelieving father or an unbelieving mother; and they would also be unclean because of the foods they ate that had been consecrated to idols. But now, while the believer lives together with the unbeliever, perhaps their children imitate the believer and are holy.

But if the unbeliever—whether man or woman—departs from the believing partner, unwilling to believe, let that person depart; that is, let the person have free power to depart. Nevertheless, the believer should not cast the unbeliever away, nor depart from the faith because of that person. For a brother or sister is not subject to slavery in such a matter—that is, in such a circumstance. The meaning is that if the unbeliever does not wish to remain with the believer, the believer is not so subject to the unbeliever that he or she must follow; nor is the believer subject to guilt on this account if the unbeliever departs.

“For God has called you to peace,” that is, to harmony. Therefore, if the unbeliever who blasphemes the Lord’s name wishes to depart, let that person leave, so that the believer may have peace; that is, the believer ought not to quarrel with the one who departs.

For how do you know, woman or man, whether one will save the other, unless the Lord has assigned or arranged for each person—man and woman—the times for believing, so that first the man believes and then the woman, or first the woman and then the man? Let each person walk as the Lord has called him or her to faith; let each remain as he or she is. That is: if you have a wife, keep her; if you do not have one, you are not compelled to marry.

Was anyone called after being circumcised? Let him not put on the foreskin. What is the meaning of the Apostle’s sudden transition, while speaking about wives and married people, to circumcision and the foreskin? And how can a foreskin that has been cut off be put on? It should be noted here that he is not speaking of circumcision—that is, the removal of the skin of the sexual organ—but calls one who is free from a wife “circumcised,” and one who has a wife “foreskinned.” “Was someone,” he says, “called while circumcised”—that is, without a wife? Let him not put on the foreskin—that is, let him not take a wife, so that he does not become foreskinned but remains outside marriage. Was someone called while foreskinned—that is, without a wife? Let him not be circumcised—that is, let him not leave his wife, unless she has perhaps decided to remain chaste.

Circumcision is nothing—that is, chastity without good works is nothing; moreover, faith without works is idle—and the foreskin is nothing—that is, marriage without good works. If someone is circumcised—that is, chaste or celibate, which means without a wife—but lacks good works, his chastity benefits him nothing. If someone is married and has no good works, his marriage neither benefits nor harms him. But observance of God’s commandments does benefit him.

Let each person remain in the calling to which he was called, to the faith, whether with a wife or without a wife.

Were you called as a slave—implicitly, of a wife? You should serve and obey her will; do not be concerned, do not withdraw, and do not dismiss her, because you will not thereby lose the kingdom of God. Although you are married, you will not lose it if you serve your wife in such a way that you do not displease the Creator. But if you can become free—implicitly, from your wife—that is, if your wife dies or chooses to remain chaste, make better use of this freedom, implicitly by consenting to her, and do not take another wife.

For the one who was called in the Lord—that is, called so that he might believe in the Lord—as a slave, implicitly of a wife, is the Lord’s freedman; that is, he has been freed from the yoke of sin and has a certain small freedom from the Lord, so that he may serve his wife without displeasing the Creator. Similarly, the one who was called as a free person—that is, without a wife—is Christ’s servant. He ought not to occupy himself with earthly and marital service, but should serve the Lord wholeheartedly, because the Lord demands a greater service from him than from a married person.

You were bought with a price—that is, with Christ’s blood. Do not become servants of human beings—that is, servants of wives. Those become servants of human beings who, because of a wife, abandon the Creator and displease him by serving their wife excessively. We were bought with so dear a price that we could be redeemed by no other means than the blood of the Son of God. Therefore, just as the one who is bought ought to serve the one by whom he is bought more fully, so that at some time he may repay the buyer, so we too must serve Christ, by whom we were bought, with every effort and diligence.

Let each brother—that is, each believer—remain in the condition in which he was called to believe: if he was called with a wife, let him not dismiss her; if he was free from a wife, let him use that freedom, provided he can remain continent.

Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, because the Lord praised virginity; nevertheless, he did not command it, lest he appear to condemn marriage. Rather, he said: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX), and added: “Let the one who can accept it accept it” (ibid.).

But I give advice that does not displease others, as one who has received mercy from the Lord to be faithful—implicitly, as a counselor—and competent to give salutary advice. The Apostle Paul was God’s counselor because he had the Spirit of God, as he himself says elsewhere: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” Therefore he says: “I have received grace and mercy to be God’s faithful counselor,” and for this reason I ought not to conceal my advice from you.

I think, therefore, that this is good—that is, to preserve virginity—because of the present necessity. By “present” or “immediate necessity” he means the tribulation and distress that married people, and especially married women, endure: weariness in conceiving; pain in giving birth, by which pain women often die; great care and labor in raising and watching over children; grief at their illness and death, especially if she is deprived of all her children; and also the loss of a spouse. Similarly, a husband endures labors and griefs through the loss of children and the death of his wife. Those who preserve virginity are free from all these things, imitating the life that will exist after death.

For this reason the Apostle adds that it is good for a person to be so—that is, to live in bodily integrity and preserve virginity—so that he may be free from these necessities. But what follows is:

Nevertheless, such people will have tribulation in the flesh—that is, those who are joined in marriage. What he called above “present necessity,” he calls “tribulation” here. But I spare you, and the meaning is: I advise and counsel you to be chaste, wishing to preserve you from falling into tribulation of the flesh. Alternatively: “I spare you,” that is, I permit or consent to your entering this tribulation of the flesh if you do not wish to preserve bodily integrity.

The time—implicitly, of our life—is short, because it will soon come to an end. Therefore the people of God should no longer be propagated by carnal generation as they have been from the beginning of the world, but should now be gathered by regeneration.

It remains—that is, this is left or is still to be done—that those who have wives should live as though they did not have them. A person has a wife, but lives as though he did not, if he appears to have her today but dies tomorrow and subsequently ceases to have a wife. Therefore, in the present age he ought to imitate the life to come, in which the elect will be like the angels of God. Alternatively, a person has a wife but lives as though he did not if he knows how to discharge the obligations of the flesh without being compelled by her to cling to the world with his whole mind—namely, if he renders the marital debt in such a way that he does not displease the Creator.

And those who weep should be as though they did not weep. Anyone weeps over the loss of loved ones, over the miseries of this age, and over his own sins and those of others. But a person weeps as though he did not weep if he has consolation in the hope of heavenly reward, so that what the Lord said may be fulfilled: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V).

And those who rejoice should be as though they did not rejoice. Many rejoice in temporal advantages, but they rejoice as though they did not, because they rejoice in temporal goods while always considering everlasting torments and fearing God’s eternal judgment.

And those who buy should be as though they did not possess. Someone buys earthly estates, oxen, male and female slaves, but possesses them as though he did not, since he suddenly passes from this age through bodily death. Alternatively, many buy temporal goods and prepare for their own and others’ use what is necessary in this age, but possess them as though they did not, when they cling to earthly things in such a way that they do not lose eternal things, prudently foreseeing that they will soon leave all these things behind and never place their hope in earthly and transitory matters and possessions.

And those who use this world should be as though they did not use it. Many use the goods of this age, like kings and rulers, but use them as though they did not, since unexpectedly they abandon its gifts and desires through bodily death. Many also use the things that exist in this age, like good kings, rulers, and wealthy people—such as Abraham, Job, and David—who, because of the dignity of honor and rule they hold, cannot avoid using them. Yet they use them as though they did not, since they do not become servants of riches, nor permit these things to dominate their minds, considering that everything is transitory.

For the form of this world is passing away—that is, the world’s form and appearance will pass away through fire, while its substance, renewed and improved through fire, will remain, so that it may endure forever, in accordance with what Solomon says: “The earth shall stand forever” (Ecclesiastes I).

I wish you to be without anxiety—that is, without the excessive and superfluous care that married people have.

The one who is with a wife is divided, because he serves his wife in part and the Lord in part.

And the unmarried woman and the virgin—which are one and the same—think about being holy in body and spirit, that is, in mind. He added “in mind,” or “in spirit,” because many women possess bodily integrity but are not virgins in mind, since, if they could, they would already have married.

I say these things for your benefit, because it is holy before God and easy in this age to remain in virginity; not so that I may cast a snare upon you—that is, I do not say these things in order to bring eternal destruction upon you—but to lead you toward what is honorable, implicitly encouraging you to it. To preserve virginity is honorable; therefore everything honorable is holy, and for that reason virginity is holy, honorable, and acceptable to God.

But if anyone thinks and judges that he is being regarded as disgraceful by others concerning his virgin daughter, because she is overmature—that is, because she has reached marriageable age—fears that she may commit fornication with one of his slaves, and cannot keep her a virgin, let him do what he wishes—that is, let him give her to whomever he wishes. The virgin does not sin if she marries; if her husband sleeps—that is, if he has died—the woman may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord—that is, let her join herself to a believing man.

But she will be happier if she remains thus, according to my advice—that is, if she remains in chastity and widowhood.

## CHAPTER VIII

Now concerning the foods and drinks sacrificed to idols—implicitly, you wrote to me about these matters. Among the other things about which the Corinthians wrote to the Apostle in their letter, they also wrote about this, asking whether they ought to eat everything and whether everything was clean. Some of them, possessing the knowledge that all things created by God are good, ate in the temples of idols and scandalized the simpler brothers. These said: “If the person who has greater knowledge than I do knew that there was some divine power and deity in this idol and in the meats consecrated to it, he would certainly not sit in the idol—that is, in a temple consecrated to idols—and consume meats and other foods, or drink wine consecrated to idols.”

The Apostle will say much about this here. We know that we all have knowledge—implicitly, that all things are clean by nature—but their invocation and the consecration by which they are dedicated to them make them unclean. Knowledge—implicitly, the knowledge by which we believe that all things are clean to the clean and that all things are sanctified through invocation of the name of Christ—inflates; that is, it elevates the mind through the swelling of pride. But love builds up—that is, brotherly affection, by which we take thought for simpler brothers so that we do not scandalize them in certain matters, possesses the power of edification. Within this virtue, love, other virtues also are included: patience, humility, and simplicity of heart.

For just as undiluted wine, not mixed with some sweetness or even with water, elevates the mind, and just as unmixed and pure things do not please as much as those that are blended, so divine or human knowledge is not useful, because it elevates the mind into pride, unless it has been tempered by love of neighbor, humility, patience, and simplicity. Knowledge is then great and useful to itself when it is humbled by love, with which it also grows further.

If anyone thinks that he knows something—that is, that all things are clean and that they are lawful for believers to use—he does not yet know how he ought to know; that is, he has not yet considered that it is expedient to abstain even from many lawful things for the sake of avoiding scandal to the brothers.

But if anyone loves God and, for the sake of love, moderates his knowledge, that person is known by him—that is, that person is chosen by him.

Now concerning foods sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world. *Eidos* in Greek means “appearance” or “form”; from it comes the diminutive *idolum*, “a little form,” that is, a figure made from some metal, or from wood or stones. An idol is therefore nothing because it appears to have the image of a human being but is not a human being; it appears to have the image of some beast but is not a beast; it appears to have ears, eyes, nostrils, and a mouth, but it is nothing because it does not see, hear, smell, or speak. It is said to be a human being, but it is not a human being; it is said to be God, but it is not God. It is therefore nothing because what it is said to be, it is not. Its worshipers and devotees, and the foods consecrated to it, are also nothing, because its worship and consecration make them nothing.

For this reason also the people who worship idols are nothing, because every creature that does not cling to the one who always possesses being is nothing, as the prophet says: “All the nations that worship idols are as though they did not exist, and are accounted as nothing and vanity by him” (Isaiah XL). Idols are also nothing for this reason: a person makes a figure having a human head on one side, an ox’s head on another, a lion’s head on a third, and an eagle’s head on a fourth, with the rest of the body serpentine and the feet those of a horse. This is nothing, because God did not make any such creature.

For even if there are beings who are called gods by the pagans in heaven—Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury—or, among Christians, angels and saints, they are called so merely by name and not substantially; and on earth, by the pagans, Neptune and Pluto, or, among Christians, righteous human beings—since there are many gods in name among pagans and Christians, such as Moses, to whom it was said, “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exodus VII), and of whom it is said, “I said, You are gods” (Psalm LXXXI)—

Nevertheless, for us apostles and other believers there is one God, the Father, substantially, from whom all things exist and from whom everything received its origin, and we subsist in him—or subsist in him as though within him—because every creature exists within him, while he is both outside all things and within all things. And there is one Lord Jesus Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through whom all things were made—implicitly, and through whom we too were created and redeemed.

But not everyone possesses this knowledge—implicitly, the knowledge that there is only one true God, who has a Trinity in persons and unity in substance. Some, through conscience, still eat idol-food as though it were something sacrificed to idols—that is, something given and consecrated to idols—and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. When they see those who are stronger in faith reclining at an idol and eating food sacrificed to idols, they think that there is some divine power and religious significance in idols. Their conscience is weak either because, thinking that everything is clean, they eat food sacrificed to idols, or because they believe that there is some divine power in idols.

But food does not commend us to God—implicitly, food that we believe to be clean; that is, it does not make us acceptable to God or worthy of praise before him. For neither, if we do not eat—implicitly, from the sacrifices of idols—will we lack other foods that we can eat, nor, if we eat meats consecrated to idols, will we abound—implicitly, in such a way that we need not seek nourishment from other foods.

But take care lest this freedom of yours—the freedom by which you believe that all things are clean to the clean and that all things are sanctified through invocation of Christ’s name—become a stumbling block to the weak in faith, so that they believe that there is some deity in the idol and therefore eat meats consecrated to it.

For if someone sees the one who has knowledge—that is, one who is perfect in faith and believes that all things are clean—reclining in an idol-temple, that is, reclining in order to eat. Thus you sin against the brothers when you eat meats consecrated to idols in their presence while reclining in an idol-temple.

If food causes my brother to stumble—any simple believer who is still weak in faith—I will never eat meat sacrificed to idols, lest I cause my brother to stumble.

There were certain people among the Corinthians who, possessing the knowledge that everything was clean, ate foods consecrated to idols and provoked the simple and weak in faith to do the same. These said: “If those who possess prudence and knowledge knew that there was deity in these idols, they would certainly not do this. Therefore I too will eat, so that I may be consecrated through these meats.”

Conversely, there were others who were more perfect. Although they knew that everything had been made clean by God, they did not wish to eat food sacrificed to idols, because they knew that it was made unclean through the invocation of demons. And so that they would not scandalize their brother by provoking him to eat, they said what the Apostle speaks in their person: “Before,” he says, “I would die of hunger than cause my brother to stumble by eating food sacrificed to idols.” And I will abstain not only from those foods but also from everything by which he might be scandalized. Yet this may also have been spoken in the Apostle’s own person, so that the Apostle himself might say such things, urging them toward love.

## CHAPTER IX

Am I not free? These are the words of an angry person, and what he appears to deny he confirms. They should be read as a rebuke: “Am I not free?” Indeed I am. The Apostle was free according to his bodily lineage, since he descended from the race of the patriarchs; he was also free from all obligation to them, because he had received nothing from them.

Am I not an apostle? Some unbelieving Jews said this, and so did the Corinthians who had been led astray by false apostles: that Paul was not an apostle because he had not seen Christ. The Apostle rebukes them, saying: “Am I not an apostle sent by Christ?” Indeed I am, because he himself said to me: “I will send you far away to the Gentiles” (Acts XXII).

Have I not seen the Lord Jesus? Indeed I have seen him, when I was going to Damascus and afterward in the temple.

Are you not my work—that is, my activity and planting—in the Lord? Indeed you are.

And if I am not an apostle to others—implicitly, to Gentiles and Jews—yet I am one to you Corinthians. I brought you to faith in Christ through my preaching over the course of one year and six months. I was therefore not an apostle only to the Corinthians, but to almost all the Gentiles, as he himself said: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Galatians II). For you are the seal—that is, the sign and evidence—of my apostleship, and your faith, because through my preaching you believed in the Lord.

My defense before those who question me—implicitly, whether I am an apostle or not—is this: you are the sign of my apostleship in the Lord, and by this I defend my claim to be an apostle. For you are my defense, you to whom I preached the Gospel.

Do we not have authority—I and Barnabas—to eat and drink? Implicitly, by the office of preaching, and to receive from you what is necessary, according to the authority the Lord gave us, as he also gave it to the other apostles.

Do we not have authority—I and Barnabas—to take around a believing woman, that is, any woman who is faithful, and lead her from place to place, so that she may minister to us, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord—namely James and John, the sons of Zebedee; the Lord’s maternal aunt; and also James son of Alphaeus, Judas, and Joseph, likewise sons of the Lord’s maternal aunt; and also Cephas, who is Peter?

*Cephas* is Hebrew and Syriac; *Petrus* is Greek and Latin; *Simon* is Greek. Some who did not understand the peculiarities of the Greek language were misled by the ambiguity of the Greek word in the phrase “a woman who is a sister,” as though the apostles had wives whom they took around with them. For *gyne* means both “wife” and “woman.” Hence a *gyneceum* is called the place where many women reside.

Faithful women who possessed earthly wealth went with Peter and the other Jewish apostles, ministering to them from their own resources what was necessary, such as Mary Magdalene, Martha, and the other women who had followed the Lord from Galilee. They followed him, ministering to him. The blessed Apostle Paul did not do this, although he had the authority, because he preached to the Gentiles; nevertheless, he did not take women with him, lest scandal arise among the Gentiles, whose teachers and leaders did not have this custom.

What soldier ever serves for the life of the king or for the defense of his country at his own expense—that is, from his own resources? No one. Yet I serve at my own expense, acquiring food and clothing through the labor of my hands.

Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit—that is, its clusters? The Apostle’s vineyard was the Corinthians, whom he himself had planted in the faith of Christ, but he did not receive its fruit—namely, the expenses by which he might live.

Do I say these things according to human judgment? That is, do I speak these things according to human understanding and from my own opinion?

“You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain,” that is, you shall not deprive the preacher of his recompense. Preachers are rightly compared with oxen, because just as oxen plow the earth with a plowshare, so preachers cultivate the hearts of their hearers with the plowshare or mattock of God’s word, so that they may bear the fruits of eternal salvation.

Does God care about oxen? Indeed he does. God cares for oxen, since he cares for everything he has made, as it is said to him: “You hate none of the things that you have made” (Wisdom XI). He cares not only for oxen but also for sparrows, as is shown in the Gospel, where it is said that he feeds them (Luke XII). But he did not care for oxen in such a way that, among the commandments he gave human beings for their salvation, he commanded them to care for an ox. Nor is it necessary to instruct a person through a written law about how he should provide for his ox.

For the one who plows ought to plow in hope—implicitly, in hope of receiving fruit.

If we have sown spiritual things among you—that is, good things, namely by preaching the grace of faith and teaching—is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things? That is, if we receive from you temporal provisions, since we have bestowed eternal things upon you? This should not be read as an exclamation of reproach, but as a question.

If others—that is, the false apostles—share in your power, that is, in your means and temporal goods, why should not we do so all the more? The implied meaning is: why should we not share in your goods, since we preach to you the sacred admonitions of the Gospel? Yet I and Barnabas endure every hardship—thirst, hunger, nakedness, and every kind of want—in order not to place any obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ; that is, lest it be said of us that we preach the Gospel for the sake of profit and temporal concern rather than for the salvation of souls and eternal reward, and that we make the Gospel a commodity.

Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary—that is, in a temple of idols—by stripping and cutting up the victims, eat what comes from the sanctuary? That is, they live from what is offered there and belongs to the sanctuary; and that those who serve at the altar—that is, God’s altar—in the Law, namely the Old Testament, share with the altar? Whenever a whole-burnt offering was presented on the altar of the Lord’s house, the altar claimed the entire animal; but whenever victims or other sacrifices were offered, part of them was burned on the altar, while the ministers took part for their own use. [Col. 0553B]

So also the Lord ordained—that is, arranged and granted the authority.

Although I had the authority to live from the Gospel, I made use of none of the things I have mentioned above, because I accepted no expenses from you, so that I might not make the Gospel a commodity and might freely rebuke you. I have not written these things so that this should be done for me. They could have said: “The Apostle has written such things to us precisely so that what he did not previously receive from us he may now receive, and so that we may give him what he needs.” To this he replies: “I do not say these things for that reason—that I may now begin to do what I have not done until now—but to summon you to charity. For it is better for me not to die of hunger, thirst, and nakedness than for someone to empty or destroy my glory, which I hope to receive as the reward of my preaching, by giving me gifts.” His glory would be emptied if, receiving a reward in the present, he no longer hoped to receive another reward in the future and no longer rebuked wrongdoers. [Col. 0553D]

For even if I preach the Gospel—understand: solely for this purpose, that through the constant labor of preaching I may receive a present reward and praise from human beings—it is not glory for me, namely eternal glory in the future; for necessity—that is, the necessity of eating, drinking, and clothing myself—presses upon me. Therefore I preach, since I have no other means of living. Such things occurred in some people, as in the false apostles, but they were not found in Paul, who sought neither reward nor praise from human beings in the present, fearing that he might hear on the day of judgment: “You have received your reward,” if he had labored for that purpose. For woe is me—that is, want will oppress me and I shall endure the poverty of hunger—if I do not preach the Gospel. He does not say these things of himself, but rather of those who preached because they had no means of living except from preaching, and therefore curried favor with their hearers. [Col. 0554A]

For if I do this willingly—that is, if I preach without seeking temporal support and administer the Gospel without a temporal reward—I have a reward prepared by Christ, namely eternal recompense, and shall hear from him: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

What, then, is my reward? The Apostle asks himself what the reward of his preaching is in the present, and says, as though continuing: “I wish to preach the Gospel willingly; what is my reward in the present?” He answers himself, or someone asking him, “What is your reward?” This is my present reward and purpose: that, preaching the Gospel to the faithful and to all who wish to hear it, I may place the Gospel—understand: in their hearts—without charge, so that I may not abuse, or rather may not use, my authority in the Gospel, which I share with the other apostles; that is, so that I may accept nothing from my hearers, since a great reward is reserved for me by Christ. [Col. 0554B]

For although I was free—not only by nature, as one descended from the race of the patriarchs, but also from all human affairs, since I accepted nothing from them—I made myself the servant of all human beings, supporting everyone like a good steward; understand: a good steward supports the weak—especially you, O Corinthians—through my patience. I did this not through the cunning of craftiness, but through the affection of compassion, so that I might win more people for Christ.

I became to the Jews as a Jew—understand: as an observer of the Law—still shaving my head at Cenchreae, the port of Corinth, offering gifts in the Temple at Jerusalem, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, when he went up to the Temple after being purified (Acts XXI), and circumcising Timothy on account of the Jews, so that I might win the Jews for Christ, leading them from the observance of the Law to the grace of the Gospel.

To those who are under the Law—that is, to the Samaritans, who possess the five books of the Law—I came and became to them as though I were under the Law, that is, as though I served the Law carnally, although in spirit I was not under the Law of Moses but under the grace of the Gospel, so that I might win those who were under the Law. I did this not through the deceitfulness of pretense, but through the mercy of compassion. To those who were without the Law—that is, to the Gentiles—I became as though I were without the Law, agreeing with the Gentile philosophers at Athens that there is one God who made all things, that souls are immortal, and that human beings derive their origin from one God. Thus he appeared to them as one of themselves, although he did not worship idols, and gradually drew them toward what they believed less readily, persuading them to believe in him through whom all things were made, that is, in the Son. [Col. 0554D–0555A]

I became weak to the weak—Jews and Gentiles in understanding and intellect, who could not grasp great matters—weak by comparing and conforming myself to their weakness and smallness of mind, so that I might win the weak in sense and understanding by preaching things suited to their capacity and things they could grasp; I became all things to all peoples, namely to Gentiles and Jews, in all the ways stated above.

I became weak to the weak, a Jew to the Jews, a Samaritan to the Samaritans, who awaited the promise concerning Christ, and a Gentile to the Gentiles, so that I might save all by preaching the word of God to them.

I do everything for the sake of the Gospel—that is, for the sake of Christ, to whom the Gospel bears witness—so that I may become a participant in it, that is, a participant in the Gospel. These words seem to sound as though the Gospel were capable of rational participation, as if he were saying: “So that I may become a participant in the Gospel,” that is, so that I may deserve to obtain in the kingdom of heaven the rewards promised in the Gospel. [Col. 0555B]

Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? The distinguished preacher wishes and desires to urge all the Corinthians and all the faithful toward the course of good works, so that by laboring vigorously they may deserve to reach the prize of the heavenly calling. He then gives a comparison, by whose example we may approach the pursuit of eternal victory, saying: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium,” and so forth.

At one time there was a certain giant named Hercules, the strongest among the Greeks, powerful in every bodily virtue and also exceedingly swift and nimble in the agility and speed of his feet. With one breath he ran—and, so to speak, flew across—one hundred and twenty-five paces. Thus, in one place, he completed the distance of his run, which he called a stadium, from *stando*, “standing”; it is one-eighth of a mile. Later, a custom and longstanding practice arose among the Greeks: young men from each city, fortress, town, and even village prepared themselves so that, when the festival of the gods arrived, they could run to that stadium, which was measured at one hundred and twenty-five paces. Beyond its finish line they placed gold or silver, a horse or a cloak, or some other prize, which in Greek was called a *bravium* and in Latin may be called the palm of victory or a crown. While men and women stood around to watch the spectacle, everyone ran; but only the one who ran first received the prize, while the others ran in vain, because their running brought them no benefit, except that they provoked laughter and jeering among the people and great shame upon themselves. [Col. 0555C–D]

In a higher understanding, by the stadium in which they ran we should understand our faith, within whose boundaries we are commanded to run from the beginning of our faith until the end of this life, until we reach the promised prize, of which the Lord says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXVI).

There is, however, this difference between their race and ours: there, all who had prepared themselves for it ran, but only one who ran ahead of the others, reaching the prize first, received the reward of his victory. In our race, however, all who run well will receive the reward of their labor, and they will not regret having run in vain, since all who arrive will receive their reward. That one signifies the number of the elect, which in comparison with the reprobate will be very small, although in itself it will be complete. Hence the Lord says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX), as if he were saying: “Many begin to run, but fail and grow weary before they reach the prize; few are those who reach the palm of victory.” That one also signifies the unity of the holy Church, which is the body of Christ. For whoever is joined to the unity of the Church by faith, good works, and perseverance will reach the palm. Concerning this unity the Lord says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III), together with his body, which is the Church. [Col. 0556A–B]

Run in this way, O faithful: run in faith, believing rightly and living well, so that you may grasp the palm of everlasting recompense. The Apostle wants us to run carefully and courageously, because great is the promise toward which we strive.

Everyone who contends or labors in the contest—that is, in struggle and combat—abstains from everything contrary to his race. Those young men who prepared themselves for running abstained from all foods and drinks and from every other thing that could impede their running. They not only restrained their minds from eating and their bodies from excessive drinking, but also placed leaden plates around their loins at night so that they would not suffer an outflow of lust during sleep, since lust greatly weakens the body. If all those men prepared themselves in this way, knowing that only one would be crowned and that the promised prize would belong only to the one who arrived first, even though all the others reached the same place afterward, how much more must we abstain from everything that can impede our race, since eternal salvation has been promised to all of us? [Col. 0556C]

If, then, we ask from what things we ought to abstain, and what things, once we begin our race, overcome us and draw us back from the promised prize, let us ask the Apostle, and he himself will show us in the passage where he says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness” (Gal. V). These and similar things are contrary to our race.

Those who run within the stadium run in order to receive a corruptible crown; we, however, run within the boundaries of our faith in order to receive an incorruptible crown. What he called above the *bravium*, using the Greek term, he now calls in Latin a crown. Their crown and reward was corruptible, that is, temporal, because it passed away with time. For example, they received gold and silver, which were corruptible because they were taken from the earth and returned to the earth. They received garments, which were consumed by age and moths. They received a horse, which was corrupted by death and, consumed by worms, returned to dust. [Col. 0557A]

They were given a crown woven from earthly and withering flowers, but it passed away like the wind. Our crown and reward, however, is incorruptible and will not be corrupted by any alteration. Our crown will not be adorned with withering flowers, but, fashioned like a royal diadem and set with eternal gems, it will be preserved for us spiritually forever.

Our crown and reward, therefore, will be God himself almighty, and the contemplation of the whole Trinity. Seeing God as he is, we shall possess life enduring without end, together with every blessedness and satisfaction. For seeing the radiant one, we shall be radiant; seeing the blessed one, we shall be blessed; seeing the immortal one, we shall be immortal, and happy throughout all ages. Therefore we must run by believing, hoping, and desiring; by chastising the body; by laboring in almsgiving; by advancing from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen by us in Zion (Ps. LXXXIII). Nor should we despair of the promised reward, as the Apostle did not despair when he said: [Col. 0557B]

“I therefore run in this way, living well within the boundaries of faith, not as though running into uncertainty, because I do not doubt the reward, being certain of what has been promised to me. Those who ran in the stadium ran into uncertainty, because they were not secure concerning the prize. But so that we may be certain of the reward, the Apostle sets himself forward as an example, so that we may imitate him: ‘So I fight, not as one beating the air,’ raising and lowering his sword like a foolish soldier who, not stationed against an enemy, strikes the air and brandishes both his arm and his sword, wishing to appear to be a combatant.

Paul therefore fought against the aerial powers, about which he speaks in the Epistle to the Ephesians. He fought against philosophers, magicians, and bestial men, concerning whom he says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: ‘If I fought with beasts at Ephesus’ (1 Cor. XV). He fought not with a material sword, but by preaching, performing miracles, praying, fasting, and devoting himself to good works. [Col. 0557C]

That preacher beats the air who preaches without the effect of preaching: he merely utters words and does not adorn them with works; he preaches one thing and does another, and does not confirm what he preaches by miracles and examples. The Apostle, however, did not beat the air, because he did not utter words in vain; he fulfilled and strengthened by his works what he preached with his mouth.” [Col. 0557D]

But I chastise my body—understand: through labor and hardship, hunger and thirst, fasts and vigils, and many other such things—and bring it into servitude; that is, I make it my servant, so that I do not destroy by my works what I preach in words, but rather serve through words and examples those to whom I preach.

To chastise the body is to afflict it with the many tribulations we have listed above; it is to give it those things that advance eternal life, not those that serve luxury. It is brought into servitude when it does not fulfill its own pleasure but the will of the spirit, that is, of the soul’s rational faculty. Every faithful person ought to act in this way, chastising his body and subjecting it to servitude, fulfilling what the Apostle says elsewhere: “Walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” or of the body (Gal. V). [Col. 0558A]

The Apostle immediately explains why he subdued his body, restraining it from depraved pleasures, adding: “Lest, after I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate.” One is called approved when worthy of praise and accepted; conversely, one who is unworthy of praise and not approved is called reprobate. Thus the Lord will say to the reprobate: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV), that is, “I do not approve you as belonging to my side,” or, “I do not approve you as worthy of praise.”

Therefore, fearing that he might be rejected and appear unworthy of praise, the Apostle said: “For this reason I chastise my body and subject it to servitude, lest others, taught by my preaching, receive the palm of victory, while I myself remain alien to praise and the reward of recompense, hearing from the Lord: ‘You have received your reward.’” Lest, while caring for others, I myself remain in the wound. [Col. 0558B]

## Chapter 10

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers—understand: of this mystery, which I shall recount to you in part—that our fathers, namely the Jews, from whose ancestry I derive my origin, were all under the cloud, which went before them above by day, and all passed through the sea, because they escaped death.

And all were baptized into Moses—that is, through Moses as their leader—in the cloud and in the sea; that is, they were delivered from death. As far as the literal historical account is concerned, the Jews, when they went out from Egypt, were under the cloud, because the cloud moved or was carried over them by day (Num. IX). In a higher sense, according to Ambrose, they were under the cloud because everything that happened to them took place in obscurity and in figure.
