They were also under the cloud in the sense that they were covered by it from their adversaries, the Egyptians, when the cloud came between them and the Egyptians, while the waters were on their right and left. Later they were protected during the day by that same cloud from the heat of the sun, while they were delivered from present death. They are therefore said to have been baptized through Moses in the cloud, which was behind them, and in the sea, through the middle of which they passed. [Col. 0558C–D]

Or they are said to have been baptized through Moses in the cloud and in the sea because everything that happened to them in figure happens to us in reality. For just as they were delivered from Egypt through Moses their leader and escaped death through the cloud and the sea, so we, through Christ and through the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism, are delivered from the death of original and actual sin.

Moses signifies Christ; the cloud signifies the Holy Spirit; and the Red Sea, through which they were delivered from death as they passed, signifies baptism, which is consecrated by the redness of Christ’s blood and through which we are delivered from eternal death.

And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. He calls the manna that was given to them from heaven—that is, from this air—and the water that flowed from the rock spiritual, either because they are to be understood spiritually or because they signified the body and blood of the Lord, which are now consecrated and received in the Church. Or they are called spiritual because they were not prepared according to worldly law and custom, but by the power of God, without the mixing of ordinary elements, namely water and flour.

That food was created and given to them for a time, and likewise the water flowed from the rock for them not according to worldly custom but by the spiritual power of almighty God. That bread was therefore also called the bread of angels, because the food was created by the power of almighty God, by which the angels live and subsist without any labor, and was set before them without any labor on their part. This also signified that Christ, the spiritual bread who would feed spiritually, was to come from heaven. Hence the manna first came down from heaven on the first day, or the first day of the week, which is now called the Lord’s Day in honor of the Lord’s resurrection, to satisfy the people. [Col. 0559A–B]

They drank from the spiritual—that is, from the rock—which followed them, the same rock.

The Jews and certain simple-minded teachers argue fabulously from this passage, wishing to affirm that, after Moses struck the rock twice with his staff and the people and their animals drank, that rock continually followed them; wherever they pitched their tents, it rolled into the middle of the camp without being pushed by anyone, sending out very broad streams sufficient to satisfy the people and their animals. They say that this happened for forty years, until they came to the land of Midian, where they dug wells and found abundant water that was sufficiently sweet.

Some, even in their dreams, invent that the stone was so small that Miriam, Moses’ sister, carried it at her breast through that vast wilderness. [Col. 0559C]

But those who invent such things should say where, when, or how, according to the literal sense, what is found in the song of Moses according to the Septuagint translators was fulfilled: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hard rock.” Only then should assent be given to the claim that the rock followed them.

But since this event can nowhere be found in the Old Testament, let them lower their voice and incline their ear, so that they may be able to penetrate these matters spiritually, since they cannot follow the literal sense in them. For, as the teachers transmit, Horeb, the rock that Moses struck, is a rocky mountain whose side Moses struck. Therefore it is better for us to understand these things spiritually, as we did the preceding matters.

Hence the Apostle also calls it the same spiritual rock, because it is to be understood spiritually. For it signifies Christ, as what follows makes clear: “The rock, however, was Christ.” He did not say, “The rock signified Christ,” but as though Christ were truly the rock, although he was not so in substance but by signification. [Col. 0559D]

Similarly, when speaking of Abraham’s two sons, he did not say, “These signify the two Testaments,” but: “These are the two Testaments.” Christ, therefore, is the rock by signification, on account of his firmness, not in substance. The water that flowed from the rock signified the teaching of Christ and the grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning which he himself says in the Gospel: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink” (John VII), and so forth.

The rock is also called spiritual and following because it spiritually signified Christ who followed them. They drank from that spiritual rock that followed them because, whenever human help failed them, Christ was present, providing assistance. By his power—he who is the Word of God the Father—they were delivered from the land of Egypt and brought into the promised land. It is therefore said that the rock followed them because he came to their aid. The rock did not give that water only once; rather, Christ gave it through his power.

It should be noted that the Apostle said all these things for this reason: so that no one might trust in his baptism, or in spiritual food and drink, and think that God will spare him if he commits serious sin, unless he has earned this through worthy repentance. Therefore everyone must keep watch and labor, because the time of our life is exceedingly brief. [Col. 0560A]

But God was not pleased with most of them. For many died in the wilderness because of unbelief, not understanding God’s benefit—namely, forty thousand.

All these things that we have mentioned concerning the cloud, the sea, Moses, the food, the drink, and the rock happened as figures of us, that is, of our reality; in us they have happened in truth and now remain, because we have been led out of Egypt following their example, namely from the error of this world, so that we should not be desirous of evil things—understand: foods and vices—as they, that is, the Israelites, desired them: meat, melons, and the things they had possessed in Egypt for eating.

These words depend on the Apostle’s preceding statements, where he says that everything that happened to the Jews preceded us in figure, as what follows also makes clear, and that it was written for our salvation, so that we should not be desirous of evil foods and vices.

A question arises: since the Jews had a multitude of animals and livestock with them, why did they desire meat, and why did they not eat the meat of animals? The answer is that they did not desire the flesh of livestock, but craved the flesh of birds, which they had been accustomed to eat in Egypt. For the river Nile has along its banks and in its marshy places many kinds of birds, including kinds not found around other rivers.

Let us therefore flee evil desire and fight against it as far as we can, because—as blessed Augustine says—we can also prove by experience in ourselves that through evil desire all evils are done and perpetrated. I said “evil desire” because there is also good desire, concerning which Solomon says: “My son, desire wisdom” (Eccl. I), and the Psalmist: “My soul desired to long for your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII).

Evil desire is that which suggests to us that we should desire unlawful foods and foods beyond measure, commit homicide and theft, perpetrate adultery, and do other things of this kind. Therefore the Apostle, wishing to make us vigilant, gives us the example of those Jews who offended God in the wilderness through desire and perished. [Col. 0560B–D]

Nor should you become idolaters, as some of them did. The implied reference is to those who worshiped the calf at Mount Sinai.

As it is written in Exodus: *Eidos* in Greek means “appearance” or “form”; from it, as a diminutive, comes *idolum*, “a little form,” made from some metal, or from stones, or from fire. *Latria*, likewise a Greek word, means “service,” which belongs to almighty God alone. From these words the term *idololater* is composed: it denotes one who gives idols the honor and service that he ought to offer to almighty God alone. Hence idolatry itself is the act.

“The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Here the Apostle touches on the ancient history. After the children of Israel had gone out from Egypt and reached Mount Sinai, Moses ascended the mountain to God and remained there for several days. The people then gathered around Aaron and asked him to make gods for them to go before them, saying: “Make gods who will go before us. As for this Moses, who brought us out of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him” (Exod. XXXII). [Col. 0561A–B]

Then, as the history relates, Aaron took their bracelets and earrings and made from them a cast calf, which the Egyptians worshiped. Immediately they built altars before it and sacrificed victims to it, saying: “These are your gods, O Israel,” and so forth. When the sacrifice was completed, they sat down to eat and drink, and afterward rose up to play various games and dances; moreover, they began to fornicate.

For this reason a multitude of them was killed by their brothers, at Moses’ command and with the Lord’s will. The Apostle repeats this event so that the Corinthians might not believe themselves free from this crime, since they feasted in an idol’s temple. Every greedy person is also an idolater, since he worships money as though it were God, fearing to lose it. [Col. 0561C]

Nor should we fornicate, as some of them fornicated, namely with the Midianites, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day.

This happened in the land of Midian, and this was repaid to them when they defiled themselves with the Midianites, first worshiping idols before the doors of those houses. Balaam, the diviner, son of Beor, seeing that the minds of the Jews were inclined toward lust and prone to worship idols, was seduced and captured by love of money. He gave Balak, king of the Moabites and Midianites, the advice to place young girls and prostitutes at the doors of the houses, dressed in prostitutes’ adornment, and to place idols and altars before the doors, so that the Israelites, when they came, might be captured by love of those women and have intercourse with them, but in such a way that they would first worship the idols. Once this had happened, he knew that the anger of God would be aroused against them.

Thus it came about that twenty-three thousand were consumed by heavenly fire, and nearly all would have perished if Phinehas, moved by zeal for God, had not pierced with a spear the Hebrew man and the Midianite prostitute in their genitals. Because of this, God’s anger against the people subsided.

It should also be noted that not only are those called fornicators who satisfy their lust in whatever manner, but also those who depart from God through other vices. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. LXXVII), that is, all who depart from you. [Col. 0561D]

Nor should we tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him—understand: Moses, who bore the figure of Christ. Or they also tempted Christ himself, who was in Moses, as Moses himself says: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord” (Exod. XVI).

For Christ, who is the Word of the Father, was himself in Moses, and he himself spoke through Moses’ mouth. Both when they tempted Moses and when they murmured against him, they were murmuring against God. But what happened to them? “They perished by fiery serpents,” which both bit and, by biting, injected venom.

The Apostle therefore recalls such events and warns us, lest we be found in the same situation and be handed over to the devil, whose figure the serpents represented. [Col. 0562A]

Nor should you murmur—understand: against God, or against those set over you and your rulers—as some of them murmured: namely Dathan, Abiram, and their companions, against Moses and Aaron. And they perished by the destroyer, whether God or fire.

Dathan and Abiram, with their entire households, were destroyed from the face of the earth by God, because, at God’s command, the earth swallowed them alive. They were buried before they died, since, as Scripture relates, they descended alive into the underworld. Their companions, however, who had been like-minded in that conspiracy, were destroyed by heavenly fire.

To murmur is generally to complain and make accusations against those set over us and our rulers, often falsely and among ourselves. Sometimes, however, murmuring also arises from a just cause, when those in authority do not conduct themselves straightforwardly and rightly toward their subjects. Nevertheless, however it arises and occurs, it is evil; and woe to the one through whose action it comes about, whether that person is in authority or subject to it.

Blessed Augustine says that in no other matter did the Jews offend God in the wilderness as they did through murmuring, since they were always murmurers. Therefore we must avoid this vice in every way, lest similar things happen to us. [Col. 0562B–C]

All these things mentioned above, concerning the serpents and the fire that devoured them, happened to them in figure. Let us see how the fiery serpents to which they were handed over were figures, and also how the bronze serpent that Moses hung up was a figure: those who looked upon it were healed (Num. XXI).

Those serpents that injected venom by biting signified demons, who, by suggesting things to us, inject the venom of deadly pleasure. We are also handed over to them if we do not look upon the bronze serpent hanging on the wood, that is, Christ.

The bronze serpent, which had the likeness of a serpent but nevertheless had no venom, enabled those who looked upon it to escape temporal death from the bites of the serpents. The serpent signifies Christ, as he himself said: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish” (John III).

That serpent therefore had the likeness of a serpent but lacked venom, because Christ had the likeness of sinful flesh but lacked the venom of sin. By the fact that it was bronze, it signifies Christ’s eternity, because bronze is a durable metal. It was hung upon wood, and Christ upon the cross.

The person who looked upon it was healed from the bites and venom of the serpents; for whoever recalls and beholds Christ’s Passion with reverence, in order to put his own body to death with its vices and desires, is saved from the suggestions of demons, from the venom of depraved pleasure, and also from eternal death. [Col. 0562D–0563A]

The fire that devoured the murmurers signifies the eternal fire that will devour all who do similar things.

These things were written for our correction—that is, for our amendment and improvement—so that we may be corrected through such examples. “Upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” The ends of the ages have come upon us, because we are already situated at the end of the age, namely in its final period.

They were not written on account of those people, so that they themselves might read them—for those who did such things deserved to receive such things, and they had long since died—but for our salvation and benefit, so that, if we remain in the fear and service of God, we may receive the glory promised to them, namely the promised land, which signifies the heavenly homeland. But if we act less well or otherwise, their punishments will be doubled for us, because greater knowledge of the Law makes a person more guilty. [Col. 0563B]

Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands in the uprightness of faith, in good works, and in the knowledge by which he believes that all things are clean, should take care lest he fall into pride or become a stumbling block to his brother.

Here he silently and specifically strikes at those who, trusting in their knowledge by which they believe that it is lawful to eat everything because all things are clean for the clean, reclined at idol feasts and ate sacrificial meats, thereby causing weaker brothers to stumble. When those weaker brothers saw them doing such things, they thought that there was some divine power and deity in the idols and in those consecrated foods. [Col. 0563C]

In general, however, what he says applies to everyone: whoever stands in faith and good works should take care lest he fall.

Temptation must not overtake you except in a human way, that is, in a way that is not carried through into action. Human temptation is to think evil and to endure many temptations in the heart. Diabolical temptation, however, is to be overcome in the contest of temptation in action and to carry out evil. To desire a woman is human temptation; to commit adultery or fornication is diabolical. The same is to be understood of the other vices.

But God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can—understand, endure. God is said to be faithful [Col. 0563D] because whatever he promised to his faithful, he has fulfilled in action; he also fulfills it daily and will fulfill it. He promised heavenly kingdoms to those who love him; he will fulfill this, because he will give them to them. Therefore he does not permit them to be tempted beyond what human frailty can bear. But with the temptation he will also provide an outcome, that is, help, so that you may be able to endure; that is, he will bring about what human frailty can bear, namely, by delivering you more quickly from temptation and tribulation, as we read happened to blessed Abraham when he was delivered from the city of the Chaldeans, and likewise to the three boys in the furnace, and to Daniel when he was thrown into the lions’ den, and to an innumerable multitude of martyrs; or by granting endurance and victory within the temptation, [Col. 0564A] as he granted to blessed Job, and also to Peter on the cross, and to Andrew, and likewise to Lawrence upon the gridiron, and to many other martyrs. For who among human beings could believe that a mortal man could endure such things as Lawrence endured through God’s help? Therefore, whenever temptations and afflictions of this kind come upon us, we ought to recall these things and cast all our hope upon God, so that he himself may cause an outcome to come to us, either by delivering us more quickly or by granting endurance unto victory.

I speak as to prudent people; you yourselves judge, that is, discern, what I am saying: whether I speak what is true and good or not.

Is not the cup of blessing, which we bless, a sharing [Col. 0564B] in the blood of Christ? For this reason he first mentioned the cup, because afterward he was going to discuss the bread more fully. The cup of blessing is so called because it is blessed by priests at the altar. The cup itself is also called a sharing, as it were a participation, because all share from it and take a portion of the Lord’s blood, which it contains within itself. And is not the bread that we break at the altar a participation in the Lord’s body? Certainly. First it is consecrated and blessed by the priests and by the Holy Spirit; then, although it may already appear to be bread when it is broken, in truth it is the body of Christ. Whoever shares in this bread eats the body of Christ.

Because there is one bread—understand, Christ’s bread—and because we who eat that bread are one body of Christ, [Col. 0564C] the flesh that the Word of God the Father assumed in the virgin’s womb in the unity of his person, and the bread that is consecrated in the Church, are one body of Christ. For just as that flesh is the body of Christ, so this bread passes into the body of Christ; they are not two bodies but one body. For the fullness of divinity that was in him fills this bread also, and the very divinity of the Word, which fills heaven and earth and everything in them, fills the body of Christ, which is sanctified by many priests throughout the whole world, and causes it to be one body of Christ. And just as that bread and blood pass into the body of Christ, so all who worthily eat it in the Church are one body of Christ, as he himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6). Yet that flesh which he assumed, this bread, and the whole Church do not make three bodies of Christ, but one body. And just as those who share in the Lord’s body and blood become one body with him, so those who knowingly share in food sacrificed to idols exist as one body with the devil. All of us who share in one bread—that is, in the one body of Christ—and in the same one cup, or blood, that is, receive portions of it, become one body of Christ.

“Consider,” he says, that is, pay attention to, Israel according to the flesh, because it lives carnally and still offers carnal sacrifices. At the time when the Apostle said these things, the temple was still in Jerusalem, [Col. 0565A] in which Israel, living carnally, offered sacrifices to God. He calls it carnal because it wanted to observe the law carnally; or he calls it so in contrast with spiritual Israel, which no longer followed the ancient shadows, and of whose number the Apostle himself was. He wishes to show the Corinthians that just as those who ate what was offered on the altar were companions and participants of the altar, so these Corinthians, eating food sacrificed to idols, were companions of demons. Hence what follows: “Are not those who eat the sacrifices”—understand, the victims under the law—participants in the altar? Certainly they are. So you also, who eat meat consecrated to idols in an idol shrine, are participants in idols.

What then? Am I saying that something sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? I am not saying that it is something, because an idol is nothing, and what is offered to it is nothing. Whatever is not in him, or does not adhere to him who possesses being, is nothing. In this respect the idol is nothing because it has the likeness of a human being but is not a human being, since it possesses neither sensation nor movement; or because it is called a god but is not a god. It is said to be Hercules, but it is not. And just as the idol is nothing, so what is sacrificed to it is nothing.

But I do not want you to become companions of demons. They became companions of demons when they ate food sacrificed to idols and when they fulfilled the demons’ will. You cannot drink the cup—that is, the blood—of the Lord, understand, rightly, as it ought to be drunk, and the cup of demons—that is, rightly to be participants in the Lord’s body—and the table of demons, where sacrifices are poured out to idols. You cannot [Col. 0565C] eat the food of the demons’ table. Just as you cannot rightly serve two masters, so you cannot rightly do both: serve the devil, please Christ, and worthily receive his body.

Are we provoking the Lord? He joins himself to the Corinthians and speaks in the person of those who were saying: “Surely we imitate the Lord?” In this, then, that we go to the examples of idols and eat there with unbelievers whom we wish to win for Christ, we imitate the Lord, who came to the houses of tax collectors and sinners in order to have an opportunity to teach. “Surely we are stronger than he?” As if he were saying: “Surely you are stronger than he in this respect?” You are not. In this they wanted to be stronger than Christ, because they wanted to do what he did not do. For they went to the houses of pagans; we do not read that Christ went to the house of any Gentile. “All things”—understand, foods—are permitted for me to eat according to nature, but not all things are beneficial, that is, not all things are useful.

“All things are permitted for me,” but not all things build others up in the faith; rather, they destroy the simple through scandal.

Let no one seek only what is his own in this matter of eating everything, but what belongs to another, that is, what benefits the simpler people; just as Christ did not seek what was his own, but what was ours.

Whatever is sold in the meat market—literally, whatever comes into the market—eat, asking no questions for the sake of the conscience of the person whom you ask. The market is called *macellum* from *mactare*, “to slaughter,” because meat is slaughtered there. The Apostle therefore forbade them to ask anything about the meat, whether it had been consecrated to idols or not, because if they asked, the person questioned might say by way of insult and mockery: “All this meat that you see in the market has been dedicated to idols.” If one of the faithful heard this and afterward bought it, that pagan would mock him in his mind and conscience, saying: “Look what that Christian has done! He forbade me to offer victims to idols as though it were evil, but now he has bought meat consecrated to idols and eaten it as though it were holy. If he did not recognize some divine power in idols, he certainly would not do this. As long as I see him doing such things, I will not convert to Christianity.”

[Col. 0566B] If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you wish to go—understand, to his house—he neither commanded you to go nor forbade you, but granted permission. Dinner is called *coena* from the fellowship of those who eat, as it were, a common banquet and common food or refreshment. The Greeks call “common” κοινόν (*koinon*). Hence those who share together are called “communicants,” because they ate commonly, that is, together. Among the ancients it was customary to dine at the ninth hour, not in secret but openly, lest separateness produce luxury.

But if someone says, “This was sacrificed to idols,” that is, “It was consecrated to idols,” do not eat it for the sake of the conscience of the other person who judged it so, and of those standing around, lest they mock you, as was said above. “Why should my freedom”—by which I believe all things to be clean—“be judged,” that is, reproved, “by another’s conscience?” That is: If I eat everything, what concern is it of anyone else to reprove me, or what harm does his reproof do?

If, then, I share with thanksgiving—understand, thanksgiving to God—or eat, why am I blasphemed for giving thanks to God? He speaks in the person of those who were saying such things, as though the Apostle were adding: You ought not to say this. Even if you sanctify what you receive by the sign of the cross and by invoking the Lord’s name, you ought nevertheless not to eat it, because from this the Lord’s name is blasphemed, and you yourselves are blasphemed.

Do everything for the glory of God, that is, with invocation of God’s name, and with propriety, so that God may be glorified through you. We read somewhere that once a certain little man, overcome by excessive sadness, wanted to hang himself with a noose and said, “God, help me,” a phrase he habitually used. Blessed Paul the Apostle stood by and said: “Unhappy man, do you wish to tie yourself with a noose and presume to invoke the Lord’s name?” But because you invoked it, be freed from this present sadness and death, for everything will turn out prosperously for you.

Be without offense, that is, without scandal and reproach, to Jews, who curse idols, and to Gentiles, both faithful and unbelieving: “Just as I also please everyone in everything”—understand, in everything I do. Since the Apostle says elsewhere, “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1), one must ask why here he says that he pleases everyone in everything. The answer is that where he says, “If I were pleasing people,” he means by “people” heretics, unbelieving Jews, pagans, and persecutors. But here, where he says that he pleases everyone, one must understand good and religious men. “If,” he says, “I were pleasing unbelieving people—Nero, that is, heretics, unbelieving Jews, and persecutors—I would not be a servant of Christ, because I would have denied Christ. Yet although I do not please them, I do please good and religious people: not seeking what is useful only to me, because I do not receive food and clothing from you, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved.” Just as Christ did not seek what was his own, because he was not scourged, spat upon, afflicted, and killed for himself, but sought what was ours, so Paul was not content with his own salvation, because he did not seek what was useful only to himself, but what was useful to others, willingly enduring many adversities and insults for the salvation of others.

## CHAPTER XI

Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ; that is, just as I am an imitator of Christ, not seeking only what is useful to me but what is useful to another, so you also imitate me. For just as God the Father sent Christ so that his apostles might be imitators of him, so Christ sent us apostles so that we might be their imitators.

Now I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in every respect. He says this ironically: what he appears to affirm, he reproves and denies, as though he were saying: “I do not praise you, because you do not remember me and do not keep the commandments that I delivered to you.”

But I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man. Christ is the head of every man, that is, his ruler and source, because man was created by him who is the Word of God the Father; and not only according to his divinity, but also insofar as he is man and assumed our flesh, he is head and ruler of all human beings. The head of a woman, that is, the beginning and ruler of a woman, is a man, because she was made from his rib and subjected to his authority. But the head of Christ, that is, his source and beginning, is God the Father, because he has his origin and beginning from him, both according to his divinity and according to his humanity.

Every man who prays or prophesies in the Church—that is, teaches the prophets or explains them—with his head veiled dishonors [Col. 0567D] his head, that is, disgraces it. Or “prays” means reciting the Lord’s Prayer, and “prophesies” means reciting the Apostles’ Creed, in which Christ’s coming to judgment is prophesied. If a woman is not veiled—that is, if she does not wish to cover her head with a linen cloth—let her be shorn. Why did the Apostle command this? Because there was then a bad custom: women did not want to bind their hair or cover their heads. And lest the flowing of their hair provoke men to lustful love, he therefore commanded them to veil and bind their hair.

A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God. Man is the image of God because, just as all things took their origin from one God and were made by him, so the whole human race proceeded from one man, Adam. He is also the glory of God because God is glorified by having made rational man. Therefore he ought not to veil his head, so that he may show that he is not subject to a woman but has authority over her. A woman, however, is subject to a man, as what follows makes clear: “A woman is the glory of a man,” because she was made from him, or because she is subject to him, and in this the man has glory.

For the man, the first Adam, was not made from the woman, but the woman from the man. Indeed, the man Adam was not created for the woman, because the woman had not yet been created, but the woman was created for the man, that is, for the man’s assistance. Therefore—understand, so that she may recognize that a woman is under a man’s authority—a woman ought to have a veil over her head because of the angels. In Greek, *angelus* is called “messenger” in Latin. By this term the Apostle wishes to indicate bishops, priests, and all the orders of the altar, who ought to be angels by announcing to the people what they should seek and what they should avoid. Because of these angels, women standing in church ought to have veiled heads, lest one of them, looking toward the people, be captivated by love of their beauty.

Let us also explain it another way, following Augustine. When he says that a man ought not to veil his head because he is the image of God, but that a woman ought to veil her head because of the angels, we can understand “man” here in one way as any preacher who is spiritual and acts manfully, whose head is his wisdom. For just as the head governs the other limbs, so wisdom governs the mind. Such a man, the preacher, ought not to veil this head, namely wisdom, because he ought not to conceal or hide it, but to reveal it to others. By teaching, preaching, and devoting himself to good works, he ought to make himself worthy of imitation.

By “woman,” however, we should understand anyone in the Church who acts in a womanly and foolish manner. His or her head is ignorance and folly itself, which should not be openly displayed to others, lest the person make himself or herself worthy of imitation. Rather, it should be covered and referred to the angels—who are also called men—that is, to preachers, so that through their exhortation and teaching the person may be saved. Or such a person ought to veil his or her foolishness and ignorance because of preachers, since one ought to humble oneself before them.

Another interpretation: a human being consists of body, soul, and mind, which is also called the rational faculty of the soul. Although soul and mind are one, let us here distinguish the soul, which gives life to the body, from the mind, which governs the soul, because it distinguishes between good and evil, between vices and virtues. According to Augustine, by “man” here we should understand the rational faculty of our soul, that is, the mind, which is the image of God; for just as God knows the difference between good and evil, so does the mind according to its measure. The head of this man, that is, of the mind or rational faculty, which is one, is its good intention. This it ought not to veil, because it ought not to restrain it from contemplation of God. The more it understands about God, the more it ought to allow it to rise toward contemplation of God, until it reaches the point where what it now sees in hope and in a mirror it may one day see in reality, contemplating God as he is.

By “woman” we can understand the soul, whose head is its intention, by which it often directs itself beyond measure toward earthly things. This head, that is, this intention, we ought to veil, because we must restrain it so that it does not occupy itself beyond measure with earthly things. For the soul that gives life to the body often desires things beyond what is necessary, things in which the body takes delight while seeking earthly matters.

Nevertheless, neither was man created in God’s presence without woman—understand, nor was he created without her—nor was woman created without man in the Lord, that is, through the Lord.

For just as the woman Eve came from the man, that is, from Adam’s rib, so the man Cain came into being through a woman. But all things—understand, all classes of human beings—were created by God, namely Adam, Eve, and Cain; or “all things” means the bodies of men and the bodies of women, and likewise the souls of men and women.

You yourselves judge, that is, discern what I am about to say.

Hair was given to a woman in place of a veil, that is, as an adornment.

But if anyone appears to be contentious, saying, “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos,” and does not wish to obey our admonitions, we—believing Jews and apostles—do not have such a custom, that we should contend, because the law forbids anger and contention; nor does the Church of God, which possesses the Gospel, have such a custom.

But this I command, not praising—understand, not praising the fact—that you are contentious.

[Col. 0569C] First of all, when you come together in the Church, and the assembly of the faithful on the Lord’s days, I hear from those who belong to Chloe that there are divisions among you, that is, dissensions and disagreements; and in part I believe that what I hear is so.

For there must be heresies, that is, it is necessary that there be heresies, so that those among you who are approved in faith and good works may become manifest, and so that those who are imperfect and double-minded may also be revealed. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is necessary that scandals come” (Matt. 18), that is, it cannot be otherwise. And indeed heresies have provided great benefit to the holy Church—not in themselves, but because they stirred up teachers who were, as it were, asleep. For the holy Church would by no means have such a wealth of books and such knowledge [Col. 0569D] of God if heresies had not arisen. They roused Jerome, Augustine, Hilary, Gregory, and other holy teachers, who wrote much against heretics.

When you come together into one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s Supper. It is called the Lord’s Supper because on that very day the Savior supped with his disciples, completing the Passover of the Old Testament and handing over to the apostles the mystery of his body and blood.

The Corinthians—who are also called Achaeans—came to faith in Christ through the preaching of the Apostle Paul. Among the other things that the Lord did, they had received from him the sacrament of the Lord’s Supper. After Paul’s departure, in memory of the Lord’s Supper, every year on the Thursday before Easter they all assembled at the Church. The noble, powerful, and wealthy each came bringing bread and wine, which they gave to the priest so that he might consecrate the body and blood of the Lord. Once the mysteries had been consecrated by the Lord’s priest, each person took from the altar what he had brought. He quietly consumed it with his own household, so that those arriving later would not find anything to eat or with which to communicate; or he carried everything he had brought to his house, so that he might consume it with his household.

Because of this, there were great dissensions among them, which the false apostles had sown. Although the offerings of all had been consecrated with one blessing, each took his own, even though they ought to have been common, and thereby caused the greatest embarrassment [Col. 0570B] to those who, as often happens, had not brought anything, even if they possessed it, or to those who had nothing to bring. Many did this after they had already gorged themselves on food supplied by others.

The Apostle called this reception of the Eucharist the Lord’s Supper in one sense. In another sense, all the rich, powerful, and noble were also accustomed to assemble at the Church on that day and prepare meals and banquets for themselves in the Church, at its doors, and in its courtyards. They ate and drank and became drunk until evening in the sight of the poor and needy, who had no means to prepare similar food. They received nothing from those rich and powerful people, but waited fasting and shamefacedly for the time when it might please those rich and powerful people to have the body of Christ blessed by the priests, so that they could communicate.

But after those rich people had been filled with every kind of food and drink, even to vomiting, they finally received the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood, saying: “Christ handed his body and blood to his disciples, our teachers and masters, after other food had been consumed, and so we wish to receive it.” When the Apostle heard this, he wrote to them, among other things, what is now before us, wishing to rebuke them: “When you come together in the Church, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s Supper,” that is, you are not permitted to eat the Lord’s Supper in the way you eat it.

We can understand that the Apostle called it the Lord’s Supper in two ways: either the reception of the Eucharist, in which each person claimed for himself the portions he had brought, not sharing them with others, or receiving the same Eucharist after other food; or, in another way, he calls those preparations of banquets and meals the Lord’s Supper, which they consumed without charity, giving nothing from them to the poor.

The sacrament of Christ’s body is therefore called “supper” from the fellowship of the meal, because it ought to be common to all faithful and righteous people. For the whole Church is signified by one bread. Since we are one, we ought all to partake of one bread. Although that bread is brought from many places and consecrated by many priests throughout the whole world, the divinity that fills all things also fills it, making it one body of Christ; and all who worthily receive it make one body of Christ, not two, because he himself said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6).

Therefore whoever wishes to imitate the Lord’s Supper by receiving his body, or even by receiving other food, ought to use it communally, because the Lord’s Supper was common to all who reclined at table, not only to the good but also to the betrayer Judas. Yet someone may reasonably ask why our Savior, after the supper of his body and blood, handed the sacraments to the apostles, or from where the universal custom of the Church arose by which we are taught to receive these sacraments while fasting, since the apostles received them after they had already supped, and the Lord did not establish the practice as it is now observed.

The answer is that the apostles communicated after supper at that time because it was necessary first to complete that typical Passover and thus pass over to the sacraments of the true Passover. The Lord also did not himself establish that we should receive the sacraments while fasting, so that his apostles might have the honor of ordering something in the holy Church. After his Ascension, taught by the Holy Spirit, they ordered, in honor of so great and terrible a sacrament, that we should first be fortified by participation in the Lord’s Passion while fasting, and first be inwardly and outwardly sanctified by spiritual food; afterward the body should be refreshed with earthly dishes and lowly foods, with thanksgiving, moderation, and sobriety.

[Col. 0571C] For each person presumes to eat his own supper. This too can be understood in two ways: either the supper is understood as the sacrament of the Eucharist, which each person claimed for himself, or the preparation of banquets, both of which they consumed as their own, not sharing anything from them with the poor. We briefly said above that supper is called from the fellowship of those who eat, as it were, a common banquet and common food and refreshment. For the Greeks call “common” κοινόν (*koinon*). Hence those who share together are called “communicants,” because they eat commonly or together. Among the ancients it was customary to dine at the ninth hour, not in secret but openly, lest separateness produce luxury.

And one of you is hungry—namely, the person who, oppressed by poverty, lacks wheaten bread and wine to bring for consecration, from which he may communicate, or with which he may prepare a banquet for himself. But another, some rich and powerful person, is drunk and gorged both on other foods and also on the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood.

Do you not have houses, O Corinthians, in which to eat and drink ordinary food? Or do you despise the Church of God, that is, make it contemptible and regard it as nothing, preparing shameful banquets for yourselves in it, and do you put to shame—that is, cause embarrassment to—those who do not have food from which Christ’s body and blood may be consecrated, or with which they may prepare a supper for themselves in the Church, as you do, who abound in riches? [Col. 0572A] What shall I say to you, O Corinthians? That is, what can I say to you because of my excessive sorrow? I praise you—understand, in those matters in which you do what is good; but in this I do not praise you. You despise the Church of God, and, already drunk in this manner, you receive the Lord’s body and put the faces of the poor to shame.

For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that is, the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood: how you ought to receive it, just as he revealed it to me, so I delivered it to you. Moreover, he also revealed what that sacrament signifies, as he will say in what follows, when he was traveling to Damascus and was struck blind. Or the Lord revealed this to him then, among other things. Or it was when he was placed in a spiritual ecstasy while he was in the temple. Finally, he delivered it to the Corinthians when he stayed with them for a year and six months.

For the Lord Jesus, on the night on which he was betrayed—that is, on the very night when he was to be betrayed by Judas—took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said to his disciples: Once the solemn rites of the ancient Passover, which were performed every year in remembrance of the ancient liberation of God’s people from Egypt, had been completed, he immediately passed over to the new Passover, as we said above, which he left to his Church to celebrate in memory of his Passion and our redemption. He himself broke the bread that he had offered to the disciples, to show that the breaking and Passion of his body would not come without his own will, as he had earlier said: “I have power to lay down my life.”

Take and eat: this is my body, which will be handed over for you. Just as Christ’s flesh, which he assumed in the virgin’s womb, is truly his body and was killed for our salvation, so the bread that Christ handed to his disciples and to all predestined for eternal life, and which priests daily consecrate in the Church through the power of divinity that fills it, is truly the body of Christ. Those flesh and that bread do not constitute two bodies, but together make one true body of Christ, so completely that while the bread is broken and eaten, Christ is sacrificed and eaten, yet remains whole and alive.

And just as that body which he laid down upon the cross was sacrificed for our salvation and redemption, so this bread is offered daily to God for our salvation and redemption. Although it appears to be bread, it is the body of Christ. For the Lord and our Redeemer, taking account of our weakness because he knew that we are frail in sinning, handed this sacrament over to us so that, since he can no longer die while we sin daily, we might have a true sacrifice by which we could be cleansed.

Therefore, because they make one body and are offered for our redemption, he said: “This is my body, which will be handed over for you,” and he added: “Do this,” that is, sanctify this body in remembrance of me, namely, of my Passion and of your redemption, because I redeemed you with my blood. In leaving this saving sacrament to all unbelievers, the Lord acted like any person who, approaching death, leaves some precious gift to a friend, saying: “Keep this carefully with you in remembrance of me, so that whenever you see it, you may remember me.” If that friend receives the gift of his dearest friend and has loved him with all his heart, he cannot fail to grieve for him and mourn his death whenever he sees the gift left to him.

Similarly, whenever we approach to consecrate or receive the sacrament of the eternal gift that the Lord, about to suffer, left to us to hold in remembrance of him, we ought to approach with fear, compunction of heart, and every reverence, recalling how greatly he loved us, who offered himself for us in order to redeem us.

Likewise the cup—understand, he handed it to them—after he had supped, saying: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood.” That is, the cup that I hand to you signifies the New Testament, as Fulgentius says; or it confirms the New Testament in my blood, or through my blood. He calls it the cup of the New Testament to distinguish it from the Old Testament, which was confirmed by the blood of goats and bulls, as is found in Exodus, where Moses, having collected the blood of goats in a cup or dish, sprinkled the same people with it, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that the Lord has commanded for you.” That is: This blood is the witness of God’s words and promises to you, and the witness of your words, by which you promised that you would be obedient to him.

Likewise the New Testament, that is, the Gospel, in which the promises of our redemption and of the heavenly homeland are contained, was confirmed by the blood of Christ’s Passion, which is celebrated daily in the Church. For every testament is confirmed by the death of the testator. As for what he added—“Do this,” or “sanctify it whenever you drink, in remembrance of me”—the sense is the same as was stated above concerning the body.

For whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he himself comes to judgment. We proclaim the Lord’s death, already celebrated for our redemption, in two ways: either by celebrating the mystery itself, in which we repeat his Passion, or by preaching it to others. We ought to do both, receiving and preaching.

This too must be known: the flesh of our Savior was for the salvation of our body, but his blood was poured out for our soul, because the seat of the soul is located in the blood. In remembrance of this we receive his body and blood, because, in order to save and redeem the whole human being, he permitted his blood to be poured out.

Therefore whoever eats this bread and drinks the cup—that is, the blood of the Lord—unworthily, that is, whoever receives the Lord’s blood and body unworthily, will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord; that is, he will pay eternal penalties for it, unless he expiates it by worthy repentance and other good works.

“Unworthily” means without observing the proper order: namely, whoever celebrates or receives that mystery in a manner different from that handed down by the holy Fathers; or whoever believes that there is no difference between that body of Christ and other foods; or whoever, stained by more serious crimes, presumes to receive it. Whoever eats and drinks it unworthily in this way, as we have said, receives it and will therefore pay the penalty for it. The Apostle therefore explains how we ought to receive it.

Let a person examine himself, and then eat from that bread, that is, from the Lord’s body, and drink from the cup, that is, from the Lord’s blood. Let him examine himself, that is, scrutinize himself and determine whether he is worthy or not, and make himself approved, lest he receive judgment and condemnation from the very thing from which others receive a remedy, receiving it unworthily, as Judas the betrayer did.

For while the other apostles received that terrible sacrament for their own remedy and salvation, he who was unworthy of so great a mystery received it for his own condemnation. The devil had previously held him through suggestion and temptation, but afterward entered him more fully, so that he could think or do nothing except what the devil’s will was. For the Evangelist says that after the morsel Satan immediately entered into him, so that he might complete, at the devil’s prompting, the evil which he had planned at the devil’s instigation.

Whoever eats and drinks unworthily, as we said above, eats and drinks judgment upon himself—that is, he receives it to his own condemnation—not discerning the body of the Lord, that is, not distinguishing it from other foods. We must approach that awesome sacrament with fear and trembling, so that the mind may know that it must show reverence to him whose body [Col. 0574C] it approaches in order to receive.

Therefore—that is, because you presume to receive the sacrament of salvation unworthily—there are among you, O Corinthians, many who are weak, that is, sick and feeble, that is, feverish; and many sleep—not the sleep of peace and rest, but the death of condemnation. That is, they have died an eternal death on account of this sin. Wishing to demonstrate that those who receive the Lord’s body unworthily thereby receive judgment and condemnation, he shows that some among the Corinthians had already suffered punishment in the present life: they had received it thoughtlessly and irreverently, and consequently had been afflicted with many fevers and illnesses, while some had even died. Thus, by their example, the others might learn that they must not receive the Lord’s body unworthily and negligently.

[Col. 0574D] But if we judged ourselves—that is, examined and tested our life to see whether we were worthy or not—and if we ourselves corrected our errors, we would certainly not be judged, that is, we would not be condemned by Christ, either in this age or in the age to come.

But while we are being judged—not merely in a few cases, namely, in those who become weak and feverish in the present life and also in those who die—we are chastised by the Lord, and through them we are scourged in the body, so that, terrified by that very fear, we may not be eternally condemned with this world, that is, with unbelievers and lovers of this world. For there is no difference between an unbeliever and one who, irreverently defiled by all the grave sins, [Col. 0575A] presumes to approach the Lord’s table; indeed, he is worse than that person and deserving of a greater punishment, because it is better not to have known the way of truth than, after acknowledging it, to turn back.

Therefore, my brothers, when you assemble in the Church to eat the body and blood of Christ, wait for one another, so that the offering of many may be celebrated together and all may share together from one bread. For that offering is one bread and ought to be common to all.

If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—that is, let the person who is impatient and unwilling to fast with the others eat earthly bread at home—so that you may not assemble for judgment, that is, so that you may not receive the body of Christ reprehensibly, to your condemnation. As for the remaining matters—that is, [Col. 0575B] the things that remain disordered—I shall arrange them when I come.

## CHAPTER XII

Concerning spiritual matters—that is, mysteries—I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers; that is, I do not want to leave you ignorant.

You know that when you were Gentiles. The Apostle recalls to the Corinthians the conduct of their former life, so that, by considering it, they may grow into a new way of life. For just as, while living as Gentiles, they burned with zeal for falsehood and error, since that worship was nothing, so now that they had become Christians they ought to obey the divine commandments with fervent devotion.

“Gentiles” (*gentes*, or *gentiles*) are those who do not change from the error of their fathers, in which they were born, to the religion of a better life. Hence a people that [Col. 0575C] remains as it was born is called a *gens*. These are the pagans, who do not approach the worship of God. He now calls them “Gentiles,” not because they were pagans at the time when he said these things, but because they had been so before learning the faith. This is what he says: “when you were Gentiles,” with the implied addition, “and now you are no longer so.”

The word “people” (*gens*) is also used in a good sense, as in: “not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God” (John XI).

You were being led away to mute idols. The implied sense is: “you were going.” They are called “idols” (*simulacra*) because they are said to imitate something: they imitate a human being, although they are not human; a horse, although they are not a horse; and other things of this kind. They are therefore called mute because, as the Psalmist says, “they have a mouth, but they will not speak; eyes, but they will not see” (Psalm CXXXIII). For there is no spirit in their mouths. If any word [Col. 0575D] is heard from idols, it must be attributed to the deception of demons, not to the sensory capacity of the idols.

You were driven to worship these idols by demons, diviners, and foolish philosophers. The meaning is this: just as, when you were Gentiles, you frequented the temples of demons without resistance, being led wherever you were led, so now, while you are guided by the Holy Spirit according to sound doctrine, approach the Church of God and strive to obey the commandments that bring salvation with complete humility.

By saying “as you were led,” he shows that they had displayed such great reverence toward idols that they in no way recoiled from their worship, regardless of the persons by whom they were urged, advised, or led to it. In the same way, now that they have been converted, he admonishes them to love God and [Col. 0576A] not to despise his fellow apostles, who care for their salvation.

Therefore—that is, because you have come to know God, and because I do not want you to remain ignorant of spiritual mysteries—I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God, that is, no one who possesses the Holy Spirit and speaks through the Holy Spirit, who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, says, “Jesus is accursed” (*anathema Jesu*).

In the decrees of the emperor Justinian, *anathema* is called separation from God. It is also used in the canons for a curse. It is used also for killing, as the Apostle himself says in the Letter to the Romans (chapter IX): “I could wish myself accursed for my brothers,” that is, “I could wish to be killed for them according to the flesh.” It is also used for an abomination. Here, however, it means separation.

Thus no one inspired by the Spirit of God [Col. 0576B] says to Jesus himself, “You are accursed”—that is, “separated from God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and inferior in some respect.” Certain mad heretics did not fear to say this in their frenzy; therefore they were struck by the Church with anathema, that is, separation from God.

And no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit. In sacred Scripture, “to say” sometimes means ordinary speech, as in: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VII). Sometimes it refers to the reality and deed itself, as King Hezekiah says to Isaiah: “There was no word”—that is, no matter—“in my house that I did not show them” (Isaiah XXXIX).

So here too it refers to the reality and deed. “No one,” he says, “can say”—that is, confess with heart and mouth, practice deeds worthy of faith, love Jesus, and affirm him as Lord—[Col. 0576C] unless he has been inwardly taught by the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the one who says that Jesus is Lord is the one who believes that he is coequal and co-omnipotent with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and confesses him by keeping his commandments, through which true love is proved.

We may also state this briefly as a conclusion: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord’”—with the implied qualification, “as he ought to be called, in heart, mouth, and deed”—unless he has been enlightened by the Holy Spirit.

There are different kinds of gifts (*divisiones gratiarum*)—the implied qualification is, not different kinds of merits—but the same Holy Spirit remains ever one and undivided in all. It should be noted that he does not say, “There are divisions of merits,” but “of gifts,” because God’s gifts are freely given and are not attributed to human merits. Hence he says to the Romans: “Who has first given to him”—that is, [Col. 0576D] to God—“his faith or anything else, so that it might be repaid to him?” (Romans XI).

For the Holy Spirit remains in himself one and the same, that is, infinite, undivided, and inseparable with the Father and the Son. But his gifts are divided because they are not bestowed equally upon all. Therefore we must acknowledge that, although God is everywhere through the power of his divinity, he is not everywhere through the grace of indwelling; and where he dwells by grace, he does not dwell equally.

Just as the sea is infinite, and those who come to it draw water according to the capacity and differences of their vessels, while the sea is neither emptied nor exhausted; and just as many lamps are lit from one lamp, while that lamp itself does not diminish—so the Holy Spirit, being infinite, distributes his grace to the righteous [Col. 0577A] according to what seems good to him. Yet he remains almighty in his infinity: he gives as much as he wishes, to whom he wishes, when he wishes, and how he wishes, and nevertheless possesses no less, because he gives to no one anything outside himself.

There are also different kinds of ministries. For example, bishops, priests, deacons, and the other orders are appointed as ministers of the Church through the distribution of the Holy Spirit, not by a human decision of their own, but through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit. Yet the same Lord—the implied qualification is, remains undivided in all.

There are also different kinds of workings, because one works great deeds through the Holy Spirit, another intermediate deeds, and another small deeds. Yet it is the same God who works all things in all.

The one whom he earlier called “the Spirit” he now [Col. 0577B] calls “Lord” and “God.” By saying the same thing three times, he shows that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit, but he does not thereby separate the Father and the Son. For those whose power of nature is one and whose substance is one also have one undivided operation. This God works all good things in all people.

These words remove human arrogance, since without the Holy Spirit our weakness cannot perform either great or small good deeds. The Apostle more profoundly warns that no ranks are to be established within the Trinity: he places the Holy Spirit first, the Lord Christ second, and God the Father third, while the one God distributes his gifts and remains undivided in himself.

But to each one—the implied qualification is, each of the faithful—the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good: for the benefit both of the person who [Col. 0577C] receives the gift of the Holy Spirit and of others, who are either taught by that person or instructed by his example in a better life and stirred to praise God, as the Lord commands: “Let your light shine before people” (Matthew V), and so forth.

The “manifestation of the Spirit” is understood as the gift itself, which makes it manifest to the person that it has been given for his benefit, so that he may believe rightly and live holily, and so that others may derive benefit from him. Alternatively, it is called the manifestation of the Spirit because wherever he is present through his gifts, he is immediately manifested through the work of righteousness. Hence it is written: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

To one, through the Spirit, is given a message of wisdom. He now begins to explain the divisions of gifts [Col. 0577D] and ministries that are given through the Holy Spirit.

Wisdom is understood as consisting in avoiding evils and pursuing good things, while knowledge consists in arranging and ordering human affairs. For cultivating estates or fields, prudently building a house, and properly ordering a household appear to belong to knowledge.

Alternatively, wisdom pertains to eternal knowledge, by which we believe that God is a Trinity in persons and a unity in substance; knowledge, however, concerns human affairs, as we said above.

Or wisdom, according to Gregory, is present when someone reads the books of the Old and New Testaments, understands them, and expounds them for the benefit of others, as Jerome, Augustine, Hilary, and Gregory himself did. Knowledge is present when their expositions [Col. 0578A] are read and understood, and when the Old or New Testament is transmitted according to them.

There is also wisdom by which a person abstains from an evil deed, while knowledge is present when he abstains from an evil thought. Thus, whether we possess wisdom concerning divine things or knowledge concerning human affairs, we receive it not from ourselves but from the grace of the Holy Spirit, who gives it.

When he says “according to the same Spirit,” this means nothing other than as if he had said: “To another is given a message of knowledge according to the will of that same Holy Spirit,” or “through that same Spirit.”

To another—the implied phrase is, “is given”—faith in the same Spirit, that is, through the same Spirit. The Lord speaks in the Gospel concerning the person of the Father: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent.” And the Apostle says that faith is given through the Holy Spirit.

From this it is understood [Col. 0578B] that what the Father gives through the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit himself also gives with the Father and the Son, because he has one power and one operation with them. Therefore the faith by which we believe in God is given by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. It is not naturally present in a human being but is given by God; for if it were natural, everyone would possess faith.

To another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit. By “gifts of healings” he means the gift by which the sick and infirm are healed.

To another, the working of powers, in casting out demons and performing mighty deeds; to another, miracles; to another, prophecy, by which someone filled with the Holy Spirit predicts future events or expounds the books of the prophets; to another, the discernment of spirits, so that a person may know who is speaking from the Holy Spirit and who from the human or evil spirit.

Such was the case with the girl who brought [Col. 0578C] great profit to her masters, from whom Paul cast out a pythonic spirit; and such was the case with magicians and enchanters.

To another, kinds of tongues—that is, varieties of speech—as occurred among the apostles and believers at the beginning of the faith; to another, the interpretation of tongues, as in the case of Jerome, who translated the divine Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin.

All these things that we have enumerated, and also more than we have enumerated, are worked by one and the same Spirit, for the benefit, namely, of the whole Church. In this the Father and the Son are understood, because their operation is inseparable. He divides his gifts among the individual elect as he wishes, yet he himself is not divided, because he is almighty.

For just as the body is one and has many members, [Col. 0578D] and so forth, so also is Christ—that is, with the Church forming one body. By these words he teaches that no one should be puffed up against another, because even if someone is not a great member, he is nevertheless a small member of the Church.

And just as all the members, whether large or small, honorable or dishonorable, form the human body, so people of different degrees of merit build one Church and constitute one body of Christ. For the Church itself is understood together with Christ, who is the head of the Church, and the Church is his body.

For in one Spirit—the implied qualification is, the Holy Spirit—of whom it is written: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew III), and: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John III)—we were all baptized into one body. That is, we were baptized for this purpose: that we might be one [Col. 0579A] body with Christ, our head. And we were all given to drink of one Spirit.

It is as if he had said: “We were given to drink,” or “we drank one Spirit,” because at the time of baptism we all received one Holy Spirit.

For the body is not one member but many. One member does not make a body; rather, many members joined together by sinews do so. In the same way, all believers—whether they are exalted in the merit of their life or of lesser stature—form one body, joined together by the power of the Holy Spirit.

If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,” would it for that reason not be of the body? This must be read as a question, with the implied answer: “Certainly it is of the body.”

Christ is the head of his body, that is, of the Church. [Col. 0579B] The eyes of this body are to be understood as the apostles, concerning whom it is said: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine” (Genesis XLIX). They are also the preachers who provide spiritual things for themselves and others.

The ears are the faithful hearers. The nostrils are those who possess the power of discernment between the fragrances of virtues and the stench of vices. The mouth consists of those who pour forth the divine words for others, that is, teachers. The hands are those who work so that others may live. The feet are those who run about in secular affairs for the benefit of the rest.

If such a foot should say, “I am not a hand because I have nothing to give, or because I cannot work so as to provide others with their livelihood; therefore I am not part of Christ’s body,” would it for that reason not be of the body? The implied answer is: “Certainly it is part of Christ’s body.”

The same must be understood of the ear and the eye. Even if a good hearer says, “I am not an eye”—that is, “a preacher”—and therefore “I am not part of Christ’s body,” [Col. 0579C] he will not for that reason cease to be part of Christ’s body. He will be a member of the Church.

But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he wished. By these words he removes presumption, so that no one may regard God’s gift as his own merit. Whoever is an eye in the Church was made an eye by God, not by himself. The same is to be understood of the other members. Hence he says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians IV).

And if all the members—the implied phrase is, all the members—were one member, where would the body be? The body consists not of one member but of a variety of members. And if everyone were an ear or an eye—that is, merely hearers or merely preachers—how would there be a body of the [Col. 0579D] Church, since it would not consist of a variety of members?

The eye cannot say to the hand, “I do not need your work,” because every preacher needs sustenance from the labor of those represented by the hands. Nor can the head say to the feet, “You are not necessary to me.” In the same way, one who presides over subjects cannot say to his subjects in their temporal activities, when he needs their work, “You are not necessary to me.”

But rather, the members of the body that seem to be weaker—such as the feet and hands, which perform the more menial services—are necessary, because they work for the whole body. And we surround with greater honor [Col. 0580A] those members of the body that we consider less honorable.

The less honorable members to which we give greater honor are the hands and feet, to which we apply ornaments such as shoes and bracelets. And our dishonorable members possess greater propriety.

Our dishonorable members are the private parts, which we are ashamed to see naked and to which we provide greater propriety by clothing them in garments of various colors.

Our honorable members—that is, the eyes, nostrils, and other such parts—need no ornament. But God tempered, that is, fashioned, the body, giving honor to the member that lacked it—the implied qualification is, giving it greater honor. He supplied external honor to the member through the addition of clothing and ornaments, because it does not possess that honor inherently through the beauty of nature.

[Col. 0580B] So that there may be no schism—that is, division—in the body, with some members beautiful and others remaining dishonorable, but so that the whole body may now be honorable, both by nature and through the grace of ornament; rather, the members should be mutually concerned for one another, each for the other, just as the eye sees for the whole body and the foot walks for the whole body, and so forth.

You are the body of Christ and members derived from a member. Just as the elbow, hand, and fingers proceed from the shoulder, and the feet and joints from the thigh, so members are taken from a member—that is, they depend upon those set over them.

First, God placed apostles in the Church. They were placed in the Church in Christ’s stead, as the Apostle says: [Col. 0580C] “We beseech you through Christ”—that is, “in Christ’s stead”—“be reconciled to God.”

In their place, bishops were appointed. But the apostles, by the Lord’s command, were compelled to pass from kingdom to kingdom, whereas bishops are commanded by canonical authority to remain in their own Churches for the benefit of those entrusted to them.

He calls “prophets” those who proclaim future events, such as Agabus and the apostles themselves, or those who explain the words of the prophets. “Teachers” are those who instruct the little ones. “Powers” are those who cast out demons and perform other miracles. “Gifts of healings” are those who restore the sick to health. “Helps” are those who assist others by word or deed. “Governments” are found among rulers and kings, bishops and leaders. “Kinds of tongues” occurred at the beginning of the faith.

[Col. 0580D] Do all interpret the Scriptures, as Jerome did?

But strive after the better gifts. By these words the Apostle shows that the things mentioned above are good: prophecy, teaching, the casting out of demons, and so forth. But the things that follow are better insofar as the benefit of the elect is concerned. For through the things listed above, only God’s power is demonstrated, through whose name and invocation they are performed. Through these things that follow—that is, charity, faith, and hope—the righteousness of a person is established.

The Corinthians boasted as though they possessed the fullness of righteousness because some of them cast out demons and bestowed the gift of healing upon the sick. But the Apostle shows that better things were lacking in them, and that for this reason they were not yet perfect. Therefore he [Col. 0581A] exhorts them, saying: “Strive after the better gifts,” that is, “strive after the better gifts of grace.”

For the gifts mentioned above may be possessed by the wicked as well as by the good, just as Judas was an apostle. Caiaphas, like Balaam, prophesied although he was evil. Many will say on the day of judgment: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, perform many mighty works in your name, and cast out demons?” (Matthew VII). But they will hear: “Truly I tell you, I do not know you” (Matthew XXV).

And I show you an even more excellent way. By this, charity is understood, in which commandment the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew XXII). It becomes a way for us because through it we reach the heavenly homeland. He now begins to explain its greatness, saying:

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0581B] If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I am useless.

These words depend upon the Apostle’s preceding words, where he says: “Strive after the better gifts” (1 Corinthians XII), and so forth.

If I speak in the tongues of all human beings—namely, the seventy-two tongues that were divided at the building of the tower—and if I speak also in the tongues of angels, but do not have charity, that is, love of God and neighbor, I am nothing.

When he says that he speaks in the tongues of angels, he is understood to have said this to heighten the force of what he wished to demonstrate, namely, the power of charity. For angels have neither tongue nor palate nor teeth with which to form words, since they are spirits.

When they appear to human beings, having assumed aerial bodies, they speak according to [Col. 0581C] the language of those to whom they appear. For their speaking to God means nothing other than being in his presence; and God’s speaking to them means nothing other than the presence of his countenance, which they enjoy, as they attend to what he wishes to reveal to them. Their voice in praise of the Creator is itself the inward wonder of contemplation.

Angels also speak with one another ineffably. Yet their mutual conversation is the concord of a good will; there is no need for words to sound where, in the contemplation of God, the good will of all the angels is harmonious.

Thus the Apostle says: “Even if I could speak in the tongues of angels, it would profit me nothing without charity.”

[Col. 0581D] Angels may also be understood as highly educated speakers, who, instructed in the liberal arts, express in polished words what they know; “human beings” may refer to those who speak simply.

Whether someone argues simply, as many seek to do because such speech can edify everyone, or eloquently, as many desire, if he does not have charity he becomes like resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. For just as bronze resounds or a cymbal clangs without benefiting itself, because it provides no benefit to itself, so it is with a person who speaks in tongues without charity.

Indeed, just as bronze resounds and contributes nothing to itself but helps—that is, delights—those who hear it, so it is with a tongue deprived of charity.

Bronze and a cymbal do not sound by themselves unless they are struck by someone or moved by the impact of something. In the same way, the person who speaks in tongues does not speak from himself; rather, the power of the Holy Spirit speaks through him.

[Col. 0582A] But the one who practices the commandment of charity acts with God’s help.

And if I have prophecy—that is, if I proclaim future events, as Balaam prophesied concerning Christ: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and this one shall rise from Israel” (Numbers XXIV)—and if I know all mysteries, that is, the secrets of the Old and New Testaments, and all knowledge, that is, knowledge both of divine and human affairs; and if I have all faith, that is, perfect and complete faith, which the Lord compares to a mustard seed—not because of its smallness, but because of its fervor, since when crushed it reveals the strength that it possesses; so faith, when crushed by adversity, shows what strength it has—

so that I could move mountains from one place to another, or cast out demons from those possessed; if I do not have charity—that is, [Col. 0582B] love of God and neighbor—I am nothing. That is, it will provide me with no benefit.

It is understood that some of the Corinthians performed these deeds by invoking God and therefore regarded themselves as perfect. But he exhorts them toward what is primary, namely, charity.

And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, according to the Lord’s command: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor” (Matthew XIX); and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, as Lawrence was burned; but if I do not do this for the sake of love—namely, love of God and neighbor—it profits me nothing. The Apostle uses himself as a representative of everyone.

Charity is patient.

How can charity, [Col. 0582C] which is a virtue, be patient? He seems to speak as though he were speaking about a thing possessing a soul. For charity is a virtue that does not suffer in itself, and therefore is not itself patient. Consequently, by “charity” we must understand a person who possesses charity.

Thus the person who has charity is patient, enduring adversity, because through tribulations he knows how to reach the joys of the kingdom.
