It is kind—that is, very good—because it not only does not repay evil for good, but moreover returns good for evil, feeding and giving drink to an enemy.

Charity does not envy. Above he said: “Strive after the better gifts,” that is, “make an effort to pursue them.” Here, however, he says: “It does not envy,” that is, “it does not pursue” in the evil sense. It envies no one and is not tormented by another’s happiness.

It does not act perversely, that is, it does nothing crookedly. Anything done outside uprightness, because it is crooked, [Col. 0582D] may be called *perperam*—“perversely”—as an adverb.

It is not puffed up, that is, it is not exalted and does not raise itself into pride.

It is not ambitious. To “ambire” means to desire, and anyone filled with charity does not desire or seek to exercise power over others, because he does not wish to appear greater than the rest.

It does not seek its own—that is, what is useful only to itself, but what is useful to others.

Alternatively, “it is patient” and “does not seek its own” may mean that it does not seek vengeance, because it does not repay enemies in kind.

A question arises here. Since John says, “God is charity” (1 John IV), why does the Apostle say, “Charity does not seek its own”? This can be understood in three ways.

[Col. 0583A] Charity is to be understood one way according to John’s words and another way according to Paul’s.

According to John, charity means God himself, who pours charity into the hearts of the faithful, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “God’s charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans V).

According to Paul, however, “charity” means a person who possesses charity, who does not seek only what is his own and what is useful to himself, but what is useful to others.

For even God himself, who is charity, does not seek what is his own. When he came into the world through the mystery of the incarnation, he did not seek what belonged to him—that is, he did not seek the righteous but sinners, who were held under the power of the devil. Hence he himself says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke V).

Let us also state it [Col. 0583B] in a third way: Charity—that is, God himself—when coming into the world did not seek what belonged to him. What was his own? That he should be worshiped, glorified, and revered by every creature as God, the Creator of all.

But he did not seek these things that were his and that suited him. He did not seek honor, kingship, or fear from human beings, but what belonged to thieves, murderers, and evildoers: spitting, blows to the face, slaps, mockery, scourging, the cross, and death.

And just as he did not seek what was his own, so we too ought not to seek what is ours, but what belongs to others.

It is not provoked—that is, even if it has been injured, it is not stirred to anger or rage; it is not driven to vengeance, so as to repay evil with evil.

It does not think evil, that is, it not only [Col. 0583C] does not do evil, but does not even think of harming another.

It does not rejoice over iniquity, but rather grieves when it sees anyone fall through some crime. It rejoices with the truth—that is, with works of righteousness—or even with the person who is faithful in truth and not hypocritically.

It bears all things—the implied qualification is, it patiently bears all adversities. It believes all things contained in the Old and New Testaments, or all things promised by God to the elect in the future kingdom, and believes them to be true.

Therefore it hopes for all things, because unless it believed, it would not hope. For hope is the expectation of future goods, and in consideration of them it endures every adversity.

Charity never fails—that is, it never slips away from a person who possesses it and never falls.

Or, “prophecies will be abolished.” Prophecy is speech concerning the [Col. 0583D] future. When the future arrives, there will no longer be a need for it to be prophesied. Let one example stand for all: Christ is prophesied as coming for judgment. When he comes, it will no longer be necessary for this prophecy to be recited. The same is to be understood of the rest.

Or, “tongues will cease,” because, just as before the tower of Babel there was one Hebrew language, as some teachers think, so after judgment that one language will remain. Indeed, the diversity of languages involves variety, and where there is variety, there is dissension. In the kingdom of the saints there will be no dissension; therefore there will be no variety of languages.

Or, “knowledge will be destroyed.” Present knowledge, which is now possessed only in part, will be destroyed—or rather, changed for the better—when the fullness of knowledge arrives, because present knowledge is imperfect.

[Col. 0584A] For we know in part, not in whole, concerning God and the blessedness of the saints, and we prophesy in part. Since what we know is partial, what we prophesy is also partial.

But when what is perfect has come—that is, what is complete and whole—when the elect contemplate God with unveiled face, just as he is, then what is partial will be as though emptied and annihilated. As John says: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him just as he is” (1 John III).

When I was a child, I spoke as a child.

He gives the comparison of natural growth and introduces a human example, by which he shows that the knowledge we [Col. 0584B] possess in the present is like infancy, while the knowledge of the future will be like the strength of adulthood, possessing perfect fullness.

“When I was a child,” he says, “I spoke as a child,” stammering and producing incomplete words; “I understood as a child,” namely, things that were trivial and unsuitable; “I thought as a child,” namely, about places and matters suitable for laughter.

But when I became a man and began to understand more perfectly, I put away—that is, I despised—the things that belonged to childhood, because I began to shun what I had previously desired.

In this life, therefore, we are children in comparison with the future life. For just as this life is imperfect, so also is its knowledge.

We now see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. The comparison made above leads to this: just as someone sees his own face in a mirror [Col. 0584C] and, departing from it, forgets what he looked like, so we too perceive only a little of God and of the future life. And this is “in an enigma,” that is, in obscurity, because, being carnal, we cannot grasp clearly those things that are purely spiritual. But then—that is, in the future—face to face: that is, being present, we shall see God who is present. Now I know God in part; but then I shall know fully, just as I also have been known—now by God, who knows me entirely, inwardly and outwardly. It must be understood, however, that “as” is not always used to indicate equality. We are known by God in one way, and know him in another: he knows all things as God, whereas we know him as creatures, through his gift. Nevertheless, just as he knows us wholly, so we shall know him wholly. He has known us [Col. 0584D] in the manner proper to God; we shall know him in the manner suited to glorified creatures.

Now faith, hope, and charity remain—these three. At present these three virtues are joined to one another and are so closely united during the time of this life that one cannot stand without the others. For whoever believes in God hopes to receive what he has promised; and the more one hopes, the more one believes in him, and therefore possesses charity, because one loves him and one’s neighbor. For the things that we believe have been promised to us, we also hope to receive. Delighting in these things, we burn more ardently with charity. Indeed, we cannot truly believe unless we hope for the things that have been promised; nor shall we be able to endure the promises if firm fidelity is lacking in faith. Nor will the fruit of hope, or the stability of faith, be present unless the perfect charity of Christ is in us—a charity that assists faith so that it may precede, and strengthens hope through expectation.

But greater than these—namely, than faith and hope—is charity. Surely the Son of God became man and the Redeemer of the world through charity, that is, through love, and not through our merits: he loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance. Through this love God the Father sent that same Son into the world; this love the Holy Spirit pours into the hearts of the elect.

Faith is that by which we believe that God is threefold in persons and one in substance, and also believe the mysteries of the incarnation and passion of the Son of God. Hope is the expectation of future blessings, which we have not yet seen and have not yet obtained in reality. Charity is that by which we love God and our neighbor.

When the elect see face to face the God in whom are the rewards for which they wait, nothing will remain for them to believe concerning the future, nor will they have anything further to hope for. But through charity they will love the giver of every good work; and they will love their neighbor, rejoicing in them as in themselves. Charity is therefore greater than faith and hope because, when those cease and fail, it will remain. In the present age it exists together with them, but it alone will endure forever. It alone will lead us to Christ; it alone will enjoy everlasting joy and the most immediate presence of almighty God, and so forth.

## SERMON AND TREATISE ON THE FOREGOING

Let us now learn, with the Apostle as our teacher, what kind and how great charity is—not by a way of the feet, but by a way of conduct. “If I speak,” he says, “with the tongues of men and of angels” (1 Cor. XIII), and so forth.

We should understand “the tongues of men and of angels” as signifying the empty eloquence of certain men, who carefully and eloquently express whatever they wish. But although they argue elegantly and at length, they undertake the task of teaching more from the vanity of pleasing than from the charity of giving help—not in order to teach others, but to display themselves as learned; not to seek improvement, but applause from their hearers. If they transfer all the diligence of knowledge to a deceitful tongue and are more eager to cultivate eloquence than their lives, lifted up by the pride of vain loquacity, they desire their words to be praised rather than put into practice. They are concerned not with the holiness of their deeds, but with the beauty of their polished speech.

Are such men not rightly compared with sounding brass or a clanging cymbal? Like sounding brass or a cymbal, they prefer to make every splendid thing resound rather than do it; or they are ashamed to differ from their own preaching by living otherwise. In order somehow to obscure the disgracefulness of their conduct, they do not cease to preach honorable things—not so that their hearers may advance through their preaching, but so that they themselves may appear to care about what they preach.

But let us see what the Apostle adds to this: “If I have prophecy,” he says, “and know all mysteries” (ibid.), and so forth. This is not said as though someone could not possess certain good things without charity, but because those things do no good to their possessors if they fall away from charity. Charity itself is necessary for this reason also: so that all good things may benefit those who possess the highest good, namely charity. Charity itself will remain perfect when it has led all who persevere in it to the vision of God.

Prophecy, however, and knowledge or understanding of all mysteries, and faith itself, together with other such things—which are judged necessary not only for the perfection of the faithful but also for their weakness—will not be needed by those who are advancing toward that perfection of the saints in which they are rooted in charity, once things incomparably better and more perfect have succeeded them. Prophecy will not be needed there, since it will have led them to the fulfillment of what it promised would come; nor will knowledge be needed, which, like a lamp in the night of this age, illuminates the faithful, when the living sun shines perpetually in the day of that life. Nor will knowledge of mysteries, or faith itself, be necessary, when Christian perfection has reached, in reality, the things that were signified by mystery and believed through faith.

Charity, however, is necessary here: it separates us from the devil, purifies us from sin, and reconciles us to God. There it will be perfect, when it has joined the perfected to God, from whom it was given to them.

Again, as he enlarges upon the praise of divine charity, the Apostle adds: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (ibid.). And rightly so. For if at that final examination it is asked not what we do but for what purpose we do it, what will almsgiving or the handing over of one’s own body to death benefit those who do not have charity? Charity, therefore, must be possessed; it must be pursued. Without it, neither almsgiving, nor the mortification or killing of the body, nor all the things mentioned above, nor any other good, leads anyone to salvation, because no good action or suffering can benefit us if it does not arise from faith working through love.

Therefore nothing of damnable sin can remain in such people, and nothing good will be lacking to those in whom charity is present—the cleansing of every impurity and the mother of every good. For “charity is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (ibid.). In those in whom it exists, it distributes all these qualities that it possesses.

And what can be more perfect in this life than those who abound in such virtues, with charity reigning within them? Therefore, when we see people firmly established in great patience, presenting an unshaken breast against raging evils; enriched by an abundance of holy kindness and wishing to share their good with everyone; not being consumed by the flames of burning envy; not acting wrongly, but dealing simply with all to whom the unity of charity ought to be shown; not being inflated by any pride of destructive vanity; not coveting anything that belongs to others through criminal desire; not seeking what is their own, but what belongs to the good of pious fellowship; thinking no evil of anyone, however provoked by injuries; rejoicing not over anyone’s wickedness but over the truth [Al.: virtue]; bearing all disturbances and all troublesome people with a firmly established tranquility of mind; believing without fear the punishments divinely threatened after this life; hoping with joy for the promised rewards; desiring the revelation of the children of God and enduring steadfastly—when, therefore, we see people able to do these and similar good things, let us recognize that they are not able to do what they ardently wish and accomplish through the greatness of their own virtue, but through the gift of that charity which is not from us, but has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. V).

## CHAPTER XIV

“Pursue charity,” that is, follow after it. This word signifies the continuation of an undertaking, as also in: “Pursuing hospitality” (Rom. XII). “Be zealous for spiritual things”—that is, for spiritual gifts; imitate them, strive to seek the spiritual gifts that are given through the Holy Spirit, so that you may exercise powers by speaking in tongues and casting out demons. But be especially zealous and eager to prophesy—that is, to expound openly the prophets and the other books of the Old and New Testaments. Whoever does this is a prophet, because through the charity by which he gives counsel to others, he possesses the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets.

For whoever speaks in a tongue—meaning an unknown and foreign tongue, or in an obscure manner of speech—does not speak to human beings, because what he says is not understood, but to God, who knows all tongues, and knows even those that have not been uttered. No one hears—that is, none of those standing by understands—what he says. For the Spirit—understand, the Holy Spirit—speaks mysteries, that is, hidden things, through the person in whom he dwells, to whom he has imparted knowledge and understanding of that language. Those who hear, however, do not know the language, and so those same mysteries remain hidden from them.

But whoever prophesies—that is, whoever teaches the prophets and other Scriptures in clear speech—speaks to human beings for the edification of their understanding, because they understand what is put forth by the teacher and learn the solution of questions. He also gives exhortation, because he exhorts others to desire the ability to explain and to be able to expound for others; and he gives consolation, which they receive in a language known to them, whereas others are exalted in one that is unknown.

Whoever speaks in a tongue—understand, one unknown to others, or in an obscure manner of speech—edifies himself and not others, because he alone understands what he is saying. But whoever prophesies, speaking openly by explaining the prophets, edifies the Church of God, that is, the assembly of the faithful. So that the Corinthians would not say, “You begrudge us, Apostle Paul, the speaking of tongues,” the same Apostle adds:

“I want you all to speak in tongues”—understand, various tongues—“but I would rather have you prophesy,” that is, bring the obscure sayings of the sacred Scriptures into the light by explaining them openly. For the one who prophesies—that is, who teaches openly by explaining the prophets—is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets in plain speech what he says in another tongue, so that the Church may receive edification from his interpretation. If the one who speaks in tongues can interpret, he will not be less than the one who explains the prophets, because he likewise edifies the Church. For that is greater which benefits everyone.

But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I be to you? Understand: if I speak in an unknown tongue, unless I speak to you either in revelation—that is, in interpretation and clear speech—or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching. These four expressions signify one thing.

Yet even lifeless things that give sound—whether flute or lyre, that is, a *rota*—if they do not produce distinctions among their sounds, so that the sounds are distributed according to the higher or lower pitch of the voice, how will what is played on the flute or what is played on the lyre be recognized? He says this about musical instruments, because just as the sound of the lyre and flute is unpleasant unless it resounds distinctly, so the voice of a preacher or teacher offers no benefit and does not delight the hearers if they do not understand what he says.

For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? It was the custom among the Jews to sound trumpets at the beginnings of the months and at the solemnity of the Feast of Tabernacles. Hence it is also called the feast of trumpets, as the Psalmist says: “Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemnity” (Ps. LXXX). It was also customary to sound trumpets when war was impending, and there was a difference in the sound between the call to war and the summons to a festival. If, therefore, someone heard trumpets sounding confusedly, how could he know for what purpose he ought to prepare himself? So, when a teacher speaks in an unknown tongue or obscurely, how will the hearer be able to understand? It is as though he were saying: Just as, when the trumpet’s voice is uncertain, no one can distinguish whether it is the voice of a solemnity or of war, so, if you begin to speak in various tongues, your hearers will not understand your preaching. Your speech, however, must be understood, so that it can prepare Christ’s soldiers for spiritual battle.

For you will be speaking into the air—that is, pointlessly.

There are, so to speak, many kinds of tongues—that is, however many kinds of tongues there are in this world—and nothing is without a voice. It will be so for the hearer if you speak in a tongue unknown to him, as though you were uttering all tongues, because just as speaking everything to him would be of no benefit, so you offer no benefit by speaking in one or two unknown tongues. In those tongues nothing is without a voice, and yet their voice is not grasped by those who do not possess knowledge of the language. Therefore speech that is not understood is uttered pointlessly.

If, then, I do not know the power, or meaning, of the voice that is heard, I shall be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak, and the one who speaks to me will be a barbarian. For example: I am a Greek and you are a Hebrew; if I begin to speak Greek to you, I will seem a barbarian to you. Likewise, if you speak Hebrew to me, you will seem a barbarian to me. In another case: I recite the Creed in Greek because I found it written that way, and I am a Latin, not a Greek; I am a barbarian to you. Again, if you have learned something of the Greek language and likewise begin to speak, I, who at first seemed a barbarian to you, perceive you as something like a barbarian to me.

So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts—that is, since you are eager for spiritual gifts for the edification of the Church—seek to possess those gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that you may abound, bearing fruit for others. For whoever speaks in a tongue—understand, an obscure and unknown one—should pray that he may interpret: that is, he should ask God to give him the power of interpretation, so that what he says in one tongue he may be able to explain to others in another.

For if I pray in a tongue—understand, an unknown one—and in an obscure manner of speech, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit. That is, the power of my soul—namely, the soul itself, which gives life to the body—utters the word, but the understanding of my soul is without any benefit, because I do not understand what I say. That “spirit” means “soul” is shown by the Evangelist, who says of the Lord: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John XIX), that is, his soul.

It is clear that our mind, or understanding, is ignorant when the tongue speaks what it does not know, as Latin people are accustomed to sing in Greek, delighted by the sound of the words, though nevertheless unaware of what they are saying. Such singing is without the fruit of understanding, which cannot be possessed by one who does not know what he is saying.

What, then, is there for me to do? Understand: what is useful and necessary? “I will pray with the spirit,” that is, I will speak with the soul; “I will pray also with the mind,” that is, I will speak with understanding. For those things must be said that are both usefully uttered and clearly understood.

But if you bless with the spirit, who occupies the place of the unlearned person? That is, if, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, you teach well and speak well to your hearers in an unknown tongue, who will take the place of—or fill the role of—the person who hears you but does not understand your words? *Idios* means “one’s own”; hence an *idiot* is one who knows only his own language, the language in which he was born and raised.

If, therefore, such a person stands before you while you are solemnly celebrating the mystery of the Mass, or delivering a sermon, or even giving a blessing, how will he say “Amen” to your blessing when he does not know what you are saying? That is, how will he answer with the confirming word “Amen” when he, who knows only his own language, does not understand that you are speaking in that barbarous tongue? No one else will be present in his place who knows what you are saying and can answer, “Amen”—that is, “What you have said is true,” or “Let it be so.” For he does not know where the conclusion of the speech comes, since he does not know what you are saying.

You indeed give thanks well—understand, to God—in a language known to you; but the other person, who does not know what you are saying, is not edified. And so that the Corinthians would not say of the Apostle that he himself lacked a variety of languages and did not want us to possess it, he added:

“I give thanks to God that I speak in the language of all of you.” There are five differences of the Greek language, as a careful reader can discover in the writings of Priscian. The Apostle knew all of these and several others. “In the church I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so that I may instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue”—understand, one unknown to others, or in an obscure manner of speech.

Take it simply: “I would rather,” he says, “speak five words in the assembly of the faithful so that others may understand, than ten thousand without benefit to others.” He declares it more useful to speak a few words in clear language, which everyone understands, than to deliver a lengthy speech in obscurity.

Do not become children in your understanding. The person who is childish in understanding—that is, who acts childishly—is one who seeks to speak in an obscure and polished manner for the sake of boasting. But “be children in malice,” that is, be free from malice, as children are. “But be mature in understanding.” A person is mature in understanding who seeks another’s benefit as much as his own.

“With other tongues and other lips I will speak to this people” [Col. 0590B]: the expressions “tongues” and “lips” signify one thing. This is written in the book of Isaiah (Isa. XXVIII), which is now called the Law, and this prophecy was spoken beforehand concerning the New Testament.

Under the Law of Moses, sinners were punished in various ways at the Lord’s command. God speaks in another tongue in the Gospel, because he does not command sinners to be killed but urges them to repentance, saying: “Repent” (Matt. III), and so forth. There he commended circumcision; in the Gospel, baptism, saying (Matt. XXVIII): “Go, baptize all nations.” There he commended the Sabbath; here, the Lord’s Day and rest from sins. There, sacrifices of animals; here, the mystery of his own body and blood. Yet even then the unbelieving Jews did not listen to the Lord—that is, they did not obey him.

Or otherwise, according to the Apostle’s preceding discussion: On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon the believers in Jerusalem, and they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance. Jews were present from every nation under heaven. Those who had been predestined, struck with amazement, believed in Christ and were saved. The others, although they heard such marvelous things, did not wish to believe in Christ through his apostles speaking in tongues.

Tongues are for a sign—that is, they are a miracle—not for believers who know that nothing is impossible for God, but for unbelievers who doubt God’s power. For example, Paul spoke in all tongues not for his own sake, but for the sake of unbelievers from different nations whom he wished to win for Christ. Prophecies, however—that is, interpretations of the Scriptures—are not for unbelievers who do not listen to the Scriptures, but for believers who love them.

If, therefore, the whole Church comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, each in his own language, while the unlearned enter—that is, those content with their own language—and unbelievers, or pagans, enter as well, will they not say, “What are you doing? Are you insane?” That is, “Why have you been turned to madness or frenzy?” This is because you are all speaking confusedly, and they do not understand what you are saying.

But if all prophesy—that is, explain the Scriptures of the prophets—and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, one content only with rustic speech, he is convicted by all—understand, convicted as an unbeliever or an unlearned person—and is judged by all; it is shown that, unless he repents, he is to be condemned. The secrets of his heart are made manifest: that is, his evil thoughts and vices, which he supposes those preachers do not know. For while they argue against vices, these become manifest in him, because he says, “In truth, I recognize all these things as existing in me.”

Blessed Augustine reports in one place that once, while he was delivering a sermon to the people, a wicked man entered; and immediately, without his intending it, his sermon turned against that man’s vices. The man, realizing that God had revealed him to the bishop, was converted, and by repenting obtained salvation. Likewise, in the life of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, it is read that the Holy Spirit so arranged his sermon that it shook the consciences of all through his words, as though all the hearers had disclosed their consciences to him or he had them written out before him [Col. 0591B]. Falling on his face, the unbeliever or unlearned person, humbling himself, will worship God, declaring that God truly is among you, since he has also revealed his conscience to you.

Each of you has a psalm about which he ought to speak; he has teaching—that is, an exposition of the books; he has an apocalypse—that is, a revelation manifested by God in his heart, through which he is able to understand the divine Scriptures; he has a tongue to utter; and he has an interpretation, saying, “This speech is said in that language, and this is how it is explained in ours.”

If someone speaks in a tongue—namely, an unknown one—let the address be made by two, or at most three. That is, let it be made by three at the most, and let them speak in turn—not all at once—so that they do not appear insane if they all begin together. And let one interpret: that is, let there be one interpreter who explains and interprets their obscure language. Or he commands them to speak in turn so that the interpreter may interpret each one individually. The meaning is this: In the assembly, let one, or two, or three speak—not all at once, but in turn—so that whatever each one says may be made clear to those present by the interpreter.

But if there is no interpreter, let the one who has the unknown tongue be silent—understand, the teacher who possesses it—and let him speak to himself and to God by praying and reading, since all the words of tongues are known to God.

Let the prophets—that is, the interpreters—speak, whether two or three. For “in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.” But let the others—understand, the prophets and teachers, or interpreters of the prophets—judge whether anything more or less needs to be said, and let them also discern whether those who teach are teaching according to the truth of the faith.

But if something else, or something different from what the speaker is saying, is revealed by the Holy Spirit to another who is sitting, let the one who was speaking first be silent for a while. He speaks according to the custom of the Jews, who sat in their synagogues in this order: scribes, Pharisees, and teachers of the Law sat in chairs; those of lesser rank sat on benches and stools. The common people and ordinary persons sat on the floor and on mats. Hence the Apostle says: If something is revealed to the one sitting in the chair, different from what the interpreter is saying, or to one of those sitting on benches or on the floor, let the one who was speaking previously be silent.

For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be exhorted. Just as teachers are not endowed with equal knowledge, so hearers are shown to differ in their capacity for understanding. Therefore those who are thoroughly instructed should teach hearers who are thoroughly capable of understanding; those who are less instructed should instruct those who are less capable. Thus each may prophesy—that is, teach one by one—so that one speaks after another and the preaching may be completed in due order by all.

The spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets. The Holy Spirit who spoke through Isaiah, Jeremiah, [Col. 0592B] and the other prophets of the Old Testament, and also through the prophets of the New Testament—such as the apostles and interpreters of the prophets, who are rightly called prophets—in some manner is subject to all of them, because he does not suddenly compel them to burst into speech, as an evil spirit does with the possessed and frenzied. Rather, he grants their authority over when they should speak and when they should be silent.

For example, a prophet—that is, any preacher—wishes to deliver a sermon to the people, just as Jerome might wish to explain the book of one of the prophets. The Spirit is present with him so that he may instruct and speak through him when he begins to speak; yet he does not immediately cause him to burst into speech like a madman as soon as he touches the book. And rightly the same Holy Spirit who once dwelt in the prophets is said to be in their interpreters, since otherwise they would not have been able to explain the words of the Holy Spirit or bring their obscurity into the light.

Alternatively, if we read the phrase in the plural—“the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets”—we must understand “spirits” as the gifts of the Holy Spirit: tongues, powers, the casting out of demons, wisdom, counsel, and the rest. These gifts are subject to the elect in such a way that they exercise them when they wish and, when they wish, keep them hidden as it were. These words make it understood that, although many teachers may be present at the same time and know through the Holy Spirit what they ought to say, they are not driven by that same Holy Spirit in such a way that, while one is speaking, the others are unable to remain silent.

For God is not a God of dissension but of peace, because God taught peace and not dissension. When one person, swelling up against another, attempted to speak while the other was still speaking, he caused dissension, and this was detestable to God. As in all the churches, so also I teach you—understand, you as well—that one, or two, or certainly three should teach in the assembly, and in turn, so that one may interpret; and if there is no interpreter, they should remain silent.

Let women be silent in the church, lest they sow error, as Eve, the first woman, did (Gen. II); but they ought to be subject to men, because woman was taken from man, not man from woman, and because the man was deceived through her. As the Law also says—that is, God says through Genesis: “You shall be under the authority of the man” (Gen. III).

Did the word of God proceed from you, O Corinthians [Col. 0593A]—understand, to others? The Corinthians were puffed up, as though the other nations had believed in Christ unwillingly, following their example, and as though the faith had been spread by them. Therefore the Apostle says: “Did the word of God”—that is, the faith of Christ or his Gospel—“proceed from you to other nations?” They were also inflamed by the thought that the salvation which is in Christ had been promised through the patriarchs and prophets to them alone. This is what he says: “Or did the word of God come to you alone?”

If anyone thinks he is a prophet—that is, a wise teacher and interpreter of the Scriptures—or spiritual, that is, able to grasp spiritual things, let him recognize what I am writing, because they are the Lord’s commandments; that is, let him understand and approve that this is the Lord’s commandment. The pseudo-apostles spoke from themselves and from the devil, but the Apostle Paul and the other servants of God put forward the commandments of God. By these words, therefore, he touches those who, for the sake of temporal profits and human desires, taught earthly rather than divine things.

But if anyone is ignorant—understand, of these commandments of the Lord—he will be ignored; that is, if anyone rejects or does not approve these commandments of the Lord, he will be rejected and will not be approved by the Lord on the day of judgment.

Therefore, my faithful brothers, be zealous—that is, strive and love—to prophesy, that is, to interpret Scripture and explain it openly. And if anyone wishes or is able to speak in tongues, do not forbid him, provided that he has an interpreter. But let everything among you be done properly, that is, with decorum.

## CHAPTER XV

Now I make known to you, brothers—that is, I call back to your memory—the Gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, and through which you are also being saved. The Apostle had been among the Corinthians for one year and six months, preaching the Gospel to them. But after his departure, pseudo-apostles entered among them who denied that Christ had been born of a virgin, had suffered, and had been raised from the dead; they also denied that there would be a general resurrection. For this reason the Apostle, compelled by the situation, recapitulates what he had taught them while present.

Hence he says: “I make known to you the Gospel that you received”—or accepted—from me; or, “that you have received as something entrusted to you”—“in which you also stand.” In every faithful congregation there are two peoples: the perfect and the imperfect. Here he addresses the perfect in faith. Then, turning against the imperfect, he adds: “In what manner I preached to you, if you hold fast to it, unless you believed in vain.”

The wording of this verse seems to convey somewhat less meaning, because it sounds more elegantly in Greek. It should also be noted that it must be read interrogatively and reproachfully. It should therefore be expressed as follows: “What benefit did you receive from what I preached to you, if now, deceived by the pseudo-apostles, you hold something else, except that you believed in vain or pointlessly, in that you have departed from the faith?” Thus he says: “In what manner, or with what benefit, did I preach the word of faith to you, if you hold it”—understand, now in a different way from what you then heard—“unless you believed in vain? Did you acquire, when I preached, a useless faith and not a true one?” It is not so, because I taught what was true and not false, and a true faith and belief. Therefore, as to how or with what benefit I preached to you, if you hold it otherwise, I know only that you believed in vain. One believes in vain who later departs from the faith itself. In what follows he now explains what he preached.

For I delivered to you first—that is, at the beginning of my preaching—what I also received, understand, from Christ: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. He recalls the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which foretold Christ’s future passion. Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter, and like a lamb he will not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). And because he was buried—understand, according to the Scriptures—the prophet says: “He will give the wicked Jews for his burial, and a rich man for his death” (ibid.); and again: “His tomb will be glorious,” he says (Isa. XI). No one doubts that he died and was buried.

And because he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up.” And because he was seen by Cephas: *Cephas* is Syriac and Hebrew; *Peter* is Greek and Latin. Although the Evangelists do not specify a definite place where he appeared to him, it must nevertheless be believed that he appeared to him. And afterward to the eleven: namely, on the eighth day after his resurrection, when Thomas was with the others.

Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once—that is, believers. This too is true, although the Evangelists do not mention it. Of these, many remain in the body even to the present—understand, people whom you can question if you wish. But some have fallen asleep—that is, have died. He says this because they will be raised by Christ from the sleep of death more easily than someone can be awakened by his companion from sleep in bed.

Then he was seen by James, who had promised at the Lord’s Supper that he would neither eat nor drink until he saw Christ risen from the dead. Then he was seen by all the apostles, on the mountain where he had appointed them to go, and when he ascended to heaven.

Last of all, as though to one born prematurely, he appeared also to me. One born prematurely is someone who is born outside the proper time of birth: either before the suitable time, before he ought to be born, or afterward. Julius Caesar was such a one, who was born after the proper time, with hair, after his mother’s womb had been cut open. In the same way the Apostle was, in a certain sense, born prematurely, because he was born in Christ after the appropriate time: he was not called by him while he was still in the flesh, but when Christ had already been placed at the right hand of the Father.

Or he is called premature because, just as one despairs of the life of a prematurely born child, so the faithful despaired of Paul’s life when he was persecuting them. Indeed, he would have incurred everlasting death unless Christ had come to his aid. Christ appeared to him from heaven after a considerable time had passed since his ascension, when Paul was blinded on the road as he was going to Damascus (Acts IX), and afterward when he was praying in the temple.

For I am the least of the apostles. He says this out of humility, as Matthew also calls himself a tax collector. Or he is least in time and calling, because he was called last [Col. 0595A]. But he is greatest in labor, dignity, and preaching, as he himself makes clear in what follows, where he says: “For I labored more abundantly than all of them.”

But by the grace of God I am what I am—that is, I believe that my being an apostle and preacher of the Gospel is wholly the work of God’s grace. And his grace toward me was not ineffective. Through free will he cooperated with God’s grace. Nevertheless, grace preceded him, so that he might will, and followed him, so that he might be able to accomplish what they willed; and he joined his will to God’s will. Therefore he is worthy of reward.

But I labored more abundantly than all of them, because they preached only to the Jews and within particular provinces. Paul, however, preached both to Jews and Gentiles, traversing nearly the whole world [Col. 0595B], either personally or through his letters. Or he labored more than they in this respect: they received their sustenance from preaching, according to the Gospel; Paul, however, did not use this right, but lived by the labor of his hands.

Or he labored more because they preached to Jews—who possessed the Scriptures by which vices were condemned and virtues encouraged—and, since they performed miracles, their teaching was readily accepted, because the Jews already possessed knowledge of the one God. Paul, however, preached to Gentiles who knew neither vices nor virtues. They preached to Jews who possessed prophecy concerning Christ, and the things preached about Christ agreed with that prophecy. Paul preached to Gentiles who possessed no prophecy concerning Christ.

But not I alone, he implies, labored; rather, the grace of God labored with me. Now, if Christ is preached through miracles, by touching and enlightening the hearts of the hearers so that they believe, and by supplying me with the word of preaching—

Whether, then, it was I or they—that is, the other apostles—we preached, he implies, as I have mentioned above: that Christ died, rose again, ascended into heaven, and so forth.

But we are also found to be false witnesses of God—that is, witnesses bearing testimony on God’s behalf, yet found to be false—because we have testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, he implies, if, as some say, the dead do not rise.

In these passages the Apostle uses dialectical syllogisms, and appears to deny what he affirms. For the apostles are not false witnesses, since Christ did rise and the dead will rise. And if [Col. 0595D] it is as some of you say, you are still in your sins, because you were baptized in faith in the death and resurrection of Christ so that you might receive forgiveness of sins. Therefore, if you do not believe that Christ rose, you remain in your sins, because baptism is of no benefit except in faith in Christ.

Therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ—that is, those among you who believed in Christ and have already died—have also perished, he implies, if matters are as you suppose. By denying such things, he speaks dialectically.

If in this life alone we have hope in Christ—that is, and not in another life that will exist after the resurrection—we are more pitiable, or more wretched, than all human beings, the unbelievers. For they enjoy this life [Col. 0596A], indulge themselves, feast, become drunk, rejoice even when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things. We, by contrast, who believe in Christ, fast, keep vigil, abstain from wives, avoid unlawful things, and endure many adversities and hardships for Christ.

But the saints hope in Christ in this life, believing that they have been cleansed by him from their sins; and in the other life they hope for resurrection and everlasting blessedness. They are so firmly established in this hope as though they already possessed all of it in reality.

But now—that is, in this age in which we are—Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep.

He calls Christ the firstfruits of those who sleep because he himself is the head of all the elect. He was the first to rise by his own power, and he rose from the dead so as never again to die [Col. 0596B]. For just as through one man, Adam, came the death of soul and body, so through one man, Christ, came the resurrection of the dead, both good and evil.

But each in his own order. He says this lest they should say—and perhaps they did say—“Why did the righteous who died before Christ not rise before him?” For he by whose power some of them rose, and all human beings will rise, had to be the firstfruits of those who sleep—that is, he had to rise first, as he did. Then all in their own order, he implies: some have already risen, while others will rise, after Christ, who rose first.

Then those who belong to Christ, at his coming. Some manuscripts read: “Then those who belong to Christ, who believed at his coming” [Col. 0596C]. But this is written incorrectly. “Then,” he says, “those who belong to Christ will rise at his coming, when he comes for judgment.” Those belong to Christ who believe in him and who believed before his coming.

Then the end—that is, the end of the world—will come. For the resurrection will be the end of the world, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father. God the Father delivered all things to the Son, as he himself says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matthew 11). Paul says that the end of the world will come when the Son delivers the kingdom to his Father, who is God.

But because this kingdom is delivered by the Father to the Son and by the Son to the Father in such a way that it is possessed jointly by both, it should be stated briefly that the Father delivered all things to the human Son, assumed from the Word, so that, just as divinity and humanity are one person in the Son, so also there might be one possession [Col. 0596D]. He delivered all things to that man when he willed him to be received by his Only-Begotten Son.

The same Son will deliver the kingdom to God the Father at the end, when he has led his elect, whom he acquired with his own blood, to the contemplation and knowledge of God the Father, showing that God the Father reigns together with himself and the Holy Spirit. Then they will clearly know how God the Father, with his Only-Begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, reigns without end, immeasurable and almighty; and how the Trinity exists in persons and unity in the substance of divinity.

Or certainly the Son will deliver the kingdom to God the Father—that is, all the elect—because he himself will appear in human form at the judgment. After condemning the reprobate by a just sentence, he will present all the elect with himself before the Father’s face [Col. 0597A], so that those who saw the human judge with a pure conscience may contemplate the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

When he has abolished every principality, he implies, then the end will come. In the divine spirits, the archangels rule over the angels, as their very names indicate, and the remaining names of the orders make clear. Human beings also rule over human beings. But then there will be one ruler, God the Trinity, because all power of creatures—among angels and human beings—will cease. Fear will cease, and perfect charity will reign. There will no longer be any disagreement between rulers and subjects. Therefore the one God will be the ruler of all good spirits and all the righteous, when what is written has been fulfilled: “And the Lord alone will reign on that day.” Hence what follows:

[Col. 0597B] “But he must reign until he has placed all his enemies beneath his feet.”

“Until” is sometimes used in place of “so that,” as in the Psalm where it says: “So our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Psalm 122), meaning “so that he may have mercy on us.” “Until” is also used in place of “and,” as in the Gospel concerning Mary and Joseph: “And he did not know her until she had borne” [a child], meaning “and she bore her firstborn son” (Matthew 1).

It is used to mean “always” and the continuation of time, as in this passage. The meaning is: “The Son must reign until God the Father places all his enemies beneath his feet”—that is to say, “The Son will reign forever, because God the Father will forever subject his enemies beneath his feet.”

If by the head of Christ his divinity is understood, as the Apostle says, “The head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11), then by his feet his humanity may appropriately be understood, since it appeared to be humbled like feet. His enemies, or unbelievers, are subjected to him in two ways: either they are converted, by God’s inspiration, and believe in Christ, who suffered in human form, died, and escaped from the underworld through the glory of his resurrection; or, persisting in their hardness, they will at least recognize him as judge on the day of judgment, of good and evil, and will see themselves condemned by his just judgment to the punishments of torment.

Finally, death, the enemy, will be destroyed, because after all have risen, death will be destroyed in the resurrection itself. After its destruction, the human race will suffer no hostility of the present life. For where there is eternal life, death will have no place [Col. 0597D].

“But he subjected all things beneath his feet”—that is, beneath the feet of the Son. He subjected all things that have been and will be: hostile and friendly, earthly and spiritual, or heavenly; he subjected them to his power. When he says this, he implies, the Psalmist David is speaking.

“All things have been subjected to him”—without doubt, except the one who subjected all things to him. For it is not the Father who ought to be subject to the Son, but the Son who ought to be subject to the Father, insofar as he is man. For insofar as he is divine, he is of one power and one divinity with the Father, just as he is of one essence with him.

But when all things have been subjected to him—that is, to the Son—then the Son himself will also be subject to him, that is, to God the Father, who subjected all things to him. Indeed, all things are now subject to the Son [Col. 0598A], but many do not attend to this, nor consider that they are held under his power by a certain ignorance. On the day of judgment, however, no one will be ignorant of it.

Then the Son himself will also be subject to God the Father—namely, the head together with his body, which is the Church. Hence it is said elsewhere: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring,” that is, “you belong to the one Christ,” or “you are one Christ.”

“So that God may be all in all”: that is, God will be all things in all the elect, because he will be their satisfaction and joy, gladness and exultation, and life. As he himself says through the prophet: “I will be their God” (Leviticus 25)—that is, “I will be that from which they are satisfied and that in which they rejoice.”

For the presence of God will be so fully enjoyed, and all the elect will be so filled with every good and every virtue, that each will possess all good things in him. At that time God will be patience in each person, as he was in Job; obedience, as in Abraham; gentleness, in Moses; virginity, in Daniel; wisdom, as in Solomon; and the other gifts that are now distributed among the elect, but which then each will possess in their entirety.

Otherwise—that is, if the dead do not rise—what will those do who are baptized for the dead?

There were some among the Corinthians who did not believe in the resurrection, while others believed that those who died baptized would rise; but they believed that those who died without baptism either would not rise or would rise in an evil condition. If a relative of one of these people had departed from the world without the grace of baptism, a living person would be baptized in his name, and they thought that baptism performed by the living benefited the dead.

The Apostle mentions this practice [Col. 0598C], not to approve that something of this kind benefited the dead, but, by this example, to persuade those who did not believe in the resurrection and to demonstrate that belief. For if they did not believe in the resurrection, they would certainly not baptize the living for the dead.

The meaning is: “O Corinthians, if the resurrection did not first occur in Christ and in certain others who rose with him, and if it will not occur generally for everyone, what does this practice among you mean, in which the living are baptized for the dead?”

As we have said, they did this for two reasons: either because they thought that no one would rise unless baptized, or because they believed that no one would live happily after the resurrection unless baptized, as the truth actually teaches.

“Why are we apostles also in danger?”—that is, why do we suffer dangers every hour, in hunger, thirst, and the other hardships?

[Col. 0598D] “Every day I die, by your glory, brothers.”

The Apostle swears so that his hearers may believe him more readily, and says: “I swear by your glory”—not by the glory that you will possess, but by that which I will possess through the labor I have undertaken among you. And if he died every day, how did he live?

“Every day,” he says, “I die”—that is, I endure the dangers of death. If we say, “Every day,” he says, “I die for your glory,” as some manuscripts read, it must be understood that he endured the dangers of death so that they might be glorified in the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

The meaning, referring back to what precedes, is: “Even if you do not wish to advance, I nevertheless possess the reward of my labor.” Hence he also says: “By that glory I swear which I have in [Col. 0599A] Christ Jesus.” Secure and firm in hope, he spoke as though already possessing what he was to obtain in the future.

“If, as a man, I fought with beasts at Ephesus”—that is, if I fought as far as a human being can fight, or endured as much as a human being can endure—“what benefit is there for me if the dead do not rise?”

In this passage he calls “beasts” human beings living in a beastlike manner, who stirred up a popular riot against him at Ephesus on account of the idol of Diana, whose worship the Apostle preached must be destroyed (Acts 19). All the labor of the saints is directed toward this: that they may deserve to receive the glory of the resurrection.

“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”

This was the voice of the despairing Jews when captivity under Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar was imminent [Col. 0599B], and it is a testimony expressed by Isaiah. Placed in the crisis of death, they said: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah 22). The Apostle applies this to those who doubted the resurrection.

“And if it is as you suppose,” he says—that is, if there is no future resurrection—“let us eat and drink now, because tomorrow we shall die, and afterward we shall suffer no evil.” Indeed, if there were no resurrection of the dead, one ought to eat and drink.

“Do not be deceived”—that is, do not be misled by the pseudo-apostles who deny the resurrection, nor by the devil, who wishes to deceive you.

“Evil conversations corrupt good morals.” By these words the Apostle shows that conversations with wicked and dissolute people can overthrow a good purpose. Constant association with evil conversation corrupts the mind. Therefore such people must be avoided, because evil conversations corrupt and deprave a good life and honorable, modest conduct; for the speech of evil people is the corruption of what is good.

“Awake righteously, and do not sin.”

Some manuscripts read: “Awake, righteous ones,” as though he were commanding those who are righteous to awake. But this is written incorrectly, because those who are righteous do not need to be admonished to awaken from the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of error.

He spoke adverbially: “Awake righteously”—you who are asleep in error and unbelief and do not believe in the resurrection—and “do not sin,” so that, conducting yourselves righteously in good works, you may be able to rise to glory.

“For some have ignorance of God”—that is, some of you are ignorant of the words of God, which are spoken in the Gospel: “The hour will come when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth” (John 5), and so forth.

“I speak this for your reverence”—that is, for your benefit—so that you may fear God and, by fearing him, love him. Cassiodorus says that reverence is fear mixed with love.

But someone among you will say—he implies, someone doubting the resurrection—“How will the dead rise? And with what kind of body will they come?”—he implies, to judgment.

“Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.”

He uses a natural explanation, giving the example of a grain of some seed. It dies in the earth when it is sown, because it becomes milky, and afterward, [Col. 0600A] through the power of almighty God, it is made alive and produces many grains from itself. By these words he wishes to show that dead bodies will again be restored to life.

“And what you sow is not the body that will be, but a bare grain.” Here it is made clear that the God who by his power raises the pure, bare grain, stripped of its awns and stalk, into roots, stalk, blades, ears, grains, and awns will likewise, by his power, raise the bodies of the saints—not bare, but clothed with immortality and incorruption, animated by their own spirits.

And just as it is not another grain but the grain that was sown that will spring up from the earth, so each human being will rise not in another person’s body but in his own, as Job says: “In my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19)—the one whom I myself shall see, and not another.

[Col. 0600B] “Not all flesh is the same flesh, but one kind belongs to human beings, another to animals.” That is, all flesh is not one and the same kind of flesh.

All flesh is indeed formed by a mixture of the four elements, but creatures of different origins occupy different regions: birds the air, human beings the earth, and fish the streams of the waters. Therefore, just as each animal has its own body and cannot have another’s, so each human being will take up his own body, not another’s, on the day of judgment.

And just as, from one material, the flesh of living creatures differs, so human beings, though of one flesh, will differ in dignity at the resurrection, so that each person will appear according to what he has merited.

“There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies.” Heavenly bodies are those of flying creatures; earthly bodies are those of human beings and animals that inhabit the earth.

Or “heavenly bodies” means the sun, moon, and stars, which are corporeal, being fiery. For the glory—that is, the dignity or splendor—of heavenly bodies is one kind, and that of earthly bodies another, each in its own condition.

“For star differs from star in glory”—in brightness, magnitude, and speed. The brightness of the sun is one kind, that of the moon another, and so forth.

Just as the sun, moon, and stars, although of one kind, will nevertheless rightly differ in glory, so he himself makes clear when he adds: “So also is the resurrection of the dead.” Since there are many dwellings in the Father’s house, and the recompense of heavenly rewards will correspond to the diversity of merits, this does not mean that one will be rewarded in one place and another elsewhere. Rather, just as the sun, moon, and all the stars, differing from one another in brightness, are nevertheless in one heaven, so the elect, differing in merits, will all be crowned in one kingdom.

“It is sown”—that is, the body is buried—“in corruption,” because it is corrupted by worms, swarms with them, and decays; “it will rise in incorruption,” because afterward it will be subject to no labor or corruption [Col. 0600D].

“It is sown in dishonor”—that is, it is buried in disgrace; “it will rise in glory”—that is, in incorruption and freedom from suffering.

Something dishonorable is so called as though it were “without a name.” A dead person is without a name, because he is no longer a human being but a corpse, which is called *cadaver* from *cadere*, “to fall.” Or “dishonorable” means without the name of dignity. For what is more dishonorable than dead flesh? Or what is more glorious among created things than flesh rising and receiving incorruption?

“It is sown in weakness,” because it cannot move itself, having been rendered immobile; “it will rise in power”—he implies, the power of God—or in the power by which it can no longer die, because it will live through the power of angelic eternity.

“It is sown an animal body,” which possessed a soul; “it will rise a spiritual body.” Just as an animal body is not a soul but a body, so we must not think that a spiritual body is a spirit, but a body.

For, as Pope Gregory says, the bodies of the elect in that resurrection will be tangible according to the reality of their nature, just as the Lord’s body was after the resurrection. They will possess true flesh, but it will be more subtle through the effect of divine power. They will not be spirits, so that they cannot be touched or seen; rather, they will be spiritual in this respect: just as our spirit—that is, our soul—cannot die and does not need food or drink, so those bodies will be immortal and will not need food or drink.

Therefore he says: “The body is sown”—that is, it is buried—because it will be endowed with the greenness of resurrection, like a grain.

“If there is an animal body now in this life, there is also a spiritual body”—that is, it will be spiritual in the other life and will not be able to die. Such a body already exists in Christ, and it will be a spiritual body in the manner we have described above.

“The first man, Adam, became a living soul.” This is written in Genesis. But what follows—“the last Adam became a life-giving spirit”—the Apostle added on his own.

Adam was made a living soul—that is, he was made an animal being, and his body was animated, so that, if he sinned, as he did, he could die. Therefore he became mortal.

The last Adam—that is, Christ—was made a life-giving spirit, because the spirit that he released with bowed head made his body alive in the resurrection.

Thus Adam had an animal body—that is, a mortal one—but Christ had a spiritual body, which was glorified through the resurrection.

But we must consider why Christ is called either the last Adam or the second, when many existed between Adam—who is unquestionably the first—and Christ.

The answer is that all sinners are included in Adam the sinner, who begot all sinners, up to Christ. Christ, however, without sin, makes his faithful sinless in baptism, because he completely removes the bond of death.

Thus he is rightly called the second or last Adam, not according to chronological order but according to imitation of the deed, because until you pass over to Christ through faith and baptism, you belong to the first [Col. 0601D] Adam; afterward you belong to the second Adam, who remits the transgressions of the first.

You too are the first Adam until you are baptized; you are the second when you are baptized.

“But not first what is spiritual, but what is animal; afterward what is spiritual,” because the first human being is mortal, but afterward becomes immortal.

“The first man, Adam, was from the earth, earthly; the second man, Christ, was from heaven, heavenly.”

Hence he himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John 3). The man himself did not descend from heaven by himself, but he did so in his divinity, with which he is one person.

He is called heavenly because his incarnation, birth, resurrection, and other such deeds that he accomplished while present in the world in the flesh were heavenly [Col. 0602A]. His teaching and miracles were also heavenly.

“Such as was the earthly one, Adam, such also are the earthly”—that is, mortal sinners. “And such as was the heavenly one, Adam”—that is, Christ—“such also are the heavenly”—those who belong to Christ, namely the immortal and sinless.

They are so now in hope; in the resurrection they will be so in reality.

“Just as we have borne the image of the earthly man”—that is, sin and mortality—“let us also bear the image of the heavenly,” walking in newness of life in faith and hope and possessing the hope of resurrection.

“Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.”

In Scripture “flesh” is sometimes understood according to nature, as in: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2). Sometimes it is understood according to corruption, mortality, or weakness, as in: “He remembered that they were flesh” (Psalm 77)—that is, fragile and wretched.

Sometimes it is understood according to guilt and transgression. In this passage it is understood both according to corruption and according to guilt, just as God is said to tempt the elect in the passage: “The Lord your God is testing you.” And just as it is said, “God tempts no one,” so it may be said: “Flesh will possess the kingdom of God,” and “flesh will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Thus, among the elect, flesh and blood will possess the kingdom of God according to the truth of nature; yet flesh will not possess the kingdom of God according to corruption and mortality, because they will be immortal and incorruptible. Or flesh and blood will not possess it according to guilt, because there will be no guilt or transgression there.

Therefore flesh—that is, mortality—and blood—that is, corruption—or a human being devoted to carnal desires, will not possess the kingdom of God. Yet flesh and blood will possess the kingdom of God in the glorified truth of nature.

“Nor will corruption possess incorruption,” or “the incorruptible”: that is, corruption will not possess the resurrection, because mortality and corruption will no longer exist in those raised to life.

“Behold, I tell you a mystery”—that is, a secret and hidden thing concealed from unbelievers, or something that has until now been hidden from you.

For *mystery* is Greek; in Latin it is called a *secret* and a *hidden thing*.

“We shall all indeed rise”—that is, both good and evil—but “we shall not all be changed” [Col. 0602D]—he implies, into glory. That is, we shall not all be glorified. Those will not be glorified who will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

“In a moment.” A moment is a very small and extremely brief period, so called from the movement of the heavenly bodies and stars; it signifies the briefest span of time. It is the extremity of an hour in short intervals, when one thing yields and succeeds another.

“In the twinkling of an eye.” The twinkling of an eye is the movement by which the eyelid strikes—that is, touches—the eye. Or, as Augustine more aptly wishes, so that there may be no such delay in the judgment, the twinkling of an eye is understood as the sudden striking of the eye by the sun’s brightness, so swift that it can scarcely be imagined.

“At the last trumpet”—that is, at the angelic voice—because the Lord will descend from heaven at the command of God the Father and amid the trumpet blasts, that is, the proclamations of the angels [Col. 0603A].

It must not be understood that an angel takes up a bodily trumpet, or that the judge himself emits a human voice. Rather, the angels’ voice is called a trumpet because of its greatness. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “God has gone up amid jubilation, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm 46).

The trumpet there therefore means the voice of the angels, which will sound and say: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

Or when he says “in the trumpet,” he means “in manifestation,” in accordance with: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you” (Matthew 6)—that is, do not perform it publicly.

“For the trumpet will sound”—he implies, the angel will sound the trumpet, or “with the trumpet,” meaning that the angelic voice will resound—“and the dead will rise incorruptible,” that is, complete in body, without loss of limbs, and immortal. “And we faithful will be changed”—he implies, for the better, into glory, because we will be glorified with the immortality of eternal life.

“For this corruptible thing”—he implies, this body—“must put on incorruption.” That is, since the resurrection will truly occur, corruption must be removed and incorruption given.

“But when this mortal thing has put on immortality”—as though pointing to and indicating his own body with his finger, the Apostle said this.

He says “this mortal thing” because he will receive no body other than the one he will lay aside.

“Then the saying will come to pass that is written”—he implies, in Hosea, according to the Septuagint—“Death has been swallowed up in victory,” that is, in the glory and power of the resurrection.

Just as a very small drop of water, thrown into a powerful fire, is swallowed up so that it is no longer seen, so death will be swallowed up and devoured in the victory and power of the resurrection, so that it will no longer be felt. For the destruction of death will be the glory of the resurrection.

“Where, O death, is your victory?” This is the voice of the saints who have been raised, taunting death.

“Where,” they say, “is your victory, O death, by which you subjected the human race to yourself, and by which you also wished to rule over the Son of God made man?” The meaning is: “Do not boast any longer, because we have now risen, we who once experienced your bitterness.”

“And what benefit did it bring you, O wicked death, that you boasted? Behold, those who passed through you will reign happily in eternal life with Christ, who overcame you.”

“Where, O death, is your sting?”

These words seem to sound as though a sting proceeds from death. But because this sting is sin, it is understood that death proceeded from the sting—that is, from sin.

For the first man could not have died if he had not sinned. He sinned, and therefore incurred the death of soul and body.

He does not, however, say to death, “O death, where is the sin for which you condemned the world?” but “Where is your sting?” Thus, explaining what he called the sting, he adds: “The sting of death is sin.” That is, the sting that produces death is sin.

Sin is rightly called a sting, because just as a sting pierces the flesh, so sin pierces and wounds soul and body.

“But the power”—that is, the strength—“of sin is the law,” he implies, because in some way the law supplies strength to sin by inflaming a person toward sin while prohibiting it. It is natural to human weakness that whatever is more strongly prohibited is desired more ardently.

Or the law is the power of sin because through the law the magnitude of each sin is recognized, however great it may be. One who sins without the law seems to himself to sin with impunity; but when he has come under the law, if he sins again, he recognizes how great the power of sin—that is, how great the magnitude of sin—is.

“But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory”—he implies, the victory over death in hope—“through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The Apostle praises God the Father on behalf of the saints because they already possess in hope the victory over death and the gift of resurrection.

[Col. 0604B] Therefore, my brothers, beloved in faith—that is, greatly beloved—be steadfast, or firm, and immovable, so that you may not be moved from the uprightness of faith by the deception of corrupt people. Be abundant, or grow, in every work of the Lord always; that is, make progress at all times in the commandments of righteousness, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XVI

Concerning the collections made for the saints.

Paul and the other apostles always cared for the saints among those whom they taught, namely those who were in Jerusalem. These had been stripped of their possessions by unbelievers because they had abandoned the traditions of their fathers and believed in the Crucified One.

Therefore the apostles instructed them to assemble on Sundays, and for each person to give whatever seemed appropriate for their support. Expenses were collected in each church so that, after being gathered, they might be sent to them.

“As I arranged in the churches of Galatia”—that is, among the Galatians—“so also do you: on the first day of the week, let each of you set aside privately and store up whatever he has willingly chosen, so that collections may not be made when I come.”

He calls Sunday “the first day of the week,” because among the Jews it was called *una sabbati*, or *una sabbatorum*, or “the first of the Sabbaths.” Now, out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, it is called the Lord’s Day.

On that day he commanded the whole people to assemble in the church and to gather individually, according to each person’s will, for the benefit of those who were in Jerusalem. Each person was to store this up privately, as though in a treasury, so that when the Apostle came they would have everything prepared that they wished to send [Col. 0604D].

For what is collected gradually is not burdensome, and in the end is found to be much.

He instructed them to bring this to the church because he wanted each person to state: “I wish to send this from my share to the saints who are in Jerusalem,” so that others might be encouraged by his good example to do the same.

Nevertheless, lest those gifts perish through dishonest ministers if they were left with the church, he instructed them to take them back with them and place them in a secure location until he came.

“But when I am present, those whom you approve”—that is, those whom you judge suitable or show to be praiseworthy; at this point there is a medial pause, and what follows is to be supplied immediately—“I will send by letters,” he implies, my letters and your letters of commendation concerning your good will, or letters of recommendation by which I will commend them to the faithful in Jerusalem, so that they may be received peacefully.

“And if it is worthy that I go”—that is, if the sum is large enough for me, as an apostle and bishop, to carry it honorably—“they will go with me.”

For I do not wish to see you merely in passing, because there were many things in you that needed correction and could not be corrected in passing. Therefore he says: “I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost.”

He does not mean the Pentecost of the Jews, as is supposed, but that of the Christians, when the Holy Spirit came upon the multitude of believers.

“For a great and evident door has been opened to me”—that is, many human hearts are prepared to believe [Col. 0605B], and it is already clear that there is no doubt about their faith—“and there are many adversaries,” he implies, those who oppose me on behalf of their relatives and friends whom I have joined to Christ.

“If Timothy comes to you”—he will bring you this letter—“see that he is without fear among you.”

Perhaps he was already among them in fear, because the pseudo-apostles were stirring up persecution by the pagans against the faithful.

“For he is doing the work of the Lord, as I also am”—that is, he is carrying out teaching and the power of miracles for the salvation of your souls.

Therefore let no one despise him, because perhaps they had already despised him.

“Concerning the brother Apollos I make known to you, brothers.”

He had been ordained bishop of the Corinthians by Paul [Col. 0605C]. But when they began to say, “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” and “I am of Cephas,” and he was unable to calm them, he left them and went to Ephesus, to the Apostle Paul.

When the Apostle afterward asked him, as is said here, to return to Corinth, he refused because he still knew them to be uncorrected.

“He will come when he has opportunity”—that is, when he hears that you have been corrected.

“Be watchful.” The person who keeps the eyes of the mind open toward the sight of the true light is watchful. The person who preserves through his deeds what he believes is watchful.

“Stand in the faith,” so that you may not fall, deceived by unbelievers, and so that you may be able to hear with Moses: “But you, stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5).

“Act manfully”: do not fight softly or effeminately, but fight firmly against the temptations of the devil.

“Be strengthened”—he implies, in the Lord, not in your merits or in your own power [Col. 0605D].

“Let all your affairs be done in charity”—that is, in love of God and neighbor—not with a divided mind and not for the sake of empty glory.

“You know the household of Stephana and Fortunatus.”

Stephana was a certain noble matron whose household had become a church; the same was true of Fortunatus’s household.

“For they are the firstfruits of Achaia,” because they were the first of the Achaeans to believe, and they organized themselves to minister to the saints who are in Jerusalem.

“But I ask that you also be subject to such people”—that is, be imitators of those who minister to the saints—“and be subject to, or imitators of, everyone who cooperates and labors,” he implies.

I rejoice, however, at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus.
