It is to be understood that these three—namely Stephanas, Fortunatus, and also Achaicus—after completing all their ministry among the saints in Jerusalem, came to Paul before they returned to Corinth. For they were Corinthians by origin, and the Apostle rejoiced in their presence. For they themselves supplied what was lacking among you; here it is understood that they ministered to the Apostle from their own resources, something which the other [Col. 0606B] Corinthians to whom he was writing had not done. Hence he says: “What was lacking among you, they themselves supplied,” namely, by ministering to me.

For they refreshed my spirit as well, which had certainly been wearied by hunger, thirst, and labors; and they refreshed yours too, since you rejoiced when you heard that they were ministering on behalf of all of you. Therefore, recognize those who are such—that is, love, esteem, and imitate such men. Or, “recognize” means: submit to them with humility, because they do such things.

All the churches of Asia greet you—that is, they wish you well; as though he said: You ought to imitate these churches, which minister from their resources to me and to the saints who are in Jerusalem.

All the brothers greet you. Here he refers to all his assistants. Greet one another with a holy kiss—that is, a chaste and sincere one.

The greeting in my own hand—Paul’s. Someone else had written this Epistle, as he had written the others; but the Apostle himself added this at the end in his own hand.

If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed. *Anathema* in Greek means “destroyed” or “condemned,” that is, alienated and separated from God. He adds *maranatha*, which is more properly Syriac than Hebrew, although, because the two languages border upon one another, it also has something of a Hebrew sound. It is interpreted as “Our Lord has come.” The sense, therefore, is: “Accursed”—that is, destruction—are those who do not love him at the Lord’s coming, whether they do not believe that he has come or that he is to come.

[Col. 0606D] The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you; that is, faith, the forgiveness of sins, and all the gifts of God that are freely given to the faithful.

My love be with all of you; that is, with the love by which I love you, love one another; and with the love by which I love God, love him. Amen—that is, “May what I desire come to pass”; or, “May everything I have said above be true.”

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0605]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0605D]

When the Apostle had departed from the Corinthians and heard that they had been led astray by false apostles and were also suffering from dissensions, he wrote them the First Epistle. In it he sharply rebuked those who were sowing disagreements among the brothers, as well as those who were in fellowship with that man who had taken his father’s wife. He ordered that the latter be expelled from the association of all the faithful, handing him over to Satan for punishment. In that Epistle he also handed on to them the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, instructed them that they ought to receive it, and taught how men and women ought to stand in church. He instructed them concerning the resurrection and many other matters as well.

After he learned that they had repented of their errors and had also excluded from their fellowship the man who had committed incest by taking his father’s wife, he wrote them this laudatory and consolatory Epistle from Troas. In it he says that they have obtained mercy, and he recalls that wretched man whom he had previously handed over to Satan, reconciling him to the Church. He also exhorts them always to advance toward better things.

## CHAPTER ONE

Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ. This has already been sufficiently explained above.

By the will of God. Of the Father and of the whole Trinity, since just as the Trinity has one substance and an undivided majesty, so also it has an inseparable will.

And Timothy, a brother in faith, or a companion in preaching, though not his equal in rank.

To the Church of God that is at Corinth. Perhaps they did not yet have a bishop as their prelate; therefore he addresses the whole Church.

Blessed be God—that is to be understood as “the Father, Creator of all things”—who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, both according to his divinity and according to his humanity. Alternatively: “Blessed be God the Son,” who was in the beginning the Word with the Father, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, of the man assumed by him. For that man was created through the work of the whole Trinity. Nevertheless, it must be understood that we distinguish the persons but do not separate the substance.

The Apostle began with blessings and praises in the manner of the patriarchs and holy Fathers; wherever this is found, the things that follow proceed favorably.

The Father of mercies—that is to be understood as “blessed be he”—who, according to the multitude of your errors and crimes, bestowed upon you who were doing penance manifold mercies, forgiving your committed wickedness; and the God of all consolation—that too is to be understood as “blessed be he.” He is rightly called the God of all consolation, because all who deserve to be consoled are consoled by him and through him.

So that we too may be able to console those who are in every affliction. The Apostle therefore consoles us by delivering us from the afflictions of our persecutors, so that we in turn may console by our word and example those who are in every affliction and distress. And how? Through the exhortation with which we exhort them—that is, teach them—to be delivered, and they themselves also by God. Exhortation is a form of teaching. For example: when, either by a simple word or by one’s own or another’s example, we console someone so that he does not despair of salvation but remains confident of pardon.

I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, about our tribulation [Col. 0608A] which took place in Asia. If we divide the world into three parts, we find that Asia is half of the whole world, while the other half lies between Europe and Africa. If, however, we divide it into four parts, its regions will be Europe, Africa, Greater Asia, and Lesser Asia. In the latter the Apostle endured many tribulations. Yet all of it is generally called Asia: Greater Asia and Lesser Asia. It was named after a certain woman who held rule over the entire eastern kingdom and called it Asia after her own name. From the Indian Sea as far as Britain, all those islands are called Asian.

So that the Corinthians, who were suffering persecution from unbelievers, would not falter, the Apostle gives them himself as an example, saying: “I do not want you to be ignorant of the tribulations that we endure, so that you may be strengthened by our example.” For what wonder is it if disciples are beaten when their teachers are beheaded, crucified, and stoned?

We were burdened beyond measure and beyond our strength. Since the same Apostle says in the First Epistle, “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able,” one must ask why he says here that he was burdened beyond measure. The answer is that although they were burdened beyond measure—that is, beyond the human measure and beyond what human frailty can bear by its own strength—they were not burdened beyond divine power, which granted them endurance to bear and strength to overcome. Thus, he says, we were burdened so that we were even weary of living.

Weariness is anxiety of spirit. At times it denotes aggravation, and at times hatred, as here. “We were so burdened,” he says, “by pressures that we hated the present life and preferred to die rather than live.” But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we would not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead.

What kind of death can speak and give a sentence? “We ourselves,” he says, “had within ourselves the sentence of death.” That is, death itself, tribulation, and distress said to us in our hearts while we were being tormented: “Do not trust in yourselves, but in God, since you cannot overcome these torments by your own strength or by that of other human beings. Place your trust and hope in God, and he who raises the dead will certainly be able to rescue you.” For it seemed to them that they were being recalled from death to life.

With your assistance in prayer for us—that is, with the prayer understood as being made for us—so that we too may be delivered from the distress of this world, so that thanksgiving may be offered for us by many, on account of the gift that is in us, from the persons of many faces.

Here the sentence is confused. For the Apostle was unskilled in speech, though not in knowledge, as he himself says about himself. The construction of this verse is as follows: “Through your prayers he will deliver and rescue us from the pressures of our persecutors, so that thanksgiving may be offered to God for us by many persons of many faces,” that is, by many people, “on account of his gift”—that is, the gift that is in us. The meaning is this: God will therefore deliver us through your prayers, so that, once we have been delivered, many people to whom we have been and are and may be of benefit may give thanks to him, because he has heard you on our behalf by delivering us.

[Col. 0609A] For when he says “of many faces,” this is what he means by “from persons.” By “his gift” he means the grace by which they were delivered.

For our glory—that is, our honor and magnificence—is this. What is it? The testimony of our conscience, because our conscience, that is, our mind, bears witness to us that we believe rightly, teach well, live holily, and that we have conducted ourselves in this world in simplicity of heart and sincerity toward God—that is, in truth and not with a divided mind—but in the grace of God, that is, in the wisdom given to us by God’s grace.

The false apostles conducted themselves with a divided heart, because they taught one way but lived another. Or rather, they devoted themselves to preaching for the sake of temporal profits than for the love of God and the salvation of others. The philosophers too preached in carnal wisdom—that is, philosophically and with affected speech—wishing to appear wise. Or they did so because they denied that Christ had suffered, died, and risen from the dead.

But I conducted myself toward you with still greater simplicity, because although I had received something from other churches, I received nothing from you, so as not to give the false apostles an opportunity to accept gifts, and so that I might rebuke you more freely.

For we do not write to you anything other than what you read in the First Epistle, and you have recognized, from my life and preaching, what you will recognize until the end of our life, or until the day of judgment: what we wrote and what we preached to you. Just as you have recognized us in part, [Col. 0609C] not in every respect—for we could not minister and disclose to you everything that we understood about God, since you were still infants in understanding—you are our glory, because you can glory in having holy and truthful preachers. And you also will be our glory on the day of the Lord, that is, on the day of judgment, when we receive the crown of eternal reward on your account.

With this confidence, or hope, being secure concerning you, I first wished to come to you when I sent you the First Epistle, so that you might have a second grace. You had one grace when I first came to you, when you quickly came to the faith; and I ought to come again to chastise and rebuke you, so that, correcting yourselves, you might also have a second grace.

But for this reason I did not come, because I feared that, if I came, I would not be able to rebuke you in my presence as I wished, lest perhaps you should be impatient, just as I admonished you more gently in words through letters.

Since, then, I had wished this—that is, since I had wished to come to you—when I did not come, did I act frivolously? One is said to act frivolously when one does not carry out in deeds what one permits or promises in words. The Apostle would then have acted frivolously if he had promised that he would come and had not fulfilled his promise. But since he did not promise, although he wished to come, he did not act frivolously.

Or, “What I plan, do I plan according to the flesh?” That is, carnally and humanly. He plans according to the flesh who, for the sake of friendships and the honors of rulers, or for the sake of the temporal profits that he hopes to receive from the wealthy and powerful, delays fulfilling what he promises to someone, not keeping his promise, so that “with me there is both yes and no”—that is, so that I promise to come and do not come, and appear to speak truth while lying? Certainly not.

But God is faithful—that is, he is truthful, because whatever he promises he fulfills in deed. And he himself, who is truthful, knows that our word, which was with us when we preached to you, or which now concerns my coming to you, is not in him—that is, in that word there is no “yes and no,” truth and falsehood, or any changeability, so that I might appear to speak the truth while it was not true. Rather, it is “yes” in that word; that is, truth is present there, because I spoke in truth. It is as though he said: For this reason I am not moved by the breath of falsehood, because I do not succumb to the fault of fickleness.

For the Son of God, namely Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by me and by Silvanus and Timothy, is not “yes and no.” Silvanus is the same as Silas and Syleas, just as Lucius is the same as Lucas. Why, then, is Silvanus placed before Timothy? Because he was chosen to the faith earlier and was associated by the Apostle Paul with the ministry of preaching before Timothy was.

Therefore, he says, because Jesus Christ is the Son of God, there was not in him—that is, in Christ—“yes and no,” that is, any changeability, or truth combined with falsehood. Rather, there was “yes,” that is, truth, in him; as he himself said: “I am the truth” (John 14).

For however many promises of God the Father were made through the prophets concerning Christ’s birth, passion, death, [Col. 0610C] resurrection, and ascension, and also concerning the salvation of the nations, in him—that is, in Christ—they have been truly fulfilled. He always possesses being, and in him is the truth of the promises. Hence, while hanging on the cross, he himself says: “It is finished” (John 19), that is, everything that had been foretold about me has been completed.

Therefore, through him also comes the Amen to God for our glory. Because those promises were truly fulfilled in Christ, through him—that is, through Christ—truth is to be attributed to God the Father, to our glory, because we are his apostles and ministers. Some have added before “Amen” the words “we say Amen,” which does not seem to belong to the text but to a gloss.

How, then, is truth to be attributed through Christ to God the Father for the glory of the promises themselves? Because what Christ fulfilled in himself, he also preached and handed on to the apostles; and while they preached, God the Father showed by performing miracles that what he himself had promised and what they preached was true. In this consisted their glory.

But he who confirms us Jews with you in Christ—that is, in the faith of Christ—and joins two peoples in the one cornerstone, and who anointed us by the grace of the Holy Spirit—that is, who gave us the forgiveness of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit—is God, who is to be understood as true.

In the Old Testament, priests and kings were anointed with visible oil. In the New, all the faithful are anointed not so much with visible oil as with invisible grace, namely, that of the Holy Spirit in baptism. Through the laying on of hands they are made kings [Col. 0611A] of souls and priests of peoples, so that they may sanctify them, in accordance with what Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2).

He also sealed us—that is, he marked us as his own—by giving us his sign. When Christ said, “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 6), he placed his sign upon them and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.

A *pignus* is properly something given on account of a trusted matter, so that, when that matter has been fulfilled, it may be returned. But here the Apostle uses it rather for a pledge (*arrha*), which is given to God so that he may be certain of the promise and so that what is lacking may be completed. We therefore have received a pledge, or earnest, namely the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism, so that we may have security and certainty concerning the promise of our eternal homeland.

I call God as witness against my soul; that is, if I lie, I call upon him against my soul: it was out of sparing you that I did not come again to Corinth. That is, so that I would not be a burden to you and grieve you by my arrival, I spared you by not coming to Corinth again—that is, after I had departed from you.

Not that we lord it over your faith, like emperors, because you and we already share one faith; rather, we are helpers of your joy—that is, we rejoice in your faith and good works. For you stand firm in faith, and for this reason we do not lord it over you.

This is how prelates ought to act: when they see those subject to them agreeing with them in good conduct, they ought not to place themselves above them but on an equal footing. But when they see some straying from the way of righteousness, they ought to display toward them the authority and power of their office. Peter demonstrated both forms in Cornelius and Ananias: he humbled himself toward Cornelius, while with a single word he destroyed Ananias and his wife.

## CHAPTER TWO

For if I make you sorrowful, who is there to make me joyful except the one who is made sorrowful by me? That is, if I make one of you sorrowful by rebuking and correcting him severely, who is there to make me joyful except the one who is made sorrowful through my admonition and is thereby moved from his guilt to repentance? For when he is sorrowful over his sin and does penance, then he makes me joyful.

Thus every preacher and prelate is made more joyful the more he sees those subject to him sorrowing over their guilt and mourning as they do penance, being assured of their salvation.

[Col. 0611D] So that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow. At present, hearing that you are entangled in various errors, I have sorrow; but if I come to you and find you uncorrected, then I will have sorrow upon sorrow. Therefore I admonish you to correct yourselves.

For out of much tribulation and anguish of heart—which amount to one thing—I wrote to you the previous letter with many tears; that is, almost as many tears as there were syllables that I dictated or wrote, I seemed to shed.

When the Apostle heard that some of the Corinthians had returned to their former vices and to fornication without doing penance, and, moreover, that one of them had taken his father’s wife, he was overcome by immense sorrow and mourned for them greatly. Therefore he also sent them the previous letter, in which he severely rebuked [Col. 0612A] them and ordered that the man who had committed incest be excluded from the fellowship of all.

They obeyed his words, did penance, and separated that man from themselves. When the Apostle learned this, he rejoiced greatly, yet he recalled to them how he had mourned for them and still addressed them, saying: I am not writing this now so that you may be sorrowful—you who have done penance—but so that you may know how abundantly I love you, after I heard that you had done penance.

But if anyone has caused me sorrow—whether the man who took his father’s wife or those who returned to their former vices—he has not caused me sorrow alone, but in part he has caused sorrow to you, who grieved over their guilt and who are united with me in love.

He continues: So that I may not burden you all. To burden is to impose some load or weight. The meaning is this: I did not rebuke the offenders or excommunicate them in the previous letter in order to burden you who are living perfectly with that correction. Nor am I recounting these matters now in order to burden you by excommunicating and rebuking you, but so that those who have strayed from the way of righteousness may be corrected.

This rebuke is sufficient for him—the fornicator, that is, the man who took his father’s wife—namely, the correction and reproof made by the majority. That is, the general correction and reproof, and the fact that he has been excluded from the fellowship of all of you, are sufficient for him for repentance.

For in the previous letter he ordered that he be expelled from the fellowship of the faithful, saying: “Cleanse out the old leaven” (1 Corinthians 5): expel and drive from your fellowship that sinner who took his father’s wife.

But lest he should fall into despair if he were always excluded from the fellowship of the faithful, he now reconciles him, recognizing that he has been cleansed in this way: he sinned because the devil suggested it, and he was cleansed when the devil scourged him, when he was handed over to the devil’s power.

So that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive him—that is, the reproof made by all of you will then be sufficient for him if, on the contrary, you forgive him his offense and console him, lest perhaps, being excluded from you, one who is such should be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. That is, lest perhaps, falling into despair, he should strangle himself with a noose or surrender himself to the pleasures of this age, saying within himself: “Since I am now excluded from the fellowship of the faithful both in the present and in the future, I will plunge myself into every delight and pleasure.”

Forgive him and console him, so that he will not despair of pardon and salvation.

For this reason—that is, lest he should be swallowed up by excessive sorrow and slip into despair—I beseech you, Corinthians, to confirm your love toward him by receiving him into your fellowship and communion.

For this reason I also wrote to you—that is, concerning the reception of this brother—so that I might learn the result of your conduct, that is, so that I might test whether you are obedient in all things that I command you.

Previously you had been obedient to him when you expelled him from your fellowship, [Col. 0613A] and when he ordered that men should stand in church with their heads uncovered and women with their heads covered. He still wished to test your obedience in this matter, namely, that you should recall the expelled man.

But to whomever you have forgiven anything, I forgive as well. While the Apostle Paul was staying among them, they forgave someone who had sinned, and the Apostle himself, so that he would not seem to separate himself from their fellowship, also forgave him.

Hence he says now: To whomever you forgave—that is, remitted—when I was with you, I likewise forgave and remitted. It is customary to say, “He forgave me my sin,” meaning that he remitted it.

The Apostle therefore wishes to urge them to reconcile the expelled man and forgive him. He wants to show that just as he forgave the sinner when they forgave him, so they should forgive while he himself forgives. Therefore he adds:

For whatever I have forgiven—or remitted—if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sake, because you wished to forgive him; and I have forgiven it in the person of Christ, that is, in Christ’s place, who gave us apostles the power to bind and to loose.

The Apostle did not lightly grant forgiveness to those who sinned, except to one whom he saw to have been loosed by Christ and whose repentance had been accepted by God.

So that we may not be deceived—that is, tricked—by Satan. For this reason, he says, I command you to forgive the sinful brother, just as I forgive him, so that we may not be deceived by Satan, who desires to generate dissensions.

Often, when one person wishes mercy to be shown to a sinful brother by forgiving what he has done and reconciling him to the assembly of the faithful, another, persuaded by the devil, does not wish to forgive him, remaining hardened in his own heart. Hence dissensions and quarrels often arise among those who disagree and are divided in judgment.

For we are not ignorant of his thoughts—that is, we are not ignorant of the devil’s cunning, deceit, and fraud; rather, we know them.

When I came to Troas. Troas is a city of the Greeks, which was once called Troy; the expression is used improperly. Phrygia is a province of the Greeks; Troy is a region within Phrygia, while the city itself was called Ilium, as is found in Virgil: “And proud Ilium fell.” Frequently the name of a region is used for a city, and so it is called Troy.

For the Gospel of Christ—that is, to preach the Gospel of Christ—and a door had been opened to me in the Lord—that is, many human hearts had been prepared by the Lord to believe—I had no rest in my spirit, that is, in my mind, because I did not find Titus, my brother. But bidding them farewell—that is, greeting them—I departed for Macedonia, another province of the Greeks.

Saint Jerome says: Because the Apostle did not find his “flute,” that is, Titus, his interpreter, he therefore departed.

But there is a question here. If the Apostle could speak in the languages of all nations, as he himself says in the First Epistle, “I thank God that I speak in the languages of all of you” (1 Corinthians 14), why did he leave Troas merely because Titus was absent, especially since many hearts there were prepared to believe?

This is resolved as follows: although, when he came to Troas, he found many hearts prepared to believe, he also found many adversaries and opponents—namely, philosophers, magicians, and very many others. He himself could not manage both tasks alone: resist the philosophers and preach the word of salvation to those who wished to believe.

If he had found Titus there, as he hoped, Paul himself would certainly have resisted the adversaries, while Titus would have preached to the simpler people who desired to believe.

A Macedonian man also appeared to him in that same place, saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16). This man is believed by the teachers to have been a good angel appointed over that people.

But thanks be given to God the Father, who always triumphs over us—that is, who always makes us triumph and have victory—in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus, by destroying unbelief, planting faith in the hearts of believers, making the unbelieving faithful, and manifesting through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place, among Jews as well as Gentiles.

By “fragrance” in this passage he means knowledge of the holy Trinity. Thus, just as aromatics and ointments, although they are in one place, give off their fragrance elsewhere, so, when the apostles preached the faith of the holy Trinity and the knowledge of the divinity of almighty God, although the divinity itself was not seen, since it is invisible, those who received faith in it through the apostles’ preaching in a certain way perceived the fragrance and knowledge of that divinity.

For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are perishing and among those who are being saved.

We read in Genesis that, when Noah offered sacrifice after the flood had ceased, the Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness, to such an extent that he blessed him and his sons. We must not therefore understand childishly that God, who is spirit, takes pleasure in the smell and smoke of meat. Rather, holy Scripture calls the intention of that good man a fragrance of sweetness, because God was pleased with it.

Similarly, in this passage we must understand “fragrance” to mean zeal, good will, and intention. “We are,” he says, “the good fragrance of Christ to God”—that is, we who believe in Christ and have been led forth by Christ, preaching the mystery of his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, as well as the mystery of the holy Trinity.

We are his good fragrance because we proclaim his good reputation and the glory of the whole Trinity, pleasing God the Father, as is to be understood, by doing such things.

It should also be noted that he adds: “Among those who are being saved by our preaching, and among those who are perishing, we are the good fragrance of Christ,” pleasing God the Father. For just as God is pleased by the good zeal that we devote to those who are being saved, so he is also pleased by what we devote to those who are perishing, since our will is such that we would wish to save everyone, if we could. Therefore he delights in the fragrance of our intention.

Whether, then, among those who are being saved or among those who are perishing, the apostles were a good fragrance pleasing to God the Father, because they preached sincerely and without flattery.

To some, indeed, we are the fragrance of death unto death—namely, to those to whom we preach if they despise believing; but to others, the fragrance of life unto life—to those who hear and believe.

Although the apostles offered the same preaching to all, both to those willing to believe and to those unwilling, that preaching was for some a taste and fragrance of death unto eternal death rather than unto the present death that we share with animals and cattle, because they were eternally condemned for refusing to obey the words of the Gospel. But for others it was the fragrance and taste of life, leading them to receive eternal life, because they were saved through it.

For just as believers were saved through it, so unbelievers were condemned, because they were without excuse.

And for discerning these things, who is so capable and suitable a preacher that he can discern who will be saved and who will be condemned through his preaching? No one. Therefore the word of preaching must be offered to everyone.

For we apostles are not like the many who adulterate the word of God. Here he attacks the false apostles. For just as an adulterer commits adultery with another’s wife not out of love for her children but to satisfy his own lust, so the false apostles adulterated the word of God: they preached falsely, not in order to acquire spiritual children for God or for the reward of the heavenly homeland, but for temporal profits and human favor. They also adulterated the word of God because they did not teach it rightly or truthfully, saying that Christ had neither died nor risen from the dead.

But the apostles did not adulterate it, because they desired to acquire spiritual children for God and devoted themselves to preaching not for temporal profits but for the reward of eternal blessedness, preaching most rightly, neither for human favor nor praise, as the same Apostle adds: “But from sincerity”—that is, from purity and truth—“we preach; but as from God,” that is, as we have received from the Holy Spirit, so we preach. Since he is one God, existing in one substance with the Father and the Son, “before God,” that is to be understood, “we speak”: we preach as though we were always set in God’s presence and he were our helper. For indeed he is present everywhere. “In Christ Jesus we speak,” that is, for the honor and glory of Christ Jesus.

## CHAPTER THREE

Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? That is, to praise ourselves. Surely he did not already praise both himself and others a little earlier? Indeed he did, both above and again in this passage and in what follows.

But since Wisdom says through Solomon, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Proverbs 27), why will the Apostle praise himself? Certainly in order to draw the Corinthians away from love of the false apostles and back to love of himself and of the other truthful apostles.

Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation? That is, letters of praise, sent to you from other peoples and churches, or from you to others, which might offer you testimony of our praise and holiness, as some do—namely, the false apostles and Jews, who receive commendatory letters from the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests of the Jews, so that they may be regarded as holy and religious by the preachers?

We do not need your praise, nor letters of recommendation that might offer testimony on our behalf. He therefore explains why he does not need them, saying:

You are our letter, written in our hearts. A letter is a sign of salvation, because it contains the salvation of the one who sends it and speaks of the salvation of the one to whom it is sent.

“You,” he says, “Corinthians, are our letter, written in our hearts,” because day and night we meditate and think about your salvation. The very intention of our heart bears witness to you, a letter that is known and read by all people—that is, it is known and read by all people not with bodily eyes but understood by the mind. That letter is the fact that we always think about your salvation.

You have been shown to be Christ’s letter. This depends upon what precedes: you who are our letter, written in our hearts, have been shown to others to have come to the faith through our preaching, because you are Christ’s letter.

Ministered by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. What is written with ink can be blotted out or erased; but the faith written by the Holy Spirit, who always lives, is eternal. For just as that Spirit is eternal, so that faith is eternal.

“You have been shown,” he says, “to have believed through our preaching, because you are Christ’s letter,” that is, you possess his faith, from whom you are called Christians. This faith was ministered by us, because “faith comes from hearing” (Romans 10), and it was written by the Holy Spirit in your hearts, because “to one is given faith in the same Spirit.”

That faith was not written on tablets of stone, as the law of Moses was, but on tablets of fleshly hearts. Almighty God, foreseeing the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, wrote on stone the same law that he gave them, so that the hardness of their hearts might be signified through the stone.

By the stone tablets, therefore, we must understand the hard and insensible hearts of human beings, in which the faith of Christ is not written, because they cannot be softened by any preaching or any terrors.

But by what he says, “on tablets of fleshly hearts,” we must understand a tender and perceptive heart, one that feels and is moved toward gentleness, understands what is said, receives it, and retains it. On such hearts Christ’s letter—that is, faith in the Holy Spirit—is written.

Such confidence we have through Christ toward God. In this passage the Apostle wishes to establish a difference and distance between Moses, the lawgiver, and Christ, the giver of the Gospel; between the Law and the Gospel; and between the teachers of the Law and those of the Gospel.

He shows that just as great as the distance is between Moses and Christ, so great is the distance between the Law and the Gospel, and between the teachers of the Law and the teachers of the Gospel. He also demonstrates that we are nothing unless we are governed by the Lord’s mercy and grace.

“Such confidence,” he says—that is, such boldness and faith—we have through Christ our Lord, by whose passion we have been redeemed and reconciled to God, that is, before God the Father. I shall now state and write in what follows what kind of confidence this is.

[Col. 0617A] Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God. Here he destroys all confidence in free choice, by which many suppose that they can do some good without the grace of God. For this reason he says all these things, to show that no one can think or do anything good by his own power and wisdom. He therefore says: We do not have such confidence or boldness as though we were sufficient—that is, as though we could think of anything good by ourselves concerning your salvation or ours, as though something good could come to you from us without the grace of God. Rather, our sufficiency, in its abundance, is from God, who gives the will and the ability—that is, we are not merely unable to accomplish any good without the mercy and preceding and following grace of God; we are not even able to think of it. For the grace of God precedes us, so that we may will, and follows us, so that we may be able. Hence the Psalmist prayed, saying: “His mercy shall prevent me” (Ps. LVIII [59]), and: “Your mercy shall follow me” (Ps. XXII [23]). For if we are unable even to think, how shall we be able to accomplish anything?

He—that is, God—made us fit, that is, suitable and appropriate, ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit. That is, he did not make us ministers of the letter of the law, so that we should preach circumcision as something to be observed bodily, or the rest of the Sabbath, or the rite of new moons or sacrifices as something to be celebrated; rather, he made us ministers in the spiritual understanding of the Gospel, which must be understood spiritually and whose observance bestows the Holy Spirit at the time of baptism.

As for his saying that he and the other apostles were made fit ministers, understand it in this way: a fit minister is properly one who is suitable, useful, and adapted to the matter under discussion. “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” This is to be understood in two ways.

The letter of the Mosaic law kills a person bodily by commanding but not helping. For when the law says, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” whoever kills, or commits adultery, or perpetrates anything of this kind, will be guilty in judgment—that is, he will be killed, burned with fire, crushed by stones, or hanged on the gallows. Since it does not help him to fulfill what it commands, it undoubtedly kills the person, for it gives the judgment that he should be killed, although it is not itself the cause of his death.

But the spirit gives life. The Gospel, which is understood spiritually and which grants the Holy Spirit, not only does not kill a person in the present life; it also gives life, that is, it grants eternal life. Nowhere does the Gospel command a person to be killed. Rather, after sin it summons him to repentance, promising eternal life: “Do penance,” it says, “for the kingdom of heaven shall draw near” (Matt. III).

In another sense: before the Lord’s coming there were certain works of the law that cleansed their observers from lesser sins. For example, circumcision removed original sin, although it did not open the entrance to the heavenly homeland. There were also many other matters for which burnt offerings were offered (Lev. XII), concerning which it was said: “If anyone does this or that, let him offer a ram or something of the kind, and he will be cleansed.”

After the Lord’s coming, in which all those figurative and shadowy things were fulfilled in truth, whoever wishes to observe that same law bodily will die in soul, because “the soul that sins shall die.” Hence the same Apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians: “I truly say to you, if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V); and we know that those to whom Christ is of no benefit are dead in soul.

But whoever wishes to observe that same law spiritually—by circumcising himself spiritually in baptism, where there is the true stripping away of vices; by observing the Sabbath, that is, by resting from evil works; by offering spiritual sacrifices to almighty God; and by mortifying himself together with his vices and desires—he lives and will live in eternal life. Hence the Apostle says: “The letter kills in the soul now,” that is, the literal understanding of the law; “but the spirit gives life,” that is, the spiritual understanding grants eternal life.

If, then, the ministry of death—that is, if the law which was the minister of death, as we have just said—was formed or written in letters upon stones, and was given to Moses in glory, through the brightness of his face, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon his face because of the glory of his countenance, a glory or brightness that is brought to an end, how much more will the ministry of the spirit—that is, the spiritual teaching and preaching of the Gospel—be in glory, for its ministers and observers?

Here he wishes to show what difference there is between the law and the Gospel, and between Moses and the teachers of the Gospel, as we have already said above. We read in Exodus (Exod. III, IV) that, when Moses descended from the mountain, his face was horned through his converse with God—that is, it sent forth certain rays of brightness like the sun—so greatly that the children of Israel could not gaze upon his face. But whenever he went out to the people, he placed a veil over his face.

Perhaps someone asks: Why could they not gaze upon the glory and brightness of a mortal man? The answer is that Moses was holy and just, and therefore shone forth; he himself was able to bear his splendor. But those who were sinners and unbelieving were not worthy to contemplate his radiance.

The meaning, therefore, is this: If Moses had such brightness in his face when he gave the law to the people—a law that was the minister of death because it threatened death—how much greater glory will the ministers of the Gospel have, since they minister virtue and righteousness, which grant eternal life? They will have much greater glory and brightness, for they will possess the same glory that the Lord displayed on the mountain to the three disciples, when Moses and Elijah were seen with him in majesty and brightness.

For they will see with bodily eyes the glory and brightness of the glorified humanity of the Son of God, as blessed Leo says; and they themselves will possess that same glory. But the glory of the Divinity and of the whole Trinity they will contemplate only with the mind, because “God is spirit,” that is, he must be seen spiritually. Blessed Leo says in his exposition of that Gospel that the brightness and glory were not the glory of the Son of God’s divinity but of his humanity.

Otherwise, how would what he said to Moses be true: “Man shall not see me and live” (Exod. XII), when Moses said: “Show me yourself,” that is, your invisibility?

[Col. 0619A] In a higher understanding, therefore, Moses, who placed a veil over his face so that the children of Israel would not gaze upon him, signifies the law itself, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel when he says that Abraham said to the rich man: “They have Moses” (Luke XVI), that is, the law.

That veil signifies the literal understanding and historical sense by which the law is overshadowed, as well as the unbelief and ignorance of the Jews’ hearts. The veil, therefore, that Moses placed over his face did not allow them to perceive the glory of his countenance, because their unbelief, ignorance, and sin, together with the literal understanding and historical sense, did not permit them to penetrate and understand the glory of the spiritual understanding that lay hidden in the law.

When he says that the glory and brightness of Moses was brought to an end, he speaks according to the letter: for after Moses died, his face, which had previously sent forth rays of brightness, was changed into pallor.

In a higher and more elevated sense, according to Augustine, the glory of the law that appeared in festivals and works was brought to an end when Christ came, whom the law signified. Or again, the spiritual understanding that certain people possessed—such as Moses, Joshua, Samuel, David, and others of this kind—was brought to its fulfillment and made fully manifest to the apostles when Christ came. As soon as fullness arrived, what had been partial was brought to an end—not so that the spiritual understanding should cease entirely and perish, but so that it might advance to something better and receive increase.

For example, infancy and childhood are brought to an end when adolescence arrives, and adolescence is brought to an end when youth arrives, as one stage advances toward something better. This does not happen in the Gospel, however, because the Gospel is understood spiritually in its entirety and is not brought to an end, since it is eternal.

If, then, those who fulfilled the law in works understood it spiritually in part—and that partial understanding was brought to an end—nevertheless possessed such great glory in the present age that they received the promised land and afterward became victors over their enemies, how much greater will be the glory obtained by those who spiritually understand, observe, preach, and teach the law and the Gospel, which is never brought to an end?

For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, the ministry of righteousness abounds much more in glory. This is a repetition of what was said above, with a change of wording. If the ministry of condemnation is glory—that is, if the law, which was the minister of condemnation and death, bestowed such great glory upon Moses, its minister, and upon its other observers—then the ministry of righteousness, that is, the Gospel which justifies human beings, abounds much more in eternal glory.

The Gospel, therefore, is the ministry of righteousness, because through it righteousness, salvation, and eternal life are ministered to us at the time of baptism, as the Lord says to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII), that is, minister the Gospel to them. “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” with eternal salvation, because he will be cleansed from all sins and will be made righteous.

The glory of the Gospel, finally, which is given to its ministers and observers, is greater than the glory of the law that shone in Moses’ face. The former was temporal and could be borne and seen by anyone; the latter will be eternal. Nor could the apostles bear it when it was shown by the Lord on the mountain, because they immediately fell to the ground as though dead.

Therefore all must labor to become observers of the Gospel, so that we may be worthy to reach that glory which it promises.

For even that which was glorified in this part was not glorified because of the surpassing glory. By “this part” he means Moses, or what the Book of Exodus narrates in this section concerning the brightness of his face; and by “the surpassing glory” he means the glory by which the Lord was glorified on the mountain and by which all the elect will be glorified.

The meaning is this: That which shone in Moses’ face was not glorified—that is, it was not true glory, because it could be brought to an end by his death. Nor was it glorious in comparison with this glory, which will remain eternally and will be much greater. For since the glory of his face benefited no one, it was as though it were not glory, because it bore no fruit of glory.

In another sense: when he says “in this part,” it is as though he meant “with respect to this part.” That which shone and gleamed in Moses was not glorified in this part—that is, insofar as this part of the glory of the Gospel is concerned, it is not glorious because of this greater glory.

For if that which is brought to an end is in glory, much more is that which remains eternally in glory. That is, if the law, which could be brought to an end, was in glory for Moses and his observers, much more is the Gospel, which remains eternally, in glory for its ministers and [its] keepers. For as great as the difference between the image and the truth, so great is the difference between the glory of Moses’ face and the glory of Christ, to whose likeness all the elect will attain in glory.

Having, therefore, such hope of seeing and receiving glory—not such as was in Moses’ face, but that which the three apostles saw on the mountain when the Lord revealed himself—we use great confidence in preaching, secure concerning the reward.

And just as Moses placed a veil over his face so that they would not gaze upon him, so Christ does not place a veil over the law in the Gospel. The veil of the law is brought to an end: Christ does not place the veil of literal understanding and obscurity over the Gospel, so that the faithful cannot penetrate the glory of spiritual understanding, as Moses placed the veil so that they would not gaze upon the glory of his face. That veil signifies the obscurity and shadowing of the law, which is brought to an end when it is revealed by Christ and that same law is understood spiritually.

Or, Christ will not conceal his glory from the elect in the way Moses concealed his face by placing a veil over it. That veil is brought to an end—or, rather, was brought to an end—when Moses died.

But their senses were dulled. That is, although the veil signifying the obscurity of the law was brought to an end by Christ, and although there is no veil in the Gospel, the Jews do not for that reason penetrate the glory of the spiritual understanding hidden in the law. Their senses have been dulled and struck blind by the obstinacy of unbelief and by ignorance, because they do not wish to believe in Christ; instead, they always wish to follow the letter.

[Col. 0621A] For even to this day that same veil—that is, the obscurity and ignorance—remains in the reading of the Old Testament, among unbelieving Jews, not having been revealed to them, because their unbelief and sins strike their understanding, and they are unable by themselves to penetrate it. For in Christ it is brought to an end: through faith in Christ the veil of ignorance will be taken away, not through their own knowledge, nor will it be revealed to them unless they believe.

But even to this day, when Moses—that is, the law given through Moses—is read by unbelieving Jews, a veil is placed over their heart, that is, ignorance and blindness of understanding are in the hearts of the Jews, so that they cannot penetrate the spiritual understanding of the law, which was obscure and hidden from them until, by believing in Christ, it is stripped away for them by Christ.

But when he shall have been converted to God—that is, when that people shall believe in Christ—the veil will be taken away: the obscurity will be removed from the law through Christ and through the grace of the Holy Spirit, who begins to dwell within us at the time of baptism.

But the Lord is the Spirit. And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. No one who holds the faith of the Holy Trinity doubts that the Holy Spirit is God, because he is the third person of the Trinity; yet there are not three Lords, but one Lord. It is known to all the faithful, through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that the law and the Gospel were written down. Therefore the Holy Spirit is Lord of the law and of the Gospel, and nothing in the law or Gospel is hidden from him.

With the cooperation of that same Holy Spirit, through faith in the Lord’s passion we are freed in soul from all sins. Concerning this freedom the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed” (John VIII). Through him also the faithful are given the ability to understand the divine Scriptures.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is Lord of the Scripture of the law and of the Gospel. Nothing contained there is hidden from him, nor is any veil of obscurity or doubt set before him; rather, he himself reveals what lies hidden there, as what follows makes clear. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom of soul and the ability to understand the Old and New Testaments.

That is, whoever the Holy Spirit fills through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ possesses freedom of soul and the ability to examine the obscurities of the law and to penetrate the grace of the Gospel.

But we all—that is, the apostles, believing Jews, and all who have obtained freedom of soul and the ability to understand the divine law—with the face of our heart unveiled, that is, with the mind’s understanding made manifest through faith in Christ and understanding of the Scriptures, contemplate the glory of the Lord that he showed to the three disciples and that all the elect will receive. We are “contemplating” it—that is, we see it by faith and hope in the mirror of the mind.

There is a difference between a watchtower (*specula*) and a mirror (*speculum*). A watchtower is a tower in cities, a place from which one watches from afar to see from what direction enemies may come. A mirror, however, is where people customarily contemplate their own images and faces and those of others. Here it is the mirror that is meant.

Our mirror, therefore, is our mind. For just as an image and shadow are contemplated in a mirror, so in the present life we see and contemplate in the mind that glory which we shall receive in reality.

We are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory. In Greek, as blessed Augustine says, it reads: “We are transferred from form to form.” As it is stated in Genesis (Gen. I), the human being was made in the image of God: holy, just, immortal, and incorruptible. Through sin he lost that image and fell into the form of mortality, corruption, and injustice.

From that image and form of righteousness, therefore, we are now transformed and transferred in hope and faith into that same image and form which we lost: from the form of creation to the form of justification; from the form of mortality and corruption to the form of immortality; from the form of sonship, by which we are now sons of God in hope, to the form of contemplation and vision; from an obscure form to a luminous form.

Concerning this John says: “We are sons of God in hope, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be in reality” (1 John III). From this obscure form we shall be transferred to the luminous form when we shall be like God, because “we shall see him as he is.”

We are also transformed from the brightness of hope to the brightness of direct vision, and from the brightness of faith to the brightness of reality, so that what we now possess in hope and believe we shall attain, we may someday possess in reality.

And rightly, after saying that we are transformed from the brightness of hope into the brightness of direct vision and reality, he adds, “as from the Spirit of the Lord,” to show that such glory is given as corresponds to the majesty of the giver. For the glory and brightness of Moses was neither as great as that of Christ on the mountain nor everlasting.

God has granted his faithful so much that he gives them the Holy Spirit as a pledge of the glory he has promised. For just as one who receives a pledge or earnest is secure concerning the payment that remains to be made according to the promise, so the faithful who receive the Holy Spirit as a pledge and earnest at the time of baptism are secure concerning the promises of the heavenly homeland, because through him they are transformed in hope [Col. 0622D] toward that glory.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, since we have this ministry—that is, of hope, since we possess the confidence and hope of being transformed, a hope and confidence ministered to us by the Holy Spirit according to the mercy we have received, not according to our merit—we do not fail amid the adversities of this age. Rather, we use great confidence in preaching, enduring all hardships courageously and secure concerning the reward and glory.

But we renounce the hidden things of shame—that is, we reject and cast away from our heart, mouth, and works all disgraceful things, which are especially accustomed to be done in secret—not walking in cunning, that is, in the craftiness of this age. Cunning is said to derive from *hasta*, “spear,” that is, from sharpness, because it is exceedingly sharp in deceiving people.

Nor do we adulterate the word of God, as the false apostles do in many ways. Rather, in the manifestation of truth—we understand, we preach the word of God—not with affected speech or philosophical language, but simply, so that all the simple may be able to understand it. We commend ourselves to every human conscience, that is, we make ourselves commendable to all people by living holily and preaching well, before God—that is, in the presence of God, who is pleased with what we do.

Or “before God” because, just as it is given to us by him, so we preach in the presence of him whom we know to be present with us.

Someone might say: How do you preach in manifestation, when not everyone understands what you say or believes? To this the Apostle added the following:

If our Gospel is veiled—that is, if it is closed and obscure so that it is not understood—it is veiled among those who are perishing. He means: It is veiled for those who are perishing in unbelief, because the Holy Spirit does not inspire them and they do not wish to believe; but for those who wish to believe, it is manifest.

All heard the apostles’ preaching, but it was manifested to those who wished to believe; to those who remained in unbelief, it was concealed.

In whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers. Certain heretics, including Marcion and other false apostles, incorrectly dividing this verse, said that “the god of this age” meant the devil, concerning whom it is said: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. XCV [96]); although they are called gods, they are not gods.

The verse should instead be divided in this way: “In whom”—that is, in those who are perishing—“God,” the true God; and then, farther on: “has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age,” since he has not enlightened them. This is like the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart, when he did not soften it, so that the illumination of the Gospel would not shine in them—that is, the faith and teaching of the Gospel and the glory of Christ.

The Gospel is the glory of Christ because it recounts his divine and human birth, the power of his miracles, his passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and coming to judgment. Christ is the image of God the Father, that is, like him in all things according to his divinity.

For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ [Col. 0623D] our Lord. That is, we do not seek our own praise or temporal profits; we preach and seek the glory and honor of Christ, so that we may be rewarded by him.

The person who preaches himself is the one who speaks in affected language and seeks to falsify the truth of the Gospel so that he himself may be proclaimed wise and praised, and who devotes himself to preaching for the sake of temporal profits rather than for the sake of eternal life.

For God, who said at the beginning of creation that light should shine out of darkness—saying, when darkness still covered the face of the abyss, “Let there be light,” and light came to be (Gen. I)—himself has shone in our hearts with the light of faith and teaching. We who were formerly darkness have been enlightened for the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

The order is this: God, who said, “Let there be light,” when darkness still existed, and light came to be, has shone in our hearts with the light of faith and teaching in the face of Christ—that is, in the presence of God—and through the presence of Christ, for the illumination and manifestation of the knowledge of his divinity.

Through Christ’s presence, therefore, knowledge of God the Father and of the whole Trinity was made manifest, as Christ himself said: “Father, I have manifested your name to the human beings whom you gave me” (John XVI)—not the name by which you are called God, but the name by which you are called Father.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels. Here “treasure” means a container and repository of gold. The Apostle calls the sacrament of the knowledge of the Holy Trinity and the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God a treasure in this passage.

For just as a treasure is placed in a hidden and secret place, so this mystery was stored up in their hearts. He calls fragile bodies “earthen vessels,” since they were made from the clay of the earth and are subject to various sufferings and weaknesses: hunger, thirst, nakedness, and other such things.

Thus the surpassing power may be God’s in us and not from us. That is, the height of God’s power is proclaimed and appears through us because neither that wisdom nor the power of miracles is from us, but from God, although it is ministered through us.

It is as though he said in other words: The treasure of spiritual grace that we preach, and the signs of miracles that we perform, we carry in a fragile body; and although we often heal others, we ourselves are weak, subject to hunger and thirst, so that it may be understood that what we do is not accomplished by our own power or merits, but is the surpassing power of God.

In every way and in every place we suffer various tribulations, but we are not distressed. That is, although we endure tribulations and hardships, we are not so constrained or pressed that we abandon the work of preaching and cease from our purpose.

We are driven into perplexity, that is, we are cast down and endure reproaches—or, what is better, we are rejected as though we were poor—but we are not abandoned. That is, we are not forsaken by God; although placed in poverty and want, God our shepherd is present with us.

The Greek word *aporos* is called “poor” in Latin; hence *aporiare*, properly meaning to cast someone away as poor. [The Greek-derived wording is somewhat uncertain in the transmitted text.]

Always carrying about in our body the mortification of Jesus, or bearing it—that is, we are always mortifying our members together with our vices and desires—so that the life of Jesus, by which he now lives immortally, may also be manifested in our bodies after the general resurrection.

Alternatively: just as Christ is fed and nourished in his own people, as he will say to the elect, “As long as you did it to one of these my least ones, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV), so he is killed, mortified, scourged, and persecuted in his own people.

Was he not persecuted and stoned in Stephen when he said, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX). He said likewise to Peter: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again in you.”

“Always,” he says, “we are carrying about or bearing the mortification of Jesus in our body.” That is, Jesus is always mortified and killed in us, so that, just as he is now killed in us and we too are killed for him, so he may also live in us and we may live in him.

And just as he now dies no more but always lives, so after the resurrection may we live immortal and incorruptible.

For we who live in the present age by faith and good works are always delivered over to death for the sake of Jesus. That is, we endure the dangers of death for the sake of Christ’s name and faith, which we preach, so that the life of Jesus, by which he now lives, may be manifested in our mortal flesh.

Thus the life by which Christ rose from the dead and by which he now lives may grant immortality and incorruption to this mortality of ours, so that after the promised resurrection we may not fear to die.

[Col. 0625B] Therefore death works in us—that is, what belongs to death—because it constantly mortifies us through many tribulations and hardships; but life—that is, the faith by which the righteous person lives—works in you what belongs to it, and draws you toward eternal life.

The meaning is: For the sake of the eternal life that we preach to you and the faith that we minister to you, we die and are killed, enduring the dangers of death each day.

But we apostles and the other believers have the same Spirit of God—that is, the Spirit possessed by the fathers of the Old Testament—for what they foretold as destined to be fulfilled concerning Christ, we believe has already been fulfilled.

Likewise, concerning the salvation of the Gentiles, we know that God the Father, who raised Jesus, will also raise us with Jesus on the day of judgment, that is, through the power of Jesus, and will establish us with you in eternal glory.

For we endure all things—that is, all the adversities of this age—for your sake, O Gentiles, because we preach faith and eternal life to you, so that abundant grace may abound through many in thanksgiving, to the glory of God.

He calls “abundant grace” the great divine wisdom that was freely given to them. The order is this: We therefore endure the adversities of this age for your sake, so that the great divine wisdom freely given to us may abound through many believers to glory and praise of God with thanksgiving—that is, so that very many believers, through our teaching, may offer thanks and praise to God.

Some manuscripts read: “so that divine wisdom may abound through many acts of thanksgiving to the praise of God.” This does not differ from the sense.

[Col. 0625D] Therefore—that is, so that divine wisdom may abound through many believers to the praise of God—we do not fail in the faith amid the dangers of death.

But although our outward person is corrupted, the inward person is renewed day by day. The outward person is called the body, while the inward person is the soul.

Although the human being consists of two substances and natures, there are nevertheless not two human beings, soul and body, but one human being. The outward person, namely the body, is increasingly corrupted by torments and tribulations; by that very fact the inward person, that is, the soul, is increasingly renewed and becomes more purified.

For the momentary and light affliction of the present works for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory. A moment is the shortest interval of time, named from the swift movement of the stars.

The meaning and order of the words is this: Every torment of our affliction, which is present, momentary—that is, very brief—and light to endure, works in us an eternal weight of glory, that is, a greatness of glory in the sublimity of the heavenly homeland, beyond measure and beyond every standard.

For the magnitude of that glory cannot be comprehended or measured by time, since it will exist eternally without end or limit. We do not contemplate what is seen, but what is not seen.

That is, we do not consider or attend to the honors, riches, and temporal profits that are seen and promised to us by the lovers of this age. Rather, we consider the joys of the heavenly homeland, which are not seen by bodily eyes.

Someone might say: Why do you not consider these temporal things? To this the Apostle adds: The things that are seen are temporal and transitory, but the things that are not seen except through faith are eternal. Therefore we set the former aside and embrace what will remain.

## CHAPTER V

For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved—that is, if our earthly, mortal, and corruptible body, in which our soul dwells, is dissolved through illness and the greatest tribulations and is reduced to dust through death—we have an edifice from God, or from God himself: a house not made by human hands, but eternal in the heavens.

By “edifice” he means a house not made by human hands, namely the mortal body, which will not be made by the hand—that is, by the union of male and female, as this present body is—but will be restored through the power of almighty God, so that it may be immortal and eternal and remain always in heaven.

The order and meaning are therefore this: If this mortal body, in which the soul now dwells, is dissolved through death, we know and are certain that we have from God in heaven an eternal edifice and a house not made by human hands—namely, an immortal body restored by the power of God.

For in this also—that is, in this mortal body—we groan, asking with a groan to be released from this mortal body, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling that is from heaven, that is, desiring to receive an immortal body.

It is said to be from heaven because it will be heavenly and will dwell in heaven. To be clothed over means to be clothed over the soul, just as the soul is now clothed with this mortal body.

If only we are clothed—that is, clothed by Christ—and are not found naked by him. The meaning is: Then we shall receive an immortal body for glory, and then it will be heavenly, if on the day of our death or on the day of judgment we are clothed with Christ, so that he may be with us, and if we are not found naked by him and alienated from his protection.

All the elect are clothed with Christ, because he is their protection, as the Apostle says: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III), that is, you have Christ as your protector.

For even we who are in this tabernacle—that is, in the mortal body, like travelers in tents—groan, that is, we grieve because we are burdened by hunger, thirst, nakedness, and other dangers.

We do not wish to be stripped of this mortal body; rather, we wish to be clothed over with immortality, without death intervening, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

That is, we wish that what is mortal and corruptible in us might be devoured by the immortality and enduring life, just as a tiny drop of water is consumed when thrown into a great fire.

It is as though he said: We therefore groan in this mortal body, which is burdened by various hardships, because, if it could happen, we would not wish to die; rather, we would wish death itself to fail within us, and we would receive immortality in the present age so that we might never die. But this will in no way happen in the present age.

Now the one who accomplishes this very thing for us—the one who will perfect us as immortals in the other life—is God, the Almighty, who gave us, as believers in him, the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

That is, at the time of baptism he gave us the grace of the Holy Spirit as a security or earnest, so that we might be certain of the promised glory of the inheritance. If the pledge is so great, how great will the inheritance and the fulfillment of the promise be?

Therefore, being confident always—that is, possessing confidence and daring to say that we have the pledge of the Holy Spirit—we know that while we are in this mortal body, we are absent from the Lord, that is, far from the Lord.

Yet the same Apostle says elsewhere, confirming the statement of a certain Gentile, that “in him”—that is, in God—“we live and move and are” (Acts XVII). Since God is everywhere and every place is in him, and therefore he is present everywhere, why does he now say that we are far from the Lord?

He says this for the following reason: the proper dwelling-place of almighty God is called heaven, and there he is always seen by the holy angels and righteous human beings. Since we are placed here, where he himself and the glory of eternal blessedness are not seen, we are said to be far from him and to be traveling as strangers from that glory.

For we walk by faith and not by sight, that is, by faith and hope we make our way toward the heavenly homeland, and not by sight or by possession, because we do not yet see what we shall be.

Yet we dare, with “to say” understood, and have the good will rather to be absent from the body and present with God in the soul, than to be present in the body and absent from God in the soul; that is, we already desire more to be in God’s presence, separated from this mortal body, than to be in this mortal body, where, while remaining here, we are far from contemplating God.

And therefore, because we have this will, we strive and labor to please him, whether we are absent, remaining in the mortal body, or present in soul; for whoever pleases God while situated here will not displease him there.

For we must all be made manifest and presented before the tribunal of Christ. A tribunal is the elevated seat of judges and governors who, when pronouncing judgments upon peoples, sit in a high place so that they can see the guilty and the innocent, [Col. 0628A] and so that they themselves too may be seen by all. The greatness of the tribunal and of the judgment must therefore be assessed according to the greatness of the power and of the judge, because that eternal power will appear exalted above heaven and earth, so that it can be seen by all, both the good and the rejected, “so that they may look upon him whom they pierced”; so that each person may render—that is, carry away or receive—the things proper to the body, with “merits” understood, according to what he did, whether good or evil.

Since many and very great sins are committed by the mind alone, such as hatred, envy, pride, and what the fool said in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. XIII), why does he say that a person will be judged only for what he has done with the body, namely, for murder, adultery, and other such acts? What he says—“that he may receive the merits proper to the body”—is to be understood in this way: that he may receive the merits proper to what he did during the time when he was in the body, so that “body” may be understood as the time of bodily existence.

From this passage also Bishop Paulinus of Nola proposed a question to blessed Augustine: what benefit did prayers and almsgiving bring to a dead person, when his parents and friends offered them after his death for the relief of his soul, if a person was to receive only his own merits, which he had acquired during the time when he was in the body? Blessed Augustine answered him that what is done after death by a person’s parents benefits the one who has already died in no way at all, unless, while situated in this life, he had earned by good intention, will, and beginning of action that those things performed by his parents after his departure should be acceptable to God.

Agreeing with this opinion, blessed Gregory says: “It must be known that no one will obtain any purification after death, even from the least things, unless, while situated in this life, he has earned the favor that he may obtain forgiveness there.” There are three things, however, that are beneficial after death, as blessed Augustine says in the book *Enchiridion*: fasts, almsgiving, and prayers. Those performed on behalf of the very good are acts of thanksgiving; on behalf of the not very good, who have been placed in some purification, they are acts of propitiation; and on behalf of the very wicked and eternally condemned, they are purifications. And if there are no aids for the dead, they are nevertheless consolations of whatever kind for the living. For those whom these things benefit, they either benefit them so that complete remission may be granted, or so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.

The mildest punishment of all will certainly be that of those who, apart from the sin they brought with them from their origin, added no further sin; and among the others who added sins, each person will have a condemnation there that is the more tolerable the lesser the iniquity he committed here.

Knowing, then, the fear of the Lord—not the fear by which he himself is afraid, but the fear by which he is to be feared, and by which all will be terrified on the day of judgment—we persuade people to turn away from evil and to do good, so that they may escape God’s vengeance.

But we are manifest to God. I hope, however, that we are manifest in your consciences, O Corinthians; that is, your very consciences bear witness on our behalf, because we believe rightly, live holily, and preach well. We are manifest to God.

Here he returns to the matters of which he spoke above: namely, that the false apostles were judging the true apostles and saying that Paul and Barnabas were deceivers, wishing to place not only Peter and the other apostles but also themselves above them—as if blessed Paul were saying: “To those who disparage us we are unknown, because they do not know what kind of men we are.” [Col. 0629A]

We are not again commending ourselves to you—that is, we are not again praising ourselves to you, as though we gained some advantage from that praise—but we are giving you an occasion to boast on our behalf, so that you may have something to say to those who boast in appearance and not in heart. That is, we give you grounds for boasting against the false apostles: that we are good and truthful apostles, that is, preachers.

The pseudo-apostles boasted in appearance, or in the presence of many, and not in heart; for, having no basis on which they could boast in their hearts, they praised themselves before others as being what they were not. The elect, however, boast in their hearts and not in appearance, because, knowing that they please God, they rejoice inwardly and nevertheless do not seek to be praised in public, lest perhaps they lose through vain glory the good that they possess.

For whether we are beside ourselves—that is, whether we act contrary to our mind, preaching one way and living another, or whether we boast of ourselves arrogantly—we are to be left and reserved for God, with “not to be judged by any of you” understood; or whether we are sober—that is, whether we have sound doctrine, or whether we live soberly and temperately—we preach to you, with “we are of benefit” understood.

For the love of Christ constrains us: that is, the love by which we love Christ compels us to say such things, namely, to praise ourselves to you, wishing to turn you back from love of the pseudo-apostles to love of Christ and of us. We judge this, and hold it as certain: if one—that is, Christ—died for all, then all are dead, both those who preceded his coming and those who followed it; and Christ died for all.

The entire human race, because of the original sin it brought from Adam, died both in body and in soul, since it was said to Adam: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Gen. II). He died on the day when he ate: he became mortal in soul and body, because afterward he died. Therefore, just as no human being exists outside Adam’s offspring, so no one exists outside his sin and death, except Christ alone.

Christ therefore came, born without sin, living in the world without sin, and died innocently for all who were predestined to life. As Prosper, John Chrysostom, and other teachers say, although not all believe, and although not all believers will be saved, he nevertheless did what belonged to him by dying for all.

For example: just as some physician, preparing a potion against every illness, might come into a certain city and say to everyone, “Whoever drinks from this potion will be saved from whatever illness he is afflicted with,” and whoever drinks is healed—even if all those unwilling to drink are not healed, he nevertheless brought the potion to all of them and did what pertained to him—so Christ died for all.

He died for all so that those who live in faith might no longer live for themselves, [Col. 0630A] but for him who died for all and rose again. The person lives for Christ who seeks not only his own advantage but that of others, and who does not hesitate to die for his brothers, just as Christ did not seek what was his but what was ours, because he died for all.

The sense is this: Christ died innocently for all; therefore I and the other apostles must not cease to bestow upon our brothers what we have received from him, and, if necessity requires it, to lay down our lives for their salvation.
