Therefore, from now on we know no one according to the flesh. He is addressing the perfect among the Corinthians. But were they not in the flesh when he said these things? Certainly they were. It must instead be understood as follows: “From now on”—that is, from the time when you were called to faith—“we know that none of you who are perfect lives according to the hope of fleshly and temporal things, but according to hope in heavenly rewards.” [Col. 0630B]

And if we have known Christ according to the flesh—that is, as mortal and corruptible—yet now we no longer know him as mortal and corruptible, but as immortal and incorruptible. The sense is: You have therefore not been placed in hope of fleshly and temporal things, because in hope and faith you are already immortal and incorruptible, secure of your reward.

If, therefore, anyone is a new creation—that is, a new people through faith and through the water of regeneration—the old things have passed away for them: namely, the law of the Old Testament in sacrifices, circumcision, the rest of the Sabbath, and other such things. Behold, all things have become new in the Gospel: circumcision, namely spiritual circumcision, which takes place in baptism, where the true stripping away of sins occurs.

The same is to be understood of the other matters as well. Alternatively: the old things have passed away—unbelief, sin, and the other things that belong to the old man, Adam—and the new things have come to be: faith, namely, righteousness, obedience, love, and the other virtues belonging to the new man, that is, Christ.

Another interpretation is this: if anyone is a new creation—that is, a new people—the old things have already passed away for them in hope, namely mortality and corruption, and the new things have likewise come to be in hope, namely immortality and incorruption. Or he has used the past tense for the future, meaning: “the old things will pass away, and all things will become new,” in accordance with what John says: “All things will be new.”

All things—that is, every kind of renewal—proceed from God the Father, who reconciled us to himself [Col. 0630D] through Christ, that is, through Christ’s passion, and gave us apostles the ministry of reconciliation.

Those are reconciled who were previously enemies. We too were enemies of God the Father, not by the nature that he made holy and good, but by the vice that we added. When, therefore, the sin that we added was removed, nature was restored through Christ’s blood as it had been created, and we were reconciled to God the Father.

Christ therefore, securing reconciliation for us through his passion, returned to God the Father, from whom he had come. But so that what he had secured for us should not remain incomplete or unfinished, he gave the ministry of reconciliation to his apostles, so that they might announce to us that we had been redeemed by Christ’s blood and reconcile us through their preaching. For he himself said: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John VI); “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII).

For God the Father was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself through him. God the Father was in the Son, and the Son in the Father, as the same Son says: “I and the Father are one” (John X); and, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV).

He was therefore in Christ in one way, and in the prophets and apostles through whom he spoke in another. In them he was present by grace; in Christ he was present through unity of substance, because they are one.

He reconciled the world to himself through Christ—that is, all those predestined to eternal life—not counting their sins against them, that is, against believers, after they had come to faith. For he did not regard what they had previously been, [Col. 0631B] but what they were going to become; and he placed in us the word of reconciliation, that is, the teaching of the Gospel.

Therefore, we act as ambassadors for Christ—that is, we perform the mission of Christ in his place—as though God were exhorting people through us, with “to believe” understood. We entreat on behalf of Christ—that is, in Christ’s place: be reconciled to God the Father through faith and righteousness, removing from yourselves every sin that separates you from God.

God the Father made him, that is, Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us—that is, a sacrifice for sin. For this is what the sacrifice for sin is called, especially in the Septuagint translators, who are accustomed to say: “For he shall place his hand upon the head of the sin” (Lev. I), that is, upon the head of the sacrifice for sin.

But a question arises in this passage: How can God judge and avenge sin in a human being if he himself did not know sin? It is resolved as follows: he knew through wisdom that sin is evil, but he did not know it by experience, as though he had ever sinned.

For example, we say that the evangelist John, when he wrote his Gospel, knew how to lie—that is, he knew falsehood through wisdom—but he did not know it through the will, as though he wished to lie, nor through experience, when he wrote it.

Therefore God the Father made Christ a sacrifice for sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him—that is, so that we might be made righteous through the mercy of God the Father in him, that is, through Christ; or “in him,” that is, joined together in the body of Christ, while assisting you through our preaching and example.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0631D]

We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. Exhortation is a form of teaching, when someone provides consolation to another by word or example.

For example: one of us sees his brother placed in grief and sorrow because of the loss of children and wife, or because of the loss of temporal possessions. If he recalls to him, as an example, how much and what kinds of things blessed Job patiently endured, and how afterward he deserved, because of his patience, to receive everything back twofold, such consolation and admonition is to be called exhortation.

He also sees someone grieve and suffer because he has lost the sight of his eyes. If he recalls blessed Tobit to him and thereby offers him some consolation, that too is exhortation.

If he sees another being crushed by excessive grief because of his sins and almost falling into despair, and by word or example offers consolation so that he does not despair of pardon or salvation—giving him the example of Mary the prostitute, to whom the Lord forgave all her sins (Luke VII), and of the thief on the cross, who at a single utterance deserved to hear, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII)—that is good exhortation and consolation.

Let us explain it in another way. Suppose someone is placed in single combat with his enemy, and one of the bystanders says to him, “Fight bravely; do not hesitate; do not give up; you will obtain victory.” He offers him exhortation and courage. Likewise, whoever admonishes someone engaged in the contest of good works against the devil and the vices of the flesh not to give up or cease from the work he has begun offers good exhortation.

Accordingly, the Apostle now addresses the Corinthians, and in them all the faithful: We exhort you by our preaching, our example, and in every way, not to receive the grace of God in vain—that is, emptily and uselessly.

All good things given to the human race are called the grace of God, because they are granted to it freely. The grace of God is to possess faith, hope, love, divine or human wisdom, and temporal goods.

A person therefore receives this grace of God in vain if, coming to faith and receiving remission of sins in baptism, he proves disobedient to God’s commandments and does not apply himself diligently, with God’s help, to fulfilling them, since “faith without works is dead and empty” (James II).

He also receives temporal goods given freely by God in vain if he does not endeavor, with a cheerful spirit, to distribute them to the poor for the love of God.

So that we do not prolong the discussion, let us mention one example among many of how the grace of God is received in vain. The Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations the faith of the holy Trinity, baptizing them and teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII). Whoever comes to faith and does not observe what is contained in the Law and the Gospel receives the grace of God in vain.

For he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” The prophet Isaiah spoke this in the person of God the Father speaking to the Son.

The acceptable time for God the Father, and the day of salvation for the human race, was the time of Christ’s passion, in which God the Father decreed, arranged, and predestined to save and redeem the human race through the passion of his Son.

At this acceptable time God the Father heard his Son, because whatever the Son prayed for the salvation of the human race, he obtained in its entirety. For we read in John’s Gospel that, as his passion approached, he prayed, saying: “Father, I will that those whom you have given me should be where I am, and that they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory” (John XVII).

If any of the apostles claims that this was said only about the apostles, let him consider that Christ elsewhere says: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (ibid.).

He also heard him concerning his prayer when he prayed, saying: “Father, glorify your Son.” And a voice came from heaven, crying: “I have glorified him”—with “at the time of baptism and on the mountain before the disciples” understood—“and I will glorify him” by raising him from the dead on the third day.

Nor was he heard only on behalf of others, but also on behalf of his persecutors, for whom he prayed while hanging on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). For many thousands of them believed through the apostles’ preaching after his ascension.

He also heard him on the day of the salvation of the human race, because, having conquered the power of death on the third day, he recalled him from the dead.

Just as we have referred these words to the head of all the elect, that is, to Christ, so let us refer them also to his members. The acceptable time in which we can be heard, and the day on which we can secure eternal salvation for ourselves, extends from the beginning of the Lord’s preaching, but especially from his resurrection until the day of judgment. During this time, through good works, we can be acceptable to God the Father, please him, and be heard by him.

Concerning this time the Apostle adds: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” The acceptable time for doing penance is the present life, lasting until the day of judgment. It is also called the day of salvation, in which we can earn eternal salvation for ourselves, because it is suited to working.

Concerning this day the Lord says: “Walk while you have the light” (John XII). Night follows this day, namely the eternal darkness of condemnation, in which no one can work, as the Lord says: “The night is coming, when no one can work” (John IX). And the same Apostle says: “While we have time, let us do what is good” (Gal. VI).

Now we sinners can make progress toward forgiveness; now we can obtain pardon, because, according to what the prophet says, “In hell no one will confess to God for forgiveness” (Ps. VI). There will indeed be repentance, but it will be late and delayed.

Giving no offense to anyone. Properly speaking, an offense is a scandal, a fall, or an impediment to the foot; but in this passage it is used especially for an occasion. “Let us,” he says, “give no one any offense”—that is, no occasion for sinning, whether in word or in the example of an evil action; let us scandalize no one in any speech or deed—so that our ministry may not be reviled.

The Apostle speaks in his own person and in that of all preachers, joining himself to the Corinthians. The ministry of preachers is reviled and despised if they destroy by their deeds what they preach should be done in words, preaching one thing publicly and doing another in secret: teaching good things openly, but practicing shameful things in private.

But in all things—with “our acts and words” understood—let us present and prepare ourselves as ministers of God. A minister of God is one who serves and fights for God through the word of teaching and the fruit of good works.

Whoever wishes to be a minister of God must minister to God in all things, so that in everything he does he may be recognized as a worshiper of the true God. For example, he should teach the ignorant, feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, warm the cold, gather the wandering, visit the sick, [Col. 0634A] and bury the dead. In all these things he should seek not human praise but the grace of God; he should seek not to please human beings but to obey God’s commandments.

Whoever does these things will minister to God and will deserve to hear from him, together with the elect: “As long as you did it to one of these least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV).

In great patience. Patience is not giving up amid the adversities of this age, such as the holy martyrs possessed. “Not in little or moderate patience,” he says, “but in great patience let us present ourselves as ministers of God.”

Patience also consists in patiently bearing with offenders, just as blessed Paul endured the Corinthians. After they had come to faith, they returned to their former vices; he reproved them sometimes gently and sometimes severely, until he recalled them [Col. 0634B] to faith.

In tribulations—with “let us be in great patience and present ourselves as ministers of God” understood. By tribulations he means hunger, thirst, nakedness, and other afflictions.

In necessities. A necessity is so called because it is placed in *nece*, that is, in danger of death, where the Apostle commands patience to be maintained in straits. Every need and want is called a strait.

In blows, in prisons. The Apostle was often beaten with rods and swords, and often confined in prisons for Christ’s name. There he did not cease to preach God’s gift, disregarding his own safety.

He admonishes us, with great patience, that if necessity should require us to suffer such things for the love of Christ and the salvation of our brothers, we should endure what he himself endured, even to decapitation.

In riots let us be in great patience. Riots properly concern citizens and are disturbances, disorders, or contentions.

In labors. The Apostle Paul labored not only in preaching but also toiled with his hands. Thus he acquired food and clothing through his work, specifically through the labor of the tentmaking trade, so that he would not be burdensome to his hearers if he accepted anything from them, knowing that this would benefit him before God.

In vigils let us be devoted. He not only did not cease from labor or rest during the day, but was also so concerned with the duty entrusted to him that he did not cease at night either from preaching or from other work.

Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles that he prolonged his discourse until midnight (Acts XX), when Eutychus—whose name means “mad”—fell from the third story, because he had been negligent in his eagerness to hear the word of God.

In fasts let us be patient. Sometimes he fasted voluntarily and sometimes unwillingly, and so that he would not be bent toward concern for his stomach, he gave thanks to God. For just as the medicine of the chief physician is necessary for wounds, so fasts are necessary for our soul.

In purity of mind and body. Purity of body consists in being kept immaculate and undefiled from every pleasure of lust. Purity of mind is integrity of faith, because true purity is that which is not polluted even in the mind.

Or when he says “in purity,” he means that we should be devoted to the sincerity and integrity of the word of God, so that we do not adulterate God’s word; so that we seek not our own glory but God’s; so that we do not devote ourselves to preaching for temporal profits but for eternal recompense; so that we do not preach one thing publicly and do another secretly; and so that we do not interpret Holy Scripture perversely.

In knowledge of the Old and New Testament let us be occupied, not in pretense, nor in human wisdom, which inflates a person without love.

In long-suffering. Long-suffering is prolonged perseverance of spirit and patience amid the adversities of this age.

In gentleness, so that we generate bitterness in no one, not only by our deeds but not even by our words.

In the Holy Spirit—that is, let us present ourselves as people who are a temple of the Holy Spirit.

In unfeigned love. Love is feigned when someone sees his brother placed in need and abandons him, although previously he professed that he loved him with all the effort of his mind. Love is also feigned when someone sees his brother sinning but does not rebuke him out of a desire to flatter.

Love is firm, however, if we love our neighbor as ourselves, and if we do not abandon the one to whom we appeared to cling in prosperity when the time of persecution comes. The apostle John says concerning love: “Beloved, let us not love only in word and tongue, but in deed and truth.”

In the word of truth. Let us be occupied—that is, in the teaching of the Gospel—or certainly in the word of truth, so that we speak the truth with our neighbors.

Let us place our hope in the power of God, not in our own boldness or in the power of any human being, because “cursed is the person who trusts in a human being” (Jer. XVII).

Or when he says “in the power of God,” he means that we should not attribute to our own merits whatever good we do, but to the power of God, with whose help we are able to fulfill every good work.

Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left—that is, let us proceed through the weapons of the virtues in prosperity and adversity.

The person who possesses the weapons—that is, the guardianship of the virtues—on the right is one whose mind the prosperity of this age does not raise up into pride or soften. He also possesses weapons on the left who is not cast down or broken by adversity.

Paul therefore carried weapons on the right and on the left, and proceeded securely in the midst when he said such things, because he was humble in prosperity and exceedingly strong in adversity.

Confidence and certain hope should therefore always be present to our minds in adversity, and fear in prosperity, lest either adversity drag us into despair—as it did Cain and Judas the traitor—or prosperity raise the mind into the swelling of pride and deceive it through confidence in itself, as happened also to Nebuchadnezzar when he said: “Is this not that Babylon which I built?” (Dan. IV.)

Through glory and ignobility. Just as a noble person is called *nominabilis*, “worthy of being named,” so an ignoble person is one without a title of dignity.

The holy apostles were regarded as glorious among the faithful, who praised them as truthful, holy, and righteous; but among unbelievers they were ignoble and without any praise.

Hence the Apostle says: “Through the glory of the faithful and the ignobility of unbelievers.” Or: let us proceed patiently as ministers of God among those by whom we are called glorious and among those by whom we are called ignoble, so that we are neither lifted up by the favor and praise of the faithful nor cast down by the disparagement of unbelievers.

Alternatively: through the glory of divine wisdom and the glory of virtues or miracles, and through the ignobility of scourging, contempt, and prisons, let us proceed patiently through dishonor and good repute.

Dishonor is a bad reputation; good repute is a favorable opinion and praise. What he said above, “through glory and ignobility,” he repeated by way of explanation when he said: “Through dishonor and good repute let us proceed patiently,” maintaining the guardianship of the virtues on the right and on the left, trusting our own knowledge of what we are more than the words of others.

As deceivers and truthful. He now explains what came before. By unbelievers they were called deceivers, magicians, and sorcerers; by believers, however, because of their sound doctrine and the power of their miracles, they were regarded not only as truthful and righteous but even as gods.

Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XIV), when they brought crowns to Paul and Barnabas, saying: “They are gods hiding in human form.”

And what wonder is it if the apostles and servants were called deceivers, when the Lord himself, the teacher of all, was called a deceiver, when the Jews said to Pilate after his death: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said while he was still alive: ‘After three days I will rise again’” (Matt. XXVII).

Let us proceed patiently as deceivers among unbelievers and as truthful among believers, protected on every side by the weapons of the virtues. As those who are unknown to unbelievers and known to believers—that is, let us proceed among those who do not know our way of life and cannot penetrate our teaching, and among those by whom we are known to be true worshipers of God—most patiently fortified with the weapons of righteousness: [Col. 0636C]

As dying, and behold, we live. The holy apostles and martyrs seemed to be dying when they were afflicted by many tortures and sufferings almost to the point of death. But while they were placed in such danger of death and in despair of life, through scourges, beatings, and stonings they were suddenly strengthened and comforted by God’s power, and as though from the dead they received life.

Thus we read concerning blessed Paul: after he had been scourged and buried under stones at Lystra for a long time, and dragged through the streets of the city until he was left as though dead, at dawn, when that same night had passed, he began publicly to preach the word of God in Derbe.

Those who were beheaded seemed to die while passing from this age, but that death was temporal, and perpetual life followed it.

As chastised, by blows and by words, but not put to death. When the holy apostles and martyrs were scourged, God indeed chastised them so that they would not exalt themselves on account of the greatest grace granted to them, but he did not permit them to die until the time when it pleased him.

In this passage we can understand chastisement as scourging, just as we read that Pilate said concerning the Lord: “Having chastised him, I will release him” (Luke XXIII).

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. When the apostles and holy martyrs wept amid scourges and terrible torments, they appeared sorrowful in their faces, but they rejoiced in their hearts, secure in the hope of heavenly rewards, knowing that the sufferings of this time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in them, and that their sorrow would be turned into eternal joy.

Whatever tribulation and persecution the elect endure is, as it were, for them—that is, as though it were not—because if they are struck with rods, flayed, or even killed, all these things are “as though”: they are transitory and temporal. Their reality will come, namely eternal joy and life that will endure without end.

For just as someone who sows, having awakened, is accustomed to say, “As though I saw people riding; as though I saw many feasts set before me,” and says “as though” throughout because there is no reality there, but they have passed away like a shadow, so in all that the saints suffer in this age there is an “as though,” because it is transitory.

They appeared to die amid punishments; they appeared to be sorrowful according to their weakness, but it was only “as though,” because inwardly they rejoiced. And if they died for a time, their death suddenly passed into eternal life.

For the rejected, however, who place all their hope in earthly and transitory things and do not strive toward eternal joys, but rejoice in the prosperity and happiness of this age, it appears that they possess what is real, but it is not real, because it is transitory and temporal. When they have passed from this life, they will find nothing of those things that appeared to them here as though real, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV). [Col. 0637C]

Their “as though” reality will therefore pass away; it was not real. Their woe will come, that is, eternal punishment.

As poor, yet enriching many. They appeared poor in the riches of this age, but they abounded in spiritual riches through preaching and miracles, by which they enriched others.

Or they truly appeared poor in temporal substance, but they made many rich, such as the saints who were in Jerusalem, who had abandoned all their possessions for Christ or had been stripped of them by the Jews because they had believed in a dead man. The Apostle addresses them in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “You joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions” (Heb. XII); and Isaiah says of them: “The one who withdrew from iniquity and evil was exposed to plunder” (Isa. LIX).

The apostles therefore enriched and made these people wealthy, because from every place where they preached they supplied them with what was necessary. Hence the same Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Now I will depart for Jerusalem to minister to the saints” (Rom. XV). [Col. 0637D]

As having nothing, and possessing everything. They were as having nothing because they possessed nothing as their own. Yet they possessed everything, because all things were common to them (Acts II, IV). Monks too should be as having nothing of their own and possessing everything in common.

Or they were as having nothing because they possessed neither estates, nor gold, nor silver, nor male or female slaves, and yet they possessed all these things in their owners, whom they had subjected to themselves through the weapons of preaching and the power of miracles. [Col. 0638A]

For in the possessors they possessed everything that belonged to the possessors. Just as a certain Roman commander named Tarquinius replied to the envoys of a certain people who wished to offer gold in exchange for peace and liberty—namely, that the Romans preferred to rule those who possessed gold rather than to have or possess gold themselves—so the holy apostles desired more to possess the owners of riches through the faith and teaching of Christ than to possess anything as their own.

We may also say that in this age the apostles were as having nothing, but in their head, Christ, they possessed everything, in accordance with what the same Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans concerning God the Father: “He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also, together with him, give us all things?” (Rom. VIII).

Let us therefore also be as having nothing in this age, placing no hope in transitory and perishable things.

For we possess all things with Christ, and, moreover, we shall possess Christ himself with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. For, as Solomon says, whoever is faithful possesses the whole world as his wealth, because he does not desire the things that are in the world, knowing beyond doubt that the world and its desire will pass away; and because he does not desire or seek to have anything except what he has, he possesses, as it were, everything. No one has more than the person who needs nothing; yet although the rich possess many things, they need many things because they desire to have more than they have. But the person who needs nothing is the one who, apart from [Col. 0638C] the necessities of food, clothing, and footwear, requires nothing and is content with what he has. In all these things, therefore, let us imitate the holy apostles, our teachers and patrons, as good sons imitate good fathers, so that amid adversity and prosperity we may proceed patiently, presenting ourselves as God’s ministers; for if we share in their deeds in this world, we shall surely be participants in their eternal rewards.

“Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.” That is, the disposition of our mind and the intention of our heart. The preaching of our mouth is also open and already prepared for preaching and ready to teach you. The mouth of the person whose will is perfect, whose preaching is holy, and whose conduct is good is open and ready for preaching. But when someone’s will is [Col. 0638D] crooked and his conduct and life are depraved, even if he seems to possess some understanding, his words fail together with his meaning. Therefore, his mouth is not open for preaching, because he is afraid to rebuke in others what he knows is perceived in himself by others.

“You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own inward parts.” The meaning is this: O Corinthians, if you have a narrow and constricted understanding, so that you cannot receive the breadth of the divine mysteries, do not attribute this to us, since it does not rest with us, who ought to minister to you, but with you, who ought to receive. We can indeed say many things to you, and we have the will to do so, but your understanding and will are constricted [Col. 0639A] in your inward parts, that is, in the interior of your heart.

“Having the same reward”—understand, “prepared”—“as we do,” because you have the same faith, “you too be enlarged,” that is, extend your understanding and intellect, lest, because of the narrowness of your understanding, you be unable to penetrate and receive the divine mysteries.

“Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers.” In a yoke two animals are joined and made equal. Here, however, we must understand the yoke of the devil and the power that he exercises over the faithful, as though he were saying: Do not take upon yourselves the devil’s yoke, nor be made equal or joined to unbelievers, lest you become like them. “For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity?” That is, what fellowship does a righteous person who possesses righteousness have with an unrighteous and pagan person? None. “What fellowship has light”—that is, the faithful person—“with [Col. 0639B] darkness”—that is, the unbeliever? None. This is the light, and these are the darkness, of which the same Apostle says: “You were once darkness,” that is, unbelievers, “but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V), that is, believers.

“And what agreement has Christ with Belial?” Belial is interpreted as “without a yoke,” signifying the devil, who shook the yoke of almighty God from his neck. It is also said in the Book of Samuel: “The men of Belial,” that is, “without the yoke of God.” What agreement, or what fellowship, does Christ have with the devil? None.

“And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” That is, what agreement should the faithful, who are the temple of God, have with idolaters, who are temples of demons? None. In this passage he strikes at those who, reclining in [Col. 0639C] idol temples, ate sacrificial meat, although they ought to have been faithful and the temple of God. “For you are the temple of the living God,” not of gods who do not live. God is called living in distinction from those gods who do not live, although they are called gods. As God says through Jeremiah: “I will dwell in them,” through faith, love, and my grace, “and I will walk among them.” The Son of God, who spoke these things about believing and chosen people, walked among human beings, as it is said: “He was seen upon earth and lived among human beings”; and he himself dwelt in us, as John says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). “And I will be their God, and they will be my people,” just as Israel formerly was.

[Col. 0639D] “Therefore come out from among them.” The prophet Isaiah foretold this long before the Babylonian captivity, and the Apostle related it to the Corinthians. The prophet speaks in the person of God, addressing the Jews returning from captivity after seventy years: “Therefore”—because you are my people—“come out from among the Chaldeans, so that you may be separated from them, and do not touch what is unclean,” that is, the idol, than which nothing is more unclean; do not worship it. “And I will receive you” into the land of promise.

Let us also refer this to the Corinthians and see how those who had believed could leave their wives, children, and all their possessions, when they were still imperfect and could not fulfill what the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything that you have” (Matthew [Col. 0640A] XIX), and so forth. The Apostle therefore did not command them physically to withdraw completely from those unbelievers who were still among them, but rather to separate themselves from them in mind. “Come out,” he says, “from among the pagans”; but if you cannot do so physically, then at least do so mentally. Separate yourselves from them in your will, and do not touch an unclean person. The person who imitates a sinner touches an unclean person. “And if you do this,” says the Apostle, “I will receive you into complete fellowship,” and the Lord will receive you into eternal blessedness.

# CHAPTER VII

Since, therefore, we have these promises, beloved—namely, those mentioned above, that we are God’s children and that he is [Col. 0640B] our Father—“let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit.” He did not simply say, “Let us cleanse ourselves from defilement,” but “from every defilement of flesh and spirit.” Defilement of the flesh is fornication, adultery, murder, and the other vices performed through the body. Defilement of the spirit, that is, of the mind, is anger, envy, pride, evil will, and the other evils conceived in the soul. “Let us complete sanctification in the fear of God.” The person who cleanses himself from every defilement of flesh and spirit completes sanctification in fear, that is, through the fear of God.

“Receive us,” that is, understand what we say; or, become capable of our speech; or, imitate us. We have injured none of you by word or example; we have stripped none of you [Col. 0640C] through our flattery; we have corrupted none of you by a perverse understanding or example; we have defrauded none of you in business in order to empty your purses. It is as though he were saying: What we did not do, the false apostles did; therefore you are not acting rightly when you place them before us.

“I do not say this for your condemnation,” that is, I do not praise myself and the other apostles to your reproach, but for your correction. Or: I do not cast you away by saying such things, but admonish you so that you may correct yourselves. For we said in the previous Epistle that you are in our hearts, or in our will, “to die together in the present life and to live together in future glory.” That is, we are led by such great love and longing for you that, if it were possible, you would endure with us in this world martyrdom through [Col. 0640D] many torments for Christ’s name, so that you might receive with us the crown and reward of martyrdom.

I have great confidence in you—understand, “and therefore I speak such things,” hoping that you will obey me. “I overflow with joy in all our tribulation,” that is, when I hear of your correction and good conduct, I am so filled with joy that, even though I were confined in prison and chains, I would feel no pain.

For when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest; but what the flesh did not have, the spirit had, since it rejoices amid adversity. Macedonia is a region of Achaea. When Paul and Silas came there and began to preach and perform miracles, [Col. 0641A] a certain girl who had a pythonic spirit—who brought her masters considerable profit by divining—walked through the streets crying out: “These men are servants of the Most High God” (Acts XVI). Paul took pity on her and drove the evil spirit out of her. When her masters saw that the hope of their profit had disappeared, they stirred up a considerable riot against Paul and Silas, so that, after being scourged for a long time, they were thrown into the depths of the prison.

He adds: “Our flesh had no rest,” he says, “but we suffered every tribulation.” “Outside,” understand, there were conflicts; “inside,” fears. The conflicts were outside, in the body, while they endured blows and scourging; the fears were inside, in the mind, because they feared that those who had believed might be scandalized by their suffering and withdraw from the faith. [Col. 0641B]

Alternatively: “Outside,” that is, outside the prison, in public, there were conflicts against the believers, who were being attacked by unbelievers; “inside,” in the prison, there were fears, since the apostles were bound there and feared that they would be killed by their persecutors.

He reported to us your longing, by which you desired to correct yourselves—or by which you desired to see us; your weeping, by which you lamented those who had withdrawn from the faith; and your zeal for me, that is, your love for me, by which you were ardently determined to defend strongly the truth of my preaching, and you rejected the false apostles from among you. Thus I rejoiced more—understand, over your correction—than I grieved over my chains.

“Not because you were saddened”—understand, when you received [Col. 0641C] the Epistle—“therefore do I rejoice”; for you were saddened according to God. The person who is saddened according to God is the one who desires to appease God toward himself through repentance. “So that you might suffer no harm from us,” that is, so that you might receive no harm in any of the things that we command you. For although we saddened you through the Epistle, it benefits you greatly.

For “the sorrow that is according to God”—that is, the sorrow of one who desires to please God—“produces repentance leading to enduring salvation,” that is, to eternal life. “But worldly sorrow,” that is, sorrow over the loss of temporal things or over some pain belonging to a temporal matter, “produces death,” understand, eternal death, that is, the condemnation of the soul; often also bodily death, as is known to have been experienced by many.

[Col. 0641D] For behold, this very thing—namely, this sorrow, your being saddened according to God—produces how great a diligence, that is, how great a concern, lest you fall again into similar sins. Where there is diligence, there is no sleepiness, security, or inertia. It produces defense, understand, so that you may be able to defend yourselves against the attacks of demons. It produces indignation, because a person becomes indignant with himself when he sins. The person who exercises good care also becomes indignant against sinners, or patiently endures the indignation of others. It produces fear of God; it produces longing for the heavenly homeland; it produces zeal, that is, love of God, good earnestness, and imitation of good works; and it produces vengeance upon oneself, because one afflicts oneself on account of one’s offense.

[Col. 0642A] Blessed Augustine says that although the conjunction *sed* (“but”) in this passage does not yield a complete sense, it nevertheless sounds very well in Greek. “In everything in which I instructed you, you showed and prepared yourselves to be undefiled by the matter,” that is, to be unstained by my command, because you obeyed me. A disciple makes himself undefiled by his teacher’s command when he obeys the teacher’s order. If, however, he proves disobedient in some matter, then, even if he is free from every other fault, he is nevertheless stained by his disobedience.

Alternatively: In this you prove yourselves free from the guilt of others, because you rebuked their error vigorously. A defiled person does not possess the authority to exact punishment from others.

Therefore, although I wrote the previous Epistle to you, I did not write it only because of the man who committed the wrong against [Col. 0642B] all of you by taking his father’s wife, or because of those who defrauded their brothers, but to make our concern for you manifest. For this reason he adds: “Therefore we have been comforted” by your correction, obedience, and reception of Titus.

“His inward parts,” that is, those of Titus, “are more abundantly inclined toward you.” Whatever is contained within the skin may be called *viscus* (“inward part”). Children are also called “inward parts.” The term is likewise used for an affection of excessive love, as here. “His inward parts,” that is, his exceedingly abundant love and charitable affection toward you have increased all the more.

“I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you,” understand, because you will obey me.

# CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0642C]

We make known to you the grace of God, that is, faith and other such gifts freely given to the faithful, which grace was given to the Church of Macedonia. In the midst of a severe trial of tribulation—understand, both ours and theirs—their abundance of joy, and their very deep poverty, abounded and overflowed into the riches of their simplicity. The blessed Apostle, knowing that the Corinthians were avaricious and extremely tight-fisted, sets before them as an example the charity and good will of the Macedonians, which they had shown toward the saints who were in Jerusalem.

For those Macedonians had been exceedingly poor before they came to the faith by believing in Christ. Their great poverty [Col. 0642D] overflowed into many riches because, from that same poverty which they possessed, as soon as they believed they resolved to send necessities to the saints who were in Jerusalem. They did this simply, that is, with good will and intention. He is therefore about to speak at length in what follows concerning the almsgiving and gift that the Apostle wished the Corinthians to send to those who were in Jerusalem.

“For I bear witness to them according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing.” The order is confused and inverted: “I bear witness to them”—namely, to the Macedonians—“because beyond their ability they were willing,” that is, they desired more than they were able to give, and they gave according to the measure of their ability.

“With much exhortation, begging us”—understand, “to accept from them [Col. 0643A] the grace,” that is, the gift which they were freely giving, “and the fellowship of the ministry” that is performed for the saints who are in Jerusalem.

“And not as we hoped, but they gave themselves.” That is, they did not act as we feared when they first put us in prison. Here he uses “hope” for “fear,” just as it occurs in Virgil:

> “If only I had been able to hope for so great a grief,”

where the meaning is “to fear.” First they gave themselves to the Lord, coming to the faith and correcting their errors; then they gave themselves to us, submitting themselves to our teaching. Thus—understand, they gave themselves wholly to the Lord, and they became subject to us—so that we might ask Titus, when we sent him to you, to complete in you this grace of generosity and almsgiving: that you might willingly send temporal goods to the brothers who [Col. 0643B] are in Jerusalem, just as these people freely and willingly send them.

“I do not speak as one commanding”—understand, such things—but, through the concern shown by others, also testing the good disposition of your charity. That is, I wish, through the generosity of these people, to be able to approve the good disposition of your charity, so that, if these poor people have sent so much, you may send more.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he bestowed upon you. All the good things given to the human race are the grace of God. Although he was rich according to his divinity, possessing all things with the Father, for your sake and for the sake of all believers he became needy and poor, so much so that he did not have what the foxes have, so that through his poverty you might be rich [Col. 0643C] in heaven. He became human so that he might make us gods, in accordance with what he says through the Psalmist: “I said, You are gods” (Psalm LXXXI).

“And I give counsel in this matter”—understand, that you should imitate his poverty. For this is useful for you—understand, to do what I say—you who began not only to do but also to desire it from the previous year, or from last year. There were some among them who had the will to send something to the brothers in Jerusalem, but did nothing as a result. There were also others who did something toward this end, but did not bring it to completion. He now exhorts them all, saying: “This is useful for you to do, who began to desire it and who have done it in part.”

But now complete it in deed, that is, fulfill it through action.

[Col. 0643D] For if the will to give is ready and prepared, it is accepted according to what one has—understand, and gives—not according to what one does not have, because one cannot give what one does not have, even if one wishes to do so. This is so among human beings; but with God the good will itself is rewarded.

“For it is not”—understand, “for this reason that I command such things”—so that there might be relief for others, that is, abundance and refreshment, but from equality. Understand, this is what you ought to do. For example: Let the person who has one hundred solidi retain fifty for himself and send fifty to those who are in Jerusalem. Or, “from equality,” let him send something to them and retain something for the needs of himself and his household. A cheerful giver is rightly characterized by good will, which regulates his generosity in such a way that both the refreshment of the poor [Col. 0644A] may rejoice in it and domestic sufficiency may not suffer.

It should be noted that the distinction occurs where he says, “but from equality”: “At the present time,” that is, in this life, “let your abundance supply their need,” so that their abundance, which is spiritual, in fasting and prayers, may also be a supply for your need. That is, let them provide you with what you possess less of in spiritual matters, while you provide them with what they do not have in temporal matters, so that there may be equality between you and them: you giving them what they do not have, and they giving you what you do not have—you giving them temporal things, and they giving you eternal things.

“He who gathered much did not have too much, and he who gathered little did not have too little.” Literally, this was said about the manna. For when the Lord commanded that a full [Col. 0644B] *gomer* be gathered for each person—a measure containing three sextarii—some gathered more and some less. But when they had prepared their food for themselves in a mortar with a pestle, both the one who had gathered more and the one who had gathered less afterward found one measure, namely, a full *gomer*.

Spiritually, however, he wishes to show here that if there are two people, one rich and the other poor, then although the rich person possesses much and distributes more to the poor than the poor person does, the rich person’s almsgiving does not surpass the generosity of the poor person. Often the poor person’s small gift is more acceptable to God than the rich person’s large gift, because the poor person gives from his own sustenance, while the rich person gives from what he has in abundance.

The Lord confirmed this in the Gospel when, seeing the rich putting much into the treasury [Col. 0644C] and a widow putting in two small coins (*duo minuta*), which is a *quadrans*, that is, a quarter of a denarius, he said (Luke XXI): “This widow has put in more than all the others,” because they retained much for themselves, whereas she put in all her sustenance, keeping nothing for herself. For God weighs the heart, not the substance; nor does he consider how much is brought into his gift, but with how much love it is offered.

“For he received the exhortation”—understand, from me—which he ministered to you.

“With him,” that is, with Titus, “we sent the brother whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches.” [Col. 0644D] Luke, who is also Lucius, is understood here though his name is not explicitly given. He already possessed a Gospel written with remarkable skill, which was read throughout all the churches, and also the Acts of the Apostles; through this labor he had the praise of all the faithful.

He was not only praised throughout all the churches, but was also appointed as the companion and associate of our pilgrimage.

“We avoid and take precautions against this, lest anyone blame and reproach you in this abundance”—understand, of doctrine and miracles—which is administered by us. That is, lest someone should be able to say: “Paul, Barnabas, Timothy, their companions, and many others indeed preach well and perform thousands of miracles through the Lord’s power; but in this they do not act well, because they do not care for the poor saints who are in Jerusalem, as the other apostles do, and as the apostles commanded Paul and Barnabas when they were sent to the [Col. 0645A] Gentiles.” Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The apostles appointed,” he says, “that we—I and Barnabas—should go to the Gentiles and devote ourselves solely to preaching, provided that we remembered the poor.”

“Providing what is good not only before God but also before human beings.” The Apostle Paul and the others provided what was good before God because in everything they did they sought to please God. They provided what was good before the Corinthians because they sent to them such brothers to receive the gifts that were to be sent to the saints in Jerusalem—those who had likewise abandoned their possessions for Christ and were not greedy for wealth or lovers of earthly things—lest the Corinthians should find an occasion to say: “We sent much, but those whom he sent to us stole it, when they ought to have [Col. 0645B] increased it.”

Alternatively: As we have said, the person who desires to please God provides what is good before God; and before human beings is the person who avoids blame, so that he may not be excessively righteous, but may be considered irreproachable by everyone in his entire life and conduct.

“With them”—namely, with Titus and Lucius—“we sent our brother,” understand, Apollos, who had already remained with you for a long time. We have found him to be concerned—understand, concerned for you—after he had departed from you because of the bad conduct and harshness of certain people. But now we have found him much more concerned—understand, concerned for you—because he heard that you had been corrected and reformed. At this point the passage should be punctuated, and one should then proceed to what follows: “I have much confidence”—understand, “in you.”

[Col. 0645C] Either on behalf of Titus, who is my partner in preaching and your helper in teaching, just as I am, or on behalf of our brother apostles—understand, your helpers—they reported to me your correction and holy conduct.

“Show your charity toward them”—that is, toward Titus, Luke, and Apollos—“in the presence of the churches,” that is, in the presence of the faithful.

# CHAPTER IX

For concerning the ministry that is performed for the saints, it is superfluous—that is, more than necessary—for me to write to you.

“For Achaia”—that is, the part of Achaia—“has been ready since last year,” namely, those who live outside Corinth, the metropolitan city.

“So that we do not speak of you in this substance.” [Col. 0645D] There is a considerable deficiency of wording and sense in this passage, of this kind: “So that we do not speak of you in this substance”—understand, in this carnal and temporal matter—as having done less, since you are perfect in all things and flourishing in good will.

I considered it necessary to ask the brothers—namely, Titus, Silas, and Apollos—to go ahead of us—understand, to you. The meaning is: Give that gift as a blessing, that is, as good will arising from charity; give it not as though it were avarice, that is, not grudgingly, but willingly.

“He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.” *Parce* (“sparingly”) is sometimes used for “forgive,” as in Virgil:

> “Spare your fear, Cytherea,”

that is, “dismiss your fear.” At other times it is used for “preserve,” as in the passage: “Here I shall begin to sing how great the skill is of the sparing bees.” The bees are called *parcae* (“preservers”), as it were, because they [Col. 0646A] preserve their honey.

In this passage, however, by using *parce* adverbially, he wishes to signify the avaricious person, from whom something is extracted by force so that he may give it. Therefore, “he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly,” that is, the person who gives little to the poor will receive little reward, just as, literally, the person who sows little gathers little.

“And he who sows in blessings”—that is, the person who gives alms to the poor with good will and distributes temporal goods with sincerity of mind, seeking neither human praise for it nor wishing to make the person to whom he gives subject to himself through the gift—“will also reap from blessings.” That is, from the good will of his mind he will receive the reward of eternal blessedness. The person sows in blessing who acts with good will in the hope of eternal reward.

“Each person should give as he has determined in his heart, not from sadness or compulsion.” That is, let him give to God and to the poor as much as he has resolved [Col. 0646B] in his mind to give, since it is better not to promise in one’s heart or by word than not to fulfill what has been promised. The Apostle teaches that this same almsgiving or vow should be fulfilled with a joyful spirit, because among all those who offer something, God has chosen for reward the person who performs this with a devoted heart.

Hence he commands that none of you should do this “from sadness,” he says, or from compulsion—that is, constrained or unwillingly—and not from spontaneous desire. The person fulfills this from sadness and compulsion who does not hope to receive a reward, but does it unwillingly because of present embarrassment and shame, lest, while others do it, he himself should appear avaricious [Col. 0646C] and disgraceful. Therefore he will not enjoy an eternal reward for this.

Blessed Augustine says that if you give bread sadly, you lose both the bread and the merit, because you lose what you give in the present and will lack the reward in the future. The person gives alms to the poor with a joyful spirit who is certain of the reward of eternal goods, which the Lord has given him with whom he stores up treasure. “God loves a cheerful giver.” The person who lends to the Lord ought to be cheerful; the person pleases God who afterward does not grieve over what he has given as though it were lost, but rejoices as though it had been doubled.

“For God is able to make every grace abound in you, so that, always having every sufficiency and abundance in all things, you may abound in every good work.” Do not distrust or despair of reward, he says, if you spend alms with a cheerful spirit, because God is able to make every grace abound in you, so that in the present you may abound in faith, hope, charity, divine knowledge, and every temporal possession, and, moreover, that in the future he may grant eternal [Col. 0646D] happiness.

For this will be to abound in every good work: to retain for oneself what is sufficient to meet one’s own needs and those of one’s household, and to spend the rest for the use of the saints or the poor.

As it is written in the Psalm concerning any righteous person who gives alms and cares for the poor: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever” (Psalm CIII). Here he calls the generosity of temporal substance [Col. 0647A], or the reward of that distributed substance, “righteousness.” This generosity is rightly called righteousness because it is just that, just as God gave the earth to all human beings in common for possession, and just as the heat of the sun and the moisture of the rains are granted by God to all in common, so also the things that are born on the earth by God’s gift should be distributed and used in common. This is righteousness: since God freely gives those things, a human being should in turn give from them to the person who lacks them.

It should be noted that this is said of the holy man: he scattered and divided among the poor the substance given to him by God, and gave to the poor, who had nothing with which to repay him in the present—not to the rich of this world, from whom he might hope to receive the same or more in return. And because he followed the Lord’s command: “Make friends for yourselves [Col. 0647B] from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke XVI), therefore “his righteousness”—that is, the reward of his generosity and the recompense for that righteousness—“remains forever,” because he placed his riches there and stored up his treasure where thieves do not break through and steal.

“Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness.” This can be understood in two ways, both literally and spiritually.

Almighty God, who supplies a person with seed for sowing, will, if that person is devoted to almsgiving, also supply him with bread for food from the seed, and will multiply his seeds in the earth, so that the person who sowed five *modii* may gather fifty, and the person who sowed ten may gather one hundred. “And he will multiply the increase of the fruits of your righteousness,” that is, of your substance, which is rightly called righteousness.

Alternatively: God, who supplies a person with seed for sowing—that is, temporal [Col. 0647C] substance from which he can give alms—will certainly supply him in the future with bread for food, namely, eternal satisfaction, which will be the vision of the most present face of almighty God. Concerning this bread the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed is the one who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke XIV). And the Psalmist says concerning the same satisfaction: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed to my soul” (Psalm XVI).

And he will not only provide eternal satisfaction there, but here he will also multiply his substance, as we said above, so that he may have the means to give more abundant alms, through which his increase will be enlarged—that is, his reward and the [Col. 0647D] recompense of his righteousness.

Therefore, since all the good things we have belong to God—both the seeds and the things that grow—and since God nourishes, causes them to sprout, and multiplies them for human use, and has commanded that we share them with those in need, we ought to give these temporal things so that we may deserve to receive eternal things. Many of the saints have done so; among them, the most blessed martyr of Christ, Lawrence, received a share in blessed reward. As a true steward of temporal riches, he deserved to possess heavenly, eternal, and unfading crowns.

“So that, enriched and made rich in all things, you may abound in complete simplicity,” which simplicity produces thanksgiving to God through us, who are his [Col. 0648A] preachers. A person ought to give alms with such intention and simplicity that he neither seeks to make subject to himself the person to whom he gives nor seeks praise from human beings.

“Glorifying God in the obedience of your confession.” Obedience gives a person’s confession when it is fulfilled. For although the person who is commanded remains silent, in the fact that he obeys, his deed shows and confesses him to be very obedient. For example, someone is commanded to go only as far as the lectern. Although he gives no verbal response to the command, if he goes there to sing, the singing itself bears witness to his obedience and confesses him to be very obedient.

In the Gospel of Christ also, glorify God, because the [Col. 0648B] Gospel commands: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity”; and in the simplicity of your heart—understand, glorify God. We spoke of this simplicity a little above.

And in their supplication for you, whom you have assisted with alms, glorify God, because they will entreat God and praise him on your behalf.

# CHAPTER X

But I ask you—understand, to correct yourselves—so that, when present, I may not dare to rebuke you with the confidence, that is, the authority, with which I am thought to be bold against certain people—understand, those who have sinned—who suppose that we walk according to the flesh, that is, that we live carnally and give carnal commandments.

“For although we walk in the flesh,” that is, although we lead our life in the [Col. 0648C] body, “we do not wage war according to the flesh,” that is, we do not live carnally, but spiritually. The person lives and wages war spiritually who does what pleases God. But the person lives carnally and wages war according to the flesh who obeys the desires of the flesh.

For the weapons of our warfare, with which we fight against philosophers and demons, are not carnal, such as a breastplate, helmet, sword, spear, blade, shield, and other things of that kind, but the power of God. Some manuscripts read “the power of God,” while others read “power toward God”; either reading can be understood in this way: “Our weapons,” which are carnal weapons, as though we were speaking of them individually—our sword is not carnal, but the power of God; that power itself is our sword, because through its strength and power we overcome demons and wicked men.

[Col. 0648D] Alternatively: our weapons are carnal—that is, weak, corruptible, and pliable—namely, the power of God is our weapon; that is, through God they are effective and strong for battle. The weapons of the apostles, therefore, with which they fought against philosophers, were the word of preaching, of which it is said elsewhere: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6). The power of miracles was also their sword.

Against demons, however, they fought through prayer, fasts, and vigils, for the destruction of strongholds—that is, of demons and philosophers. And we are prepared for these things, destroying the plans of philosophers and the plans of demons, who inspired the hearts of persecutors to stir up persecution against us; and destroying every height—that is, every pride—that raises itself against the knowledge of God.

[Col. 0649A] And we are bringing every human understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ—that is, into his worship and religion. This captivity must be understood in a good sense. The devil, therefore, took the first human captive by persuasion, when he subjected him to himself, and afterward the whole human race to such an extent that he persuaded it to worship idols instead of the true God. But the captivity of the human race, which the devil had taken captive for death, the apostles took captive for Christ and eternal life through the weapons of preaching and the power of miracles.

For just as any earthly emperor arms his soldiers so that through them he may subjugate kingdoms, regions, and provinces to himself, so Christ armed his soldiers, the apostles, with spiritual [Col. 0649B] weapons, and through them subjected nearly all nations to himself.

And we are ready—that is, we have an evident willingness—to avenge every disobedience when your obedience has been fulfilled. This should be punctuated in this way, and what follows should then be connected with it. It can also be understood in two ways. First, it may mean: “We have this intention, that your disobedience, which you have hitherto had, may be avenged through your good obedience.” For disobedience is then corrected and avenged when obedience is placed above it.

Alternatively: “We have this intention,” he says, “that when you, who are more perfect and of good will, have fulfilled your obedience and obey us in all things, then through us the disobedience of those who have disdained to send anything with you to the saints who are in [Col. 0649C] Jerusalem, so that they might share in your gifts, may be avenged.”

“Those things which are according to appearance, observe”: that is, understand and weigh what is said by us above and below in our presence.

But so that I may not be considered—that is, by you—as though I wished to terrify you through these letters, since, they say, “the letters are weighty and severe in correction, and powerful in enforcement; but his bodily presence—that is, his outward appearance when present—is weak or unimpressive, and his speech contemptible or despicable.” He speaks in the person of certain people who said such things about him; and therefore he says, “since, they say”—that is, those people.

For we are not, as though we lacked the authority to reach you, extending ourselves beyond our measure in preaching, preaching all the way to you. Indeed, we have reached you by preaching the Gospel of Christ from Jerusalem. We also hope, in the abundance of your faith, to evangelize those places beyond you—understand, “those places”—but we neither hope nor wish to glory in another’s rule, that is, in those who believed through another’s preaching and received the rule or rectitude of faith. Nor do we wish to glory in places prepared by others, lest we appear to build upon another’s foundation.

This sentence, although it is wholly confused and joined together in the Latin wording, with much left implicit, is found among the Greeks more fully and more clearly [Col. 0650A] in meaning. It is also true that he himself said: “And even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge.”

“Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.” The blessed Apostle, knowing that we possess from God every good thing that we can possess—whether by nature, because we were made by him; by formation; or in every holy manner of life, in faith, hope, love, good works, justice, and the fear of God—and knowing that everything comes from his gifts without any merit of our own, removed human glory and pride, by which many say that they possess what they have from themselves and their own merits. He says: “Whoever glories in faith, preaching, the power of miracles, or any good that he possesses, should not glory in himself, but in the Lord”—that is, he should refer everything to the glory of God and reckon it as coming from the grace of the one from whom he received it.

[Col. 0650B] That we should exist, therefore, is the mercy of God. If, then, we were nothing at all before we existed, we earned nothing from God so that we might exist. He made us so that we might exist, but he did not himself make us so that we might be good. He himself gave us existence, and someone else could have given us goodness. If he gave me existence, and someone else gave me goodness, the one who gave me goodness is better than the one who gave me existence. But since no one is more generous in mercy than the one from whom we received existence, we received goodness from him as well. Therefore we must all say with the Psalmist: “My God, my mercy” (Ps. 58).

“For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends.” Commendation is generally used for praise, as in this passage and elsewhere, where the same Apostle says: “I ought to have been commended by you” (2 Cor. 12)—that is, praised—and, “We do not commend ourselves to you”—that is, we do not praise ourselves before you. “Approved” means both upright and praiseworthy, or worthy of praise. The Apostle says: “It is not the one who commends and praises himself before men who is approved or worthy of praise, because he suffers from empty glory; but the one whom God commends”—that is, whom he makes praiseworthy—is worthy of praise.

## CHAPTER XI

“I wish that you would bear with a little of my folly.” After the pseudo-apostles came to Corinth following the Apostle’s departure and said that the Apostle had not been sent by God, because he had not been called by Christ before his ascension nor instructed by him, and moreover preached things contrary to the preaching of the other apostles, whom they called the great apostles, they turned many away from the Apostle’s love and drew them to their own love. They said that they had been sent by the great apostles—by Peter, Andrew, James, and the other apostles.

The Apostle, therefore, wishing to separate them again from their love and bring them back to his own—the one who had first implanted the faith of Christ in their hearts—praised himself under compulsion in words, but not in heart or intention. He knew that he gained nothing from human praise except that they should not withdraw from his preaching. Moreover, since among human beings it is considered foolish and senseless for someone to praise himself, especially when Solomon says, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Prov. 27), he wished to praise himself for the reason stated above, so as not to give others an occasion for praise, and said:

“I wish that you would patiently bear with a little of my folly, O Corinthians”—that is, with a little of my folly in praising myself—“but also bear with me,” that is, tolerate my folly in this matter of praise. It is as though he were saying: “If you are willing to bear my words patiently, I will speak; and if you are unwilling, I will nevertheless not omit saying what I have resolved in my mind.” And why is this?

“For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God.” To be jealous means to envy, imitate, love, or be zealous; but here it is used for “to love.” “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God,” that is, “I love you with the love of God.”

“For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” The Apostle Paul betrothed the Corinthians not to himself but to Christ through his preaching and faith, just as Moses betrothed the Israelite people in Egypt not to himself but to God (Exod. 3). For this reason he was commanded to remove his sandals from his feet. The sign and ring of the betrothal by which the Apostle betrothed the Corinthians to Christ was the faith of the Lord and Savior, which he ministered to them.

Hence he says: “I betrothed you to one husband, Christ, wishing to present you to him as a chaste virgin”—that is, so that you might prepare yourselves as a chaste virgin for him, preserving the integrity of the faith. This virginity is more properly the integrity of the mind than of the body. If, therefore, we consider bodily virginity, there are many more virgins in the Church [Col. 0651C] in mind than in body; and many of those who still preserve bodily integrity have already married in mind and desire.

Therefore it is better that the universal Church—which consists of both sexes and both orders—should be called a chaste virgin. She is also Christ’s bride, of whom John says: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). Whoever in the Church possesses the integrity of faith and adorns it with good works is a chaste virgin, even if not in body, nevertheless in mind; and therefore is Christ’s bride.

But whoever, by God’s favor, has preserved both kinds of virginity chastely and inviolate, as many saints of both sexes have done, will surely receive the palm which none of the married will possess. And if the female sex, which is so weak and inclined to fall, observes this, how much more will those do so who are called men on account of their strength.

“But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning”—that is, just as the devil, clothed in a serpent, deceived the woman by his craft and through the woman deceived the man—“so your minds may now be corrupted by the pseudo-apostles, who are ministers of the devil, and may fall away.”

“You gladly bear with fools, since you yourselves are wise.” When the Apostle had passed from the Corinthians to other nations, pseudo-apostles coming from the Jews corrupted them. They are called fools here because they wished both to observe circumcision, the Sabbath rest, and the other carnal commandments of the Law, and to retain the grace of the Gospel.

They are also called fools [Col. 0652A] because they did not persist in preaching for eternal reward or for the salvation of their hearers, but for temporal profits, so that they could strip them of their possessions, and for human praise. They said that the Apostle was not a true preacher because he had not been called by the Lord through the presence of his flesh. They said such things in order to draw the Corinthians away from love of the Apostle to love of themselves; and they succeeded, deceiving many of the simple.

The Apostle addresses these people ironically when he says: “You gladly bear with fools, since you yourselves are wise.” Although some explain this verse as though he were genuinely calling them wise, saying, “I wonder, since you yourselves are wise, why you gladly tolerate fools,” blessed Augustine explains it differently. He rejects that interpretation and understands them to have been called “wise” ironically. “Since you,” he says, “O Corinthians, are fools who think yourselves wise, it is no wonder that you patiently tolerate the foolish pseudo-apostles.”

“For you bear with it if someone enslaves you.” The Jews who had come from Judea wished to do both things—to Judaize and to observe the Gospel—and wanted to reduce believers to slavery under the Law, so that they would observe the Sabbath rest, go to Jerusalem to offer the legal sacrifices, and above all observe circumcision. They said that no one could be saved without circumcision, especially since this was not only a commandment of the Law, but long before the Law God had said to Abraham in familiar speech: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17).

The Jews therefore wished to reduce the Corinthians to this slavery of the Law and this impediment of the flesh. To them he says: “You bear with it”—that is, you patiently tolerate it—“if someone wishes to reduce you to slavery under the Law.”

“If someone devours”—understand, “your possessions”—you bear with it. Through their flatteries and praises, the pseudo-apostles stripped those whom they deceived and plundered their goods at many banquets; and those people were content to have their possessions devoured by their deceivers.

“If someone takes”—as though he were saying: “If someone snatches your possessions from you and takes them for himself, you patiently tolerate it.” Hence the very rapacious birds that are called *accipitres* in Latin are called Greek *harpies*, that is, “snatchers,” because they take for themselves and seize from others. In this way, “to take” means to acquire something deceitfully.

“If someone is lifted up in pride.” Exaltation is pride. The Apostle says: “You patiently tolerate those who exalt themselves because of their knowledge of the Law, who raise themselves up in pride because of the nobility of their lineage.”

What follows—“If someone strikes you in the face”—must be punctuated here, and what comes afterward must then be supplied: “I speak according to dishonor”; and that phrase must likewise be punctuated. Although each sentence can be delivered separately with its own punctuation, when he said, “If someone strikes you in the face,” he explained what it means to strike someone in the face when he added, “I speak according to dishonor.”

To strike someone in the face means to reproach him with the dishonor of his lineage, just as the Jews reproached the Corinthians for being lowborn, since their fathers had always been idolaters, venerating demons and stones instead of God. The Jews, by contrast, set themselves above them, boasting that they derived their origin from the line of the patriarchs and prophets, from whose stock Christ had been born according to the flesh.

It is indeed great folly and dishonor for someone who through the regeneration of water and the Holy Spirit has been made a son of God to boast of anything concerning the nobility of his lineage, especially since the Lord says that we are all brothers.

Some, however, explain this verse as though it referred to the Apostle, so that the sense would be: “I am acting dishonorably by exalting myself over something concerning the nobility of my lineage.” This interpretation is not appropriate, because he has not yet reached the place where he will say that he is descended from the patriarchs. It should instead be understood in the manner we have stated.

And lest someone should perhaps think that he was saying they were struck in the face of the body with fists or in some other physical manner, he spoke as follows: “If someone,” he says, “strikes you in the face”—that is, in your presence—by reproaching you with something concerning the dishonor of your lineage, you patiently tolerate it and place them above us.

“I speak according to the nobility of lineage”: I say that you are struck in the face, or in your presence, not with fists, as though we were weak in this matter—understand, in the matter of lineage. In this way they set themselves above us, and in this way you count us as nothing in comparison with them.

Speaking of himself and for his own case, the Apostle introduces the person of his companion Barnabas, who also belonged to the same Jewish lineage. Thus the false apostles from among the Jews placed themselves above the Apostle Paul and Barnabas, as though they had been born from a nobler lineage than those two, and as though those two had been born from an inferior stock. In this way they despised them.

Therefore the Apostle says: “As though we were weak and lowborn in the dishonor of our lineage, so they place themselves above us; and so you too place them above us. But in reality they are weaker in that aspect of lineage in which they boast. For although they say that they are sons of Abraham according to the flesh, they are not truly sons of Abraham through faith and works, because they are not his imitators. We, however, are strong and noble, because although we are sons of Abraham according to the flesh, we are also his sons through imitation of his faith and works.”

This verse must be delivered and punctuated on its own: “In this matter”—understand, “in this undertaking”—“who dares”—understand, “to glory”—“I also dare to glory in folly.” It is as though he were saying in other words: “They dare to glory in the nobility of their lineage; although I speak foolishly, I too dare to glory in the nobility of my lineage.”

He says, “I speak in folly,” because, insofar as human beings are concerned, it seems foolish for someone to give himself testimony of praise on the basis of anything. Yet the Apostle was not foolish, because he was not doing this willingly but under compulsion, and not for human praise, but so that through his praise he might draw the Corinthians back to love of him from love of the pseudo-apostles.

Alternatively, he says in folly that he dares to glory in the nobility of his lineage in order to empty the glory of those who boasted that they were sons of Abraham, since they were acting foolishly.
