He also declares himself imprudent and foolish in praising himself in this matter, lest those who exalted themselves because of the nobility of their lineage appear wise and noble in this respect.

[Col. 0654A] “They are Hebrews, and so am I.” The Hebrews are called after their patriarch Heber. Therefore the Apostle says: “They glory in the nobility of the flesh because they are Hebrews, and I too am a Hebrew.”

“They are Israelites,” from the lineage of the patriarch Jacob, who was also called Israel. “And I am truly an Israelite,” because I contemplate God with the mind.

“They are the seed of Abraham; so am I.” They are “ministers of Christ”—and so am I. Whoever preaches the Gospel is called a minister of Christ.

“I speak as one less wise: I am more so.” Understand: “I am more of a minister of Christ than they,” because I labor more than all, and whatever I preach I adorn with works. Although they may appear to preach well in certain matters, they are not true ministers of Christ, because what they preach with their mouths they destroy by their works.

He calls himself less wise in this matter because he was praising himself by saying that he was more of a minister of Christ than they; and in the same way that he earlier said he was acting foolishly, so now he says that he is less wise.

“In many labors”—understand, “I serve Christ.” The meaning is: “It is evident in this that I am more of a minister of Christ than they: although those who place themselves above me have always labored in some way, I have labored more, because I devote myself day and night to very many labors.”

The holy teachers relate that the Apostle applied himself to manual labor from morning, or from cockcrow, until the fifth hour, in order to acquire his livelihood; from then until the tenth hour he debated publicly. Often, however, he prolonged his speech into the night (Acts 20), as he did when Eutychus, weighed down by sleep, fell through a window from the upper room.

“In prisons more abundantly”—understand, “I was confined”—than they; and the meaning is: “Even if those whom you exalt, O Corinthians, were in prison, I was there more than they.”

“In blows beyond measure”—understand, “I have been afflicted.” The Apostle was often beaten by Jews and Gentiles, and often struck with rods; and he says: “If they were beaten, I was beaten more.”

There is a question here. Since the Apostle says elsewhere, “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10), why does he say here that he was afflicted with blows beyond measure?

The answer is that he himself endured many things beyond human measure and beyond the strength of human frailty, but not beyond divine strength. Therefore he was able to endure and overcome them, because the power of almighty God supplied him with strength to suffer.

“In deaths frequently”—understand, “I was placed.” If he was often in deaths, how did he live? By “deaths” he meant situations of mortal danger and the extremity of life.

“From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one.” Deuteronomy had commanded that when judges flogged someone who had committed an offense, they should regulate the punishment so that the number of lashes did not exceed forty, lest their brother, shamefully lacerated, lie before them.

The Apostle briefly refers here to what happened to him five times. For when he was flogged five times by the Jews, he received thirty-nine lashes according to the Law of Moses, as though he were a transgressor of that same Law (Acts 16).

Blessed Bede relates that a book was brought from Rome by Chidonius, bishop of the East Angles, in which all the Apostle’s labors, sufferings, and punishments had been depicted in their appropriate places. Among these images the Apostle was shown lying naked on the ground, while a torturer stood over him holding a four-thonged whip in his hand. He retained one of the thongs in his hand, while the other three were stretched out for striking.

If he struck with all four thongs ten times, he would inflict forty lashes. If he struck eleven times, he would complete forty-four blows. Or if he struck nine times with all four thongs and the tenth time with three, he would give thirty-nine lashes, one less than forty.

“Three times I was beaten with rods”: he suffered this at the hands of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0655B] These events are not all found in the Acts of the Apostles, since those Letters likewise do not contain everything that is included in that history. We do find there, however, that when he came into the region of Macedonia and was in the city of Philippi, he was ordered to be beaten with rods. On another occasion the tribune ordered him to be brought into the fortress, flogged, and tortured with whips.

“Once I was stoned.” He was stoned at Lystra, a city of Macedonia, because of the girl from whom he cast out a spirit of divination, which had brought great profit to her masters.

“Three times I made shipwreck.” Shipwreck means the breaking of a ship. When he says, “Three times I made shipwreck,” the words seem to sound as though he himself had caused the shipwreck; but the meaning is: “Three times I suffered shipwreck.” Since he traveled by ship across the sea very frequently, it is not surprising that he suffered shipwreck so many times.

“Night and day I was in the depths of the sea.” Although some say that the Apostle was not submerged in the sea and deny that he remained day and night in the depths of the waters, the established tradition of the holy Fathers must nevertheless be maintained: in reality, by accident he fell into the depths of the sea, where, surrounded by waves day and night alike, he afterward returned safely to land under God’s guidance.

Could the one who, at the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, divided the sea into sections, and afterward the Jordan and the torrent of Arnon (Exod. 14), who also preserved Jonah in the belly of the whale (Jonah 2) and made the sea passable for Peter (Matt. 14), not also preserve his distinguished soldier and preacher Paul in the depths of the sea, so that he could neither be suffocated by the surrounding waters nor devoured by sea creatures?

The Almighty was certainly able to do this, and therefore he did it. Indeed, it is no more astonishing that Peter walked over the waves of the sea without his feet sinking into them than that Paul was preserved unharmed day and night in the depths of the sea.

Mystically, Paul’s being in the depths of the sea day and night, yet reaching the land safely under the Lord’s protection, signifies those righteous people who are daily brought out by the Lord from the depths of the dangers and disturbances of the world, but will be delivered more fully on the day of judgment and brought to the shore of eternal stability. Placed amid the waves of this age, they did not doubt God’s mercy in faith.

Peter, however, who at first walked without his feet sinking into the water but afterward, when he doubted, fell amid the waves, and was then raised up by the Lord and brought to land, signifies himself: he doubted when he denied the Lord, but was restored by the Lord to faith. He also signifies all martyrs and all the righteous who at the beginning of faith advance courageously, counting the cruelty of persecutors as nothing, but afterward, when a very severe storm of persecution arises, doubt in some respect. Protected by the Lord’s grace, they are lifted up lest they fall entirely into despair and be overcome by the storms, and they are brought to the land of the elect.

“In journeys often, in dangers from rivers”—understand, “I was.” He turns again to other dangers that must be remembered, wishing to show that according to the flesh he was afflicted for Christ on land and sea, and that he endured much more than the pseudo-apostles.

During winter and rainy seasons rivers often overflow their channels and make passage exceedingly difficult for travelers. Since the Apostle was accustomed to go on foot from place to place in winter, he often encountered the dangers of rivers.

“In dangers from robbers I was often exposed.” The pseudo-apostles and unbelieving Jews sent robbers against him, because, unable and unwilling to kill him publicly themselves, they wanted him to be killed by their agents.

“In dangers from my own people.” He endured dangers from the Jews, his brothers according to the flesh, who were distressed that, having abandoned the Law, he had turned to the Gospel. Thus we read that on one occasion Ananias, the high priest, ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth (Acts 23); and it would take too long to recount how often this happened.

“In dangers from the Gentiles.” He suffered many hardships from the philosophers and rulers of the Gentiles because of the mystery of the Son of God’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, and because of the worship of the one God that he preached.

“In danger in the city.” He often experienced this, though it would take too long to recount.

“In dangers in the wilderness.” He endured dangers in the wilderness from the Jews, when they laid ambushes and wanted to kill him on the road. Or he encountered dangers in the wilderness because the devil, envious of him, persecuted him not only through human agents but also stirred up the fiercest beasts against him, so that he would not dare to pass from one place to another.

“In dangers at sea.” Not only when he suffered shipwreck three times and when he fell into the sea, where he remained unharmed among the waves day and night, but also very often he endured dangers at sea.

Thus on one occasion they drove the ship onto the shore, when the prow remained fixed and immovable while the stern was being broken apart by the force of the sea; and when the soldiers wanted to kill all the prisoners, lest anyone be able to reach the shore by swimming, the centurion prevented this because of the Apostle, wishing to preserve him (Acts 27).

“In dangers from false brothers.” He often experienced this. These are the people of whom he says in the Letter to the Galatians (ch. 2): “False brothers came in secretly to spy out our freedom.” They were partly Christians and partly Jews, but perfect in neither respect. Envious of the Apostle because of their zeal for the Law and circumcision, they laid traps for him.

“In labor and hardship.” Hardship is misery and sorrow. There can be labor without hardship—that is, without annoyance, misery, or any weariness—and therefore he added “hardship,” to show that the Apostle’s labor was not without distress and affliction.

People sometimes labor in gardens and orchards with enjoyment, for the sake of exercise, as we read concerning the first-created man: God placed him in paradise to work it and guard it (Gen. 2). That labor was without any distress.

“In many vigils.” Sometimes he kept watch willingly and voluntarily; at other times unwillingly, out of necessity, because, placed under pressure and distress, he needed to keep watch while imploring God’s help. Thus, when he was in prison, he sang hymns to God with Silas; and when the jailer saw the light in the prison and the door open, he wanted to kill himself, thinking that all the prisoners had escaped, but the Apostle prevented him (Acts 16).

“In hunger and thirst.” He was pursued by the Jews from place to place, and therefore often suffered hunger through want and thirst.

“In many fasts.” He endured many fasts, sometimes willingly and sometimes unwillingly.

“In cold and nakedness.” He endured extreme cold and the greatest deprivation because of his nakedness when he was being taken by ship to Rome, having appealed to Caesar. When they disembarked from the ship and came to the island of Malta, he gathered a large quantity of branches to warm himself; a viper, coming out from the heat of the fire, fastened upon his hand (Acts 27).

Besides those things which are external—that is, besides the dangers which I endure in the body—there is my daily burden, that is, my perseverance, and my concern for all the churches. Since it would have taken too long to recount all the dangers, hardships, and tribulations that he had suffered, he brought them to a conclusion by saying:

“Besides those things which are external, which I endure in the body, my perseverance consists in always being concerned for all the churches in which I have preached.” For he feared that those to whom he had preached might perhaps be deceived by false apostles, or that, because of the excessive tribulations which they saw and heard the Apostle suffering, they might fall away from the faith.

“Who is weak, and I am not weak?” Because of his exceedingly great love, he sympathized with the weak to such an extent that he himself seemed to become weak, counting their weakness as his own, acting like a physician and caretaker who, seeing a sick person saddened and in pain, shares in that person’s pain and sorrow.

“Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?” So far as this passage is concerned, to be scandalized means to suffer the desire of the flesh, to be saddened and afflicted by bodily heat, and to be inflamed by the burning of vices. Likewise, to be burned means to be heated by lust and to be consumed by the heat of the whole body.

Someone is therefore scandalized when, unwillingly and without having anticipated it, he is enticed by the beauty of a woman or by the heat of his own flesh and provoked to commit lust; but while doing this unwillingly and without prior deliberation, he is scandalized at himself, becomes angry with himself, and is saddened.

Considering this weakness of human nature, which is exceedingly frail, the Apostle says that he is burned, so that, sympathizing with those who suffer such things, he may counsel them. He does not condemn those who endure such experiences; rather, in humble language he reminds them that he suffers similar things. Thus, if one who had received such great grace and was the teacher of the Gentiles still suffered the desires of the flesh, those who still possessed a weaker grace should not despair if they suffered such things. Instead, in hope of the promised reward, they should resist the impulses of the flesh as he resisted them, lest those who heard these things from him, overcome by the desires of the flesh, fall into despair.

For to be burned is more than to be scandalized. It is as though he were saying: “Someone suffers and is afflicted by desire and the excessive heat of lust, and I am not only afflicted but also—and this is greater—I am burned, and in a certain sense set on fire.”

He suffered excessive desire of the flesh when he said: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7). And also: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive”—that is, seeking to take me captive—“under the law of sin which is in my members” (ibid.).

Therefore, if we wish to be crowned with the Apostle Paul, let us strive manfully, as he strove, so that we may overcome every pleasure; for no one can be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of the things that are my weaknesses—that is, in these things I will boast. He certainly had to boast and enumerate his sufferings, not for his own sake, as though he might thereby gain something before God, but for the salvation of those whom he wished to recall from love of the false apostles to his own, and also so that he might offer himself to others as an example and someone to imitate. By the term “weakness” are included all the hardships, persecutions, and sufferings that he willingly endured for Christ. The meaning is this: If those who lead you astray and withdraw you from my love wish to boast, by disparaging me, let them boast in the things in which I also boast, although unwillingly and under provocation.

It is evident, however, that they cannot boast in the weaknesses and sufferings that they have endured for love of Christ, for an eternal reward, and for the salvation of their brothers; rather, they boast only of the nobility of their lineage, because they are sons of Abraham. I do not wish to boast of this, although I too derive my origin from the same stock.

Some ask, since God said through Solomon, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Prov. 27), why just and perfect men sometimes recount the good deeds and virtues that they have received from God—for example, the blessed Job, who said, “I was the foot of the lame and the father of orphans, and I diligently investigated the case that I did not know” (Job 29), and other things of this kind; and David: “If I have repaid those who rendered evil to me” (Ps. 7), that is, “I have not repaid them.” The Apostle does so in many ways in this passage as well.

The answer to them is that when the perfect proclaim their own virtues and praise themselves before human beings, they do not do this so that they themselves may gain something before people through such self-display, but so that by their example they may draw those to whom they preach toward life. In this too they imitate almighty God, who speaks of his own praises to human beings so that he may be recognized by them. For the God who forbids us through Scripture, saying, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth,” himself speaks of his own praises throughout the sacred Scriptures, saying to Moses, “I am God almighty, and I did not reveal my name Adonai to them” (Exod. 6); and through Isaiah, “Before me no God was formed, and after me there will not be one” (Isa. 43).

Why, then, does he himself do what he forbids? Surely, if he kept silent about his virtues and miracles, no one would ever know him. If no one knew him, no one would love him. If no one loved him, no one would return to life. Hence it is said of him through the Psalmist: “He will announce the power of his works to his people, to give them the inheritance of the nations; the works of his hands are truth and judgment” (Ps. 110).

He therefore announces his own virtues, not so that he himself might gain anything from praise or stand in need of it, but because, while he tells us of his greatness, he raises our ignorance toward himself. Thus the just are not blameworthy when they proclaim their virtues, because, while they recount their own life, they seek the life of other souls.

It must nevertheless be understood concerning them that they never disclose their own good deeds unless either the benefit of those near them or some great necessity compels them, just as necessity then compelled the Apostle. Hence he himself said, “If it is necessary to boast”—and indeed it was necessary. Therefore, if a Christian must boast, he must boast in humility.

## “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ knows that I am not lying.”

As he is about to state something almost incredible—that the unbelieving Jews had stirred up the rulers of the nations against him, and that the kingdoms of the earth had risen against him, yet had done him no harm—he calls upon God as witness, so that he may be believed more readily. For this reason he recalls such events: to show how great the difference is between the true apostles, who endured so much for the love of God while seeking the salvation of their hearers, and the false apostles, who stripped their hearers of their possessions and did not seek their salvation.

## “The governor of King Aretas’s nation in Damascus was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me.”

Damascus is the metropolitan city of Syria. Damascus, the servant of Abraham, built it, and its name is interpreted as “drinking blood,” which aptly suits that place, because there the blood of Abel was poured out.

The things said here about the Apostle occurred at the beginning of his faith, when, having been blinded by the Lord on the road, he was brought to Damascus, where he remained for three days without drinking or eating. Afterwards, having been baptized and strengthened by receiving bread, he immediately entered the synagogue of the Jews and began publicly to preach the name of the Lord Jesus.

When the Jews saw this, they were inflamed with zeal and sought an opportunity to destroy him. But since they did not dare to do this by themselves, they approached the governor of the city about the matter, so that with his assistance and permission they might be able to kill him. Wishing to please the Jews and to appear diligent in the office entrusted to him, he ordered the city to be guarded on every side, so that Paul could not escape alive in any way. But, with God’s assistance providing the means, he escaped in the manner that the following words make clear.

## “And through a window,” he says, “I was lowered in a basket through the wall, and so I escaped his hands.”

A basket is a vessel woven from rushes and palm leaves. In it he was lowered down the wall with ropes by faithful brothers.

A question arises here: Why did the Apostle flee from Damascus, when he said, “I am ready not only to be bound in Jerusalem, but also to die for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 21)? The answer is this: He did not flee because he dreaded accepting martyrdom; rather, he preferred to seek the field of combat and the breadth of the nations instead of being confined within the walls of a city and killed there, where there were very few believers to be strengthened and instructed by his martyrdom, so that they would not hesitate to suffer similar things. He later fulfilled this purpose himself by enduring martyrdom and instructing many to do the same.

Thus he fulfilled the Lord’s command: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. 10). In truth, he preserved both the example of martyrdom and the usefulness of his preaching, which he later fulfilled. From his example, therefore, we learn both to approach the battle with our adversaries steadfastly and, at times, to withdraw from it prudently.

# CHAPTER TWELVE

## “If it is necessary to boast, it is not expedient.”

If it is necessary for me to boast for the salvation of others and because of the necessity mentioned above, by which I am compelled, I can boast in this: that I escaped the hands of my persecutors. Yet it is not expedient—that is, it is not necessary for me to boast—for I have not chosen pride and vainglory, but humility.

## “I shall come to visions and revelations of the Lord”—that is, to those things about which I shall be able to boast.

He calls them “visions and revelations of the Lord,” although this is one and the same thing: the visions that the Lord showed him. In what follows he is now going to say to what height he was carried, so that from this we may understand how great and what kind of things were shown and spoken to him. Otherwise, as it seemed to the false apostles and other unbelievers, he might be regarded as lesser than the other apostles in grace, even though he was called last and had not seen the Lord present in the flesh.

## “I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—caught up to the third heaven.”

It is the custom and established practice of writers who provide us with the sacred Scriptures that, whenever one of them recounts a story and comes to himself, he speaks of himself as though of another person. Thus Moses did this when he said, “Now Moses was a very meek man, more than all the people who were upon the earth” (Num. 12); and Job: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job” (Job 1). Likewise, when the blessed Matthew came to himself in the text of his narrative, he said, “He saw a tax collector named Matthew” (Matt. 9). He did not say, “He saw me,” but inserted himself into the order of his narrative as a writer of events, not as one proclaiming himself.

The blessed Apostle did this in a less customary way—not in a history, where the account of events is being set forth, but in an Epistle. This is evident in the present passage, where, for the sake of humility, he speaks of himself as though of another, saying: “I know a man remaining in Christ, caught up to the third heaven fourteen years ago.”

Fourteen complete years elapsed from the time when the Apostle was caught up to the third heaven until the time when he wrote these things. It is therefore plainly evident that great necessity compelled him to disclose what he had concealed for so many years in the innermost secret of his heart.

Different people understand these words of the Apostle differently. It would be too lengthy to insert and recount all their opinions here; for the present, only a few of the many will be mentioned.

Julianus Pomerius, a man of sound judgment, says that the first heaven in this passage is the aerial heaven, from which birds are called “birds of heaven”; the second is the stellar heaven, in which the twelve signs and the other stars are contained, apart from the seven planets, and which is also called the firmament. He understands the third to be spiritual or intellectual, where angels and the souls of the saints are placed in contemplation of God, contemplating above themselves almighty God, who presides over every creature—presiding in such a way that, by presiding, he sustains everything; by sustaining, he surrounds everything; and by surrounding, he fills everything.

According to his interpretation, the Apostle was caught up to this third, intellectual heaven. In this he judged correctly. But according to the blessed Augustine, it is still necessary to ascend higher and investigate deeper, for in elucidating questions he surpasses all teachers after the Apostles.

Since, therefore, the Apostle says that he is recounting neither human nor angelic visions, these matters must be investigated more profoundly.

There are plainly three kinds of vision. There is bodily vision, which takes place through bodily eyes, by which we see the heaven and the earth and all visible and corporeal things. There is spiritual vision, by which we store in memory the things that we see and hear in the present, and by which we now behold as though present the things we once heard or saw.

Even when the things that we saw bodily have been located somewhere away from us, we now see them as though present. For example, I am now physically present in Rome, and yet I see Carthage, which I saw long ago, as though it were placed before me, although I am far removed from it.

These two kinds of vision are common to us with beasts and birds. They see through the body, and their spirits are formed by the things they see imaginatively. Thus beasts recognize their mangers, and birds return to their nests. For unless they possessed a part of spiritual vision—that is, memory, which exists solely in the soul—birds, once they had departed from their nests, would never remember them, nor would animals recognize their mangers.

There is also a third kind, intellectual vision, which is nothing other than the rational capacity and excellence of the soul. Through it we distinguish by understanding the things that we see bodily and retain imaginatively in memory. Through understanding we distinguish that one thing is a body, another the likeness of a body, and often what something signifies.

Beasts and birds do not possess this intellectual vision in any way, because they neither understand themselves nor the things they see with their eyes.

Finally, bodily vision cannot exist without spiritual vision, which exists only in the soul. Spiritual vision, however, can exist without bodily vision. Thus we remember people who are absent, and in darkness we imaginatively see the things that we have seen; dreams belong here as well.

Intellectual vision, moreover, needs neither bodily nor spiritual vision. Through the intellect we see neither a body nor the image of a body. Through it we perceive justice, love, God himself, and the human mind itself, which has no body or bodily solidity. Therefore intellectual vision transcends and precedes the two mentioned above, namely bodily and spiritual vision.

We can prove this from the book of the prophet Daniel. We read there that when Belshazzar was feasting and drinking lavishly or splendidly from the vessels of the Lord’s temple that his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem, he saw the fingers of a hand writing on the wall of the royal hall.

He saw this with bodily vision, and immediately, through the bodily sense, the image of the bodily event was impressed upon his spirit. When he turned to other things, although he no longer perceived it bodily, he saw it through spiritual vision and memory; he saw it in his spirit—that is, in his soul—but he did not understand what it signified, because he did not possess intellectual vision fully, although he possessed something of it.

From this it is evident that intellectual vision is not equally active in all human beings. He understood that what he saw was a sign, and this he had through the activity of the mind—that is, through intellectual vision. And because he sought what it signified, the intellect of the mind was also at work in that very inquiry.

When he could not discover the meaning, Daniel came forward. Because he possessed intellectual vision, his mind having been enlightened by the prophetic spirit, he explained to the troubled king what that sign foretold. The prophet himself, through this kind of vision that belongs properly to the mind, was able to understand and say what it signified, rather than the man who had seen the sign bodily and contemplated its image in his spirit while thinking about it, but who could understand nothing intellectually except that it was a sign and had to inquire in order to understand what it signified.

Thus the three heavens may not improperly be understood as the three kinds of vision of which we have spoken. Yet by the first vision we are to understand everything contained within the expanse of the stellar heaven, together with the stellar heaven itself, which is also called the firmament. By the second heaven we are to understand the spiritual realm, where the angelic nature and the souls of the saints are placed in contemplation of God. By the third heaven we are to understand intellectual and rational vision, through which, by understanding, one perceives love, peace, joy, patience, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control, and other things of this kind by which one draws near to God—and through which God himself is seen: from whom all things come, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things are.

To this intellectual vision, which is represented by the third heaven, the apostle Paul was caught up and elevated. There, that is, in intellectual vision, he not only saw by understanding those things that are in the spiritual heaven, but also contemplated the very substance of God, the Word of the Lord through whom all things were made, in the love of the Holy Spirit—not through the body, not through the likeness of a body, but as the Truth itself is.

In this life he contemplated that almighty God is a Trinity in persons and a unity in substance, just as he will be seen by all the saints after the general resurrection.

A considerable question arises here: How could the very substance of God have been seen by certain people living in this life, in view of what was said to Moses, “No one can see my face”—that is, my invisibility—“and live” (Exod. 20), and in view of the statement, “No human being has ever seen God” while wholly in mortal life?

The answer is this: The human mind—that is, the intellect and rational capacity of the soul—can be divinely snatched away from this life into angelic life before it is separated from the flesh by the common death, as must be believed concerning the blessed Apostle. In his case, God caused a certain withdrawal of the mind’s attention from the senses of this life.

The vision was so evident and so manifest that he himself professes not to know whether, when he was caught up, he was in the body—that is, whether, as the soul is in the body while the body is said to be alive, his mind was removed from the senses in a violent ecstasy or rapture while the bond with the body remained—or whether such a dissolution took place as occurs in complete death, with the soul departing from the body.

Therefore we must neither inquire into this nor act against what is said in Ecclesiasticus 3: “Do not seek what is too high for you.” Thus both statements are true: “No one can see my face and live,” because the mind or intellect must be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the ineffability of that vision. Nor is it incredible that this excellence of vision was granted to certain saints who had not yet died completely, in such a way that only their corpses would remain to be buried.

# EPILOGUE OF THE FOREGOING

The three heavens signify three kinds of vision. The first is bodily vision, by which we see the heaven and the earth and the other corporeal and visible things. The second is spiritual vision, which takes place in the soul without understanding, when we store the images of the things we see in memory and, in darkness, imaginatively behold the things we have seen. We also see dreams, buildings, and people whom we saw long ago through spiritual vision in the soul, as though they were present to us.

These two visions are common to us with beasts and birds, which see bodies and recognize their proper places. Thus beasts recognize their mangers, and birds return to their nests because they remember them.

There is also a third, intellectual vision, which beasts and birds do not possess in any way, but which angels and human beings who use reason possess. Hence there is intellect—that is, reason—although it does not operate equally in all human beings.

By intellect, even without reasoning, we distinguish that one thing is a body and another the likeness of a body. Through this vision justice, love, and God himself are seen.

To this intellectual vision, therefore, which is the third and is signified by the third heaven, and which in its excellence also transcends the two mentioned above, the Apostle was divinely caught up and elevated, so that he might behold God—not through the body, not through the likeness of a body, but as the Truth itself is—and as he will be seen after this life by all the elect.

This vision was so evident and so manifest that the Apostle himself professes not to know whether, when he was caught up into the third heaven, he was in the body—as the soul is in the body when the body is said to be alive, whether awake, asleep, or separated from the bodily senses in ecstasy—or whether he had altogether departed from the body, so that the dead body lay there until, after that revelation had been completed, the soul was restored to its dead limbs; and not as though he had awakened from sleep or returned again to his senses after being separated from them in ecstasy, but as though the dead had wholly come back to life.

## “And I know such a man, whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—because he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak.”

The Apostle says that he was caught up twice: first to the third heaven, and afterwards into paradise—not into that earthly paradise where the first-created human being once dwelt, but into the heavenly paradise.

For “paradise” is interpreted as “a garden of delights,” and it signifies the blessedness of the elect, namely the heavenly rest. The Apostle says that he was caught up to it in the same way as to the third heaven. He heard secret words—that is, hidden, concealed, and ineffable words—which it is not permitted a human being to speak.

Among spiritual men who lead a heavenly life, some are certainly more capable and better than others, to such an extent that they have reached things that it is not permitted them to speak to others. The Apostle was one of these. In paradise he heard ineffable words that it is not permitted a human being to speak.

This means either that the one who heard them cannot recount them to others because of their ineffability, or that he is not permitted to do so; or, if he is of such dignity that he is permitted to speak and is able to recount them to others, those who hear them are not permitted to speak of them, because they are unable to grasp them on account of the greatness of the mysteries.

For such things—that is, for these most manifest visions of God—I will boast, rejoice, exult, and be glad. But for myself—that is, for my own exaltation and praise, or for my own merits—I will boast in nothing, because by the grace of God I am what I am, except in my weaknesses.

By the term “weakness” he includes all the hardships and sufferings that he endured for the name of Christ, in which he himself boasted.

For even if I should wish to boast—that is, because of the merit that I have before God—I would not be foolish in recounting it. Why? “For I shall speak the truth.” He says this because, if he professes the merit that he has before God, he will not be imprudent, since he speaks the truth.

Therefore, if someone recounts with humility, for the usefulness and edification of others, the good that has been divinely granted to him, he does not act foolishly, because he speaks the truth. But whoever proclaims to others the good that he possesses for the sake of vainglory, attributing it to his own merits, or says that he possesses what he does not possess, is foolish and exceedingly imprudent, because he speaks a lie.

“But I spare”—that is, I refrain from recounting—“my glory, merit, and grace, lest anyone think more of me than what he sees in me or hears from me.” The Apostle did not wish to recount the grace bestowed upon him, because he did not wish to appear greater or holier than he was.

Hence he says: “For this reason I do not wish to boast, and I refrain from mentioning all the grace granted to me, lest anyone think that I am better and holier than what he sees in my conduct, or more than what he hears from others about me.”

## “And lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me”—that is, into pride—“there was given to me by the Lord a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.”

Some say that the Apostle suffered from headaches; others say that he was tempted and afflicted by the devil through the heat of lust. The latter is more likely.

Therefore, lest he be lifted up into a swelling of pride, he was permitted to be tempted by the devil through the heat of lust, which he calls a thorn in the flesh. As the teachers say, a thorn properly refers to swelling and lust. He calls the very thorn in the flesh by which he was pierced and inflamed “an angel of Satan,” that is, a messenger of the devil, because that stimulation of desire was introduced into him by the devil.

Whenever the Apostle suffered that stimulation, he knew that it was being inflicted upon him by the devil. But the Lord, who permitted him to be buffeted—that is, afflicted and troubled—by the devil’s temptation, guarded him from falling into the vice of lust by enabling him to recognize his own weakness and thus preventing him from being lifted up into pride.

Hence it is evident that he drove out poison by means of poison. By the poison of lust and the temptation of the flesh, he drove away from him the poison of pride.

For the Lord gave him a medicinal antidote, *tyriacum*, which is made from a serpent called *Tyrus* or *Tyriacus*, from which the name *tyriacum* is also derived; it drives out another poison. From the very source by which he was tempted with lust, he was healed of the vice of pride, because he had received from the Lord, against the poison of pride, a *tyriacum* antidote which, when tasted, expels poison.

Wishing to instruct his elect and preserve them in the humility of virtues, the Lord often permits them to be tempted. Thus he permitted the outstanding preacher to be tempted by the devil, lest he be lifted up by the greatness of his revelations. He orders the temptation itself in such a way that those who might have perished through exaltation are kept from destruction and ruin by remaining in a state of humility.

Therefore, if anyone endures some temptation, he must neither despair nor give up, but must struggle with God’s help in order to conquer.

## “For this reason”—that is, because of the impediment of lust—“I asked the Lord three times that the thorn in my flesh, or the angel of Satan, might depart from me.”

A question can be raised here. Since the Lord says through the prophet concerning any one of the elect, “While you are still crying out, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. 58), and in the Gospel, “Whatever you ask in my name will be done for you” (John 14), why was the foremost of the Apostles not heard when he prayed to be freed from the devil’s temptation and the stimulation of the flesh?

It must be understood that he was not heard because he was not asking in the name of Jesus—that is, he was not asking for what pertained to his salvation. He did not know how to ask for what was useful to him, just as he says elsewhere: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Rom. 8).

If he had been heard and the devil’s temptation had departed from him, it might have happened that he would quickly have been lifted up into pride. And lest he be excessively saddened, let us hear what the Lord said to him, whether through an angel, in his heart, or by some other revelation:

## “My grace is sufficient for you.”

In this passage “grace” means everything that was freely given to the apostle Paul: that he was called from heaven; that he received faith so that he might believe; that he received remission of all sins in baptism; that he was chosen for the grace of apostleship and the preaching of the nations; that he received from God wisdom surpassing that of all the other apostles; that he was caught up to the third heaven for visions and revelations of the Lord; and that he heard ineffable words in paradise.

Concerning this grace the Lord said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you.” Therefore, do not pray for the thorn in the flesh, lest you perhaps fall into pride.

“For power is perfected in weakness.” Power—that is, the perfection of virtues—is perfected in weakness of the flesh, in toil, and in temptation, if the weakness itself is endured patiently and one fights manfully against the temptation of desire.

“Therefore I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

After he understood that what he had thought harmful was beneficial to him, and after he received from the Lord the answer that the perfection of life and of all virtues is perfected in weakness, he says that he gladly boasts—that is, rejoices and is glad—in his weaknesses: in the sufferings that he endured for Christ, so that the power and grace, or perfection, of all Christ’s gifts might deign to dwell in him.

Therefore, since we cannot possess perfection of virtues in any other way unless we patiently endure temptations and the allurements of the flesh, let us nevertheless fight against vices and struggle with the Apostle, so that the power and grace of Christ’s gifts may dwell in us and so that, together with him, we may be crowned in the heavenly kingdom.

## “For this reason”—that is, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me—“I am pleased with my weaknesses.”

I am pleased not with prosperity and the riches of this age, but with insults—that is, with beatings or reproaches; not with the honors of this age, but with necessities; not with feasts or leisure, but with persecutions; not with greetings, but with hardships; not with boastful pride. And I endure all this for Christ, not for some crime.

“When I am weak”—that is, in body—“then I am strong”—that is, in soul. From the very point at which the flesh is worn down, afflicted, and weakened, the soul is strengthened and grows.

## “I have become foolish”—that is, by recounting my own merits and virtues—“but you compelled me to do so.”

He says this to those whom he wished to bring back from love of the false apostles to his own love. He calls himself foolish, but he is certainly not foolish, because he spoke the truth. Although he was compelled to recount his virtues for the salvation of others, he nevertheless did not fall from the state of humility.

“For I ought to have been commended by you”—that is, praised. “For I was inferior in nothing in preaching and in the power of miracles to those who are apostles beyond measure”—that is, to Peter, James, and my other predecessors, whom my detractors say are apostles of extraordinary greatness, greater than I am.

“Even though I am nothing”—that is, although I am nothing in comparison with them—“the signs of my apostleship were nevertheless performed among you,” or “in your midst,” because I raised your dead and healed your sick.

## “For what is it in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I did not burden you?”

I took nothing from you. “Forgive me”—that is, indulge me in this injury, if it is to be called an injury. He speaks ironically. In reality it was not an injury, but consideration.

## “Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you.”

A question may be raised: Since we do not read that he came to them except once, when he stayed with them for a year and a half, and since after departing from them he did not come again—as he himself says in the earlier Epistle, “I call God as witness that I did not come to Corinth after I departed from you,” sparing you, that is, so as not to be a burden to you—why does he now say that he is coming a third time?

It must be understood that he came only once in the presence of his flesh, when he preached to them. He came a second time through the earlier Epistle, not in person. Through this second Epistle he says that he is coming a third time, as though he himself were coming in his Epistles.

“And I will not be a burden to you”—that is, I will take nothing from you. “I do not seek what is yours, but you”—that is, your salvation.

## “I will most gladly spend”—that is, spend everything that is mine for you in preaching and miracles—“and be spent,” that is, give myself over to death for your souls, “although, loving you more, I am loved less”—that is, by you.

But suppose it is so: I did not burden you. “Suppose” (*esto*) is properly an adverb of concession and is used in place of “if.” In this passage it has the following sense: “But suppose”—that is, even if I am loved less by you—“I nevertheless did not burden you in anything.”

“But being crafty,” he says, “did I catch you by deceit?” This should be read reproachfully and interrogatively: “Although I was clever and ingenious, did I capture you by deceit and fraud for the faith of Christ?” No; by true preaching and the power of miracles, with Christ cooperating, I brought you to the faith.

## “Do you think that we are excusing ourselves to you from long ago?”

The implied answer is: We are not doing so, because it is unnecessary.

This can be understood in two ways. First: “Have you for some time been in doubt about us, thinking that we speak such things as though we were not acting toward you sincerely, and that for this reason we are excusing ourselves?” We do not speak such things in order to excuse ourselves, because we proceed sincerely.

Alternatively: “Do you think that we have been excusing ourselves to you from long ago?” The meaning is: You have known our conduct and our preaching for a long time, and therefore we do not need to excuse ourselves.

“Before God, the Father, in Christ we speak”—that is, seeking the honor of Christ. He assures them, in order to satisfy them, that he speaks the truth: “God the Father and Christ, whose honor I seek, are my witnesses, because I act sincerely toward you.”

“But we endure everything”—that is, all hardships—“for your sake.”

“Lest, when I come again, God humble me before you”—that is, afflict me with fasts and tears because of your lack of correction. The Apostle had no sins of his own to mourn, and therefore he mourned the sins of others.

# CHAPTER THIRTEEN

## “Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you.”

First in person, and then twice through my Epistles, “so that every word may stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses.”

He compares his three visits with three witnesses. Just as under the Law someone was defended by three witnesses or convicted by three witnesses, so these people were either corrected and reformed by his third coming and were praised, or, if they remained uncorrected, they were more severely rebuked by the Apostle and received punishment.

## “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me, who is not weak among you, but is powerful in you?”

It is as though he said: Are you seeking proof whether Christ, who speaks in me, is able to punish your sins through me, since he is not powerless among you when it comes to performing miracles and mighty works? Certainly he is able.

## “For even if Christ was crucified from weakness of the flesh, he lives by the power of God.”

That is, in his divinity he remains beyond suffering.

## “For we too, the apostles, are weak in him”—that is, we endure tribulations and hardships for his sake—“but we shall live with him by the power of God among you,” that is, for your sake, to whom we preach.

We already live with him in hope through the power of God that is in us; or, for your sake, we hope to have life with Christ.

## “But we pray not that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good, while we may be as rejected.”

A judge appears approved or proven when he finds something in his subjects to punish, by which he may display his authority. He appears rejected, however, when he finds nothing to avenge, nowhere to display his authority, and nowhere to demonstrate his judgment.

It is as though he said: We do not pray that we may find something in you to punish, but that you may do what is good and that we may be found rejected in this respect, finding no place where we may display our authority.

## “We cannot do anything against the truth, but for the truth.”

That is, we cannot display our authority against a person who possesses the truth, but we struggle on behalf of the truth.

## “We rejoice because we are weak.”

Not in body, but in authority, because a judge is then like one who is weak when he cannot display his authority. Subjects are then powerful when they do not fear the judge.

## “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship”—that is, the partnership and conjunction—“of the Holy Spirit be with you all.”

The implied words are: “May it be so.” Amen. “Let it happen as we have said,” and so forth.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 0669]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0669A]

First, at the beginning of this Epistle, we must ask why the Galatians were so called. The king of Bithynia, which is a province of Greece, being at war with his enemies, sent to the Gauls living near the sea, promising that if they came to his aid, he would divide the kingdom with them once the war had been concluded and victory won. When they came and gained the victory, he divided the kingdom with them as he had promised, and they were first called *Gallo-Greeks*—that is, Gauls mixed with Greeks. The part of the kingdom which they themselves had held was called *Gallo-Greece* (*Gallograecia*)—that is, Gauls dwelling in Greece. Later, however—as wiser authorities think—they were called *Galatians* because of the whiteness of their bodies, for in Greek milk is called γάλα (*gála*). Hence the white band of the sky which in Latin is called the Milky Circle is called in Greek γαλαξίας (*galaxías*), as Martianus affirms.

They are therefore extremely vigorous warriors, but foolish and easily turned away from their purpose of mind. Thus, after they had received the word of preaching from the Apostle, and the Apostle had gone on from them to others, they were led astray by false apostles and by Jews who wanted them to follow circumcision and the legal sacrifices. They said: “Although you have been baptized and believe in Christ, nevertheless you cannot otherwise be saved through the passion of Christ unless you are circumcised and offer the legal sacrifices.” When the Apostle heard this, he wrote this Epistle to them from Ephesus.

## CHAPTER ONE

**Paul.** He places this name of his first in the title of all his Epistles. He did so on account of his authority, just as the kings and princes of this world customarily do.

**Apostle.** This is a name of dignity and is Greek, although some say that it is Hebrew. There are four kinds of apostles.

The first is that which comes neither from human beings nor through a human being, but from God alone. Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and very many other prophets belonged to this number, though not all of them; so did the apostles, who, although they were sent by the human Christ, were sent by one who was also true God.

The second is that which indeed comes from God, but through a human being. Joshua belonged to this number: by God’s will he was sent through Moses. Many others are chosen by the election of the people on account of the merits of their life, by God’s will, because the will of God is sometimes the will of the people.

[Col. 0669D] The third occurs when someone is chosen by a human being alone and not by God, with the favor of human beings—not on account of good conduct, or when someone is installed in the priesthood in return for payment. Concerning such men blessed Ambrose said: “O bishop, surely, if you had not given a hundred solidi, you would not be a bishop today.” Concerning them it is also said in the Book of Kings (III Kings XIII): “In the days of Jeroboam, whoever filled his hand with gifts became a priest of idols.” Such men must therefore be reckoned among those of whom the Lord says through the prophet: “They kept coming, and I was not sending them” (Jer. XXIII). “All who came are thieves and robbers.”

The fourth kind is that which is made neither by God nor through a human being, but by the person himself—as with false prophets and false apostles, who say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord has not sent them.

It should also be known that among the prophets themselves there are some of such great dignity that they are both prophets and apostles, such as Moses, Isaiah, John the Baptist, and the apostles; others are prophets only.

Since there were among the Galatians certain Jews who said that blessed Paul was not a true apostle of Christ or a teacher of the truth, because he had not been called and taught by Christ as the other apostles had, the Apostle therefore wished to confirm the Galatians in his teaching, to show himself a true apostle [Col. 0670B] and preacher of Christ, and said that he had not been taught and appointed by a mortal human being on earth, but by the almighty God from heaven—not as though he denied that Christ was truly human, but because Christ had by then become immortal. Therefore, the one who taught Peter by his presence on earth while he was still mortal taught Paul from heaven after becoming immortal. Hence he says: “Not from human beings”—that is, I was not appointed as Matthias was, who was chosen by lot by the apostles—“nor through a human being”—that is, not through one who was already mortal—but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, because the Father and the Son have one operation.

To show that those two persons possess one dignity, he placed the person of the Son before the person of the Father, and at the same time he destroys the error of the Arians, who say that the Son is a creature and therefore lesser than the Father.

**Who raised him from the dead.** God the Father raised his Son from the dead on the third day; the Son himself also raised himself by the power of the Word by whom he had been assumed.

**And all the brothers who are with me**—that is, all fellow disciples and believers—sharing the same opinion concerning circumcision.

Why is it that in his other Epistles he gives the names of certain of his disciples, whereas here he does not mention any one of them specifically, but includes all of them generally? He did this so that his Epistle might possess greater authority, or to show that all were grieving over the Galatians’ deception and that all held the same opinion concerning circumcision: that they should not be circumcised or offer the legal sacrifices.

Why also does he make no mention in this Epistle of bishops, presbyters, or deacons, as he does in the others? Because they did not yet have ordained bishops or other rulers. For this reason they could be led astray more easily.

**Grace to you and peace.** By this we are reconciled to the Lord, who handed himself over to death for our sins, in order to rescue us from the present evil age.

“Age” (*saeculum*) is said to derive from *sequendo*, “following,” because it always follows and revolves back upon itself. The age therefore cannot itself be evil or bad, because it always preserves its own order and course according to God’s arrangement, with days and nights alternating. But just as one speaks of a bad house—not because the house itself is bad, but because it has bad inhabitants—so the age or time is called evil, not because it is evil, but because it contains within itself the worst and wickedest people.

He rightly added, “according to the will of God the Father,” because it was the will of God the Father that the Son should restore the human race through his passion.

**Amen.** “Amen” is Hebrew, and it is a confirmation of the Epistle. Thus *Amen* means “truly,” or “faithfully,” and “let it be done.”

**I am amazed that you are transferring yourselves so quickly.** The Apostle says that he is amazed that they could so quickly be led astray by mere words from the truth of the Gospel, and be reduced from freedom to slavery; and that they could be changed and transferred from the Gospel of Christ which he had delivered to them into another [Col. 0671B] Gospel—that is, into another doctrine.

**Which is not another**—understand, “Gospel”—because of what I preached. The Gospel means “good proclamation.” If there is any doctrine which the Lord himself, or someone acting on his behalf, has not given, it can no longer be called the Gospel, but is error.

**You are transferring yourselves**—that is, you are being led away or deceived by him, namely by God the Father, who called you into grace—that is, into the remission of sins—which God the Father freely gave us, either through the passion of his Son or through baptism, into another Gospel.

There is no other Gospel except Christ’s. Therefore the tradition of the Jews and the doctrine by which they said that circumcision had to be preserved, along with the other things prescribed by the Law in its mysteries, are error after Christ has come.

**Unless there are**—that is, there are certain people who disturb you, namely, move you away from the straight path of faith, and want to convert you. They do indeed want to change the Gospel of Christ from spiritual things to carnal things, but they cannot, because it is most firm and true. If the Gospel is changed, it will no longer be the Gospel. Although some may be turned away from the straight path of the Gospel, the Gospel itself always remains unchangeable.

**But even if we**—that is, I and the apostles of Christ, Peter and the others—or an angel from heaven, Michael or Gabriel, should preach to you something beyond—that is, something other than this Gospel—let him be accursed.

“Anathema” has various meanings. Sometimes it is used for killing, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “I could wish that I myself were accursed for my brothers” (Rom. IX)—that is, “I wished to be killed bodily for them.” Sometimes it means a curse, as is found in the canons: “If anyone does this or that, let him be anathema”—that is, let him be accursed. Elsewhere it means separation, as here.

**As I said before**—understand, “when I was present”—“so now, while absent”; or, “as I said shortly above in the preceding verse, so now I say again: beyond what you received”—understand, “from me.”

**For now am I persuading human beings, or God?** The meaning is this: “Am I now persuading”—that is, exhorting—human beings to believe in Christ and persevere in his faith, or am I persuading God to do something new, although all past and future things are open to him?

He persuaded human beings to believe in Christ, but he was not persuading God to do anything new. The Apostle would then be persuading God to do something new if he himself were the first to abolish circumcision. But because Christ, by fulfilling the Law, rendered it void, the Apostle was not persuading God; rather, he declared that the things which Christ himself showed ought to be observed were to be observed.

**If I were still pleasing human beings**—that is, if I were pleasing the Jews from whom I originated by remaining in Judaism, or wicked people such as heretics—I would not be Christ’s servant.

Every preacher must attend to this: he should seek to please his hearers with Christ and his preaching, not with himself. If both can be done, so that God is loved and the preacher himself is good, then both should be done. But if Christ does not please them, the preacher himself must not make himself pleasing to them.

**I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was evangelized by me**—that is, preached and proved—because it is not according to human beings, meaning according to the tradition of the scribes and Pharisees. The Gospel which is said to be according to human beings is not the Gospel. For every human being is a liar, and whatever truth is found in a human being comes not from the human being but from God through the human being.

For I did not receive it from a human being—that is, from any of the apostles. And if I received it from the Lord Jesus Christ, he was already immortal.

There is a distinction between receiving the Gospel and learning it. One receives the Gospel when it is first imparted to him and he accepts its faith. One learns it when, with God revealing or a human being teaching, he is able to penetrate those things which the Lord uttered in it through enigmas and parables. But I learned the Gospel through the revelation of Jesus Christ—that is, through its manifestation.

What revelation does he mean? The teachers say that Paul learned the fullness of evangelical teaching during those three days, when the Holy Spirit revealed it to him, while he remained in Damascus for three days, seeing neither the light of the sun nor that of day, and neither eating nor drinking. Or he received it at that time when—as he himself says—one day, while he was in the temple, he was placed in an ecstasy.

For you heard about my conduct: how I lived without reproach in the Law, as it seemed to me, when I adhered to the Law and observed circumcision and the Sabbath and the other things prescribed by the Law, and for that reason did not know Christ. For I persecuted the Church of God—that is, those who believed in Christ—beyond measure, that is, more than all the Jews, and attacked it—that is, fought very fiercely against it.

I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries—that is, beyond all those of the same age as I. I advanced in the teaching of the Law according to the tradition of the Pharisees, from whose group I had originated. No one could equal me in zeal for reading and disputation, nor in the persecution of Christians; no one could advance so far in support of the position of the Synagogue.

In my own group—that is, the group of the Pharisees—I was more abundantly zealous—that is, more ardent—as an imitator and devoted student, for the establishment of the Synagogue and of the traditions of my fathers—that is, of the Pharisees.

[Col. 0673A] **But when it pleased him who**—that is, who caused me to be born from my mother’s womb, or who set me apart in his presence and separated me from my mother’s womb—for the preaching of his Gospel; or, “from my mother’s womb,” that is, he drew me away from the company of the Synagogue and called me through his grace—that is, through his mercy—to preach his Gospel,

**to reveal his Son in me**—that is, through me, to the Gentiles—**so that I might preach him among the Gentiles immediately**, that is, as soon as it pleased God the Father to reveal his Son through me among the Gentiles, **I did not consult flesh and blood**—that is, I did not consent to remain in Judaism.

Or, “I did not consult flesh and blood”—that is, the scribes and Pharisees from whom I originated. Some wish to understand the apostles by this phrase, but that is false.

Blessed Jerome divides this verse according to the following meaning. Peter and the other apostles, after they were called by the Lord, did not immediately go out to preach, nor even after his resurrection, until they had received the Holy Spirit; therefore they made what was, as it were, a lengthy delay. Paul, however, as soon as he had been baptized, without any delay entered the synagogue of the Jews and began to preach publicly.

Nevertheless, the phrase “immediately” can also be joined to what follows. But it is better understood as we have explained it: “to reveal his Son in me”—that is, through me.

Alternatively: The Word of God the Father, namely the Son, contains heaven and earth with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and fills all things. There is no place which he does not fill through the fullness of his power; and thus, since he is everywhere through the power of his divinity and fills all places, he was also in Paul, although Paul did not know it.

When, therefore, he gave Paul faith in his Son, he then manifested his Son to him; and the Son himself was there where he revealed himself. For example, he was in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and there he assumed flesh.

**Nor did I go to Jerusalem.** The question is why he says that he did not go to Jerusalem until after three years, when the Acts of the Apostles says that, after he was baptized, he began to preach in the synagogues of the Jews, and that the Jews rose up against him; because of their persecution he came to Jerusalem.

The question is resolved as follows: “I did not go,” he says, “to Jerusalem in order to visit the apostles, nor for the purpose of learning, as is also not stated here. I came to Jerusalem because of persecution, just as I would go to any other city if it lay on my route—for example, to Samaria or Bethlehem.”

Luke speaks of this occasion in the Acts of the Apostles: “I came to Jerusalem to my predecessors, the apostles”—understand, “neither for the purpose of learning nor of visiting them on this occasion”; but “I went away into Arabia,” having fled from Jerusalem—understand, “having fled from Jerusalem.”

Blessed Jerome says: “What benefit is it to me if I hear that Paul went away into Arabia and returned from there to Damascus, if I do not know what he did there? Perhaps he was forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word there, as he was in Asia. For this reason Scripture did not say what he did there. But if we carefully consider the interpretation of the names of his going and returning, we may find a little benefit.”

That Arabia signifies the Old Testament is shown by the Apostle himself elsewhere, where he speaks of Hagar and Sarah (Gal. IV): “For these,” he says, “are two covenants, and Mount Sinai is in Arabia.”

Damascus, however, which is interpreted as “drinking” or “shedding blood”—because Abel was killed there by Cain, and because Abraham’s servant later built that city there, naming it Damascus after himself—signifies the New Testament, in which the passion of Christ is contained.

The Apostle therefore went into Arabia because, after searching the Law and the Prophets, he found Christ promised there, though not yet given. He returned to Damascus because he passed over to the Gospel, where he found Christ already having suffered, and believed in him.

**For fifteen days.** The number fifteen pertains to the Old and New Testaments because of the numbers seven and eight. The number seven refers to the Old Testament because of the Sabbath; the number eight refers to the New Testament because of the Lord’s resurrection, which is celebrated on the eighth day.

Since the Apostle was filled with the teaching of the Old and New Testaments, he did not need to remain longer with Peter than fifteen days.

**And again I returned to Damascus**, and so forth, up to “I remained with him fifteen days.” He went into Arabia; from Arabia he returned to Damascus; and, after completing three years in Arabia and Damascus, he came to Jerusalem a second time to see Peter—not in order to learn, but to commend charity, and to offer others an example of humility by showing honor to the earlier apostle.

From this it is clear that he did not come in order to learn, because he could not have been taught in so few days. Since someone might also say, “What if he did not learn from Peter but learned from others?” the Apostle added in response:

**But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord**—namely, the son of Mary of Clopas, the Lord’s maternal aunt, who bore him to Alphaeus.

**Behold, before God, I do not lie**—that is, these things are worthy of God’s sight because they are true.

**Then I went into the regions of the province of Syria and Cilicia**, understand, “my homeland,” where Tarsus, Paul’s city, is located.

The Apostle came into Syria, which is interpreted as “the elevated one,” in order to humble it to Christ. He came to Cilicia, which is interpreted as “lamentable assumption,” in order to raise it up to the faith of Christ and teach it the discipline of repentance and mourning.

**I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea**, and so forth. He was indeed unknown by face, but known by name and reputation. He had already been preaching the Gospel for fourteen years.

He does not use the plural “churches” because Jews and Gentiles were mixed together, but because the multitude of believing Jews was so great that they formed several churches. For the one who once persecuted us—that is, those who believed in Christ—now preaches the faith which he once attacked, that is, against which he fought very fiercely.

**And they glorified God in me**, in accordance with the saying: “That they may see your good works” (Matt. V), and with the fact that God made a preacher out of a persecutor (I Tim. I).

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0675A] **Then after fourteen years I again went up to Jerusalem.** The three preceding years, joined to these fourteen, make seventeen. From this it is gathered that it was the seventeenth year of his preaching when he came to Jerusalem for the third time.

But what occasion arose for him to go to Jerusalem? There was dissension between believing Jews and Gentiles. The Jews were saying: “You have been baptized and believe in Christ, but you cannot otherwise be saved unless you are circumcised and observe the Law.”

Therefore, in order to suppress this dissension, after the Holy Spirit had revealed it to him, he went to Jerusalem with Barnabas. Barnabas was a Jew and circumcised; Titus was a Gentile and uncircumcised.

He therefore went up with these two so that, if the apostles and the other Jews [Col. 0675B] said that he was not preaching correctly among the Gentiles, he could defend himself by their testimony, when they said to them: “Truly, our teacher preaches just as you do; and he holds the same faith in every respect as you do.”

Hence he says: **And I conferred with them about the Gospel**, so that he would not appear to have received something from others. There is a distinction between conferring with one another, teaching, and learning: equals confer with one another, while superiors teach and inferiors learn.

**I conferred with them**—that is, with Peter, John, and James.

**Privately, however, with those who seemed to be something**, I spoke—that is, with Peter and the other apostles—not in an assembly of the Jewish people, but separately.

Why separately? Because he knew many things which the general multitude could not grasp. Or, separately, so that, if he completely forbade circumcision, he would not stir up the persecution of the Jews against himself.

**Those who seemed to be something**, he says, **of themselves.** They seemed to possess doctrine and power from themselves, but they had neither doctrine nor virtues, nor anything good, from themselves or from their own merits. Therefore, although they seemed to the people to be something, they were nothing.

**Lest perhaps I should be running, or should have run, in vain?** Although this may seem harsh, blessed Jerome says that the verse should be read interrogatively. Its meaning is: “Did I therefore confer with them privately because I feared being reproved by them, as though my doctrine were not true and needed their confirmation, or as though I were running about preaching from place to place without purpose?” No. Rather, I did so so that they might hear from me lofty and profound mysteries, which those less capable could not grasp, and so that they could not say to the Galatians: “Do not believe Paul, because he preaches lies. He preaches or teaches one thing among us and another among you. Among you he preaches that circumcision should not be observed; among us he circumcises Titus.”

Therefore, wishing to confirm them in the faith and lead them away from circumcision, the Apostle said: “If Titus, while he was with me, was not compelled by the apostles to be circumcised—not even by threats, terrors, or the multitude of Jews—why are you being led astray by words alone?”

**But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised.** When the Apostle came to Jerusalem, the Jews, out of curiosity, secretly sent men into a hidden place—men whom no suspicion could attach—to observe whether the Apostle, terrified by fear of them, would circumcise Titus.

**They entered to investigate our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus.** Freedom is greatest in Christ Jesus—that is, in the faith of the Gospel—because through faith in the Lord and Savior we are made free in baptism, not only from sins but also from slavery to the Law.

**We did not yield even for an hour**—that is, we did not consent to them even for a time, lest we be subjected to slavery under the Law—so that the faith of the Gospel which we preached to you might remain always in you, and you might not be circumcised.

**But from those who seemed to be something.** By “those” he means Peter, James, and John, who, as we said above, seemed to be something of themselves. What they had once been, before they were strengthened by the coming of the Holy Spirit, is not for me to say. I will say only this: it makes no difference to me—that is, there is no distinction between them and me—and this because God is not a respecter of persons.

Paul was a persecutor of Christians; Peter denied Christ after he had been taught by him. John and James, at the time of the passion, abandoned him and fled with the other apostles.

**Those who seemed to be something**—that is, Peter, James, and John—**contributed nothing to me**, but, on the contrary—understand, “I contributed to them.”

Or alternatively: although some of my critics had thought that they would reproach me, they proved to be not reprovers but praisers and supporters of my preaching.

Augustine and Jerome divide and distinguish this verse in the following manner, with this understood addition: “When James and John, who seemed to be something, had seen”—understand, “from what follows”—“that the Gospel of the uncircumcision,” that is, of the Gentiles, “had been entrusted to me just as the Gospel of the circumcision,” that is, of the Jews, “had been entrusted to Peter.”

**And when they recognized the grace that had been given to me, they gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas.** The remaining words are said parenthetically, as in the phrase “the Gospel of the circumcision entrusted to Peter.” The Apostle has the custom of calling the Jews “the circumcision” and the Gentiles “the uncircumcision.”

For the one who worked through Peter in the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles. The meaning is: The one who made Peter teacher and leader of all believing Jews also appointed me to the office of preaching to all the Gentiles.

Blessed Augustine says in one place that the blessed Apostle was granted greater wisdom than all the apostles. This was so because, since he was going to preach to all Gentiles and philosophers, his preaching might be sufficient for all Gentiles and philosophers.

But someone may say at this point: “If Peter was the teacher of the Jews, then, when he saw a Gentile wishing to convert to the faith, did he refuse to receive him unless he was circumcised? Or did Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, receive a circumcised Jew?”

Certainly Peter received a Gentile without compelling him to be circumcised, as in the case of Cornelius; and Paul did not reject a Jew on account of circumcision. He taught only that the legal observances were not to be observed in a carnal manner.

**Those who seemed to be pillars.** Blessed Augustine says: “They seemed to be pillars, but they were not.” Let us see, however, what the most solid pillars are.

Solomon says: “Wisdom”—which is the Word of God the Father—“built herself a house; in the virginal womb she hewed out seven pillars” (Prov. IX), that is, the seven churches to which John wrote in his Apocalypse (chapter I). These seven churches, or pillars, constitute one Church and one pillar, of which the Apostle says to Timothy: “That you may know,” he says, “how it is necessary for you to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the pillar and foundation” (I Tim. III).

If these men were not pillars, what does the Lord mean when he says: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in my temple” (Rev. III)?

As the Apostle says, and blessed Augustine agrees, they were not pillars of themselves, although they seemed to the simple-minded to be what they were not from themselves. They were pillars solidified by the Lord without their own merits; they were founders of the Church and its supports.

**They gave me the right hands of fellowship.** When he says that they gave the right hands of fellowship to him and Barnabas, this means nothing other than that they received us into their fellowship and friendship.

This expression is drawn from merchants. When they come to foreign regions for the sake of trade, as soon as they arrive, the governor of the place and the people who live there approach them and ask the one who presides over them: “Is your arrival peaceful?” And he replies: “Peaceful.” Then they give their right hands to one another, kiss one another in turn, and thereafter carry out their business in peace, walking freely and securely before their judgment.

So these men also made peace with the Apostle, so that he and Barnabas might preach among the Gentiles, while they themselves preached among the Jews.

**Only this**—understand, “they commanded us”: that we should remember their poor—those who had abandoned their possessions for Christ, or who had been stripped of them by the Jews, such as Nicodemus and others.
