This was also the very thing I was eager to do, sending them what they needed and receiving small gifts from believing Gentiles.

**But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face**—that is, in his presence—**because he was blameworthy**, that is, deserving of blame.

For before certain men came—understand, Jews—from James, that is, from Jerusalem, where James had been appointed bishop over those who believed through the apostles, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision—that is, fearing to be reproved by them.

**But when I saw that they were not walking rightly.** They were not walking rightly because they separated themselves from the Gentiles as though they were unclean, since they had not been circumcised.

**I said to Cephas before everyone.** He rebuked him publicly because he had sinned publicly, so that the others too might be strengthened in the faith through his correction. For a public fault requires public correction before everyone, as is stated in the canons.

**How do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?** He did not compel them to be circumcised by words but by actions, through his separation from them. The Gentiles could say: “If we had been saved and cleansed through baptism, he would certainly not regard us as unclean. It is therefore better that we be circumcised.”

**If you, although you are a Jew**—Peter was a Jew by nature, and lived like a Gentile, not worshiping idols, but not believing that anyone could be saved through circumcision; rather, he believed that salvation came through baptism, just as the Gentiles were saved not through circumcision but through baptism—

**we are Jews by nature and not sinners from the Gentiles.** Gentiles were called sinners. The meaning is: “O Peter, if we, who are Jews by nature, have not been justified by the Law, why do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize—not by word but by action—so that they believe they cannot be saved through baptism without circumcision?”

**We know that a person is not justified by observance of legal commandments.** When he says, “by the works of the Law,” he means by the offering of carnal sacrifices, by observing the commandments, and by circumcision. “By the works of the Law no human being will be justified”—that is, no one will be justified.

**But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ**—that is, in the faith of Christ, in baptism—we who are Jews by nature were found to be sinners when we came to baptism, did Christ make us sinners so that we would have sins and he would find in us something to cleanse? Certainly not.

Rather, because the Law could not justify us, we came to Christ so that, by believing in him, we might be justified.

**For if I rebuild the very thing that I destroyed, I constitute myself a transgressor.** That is, if I again preach that circumcision, which I preached should be abandoned, must be observed, I make myself a transgressor both of the Mosaic Law and of the Gospel. For if circumcision could justify, then, indeed, when I destroyed it, I became a transgressor; and if, after coming to the Gospel, I returned again to the carnal Law, I likewise became a transgressor.

It should be noted that he was speaking these things against Peter, who compelled the Gentiles to be circumcised not by word but by action, withdrawing from them, although Peter himself had preached that circumcision should not be observed.

**For through the Law**—understand, “the Law of the Gospel”—**I died to the Law of Moses**, that is, I owe it nothing because I am not subject to it.

Or, through the spiritually understood Law I died to the carnal Law, because I do not observe it in a carnal manner, **so that I might live for God through faith and righteousness.**

**I have been crucified with Christ**—that is, I have been fastened to the cross of Christ, because my sins were fastened to his cross, that is, erased and put to death.

**But I live—now no longer I.** He did indeed live in substance, but wickedness did not live in him; righteousness lived in him. The most savage persecutor had been extinguished and put to death in him, while the most devout preacher lived in him.

Christ lives—or reigns—in me through faith and through all virtues.

**I do not reject the grace of God**—that is, I do not repel the faith of Christ, the Gospel, or the remission of sins, all of which have been freely given to us.

For if righteousness comes through the Law—that is, if the Law could justify—then Christ died without cause, and his passion neither benefited nor harmed anyone.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0679A] **O foolish Galatians.** Every nation has its own distinctive character in conduct and morals. Thus it is characteristic of the Galatians that, although they are fierce, they are also dull or foolish, and can easily be transferred from one thing to another.

**Who has bewitched you?** That is, who has harmed you, or who has deceived you? Children, small animals, and young birds are said to be bewitched by the gaze and incantation of human beings.

**Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was portrayed as crucified among you.** Christ Jesus had been portrayed as crucified before their eyes because they possessed not only the four books of the Gospel, in which Christ’s passion is fully contained, but also the books of the Old Testament in Greek according to the Seventy Interpreters. In those books Christ’s passion was announced and preached, and Christ crucified was, as it were, before their eyes.

**Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed in the flesh?** That is, although you had begun to conduct yourselves spiritually, or had begun through the Holy Spirit to speak in various languages, are you now failing through carnal observance, setting aside all spiritual things and turning to carnal observances—that is, to circumcision of the flesh and legal sacrifices?

Alternatively: At the beginning of the faith, all who believed in Christ received the Holy Spirit, as they do now, and in addition received a diversity of languages, by which it was shown that they possessed the Holy Spirit.

This can be proved by no example better than the one stated in the Acts of the Apostles: when Paul said to certain baptized people, who had been baptized with John’s baptism, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” they replied: “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit in us, because we cannot speak in all languages.”

When he had baptized them in the name of Jesus, they began to speak in various languages. These Galatians did not receive the Holy Spirit and the diversity of languages from the works of the Law, but because they believed in Christ, after hearing the Apostle preach the faith of the Lord.

He says, “from the hearing of faith,” because a person hears what he ought to believe, and at the font is asked how he believes, and thus is baptized.

**Have you suffered so many things without cause?** They had suffered many evils from the Jews and persecutors on account of the faith of Christ [Col. 0679D], because they did not wish to observe circumcision.

**If indeed it is without cause.** This is an affirmative conjunction: “Certainly you suffer without cause, if you return again to carnal desires and to observing circumcision.”

**Therefore, the one who supplies the Spirit to you**—understand, “the Holy Spirit”—**and works powers in you**—understand, “miracles and languages”—does he do this **from the works of the Law**—understand, “does he do this on account of the observance of the Law”—or **from the hearing of faith**?

The understood answer is: “He did not grant this to us because of observing the Law, but because of faith, since through faith we have been justified and are pleasing to God.”

**Therefore, those who are of faith will be blessed with faithful Abraham**—that is, those who possess Abraham’s faith will obtain Abraham’s blessing.

Whoever, then, are of the works of the law are under a curse [Col. 0680A]—that is, those who think they are justified through the law are under the law’s curse, because they cannot fulfill everything contained in it. Hence Peter says to the Jews: “Why are you trying to impose upon us a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” Under what curse are they? Under this one: “Cursed is everyone,” and so forth. The law, however, is not based on faith; faith consists in believing and hoping for what is not seen. The law, therefore, was not fulfilled by faith but by works. The Gospel, on the other hand, is fulfilled more by faith than by works, because faith alone saves. Whoever, then, did the commandments prescribed by the law lived by them, because his present life was prolonged for him until the end appointed by God. Whoever, however, was a transgressor of the law was ordered to be killed, since the law says: “Whoever does this or that shall be put to death.”

[Col. 0680B] Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. From what curse? From the one spoken to Adam: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Gen. II). From this curse—that is, from this death—he redeemed us by restoring us to life, because by his single death he destroyed our double death. And how? By becoming a curse for us. He did not himself become accursed, as blessed Ambrose says, as though he had sin; rather, he became a curse—that is, a sacrifice for the accursed and for sinners, namely for us, who were held under the curse of the first man and under death. Or, as blessed Augustine says: “He became a curse”—that is, he became mortal as we are, although he was without sin.

For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Euticus explains this verse in the following way: [Col. 0680C] “Cursed is every guilty person who hangs on a tree because of his own guilt and sin; but whoever is innocent, if he has been unjustly hanged, will not therefore be accursed.” What, then, if Mordecai had been innocently hanged on the tree that Haman had prepared for him—would he for that reason have been accursed? Certainly not. So also Christ, although he endured that curse—that is, suffering and torment—and took upon himself our sins, was nevertheless not for that reason accursed or a sinner, because he took our sins upon himself not in order to possess them but to destroy them. Or again, in the eyes of the Jews he was accursed—that is, a sinner.

“Brothers, I speak according to human considerations”—that is, according to human custom and human law—“yet no one rejects a human testament once it has been confirmed.” A testament is so called from the witnesses whose names are written in it and by whom the testament is confirmed; or it is the charter or written document that a father makes concerning his possessions for his sons, specifying what each one is to possess of the paternal inheritance after his death. No one despises such a testament by interpreting and dividing it otherwise, or by arranging it differently from the way the living father arranged it.

“Promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He says in the singular: “The promise was spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” But because many promises were made to him, both concerning the promised land and concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, he therefore spoke in the plural: “Promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” Let us see and consider what those promises were, in case we find that something concerning us Gentiles was promised to him. The first promise was made when the Lord called him, promising that, if he departed from his land, he would become a great nation: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and go into the land that I will show you, and I will make you into a great nation.” Then he said to him: “Blessing I will bless you, and I will multiply you,” and so forth; and again: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed”; and: “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Gen. XII).

What is added, “and to his seed,” is to be understood as “the promises were spoken”; although the Apostle specifically understands Christ as Abraham’s seed, we may nevertheless in a simple manner take his seed to be Isaac, his son, and Jacob, his grandson, [Col. 0681B] to whom also we read that promises were made. For we read in Genesis that, while Jacob was sleeping, God appeared to him in a certain place, saying: “The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed.”

Let us now speak according to the Apostle: “Promises,” he says, “were spoken to Abraham and to his seed”—that is, to Christ. What are those promises that were spoken to Christ or in Christ? They are that all nations would be blessed in him, according to what we have already said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” Christ, then, is Abraham’s seed, because Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac Jacob, and Jacob Judah; from Judah’s tribe and lineage the Lord assumed flesh in the virginal womb of blessed Mary, and he came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber.

But one may ask why all nations are said to have been blessed in Christ, since not all nations yet believe in him, and since there is no doubt that no one deserves to be blessed except the one who has faith in him. This can be resolved in two ways. It can be understood synecdocically—that is, as the part from the whole—because, although not all believe, nevertheless there are believers from every nation. Or, all who deserve blessing are blessed in Christ.

The Apostle therefore adds and says: “He does not say”—understand, “Promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seeds”—but it is said in the singular, “to his seed.” Scripture does not say: “In your seeds all nations shall be blessed,” but “in your seed,” so that we may understand it to have been spoken of Christ. For if he had said “seeds” in the plural, someone might perhaps have argued that it was spoken of David and of other Jews. In one place blessed Jerome, who had mastered all the sacred Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments in meaning and memory, says: “Nowhere was he able to find the plural form *seeds* used when the matter concerns the propagation of children. But when it refers to the seed of crops, it is found in the plural, as it is written in Genesis: ‘Joseph commanded the Egyptians to collect seeds and sow them, lest the land be reduced to nothing’” (Gen. XLVII).

This testament, then—that is, the promise that had been made to Abraham—I say was confirmed by God. Teachers distinguish this verse in various ways in their writings. Some make a complete division where it says “by God”; others make a medial division. Both readings can be accommodated. Here he calls the promise made to Abraham a testament: that in his seed, that is, in Christ, all nations would be blessed. How was this testament or promise confirmed? Christ was born of the Virgin Mary from the seed of Abraham; he preached in the world and performed miracles; by his passion he redeemed the human race; he sent his disciples to preach and baptize. What he promised to Abraham was fulfilled when the apostles went forth preaching everywhere, with Christ himself cooperating, so fully that their sound went out into all the earth and the fame of his name was proclaimed to the ends of the world. Then all nations were blessed in the seed of Abraham—that is, in Christ—in the manner we explained above, and his promise was fulfilled.

[Col. 0682B] The law, which was made—or given on Mount Sinai—after four hundred and thirty years, did not invalidate, that is, did not abolish or destroy, the testament, or promise, of Abraham. An invalid thing is empty and void; for example, the husks of a grain of wheat, or of chickpeas, or of some other legume or seed, can be empty. The law, therefore, which was given to the children of Israel after the promise had been made to Abraham, did not make that testament empty and void, so that the promise would be annulled.

Concerning this number of four hundred and thirty years, teachers argue in various ways, gathering the whole period through lengthy and circuitous calculations. But, passing over all that briefly, let us use a concise solution by counting the years themselves. From Abraham’s call out of the land of the Chaldeans until Jacob’s entry into Egypt, two hundred and fifteen years are reckoned. Again, from Jacob’s entry into the land of Egypt until the departure of the children of Israel from it, another two hundred and fifteen years are likewise reckoned. Joined together, these complete the number of four hundred and thirty years, after which the law was given, counting from the time the promise was made to Abraham.

It must also be explained how we should understand what God says to Abraham in Genesis: “Know with foreknowledge that your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and they will afflict and mistreat them for four hundred years” (Gen. XV). For we cannot find how they were afflicted and mistreated for four hundred years. Scripture relates that after Joseph’s death a king arose in Egypt who did not know Joseph, and he began to afflict the children of Israel. [Col. 0682D] But it must be understood that the words “Your seed will be a stranger in a land that is not theirs” refer to the entire period of four hundred years, during which Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were strangers and sojourners in a land that was not theirs, and their sons after them for a long time. What follows—“They will be subjected to servitude and mistreated for four hundred years”—refers to the final part and end of the four hundred years, during which they were afflicted from Joseph’s death until their departure from Egyptian slavery.

For if the inheritance were from the law and no longer from the promise—that is, if the inheritance of the promised land, which Abraham possessed in his sons, [Col. 0683A] or the inheritance of the whole world, which he possessed in Christ who was born from his seed, had been given to Abraham through the law—then that inheritance would no longer be a gift of promise but of law. Abraham possesses the inheritance of the whole world in Christ. God did not give Abraham the inheritance of the whole world through the law; rather, through the promise the seed was given, which is Christ, in whom all nations are blessed.

What, then, is the purpose of the law? Blessed Augustine, explaining this Epistle to the Galatians, first distinguished the passage in this way: “What, then?” But afterward, rereading what he had dictated, he corrected his error in the book of the *Retractations*, and prescribed that it be distinguished as follows: “What, then, is the law?”—that is, “Why did the law come?” or “What benefit did it bring?” or “Why was it given, if Abraham’s inheritance was given through the promise?”

The Apostle himself answered these questions, saying: “It was added because of transgressions until the seed should come”—that is, Christ, to whom, or to which seed, he had promised—understand, that in him all nations would be blessed. To transgress is to go beyond and to violate. Therefore the law was given after the promise in order to restrain human beings and keep them from sins, since they were inclined to transgress the commandments of almighty God and the natural law.

As soon as the people had gone out from the Egyptian prison, before they crossed the sea, they murmured; and after crossing the sea they murmured again. When they reached Mount Sinai, after receiving the Ten Commandments, they worshiped the head of the ox that the Egyptians adored and bowed down before it. The law was therefore given because of such transgressions and others like them, in order to prohibit such acts, while God threatened those who committed them with death.

“Established through angels”—that is, arranged, written down, and dictated—the law itself was given through an angel. God spoke to Moses through a subordinate creature, that is, through an angel, just as Stephen says to the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles: “This is the Moses who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai” (Acts VII).

“In the hand of the Mediator”—that is, in the power of the Word of God, namely the Son of God, who afterward, by assuming flesh, became our mediator. For unless he had assumed humanity, he could not in any other way have been our mediator. By assuming the flesh of our weakness, he became our mediator, now standing before the face of God on our behalf; through him we direct our prayers to God the Father.

Some wished to interpret “mediator” here as Moses, because he himself said: “I was intermediary and mediator between God and you at that time.” But, according to blessed Augustine, it is better to understand it in the way given above, referring it to Christ, by whose arrangement the law itself was given through the ministry of angels. Just as by his authority the prophetic oracles were spoken by the prophets, who said, “The word of the Lord that came to Joel,” or “to Isaiah,” so by his arrangement the law was written.

A mediator, however, cannot be of one alone—understand, of the Father—but must be between two or between several, so that he may stand in the middle. Yet God is one. The Apostle added this lest anyone suppose that Christ had been entirely separated from the unity of the divine nature because he assumed the office of mediator. Although he is our mediator according to his humanity, he is not cut off from the nature of divine fatherhood. He himself, who is true God and true man, always remains one in nature; he remains equal to the Father in the nature and power of divinity.

Is the law, then, contrary to the promises of God? That is: Is the law therefore contrary to the promise of almighty God that was made to Abraham concerning Christ—that in his seed all nations would be blessed? Certainly not. It must not be believed that the law is contrary to this promise in such a way as to annul it.

For if a law had been given that could give life—that is, justify—a soul lives for God so long as it does not sin, but dies when it entangles itself in crimes. That Mosaic law could not raise a person from this death, because it showed sins but did not remove them. It was indeed impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of goats. If it could give life to a person and open the gates of the kingdom, then righteousness would truly be from the law—that is, the promise would be thought to have been excluded. For if the law could cleanse and justify us, what need would there have been for Christ to come? But because the law could not do this, Christ’s coming was therefore necessary for us.

But Scripture confined all classes of human beings, and all Jews, under sin—that is, it showed that no one was able to fulfill the law. For the law said: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not do this or that,” because if you did so, you would die the death of the soul. It foretold what must be avoided; but if such acts were committed, it did not remove them. While someone was perpetrating them, the law showed [Col. 0684C] that he was a sinner.

If, then, the law showed sins but did not remove them, was it the author of the crime and guilt of sinners? Certainly not. For example, the law itself was like a certain king, or like any earthly authority, which establishes and publishes a law and edict so that, if anyone does this or that, he may either be sent to prison or beheaded. Someone violates that edict and is put in prison—is the king therefore the author of his guilt? If he is freed from prison, that is the king’s grace and mercy.

The law showed sins and prohibited them, but did not remove them, so that the promise made to Abraham through faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers, so that all nations might be blessed in his name and justified through faith in him. It would be his grace and forgiveness, so that those whom the law could not save he himself might redeem; and we, who through the works of the law were not worthy to be saved, might obtain justification through faith in him, and so forth.

## CHAPTER IV

### How long the heir is a child

Here the Apostle speaks according to the custom of human law. Fathers who are about to die commonly entrust their young sons, whom they leave as heirs, to guardians and administrators until the time when the sons themselves are able to manage their own property—that is, according to Roman law, until the twenty-fifth year. These guardians too ought to be appointed with the counsel of the *scabini* in a general assembly. As long as a child is under their guardianship, he differs in nothing from a slave, even if he is the master of slaves and the son of a king, count, or some other prince, because just as a slave is flogged, so is he, often even by a slave.

Guardians are defenders of property, legal representatives, and advocates. Concerning the word translated here as “administrators,” certain teachers say that *auctores* is better at this point, because an *auctor* himself is a guardian or advocate. An *actor*, however, is a patron or fosterer, one who nourishes the child in a fatherly manner. It belongs to the guardian to defend and administer the child’s property and to provide food and clothing; it belongs to the *auctor* to provide discipline and uprightness of conduct and way of life.

Similarly, as long as the Jews were children in understanding, they were under guardians and administrators, until the time appointed by God the Father came, when he sent them his Son. Their guardians were kings and princes, such as David and Zerubbabel, because they defended the inheritance. Their administrators were the priests and prophets, who instructed them according to the law and compelled them not to depart from the worship of God if anyone wished to worship idols.

So also, when we were children, we were serving under the elements of the world. “Elements” are so called as if from “elevations,” because all corporeal and visible things are raised up from them. As for the statement here, “we were serving under the elements of the world,” it can be understood in two ways with reference to the Jews.

In the first understanding, the elements are called the law and the prophets, because just as the elements are the beginning and foundation of all corporeal things, so the law and prophecy are the beginning and foundation of all divine utterances. Thus also in the Epistle to the Hebrews he calls the law “elements.” They were serving under the law and prophecy.

Alternatively, they also served under the elements because they lived under observance of the sun and moon, celebrating new moons and other festivals. It should be noted that he did not say, “We were serving the elements,” but “We were under the elements”—that is, under observance of the law and prophecy, or under observance of the seasons, attending to the course and age of the moon. For the sun and moon are elements. The Gentiles, however, were serving the elements.

But when the fullness of time came—that is, the time predetermined by God the Father, at the end of the fifth age and the beginning of the sixth—God sent his Son, made from a woman, that is, created from the seed of a woman by the work of the Holy Spirit. Some wish to say “born,” but “made from a woman” is better because of the heretics who maintain that, as he entered the virgin, so he immediately came forth.

“Made under the law.” He was made under the law because he was circumcised on the eighth day; on the fortieth day legal offerings were presented for him. This was done to demonstrate that the law was holy, just, and good; or so that he might redeem those who were under the law—that is, those subject to the law, sinners unable to be cleansed through it—in order that we might receive adoption, that is, the choosing of sons, understand, of God, which we had lost in Adam.

And because you are adoptive sons of God, not natural sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son. The Holy Spirit is common to the Father and the Son, and when he is sent by the Father, he is also sent by the Son.

“Crying,” that is, causing us to cry: “Abba, Father”—understand, “have mercy on me.” *Abba* is Hebrew and Syriac; “Father” is Greek and Latin.

Therefore whoever has the Spirit of Christ is not a slave—understand, of sin—but a son—understand, of God. And if a son—understand, of God—then an heir—understand, of eternal life—not by his own merit but by the grace of God, through whom he has been redeemed.

“Become like me, because I too”—understand, was—“like you.” The Galatians were unbelievers and sinners, alienated from God, just as the Apostle himself once was when he persecuted the Church of God. But by God’s grace he was now faithful and justified. Become perfect in faith, as I now am, and do not despair of forgiveness, because I too was once an unbeliever and sinner, as you are now, and even more so.

I beseech you, brothers—understand, that you listen to me patiently. You have done me no wrong—understand, when I first preached the Gospel to you. And just as you did me no wrong then and listened to me patiently, so now do not wrong me, but listen patiently to what I am about to say.

For I bear witness to you that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me, without injury to yourselves. That is: if it had been possible for me, through the eyes of the body, to know greater things about God and to penetrate more deeply into the light of his mysteries through bodily sight, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. Such was the love you had for me, and so greatly did you desire to hear the word of God through me.

“My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” To be in labor is to wish to give birth. Blessed Paul had already given birth to the Galatians in faith through the Gospel, as he himself said: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (I Cor. II). But they had departed from the faith and followed false apostles. The Apostle, grieving over their misery and wishing to call them back to the faith of Christ, was in labor over them—that is, he wished to give birth to them again by word and example. Hence he also says: “My little children, whom I wish to bear again through my preaching in the faith of Christ, just as I bore you formerly when I brought you to the faith, until the faith of Christ is formed in you.” Christ is formed in us when he is believed by us as he ought to be believed.

For it is written that Abraham had two sons. The Apostle did not recall Abraham’s deed without reason. The Jews especially gloried in this, that they were Abraham’s sons according to the flesh. Therefore, when the Lord had said to them in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John VIII), they answered him: “We are Abraham’s sons, and we have never been slaves to anyone” (ibid.).

The Apostle therefore wished to make the Galatians concerned, lest they be led astray by the Jews who taught them to observe circumcision and offer the legal sacrifices, saying: “You cannot be saved through Christ’s passion or through baptism unless you are circumcised and offer the legal sacrifices.” He showed them how Abraham did not deserve to be justified and called God’s friend through observance of the law, but because of his most sincere faith and his most approved works.

[Col. 0687A] “But the one from the slave woman”—that is, Ishmael, who was born from Hagar according to the flesh, that is, according to the usage of human custom. Blessed Augustine says that it is the custom of human nature for an old man joined sexually to a young woman to beget children; conversely, when an old man and an old woman are joined, it is natural that they cease to bear children. If, however, a young man has intercourse with an older woman, he says that they too can produce children, although this occurs very rarely in practice.

According to this manner and the natural custom we mentioned first—namely, that if an old man is joined to a young woman, the young woman can conceive—the Apostle says that Ishmael was born.

“But the one from the free woman”—that is, Isaac from Sarah—“through the promise,” understand, of God, which was made to Abraham, not according to human custom. But a question arises here: why does the Apostle say that Isaac alone was born through the promise, when we also read that a promise was made concerning Ishmael? For we read in the book of Genesis (Gen. XVI) that, when Hagar was in the desert of Shur, the angel of the Lord appeared to her, saying: “Hagar, slave woman of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?” She answered: “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.” The angel said to her: “Return and humble yourself under her hand.” And again: “I will multiply your seed exceedingly. Behold, you shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael. He will be a wild man. His hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him.”

The answer is that, when this promise was made, Ishmael had already been conceived. But the promise that was made concerning Isaac was given to Abraham before Isaac was conceived, as we can prove from the angel’s words when he said to Abraham: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. XVIII). Hence it is clear that Isaac was not born according to the course of human custom, but through the promise, from an aged father and an old mother; and what is more, he was born from a barren woman through God’s action.

These things were spoken allegorically—that is, the things said above concerning Hagar and Sarah. They were also spoken spiritually concerning Ishmael and Isaac and require a spiritual exposition. Blessed Paul has the custom of calling spiritual understanding “allegory.” Allegory, properly speaking, belongs to grammarians. It is a trope by which something other than what is said is signified. The things said here are to be understood allegorically, as what follows makes clear.

“These,” he says, “are two testaments”—that is, the things mentioned above signify two testaments. For as far as the literal meaning is concerned, Hagar and Sarah were two women, and Ishmael and Isaac were two men. As far as spiritual understanding is concerned, Hagar the slave woman, who bore a son in slavery, signifies the law, which brought forth and held the Jewish people under the yoke of slavery.

In what respect, then, was the Jewish people enslaved? In this respect: they were compelled to serve the law, to observe circumcision, to offer legal sacrifices, and to keep countless other commands that could not be transgressed with impunity. The transgressor was subject not only to corporeal punishment but also to the curse contained in the law itself: “Cursed,” it says, “is everyone who does not remain in all these things” (Deut. XXVIII). While he was bound by such commands, he was in a certain sense a slave.

Sarah, however, the free woman who bore a free son, signifies the grace of the New Testament, which brought forth a Christian people liberated in baptism—not only from original and actual sins but also from every servitude to the law—which will inherit the inheritance of Christ, that is, Christ’s homeland.

Abraham also had two other sons from Keturah, whom the Hebrews say was Hagar. Nevertheless, they were not worthy to be admitted to the paternal inheritance. Similarly, in the holy Church there are many who are reborn in baptism and who appear to be sons of Abraham; but because they do not possess Abraham’s works, following various errors and different schisms and entangling themselves in various crimes, [Col. 0688B] they will not deserve to enjoy the inheritance of the heavenly homeland with the elect. Concerning such people the evangelist John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II).

“These,” he says, “are two testaments.” A testament is so called from testators. The Old Testament had as its testators angels, Moses, and the other prophets. The New Testament, however, had one most true Lord, Jesus Christ, and the apostles, through whose ministry it was proclaimed throughout the fourfold world.

“One”—understand, one testament—“was given on Mount Sinai, generating”—understand, the Jewish people—“for slavery.” This is Hagar, that is, the people signified by Hagar. Through the teachers of the synagogue, the law generated the people into slavery to itself.

For Sinai is a mountain in the province of Arabia, which is joined to what is now Jerusalem—that is, it borders the promised land in which Jerusalem is located. Jerusalem itself is in slavery with her children—that is, with the priests and teachers who lived chiefly in Jerusalem, together with their subjects, under legal servitude to almighty God.

Arabia is a province containing many nations and regions, namely the Ammonites, Moabites, Philistines, Idumeans, and many others. In this province is Mount Sinai, of such size and length that it borders the promised land, just as, for example, the mountains that surround Italy and separate it from other kingdoms do.

The Apostle set forth everything mentioned above in order to arrive at what he now says about Mount Sinai, which is near the land of the Jews, so that he might show that the Jews were slaves not only because of the law they received but also because of the proximity of the places and because the mountain adjoined them—the mountain on which they received the law of slavery.

But the Jerusalem that is above—Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifies the holy Church that sees God with the mind. It consists of angels and human beings: part of it already reigns with Christ, while part of it is still a pilgrim away from God on earth.

As for the part that already reigns with Christ—in angels and righteous human beings, partly in body and partly in soul—there is no doubt that it is above, in heavenly blessedness. But concerning the part that is still a pilgrim on earth, we must ask how it is above. It is said to be above because, although it dwells bodily on earth, it dwells in heaven in mind, saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). It continually performs heavenly works, that is, those by which it can attain the heavenly kingdom.

It is also rightly called our mother, because the apostles, martyrs, and holy preachers who went before us begot us in the faith of Christ through their teaching, writings, and examples. Concerning this generation the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (I Cor. IV).

For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear,” and so forth. This testimony is found in Isaiah, the most renowned of the prophets. It can be understood in two ways.

He speaks, then, to the Church from the Gentiles, which for a long and extended time remained barren of good works and did not beget children for God—that is, from the destruction of the tower of Babel, which is now Babylon, until the coming of the Lord. For there the speech of the whole earth was divided, and knowledge of God remained only in the house of the Hebrews.

Let it therefore be said: “Rejoice”—that is, “be glad and exult”—O Church from the Gentiles, who formerly were barren and did not bear children for God. Break forth into joy and cry out with exceeding gladness, you who did not bear, because you will have more children acceptable to God than the synagogue, which once had almighty God as its true protector, or which now boasts and thinks that it has the true God, although it lost him after saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX).

Let us also speak more deeply according to blessed Augustine, referring these words to the Church that already reigns with Christ in heaven. It is called barren not with respect to good works and praise of its Creator, but with respect to carnal propagation. For because of sin death came, and death is nothing other than the dissolution of the elements; and because of death the succession of children came.

In the present life, children of the flesh must necessarily be procreated to succeed their fathers, once their fathers have died or are about to die, in the inheritance. But in that blessedness where no one dies, there is no need for a succession of children through the propagation of the flesh. Therefore it is called barren, and the prophetic voice addresses it in rejoicing: “Rejoice, O Church, barren with respect to carnal procreation, who do not bear fleshly children with pain and great anguish, because more children of the Gentiles who were once forsaken will come to you than from the synagogue, which formerly had almighty God as its husband, or which now boasts that it has him.”

It is evident to all that more people from the Gentiles pass into eternal glory than from the Jews. Similarly, in the present Church there are more faithful children from the Gentiles than from the synagogue. For throughout nearly all cities and regions, and even villages and hamlets, the Gentiles proclaim that they believe in Christ; among the Jews, however, scarcely anyone—or no one—is found who confesses belief in Christ.

But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac. The Apostle joins himself to the believing Galatians and says: “But we, brothers”—that is, I and you—“are children of the promise according to Isaac.” This means: just as we who believe in Christ are sons of Abraham, since the Lord said to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII), and just as Isaac was born according to the promise, so we are children of the promise.

But how then could he who had been born according to the flesh, etc.? The Apostle addresses the Galatians, urging them to guard themselves against the Jews lest they be led astray by them: “O Galatians, beware of and withdraw from the Jews. For just as Ishmael, who had been born according to the practice of human custom, in the manner we explained above, was then persecuting Isaac, who had been given to Abraham according to the spiritual promise, so now also the Jewish people—represented by Ishmael, born of the slave woman—persecutes the Christian people and the others represented by Isaac, born of the free woman, in order to bend them toward subjection to the law.” [Col. 0690B]

The Jews offer various explanations concerning the game of the boys Ishmael and Isaac. Some say that Ishmael wanted, in a certain kind of game, to challenge him to leap, holding a staff in his hand, with the intention of weakening him so that he would become unworthy of the honor of the firstborn and of his father’s inheritance. Others say that he wanted to persuade him to join in certain shameful acts, so that he would become notorious and despised by his father and mother and, as we have said, be made unworthy of the honor of the firstborn. For he knew that he could in no way attain his father’s inheritance and the dignity of the firstborn, since he was born of a slave woman, even though he was the firstborn, unless they made him so blameworthy either in body or in the frivolity of his mind that he would be regarded as worthless by his father and mother. But whatever the matter may have been, it is plainly evident [Col. 0690C] that the game was not an innocent one; for this reason the mother became indignant and ordered that the slave woman together with her son be expelled from the house and from the company of the freeborn son.

The blessed Apostle also, who had been taught at the feet of Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, and who had understood all the knowledge of the law and the prophets that could then be penetrated, knew likewise that the game was not an innocent one; he called it persecution. For Ishmael wanted to make Isaac frivolous and scurrilous, deprive him of his dignity, and exalt himself.

But what does Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son.” As far as the literal meaning is concerned, because of the cause we have mentioned, the mother ordered her to be expelled. As far as the spiritual understanding is concerned, so long as the Jews wish to remain sons of the slave woman and to persecute the son of the free woman—that is, so long as they wish to remain subject to the law in circumcision and the legal sacrifices, refusing to believe that they can be saved through the passion of Christ—and so long as they wish to persecute us, who have already been made free, they are to be driven away from the inheritance of the Church. For the son of the slave woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman. This means that the son of sin and evil desire, which may be understood through the slave woman, and the carnal son of the law, who strives to observe the law carnally, will not be heir in the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland with the free sons, who are made free in baptism—not only from original sins but also from every servitude to the law.

Therefore, brothers, we are not sons of the slave woman but of the free woman. That is, we are no longer sons of the law, which makes its observers slaves, but sons of the new grace and sons of the Gospel [Col. 0691A] through baptism and through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which we received both in baptism and through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, and through participation in the body and blood of the Lord, in which we share. We are free with that freedom by which Christ freed us through his passion and through the grace of baptism.

Everyone who has the faith of Abraham and proves to be an imitator of Abraham’s works is certainly a son of Abraham—not by nature but by imitation—as the Apostle says elsewhere: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Galatians 3). But whoever does not adorn the faith he possesses with good works will certainly not be counted among the sons of Abraham, nor will he receive the heavenly inheritance with them. Therefore, we must all labor so that we may strive to adorn the faith we possess by the performance [Col. 0691B] of good works, having become true imitators of him.

## CHAPTER V

“But I say in Christ: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” Concerning this reading, different teachers do not hold the same opinion. Some say that the Apostle is speaking here of the human spirit, as Cassian, a most prudent man, does in the *Conferences of the Fathers*; others say that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit, as the blessed Augustine does. Both interpretations can be accepted without impropriety and without contradicting the soundness of the faith.

Let us therefore speak according to Cassian: “Walk by the Spirit,” that is, live with the Spirit as your guide. What, then, is the human spirit? It is the ruling faculty of the soul, which is also called the rationality of the mind, through which we are able [Col. 0691C] to know what we ought to desire and what we ought to avoid. “If,” he says, “you live by the spirit”—that is, if you live according to the rational faculty and understanding of the mind—“you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” that is, the desires of the carnal person, evil concupiscence, and the desires of perverse pleasure. What the desires of the flesh are will be made clear below.

Let us also speak in another way, following the understanding of the blessed Augustine. It is known among the learned that the sacred Scriptures were written under the dictation and revelation of the Holy Spirit, who is of one substance with the Father and the Son, and that all the divine words and commandments contained in the law, the prophets, and the grace of the Gospel were given by him. For this reason the Apostle says: “Walk by the Spirit,” that is, live and conduct yourselves as the Holy Spirit teaches and commands in the divine Scriptures, walking and advancing from virtue to virtue, from faith to hope, from hope to charity, and from charity to perfect action. If you do this, you will not fulfill the desires of carnal concupiscence. What does the Apostle say?

“Flesh desires against the Spirit, but the Spirit against the flesh.” Can the flesh desire anything if the spirit is absent? No. This can be proved from dead bodies. After they have breathed out their spirit, they are not only unable to desire anything but also cannot move any of their members by themselves. He therefore calls the person “flesh”—the person who seeks only carnal and bodily things, as well as carnal habit and pleasure. Although the flesh is unable by itself to accomplish anything if the spirit is absent, nevertheless, so long as it is given life by the spirit, it always appears to be opposed to the spirit, that is, to the rationality of the mind. Therefore the Apostle says: “The flesh desires,” and so forth.

Let us hear how the flesh desires against the spirit. The flesh always desires to be filled with food, to become drunk, to indulge in lust, and to remain in every pleasure, always seeking what belongs to it. Behold how the flesh desires against the spirit. Conversely, the spirit desires against the flesh because it delights in fasting, abstinence, chastity, and those things opposed to the flesh. The spirit must always be followed, because it seeks that by which the soul lives for God.

We can speak similarly of the Holy Spirit. When carnal pleasure desires to transgress God’s commandments, it desires against the Holy Spirit; and when the Holy Spirit forbids in the law, the prophets, and the Gospel what the flesh desires, he desires against the flesh. Hence the Apostle adds: “These,” he says—that is, the flesh and the spirit—“are opposed to one another,” and so forth. The flesh and the spirit are so mutually contrary that what the flesh wants, the spirit does not consent to, and what the spirit wants, the flesh does not consent to, because the flesh delights in serving vices, while the spirit delights in serving virtues.

“But if you are led by the Spirit”—that is, if you live and conduct yourselves rationally—“you are not subject to the law,” and the law is not necessary for you, because the law was not established for the just but for the impious and sinners. Alternatively: “If you are led by the Spirit,” that is, if you are governed by the Holy Spirit and live according to what the Holy Spirit teaches in the holy Scriptures, “you are not subject to the law”; rather, you are alien to it [Col. 0692C] and owe it nothing.

Now the works of the flesh are manifest, and they are as follows. To all who believe in Christ, and especially to those who pursue a spiritual life, they are so well known that they even make themselves strangers to them, knowing that they produce death.

“Fornication” is called *fornicatio* from *fornices*, that is, from the theatrical places and brothels constructed with *fornices*, or arches. Although these places were then also called arenas, prostitutes were present there, and the most depraved men had intercourse with them. To commit fornication is to have intercourse with unmarried girls or with widows not yet consecrated to God. “Uncleanness,” “immodesty,” and “lust” may be called by these names in whatever form they occur. Lust, however, is a harmful excess of bodily fluid.

“Service of idols” is idolatry, which at that time existed among almost all peoples. We may also understand avarice in a higher sense through the phrase “service of idols.” Thus, in the Epistle to the Colossians, “sorceries” are evil practices—that is, magical arts—by which wretched people are often compelled to love and be loved. They are called *veneficia*, as though infected with poison.

“Hostilities” are evil intentions. “Contentions” often arise from pride, because people wish to dispute about questions of divine and even human Scripture, so that, when they emerge as victors, they may be glorified. “Jealous rivalry” is envy, concerning which it is written that Joseph’s brothers, envying him, sold him. “Anger” is a great disturbance of the mind. There is this difference between an angry person and an irascible person: an angry person is angry for a time, [Col. 0693A] whereas an irascible person becomes angry easily and is always inclined to anger.

“Quarrels” are disputes and contentions that often arise without cause. “Dissension” is discord, which commonly arises between husband and wife, and also between brothers, housemates, or fellow soldiers. “Sects” are divisions. Heresies are the same thing. They are called sects either from *secare*, “to cut,” that is, “to divide,” because they divide themselves from the communion of others, as heretics did when they separated themselves from the unity of the Church—of whom John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2)—or they are called sects from “following,” just as heresies are named from “choosing” or “clinging,” because from many errors they choose one and follow it.

“Envy.” Envy is divided into two forms of passion: either someone who is in a position of honor, seeing another striving attentively, envies him lest he should attain the same honor; or someone is tormented by another’s happiness, seeing that person superior to himself.

“Drunkenness.” In the masculine gender we say *briam* for a cup suitable for drinking wine. “Revelry” is called a contribution to the table or an alternation of the table. There are banquets that are held by turns and prepared by companions on successive days and in rotation; there are others that are prepared by contributions, when one person brings bread, another wine, and another something else. They are therefore called *comessationes*, that is, contributions to the table, because just as everyone uses his own and common foods, so each person, according to his own inclination, speaks whatever scurrility and idleness pleases him. For this reason they are called shameful banquets. [Col. 0693C]

“And things like these”—that is, sins understood—“are works of the flesh, which I warn you about now, just as I warned you before.” Where did he warn them before? “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6), because those who do such things—that is, who perform such works—“will not obtain the kingdom of God.” He did not say, “Those who have done such things,” but “those who do such things,” that is, those who remain in such things until the day of their death will not possess eternal life. Thus the Lord will also say on the day of judgment to the rejected: “Depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matthew 7)—not, “you who have worked iniquity,” but “you who have ended your life in sins.”

“But the fruit of the Spirit is charity.” *Charitas* is Greek and is translated in Latin as *dilectio*, “love.” It is called *dilectio* because it binds two together: God and the human being, or two neighbors. It rightly holds first place among the virtues, because it binds the other virtues together. Charity is the love and affection by which God, one’s neighbor, and even one’s enemy are loved for God’s sake.

“Joy” is gladness of heart. There is this difference between joy and happiness: joy is an excessive exultation of heart and body, whereas happiness is moderate and takes place only in the heart.

“Peace” is rest and tranquility, or gentleness, of mind. Solomon received his name from this, namely “peacemaker,” because in his days rest was given.

“Long-suffering” is perseverance in good work and endurance amid adversity. Every believer ought to be long-suffering in order to attain the promised reward, according to what the Lord says: “Whoever perseveres to the end,” and so forth. [Col. 0694A]

“Goodness” is a good will. “Kindness” is a most ready will, tempered by good character and gentle speech. It invites not only those who are well disposed to be loved but even those who appeared to be opposed. Hence someone is called *benignus*, as though “very and exceedingly good.”

“Faith” is that by which we believe that almighty God has a Trinity in persons and unity in substance, and by which we hope for and believe in those things that we do not yet see. In the things we see there is neither faith nor hope, but only in those that have not yet been seen by us. For example, we believe that the Lord Jesus suffered, rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven, and that he will come to judgment to render to each person according to what he deserves. Faith is also the belief by which we hope for things that we do not see with the eyes of the body.

“Moderation” is gentleness and mildness of mind, which, when injured, is not easily angered.

“Self-control” is abstinence by which a man restrains himself from intercourse, and by which a widow likewise abstains from every enticement. “Chastity,” properly speaking, belongs to virgins; hence *castitas* is said to be derived from “castrated.” There is this difference between self-control and chastity: self-control can belong to married people, widows and widowers, and virgins, whereas chastity properly belongs to virgins.

“Against such things there is no law.” That is, for people of this kind, who perform such deeds, the law is neither opposed nor necessary, for they are alien to it. Why is the law not necessary or opposed to them? It says: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill.” They not only do not do these things but also preserve chastity [Col. 0694C] and guard themselves not only from murder but even love their enemies.

“Those who belong to Christ”—that is, those who belong to Christ’s portion—“have crucified the flesh with its vices and evil desires.” For as many sins as we drive out from ourselves, so many vices do we continually kill within ourselves. We crucify and mortify the flesh when we do not consent to perverse pleasure and a crooked will.

## CHAPTER VI

“If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.” Here he is speaking of the Holy Spirit: “If,” he says, “we live by the Spirit”—that is, if through the Holy Spirit we have the life by which we live for God—we ought to conduct ourselves and live spiritually, walking from virtue to virtue, pursuing virtues and rejecting vices.

The life of the soul is faith, by which we believe in almighty God. Just as the body lives by the soul, so the soul lives by faith, according to what the Lord says through the prophet: “But my righteous one lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2). “But if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased.” This faith is bestowed upon us through the Holy Spirit, who is of one substance with God the Father and the Son. The Spirit gives us not faith alone; whatever good we possess is also administered to us by him.

“Let us not become desirous of empty glory.” What is empty glory? Human praise and earthly favor, concerning which Christ says: “If I seek glory from human beings, my glory is nothing” (John 8). It is rightly called empty glory because it is devoid of every useful benefit.

There is nevertheless a useful glory, concerning which the Lord says: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify” (1 Samuel 2). Who, then, are desirous of empty and earthly glory? Those who, through what they do, do not seek to please God or to receive from him the reward of eternal recompense, but seek temporal glory and praise. Of such people the Lord says: “They do all their works so that they may be glorified by human beings” (Matthew 23).

Such people will hear on the day of judgment: “You have received your reward” (Matthew 6). For many seek to be praised not only for what is good but also for what is evil; and not only do they seek praise from others, they even exalt themselves and glory in their virtues.

True and complete glory is for a person, in his heart, to desire to please almighty God for the good he does, to expect his reward from him, and to rejoice in his heart that he pleases his Creator. He should act so that the good work he performs is public, while his intention remains hidden. Whoever does this is not desirous of empty glory.

“Provoking one another to anger, to quarrels, to contentions, envying one another.” Some of the Galatians had been led astray by false apostles and by Jews, disputing about genealogies and questions of the law. Some of them said: “Circumcision is better than baptism.” Others, conversely, said: “Baptism is better than circumcision.” Still others said: “Allegory is better than history, because allegory—that is, spiritual understanding—gives life, whereas the letter kills.” Conversely, others said: “History, in which the truth is contained, is better than vain and shadowy allegory.”

[Col. 0695C] “Brothers, and if a person is overtaken in any offense.” To overtake is to come beforehand; hence it is sung in the psalm: “Let us come before his face in confession” (Psalm 94), that is, let us precede him in confessing our sins.

A person is therefore overtaken in sin when he sins suddenly and unexpectedly, without having previously premeditated it. But when he premeditates how he will commit murder, adultery, or something of that kind, it is not being overtaken but premeditation and perpetration of a crime. The one who sins unexpectedly, without having previously premeditated it—that is, who is overtaken by sin—must be reproved differently from the one who has long premeditated it. The former should be corrected with gentleness of mind lest he fall into despair; the latter requires sharper correction.

He rightly added “person,” because the human being is frail and transitory, quick to slip into guilt, especially one who possesses simplicity without cunning. “You who are spiritual,” who lead a spiritual life and are concerned with faith and teaching, should instruct and correct those who are overtaken and are more simple-minded with gentle affection and sweetness of mind, promising them forgiveness, lest they perhaps fall into the collapse of despair.

“Considering yourself,” because you are a human being of fragile nature, just as he is; therefore you can also be tempted and overtaken by sin as he was. When you consider that you can be tempted and fall into sin, then, just as you would wish to be corrected and chastised with gentleness of mind if you were doing such things, so correct and admonish him.

“Bear one another’s burdens.” There are burdens of a certain weight, and there are burdens of sins, concerning which the Psalmist says: “My iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden” (Psalm 37), and so forth. This is the burden referred to here, and the meaning is: If you wish to be patiently carried and supported when you sin, and to be corrected with moderation, then likewise patiently carry your brother if he has sinned.

This can also be understood in another way, according to the meaning of the blessed Jerome: “Bear one another’s burdens,” that is, you who abound in riches and temporal goods, support your poor brother. For example: I have a very poor sister whose poverty is my burden; by providing her with food and shoes, I support her burden. I have a wife because I cannot be continent, but I am oppressed by extreme poverty. You who, by God’s gift, are continent and abound in temporal goods, bear my burden.

Consider the comparison of the stags in the Epistle to the Colossians, which the blessed Augustine gives from this passage. If this occurs even among animals that do not possess reason, how much more ought it to occur among human beings? “If,” he says, “you do this, you will fulfill the law of Christ,” that is, Christ’s pact, which he gave to his disciples when he said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15); and: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13).

For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing—that is, if, trusting in his virtues and merits, he disdains to bear his brother’s burden by correcting him with gentleness and sweet admonition—although he himself is nothing before God, and although his works do not please God, he deceives and misleads himself.

He is said to be nothing because he does not cling to the one who substantially possesses being, and who, having compassion on our frailty, deigned to humble himself for us although he was God. Every creature that does not cling to the one who always possesses being is nothing.

“But let each person test his own work,” that is, let him consider what good he has done, and let him rejoice in his heart because he pleases his Creator, without seeking another’s praise.

“For each person will bear his own burden.” These words seem contrary to those above, where he said: “Bear one another’s burdens.” But we should understand that the former refer to the time of the present life, whereas these refer to the day of death, or generally to the day of judgment. The meaning is: Whatever each person has done, he will receive accordingly. If he has done good, he will receive good; if evil, he will receive eternal condemnation.

It should also be noted that “burden” can be understood here in both a good and a bad sense, since it applies to the elect and the rejected. The burden of the saints will be the greatness of glory; the burden of the rejected will be ineffable misery and torment.

“But let the one who is catechized in the word of God share with the one who catechizes him in all good things.” That is, the disciple, or any hearer who is instructed and taught by the word of doctrine, should share with or provide for the teacher or preacher who instructs and teaches him in all good things.

He admonishes hearers and disciples to strive to provide temporal goods for their teachers, from whom they receive the word of life and faith—that is, food and clothing—because “the laborer is worthy of his wage,” and because the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.

By “word” we can also understand the fruit of devotion and the substance of good work and study, as in the passage concerning Moses: “How did this word become publicly known?” (Exodus 2). We may refer this to the disciple: “Let him share,” that is, let the disciple, or the one being catechized, make himself pleasing to the teacher who instructs him, through zeal and the fruit of devotion, and let him be teachable and obedient in all good things that do not displease God.

One of the disciples might say: “I have nothing with which to provide for my teacher, because my field—that is, my grain—has withered from drought; my vineyard has been destroyed by hail; my sheep have been struck by disease; my pigs, swollen with fattening, have died.” But so that the Apostle might remove every excuse, he said:

“Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.” This means: Do not lie, because a human being can accept a lie, but God cannot; and God, who penetrates all the secrets of hearts, cannot be deceived.

You say, whoever you are among the hearers: “I could not provide expenses for my teacher because extreme poverty presses upon me.” Do not deceive yourself as though you could deceive God. From the source by which you live, support your teacher also. If you do not have crops from the present year, you have some from the previous year; you can also borrow from your neighbors against the future.

“For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.” This means that whatever he has done, he will receive accordingly.

We have two fields: the body and the spirit. If we have sown in the flesh—that is, if we have performed carnal works and followed carnal desires—we shall reap corruption from that same flesh. That is, we shall receive condemnation and, on the day of judgment, be handed over to the punishments of hell, where we shall be tormented by worms and everlasting fire.

But if we have sown in the spirit—that is, if we have fulfilled spiritual works and obeyed the commands of the Holy Spirit—we shall receive eternal life from the spirit, through spiritual works and through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

“Let us not grow weary in doing good.” That is, let us not cease from the good work we have begun, but persevere in it so that we may obtain the salvation that the Lord promised, saying: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24).

“In its own time,” that is, at the suitable and appropriate time, “we shall reap,” meaning that we shall receive the reward of our labor, without failing to obtain the reward of our work. Now is the time for sowing, that is, for doing good; on the day of judgment or on the day of death there will be the time of reaping and gathering.

That harvest will never fail, because that life remains without end, and as the years pass it is forever renewed and flourishes.

“Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all.” The present life is the time for sowing and practicing virtues, because after this life there will be no time or opportunity for repentance and salvation. Concerning this time the Apostle says elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6).

In this time we ought to do good to all human beings—to brothers, heretics, and pagans—both in the duty of almsgiving [Col. 0698A] and in the teaching of the word. Mercy must be shown to all people, and we must imitate our Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil (Matthew 5).

Above all, however, we ought to do good to the household of faith. Members of a household are called *domestici* from *domus*, “house,” because they are nourished and live together in one house. We ought indeed to do good to all—to heretics and pagans—but especially to those who are with us in one house, that is, in the unity of the Church, who share the same faith, and above all to those who show us the path of righteousness by word and example.

“See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.” At the end of all his epistles the Apostle wrote his name in Hebrew letters, lest his words be corrupted by the false apostles. In this epistle, however, as the teachers relate, he wrote from this point to the end with his own hand, so that he might draw them more fully to the faith of Christ when they saw his love for them.

“For all who wish to please in the flesh, they compel you to be circumcised.” That is, those who wish to please in carnal circumcision their scribes and Pharisees, their ministers, compelled the Gentiles to be circumcised, and this so that they might not suffer persecution because of the cross of Christ.

For Octavianus, Gaius, and other emperors had decreed that wherever Jews were found, they might use their own laws. The Jews who wished to hold both the law and the Gospel therefore circumcised themselves so that they would not be persecuted on account of Christ’s name, saying that they were Jews, circumcised, and keepers of the law. But they did not keep it, because they were murderers, adulterers, envious, greedy, and full of other vices. [Col. 0698C]

“That they may glory in your flesh.” The Jews gloried, saying: “Yesterday I compelled so many Gentiles to circumcision; today, so many.”

“But far be it from me to glory.” I do not wish to glory in the riches and dignities of this world, but in the cross of Christ—that is, in his passion, which was accomplished on the cross. In it I shall glory, because from it comes my redemption and salvation.

Or: “I shall glory in the cross of Christ,” that is, I shall glory if I am able to imitate Christ’s passion, so that whatever he endured for me, I may endure for his name.

“Through whom”—with “cross” or “Christ” understood. The blessed Jerome says that *cross* is masculine in Greek, and that the translator of this Epistle transferred into Latin the same article and gender that he found in Greek. The phrase may also be referred to Christ, or understood as meaning “for love of his passion.”

“The world is dead to me, and I to the world,” because I neither seek nor love the things that are in the world, and the world—that is, the lover of this world—neither seeks nor loves me. For example, it is like two dead people, neither of whom touches or loves the other.

“In Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any force,” that is, whether someone is circumcised or uncircumcised neither benefits nor harms him in the faith of Christ, provided that through circumcision he does not believe that he can be saved. If he believes this, then it harms him.

“Upon the Israel of God”: not upon carnal Israel, but upon all the nations who are true Israelites, who see God with the mind.

“Let no one trouble me,” that is, let no one raise questions with me about circumcision and the legal sacrifices, because I have often discussed all these matters with you.

“For I bear the marks of Jesus in my body.” The marks are signs of servile punishments, with which fugitive slaves, when captured by their masters, are usually bound. The blessed Apostle also bore the marks or signs that he had endured for Christ, because the wounds from rods and lacerations were still visible on his body, and because he had been bound in chains and dragged through the streets, and so forth.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 0699A]

## INTRODUCTION

[Col. 0699B] Ephesus is a city of Asia and Greece, whose inhabitants are called Ephesians, after the name of the city in which they live. Having received the word of truth from the Apostle, they persevered in the faith and did not accept false apostles, as the Galatians and others did.

When the Apostle therefore came to them, he remained with them for one year and six months, diligently preaching the word of the Gospel and strengthening those who believed in the faith. Magicians and philosophers, Jews and Gentiles, were also mingled together in the same city. Against them the Apostle fought manfully for the truth of the Gospel, as though against beasts, as he says elsewhere: “If I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead are not raised?” (1 Corinthians 15).

He called them beasts because of their savagery and beastly character. Ephesus is interpreted as “will in it”; and where the anger of almighty God had once rested because of idolatry and magical practices, there, through the Apostle’s preaching, the will of almighty God came to rest.

It should also be known that he sent this Epistle to them from Rome, while placed in prison, through Tychicus the deacon. It is more difficult than almost all the other Epistles, because, just as the heart lies in the middle of the belly, so this Epistle stands in the middle of the body of the Epistles.

## CHAPTER I

“Paul.” Many ask why the Apostle, who was previously called Saul before he came to the faith, was afterward called Paul. The authority of the Fathers differs concerning this question.

The blessed Jerome says that he was called Paul from the first spoil that he took from the devil and brought to the Church, namely Paul Sergius, a prudent man whom he won for Christ.

The blessed Jerome also says that he called himself Paul for the sake of humility, as though “small.” For *paulum* or *paululum* means “a little,” as appears in Virgil concerning Achaemenides fleeing from Polyphemus:

“Then, terrified by the sight, he halted some distance away.” For *paulum* he used *paululum*. So too the Apostle himself says elsewhere: “To me, the very least of all, grace was given” (Ephesians 3), and: “I am the least of the Apostles” (1 Corinthians 15).

Some also say that he had two names, like Claudius; but this is not supported by the authority of the Fathers. He placed his own name in all his Epistles for the sake of authority, except in the Epistle to the Hebrews, just as kings customarily do in this manner: “The Emperor Nero sends greetings to his Seneca.”

**Apostle.** This is a Greek name, although some say it is Hebrew, and it means “sent.” And rightly does he call himself an apostle, because he was sent by the Lord, who said to him: “Behold, I will send you far away to the regions and nations” (Acts 22). He also used the title “apostleship” to indicate dignity, so that his Epistles might have greater authority among their hearers.

There are four kinds of apostles. The first is that which is neither from human beings nor through a human being, but from God alone. Moses and Isaiah, and very many other prophets and apostles, belonged to this number. Although they were sent by the human Christ, he was himself both human and true God. Moses was told: “I will send you to Pharaoh” (Exodus 3); and Isaiah was asked: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6). He replied: “Here am I; send me.” And the Lord said: “Go to this people” (Exodus 19).

The second kind is from God, but through a human being. Joshua belonged to this number: at God’s command, he was sent through Moses. Many others also belonged to it—men who, by the will of God, were chosen for the merits of their lives through the votes of the people, because the will of the people is sometimes the will of God.

The third kind is from a human being alone and not from God. This occurs when someone is chosen with the favor of human beings—not for good conduct or on account of religion, but appointed to the dignity of the priesthood in exchange for money. To one of this number blessed Ambrose said: “O bishop, truly, unless you had given a hundred solidi, you would not be a bishop today.” Those of whom it is said in the Book of Kings that, in the time of Jeroboam, “they filled their hands” and became priests of idols (1 Kings 13) also belonged to this number.

The fourth kind is made neither by God nor through a human being, but by the person himself. Such are the false prophets and false apostles who say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord has not sent them.

It should also be known that among all these there are some of such great dignity that they are both prophets and apostles, such as Moses, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and John the Baptist, of whom it is said: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mark 1). Among these were the apostles, who foretold to their hearers the rewards of the elect and the evils of the reprobate. Others, however, perform only the office of prophets.

**Of Jesus Christ.** Jesus is the name of the human being assumed by the Word, just as the angel said to Mary: “His name shall be called Jesus” (Luke 2). Christ, however, is the name of dignity. He is called Christ from *chrism*, that is, from anointing. For just as among the Romans the diadem and purple make kings, so in ancient times among the Jews the anointing of chrism made kings and priests. Through that visible anointing they were deemed worthy to receive the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit—for example, just as believers now receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit in baptism.

Christ, however, was not anointed with visible oil, but was filled with the fullness of the Holy Spirit. Of him the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 44).

Paul, therefore, is an apostle of Jesus Christ, because he was chosen by him and sent by him, through the will of God—that is, of the Father. He says “through the will of God the Father” because the will of the Father and of the Son is one.

The entire salutation of these Epistles may also be punctuated with an intermediate distinction at the point where he says “in Christ Jesus,” as some simple-minded people say, with “Grace to you” then following. But it is better and more appropriate to place a complete distinction there, understanding an omitted word of greeting—“salvation”—and then beginning another verse: “Grace to you and peace.” For when he says “to all the saints who are in Ephesus,” he wishes them salvation; this is in the third person, as every salutation requires. But when he adds “Grace to you,” he has already turned to the second person, to whom the subsequent language of the greeting properly applies.
