Why does he say “with all the saints and faithful”? Because not all faithful people are saints. Catechumens are faithful, since they believe in the true God; but because they have not yet been baptized, they are not saints. He therefore added “in Christ Jesus,” because there are many who are faithful but not in Christ Jesus. Thus there are slaves who are not faithful to their masters in order to find the grace of Jesus Christ, but only the favor of their masters, since they fear being beaten by them.

To these, then, the Apostle wishes the salvation by which they have been sanctified in baptism and are faithful in Christ Jesus—that is, they possess faith in Jesus Christ—and they adorn the faith they possess with good works.

**Grace to you**, with *let it be understood* “may it be,” that is, faith, salvation, and the remission of sins, which has been freely given to you in baptism; **and peace**, by which we have been reconciled to God through the passion of his Son, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Some wish to interpret the passage in this way: “Grace to you from God the Father,” who freely sent us his Son, “and peace from the Lord Jesus Christ,” through whose passion we have been reconciled to God and the angels. But we may refer both expressions to both persons and say: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father, and grace and peace from the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Some nevertheless think that the Apostle has omitted the person of the Holy Spirit. But to those who examine the matter carefully it will be clear that he has nonetheless mentioned the whole Trinity. For in saying “Grace to you” he includes the person of the Holy Spirit, since we received grace—that is, the remission of all sins—through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Alternatively, wherever one person of the Trinity is named, the whole Trinity is understood, because just as the substance of the Godhead is inseparable, so the power of its operation is inseparable.

**Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.** This may be understood in two ways. “Blessed,” he says, is God, the Creator of all things, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and who begot him before all ages in the nature of divinity.

Alternatively, “Blessed” is God the Son, who was the Word in the beginning and who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, of the human being assumed by him. For the human being assumed by the Word was formed in the virgin’s womb through the operation of the whole Trinity.

It should also be noted that the Apostle begins with praises and blessings, as the holy Fathers were accustomed to do; and he blessed God, from whom all things that deserve to be blessed receive their blessing.

**Who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.** When he said “with every blessing,” why was it necessary to add “spiritual,” or “in the heavenly places,” or “in Christ”? Because there is a temporal blessing, which is not heavenly or in Christ, and there is an earthly blessing.

A temporal blessing is a multitude of sons, servants, and maidservants. An earthly blessing is an abundance of riches and crops. This blessing even extends to animals, as we read in Genesis, where God blessed every creature, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1).

A spiritual and eternal blessing, however, consists in faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues. “In the heavenly places” is added as though to say “from heavenly things,” because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1). He also added “in Christ,” as though meaning “through Christ,” because whatever good we have, we have not through our own merits but through him and from him.

A question arises: why did he say “with every spiritual blessing,” since no human being can possess all blessings in the present age—that is, all the virtues or all the gifts of the Holy Spirit—until what the same Apostle says elsewhere is fulfilled: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father, then God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15)? In the present age the gifts of the Holy Spirit are distributed individually; nevertheless, not all are given to each person. “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge,” and so forth, until he adds: “All these things are accomplished by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

This question is answered in three ways. First, because whatever each person possesses inwardly, he possesses within the totality, since brotherly charity makes this so. For example, one has charity, another chastity, another abstinence, another gentleness, and another wisdom. Second, because in every blessing we possess, we are blessed by him. Third, the past tense may stand for the future, so that the meaning is: “He will bless us, after the general resurrection, with every spiritual blessing.”

**As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love.** This depends on what came before. “Thus,” he says, “he blessed us as he chose”—that is, predestined and foreordained—“in him,” that is, in Christ.

Therefore, before every creature, spiritual and bodily, the almighty Father predestined all believers in Christ, so that he might be the head of all who believe in him, and all believers might be his members. He did this so that we might be holy and blameless before God the Father in the charity and love by which God and our neighbor are loved—or also in that charity by which he himself loved us, in which he predestined us.

He loved us so greatly that he gave his only-begotten Son for us, as John also says: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world” (John 3).

There is this difference between “blameless” and “holy”: a child, or any human being, is blameless when he is cleansed from all stains of sin in baptism; but he becomes holy through labor and discipline, when he delivers his body to various torments for the name of Christ, as the holy martyrs did, or when he puts to death vices and desires along with the passions of the flesh.

Alternatively, he chose us so that we might be holy and blameless, although we were not yet so. When he said “as he chose us,” he meant “he foreordained us by his disposition,” because it was to come about that we would believe in Christ. He “predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the purpose of his will.”

To predestine is to foreordain and determine in advance: when we decide far beforehand in our heart what we are going to do, and when and how we will accomplish it in action. Adoption—or *option*—means election. Hence we say *optimum*, that is, “chosen.”

Thus God the Father determined beforehand and established in his will and disposition that we should be received as his sons by adoption through Jesus Christ—that is, that by believing in Jesus Christ we should become sons of God through grace, although we were not so by nature.

**According to the purpose of his will**, that is, according to what he arranged in his will; **for the praise of the glory of his grace**, in which he favored us in the love of his Son.

He speaks of glory and grace as belonging to God. Glory is to be referred to our redemption, by which he redeemed us; grace to the remission of sins, which he freely gave us in baptism through faith in his passion and through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Thus he chose us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for the praise of his glory and grace, so that he might be praised and favored by every rational creature. In that grace, with *let it be understood* “in that grace,” he favored us—that is, he freely redeemed us and gave us the remission of sins. In this way he afterward made us grateful and acceptable to himself, and this through the passion of his beloved Son.

Blessed Jerome says that in the Greek text the words “of his Son” are not present, but only the absolute expression “beloved,” so that he might show that he is beloved by every rational creature. Thus one says *gratificare*—“to favor”—from *gratia*, “grace,” just as one says *justificare*—“to justify”—from *justitia*, “justice.”

**In whom**, that is, in Christ, or **through Christ**, we have all redemption or liberation from death to life through the blood of his passion, and the remission of sins in baptism through faith in his passion, as John says: “He loved us,” he says, “and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation 1)—that is, through his passion and through faith.

**According to the riches of his grace**, with *let it be understood* “we have redemption and the remission of sins.” That grace, with *let it be understood* “the grace,” overflowed—that is, increased abundantly—in us with all wisdom and prudence.

The riches of his grace are mercy and compassion. They increased in us to such an extent that he not only redeemed us and gave us the remission of sins through the Holy Spirit, but also revealed to us the mysteries of his knowledge contained in the New and Old Testaments: all wisdom concerning divine and human, visible and invisible things, and all prudence concerning visible, mortal, and transitory things.

For wisdom is, as some say, knowledge of divine and human things, visible and invisible, mortal and immortal. Prudence, however, concerns visible, human, and transitory things.

Alternatively, wisdom is knowledge of the Holy Trinity; prudence is knowledge of visible things and of the elements, so that a person may know that the world was made by God when it pleased him and in the manner that seemed good to him. He may also know, insofar as human frailty permits, the course of the stars, the order of times, how these things were made, and toward what end they are directed.

**To make known to us the mystery of his will**, God the Father did this **according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him**, that is, in Christ.

A mystery is a secret matter, that is, something hidden. What was this mystery that God the Father revealed to us? It was the mystery of Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection, and of our redemption.

For the will of God the Father was what he purposed—or arranged or decreed—to accomplish in Christ or through Christ: that we should be redeemed through the coming of his Son. God the Father therefore revealed these mysteries of his will to us through the incarnation of his Son, according to what pleased him and according to what he himself decreed in him.

He also revealed when this took place, saying: **in the dispensation**, that is, in the arrangement or ordering of the fullness of times, God the Father himself determined **to restore all things in Christ**, or through Christ.

Blessed Jerome says that because of the excessive love with which the Apostle loved Christ, he often mentioned his name in an unusual position, just as the Apostle himself says of himself: “I was unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge” (2 Corinthians 11).

To restore is to bring back to its former condition something that had fallen. God the Father therefore restored through his Son all things that are in heaven and on earth when he repaired the angelic and human natures.

He repaired the things in heaven when he completed the number of angels, which had once been diminished by the fall of an angel, through the restoration of the human race; and he restored to them the joy that they had lost when human beings sinned.

He repaired the things on earth when he redeemed the human race, which had fallen into death through sin, and brought it back from death to life through his passion.

Alternatively, by heaven we may understand the Jews, who had received heavenly commandments; and by earth, the Gentiles, who thought about and sought only earthly things and worshiped idols instead of God.

God the Father therefore restored through the passion of his Son all things that are in heaven and on earth, when he completed through the multitude of Gentiles coming to faith what had perished among the Jews who remained in unbelief. He did this in the dispensation of the fullness of times—that is, in the sixth age of the world—which God himself had decreed and established.

Concerning this fullness of times the same Apostle says elsewhere: “When the fullness of time had come”—that is, the sixth age—“God sent his Son” (Galatians 4). Here he says “times” in the plural, while elsewhere he says “time” in the singular; but the time is one and the same.

**In whom**, that is, in Christ or through Christ, **we have been called by lot or by election**, with *let it be understood* “to eternal life,” having been predestined or foreordained according to his purpose—that is, according to the disposition of God the Father, who works all things according to the counsel of his will, that is, according to what he himself wills and orders.

Therefore we have been predestined or foreordained to eternal life, so that we may be for the praise of his glory, with *let it be understood* “we Jews who previously hoped in Christ,” that is, so that he may be praised and glorified by all.

He is to be praised not only for the salvation of the Gentiles but also for ours, when we have been justified through baptism and through faith in his passion—something we could not achieve through the Law, which brought no one to perfection.

It should be known that he does not need our praise; rather, we need to praise him in order to attain his grace. For example, the sun does not need our sight in order for us to see its brightness and splendor; we, however, need its warmth and illumination so that we may be illuminated and warmed by it.

**In whom**, that is, in Christ or through Christ, **you also**, with *let it be understood* “you Ephesians,” **when you heard the word of truth**, that is, the Gospel of your salvation, with *let it be understood* “you received faith in him”; **in whom**, that is, believing in Christ, **you were marked**, that is, sealed or assigned, **with the Holy Spirit of promise**, that is, through the Holy Spirit who was promised by the Lord to the apostles, and through whom we possess the promise of life in baptism.

We have therefore been assigned to God through the Holy Spirit, whom we received in baptism, because in baptism we receive the seal of the likeness of God that we lost when our first parent sinned. This means innocence and holiness of soul, in which the human being was made in the image and likeness of God. That likeness and image was not in the body but in the soul.

We possess the innocence of the soul, having been cleansed from every stain of sin, and we already hold immortality in the body in hope.

**He**, with *let it be understood* “the Holy Spirit,” **is the pledge of our inheritance for the redemption of the possession**.

Blessed Jerome says in his explanation of this Epistle that it is better to say “who is the earnest of our inheritance” than “the pledge,” because this is how it appears in Greek. The translator who rendered this Epistle from Greek into Latin, not understanding the precise meaning of the word, translated *arrha* as *pignus*.

A *pignus*—a pledge—is one thing, and an *arrha*—an earnest—is another. A pledge is a security or bond given so that it may be recovered. People customarily give such a pledge when their animals are found in another person’s crops or vineyards, or when they have caused someone some other damage. An earnest, however, is what merchants customarily give to those from whom they purchase something; it is given not to be recovered, but so that what remains of the price may be completed. Hence *arrha* is said to derive from the matter to be completed, for which it is given.

The Holy Spirit is therefore an earnest to believers, because through him they receive the working of miracles and other virtues—namely, hope, faith, and charity, the interpretation of languages, and other things of this kind.

If in the present we possess such great glory from him while we still hold only the earnest, we should consider how great our dignity will be when, in eternal blessedness, what is now lacking in us has been completed, and we shall enjoy the presence of God without end.

It should also be noted that we possess the earnest of the Holy Spirit **for the redemption of our possession and for the praise of Christ’s glory**, because through him we are acquired for God, redeemed by his blood—that is, by Christ’s blood—and baptized in faith in him, so that God almighty may be praised and glorified.

**Therefore**, with *let it be understood* “because you possess the earnest of the Holy Spirit, you have been acquired for God,” and I, hearing of your faith—which you have in the Lord Jesus—and of your love for Christ—which you have for all the saints, that is, for all those sanctified in baptism—

**do not cease giving thanks for you**, with *let it be understood* “to God,” **making mention of you in my prayers**, first for myself and then for you, **so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ**, that is, God the Father, who is God of the human being assumed by the Word, **and the Father of glory**, that is, the Father of the Word, **may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation**, or manifestation, **in the knowledge of him**, that is, in the knowledge of God the Father.

Why did he say, “I do not cease giving thanks to God for you”? Could he always have remained engaged in praises and prayers? No; he spoke in this way because of his great constancy and continual devotion.

We said that God the Father is the God of the human being assumed by the Word because this is truly what Scripture says, just as Christ speaks from the perspective of his humanity during his passion: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27). And after rising from the dead he said to Mary: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20).

The **Father of glory** is the Father of the Word, because the Son himself is called Glory. The Father says to him: “Rise, my glory; rise, psaltery” (Psalm 56), that is, the choir of all virtues. Through him God the Father was glorified.

**The eyes of your heart having been enlightened**, with *let it be understood* “and may he give you this,” **so that you may know what is the hope of his calling**, in what follows, **among the saints**, that is, so that you may have the hope of receiving eternal life.

It follows: **And he subjected all things under his feet.** What does “all things” mean? Namely, the various kinds of human beings, and everything contained on earth and in heaven.

A question arises here. The Psalmist says that all things are subject to the power of the Son of God, and the same is said in this passage; why, then, does the Apostle say in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him” (Hebrews 2)?

This question is resolved as follows: there are two kinds of subjection—voluntary or spontaneous subjection, and forced or authoritative subjection.

The Apostle says to the Hebrews that all things are not yet subject to him in voluntary subjection, through faith and the will, because not all nations have yet believed in him.

But the Psalmist says that all things are subject to him in forced or authoritative subjection, because through his power, whether they wish it or not, Jews, pagans, and demons are subject to him. Demons are driven from possessed bodies through the invocation of his name; and pagans, by his permission, invade the kingdoms and lands of others.

**And he gave him**, that is, Christ, **as head**, that is, ruler, **over the whole Church, which is his body**, with *let it be understood* “which consists of angels and righteous human beings.”

Christ is therefore the head or ruler of the Church, because just as the members are governed by the head and the body is given life by the spirit, so all the elect are governed and given life by Christ.

And just as a body consists of bones and of fleshy, strong, and weak members, yet all are given life by the spirit, so the Church contains within itself those who are strong in faith and good works, as well as sinners who are weak in faith and virtues. Nevertheless, Christ, who is their head, gives life to them all by calling them to faith.

**And the fullness of him who is filled completely in all things.** Omitted words of this kind are necessary here: “That Church which is the body of Christ is his fullness,” with *let it be understood* “the fullness of Christ’s body,” which is filled—or increased—through all the kinds of human beings in all nations.

For every day, as people from each nation come to the faith of Christ through baptism, his body is increased every day. For example, one speaks of a king as becoming greater when armies and peoples of diverse nations come together under him.

**CHAPTER II.**

[Col. 0707C] **And you**, with *let it be understood* “Ephesians,” **when you were dead in your trespasses and sins**, in which you once walked according to the age of this world—that is, according to the desires of those who love this world—according to the prince of the power of this air, that is, according to the will of the devil. For the spirit—that is, the devil, whom he above called the prince—is kept in the darkness of this air to be punished; he now works his own will in the children of unbelief, that is, among pagans, heretics, and Jews, who do not possess right and perfect faith.

There is this difference between a trespass and a sin: we commit a trespass when we omit things which God commands us to perform, such as: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19). When we do not love him or honor our parents, we trespass. Hence it is called *delictum*, as though *derelictum*, “something left undone.” Sin, however, occurs when a person performs what God commanded him to avoid, for example: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Deuteronomy 5), and so forth. Alternatively, a trespass is in thought, a sin in action.

[Col. 0707D] The Jews and Gentiles, therefore, were dead in trespasses and sins, because “the soul that sins shall die,” not in substance but through sin, on account of which it withdraws from God, who is the life of the soul. For just as the body dies when the soul departs, so the soul dies when God departs. When he says, “in which”—that is, in trespasses and sins—“you once walked,” he says this by way of encouragement, and it is like the saying: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

It follows: **In which**, that is, in trespasses and sins, **we all**, with *let it be understood* “we Jews,” **once lived in the desires of our flesh**, that is, in fleshly lusts and earthly pleasures, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts—that is, carrying out in action what we conceived in our heart: adultery, fornication, theft, and so forth. And we were by nature children of wrath and children of vengeance, as also were the rest of humankind.

[Col. 0708A] We must not suppose that human nature was created and established evil by God, for it was made good, holy, and immortal, but was corrupted and depraved by its own vice. Humanity was made in the image and likeness of God in the soul, not in the body; but by sinning it lost the image it possessed in holiness and innocence, and the likeness it possessed in immortality. A human being did not beget a son in that likeness in which he himself was made, but in his own image and likeness as he now possessed it—that is, sinful and mortal, as he was himself. Therefore, since we were born sinners and mortal from our first parents, who had already become like us, we were, as it were, by nature or naturally children of vengeance, because we deserved to receive vengeance for the transgression of God’s commandments which we committed in our parents.

[Col. 0708B] But God, who is rich—that is, abundant and manifold—not only in power and strength but in mercy, because of his excessive or surpassing charity and love by which he loved us when we were dead in sins, in the manner stated above, made us alive together with Christ in baptism through faith in the passion of his Son. Thus, just as Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more (Romans 6), so we, rising from sin, may live in virtues. By whose—that is, Christ’s—grace you, O Ephesians, have been saved, not by your merits; and he raised us together and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ, that is, through Jesus Christ.

This may be understood in two ways. “He raised us together,” that is, he raised us together with Christ in baptism, when, for example, we descend into the font and there die to sin, just as Christ died on the cross and was laid in the tomb. We rose from death to life, from uncleanness to innocence, coming forth from the font purified and cleansed from all sins, just as Christ rose from the tomb; and now we sit in heavenly places through faith and hope, according to what he promised the apostles: “You shall sit upon twelve seats” (Matthew 19). For when the Apostle spoke these words, he was in prison, yet he spoke with confidence.

[Col. 0708D] We may also understand it otherwise, taking the past tense for the future: God the Father will raise us through the power of his Word on the day of judgment, and through Christ Jesus will make us sit in heavenly places. This love is ineffable: God the Father deigned to send his Son not only for the righteous but also for sinners, and, what is greater, for rebels, in order to show—or because he is to show—in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace upon us who believe in him, in goodness or mercy, in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ.

[Col. 0709A] The ages are so called because they follow one another and revolve within themselves. He says “in the ages to come” or future ages because after the day of judgment there will be many and innumerable ages and times, although the day is continuous. For the sun will not suffer setting, according to the saying: “Your sun shall no more go down.” These, then, are the riches which he will show upon us, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2): namely, the joys of eternal life, to endure without end. They will then be shown to us through Christ in the ages to come, because in the present age they cannot be seen.

[Col. 0709B] For by God’s grace you have been saved from death to life through faith in baptism, not by your merits. And this—that you have been saved and possess faith—is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift that you may be saved and have faith. Hence the Lord says: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him” (John 6). If it is the work of God, it is not from us. For from ourselves we have neither faith nor salvation nor anything good; rather, God works in us both willing and accomplishing (Philippians 2).

Because many are accustomed to say, “I came to faith because of my good works,” the Apostle therefore adds: “not from works”—with *let it be understood* “you received faith”—“so that no one may boast,” but through God’s grace. Faith comes first; action follows afterward. Those who boast of their works also customarily cite Cornelius the centurion as an example, saying that because of his good works he deserved to receive faith when instructed by Peter.

[Col. 0709C] They must be answered that Cornelius the centurion was one of the Jews, possessing knowledge and awareness of the one God. He hoped and believed that he would be rewarded by God for his good works; and because he had already received some faith, which he adorned with good works, he deserved to be instructed by Peter concerning knowledge of the whole Trinity and to be baptized with the sacrament of baptism, without which no one can be cleansed from sins.

For we are his workmanship: that is, with Christ himself assisting us, we have become good and have been made innocent, created or renewed for good works in Christ Jesus—that is, through Jesus Christ or through faith in Christ Jesus—which good works God prepared so that we might walk in them, advancing from virtue to virtue. He is not speaking here of that making by which we were made in the beginning so as to exist, but of that by which, when we were evil, we were made good through his working.

Therefore—understand: because you have been renewed in good works—remember that at one time, that is, before you came to faith, you were Gentiles in the flesh, that is, in carnal conduct. You were called “foreskin” by that people which is called “circumcision” by you, a circumcision made with hands in the flesh. Because of circumcision, the Jews were called “circumcision” by the Gentiles; and because they were uncircumcised, the Gentiles were called “foreskin” by the Jews, who are sinners and alienated from God. [Source cols. 0710A–0720A.]

It is rightly said that circumcision is both “circumcision” and “made with hands,” because that circumcision was performed by the work of human hands upon only one bodily member. Our circumcision, however, does not consist merely in the removal of one member, but extends throughout the whole body and all the senses of the body, since we circumcise from ourselves vices, the pleasures of the flesh, and evil desires, stripping ourselves of every sin of pleasure and action.

It follows: “You were at that time”—before you believed—“without Christ,” that is, without faith in Christ or without the promise concerning Christ; “alienated from the society of Israel,” that is, strangers and foreigners to the fellowship of the Jews, because you did not observe circumcision or the Sabbath, nor offer the sacrifices prescribed by the Law; “and guests of the covenants”—understand: you were guests.

A guest is so called as though from *ostii pes*, “the foot of the doorway,” because when people were received into a house, the master of the house and the one being received placed a foot upon the threshold; and, giving their right hands, he swore that his entrance was peaceful. Thus Gentiles who passed over to Judaism, although they were circumcised and offered the sacrifices prescribed by the Law, were nevertheless not regarded as citizens; they were called proselytes and newcomers and were treated almost as guests.

Therefore the Apostle says that they were guests, newcomers, and proselytes of God’s covenants, lacking the hope of the promise of eternal life—or of that promise made to Abraham, namely, that in his offspring, that is, in Christ, all the nations would be blessed (Genesis XXII). Although that promise had been made concerning them, they nevertheless had no hope that they could attain fellowship with the Jews, because they did not possess the Law and the Prophets, in which that promise was contained; and they were “without the true God”—understand: they had no knowledge of him, because the gods whom they worshiped were not gods, but demons and the works of human hands (Psalm CXIII).

But now, in Christ Jesus—that is, through Christ Jesus, or in faith in Jesus Christ—you Gentiles, who were once far away—understand: far from God, not in place but in merit—have been brought near through the blood of Christ, that is, through faith in Christ’s Passion.

For Christ himself is peace, that is, our reconciliation, because through the blood of his Passion he reconciled us to God. And because he made both kinds of people—namely, Jews and Gentiles—one, that is, one flock, and one body in the unity of the Church and of faith, just as he himself promised in the Gospel: “There shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John X), he, by abolishing—that is, destroying and removing—in his flesh, that is, in his Passion, the dividing wall of the barrier, namely, the hostility that existed between the two peoples,

abolished the law of commandments in decrees, that is, by the commandments and ordinances of the Gospel he abolished the Law, so that he might create, perfect, or build the two peoples in himself, that is, in the unity of his faith.

Here he calls the legal commandments—the circumcision, the observance of Sabbaths, the festivals of new moons, and the sacrifices—the dividing wall, because they separated the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, just as a wall divides and separates two people or two things. And what he called a “wall” he explained when he said “hostility” and “the law of commandments,” because on account of the Law and its observance there were hostility and disputes between the two peoples, since the Jews regarded the Gentiles as unclean.

But he himself destroyed that wall, or hostility, or law of commandments, in his Passion, when he was sacrificed for all, calling the Gentiles to faith and redeeming the Jews as well. Moreover, in the ordinances of the Gospel he abolished the Law in its mysteries, because after he had suffered—he whom those sacrifices prefigured—he commanded neither Jew nor Gentile to offer sacrifice or to be circumcised. Thus he made peace in one new man, that is, in himself.

How did he himself become the new man? In that he became human, born from a virgin without male seed, and lived in the world without sin—something no one had done either before or afterward—in order to reconcile both peoples to God the Father through the cross, that is, through the Passion of his cross, in one body, that is, in one Church, one faith, and one fellowship. Or “in one body” means that all believers from Jews and Gentiles should be one body in him, while he killed, destroyed, or abolished the hostility in himself.

What hostility did he destroy? That which existed between Jews and Gentiles on account of circumcision and the sacrifices prescribed by the Law. He abolished it in himself when, by enduring his Passion, he fulfilled in reality what had existed in the mysteries; afterward he did not command those things to be offered or observed.

Coming into the world through the mystery of the Incarnation, he proclaimed through angels, through himself, and through the apostles peace to you Gentiles who were far away from God—not in place but in merit—and peace to those who were near, namely, the Jews, who were near through the knowledge of him that they possessed. For through Christ himself both peoples have access to the Father in one Spirit—understand: confessing him.

Or, reborn through Christ, we approach God the Father, because Christ is the mediator in that he is both God and man (1 Timothy II). Through him we direct our prayers to God the Father, and through him we are brought into his presence, as he said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV).

Therefore, brothers, you Gentiles are no longer guests and newcomers, proselytes, or strangers to the fellowship of the Jews, as you once were, in the manner we explained above; rather, you are citizens of the saints—patriarchs, prophets, and the other righteous—and members of God’s household.

They are called citizens because they belong to one city and fellowship; they are called members of a household because they live together in one house. Thus the Gentiles are fellow members and citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, because they strive to reach the one heavenly city, Jerusalem, and dwell in the one house, which is the Church of God.

## Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets

The foundation of the apostles, the prophets, and all the faithful is Christ, because they are founded and established in faith in him, just as he himself said: “Upon this rock,” that is, upon me, “I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI), which consists of angels and righteous human beings.

Everyone who has faith in Christ is founded upon him, Christ Jesus himself being the supreme cornerstone. How is Christ both foundation and cornerstone? Because faith begins from him, exists in him, and is perfected and completed by him; therefore all the elect are founded in him.

He said “in him” in place of “because of him.” He is also called the cornerstone because, just as a cornerstone joins two walls, so Christ joins and holds together two peoples in the unity of his faith.

In Christ the whole structure of the Church is joined together and built up, growing into a holy temple in the Lord. In Christ, because people from all the nations come daily to the faith of Christ, faith grows within the Church itself, which is Christ’s temple, as it is said elsewhere: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians III).

Although almighty God is everywhere through the power of his divinity, he nevertheless dwells differently in the elect and in the reprobate.

In Christ—that is, in whose faith—you too are built together into a dwelling place of God, so that by growing from virtue to virtue you may be the temple of the living God; and this takes place in the Holy Spirit, that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER III

For this reason—that is, because you are citizens of the saints and are founded upon Christ—I, Paul, am a prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles.

“I am a prisoner” means that I am bound and shackled for the faith of Christ and for you Gentiles, to whom I proclaim the word of salvation. Or, “a prisoner” means that I am held in prison through love of Christ for you Gentiles. The sense is this: If I had wished to remain in Judaism and cease preaching the name of Christ, I could have been wealthy and been called a teacher of synagogues. But because I preach Christ to you, I am now held fast in poverty—if indeed you have heard of the dispensation, or administration, of God’s grace that was given to me for your benefit.

If in this passage the conjunction is affirmative rather than doubtful, the meaning is simply: “Certainly you have heard of the task of my preaching, which was given to me through God’s grace for your benefit.”

For according to God’s revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote to you above briefly, so that, when you read my words, you may understand my insight into the mystery of Christ. This Epistle is considered almost more difficult than all the others because it contains great and hidden mysteries, compressed into a brief discourse.

What mystery he means—what was revealed to Paul through God’s revelation—is disclosed in what follows: namely, that the Gentiles would enter into fellowship with the Jews without any distinction. Hence it continues: “The mystery or sacrament that was revealed to me.”

Was it not revealed to the patriarchs and prophets? Certainly it was. It was revealed to them only in the Spirit, that is, through the Holy Spirit, who were sons of God by adoption, as Paul also was—not to those who were sons and lovers of this world.

Alternatively: to other generations of human beings, that is, to patriarchs, prophets, and other people, the mystery of the faith of the Gentiles was not made fully manifest in the same way as it was to the apostles and prophets of the New Testament, such as Agabus, through whose preaching the Gentiles came to faith.

This can be proved by what the Lord said to the apostles: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matthew XIII). The apostles possessed greater wisdom than the patriarchs, because what the patriarchs saw from afar in the Spirit, the apostles saw both with the mind and with bodily eyes.

Indeed, the Jews could in no way believe that the Gentiles would enter into fellowship with them. They said to those who became proselytes: “You will certainly receive eternal life, but you will not have as great a rank in glory as we do.”

What, then, was revealed to the apostles? That the Gentiles would be co-heirs with the Jews in the heavenly homeland, in eternal glory; that they would be members of the same body, that is, would be one body in Christ, or would be joined together in the one body of the Church; and that they would be fellow-partakers of his promise in Christ, that is, sharers in the promise of God the Father that all the nations would be blessed in the offspring of Abraham.

To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to proclaim, or preach, among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten everyone.

Why does he now say, “To me, the least of all the apostles, grace was given,” when elsewhere he says, “I labored more than all of them”? Both statements are true. One refers to labor, when he says, “I labored more than all”; the other refers to the time of his calling.

He labored more than all the apostles because, while the others preached in the places assigned to them, he preached not only to the Jews but also to all the Gentiles among whom he had been appointed teacher and preacher (1 Corinthians XVI). When he says “the least,” it is as though he were saying “the latest and last.” He himself was the last of the apostles to be called to the grace of the Gospel: the others were called by the Lord before his Passion, but he was called from heaven after his Ascension.

To evangelize means to proclaim good things, because the Gospel is good news. Therefore one evangelizes not only by preaching the Gospel spoken by Christ’s mouth, but also by proclaiming good things and promising the joys of the heavenly homeland, which are contained in the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the sayings of the holy Fathers.

What are these unsearchable riches of Christ, to proclaim which the Apostle was sent among the Gentiles? Surely they are the riches of which the same Apostle says elsewhere: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians II)—that is, the joys of the heavenly homeland and life that will endure without end.

What he calls “riches” in this passage he later calls “the mystery.” Therefore, by “riches” we may appropriately understand the mysteries of Christ’s Incarnation and Passion, the redemption of the human race, the faith of the Gentiles, and the fact that there is no distinction between Jews and Gentiles in God’s grace.

All these things are rightly called a mystery, because before Christ’s coming they were hidden and secret.

But if the riches themselves are unsearchable, how was the Apostle sent to proclaim them? For something is unsearchable if it cannot be investigated or comprehended.

This can be resolved in two ways. They were unsearchable before the Lord’s coming, because no one could know them fully; but what had previously been unsearchable became, when the Lord came, traceable and comprehensible. Alternatively, they are unsearchable by their nature, but through the grace and revelation of the Holy Spirit they become traceable to faithful people.

For example, Nebuchadnezzar could not understand what the statue prefigured, but through the revelation of the Holy Spirit it became traceable and comprehensible to Daniel, who interpreted it.

The Apostle was also given grace to enlighten through faith all who wished to believe. Just as the unbeliever and disbelieving person remains in darkness, so the faithful and believing person rests in the light.

He was given grace not only to enlighten, but also to proclaim what is the dispensation—that is, the distribution or administration—of the mystery hidden in God, who created all things.

Here he calls “mystery” what above he called “riches”: the mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God, the faith and salvation of the Gentiles, and the joys of eternal life, which had been hidden from the ages—or from the beginning—in the true God who created all things.

It should be noted that he does not say that it was hidden from God, but that it was hidden in God until he determined to reveal it through himself. Hence it is called a mystery, which is a secret and hidden reality before it is brought into public view.

So that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known—that is, might become manifest and known—to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places through the Church.

The wisdom of God is called “manifold,” as though it had many kinds, appearances, and forms. Let us see how it is manifold.

The Son of God was born from a virgin without male seed; he cried in a manger as an infant, yet was glorified by the angels as God in heaven. Herod sought to kill him as a human being, yet the Magi, guided by a star, sought to worship him as God. He died as a human being, yet rose again through the power of his divinity. After rising from the dead, he appeared to the disciples in human form, yet gave them the Holy Spirit as God.

Behold how manifold the wisdom of God is.

In order, therefore, that this manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places—whom blessed Jerome understands as the angelic powers dwelling in heaven—the Son of God, coming into the world, revealed it to his apostles. Through the Church, that is, through the apostles preaching in the Church, he made it known to the angelic powers.

Blessed Jerome said that there were certain angelic ranks that did not fully understand the mysteries mentioned above until Christ’s Passion had been completed and, as the apostles preached throughout all the nations, they began through their preaching to draw the Gentiles to the faith.

This can be proved by the fact that the angels, wondering, said when Christ ascended to heaven by his own power: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” (Isaiah LXIII)—that is, from the bloody and bloodstained world. And in the Psalms: “Who is this King of glory?” (Psalm XXIII).

Those who possess greater dignity, through whose ministry these things were commanded, knew them—such as counselors and messengers. But it is possible that those of lesser dignity knew them only in part; and this passage reveals that possibility.

According to the determination, or preordination, or predestination of the ages—which are one and the same thing—which determination he made or fulfilled in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus.

As God the Father preordained everything before all ages, so he completed and revealed his manifold wisdom through Christ.

Therefore, because you have faith in Christ and access to God the Father through him, I ask you not to lose heart in my tribulations for you, that is, not to depart from the faith of Christ when you see me suffering for you. For this tribulation is your glory.

More appropriately he would have said, “these tribulations are your glory.” The Apostle suffered on their behalf because, while preaching the word to them, he was seized by persecutors. But his tribulation was their glory, since they were strengthened in the faith and acquired eternal glory through his suffering.

For this reason—that is, so that you might not depart from the faith of Christ—I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Just as there are external eyes of the body and external knees and other members, so there are also said to be interior ones. Therefore the Apostle is not speaking here of external knees. By “knees,” then, we must understand only the submission and humbling of the mind.

“I bend my knees,” he says—that is, I submit and humble the disposition of my heart, praying to God for you.

The words that follow, “before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” are not found in the Greek text, which has only “before the Father,” so that he may be understood simply as the Creator of all things. What has been added in the Latin manuscripts—“of our Lord Jesus Christ”—is nevertheless appropriate, because he is Christ’s Father properly and naturally, whereas he is our Father by adoption.

It continues:

From him, God the Father, every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.

Just as in the present age we have those whom we call fathers and there are those by whom we are called fathers, so in that assembly of holy spirits there are those who like to call other archangels “fathers,” as prelates. For example, the angels love to call the archangels fathers; the same is to be understood of the other powers.

Therefore he said, “From him every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named,” because both the angels in heaven and human beings on earth received their beginning from him, and from him, who is the Father of all things, they received the name “fathers” of others.

May he grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and may Christ dwell through faith in your hearts.

For this reason, he says, I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord, so that he may grant you power according to the abundance of his glory, so that you may be strengthened in faith and Christ may dwell through faith in the inner person, that is, in your hearts.

Although almighty God is everywhere through the power of his divinity, he is nevertheless said to dwell especially in those who have faith in him.

Rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able, together with all the saints, to comprehend within yourselves what is the breadth, length, height, and depth.

These words depend upon what precedes. For this reason I also submit the dispositions of my heart to God, so that you may be rooted in love, just as a tree firmly planted by its roots is established in the earth, so that it may have moisture and not easily be uprooted by the wind.

And not only rooted, but also founded in love itself, as upon the most solid rock, so that you may understand the breadth of love.

The breadth of love is that by which one loves God, and not only a friend but also an enemy. Concerning this commandment the Psalmist says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm CXVIII).

The length of love is perseverance in good works. The patience, or length, of love is also the period from the beginning of faith to the end of hope, until we reach the point at which what we now hold in hope we then possess in reality, enduring patiently, for the love of God, the adversities of this age.

The height, or loftiness, of love is that, on account of all our good works—both the breadth of love and patience, endurance, and perseverance in good works—we seek the height of the heavenly homeland, hoping that God will reward us.

The depth, or hiddenness, of love is that we believe all the good things we possess come from the lofty gift and inspiration of God.

We can understand all these things in the cross, or in the love of Christ.

And to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge.

May he also grant you to understand the love of Christ, which surpasses human knowledge; that is, may he grant you knowledge sufficient to understand how great is the love of Christ, who died for us. This love transcends and surpasses all human knowledge, and not merely human knowledge, but even the divine knowledge that he bestows upon human beings.

How can we know it, if the knowledge that is granted to all surpasses us? We must know it in this way: by recognizing that we do not know it. For what mortal human being can comprehend how great was the love of God the Father, who permitted his only Son not only to become incarnate for us but also to die?

It continues:

So that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.

For this reason, he says, I pray that you may know the love of Christ, so that you may be filled with virtues and deserve to be counted among the number of the faithful, from whom the body of Christ is filled day by day.

For the fullness of Christ’s body is the Church, which is filled daily from all the nations.

Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, for ever and ever. Amen.

“To him,” that is, to God the Father, who is able to do abundantly all that is necessary for you—more than we ask; that is, who is able to grant us more than we know how to ask for or dare to request—and this according to the power of his divine might.

This divine power works in us miracles, faith, virtues, and teaching. To him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus.

The glory of God the Father is in the Church because the multitude of the faithful glorifies and praises God the Father in all that he does. He is also glorified through the Church, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father” (Matthew V).

The glory of God the Father is also in Christ Jesus, because everything that the Son himself accomplished he referred to the praise and glory of the Father, saying: “The Father who dwells in me performs the works” (John XV).

May glory be given to God the Father throughout all generations, that is, present and future generations; or among the generations of the Gentiles and the generations of the Jews, throughout all future ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore I, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.

“I beseech”—that is, I implore—you, I who am a prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthily and live holy lives according to the calling with which you were called in baptism.

You were called to be holy and without blemish. Live in a holy and blameless manner, walking from virtue to virtue.

What he says, “I, a prisoner,” can be understood in two ways: either as one bound with chains and placed in prison in the Lord—that is, for the Lord or for love of the Lord—or as one bound, that is, held fast by the love of affection for you because of God.

Understand: walk and conduct yourselves worthily.

With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.

A humble person is called *humilis*, “inclined toward the ground.” Gentleness is the mildness and tranquility of the spirit.

“Walk,” he says, “and conduct yourselves with complete humility and gentleness of mind, bearing with one another in love,” or in the love of God and neighbor, in accordance with the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens,” imitating the nature of servants.

For example, let the person who is rich in the resources of this age support the one who is poor in present possessions but rich in spiritual virtues; and conversely, let the person who is holy support the sinner by his holiness and prayers; or let the rich support the poor through his almsgiving.

Be diligent—that is, earnest, cautious, and attentive—always to preserve the unity of the Spirit, so that you may be of one mind concerning Christ and have one faith. Let there be no schisms or heresies among you. Do this in the bond of peace, that is, in the love of God and neighbor, or in fraternal harmony.

Love is rightly called a bond because it binds and joins two together: namely, God and a human being, or two neighbors.

You are one body of Christ, and one Holy Spirit dwells in you, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. You were called as saints, united in baptism, according to the saying: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus XI). Therefore you ought to live holy lives.

He rightly says, “You were called in one hope of your calling,” because all the faithful have one hope of reaching the heavenly homeland.

There is one Lord of all creatures; there ought to be one faith among all believers, who have one baptism.

Although some have greater faith and others lesser faith, understanding greater or lesser things about God, faith is nevertheless said to be one because they believe in one God who has a Trinity of persons and unity of substance.

There is one baptism because throughout the whole world all who receive the seal of faith are baptized equally.

There is one God of all creatures and Father of all things, that is, Creator, who—the Father, understand—is exalted above all creatures. He is through all things the Son, because all things were made through him (John I) and restored through him; and he is in all of us—the Holy Spirit, understand—who has been poured into the hearts of the faithful, and is in all creatures, according to the saying: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wisdom I).

But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

Here the Apostle speaks in his own person and in that of the other apostles, or of all believers.

Grace was given: faith, the forgiveness of sins, redemption, and whatever good we possess. Grace is so called because it is given freely.

All these things were bestowed upon us as a free gift of almighty God, according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Here we should understand the gift or donation of the Father and the Son to be the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God” (John IV), that is, the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

But when he says, “It was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift,” the words seem to imply that the Holy Spirit has a measure and can be measured. But how can he be measurable, when it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world”?

It should therefore be noted that, just as God the Father is immeasurable, who says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah XXII), and the Son is immeasurable, who is the wisdom of God the Father and “reaches mightily from end to end,” so the Holy Spirit is immeasurable.

Because there are three persons, we must refer this “measure of the gift” to our capacity. According to what we are able to receive, a measure is given from the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

For example, the sea is immeasurable in its length, depth, breadth, and abundance of waters. When inhabitants come to it, each carries away water according to the measure of his vessels—one more, another less—yet the sea remains immeasurable. So we too receive from the gifts of the Holy Spirit according to the measure of our capacity, while the Spirit himself remains immeasurable in his nature.

Therefore, because grace was given to each according to the measure of Christ’s gift—greater to one, lesser to another—the Psalmist says: “Ascending on high, Christ led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings.”

A certain teacher explains this verse in a way that does not depart from the truth, calling the devil “captivity,” because he took the human race captive from paradise.

“Ascending on high,” that is, onto the cross, in accordance with what he himself also said: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man” (John VIII), and so forth—then he led captivity captive, that is, he took the devil captive, depriving him of the power that he held in this world, according to the saying: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII).

But what did he do afterward? Rising on the third day, he gave the gifts of the Holy Spirit to the disciples by breathing upon them and saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XXIX).

Alternatively: “Ascending on high,” that is, into heaven on the fortieth day after his Resurrection, Christ led captivity captive when he himself took captive the human nature that had been captured by the devil from paradise, drawing it away from the devil’s power and recalling it to the heavenly places. Then, on the tenth day after his Ascension, he gave the gifts of the Holy Spirit to the disciples.

One may ask: since above he said in the singular, “Grace was given according to the measure of his gift,” why does he now say in the plural, “He gave gifts to human beings”?

The answer is that although the Holy Spirit is called “gift” or “donation” in the singular, the gifts of that same Spirit are distributed according to the quality of people’s merits. Hence the Apostle says (1 Corinthians XII): “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge,” and so forth, until he adds: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills.”

But what does “he ascended” mean except that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth?

The Apostle questioned himself and said: “What does it mean when I say, ‘He ascended’?” How can God ascend, when he is everywhere? Certainly it means nothing other than that he also descended. First he descended into the lower parts of the earth, to the underworld, and afterward he ascended into heaven.

Therefore he neither ascended nor descended according to his divinity, which fills all things, but according to his humanity. In his soul alone he descended into the underworld, and afterward in body and soul he ascended above all the heavens.

It should be noted that by saying, “He descended into the lower parts of the earth,” he shows that the underworld is beneath the earth. Hence it is called *infernus*, because it is below the earth, or beneath the earth.

He who descended—understand: into the lower parts of the earth—is the same who ascended above all the heavens, namely Christ, in order to fulfill all things.

This means either the prophecies of the Law and the Prophets that had been written concerning him, or “all things” means certain dispensations that he had arranged with the Father and that he alone with the Father knew.

Alternatively, he ascended in order to fill all heavenly and earthly things with the knowledge and revelation of his divinity. Before his coming, all these things were, in comparison with the knowledge of his divinity that they later received, almost empty.

The heavenly things were filled because there were certain angelic powers that did not fully understand the mysteries of Christ’s birth, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven until these things had been accomplished. Hence, in wonder, it is said in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory?”

He also filled earthly things because among human beings who did not know God he bestowed his knowledge and filled them with his grace.

And he gave some as apostles—such as the twelve and the seventy-two disciples; some as prophets—such as Agabus, the others from Antioch, and the four daughters of Philip; others as evangelists—such as Luke and Mark, and also John and Matthew, who were apostles as well; and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting, that is, the completion, of the saints, so that those who have been predestined to eternal glory might be perfected through their preaching and examples.

At the beginning of the faith there were evangelists, prophets, pastors, and teachers; they still exist in the Church today. Whoever announces good things is an evangelist; whoever announces to his hearers the joys of the elect and the punishments of the reprobate is a prophet.

When the blessed Augustine was asked by Paulinus about the title “pastors and teachers,” he replied that one person is both pastor and teacher. For a pastor cannot be one unless he possesses the teaching by which he feeds the flock entrusted to him. If he lacks teaching, although he may have the name of pastor, he nevertheless lacks the office.

The pastors and teachers of the Church—which is one office—are bishops, priests, and the other rulers and ministers of the Church. They have been appointed for the work of ministry and for the building up of Christ’s body until we all attain to a perfect man and to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God. They have therefore been appointed as pastors and teachers so that they may build up Christ’s body, which is the Church. The Church is built up daily from the number of believers who come to the faith, so that we may have life after the resurrection and that we may all know God equally.

In the present age, just as there is a diversity of knowledge, so there is a diversity of faith: one understands more about God, another less; and according to what each understands and knows concerning the divinity of almighty God, so does each possess faith. After the resurrection, however, there will no longer be a diversity of faith, because just as all will see God equally, so they will possess equal faith. For God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

“Into a perfect man, into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” These words depend upon what has already been said. “He,” he says, “gave pastors who build up his body until we all attain, after the general resurrection, to a perfect man.”

Some understand this to mean that at the general resurrection everyone will rise at the same age at which Christ rose, whatever age they may have been; and that women too are included under the designation “men.” Although the phrase “into a perfect man” is not contrary to the faith, it is better that we understand it otherwise. He calls Christ with his entire body “the perfect man”; and that body will not be perfect until all the elect have been gathered in. Once the number of the elect has been completed, we shall all attain to the perfect man: that is, all the elect will meet their head, Christ, so that thereafter there will be one man—Christ and the Church—perfect and complete.

“And into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” Just as a human being grows through each stage of life until he is a perfect man, so Christ grows daily until the day of judgment—not in himself, but in us, who are his body. Once the measure of his stature has been completed, that is, once the perfect and complete number of the elect from whom the fullness of the body is constituted has been reached, we shall meet him.

So that henceforth—that is, after the resurrection in which Christ will be perfect—we may not be, understood as to our understanding, little children, wavering and wandering here and there, falling now into one vice and now into another, and be carried about by every wind of doctrine.

With respect to the wisdom of the present age, the blessed Apostle was not a child in understanding, because he was wiser than all mortals. But with respect to that perfection of wisdom which the saints will possess after the resurrection, he was a child in understanding and imperfect in intellect.

When he says, “nor be carried about by every wind of doctrine,” he calls dialectic and worldly wisdom “the wind of doctrine.” It is of no use, and by it we are carried about and driven, because we are often led astray through it, supposing things that are false to be true. These Ephesians were dialecticians, and by dialectic they led the simple astray, making them believe through their inventions and cunning that false things were true.

Hence he continues: “In the wickedness,” that is, in the malice, “of men and in their cunning, we are circumvented for the deception of error.” The blessed Jerome says: “What benefit is there in persisting continually in the art of dialectic and composing the syllables of iambics into various poems, when there is no truth there, but only human seduction and error?” This may exist in the present age, but after the resurrection it will cease.

“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in justice and holiness of truth.” These words of the Apostle depend upon what precedes. For he is speaking to the Ephesians: “Put off,” he says, “according to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error”; and then he adds: “But be renewed in the spirit of your mind.”

The former way of life is sin and remaining in sins; the old man, however, is the way of life of the old man Adam. Whoever remains in sin possesses the way of life of the old man. That man—that is, that way of life—is corrupted and depraved according to the desires of errors and vices.

“Be renewed, therefore, in the spirit of your mind.” According to the blessed Augustine, we should take “spirit” and “mind” as referring to one thing, namely, the rational faculty of the mind.

There are two renewals. One is sudden, taking place in baptism, in which we are renewed from all original and actual sins. The other takes place over a period of time, through continual reading and through the practice of good works; it is this renewal that is meant here. For when the mind daily understands through devoted reading things about God that it previously did not know, and when it advances daily from virtue to virtue, it is renewed each day.

The meaning is therefore as though he said: “You have been renewed in baptism; be renewed daily through devoted reading, understanding about God the things that were formerly hidden from you, and advancing from virtue to virtue.”

“And put on the new man.” By “the new man” he means either the way of life of the new man or the Lord Jesus himself. Let us see how he himself is the new man and has been created according to God.

He was conceived in a virginal womb by the work of the Holy Spirit, from the seed of a woman and without the seed of a man; this was new. He performed miracles such as no one else performed. He lived in this world without sin. He is true God and true man. He rose from the dead. All these things were and are new.

He was “created according to God in justice,” because he is just; and “in the holiness of truth,” because he is just and true. He is not merely just, holy, and true; he is justice itself, truth itself, and holiness itself.

Thus, when he says, “Put on the new man,” the meaning is as though he said: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ”—that is, the way of life of the new man and all the virtues that you understand to exist in Christ. Whoever assumes justice, holiness, truth, wisdom, charity, and all the virtues that he recognizes to exist in Christ has indeed put on Christ.

Therefore, putting away all falsehood, let each of you speak truth with his neighbor, because all falsehood comes from the devil, who is a liar and the father of falsehood.

All who are children of truth ought to put away and cast off every lie, deceitfulness, and duplicity, and speak truth from a pure heart with every person—not only with a Christian, but also with a pagan and a heretic—for all are our neighbors.

And why ought we to speak truth with our neighbor? Because we are members of one another. Christ is the head, and his members are the elect. Just as the members of our body are necessary to one another and minister to one another, so the members of Christ ought to minister to one another what is necessary.

For example, the eyes are necessary to the hand and foot, and the hand and foot to the eye. Therefore the eye ministers to the hand and foot the light by which they see, while the hand wipes and washes the eye from impurities. So in the holy Church every preacher ought to minister the light of knowledge and preaching to others, who are the hands and feet—that is, to those who give alms, those who run to bury the dead, and those devoted to the active life.

Conversely, these people ought to support the eye, that is, the preacher, from their own resources, providing him with food and drink and supplying him with the other things necessary for him. By doing this they will be members of one another.

It follows:

“Be angry and do not sin.” We can understand this in two ways. If, whenever you sin and, persuaded by the devil, depart from the way of righteousness, you become angry with yourselves and are indignant, so that you do not do such things again, chastising your body with vigils and fasts.

Alternatively: “Even if,” he says, “you become angry, do not carry it through.” He permits anger, which is human, but forbids seeking vengeance, which is no longer human, because “the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1).

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” This too can be understood in two ways. Let us take it simply: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger,” that is, if you have been stirred up for a time against your neighbor, be reconciled before sunset, and let anger depart from you.

Alternatively, Christ is called “the Sun” in the sacred Scriptures, as in the words: “For you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4). This Sun of righteousness often sets for us because of anger that seeks vengeance and because of discord—that is, he withdraws from us—just as he set for the false prophets, concerning whom it is said: “The sun set for them while it was still midday” (Jer. 15).

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger”: that is, beware lest on account of your anger and your sin the Sun of righteousness—Christ—withdraw from you.

“Do not give place to the devil,” that is, do not seek vengeance and do not become excessively angry, lest the Sun—Christ—withdraw from you and the devil, the prince of darkness, arrive. Whenever we sin, we give the devil a place in us.

“Let the one who was stealing the property of others steal no longer.” Or the one who was stealing words and the teaching of the Gospel through heretical depravity, like the false prophets of whom it is said: “Those who stole words for themselves, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ although the Lord had not sent them”—let him steal no longer, but let him depart from his error.

Rather, let him labor, working with his own hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to one who is in need. The one who previously stole ought not merely to cease from theft; he ought to work with his hands so that he may have something with which to support others who are suffering want.

“Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were marked and sealed, and designated for God on the day of redemption.” This means: Do not drive the Holy Spirit from you by evil works. He began to dwell in you on the day of redemption—that is, on the day of baptism.

Just as a person is grieved when he is expelled from the house he built for himself so that he might dwell there in peace, so the Holy Spirit is said to be grieved when he is expelled by evil works from the person whom he cleansed for himself in baptism.

Alternatively: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God,” that is, do not grieve spiritual people, in whom the Holy Spirit dwells, through your evil works. Spiritual men, whenever they see others sinning and departing from the way of righteousness, are grieved by their misery and suffer with others as with themselves.

## CHAPTER V

“Be imitators of God, as beloved children.” The Apostle exhorts the Ephesians to be imitators of God, as beloved children. To imitate is to follow. Imitation is a kind of representation—for example, when a student attempts to imitate his teacher in some work.

How, then, can we imitate almighty God? Let us see. He is wise, prudent, merciful, just, and true. Let us also, according to the measure of our capacity, be wise and prudent; let us be just, truthful, and merciful, loving our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake.

Just as a beloved son imitates a good father in every way of life, in gentleness of mind, and in integrity of conduct, so you too should imitate your Father, almighty God, according as he has granted you assistance for good will and good action. I call him Father not by nature, but by adoption.

It follows:

“And walk,” that is, live, conduct yourselves, and grow, “in love of God and neighbor, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.”

Great, wondrous, and unspeakable was the love by which the only Son of God gave himself to death: the Lord for servants, the Creator for the creature. Since he laid down his life for us, so we too, if necessity should arise, ought to lay down our lives for his name—and not only for his name, but also for our brothers, because of the love of his name.

When the Apostle says that he “gave himself as a sweet-smelling fragrance,” although we read in Genesis (Gen. 8) that the Lord smelled the sweet fragrance in the sacrifice offered to him by Noah after he came out of the ark, we must not suppose that almighty God, who is spirit, delights in the smoke and odor of bodily things.

Rather, by “sweet-smelling fragrance” we should understand the intention of good will and the affection of the mind, in which God delights. Thus, in this passage also, the Apostle calls the intention of the mind and the affection of the most sincere love with which the Son of God loved us a “sweet-smelling fragrance,” because God the Father delighted greatly in these things, as though many spices had boiled forth in his sight.

He himself was the offering and the sacrifice; he himself was the priest and the one who offered the sacrifice, offering himself to God the Father on the altar of the cross for us.

“But fornication and every impurity, or greed, must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints.”

Fornication is so called from *fornices*, that is, from brothel-like and theatrical places, which are constructed with *fornices*, that is, arches; these places are also called arenas, and prostitutes were found there, with whom the most depraved men had intercourse.

To fornicate is to have intercourse with unmarried girls and with widows who have not yet been consecrated to God.

Every impurity means every form of lack of self-control relating to lust. In whatever manner it occurs, it may be called impurity, immodesty, or luxury.

“Greed” can be understood in this passage in two ways. It may be taken for the love of money; it may also be taken for adultery, which the Apostle elsewhere calls “business,” when he says to husbands and wives: “Do not defraud one another” (1 Cor. 7), and “Let no one circumvent his brother in business,” that is, in adultery (1 Thess. 4).

The Apostle commands that the things we have mentioned should not only not exist among us, but should not even be named. For if they exist, they will be named; and if they are named frequently, except for the sake of edification, the mind will more easily turn toward them. “Evil conversations corrupt good morals.”

“But be as is fitting for saints.” What is fitting for saints? To preserve integrity of conduct, pursue virtues, and avoid vices.

“Or obscenity.” Obscenity occurs when the impulses of our flesh are excessively inflamed toward lust, although they are often restrained because of the death of God and fear of punishments.

“Or foolish talk.” Foolish talk is idle speech of no usefulness, when, leaving aside profitable and useful matters, one discusses empty and useless things.

“Or jesting, which is not appropriate, but rather thanksgiving.” Jesting is playful speech that ordinarily provokes laughter.

The difference between foolish talk and jesting is that foolish talk is of no usefulness and contains no wisdom, whereas jesting often proceeds from the mouth of the wise and displays a certain urbanity, as in Virgil:

> Let him who hates Bavius love your poems, Maevius;  
> and let him yoke foxes and milk he-goats;

and other such expressions, which contain nothing evil in themselves, except that they are idle and do not pertain to a perfected purpose. Rather, they are a kind of thanksgiving—that is, such jests are uttered so that the delivery may be agreeable to serious hearers.

Therefore the Apostle commands that such things be avoided, because people will have to give an account of every idle word.

The phrase “but rather thanksgiving” can also be understood differently. Let not the things we have mentioned exist among you, nor even be named; but rather let thanksgiving exist among you, so that you give thanks to God in all that you do and possess. Or let yourselves be gracious and acceptable to God and to human beings.

“For you know this, understanding that every fornicator, or impure person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.”
