We have already spoken above about these vices. Let us now see why he says that greed is the service of idols.

Greed is said to be the service of idols because, just as the person serves the devil who, insofar as he can, takes away from almighty God the worship and religious devotion that belong to him alone, as well as the unique name by which he alone is called God, and gives them to demons, so also the person serves the devil who wickedly appropriates for his own use the common possessions of almighty God that have been given commonly to all human beings.

Alternatively, greed is rightly compared with idolatry because, while people serve immoderately the metals of gold and silver from which idols are made, and set up coins bearing the images of emperors, they venerate gold and silver in place of God, because they are servants of wealth.

Or, in a third way, he compared greed with idolatry in order to show that nothing is more wicked than it. For greed is the root of all evils.

It should be noted that, when speaking of obscenity, foolish talk, and jesting, he does not add that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of Christ, as he does with fornication, impurity, and greed. By this he shows that the former are indeed sins, but that the latter are worse because they separate people from the kingdom of Christ.

He called it the kingdom of Christ and of God the Father because, just as the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, so there is one power, one Trinity, and one kingdom.

“Let no one deceive you with empty words.” Those who say that no punishment is suffered in hell except to be tormented by one’s own conscience speak empty words—that is, words of no usefulness. They do not attend to what Isaiah says at the end of his book concerning the reprobate: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. V).

There will indeed be punishment within their conscience, by which they will be gravely tormented, and there will also be externally a worm and fire, by which they will be harshly tortured.

Those also speak empty and seductive words who say: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16), even if he does evil works. This is entirely false.

“Because of these things”—that is, because of fornication, impurity, and greed—“the anger of God comes upon the children of unbelief,” or of the devil: that is, upon those who perished in the Flood and afterward in Sodom and the other cities.

Those who perished in the Flood perished because, contrary to the Lord’s commandment, they took several wives and ate flesh. In a certain sense they perished with a lighter punishment than the Sodomites, who were burned in fire, because they did not take several wives but, in addition, fornicated contrary to natural use.

The devil is called “unbelief” because he makes human beings become distrustful and fall into despair.

“Therefore do not become partners with them,” that is, do not imitate them, because if you are partners in the deed, you will also be partners in the punishment.

“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5): that is, before you came to the faith, you were sinners, ignorant of God, and children of the devil, the prince of darkness. Now you have been justified by faith and by baptism, and you are children of God by adoption—he who said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8).

Therefore, “walk as children of light,” that is, as children of life, and conduct yourselves holily and without blemish, advancing from virtue to virtue (Ps. 83).

As great as the difference is between light and darkness, so great is the difference between the light of faith and knowledge of God, together with good works, and the darkness of unbelief, ignorance, and sin.

“For the fruit of light”—that is, the good practice of conduct and faith—is to live in all goodness, justice, and truth: whoever possesses faith and the light of the knowledge of God should pursue every good work, live justly, and speak truth to his neighbor, attending to what the Apostle adds: “Testing what is pleasing to God.”

Just as a money-changer tests metals by weight, purity, and sound, so we ought to test our works. We should test them by weight, considering how substantial and how great they are; by purity, asking whether they are performed with a pure and simple mind and with good intention; and by sound, asking whether they produce a good reputation.

“All things”—understand, all works—“that are reproved,” that is, condemned by good and holy people in the wicked, “are manifested by the light,” that is, by those who are children of light, as not being good.

As long as evil works are not reproved by the good, they appear good to the wicked. But when the good begin to reprove them, they are shown not to be good.

“For everything that is manifested is light”: that is, every evil work that is manifested through confession or penance is light. It begins to be light because it is good for sins to be manifested through confession and penance.

Therefore he says: “For this reason, he says, ‘Who is the one who says this?’” The blessed Jerome says that this verse is found neither in the Old Testament nor in the Gospel, except only in this passage—unless perhaps it was taken from here by teachers and placed elsewhere as an example.

But when the Apostle was dictating this Epistle, the Spirit suddenly spoke through him, as he did many other things. Therefore he says: “For this reason”—that is, because everything manifested through confession has already begun to be light—“the Holy Spirit says,” understood, “through me”:

> Rise, you who sleep,  
> and arise from the dead,  
> and Christ will illumine you.

The one who lies in sin is said to sleep and to be dead, because “the soul that sins shall itself die.” Rise from vices to virtues, you who now sleep in sins; rise from the dead to life, from sin to good works, and Christ will provide you with the light of faith and of his knowledge, and the light of good action.

“Brothers, see how carefully you walk, not as unwise but as wise.” The Apostle addresses the Ephesians, and in them all human beings, exhorting them to live carefully and thoughtfully as wise people, and not as unwise.

He calls them brothers in faith and in the fellowship of love, because we all have one Father, almighty God—not by nature, but by adoption.

“See, brothers,” that is, consider how carefully you walk, how orderly you live and conduct yourselves amid a crooked and perverse nation—not as the unwise, that is, unbelievers who do not possess true wisdom, with Christ dwelling in them, but as wise believers who possess within themselves substantial wisdom.

For as great as the difference is between light and darkness, and between a believer and an unbeliever, so great is the difference between the wise and the unwise, because light and wisdom cannot exist in one who does not possess faith in almighty God.

“Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” How can time be evil, when, according to God’s ordering, it continually revolves through months, days and nights, hours and passing moments?

Just as a house is called evil because it has evil inhabitants, so days are called evil in which evil things are done by evil people.

What does “redeeming the time” mean? Make it your own. For example, others sell it by doing evil works to their own harm; you redeem it from them by doing such works as will earn you a reward.

Whoever does what is useful to himself redeems and acquires time for himself, because he makes it his own and employs it for his salvation.

“Therefore”—understand, because the days are evil—“do not become imprudent, but understand what the will of God is.”

A prudent person is so called as though he were one who sees ahead: he considers from a distance what outcome his works will have; he knows what he ought to seek and what to avoid; and he considers what pleases or displeases God.

Conversely, the one who does everything inconsiderately and improvidently, who does not consider toward what end he is directing his works or what pleases the will of God, is called imprudent and foolish.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Because the days are evil, in which many evil things are done, do not become imprudent,” that is, unreflective, “but understand what the will of God is”—that is, what pleases God and in which works the will of God is fulfilled.

“And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is luxury, but be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

By “luxury” we should understand all the vices that ordinarily arise through drunkenness, because, as a certain teacher says, drunkenness excuses no vice.

It should be noted that just as those who are filled with wine are filled with shamelessness, impatience, lust, immodesty, pride, and the other vices, so those who are filled with the Holy Spirit are filled with chastity, humility, gentleness, and the other virtues, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

We speak to one another in psalms when we sing the psalms antiphonally. Psalms are so called from *psallere*, “to play or sing to the accompaniment of an instrument”; they are found in the psalms, that is, in the psalter.

“Hymn” is Greek; in Latin expression it signifies “praise of God.” If a hymn is composed but not sung, it is not a hymn; if it is composed and sung but not in praise of God, it is not a hymn. Ambrose and Hilary, men of great renown, composed Latin hymns especially.

Appropriately, when he said “songs,” he added “spiritual,” because there are songs that are not spiritual and are not sung in praise of God, such as the songs of worldly people.

Spiritual songs are those composed by the prophets, inspired and filled with the Holy Spirit, such as the songs of Moses, Hannah, Deborah, Isaiah, Hezekiah, and the other prophets.

The difference between a song and a psalm is that a song is produced and sung only by the mouth, whereas a psalm includes a certain instrument of musical art, namely, the psaltery.

“Singing and playing in your hearts to the Lord.” He said “in your hearts” because there are many who sing with their mouths although their minds do not agree with their voices. They pay more attention to the sweetness of their voices, so that they may please their hearers, than they consider in their minds what they are saying.

Those sing in the heart whose minds agree with their voices, in accordance with the saying of the blessed Benedict: “Let us stand for psalmody in such a way that our mind may agree with our voice.”

“Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father.” We ought to give thanks to God the Father for all the benefits given to us by God, or for all prosperous and adverse circumstances. He is God the Father of all creatures—that is, their creator and maker.

And how should we give thanks? In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, saying to him: “We give thanks to you, holy Lord and Father, because through your Son you made us and redeemed us, and opened for us the way to our heavenly homeland.”

Therefore we ought to give thanks to God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, because through him, who is our mediator, we offer and transmit our prayers and sacrifices to God the Father, saying: “Receive, Lord, the prayers of your people, through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“Being subject to one another in the fear of Christ.” Just as hearers and subjects are subject to their superiors because of obedience and reverence, so superiors too ought to humble themselves toward their subjects insofar as they see them to be their equals in virtue and the merits of their lives.

But insofar as they see them rising up in pride against them and pursuing vices, they ought to exercise the office of their authority, and rebuke and reprimand them firmly. This can be demonstrated from the deeds of the Apostle Peter.

When he saw the centurion Cornelius and his entire household humbly wishing to worship him, Peter, on the contrary, humbled himself before him, saying: “Rise, for I too am a man” (Acts 10).

But when he saw Ananias and Sapphira departing from the way of truth and subject to vices, he displayed the power of his office and authority, killing them by his word alone (Acts 5).

All these things, however, must be done in the fear of Christ—that is, for the love of God—not for the sake of flattery or patronage, as some do in order to win the favor of their superior and to carry out more freely whatever pleases them.

“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, so that he might sanctify her.”

Just as Christ loved his bride, the Church, to such an extent that he gave himself for her to the Jews in order to sanctify her—that is, to make her holy through her faith, through the sacrament of baptism, and through the remission of sins—so a husband ought to love his wife and keep her chaste, so that she may be holy. And if necessity should arise, he ought to lay down his life for her.

It follows concerning the Church: “Cleansing her by the washing of water,” that is, by the washing of baptism, “in the word of life,” that is, in the sanctification of his name, through which sanctification a person receives eternal life.

After the renunciation of the devil, the priest sanctifies the person, saying: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

And why did Christ do this? Why did he cleanse her, and why does he cleanse her daily in the washing of baptism through the invocation of his name? “So that he might present the Church to himself in glory, not having a spot of sin or a wrinkle of duplicity of mind or anything of this kind”—that is, anything vicious—but so that she might be holy and immaculate.

In the present age, the Church can be called and be glorious in one respect: namely, because she has the kings and princes of this age subject to her and contains within herself various orders and ranks. Yet she cannot be without the spot of sin and the wrinkle, because there are many penitents within her.

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1), and so forth. “There is no human being upon earth who does good and does not sin” (1 Kings 8).

Therefore it is better that we refer these words to the general resurrection, when the Church will be glorious, because she will shine like the sun in the kingdom of her Father and will be without the spot of sin and without the wrinkle of duplicity: she will be incorruptible in body and unchangeable in soul.

By saying “without spot and wrinkle,” he also shows that the Church is Christ’s garment, in accordance with what the Father says to her through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with a garment” (Isa. 49).

A garment usually has spots and certain marks from some dye, and it is usually wrinkled—that is, folded and doubled in places. There is another garment, however, which has neither spot nor wrinkle, such as a linen cloth stretched out well.

After the resurrection, the Church will be without spot and wrinkle, because she will be without sin and stretched out in the contemplation of almighty God like a linen cloth.

“No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.” This can be understood in two ways.

The meaning may be: Just as no one hates his own flesh, so no one ought to hate his wife, because she was made from his body.

Alternatively, “flesh” here means the wife, who was taken from the man’s body. No one has hated his own flesh—that is, no one ought to hate his wife—but ought to nourish and cherish her, just as Christ cherishes and nourishes the Church both bodily and spiritually.

“For we are members of his body.” Just as the whole Church in general is Christ’s body, so each of the elect individually is a member of his body—that is, a member of the Church.

We are not members of the body that he assumed in the virginal womb, but members of the Church, which is his body.

One person in the Church is an eye, such as any preacher; another is an ear, such as a good hearer; another is a hand, such as one who gives alms; another is a foot, such as one who cares for the sick and the dead.

“We are of his flesh and of his bones.” This can be understood in two ways.

We are of his flesh and bones because, just as we are constituted from flesh and bones, so he too has a true body of flesh and bones.

Alternatively, within the Church there are people who are strong in faith, work, and preaching. These are represented by the bones, such as the apostles and martyrs, and today bishops and superiors. There are also the weak, represented by the flesh, who need to be supported by the strong, just as flesh is supported by bones.

The strong and the weak, since they are called his members, are therefore also rightly called his bones and flesh.

For this reason—that is, because of this love which a husband ought to have for his wife—a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh. As far as the literal sense is concerned, this is what happens: a man leaves his father and mother, joins himself to his wife, and the two are one flesh—that is, from one flesh. Or again, in that union of intercourse, when they come together, he leaves [his parents], and they are one flesh. Spiritually, however, this can be referred to Christ and the Church, [Col. 0730D] who, because of his love for the Church, left God the Father by appearing not in the form of divinity, which is equal to the Father, but by emptying himself—and clung to his wife, the holy Church, by love and by the flesh which he assumed. Thus Christ and the Church are now two in one flesh, because they are from one flesh: Christ is truly human, possessing in himself a true human body, and the Church likewise. The prophet Adam first prophesied this about Christ and the Church.

This sacrament—or, understand, what I have just said—is great. There are greater sacraments, and there are lesser ones. Therefore, to show that the Apostle intended this to be understood both according to the literal sense and according to the spiritual sense, he added: “This sacrament, or mystery”—namely, what I have said, that a man leaves his father and mother, and so forth—“is great,” because it pertains to Christ and the Church. Hence he also adds: “But I speak in Christ and in the Church,” meaning, understand, that this is fulfilled in them.

## CHAPTER VI

“Brothers, henceforth be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.” After the particular precepts in which the Apostle admonished husbands and wives, fathers and children, masters and servants, he appended these general instructions—not only for the Ephesians, to whom he was sending this Epistle, but for every sex and every condition—and said: “Henceforth,” that is, from now on, and in addition to what we said above, my brothers in faith and love, and you who have one almighty God, “be strengthened in the Lord,” and in his faith, and in the power of his might. Do not trust in your own strength, or in your merits, or in the power of the rulers of this age, but be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.

“Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil.” In the term “armor” are included all instruments of war—namely, breastplate, helmet, shield, spear, missiles, and the other implements of arms. Spiritually, however, what should we understand by the armor of God? The Lord Jesus Christ, by whose protection all the elect are defended, and whom they put on, according to what the same Apostle said elsewhere: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III). For the elect put on Christ when, through his help, they assume the virtues that are in Christ. Therefore, when he says, “Put on the armor of God,” it is as though he said: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, assume in yourselves all the virtues which you know to be in him. For example: he was called just, true, patient, chaste, and gentle; he was also called a lamb, a lion, and a calf. Put on justice, truth, patience, charity, chastity, and gentleness. Be a lamb—that is, be meek; a lion—strong in faith and good works against the devil; and also a calf, mortifying yourselves together with vices and desires, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil.

The devil lies in wait for us in many ways. Indeed, he lies in wait through evil suggestions; he lies in wait through the vices of our flesh and the incitements of evil pleasures; he lies in wait through his ministers—namely, heretics, false brothers, and pagans. Against all these we must fight manfully, lest we be overcome. Someone might say: “O Paul, why do you command us to put on the whole armor of God?” To this he added: “Because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.”

In this passage the Apostle calls “flesh and blood” all who consist of flesh and blood, by whom we are often attacked at the devil’s prompting. He says: “Our struggle is not against them alone, but against demons who rule over evil men, exercise power over them, and direct them toward evil rather than good. These are called ‘spiritual beings’”—understand, demons—“of wickedness,” that is, of evil, who dwell in this air. In the Holy Scriptures the air is called “heaven,” and therefore birds are called “the birds of heaven.” As the prophets said, and as our teachers also believe, the air is so full of demons and evil spirits as a sunbeam is full of the smallest atoms—that is, indivisible particles.

We must therefore fight against these rather than against human beings composed of flesh and blood, because whatever evil men devise against us is suggested by them. If we overcome those who are the leaders of the army, at whose prompting the vices of our flesh rage against us, then we shall easily be able to overcome all their ministers—for example, just as, once the commander has been defeated, the army is easily put to flight. This can be proved from the Book of Judith, where, according to its account, when Holofernes, the commander of the army, had been killed, the multitude of the armies was put to flight and was very easily overcome by the Jews (Judith X).

But one may ask how we can fight against demons, since they are spirits. Is it not clear to everyone that one cannot fight against a spirit with material weapons, because spirits are invisible? It is therefore necessary that spiritual weapons be fashioned—namely, those mentioned above—and that we fight in the manner in which we read that Jacob wrestled with the angel (Gen. XXXII): by praying, fasting, keeping vigil, and applying ourselves to other good works. Thus, just as Jacob deserved to be blessed by the holy angel with whom he wrestled in prayer, so may we deserve to be blessed by the Lord after overcoming the devil.

Furthermore, one may ask where the Apostle obtained the idea of calling demons and evil spirits “principalities,” “powers,” and “rulers of this darkness”—that is, of unbelieving men who do not know God and are sinners—of whom those to whom he once said, “You were once darkness” (Eph. V), that is, unbelievers and sinners ignorant of God, had been part. We must answer that he took this from the Book of Daniel, where we read of “the princes of the Greeks and the princes of the Persians” (Dan. X); and also from the Book of Ezekiel, where it is said to the prince of Tyre: “You were the seal of likeness in the paradise of God” (Ezek. XXVIII), together with the other things said there about him and about the princes of other nations—namely, the Egyptians, Assyrians, and Idumeans. For those princes—that is, demons—are understood to have been set over those nations.

Just as each of the faithful has an angel assigned to guard him, so pagans have evil beings who rule over them by God’s permission. Just as Michael is set over the nation of the Jews, or of Christians, concerning whom it is said, “And no one is my helper except Michael, your prince” (Dan. X), so the nations that remain in unbelief have evil princes.

Let us speak still more deeply. The Apostle, filled with the grace of God, came to know through the Holy Spirit that just as the good kings of the Israelites signified the Lord Jesus and the rulers who are in the Church—for example, David, whose name is interpreted “strong of hand” or “desirable,” and many others—and just as the people of Israel signified the people of believers, who are the true Israelites, so the evil kings and rulers, together with their nations, who fought against the people of God—such as the kings of the Ishmaelites, Assyrians, Idumeans, and Philistines—signified the demons who rule over pagans and heretics, who continually attack the Church of God.

Therefore—understand, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against principalities—take the armor of God, the armor of which we spoke above, that is, all the virtues, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in all things. This means: persevere firmly in faith and good works in all prosperous and adverse circumstances. He calls the present time “the evil day,” not because it is evil in itself, but because many evils occur in it. Or he calls the day of judgment “the evil day,” on which all the wicked will be condemned.

“Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth.” We gird our loins when we restrain lust. “Stand,” he says, in faith and good works, and restrain your loins from lust, where it is especially vigorous; and do this in truth, not in falsehood, not through hypocrisy, and not so that you may win human praise. Or by “in truth” he means as though for the love of the name of Christ, who is the truth.

“Having put on the breastplate of righteousness.” Righteousness is rightly compared to a breastplate, because just as a breastplate is woven from many rings, so righteousness consists of many virtues. In another way, righteousness can be compared to a breastplate because, just as a breastplate protects the chest, tightens the belly, and shields the thighs, so righteousness drives away the superfluous thoughts that usually circulate in the chest, restrains the gluttony of the belly, and also suppresses lust.

“And let your feet be shod”—understand, let them be shod—“for the preparation of the gospel of peace.” The meaning is this: just as one who has shod feet despises serpents and considers thorns and every hardship of life as nothing, so you too should despise the ancient serpent, the devil, and thorns—that is, the pricks of sufferings—and every hardship of this life; and go freely toward preaching the gospel.

In another way, by the footwear made from dead animals we should understand the words and examples of the holy fathers who preceded us. We have shod feet, therefore, when, fortified by the words and examples of our preceding fathers, we approach the preaching of the gospel of peace confidently. The gospel is called “of peace” because it contains the peace that Christ commended to the apostles and, through the apostles, to all believers; or because, by observing the gospel, we deserve to be reconciled to God.

“In all things”—understand, in all disciplines and struggles—“take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one.” Anything that is thrown or launched may be called a missile; properly, however, the term refers to something extended lengthwise, such as a spear. For the Greeks call a long thing *telon* [Greek: “long”]; hence *mustela* is said to mean “a long mouse.” Just as a shield protects the one who holds it and repels missiles, so faith fortifies a person and repels from him the arrows and attacks of the devil—provided, however, that faith has been adorned with good works.

The devil’s missiles he calls “fiery” because they are evil suggestions which set us on fire to perform evil works and which are extinguished through the power of faith.

“And take the helmet of salvation.” The helmet is placed on the head and protects and guards all the bodily senses: sight in the eyes, hearing in the ears, taste in the mouth, smell in the nostrils, and touch throughout the body. What, then, should we understand by the helmet, which, as we have said, protects all the bodily senses? The Lord Jesus Christ and his protection. By the head we should understand the mind, because just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind.

Let us therefore place the helmet on our head—that is, let us store Christ’s protection in the secret place of our mind, trusting in him and not in ourselves. He will guard all our senses so that they cannot be wounded by the ancient enemy, the devil.

“And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”—understand, take it up. The word of God is understood as the sword of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says; that is, it is the teaching and knowledge of the divine Scriptures, which are granted to us through the Holy Spirit. It is called a sword because, just as enemies are driven away by a sword, so through knowledge of the divine Scriptures we can drive away all the snares and plots of the devil, pursuing what Scripture teaches and avoiding what it forbids. Through its knowledge and with God’s help, we can not only overcome demons, but also refute heretics by its authority and destroy their error.

“Grace”—that is, faith and the forgiveness of sins—“be with you in incorruption,” that is, in integrity, together with all who love the Lord Jesus Christ. In another way: may grace—that is, faith and the forgiveness of sins—be an eternal fellowship for you with all the saints in incorruption, that is, in the general resurrection, where all the elect will receive incorruption in the body and immortality in the soul, shining like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, with whom they will remain blessed forever and ever. Amen.

# ON THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 0733]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0733D]

The Philippians are Macedonians, that is, Greeks. For Greece received different names from different kings. It is called Macedonia from King Macedon, Aemathia from Aemathus, and Thessaly from Thessalus. In general, however, the whole land of the Greeks is called Greece from King Graecus, as Servius says: After the Philippians received the word of preaching from the Apostle, they were strong in faith and did not accept false apostles, as is shown in the Argument.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0735A]

“Paul.” Why did he place his name at the beginning of the Epistle? So that the Epistle might have greater authority. Kings and princes are accustomed to act in this way. Why did he not preserve his usual practice of placing the name of his apostleship in this Epistle, as he did in all the others except the one to the Hebrews? In that Epistle he omitted it so that the benefit of reading might not be delayed.

The Philippians, then, as we have said, after they believed through him, did not doubt that he was the Apostle and teacher of the nations. Therefore, when writing to them, it was not necessary for him to call himself an apostle. The Corinthians, however, having been led astray by false prophets, departed from the faith and doubted that he was an apostle chosen and sent by God, saying: “Paul truly did not see Christ in the flesh, nor is his teaching true.” For this reason he judged it necessary to call himself an apostle, saying: “Paul, an apostle not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Gal. I).

It should also be known that it was revealed to blessed Paul in a vision that he ought to preach the word of God to the Philippians. For, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (chap. XVI), a Macedonian man appeared to him, beseeching him and saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.” This man is believed to have been an angel of God assigned by God to that people.

“And Timothy.” Why did he insert the names of his disciples in his Epistles? So that they might have greater authority, in accordance with what the Lord said: “Let every word stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XXVII); so that no one might say, “These things have been devised falsely”; and also so that he himself might fulfill what he had taught, saying: “If something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (I Cor. XIV). For when he dictated his Epistles, all his disciples were present. If something else had been revealed to any of them which he himself did not say, or if it had been revealed differently from what he said—since the same Holy Spirit was in the disciples as in the teacher—Paul would set it in order just as it was spoken by that disciple. The good teacher did not begrudge his disciples; moreover, he placed that disciple’s name at the beginning together with his own, because the disciple had a share in the work.

“Servants.” Just as someone took pride in calling himself the servant of an emperor, as Andromachus called himself the servant of Octavian, so the Apostle, in order that his Epistle might be more firmly established, said that he was a servant of Christ, writing to all the saints—that is, to all who had been sanctified in baptism and remained in that sanctification—who were at Philippi, together with the bishops—that is, the presbyters, since one city cannot have several bishops.

Philippi is a city of Greece, which Philip, the adoptive father of Alexander, built and called Philippi after his own name; and to the deacons—understand, may salvation and the forgiveness of sins be given.

“I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you.” That is, at the remembrance of your faith, in which you remain steadfast, I give thanks to God; or, always mindful of you in my prayers, I give thanks to him who continually confirms you in faith.

“With joy”—understand, spiritual joy—“making my prayer,” not with sorrow. For those who persevere in the faith and adorn the faith they hold with good works, it is not necessary to pray with sorrow, but to give thanks to God. For those who fall away, however, one must pray with groaning and sorrow.

“For your fellowship”—that is, concerning the fellowship which you have with us; or because you received the gospel and shared in its faith; or also concerning the fellowship and participation by which you shared with us in preaching, because you now preach as we do—from the first day, that is, from the beginning of your faith—we are confident in the Lord Jesus, that he who began a good work in you”—that is, Christ, who gave you the beginning of faith and good conduct—“will also grant perseverance until the day of death,” or until the day of judgment, through succession.

“As it is right for me”—that is, it is right for me to understand this concerning you, because you will remain in the faith of Christ. Therefore I ought to rejoice and to think this—that is, understand it—because I have you in my heart and in my bonds. Understand: I remember you.

“God is my witness, how I long for you in the bowels of Jesus Christ.” Children are called “bowels,” and whatever is inside the skin is called *viscus*. Therefore this can be understood in two ways. “I long,” he says, “for all of you to be children of God”; or, “I long for him to be your temple, and for you, sharing in his body and blood, to remain in him.”

“And this I pray, that your charity,” and so forth. Just as faith has a beginning, an increase, and perfection, so does charity. “I pray,” he says, “that your charity may extend not only toward God and your neighbor, but also toward your enemies—in knowledge,” understand, of the law, “and in all understanding,” that is, in the teaching of the gospel, “so that you may approve”—that is, understand—“the greater things concerning God, so that you may be sincere,” that is, perfect in God, in faith, and in every goodness.

A sincere thing is solid and firm, not stained by any variation of matter; faith likewise ought to be solid. “Without offense,” that is, without stumbling, until the day of judgment, “filled with the fruit of righteousness.” That is, may you be filled with all the virtues of which the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace” (Gal. V), and so forth. “For the glory and praise of God,” so that God may be glorified in you and the Lord Jesus praised, through whom we have every good thing.

“I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has come rather for the advancement of the gospel.” Knowing that the Philippians were saddened by his tribulations and grieving over his sufferings, and fearing that they might fail in faith when they heard that he was enduring such things, blessed Paul wrote to them: “I know indeed that you suffer with my afflictions, but I want you to know that what has happened to me”—namely, bonds, prison, and stocks—“has come rather for the advancement,” that is, for the benefit and increase, “of the gospel,” than for its opposition.

“So that my bonds in Christ”—that is, bonds which I endure not for some other crime but for Christ—“have become manifest in the whole praetorium and in all other places.” The term *praetor* is derived from *praeire*, “to go before,” and is almost equivalent to “preceptor,” because he gives commands to the people. A praetorium is so called as though it were a *praeceptorium*, because praetors, or commanders, and prefects sit there to investigate certain matters and issue commands.

When blessed Paul came to Rome, bound for Christ’s name, and was confined in prison in the emperor’s household, he began to teach, heal the sick, and perform many miracles. Many believed, to such an extent, as blessed Jerome says, that he made the house of the persecutor Nero into a church of the Redeemer. Then it became manifest throughout the praetorium—that is, to the emperor and to all the consuls and princes—and in every place that he was enduring such things because of Christ.

“And most of the brothers”—that is, of those who believed in the Lord—“having confidence in my bonds,” that is, strengthened by the example of my bonds, when they saw blessed Paul suffering such things, cast away all fear of death. Strengthened and encouraged by the example of his bonds, they began to preach the word of God more boldly and without fear.

“Some indeed through envy and contention, but some also through good will.” These four forms that follow can, as it seems to the teachers, be reduced to two categories: the first and last forms being counted as one, and the two middle forms likewise as one. But let us attempt to trace the meaning of each individually.

When he says, “Some indeed through envy and contention,” understand that they proclaim one Christ. There were some among the believing Jews and Gentiles who envied blessed Paul because he was said to be the sole teacher and preacher of the nations. They said: “Is Paul alone called the teacher of the nations? We have teaching; we shall preach as he does, so that we too may be called teachers of the nations.” They did this because they wanted to contend with him.

The second form is: “Some through good will,” that is, with good intention, desiring to save others just as they themselves had been saved.

The third form is: “Some through charity”—understand, the charity with which they loved God—and they desired to save others; and also through the charity with which they loved the Apostle, wishing to provide him assistance in preaching.

The fourth form is: “Some through contention, not sincerely.” A sincere thing is solid and firm. There were some who preached not sincerely—that is, not with a pure conscience—because they devoted themselves to preaching for the advantages of the present life and for temporal profits, so that they might receive food and clothing from their subjects, saying: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should live from the gospel” (I Cor. IX). And because of the opportunity for contention, the Apostle, placed in prison, did not cease; he even sent his disciples throughout the whole world to preach. Some wanted him to be killed, so that, once he had been killed, they might more freely strip his hearers of their possessions.

“Knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel”—that is, for the defense which we described a little above—“not sincerely,” that is, not with pure intention, “supposing that they will raise up affliction,” that is, a greater persecution, “through my bonds.”

“For what does it matter?” That is: Why should I be saddened, or why should I be disturbed by sorrow? “Whether through occasion”—that is, through envy and not sincerely—“or through truth”—that is, through good will and charity—“Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice,” because the name of Christ is preached through good will and charity. “But I will also rejoice,” understand, for this reason: because I do not envy them.

“For I know that this will turn out for my salvation.” What I endure for Christ’s name will turn out for my salvation, that is, for eternal life. Or it will turn out for my salvation because I do not wish evil upon those who envy me and raise persecution against me. “And for the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,” that is, with Christ and the Holy Spirit supplying and providing assistance to me.

“According to my expectation and hope.” Expectation and hope are one thing, because hope is expectation of future goods. Blessed Paul was certain that he would receive the reward of eternal recompense for what he endured for Christ; and he also expected a reward because he wished good things for his envious persecutors. “Because I shall be put to shame in nothing”—that is, in none of the things they do to bring a greater persecution upon me, or in the things I shall endure. Although already placed in bonds, I am not ashamed.

“But with all confidence”—that is, with all my faith—“as always, so now Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death.” If I endure torments, all who hear of it will say: “Great is this God, for whose name his servants do not fear to die.”

“For to me to live is Christ.” That is, if I live, Christ is life to me; or, if I live, I shall increase his body through my preaching. “And to die is gain.” If I die under punishments, it is the greatest gain for me, and he will be preached more and more. Or it is gain for me to die because, if I die, I shall receive the greatest gain, namely, eternal life.

“To live in the flesh is the fruit of work for me.” The longer I live, the more I shall increase my reward. “And what I should choose I do not know”—that is, whether I should desire death or wish to remain still in the flesh.

The punctuation should be understood as follows: “And what I should choose I do not know; to be with Christ is much better.” When he said that it was much better to depart and be with Christ, and then added that remaining in the flesh was necessary, he showed what he preferred. Remaining here is indeed good, but remaining with Christ is better and best.

[Col. 0738D]

“And being confident of this, I know that I shall remain”—that is, I am confident and believe that I shall remain as long as it pleases the Lord—“and I shall continue,” that is, I shall remain until the perfection and strengthening of your faith, for the benefit of all of you, that is, for your usefulness, and for the joy of faith, that is, so that both you and I may rejoice in your faith.

“So that your rejoicing”—that is, your joy—“may abound in Christ Jesus through me, by my coming again to you.” To rejoice is to rejoice together and to give thanks. The meaning is: “You will rejoice,” he says, “at my coming and give thanks to God, who has restored me safely to you, freed from my bonds.”

“Only live worthily in the gospel of Christ”—that is, live and persevere worthily in it. To live worthily in the gospel is to believe Christ according to what the gospel teaches, to teach, to live according to his commandments, to hope for what he promises, and to do everything according to his commands.

“So that whether I come and see you”—understand, that I may rejoice at your faith, because you stand, persevere, and are firm “in one Spirit,” with one will. Hence Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV), that is, one will and one faith.

“United in soul”—that is, in one spirit—“working together,” that is, laboring together in the faith of the gospel by living well, believing rightly, and teaching rightly.

“And in nothing be terrified,” whether by an action or by a circumstance. By “be terrified” he means: do not fear the threats and errors of heretics, pagans, and false Christians, because the affliction with which they trouble you will be condemnation for them and the rewards of eternal recompense for you. This affliction and tribulation of yours is condemnation for them. And this will be done to them by God for condemnation, and to you for salvation.

In another way: “This,” he says—understand, what God has granted you—has been granted so that you may persevere by suffering such things for his name, so that you may obtain the palm of martyrdom, which he grants only to his lovers, whom he causes to love him. “And that you should also suffer for him,” that is, by suffering for him you should obtain perseverance and afterward the palm.

“Having the same struggle”—that is, the contest against heretics, pagans, and false Christians. If necessity arises, may you endure the sort of things I endured among you, when I was beaten because of the pythoness woman from whom I expelled the evil spirit and who had provided her masters with great profit.

## CHAPTER II

“And now you have heard about me”—understand, what I endure while placed at Rome.

“Complete my joy by thinking the same thing.” That is, think as we do in faith, in work, and in teaching; or have one will, possessing the same charity, united in soul—that is, of one will—and thinking the same thing, that is, understanding what we understand.

Or, since you are wiser and understand more about the faith of the Holy Trinity, make those who are less capable understand the same thing through your zeal and preaching.

“Do nothing through contention.” Here he forbids every kind of contention, both voluntary and necessary. There were contentious people among the Philippians who disputed about questions of the law and genealogies, doing this so that, when they defeated others, they themselves might appear glorious.

“Nor through empty glory”—that is, vain glory—“but in humility, considering one another superior to yourselves.” We must all consider others better and superior to ourselves. If we see someone enslaved to some vice and nevertheless possessing some virtue, because of the one virtue he has we ought to prefer him to ourselves. And even if we see no virtue in him, he may nevertheless possess some good that is hidden from us.

“Not each one considering his own interests.” They ought not to seek only their own advantages and their own usefulness, but also those of others. The usefulness of many benefits many, whereas the usefulness of one benefits only one. We must also seek those things which belong to others—that is, which pertain to the usefulness of many.

“For let this be your mind among yourselves,” that is, understand, think, and complete within yourselves what you understand to have been completed in Christ, “which was also in Christ Jesus.” Just as Christ did not seek his own interests but ours, so we should not seek only our own interests but also those of others.

“Who, although he was in the form of God”—that is, in the equality of the Father’s divinity, consubstantial with and equal to him in all things—“did not regard it as robbery to be equal to God.” Robbery occurs when someone usurps another’s property by violence, although it does not belong to him. The Lord Jesus did not commit robbery when he said that he was equal and coequal with God the Father, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X). If he were not truly the Son of God, he would not be equal to him in all things.

But when his forerunner, questioned by the scribes, Pharisees, and people about whether he was the Christ, said, “I am not the Christ” (John I), if he had said, “I am the Christ,” he would have committed robbery. Simon Magus therefore committed robbery when, although he was the son of the devil, he said (Acts VIII): “I am the son of God; I am the Paraclete; I am the son of God.”

“But he emptied himself,” that is, humbled himself, and, as it were, contracted and diminished himself. Emptying occurs when something great and incomprehensible is contained in a small form. For example, if some artist wished to contain in a very small image, in comparison with the magnitude of the world, the whole structure of the world and all that is in the world—human beings, beasts, birds, mountains, trees, cities, rivers, and fish—in a painting or in wax, this would be an emptying.

Similarly, the Word of God the Father, who is everywhere through the invisibility of his divinity, when he deigned to appear visibly in the small form of a human being, as it were emptied and humbled himself and, so to speak, contracted himself in some way. For he is above all things, outside all things, beneath all things, and whatever exists is within him.

For example, as blessed Augustine says, giving an analogy from a sponge and the sea: just as a sponge placed in the midst of the sea and rivers is surrounded everywhere by water—above, within, and on every side—and water penetrates through its hidden passages, so, in comparison with divinity, the world is almost nothing; and divinity surrounds and penetrates all things as the sea surrounds and penetrates the sponge.

“Taking the form of a servant,” that is, truly assuming a human being. “Being made in the likeness of human beings.” Here “likeness” is used for the reality itself: he became a true human being, because “the Word became flesh” (John I), that is, God became human.

“And being found in habit as a human being.” We speak of “habit” in many ways. First, habit is an accident belonging to us which changes the one to whom it happens but is not itself changed. Such is wisdom, which changes a person by making a foolish or dull person wise, while wisdom itself is not changed.

Second, habit is something which changes a person and is itself changed, such as food, which changes us from weakness and languor into strength and health, while it is itself changed when eaten by us.

Third, habit is something which neither changes nor is changed, such as a ring placed on a finger. This form is found very rarely.

The fourth form occurs when things that happen neither change nor are changed, but nevertheless take on another appearance and form, as a garment, which has one appearance when folded or wrapped together and another when worn. This form corresponds to the present comparison. For just as a garment, when put on, adheres to the body but is not changed in its nature—so that it remains a garment forever, although it assumes another appearance and greater honor than it had before—so the Word of God the Father, by assuming humanity, was not changed into a human being, nor was the humanity assumed by the Word changed into the Word. Yet it assumed another form because it became greater in honor and dignity than any other human being, since he was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV).

“He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.” He became obedient to God the Father, whose will was that he redeem the human race; and not only to the Father but also to his mother, as the gospel records, for he came to Nazareth and “was subject to them” (Luke II).

“Even death on a cross.” They crucified him because death on a cross is more savage than all other deaths, on account of its prolonged torment. If they had pierced him with a sword, it would have ended quickly; or it pleased him thus because, since the human being sinned through a tree, he should be redeemed through a tree.

Therefore, on account of which—that is, on account of the torment—or because he was obedient to God the Father, God the Father exalted him: the man assumed by the Word, raising him from the dead on the third day and lifting him up to heaven on the fortieth day, or establishing him above all things. And he gave him the name that is above every name.

What name did he give him? That he should be called and should be the Son of God, he who was the Son of Man, as the paternal voice made known on the day of his baptism, saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). Likewise on the mountain. Or he also gave him the name that is above every name, so that he should be called Jesus, that is, “Savior.” For although we read that human beings in Genesis, and angels in the Book of Blessed Job, were called “sons of God,” nevertheless none of them was called “Savior,” nor properly “Son of God,” but only abusively, because none of them was able to save the human race, except him alone.

So that at the name of Jesus—that is, at the invocation of the name of Jesus—every knee should bend: that is, every class of human beings is subject to him—those in heaven, that is, the angelic powers; those on earth, that is, human beings and creatures; and those in the underworld, that is, demons and the souls that dwell in hell. Alternatively: all the heavenly beings and all those beneath the earth, who are said to be in the underworld, serve his judgment, command, nod, and authority.

And every tongue should confess—that is, every human being should confess—that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father, equal in power and in the nature of divinity.

[Col. 0742A] Therefore, my beloved, in faith and love, just as you have always obeyed—namely, the Lord and me—so now obey our words, not only in my presence, that is, just as you were always obedient in my presence when I was among you, but much more in my absence. For there are many who are obedient in their master’s presence but disobedient in his absence, like servants who serve merely to be seen.

Work out your salvation with fear—that is, with fear of heart—and trembling—that is, with trembling of body—that is, prepare eternal life for yourselves.

For it is God who works in you. Lest he seem to exclude God from our salvation, as though we could be saved without God’s help, he added: “For it is God who works in you,” and so forth. Therefore, every good thing that we have—both good will and good action—is not from ourselves but from God.

But the question arises: If he himself gives the will and the ability, what reward are we worthy of? Indeed, God’s grace and mercy precede us, and we must obey his will; afterward he grants the ability. We must therefore, by obeying, cooperate with him. When we join our will and obedience to his will and ability, the one who goes before us, grants ability, and bestows perseverance is to be praised, so that we may be worthy of eternal reward.

“And to will,” that is, to have good will, “and to accomplish,” in accordance with good will—that is, so that we may always will what is good.

Do everything without murmuring—that is, without murmuring about the good things that the Gospel commands—so that you do not say, “The things that God commands are excessively burdensome.” Without hesitations, that is, doubts: do not doubt in the faith, nor doubt those things that the Gospel promises.

[Col. 0742C] So that you may be without complaint—that is, without reproach—and simple, like the sons of God. Just as God is simple, so his sons ought to walk with a pure and simple heart.

Without reproach—that is, without guilt—in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine. When the Apostle was writing these things to the Philippians, not all of them had yet been reborn or become believers; rather, many were unbelievers, heretics, and false Christians.

Among all of them you shine. The Apostle desired that those among them who were believers should live in such a way that, just as the sun drives away darkness and the moon and the other stars illuminate the night, so they, by shining through faith, works, and teaching, might drive away the darkness of error and the clouds of unbelief from the hearts of unbelievers through their example and teaching.

Like lights—the sun, the moon, and the other stars—in the world, or in this life.

Holding fast the word of life. That is, the right faith by which the just person lives; or the memory of that Word of whom it is said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1).

For my glory on the day of Christ. For it will be a reward for you if you live in this way, and glory for me on the day of judgment, since I ministered the word of life to you.

For I did not run in vain—that is, from place to place preaching—nor did I labor in vain through the exertion of my bodily tongue. And this also is for my glory.

[Col. 0743A] But even if I am poured out—that is, killed by Nero. Nero himself was the priest of Peter and Paul, because he slaughtered them. He slaughtered them, certainly, but he did not offer them, because they offered themselves.

Upon the sacrifice. I rejoice, because I offered you as a sacrifice to God.

And over the service of your faith—that is, over the worship and religion of faith that I taught you.

Blessed Paul, who freed the Philippians from unbelief and sanctified them by cleansing them from sins in baptism, himself offered them, and they themselves were his sacrifice. He also calls worship and religion “service,” as elsewhere: “Let your service be reasonable” (Rom. 12). The meaning is: “Even if,” he says, “I am killed by Nero, I do not feel the punishments or fear death, rejoicing together with all of you, because I offered you as a sacrifice to God and because I taught you the religion of faith.”

And in the same way you also rejoice—that is, just as I rejoice over your faith, so you too should rejoice together with me over my reward, which I am about to receive on your behalf.

I hope in the Lord Jesus Christ to send Timothy, and so forth. Timothy was the Apostle’s disciple, adorned with complete faith, teaching, and good works, and for this reason exceedingly dear to the Apostle, so much so that he is said to be *unanimis* with him—that is, of one will.

He also had others who loved him with the same affection, such as Titus, Luke, Clement, and others. But when he sent this Epistle to them, he had no one with him among the more perfect except this man, for all the others had been dispersed to different places on account of preaching. Therefore he says that, at present, he has no one who is of one mind with him.

Or it may have been that Timothy loved the Philippians more than all his other disciples.

Soon—that is, shortly—to send him to you, so that I too may be of good cheer—that is, may be tranquil and secure in mind—when I have learned through him what concerns you, that is, what is happening among you, both in faith and in conduct.

For I have no one—that is, no one with me at present—who is concerned for you with sincere affection, that is, pure and steadfast affection. The will that was in the Apostle toward the Philippians was also in Timothy. Therefore he says: “I have no one so like-minded who has the same disposition toward you and is so concerned for you.” For this reason he must be sent: he is exceedingly dear to me and takes the greatest care of you.

For all seek their own interests—that is, their own advantages—not those of Jesus Christ. Here he shows why the others who were with him were not so closely united to him as this man. For they all seek their own advantages or their own ease, unwilling to suffer for the salvation of others, unless they receive temporal profits from them; they do not care about eternal recompense.

Know his proven character—that is, his tested worth—because, like a son with his father, he served with me in the Gospel. “He did not serve me,” he says, “but served with me in Christ, in the preaching of the Gospel.” Nevertheless, he also served Blessed Paul.

I therefore hope to send him to you as soon as I see what concerns me. The Apostle, placed in chains, was uncertain whether Nero would behead him or release him from prison. Therefore he said: “When I learn what has happened to me.” If I emerge unharmed from prison, I will send him to you.

But I trust in the Lord that I myself will come to you soon. It should nevertheless be understood that afterward he did not come to them.

[Col. 0744A] But I considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you. Since I cannot send Timothy until I learn what concerns me, I think it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you. He is called Epaphras elsewhere, just as Lucius is called Luke. The Apostle did not concern himself with the exact form of names.

My fellow worker—that is, one laboring together with me in preaching—and fellow soldier, or comrade-in-arms, in the camp of God for the faith.

But your apostle: either the one whom I am sending to you, or the one whom you chose from among your own people and sent to me as an apostle.

And minister to my need and desire: he ministers to what is necessary for me now that I am imprisoned, and, in addition, devotes himself to preaching. He calls him an apostle because he was sent by him. For everyone who is sent is called an apostle.

Because you had heard that he was ill—for indeed he became ill to the point of death—but God had mercy on him, that is, he drew him back from the jaws of death to life.

And not only on him—that is, God had mercy not only on him—but also on me. Why? So that I would not have the sorrow of his death added to the sorrow of his illness.

The blessed Apostle was grieved over Epaphroditus’s illness. But if Epaphroditus had departed from this life, the sorrow of his death would have been added to the sorrow of his illness. Or, because Paul himself was held fast in chains, if Epaphroditus had happened to die—the man who provided what Paul needed—he would have had the sorrow of his death added to the sorrow of his chains.

So that when you see him again you may rejoice. The Apostle’s joy was the Philippians’ joy, just as his sorrow was theirs; likewise, the Philippians’ sorrow was the Apostle’s sorrow, and their joy was his joy, as he himself had said: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep” (Rom. VII).

And I may be without sorrow—that is, when I learn that you have been gladdened by his presence and learn through him what is happening among you.

Therefore receive him with joy in the Lord, and hold such men in honor. That is, receive with spiritual joy not only the one who is your apostle, but all who hold the same faith and devote themselves to good works, as he does.

For on account of the work of Christ he came close to death—that is, on account of his love and preaching of the Gospel he came close to death, preaching and ministering to me contrary to the commands of the authorities.

Handing over his life—that is, to the danger of death—in order to fulfill what was lacking from you in your service to me. The Philippians had heard from the Apostle the word of preaching through which they were saved. If they had possessed the means, and if the length of the journey had not prevented them, they ought themselves to have supplied and ministered to him all temporal assistance.

[Col. 0745A] What they were therefore unable to fulfill, Epaphroditus alone fulfilled on their behalf. Contrary to the emperor’s orders, he remained with Paul in prison and provided him with food and clothing; moreover, he became his companion in preaching. Thus he handed over his life to the danger of death because, as we have said, he approached Paul contrary to the emperor’s command. By ministering to him, he fulfilled what was lacking from them, because he himself did what they ought to have done, as the Apostle declares.

To fulfill what was lacking from you—that is, what you were unable to fulfill because the distance of the lands prevented you—he fulfilled it on your behalf.

## CHAPTER III

Finally—that is, henceforth, and in addition to the things said above—my brothers in the faith, rejoice in the Lord, [Col. 0745B] not in temporal, earthly, and transitory things.

To write the same things to you—that is, the things I taught when I was present—for they are necessary both to you and to me does not trouble me; but see to it that it does not trouble you to read and fulfill them.

Beware of dogs—that is, be on your guard against them and avoid them. He calls the Jews “dogs,” and he calls the same people “evil workers” and “the circumcision,” because it is his custom to call the Jews “the circumcision” and the Gentiles “the uncircumcision.”

He therefore calls them dogs because, just as a dog barks and then bites, so they barked through their speech and, by seducing people, bit them harshly. They were evil workers because they wrongly persuaded the Philippians to practice these things, saying: “You cannot be saved through baptism unless you are circumcised, as the law commands” (Acts 15), because it is written: “The male whose flesh has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. 17).

For we are the circumcision. We—that is, all who believe rightly—are spiritually circumcised, serving God in the spirit, that is, spiritually and not carnally. Or they serve God with the mind, as it is written in the Gospel: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit,” that is, in the mind (John 4).

And we glory in Christ Jesus—that is, in faith in Jesus Christ—and do not place confidence in the flesh, that is, in carnal circumcision, because all the senses of our body have been circumcised.

Although I too have confidence in the flesh—that is, I could have confidence in carnal circumcision, if there were any confidence to be placed in it.

[Col. 0745D] But if anyone else among you Gentiles seems to have confidence in the flesh, I have more. Someone might say: “You are not circumcised, nor were you ordered to be circumcised; why then do you give such commands?” To this he replies: “I do not give such commands because I am not circumcised and cannot place greater confidence in my own glory than any of you Gentiles could, if there were any confidence and righteousness in it after Christ came. Rather, because there is no ground for glorying in it, I do not want you to be circumcised by the Jews.”

Of the stock of Israel—that is, I was born of Israel—of the tribe of Benjamin, which none of you is.

A Hebrew of Hebrews—that is, born of the tribe of Benjamin.

According to the law, a Pharisee—that is, a teacher of the Mosaic law.

According to zeal, persecuting the Church of God. “I was,” he says, “a teacher of the law, and out of devotion and love for the Synagogue, which I wished to establish, I persecuted the Church of God.”

An *aemulus* is called an envious person, an imitator, or a zealous person; in this passage it means “a zealous person.” The blessed Apostle was therefore a zealous adherent of the law, wishing to establish the Synagogue and destroy the Church of God by persecuting the saints.

According to the righteousness that is in the law. If there is any righteousness in the law now, I lived according to it—that is, I lived without guilt and without reproach, as it seemed to me and to others—because I was circumcised on the eighth day, because on the fortieth day the legal offerings were presented on my behalf, and because I observed the festivals, Sabbaths, and all the other things that the law commands.

But whatever things had been gains for me—that is, whatever things I thought would provide me with great profit and reward—I understood all these to be loss to me if I observed them carnally on account of Christ; that is, after I believed in Christ, or on account of the faith in him that I hold, I regard all those things as loss and detriment to those who observe them.

This is on account of the Gospel of Christ, according to whose teaching we ought to live, which surpasses and transcends every Scripture of the divine utterances in dignity and truth.

Nevertheless, I consider everything—that is, the legal precepts—to be loss, that is, harm, to those who hear them, because of the surpassing knowledge—that is, because of the Gospel. For its sake—that is, for Christ’s sake or for the sake of his faith—I have considered as loss all the things that the law commands to be observed carnally, and I count them as nothing, so that I may gain Christ and acquire him, and be found in him—that is, perfect in his faith—not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law, but that which comes from faith in Jesus Christ.

The righteousness that was in the law was called human righteousness because it was practiced by the hands, namely in circumcision and the offering of gifts. The Apostle rejected this righteousness and no longer wished to possess it, but rather desired to be found in the righteousness of faith and the Gospel. This is not human righteousness but God’s, because it is brought about spiritually in baptism and in the mind.

The righteousness that is from God—that is, I say, righteousness in faith, for God is known through faith adorned with good works.

The power of his resurrection—that is, the power of his resurrection is to be known. What is the power of the resurrection? Just as Christ died and rose again and no longer dies, so we too should die to sin in the baptismal font, rise to life, and always walk in newness of life.

This power is known through faith, and through faith in him one comes to participation in Christ’s sufferings, because unless we had faith, we would by no means imitate his suffering. We ought also to imitate it by offering our lives on his behalf, if necessity should arise; or, even within ourselves, we ought to put vices and sins to death.

I have been conformed to his death—that is, I am an imitator of his death and passion.

If somehow—that is, in some way—I may attain to the resurrection of the elect. This resurrection will not belong to all who rise, but only to the elect. Although all—the just and the wicked alike—will rise in an instant on the day of judgment, only the just will meet the Lord, carried by angels into the air, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “We shall be caught up to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thess. 4).

But the wicked will remain on earth until they receive that terrible sentence of the judge: “Go away, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

The resurrection—that is, the resurrection that is to come from the dead on the day of judgment.

Not that I have already received it—that is, I am not saying these things about the resurrection because I have already received perfection, for I am not yet perfect, nor am I already perfectly justified.

As far as concerns that wisdom which is given to mortal human beings, the blessed Apostle was the wisest of all the people who at that time dwelt in the flesh. But as far as concerns the perfection that the saints will receive after the general resurrection, he was not yet perfect, because “now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13), for “we shall see God as he is” (1 John 3).

But I pursue—that is, I will imitate Christ—if somehow I may apprehend perfection, for which I too have been apprehended. All the elect, predestined to eternal life, have been apprehended in the Lord’s passion, because through it they were redeemed—not only those who were to be saved and cleansed through baptism after his resurrection, but also all the righteous who preceded his coming.

But someone may say: “If I have been apprehended in his passion—that is, redeemed—and cleansed in baptism, why do I not at present possess the perfection of faith, wisdom, and righteousness?” The answer is that, because you have defiled the renewal of baptism by living badly, you will not be able to obtain that perfection until, cleansed again through repentance, you come to the one who cleansed you in baptism.

Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended perfection, because in the present age we cannot be perfect.

But one thing—that is, I will say one thing—for my part: forgetting what lies behind. What are the things that lie behind? All temporal and transitory things: estates, riches, and the advantages of the present life. They are said to lie behind because, when we pass from this life through the death of the flesh, we shall leave them all behind us.

Straining forward to what lies ahead. What are the things that lie ahead? The rewards and joys of the heavenly homeland that are to come to us and will remain without end.

Alternatively, the blessed Apostle counted all the good things that he possessed in this world as nothing in comparison with eternal things, and lived each day as though he were always unknowing. Therefore he said: “I forget what lies behind,” always desiring to press on toward other things.

I pursue the goal—that is, I strive toward what has been promised—toward the prize, that is, the crown of heavenly recompense, in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus.

Therefore, as many of us as are perfect, in comparison with others, let us think this way—that is, let us recognize that we are not perfect.

As many of us as are perfect—that is, those who consider themselves perfect in comparison with believers and those of lesser understanding—let us hold this conviction: we are not perfect in comparison with the perfection that we shall receive on the day of judgment.

And if you think or understand anything differently regarding what we have said, this is not from yourselves; rather, God will reveal it to you.

Blessed Bede, speaking in one place from the Apostle’s words, says: “Let each person abound in his own understanding, and if you understand anything else, God will reveal this also to you.” What then? If someone is a heretic, should he abound in his own understanding? Certainly not. I am not speaking about a heretic but about a Christian.

“Let each faithful person,” he says, “abound in his own understanding,” that is, let him strive to fulfill in works what he believes and to abound in virtues. And if he understands something else that is contrary to the faith, God will reveal it to him because of the good works that he possesses, so that he may correct it.

This is what happened to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who gave only one immersion to those being baptized, doing this in ignorance. But because he devoted himself to good works and fulfilled in action what he understood, he deserved to receive a revelation from the Lord, so that he would give three immersions to those being baptized.

To the point we have reached—that is, in the faith to which I have come, with the Lord teaching and my preaching to you—let us remain, walking from virtue to virtue, so that we may understand the same thing—that is, concerning Christ; in other words, let us have one faith and remain in the rule, that is, in the rightness of the faith.

Brothers, be imitators of me. Imitation is a certain knowledge of whatever is imitated; to imitate is to follow. The meaning is: If you cannot imitate and follow Christ, at least imitate me, his disciple, in faith, in works, and in teaching. Just as I believe, act, and teach, so may you believe, act, and teach.

And observe them. The word “observe” has various meanings. Sometimes it means “to avoid and beware of,” as in: “Observe those who cause dissensions and offenses,” that is, avoid them. Sometimes it means “to plot ambushes,” as in: “They too were watching,” that is, laying ambushes. Sometimes it means “to imitate,” as here: “Observe”—that is, imitate—those who possess the form of our teaching, who believe, live, and teach in this way, who walk in this way, that is, who live as I do, just as you have the form of our teaching.

For many walk—that is, do not live rightly—like the pseudo-apostles, whom I often told you about, that is, whom I often preached that you should avoid, when I was present among you.

But now, even weeping, I say this. The Apostle’s love is to be imitated: he even mourned the enemies of Christ’s cross, just as Samuel mourned his enemy Saul, and just as the same Apostle elsewhere mourned the Corinthians who did not repent after fornication.

Weeping, I say, over the enemies of Christ’s cross, so that you may avoid those whose end—that is, the death of the present life—is destruction for them, that is, eternal perdition. For when they have passed from this life, they will be handed over to everlasting punishments.

He calls Jews and other unbelievers “enemies of Christ’s cross,” because they said that a person could not be saved through faith in the Lord’s passion without circumcision.

Their god is their belly—that is, avoid those whose god is their belly. Whose god is their belly? The god of those who preach for the purpose of filling their own belly.

And their glory is in their shame—that is, in their shameful and disgraceful genital member, because they glory in being circumcised.

Those who set their minds on earthly things—that is, those who understand the law not spiritually but carnally; or those who wish to observe carnal circumcision in themselves and in others.

But our citizenship is in heaven. He joins himself to the other saints, who inhabit the earth in body but heaven in mind. From there—that is, from heaven—we also await the Savior, who is to come for judgment.

He will transform—that is, by renewing, he will form anew—the body of our lowliness. Our body is a body of lowliness, since through death it can be humbled into dust and worms. He first formed this body in the mother’s womb, but he will form it anew through the glory of the resurrection.

Conformed—that is, made like—to the body of his glory, that is, in glory and immortality. The bodies of the saints will possess after the day of judgment the glory that Christ’s body possessed when it was glorified on the mountain, for we shall be like the angels.

Someone might say: “How will he be able to reform our bodies, which will have been corrupted by worms and reduced to dust?” To this the blessed Apostle replies: “According to that power by which he raised himself on the third day, and by which he was able to subject all things to himself, he will also reform our bodies on the day of judgment according to his glory.”

According to the operation by which he is able—that is, by which he can or could—subject all things to himself.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, my brothers in the faith, most beloved in love, and greatly desired in work or affection, my joy—that is, my joy in the present—

and my crown—that is, my crown in the future, because I acquired you for God—stand firm; that is, persevere in faith, in works, and in teaching, as you heard and saw from me.

I urge Euodia and I beseech Syntyche to think the same thing in the Lord—that is, to think what we think: I and the other faithful, who think and believe perfectly as I do.

They were wise and religious women among the Philippians, who preached at home within their own sex. They also taught little boys and little girls, but not in the church, because the same Apostle commands that women should be silent in the church.
