And I ask you also, loyal companion. Germanus was his companion in faith and in the office of preaching, and yet he was wealthy. Therefore he instructed the man who abounded in resources to assist them, whether in material wealth or even in preaching.

Companion—one who shares faith and service.

Help them—that is, the women mentioned above—who labored with me, teaching within their own sex.

Together with Clement. Clement was a philosopher, but afterward became a disciple of the apostles Peter and Paul. He presided as bishop over the Church at Rome and was thrown into the sea for Christ’s name.

And my other fellow workers. Lest the Philippians take it badly that their names were not included in this Epistle, he added: “And my other fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.”

The meaning is: “O Philippians, do not take it hard that I have not named all of you in my Epistle. For even if you are not written in my Epistle, you are nevertheless contained in the book of life, because you are my fellow workers.”

This is the book of life of which the Lord says: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10)—that is, in the book of life, that is, in the memory of almighty God.

Rejoice in the Lord always. You who do not rejoice in temporal things, earthly business, or things that are perishable and transitory, rejoice in the Lord—in faith, in speech, and in work—in mind and body.

Let your moderation—that is, your gentleness and humility—be known to all people, faithful and unfaithful, heretics and false brothers.

Let it be known to the faithful, so that they may be strengthened in every goodness by your example, becoming imitators of you, so that you may receive a reward.

Let it be known to the unbelievers, so that, seeing your religion and good conduct, they may not be able to defame your faith and the name of the Lord Savior, but rather may be recalled from error by your example.

The Lord is near: near to all who believe rightly, live justly, teach well, and have an undefiled heart; or he is near because he is about to draw you from this life through the death of the flesh; or he is near because he is about to come for judgment.

Do not be anxious about worldly and earthly things. Anxiety is excessive care. But the just ought not to have excessive care for transitory things; they should place all their hope in the Lord, according to what the Psalmist says: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Ps. 54).

But in every prayer and supplication with thanksgiving. Prayer is for past offenses and sins; supplication is for obtaining future things; thanksgiving is for benefits already bestowed.

Therefore we ought to give thanks to almighty God for the benefits he has bestowed, so that, when we are found not to be ungrateful for gifts received, we may not be judged unworthy of those we are to receive.

Let your requests be made known before God. “Do not,” he says, “take on excessive concern for temporal things, but let your requests be made known before God,” that is, let them become known to God through the ministry of the angels.

If almighty God knows not only past and present things but also future things, and discerns not only works but also thoughts, and is wholly present everywhere, what need is there for the things we do to be reported to him through the ministry of angels?

They do not announce these things to him because anything is hidden from him, in accordance with what Solomon says: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men.” Rather, they do so in order to fulfill their office and ministry, because they are messengers.

And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding. It surpasses—that is, transcends—the understanding both of angels and of human beings, though not God’s understanding.

What peace is he speaking about? The peace by which we have been reconciled to God through the passion of his Son. Before the Lord’s coming, we were far from God and at odds both with God and with the angels; but through the passion of the Son of God we have been reconciled to God.

This reconciliation must always guard us. It surpasses every understanding except the Lord’s, because no angel and no human being can penetrate the mystery of the passion of the Son of God, our reconciliation, or the greatness of the love that was in him, since, although he was God, he deigned to become human for you.

May it guard your hearts and your understandings. “Heart” and “intellect” are to be understood as one and the same.

In Christ Jesus—that is, through Jesus Christ, or in the faith of Jesus Christ.

Finally, brothers, in addition to the things mentioned above, whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovable—that is, all the things contained in the Gospel—think about these things, and fulfill them in action through your thinking, because these things are true.

All true things are chaste and pure, because they are free from every lie, inviolate and incorrupt. Those things are just and holy that teach holiness and righteousness.

Whatever things are of good repute—that is, whatever things cause us to have a good reputation—think about and accomplish all these things.

If there is any virtue—that is, of faith, action, or teaching—and anything by which God can be praised, apply those things to God, not to your own merits.

What you have heard—that is, through our letters or from me personally—and seen in action, do these things. And the God of peace will be with you—that is, the God who is the Father of peace, namely, of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is our peace and who made the two one.

I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that at last, and so forth. At the beginning of the Apostle’s preaching, when the Philippians believed, they showed him the greatest kindness, supplying cheerfully whatever was necessary for him. But when they began to suffer persecution from their unbelieving fellow citizens and to be troubled by their persecutors, they ceased their ministrations.

For, placed amid revolt and persecution, they could not fulfill the duty of charity in the same way as in a time of peace. But when tranquility was restored to them with the Lord’s assistance, they returned to their former way of life and began to supply the Apostle and the other saints with what was necessary.

Therefore the Apostle rejoices together with them over their goodness and says: “I rejoiced greatly, because at last”—that is, in the end, or scarcely after some time—you flourished again, that is, produced the flower of virtues, returning to your former way of life and practice.

You flourished—that is, you produced the flower of good action; in other words, you began to display toward me the affection of love, as you had done before.

But you were occupied—that is, in the persecution by your fellow citizens.

He excuses them here, saying: “I forgive you if for a time you omitted this, because you were held back by the persecution of your enemies.”

Not as though I speak because of want—that is, need—for I have learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be self-sufficient. That is, I know in what circumstances I can have sufficiency, because I know how to bear want patiently and how to manage abundance with moderation.

There are many who, placed in poverty, do not know how to bear it patiently; and there are many who, placed in abundance, do not know how to practice moderation. They eat and drink beyond measure and use what they possess excessively. The Apostle was far removed from their number.

I know how to be brought low—that is, I know how to endure want patiently—and I know how to abound, that is, how to be temperate in abundance, lest I be corrupted by it.

In every circumstance I have been instructed, both to be filled—that is, to abound—and to be hungry, that is, to suffer want.

I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Lest he seem to attribute this to himself, as though he were able by his own strength to endure poverty patiently and to remain temperate in abundance, he says: “I can accomplish all these things in him who strengthens me,” that is, in Christ, who grants me the ability.

Nevertheless, you did well by sharing in my tribulation. That is, although I lack nothing, you did well by fulfilling the duty of charity toward me, sharing in my sufferings and sending me what was necessary.

[Col. 0752B] “You know also,” etc., up to “I departed from Macedonia.” Macedonia is a province of the Greeks, named from Macedon; and Thessalonica is a city named after King Thessalus. In this, therefore, when he praises the Philippians who sent him what he needed, he reproves others who offered him no service. “In the account of giving and receiving.” Whatever is received or given can have an account attached to it. The account of giving is that the giver knows what he gives, or how much he gives, or to whom he gives it—whether he gives gold or clothing, a pound of gold or a horse. The account of receiving is that the one who receives some metal or clothing knows how much he receives and from whom he receives it. The meaning is therefore: From all those things concerning which there can be an account of giving and receiving, they did not minister to me, because they gave me nothing and I received nothing.

[Col. 0752C] “I do not seek the gift”—understand: alone—but I seek the fruit, that is, the goodwill and kindness of spirit, abounding in your prayer, that is, for your benefit. Some manuscripts read: “Abounding in your prayer.” The Apostle’s prayer was the prayer of the Philippians, because he prayed for them. And whenever anyone prays for another, if the life of the one for whom prayer is offered has been pure, it lifts up the prayer of the petitioner, so that he may be heard by God; conversely, the evil life of the one for whom prayer is offered hinders the prayer of the one praying for him. Hence the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Do not pray for this people, because I will not hear you” (Jer. VII). Therefore the prayer of blessed Paul, which he poured out for them, was lifted up by their good life. Hence he says: “I do not seek only the gift, but I seek the goodwill and kindness of spirit abounding in your prayer,” that is, so that your good will may lift up the prayer that I pour out for you.

“I have everything, and I abound.” He has everything who needs nothing and seeks nothing beyond what is necessary. “I have been filled,” he says—understand: with every abundance—having received from Epaphroditus—understand: gifts—which you sent me. The Philippians had sent him, through Epaphroditus, either gold, silver, or clothing; and he rejoiced and gave thanks greatly over these things, not so much for his own need as for the need of others. “As an odor of sweetness.” An odor of sweetness before God is the good intention and most ready will of the one offering; concerning this we read in Genesis that “the Lord smelled the odor of sweetness” [Col. 0753A] when Noah, having come out of the ark, offered sacrifice to God. For it must not be thought that the almighty Lord takes pleasure in the sacrifice of victims, the smoke of flesh, and the smell of fat, but rather in the good intention and most ready will of the one offering. For if he delighted in smoke and the smell of flesh, he would certainly not have said through the prophet: “My soul hates your sacrifices.”

“Now may my God fulfill all your desire.” The Philippians had such a desire that they might deserve to become companions and fellow-partakers of the blessed Apostle; and the meaning is: May my God grant and provide that, just as you are partakers of my suffering and suffer with me in my tribulations, so you may be partakers of my rewards and rejoice with my joy. And how will this happen? “According to his riches in eternal glory.” What are those riches? Those “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart,” that is, eternal joys and rewards that will remain without end. And this is “in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ Jesus.

“Now to God and our Father,” that is, to the holy Trinity, which is one God, “let honor remain for ages of ages,” that is, through all future ages.

[Col. 0754A] “Greet every saint,” that is, everyone sanctified in baptism, or those who flourish without crime and without serious sin. “But especially those who are of Caesar’s household.” Why did he add, “But especially those who are of Caesar’s household”? So that he might sharpen and urge the Philippians to preserve the faith and labor in good works, as if he were saying: O Philippians, pay attention: if those who are the emperor’s attendants and must always stand before him in his palace come to the faith, regarding the emperor’s anger as nothing, and labor manfully in faith and doctrine, how much more ought you to preserve the faith with fervent spirit and persist in good works—you who are far removed from the royal court and are not terrified by the command of wicked rulers? For while the Apostle remained imprisoned in the emperor’s household, many from Caesar’s household came to him; and, instructed by him, they were baptized, so that—as we have already said—they made the house of the persecutor into the Church of the Redeemer.

“May the grace of the Lord”—that is, faith or salvation, redemption and forgiveness of sins—“remain with your spirit,” that is, in your heart and mind; for if it remains in the mind, it will also remain in the heart, and so forth.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

[Col. 0753]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0753B]

[Col. 0753C] “The mystery that was hidden from ages and generations.” The mystery of the incarnation and passion of the Son of God, and of the redemption of the human race, was hidden from the wise of this age from the beginning of the world; but it was revealed to the patriarchs, prophets, and many other righteous people.

“Which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.” Christ is the hope of the glory of the elect, because whoever firmly believes in him hopes to receive eternal life and the glory that he himself promised.

“Correcting every person.” Here we must understand “every person” as Jew and gentile, lord and servant, rich and poor, and every sex and condition of people to whom the apostles were commanded to preach. But what he says, “admonishing every person,” applies to the ungrateful and proud; and what he says, “teaching,” applies to the humble and submissive. “In all wisdom,” that is, in faith in the holy Trinity, in which all wisdom exists. “Perfect in Christ Jesus,” that is, in the faith of Jesus Christ, insofar as any elect person can be perfect in the present age. In the present age, indeed, no one can be perfect in comparison with eternal perfection. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “As many as are perfect, let us have this understanding” (Philipp. III), because—understand—we are not perfect. For what we now see in a riddle and hold in hope, we shall then possess in reality, since “we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

[Col. 0753D] “In which I also labor, contending.” He mentions two things, labor and struggle: one refers to preaching, the other to conflict with enemies. “I labor,” he says, [Col. 0754B] in preaching, “contending” against the enemies of Christ; and this not by my own powers or strength, but according to the help that he grants me.

## CHAPTER TWO

“I want you to know, O Colossians, what concern I have for you.” Concern is the greatest care. Blessed, therefore, the Apostle had the same concern and zeal for those who were taught by his disciples and to whom he sent letters, although he himself had not seen them bodily, as he had for those whom he taught with his own mouth. He spoke in such a flattering way so that he might soothe their minds and they might receive his Epistle. “And for those who are in Laodicea.” Laodicea is a city of Greece. “Instructed,” that is, strengthened and taught. “In love,” that is, in love of God and neighbor, “unto the knowledge of the mystery of God,” that is, unto knowledge of the holy Trinity and faith in the Lord and Savior, believing that he came in the flesh for our salvation.

“In whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” Wisdom refers to human matters, knowledge to divine matters; and in Christ Jesus there is wisdom concerning how he should administer temporal and human affairs, and knowledge of how he should order divine things. Or wisdom in human matters and knowledge in divine matters are hidden, because they are not evident to everyone. Before the Lord’s coming, the name of the Lord the Father was unknown to all previous generations—not the name by which God is called, but the name by which he is called Father, as the Son himself says: “Father, I have manifested your name” (John XVII).

[Col. 0754D] “Now I say this”—understand: so that you may be strengthened in love—“so that no one may deceive you by subtlety,” that is, by fineness of speech, “and by cleverness,” or by syllogisms. Some manuscripts read “by sublimity,” which has the same meaning as “height.”

[Col. 0755A] “For even though I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing in your faith and seeing your order,” that is, because the Holy Spirit who is in me reveals it, I know everything that is being done among you in faith and good works, as though I were present in body. Blessed Jerome says in one place that such grace was given to him that he knew everything that was being done among those whom either he himself or his disciples had taught. “And its firmness.” He calls the firmness of Christ’s faith the firm and perfect faith that is ordered by good works.

[Col. 0755B] “Therefore, as you received,” that is, as you have received and retained, “him,” that is, his faith, “walk, rooted.” By “rooted” he means built upon Christ and confirmed in his faith; and this amounts to one thing: adorn the faith you possess with good works. “As you have also learned”—understand: from our disciples—“abounding,” that is, in his faith, “in thanksgiving,” that is, always giving him thanks for everything you possess.

“See that no one deceives you through philosophy,” that is, through human wisdom and empty deceit by which people are deceived. The Apostle foresaw that there were philosophers among the gentiles and also among the Jews who wanted to separate the Colossians from the faith through the sublimity of human wisdom. For they said that, just as nothing bodily can produce a body by itself without the mingling of a bodily substance that is female, so a woman cannot give birth without the mingling of a man. They said this by attending to the nature of the elements, not to the power of divinity, which can change the nature of the elements. By “nature” I mean order. For nature is that every creature should obey its Creator.

They also said that, if blessed Mary the virgin conceived and gave birth as a virgin, nevertheless she was not a virgin after the birth. Therefore he addresses them so that they would not be deceived by such people. “For in him,” that is, in Christ, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” He does not say “bodily” because divinity itself is a body, although it is a living substance; rather, he used “bodily” in the sense of truly, substantially, and fully. For divinity dwells in each of the elect in one way and in Christ in another: to them the Spirit is given according to measure, but in him fully. It dwelt in Solomon through wisdom, in Daniel through chastity, in the prophets through holiness, in Moses through gentleness, but in Christ through every virtue and innocence. Alternatively: “Bodily,” that is, as in his temple, because the body of Christ was the dwelling place of the whole divinity. It dwelt in him more fully than in the temple of the Jews.

“And you are filled in him,” that is, in Christ, or you are filled through him by faith. “Who is the head,” that is, the principle and beginning, because he holds primacy over all heavenly and earthly things. “Of every principality and power.” [Col. 0756A] Powers are those through which the saints cast demons out of possessed bodies; principalities are those that rule over the other orders.

“In whom,” that is, in Christ, “you were circumcised,” that is, cleansed from all sins in Christ’s baptism—not by the handmade circumcision with which he himself was circumcised on the eighth day according to Jewish custom. That circumcision was made with stone, whereas this cleansing is through Christ, who is the rock.

“Buried with him,” that is, buried together with him in baptism, “in whom,” that is, in Christ, “you also rose again from sin and vices through faith.” How were we buried with him? By way of example: Christ died on the cross, was placed in the tomb, rose alive from the tomb, and now dies no more. Likewise, when, while standing beside the font, we renounce the devil and all his pomp at the priest’s questioning, it is as though we then die; when we descend into the font, it is as though we are then buried in the tomb; and when we come out of the font cleansed, then it is as though we rise again. But we must take care that, just as Christ now dies no more, so we too may not die in sin. “Through faith in the operation of God.” The power of the Divinity that raised Christ on the third day itself works faith in us.

[Col. 0756B] “And you, when you were dead in transgressions and in the uncircumcision of your flesh.” “Transgressions” and “uncircumcision” refer to one thing, namely, carnal sins; or they refer to transgression, forgiving sins committed afterward, that is, granting pardon.

“Blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us.” A *chirographum* is called a handwritten document. For χείρ (*cheir*) means “hand,” and γραφή (*graphē*) means “writing.” By “decree” he means the law and statute that God commanded Adam, saying: “Eat from every tree of paradise,” etc., “you shall surely die” (Gen. II). The sin, therefore, that our first parent committed—in which we all sinned and became mortal—he now calls the handwriting of the decree, because it remained written in the memory of almighty God until the Son of God came and removed it. Hence God is said in the Psalms, in the Song of Moses, to say: “Are these things not stored up with me and sealed in my treasures?” (Deut. XXXII).

For “hand” signifies action; and when he extended his hand to touch the forbidden tree, it was as though he then wrote the handwriting of the decree, that is, the handwritten record of what he was doing against God’s decree. [Col. 0756D] That handwriting was against us because it drew everyone to death, and no one could be justified until it was erased by the Lord. How, then, did he erase it? By living innocently and without sin in the world, or by dying innocently on the cross for sinners. And he took it itself—understand: the handwriting or the sin—out of the midst, fastening it to the cross, because, as we have said, he crucified it, that is, killed it in himself, when he lived without sin, or when he, innocent, died for sinners. Another translation reads: “Stripping himself of the flesh by dying on the cross,” and “he set forth an example,” that is, he gave an example by living innocently, “triumphing over the principalities and powers of darkness.” And he took it itself out of the midst—understand: out of our midst—[Col. 0757A] because, having become our mediator, he removed our sins, which were as if in our midst when they separated us from God.

“Stripping the principalities,” that is, he stripped the demonic powers of the souls of the dead, and removed their power from this world; and he “led the powers in triumph,” that is, he overcame them confidently, openly triumphing over them in himself, because he lived innocently by himself and was openly crucified. “Triumphing”—conquering and overcoming in himself, in the same ways that we have described.

“Therefore let no one judge you,” that is, do not heed anyone’s judgment in this matter: that you should abstain from what God has commanded. For “it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person” (Matt. XV). “In food or drink, or in a part of a feast day,” with some saying that certain days are feast days. They spend the days and observe Sabbaths by resting from vices and passing from vices to virtues.

[Col. 0757B] “Which are a shadow of future things”—understand: all the things mentioned above concerning food and drink, which are found in the law, are shadows of other things that have been and are being fulfilled in Christ and in the Church. “But the body of Christ,” that is, the truth and substance of those things or shadows, “is Christ and the Church.” For there were Jews who wanted to observe the law and the Gospel together, and they urged the Colossians to do likewise—in circumcision and in the observance of the legal festivals. They said: “You have been baptized; you ought to be circumcised. You have already shared in the body and blood of the Lord; you ought to offer the legal sacrifices. You ought to eat what the law commands and abstain from what it forbids; and if a mouse falls into a well, you must not drink.” But so that they would not be led astray by them, the Apostle wrote such things to them, because at the Lord’s coming everything was cleansed and the law ceased in its mysteries.

[Col. 0757C] “Let no one deceive you,” or separate you from the faith, “desiring”—understand: desiring to deceive you—“in humility,” that is, in order to deceive your understanding. A person is called humble from being inclined toward the ground. “Desiring to deceive you in humility,” that is, through a humble understanding and humble teaching that has no usefulness, such as distinctions among foods and observance. “And in the religion of angels,” that is, in the worship of angels. There were gentile philosophers and some Jews who said: “Just as there are four elements, so there are four angels who preside over the individual elements.” These people therefore said to those who had believed, wishing to appear religious: “Since you are constituted from the four elements, you ought to offer some worship and sacrifices to those angels who preside over the elements.”

But because what they said was nothing, the Apostle added: “Which he has not seen”—understand: teaching and walking in vain, puffed up by the understanding of his flesh, that is, walking puffed up by his own error and falsehood. Because he appeared to know something, he was proud in his mind, displaying humility in his expression. Or, as another edition reads, “which he has not seen, inculcating,” that is, repeating it in vain. Although some people had indeed seen that false religion being practiced, they had not seen the angels themselves, nor the things they taught.

“And not holding fast to the head,” that is, not clinging to the head, namely Christ, who is the head of all the saints. From him the whole body is supplied, that is, the multitude of holy angels and the multitude of human beings are increased. “And is constructed through bonds,” that is, through bonds, connections, and joining together, “and grows with the increase of God.” Just as a body is constructed from many members and many joints, so it is increased and grows from many peoples, many provinces, and many kinds of human beings when the number of believers grows daily.

“If you have died with Christ”—understand: at the time of baptism—“to the elements of this world,” that is, to its errors and pomps, “why, as though living in the world”—understand: for the world—“do you make decrees,” that is, why do you make distinctions among foods? Alternatively: “If you have died to the elements of this world,” the elements of the world are all bodily, visible, and transitory things. When the gentiles did not know God, they served the elements of the world, because they served and worshiped them. But when they came to the faith, they died to the elements of this world, that is, to errors and superstitions, or to various and empty forms of worship, renouncing the devil and all his pomps and errors.

We may also understand by the elements of the world the law that commanded distinctions between animal and animal and between food and food. But after the Lord said, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person” (Matt. XV), all that distinction immediately ceased. Hence the Apostle says to both Jews and gentiles: “If you have died with Christ to the elements,” that is, to errors, pomps, and empty religions, at the time of baptism, “why do you still make distinctions among foods, when God has said that all things are clean?”

“Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.” This is the voice of those who said: “Do not touch or handle a dead person, nor the stool on which a menstruating woman has sat, because you will be unclean; and do not taste pork or hare meat, because it is unclean,” and other things of this kind.

“All of which”—understand: all that the law permits or prohibits—“are for destruction by use,” that is, by the very habit of eating, they pass into destruction, because everything is reduced to excrement as soon as it has been eaten. “Which indeed have a rationale of wisdom”—understand: worldly wisdom—“according to the precepts and teachings of human beings,” that is, according to the tradition of the scribes and Pharisees, [Col. 0758D] and according to those who, because of bodily weakness, do not want to eat such things, saying: “I do not want to eat pork because I am melancholic, nor eel.” But this wisdom is not according to God, because it does not pertain to religion in superstition and humility—understand: which is also found in superstition—that is, in empty religion and excessive fear. For this is superstition—understand: a humble understanding. Excessive fear is empty religion and a humble understanding: refusing to eat and calling unclean what God has sanctified, unless someone abstains from these things for the sake of discipline, just as from wine.

[Col. 0759A] “Which are also not for sparing the body,” that is, not for preserving the body’s health. For when someone does not want to eat what he has and desires what he does not have, saying, “Do not eat this, because it is unclean; but if I had mutton, I would eat it,” the person who is sustained by such foods becomes weak and debilitated. “Which are also not in any honor,” but for the satisfaction of the flesh; that is, a ram offers no greater honor to the body than a hare would offer if he ate it, provided only that the belly is filled.

## CHAPTER THREE

“Brothers, if you have risen together with Christ,” that is, from death to life at the time of baptism, “set your mind on the things above,” that is, on the joys of the heavenly homeland. Christ dwells above in the fullness of the Father’s majesty, and wherever he is, there we ought to aspire to be. “Set your mind on the things above,” that is, weigh and understand them and place your mind upon them, not upon the things that are transitory above the earth.

[Col. 0759B] “For you have died.” You have died to sin at the time of baptism, as we said a little above, “and your life,” that is, your blessedness, “is hidden with Christ in God.” For Christ is your life and blessedness, as he himself said: “This is eternal life, that they know you, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII). Therefore, where he is, there our life and blessedness are hidden—not so that they may be denied or concealed from us, but so that they may rather be preserved for our salvation.

“When Christ, your life, appears”—understand: glorious and radiant in judgment—“then you also will appear with him in glory,” glorious and radiant, as he himself promised.

[Col. 0759C] “Therefore put to death your members,” that is, the evil uses of your members. In the Epistle to the Corinthians the Apostle calls the multitude of sins “the body,” saying: “So that the body of sin may be destroyed” (Rom. VI). For just as many members make one body, so many sins make one body, that is, one totality. The meaning is: Put to death your members, that is, the evil uses of your members and the evil habit of sinning, showing the effect through the agent that produces it. He does not command us to kill our body and members with a material sword, but to kill sins. We put our members to death when we cease to sin; and however many sins we put to death in ourselves, we kill, as it were, that many members, which are upon the earth—that is, as long as you are in the world.

[Col. 0759D] “Fornication.” Fornicators are those who have intercourse with unmarried girls, or with an animal, or do something of that sort. To commit adultery is to violate another person’s bed, that is, to have intercourse with another man’s wife or with a woman consecrated to God, who is God’s wife. “Lust.” Every lack of self-control is called lust. “Evil desire.” He says “evil desire” because there is also good desire, of which it is said: “Son, desire wisdom; keep the commandment,” and: “I desire to depart and be with Christ.” Evil desire is desiring evil things.

“And greed, which is the service of idols.” How is greed the service of idols? Because, just as the one who takes away from the omnipotent God, insofar as he can, the worship and religion that belong to him alone, and his unique name by which he is called God, and gives them to demons, serves the devil, so the one who appropriates for his own use the good things of almighty God, which have been given equally to all human beings, serves the devil. Greed is also rightly compared with idolatry because, while people serve metals—gold and silver—from which idols are made, they venerate gold in place of God (Exod. XX), because they are slaves of riches. Or, in a third way, he compared greed with idolatry in order to show that nothing is more wicked. For greed is the root of evils, and therefore he urges that it be avoided by every means.

[Col. 0760A] “Because of these crimes”—that is, those mentioned above—“the wrath of God came upon the sons who perished in the flood and in Sodom and other cities, and upon the sons of unbelief,” that is, upon those six hundred thousand who died in the desert, possessing unbelief of heart. “Among whom”—understand: in those sins—“you too once walked when you were living” in sin before faith, and were dead to God; but now you no longer walk in them.

[Col. 0760B] “But now you also put away everything”—understand: both the things mentioned above and those that follow—“anger,” because “the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God”; “indignation,” that is, do not become indignant at those of lesser status when they rebuke you; “malice.” Malice is an evil will. “Blasphemy,” that is, mockery directed against God and neighbor; “shameful speech,” that is, an idle or joking word from your mouth—understand: put all this away.

“Do not lie to one another.” Every lie is from the devil, because he is a liar and its father; therefore the children of truth ought to speak truth with their neighbors, [Col. 0760C] “stripping off the old person.” Here he calls the conduct and life of the old person the “old person.” What is the conduct of the old person? Unbelief, disobedience, evil desire, robbery, adultery, murder, and other things of this kind. Until a person is renewed in the baptism of regeneration, he will always remain in oldness, because he is held liable by original and actual sins. But he ought to be baptized and put on the new person, that is, a new mind and the new conduct of the new person. What is the conduct of the new person? To pursue virtues and possess every good thing within oneself.

And lest we think that he commanded the outward person to be renewed according to the likeness of something, he added: “I command that person to be renewed who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him,” that is, the inner person: the soul and mind that was made in the image of God, holy, just, rational, and immortal. But the outward person, that is, the body, was not made in the image of God, because God is spirit.

There are two renewals: one instantaneous, which takes place in baptism; the other takes place daily, when, through diligent study of the holy Scriptures, a person strives to understand concerning God what he previously did not know, and the mind is therefore renewed each day. A third renewal can also take place after a fall through repentance, “in knowledge,” that is, unto the knowledge, “according to the image of the one who created him,” because the human being was made in the image of God.

[Col. 0761A] “Where there is neither gentile nor Jew.” “Where,” that is, in the human mind where the image of God is, sex, condition, race, or province is not given precedence before God; that is, there is no distinction among human beings before God, because there is no sex in the soul. Only good conduct together with right faith is required. “Barbarian and Scythian.” A Scythian is more foreign to us than a barbarian. A barbarian can be anyone whose language we do not know; but a Scythian is so called from Scythia, a province remote in the north, stiff with cold, and barbarous in its customs. “But Christ is all and in all.” Therefore there is no distinction, because all—understand: all kinds of faithful human beings—have Christ as their head, and Christ is in all of them.

[Col. 0761B] “Holy, beloved”—one thing is understood. “Bowels of mercy,” that is, a merciful will. Children are called “bowels.” *Viscus* can also signify, in the singular, a most ready and good will. “Kindness,” that is, a great and good will; “modesty,” that is, gentleness; “patience”—understand: in enduring adversities.

“Supporting one another.” The Apostle commands us to support one another according to the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens.” By way of example: the person who is continent, without wife and children, and abounds in riches and temporal goods, ought to sustain the person who is incontinent and has a wife and children, if there is need. The same should be understood concerning other needs, imitating deer that, when crossing some strait to an island or to the far side of a river, sustain and support one another, the one following placing his chin upon the haunches of the one in front; and when the one who was going first becomes tired, he gives way so that another may cross, and that one in turn places his chin upon the haunches of the last.

“And forgiving,” that is, pardoning, “if anyone has a complaint against another,” that is, a genuine cause of complaint. By way of example: someone has taken away my horse; when I remember that the Lord said, “If anyone takes away what is yours, do not demand it back,” I ought to forgive him. The same applies to every possession and offense. “As the Lord forgave you, so also do you.” Just as Christ, although he had nothing that could be forgiven him, forgave us all our sins in baptism, so we too should forgive the neighbor who sins against us, since we have something that must be forgiven both by God and by our neighbor.

[Col. 0761D] “Above all these things mentioned above, have love, which is the bond of perfection.” Love is the bond of perfection, because through it all good things are bound together so that they do not perish. Thus a person does everything out of love of God and neighbor. Hence it is called *dilectio*, “love,” because it binds two people together, or a person and God. “In which”—understand: in peace or love—“you were called in one body,” so that you may be one body of Christ, “and be grateful,” that is, gracious and acceptable both to God and to human beings.

“And let the word of Christ,” that is, evangelical teaching, “dwell in you,” that is, in your heart, mouth, and works. “And let the peace of Christ rejoice,” and likewise you, insofar as human frailty can preserve it, remaining without the stain of sin, so that you may have the Holy Spirit within you, [Col. 0762A] “in all wisdom,” in all the teaching of the Gospel and in faith in the holy Trinity, “teaching and admonishing yourselves.” You who are wiser should teach, admonish, and exhort one another, “in psalms”—understand: those of David—“and hymns,” those of the three youths and of the saints, “singing in grace,” that is, always giving thanks to God, so that what you sing with your mouth you understand with your heart, and your mind may agree with your voice.

“Whatever you do in word,” that is, in teaching, “or in deed”—understand: in any deed—“in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” always say in everything: “O God, attend to my help” (Ps. LXIX), and always invoke the name of the Lord, “giving thanks to God and the Father through him,” that is, through Christ, because he is our mediator and we are saved through faith in him.

[Col. 0762B] “Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.” Woman, because of guilt, is subject to man, as is fitting in the Lord, just as the Lord commands in Genesis: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III). At the beginning of the faith there were indeed many women who, for the sake of religion, abstained from intercourse with their husbands. The Apostle now addresses them specifically, so that because they abstained from intercourse with men they would not resist, rebel against, or oppose their husbands. For just as the holy Church is subject to her spouse and husband, Christ, so every woman ought to be. There were also many men who likewise abstained from intercourse, or who had intercourse with other women, and beat their wives so that they would not behave similarly with others, nor dare to murmur against them. He addresses these men in the same way.

[Col. 0762C] “Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them,” that is, if you abstain from intercourse for a time for the sake of religion, or because you have intercourse with other women, do not therefore provoke your wives to bitterness. But a question arises here: Why does the Apostle proclaim that a wife should be loved, when the Lord says: “Whoever does not hate … his wife … cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV)? This is resolved in the following way: insofar as father and mother, brother and wife, are close to us through the kinship of the flesh, we should love them; but insofar as we recognize them as adversaries on the way of God, we should hate their evil and, by fleeing it, cease to know them [reading uncertain].

[Col. 0762D] “Children, obey your parents,” that is, father and mother, “in everything”—understand: in whatever pleases God. But if they command you to commit murder, theft, robbery, or anything of that kind, do not obey them. “For this is pleasing in the Lord”—understand: that you obey them.

“Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, so that they may not become fainthearted,” that is, so that, exasperated by you, they may not become irritable, quick to anger, but may learn through your example to be patient.

Servants, obey your masters in everything, that is, in matters which do not displease God. Servants are not so by nature, but through guilt and because of sin, as in the case of Canaan, the son of Ham. For captivity came because of sin, and through captivity came servitude. Hence those who were kept by enemies were called *servi* (“servants”) from *servare* (“to preserve”), and *mancipia* (“bondservants”), as though captured by hand, because they were seized by hand. [Col. 0763A] Do not serve merely for appearances. He serves merely for appearances who does something else in secret, and in the master’s presence performs his service in whatever manner; but when the master is absent, he does not care about his welfare. Rather, serve in singleness of heart, that is, not with a divided mind or evil intention, as though serving the Lord and not human beings. A servant who serves his earthly master for the love of God, hoping thereby to receive a reward from God, renders that service not to a human being but to God. Therefore, even if he does not receive a present reward from his master, he ought not to withdraw from his service; his reward is the inheritance of eternity, that is, an eternal recompense. Serve the Lord Christ: although you render temporal service to human beings, fulfill it for the love of Christ.

[Col. 0763B] For whoever does wrong—that is, if a master unjustly oppresses a servant and does not give him a fitting wage—will receive condemnation for it. And if a servant is thievish and has in some respect withdrawn himself from his master’s service, he too will be condemned for that. Let servants not say, “Since we are servants, we shall not deserve to come to the glory of the saints.” The Apostle says: “There is no acceptance of persons with God”; that is, if the master has acted badly and the servant well, the master will be condemned and the servant glorified.

## CHAPTER IV

Masters, provide your servants with what is just and fair; that is, do not hold them as slaves, but be to them as fathers. For certain men were called *patresfamilias* (“fathers of households”) because they loved everyone in their household with equal affection as sons [Col. 0763C], and likewise their servants.

Persevere in prayer, keeping watch. A person keeps watch in prayer and in giving thanks to God when he does not perform it according to the hour or with laziness, but with cheerfulness. For if what is requested cannot be obtained from a human being when it is done lazily, how much more is this true with God?

Praying also for us—that is, for us who have administered the word of life—so that God may open to us a door for the word; that is, so that he may open the hearts and understanding of our hearers, so that what we say and send forth from our mouths may enter their hearts and understanding, and so that they may understand what we teach. We read something similar in the Acts of the Apostles concerning a woman named [Col. 0763D] Lydia, a seller of purple from the city, whose heart the Lord opened so that she might understand what was being said by Paul. Or otherwise: “so that he may open to us a door of speech,” that is, the meaning and understanding of the divine utterances, so that we may be ready to speak of the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation and divinity, on account of which—that is, the Gospel—we should speak as I ought to speak: that is, so that I may know to whom, what, when, and how much I ought to say.

Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside; that is, in faith in the holy Trinity, in which all wisdom exists, and live and conduct yourselves there in good behavior toward those who are outside—that is, toward pagans, heretics, and false Christians—so that they may not be able to reproach you. Redeem the time; that is, make it your own, gaining it for yourselves by living well [Col. 0764A] and speaking rightly. For the person who works for his own advantage in time redeems it for himself.

Let your speech always be seasoned with grace, with salt; that is, let it always offer grace and benefit to your hearers, and be pleasing to everyone. Just as salt gives flavor to every food, so let speech season the minds of all, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person—that is, how to answer a heretic and how to answer a Christian. If a heretic questions you, answer that you believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that these three possess a Trinity in persons and unity in substance; and that the Lord Jesus Christ is true God and true man. A Christian likewise must be answered in this way.

[Col. 0764B] Tychicus will make known to you everything concerning me—my bonds and my imprisonment. He was a preacher of the Colossians, most beloved—that is, in the faith, because we share one faith—a minister—that is, in the preaching of the Gospel—and a fellow servant in labor, because we labor together in preaching. And may he comfort your hearts with consolation; that is, by his arrival and by my example, so that you may not fail in faith but rather be strengthened, and, if necessity should arise, may be able to endure such things as I also endure, together with Onesimus, the most beloved. Here it is shown that Philemon the Colossian was the master of Onesimus, and that Onesimus himself was with him. “He will make known to you”—that is, Tychicus and Onesimus will do so.

Aristarchus greets you. Aristarchus was a disciple of the blessed Paul and a companion in preaching, my fellow prisoner [Col. 0764C]—that is, one held in bonds as I am for the name of Christ—and so too is Mark. This is the man over whom disagreement arose between Paul and Barnabas, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles. He withdrew from the blessed Paul during a certain conflict that Paul had with the persecutors. Some say that Mark himself wrote the Gospel, because although he had been with the blessed Paul, he had also been with the blessed Peter. He is a cousin of Barnabas. Cousins are called *consobrini*, as though “sister’s sons,” because they are born from individual sisters. He says that Mark is his cousin so that Mark might be held in greater honor among them because of Barnabas; and unless he had said, “Receive him,” they would by no means have dared to receive him, because they had already heard that he had departed from Paul. Once corrected and reformed, he was again associated with him. Concerning Mark, therefore, you have received instructions—that is, written instructions [Col. 0764D]—because they are now returning to us. These alone are the ones mentioned above who are from the circumcision, that is, from the Jews.

They alone are my hearers in the kingdom of God—that is, in the preaching of the Gospel, which brings those who observe it to the kingdom of God. May you stand perfect—that is, perfect in faith—and full of good works.

And those who are in Laodicea, which is a city of Greece; Hierapolis is a city of Greece.

Luke the physician greets you. This is Luke who wrote the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, and who was Syrian by birth; and Demas also greets you. He departed from him for a time, but, having been corrected, returned.

Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea. To greet is to wish salvation [Col. 0765A]; and greet Nympha also. Nympha was a certain noble matron, in whose house there was a multitude of the faithful.

And when the Epistle has been read among you, arrange that it also be read in the church of the Laodiceans. He therefore commands that this Epistle, which he addressed to the Colossians, be read in the church of the Laodiceans, and commands that the one which belonged to the Laodiceans be read by the Colossians, because although it is very short and is not included in the canon, it nevertheless contains some benefit.

Say to Archippus: Archippus was their bishop. “Watch over your ministry”; that is, guard and understand your episcopate.

[Col. 0766A] The greeting is by the hand of Paul, which is the sign in every Epistle of mine. Remember my bonds; that is, take me as an example, so that just as I am not afraid to endure bonds and imprisonment for the name of Christ, so you too may not be afraid if necessity should arise. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen. Grace is called something given freely; and grace is that by which we received the remission of sins in baptism. The meaning is: May the grace of the Son of God, together with salvation and the remission of sins, remain always with you. Amen.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0765]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0765B]

Macedonia is a province of the Greeks, in which there is the metropolitan city of Thessalonica. After it received the faith from the Apostle Paul, although its inhabitants endured many dangers from their fellow citizens who did not believe, and although they wished to be led astray by pseudo-apostles, they nevertheless in no way departed from the truth of the faith. The Apostle praises them highly, writing to them from Athens through Timothy, and so forth.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians: greeting. He places his own name and those of his companions at the beginning of the Epistle for reasons mentioned in other Epistles. He writes generally to the whole church, because perhaps at that time they did not have a bishop appointed for themselves [Col. 0765C]. Although among the Jews the names “Synagogue” and “Church” were in use, as we read in the Book of Kings that Solomon blessed the whole assembly of Israel, nevertheless the apostles preferred to insert the name “Church” rather than “Synagogue” in their Epistles, because of the interpretation of the names. For “Church” (*ecclesia*) means “assembly,” which cannot be formed except from a rational creature; whereas “Synagogue,” which means “gathering,” can consist of something irrational and inanimate, just as a flock of sheep is gathered and stones are gathered. He wished to show that believing Gentiles are more rational than unbelieving Jews, who make the greatest use of the name “Church.”

We give thanks to God—that is, we render him praises—always for all of you. And not only for the Thessalonians [Col. 0765D], but also for all who received their preaching.

Remembering the work of your faith. He joins two things together, work and faith, which make a perfect human being. For faith adorned with good works pleases God; but faith without works is dead and empty. And remembering the endurance of the hope of our Lord. Endurance means expectation. Hence we say in the Psalms (Psalm XXIV): “Indeed, those who endure you”—that is, those who await you—“will not be put to shame.” He calls the endurance of the hope of our Lord the expectation of future goods, which are given through the Lord, and the expectation of the Lord’s coming for judgment. Before God—that is, in the presence and sight of God the Father—for the Son will judge the world in the presence and sight of God the Father.

But knowing—that is, we know—your election, by which you were chosen by God before the foundation of the world, because our Gospel was not only in speech or in the word, but in power and in the Holy Spirit; that is, in the power of the miracles which we performed through the Holy Spirit, and in great fullness of teaching and good works. You know what sort of people we were among you; that is, we were humble for your sake, so that we might win you for God. And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, because what the Lord endured, and what we endured from our fellow Jews, you likewise endured patiently [Col. 0766C], receiving the word of faith and teaching amid much tribulation with the joy of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit who was in you made you rejoice amid the tortures of persecution, so that you became a pattern and example of faith and teaching to all believers in Achaia and Macedonia, the two provinces.

[Col. 0766B] For the word of God has been reported abroad from you. “Reporting abroad” is used chiefly in the sense of blame and in the contrary sense. But the Apostle, not attending to the proper meaning of the words, when he ought to have said, “The word of God has been made manifest and proclaimed by you,” said “reported abroad.” There is no need for us to say anything to you—that is, because you have become preachers of God. In every place—that is, in every place near you—and so forth.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0766D]

Our exhortation—that is, our teaching—was not from error, that is, from falsehood, nor from uncleanness, because we were not lustful, nor in deceit, that is, fraud or cunning; nor in hypocrisy, that is, pretense, so that we might strip you bare.

Thus we speak, not as pleasing human beings—that is, evil ones. He seeks to please human beings who flatters them and favors their sins; but the apostles did not act this way toward anyone. Rather, they rebuked publicly.

[Col. 0767A] Nor did we preach on the pretext of greed, or preach to you because of covetousness.

As a nurse cherishes her own children—that is, not children belonging to someone else—so we love you. Wealthy, incontinent, and lustful women commonly entrust their children to other women for nursing. Although these women provide them with nourishment, they do not love them with the affection with which they love their own children, but so that they may receive a temporal payment. Thus the pseudo-apostles did not love them with maternal affection, but in order to receive temporal profit from them. The Apostle Paul and his companions, however, did not love them as a hired nurse loves another woman’s children. Rather, just as a mother cherishes her only son with maternal affection, so he loved them, because he himself had first begotten them in the faith of Christ.

You remember, brothers, our labor and toil. [Col. 0767B] The Apostle labored in preaching and in the work of his hands, in the manner we have often described. And why did he labor? So that he would not be idle. Every idle person is given over to desires; and so that he might avoid depraved desires, he devoted himself to the labor of his hands.

When you received the word you heard from God, you received it not as the word of human beings. The word of preaching which the Apostle proclaimed he had heard from God. And the Thessalonians received it as though they were hearing it from Christ himself, present among them.

For you suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they themselves did from the Jews. Those are called *contribules* (“fellow tribesmen”) who are from one tribe. As the faith of the Lord increased in Judaea, believers endured persecution from unbelievers: Reubenites from Reubenites, Gadites from Gadites, and likewise from [Col. 0767C] all the tribes. In the same way, the believing Thessalonians were persecuted by their unbelieving fellow tribesmen—that is, by their fellow citizens and neighbors.

So that they may fill up—that is, the Jews may fill up—their sins. When the period of forty years, which the Lord granted the Jews for repentance, had been completed, their sins were filled up after his Passion, because they refused to believe. Concerning this completion the Lord said to them: “Fill up the measure of your fathers.” But when the Apostle was saying these things, Jerusalem and the Temple were still standing; therefore their sins had not yet been completed. They were completed when the Romans came. Hence what follows: “For the wrath of God has come upon them to the end”—that is, the vengeance of God has come upon them to the end. He calls the arrival of the Romans God’s vengeance, when they were destroyed by famine, pestilence, the sword, and captivity. This vengeance will remain upon them until the end of the age, because they will always be captives. Or, if we read, “the wrath of God has overtaken them,” or “come before them,” as certain manuscripts have it, the meaning will be: God’s vengeance overtook them in this age and will remain until the end. It is said to overtake them because this temporal vengeance precedes the vengeance of the future judgment, in which they will be condemned eternally.

Bereft of you in speech—that is, in familiar conversation—and in sight, that is, in bodily presence, but not in heart, that is, in the affection of love.

## CHAPTER III

It pleased us to remain alone—that is, me and Silas or Silvanus [Col. 0768A]—at Athens, and we sent Timothy to you.

For you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this—that is, by God—so that we should patiently endure the persecutions and tribulations of this age, in order that through these temporal things we might arrive at eternal joys.

## CHAPTER IV

We ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus. After the Apostle praised the Thessalonians for their perseverance in the faith which they had maintained, refusing to receive false apostles, he began to exhort them always to advance toward what was better and to adorn their faith with good works, saying: “We ask and exhort.” The Apostle has the custom of doubling and tripling his words when they have one meaning, as in this passage. For what it means here to ask is also what it means to exhort; and when he says “in the Lord Jesus,” it is as though he said “through the Lord Jesus.” Something similar is found in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “He spoke to us in the Son” (Hebrews I), that is, through the Son. Just as you received from us—by hearing and understanding from me and Silvanus how you ought to walk, that is, live, and complete the course of this life in good works, and please God by adorning the faith you possess with good works—so indeed you are walking, living, and conducting yourselves now; therefore abound more and more, that is, grow increasingly in faith and good works. For the person who adorns the right faith he possesses through the practice of virtues pleases God. And the person abounds well who, as the age of faith in him increases, also strives to abound in [Col. 0768C] holy works and in the pursuit of virtues.

For you know what commandments I gave you through the Lord Jesus—that is, in the Lord Jesus speaking through me. What were the commandments which he gave them? They were commandments of faith and Christian conduct, in which he exhorted them to serve the living and true God and to await his Son from heaven for judgment, the Son whom God the Father raised up. I mean Jesus, who rescued us through his Passion and through his grace from the coming wrath.

For this is the will of God: your sanctification; that is, it is God’s will that you sanctify yourselves in the manner that the following words make clear, namely, that you abstain from fornication. “Fornication” can be understood in this passage in three ways. To fornicate is to depart from God through the worship of idols and to worship idols in place of the true God [Col. 0768D]. Concerning this fornication the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Psalm LXXII). And: “Israel fornicated with the nations,” that is, he worshiped idols. In another way, fornication occurs when a person places the love of earthly things—namely, children, possessions, or riches—before the love of almighty God, and through such things departs from God, who is the husband of the soul. Third, there is bodily fornication, by which someone has intercourse with prostitutes or satisfies his lust in any manner.

That each of you may know how to possess his own vessel—that is, his own body and his wife’s body—in sanctification, that is, in chastity, and in honor. A person honors his own body and his wife’s body [Col. 0769A] when he abstains from intercourse, because by keeping the body chaste, his prayer is chaster and more acceptable to God. Not in the passion of desire. The passion of desire occurs when a person, like a horse or mule, which lack understanding, rushes headlong into lust and does not restrain the heat of lust through regard for and fear of almighty God. Such are the nations who do not know God. The nations who do not know God are fornicators and excessively devoted to lust, since they lack knowledge of God. Such are the Moors, Vandals, and especially the Saracens, to such an extent that many of them have sixty wives or more. The meaning is: Be careful and take heed that, by serving lust excessively and without restraint, you do not become like the nations, who do not know the God who loves chastity, and are condemned together with them—and even more severely, because “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows.” It is better not to know the way of truth than afterward to turn back from it.

[Col. 0769B] And that no one should overreach or defraud his brother in this matter. The blessed Apostle and his companions preached and urged their hearers, on feast days and days of fasting, to abstain by mutual agreement from all intercourse; and many obeyed his commandments and admonitions. But lest someone, after devoted continence, should be provoked by the devil to intercourse on those days on which they had vowed to maintain continence, the Apostle says: “And that none of you should overreach or defraud another in this matter of intercourse”; that is, no one should by any deception inflict violence [Col. 0769C] upon his partner who wishes to keep the vow, by provoking him to intercourse. Rather, by mutual agreement they should abstain from all intercourse, as they vowed, because it is better not to make a vow than not to fulfill a vow. Although pure prayer pleases God at all times, it is then more acceptable and pleasing to God when it is poured out with a pure heart and body, namely, on days of fasting. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room” (Joel II). In this passage we must understand “bridegroom” and “bride” to mean married people. For the blessed Jerome says that repentance is assumed in vain in voice and dress unless one also abstains from the pleasure of the flesh and from intercourse.

This may also be understood of every business and commercial transaction, so that no one should defraud his brother or [Col. 0769D] deceive him. For the Lord is an avenger of all these things—not only of fornication and public disgrace, but also of the transgression of every good intention. For example, this applies to those who vow to abstain by mutual agreement from intercourse during a period of fasting and afterward do not fulfill their promise. As we said to you earlier—that is, when we were present—and testified, so the Lord will be the avenger of all such things.

For God did not call us to his faith and grace, and to the heavenly homeland, for uncleanness, so that we should serve uncleanness, but for sanctification, so that we might live holy lives and be holy, imitating him who said: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus XI). By the name “uncleanness” is understood every form of incontinence [Col. 0770A] and impurity, and every way in which someone pollutes himself. This sanctification consists in prayers, fasts, almsgiving, hospitality, charity, and the other virtues.

The blessed Apostle, following the custom of the holy Fathers, wished to sanctify the Thessalonians, just as we read that Moses the lawgiver, when he was about to give the Law, sanctified the people; that is, he warned them to live holy lives and remain clean, so that they might be worthy to hear the voice of the Lord and receive his commandments, saying: “Sanctify yourselves, wash your garments, and abstain from your wives.” If, then, God called them to sanctification, how much more has he called us to sanctification, whom he redeemed with his blood and cleansed through the grace of baptism, so that we might be able to approach worthily the sacrament of his body [Col. 0770B] and blood?

Likewise, the blessed Job sent to his sons each day—who perhaps lived outside his house with their wives—and sanctified them; that is, he admonished them to live holy lives, so that their sacrifices and vows might be acceptable. Samuel too, when he came to anoint David to the kingship, summoned Jesse and his sons to the sacrifice and sanctified them; that is, he warned them to prepare themselves in such a way that they might be worthy of so great an honor, since their brother had been chosen by God for kingship. In this way the apostles and holy teachers sanctify us every day by admonishing us through their words to live holy lives, so that we may be worthy not only to be called Christians but also sons of God, and so that almighty God may deign to dwell in us.

[Col. 0770C] Therefore, whoever rejects, despises, and scorns these things—that is, these words—does not reject a human being; that is, he does not despise me, but God, whose words I recite and who speaks through my mouth.

We do not wish you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. Philosophers and pagan unbelievers, who did not believe in the resurrection, deceived many people in this matter by denying the resurrection, and caused them to grieve and mourn over the death of their relatives. Not only unbelievers, but also many of the faithful among the Macedonians and Thessalonians grieved over the death of their parents, not believing that they would rise again. Pagans and unbelievers therefore rightly grieved over the death of their own people, because through temporal death they were reaching eternal death. But believers and unbelievers rightly grieved over the departure [Col. 0770D] of the faithful, because through temporal death they were reaching eternal life. Therefore, wishing to assure them concerning the resurrection and to console them over the death of their relatives, the Apostle said: “I do not wish you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep,” because they will rise again, so that you may not grieve over their death like unbelievers, who have no hope of rising.

For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God the Father will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. The Apostle says something remarkable. He calls Christ, who now lives and, having risen from the dead, dies no more, “dead,” and he calls the chosen dead “those who sleep.” He calls Christ dead so that, when we hear and know that he was dead and rose again [Col. 0771A], we too may hope to rise through the power of his divinity. He calls the chosen “those who sleep,” because no human being can awaken his companion from sleep as easily as all will be raised from the sleep of death.

When he says that God the Father will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus—that is, with Jesus—to judgment, the meaning is as follows: Those who have fallen asleep in Jesus—namely, those who died before his coming and afterward died in faith in his Passion, who were marked with the sign of the cross and, on the day of their death, fortified with the sacrament of his body and blood, believing that their salvation was contained therein—will come with Christ in glory to judgment. The blessed Augustine says that it is rightly for such people that sacrifice is offered to God after death and the Lord’s body is consecrated, because while they lived in the world they received it with the greatest devotion.

[Col. 0771B] For we say this to you by the word of the Lord—that is, according to the Lord’s meaning, because almighty God speaks through our mouth—namely, that we who live, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep in Christ, in the manner described above. These words of the Apostle seem to indicate that in his own time the Apostle showed that the day of judgment was about to come. Hence the Thessalonians, when reading this Epistle, thought that the day of judgment would come in the Apostle’s time. Therefore, in the second Epistle, he addresses and exhorts them, saying: “Do not be terrified by a letter, as though the day of the Lord were at hand.”

It must therefore be considered that he speaks in the person of the chosen, who will be found alive in the body at the Lord’s coming. They are said to be “those who remain” [Col. 0771C] after the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all the saints who preceded them through the intervals of time, who now precede them, and who will continue to precede them until the day of judgment, for the repose of souls, because they will be left after them. The resurrection of the chosen dead will therefore be so swift and exceedingly rapid that those who are found alive in the body and upon the earth will not be able to precede them as they go to meet the Lord in the air, although the others had been lying in the dust of the earth.

[Col. 0771D] For the Lord Jesus himself will descend from heaven with a command—that is, at the command of God the Father—and with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God he will descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ, dead in the manner described above, will rise first. He says “with a command” because the Son will come to judgment at the command and disposition of God the Father. According to Augustine, by “one archangel” we ought to understand all the angelic powers, because the angels will sound forth with their voices when he comes.

“Trumpet” may be understood in one way as the great voice and sound of the angels, concerning whom Matthew says: “The Son of Man will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice” (Matthew XXIV). That the trumpet signifies the voice of the angels is shown by the Psalmist when he speaks of the Lord’s ascension: “God has ascended with jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm XLVI). Just as there he calls the voice of the angels a trumpet—those saying, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts I), and so forth—so in this passage he compares the voice of the angels to a trumpet, when they say: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” [Col. 0772A] (Matthew XXV), and: “Rise from your graves; go to meet your Redeemer in judgment.” This voice by which all will be raised can rightly be called a trumpet.

In another way, “trumpet” is used for manifestation, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you” (Matthew VI); that is, do not do it openly, lest you be praised by human beings like the hypocrites. Thus the Lord will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God—that is, he will come openly to judgment, so that he may be seen by all, according to the saying: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III).

Although some have understood childishly what was said by the prophet Joel—“The judgment of the Lord will come in the valley of Jehoshaphat”—as though he would judge all the nations in that valley, it should not be understood in this way. The prophet used that name not for a place but for its interpretation. For *Jehoshaphat* means “valley of judgment.” The Lord’s coming for judgment will be “in the valley” for the reprobate, because, when the chosen have been raised to the heights with the Lord, the reprobate will remain below, in the depths and lower regions of hell.

[Col. 0772B] Let us also give a third interpretation, according to the blessed Ambrose, of the statement that he will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God. We read that Moses the lawgiver, at the Lord’s command, made silver trumpets, and that afterward Solomon made them for the Temple of the Lord. They were sounded at solemn celebrations and in battles, as happened when the walls of Jericho collapsed, and later in the time of Gideon. Concerning solemn celebrations the Psalmist says: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon” (Psalm LXXX). It is therefore rightly said that the Lord will come to judgment with the trumpet, because he will come for this purpose: as in battle, to overthrow his adversaries [Col. 0772C]—the Jews, pagans, heretics, and false Christians—and to gain victory over them, saying: “Go into the eternal fire.” He will also come to reward his chosen by bringing them into the solemn celebration of eternal glory and blessedness.

Then we who live, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord. He speaks in the person of those who will be found alive, as above, who say: “We shall be caught up together with them”—that is, with those who preceded us to the repose of souls—but then we shall come together to meet the Lord. The word “to catch up” is often used to signify speed. In this passage it signifies the extreme swiftness of the resurrection and the day of judgment, about which we have already spoken above. For [Col. 0772D] just as God made all things in a moment, so in a moment he will judge all things.

When he says, “We shall be caught up by the angels with them who preceded us to meet the Lord in the air,” he shows that the Lord will not descend to the earth, but will sit in the heights of this air to judge. When he adds, “And thus”—that is, having been made immortal in body and soul—“we shall always be with the Lord,” we should not think that we shall reign with the Lord in the air. For when the judgment has ended, he will return with all the chosen to eternal blessedness, from which he descended for judgment.

If the chosen who are found alive will be caught up by the angels into the air to meet the Lord [Col. 0773A], it must be asked how this agrees with what God said to the first man, Adam, and in him to all his descendants: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” since they will not have experienced death. This is resolved in the following way, according to the blessed Augustine. The human being was made from earth in the body; and before the Lord breathed into his face the breath of life—that is, before he gave him a soul—that body was earth. The chosen who are found alive will likewise, in the very act of being caught up, suddenly die while they are being carried by angelic hands, and suddenly rise again. As the soul leaves the body in that very act of being caught up, the body will remain earth; but death itself will last for an exceedingly brief interval, so brief that it cannot be conceived or measured.

Therefore, O Thessalonians, console one another with these words concerning the resurrection, and do not grieve over the death of your parents.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0773B]

Concerning the times—that is, the day of judgment—and the moments, whether it will come in summer or winter, spring or autumn, or at what hour of the day or night, you have no need for us to write to you. Why? For you yourselves know carefully that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night; that is, just as a thief comes suddenly and unexpectedly in the deep night while the master of the house is sleeping, so unexpectedly will the day of judgment and the Lord’s coming arrive.

After the resurrection, when the apostles asked the Lord about that day—that is, about the kingdom of the chosen—saying, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” he said: “It is not yours to know the times or moments” (Acts I). And before his Passion he said concerning the same day: “Concerning that day,” he said, “no one knows [Col. 0773C], neither the angels who are in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Matthew XXIV). Therefore, if the Father knows, surely the Son also knows, since he is of one substance with him. But the Son is said to be ignorant because he left the disciples in ignorance.

For when they say—that is, the reprobate say—“Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them; that is, the sudden ruin of the day of judgment, as labor comes upon a woman with child—that is, the pain of childbirth—and they will not escape. Just as a pregnant woman, when tribulation and persecution are imminent, cannot escape the plots of her pursuers, so they will not be able to escape. Concerning them the Lord says: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Mark XIII).

[Col. 0773D] As we find in the words of the prophet Daniel, when the Antichrist and his ministers reign for three years and a half, and when Elijah and Enoch have been killed by him, as is recorded in the Apocalypse, there will be a persecution such as never was before and will never follow afterward. The Antichrist himself will be killed, and the greatest part of his members, by Michael, as the blessed Gregory says; and, as the blessed Paul says: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth,” that is, with his word and his power.
