Both statements can be true, because if Michael kills him, it will not be Michael’s power but God’s power and command.

After his death, forty-five days will remain, during which there will be much peace, so that during those days the chosen who faltered in some respect during the persecution may repent and be saved. But the ministers of the Antichrist who remain [Col. 0774A] after his death will rejoice throughout those forty-five days, taking wives, holding banquets, and engaging in various kinds of amusements, saying: “Although our prince is dead, now we shall have peace and security.” And when they have said such things, sudden destruction will come upon them.

But you are not in the darkness of unbelief. For those who sleep and rest in sins sleep at night—that is, they rest and lie in sins and vices. Clothed with the breastplate of faith and charity, and with the helmet of hope and salvation—that is, we have faith in God, charity toward God and neighbor, and hope and expectation of future goods upon our head—for salvation will come to us from heaven; armed with these weapons, we shall be secure and free at the Lord’s coming.

[Col. 0774B] God has not appointed us for wrath—that is, God did not place us in his faith, in the Church, and in his knowledge so that he might exercise his vengeance upon us—but he appointed us for the acquisition of salvation, so that we might find salvation through faith in Jesus Christ; so that whether we keep watch, that is, live in this world, or sleep, that is, die in the body, we may live together with him—that is, with Christ—in soul and in the hope of resurrection.

Therefore—that is, because of what we said above concerning the resurrection—comfort one another. We ask you to know them—that is, to love them, honor them, and minister what they need to them—those who labor among you in preaching and teaching.

We ask you: correct the unruly, comfort the fainthearted. Among the Thessalonians there were certain [Col. 0774C] wanderers, or, so to speak, gyrovaghi—people living idly and not working with their hands to provide their livelihood, nor devoting themselves to prayers or psalmody. Instead, they went around other people’s houses and traveled from place to place, seeking means by which they might live; for this reason they disturbed many people. Or he also calls proud people “unruly,” because through their pride they disturbed others.

There were also others who were fainthearted and timid. They were afraid to begin a good work, lest perhaps they should be unable to bring it to completion; or, if they began it, they did not do it freely, but were ashamed of it in the presence of others. They were themselves fainthearted because they were unwilling to endure patiently the adversities of this world, and they were quickly scandalized by the words and deeds of others.

The Apostle therefore commands that the unruly—that is, the wanderers, the idle, and the unstable, [Col. 0774D] or the proud who troubled others—be corrected by prelates and teachers, so that they might cease from idleness, which is the enemy of the soul, and lay aside pride, the root of all vices. But he commands that the fainthearted be comforted gently, so that through the exhortation and consolation of their superiors they may be strengthened in every good thing.

Receive—understand, into the service of charity—the weak in faith and in body. Be patient toward all. Now he admonishes prelates to endure patiently the wickedness and impatience of their subjects when they murmur against them in some matter. For the unruly, immoderate, or impatient often rise up against prelates when they are corrected, and bear their correction impatiently, unwilling to be corrected by them and wishing instead to fulfill their own will. Prelates ought for a time to endure their rebelliousness, and then, at a suitable and appropriate time, to correct it with counsel and assistance.

See—that is, beware—lest any of you repay evil to anyone for evil. The Apostle wishes to show in this passage that we must not only refrain from repaying evil for good, but also from repaying evil for evil.

There are four ways of repaying: good for good, evil for evil, good for evil, and evil for good. Good is repaid for evil when, for example, our Redeemer redeemed us—who were dead and lost, and alienated from God because of our sins—through his passion and the grace of baptism.

Good is repaid for good when, for example, on the day of judgment he will give the elect what he promised, saying to them: “Because I was hungry and you gave me food, receive the kingdom [Col. 0775B] prepared for you” (Matt. XXV).

Evil is repaid for good as Judas and the Jews repaid it to the Lord. Therefore he said to them through the prophet Zechariah: “If it is good in your eyes, bring my payment”; and the meaning is: I healed your sick, cleansed your lepers, raised your dead, and fed your hungry. Give me payment for this, if it is worthy and good. “And they weighed out my payment, thirty pieces of silver” (Zech. XI).

The Lord will repay evil for evil to the reprobate on the day of judgment, saying to them: “Because I was hungry and you did not give me food, depart into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore we ought not seek vengeance in order to repay evil for evil, because we cannot do this with a peaceful mind. Rather, we ought to reserve it for him who always remains the same and equal, and who said: “Reserve vengeance for me, and I will repay” (Rom. XII)—punishments for them, but rewards for you.

To repay evil for evil is not good; but to repay evil for good is exceedingly and profoundly evil. Always pursue what is good—that is, imitate and accomplish it—among one another, or with one another, and toward all. This means not only toward believers but also toward unbelievers, because we are all brothers according to the flesh.

Always rejoice. Rejoice not in perishable riches and temporal honors, but in the Lord and in good works, because you are children of God.

Pray without interruption. What mortal human being can always persist in prayer? Either the Apostle has put the whole for the part, so that he calls the one who observes the canonical hours according to the custom and practice of the holy Fathers one who always prays; or he means the one who always thinks about God and desires to please God.

For as long as someone thinks rightly and desires what is good, he always prays. Whatever the righteous person does that is good must be referred to prayer, and he will never cease praying unless he ceases to be righteous.

In everything give thanks—that is, in faith, hope, charity, and the other good works; and in prosperity and adversity always give thanks and praise to God, because neither prosperity occurs unless he grants it, nor adversity unless he permits it.

For this is the will of God in all things in Christ Jesus—that is, through Christ Jesus—from whom every good thing is granted to us, and without whom we are able to do nothing good, as he himself said: “Without me [Col. 0776A] you can do nothing” (John XV). This, he says, is the will of God: that you not repay evil for evil, that you always pursue what is good, pray without interruption, rejoice in the Lord, and give thanks to him in all things.

Do not extinguish the Spirit. Let us explain this according to Ambrose’s interpretation: “Do not extinguish the Spirit”—that is, if the Holy Spirit has filled someone for a time with his grace so that he can interpret the divine Scriptures and speak of divine mysteries, do not prevent him from speaking and teaching. For God, who opened the mouth of the she-ass, often reveals to a younger person what he does not reveal to an elder—which is better.

Alternatively, according to Augustine: the Holy Spirit, who in his nature is of one substance with the Father and the Son, cannot be extinguished; but through our vice we extinguish him in ourselves when, by sinning, we exclude him from ourselves. “The Spirit of discipline,” he says, “will flee deceit.” Therefore, when we surrender our body to lust and join it to a prostitute—our body, which at the time of baptism and the laying on of hands became a temple of the Holy Spirit—we exclude him from ourselves and drive him away. Insofar as it depends on us, Augustine says, we are his extinguishers.

But so that we may not do this, the Apostle says: Do not drive away from yourselves the Holy Spirit, who began to dwell in you at the time of baptism, nor extinguish him in yourselves by sinning and surrendering your body to various forms of shame, since it ought to be his temple.

Do not despise prophecies—that is, if someone is able to explain the sayings of the prophets, as Jerome and the other teachers speak and preach for the edification of their hearers, do not look down on him or despise him, but attend humbly to what he teaches.

But test everything; hold fast to what is good. That is: attend to everything he says. Test whether his sayings and words agree with the sayings of the Gospel, the sayings of the prophets, and the sayings of the apostles. If you have tested them and found that his words do not differ from the understanding of the holy Fathers, hold what is good in your heart and fulfill it in action.

Abstain from every form of evil—that is, abstain from every evil thing, from wicked thought, and from perverse action.

May the God of peace himself—that is, the Lord Jesus, who left peace to his disciples, saying to all of us, “I leave you peace” (John XIV), and who also made peace between us and reconciled us to God the Father through his passion—sanctify you in every way. That is, may he make you holy in everything you think and accomplish in action, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When he says, “so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole,” we can understand it in two ways. A human being consists of body, soul, and spirit; nevertheless, these are not three substances in him, as Didymus argues, nor is spirit a third substance in the human being. Rather, the spirit itself is the soul. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John XIX).

For this reason the soul is called spirit, either because it is spiritual in nature or because it breathes in the human being. It is called soul because it animates the body in order to give it life and is given to the body for seeing.

Likewise, the rationality and excellence of the soul by which we have understanding and are distinguished from other creatures is commonly called spirit, as is shown there: “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Dan. III). Yet because spirit and soul are one, this is evident: with the body we walk, by the soul we live, and by the spirit we understand and have wisdom.

It is concerning this spirit, or rationality of the soul—which rationality is also called the mind—that the Apostle speaks here when he says: “So that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole,” and so forth.

The Apostle therefore prays that our spirit—that is, our rationality—may remain whole, incorrupt, and inviolate; and likewise that soul and body may remain [Col. 0777B] incorrupt and undefiled until the day of our death or the day of judgment, just as we were cleansed from every pollution of sins at the time of baptism.

Since the body can be clean while the soul and spirit are polluted by evil thought and desire, he therefore says that the whole human being must be clean.

Alternatively: “spirit” is often used for grace and its gifts, as in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “The spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets” (1 Cor. XIV)—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because they do not compel a person to speak like someone possessed or demonic.

In this passage also, “spirit” can be understood as the grace given to us at baptism, by which we are cleansed from every pollution of vice. The Apostle prays that this grace may remain in us whole, incorrupt, and undefiled, lest through our fault and uncleanness it be corrupted, diminished, or driven away from us.

For if an evil life or thought intervenes, the grace itself is no longer whole, because it abandons a person who is subject to sins. While a person does what the Holy Spirit hates, his grace either departs from him entirely or is diminished in the one who sins.

“May the God of peace,” he says, “sanctify you in every way”—that is, the whole human being—so that the grace of the Holy Spirit which you received at the time of baptism may not depart from you, but remain whole; so that your soul may be incorrupt, your body undefiled, and the whole cleansed human being may be preserved complete and blameless.

He does not say “without sin,” because there is no human being who does good and does not sin, and “in many things we all offend” (James III). “If we say that we have no sin, the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

He is faithful—that is, truthful in his promises—who called you to his faith and grace; he will also do—understand, what he promised. He calls God faithful in his promises so that they may conduct themselves rightly with confidence concerning their reward.

# INTO THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0777]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0777C]

When the Thessalonians received the first epistle and, while reading, came to the passage where the Apostle speaks in the person of the elect who will be found alive on the day of judgment, saying, “Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thess. IV), they were disturbed and exceedingly frightened. They thought that the Apostle had spoken as though, in his own time and theirs, the Lord would come to judgment. They feared that they would be sent with the devil into the prison of eternal punishment because, having come late to the faith, they were imperfect.

Therefore, when the Apostle learned that they were distressed about this, he wrote this second epistle to them. In it he indicated that the day of judgment was not yet imminent in their time, [Col. 0777D] and showed them—although secretly and obscurely—that the Roman kingdom would first have to be destroyed. For he did not dare to write openly about the abolition of the Roman kingdom, lest he perhaps provoke persecution against the believers.

He also announces the coming of Antichrist and his death.

## CHAPTER ONE

Paul and Silvanus. The beginning and meaning are the same as those we explained in the preceding epistle.

Your faith is increasing. Faith requires increase; hence the apostles say to the Lord: “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII). And someone else says: “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief” (Mark IX).

[Col. 0778C] Let us glory in the tribulations that you endure as an example of the righteous judgment of God. As we can gather from the words of Prosper and other teachers, nothing happens in this world except either by God’s action or by his permission.

Therefore the holy martyrs and other faithful people, by God’s permission, suffered many dangers and adversities in this world as an example of God’s righteous judgment. For it was shown in them that if those who were beloved by God suffered such things, the reprobate and his enemies will receive far greater and more severe things on the day of God’s righteous judgment.

He calls it God’s righteous judgment because then God will judge the world in equity.

If indeed it is just with God to repay evils to the wicked and good things to the good. If the causal conjunction “if” in this passage is not used to express doubt but affirmation, as though he were saying: Since it is just for God to act in this way, then this is what follows:

At the revelation—that is, at the manifestation—of the Lord Jesus coming from heaven for judgment with the angels of his power, as he himself said: “When the Son of Man comes, and all the angels with him” (Matt. XXV); and at the revelation of the Lord Jesus when he gives vengeance to the reprobate in a flame of fire: to those who did not know God—that is, the pagans—and to those who do not obey the Gospel—that is, heretics, false Christians, and Jews.

He rightly says that the Lord will give vengeance to the reprobate in a flame of fire, because fire will go before him, occupying as much of the air as the water occupied in the flood. It will burn the earth and the density of the air and cleanse the elect. But the reprobate, hearing from the Lord, “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), will be enveloped by this fire and dragged to the punishments of hell.

Those reprobates will suffer eternal punishments in destruction. They will give punishments to others, but to themselves they will give and inflict them, because they did the evil deeds for which they will receive such things.

“Give” is also sometimes used for “endure,” as in Virgil:

“And Scylla pays the penalty for her purple hair,”

that is, she endures the penalty. So these too will give penalties—that is, they will endure them.

When he comes to be glorified in his saints—that is, to appear glorious and gracious to them, but terrifying and fierce to the reprobate. Because our testimony was believed among you—that is, because our Gospel and preaching were received and believed by us and by you—on that day, that is, because of that day, so that the Gospel may bear witness on that day to your faith, and you may receive an eternal reward.

In which—that is, in which matter—we pray, or for this we always pray for you, and so forth.

## CHAPTER TWO

We ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him. We read of two comings of the Lord: the first in humility, the second in power, when he will come to judgment. It is the latter that is discussed here.

He calls his gathering the multitude of the elect, either those who will come with him or those who will go to meet him at the judgment. He says “to him,” as though he meant “in him,” because all the elect are in Christ, being members who adhere to him.

We ask you, brothers, by the coming of the Lord Jesus to judgment and by the coming of our gathering to him—that is, of all the saints who remain in him—not to be quickly shaken, that is, not to be quickly disturbed, nor terrified as though the day of the Lord were imminent.

Do not be terrified by spirit—that is, if someone claims to have been warned by the Holy Spirit that the day of judgment is near, do not believe him or be frightened by his words.

Nor by a word—that is, by a treatise. If some interpreter and expounder of prophecies says to you, “I have gathered the meaning of the prophet Isaiah, Daniel, and the other prophets, and I foresee that the day of judgment is near and that Christ is coming to judgment,” do not therefore be afraid.

Nor by a letter supposedly sent by us. If some false apostle has fabricated such a letter, do not believe him.

[Col. 0779D] For unless the falling away comes first—that is, unless all kingdoms depart from the kingdom and empire of the Romans—and the man of sin is revealed or manifested—namely, Antichrist, who, although he is a human being, will nevertheless be the source of all sins—and the son of perdition—that is, the son of the devil, not by nature but by imitation.

He is called perdition because through him perdition comes, and he himself destroyed the human race.

He is the one who opposes—that is, who is contrary to Christ and all his members—and who exalts himself, or raises himself in pride, above everything that is called God or is worshiped.

It is not true that the Apostle means “what is called God” or “what is worshiped” in the same way. Antichrist will exalt himself above everything that is called a god—that is, above all the gods of the nations: Hercules, Apollo, and Jupiter, who are falsely called gods—and above all the elect who are called gods by designation, such as Moses, of whom it is said, “Behold, I have appointed you as god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII); and in the Law, “You shall not revile the gods” (Exod. XXII), meaning the priests; and, “I said, You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI).

Thus Antichrist will exalt himself above all these and will say that he is greater than all of them—not only above them but also, which is greater, above everything that is worshiped, that is, above the holy Trinity, which alone is to be worshiped and adored by every creature.

He will exalt himself in such a way that he will sit in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God. This can be understood in two ways.

Antichrist will be born in Babylon, from the tribe of Dan, in accordance with what Jacob says: “May Dan become a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path” (Gen. XLIX). When he comes to Jerusalem, he will circumcise himself and say to the Jews, “I am the Christ promised to you.” Then all the Jews will flock to him and rebuild the temple, which was destroyed by the Romans, and he will sit there, claiming to be the Christ.

Or he will sit in the temple of God—that is, in the Church—displaying himself as though he were God. For just as the fullness of divinity dwelt in Christ, so in that man who is called Antichrist because he is contrary to Christ, the fullness of evil and all iniquity will dwell. For in him will be the head of all evils, the devil, who is king over all the sons of pride.

By these words the Apostle showed the Thessalonians that the Lord would not come to judgment until the human kingdom had fallen—a fall that we now see fulfilled—and that Antichrist would appear in the world, who will kill Christ’s martyrs.

Do you not remember that while I was still with you I used to tell you these things? He means concerning the coming of Antichrist and the day of judgment.

And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. He says, “You know what restrains him,” but he does not explain what it is. Nothing can be better understood there than his intention to signify the destruction of the Roman kingdom, about which he spoke obscurely here, lest perhaps some Roman should read this epistle and provoke against himself and the other Christians the persecution of those who thought they would reign forever throughout the whole world.

You know, he says, what restrains Antichrist and delays him: the Roman kingdom has not yet been destroyed, nor have all the nations departed from it. He will be revealed, or manifested, in his own time—that is, at the appropriate time appointed by God—after all kingdoms have departed from the Roman Empire.

For the mystery of iniquity is already at work. “Mystery” is a Greek word; in Latin it means something hidden and secret.

He therefore calls the mystery of iniquity the killing of the holy martyrs and the persecution that Nero and his rulers inflicted upon Christ’s faithful. It is called a mystery because what the devil will openly accomplish through Antichrist, by killing the holy martyrs Elijah and Enoch and many others, he is already accomplishing secretly through his members, [Col. 0781A] Nero and his rulers, killing the apostolic martyrs through those rulers.

This mystery of iniquity began with Nero, who, secretly instigated by his father the devil, killed the holy martyrs out of zeal for idols. It continued as far as Diocletian and Julian the Apostate, who killed very many saints.

Therefore, just as Christ, who is the head of all the elect, was prefigured long before his coming, secretly and through a mystery—as in the death of Abel, the sacrifice of Isaac, and King David, who killed Goliath, who signified the devil whom Christ conquered in his death and passion—so the devil, who will be in Antichrist, was secretly and mysteriously prefigured in his evil members, namely wicked kings.

Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain until he is removed from the midst. [Col. 0781B] That is, only this remains: that Nero, who now holds the empire of the whole world, should continue to hold it until the power of the Romans is removed from the midst of the world.

In Nero he includes all the Roman emperors who held the scepter of the empire after him. He says, “until he is removed from the midst,” because people came to Rome from every nation, and it was, as it were, in the middle of the world, with all nations surrounding it; or whatever is contained between a beginning and an end can be called “the middle.”

And then—understand, when power has been taken away from the Roman Empire—the lawless one will be revealed, or manifested: Antichrist, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth; or, if the Lord Jesus himself kills him by the power of his command, or if Michael kills him, he will be slain by the power of the Lord Jesus, not by Michael’s power.

He will be killed, as the teachers transmit, on the Mount of Olives, in Babylon and in his throne, in that place opposite which the Lord ascended into heaven.

When the Apostle says, “Then the lawless one will be revealed” after the Roman Empire has been destroyed, this must not be understood as though he meant that Antichrist would come immediately: first the Roman Empire must be destroyed, and then Antichrist will come at the time appointed by God.

And by the brightness, or splendor, of his coming the Lord Jesus will destroy him—that is, Antichrist.

His coming is according to the activity of Satan. This pertains to the day of judgment itself, when Antichrist will be destroyed together with all his members. For they will hear from the Lord: “Go into eternal fire.”

It must be noted that the Lord will not come to judgment immediately after Antichrist has been killed, but, as we understand from the Book of Daniel, after his death forty-five days will be granted to the elect for repentance. However long the interval of time may be until the Lord comes, it is entirely unknown.

When he says, “His coming was according to the activity of Satan,” this must be understood to mean that whatever he accomplishes, he will fulfill with the devil’s instigation and cooperation. The devil will possess him completely; nevertheless, he will not lose his reason and say unknowingly that he does not know God, nor will he be tormented by the devil like the deranged.

For if that were the case, whatever he did would in no way be sin, just as those who suffer from delirium are not guilty of the actions they perform because they do not know what they are doing.

In all power, signs, and lying wonders—understand, the coming of Antichrist will be manifested in these. “Signs” and “wonders” are taken as one expression. He will operate through lying signs and wonders, because he will appear to raise the dead and perform many other signs; but they will be lies and separated from the truth, because through magic and illusion he will deceive people, just as Simon Magus deceived the man who, thinking he was killing him, beheaded a ram in his place.

Or his coming will be manifested in lying signs and wonders because, through the false signs and wonders that he will appear to perform, he will hand people over to the worship of falsehood—that is, to himself, who is a liar and the father of lies.

And with every seduction or deception of iniquity for those who perish—that is, for Jews and pagans—because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved.

That is, the Spirit of Christ, who said, “I am the truth” (John XVI), and through whom the love of God and neighbor is poured into our hearts.

Because they were unwilling to receive either Christ or the Holy Spirit, God will send them the activity of error—that is, he will permit the worker of falsehood, Antichrist, to come to them.

He says “activity” rather than “worker,” which is stronger, because he will send them the thing itself—that is, falsehood itself and the father of all malice and iniquity.

So that they may believe the lie—that is, the devil—and so that all who did not believe the truth, Christ, but consented to iniquity, the devil, may be judged or condemned.

God chose us apostles as the firstfruits for the salvation of all nations. The apostles were the firstfruits because they were the first to believe.

For the acquisition of the glory of the Lord Jesus—that is, so that you, acquired for the faith through our preaching, may increase the body of Christ, and so that he may be glorified and praised through you, according to the saying: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

May God the Father, who loved us so greatly that he gave his Son for us, and who gave us eternal consolation by promising us the kingdom of heaven and a good hope—the expectation of future goods—in his grace, not through our merit, exhort—that is, teach—our hearts.

## CHAPTER THREE

Finally, pray for us, so that the word of God may run from our mouth to your ears, and from your ears to your heart, and thus be transformed into action.

So that we may be delivered from troublesome people, who do not stand in the harbor of peace.

But may the Lord direct your hearts—that is, if there is any strength in you, may he increase it, make you walk by the straightness of life, and establish straight steps in good works—in the charity of God and neighbor, and in the patience of Christ.

May you be patient amid the adversities of this world, just as Christ patiently endured insults, mockery, scourging, and the cross; or, as some manuscripts read, “in the expectation of Christ,” so that you may await Christ’s coming to judgment.

We did not eat bread without payment—that is, without labor.

[Col. 0783A] If anyone does not obey the word—understand, our word or yours—so that he may not be idle, mark him out for us by a letter—understand, your letter—and we will rebuke him severely.

My greeting with the hand of Paul, which is the sign in [Col. 0784A] every epistle. At the end of all his epistles he wrote his name in Hebrew letters and in the Greek language, so that what follows could not be corrupted by some false apostle.

I write in this way. How? “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all. Amen.”

# INTO THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0783]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0783A]

Timothy was the son of a widow, begotten by a Gentile Greek father. When his mother wished to circumcise him according to the commandment of the Law, his father, who was uncircumcised because he was a Gentile, prevented her.

When he was handed over to letters, he was educated both in the divine Scriptures and in the liberal arts. He was associated with blessed Paul and became his companion in preaching; afterward Paul ordained him and appointed him bishop.

To him the Apostle directed this epistle, instructing him concerning the ordering of the episcopate, the diaconate, and the whole discipline and order of the Church, as well as how he ought to teach the people.

## CHAPTER ONE

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus according to the command of God—that is, according to the command and will of God the Father, our Savior—and according to the command of Christ Jesus, our hope.

He refers salvation to God the Father and our hope to Christ, because God the Father gave us salvation through his Son, whom he graciously sent to us, and through the Holy Spirit, whom he bestowed upon us at the time of baptism and at the time of the laying on of hands.

Through Christ we have hope—that is, expectation of future goods—because just as he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, so we hope for a resurrection that will benefit you through him, and that we shall ascend to the glory of eternal blessedness.

To Timothy, beloved son in spirit, in teaching, and in faith, not according to the flesh. Grace, by which sins are freely forgiven; mercy; and peace, by which we are reconciled to God the Father.

He inserted mercy between the two, to show that grace and peace are conferred upon us through the mercy of God, not through our merit.

Just as I asked you to remain in Ephesus, which is the metropolitan city of Asia, when I was going to Macedonia, the province of the Greeks, so that you might charge certain people—that is, Judaizing Jews and those who did not believe rightly—not to teach otherwise, understand, than we teach, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies—that is, generations without end.

These myths and genealogies provide questions rather than God’s edification, which is in faith.

He is speaking about the Jews, who, besides the Pentateuch, the prophets, and other Scriptures, possess certain traditions—not written down but committed to memory through the tradition of their ancestors—which the Apostle calls myths, that is, inventions and imaginings. These have no usefulness in themselves except that they generate disputes and questions.

[Col. 0784A] Let us mention a few examples from among many. Their tradition says that at the beginning two women were created, Eve and another woman, and they claim that many children were born from them; but sacred Scripture nowhere relates this.

Those people too were like the ones of whom the Lord says [Col. 0784B] (Matt. XV; Mark VII): “Woe to you, Pharisees and scribes, who set your traditions beneath the commandments of God,” saying to their father, “Corban”—that is, “a gift” or “an offering”: whatever might profit you from me is a gift or offering—and many similar things.

Likewise, they raised questions about genealogies: how many years Methuselah, Eber, Noah, and the other fathers lived; what they did, and how or when they did it. Hence they raise the question: if Solomon was anointed king in the twelfth year of his age and reigned for forty years, and Rehoboam, his son, likewise assumed the kingdom in the fortieth year of his age, how could Solomon have fathered a son at twelve?

Such traditions and genealogies provide no edification of God, which is in faith—that is, which pertains to faith in God.

God’s edification occurs when someone speaks things that have some usefulness, through which he prepares and builds a temple for God in the hearts of his hearers. But the inventions of the Jews, which they recite from memory, have no usefulness.

For blessed Jerome says: “What does it profit me to know how many years Methuselah, Noah, Shem, and the other fathers lived?” Nothing.

The same must be understood of their inventions, from which the Apostle commands them through Timothy to desist.

For the end of the commandment is charity. “End” means a boundary; “end” also means the consumption by which food is consumed, so that what was there is no longer present. Thus we say, “The food is finished.”

“End” also means completion, perfection, and consummation, by which a woven fabric is completed. Thus we say, “The fabric is finished,” that is, it has been perfected and completed through weaving.

[Col. 0784D] In this way, the end—or perfection and completion—of the commandment is charity.

Charity securely possesses the whole magnitude and breadth of the divine utterances, through which we love God and neighbor. Therefore the end or completion of every commandment is charity: every commandment is referred to charity, because whoever loves God does not sin, and whoever loves his neighbor as himself does not transgress.

He does not commit adultery with his neighbor’s wife, because he does not wish his own wife to be violated; he does not kill another, because he does not wish to be killed. The same must be understood of the other commandments.

And charity itself must come from a pure heart, not from a feigned one, and from a good conscience and unfeigned faith.

“Conscience” is often used for “hope,” as in this passage. Charity must therefore proceed from good hope, because one ought to love God and neighbor in the hope of receiving eternal rewards in return.

It must also proceed from unfeigned faith, so that what one believes and understands may be fulfilled in action. For faith is feigned when it confesses with the mouth but is not held in the heart or adorned with works. Many possess such faith, of whom it is said: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him.”

True faith, however, is held in the heart, professed with the mouth, and perfected in action.

From these virtues—understand, from charity, good hope, and unfeigned faith—some converted Jews have gone astray into empty talk, speaking things that are vain and contain no usefulness in themselves.

Desiring to be teachers of the law, they understand neither the things they speak nor the matters about which they make assertions [Col. 0785B] as they ought to be understood. Whenever the Jews began to be reproved and convicted concerning their wicked and false opinion, and concerning their fables and empty traditions, they attempted to defend what they had said with the utmost recklessness of judgment and thought, as well as with the most blatant falsehood. They tried to produce the same books of theirs from which they claim to prove it; or else, from memory, they recited many words which they thought could serve as testimony, understanding neither the things they spoke nor the testimonies they produced as they ought to be understood, although they wished to establish their falsehood by them, adducing inappropriate examples.

But we know that the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully. The person who uses the law lawfully is the one who understands why it was given: namely, for the restoration and strengthening of the natural law, which the human race had already trampled underfoot; who understands how long it was to be observed—that is, figuratively, until the coming of Christ; and who understands spiritually, after the Lord’s coming, the things commanded in the law that were formerly understood carnally and figuratively, and now fulfills them—not in figure but in truth. Thus he is to circumcise himself, that is, through baptism and repentance to strip himself of all sins; to celebrate the Sabbath spiritually by resting from evil works; and to keep the moral commandments. For one who uses the law in this way, the law is good.

Knowing this: the law was not laid down for the righteous—that is, for one justified by faith and the grace of baptism—and the law was not laid down for one who wishes to fulfill it, that is, it was not imposed [Col. 0785D] so that it might stand over him. Rather, he is in it, and with it, rather than under it, because he is a friend of the law. Hence, if everyone were righteous, the law would never have been given. But the law was given to the righteous and to sinners, so that sinners might cease from sin through fear of it. “For kidnappers”—the law is understood to have been laid down for them—are seducers who, by deceiving people, steal and sell them.

A faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came to save sinners, of whom I am the first. In Greek, it reads “a human saying,” that is, a pleasant, gracious, and welcome saying. For what is more pleasant, more gracious, or more welcome than to hear that Christ Jesus came to save sinners? If, then, it is human, is it also divine? Certainly, for unless it were divine, it could in no way have saved sinners. But he called it human in another sense, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”; or “a faithful saying” means that it is true and worthy to be accepted by all, because Christ Jesus came to save sinners. As he himself said: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX), to repentance; and the Son of Man came to save what had been lost.

But it must be asked why the Apostle says: “of whom I am the first.” Was Cain not a sinner before him? Were the Sodomites and the Jews who crucified the Lord not sinners before him? Or did Christ come to call and save him first? Were Peter and the other apostles, and many believers, not called and saved before him? They certainly were.

It should be noted that just as someone is called “first” among others in what is good, so he may also be called “first” among others in what is evil; and the word is sometimes used with reference to order or rank. But in this passage the Apostle called himself first out of humility, as though he were worse than the others, or the worst of all. We are accustomed to speak in this way. For example, when a king or any authority passes through a certain place and finds a band of robbers, he says: “Who is first among you? Bring him here”—that is, let the one who is foremost in evil be brought, by whose authority the others practice robbery. Likewise, when someone finds craftsmen at work, he says: “Who is first here?” He is not asking who is older in age, but who is foremost in his craft. Just as that man is first in his craft, so the robber is first in wickedness.

In this way the blessed Apostle speaks of himself, out of humility: “of whom I am the first,” that is, among those sinners whom Christ came to save, I am the worst. For he was truly deeply steeped in wickedness, since he was persecuting Christ, already seated in heaven, on earth in his members.

But for this reason I received mercy: so that Christ Jesus might first display in me all power [Vulgate: patience], as an instruction, or example, for those who were going to believe in him for eternal life. He explains the reasons why he received mercy. Christ, he says, intending to forgive sinners who turn to him, extended his charity even to his enemies. He first chose me, a particularly fierce enemy; and, when he healed me, the Lord acted so that no one might despair in other cases [the printed reading, *ne me in caeteris desperaret*, is uncertain], after the manner of a most skilled physician. When such a physician comes to a place where he was previously unknown and where there are many sick people, he takes first for treatment whoever he finds suffering from the more serious illness and lying in a state of despair. In that person he displays the skill of his art, so that the other sick people, seeing him healed who had been weighed down by the more severe disease, may not despair of recovery. Instead, each one in that place says to his neighbor: “Go to that physician; be confident—he will heal you.”

So the Lord Jesus Christ, the true physician, displayed in blessed Paul the grace of his healing—that is, the mercy of his compassion—by healing him from the sickness of unbelief and the disease of vices. He did this to show in him that if he had mercy on one who had persecuted him [Col. 0787A] in his holy martyrs, he would certainly also have mercy on others.

To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Some understand “King of the ages” in this passage as God the Father, because the Apostle calls him invisible. They say that in the Old Testament the Father’s person was not shown through some created being or likeness, whereas the Son’s was shown, as it was shown to Isaiah, who saw him seated in the appearance of a reigning king, and to Daniel, who said (Dan. VII): “I watched in the night vision, and behold, the Son of Man came, and authority was given to him.”

The blessed Augustine rebukes them, affirming that the invisible King of the ages is the holy Trinity: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This Trinity of persons constitutes the unity of the Godhead, which is one God. Just as the Father is invisible, so the Son is invisible, and the Holy Spirit is invisible, because God is spirit.

Therefore, those who say that the Father’s person was not shown in the Old Testament should consider what Daniel says: “I watched,” he says, “and behold, the Ancient of Days sat” (ibid.). Consequently, the King of the ages is the holy Trinity, which is the one true God, immortal, unchangeable, and invisible in his substance. The Father, then, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, the King of past and future ages. The man assumed by the Word has been king of future ages from the time he was assumed by the Word; for he was not king of past ages, because that man did not yet exist. To God alone—that is, to the holy Trinity—be honor, praise, jubilation, and glory throughout all ages of ages.

This commandment, stated above—namely, that Christ Jesus came to save sinners—or else this commandment that I am about to give you, son Timothy, I entrust to you in accordance with the prophecies previously given concerning you, so that you may wage a good warfare in them. He calls the preceding prophecies the understanding of the prophets that Timothy possessed before he was ordained bishop. “I entrust,” he says, “this commandment to you”—the understanding of the prophets is understood—“which preceded in reality, before you were ordained bishop by me, so that you may wage,” that is, fight, “a good warfare in those prophecies”: that is, a battle, by teaching yourself and others what you proclaim with your mouth and fulfilling it in your works. For *warfare* means battle, and a soldier is a fighter.

Having faith—the right faith is understood—and a good conscience, that is, a good hope, which is understood by “conscience,” as we said shortly above. Therefore, the person who has good hope is the one who performs such works as give him hope of receiving eternal rewards. Some, by rejecting it—that is, faith or hope—have suffered shipwreck with regard to the faith. A shipwreck is called a broken ship; and just as the person who suffers shipwreck is stripped of the possessions he had on the ship and, moreover, perishes himself, so those who reject the faith are stripped of the truth of faith and, in addition, perish in eternal destruction. They have suffered shipwreck with regard to the faith, that is, they have remained naked and separated from the truth of faith, or have even perished.

Among these—that is, among those who have departed from the truth of the faith—are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I handed over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme. Alexander was a coppersmith who came to the faith of Christ but later returned to his apostasy. He was afterward at Athens making temples for Diana, when he stirred the entire city against the Apostle. Hence the Apostle himself says in his letter to Timothy: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me much harm” (II Tim. IV).

There were therefore many who departed from the faith, among them Simon Magus, Hymenaeus, and Alexander. The Apostle handed the latter two over to the devil to be afflicted and punished, through whose persuasion and instigation they had departed from the faith [Col. 0788B] and blasphemed the name of almighty God, so that others would not dare to do likewise. For the Apostle possessed such authority and such grace that by a single word he could hand over to the devil those who had departed from the faith.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, first of all I ask that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority. The blessed Apostle, directing these words to Timothy, gave through him to all bishops and presbyters, and to the whole Church, a pattern of how they ought to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass and pray for all people. The whole Church still retains this pattern or example.

For “supplications” are everything that precedes in the solemn rites of the Mass up to the point where the priest begins to consecrate the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, saying: “Therefore, most merciful Father, we ask you . . .” “Prayers” are those which the priest pours forth during the consecration of the Eucharist up to the breaking of the Lord’s body, namely, when the priest places a certain particle into the chalice.

“Petitions” are the episcopal blessings which the bishop pronounces over the people, invoking the name of God upon them; this practice is taken from the Old Testament. For through Moses the Lord said to the priests: “You shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them” (Num. VI).

“Thanksgivings” are the praises which, after the people have received communion, the priest offers to God the Father, who has deigned to give them the mysteries of the body and [Col. 0788D] blood of his Son for salvation and redemption.

And lest someone should perhaps say, “We ought not to pray for unbelieving kings, judges, and rulers, because they are pagans,” the Apostle, inspired by the same Holy Spirit as the prophet Jeremiah, commanded prayer for all people. Jeremiah sent a letter to the Jews who were in Babylon, instructing them to pray for the life of King Nebuchadnezzar and his sons, and for the peace of the city to which they had been led as captives. He said (Jer. XXIX): “You must pray for them, because in their peace there will be peace for you.”

Similarly, the Apostle gives reasons why he commands such prayers: “so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet”—that is, peaceful—“life in all piety and chastity.” Piety is the worship and religion of almighty God. Therefore the servants of God ought to pray for the king’s life and for the peace of the kingdom, so that they themselves may devote themselves more freely to the worship and religion of God. For often, when enemies drive God’s servants from their homes and wars and seditions rage throughout kingdoms, they cannot devote themselves entirely to the worship of God as they can in time of peace.

Piety also means the mercy which we ought to bestow upon the poor and needy. If we are plundered by enemies, we cannot perform works of mercy, because one who has no means of sustaining his own misery or himself cannot bestow mercy upon another. Therefore, so that we may have something from which to give alms, we ought to pray for the life of the king and rulers, for the peace of the kingdom, and so that we may lead our life—that is, conduct it—in complete bodily chastity.

In time of peace, chastity can be preserved somehow and with very little difficulty. When, however, a kingdom is plundered by brigands and enemies, it cannot be preserved at all, because the lords who have taken captives satisfy their desire and impurity upon them as they please, and the captives are unable to resist. Therefore one ought to pray for the safety and life of faithful kings and rulers, so that, preserved for a long time, they may have peace and the kingdom, and may advance increasingly toward what is better. One should also pray for the unhappy, so that they may recover from unbelief and pass over to the faith.

For this is good in the sight of God our Savior—the implied meaning is, that we should pray for all people—who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Since the Psalmist says, “The Lord has done whatever he desired” (Ps. CXIII), and the Apostle says, “who wishes all people to be saved,” it must be asked why all people are not saved.

The answer is that what the Psalmist says is true: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII). Likewise, he wishes to save all the people who are saved and who seek to be saved through mercy. The Apostle has placed the whole for the part, just as in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII). He did not draw, nor does he draw, all people to himself, but “all things”—the elect are understood—from every kind and nation, from every sex and condition, from kings even to beggars, from the perfect even to a boy or an infant of one day.

Nevertheless, no one can be saved unless the Lord wills it, because “he has mercy on whom he wills” (Rom. IX). If all people had remained in their destruction, God’s judgment would have been just. But so that his mercy and power might be revealed—for he is powerful enough to save all people—in those who perish he displays his just judgment, and in those who are saved his mercy.

His grace precedes us so that we may will; our will ought to agree with his will, and then he himself will grant the power to act. Through joining our will to his will, we become worthy of reward. Yet everything good that we do must still be attributed to his grace. “Who wishes,” he says, “all people to be saved”—those who are saved are understood—and to come to the knowledge of the holy Trinity, which is the supreme and substantial truth.

For there is one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. The Lord Jesus is true God and true man in one person. If he were God alone, he could not be our mediator, because in the nature of his divinity he is of one substance with the Father. Conversely, if he were merely a pure human being, he could in no way be mediator between us and God the Father, because he would be a sinner and like all of us.

Therefore, he who was God took our humanity. Because he was conceived, born, and lived without sin, being true God and man, and died innocently for us, he became our mediator. For there is no one who is God and man except him alone, since a mediator can exist only between two parties.

There is also a bad mediator, who creates discord between two people; but a good mediator creates and secures peace, as the Lord Jesus does between us and God the Father.

Who gave himself as a ransom for all—the elect are understood. What ransom? Himself. He also gave testimony—the resurrection and our ascent to eternal blessedness are understood—at the proper time, that is, at the time when he rose and ascended into heaven. He gave testimony to the resurrection because, just as he himself died, rose on the third day, and afterward ascended into heaven, so we believe that we shall rise on the day of judgment and pass into the joys of the heavenly kingdom, as he himself promised.

[Col. 0790C] For this testimony—that is, in the hope of the resurrection—I was appointed a preacher, so that I might proclaim it.

Therefore I wish men to pray in every place. If the Apostle wishes this, God wishes it, since he dwells in him; for he is the vessel of election. Lest some people should perhaps think that prayer ought to be offered only in the Church, the Apostle says: “I wish men to pray in every place”—in the fields, in the woods, in houses, and on the road.

Nevertheless, he does not command prayer in disgraceful places, such as a dung heap, nor in public places, namely in the forum or the streets, except when one is traveling and is on the road, lest such a person be reproached along with the Pharisees, to whom the Lord said: “Woe to you, hypocritical Pharisees, who pray in the corners of the streets.”

They should lift pure hands toward heaven, free from murder, robbery, theft, and perjury, without anger and dispute—that is, discord.

Likewise, I wish women to pray in becoming attire, not adorned with gold, gems, or pearls. But he says “adorned,” meaning suitably dressed, because nothing is more suitable than white clothing, such as a linen garment. They should have the clothing that becomes women—the implied meaning is that they should have that garment—professing piety through good works, that is, showing through good works that they maintain the worship and religion of God.

Let a woman learn in silence—the thing she does not know is understood—with complete submission, not in the church and not with pride, but at home.

But I do not permit a woman to teach. A woman is permitted to teach within her own sex in her own home, and also to teach children; but in the church she is prohibited from doing so. And why? Because she ought to be subject to the man, since she was made from his body. Or she is not permitted to teach for this reason also: she is weaker in sex than a man, and care must be taken lest, just as Eve through the serpent brought death into the world after being deceived, she too, easily falling into error, lead others into the same error.

Adam was not deceived—the first Adam is understood—by the serpent; but the woman, the first woman being understood, was deceived and became subject to the transgression, that is, to the penalty of transgression.

But she will be saved—the woman is understood—through the bearing of children, if that woman remains in perfect faith, in love of God and neighbor, and in sanctification, so that, apart from her husband, she knows no other man, with sobriety or self-control.

A woman will be saved through the bearing of children—that is, through good works—if she possesses charity, mercy, hospitality, and other such virtues, which the blessed Gregory wishes to be understood by “children.”

Alternatively: will a woman not be saved all the more if she remains chaste? Certainly. But if she has borne children, brought them up in the faith and religion of almighty God, and led them to the perfection of a good life, then, if she has sinned in anything, she will be saved on account of the labor which she diligently devoted to them.

“A faithful saying,” that is, a true saying, whether the preceding or the following one; or “a human saying,” as it is found in Greek, that is, a pleasant, gracious, and welcome saying.

## CHAPTER III

If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work. It is work, not rank; labor, not honor. Therefore one ought to desire the episcopate in order to proclaim the teaching of the word of God to others, to provide a good example, and, if necessity arises, to be the first to run toward the palm of martyrdom.

A bishop must be blameless, that is, without a crime or a capital sin. He did not say “without sin,” because there is no human being on earth who does good and does not sin. He must be adorned with morals, virtues, and teaching, not with gold-embroidered garments or beaver furs; temperate, that is, chaste from every impurity; hospitable.

If a layman or any member of the clergy takes in two or three poor people as guests, he fulfills the duty of hospitality. But if a bishop does not receive everyone, he is considered inhospitable.

He must not be violent, so that he is not a fighter, like the judges of this age; or, if he is struck, he must not return the blow; nor, by a bad example or perverse teaching, must he strike the hearts of those subject to him.

He must not be greedy, suffering among all people from the disease of greed. He must be the husband of one wife: before he is ordained, he must have one wife, so that he is not twice-married or thrice-married; afterward he must abstain entirely.

He must rule his own household well—that is, his family, before he is ordained. He must not be a novice, that is, a recent convert, newly come to the faith, or one who has only recently abandoned secular military service, lest, being lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil—that is, into the condemnation into which the devil fell through pride—and say: “My Church needed my wisdom or my help; therefore it brought me to the faith and set me over itself.”

He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside—that is, from heretics and pagans who are outside the Church. He ought to have a good reputation among them, as we read concerning the blessed Basil.

Likewise, deacons—the need for them to be temperate is understood—must be temperate. Why did he remain silent about presbyters? Because presbyters are included in the episcopal order. For every bishop is a presbyter, although not every presbyter is a bishop. They must not pursue dishonest gain. Dishonest gain consists in accumulating temporal profits through usury and various devices.

Holding the mystery of the faith in a good conscience. A mystery is an hidden matter, and here he calls faith itself by the name “the mystery of faith”—the faith by which we believe in God—which is hidden because it is seen only in the heart. By “a good conscience” he means a good hope, so that through good works they may hope to receive eternal rewards. Holding the mystery of the faith means holding perfect faith in good hope.

Likewise, women must be temperate. Some have wished to understand deaconesses here, but that is not the meaning, as the blessed Augustine says.

You should know how one ought to behave in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. It is called the Church, the pillar, and the foundation of the truth because it is one through the firmness of faith, and because it has been strengthened by heavenly teachings and divine miracles.

And plainly great is the mystery of piety: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit. A sacrament is called a hidden matter; it is the same as a mystery, or something mystical. In this passage the Apostle calls the Word of God the Father a sacrament. In the nature of divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, he remains invisible.

He calls it the sacrament of piety—that is, of religion and true worship—because holy religion belongs to him alone, and he alone is fitting to be venerated. This great sacrament of piety is manifest—that is, it has been revealed in the Church and in the hearts of the faithful—that he is the Son of God.

And this is what follows: “he was manifested in the flesh.” That is, this sacrament, which could not be seen in the nature of divinity, became visible through the flesh, through heavenly teaching, and through divine miracles. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Jesus made this beginning of signs, and manifested his glory” (John II).

This sacrament was justified in the spirit, that is, it appeared to be righteous through the fullness of divinity that was in him and that guarded him from sin. He appeared to angels—that is, to apostles and preachers—through the flesh and miracles. He was preached among the nations by the apostles when they went forth preaching everywhere. He was believed in the world, that is, by the inhabitants of the world, who believed that he was the Word of God. He was taken up in the glory of the Father’s majesty.

The order is reversed: he appeared first to the apostles, then was taken up to the right hand [Col. 0793A] of the Father, and afterward was preached by the apostles and believed by the nations.

## CHAPTER IV

The Spirit plainly says—the words “through me” are understood—as though he were saying: “The Holy Spirit says these things through me.” In the last times—that is, in this final age in which we now live—some will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error, that is, to demons drawing them into error.

The same meaning is expressed in what follows: “and attending to the teachings of demons who speak falsehood in hypocrisy,” that is, in a pretense of truth. For demons speak through the mouths of heretics deceptively, as though their preaching were true; and they have their conscience branded.

A cautery is a physician’s instrument by which human skin and flesh are corrupted and burned. Just as the skin and flesh are corrupted by a cautery, so the mind of those who depart from the faith is corrupted by wicked teaching and perverse conduct. This is what the Apostle says: “having a corrupted mind.”

Forbidding marriage—that is, the celebration of weddings—and saying that marriages were invented by the devil. They do not recall or understand what the Lord said to the first human beings: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I), and “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife” (Gen. II).

In these passages the Apostle, through the Holy Spirit, identified the heretics who arose after his departure: Marcion, Ebion, Cerinthus, Manes, and the other teachers of perverse doctrine.

But avoid foolish and old-womanish fables—that is, fables unsuitable and inconsistent with the faith. He calls “old-womanish fables” the delirious inventions which old women and little old wives are accustomed to devise and tell to young women.

Exercise yourself for piety, that is, devote yourself to the worship and religion of almighty God, and to mercy.

For bodily exercise is useful to a small extent, that is, it is useful to some degree. This is true because bodily exercise undertaken in some activity provides relief to the body.

Alternatively, bodily exercise undertaken in fasting, vigils—that is, abstinence—and the restraint of the body benefits little the person who has the means to give alms to the poor but withholds them.

But piety—that is, the work of mercy—is useful for everything, possessing the promise of the present life, which now is, and also of the life to come. God provides temporal assistance in the present to the person who takes care to give alms to the poor, and eternal life in the future. This is what he says: “possessing the promise of the present life and of the future.”

He is the Savior of all people, especially of the faithful. Just as almighty God is the creator of all creatures, so he is also their savior, because he saves them in this age. Yet he is especially the Savior of the faithful, whom he saves both in this age and in the future.

Let no one despise your youth. Adolescence and youth are understood as one and the same. Timothy was already a young man; therefore he says: “Show yourself in such a way that no one can despise your age.” You are young in age; be old in mind and conduct.

Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Here he calls faith, wisdom, the remission of sins, and the grace of the episcopate “grace.” It was given to him through prophecy because, by the Spirit of prophecy revealing it, the blessed Paul recognized Timothy as worthy of episcopal honor.

## CHAPTER V

Do not rebuke an older man, because old men are accustomed to take it harshly when they are rebuked by younger people. But the blessed Gregory says that although the Apostle says, “Do not rebuke an older man,” a foolish old man must nevertheless be severely rebuked, and so forth.

Honor widows who are truly widows—that is, one who is sixty years old, has been the wife of one man, and has been left desolate of sons, daughters, and every possession. Here “honor” is understood as gifts and provisions.

For a widow who lives in sensual pleasure in the body is dead in soul before God, although she appears to live before human beings.

If any believing man, or any believing woman, does not care for his or her own children, and especially for members of the household who are in the home, so as to teach them to live and conduct themselves rightly, that person has denied the faith through evil works and is worse than an unbeliever. For it is better not to know the way of truth than afterward to depart from it.

[Col. 0794C] Let a widow be chosen—the words “to be supported from the resources of the Church” are understood—who is not less than sixty years old, that is, a woman of sixty.

When the younger widows have become wanton, they wish to marry in Christ, that is, in the faith of Christ, and to take a faithful Christian as husband. Many women, when their husbands have died, are accustomed to promise God widowhood and chastity and to take a veil upon their heads. Later, however, they join themselves to their servants and to other men and fornicators, and finally they wish to marry in Christ, that is, to take a Christian as husband, saying: “Because I cannot control myself, I will marry a faithful Christian.”

The Apostle commands that such a young woman be avoided, since they incur condemnation by nullifying the first faith and promise which they made to God—to remain in widowhood—when afterward they take a husband.

I wish them to give no occasion to the adversary; that is, I wish them not to give the devil an occasion or cause for reproach, so that they may be cursed and blasphemed by them.

If any believing woman has widowed daughters or granddaughters, let her provide them with what is necessary.

Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor. He commands that a double honor be shown to presbyters: in greetings, namely, so that those subject to them humble themselves before them, and in the provision of gifts and temporal assistance.

Do nothing with prejudice by turning aside to one side or the other; that is, do nothing unless you first examine and discern by your own judgment whether it ought to be done or not.

Lay hands quickly on no one, until you have examined his life and faith: whether he holds the right faith and possesses the teaching by which he can teach the people. Without these three things no one is to be ordained bishop or presbyter: without Catholic faith, good conduct, and sound teaching.

Nor share in the sins of others. A bishop shares in another’s sins—that is, becomes a participant in them—when he knows someone to be genuinely guilty, or hears that person’s evil reputation, and nevertheless ordains him bishop or presbyter.

But if he does not know that person’s sins, does not hear his evil reputation, and does not see him confessed or convicted by witnesses [Col. 0795B], then, even if the person ordained is a sinner, the bishop is not a participant in his sins.

Do not continue drinking only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses. People who have been nourished with wine are accustomed to become ill when they abstain from wine, because drinking wine is almost natural to them.

The same applies to other things with which a person has been nourished and which he has habitually used: whenever he abstains from them, the body becomes weak, and he is no longer able to perform the divine office as well or devote himself to the service of God.

Therefore, lest Timothy, by abstaining too much from wine, become even more infirm and later be unable to devote himself to divine work, the Apostle commands him to use a little wine, since when someone drinks wine with moderation and sobriety, it provides relief to the body.

But why did the Apostle heal Publius’s father, who was suffering from dysentery, by a mere word, while he did not heal his disciple Timothy, but merely showed him, in a certain way, a medicine by which the body might be somewhat relieved? Publius’s father was an unbeliever and needed to be healed by a miracle, so that through the bodily health granted to him he might attain the health of the soul. Timothy, however, who was a believer, did not need to be healed by a miracle, because he was exceedingly faithful.

## CHAPTER VI

If anyone teaches otherwise—the teaching that faithful servants ought not to serve unbelieving masters is understood—and does not assent to the sound, or true, words of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor to the teaching that is according to piety, that is, according to religion—the matter of life is understood.

In this passage he criticizes the Jews, who said that a servant should not be kept in service except for six years, according to the commandment of the law. But the blessed Augustine says that this must be understood spiritually, and that it contains a great mystery: what they observed carnally, he says, means that a servant ought to serve his masters for the entire time he lives, unless he earns freedom from them.

Such a person is proud, teaching otherwise while knowing nothing good, but sick in mind over disputes and quarrels about words, which are one and the same thing. From these disputes arise blasphemies, because he blasphemes sacred Scripture through a bad interpretation; evil suspicions toward one another, because one suspects that another does not understand correctly; quarrels among people whose minds are corrupted, because by fighting with one another over questions they corrupt people’s minds.

Such people are deprived of the truth, that is, separated far from it, because they think that temporal gain or profit is piety or preaching—that is, they preach in order to receive temporal profit from their hearers.

But piety with contentment is great gain. It is as though he were saying: “Do you wish to know, Timothy, what constitutes great profit or gain? Piety—that is, faith and knowledge of the holy Trinity—is great gain with contentment, when a person does not desire to have more than is necessary to meet the needs of the body.”

For those who desire to become rich fall into various temptations, because day and night they think about how they can become wealthy; and they also fall into a snare, that is, into the devil’s condemnation.

The root, or beginning, of all evils is greed—that is, love of money and of honor—which is also called avarice, because all evils proceed from it. Let us see how. For example: “I want to commit adultery”; I kill the woman’s husband—and greed brings this about. “I want to abound in riches”; I take away someone’s horse and rob others—and here too there is greed. The same is to be understood of the other vices.

But there is a question at this point: why does the Apostle say, “The root of all evils is greed, or avarice” [Col. 0796C], when Wisdom says, “The beginning, or root, of every sin is pride”? How, then, can both be true—that avarice is the root of sin and pride its beginning? Both are true, because these two are joined together, and neither can exist without the other. For avarice concerns not only riches but also elevation and rank. Every proud person exalts himself so that he may appear greater than others, while the avaricious person gathers riches so that he may be higher and more powerful than others in status and may surpass them in the multitude of his riches. Some, desiring—or, that is, seeking beyond measure—this greed or avarice, have wandered from the faith, and so forth.

“Take hold of eternal life,” by teaching rightly and living well, “to which you were called and for which you confessed the good confession before many witnesses.” “Take hold of eternal life.” When Timothy was baptized, he was of such an age that, when asked whether he believed in God Almighty and how he believed, he could confess with his own mouth that he did believe.

“I charge you before God the Father, who gives life to all things”—understand, to all things that are given life—and before Christ Jesus, who gave the good confession as his testimony before Pontius Pilate. What was that testimony, or confession? It was this: when Pilate asked whether he was the King of the Jews, he said, “You say so.” There is the testimony. Likewise, when he said, “I bear witness to the truth.”

And what do I charge you to do? [Col. 0797A] To keep the commandment entrusted to you by me, without stain and irreproachable, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, until you are summoned by him through the death of the body—or until the day of judgment, when each of the faithful must keep this commandment that I have commended to you above. This coming of our Lord Jesus Christ the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will be shown at its proper times—that is, at the fitting and appointed times. Here we should understand “the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords” as the holy Trinity: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one almighty God. He shows at the appropriate times the coming of the man assumed by the Word.

He alone possesses immortality—that is, unchangeability. [Col. 0797B] Angels and human souls are immortal, but in comparison with almighty God, whose unchangeability has neither beginning nor end, they are not immortal, because their immortality began in time. Or, to put it more fully: because angels and souls could be changed, they were, as it were, not immortal. For when an angel sinned by lifting himself up in pride, and was thereby changed from good to evil, he fell, as it were, into death, because he could be changed. Likewise, when a human being was changed through sin from good to evil and fell into the death of body and soul, this is why only almighty God remains immortal forever.

“And he dwells in inaccessible light.” Almighty God is substantial light, because he illuminates every human being. But if he is inaccessible, why does the Psalmist say, “Draw near to him, and you will be enlightened” (Psalm XXIII)? He is therefore inaccessible in this respect: no one can draw near to him unless he is drawn by God. To the one who is drawn by God, however, he is accessible.

“No one has seen him”—understand, with bodily eyes—“nor can see him” as he is with bodily eyes. Yet he is seen in part by the perception of the mind.

Command the rich of this age not to think highly of themselves—that is, not to be proud or lifted up in pride—and not to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches. [Col. 0798A] The riches of this age are uncertain because they are transitory. A person will often lose them before death, and entirely at death itself. Therefore no one ought to place his hope in them, but in God—understand, he ought to hope in God—who provides us abundantly with all things for enjoyment; that is, he supplies us with every good thing, which we can arrange in the present in such a way that in the future we may enjoy their reward.

Command them also to do good—that is, to act well—to be communicative, meaning that they should remember that they are mortal and that, in their frailty, they are companions of other human beings; and to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future—that is, to prepare riches for themselves in the future by making friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven; where your treasure is, there also is your heart.”

O Timothy, guard the deposit, or what has been entrusted to you—that is, the grace of faith and the teaching of wisdom that I have commended to you—avoiding, or turning away from, profane—that is, irreligious—novelties of words. For there are novelties of words that are not profane but religious, as we read that the Christians were first called Christians at Antioch, and as the holy Fathers at the synod devised a certain new term, *homousion*—that is, “of one substance”—which had not previously been found throughout the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures. Such novelties of words are not contrary to religion but are religious, because they pertain to religion.

Conversely, there are profane novelties of words, which heretics devised; from these the Apostle commanded Timothy to turn away. And avoid disputes [Col. 0798C]—that is, questions concerning knowledge falsely so called—the questions of the Jews that they are accustomed to raise. They appear to be questions of knowledge, but they falsely bear the name of knowledge, because there is no knowledge in them. Some, promising—or, that is, presenting—knowledge falsely so called as though it were true knowledge concerning the faith, have fallen away—that is, have become alien and have sworn falsely—regarding the faith.

“Grace be with you,” understand, “may it be with you.” Amen—that is, “May what I ask come to pass,” or, “What I have said up to this point is true,” and so forth.

# On the Second Epistle to Timothy

[Col. 0797]

## Argument

[Col. 0797D]

Paul wrote the Second Epistle to Timothy from the city, from prison, concerning the exhortation to martyrdom, what would happen in the last times, and his own suffering; and in order that Timothy might persevere in the duties of right preaching and in holy action, and so forth.

## Chapter One

Paul, an apostle. Whose apostle? An apostle of Christ Jesus, by the will of God the Father, according to the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus.

God the Father Almighty willed that Paul should be chosen through his Son as an apostle, so that through him he might announce the promise of eternal life, which is in Christ Jesus—that is, which is given through faith in Christ Jesus to the elect.
