Eternal life is given through Christ because it subsists in him, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV); and, “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII).

To Timothy, a most beloved son—in Greek, it is found as “most genuine brother”—“I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my ancestors,” or “from my fathers,” with a pure conscience—that is, with a mind pure from every fiction and pretense—because I remember you without ceasing.

Some manuscripts have *quam sine intermissione* (“… without ceasing”), but it is better to say what we read in Genesis (chapter XIV): when Abraham returned from the slaughter of the four kings, Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, met him and offered him both bread and wine. Abraham gave him tithes from the spoils of all his enemies. The same Apostle Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews that Levi, who received tithes from his brothers, was himself tithed in his forefather Abraham. For he was still in Abraham’s loins when Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek the priest.

Thus it must be considered that, just as Levi was tithed in his forefather, so the Apostle served God in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other fathers. This is what he says: “I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my ancestors.” He says this in order to show that he and the other apostles possessed the same faith as the ancient fathers who preceded the Lord’s coming; that faith descended from those fathers to the apostles, and from others to us, just as from us it descends to those who will come.

He gives thanks to God because, by God’s gift, he was always mindful of his disciple Timothy and could not forget him. Or he also gave thanks to God for this reason: because he served God from his ancestors, while desiring to see Timothy so that he might be filled with joy at his arrival, remembering Timothy’s tears, which he shed when departing from Paul.

When the Apostle knew these things, Timothy was across the sea, while Paul himself lay bound in prison, fettered with chains and confined in the stocks. Therefore he desired him so greatly that he might find some consolation in him. For when Timothy departed from him, he shed very bitter tears.

“I remember,” or “I have in mind,” your faith, which is sincere—that is, because you adorn it with good works—which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice. The Apostle recalled Timothy’s genealogy [Col. 0799C] in order to show that his love was directed not only toward Timothy but also toward his parents, whose memory he retained. “I am certain,” understand, “that this same faith dwells in you also.”

For this reason—that is, because you have true faith—I remind you to rekindle the grace of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands. Because Timothy was extremely gentle and exceedingly patient, the Apostle exhorts him to stand firm in the duty of preaching and to rebuke the negligent boldly, saying: “For this reason I remind you to awaken God’s grace in yourself, so that you may preach without fear and correct sinners.” He calls faith, teaching, and action the grace of God, because all these are given freely.

[Col. 0799D] “For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power.” There are two kinds of fear, one good and the other bad. Bad fear is that which is instilled by the devil; Peter had it when he denied the Lord. Concerning it the Lord says, “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew X). Good fear, however, is given by God; Isaiah says that it rested upon the Lord: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord will rest upon him” (Isaiah XI). Concerning this fear the Lord says in the Gospel: “Fear him who can destroy both soul and body.”

It is therefore of the bad fear, by which a person departs from the faith, that the Apostle speaks here: “God did not give us a spirit of fear,” so that we should fear the persecutors of this age and on that account cease from preaching, “but a spirit of power”—that is, of strength—so that we may steadfastly proclaim the word of faith and love, loving God and neighbor; “and of sobriety,” so that we may act soberly and temperately in all things.

Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord. At that time there were some who were ashamed to say that Christ was truly human, had died, and had suffered. Some even denied that he had been born of a virgin and had risen from the dead. Therefore he addresses Timothy, saying: “Do not be ashamed to bear witness to Christ: that he was born of a virgin, that he suffered, that he died, that he rose again, and that he ascended into heaven, where he now sits in the Father’s glory.”

Nor should you be ashamed of me, his prisoner, or despise me, because I am not held and bound in chains on account of theft or murder, [Col. 0800B] but for the sake of the truth. But “share in the labor of the Gospel.” I labor; you labor with me, according to the power of God, who delivered us from death and called us with his holy calling.

Here he joins himself to all the apostles, because they were called by the Lord. For just as Peter, Andrew, James, and John were called by the Lord, who said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Mark I), so the Apostle Paul was called from heaven when the Lord said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

This calling was holy because through it they were sanctified—not according to our works, that is, he did not call us according to our merits, but according to his purpose, that is, according to what he himself determined and predestined. He called us according to the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus [Col. 0800C] before the times of the ages.

Here we should understand the “times of the ages” as the times and ages that began from the time when the world was made, together with day and night. Before that there were neither ages nor times, until the alternation of day and night and the mutability of time came into being; rather, it was as though there were eternity. Therefore, before all ages and times, grace was given to the apostles in God’s predestination, that they would become Christ’s apostles. All the elect, too, were predestined by God in Christ before the beginning of the world, as it is said in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “He predestined us in him”—that is, in Christ—“before the foundation of the world.” Concerning this predestination the Lord says in the Gospel: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had in your predestination before the world existed” [Col. 0800D] (John XVII).

This same grace has now been manifested, understand, in the final age, through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ—that is, through the teaching and miracles of him who is light and who illuminates every human being (John I). The grace that had been predestined before the beginning of the world was shown and manifested in the world by him who indeed destroyed death by rising from the dead and recalling his elect from death.

He illuminated life and incorruption through the Gospel—that is, eternal life, incorruption, and the immortality that he possesses in himself, since he rose from the dead and, having risen from the dead, dies no more. Or he showed and manifested, or illuminates, through the preaching of the Gospel, that, just as he lives, so we hope to rise and live happily without end with him. In this Gospel, understand, I have been placed and appointed as a preacher.

For this reason—understand, because I have been appointed a preacher of the Gospel—I also suffer these things, but I am not confounded, that is, I am not ashamed. What did the Apostle suffer? Persecutions, scourging, prisons, chains, the stocks, hunger, thirst, and other hardships of this kind.

“For I know whom I have believed in”—that is, Christ—and therefore I am not confounded amid torments. “And I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit until that day.” He calls what he has entrusted a deposit. What did the Apostle have entrusted to Christ? He had entrusted his salvation to him. Hence he says: “I am certain that Christ, in whom I have believed, is able to preserve my salvation until that day,” that is, until the day of judgment, because I have placed my salvation in hope and faith in him.

“Having the pattern”—that is, the example—“of sound words that you heard from me.” Words are sound, or the doctrine is sound, when what is preached is fulfilled in works.

“Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us”—that is, guard through the power of the Holy Spirit who is in us the teaching and action that I have commended to you. Or: guard the deposit that you received through the Holy Spirit.

You know that all who are in Asia have turned away from me—that is, they have withdrawn from me. If the Apostle preached in Asia for a time, until all the Asians believed, as Luke said in the Acts of the Apostles, why does the Apostle say here that all have withdrawn from him? In both passages, then, the whole is put for a part. All the elect and predestined among the Asians believed; all the reprobate and non-predestined withdrew. Among these were Phygelus and Hermogenes.

One was Phygelus and the other Philetus; nevertheless, both Phygelus and Hermogenes were apostates and companions. They are the ones mentioned here, and likewise Philetus and Hymenaeus, concerning whom there will be discussion below. Phygelus and Hermogenes therefore joined themselves to the blessed Apostle not in sincerity, but in order to test his preaching and conduct and to criticize him. But when they were unable to do this, they withdrew from him because they did not possess the right faith.

“May the Lord grant mercy to the household”—that is, the family—“of Onesiphorus.” This Onesiphorus was an Asian who had been brought to faith through the Apostle’s preaching. When he had come to Rome on his own business before the emperor—for he was a very noble man of great rank—he sought out where the Apostle was. When he discovered that Paul was in prison, he did not disdain to visit him, but comforted him and supplied what he needed. Hence the Apostle says: “He often refreshed me” through his conversation and consolation, “and he was not ashamed of my chain.”

May God the Father grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day—understand, from the Son—that is, on the day when the Son of God comes for judgment. May God the Father grant him to find mercy. This is like what is read in Genesis: “The Lord the Son rained down from the Lord the Father.”

How many services Onesiphorus performed at Ephesus—you know this better, understand, than anyone else—not only for me and for you, but also for the other faithful.

## Chapter Two

But you, my son, be strengthened in the grace of God, or in the wisdom of God, which is in Christ Jesus. What you heard from me through many witnesses, or what you heard in the presence of many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be capable of teaching others also. Divine preaching ought to be entrusted to those who are suited to that office in their entire way of life—namely, so that they may confirm by their deeds what they preach with their mouths.

No one who serves as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, [Col. 0802B] because no one can serve two masters (Luke XVI), God and the world. Secular affairs consist in acquiring temporal profits through usury and flattery, as do those who serve kings and counts for the purpose of receiving temporal benefits from them.

Bishops ought to guard themselves against such people, since, as the canons say, they ought always to devote themselves to preaching and prayers. Not only bishops, but the whole ecclesiastical order ought, as far as it is able, to keep itself free from these things. Therefore the one who serves God ought to withdraw from them in order to please God, to whom he has proved himself—that is, to whom he devoted himself at the time of baptism.

The laboring farmer ought first to receive a share of the fruits of his labor. In the literal sense, it is right that the farmer and the vinedresser should first taste the fruits [Col. 0802C] of their labor. In a higher sense, the field here is the world or the Church; the farmers and vinedressers are the preachers, who cultivate the hearts of their hearers with the plow of God’s word. They ought to receive from their hearers the fruits of their labor—that is, food, footwear, and clothing—for “the laborer is worthy of his wages.”

They ought first to satisfy their own needs from what they receive, and then afterward to minister to others from what remains. Perhaps someone may ask why the Apostle, who lived by the labor of his hands, gave such instructions to Timothy, namely, that he should receive from his hearers what was necessary for him.

The answer is that Timothy was of good will and good intention. Since he knew that the blessed Apostle lived by the labor of his hands and accepted nothing from his subjects, he wanted to imitate his teacher. But he was unwilling to work because he was burdened by an ailment of the stomach. Therefore the Apostle wrote to him that he should accept support from his subjects, taking account of his infirmity.

Hence he also added: “Understand what I say,” understand, “because these matters concern you.” For the Lord will give you understanding, not only in this matter but also in all things.

Remember that the Lord Jesus rose from the dead, from the seed of David—that is, from the offspring of David—according to my Gospel, that is, according to my preaching.

The Apostle wrote this to Timothy not because Timothy himself was ignorant of it, but because of the heretics whom he foresaw would arise, who would say [Col. 0803A] that Christ had not risen from the dead and had not been born of a virgin. For if he was not born of a virgin, then he certainly did not descend from the seed, that is, the offspring, of David. But the truth establishes that he was born from the seed of a woman without the seed of a man, and yet that the virgin remained a virgin.

“For which Gospel I suffer hardship even to chains as though I were a criminal”—that is, as though I were a thief or murderer. “But the word of God is not bound.” Although I am bound in body, the word of God is not bound, because I continue to preach while held in chains.

Therefore—understand, because the word of God is not bound—I endure every hardship for the sake of the elect, that is, for the sake of those who have been chosen and predestined to obtain salvation.

“For if we have died together with him, we shall also live together with him.” That is, if we die to sins in baptism, just as Christ died in the flesh without sin, then we shall certainly live with him in eternal life, if we remain in good works; and we shall live beyond this life in hope.

“If we endure”—understand, tribulations and sufferings for Christ in this age, just as he endured them for us—“we shall also reign with him” in eternal blessedness. “If we deny him”—understand, before human beings—“he also will deny us,” just as he himself said: “Whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father” (Matthew X).

“If we do not believe him”—understand, that he is the Son of God and true God—“he remains faithful,” that is, he remains true God. Just as almighty God has no need of our praise, so, if we cling to him, he does not increase, nor, if we withdraw from him, does he diminish, because he always remains the same.

“He cannot deny himself,” that is, he does not wish to deny himself by ceasing to be God, as the blessed Augustine says: for it is not fitting that God should deny himself.

Remind them of these things, calling upon God as witness. Do not contend with words—understand, neither with Gentiles nor with Jews—for contention is useful for nothing except the subversion or deception of those who hear. Often, when people contend over questions in the Scriptures, especially those who appear to be wise, they deceive the hearts of simple hearers, because they frequently advance things that are contrary to salvation and truth, caring only to establish their own position.

Nevertheless, if something must be debated from the divine Scriptures, it is better for the wise to engage in an exchange guided by reason than in a quarrel driven by fury.

Take care diligently—that is, earnestly—to present yourself to God as an approved—that is, tested and praiseworthy—worker who cannot be put to shame, rightly handling and explaining with truth the word of truth.

But avoid and flee profane—that is, irreligious and contrary to the truth—things, and empty talk that has no usefulness. For empty talk makes great progress toward impiety—that is, empty talk greatly advances irreligion—and their speech, that is, the speech of heretics, spreads like cancer.

Just as the disease called cancer, when it arises in a human limb, occupies the whole limb and often brings death to the entire body, because it serves, that is, grows, more and more and eats the flesh, so the speech of heretics eats the life of the soul—that is, it eats faith and kills the soul itself through its error. And just as cancer spreads—that is, grows—from limb to limb, so error grows as it passes from one person to many.

Among these heretics who possess empty or meaningless talk are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away, or fallen, from the truth of the faith, saying that the resurrection has already taken place.

Two resurrections have been proclaimed by the Lord and believed by us. The first takes place in the soul and in faith, when a person who is dead in unbelief, disobedience, unrighteousness, and every sin comes to baptism and, through faith in almighty God and through the grace of baptism, rises to faith and obedience. Concerning this resurrection the Lord says: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who hear”—that is, those who obey—“will live” (John V).

The other is the general resurrection of bodies, which will take place on the day of judgment. Concerning it the Lord also says: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth” (ibid.).

Here the Apostle is speaking of the resurrection that takes place in the soul and in faith, which Hymenaeus and Philetus said had already occurred. Were they not speaking the truth? Certainly they were, and the Apostle does not rebuke them for that reason. He rebukes them because they confessed only this resurrection while denying the other, which will take place in the body.

For all sects that have dared to implant their error in human beings have not denied this resurrection of minds, as the blessed Augustine says, but the resurrection of bodies. Otherwise people would say to them: “If the soul will not rise, why do you say such things to me? What do you intend to do in me? If you do not make me better from worse, why do you speak to me?””

Many nevertheless denied the resurrection of the flesh, like Hymenaeus and Philetus, who, having withdrawn from the faith and fellowship of the blessed Paul, sowed this sort of error: “Whoever has been baptized has already risen in the soul. No one needs to fear, because there will be no resurrection of bodies.”

But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal. Someone might say: “And who will be able to resist them—Philetus and Hymenaeus?” Therefore he immediately added: “But God’s firm foundation stands.” He calls the firm foundation of God the firm faith by which we believe in almighty God as we ought to believe, and by which we believe in the resurrection of souls in the present and of bodies in the future.

This foundation stands in the hearts of the faithful, bearing this seal—understand, the words that follow: “The Lord knows those who are his.” This is the impression of the seal, because the Lord knows—that is, chooses—those who belong to his inheritance. This is the seal of faith, because while others depart from the faith, those who are elect can in no way be led astray. For to know in God means to choose.

And if this is so—that is, if the Lord chooses those who are his—“let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity,” that is, from iniquitous people, and, if he cannot do so bodily, at least in mind. Or again: let every elect person who names the name of the Lord, as it ought to be named, depart from every iniquity and error—with the heart, the mouth, and the work.

In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay. In the literal sense, in the great house of a king or some great person there are golden and silver vessels for honor, from which he eats and drinks; there are wooden and earthen vessels for dishonor, in which meat is cooked and other things are carried.

In a higher sense, this great house is the holy Church, which is so extensive that it stretches from east to west and from south to north. In it there are golden and silver vessels, the elect; and wooden and earthen vessels, the reprobate.

By gold are understood those who possess spiritual understanding; by silver, those of lesser rank who possess eloquence and speech. These are for honor because they will be raised to the honor and glory of the heavenly homeland. The wooden and earthen vessels are the reprobate, who are plunged into the punishment of condemnation.

Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things—understand, from heretics and errors—he will be a vessel for honor.

But avoid and flee youthful desires—that is, adultery, uncleanness, luxury, theft, robbery, hunting, vagrancy, and every kind of wantonness. Pursue—that is, embrace—righteousness, so that you may live rightly. It is as though he said: “In place of youthful desires, implant these virtues.”

Avoid foolish questions of Jews, heretics, and Gentiles, and questions that are without discipline—that is, without any usefulness—because they produce quarrels, and quarrels produce hatred.

But the servant of the Lord ought to be teachable. As regards the proper meaning of the words, there is a difference between *docilis* and *docibilis*: *docilis* is one who can teach others; *docibilis* is one who can easily be taught. Hence it is said, “They shall all be taught by God” (John VI), that is, “They shall easily be taught by God.”

But the Apostle, not attending to the proper meaning of the words, appears here to have used *docibilis* in place of *docilis*, because a bishop ought to be *docilis*—that is, he ought to teach others.

He should correct those who resist the truth with gentleness, lest God perhaps grant them repentance—understand, from their former errors and sins—so that they may acknowledge the truth. [Col. 0805D] The expression in which he says “lest perhaps,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “lest at some time God grant them repentance,” was formerly used in place of “if perhaps,” but is now considered unusual.

“Correcting them,” he says, “with gentleness, if perhaps God should grant them repentance.” And may they recover from the snares of the devil—that is, may they withdraw from the devil’s errors, by which they are held ensnared, and begin once more to understand the truth. For *resipiscere*—“to recover”—is as though it meant *resapere*, “to understand again.”

From whom—that is, from the devil—they are held captive in order to carry out the devil’s will.

## Chapter Three

In the last days—that is, in the final age—there will be people who love themselves, understand, and not God. A person loves himself when he pleases himself and fulfills his own desires and wishes rather than God’s; nor can he truthfully say with Peter, “You know that I love you” (John XXI). For the person who loves God does not seek his own will but God’s.

The Apostle Paul was a prophet, and therefore he prophesied what now exists in the Church and what is still to come. Those who feed Christ’s sheep with the intention of making them their own rather than Christ’s are shown to love themselves, not Christ.

“And they will be greedy,” that is, lovers of money; “arrogant,” wishing to dominate others; “proud,” boasting of the honors they receive from their subjects; “blasphemers,” blaspheming God through heresies; “disobedient to parents,” that is, to spiritual fathers or even to father and mother; “ungrateful” for God’s benefits, or returning evil for evil; “wicked,” not honoring father and mother, exceeding the measure of sin, or killing their own and others’ souls; “without affection,” that is, without love, not sympathizing with the weak; “slanderers,” that is, detractors, trying to stain the reputation of the saints; “without self-control,” that is, not restraining their worst desires; “savage,” that is, cruel, producing quarrels; “without kindness,” that is, without benevolence, neither knowing nor wishing to help others; “traitors,” that is, revealing and making known to enemies the deeds of good people, which ought to be kept hidden—for there is no person who does good and does not sin; “insolent,” that is, impudent, disturbing human modesty with shameless inventions; “lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God,” that is, preferring temporal joys to spiritual delights and fulfilling the desires of the flesh.

All these vices sprout from that root: people love themselves.

They have the appearance of piety—that is, the model or form of religion—but deny its power. The power of religion or piety is the goal or fulfillment of the commandment: love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith—that is, love together with faith and hope and with the performance of good works.

For among these—understand, among the heretics—are those who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins. Filled with the Holy Spirit, the Apostle foresaw that the heretics called Manichaeans and others would arise, and he speaks of the future as though it were present.

For the Manichaeans entered women’s houses and deceived them, especially in Persia. Hence the Apostle says: “There will be some who will enter women’s houses and lead captive little women, burdened with sins, from the right sense of faith to a perverse sense.” They are led by various desires and errors, “always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth.” They appear to devote themselves to study, but they do not reach the point of distinguishing truth from falsehood or good from evil.

Just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth. The disposition of heretics is always restless. To show what efforts Pharaoh’s magicians made, the Apostle mentions Jannes and Mambres. They were two brother magicians whose names the Apostle did not find in the divine books but in apocrypha—that is, hidden writings—which are not to be read by everyone, because, amid much truth, they also contain falsehood.

These two magicians resisted Moses when they turned their staffs into dragons, just as Moses had done, and turned water into blood. But when they came to the third sign—that is, to the gnats [*cymphes*]—they failed there, saying, “This is the finger of God.” Once the sign had been removed from the earth, their magical evil-working was also removed. And it was fitting that they were defeated at the third sign, because their evil-working was overcome by the power of the Holy Spirit, who is the third person of the Trinity.

I say that they will be people corrupted in mind and disqualified concerning the faith—that is, not upright—but they will not be able to proceed further, understand, in resisting, if the truth is brought forward. This happened immediately when heretics came into the council of true teachers and began to converse with them: they could no longer overcome others through their errors, as Elvidius was overcome by the blessed Jerome and other heretics by other true teachers.

But you have followed my teaching and instruction, which is the same thing. “To instruct” is said as though it meant “to establish inwardly.” You have also followed my purpose of living well.

All who wish to live piously—that is, religiously and justly—in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution, either from the devil, or from evil people, or even from their own members.

Every Scripture inspired by God—that is, given by God—is useful for teaching others, for reproving the negligent, for correcting those who wish to persist in wickedness, and for instructing in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work. [Col. 0807C]

## CHAPTER IV

I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, by his coming and his kingdom: proclaim the word of the Gospel. Be persistent in admonition, at the proper time with those who are willing and stand in the harbor of rest, and at an inconvenient time with those who are unwilling. Convict sinners; entreat those who labor well to advance toward better things; rebuke those who do not wish to correct themselves, with all patience and instruction.

Why is it that, when writing to Titus, he commanded him, saying, “Rebuke with all authority,” while in addressing a letter similarly to Timothy he says, “Rebuke with all patience,” unless it is because he was the physician of both? Titus possessed excessive patience; therefore he commanded and urged him to rebuke with all authority, lest, because of his gentleness, he fail to correct those who were sinning. Timothy, however, because he had a harsher disposition, needed to be admonished to rebuke sinners with all patience, lest by rebuking too harshly he drive some fainthearted person into despair. [Col. 0807D]

They will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires—that is, despising teachers of the truth, they will gather teachers who say what they themselves desire and what accords with their wishes—and they will have itching ears. To itch is to scratch; those have itching ears who always keep their ears intent on hearing something new.

[Col. 0808A] Do the work of an evangelist. The work of an evangelist is to teach and to act, as we read of Christ, that “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). Therefore, someone who announces some good thing but does not himself carry out the very work that he teaches may indeed be called an evangelist, but he does not perform the work of an evangelist.

Fulfill your ministry. His ministry was to teach others, so that when he departed from the body, someone would remain who could be appointed in his place. The meaning is: “The time of my passion is now near; your departure too is imminent. Therefore, just as I taught you so that someone would remain after me to fulfill my ministry, so instruct others who may succeed you.” It is as though Timothy had said to him, “Why do you command me to fulfill my ministry?” He added:

[Col. 0808B] For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand, or, “is imminent.” We use “to pour out” to mean “to taste,” “to pour forth,” or “to sacrifice”; hence the forms *delibo* and *delibor* are derived. Here it is used of sacrifice and offering, as though he were saying, “For I am already being sacrificed.” Nero became the priest of Peter and Paul, but his sacrifice was not counted as grace; their death, however, was a most acceptable sacrifice to God.

I have fought the good fight—that is, “I have fought well”—and I have finished the race. Just as one who ran in the stadium, when he reached the appointed place, received the prize promised to him, so the blessed Apostle, running between the boundaries of faith, reached the crown of his labor. Hence he himself says, “I have kept the faith.”

[Col. 0808C] Henceforth—or, “for the future” or “from now on”—there is laid up and reserved for me with God the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, that is, on the day of judgment. He speaks of the day of judgment without qualification, as though it were known to everyone. In truth, that day ought to be certain and known to all, and awaited by all.

And not only to me—understand, “will he give the crown”—but also to those who love his coming. Those love his coming who, secure in their hope of the reward, expect to be recompensed by him. Just as any king or emperor once gave a crown to one of his commanders who returned victorious from his enemies, so the Lord will grant his victors and soldiers eternal rewards and prizes that will endure without end.

[Col. 0808D] Demas has abandoned me, loving this present age more than God, and has gone to Thessalonica. He had remained with the blessed Apostle for a long time, but when the time of persecution arrived, he withdrew from him and became an apostate.

Crescens has gone to Galatia. He was faithful and, for the sake of preaching, went to other nations at the Apostle’s direction; Titus did likewise.

Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in the ministry of preaching. This is Mark the evangelist, who remained with Peter and Paul for a long time, sometimes staying with Peter and sometimes with Paul.

Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come, [Col. 0809A] and the books that I left there; especially bring the parchments on which I may write my letters. The *paenula* was a consular garment, worn by Roman consuls when they entered the senate-house. But someone may perhaps ask how or from where this kind of garment came to the blessed Apostle. The answer is that, before the Lord’s coming, when the Romans were acquiring the monarchy of the whole world, they had the custom that whatever nation met them with peace and crowns, they would grant it freedom, to such an extent that its members were called their brothers and were designated Roman citizens. They also granted them the power to build a senate-house and to have consuls, just as the Romans themselves did.

Paul’s father, therefore, was from the town of Giscala in the Promised Land, where he was born; he was later transferred to Tarsus in Cilicia. At a certain time, when the Romans were coming through Cilicia, he himself met them with the other Tarsians, since he was regarded as a nobleman among them, and received them peacefully. Then the Romans granted them the freedom mentioned above and the power to build a senate-house and to wear consular garments, so that, clad in *paenulae*, they could enter the senate-house according to Roman custom. There Paul’s father earned the right to receive a *paenula* because of his dignity. After his death, the Apostle retained this garment in memory of him. [Col. 0809B]

Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils. This is the Alexander of whom we spoke above, who returned to apostasy. Since he was an artisan, he made shrines of Diana at Athens, and for this reason he himself stirred up the whole city against the Apostle, [Col. 0809C] resisting his preaching vigorously.

The Lord will repay him according to his works. He does not say, “May he repay him,” in the optative manner, but “he will repay him,” in the indicative; this is the language of one announcing what will happen, not of one uttering a curse. He speaks similarly of that hypocrisy of the Jews whose overthrow he foresaw as imminent: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII). For prophets often foretell future events, especially in the form of a curse, just as they frequently sing of things that were to come in the figure of the past tense.

[Col. 0810A] At my first defense no one stood by me. Here he calls “defense” the persecution and oppression that he endured when, at the beginning of his faith, he was sent with Barnabas by the Holy Spirit to preach. He rightly calls that persecution a defense, because temporal tribulation will defend the elect from the punishments of hell on the day of judgment.

May it not be counted against them that they all abandoned me. He does not pray for Alexander, who had sinned by attacking brotherhood through envy, but for those who had not destroyed love, though they had succumbed through fear, so that they might be forgiven. Therefore, there is a great difference when, after the knowledge of God, someone attacks brotherhood and is inflamed by the fires of envy against the very grace by which he was reconciled to God.

[Col. 0810B] But the Lord stood by me, so that through my mouth the word of preaching might be heard by all the nations, and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion—that is, from the devil’s ambushes. Peter says of him: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter V).

Alternatively, he calls Nero a lion, from whose hands the Lord delivered him when he came to Rome, brought there by those who governed Judaea because he had appealed to Caesar. When he came to Rome, he remained for two years in free custody, in a lodging of his own, and afterward went on to other nations that lay around Rome. When he wrote this, he was in free custody; and because he was not killed immediately after he was brought there, he says that he was delivered.

[Col. 0810C] May the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. The Lord Jesus Christ is God and man; therefore the Apostle prays that the Word of God the Father—namely, the Lord Jesus—may be with Timothy’s spirit. And if he is with the spirit, he will also be with the body.

Grace be with you—that is, the forgiveness of sins, reconciliation with God the Father, and all the good things freely bestowed by God—may they be with you. Amen. That is, “May it be so,” or, “May the things I have written thus far be true,” and so forth.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

[Col. 0809]

## Argument

[Col. 0809D]

As the Apostle was passing from the island of Crete to other nations and the inhabitants of their cities, he left his disciple Titus in Crete in his place, so that those who had recently come to the faith might have a protector and not be overturned from the stability of the right faith by the chatter of the Jews or the barking of heretics. But in order to make him more diligent—especially since correction or exhortation by zealous teachers makes disciples more zealous—he reminds and fully instructs him concerning the establishment of the presbyterate, spiritual conduct, and the avoidance of heretics who believe Jewish fables. He wrote to him from the city of Nicopolis.

## CHAPTER I

Paul, servant of God. Since our Lord and Redeemer said to his apostles, “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John XV), one may ask why the distinguished preacher and teacher of the nations later called himself a servant. But if we carefully consider the matter, it will plainly become clear that there are two kinds of servitude, just as there are two kinds of fear, and that he was certainly not contradicting the Lord’s words.

There is a servitude of fear, in which a servant fears his master and a maidservant her mistress, fearing that they may be flogged by them. There is also a servitude of love, in which a good son fears his father, being afraid of offending him in anything and thereby being deprived of his inheritance. Concerning that servitude which pertains to fear of punishment, he says to the apostles: “I will no longer call you servants of fear, but servants of love.” Concerning the servitude that pertains to the love of sons, he says elsewhere: “When you have done everything that has been commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XVII). The Psalmist likewise says: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever” (Psalm XVIII).

The holy angels also possess this fear; indeed, the apostles possessed it through the coming of the Holy Spirit, through whom charity was poured into their hearts. We too ought to possess it with the greatest devotion.

One may also ask why, in the Epistle to the Romans, he calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ, while here he calls himself a servant of God the Father. When Paul says “servant of God,” the name “God” refers to the person of the Father. The answer is that, to demonstrate that the three persons possess one essence, one divinity, and one power, he openly called himself there a servant of Jesus Christ and here a servant of God the Father. For just as those three persons reign over and rule every creature, so inseparably they possess every servant devoted to them. Consequently, whoever is a servant of Christ is certainly a servant of the Father and of the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle of Jesus Christ. Just as the Apostle’s servitude is referred indiscriminately to the whole Trinity, so his apostleship must likewise be referred collectively to the whole Trinity. For the whole Trinity chose him for the grace of preaching, saying to the apostles: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have taken them” (Acts XIII).

Yet he carefully distinguished servitude from apostleship, because not everyone who is a servant is immediately also an apostle, whereas whoever is an apostle is certainly also a servant.

According to the faith of God’s elect. Here we must understand “the elect” to mean those of whom the Lord says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV), and of whom the same distinguished preacher says, “He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians I). These are those who were not merely called but were also chosen for eternal glory. According to the faith of these elect, Paul is an apostle of Christ Jesus, because he was sent to preach to the nations the rectitude of faith that the apostles themselves held.

And the knowledge of the truth that accords with piety. This depends on what precedes, as follows: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the faith of God’s elect and according to the knowledge of the truth”—a truth that accords with piety.

The truth is Christ, who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John VII). According to knowledge of him, Paul fulfilled the office of apostle—or rather, according to knowledge of the whole Trinity, which is the supreme truth. The Apostle existed according to knowledge of the truth because he recognized that almighty God has a trinity of persons and a unity of divine substance.

This knowledge of the truth is rightly said to accord with piety—that is, with the worship and religion of God—because it teaches and embraces through love those things that pertain to the religion of the true God. There is, however, a truth lacking piety, as in the liberal arts. Grammar and dialectic possess truth in speaking correctly, and dialectic distinguishes between false and true through the reasoning of syllogisms; yet they do not contain within themselves knowledge of piety, since they do not discuss the religion of the true God or the salvation of the soul.

Geometry, too, and arithmetic, as well as music, which consist in the subtlety of numbers, possess knowledge of truth in themselves, but that knowledge is not knowledge of piety. Therefore, to show that the Apostle possessed knowledge of the truth that accords with piety, he appropriately set these words forth. It follows:

In hope of eternal life. The faith of the elect and the knowledge of the truth that accords with piety are directed toward the hope of the reward of eternal life. Whoever possesses right faith and knowledge of almighty God, adorning that knowledge by living piously and religiously, certainly possesses the hope of an eternal reward. For no one can possess faith and knowledge of the truth if a sure hope is lacking.

Which God, who does not lie, promised before the ages. [Col. 0812B] It is certain to all the faithful that every human being is a liar, while God alone is truthful; he can fulfill everything that he has promised. Therefore he who does not lie, because he is supreme truth, promised his faithful eternal life before eternal times.

The term *saecularia* (“the ages”) is said to derive from *sequendo*, “following,” because they resolve themselves within themselves, as Varro attests. The ages are reckoned from the time when formless matter was distinguished into separate forms and from the time when God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Genesis I). From that point the diversity of time, the succession of hours, and likewise of days began to resolve themselves within themselves.

Before that, however, as the teachers say, there was not time but eternity, which simply possessed being. The difference between time and eternity is that eternity is stable, whereas time is mutable.

[Col. 0812C] But if God promised human beings eternal life—and there is absolutely no doubt that he did—how did he promise it to those who had not yet been created, before eternal times? He did so because, in his eternity, through foreknowledge and predestination, that which would occur at the appropriate time was already fixed.

Although human things cannot be compared wholly with divine things, let us offer an example so that what is being said may be understood more clearly. A man who desires a son, long before he has one, prepares houses, household servants, and landed possessions, arranging in his mind to give all those things to his son, although he has not yet been born. So almighty God, in his foreknowledge and predestination, promised his faithful and elect, before all times, that he would give them eternal life. It follows:

[Col. 0812D] But he manifested his word at his appointed times in the preaching entrusted to me according to the command of God our Savior. The Word of God the Father is the Son, concerning whom John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I).

God the Father manifested this Word, which was invisible in the nature of divinity, through human nature. In that nature, having become man, he appeared visible to the world at his appointed times—that is, at times appropriate and arranged by him. Concerning these the same Apostle says elsewhere: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Galatians IV), and so forth.

Therefore, the eternal life that God the Father promised to the elect before all ages is his Word, concerning whom he said of himself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John VI). Whoever is worthy to have the Son, who is life, certainly has the Father with the Holy Spirit, since the whole Trinity is one eternal life, as the Lord himself says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII), together with the Holy Spirit, as one true God.

God the Father therefore manifested the eternal life that he promised before all ages—namely, his Word—at his appointed times, in the manner that has been stated. He also manifested it to us, since we saw him present in the preaching or teaching of the Apostle Paul, which was entrusted and commended to him according to the command of our Savior God, who said to the apostles: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have taken them” (Acts XIII).

“God our Savior” is understood to be none other than the Son. For he, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true Savior and God.

[Col. 0814A] To Titus, my beloved son. He calls him his son in doctrine, example, instruction, and discipline, but not by nature. Titus was his son in the same way as the Corinthians, to whom he himself said, “Through the Gospel I gave you birth” (1 Corinthians IV). For he had brought Titus himself to faith in Christ.

According to the common faith. Titus was not his son according to the faith of all believers, since not everyone’s faith is perfect. Rather, he says “according to the common faith,” that is, according to his own faith and that of those whose faith was most perfect.

Grace and peace from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Savior. Amen.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

[Col. 0813]

## Argument

[Col. 0813B]

While the blessed Apostle was sounding forth the Gospel through preaching in Asia, among others a certain nobleman named Philemon believed, enlightened by divine grace, and was baptized in the sacred and life-giving font. When the Apostle departed from those regions, Philemon did not follow him but remained in his own country, ministering from his resources to the faithful. For he was rich and abounded in many possessions.

He had, however, a servant named Onesimus, still an unbeliever, who fled from him and stole his property. Since his master was a man of great power and nobility, Onesimus feared being captured and subjected to many tortures, especially because he had caused him no small loss. He crossed the sea and came from Greece to Rome. [Col. 0813C] There he found the Apostle confined in prison for his faith in Christ and approached him, since the Apostle recognized him. Instructed by the Apostle, he believed and was baptized, and he ministered to him.

Because the Apostle preached that servants ought to be subject to their masters, he considered it unworthy to keep another man’s servant with him without the master’s consent. Therefore he sent him back to his master, writing him a friendly letter from prison through that same servant, so that he might receive him with loving affection and not inflict punishment for the goods he had taken from him. The beginning of this letter is as follows.

## SOLE CHAPTER

Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ. The name “Apostle” has often been discussed in the other Epistles. [Col. 0813D] Let us now see why, at the beginning of this Epistle, he calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus and omits the title of apostle, which he customarily placed in the others.

He seems to say more by calling himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus than by calling himself an apostle, since many claimed to be apostles of Christ while they preached, but did not wish to be prisoners of Jesus Christ, avoiding the suffering of passion. [Col. 0814B] Yet not everyone who is imprisoned can be called a prisoner of Christ Jesus, since many deserve to be sent to prison and bound in chains for robbery, sacrilege, or some other offense. Those who are bound for the truth of the faith, however, unquestionably are prisoners of Christ Jesus, like Paul and the other apostles, who gloried in being called prisoners of Christ Jesus. For they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

He therefore says that he is a prisoner of Jesus Christ, so that he would in no way dare to leave unfulfilled or refuse what the soldier of so great a king was asking.

And Timothy, a brother. Timothy was his fellow bishop, ordained by him, and therefore a brother in the faith. He places the name of his fellow bishop alongside his own name so that the letter might possess greater authority.

[Col. 0814C] It may also be understood in another way. Whenever the Apostle dictated his letters, his disciples sat around him. If something was reported to one of them, he would place it in the body of the letter as though it were his own words, remembering that the Lord often reveals what is better to a younger person. Therefore, because Timothy was a participant in that letter, he placed his name in it as his own.

To Philemon, beloved and our fellow worker, and to Appia, our most beloved sister. In Greek, “beloved” is not found, but rather “worthy of love” (*diligibilis*). Someone who is loved but does not love cannot be called “beloved,” nor is he worthy of love. One who is worthy of love, however, is both loved and loving, and is therefore worthy of love. This fits Philemon very well. He was worthy of love and was therefore loved by the Apostle, while he himself loved the Apostle.

He calls him a fellow worker because he collaborated with them in the work of preaching and assisted the faithful through the administration of his resources.

[Col. 0814D] Appia, whom he calls his most beloved sister, is believed to have been a religious woman. He calls her a sister in the faith because of her dignity, not because she was actually his sister according to the flesh. She was either truly Philemon’s wife or his natural sister.

Her name is inserted between two apostolic men, between Paul’s fellow worker, Philemon, and his fellow soldier, Archippus, so that, supported by such companions on either side, she might not appear to possess merely the status of her sex, but also that of merit.

[Col. 0815A] This Archippus should be understood to have fought at some time with Paul and Timothy against the adversaries for the name of Christ and to have emerged victorious. Therefore he is now called their fellow soldier, either because he was victorious in the same contest and warfare or because he was still fighting alongside them in constant preaching.

And to the church that is in your house. When Philemon came to the faith, his wife, children, and the greater part of his servants believed, and the Apostle addresses words of greeting to all of them. Since they were many, he designates them by the name “church.” In Latin usage, “church” means an assembly of the faithful.

Therefore, to make it clearer that the reference was not to the person of Archippus but to that of Philemon, he explicitly says, “which is in your house,” O Philemon!

[Col. 0815B] Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ—understand, “may they be.” In all his Epistles he gives an identical opening, wishing grace and peace to those to whom he writes.

Grace is faith and the forgiveness of sins, which we freely receive in baptism. Peace is that by which we are reconciled to God the Father and to the angels.

It may indeed also be understood that the words “grace to you from God our Father” refer to God the Father, while “peace” refers to the Lord Jesus Christ, who through the blood of his passion became our peace and reconciliation. But since the nature of the Father and the Son is one, it is better to refer both grace and peace together to both, just as we have more fully explained in other Epistles. The person of the Holy Spirit is understood in his gifts; or, wherever one person of the Trinity is heard, the whole Trinity is understood.

I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers. Thus far Paul and Timothy have written jointly to Philemon, Appia, and Archippus. In what follows, however, it is shown that the Apostle writes only to Philemon and converses with one person.

We can find this practice in his other Epistles as well: several people are named in the preface, but afterward one person is introduced as speaking throughout the whole body of the letter.

When he says, “I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers,” this should be understood to mean that he always gave thanks to God for the salvation of those whom he had acquired for the Lord and always remembered them in his prayers, so that they might persevere in right faith and good works. It is not surprising that the one who urges others, saying, “Give thanks in all things, and pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians V), should himself first have fulfilled this in practice.

[Col. 0815D] It should also be noted that, when he said, “I give thanks to God,” he immediately added “my,” because, although almighty God is commonly the God of all, he is said to be specially the God of those who venerate and worship him through faith and the merit of their life, as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Concerning them he himself said to Moses, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus III)—that is, by right faith and the merit of their life.

Because the blessed Apostle possessed an unwavering faith, through which he knew that God would be favorable to him, and a meritorious life, which he knew pleased God, he said confidently, “I give thanks to my God,” that is, “I offer him praise with thanksgiving for your salvation.”

[Col. 0816A] Hearing of your love and the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints. Philemon, who was worthy of such great praise from the Apostle, undoubtedly possessed love for God and his neighbor. He also possessed faith in the Lord Jesus by believing in him and in all the saints, becoming an imitator of their faith.

For the person who turns that love and faith into action possesses faith and love toward God and all the saints. It follows:

So that the sharing of your faith—understand, “which you share and in which you participate with the apostolic faith”—may become evident in the knowledge of every good work in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 0816B] The preceding words may therefore be joined as follows: “I give thanks to my God, hearing of your love and the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, and I always make mention of you in my prayers, so that the participation by which you participate in the apostolic faith may become evident as possessing every good thing.”

Here “sharing” is understood as participation in the apostolic faith, in which he participated. It may also refer to the communion by which he shared his resources with the faithful.

For I had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother. The blessed Apostle was in prison, and there he heard of Philemon’s reputation, because he provided the greatest refreshment to saints placed in tribulation.

For this reason he emphasizes more fully why he said, “I give thanks to my God, making mention of you in my prayers.” It was certainly fitting to give thanks to his God for the love of one who, through the inward and profound affection of his heart, had refreshed the spirits of the saints by receiving their requests.

The word “hearts” (*viscera*) is sometimes used for children and sometimes for an inward and immense affection of love. Here it may be understood in both ways. “The hearts of the saints,” he says, “have been refreshed through you, brother”—that is, the children of the saints, placed in tribulation and poverty, received refreshment through your consolation and the assistance that you provided them; or, the inward feelings and great affections of the saints were refreshed through you.

Those placed in tribulation and poverty receive great refreshment when they find someone who consoles them. Philemon plainly fulfilled this role.

[Col. 0816D] For this reason—understand, “because their inward affections have been refreshed through you”—although I have great confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what pertains to the matter, that is, to your benefit, I appeal to you on the basis of love. Since you are such a person, I appeal as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

He repeats so often that he is a prisoner of Christ Jesus in order to make Philemon most perfect in faith, so that he would not despair if some opposition arose against him. Alternatively, he does so because, since he could not otherwise assist Philemon while he was in tribulation, he might at least more easily obtain what he requested for the servant.

He could have commanded him, as he himself makes clear, since he was an Apostle and Philemon was subject to him, especially since Philemon had come to the faith through the Apostle’s efforts. But because he possessed the greatest love toward all the saints, he preferred to appeal rather than command. It was not necessary for him to command Philemon by apostolic authority.

By saying, “since you are such a person, as Paul, an old man,” he shows that Philemon was his contemporary and thus addresses him almost more honorably than he would have addressed someone younger in age.

[Col. 0817A] I appeal to you for my son, whom I have begotten in chains, Onesimus. Wishing to obtain what he requested, he now pleads not for Philemon’s servant but for his own son, so that, when Philemon heard him called a son by the Apostle, he might love him more as a brother than punish him as a servant for his flight and theft.

He had begotten him while he was in chains, not through the flesh but through preaching, just as he had begotten the Corinthians, to whom he said, “Through the Gospel I gave you birth” (1 Corinthians IV).

[Col. 0817B] He was being held in chains when Onesimus came to him—Onesimus, who was once useless to you but is now useful both to me and to you. He was useless to his master Philemon when he not only withdrew from his service by fleeing but also stole his property.

“To you alone,” he says, “he was useless, not to others.” Now, conversely, through the recompense of usefulness by which he is useful both to his master and to Paul and to others, he merits more love through Paul than he had previously merited hatred.

He was already useful to his master in this respect: he served the Apostle in place of his master, something his master ought himself to have done if he had been present. He was useful to the Apostle in this respect: while the Apostle was in prison and detained in chains, Onesimus ministered to him in temporal matters and, moreover, in spiritual matters, carrying the Apostle’s letters here and there.

[Col. 0817C] Receive him as my own heart. As we have already said, “heart” signifies inward affection, a complete willingness proceeding from the soul, when everything that is within us is received by the one making the request. Sometimes, however, “heart” also means children.

“Receive him,” he says, “as my own heart”—that is, as my most beloved son; or, “receive in him the inward affection of my love.”

I wanted to keep him with me, so that he might minister to me on your behalf in the bonds of the Gospel. He repeatedly calls him his son, the son of his bonds, and the minister of the Gospel in bonds, so that Philemon, the prudent steward praised so highly in the preface, would not dare to refuse, lest he appear unworthy of the praises he had received.

[Col. 0817D] “So that he might minister to me on your behalf,” he says, because, if it were possible, you ought to have ministered to me while I was in chains.

But I wanted to do nothing without your counsel—that is, “I did not wish to keep him without your consent,” so that your good deed might not be done as though by necessity, but voluntarily.

The Apostle could indeed have retained Onesimus for his service without Philemon’s consent. But if he had done this without Philemon’s will, the deed would have been good, but not voluntary; and what is not voluntary is shown not to be entirely good. For nothing is perfectly good unless it is freely chosen.

From this we should consider the Apostle’s prudence: he sends the fugitive servant back to his master so that he might benefit his master once he had been sent back by him. Onesimus could not have benefited him if he had been retained without his master’s knowledge and consent.

[Col. 0818A] At this point some ask why almighty God did not create Adam in such a way that he could not sin. The answer is that, if he had made him unable to sin, Adam’s goodness would not have been perfect and would not have merited a reward; it would have been necessary, and he would not have possessed free will.

For God created human beings in his own image and likeness so that, just as God is good by will and not by necessity, so human beings might also be good by will and not by necessity.

Perhaps for this reason he departed from you for a time, so that you might receive him back forever, no longer as a slave, but as a most beloved brother in place of a slave. Beautifully adding the adverb of uncertainty, “perhaps,” he moderated his statement; for the judgments of God are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as though certain what is doubtful. He therefore spoke cautiously and timidly, without taking a firm position, lest he seem to give all slaves an occasion to flee and become disciples of preachers. By saying “for a time,” he used the expression in place of “for a period.” For all the time of the present life, when compared with eternity, is either nothing or a very brief hour.

“So that you might receive him forever,” he says. No master can have a slave forever, since the condition of both, and of each of them, comes to an end in death. Onesimus, however, who through faith in Christ became eternal for the eternal Philemon—for Philemon himself had also believed in Christ—having received the spirit of freedom, began to be no longer a slave but a brother in faith: from a slave, a most beloved brother and an eternal brother. Hence the Apostle also says, “so that you might receive him forever,” that is, as one who would reign eternally with Christ, “and not as a slave, but more than a slave,” that is, more than a slave, namely, a most beloved brother. For a brother pertains to us more deeply through the affection of charity than a slave does.

Some manuscripts also read: “so that you might receive him in place of a slave, a most beloved brother.” Both readings can be accepted, since when he fled he was a slave, still existing as an unbeliever; but when he returned, he was already a brother, having become faithful through faith. And so that Philemon would not disdain to keep him in the place of a brother, he added, “and especially to me”—that is, “he is a most beloved brother”—“how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the spirit?” The sense is: If he is most beloved to me, how much more ought he to be dear to you, both in the flesh and in the spirit? He is joined to me in spirit because of the unity of faith; but to you he ought to be dear in faith, in spirit, and in the flesh, because he belongs to you. In faith he is your brother, but in flesh and condition he is your slave; therefore he ought to be loved by you all the more. For when he was subject to him in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord; but now he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord. From this it follows that a slave who has believed in Christ is bound to his master by a twofold law: for a time he must be joined to him in the necessities of the flesh, and eternally united with him in spirit.

“If, therefore, you regard me as a partner, receive him as you would me,” as though he were saying: If you wish to have me as a partner, have Onesimus also, whom I regard both as a companion and a partner. If you do not wish to have him as a brother and companion, consider that you will not be able to have me either.

“But if he has harmed you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay.” I, he says, who do not write my other letters myself but dictate them, have written this one to you because of my love for you, so that I might obtain what I ask. I will repay what Onesimus took away by theft. This Letter itself bears witness to this response: I did not dictate it in my customary manner, but wrote it with my own hand. How could he have repaid him for what Onesimus had taken away, if he was being held in prison? He therefore who was deprived of temporal riches for the love of Christ was confident that he could repay him from the gift of heavenly riches. “I will repay you,” he says, “by the power of my prayers, with treasures that do not fail.” Do not delay in forgiving Onesimus; be confident concerning your reward.

“Not to mention that you owe me even your own self.” If you do this, he says, which I ask, then I will not tell you that you owe me all that is yours and that you ought to stand under my authority. For because of the word of Christ that I evangelized to you, and because I made you a Christian and a son of God, you owe me your very self. And if you are mine, not only Onesimus but everything that is yours is also mine and pertains to me. “I could have used him,” he says, “as belonging to me, but I leave the matter to your will, so that you may receive a reward for forgiving him.”

“Yes, brother”—understand, “do as I ask”—“let me benefit from you in the Lord.” To benefit from something is to use and possess it with delight. Hence it is said in the Law: “If you do not do what has been commanded you, you will beget sons and will not enjoy them,” that is, you will not see them with delight, since they will be led captive before you. “Let me benefit from you in the Lord,” he says; that is, let me take delight in your love. “Refresh my inward parts in the Lord,” that is, my son Onesimus, or the inward love and affection of my charity.

“Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.” Whoever presumes upon the person whom he is about to ask is, in a certain way, praising that person by his very presumption, so that he may not be permitted to refuse what is requested.

“At the same time, prepare lodging for me. For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” He therefore orders lodging to be prepared for him so that, when Philemon hears that he is coming to him, he may forgive Onesimus; and while he awaits him, he may more readily do what has been requested. And because wherever the Apostle was, a multitude gathered around him, it was necessary for him to have a large house, one situated away from the circus, the theater, and the public spectacles, where the licentious ran about and pursued every kind of disgraceful behavior.

“Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you.” This Epaphras, being a preacher of the Gospel, clung to the blessed Apostle and perhaps had been led captive with him from Jerusalem to Rome; or certainly at that time he was being held with him in prison.

“Mark” is the same one who wrote the Gospel. “Demas” is the one of whom he says elsewhere: “Demas has deserted me.” “Luke” is the writer of the Gospel and of the Acts of the Apostles, of whom he also says in another place: “We sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel” (2 Corinthians 8). And just as the apostles, from fishermen of fish, became fishers of human beings, so he, from a physician of bodies, was changed into a physician of souls. For whenever his words are read, they provide medicine to those who understand.

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.” Here “grace” is understood as faith, the remission of sins, and the gift of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle prays may be with the spirit of those to whom he was writing these things. By “spirit” we may understand either the soul or even the faculty of reason. For when divine grace is present in the soul, or in rationality, it fills the whole human being and makes that person spiritual, so that he clings to the Lord in mind and body, and that saying may be fulfilled which is written: “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6).

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

## PREFACE

At the beginning of this Letter it must be explained what the reason was that the apostle Paul did not observe his customary practice in this Letter—namely, that he should indicate either the title of his name or the dignity of his office.

The reason, then, was that he did not title it with his name because he was writing to Jews, his own brothers, to whom he was hateful because he himself taught that circumcision, the Sabbath, sacrifices, and the other things that the Law commands to be observed ought not to be observed in a carnal manner after the Lord’s Passion. For those Jews who had believed argued that both obligations were to be maintained: namely, that they should be baptized according to the grace of the Gospel, and also circumcised and observe the Sabbath according to the commandment of the Law.

Therefore, if the Apostle had placed his name at the beginning of this Letter, it might have happened that his opponents, reading his name at the very front, would disdain to receive it, and thus the benefit of reading would be postponed. He did not place the title of apostleship either because, since he had been appointed apostle of the Gentiles, if he had prefaced the Letter addressed to them with the title of his apostleship, calling himself an apostle, they might perhaps have thought that he wished to place himself above the apostle Peter, who had been appointed their leader by the Lord. As the same distinguished preacher says elsewhere: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Galatians 2).

They might also have said: “Why does Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, place himself above our apostles Peter and James? Let him write to his own Gentiles; we do not need him to write to us. For we have apostles appointed for us by the Lord, who can teach us sufficiently.” By doing this, he showed that he was not ignorant of their pride, and at the same time displayed his own humility.

Similarly, the apostle John also, for the same reason and out of humility, omitted his name in his Letter. Or certainly, as some say, because in this Letter he was going to call Christ an apostle, saying, “We have a high priest and apostle of our confession, Jesus the Just,” he did not wish to mention the title of his own apostleship at the beginning of this Letter. For he did not consider it fitting that, where he was going to call Christ an apostle, he should also call himself an apostle, especially in the title, lest anyone should think that he placed himself above Christ. Instead, he preferred, with his name kept silent, to instruct them concerning the figures of the Law and lead them to the truth, which is Christ.

Some say that this Letter belongs to the apostle Barnabas, some to Luke, and some to Clement, saying that if it were Paul’s, he would certainly have placed his name at the head of it in his customary manner, as he did in his other letters. But if it is not Paul’s because it is not titled with his name, then it is neither Barnabas’s, nor Luke’s, nor Clement’s, nor anyone else’s, since it bears no one’s name. To whom, then, should it be attributed? Certainly to that distinguished preacher, since its clear thought and manner of expression prove it to be his, although it is composed in a subtler and more lucid style than all his other Letters.

For it is said that the Apostle sent this Letter to the Hebrews and composed it in the Hebrew language, in which he was extremely skilled, whereas he wrote his other letters in Greek. After the Apostle’s departure, the evangelist Luke rendered it in the Greek language, from which it was later translated into Latin, as were the others.

# CHAPTER ONE

“Long ago, and in many ways, God spoke to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son.”

The whole purpose of the blessed Apostle in this Letter is to lead the Jews, his kinsmen—who are called Hebrews from Heber, through whom they were taken up by the Law of Moses—from the Law to the grace of the Gospel, and from carnal observance to spiritual observance. At the same time, he distinguishes the excellence of the grace given through the Son to believers from the legal shadows that were presented through angelic ministries.

Accordingly, he first states that the prophets spoke to the fathers in various ways and through diverse forms of expression, saying: “In many ways,” that is, through many expressions; “and in many manners,” that is, through many qualities; “long ago,” that is, in former times, God the Father speaking through the prophets to our fathers.

Then, to show how great the difference was between the grace given to them and that given to their fathers, he added: “In these last days,” that is, in the final age, “he has spoken to us through the Son.”

By saying, “He spoke in the prophets and in the Son,” he means the same as if he had said, “through the prophets and through the Son,” because the preposition *in* is used in place of the preposition *through*, just as he is found to use these prepositions interchangeably in many places in his Letter.

Let us therefore consider how God the Father spoke to the fathers of the Old Testament through many expressions and in many ways. He did not always reveal his secrets to them in a uniform manner. Sometimes he spoke to them openly and through an angel, as to Abraham, to whom he said: “At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son” (Genesis 18); and to Moses, when he gave the legal commandments: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Deuteronomy 5), and the other commandments of this kind; and to Lot, when he led him out of Sodom (Genesis 12), as well as to many others.

At other times he spoke obscurely, through riddles and through fire, as to Moses, to whom he said: “I am who I am. You shall say this to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3).

At times he appeared in the appearance of a soldier, as to Joshua. At times he spoke in the heart, as to David, who said: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Psalm 84), and likewise to the other prophets.

At times he spoke through a dream, as to Daniel, which is a kind of prophecy. Finally, that is, at the end of the ages, he spoke to us, his apostles and all other believers, through his Son.

The sense is this: Long ago he spoke to our fathers, as to servants, through his servant angels and through their fellow servants, the prophets; but in these last days, at the end of the age, he has spoken to us apostles and to all other believers through the Son, as to sons.

For just as great as the difference is between the grace of the Gospel, which was given through the Son, and the Law, which was administered through a servant, so great is the difference between the ministers and hearers of the Law. Servants were sent to servants, whereas the promise and grace given through the Son were given to sons and afterward administered through sons to sons.

The text continues: “Whom he appointed heir of all things.” An heir is called *haeres* from *herus*, that is, “lord,” because he rules over the paternal inheritance with free authority.

God the Father therefore appointed his Son heir of all things, that is, of the whole world and of all creatures—not only according to his divinity, by which he is coeternal with the Father and coequal with him in the omnipotence of the Godhead, and by which he eternally possesses all things with the Father, but rather according to the humanity assumed by the Word. In that humanity he was appointed Lord and heir over every creature, as God the Father promised him, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2).

And the Son himself, rising from the dead, speaks in the person of his humanity: “All authority,” he says, “has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28).

We do not therefore divide the persons, but distinguish the natures. Hence we must observe with careful inquiry that in this Letter the Apostle sometimes speaks of the substance of Christ’s humanity and at other times of the substance of his divinity. When he said that he had been appointed by God the Father heir of all creatures, he referred this to his humanity. But wishing to make a distinction between the nature of his divinity and his humanity, and to show what properly belongs to each nature, he added: “Through whom he also made the ages.”

The ages are called *saecula* from “following,” because they follow one another, returning and coming back into themselves. Here by “the ages” we ought to understand all things that were made in time.
