Therefore, to show that the same one who came into the world in these last days and received an inheritance temporally was with the Father before all the ages, the Apostle said: “Through him God the Father made all things that were made in time.” For what the evangelist John says—“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1)—the Apostle signified by saying, “Through whom he also made the ages,” referring this to his divinity.

Then, using a graceful progression through several ascending steps, he arrived at what is greater than all these things and proclaimed: “Who, being the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance.”

God the Father is light, as the same Apostle says when speaking of the Son: “He possesses,” he says, “inaccessible light” (1 Timothy 6). The Son is also light, and the Holy Spirit is light. Likewise, the Father is radiance, the Son is radiance, and the Holy Spirit is radiance. But how light is born from light and radiance proceeds from radiance, without an increase in number, cannot be defined.

The Son is therefore called the radiance of the Father because, just as in fire there are three inseparable things—fire, heat, and radiance—and yet fire and heat are shown to us through radiance, although human things must not be compared with divine things, so the nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is inseparably joined and united. Through his Word, as through radiance, he deigned to reveal himself, and also the mystery of the whole Trinity, as the Son himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10); and again: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

In a wondrous manner, therefore, the Apostle showed that the Father and the Son have one substance of divinity, so that he might reveal two persons in glory and radiance. Through “radiance” he declared the unity of essence with God the Father; in the name of “glory” he expressed the person of God the Father; and in “radiance” the person of the Son. Thus the Son is radiance from radiance, just as light is from light, God from God, light from light, and beginning from beginning.

The text continues: “And the figure of his substance.” As far as human beings are concerned, figure and substance are different. When the image and figure of a person is painted on a wall, that figure is not the substance itself.

But the Apostle here used “figure” for the substance itself and for equality of essence. What he called “figure” here he elsewhere called “form,” saying: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2).

“Form” there and “figure” here both declare equality of essence. Christ, therefore, is the radiance of the Father and the figure of his substance, because through him the Father was manifested, as he himself says: “Father, I have manifested your name to human beings” (John 17), and because he is equal to him in the substance of divinity.

The text continues: “And bearing all things by the word of his power.” By saying “bearing,” he wished to express the ease with which he contains all things; he used “bearing” in the sense of governing and directing. The Word of God the Father therefore bears all things that he made by the word of his power—that is, by the power of his might—and by the word of his command he governs and directs everything.

For governing the world is no less than creating it. In creation, the substances of things were produced from nothing; in governance, the things that have been made are held together so that they do not return to nothing. Therefore, while all these things are governed and things that conflict with one another are fitted together, the great and marvelous judgment of God’s power is revealed.

After such a manifestation of divine majesty in the Son, he descends to the lowliness of his incarnation and at the same time distinguishes between the nature of his divinity and that of his humanity, saying: “Having made purification for sins.”

By saying that he bears all things by his governance and the direction of his power, he referred this to his divinity. But what he added—“having made purification for sins”—belongs properly to his humanity.

How did he make purification for sins? Through the redemption of his Passion and through the water of baptism, in accordance with what John says in his Apocalypse: “He washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation 1).

“He sat at the right hand of Majesty in the highest places.” The order of the words must be considered. First he testified that the Lord procured purification from sins for us through his Passion; afterward he said that he sat at the right hand of Majesty in the highest places. Christ first redeemed us by the blood of his Passion, and afterward penetrated the heights of heaven, where he now sits at the right hand of the Father.

Here “to sit” is used in the sense of “to dwell” and “to be,” just as “right hand” is used for supreme honor and dignity. It must not be thought that the omnipotent Father, who is unbounded spirit and fills all things, has a right or left hand as we do, or that his Son sits at his right hand in the way that the sons of kings customarily sit beside their father, with a throne placed next to his. Rather, as we have said, “right hand” is understood as glory and the honor of dignity.

Indeed, the Father is also written to be at Christ’s right hand, as it says in the Psalm: “The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings in the day of his wrath” (Psalm 109). Both, therefore, are at the right hand, because there is nothing left-handed in divinity; for the human being assumed by the Word is now one with God in glory and was exalted to the heavenly places on the fortieth day.

What, then, does “he sits at the right hand of Majesty” mean except that he dwells in the fullness of the Father’s majesty? And by saying “in the highest places,” he showed that this human being had been exalted above every angelic and human creature. Hence it follows:

“Having been made so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs.” Here “made” or “having become” must be understood as “having been received,” as though he were saying: He was received by God the Father in the glory of majesty as one so much better and more honorable than the angels as he inherited a name of sonship so much more distinguished and excellent than theirs.

For just as great as the difference is between the name “son” and the name “servant,” so much greater is his dignity than that of the angels, since he is the Creator—speaking according to his divinity—whereas they are creatures.

He himself, even as a human being, is greater than every angel and every creature, because the power that existed in the Word before all the ages came to rest in that human being assumed by the Word from the time of his conception. Therefore the angels are his ministers and servants, as was shown at his temptation and Passion, and also at his resurrection and ascension. But he proved to be the proper Son and heir, as the Apostle also indicates to us when he adds:

“For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” Understand: This was said to none of the angels.

This must be understood of the Word of God, who is coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, not of any creature, although we read in the Book of Job that angels are called sons of God, and in Genesis the sons of Seth are also so called. Whenever this occurs, however, it occurs by an improper usage.

When, then, did he say to him, “You are my Son”? At the time of baptism and on the mountain, when the voice of the Father thundered from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 17). By saying, “You are my Son,” he makes clear that he was begotten from the Father’s very essence.

It must also be noted that he did not say, “I begot you before all the ages,” or “in past time,” but, he says, “today I have begotten you,” which is an adverb of the present time. In God, past things do not pass away and future things do not come into being; rather, all times are joined together for him, because he possesses all things as present.

The sense is: Just as I am always eternal, possessing neither beginning nor end, so I always have you as my Son, coeternal with me.

The same meaning is found in what he says elsewhere: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Psalm 109), that is, before the angelic creature and before all the ages.

And again: “I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son.”

Do you see how he distinguishes the twofold nature in Christ? What he said a little earlier, “Today I have begotten you,” he referred to the nature of his divinity. But what he added—“I will be his Father”—he refers without any doubt to the substance of his humanity. Accordingly, he appropriately used the future tense, saying, “I will be.”

For when God the Father said to David, “When you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring, which shall come from your loins, and I will establish his throne over your throne; he shall be my Son, and I will be his Father” (2 Samuel 7), it was still future that the Word of God would assume a human being from the Virgin’s womb in the unity of his person, so that he would truly be the Son of God—not adopted, but proper.

This statement may also refer back to what precedes, so that it is read as a question: “Again, to which of the angels did he say, ‘I will be his Father’?” The implied answer is, “To none.” Or it may be taken absolutely and affirmatively in this way: “Again, God the Father says of him, ‘I will be his Father.’”

“And again, when he introduces the firstborn into the world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God adore him.’”

Every only-begotten son can be called “firstborn,” because he is the first to open his mother’s womb; but not every firstborn is only-begotten, since a firstborn may have other brothers following him.

The Lord Jesus, however, can be called both only-begotten and firstborn, according to both his divinity and his humanity. He is only-begotten according to his divinity because, in the nature of divinity, he has no brothers following him. According to his humanity also he is the only-begotten son of blessed Mary, since she bore no others after him, as Helvidius slanders with the tooth of a viper.

He is firstborn according to the essence of his divinity, as Solomon testifies when he says: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Sirach 24). According to his humanity also he is firstborn among many adoptive brothers, of whom he says to Mary: “Go to my brothers and say to them” (John 20).

When the Apostle says that God again introduces his firstborn Son into the world, these words seem to sound as though he had already been introduced once before. But how this should be understood the evangelist John partly explains when he says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1).

The Word of God the Father, through whom all things were made, being of one essence with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is everywhere and fills all things: by encircling them he fills them; by filling them he encircles them; by governing them he presides over them; by presiding over them he governs them.

And because he was in the world, where he assumed flesh, yet was inaccessible to our sight because he was not seen, he calls that assumption of flesh another entrance. For when he who was invisible to human sight made himself visible by assuming flesh, it was as though he had been introduced again.

It must be noted that what the Apostle calls an “entrance,” the Truth himself calls an “exit” in the Gospel, saying: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 26 [probably 16]).

He rightly calls the assumption and manifestation of his incarnation an “exit,” because we were outside, expelled from God and placed beyond the court of paradise and the palace of the eternal King, imprisoned in this world and sent into exile. For example, those who incur the king’s offense are excluded from the royal court, sent into exile, and shut up in prison. But when a good mediator wishes to obtain pardon for them, he does not first bring them into the king’s court. Rather, he goes out to them and there engages with them in conversation; then, once they have been corrected and chastened, he introduces them into the king’s presence.

In the same way the Lord Jesus came out to us. He came forth to us from the presence of the Father’s majesty by assuming flesh and making himself visible; he spoke with us concerning the commandments of the eternal King; and then, after correcting and chastening us through his preaching and miracles, strengthening us by his faith, and cleansing us from sins through his Passion, he introduced us into the royal court and into the presence of the Father’s majesty when, by ascending into heaven, he opened the way of the heavenly kingdom to us.

By saying that he introduces him into the world, he signifies that he entrusts the world to him and makes him known as Lord of the whole world. For he possessed the world when he was acknowledged by all as Lord of the whole world. Understand this statement not of the substance of the Word, but of the essence of the human being.

What follows—“And let all the angels of God adore him”—is as though he were saying, “Let all my angels and his angels adore him,” because they were made through him. They adored him, therefore, when they announced his birth, when they approached and ministered to him while he was hungry, and when they guarded his tomb; they adore him daily because they obey his command.

But did God the Father command only the angels to adore him? No, rather, he commanded every creature.

“And concerning the angels he says: ‘He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire.’”

What is said—“And concerning the angels, indeed,” by God the Father or by divine Scripture—is as though it said “about the angels,” with *to* being used in place of *about*. For the Apostle does not preserve either the order or the meaning of the prepositions.

The sense is: The one whom the angels are commanded to adore makes angels from his own spirits whenever he wishes. He also makes his ministers a flame of fire, because he makes those who stand in his presence burn and blaze with his love, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “Into which things the angels desire to look.”

By saying, “He makes his angels spirits,” he expressed the words in reversed order. For he ought to have said, “He makes his spirits angels.”

It must be understood, however, that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. They are always spirits, but they are by no means always rightly called angels unless they are sent. In Greek, *angelos* means “messenger” in Latin. If you ask the name of the nature, it is “spirit”; if you ask the name of the office, it is “angel.” By virtue of what subsists, it is a spirit; by virtue of being sent, it is an angel. For example, “human being” is the name of a nature, whereas “soldier” is the name of an office.

It may also be said in another way: The angels and ministers of almighty God are the priests and prelates of the Church, in accordance with what Malachi says (chapter 2): “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

The priests of the Church are therefore spirits when they announce the joys of the heavenly homeland to their hearers, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3); and, “The righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13); and, “They will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22).

They are a flame of fire, however, when they threaten their hearers with the terror of the fire of Gehenna, saying: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3).

“But to the Son”—understand, the Psalmist says—“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.”

Observe how, and with what clarity, he distinguishes the angelic creature from the Son who created all things.

In Greek, *thronos* is called in Latin a royal seat, just as it is also called a throne. By “throne,” therefore, we may understand the kingdom in one way; by the scepter, which is a golden rod, the power of the kingdom is understood.

The Psalmist therefore speaks to the Son of God: O God, your kingdom and the power of your rule will remain forever and ever! Gabriel says something similar to Mary: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1).

This is the kingdom concerning which the crowds cried out, blessing the one who came, “the kingdom of our father David”; and concerning which the Lord himself said to Pilate: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18).

Alternatively: A throne, or seat, is customarily the place of those who judge. Hence human law also commands that judgment be given only while seated. Therefore, not improperly, by “seat” we may understand the judgment that proceeds from the seat.

This is the judgment of which the Son himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5); and concerning which the Psalmist says to God the Father: “O God, give your judgment to the king” (Psalm 71), that is, to Christ.

The throne of God will therefore remain forever and ever, because the final judgment that he will give to the elect, saying to them, “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you” (Matthew 25), and to the rejected, “Go into eternal fire” (ibid.), will stand as an eternal distinction between the two, as he testifies in the Gospel, saying: “Then these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (ibid.).

What follows—“The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom”—is understood by “the scepter of uprightness” as the rectitude of his sentence and judgment, or the just power of his kingdom, which rules the righteous in justice and strikes the impious justly and rightly, without any acceptance of persons, governing and judging all.

You loved righteousness and hated iniquity. This is the straight rod: that righteousness should be loved and iniquity hated. For no one can love righteousness perfectly unless he has hated iniquity. Iniquity, which is also called *anomia* (“lawlessness”), means whatever is done against the divine law. Indeed, love of truth is hatred of falsehood. And because the Lord loved righteousness, since he did not sin, and hated iniquity, he explains what reward he deserved to receive, saying: “Therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness” [Col. 0828C] “above your companions.”

The Psalmist addresses the Son of God and says: “O God, God the Father anointed you with the oil of gladness,” because you hated iniquity and loved righteousness. It must not therefore be understood that the Son of God, according to the nature of his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, can have God as his God, since he himself, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is the true God. But insofar as he is human, he has God the Father as his God, because he was made by him; and therefore the Psalmist says: “God, your God, anointed you with oil” (Ps. XLIV).

Christ was anointed not with visible oil, but with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, who rested upon him on the day of his baptism in the form of a dove. Nor did the fullness of the Holy Spirit remain in him only from the time of his baptism; rather, it was in him from the time of his conception, in accordance with what Isaiah says: “The spirit of the Lord will rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isa. XI) [Col. 0828D].

He says that Christ was anointed with the oil of gladness or joy because Christ, who never sinned, never experienced sadness from the recollection of sin. For what does it mean to be anointed with the oil of joy except not to have the stain of sin? The conscience of the saints becomes increasingly cheerful and bursts forth more fully into joy when it is not gnawed by the recollection of any grave sin. The Holy Spirit, who rested in Christ, guarded him, so that he would be conceived without sin, born without sin, and pass from this world without the stain of sin [Col. 0829A], in accordance with what is written about him: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Ps. XXXI).

But what does the Psalmist mean when he says of him: “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV)? Who, then, are his companions?

In the Old Testament, the patriarchs were companions of Christ in this anointing. Although they were not anointed with visible oil, but filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit, they were called *Christi*, that is, “anointed ones,” in accordance with what is written in the psalm, where the Lord says concerning Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to Abimelech and the other kings of the Philistines: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Ps. CIV).

Kings, priests, and prophets were also his companions, because anointing belonged especially to them, through which they deserved to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0829B]. For we read that Saul was anointed by Samuel, and David; Solomon, too, was anointed in Zion. Priests were anointed, as Aaron was anointed by Moses, when the Lord said to him: “You shall anoint Aaron and his sons for me as priests by perpetual right” (Exod. XXX). Prophets likewise were anointed, as Elisha was anointed by Elijah, to whom the Lord said: “Anoint Elisha the prophet in your place.”

These three orders foreshadowed the Lord, who is the true king, priest, and prophet. In the New Testament, his companions are the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and all who are cleansed by the grace of baptism, receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, and are called Christians from Christ.

Christ, therefore, was anointed with the oil of joy above all his companions, because they all receive the Holy Spirit according to a measure [Col. 0829C], whereas he received it not according to a measure but in its fullness, in accordance with this statement: “For God the Father does not give the Spirit by measure to his Son, but in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II).

And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.

After the excellence of the humanity of the Son of God, he turns again to the eternity of his divinity, saying: “You, Lord, in the beginning of creation founded the earth.” Where, then, did he found the earth? If we consider the matter carefully, we shall see that, by the divine will and arrangement, it stands founded upon nothing except itself. And when he says, “The heavens are the works of your hands,” we must not think that the Word of God the Father, who is incorporeal [Col. 0829D], works with hands, since in the nature of his divinity he does not possess bodily features as we do.

We must therefore understand “the works of his hands” as the power of his command. For by the word and the power of his might, and by his command, he brings about whatever he wills, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII). By the power, therefore, of the Word of God, heaven and earth subsist, because all things were made by the power of his command, and “without him nothing was made” (John I).

But since Moses says at the beginning of Genesis that heaven was made first and then the earth, saying, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I), the question arises why the Psalmist places the earth first and then heaven, as though the earth had been made before heaven [Col. 0830A]. The answer is that Moses placed heaven before earth, whereas the Psalmist placed it after earth. This was done to show that the two were made together; but what divine power made simultaneously, the human voice could not utter simultaneously. It was therefore necessary to mention one before the other.

They will perish, but you will remain.

Here the plural number is used in place of the singular, as in many other passages of divine Scripture. This should not be understood of the firmament in which the stars are contained, nor of the ethereal heaven through which the courses of the seven planets are carried out, but rather of this aerial heaven, from which the birds of heaven are also named.

On the day of judgment, therefore, this aerial heaven from which we draw in and release our breath will perish—not so that it will utterly cease to exist according to its nature, but it will be changed from its present form into a better one, and from its present density into the subtlety and brightness of the ether. Hence the Apostle also says elsewhere: “The form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII). If the form passes away, the substance will remain.

For as much space as the water occupied at the time of the Flood—so that it stood fifteen cubits above all the mountains under the whole heaven, and, as some say, reached as far as the circle of the moon—so much space will fire occupy on the day of judgment, accompanying the Lord’s coming, in accordance with what the Psalmist says (Ps. XCVI): “Fire will go before him; it will consume all the clouds and all the density of this air, and there will be a new heaven and a new earth.”

The Lord also speaks in the Gospel of this transformation, saying: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV). They will pass away [Col. 0830C] from their present form and appearance into something better through renewal, and they will remain in their own substance. “They will all grow old like a garment.”

Here we must understand “garment” as the human body, which is consumed by the length of time and the pain of illness and is reduced to dust. Just as the human body grows old and is reduced to dust, but on the day of judgment will be renewed through the resurrection, so this aerial heaven, through its excessive age, has in a certain way already grown old; but on the day of judgment it will be renewed through the burning of fire.

“And like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed.” A cloak is so called from *amiciendo*, “covering,” that is, surrounding. Heaven is therefore rightly compared to a cloak with which we are surrounded, because just as a cloak girds the human body on every side, so heaven surrounds the earth on every side, balanced in equal measure [Col. 0830D]. Hence it is also compared elsewhere to the skin of a living creature, as the Psalmist says: “Stretching out the heavens like a skin” (Ps. CIII).

“You will change,” he says, “the heaven like a cloak,” as if he were saying: Just as a cloak, when spread out, is easily folded, and when folded can again be easily spread out; and if it has been stained with dirt, it can readily be cleansed, so heaven is easily stretched out and arranged by you. With incomprehensible ease, therefore, on the day of judgment you will change it from its present form and appearance into something better.

And to show that thereafter the works of the Lord would thereafter remain in eternity, he added: “And they will be changed,” as though he were saying: After they have been changed, they will remain in that newness and will never return to this corruptible state.

But you are the same, and your years will not fail [Col. 0831A].

Here is the difference between temporal creation, which has been made, and the Creator, who remains equally in his eternity. In almighty God there is neither past nor future, nor any mutability; all things are present to him, and he is always immutable. Therefore the Psalmist, carefully contemplating the eternity and immutability of the Word of God, used the substantive verb of the present tense when speaking of him.

“Heaven and earth,” he says, “will be changed, but you are the same”—now as you were before all ages—“and your years,” that is, your eternity, “will not fail.” He who always possesses being says of himself to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III).

Therefore every rational creature [Col. 0831B], which is mutable and temporal in itself, ought to strive with all its strength to be joined and cleave to him who always remains the same.

To which of the angels did he ever say: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet”?

After showing that the majesty of divine eternity exists in the Son, the blessed Apostle again turns his discourse to the glorification of his humility, saying: “To which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand’?” The implied answer is: To none.

God the Father granted this glory to none of the archangels, none of the dominions, powers, or principalities, so as to say to him: “Sit at my right hand,” that is, “Dwell and rest with me in the fullness of my majesty.”

But to the victorious Son, who triumphed over the whole world through the dispensation of his incarnation [Col. 0831C], after the glory of his resurrection, on the fortieth day he says: You labored in the Passion; you labored in the redemption of the human race; rest with me in glory, “until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX).

“Until” or “until such time as” does not signify the end of any period of time here, but is used for what is infinite and everlasting, as if he were saying in other words: Dwell forever in the fullness of my majesty, because I will subject your enemies—the Jews and the other unbelievers—to your eternity.

The Lord’s feet signify the stability of his eternity, where he stands as though upon firm footprints by the power of his omnipotence. We may also appropriately understand “feet” as the mystery of his incarnation. By these feet—namely, by his eternity, or by the faith and power of his incarnation—his enemies are subjected to him daily in two ways: when, abandoning the opposition of vices and unbelief, they willingly subject themselves to him for salvation, so that they may be protected under him; or when, unwilling to believe in him, they are nevertheless forced to submit to him and are trampled under the dominion of his power. The text continues.

Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?

If all the spirits of the heavenly powers are sent for the salvation of believers, what is the meaning of Daniel’s statement: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. X)? For how can all be sent if ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him?

We must therefore understand that almighty God, who is an unbounded Spirit, fills all things and is wholly present everywhere. Thus the angelic spirit, although unbounded, wherever it is sent, runs within God and always has God present to it. Therefore those who are sent also stand before him.

Or all are said to be sent because, as Didymus the Greek says in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, they are sent from all the orders of heavenly dignities. We read that the archangels Gabriel and Michael were sent in the book of Daniel, and Raphael to Tobias; one of the Seraphim is also said to have been sent to Isaiah, when he touched his mouth and lips with a coal; and angels are frequently read to have been sent to the saints.

In general, as the teachers say, an angel is given by God to each of the faithful from the beginning of birth [Col. 0832B], or from the time of baptism, for his protection and to urge him to do good. Hence the Apostle says here: “They have been sent for the service of salvation on behalf of the elect who are to receive the inheritance of the heavenly homeland.”

In this passage, therefore, as we have said, all are sent; and those who are sent are of the same dignity as those who stand before him. Or it is because all are of the same will: while those who always stand before him agree with those who are sent, in a certain sense all stand in those who are sent, and all are sent.

The meaning is: What is surprising if the angels offer their service to the only Son of God, when it is also clear that they have been made ministers of our salvation? Therefore he said to none of them: “Sit at my right hand.”

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0832C]

Therefore we must pay much closer attention to the things we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away.

“Therefore,” he says, because the Son of God is superior to all the angels, who gave us his Gospel—or certainly because he ministers angels to us, who continually report our works to God, although he himself is everywhere—we must pay much more fully and carefully attention to the things we have heard from Christ in the Gospel and from his apostles than we formerly did to the law, which was given through a servant.

And why “much closer”? Lest perhaps we drift away—that is, lest perhaps we perish and fall away from salvation, or lest we perhaps vanish and pass into destruction like a river flowing into the sea, while our thoughts run through empty things.

As is his custom, he joins his own person to theirs. And why “much closer”? He gives the reason when he explains it in the words that follow, saying:

For if the word spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?

The word of the law and of the prophets was spoken through angels to our fathers, because he spoke through a subordinate creature to Moses and the prophets, in accordance with what the blessed Stephen makes clear in his dispute when he says concerning Moses: “This is the Moses who was with the angel speaking to him on Mount Sinai.”

The word spoken through the angel proved firm—that is, the same word was true—because everything happened as it had been foretold, whether good or evil. Every transgression or violation of the law, and every disobedience committed against that word [Col. 0833A], received a just recompense of reward, namely, the judgment of eternal condemnation, as happened to those who became disobedient by murmuring.

It should be noted that although “reward” is chiefly understood in a good sense, here the Apostle used it for evil, as is his usual practice. He does not concern himself with the strict propriety of words, but uses one term indifferently in place of another, as here he uses “reward” in an evil sense and elsewhere “captivity” in a good sense, where he says (II Cor. X): “Taking every thought captive to obey Christ.”

The Apostle therefore makes a comparison between the word of the law spoken through an angel and the grace of the Gospel given through the Son, and says: If the word of the law spoken through an angel is true in everything it promised to the good or threatened to the wicked, how much firmer will the word of the Gospel given through the Son be?

And if those who were disobedient to the law could not escape the condemnation of eternal judgment, how shall we escape God’s vengeance if we neglect so great a salvation—that is, the faith of the Gospel and eternal life, so great because it was announced and promised to us through the Son? The implied answer is: In no way.

By these words the Apostle makes clear that the law did not contain as great a salvation as the Gospel. The law promised the earth, saying: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land.” But the Gospel promises heaven, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. III).

The law provided vengeance against earthly enemies; the Gospel provides it against spiritual enemies. The law promised a long temporal life; the Gospel grants life that will remain without end.

This salvation, which had begun to be proclaimed by the Lord, was confirmed in us by those who heard it. The salvation contained in the Gospel therefore received the beginning of its proclamation from the Lord, because he first announced it himself, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near”; and, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI).

Afterward it was confirmed—that is, it was believed—by those who heard it, namely, by the apostles who were with the Lord and by their successors. Or “confirmed” means that it was strengthened and perfected in us by those who received it from the Lord himself, because the salvation given to us through the Holy Spirit remains [Col. 0833D] forever.

Because of humility, he joins his own person to theirs, saying: “It was confirmed in us by those who heard it.” Someone might have said: How was it confirmed by them? He answers: “God also bearing witness by signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.”

The same salvation, he says, was confirmed in us by those who heard it, with God bearing witness—that is, giving simultaneous testimony to their teaching and preaching—not by voice, but by power, by the manifestation of miracles, and by a diversity of tongues. For if one of the apostles said to a dead or sick person, “Rise; be alive or well,” the person immediately rose up unharmed.

Here “signs,” “wonders,” and “powers” are understood as one. But what he adds, “distributions of the Holy Spirit,” signifies the abundance of graces, which the fathers of the Old Testament did not possess and which was given after the Lord Jesus had been glorified, as the Evangelist testifies when he says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

These are the distributions or divisions that the Apostle mentions elsewhere, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (I Cor. XII), and so forth; he enumerates them in what follows until he adds: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid.). Hence he also says here, “according to his will.” For he attributes everything to the divine will and purpose, so that no one may put confidence in his own merits. The Holy Spirit himself knows what benefits each person and what is useful to each [Col. 0834B].

For he did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we speak.

This belongs to what he said above, namely, that God the Father said to the Son: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX).

By “the world to come” he means the people inhabiting the world, concerning whom it was then going to happen that they would believe in Christ, or concerning whose salvation the prophets had foretold that it would come.

“No,” he says, “God the Father did not subject to angels the world that was to believe, of which we speak,” when he said in the person of God the Father to the Son, “I will make your enemies the footstool of your feet.” Rather, he handed it over to his Son, to whom he says in the psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II) [Col. 0834C].

Therefore the Son himself, rejoicing that the believing world had been handed over to him, says: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. II), that is, by God the Father.

But someone testified somewhere, saying:

Because he does not mention the names of the prophets in this Epistle when he adduces their testimonies, he does so not from envy or from a desire to conceal them, but out of a narrator’s intention and with the aim of showing that the Hebrews, to whom he was writing, possessed extensive knowledge of the divine Scriptures—so much so that he did not even need to mention the name of the speaker.

This testimony, then, is taken from the Psalter of David. How does he speak to God the Father? “What is man?” This should be pronounced softly and with contempt: “What is man?”—that is, fragile, mortal, fleeting, and a follower of Adam, who was overcome by an inclination toward the original sin of the old transgression [Col. 0834D].

“That you remember him?” The implied sense is: so that you bestow upon him the gifts of your mercy. It is your grace, not his merit. The Lord remembers a person when he forgives his sins through gratuitous mercy and bestows the gifts of his mercy.

It continues: “Or the son of man”—the implied question is, “What is he?” The teachers refer this to Christ, who in the Gospel very frequently calls himself “the Son of Man,” that is, the son of Mary. Therefore the voice should rise in the form of a question, and the meaning is: What did that man assumed by the Word merit, so that he should become the Son of God?

What follows, “because you visit him,” refers to the human race, of which it was said shortly before under the name “man,” “What is man?” The meaning is [Col. 0835A]: Because you visit the human race through your Son and continually bestow benefits, this is not its merit but your grace; therefore it subsists because it is visited by you.

Visitation belongs to a physician and a sick person. A physician is said to perform the duty of visitation when he enters someone who is ill. God the Father visited the human race, which was sick and weak, when he sent his Son, who became flesh and dwelt among us (John I).

The blessed John the Baptist’s father, Zechariah, also speaks of this visitation: “The Dawn from on high has visited us” (Luke I). Some teachers refer the entire passage—“What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?”—to the human race; but they unanimously refer what follows to Christ.

You made him a little lower than the angels.

Through the death of the body and the shame of his Passion, God the Father made his Son lower than the angels, although according to his divinity he was equal to him in the omnipotence of the Godhead, because the angels are immortal and incapable of suffering.

He was made lower not by necessity but by voluntary choice, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II).

In that respect in which the Creator of the angels could die, he was made lower than the angels. He rightly said “a little lower,” even though he assumed a mortal body, because he nevertheless had no stain of sin.

You crowned him with glory and honor.

The Psalmist speaks to God the Father concerning the humility and exaltation of the Son of God, saying: “You made your Son a little lower than the angels when you made him mortal; but because he was obedient to you unto death, you crowned him with glory and honor” [Col. 0835C].

This is like what the Apostle says elsewhere: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (ibid.).

God the Father crowned him with glory in the resurrection, and with honor in the ascension, when on the fortieth day after his resurrection he exalted him above every creature.

Alternatively: He was crowned with glory in the multitude of believers, namely, when, after the triumph of his resurrection, he received the faith of the whole world in what concerns his humanity; and with honor in the confession of the Father’s majesty, that is, in the fact that he dwells in the fullness of the Father’s glory.

And you appointed him over the works of your hands.

Because he became human, he was appointed by God the Father over the works of his command, namely, over heavenly, earthly, and infernal things. According to the power of his divinity, just as he had created all things with God the Father, so with him he possessed all things.

By saying, “You appointed him over the works of your hands,” he shows that every creature is subject to him. For just as all things were created by the power of the Word, so the man assumed by the Word possesses all things with the Word.

You subjected all things beneath his feet—that is, beneath his eternity and power—so that every creature might adore him. This is what he himself said to his disciples when he appeared to them after the glory of his resurrection: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII).

In subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him. In this act of subjecting all things to him, he appears to have excepted neither heavenly nor earthly things, nor to have mentioned anything beyond the angelic creation. Rather, he concluded in these words: “He subjected all things to him.”

But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.

What does the blessed Apostle mean? After saying that all things were subjected to Christ, he immediately added: “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.” If all things are subject to him, how are they not subject?

We must understand this in the way explained above, where he said, “He left nothing that was not subject to him.” We must understand there a universal subjection, both voluntary—namely, through faith—and necessary, by which every creature is compelled to be subject to its Creator [Col. 0836B].

But here, where it says, “We do not yet see all things subjected to him,” we must understand only voluntary subjection. Those who do not wish to believe in him are not subject to him in this sense.

Because at the time when the Apostle was saying these things the preaching of the Gospel had not yet been spread throughout the whole world, and not all those predestined to life yet believed, he rightly said: “All things are not yet subject to him.” And not only then: even now not all the predestined have come to believe.

But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.

Here he openly shows that the glory and honor of Christ were his cross, for the sake of which he was made a little lower than the angels by dying for our salvation.

Thus elsewhere, after the Apostle had said that he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, he immediately continued: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name,” and so forth.

The Lord himself likewise urged the apostles, saying that the Son of Man should be glorified. But if he who is Lord calls the things he suffered for servants glory, you, a human being, should be even more certain that what you suffer for the Lord belongs to your everlasting glory.

“We see,” he says, “Jesus crowned,” not with bodily eyes but with the eyes of the mind, while he sits in the fullness of the Father’s majesty, “so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.”

The Son is called the grace of God the Father because he was freely given to us by God the Father and freely endured death for us. It was not owed to us on account of our merit that the Son of God should taste death for us; rather, ineffable grace accomplished this.

When he says that he tasted death for everyone, some teachers understand this absolutely, so that “for everyone” means for all for whom he tasted death—that is, for those predestined to eternal life.

Others, however, understand it generally, so that he is said to have tasted death for all believers and unbelievers alike. They say: He indeed died for everyone, although not everyone will be saved. Even if not all believe, he nevertheless did what belonged to him.

The blessed Prosper gives the following comparison. Suppose there is a highly skilled physician who comes to a populous city where many sick people are found. He prepares a potion against every kind of illness and summons everyone, saying: “Come, all you people who suffer from various illnesses, and drink this potion, which I have prepared for your salvation. I promise and solemnly assure you that whoever drinks from it will immediately receive healing.”

Those who believe his words approach, drink, and are healed. Those who refuse to drink are not healed but waste away in their illness. Thus, as far as the physician’s devotion is concerned, he prepared the potion for the salvation of all of them, even though it benefits only those who drank from it. So Christ, as far as his own action is concerned, died for all, although his Passion benefits only those who were willing to believe in him [Col. 0837B].

At the same time, it should be noted that the Apostle did not say that he “was subjected to death,” but specifically that he “tasted death,” by which he wished to show the swiftness of the resurrection. For he could be held by death only for a short time, so that, after conquering it, he might immediately rise again as victor.

For it was fitting that he, for whom and through whom all things exist, who had brought many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering.

“It was fitting,” he says, that the author of their salvation should be perfected through suffering—that is, that he should complete the salvation of all through the Passion of Christ, who is the author of the salvation of all believers, and who, even before his Passion, had brought many adopted sons into the glory of faith, hope, and love. They possessed the firm hope that they could receive the joys of the heavenly homeland and the inheritance of the eternal kingdom [Col. 0837C].

Or certainly it was fitting that through his Passion he should complete everything that had been foretold about him. Hence, while hanging on the cross, he himself said: “It is finished” (John XIX).

“For whom all things exist”: through his death all heavenly and earthly things were restored—namely, the redeemed human being and the restored number of angels.

“And through whom all things exist”—the implied sense is, “through whom all things were made,” in accordance with what John says: “All things were made through him” (John I).

Do you see how much he shares with us and how closely he is joined to us? He is the Son, and we are sons; he is the natural Son, and we are adopted sons. Yet he saves, and we are saved. Do you see how he both joins and distinguishes us? When he says, “He brought many sons to glory,” he joins us; but when he adds, “the author of their salvation,” he distinguishes us.

For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.

Who is the one who sanctifies? Christ, through faith in his Passion and through the gift of baptism. Who are those who are sanctified? All believers, who are sanctified by faith in Christ’s Passion and by the grace of baptism.

But Christ, who sanctifies, and we who are sanctified, are all from the one God the Father, because all things received their origin from him. For there is one God, through whom and from whom all things exist.

Yet he is one way, and we are another. As the natural Son, he can sanctify; we, as adopted sons, are sanctified by him. Nevertheless, we have one Father in heaven: he has him as his natural Father, and we have him as our adoptive Father.

For this reason—that is, because he and we are from one God the Father, though distinctly—he is not ashamed to call those who are adopted sons his brothers, saying: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.”

When he says that he is not ashamed to call them brothers, he shows that we share the same brotherhood of our humanity, through his great mercy and supreme humility, by which he chose us as his brothers. He also confirms this by prophetic testimony, so that it would not be thought something new and not foretold long before. For he says: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.”

After his sacred Passion and venerable resurrection, he promises that he will proclaim throughout the whole world the glory of the Father’s divinity and the name by which he was called Father.

“I will proclaim” means, “I will cause it to be proclaimed by my preachers, given to me by you.” For when he rose from the dead, he said to the women: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. XXVIII); and to Mary: “Go to my brothers” (John X), “and tell them.”

Brothers are so called both because they love and because they are loved. He adds: “In the midst of the church I will praise you.”

“In the midst of the church,” that is, in the assembly of the faithful, the Son praised God the Father when, after the apostles returned from preaching, he said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth”—that is, “I praise and glorify you”—“because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke X).

He himself also praises God the Father daily in the midst of the church, while all the faithful, redeemed by his Passion and resurrection and cleansed by his baptism, offer unceasing praises to God the Father in heart, mouth, and deed. For God must be praised in these three ways.

And again: “I will place my trust in him,” that is, in God the Father. This is the voice of the Son of God speaking about God the Father from the standpoint of his humanity.

The man assumed by the Word placed all his confidence in God the Father. Hence he said: “Father, glorify your Son” (John XII). And, praying for his faithful, he said: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII). Exhorting them to have confidence, he said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI).

And again: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.”

These two testimonies are taken from the oracle of the prophet Isaiah, who speaks in the person of the Son of God. These children are the holy apostles, to whom the Lord said: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” (John XXI). They are rightly called children because of their innocence [Col. 0838D] and humility. Concerning such people the Truth himself says: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. XIX).

Because the children shared in flesh and blood, he likewise participated in the same. This is said of the apostles and of all the faithful, because through this they became the Lord’s brothers: he had a true body and blood, just as they had. Here Manichaeus and his followers are confounded, since he dared to say that God did not have a true body, although the Apostle says that, by assuming flesh, he became a participant in theirs. For just as those children consist of flesh and blood, so do we; thus Christ too participated in flesh and blood, having become human. And just as Christ shared in our substance through the assumption of humanity, so we are participants in him through the reception of his body and blood.

But why Christ shared in flesh and blood he explains in what follows, saying: “So that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who throughout their whole life were subject to slavery through fear of death.” Here the Apostle demonstrates something remarkable: the devil was conquered by Christ through the very thing by which he held power in the world. The weapons that had once been strong against the world—namely, death—were used by Christ to strike him. It was like David taking Goliath’s sword and cutting off his head with the very weapon by which that former victor had been accustomed to prevail. Since, therefore, the devil had presumed to exercise dominion in the world through the death of a human being, he had to be defeated through Christ’s temporal death.

For this reason Christ participated in flesh and blood, so that he could die for a time. Thus, when he died—though he had committed no sin—he destroyed the devil, who had introduced sin, through which death had entered the world. Or he destroyed the devil and death in this respect also: he was always dead to sin, since he did not sin. Once the devil’s authority had been destroyed, he freed his elect, who, as long as they lived in this world, were subject—that is, indebted and bound—to the slavery of death and the devil through fear of death. They feared death because they were servants of death, since all were subject to death.

Nowhere does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. He develops further the meaning of what he had said above: that the children shared in flesh and blood, and that Christ participated in them. He wishes to show from what source he participated in them, and says: “Nowhere”—that is, in no place, neither in heaven nor on earth—did he assume an angelic creature, but he assumed a human body from the seed of Abraham. By these words he wins their favor, gently reminding them that he assumed their seed. Since it was a human being, not an angel, who was to be redeemed by the death of the Son of God, he therefore did not assume an angelic nature, which cannot suffer death, but a human nature in which he could die.

Nor was such dignity conferred upon the angels that the Son of God should be joined to their nature in one person. Divine grace, however, bestowed this dignity and honor upon human nature, so that God and man might be one person. And why did he say “he takes hold,” a term applicable to someone fleeing? Because he pursued and seized us as though we were withdrawing from him and fleeing far away.

Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect. “For this reason,” he says, “because he did not assume an angelic nature but a human nature from the seed of Abraham, he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.” What does “in every respect” mean? He was born, brought up, grew, hungered, suffered, and died, so that in all these things he might be like his brothers, who are subject and bound to such conditions.

But perhaps someone may ask why the fallen human being was restored rather than the fallen angel. The answer is that the human being did not sin as greatly as the devil. The human sinned because the devil persuaded him, whereas the devil fell without anyone persuading him, through pride. Moreover, because the human had a body, he needed to eat; but the devil, since he is spirit, is wholly without excuse.

There was also a third reason: the human being had not yet reached the place where he was to reign eternally with God, but was dwelling in an earthly paradise, from which he was to be transferred into heaven once the number of the elect had been completed. The devil, however, had already been established in heaven. Christ was made like his brothers so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. He is called merciful from a “wretched heart” (*misero corde*), namely because he bears misery and knows by experience how to show mercy.

Thus there was no other reason for him to be made like his brothers in every respect except that he might show us mercy by redeeming us, and might become a faithful, true, and powerful high priest before God the Father by interceding for us and making atonement for our sins. This was the reason for this lamentable dispensation: he saw the human race bent down toward the earth and bound by the chains of sins, and he had compassion on it as a faithful high priest, reconciling us to God the Father and cleansing us through reconciliation.

For the ministry of a priest and high priest is to be faithful, so that he may free from sins those whose priest he is. He is also called “high priest” because he provides a bridge—that is, a way—for his followers through his good example. Thus the Lord also made a bridge for us, that is, he showed us a good way, when he said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). He also made a bridge for us when he opened to us the door of the heavenly kingdom. There he now stands, interceding for us with God the Father.

[Col. 0840C] In that in which he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted. “In that,” he says, “in the humanity in which he himself was tempted by the devil, though not overcome, and suffered at the hands of his servants, he is able to free those who are bound and to assist those who are tempted, so that they may not be overcome.” He knows our temptations and sufferings not only as God, but also as a human being who proved them by experience. Therefore he can help us not only by virtue of being God, but also by virtue of being human, since the humanity assumed by the Word had the same power as the Word himself.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to him who made him, just as Moses also was faithful in all his house.

He calls them brothers both in flesh and in spirit, because they were of the same race and held the same faith. He calls them holy because they had been sanctified by faith in Christ’s passion and by the water of baptism. They were participants in a heavenly calling—that is, in the heavenly homeland—to which the Lord calls everyone, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

“Consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession.” In Greek, *apostolos* is rendered in Latin as *missus*, “one who has been sent.” The Lord Jesus is our apostle because he was freely sent to us by God the Father, as he himself testifies, saying: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” and, “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (Matt. XV; John XX). Hence the same distinguished preacher says elsewhere: “God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. IV).

He is the high priest of our confession because he presents the confession of our faith before God the Father, who is faithful to him—that is, to God the Father, who made him—in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “He was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.” It should be noted that this is said concerning the essence of his humanity, in which he himself was faithful to God the Father, obedient to him unto death (Phil. II). Was he not faithful to God the Father when he attributed everything he did not to his own glory but to the Father, saying: “The Father, remaining in me, himself does the works”?

“As Moses also,” he says, “was faithful in all his house.” Here we should understand the house of God as the people, namely the Israelite nation, over which Moses had been placed by God. Concerning this house Isaiah says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel”; and again, exhorting them: “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of God” (Isa. II, V). In this house Moses was faithful—that is, devoted and well-intentioned—defending what belonged to God and not appropriating God’s glory to himself.

For this man has been considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house. Here there is either a *hypallage* in the sense, or a sufficiently necessary ellipsis may be supplied in this way: Christ was found worthy of greater glory than Moses insofar as the Lord of the house who built that house has greater honor; or, Christ was found worthy of greater glory than Moses insofar as the builder has greater honor than the house he built. He thereby gives the reason why the builder of the house has greater glory than the house constructed by him.

For every house is built by someone. But the one who created all things is God, the implied subject. Here he distinguishes the builder from the building, wishing it to be understood that God is the author of both houses—namely, of the Israelite people and of the Gentile people.

Moses indeed was faithful—that is, devoted and well-intentioned—in his entire house, as a servant, for a testimony to the words that were to be spoken. But Christ dwells in his own house as a son, ordering and arranging it. Just as there is a difference between a servant whom the master places over his house and a son whom he leaves as heir, so great is the difference between Moses and Christ.

Moses was a faithful and devoted servant in the house of almighty God—that is, in the Israelite people—for a testimony to the words that were to be spoken through him to the people, since he was a witness both to the Lord’s words to the people and again to the people’s words to God. Christ, however, freely orders his own house, that is, his Church, as a son orders his paternal inheritance.

Concerning this house the Apostle adds, saying: “We are that house, if we hold firm to the confidence and glory of our hope to the end.” The Apostle again exhorts the Hebrews to stand firm in faith and persevere in good works, joining himself to them, as usual. “We are,” he says, “the house of God, if we hold firm until the end of our death, or until the day of judgment, to confidence”—that is, right faith—and to the glory of our hope.

The glory of our hope is that by which we glory that we are already, in hope, children of God; and what we now possess in hope, we believe we shall possess in reality. For we cannot possibly have in this punitive life the good things promised to us. Therefore, possessing right faith and certain hope, let us patiently await the rewards promised to us by the Lord.

It follows: “Therefore, the Spirit says: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,” and so forth, up to “If they enter into my rest.” A little earlier the blessed Apostle had spoken of hope: that we ought to hope for the things that are to come. He then gives a prophetic testimony, in a kind of comparison, concerning those who perished because they despaired of God’s power and concerning the few who, with certain hope, believed God’s promises and what they gained.

Since the blessed Apostle spoke obscurely, it is necessary to review the account of the Old Testament, so that his statement may become clearer. The Israelite people had been led out of Egyptian slavery through the Lord’s signs and wonders. After they had traveled a long way through the desert, been fed by the Lord with manna, given water from the rock, and protected by him, they all took counsel to send leading men from each tribe as scouts, who were to explore and inspect the land promised to them by the Lord.

They went and surveyed the land. After forty days they returned to the assembly, announcing that the land was extremely fertile and produced great crops, but that it had fortified cities and men who were unconquerable, since they were descended from the Anakim—that is, from giants.

But the Israelites were ungrateful and foolish. They ought to have remembered God’s many benefits: how he had rescued them from dangers when they were enclosed amid the great army of the Egyptians; how he had supplied them without fail with springs of water from the rock; how he had given them manna; and how he had bestowed countless other benefits upon them. Yet they neither believed God, despairing of his power, nor remembered any of these things. Terrified by a despairing fear, they murmured: “Would that the Lord did not bring us into that land! Let us return to Egypt.”

Therefore God was angry that they had so quickly forgotten his benefits and wonders, and he swore that that generation would not enter the rest and homeland once promised to their fathers. Thus the six hundred thousand who had gone out from Egypt perished, except for only two: Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun, who attempted to restrain the people’s rebellion because they believed the Lord’s promises.

It should be noted that the Apostle mentions three rests in this Epistle. The first is the Sabbath, on which God rested from his works. The second is in Palestine, into which the Israelites were to enter in order to rest from great misery and labor. The third, which is the true rest, is the kingdom of heaven. Those who happen to reach it will rest completely from the labors and hardships of this world.

It is of this third rest that the Apostle speaks here prophetically and spiritually, saying: “Therefore”—with the implied words, “because we are the house of God”—“if we hold firm to right faith and to the glory of hope, do not harden your hearts, lest you suffer what your ancestors suffered when they were deprived of the promised rest.”

By these words the Apostle exhorted the Hebrews not to be faithless and unbelieving, lest they lose the eternal rest promised to them by the Lord, just as their fathers lost the temporal rest. “Do not,” he says, “harden your hearts today”—that is, as your fathers hardened theirs in the provocation, in the bitterness, when they provoked me to bitterness, according to the day of their testing in the desert, where your fathers tested me with many trials, saying: “Can God prepare a table in the desert? And can he bring us into the land promised to our fathers?”

When he says “today,” the Psalmist is not speaking to those who died in the desert while murmuring against the Lord and remaining unbelieving, but rather to those who lived in the time of the Lord’s preaching and of the apostles, and to those who will exist until the end of the future world. “Today,” he says—that is, in the day of the New Testament, or throughout every period during which “today” is said—“do not harden your hearts.”

“Today” is used for eternity, that is, for as long as the world and the present life remain. It follows: “They tested and saw my works for forty years.” When he says that they tested his works and wonders, this should not be understood to mean that they tested them by choosing the cause of giving thanks. Rather, this testing refers to curiosity and temptation. “They tested my works,” he says; that is, out of curiosity they investigated them, testing whether I was almighty. But what happened? They saw those works for forty years and remained ungrateful.

The phrase “for forty years” may also be joined to what follows. The number forty is regarded as mystical in divine Scripture. The Lord fasted in the desert for forty days in order to triumph over him through whom those people had murmured against the Lord in the wilderness for forty years. After the whole glory of his victory had been completed through his passion and resurrection, he remained with his disciples for forty days before penetrating the heights of heaven.

In the first forty days he showed the temptation of this world; in the later forty days, the consolation with which they will be consoled in the homeland. For his body, that is, the Church, must suffer temptations in the present world (Matt. XVIII), so that afterward it may reach the joys of the heavenly homeland. Nevertheless, the Consoler is not absent even in the present life, for he said: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

It follows:

Therefore—because they tested me out of curiosity and tested my works for forty years—I was offended with this generation. To be called offended or hostile is stronger than to be called angry. For one who becomes angry can easily be removed from anger; but one who has been offended or provoked may be appeased only with difficulty or not at all. Thus almighty God, having been offended—that is, being greatly and implacably angry—was so toward those six hundred thousand who perished in the desert.

And he said to Moses and Aaron, or also to Joshua: “They always err in heart.” The Lord God almighty disciplined them in many ways, but they always erred in heart, deviating from the way of truth and uprightness. For whoever does not obey God’s will errs from the uprightness of justice.

“But they did not know my ways.” When he says “they did not know,” this means that they did not approve or choose my deeds and commandments; or they did not know because they were unwilling to know them in such a way as to hold and observe them.

“To whom I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest.” The word “if” (*si*) is sometimes used for affirmation, sometimes for doubt, and sometimes for negation, as in the present passage, where it means “not,” and in the Psalm where the Prophet says: “If I have repaid those who repaid me evil” (Ps. VII), meaning “I have not repaid them.”

The order of the words is: “They shall not enter into my rest, as I swore in my anger,” that is, in my vengeance. God’s anger is his vengeance. For God to speak is a great thing; for him to swear is exceedingly fearful. Since every word of his ought to be accepted as an oath, because he is always truthful, he is nevertheless sometimes said to swear in order to intensify the force of a matter and to strike terror into his hearers. Likewise he is said to become angry in human fashion, although he always remains the same, so that when we hear that he is angry, we may fear to sin.

When he says, “They shall not enter into my rest,” we should understand a double rest here, as was said above: one is the land promised to Abraham, which they lost because of their unbelief; the other is eternal life, of which the Apostle speaks spiritually, saying: “The Jews who remain in unbelief shall not enter it.”

See to it, brothers, that perhaps there may be in one of you an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to depart from the living God. Again the Apostle exhorts them gently, calling them brothers and giving counsel about how they may enter the true rest. “My brothers” in the flesh and also brothers in faith, “see”—that is, beware and attend with the greatest diligence—“lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil will and an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to depart from the living God,” as happened in those who erred in the desert by worshiping idols, so that you perish as they perished.

[Col. 0844D] But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. He was writing to those Jews who had already believed, among whom there were people able to exhort others in faith, hope, and good works. Therefore he speaks in this way: “Exhort one another,” he says, “and correct one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today’”—that is, throughout the whole period of the present life, in which there is opportunity for repentance.

If anyone has sinned, let him not despair of pardon as long as he lives, and let none of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin—that is, by the deception of the sin of unbelief, which produces despair, as though pardon could not be obtained through repentance. For the one who does not believe sufficiently often falls into despair, and he gives the reason why no one ought to despair of pardon, saying:

For we have become participants in Christ. We participate in Christ and are joined to him, since we exist as one with him. We participate in him inasmuch as he is our head and we are his members, coheirs and conjoined bodily with him, according to the spiritual human being who was created in him. We also participate in him because we receive his body and blood for our redemption. Therefore we must not despair.

This is so, provided that we hold firm to the beginning of our substance until the end, when it is said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts against God in unbelief, as”—with the implied words—“your fathers hardened their hearts in that provocation.”

By “the beginning of Christ’s substance” he means faith in Christ, through which we subsist and are reborn, because he is the foundation of all virtues. He aptly calls it “substance,” because just as the body subsists and is given life through the soul, so the soul subsists in the Lord and is given life through faith; without faith it is, as it were, nothing. Hence the Prophet says: “But my righteous one lives by faith” (Hab. II). And the same distinguished preacher says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI).

Faith is called the substance of Christ either because it is given by him or because he himself dwells through it in the hearts of believers, in accordance with what the same Apostle says elsewhere, praying that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person (Eph. III). Therefore we are truly participants in Christ if we hold his faith firm until the end of our death, or until the day of judgment—in every period, that is, as long as the Prophet says to us: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

For some who heard provoked him, but not all who went out from Egypt through Moses. He silently recalls that history, when, after the scouts returned, they said while murmuring (Num. XIV): “Would that the Lord did not bring us into that land!” But Joshua and Caleb glorified God, saying to the whole assembly: “The Lord is able to bring us into that land.”

Some, then, who heard the word of God concerning the promised land and the report of the scouts provoked him to bitterness through the evil of unbelief and despair—namely, the six hundred thousand whose bodies were cast down in the desert. Yet not all who went out from Egypt provoked him, since Joshua and Caleb, from so great a multitude, glorified him. Therefore they deserved not only to possess the promised land but also to distribute it by lot to others.

The Apostle’s reason for pursuing this argument is as follows: They all heard God’s word concerning the promise of the promised land, just as we have heard concerning the heavenly homeland. But what benefit did the word they heard provide them? Therefore do not suppose that entry into God’s rest comes merely from hearing the preaching, unless faith from a pure heart is added.

[Col. 0846A] With whom was he offended for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses were cast down in the desert? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest except to those who were unbelieving—that is, to those who doubted that the Lord could bring them into the promised land? And we see—that is, we understand—that those six hundred thousand could not enter his rest because of unbelief.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore let us fear lest, while the promise of entering his rest remains, any one of you should be thought to have fallen short. Let us fear, he says, their destruction and the just judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works. Let us fear lest, having abandoned and neglected the promise of faith that we gave to God in baptism—to enter the rest of the heavenly homeland—we return again to the works of unbelief that we renounced before many witnesses.

This may also be understood of the promise that the Lord made to us when he said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). He therefore promised us that rest, and we pledged at the time of baptism that we would enter it. Therefore labor, lest any one of you be thought to have fallen short of that kingdom—that is, lest any of you be found less worthy to enter God’s rest.

The Apostle speaks in the manner of travelers journeying from one region to another.
