The person who addresses everyone commonly says to them: “See that none of you remains behind on the journey, so that we may all reach together the place toward which we are traveling.” And if one person’s beast should fail through weariness, help carry one another’s burdens, lest that person remain on the road for this reason.

The elect in the present world are like travelers on the road, making for their homeland. But lest anyone remain behind and be unable to reach the heavenly homeland, the simple and weak are to be supported by the work and assistance of the strong, in accordance with the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI).

For the good news was announced to us just as it was to them. As usual, he joins himself to the Jews who existed at that time and says: The good news was announced to all of us Jews, so that we might enter the rest of the heavenly homeland, just as it was announced to those who went out from Egypt that they should enter the rest of the promised land. Yet it was announced to us through the Son, and to them through a servant.

But the word they heard did not benefit them because it was not joined to faith in those who heard it. The word that those six hundred thousand heard through Moses concerning the rest of the land of Palestine did not benefit them because it was not joined, united, and blended with faith through the promises they heard. The word they heard would then have benefited them if they had believed, for then it would have been blended with faith. But because they did not believe, it was not joined to faith. Therefore what they heard benefited them nothing, since they were not found worthy to enter it.

After these words of exhortation the Apostle added:

[Col. 0847A] For we shall enter into his rest, we who have believed, as he said: “As I swore in my anger, if they enter into my rest.” Here something must be added to complete the sense. “We shall enter,” he says, “into the rest of the heavenly homeland promised to us by God”—with the implied warning—“lest, if we are unbelieving, it be said to us as it was said to those who did not enter: ‘If they enter,’ that is, ‘they shall not enter into my rest.’”

By these words he exhorts everyone to enter the Lord’s rest, lest, because of unbelief, what was said to them be said to us. For just as it is certain that unbelievers will not enter, so it is held as certain and fixed that believers will enter.

And indeed, after the works had been completed from the foundation of the world—that is, after the world had been fully adorned—

he said somewhere concerning the seventh day: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” In Genesis God said this through Moses (Gen. II). By these words the Apostle wishes to show that there is another and better rest to which we have been called than the rest in Palestine to which the Jews were called. He does not say that we shall enter the rest that existed in Palestine; rather, he shows that they did not enter because of the hardness of their hearts—neither Palestine nor the heavenly rest.

He therefore speaks of the first rest in this way: “God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” He rested from the creation of new creatures, but he did not rest from governing what he had made, nor from producing new things from them each day. Hence Truth says to the Jews in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V). For it is no greater thing for God to create the world from nothing than to govern what has been made.

Having mentioned first the rest of the seventh day, on which God rested, he then added the second rest promised to the people of God, saying: “Concerning that rest God said through Moses in one place, and in this place he says again: ‘If they enter into my rest.’”

As has already been said, the conjunction “if” can be understood as affirmation, doubt, or negation. Above it was used in two places for negation, where he said that God swore because of their unbelief: “If they shall enter into my rest,” that is, “they shall not enter.” Here, however, it may be taken affirmatively in another sense, as John Chrysostom and other teachers explain it, as though he were saying: “If they shall enter into my rest”—with the implied meaning, “they shall prosper.” Understand this of the rest that existed in Palestine. Hence what follows is immediately added:

Since, therefore, it remains that some entered it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he says: Since it remains, or is established, that some entered into the rest of the promised land—and since only a few entered the rest that existed in Palestine, namely Caleb and Joshua alone, from all those who went out of Egypt—those to whom it was first announced, that is, the sixty thousand, did not enter it, but their corpses were cast down in the desert.

Again he establishes a certain day, “today,” in David, saying, after so much time, as was said above: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” The order of the words is this: After the great interval of time in which they murmured and died in the desert, the Holy Spirit again established, that is, fixed and determined, a certain day—the time of the New Testament—saying through David: “Today,” as was said above, where the Apostle speaks in the person of the prophet: “Today, if you hear his voice,” and so forth.

It is as though he were saying in other words: “O my fellow citizens, Jews, do not suppose that what David said—‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts’—belongs to the time when they murmured in the desert, or that he said it for the sake of those who had already died. It belongs to another time, namely, the time of the New Testament.”

For a long time elapsed from the day of their murmuring in the desert to David and to us, to whom David spoke these words. At the same time, the “day” should be understood as the time of the Lord’s coming and of the New Testament. What he says “in David” is equivalent to “through David.” He has changed the expression in his customary manner.

The statement may also be understood in this way: “He establishes a certain day”—that is, the Holy Spirit sets a limit and an end to the former period, which lasted from the day of their murmuring, and gives a beginning to another period by saying through David: “Today,” and so forth.

It follows:

For if Jesus, the son of Nun, the leader of the Israelite people, had given them rest—with “true” understood—David would never afterward have spoken of another rest, after the day when they had attained that rest. Here he shows a third kind of rest, of which David said: “Today,” and so forth. He does not mean the rest into which Jesus, the son of Nun, led the people, but another, much more excellent rest, into which the true Jesus, not the typological one, daily leads those who belong to him.

For if Jesus, the son of Nun, had given true rest to the people whose leader he was, David would certainly not have spoken afterward of another rest. It is certain, however, that some will receive the rest signified by that one, which existed in Palestine.

Therefore—understanding that Jesus, the son of Nun, did not provide true rest for the people over whom he presided—the *sabbatismus* remains, that is, is reserved for the future, for the people of God. He calls the true rest of the heavenly homeland *sabbatismus*, alluding to the name, because the Jews called rest *sabbatismus*. The heavenly Sabbath-rest is therefore reserved in the future for the people of God who truly believe: namely, eternal life, which surpasses the Sabbath of the Law. For in that Sabbath only bodies rested, whereas in this rest the souls of the people of God rest. Hence it follows:

For whoever has entered his rest—that is, the rest of almighty God, which is eternal life—has himself also rested from his works and from all earthly labors, just as God rested from his own works on the seventh day.

God’s rest should be understood as the perfection of his works: after the original creation of things had been completed on the sixth day, he ceased on the seventh day from creating new things. Through that rest of God, which is eternal, he diligently urges us to strive with all our strength toward the rest of eternal blessedness, which he calls *sabbatismus*. Whoever, therefore, enters this Sabbath of God will rest forever from every labor and work, just as God rested from the creation of new things.

Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest, so that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief. Faith is indeed a great and saving thing, since without it no one can be saved, as it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI). Whoever does not believe in God is not saved. But faith alone is not sufficient for salvation. It is necessary for faith to cooperate through love and for one to live worthily of God, because faith without works is dead.

Therefore the Apostle, considering the blessedness of perpetual life, exhorts us, saying: Let us hasten through right faith and holy action to enter the rest of the heavenly homeland promised to us, lest any one of us fall into the same example of unbelief and despair into which they fell. “Let us hasten,” he says, because faith alone is not enough; a life worthy of faith must also be added. We are sufficiently instructed by the example of our ancestors not to fall into the same example of unbelief into which they fell and thus suffer what they suffered.

For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword. The Apostle, saying and exhorting us, urges us to hasten to enter the rest of our heavenly homeland through faith and works, so that none of us may fall into the same example of unbelief into which they fell, and so that things may not happen to us as happened to them. Those who were struck down in the desert might reply: “Such things will certainly not happen to us, because we do not have prophets and judges through whose mouths the Lord may speak to us, as they had; therefore, whatever we do, we shall be excusable.” [Col. 0849C]

To this the Apostle, wishing to show that we have the same judge as they had—the one who condemned them because of their unbelief—said: “It is not so: for the word of God is living and effective.” The word of God the Father is the Son, the Word, who by his power slew those six hundred thousand in the desert because of their unbelief, since they refused to believe him. This is the word that never dies but always remains the same, according to what the Psalmist says: “But you are the same, and your years”—that is, the years of your eternity—“will not fail” (Psalm 101). This is the word that says of itself: “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John 8). For if they had kept this word of God by believing rightly and living well, they would certainly have lived both temporal and eternal life and would have entered the promised land. Likewise, if we keep his word, we shall live and enter the heavenly rest. [Col. 0849D]

This word of God the Father, who always lives with God the Father and through whom the Father judges all things, is effective—that is, ready to act, because it acts without labor. For “he spoke, and they were made”; and, “Whatever he willed, he did” (Psalms 134, 148). It is also sharper than any two-edged sword—that is, sharpened on both sides—because a material sword, sharp on both sides, can indeed divide limbs from the body and penetrate the hidden parts of the flesh, even to the point of making the soul depart from the body and reducing the body itself to death; yet it cannot divide the soul itself into minute parts, nor penetrate its hidden depths. Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10). [Col. 0850A]

The text continues: “The same word of God reaches even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and is the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” We live by the soul; by the spirit—that is, by reason—we understand. Bodily life is shared with the beasts; spiritual reason with the angels. There are some sins that pertain more particularly to the body than to the spirit, such as murder, fornication, adultery, theft, sacrilege, and other such acts, which are perpetrated through bodily action. Again, there are others that pertain more particularly to the spirit than to the body, such as hatred, anger, deceitfulness, envy, and other things of this kind, which exist without bodily action. [Col. 0850B]

Since the body is given life by the soul, we may appropriately understand bodily sins by “soul,” and spiritual sins, which move in the secret depths of the mind, by “spirit.” Again, by “joints” we should understand thoughts that are joined and connected to one another, as one follows another; by “marrow,” subtle intentions. This is why it adds, “the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart,” referring thoughts to the joints and intentions to the marrow. [Col. 0850C]

The verse should therefore be joined in this way: “The word of God is living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and the division of spirit, reaching even to the division of joints and the division of marrow, and it is the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

The word of God the Father is therefore so effective and sharper than any two-edged sword that it distinguishes between the works of the flesh and the works of the spirit, between bodily and spiritual sins, between good and evil thoughts, and between good and evil intentions. For a thought may in some way be good while its intention is evil.

For example, to speak by way of comparison: There is a widow whose hereditary property is seized by a stronger person. She approaches a judge and teacher of the law, begging him to undertake her case and assist her, so that she may recover the inheritance taken from her, promising him either one hundred solidi or even a substantial portion of that same inheritance. When this judge enters the church of God, he prostrates himself, praying and saying: “Eternal God, who judges all things justly, and who have said, ‘Judge the fatherless; defend the widow’ (4 Esdras 2), grant me help today, so that I may prevail in this widow’s case.” [Col. 0850D]

In saying this, his thought and words are indeed good, but his intention is wicked, since, unless the widow had promised him something that he hoped to receive, he would certainly not have undertaken her case. The word of God discerns and judges this subtle distinction between the thoughts and intentions of the heart, considering with what disposition and desire each person serves in his heart. The word of God and its gaze are so penetrating that all we do or think is known by it more certainly than by ourselves. [Col. 0851A]

Let us therefore always have him as a witness to our actions, thoughts, and intentions—the one whom we shall have as judge. Let us fear his presence, since we cannot in any way escape his knowledge. Hence it continues:

“No creature is invisible in his sight.” Neither angelic nor human creation is invisible in his sight. “But all things are naked”—that is, manifest—“and open to his eyes,” that is, to his presence. How, then, can anything be unknown to him by whom all things were made? Nor is it surprising that, being wholly present everywhere, he knows his whole creation. The Apostle especially terrified the Jews with this statement, saying that “all things are naked and open to the eyes of him to whom our word is addressed.” To whom is our word addressed? To whom but the Son, to whom we shall render an account of our actions, thoughts, and intentions alike? [Col. 0851B]

Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast the confession of our hope—that is, faith in his name. A little earlier, discussing the divinity of the Son of God, he said that all things are naked and open to his eyes. But now, because he is speaking of his flesh and discussing his priesthood—he who offered himself upon the altar of the cross for the sake of our salvation—he is speaking of his humanity. He himself is both high priest, or priest, and sacrifice. [Col. 0851C]

He is called *pontifex* because he provides a bridge and a way for the people. The Lord himself presented us with the way of righteousness on which we ought to walk, saying to us: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11). He also provided a bridge by which we might reach our heavenly homeland, through the blood of his passion and through the water of baptism; or else he is called so because he himself was the first to pass through the heavens.

Thus Moses, the leader of the people, to whom a transitory rest was promised, did not enter the rest that he had so often promised to the people. But this priest of ours, the guarantor of a better promise, making a way for those who believe in him, entered first into the rest promised to the people entrusted to him. Hence he calls him “the great high priest,” who possesses an eternal priesthood, always living to intercede for us. For the angel said of him to Mary: “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1). To show also that he is the Son of God, he says, “Jesus the Son of God,” something he nowhere wished to say of Moses, but rather called him God’s servant. [Col. 0851D]

The text continues:

“For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with, or feel compassion for, our weaknesses.” This means: He is not ignorant of what concerns us, for he passed through every condition of human existence without sin. Therefore, he knows the weakness of our frailty and can have mercy not only because he is God and knows all things, but also because he became our participant in the frailty of the flesh without sin; thus he knows and is able to forgive. [Col. 0852A]

Many high priests are ignorant of those who are placed in tribulation, and do not know what tribulation each person suffers. It is indeed impossible for one who has had no experience of affliction and has not endured all things sensibly to know the afflictions of the afflicted. But our high priest appropriately endured everything that was inflicted upon human misery after the first man’s sin, and then ascended within the inner part of the veil to the throne of the Father’s majesty. Hence it continues: “We have a high priest who was tempted in every respect according to the likeness”—understand, “of sinful flesh”—“without sin.” Christ was tempted in many ways, through every kind of temptation, but he was not overcome by temptations; rather, he was tested and proved a glorious victor. [Col. 0852B]

The temptations by which he was tried were these: hunger, thirst, the devil’s temptation, the persecution of many, spitting, accusations, slanders, rejection by his own people, and finally crucifixion. He was tempted in these ways according to the likeness of flesh, without sin.

But since Christ truly possessed true flesh, why does he say that he was tempted according to the likeness of flesh, without sin? Inasmuch as he became human, he possessed true flesh; but inasmuch as he did not possess sinful flesh, he possessed, without sin, the likeness of our flesh, which is sinful flesh. For “he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2). If he could have possessed sin, he would no longer have had the likeness of sinful flesh but the actual property of sinful flesh. [Col. 0852C]

Our flesh is sinful flesh because we are conceived with sin and born with sin. His flesh, however, was not sinful flesh but flesh of purity, chastity, and innocence, because he was conceived and born without sin and passed from this world without sin. Therefore, he was not tempted in sinful flesh so that he might commit sin, but in the likeness of sinful flesh so that he might remain without sin.

Let us therefore approach his throne of grace with confidence, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help. Since we have a high priest who knows how to sympathize with our weaknesses because he endured similar things, and who can help because he is God, having already passed through the heights of heaven by his own power, the Apostle urges us to approach his throne with confidence and says: “Let us approach in mind and contemplation, and also through faith adorned with good works, the throne of grace”—that is, the seat of the Son of God, who was freely given to us by God the Father. [Col. 0852D]

Sitting in the fullness of the Father’s majesty, he is able freely to forgive us our sins. The Son of God is called the grace of God because he was given to us freely, according to what the same Apostle makes clear in this epistle, saying (Hebrews 2): “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone.”

And why should we approach his throne with faith and devotion? He continues: “So that we may obtain mercy”—that is, the remission of sins and the grace of the gifts of the Holy Spirit—“and find indulgence in timely help,” that is, in the present age. For now is the timely season of his help and mercy, of which the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6); and of which the prophet says: “In an acceptable time I heard you” (Isaiah 49). [Col. 0853A]

For the one to whom he grants mercy in the present age, forgiving his sins and filling him with the grace of spiritual gifts, he promises that he will reign with him in the kingdom to come. And because our high priest sits on the throne of the Father’s glory, he grants everything that certainly brings us salvation.

## CHAPTER V

“For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, and is able to feel compassion for those who are ignorant and erring, since he himself is surrounded by weakness; and because of this he ought to offer for sins, just as for the people, so also for himself.” [Col. 0853B]

In these words the Apostle sets forth some things common to Christ and the priests of the law, and others that are higher and pertain specifically to Christ; then again, some humbler things that pertain only to the priests of the ancient law.

When he says, “Every high priest taken from among human beings,” as Aaron and Christ were, “is appointed on behalf of human beings in the offices that pertain to God,” praying for their salvation, this is common to Christ and those priests. For it is the office of a high priest to stand between God and the people and entreat God for the people’s sins. Christ did this because he is both human and God, offering himself for our sins and always living to intercede with God the Father for us (Hebrews 7). Once taken from among human beings, he always intercedes for human beings. [Col. 0853C]

Again, when he says, “to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins,” this is partly common to Christ and partly not, and there is a difference. Insofar as Christ offered a sacrifice for the people’s sins, there is a certain commonality with what those priests did. But insofar as he did not offer one for himself, whereas they offered victims for their own sins, there is no longer any commonality.

There is also a difference because they offered irrational sacrifices—oxen, rams, goats, and other such animals—whereas Christ offered a rational living being for the salvation of the whole world, namely himself, who is the spotless Lamb, according to what John says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). [Col. 0853D]

What follows is no longer common to them. For when he says, “who is able to feel compassion for those who are ignorant and erring,” that is, for those who sin and err through ignorance, “since he himself is surrounded by the weakness of the flesh,” in which he could be tempted in every respect according to the likeness of sinful flesh, without sin—this is now an excellence belonging to Christ, about which we spoke more fully above. Because he suffered similar things, he is able to sympathize; and because he is God, he is able to show mercy in both substances.

But what he adds—“and because of this he ought to offer for sins, just as for the people, so also for himself”—pertains more to the priests of the law, or to those of our own time, than to Christ, who committed no sin. The statement “since he himself is surrounded by weakness” may also be referred to the priests of the law, or to our priests, so that “weakness” is understood as sin. Since they themselves are surrounded by weakness of the flesh—that is, by sin—they need to offer both for the people and for themselves. [Col. 0854A]

By these words the Apostle wished to show what a high priest is, to demonstrate what belongs to a high priest and what his ministry is, and to identify the marks of the high priesthood, namely, that he offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, knowing how to feel compassion for those who are ignorant and erring. Then he began to discuss how one ought to approach the priesthood, saying:

“No one takes the honor of the priesthood for himself, but the one who is called by God, as Aaron was”—understand, he was called by the sign of the flowering staff, or by the sign of the burning of those who, envying his high priesthood, attempted to seize the dignity of the priesthood through their ambition. By these two signs the priest chosen by God was demonstrated. [Col. 0854B]

The blessed Apostle confounds and strikes down priests who desire honor and crave the priesthood, who voluntarily thrust and force themselves into priestly ministry, not by God’s calling or will, but rather through the intervention of gifts. They do this not for the salvation of the people but out of worldly ambition.

“So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’”

“Glorify,” “honor,” and “clarify” are three words but have one meaning; in Greek this is expressed in a single word, **ἐδόξασε** (*edoxase*, “he glorified”). Hence it is rendered differently in the variety of translators. For when the Evangelist records the Lord as saying, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8), the Apostle here calls it “clarification.” [Col. 0854C]

Christ therefore did not clarify himself—that is, he did not glorify himself—in order to become high priest by himself or to possess the honor of the high priesthood, because he was not from himself. This is what he himself says in the Gospel: “I have not come from myself, but he sent me” (John 7). And again: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who glorifies me, my Father” (John 8).

Therefore, just as he did not come from himself, because he was not from himself, and did not seek his own glory, so he did not glorify himself in order to possess the honor of the high priesthood from himself; rather, he was glorified by the Father, who spoke to him on the day of his baptism, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3). [Col. 0854D]

This clarification, or glorification, had been foretold long before through the prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit, speaking in the person of the Son of God and saying: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2). Since all future things are, for almighty God, as though already past or present, he regarded as already spoken what he would say to him after his baptism. Therefore he appropriately used the past tense, saying: “The Lord said to me.”

By “the Lord” we should understand God the Father. And so that we may believe that there is one person in Christ, he adds: “Today I have begotten you.” This means: “I, who always and eternally remain, always have you as my Son, coeternal with me.” “Today” is an adverb of the present time, which properly applies to God. [Col. 0855A]

The text continues:

“As he also says in another place: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’”

These words depend on the preceding verse, where the Apostle says that Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but that God the Father, who spoke to him—“You are my Son”—glorified him, just as in another place he himself says to the Son: “You are a priest forever,” and so forth.

It must be considered that Christ is not a priest according to the fact that he was begotten by God the Father before all ages, remaining with the Father as the coeternal and consubstantial true God with the one who begot him. Rather, he is a priest according to the fact that he was born from a virginal womb at the end of time, became human, and also according to the victim he offered for us, taking from us flesh and blood—namely, his own. [Col. 0855B]

But there are various reasons why he is said to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek and not according to the order of Aaron.

The first is that Melchizedek was not a priest according to the legal commandments, but according to the dignity of a distinctive priesthood, offering bread and wine to God rather than the blood of irrational animals. According to this order of priesthood Christ became a priest—not a temporal but an eternal one—not offering legal victims but, in the likeness of Melchizedek, bread and wine, namely his flesh and blood, of which he himself said: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6).

He also entrusted these two offerings—bread and wine—to his Church to be offered in remembrance of him. Hence it is clear that the sacrifice of animals, which belonged to the order of Aaron, has passed away, while that which belonged to the order of Melchizedek remains, because Christ confirmed it and left it to his Church to maintain. [Col. 0855C]

The second reason is that Melchizedek was both king and priest, and was anointed not with visible oil, like the priests of the law, but with the oil of the Holy Spirit. Christ remains marked by this twofold dignity. That he possesses royal dignity he himself declares when he says: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Psalm 2), that is, by God the Father. And after his resurrection he said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28). The Psalmist also says to God the Father: “Give the king your judgment” (Psalm 71). [Col. 0855D]

That he is a priest is sufficiently clear, since he offered himself for us on the altar of the cross and now intercedes with God the Father for our salvation. That he was anointed not with visible oil but with the fullness of the Holy Spirit is indicated to us by the Psalmist, who says to him: “O God, God, your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44), that is, with the fullness of the Holy Spirit.

The third reason why Christ is said to be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek and not according to the order of Aaron is that, just as Scripture speaks only once of Melchizedek and his priesthood, so Christ offered himself once as a sacrifice for us. [Col. 0856A]

The text continues:

“Who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications to the one who could save him from death, with a loud cry and tears, was heard because of his reverence.”

The Apostle does not say this about Melchizedek but about Christ, wishing to express more precisely what our high priest did in his true priesthood. What does “in the days of his flesh” mean? It means: while he dwelt in a mortal body, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him—that is, to God the Father.

The days of our Lord’s flesh are the days in which he assumed flesh, in which he was tempted and suffered, and in which he inhabited a mortal body. Everything he did in the flesh consisted of prayers and supplications for the sins of the human race. The sacred outpouring of his blood was the loud cry by which he was heard by God the Father because of his reverence—that is, his voluntary obedience and most perfect love. [Col. 0856B]

Did he not pour out prayers with tears when he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26; Mark 14), and “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”? (Mark 14; Luke 22.)

And because he voluntarily obeyed God the Father unto death, God the Father heard him by raising him on the third day, according to what the Psalmist says: “You will not permit your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15).

He is said to have poured out prayers and supplications not through fear of death, which he willingly accepted, but rather because, for the sake of our salvation, he placed the will of the Father’s dispensation above the will of his flesh, so that he might show in himself the true nature of our humanity. [Col. 0856C]

It should be noted that, according to Cassiodorus, *reverence* is understood in two ways: sometimes as love, sometimes as fear. Here, however, it signifies the highest love by which the Son of God loved us and the highest obedience by which he obeyed the Father unto death.

“And although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from what he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.”

“Although,” he says, “he was truly the Son of God, he learned obedience from the insults and torments he suffered.” He had already displayed this voluntary obedience to the Father, having experienced those things in respect of his humanity. This obedience, which the Apostle says the Son of God learned—that is, voluntarily accepted—he shows elsewhere when he says: “Although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death” (Philippians 2). [Col. 0856D]

When he says, “and having been perfected,” that is, perfected in the priesthood and in every form of obedience, “he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him,” he shows how great is the gain resulting from his passion and obedience, which suffice for the eternal salvation of all believers.

The text continues:

“Concerning whom”—that is, not concerning Melchizedek but concerning Christ—“we have much to say, and it is difficult to explain, since you have become weak in hearing.” [Col. 0857A]

The difficulty in explaining the discourse he instituted concerning the incarnate Son did not arise from ignorance on his part, since the mysteries hidden throughout the ages had been revealed to him; rather, it arose from the sluggishness of those who were weak—that is, weak in faith and fragile in understanding—when confronted with profound mysteries. Although, considering the time, they ought to have been teachers, he gives the reason, saying: “Since you have become weak in hearing,” and then adds:

“For although you ought to be teachers by this time”—understand, because from almost the beginning you have had the law and the prophets—“you again need someone to teach you the first principles of the words of God; and you have become people who need milk, not solid food.” [Col. 0857B]

He is speaking to those who, having long remained in the law, ought to have possessed an exercised understanding concerning Christ’s coming through the words of the law and the prophets, and also through the grace brought to believers through him. Although, because of the time that had passed and because they had received all the things mentioned above, they ought to have been teachers of the Gentiles, they again needed to be taught by him and by the other Apostles what the first principles of God’s words were.

The principles are so called as though they were “elevations,” because the other things take their origin from them, namely the beginnings and foundations of created things. Some also call them *elimenta*, as if they were “fabrications,” from *elimo, elimas*, as though all things had been fashioned from them. [Col. 0857C]

Here we can understand *elimenta*, or principles, in two ways: either as the actual characters and pronunciations of letters, from which speech begins, or as the very beginnings and foundations of faith. It is as if he were saying: “You need to be taught the principles of letters or the beginnings of faith, although you ought to be investigating the depths of the mysteries and to be perfect in faith.”

“You have become,” he says, “like infants who need milk,” that is, simple and rudimentary teaching, “not solid food,” that is, perfect doctrine and profound discourses or mysteries. The blessed Apostle has the practice of designating simple doctrine by the name of milk and perfect doctrine by the name of solid food. Hence he says to the Corinthians, who were still less perfect (1 Corinthians 3): “I gave you milk to drink, not food, because you were not yet able to receive it.” [Col. 0857D]

Milk, therefore, is the simple doctrine of the incarnation of the Son of God, his passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. Solid food, however, is the mystery of the Trinity conveyed in perfect discourse: how the Son is coeternal with the Father; how the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; and how there are three persons and one substance of the Godhead.

But if someone cannot understand what the Evangelist says—“The Word became flesh”—how will he be able to reach the height of his discourse, where he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1)?

The text continues:

“For everyone who partakes of milk”—that is, of simple doctrine alone—“is inexperienced in the word of righteousness,” that is, is a stranger to the discernment of perfect righteousness, because he is not yet able to penetrate the secrets of the mysteries, nor does he know how to distinguish properly between good and evil. He gives the reason: “For he is a child,” understand, in sense and understanding. [Col. 0858A]

“But solid food belongs to the mature,” that is, to those who have mature senses. It belongs to them to perceive lofty and obscure mysteries concerning the divinity of almighty God. Hence it continues: “I say that solid food belongs to those who, through the practice of reading, have their senses trained,” that is, stretched and strengthened through literary study, “for the discernment of good and evil,” and also for the discernment of truth from heretical depravity.

Just as a child does not know how to distinguish one food from another and often risks harm even in eating harmless foods unless restrained by an older person, so every uneducated person who does not know how to distinguish doctrines is easily deceived and endangered on the path of error. [Col. 0858B]

Therefore he says that everyone who partakes of milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness. What differs in milk and solid food is the same as what differs in the uneducated and the wise. Just as milk suits infants and solid food those mature in age, so humble discourse suits the uneducated, while it is fitting for the wise, whose senses have been exercised through the study of reading, to know the hidden mystery.

Through habitual reading and frequent meditation on the divine Scriptures, our senses become trained and strengthened to understand greater things. Hence the Psalmist calls blessed the man who “meditates . . . on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1).

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore, leaving aside the discourse of the beginning of Christ, let us be carried toward more perfect things. [Col. 0858C]

Because it is fitting for us to have senses exercised in the law of the Lord, let us leave aside the discourse of the beginning of Christ and be led toward the profound and lofty mysteries of his divinity. He calls the discourse of the beginning of Christ the beginning of faith: instruction concerning Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, ascension, and the grace of baptism.

Just as someone who is to be instructed in letters must first hear the principles of letters, so a Christian must first be instructed in these matters and afterward come to the mysteries of the divinity.

“Not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith”—understand, not again laying the foundation of faith—“toward God.”

He calls the foundation of repentance the instruction with which the person who is to be baptized must first be taught, provided that he has reached the age of understanding. He must believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was begotten from God the Father before all ages; that he was born from the Virgin Mary at the end of time for the salvation of the human race, without the seed of a man; that he suffered, died, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judgment to repay each person according to his works; that there will be a resurrection of bodies and an unchangeability of souls; that the good will remain in glory and the wicked in punishments; and that almighty God has a Trinity of persons and a unity of substance. [Col. 0858D]

After confessing that he believes all these things, he must confess his sins, and penance must then be imposed upon him for forty, twenty, or seven days, as we read in the passions of the saints. Afterward he must be baptized, renouncing the devil and all his pomp and all his works.

After baptism, he must be more fully instructed concerning the divinity, so that he may believe that the Father begot the only-begotten Son, and that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten but proceeds from both; and he must also be instructed in the rule of life according to evangelical and apostolic teaching, by which he ought to do good and avoid evil. [Col. 0859A]

Since the Jews to whom the Apostle was writing were already baptized and had already received the foundation described above, he exhorts them to strive toward these greater things and says that there is no need to lay again in them the foundation of repentance and faith toward God.

He calls it the foundation of repentance because, as has been said, repentance was first imposed upon those who were to be baptized. Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, blessed Peter says to the Jews who were turning to the faith: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (Acts 2).

It is also called the foundation of faith toward God because the faith by which we approach God is the foundation of all virtues. “There must not,” he says, “be a need for us again to lay the foundation of repentance from dead works and the foundation of faith, through which one approaches God, which was laid in you before you came to the grace of baptism.” [Col. 0859B]

To practice repentance from dead works is to erase through repentance the evil works that were killing the soul. The works of death are sins. For just as the soul is given life by faith and the other virtues, so it dies through unbelief and sins.

The text continues:

“Not again laying the foundation of the doctrine of baptisms.” [Col. 0859C]

The foundation of the doctrine of baptisms is the institution and teaching of baptism—namely, what baptism contains in itself and what it confers upon those who approach the faith. But when he says “the foundation of baptisms” in the plural, he uses the plural because of the variety of those who receive it; it is not to be understood that there are several baptisms, but one. For just as there is one God and one faith, so there is one baptism.

“We must not again lay the foundation of the imposition of hands.” By “the imposition of hands” he means confirmation, through which it is fully believed that the Holy Spirit is received. After baptism, this is customarily performed by high priests for the confirmation of unity in the Church.

After these matters have been perfectly received in the Church, faith in the resurrection and future judgment must be held. Hence the Apostle adds:

“And the foundation of the resurrection of the dead and of eternal judgment you must not lay again,” as though you needed to be instructed once more in faith concerning the general resurrection and the judgment that will be given alike to the just and the unjust.

It should be noted that throughout all these clauses one must always understand: “not again laying the foundation.” [Col. 0859D]

And this we shall do, if indeed God permits it—that is, we shall lead you on to greater things and teach you most fully all the matters we have enumerated, so that it will not again be necessary to lay the foundation wholly and from the beginning.

But lest anyone should in any way suppose that baptism could be performed a second or third time after sins, he immediately added:

“It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened”—that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit in the baptism of faith—“who have also tasted the heavenly gift”—that is, received the remission of sins in baptism, or shared in the Lord’s body and blood after baptism—“and have become participants in the Holy Spirit,” namely, in the distribution of his gifts; “who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God,” that is, understood the evangelical teaching, “and the powers of the age to come,” that is, the glorification of the resurrection and the future life; “and then have fallen away from the faith of Christ,” whether by denying him or by falling into criminal sins, “to be renewed again to repentance”—that is, to be made new through repentance, implicitly, from the things mentioned above—it is impossible. [Col. 0860A]

“It is impossible,” he says, “for those who, after receiving all the things mentioned above, have fallen into the uncleanness of criminal sins or even into unbelief, to be renewed again through repentance and baptism.” He did not say, “It is difficult,” but “It is impossible.” For what is difficult can somehow be done; what is impossible, however, cannot be done in any way.

What then? Is repentance after baptism and the pardon of sins excluded? By no means. There are, in fact, two kinds of repentance. One is before baptism, which may also be called the preparation for baptism. We spoke of it above: it is imposed upon those who are being instructed before they come to baptism. It is this that the blessed Apostle excludes when he says that they cannot be renewed again through repentance, so that, after repentance has been completed, they might be baptized again. The other kind of repentance is that by which sins committed after baptism are blotted out; this the blessed Apostle does not exclude. [Col. 0860B]

He therefore terrifies everyone, so that after the grace of baptism they may fear entangling themselves in more serious sins, since a second renewal through the washing of baptism cannot take place. For just as Christ, having died once and risen once, dies no more (Rom. VI), so the grace of baptism is to be received once, and cannot be repeated—unless there should be uncertainty whether someone, having been captured by enemies, had already been baptized.

By “renewed” he meant “made new.” To be made a new human being is the work of holy baptism, concerning which the Prophet says: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII).

“It is impossible,” I say, for anyone to be renewed again through the repentance that takes place before baptism, with the aim that, once repentance has been completed, he might be baptized again. Those who have received the things mentioned above have also “tasted the powers of the age to come.” What he says—“they have tasted the powers of the age to come”—means this, as though he were saying: If they have recognized that, in the resurrection of the age to come, the elect will be like the angels of God in heaven, and that “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XII, XIII), they cannot in any way be renewed again through repentance and repeated baptism if they have committed a criminal sin, as they were made new in the first baptism. [Col. 0860C]

There were indeed people who wished to repeat baptism, saying: “Whatever sin I commit does not matter to me, since I shall command myself to be baptized again, and I shall be wholly renewed as before.” The Apostle categorically denies that this can in any way happen. And because the power of baptism rests especially upon the cross and burial of Christ, he therefore added: [Col. 0860D]

“Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and making him a spectacle.” [Col. 0861A]

Nevertheless, repentance is not thereby denied. Although they are not renewed in baptism, they can still obtain forgiveness again through confession of sins, humility, repentance, almsgiving if they have the means, and forgiving those brothers who have sinned against them.

Those who wish to be baptized again, so far as lies within them, also wish to crucify Christ again and hold him up to ridicule; this is what it means to make him a spectacle. But it cannot happen. For just as Christ died once in the flesh upon the cross, so we too can die only once to sin in baptism. [Col. 0861B]

“For the land that drinks in the rain repeatedly falling upon it and produces suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated receives a blessing from God.”

By this example he rebukes the Jews, who often drank in the rain of heavenly teaching but never brought forth shoots of faith and good works. He first sets out a comparison concerning good soil and then one concerning bad soil.

“The land,” he says, “that drinks in the rain”—that is, the soul of good and holy disposition receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit and the rain of divine utterances—and “produces suitable vegetation,” that is, bringing forth good virtues and perfect faith for its preachers, by whom it is cultivated; or, for itself, it receives the blessing of eternal life or an abundance of virtues, and bears thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and likewise a hundredfold fruit. [Col. 0861C]

For nothing is more suitable than the perfect faith of God’s faithful joined with an excellent life. Having therefore offered this example of a soul flourishing in virtues and worthy of God’s blessing, the Apostle immediately added another example concerning the soul that neglects its salvation, although it can frequently receive the rain of heavenly teaching:

“But producing thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to being cursed.”

By thorns and thistles we can understand the pricks of sins by which the soul is pierced, concerning which the Lord said to Adam: “Your land shall produce thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III)—that is, your flesh shall produce for you the pricks of sins and the goads of vices. [Col. 0861D]

Alternatively, by thorns and thistles we should understand superfluous cares and anxieties of this world, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “The cares of this world and the anxieties of riches choke the word, so that it becomes fruitless” (Matt. XIII).

The soul, therefore, producing the pricks of sins and occupied with worldly cares and the anxieties of riches, is rejected—that is, unworthy of praise—and near to being cursed. It should be noted that he did not say, “It is cursed,” but “near to being cursed.” As long as it is being reserved for repentance, it is, as it were, not cursed; but if it refuses to do penance, then it will be cursed.

Hence he continues: “whose end”—that is, the end of that soul in wicked conduct and perseverance in evil until the end of life—“will be for burning,” implicitly, in eternal fire. It is as though he were saying: [Col. 0862A]

“As long as it has the opportunity for repentance, it is not indeed cursed, but is near to being cursed; if, however, it persists in its iniquity, it will be subjected to the burning of eternal punishment.”

This burning will belong only to those who have persisted in their sins until the end of their lives, because “on whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die.”

After he had sufficiently rebuked, terrified, and struck them, he addressed them once more with encouragement, so that he would not make them despair; yet he neither flatters them in everything nor strikes them in everything. He therefore says:

“But concerning you, beloved, we are confident of better things and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.” [Col. 0862B]

Since he had no present basis on which to praise them, he praises them on the basis of the future things he hoped for concerning them, as though he were saying: “We do not say this because we think you are full of thorns, but because we fear that you may become such. It is better for you to be terrified by words than to suffer grief over realities.”

“We are confident concerning you of every good work and of what benefits your salvation, although we speak in this way.” For when we spoke above of the rejected land and of its nearness to burning, we did not say this about you, because we believe better things concerning you.

He also recalled their past good works to their memory. Since he could use what was past to lead them toward every good thing, he therefore added:

“For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love that you showed in his name, when you ministered to the saints and continue to minister.” [Col. 0862C]

See how he revived and restored their spirits: he recalled their past good works to mind. Because forgetfulness cannot occur in almighty God, he does not forget the works and labors of his faithful; and he is just in this respect, because he rewards his elect who labor for him.

For if he were to forget their works and not reward them, he might somehow be thought unjust—something it is wholly impious to say. Hence the Apostle says: “God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and labor, and the love that you showed for love of his name toward one another and toward all, when you ministered to the saints and still minister according to your ability.”

He is speaking of those saints who, when they came to faith in Christ, were stripped of their possessions by other Jews. He praises them in this Epistle, saying: “You accepted with joy the seizure of your possessions” (Hebr. X). Isaiah had foretold this long beforehand, saying: “And he who departed from the evil of the Jews became prey” (Isa. LIX). [Col. 0862D]

When such people had been stripped of their possessions, those who had not been stripped of theirs ministered to them as they were able. How great and how earnest his desire was for their salvation, he partly expresses in the following words:

“But we desire each one of you to show the same diligence”—implicitly, the diligence you previously had—“toward the fulfillment of hope until the end of your life,” or until the day of judgment, “so that you may not become sluggish,” that is, lazy and negligent in good works and in fulfilling the commandments of God. [Col. 0863A]

“We desire,” he says, “that you should conduct yourselves not only in words but also in virtues. We are not condemning your past works, but admonishing you to be concerned about the future; that is, just as you were at first, so we desire you to be now and in the future.”

He did not say, “I wish,” which expresses divine authority, but, as an expression of paternal affection: “We desire each one of you always to show toward the brothers the same love that you formerly had, unto the completion of hope in the eternal resurrection.” For the fulfillment of hope is the attainment of the things that we hope to obtain.

“But we desire you to be imitators of those”—implicitly, we desire you to be imitators of those—“who through faith and patience inherit the promises.” [Col. 0863B]

Again he exhorts them to await God’s promises and the inheritance he promised to his saints with unfeigned faith and perfect patience. This can be understood in two ways: namely, as referring to the patriarchs and saints of the Old Testament, who received many promises concerning Christ and concerning the inheritance of the promised land.

Having perfect faith, by which they believed that God could fulfill what he had promised, and the most steadfast patience, by which they awaited the fulfillment of the promises not in themselves but in their children, they deserved to be God’s friends and to inherit those same promises in their children.

It can also refer to the apostles and other saints, who through faith and patience deserved to attain and inherit the promises of eternal blessing made by the Lord to themselves and to all the faithful.

“For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.’” [Col. 0863C]

To confirm more firmly what he had said above concerning the saints—that they would inherit God’s promises through faith and patience—he therefore uses examples. Yet his wisdom is marvelous. At one time he wins them over by exalting them with praises; at another he terrifies them with threats.

Above he terrified them lest they become unbelieving and insufficiently trusting in God’s promises. Now, however, by examples he exhorts them to patience and faith, so that they may believe without doubt—not merely because God spoke, but because he also swore by himself.

If it is wicked not to believe when God makes a promise, how impious it is not to place faith in God when he swears! God the Father swore to Abraham by himself, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, saying: “Surely, blessing I will bless you,” and so forth.

The repetition of the word confirms the matter. In this passage *nisi* (“unless”) is used affirmatively for “certainly” or “because,” and the sense is: “Certainly I will always bless you in your children, and I will always multiply you.”

“And thus, by patiently enduring, he obtained the promise.” [Col. 0863D]

That is, by believing and enduring for a long time through patience, he obtained in his children the promise of the promised land, which God had made to him, saying: “I will give this land to you and to your children” (Gen. XIII), and, in addition, the promise concerning Christ, of whom he said: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

He continues:

“For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every dispute among them, for confirmation, is an oath.” [Col. 0864A]

It is as though he were saying: If people place future trust in human beings, concerning whom it is said through the Prophet, “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV), how much more should belief be placed in God’s oath, since he is truth and can neither be deceived nor lie—and since he ought to be believed even without an oath!

“Human beings,” he says, “swear by one greater than themselves,” that is, by God, who is their Creator. An oath is also the end of all their contention for confirmation, because an oath is to be believed; after the oath has been completed, no complaint should subsequently be made. The end of contention should be the oath, as confirmation.

“In which”—implicitly, in the oath, or because an oath is the confirmation of a matter—“God, desiring to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise,” that is, to the fathers or heirs of the promise, “the unchangeableness of his purpose, inserted an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest consolation”—that is, so that we might firmly believe in him—“we who have fled for refuge by believing, to hold fast the hope set before us,” that is, to receive the promised remission or reward. [Col. 0864B]

Here we should understand the two unchangeable things as God’s promise concerning Christ, in which he said, “In your seed all the nations will be blessed,” and his oath, in which he said, “I have sworn by myself.” His promise is unchangeable because it could not be altered, and his oath is truthful.

Some wish one unchangeable thing to be understood as his promise and oath, and the other as the fulfillment of that matter itself. By “the hope set before us,” however, he means the truth of things accomplished—namely, the promise of the heavenly homeland, to which we flee for refuge through faith in order to attain it.

“We have this hope as a sure and firm anchor of the soul.”

Just as an anchor cast from a ship does not allow it to be driven about or endangered, even though the winds may shake it, but, when thrown out, holds the ship firmly amid storms and waves, so faith, strengthened by hope in future goods, steadies our mind amid the prosperity and adversity of this world and introduces us into the reality of the things that we now hold by faith and hope. [Col. 0864C]

Therefore the Apostle adds:

“And entering into the interior of the veil.”

By “the interior of the veil” he calls the secrets of the kingdom of heaven and the joys of the heavenly homeland. The veil that stood before the Holy of Holies signifies heaven; what was within the veil signifies the secrets of the kingdom of heaven.

Hope penetrates into the interior of the veil when, through contemplation of the mind, it sees future goods; when, without any doubt, it believes that heavenly rewards will come to it; when it hopes for them and loves them; and when it shows by its works what it believes and what it hopes for.

If we do not have this hope, we shall certainly be submerged—not only in spiritual things but also in bodily ones, just as a ship without a cast anchor will be submerged. But if we obey the voice of the Prophet who says, “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. LIV), then our hope, fixed in the interior of the veil, cannot be drowned by any unbelief.

He continues:

“Where Jesus, having become a forerunner for us, has entered, having been made high priest and appointed by God the Father forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” [Col. 0864D]

To give us a firmer hope, he added this concerning Christ. He is called a forerunner from going before and running ahead, and he is the forerunner of someone, as John was the forerunner of Christ.

It should be considered that he does not simply say, “Jesus entered into the interior of the veil,” but adds: “Where the forerunner has entered for us,” as though it were undoubtedly necessary for us to follow our forerunner. The forerunner and those who follow ought to be on the same road.

Christ, therefore, rising from the dead, went before us to the heights of heaven and became our forerunner by opening heaven for us and restoring to us the joys of the heavenly homeland. If, then, we wish to follow our forerunner, we must walk as he himself did and in the same way.

This refers to the humanity of the Son of God, in which he offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross as the sacrifice of our salvation. Why Christ is said to exist as a priest according to the order of Melchizedek was, as I believe, shown quite clearly a little above.

But when he says that Christ entered into the interior of the veil, he speaks in the manner of the Jewish high priests, who once a year entered within the veil into the Holy of Holies to pray in the temple for the people. In the same way Christ, penetrating the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, continually prays for the salvation of his faithful.

## CHAPTER VII

“For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God”—implicitly, was such—“met Abraham as he was returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him; and Abraham divided to him a tenth of everything.” [Col. 0865A]

The Hebrews report that he was Shem, Noah’s firstborn son, who at the time when Abraham was born was 292 years old, and at the time when Abraham died was 565 years old; thus he survived Abraham by thirty-five years. When these years had been completed, all the days of his life amounted to six hundred years.

It should not be considered surprising that he came out to meet Abraham, offered him bread and wine—which by the right of fatherhood he owed to his great-grandson—blessed him, and received from him a tenth of the spoil and the victory, as a priest of the Most High God, not of false gods and idols. He was also king of Salem.

Salem, as the blessed Jerome says, should not be thought to be Jerusalem, as Josephus the historian and many of our people suppose. Rather, it is near the town of Scythopolis, which to this day is called Salem or Salim. Concerning it, as the blessed Jerome attests, we read in the Gospel: “John was baptizing in Aennon near Salim, because there was much water there” (John III). [Col. 0865B]

The variation in these names arises because the Hebrews in many places write only the consonants, omitting the vowels; consequently, the word is pronounced according to the reader’s judgment, not always in one and the same way.

The palace of Melchizedek is also shown in that same town. The size of its ruins displays the grandeur of the ancient structure. Jacob is also said to have descended to this city or town, which was in the land of Canaan in the region of Shechem (Gen. XXIX).

It should also be considered that when Abraham returned from the slaughter of the enemies whom he had pursued as far as Dan, he did not have Jerusalem on his route of return, but rather the town of Salem mentioned above.

“First, he is interpreted as ‘king of righteousness,’ and then also as ‘king of Salem,’ which is ‘king of peace,’ without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life.” [Col. 0865C]

The blessed Apostle frequently introduces Melchizedek as a type of the Lord and Savior. Although almost all the saints, patriarchs, and prophets of earlier times expressed the figure of Christ in some respect, Melchizedek was a more specific type. Since he was not of the Jewish race, he preceded, in figure, the priesthood of the Son of God, concerning whom God the Father says in the Psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

We can interpret his order in many ways, as has already been said above: namely, that he alone was both king and priest; that he exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that it was not the Gentiles who received the priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the Gentiles; that he was not anointed with visible oil, as the Mosaic precepts establish, but with the oil of exultation and the purity of faith; and that he did not offer victims of flesh and blood, but consecrated the priesthood through bread and wine, a simple and pure sacrifice of Christ. [Col. 0865D]

First, however, as the Apostle says, he is made like the Son of God in this respect: he is interpreted as “king of righteousness.” For *Melchon* or *Melchi* signifies “king,” while *Sedech* signifies “just” or “righteousness.”

And who is the true king of righteousness except Christ, who says in the Psalm: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. II)? He governs and rules his elect justly and rightly, having made them lovers of righteousness.

Then he is made like the Son of God in that he is called “king of peace,” which pertains to Christ. *Salem* is interpreted as “peace.” Christ therefore justifies us, for he is the king of righteousness; and he himself makes peace among all things in heaven and on earth. By being born, dying, rising again, and ascending, he brought peace to the world. [Col. 0866A]

According to his divinity, he is a king without beginning and without end, coeternal with the eternal Father, although according to his temporal mother he was temporal. Just as we do not read in Holy Scripture of the beginning or end of this Melchizedek, so we do not know the beginning or end of the Son of God, because he has none of these in the nature of his divinity.

The likeness consists in this: neither the beginning nor the end of either is read of. In the case of Melchizedek, this is because it has not been written; in the case of the Son of God, because it does not exist at all.

For we do not read under whom Melchizedek was born, nor is it narrated when he died; rather, he is introduced suddenly, as Elijah also is. It should not at all be believed that Melchizedek was without father or without mother, since Christ too, according to both natures, had both a father and a mother.

This is said of Melchizedek because, as we have said, he is introduced suddenly in divine Scripture and his genealogy is not mentioned. It is also said of him that, having been made like the Son of God in all the matters stated above, he remains a priest forever—not in himself, but in Christ.

Melchizedek died, but his figure remains eternally in Christ. Here “likeness” is not used to indicate equality, but a figure.

“Now consider how great this man was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils.” [Col. 0867A]

He turns his discourse toward those who boast that they are sons of Abraham and claim to derive the nobility of their lineage from him. In the Gospel they even attempted to place Abraham before the Lord, saying: “Are you greater than our father Abraham?” (John IV).

To confound their pride, the Apostle said: “Consider and carefully observe how great this Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth from the chief things,” that is, from the better spoils.

By these words he wishes to show that Melchizedek was of greater dignity and honor than Abraham, and therefore that Christ’s priesthood would be greater and holier than the Jews’ priesthood. It is as though he were saying: “The one whom you consider superior to all human beings offered a tenth to Melchizedek, who preceded as a figure of Christ.” [Col. 0867B]

“And indeed, those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi have a commandment, according to the law, to take tithes from the people—that is, from their brothers—although they themselves also came forth from the loins of Abraham.”

“Such,” he says, “is the excellence of the priesthood that even those who had the same ancestor and descended from one father, because of the merit of their excellence by which they were better than their brothers—namely, Aaron, who, standing between the living and the dead, appeased the Lord’s anger—were considered worthy to attain the dignity of the priesthood.

“Therefore, unless Melchizedek had been of greater dignity than Abraham, Abraham would certainly not have given tithes to a foreigner, just as Aaron was of greater merit than his brothers of the remaining tribes.” [Col. 0867C]

He therefore says: “Indeed, those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi, as Aaron and his sons received it, have a commandment and precept according to the law to take tithes from the people—as being better than them—and this from their brothers, although they had one and the same ancestor, as the Apostle makes clear when he says: ‘Although they too came forth from the loins of Abraham.’”

“But the one whose genealogy is not counted among them”—that is, among the sons of Levi—“took tithes from Abraham, and blessed him who had the promises.”

That is, Melchizedek blessed Abraham, who had received the promises concerning the Son of God. Here he shows that an uncircumcised priest was far superior to a circumcised priest.

How is this shown? Clearly, because Levi himself, from whom the priestly race arose, was tithed by Melchizedek in the loins of his ancestor. Abraham had already been circumcised, and had already received from God the promise that all the nations would be blessed in his seed, when he was blessed by Melchizedek, the uncircumcised priest, while giving him a tenth of the entire spoil.

When Melchizedek blessed him, he said (Gen. XIV): “Blessed be Abraham by the Most High God, by whose protection his enemies were struck down by his hand,” and the other words that follow in that passage. [Col. 0867D]

“Without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the better.”

It is as though he were saying: It is evident to all, as clearly as daylight, that the lesser is blessed by the greater. Thus Abraham, as the lesser, received a blessing from Melchizedek as the better. Therefore the type of Christ is greater and better than the one who possessed the promises concerning Christ. [Col. 0868A]

“And here, indeed, mortal human beings receive tithes; but there it is testified that he lives.”

“Here,” he says—that is, in the present age, or in the temple that still stood—“mortal human beings,” namely, the sons of Levi, who are mortal and dying, “receive tithes. But there,” that is, in the other life, or in the place where it is said of Christ, “You are a priest forever,” God the Father testifies with an oath that Christ lives.

Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

“And, so to speak, through Abraham, Levi also, who received tithes, was tithed”—in his descendants, or because he has hitherto received tithes from his brothers—“for he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him.” [Col. 0868B]

How does he say that Levi was tithed by Melchizedek when Levi had not yet been born, especially since he was also the natural son of Jacob? Certainly, he was not tithed in himself, but in Abraham, from whose descendants he came.

When Abraham offered tithes to Melchizedek, all his sons gave them in him. Therefore the Apostle says that Levi, who received tithes in his descendants from his brothers, was tithed through Abraham, or in Abraham.

By these words it is shown that, unless the priesthood of Melchizedek—which preceded in the figure of Christ’s priesthood—had been of greater dignity, Abraham and all his sons would certainly not have been tithed by him. For when one priesthood is tithed by another, one is shown to be of greater dignity than the other.

“If, then, perfection was through the Levitical priesthood—for the people received the law under it—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek and not to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, there must also be a transfer of the law.” [Col. 0868C]

Here he begins to show more fully the differences of the New Testament. He says: If perfection—that is, the perfection of life and justification—was through the Levitical priesthood, what need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek?

Since there is no doubt that Aaron was the first priest from the tribe of Levi after the law had been given, he called the priesthood exercised by Aaron the Levitical priesthood; or certainly because Levi himself was joined to that priesthood in his sons.

His great-grandsons received it—namely, Moses and Aaron, together with their other brothers from the same tribe. For Levi fathered Kohath, Kohath fathered Amram, and Amram fathered Moses and Aaron. [Col. 0868D]

Therefore he says that the people received the law under that priesthood, because Moses and Aaron were leaders among the people in those times; they administered the law itself, having come from the priestly tribe.

Thus the order of the priesthood of Melchizedek, who bore the type of our priest, is much better than the Levitical priesthood. He certainly would not have said “according to the order of Melchizedek” if Aaron’s priesthood had been better—the priesthood under which the Jewish people received the law.

But if the priesthood of the law was transferred to Christ according to the order of Melchizedek, there must also be a transfer of the law; that is, it is necessary to pass from the law of Moses to the law of the Gospel.

For a priest cannot exist without a law, without a covenant, and without commandments. The Apostle labored with all his strength to make them pass from the law of Moses to the law of the Gospel, from carnal things to spiritual things.

“For the one concerning whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one attended the altar.” [Col. 0869A]

It is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priests. When he says, “the one concerning whom these things are said,” that is, the one of whom it is said here that he is a priest forever—signifying the Lord and Savior—belongs to another tribe, not the priestly tribe, namely, the tribe from which no one attended the altar.

That is, he came from the tribe of Judah. The change therefore occurred not only in order, covenant, or commandments, but also in tribe.

How was the priesthood transferred from one tribe to another—from the priestly tribe, that is, to the royal tribe—so that in Christ the same tribe might be both royal and priestly, since he is king and priest? Consider the mystery.

First, according to the sequence of this discourse, there was a royal priesthood in Melchizedek. Second, there was a priesthood that was merely priestly in Aaron. Third, there was again a royal priesthood in Christ, as at the beginning.

Hence the Church now also possesses a royal priesthood, as Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II; Matt. XXVIII). [Col. 0869B]

Thus the tribe of Judah, from which the Lord arose through the virgin Mary, although it had always been royal and never priestly, became in Christ both royal and priestly, the priesthood having been transferred completely from the tribe of Levi, which had previously been priestly.

“And it is still more evident if another priest arises according to the order of Melchizedek, who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life.”

For God testifies, the Father speaking to the Son: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

The choice of wording in this passage is sufficiently important; therefore it should now be understood in this way: “And it is still more evident”—implicitly, that the priesthood of the law has been destroyed—because Christ is said to be a priest forever not according to the order of Aaron but according to the order of Melchizedek; and this because he did not belong to the tribe of Levi. [Col. 0869C]

When he says, “if another priest arises according to the order of Melchizedek,” he is not speaking doubtfully but affirmatively, as though he were saying: “It is shown even more clearly by this that the priesthood of the law has been destroyed, because Christ, another priest, has arisen according to the order of Melchizedek. He was not made a priest according to the law of a carnal commandment, as Aaron was.”

He calls it the law of a carnal commandment because it was for the most part carnal, prescribing carnal things: circumcision, bodily purification, carnal sacrifices and offerings, distinctions among foods, days, and seasons. It said: “Remain outside the camp; wash your body; offer this or that; abstain from these foods; observe these seasons,” and other things of this kind, all of which were destined to end in death. [Col. 0869D]

Christ’s priesthood, however, is spiritual and according to the power of an indestructible life—that is, according to the power of a life that cannot fail and cannot be dissolved by any intervening fear of death.

Christ possesses indestructible life in himself. Although he was dead in the flesh for a time, he nevertheless lives forever in his divinity and, moreover, in his humanity: after rising victorious from the dead, God the Father therefore testifies with an oath that he lives, saying through the Psalmist: “You are a priest forever.” [Col. 0870A]
