The rejection, then, is of the preceding commandment—that is, of the law of Moses—because of its weakness and uselessness. The law was weak in this respect: it was unable to assist those who practiced it; and it was useless in this respect: it was unable to open the kingdom of heaven to anyone. Hence it follows: “For the law brought nothing to perfection.” What, then—did the law accomplish nothing? It did accomplish something: it cleansed bodies and remitted lesser sins. But it accomplished nothing in the sense that it could make those who served under it perfect, since it did not remove more serious sins, nor open to anyone the door of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore it was rejected, so that room might be given to grace, in which perfection consists. It was indeed useful to those who possessed faith in Christ, but not to those who placed all their hope in its carnal observances.

“The introduction of a better hope”—that is, which now exists in grace—“through which we draw near to God.” The law did have hope, but not the kind that grace provided. Those who pleased God and kept the law hoped to possess the land, according to the saying: “If you are willing, you shall eat the good things of the land,” and, to suffer no affliction and to live prosperously, as it is said: “Whoever does these things shall live.” But we hope for this: that, pleasing God and keeping the Gospel commandments, we shall possess not the earth but heaven. More than this, and better than heaven itself, we hope to stand near God, to reach the throne of the Father, and to minister to him with the holy angels, according to what the Savior says in the Gospel: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, and they will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 13:43).

This priesthood, through which we shall possess this glory, is not without an oath, so that we may believe God’s promise to be firm. Hence the Apostle adds: “And how much”—that is, how firm—“this priesthood of Christ of which we are speaking is,” namely, it is very great, because it has been confirmed by an oath. Others became priests without an oath, such as Aaron and his sons, to whom God did not swear that they would be priests forever according to the order of the law. But this one—that is, Christ—became a priest with an oath, by him—that is, by God the Father, who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” that is, he will not alter his oath, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Jesus became the guarantor, or promiser, of the better Testament to the extent that he holds his priesthood with the oath of God the Father. To the extent that Christ’s priesthood, sanctioned by God’s oath, surpasses the priesthood of the ancient law in dignity, to that same extent the grace of the Gospel surpasses the law of Moses.

And others indeed became priests because they were prevented by death from remaining in office. But this one—that is, Christ, to whom the Father said with an oath, “You are a priest forever”—because he remains forever, possesses an everlasting priesthood. Here the blessed Apostle sets forth two distinctions: our priest has no end, as the priesthood of the law did, and he is to possess his priesthood with an oath. Since the priests of the law were mortal, many priests were appointed within that very law, such as Aaron and his sons, because they were prevented by death from continuing in the priesthood. When the fathers died, their sons succeeded them. Jesus, however, because he is immortal, alone possesses an everlasting priesthood, and no successor can ever follow him, since he remains forever.

It follows: “Therefore he is also able to save forever those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for us.” Since, he says, Christ remains forever and possesses an everlasting priesthood, he always intercedes for us and is always able to save. Since some manuscripts read, “the one who draws near to God through himself,” while others read, “those who draw near,” both readings may be accepted.

Christ, then, our high priest, does not draw near to God the Father through another high priest greater than himself, but through himself; and therefore he is able to save those who believe in him. The statement, “he is able to save forever those who draw near to God through him,” may also be understood in this way: we, who are merely human beings, draw near to God the Father through him, because, being our Mediator, he stands before God’s face on our behalf, directing our prayers through himself to God the Father. Hence the priests of the Church, standing before the altar, say: “Receive, Lord, holy Father, the prayers of your people through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.” And because he always lives, he always intercedes for us.

The other high priests, who will not always exist, do not always intercede. Christ intercedes for us because he assumed human nature, which he continually displays before God’s face on our behalf, so that he may have mercy according to both substances.

For he was such a one as was needed to be our holy, innocent, undefiled high priest, separated from sinners and exalted above the heavens. We were neither worthy nor deserving to have such a high priest; nevertheless, it was necessary for us to have one who was holy in the inner person, innocent in his hands, undefiled in body, and separated from sinners—that is, free from every sin and separated from the conduct of sinners. In this he was separated from sinners: other human beings are conceived and born with sin and depart from this world with sin, whereas he was conceived without sin, born without sin, and passed from this world without sin, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

He was made higher than the heavens when, on the fortieth day after his wondrous resurrection, he was raised above all the heavens and above all the orders of heavenly spirits to the presence of the Father’s majesty. There he now sits in the fullness of honor and glory.

The statement, “He was such a one as was needed to be our high priest,” may also be understood in this way, as if he were saying: The Jews, serving God as slaves through fear of the law, had legal high priests—mortal and sinful fellow servants like themselves, who likewise needed to offer sacrifices for themselves. But we, to whom it was said, “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15), and who are sons of God, serving him with the love proper to children, ought to have an immortal high priest, separated from sinners.

It follows: “Who has no need each day, as those high priests do, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for those of the people.” Our Lord Jesus Christ did this once, offering himself. What did he do? He offered a sacrifice not for his own sins but for ours, and he did this once, not again, because, having died once for our sins, “he dies no more; death no longer rules over him” (Romans 6:9).

Here he shows the greatness of Christ’s sacrifice: offered once, it was as effective as all the legal sacrifices were not. For it was one sacrifice, offered once, and it suffices forever for taking away all the sins of believers.

The Jewish high priests were sinners, and therefore they had to offer sacrifices for their own sins. For that reason those sacrifices could not justify a human being, since it was inappropriate that an irrational animal should be offered for a rational human being. A sinless high priest and a rational sacrifice were sought, but none was found. One was found, however, who was without sin, God and human, and he offered himself as a rational sacrifice for the salvation of rational humanity.

The law appointed human beings as priests who had weakness. For the Lord says to Moses in the law: “You shall anoint Aaron and his sons for me as priests” (Exodus 30:30). But because they possessed weakness—that is, sins, by which their souls were weakened—they had to offer sacrifices both for the sins of the people and for their own. This one, however, was so powerful that he did not need to offer anything for himself; rather, once the sacrifice of his flesh had been offered, it was sufficient for the salvation of all.

The statement of the oath, which came after the law, “the Son perfected forever,” is understood to show—or to establish—a perfect priest, not weighed down by weakness, as the law established its priests. After the law, God the Father addressed David concerning Christ with an oath, saying: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” and so forth. Here he adds the name “Son” to distinguish him from the servants who were under the law. Those servants were weak, either because they were sinners or because they were mortal; but he shows the Son to be perfect because he lives forever and is forever without sin.

## CHAPTER VIII

“The chief point concerning the things being discussed” means a recapitulation of what has been said about Christ. By this statement he indicates something supreme and great, and, as though recapitulating the preceding discussion, brings the hearer to the subject itself.

“We have such a high priest”—that is, such as we said above: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and such as we are still going to describe in what follows—“who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens, a minister of the saints and of the true tabernacle which God established, not man.”

We should understand the “throne of majesty in the heavens” as the fullness of the Father’s majesty, in which the Son of God sits; this is also signified by the right hand. We must not understand this childishly, as though God the Father had a right or left hand. He is spirit and fills all things. Nor should we imagine that the Son sits at his right hand in the way that a son usually sits beside his father, a king. Rather, as we have said, by the right hand we should understand the fullness of majesty and the highest glory of blessedness and prosperity, in which the Son of God sits. The Son’s sitting is used here in the sense of dwelling.

Our high priest, then, who has taken his seat in the highest glory of the Father’s majesty, is a minister of the holy places in the heavens. This can be understood in two ways. When the Lord came into the world and manifested himself through the incarnation, he ministered to the holy apostles, to the other faithful, and also to those who would come afterward, the bread of refreshment—that is, spiritual teaching—and the drink of evangelical doctrine, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37), and: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

He also ministered to them the instruction of faith and the grace of baptism, and, beyond this, the greater sacrament of redemption through his passion and the knowledge of the mysteries contained in the law and the prophets. Later, through his ascension, he ministered to us access to the heavenly homeland. This is what he ministered to his elect when he appeared in the world.

It may also be said in another way: he will be the minister of the saints in the future, when he will minister himself to them, so that they may know him with the Father and the Holy Spirit as he is—namely, when he has handed over his kingdom to God the Father. Hence, speaking of himself in the Gospel under the figure of a householder, he says: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline at table, and, passing by, minister to them” (Luke 12:37).

He is said to “pass by” because he will cause his elect to pass from judgment into the kingdom, or from contemplation of his humanity to knowledge of his divinity. He will minister to them when he shows them himself and the Father with the Holy Spirit. For their food and life will be the vision of the holy Trinity, as he himself says to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they may know you with the Holy Spirit, and Jesus Christ whom you sent, one and true God.”

He is also the minister of the true tabernacle, which God established or constructed, not man—that is, of heaven, which he himself administers to us so that we may be illumined by the radiance of its stars. The tabernacle that Bezalel constructed in the desert, or the one that Solomon made in the Promised Land, was not true, because it was consumed by decay and age and could not endure forever. Therefore he calls heaven the true tabernacle, since it will stand forever and will not be consumed by any decay.

The statement may also be understood in a higher sense, so that the true tabernacle means the souls of the righteous, to whom the Son of God himself ministers the joys of the heavenly homeland and in whom he deigns to dwell, according to what is said through the prophet: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6:16). And the Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:17). And again: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts, and therefore this one too must have something to offer. He cannot be a priest unless he has something to offer. The ancient high priests, according to the commandment of the law, offered gifts and sacrifices for their own sins and for those of the people.

But Christ, since in the eternal nature of his divinity he had nothing to offer, took from us what he might offer for us—that is, human flesh, namely himself, whom he offered upon the altar of the cross. What, then, is so suitable for sacrifice as rational flesh for rational humanity? And what is so pure to offer for the impure as flesh without any stain?

Since four things must be considered in every sacrifice—namely, to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—we can also find all four here with considerable elegance. Since sacrifice is owed to no one but the true God alone, our high priest offered a pure victim to God the Father for us, being himself both priest and sacrifice. He also offers to God the Father an acceptable sacrifice through his Church. For while we offer the sacraments of his body, he is the one who offers.

If he were on earth—that is, an earthly priest according to the order of Aaron and not a priest according to the order of Melchizedek—he would not be a priest, since there were priests of Levitical descent offering gifts according to the law, who serve as a copy and shadow of the heavenly realities, as Moses was told when he had completed and finished the tabernacle of the testimony.

If there were on earth an earthly high priest, such as Aaron, or someone immortal and without sin according to his order, who could cleanse the human race through his sacrifices and make it perfect, then there would certainly not be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek forever, because those who offered the legal gifts would be sufficient. But because Aaron and his sons were mortal and sinful, and therefore could not make the human race perfect, Christ came without sin. He was to hold his priesthood forever and, through his sacrifice, cleanse the human race most perfectly—not like those who serve as a copy and shadow of the heavenly realities.

A copy is a figure and likeness by which something else is displayed, just as an image expressed on a wall is a copy and figure of a true human being. The Jewish priests, therefore, served as a copy—that is, as a figure and shadow—of the heavenly mysteries, because all those things were likenesses and figures of what is now enacted in the Church in reality.

By “heavenly realities” he means spiritual mysteries, which in truth lead those who observe them to heavenly things. Is not our faith a heavenly altar, on which we offer our prayers to God every day?

“See,” he says, “that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.” Since our hearing seems less suited to receiving instruction than our sight—for we do not impress upon the mind what we hear as readily as what we perceive with our own eyes—the Lord showed Moses the tabernacle on the mountain not only through hearing but also through sight, the tabernacle that he was to make with Bezalel’s assistance. Hence he says to him: “See that you make everything according to the likeness that was shown to you on the mountain.” What he says is to be understood both of the construction of the tabernacle and its vessels, and of the sacrifices and victims that they were to offer there.

But now he has obtained a better ministry, namely, the dignity of the priesthood, just as he is also the mediator of a better covenant, which has been sanctioned—that is, confirmed, established, and strengthened—by better promises.

“Do you see,” he says, “how much better this observance is than the one that was practiced at that time?” For the former was a copy and figure, whereas this is the reality, as it is said in the Gospel: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Now—that is, in this final age of the world—Christ has obtained a much better priestly ministry than the legal one, just as he is also the mediator of a better covenant. As heavenly things are better than earthly things, and eternal things better than temporal things, so Jesus is the giver and mediator of a better covenant, and this covenant has been confirmed by better promises.

The Old Testament promised earthly and temporal things, saying: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1:19). And: “Observe what I have commanded you, so that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Exodus 20:12), along with other similar promises of temporal and earthly things.

But the New Testament, given through Christ, promises and grants heavenly and eternal things, as well as perfect life through the grace of baptism and faith in the Lord’s passion—namely, the remission of all sins. For the evangelist says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3:2). And: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16). And: “The elect will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Mark 12:25). Beyond this, and greater still, is what is said in the Gospel of John: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 11:12).

Behold how Christ is the mediator and giver of the better covenant, and how it has been confirmed by better promises. He has also obtained a better priesthood because the former was temporal, whereas this is eternal. The former could neither justify a human being nor open the kingdom of heaven to those who observed it; but this one justifies a human being perfectly and immediately opens the kingdom of heaven to him.

The Lord is called the mediator of the covenant because, just as Moses was a mediator between God and the people, conveying God’s words to the people and those of the people back to God, so Christ conveyed to us the words of God the Father and conveys ours back to God.

The Apostle passes from priest and sacrifice and then finally distinguishes the covenants, saying: “For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second covenant.” That is, if another covenant of the law could remove sins, so that those who observed it would be blameless, there would now be no search for a place for a second covenant.

But because the former was not perfect, once it had been removed, a suitable place was found for the second covenant. Thus, finding fault with them—that is, not judging them worthy of praise—he says through the prophet:

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah; not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not remain in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord God.”

“Behold, the days of the New Testament and of the final age of the world will come,” says the Lord, “and I will complete”—that is, perfect—“a New Testament over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah.”

In the literal sense, the house of Israel signifies the ten tribes that separated themselves from the house of David in the time of Jeroboam. The house of Judah signifies the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, together with the priestly tribe, which remained attached to the house of David.

In a higher sense, however, by both houses we should understand all believers, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles. By rightly confessing God—*Judas* meaning “one who confesses”—they are true Israelites, that is, those who see God with the mind. To them the Lord perfected and completed the New Testament, namely, the grace of the Gospel.

It is called the New Testament in distinction from the Old. To speak more profoundly, the Old Testament is so called because it was unable to make new the human being who remained in the oldness of sin. The New Testament, however, is so called because it makes the old human being new in baptism through faith in the Lord’s passion—the old human being stained by the sin of the old Adam. It is unlike the Old Testament that he made with their fathers: the former promised earthly and temporal things and commanded carnal observances; the latter promises eternal and heavenly things and commands spiritual ones.

When he says, “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jeremiah 31:32), almighty God displays the great intimacy that he showed that people. The divine speech speaks in the manner of women, who customarily take little children by the hand, sometimes leading them along and sometimes supporting them here and there so that they do not fall, since they do not yet have steady steps.

When the almighty God saw that the people were childish and small—for they had neither the steps of good works nor the strength by which they could free themselves from the yoke of their oppressors—he extended his hand to them, offering the great assistance of his mercy. He drew them out of the iron furnace, leading them to the knowledge of himself, and loving them even more with the greatest affection. At the same time, he led them through the wilderness and brought them into a land better than all others.

But because they did not remain in his covenant—that is, because they did not observe what he had commanded in his covenant—he neglected them. This means that he left them to go according to the desires of their hearts, as the Psalmist says (Psalm 80:13).

It should be noted that when the divine word had said, “I will complete a new covenant, not like the one that I made with their fathers,” lest the Jews perhaps argue loudly that the covenant of which God said to Abraham, “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Genesis 26:4), was to be destroyed, it clearly explained which covenant it meant when it added: “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.”

For he said this about the law, which was given on Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day after their departure from the land of Egypt. Their fathers did not remain in it, but made a cast idol—the calf—at Horeb and worshiped it. But the covenant he made with Abraham was fulfilled in Christ, in whom all the nations will be blessed.

“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel”—that is, with believers—“after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws into their mind, and upon their hearts I will write them; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And no one will teach his neighbor, nor each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all will know me, from the greatest to the least of them, because I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”

There is a great difference between law and law, between writing and writing, between teachers of the law and teachers of the Gospel, and between the letter and the grace of spiritual understanding. The letter of the law was written on tablets of stone, but the grace of spiritual understanding was given to the faithful through the Holy Spirit, through whom God’s love has been poured into the hearts of believers.

What he says—“I will give my laws into their mind, and upon their hearts I will write them”—applies especially to the holy apostles. They did not have the grace of the New Testament written on tablets of stone or on parchment, but divinely engraved in their minds and hearts.

First, before the Lord’s passion, when, as Matthew relates, he ascended the mountain and there delivered to them that lengthy discourse in which the instruction of the whole perfect life is contained. Second, after his resurrection, when, as Luke testifies, “he opened their understanding so that they might comprehend all that had been written about him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:45). Then, on the tenth day after his ascension, when the Holy Spirit came upon them in tongues of fire, he revealed to them everything that mortals needed to know about God.

For how could the evangelists have written down so many miracles and heavenly words after his ascension unless they had them divinely engraved on the tablets of their hearts? This applies especially to the blessed John, who wrote the Gospel in the sixty-fifth year after the Lord’s ascension. How could he have expressed so much about Christ’s divinity—especially what the Lord himself had spoken to them on the night when he was arrested—unless he had received it in this way?

We have what they left to us written partly in our hearts, but more fully on parchment, so that by meditating on it we may exercise ourselves.

What follows—“No one will teach his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’”—does not refer to the present time, when we teach one another. Rather, as the blessed Augustine says, while the prophet Jeremiah was speaking about the Lord’s first coming, he suddenly turned the eye of his mind toward the second coming, when no one will teach his neighbor to know God, because the elect, placed in his contemplation, will see and know him as he is.

For in the present, as we have said, we teach one another. At that time also he will no longer remember their sins, because all, stripped of every remnant of mortality and bodily corruption, of mutability and sin, and endowed with the glory of the resurrection, will shine like the angels of God in heaven.

By saying “new,” he made the former obsolete. The Apostle, taking confidence and authority from the prophetic words—“I will complete a New Testament over the house of Israel”—shows more clearly that the former covenant is already destined to end. By saying, “I will complete a New Testament,” he shows that what existed previously is being reduced to old age, or made obsolete. Hence he adds: “But what is becoming obsolete and growing old is near destruction.”

It is as though he were saying: Since the divine word, by declaring that a New Testament would come and that the former was old, makes it understood that, if the former covenant is becoming ancient and obsolete, it is near its end and will soon perish.

This is to be understood not of the precepts of life and conduct, in which the law remains in agreement with the Gospel, but of the commandments concerning carnal sacrifices, in which the law was to reach its end when Christ, whom those sacrifices prefigured, arrived.

## CHAPTER IX

The former covenant indeed had ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary. The former covenant had ordinances of worship because, through divine worship, human beings were justified from lesser faults. It also had an earthly sanctuary, in which it received the people of the world—that is, Gentiles who passed over to Judaism. For it was open not only to Jews but also to Gentiles.

Thus he calls the place of the courts an earthly sanctuary, where the Gentiles stood to worship behind the Jews.

The first tabernacle was made, in which there were the lampstands and the table—understand, the table or the setting forth of the loaves—which is called holy. The Apostle is not here going to discuss the tabernacle that Moses made in the wilderness, where there was only one lampstand, but the temple that Solomon later built in Jerusalem, where there were several lampstands. Therefore the word “first” does not refer to time but rather to place.

The blessed Apostle divides Solomon’s temple into two tabernacles. He calls the first tabernacle that part of the temple where the lampstands and the table were located. Upon the table were placed twelve hot loaves, six on one side and six on the other, and above the loaves were two golden dishes full of incense, one on each side. They remained there from Sabbath to Sabbath. There was also a golden altar, where incense was offered morning and evening. With this part of the temple he includes the altar of burnt offering, which stood in the open air before the entrance of the Lord’s temple.

Into this tabernacle the priests and the other ministers were permitted to enter daily. The second tabernacle he wishes to be understood as the Holy of Holies, namely that part of the temple divided by a wall of twenty cubits and by a veil hanging before the wall. Inside it was Moses’ ark, containing the tablets of the law, a golden urn in which the manna was kept, and Aaron’s rod, which had blossomed.

The ark itself was made in a simple, rectangular form, and therefore above it was a golden slab called the mercy seat, because from there the Lord spoke to Moses and the priests. Above the ark were two cherubim, which overshadowed the mercy seat with their wings and, with their faces turned, looked upon the mercy seat.

No one dared enter this second tabernacle, that is, the Holy of Holies, except the high priest alone, once a year. Having taken blood in a vessel, he entered within to pray for the people, on the seventeenth day of the seventh month after the Passover festival. That day was called the Day of Atonement; on the following day came the festival of Tabernacles.

Spiritually, the first tabernacle, where the priests were permitted to enter, signifies the state of the present Church. There are several lampstands there, namely the holy preachers, who shine for themselves and for others through word and example. It may also signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which the hearts of the faithful who abide in the Church through faith are illumined.

The table signifies the divine Scripture, of which the Psalmist says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Psalm 22:5). The setting forth of the loaves upon the table signifies the understanding of sacred Scripture, by which the souls of the faithful are daily refreshed. We may also understand the bread as the body and blood of the Lord, which is consecrated in the Church.

After the veil, then, is the second tabernacle, understood as the Holy of Holies. It has a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold. In it was a golden urn containing the manna, Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant.

How and in what manner each of these was arranged has been explained somewhat earlier according to the literal sense; therefore let us examine the spiritual mysteries.

The veil behind which the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies was situated signifies heaven, because of its dignity, just as the Song of Songs does. Beyond it lie the inner regions of the heavenly homeland. When the veil was lifted, the high priest entered the Holy of Holies with blood to pray for the people. Likewise, our Lord, the high priest, with the blood of his passion, after completing that passion and opening heaven, entered the Holy of Holies, where he continually entreats God the Father for us.

In the Holy of Holies there was a censer because Christ remains in the hidden places of the heavenly homeland, through whom we direct our prayers to God the Father.

The ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold, is the flesh of our Lord and Savior, who is the author of both covenants. Within, he was full of divinity; outwardly, he shone with the power of miracles and heavenly words. Gold commonly signifies the brilliance of speech, as Wisdom says: “Desire wisdom as gold.”

The golden urn containing manna is Christ, in whom is the manna of divinity, who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41).

Aaron’s rod that had blossomed is the dignity of the priesthood, which always flowers in Christ; or it signifies imperial power.

The two tablets of the covenant in the ark are the two covenants abiding in Christ.

It follows: “Above them”—that is, above the ark—“were two cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat.” The two cherubim covering the ark, whose name is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” are the two covenants, in which there is the fullness of knowledge. They cover Christ, who is the propitiation for our sins, because he is hidden in the divine Scripture.

It is not now necessary to discuss one by one all the mysteries contained in these things. Perhaps he passed over them in silence because they required many words, or because his hearers were not yet capable of receiving everything.

Having thus arranged and ordered the things which we said were present both in the first tabernacle and in the second—that is, in the Holy of Holies—in the former tabernacle, namely, in that part of the temple in which the altar of incense stood, and before whose entrance there was also the altar of burnt offering, the priests continually entered, completing the duties of the sacrifices. This should not be understood to mean that they offered victims upon the altar of incense in the temple, or that they performed the sacrifices of victims there. Rather, by the duties of the sacrifices we may understand the incense, for the offering of which the priests always entered, morning and evening; or, after the sacrifice had been completed and perfected before the temple, at the altar of burnt offering, they always entered the temple with incense. It may also be understood in a third way: as we said above, when the altar of burnt offering is included together with the temple, and thus the whole is intended by reference to a part. Either interpretation, however, may be accepted as correct.

But into the second tabernacle once a year the high priest alone entered, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people. The second tabernacle, into which the high priest alone entered with blood, signifies the inner regions of the heavenly homeland. That high priest signifies Christ, who entered the Holy of Holies once, within the veil, after completing his Passion, so that he might now stand before the face of God, praying for us—not for his own sins, but for ours—unless perhaps he is said to pray for his own because of the communion which he has with his body, which is the Church. Hence, in his Passion, he says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation” (Psalm 21:1). For what are “the words of my sins” except those of his body, which we are? He himself committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22).

The Holy Spirit signified this: the way of the saints had not yet been disclosed. That is, by signifying this to Moses, the Holy Spirit indicated that Christ had not yet come, who would enter once, with the blood of his Passion, into the hidden places of heaven. It was as though he were saying in other words: The high priest entered the Holy of Holies alone, once, with blood, so that we might learn that the heavenly kingdom was still inaccessible to mortals until Christ came. When his Passion had been completed, he would open for us the entrance to the heavenly homeland by opening the veil—that is, heaven.

The way of entering the homeland of heaven had not yet been revealed, or the way of understanding had not yet been made clear, because people did not know what those mysteries signified. Nor should we think that we cannot enter where our high priest entered first. For he himself says to the Father: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24); and elsewhere: “Where I am, there my servant will be also” (John 12:26).

And because the temple was still standing when the Apostle said these things, and the legal offerings were still being presented there, although without purpose, he therefore added, saying: “While the former tabernacle still had its standing”—where “things” is understood—“it is a parable,” that is, a figure and likeness of the time that is coming or is now present. [Col. 0881C] For what was being done in the temple at that time was a figure and likeness of this truth, which is now fulfilled in the Church.

He continues: “According to which”—that is, according to the parable or figure—“gifts and sacrifices are offered,” still there by the priests, “which”—the gifts or sacrifices—“cannot perfect the one who serves according to conscience.” Conscience is called the knowledge of the heart, by which the human mind is understood. He says that those carnal gifts could not make the one serving under the Law perfect according to the perfection of the mind, because they could not justify the mind, since they did not remove the more serious sins. For the Law brought no one to perfection.

He then shows in what things the purification of the Law largely consisted, saying that it appeared to make the worshiper perfect only in foods and drinks, various baptisms, [Col. 0881D] and ordinances of the flesh, until the time of correction—that is, of improvement and amendment—when these ordinances of the flesh were imposed. These carnal ordinances concerning distinctions among foods and drinks, and concerning various baptisms or washings, were imposed until the time of the Lord’s coming, as were the other things performed symbolically. When the Lord came, however, they were corrected—that is, amended and transformed for the better.

For by the clean animals which the Law commanded to be eaten are signified clean works; by the unclean animals, unclean works are understood, from which one must abstain. By clean drinks, likewise, we should understand the teaching of ecclesiastical men; by unclean drinks, the teaching of heretics.

Concerning the baptisms of the Jews, the Gospel of Mark speaks more fully, where the Pharisees reproached the Lord and his disciples for eating with unwashed hands (Mark 7:2). All their washings are designated by the name “baptisms.” Sometimes they washed only their hands, sometimes their feet, and sometimes the whole body, whether they had touched something unclean or had approached a dead person.

But they wash their hands and their whole body in vain while they disdain to be washed in the Savior’s font. For when the prophet says: “Wash yourselves, be clean, and cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 1:16), they understood this only in a carnal manner, whereas it was spoken rather of the washing of Christ’s baptism and of purity of works. All these practices were imposed until the time of correction—that is, until the time of the Lord’s coming. Afterwards Christ changed them for the better, because while they were observed carnally they fulfilled bodily cleanliness, but when they began to be observed spiritually they likewise began to produce purity of soul.

Christ, however, being present as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands—that is, not of this creation. The Jewish high priest, who entered once a year with blood within the veil into the Holy of Holies to pray for the people, signified Christ, as has already been explained in many places. Christ, with the blood of his Passion and with heaven opened, entered the hidden places of the heavenly homeland, [Col. 0882C] where he now stands before the face of God the Father, praying for us.

He is called “high priest of the good things to come” in two ways. The future good things which he himself administered to us were the heavenly words, his Passion, resurrection, baptism, remission of sins, and complete justification. They were called future good things either because they had been prefigured in mysteries or because they had been foretold in the divine oracles. In a higher sense, however, we can understand the future good things as the joys of the heavenly homeland, which have been administered to us through Christ.

Thus he is also called high priest because, by ascending, he displayed to us the power—that is, the way of righteousness and the way to the heavenly homeland. Another translation has: “Christ, having come, the high priest of the good things to come.” For if he had not come, he would in no way have administered these future good things to us, nor would he stand before the face of God the Father for us.

It should be noted that the Apostle did not simply say that he stands before God, but that he does so “through the tabernacle,” also using the comparative degree when he says: “Through the greater and more perfect.” The tabernacle through which he stands before God the Father is his humanity, since, unless he had become man, he could in no way stand before God the Father.

The tabernacle of the Lord’s body is therefore greater than the tabernacle of Moses and also than Solomon’s tabernacle, because those were made by the hands of carnal men, whereas this was formed within the Virgin’s womb, without male seed, by the work of the whole Trinity. Or it is greater and larger than those tabernacles because the divinity of the Word, which cannot wholly be contained in a tabernacle made by hands, dwells most fully in that man.

It is more perfect, or holier, than those tabernacles because neither of them could sanctify or make perfect those who ministered in them, whereas this tabernacle can both cleanse from sins and make perfect those who approach it. When he said “not made by hands,” he himself explained it by adding: “That is, not of this creation, of which we are,” because it was not formed from male seed. This is the stone which Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands—that is, born from the Jewish people without male seed and without male intercourse.

Nor by the blood of goats or calves, but by his own blood, he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption—not with the blood of legal animals, by which perfect justification could not be given, but with the blood of his Passion he entered the heavenly homeland. By that blood all were redeemed and perfectly justified, not with a temporal but with an eternal redemption.

Concerning this redemption, Zechariah, the father of blessed John, says: “He has visited us and accomplished the redemption of his people” (Luke 1). Redemption pertains to captives, and we were captives, having been taken captive by the devil in our first parent.

For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the unclean, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ—who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God—cleanse our conscience from dead works, so that we may serve the living God?

If the blood of irrational animals could cleanse our conscience according to the flesh, and if, as it appeared at that time, someone who was unclean was sanctified when sprinkled with that blood, much more could the blood of Christ cleanse our soul and justify it most fully. But lest anyone think that complete justification and cleansing resulted from the sprinkling of that legal blood, the Apostle added that the purification of the flesh was given through it according to the Law. It was as though he said: The flesh is indeed sanctified and cleansed because of the commandment of the Law, but the soul is nevertheless not purified.

He also added the reason for the distinction, by which he showed that the blood of those animals was not unblemished, when he said of Christ: “Who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God.” The Holy Spirit, who filled that man in the virginal womb, preserved him so that he might pass from this world without sin and be an unblemished sacrifice, a pleasing fragrance to God the Father.

“He will cleanse our conscience,” that is, our mind, “from dead works.” Dead works are sins, which kill the soul. For just as the soul lives by virtues, which are called works of life, so it dies through vices and sins and is drawn at the same time toward the death of eternal destruction.

And he rightly said “from dead works.” If someone in the Law touched a dead person, he was defiled, yet he was afterwards cleansed by the sprinkling of blood. Likewise, one who imitates the work of a dead soul is defiled, yet is cleansed through faith in the Lord’s Passion. “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it”; nevertheless, he will be cleansed through faith in the Lord’s Passion—that is, if someone has been washed from dead works through repentance and the grace of baptism, but touches them again, he will be contaminated.

He continues: “To serve the living God.” Here it is shown most clearly that those who have dead works cannot serve the living and true God, because they themselves are dead and false. If someone who touched a dead person or anything unclean was not permitted to enter the temple, how much less can someone who has dead works enter heaven?

And therefore he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, with death intervening—that is, taking place—for the redemption of the transgressions committed under the former testament, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene or take place. A testament is confirmed upon the dead; otherwise—that is, in another condition—it cannot yet be valid and firm while the one who made the testament is alive.

Here the Apostle appears to touch upon human laws, according to which a testament that one person makes to another concerning his inheritance is ordinarily made ineffective until the maker of the testament departs through death. But when that testator who made the testament has died, it remains entirely firm.

In the same way, the testament of eternal life which we have received from Christ could not otherwise remain firm for us unless he strengthened it by his death. Our sin was so great that we could not otherwise be redeemed and saved unless the only-begotten Son of God died for us. And because we were unworthy to attain what he had promised, he became our mediator through his death, so that by his undeserved death he might take away from us the death which was owed to us.

And because many less perfect people might perhaps doubt the Lord’s promises, especially because he died as though he were weak, blessed the Apostle sets forth examples from the common practice of human laws. He shows that testaments are made firm and receive their force not while testators live, but when they die. For as long as the testator lives, he can change his decision and bring other heirs, one after another, into his inheritance.

Therefore, wishing the testament which Christ left us to be firm, the Apostle says: “For this reason Christ is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, with his death intervening for the redemption of those transgressions which could not be taken away or erased under the former testament, but which were erased through his Passion, those who have been called with an eternal calling may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.”

For here he is not speaking of the general calling about which the Lord says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20), but of that calling concerning which the same outstanding preacher speaks of God’s elect, whom he foreknew: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined; those whom he predestined he also called; those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified.”

In part, we already possess in the present age the title to the eternal inheritance, given to us by the Lord—namely, his Gospel, which causes those who observe it to live eternally with God, supplying the grace of the Holy Spirit, the remission of sins, knowledge of him, and the peace which he left us when he went to his Passion. “Peace,” he says, “I leave you” (John 14).

We have this title to the inheritance in the present as a kind of pledge, but it will be supplied to us more perfectly when God is all in all, when Christ has handed the kingdom over to God the Father, and when we have been brought to the joys of the heavenly homeland. There the elect will be like the angels of God in heaven, seeing God as he is. This will be the perfect inheritance of the elect, which Christ confirmed by his death.

[Col. 0885B] Therefore—that is, because a testament is confirmed upon the dead—even the first testament was not dedicated, that is, confirmed and consecrated, without blood.

For when every commandment of the Law had been read aloud by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying:

All these things were done symbolically. For that calf, which was generally the priest’s sacrifice, signified Christ, who, being the true priest, offered the calf—that is, himself—to God the Father upon the altar of the cross. This is the calf which the gracious father slaughtered for the return of the prodigal son.

The goat, too, which was offered for sin, signified the same Christ, who was offered for sinners, according to what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “God the Father made him who knew no sin to be sin for us”—that is, a sacrifice for sin.

The fact that the Old Testament was sprinkled with blood for confirmation, and likewise the people, symbolically signified that the New Testament would be confirmed by the blood of Christ’s Passion and that the believing people would be cleansed. The water with which the people were sprinkled is the water of baptism, with which the faithful are drenched.

The scarlet wool signifies the charity of Christ, who suffered for us, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world.” Hyssop is a humble herb growing on a rock, by which Christ’s humility and the strength through which our inward parts are cleansed are signified. For by the kind of herb that hyssop is, diseases of the lungs are customarily cleansed. Hyssop may also signify repentance, which, when earnestly carried out, cleanses the inner vices of the mind.

“This is the blood of the testament which God commanded for you”—as though he were saying: This is the confirmation of the testament which God commanded for you. This blood prefigured the blood which flowed from Christ’s side on the cross. With this blood Christ sprinkled us and confirmed his testament, as he himself said: “This is the blood of the New Testament, for the remission of sins” (Mark 14).

He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the mystery with blood. By the tabernacle are to be understood those of whom God speaks through the prophet, saying: “I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them.” Concerning them the Apostle also says elsewhere: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

The various vessels are the faithful in the Church, possessing different ministries. Some are vessels of preaching, such as the Apostle, concerning whom the Lord says to Ananias: “This man is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9). Others possess different ranks and various ministries, which the same outstanding preacher recalls, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another the grace of healings,” and others possess various gifts, which the Holy Spirit distributes to each one as he wills (1 Corinthians 12).

The tabernacle, therefore, and all its vessels are sprinkled with that blood, because the universal Church, together with all those who minister within it, is cleansed by the blood of Christ’s Passion.

He continues: “And almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the Law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.” Why did he say that almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the Law? Because their cleansing and remission were not perfect. Their bodies, insofar as the Law was concerned, were cleansed by the sprinkling or shedding of the blood of animals, and lesser sins were forgiven. But because that blood did not remove greater crimes or make a person perfect, the cleansing was not complete.

Perfect cleansing and remission consist in the blood of Christ, which was poured out for us for the remission of sins. Without the shedding of that blood no one is redeemed.

It is therefore necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed by these sacrifices and sprinklings. But the heavenly things themselves are cleansed by better sacrifices than these. He calls the legal sacrifices “copies,” that is, figures and likenesses. But the things now celebrated in truth in the Church he calls “heavenly,” that is, spiritual, because they are spiritual and are to be performed spiritually; or heavenly because they lead those who celebrate them in truth to heavenly things.

The copies of the heavenly mysteries and realities, which were enacted symbolically in the Law as figures of those things now fulfilled in the Church, necessarily had to be cleansed by such symbolic sacrifices and figurative sprinklings, because the true or heavenly things—that is, the spiritual things now celebrated in truth in the Church—were not yet possessed. These are cleansed by better sacrifices than the legal ones, namely, by the blood of Christ’s Passion.

Since true sacrifices were sought by which people could be perfectly cleansed, but were not found, it was necessary for those former sacrifices to remain until the true ones came.

For Jesus did not enter into holy places made by hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us. “Jesus did not enter,” he says, “into holy places made by hands”—where “holy places” means those which are copies of the true ones.

He calls the Holy of Holies “made by hands,” since it was first made by the hands of Bezalel in the wilderness and afterwards likewise by the hands of craftsmen in Solomon’s temple. Jesus did not enter that place, but heaven itself, which was not made by human hands, but extended by the command and will of the Word of God. [Col. 0887A]

Those former things, therefore, were copies and figures of the true things, because these are the true realities. The Holy of Holies prefigured the heavenly realities into which Christ entered once.

We say that Jesus entered according to what he is as man. According to what he is as God, he is everywhere and fills all things. He did not enter into things made by human hands, but into heaven itself, created by God’s command.

Nor did he set forth only this distinction, but also something concerning the high priest—“the high priest, the nearest first maker” (*pontificem proximum primum factorem*; the transmitted reading is materially uncertain)—when he says, “so that he may now appear before the face of God for us,” that is, so that he may present himself to the Father’s power and make him favorable toward us. Hence John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (John 2).

Nor did he enter in order to offer himself often, as the high priest enters the Holy of Holies every year with another’s blood; otherwise he would have had to suffer frequently from the beginning of the world. Christ did not enter the Holy of Holies for the purpose of offering himself repeatedly, as the Jewish high priest entered the Holy of Holies every year, nor did he enter with another’s blood, but with his own. For he who is both priest and sacrifice offered himself once upon the altar of the cross. Having risen from the dead, he now dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6). It is not necessary for him to die again, since his one Passion is sufficient for the salvation of all believers.

Otherwise—that is, if it were otherwise, and his having suffered once did not benefit everyone—it would have been necessary for him to be crucified repeatedly from the beginning of the world. That is, for as many elect there were and as many would come in the future, he would have had to die for each one if he wished to redeem them. But he willed to die only once, because redemption was accomplished through his one death.

Now, however, once, at the consummation—that is, at the end of the ages, in the final age—he appeared for the destruction of sin through his sacrifice, that is, through his body, which he made a sacrifice for sin. “Once,” he says, “at the end of the ages he appeared for this purpose: to destroy sin through his sacrifice.”

He rightly appeared then, when sins were abundant, in order to display the riches of his grace. For if this had happened at the beginning, perhaps no one would have believed it—and it happened once, at the consummation of the ages, through his own blood, not another’s.

And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this comes judgment, so Christ was offered once [Col. 0887D] to take away the sins of many; he will appear a second time, without sin, to those who await him for salvation.

Just as it has been appointed and decreed for human beings that they cannot die except once, and afterwards they receive judgment—that is, according to what each person has done in the body, whether good or evil—so Christ was offered once by himself to take away the sins of many. He cannot die again, nor do we need him to do so.

It should be noted that he was offered to take away the sins of many, not of all, because not all will believe. The Lord himself says something similar to the Apostles: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26).

What follows—“he will appear a second time, without sin, to those who await him for salvation”—has this meaning, as though he were saying: First he appeared through his sacrifice, that is, through his mortal body, which was a sacrifice for sin; but the second time he will appear without a sacrifice for sin, because there will no longer be a sacrifice for sin, as there was before. For he will not be able to die thereafter.

Just as each of us receives after death according to our works, so Christ, having conquered death and obtained the kingdom, will appear a second time to those who await him for salvation, in order justly to avenge his own, even as he justly suffered at the hands of others.

This appearance to those who await him for salvation is better than the general vision concerning which it is said: “Every eye will see him, and those who pierced him” (Revelation 1). To appear a second time without sin therefore means that he will no longer be seen in the likeness of sinful flesh, nor bearing the sins of others in his body upon the wood, as he did at his first coming. Nor will he intercede any longer for sins, but will exercise vengeance upon sinners.

## CHAPTER 10

For the Law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer continually year after year, make those who approach perfect.

The order of the words is: The Law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities, can never make those who approach it perfect by the same sacrifices which they continually offer year after year.

The future good things are to be understood in two ways: either as the sacraments which have been fulfilled in truth in Christ and in the Church—things which were future, awaiting their coming—or as the joys of the heavenly homeland.

He calls it a “shadow” because it is a figure and likeness, while he uses “image” for the truth. In many ways, therefore, the Law displayed the sacraments of Christ and the Church through figures, until Christ, the Truth itself, came. By giving the grace of the Holy Spirit to his Church, he disclosed the inner meaning of that same figure, and by dying on the cross he revealed all those sacraments at once.

But the Law could never perfectly cleanse those who approached it by the same sacrifices which the priests themselves continually offered every year. Every year they offered the same irrational victims—rams, oxen, goats, turtledoves, and pigeons.

He continues: “Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer have had any consciousness of sin. But in them there is a remembrance of sins every year.”

“Otherwise”—that is, if they had been freed from all sins, those sacrifices would have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer have had any consciousness, that is, memory and recollection, of the sins from which they had been cleansed once for all.

But because this could not happen, and because greater and criminal sins could never be cleansed by those sacrifices, a remembrance of sins is made every year in those sacrifices. For example, if someone had offered a sacrifice for adultery, sacrilege, or parricide in the present year, it was necessary for him to do so every year, since he could not be perfectly cleansed from that offense.

Accordingly, what took place was an accusation of sins, not their removal; an accusation of weakness, not a display of strength. In the fact that the sacrifices were always offered there was a condemnation of sins; in the fact that they were always necessary there was a condemnation of the weakness of that same sacrifice.

For this reason, he says, they were always commanded to be offered: because they could not cleanse perfectly, and so that a remembrance and condemnation of sins might be made.

What then should we say? Do not our priests also do the same thing every day when they continually offer the sacrifice? They do offer it, but they do so in remembrance of his death. And because we sin every day, we need to be cleansed every day.

And because he can no longer die, he gave us this sacrament of his body and blood, so that just as his Passion was the redemption and cleansing of the world, so also this offering might be redemption and cleansing for all who offer it in your faith and with a good intention.

In this respect our sacrifice differs from that former sacrifice, which was repeatedly offered, although ours too is repeated: ours is the truth, whereas that was a figure; ours makes a person perfect, whereas that did not; and ours is not repeated because of its weakness, as though it were unable to confer perfect salvation, but in remembrance of Christ’s Passion, as he himself said: “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 24). And this is one sacrifice, not many, as those sacrifices were.

How is it one and not many, when it is offered by many people, in many different places and at different times? We must therefore observe most carefully that the divinity of the Word of God, which is one, fills all things, and is wholly everywhere. It makes there be not many sacrifices but one sacrifice, although it is offered by many, so that there is one body of Christ together with that body which he assumed in the virginal womb, not many bodies.

Now we offer one thing greater and another less, one today and another tomorrow; but each has the same magnitude. Accordingly, this is one sacrifice of Christ, not different sacrifices as theirs were.

For if it were otherwise, since it is offered in many places, there would be many Christs. Therefore Christ is one everywhere: here he is present in fullness, and there he is present in fullness, possessing one body everywhere. And just as the one who is offered everywhere is one body, not many bodies, so also there is one sacrifice.

He continues: “For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.” What reason could there be for a rational human being to be cleansed by the blood of an irrational animal? Therefore, even if lesser sins were purified through those sacrifices, and the body was cleansed insofar as the Law was concerned, nevertheless it was impossible for criminal and more serious sins to be cleansed through those sacrifices.

Hence the Law brought no one to perfection.

Therefore, on entering the world he says:

> “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared a body for me. You took no pleasure in burnt offerings for sin; then I said, ‘Behold, I come. In the heading of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will, O God.’”

By these words the earlier sacrifices are shown to have been useless for complete and perfect [Col. 0890A] cleansing, and to have been rather a type; nor were they acceptable to God, since from the beginning he took no pleasure in them. We must not suppose that almighty God was ever delighted by the smell of flesh and the burning of animals, although he is read to have smelled “the fragrance of sweetness”; rather, he was pleased by the faith and desire of the one offering. Hence through Jeremiah he says:

> “Your burnt offerings are not acceptable to me, and your sacrifices have not pleased me” (Jer. VI);

and through Isaiah:

> “Do not offer sacrifice to me any longer,” he says; “incense is an abomination to me. Whoever slaughters an ox is like one who brains a dog” (Isa. I; LXVI).

From this a considerable question may arise: why did he command that they be offered, if they did not please him and were not his will? This can be resolved in two ways.

Almighty God, observing [Col. 0890B] that the minds of the Jews were inclined to worship idols and imitate the rites of the nations, commanded them to offer many and burdensome sacrifices, lest, sitting idle without sacrifices, they should fall into the worship of foreign gods when they saw others offering to them. He preferred that what he himself had created should be offered to him rather than to idols and demonic monsters; and he imposed these sacrifices upon them as a form of servitude, not of justification, since it is not his will that such things be offered.

In the same way the excellent preacher, following the Creator as a creature, acted in his own statements, saying:

> “I want all people to be as I myself am” (1 Cor. VII),

that is, chaste and continent; and again:

> “I want young men to marry and bear children” (1 Tim. V),

because of fornication and adultery. Behold, he established two wills, yet both are not his will. In the first statement, “I want all people [Col. 0890C] to live in continence as I myself do,” he expressed his own will. In the second, “I want young men to marry,” he spoke in this way because of necessity, on account of the frailty of the flesh. Similarly, it was not the will of almighty God that such sacrifices should be offered, but he commanded them because of their lowly condition.

Hence above he said that he not only did not desire them, but did not even wish for them. The matter can also be explained in this way: since the true sacrifice through Christ in the Church was destined to come, he commanded typological and figurative sacrifices to precede it. Indeed, it was necessary that, just as it was foretold in words, so it should also be prefigured through mysteries, so that they might pass more quickly from the figure to the truth.

But because those sacrifices did not please him, he came again, concerning whom the Apostle says:

> “Therefore,” he says, “because it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of [Col. 0890D] goats” “and because such sacrifices did not please God, it is beyond doubt that Christ says, as he entered the world: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared, or perfected, a body for me: I shall offer you that acceptable sacrifice. You took no pleasure in burnt offerings for sin; then I said, “Behold, I come,” through the mystery of the incarnation, so that by my sacrifice I might redeem the human race.’”

This entry signifies nothing other than his sending and his participation in humanity. For when he who was everywhere present, yet invisible, afterward became man, visible, and appeared to the world, he entered, in a certain sense, into the place where he was already present.

“Burnt offering” was so called because the whole offering was burned [Col. 0891A] upon the altar, as though wholly burned. For *holon* means “whole,” while *caustum* means “burned.”

But if burnt offerings for sin did not please him, one may ask how people were cleansed by them. The answer is that they were cleansed through faith and worthy repentance, just as David was cleansed from the sin of adultery and murder. Perfect cleansing, however, was given at Christ’s coming.

> “In the heading of the book it is written concerning me: ‘That I should do your will, O God.’”

The teachers dispute in various ways what is meant by the heading of this book. Some understand it as the beginning of Genesis (chap. I), where it is written that, “in the beginning”—that is, in the Son—God made heaven and earth. Others understand it as the first Psalm, which some refer to Christ and others to any chosen person, where it says:

> “His will is in the law [Col. 0891B] of the Lord” (Ps. I).

But since neither of these contains anything prefiguring Christ’s death, which is what the Apostle discusses throughout this passage, it seems better to understand this as referring to the beginning of the book of Leviticus. Since that book deals entirely with sacrifices and offerings, it first commanded a sacrifice from a calf, saying:

> “If anyone among you offers an offering to the Lord from the cattle, let him offer an unblemished male—that is, a calf from the herd, or from the cattle.”

This calf, taken from the herd and offered as a sacrifice, is Christ, born from the race of the patriarchs and sacrificed for the salvation of the human race.

Christ therefore says to the Father: “Because the sacrifices of irrational animals do not please you, since they cannot cleanse a human being perfectly, behold, I come into the world through [Col. 0891C] the mystery of the incarnation. For in the heading of the book of Leviticus it is written concerning me: ‘That I should do your will’; that is, that I should die for the salvation of the human race.”

For it was the will of God the Father that the Son should redeem the human race through his suffering. Hence the Son himself, approaching his passion, said:

> “But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do exactly as the Father commanded me. Rise, let us go from here to the passion” (John XIV).

Earlier he had said: “Because you did not desire sacrifices, offerings, or burnt offerings for sin, nor were the things offered according to the law pleasing to you, then I said, ‘Behold, I come to do, O God, your will.’” He takes away the first—that is, the former covenant, implied—by rejecting its offerings, in order to establish the succeeding covenant, that is, to make it stand and endure.

[Col. 0891D] In this will of God the Father, which the Son fulfilled, we have been sanctified in baptism through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. By saying “once,” he means as though he had said: “We have been sanctified in baptism through the passion which Christ underwent once for all.”

And every priest of the law stands ready at the altar, ministering daily and repeatedly offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins—namely, criminal and capital sins.

But this man, Christ, beyond doubt, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, thereafter awaiting the time when his enemies will be placed as a footstool beneath his feet.

To minister or to offer is a sign of ministry, by which [Col. 0892A] Christ’s humility is understood. To sit, however, is a sign of one who judges and rules, and of one to whom service is rendered; through this the exaltation and glory of the Son of God are shown. He appeared humble, but now, exalted above every creature, he dwells in the fullness of the Father’s majesty, awaiting and contemplating the remaining time when he will judge the world.

He explains the purpose of this subjection when he says:

> “So that his enemies may be placed as a footstool beneath his feet.”

His enemies are the Jews, heretics, false Christians, and all unbelievers, who must be subjected to his power. Here one may understand both a necessary subjection, belonging to the reprobate who persist in wickedness, and a voluntary subjection, belonging to the elect who abandon the way of wickedness and willingly submit themselves to Christ through faith.

Those Jewish priests, [Col. 0892B] by offering many sacrifices every day, could not take away sins; but Christ, offering himself once for all, took away the sins of the world and now sits in the glory of God the Father.

By one offering he perfected forever those who are sanctified; that is, by offering himself once, he made the sanctified perfect forever.

The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us. After he had said:

> “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will place my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds, and I will no longer remember their sins and iniquities,”

he says that the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; that is, by his testimony he confirms our words, not only through the Psalmist but also [Col. 0892C] through the prophet, that those sacrifices are no longer to be offered.

In the words that follow there is a necessary ellipsis in the sentence. It should therefore be understood in this way: after almighty God had said through the prophet Jeremiah:

> “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will place my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds,”

he immediately implied:

> “And I will no longer remember their sins,”

showing that figurative sacrifices would no longer be necessary. The Apostle also makes this clear when he adds:

> “But where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer a necessary offering for sin.”

For after the covenant that God had promised through the prophet was fulfilled, those sacrifices immediately came to an end, because when the truth arrived, the shadow departed.

It should be noted that where there is no remembrance of sins—which are forgiven in baptism through faith in the Lord’s passion—there is no longer any need for the offering of the law for sin.

[Col. 0892D] Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places through the blood of Christ, a new and living way has been opened for us through the veil—that is, through his flesh—and we have a great priest over the house of God.

Up to this point he has shown the distinction and great difference between the high priest and the sacrifices, as well as between the tabernacle, the covenant, and the promise. Now, by inviting us, he urges us to approach the things that have come to us in truth through Christ. He gives us assurance concerning the great high priest, [Col. 0893A] saying:

> “Therefore,” he says, “we have greater confidence that we are cleansed through the blood of Christ than those who offered bodily sacrifices, because our sacrifice is true and rational.”

We have confidence of entering heaven through Christ’s blood to the extent that we have become more fully coheirs. No one, however, can reach the gifts of the Holy Spirit except through faith or confidence—that is, through the new and living way which Christ opened for us. He gave us the beginning of using it.

By “new way” he means the new faith given through Christ, or the example of humility by which he himself proceeded, humbling himself even to death. We may also understand “new way” as the entrance to the heavenly homeland, opened for us through Christ. It is called new because previously it was traversable by no one. [Col. 0893B]

By calling it new, he endeavors to show that we possess all things greater and new. Now the way of faith has been opened to us, through which we receive the fullest justification, and the gates of heaven have been opened to us—something previously granted to no one.

He also called it living, that is, enduring forever or always remaining open, because true faith will remain eternally and the gate of heaven will always be open.

Christ opened this way for us—that is, he dedicated and confirmed it, or gave us the beginning of using it—through the veil, that is, through his flesh. He was the first to cut a path through it by ascending to the heavenly homeland, and it first gave us the beginning of using that way.

The Lord’s flesh is appropriately designated by the name “veil,” because [Col. 0893C] just as the veil concealed the ark and the things within it, so within Christ’s flesh the divinity of the Word of God lay hidden. And just as one reached the interior through the veil, so through humanity one reaches knowledge of divinity.

The great priest over the house of God is understood to be Christ, who was appointed by God the Father over the Church, in accordance with what he himself says:

> “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. II).

He continues:

> “Let us approach with a true heart in the fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.”

This depends upon what was said above, where the Apostle said: “Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places through the blood of Christ, let us approach him with a true heart.”

He explained what it means to approach Christ with a true heart by adding, [Col. 0893D] “in the fullness of faith,” so that we may believe that there will be a general resurrection. It is as though he said: “Now that we have confidence to enter the heavenly homeland, we must not hesitate over whether some will rise and others will not; rather, in true faith we must believe that all human beings will rise, some to glory and others to punishment.” For if anyone hesitates about this, he does not possess true and complete faith.

It may also be understood in another way: full faith is conceived in the heart, confessed with the mouth, and adorned with good works. Whoever wishes the entrance to the heavenly homeland to be opened to him must approach God with this faith.

It is also necessary that the heart be sprinkled clean from an evil conscience—that is, that we be cleansed inwardly, possessing hearts [Col. 0894A] purified from sins and evil will. At the same time he shows that not faith alone but also a life accompanied by virtues is required, since “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II).

The Jews cleansed their bodies; we cleanse the conscience.
