“And washed,” he says, “the body,” that is, possessing a body washed with pure water, namely, the water of baptism. He says that the body must be washed with baptismal water because, while the body is washed, the soul is sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering. For faithful is the one who promised.

We hold the confession of hope without wavering if we do not despair of the heavenly homeland and of all that the Lord has promised us, or if we firmly observe what we professed in baptism. For just as Christ is faithful and a true rewarder [Col. 0894B] in his promises, so he wishes us to be faithful in our promises, which we made at the time of baptism: namely, to renounce the devil and serve Christ.

Let us consider one another for the purpose of provoking love and good works. That is, let us carefully observe one another, and whenever we see someone possessing greater love and devoting himself to better works, let us be provoked by his example, so that we may imitate him earnestly, direct our attention toward him, and love him. For good works proceed from love.

Therefore love is a great good, and there is no good that is not accomplished through love, because love is the fullness of the law.

Let us not abandon our assembly—that is, the congregation [Col. 0894C] of the faithful—as is the custom of some, but let us encourage one another, as is implied.

In this passage he not only admonished but also blamed and frightened those who were splitting the unity of love. There were many who disturbed the congregation of the faithful, as though they could not live among the others because of their own holiness; they abandoned their assembly and lived alone, so that they might appear to devote themselves more freely to God. Such people, swollen with the arrogance of pride, despised the rest and disrupted love.

The Apostle both admonishes and frightens them concerning both matters, urging them not to abandon the fellowship of the faithful but rather to encourage the simpler members and strengthen them by their example. For if the fellowship of the faithful has such power that where two or three are gathered in the name of the Savior, he himself is in their midst, then Christ will be present all the more wherever more [Col. 0894D] of the faithful are gathered.

He continues: “And all the more”—always implying, “pursue love and encourage one another”—“as you see the day of judgment approaching,” on which the merits of each person will be examined, or even the final day of our life. For elsewhere he says:

> “Do not be anxious about anything; the Lord is near” (Phil. IV).

For if we sin voluntarily after receiving knowledge of the truth—that is, after receiving knowledge of the true faith and the grace of baptism—there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.

If we sin willingly and deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the true faith and after being cleansed in baptism, no sacrifice [Col. 0895A] for sin is reserved for us any longer, such as was granted under the old law, when sacrifices could be offered repeatedly for sins.

For Christ, who is our sacrifice, is not to be sacrificed again for our sins. This was done once and does not need to be done a second time. Rather, after receiving grace, we must remain in right faith and purity of good works.

You were cleansed in baptism; you were freed from crimes and every sin; you were made a son of God. If you return to your first vomit, an extremely severe judgment awaits you, as what follows makes clear, unless you are recalled through worthy repentance.

By these words he does not exclude repentance, nor the reconciliation that comes through the remedy of repentance; rather, he excludes [Col. 0895B] a second baptismal washing. He is not so hostile to our salvation as to say, “There is no repentance any longer, nor forgiveness of sins.” Instead he says, “There is no sacrifice any longer”—that is, there is no second cross, so that Christ might be crucified again and we might be baptized again.

For just as Christ died once and does not die again, so we, once baptized in faith in his death and burial, as the Apostle says elsewhere, having been buried with him through baptism into death, cannot be rebaptized.

There remains a certain terrifying expectation of judgment and the fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.

“Fury” is sometimes used for imitation and sometimes for envy; here it is understood as destruction and vengeance. The Apostle therefore terrifies everyone, so that after the washing of baptism they may fear falling back into vices, since they cannot [Col. 0895C] be rebaptized.

He also terrifies them so that, if they sin, they may immediately strive to perform worthy repentance, because whoever neglects the remedy of repentance will be devoured by the vengeance and consuming power of eternal fire. Therefore, while he has time, let each sinner flee to the remedy of repentance, lest he be handed over to eternal fire.

Anyone who makes the law of Moses void, after being convicted by two or three witnesses, dies without any mercy.

How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as profane the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?

The law is called the law of Moses either because it was given to the people through Moses or because it was given [Col. 0895D] to Moses by the Lord. In the same way we customarily say in the Lord’s Prayer to God:

> “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke XI),

not because it was ours beforehand, but because, when it is given by him, it becomes ours.

The Apostle strikes fear into Christians by drawing a comparison from the law of Moses. If anyone transgressed that law, making it void and ineffectual, and was convicted by two or three witnesses, he was judged by the authorities and immediately killed, without any mercy or pardon.

He therefore says: “If the one who transgressed the law given through a servant was killed without mercy, how much greater punishment will be endured by the one who has trampled upon the Son of God?” Insofar as Christ is greater than Moses, and the grace of the Gospel [Col. 0896A] given through the Son is greater than the law administered through a servant, so much greater punishment will be deserved by the one who has trampled upon Christ.

But how can we trample upon him who sits at the right hand of God the Father, exalted above all the heavens? When we regard his commandments as worthless and disdain to fulfill them, then indeed we trample upon him. For just as we regard as worthless the things we trample upon and assign them no honor, so those who sin freely, without fear and without repentance, trample upon Christ—or despise and scorn him—and have no fear of him as the future judge.

Or certainly anyone tramples upon Christ who receives his body unworthily.

Or, to state a third interpretation, he tramples upon Christ who by living badly drives him from the tabernacle of his heart—him who said:

> “I will dwell among them and [Col. 0896B] walk among them” (Lev. XXVI).

He also regards the blood of the covenant as profane—or, as it is found in Gregory, as common or unclean—who regards the blood of Christ’s passion as worthless, the blood by which the New Covenant was confirmed and by which he himself was sanctified at the time of baptism.

In another sense as well, to regard the blood of the covenant as profane is to receive the mystery of Christ’s blood unworthily and to make no distinction between it and other drinks, even though he was sanctified by it at the time of baptism and could also be sanctified by it daily if he received it worthily.

Of such people the Apostle says:

> “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. XI),

that is, not distinguishing them from other foods and drinks.

He also insults the Spirit of grace—that is, the Holy Spirit—by driving him out of the tabernacle of his heart through [Col. 0896C] evil living; or by refusing to believe that through him forgiveness of sins is effected in the Church; or certainly by blaspheming him, denying his works and attributing them to the devil.

Hence the Lord says:

> “Whoever blasphemes against the Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII).

He is called the Spirit of grace either because through him sins are freely forgiven us, or because, as he distributes them, the graces of spiritual gifts are divided among the faithful. The Apostle recalls these gifts, saying:

> “To one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge” (1 Cor. XII),

and so forth, until he concludes:

> “But all these things are accomplished by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (ibid.).

[Col. 0896D] For we know who said:

> “Vengeance belongs to me, and I will repay.”

Almighty God speaks through the Prophet:

> “I will render vengeance and repay those who inflict injury and insult upon me, according to what they deserve” (Deut. XXXII; Rom. XII).

And again:

> “For the Lord will judge his people.”

This was said concerning his enemies: “I will repay those who do evil,” not those who suffer evil; rather, it concerns those who live negligently and refuse to cleanse themselves through repentance, yet while doing evil approach the Lord’s table without fear.

The people whom the Lord is said to judge can be understood in two ways: the expression may refer to the chosen people or to the reprobate. For “the Lord will judge his people” means that he will separate his people and distinguish the good from the wicked, the faithful from the unfaithful.

If it is referred to the reprobate, however, [Col. 0897A] “to judge” must be understood as “to condemn.” They are called the Lord’s people not by grace but by creation.

It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

He falls into the Lord’s hands who trembles at human judgment but thinks little of God’s judgment. Whoever, after sinning, scorns the practice of repentance also falls into the Lord’s hands—that is, into the power and judgment of almighty God.

Therefore, whoever is a sinner, if he does not repent of his sins, will fall into the fearful and greatly dreaded judgment of almighty God, who will repay each person according to his works.

[Col. 0897B] But remember the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings.

The best physicians, when they have cut into a wound and increased the pain by their incision, apply comfort and a remedy to the place where the pain is present, and restore the disturbed spirit. Once they have revived the patient, they do not add another incision; indeed, they strive to soothe what has been cut with gentler and effective medicines.

In this passage the Apostle acted in the same manner. After shaking their minds and piercing them with the mention of Gehenna, affirming that those who in any way insult God’s grace would certainly perish, teaching this from the law of Moses and other testimonies, and saying that it was necessary to fear falling into the hands of the living God, he immediately [Col. 0897C] consoles them, lest they should fall into despair through excessive fear, with words of praise and exhortation, recalling their former good works to their memory.

“Remember,” he says, “the former days in which, enlightened through faith and strengthened by divine grace, you endured a great contest.” It is as though he said: “When you were introduced into the faith, when you were at the beginning of faith, you displayed such strength that you endured a great contest of sufferings for the name of Christ from your fellow countrymen.”

For some of the Jews who believed were stripped of their possessions by others who did not believe, while others were not. Those who had not been stripped supplied the needs of the others from their own resources. When the unbelievers learned of this, they inflicted many evils upon both groups.

Hence the Apostle did not [Col. 0897D] simply say that they had endured a contest, but added “great”; nor did he say “temptations,” but “sufferings.”

On the one hand, you were made a public spectacle through reproaches and tribulations, in fact or in deed; [Col. 0898A] on the other hand, you became companions of those who were treated in this way.

“On the one hand,” he says, “you were made a spectacle through reproaches”—that is, insults, mockery, or tribulations. This means that you were publicly ridiculed before many people. “On the other hand, you became companions in suffering with those who were treated in this way,” namely, the apostles and those who were stripped of their own possessions, afflicted with blows, and thrown into prison.

He shows in two ways that they labored well: either because they were publicly afflicted by various insults and tribulations—a form of suffering that the human race endures more severely when something disgraceful is inflicted before many people, whether in words or deeds—or because, when others were placed in prison, they shared their suffering and supplied them with food and clothing as far as they were able.

Thus they became their companions, because the reward and recompense that the preacher of truth, placed in prison and afflicted by other torments for Christ’s name, will receive, the person who provides him assistance so that he does not fail in his tribulations will receive as well, just as the Truth himself promised:

> “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X).

It should be noted that he did not simply say that they were afflicted by tribulations, but increased [Col. 0898B] the force of his statement by saying: “You were made a spectacle.” When someone is reproached secretly, he is indeed distressed, but much more so when it happens publicly and before many people. For the human race, just as it greatly delights in public praise, is easily captivated by reproaches openly inflicted upon it.

That they endured the things we have enumerated he now shows more clearly when he continues:

For you also had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions.

He praises them remarkably for their faith, because if they had not believed that they would receive better things in place of the possessions taken from them, they would not have accepted their seizure with joy.

As long as the promise was held out to them, they shared the suffering of those who had been stripped and those who had been placed in prison. Those who had themselves been stripped accepted the seizure and loss inflicted upon them with joy, believing that they would receive better things.

Hence he adds:

> “Knowing [Col. 0898C] that you have a better and enduring possession.”

It is as though he said: “Seeing that spiritual riches would benefit you in place of these temporal things, you endured with joy the seizure of your temporal possessions.”

All this was an apostolic deed, worthy of strong souls, so that they might rejoice in blows, as it is said in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “They went away from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

To show that this temporal possession would not endure forever, he therefore said that they possessed a better and enduring possession, as though referring to a substantial and perpetual form that cannot perish, unlike this earthly possession, which perishes.

Therefore, do not abandon your confidence, which [Col. 0898D] has a great reward. That is, do not fail in your tribulations, because the reward is great.

It is evident that they had great confidence in God, and he urges them most earnestly not to lose it. For what is preserved intact is more easily kept than what has been lost is recovered. Therefore, whatever is held and feared must possess strength.

“You have no need,” he says, “of anything except to stand firm in your faith and remain steadfast in your strength, which has a great reward with God.”

For you need endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise.

What great confidence in reward and consolation this is! It is as though someone were saying this to an athlete and contestant who had [Col. 0899A] overcome everyone and had no one left with whom to compete.

For example, if he were to say, “Now that I have overcome everyone and no one remains to compete with me, give me the crown,” someone might reply: “Wait a little until the judge comes, or even the king who will give you the prize for your victory.”

If the athlete bore this impatiently, unable to tolerate thirst and heat, saying, “Either give me what I have earned, or I shall leave,” he would be told: “Endure this short delay patiently; the emperor is about to come, and he will give you your reward.”

In the same way the Apostle urges them not to fail in their labors but patiently to await the Lord’s coming.

“You need endurance,” he says—that is, you have one task: to persevere in the contest until you receive [Col. 0899B] a crown worthy of your labor. For it is not the one who has begun who will be crowned, but the one who has persevered in the contest to the end; this person will be saved.

“In your endurance,” says the Lord, “you will possess your souls.”

“Receive the promise,” he says; that is, receive the glory of everlasting blessedness.

For yet a very little while, and “the one who is to come will come, and will not delay.”

“The one who is to come will come, and will not delay” undoubtedly signifies Christ. He consoles them as though only a short time remained until his coming. It is no small consolation in labor to hope that the judge and rewarder will come soon, rewarding the steadfastness of those who have competed.

But:

> “My righteous one will live by faith. And if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him.”

The Apostle introduced this prophetic [Col. 0899C] testimony to encourage faith and the gaining of the soul. Just as the soul is the life of the body, so faith is the life of the soul. Faith is conceived in the heart, confessed with the mouth, and adorned with works, because faith without works is dead.

If anyone withdraws from this faith, he will not please God’s will. We must not suppose that God the Father, or the Holy Spirit, or the Son possesses a soul according to the nature of his divinity. Rather, divine Scripture speaks in human fashion and, for our instruction, expresses his will by the word “soul.”

It should be considered that just as the one who hesitates will displease God, so the one who believes and lives in his right faith will please him.

“You have labored,” he says, “in the contest; await the blessed hope. Do not hesitate to seek what you hope for, because the righteous person lives by faith.”

[Col. 0899D] But we are not children of withdrawal, leading to destruction, but of faith, leading to the gaining of the soul.

“We,” he says, “are not children of those pagans and Gentiles who withdraw from the life of faith and eternal light to the destruction of their souls. Rather, we are children of the patriarchs, who were tested in faith and perfected in faith, so that they might gain their own souls for salvation, and, in addition, the souls of others through their example.”

## CHAPTER XI

Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.

The order of the words is: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, namely, the proof of things not seen.”

Faith is believing those things that are not seen. When [Col. 0900A] we believe that things we do not see either existed, exist, or will exist in truth, faith itself makes them subsist in our heart, as though before the eyes of the body.

But in things that are visible, neither belief nor unbelief can properly be spoken of; rather, they should be called knowledge. Faith, however, means that the mind is as firmly convinced about things not seen as it is about things already visible. When this occurs, faith makes those things subsist within us as objects of belief.

For example, to use at least a few examples from among many: the general resurrection has not yet occurred. Although it does not yet exist in substance, hope makes it subsist in our soul, as though we had it before our eyes.

This is what he meant when he said that faith is the substance of those things that are hoped for but not yet seen.

And if faith is the proof [Col. 0900B] of things that do not yet appear, why do some now wish to see it? The ancients used *arguere* to mean “to show.” From this comes *argumentum*, as though it were the showing and pre-demonstration of future things and of things that are not seen.

Properly speaking, an argument is a reasoning that establishes belief in a doubtful matter. It is therefore perfectly clear that faith is the proof of things that cannot appear. Things that appear no longer require faith, as we said above, but knowledge.

When Thomas saw and touched Christ (John XX), why was he told:

> “Because you have seen me, you have believed”?

He saw one thing and believed another. Divinity could not be seen by a mortal human being. He saw a man and confessed him to be God, saying:

> “My Lord and my God.”

By seeing, therefore, he believed, because as he contemplated the true man, he exclaimed [Col. 0900C] that he was God, whom he could not see.

In this faith, then, the elders obtained a testimony of righteousness. Here we must understand “elders” to mean the fathers of the Old Testament—namely, the patriarchs, prophets, and other righteous men who, in the faith they placed in God and his promises, earned a testimony of praise and righteousness. Hence, because Abraham believed God, it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called God’s friend. This faith must be understood in such a way that one believes in the heart, confesses with the mouth, and adorns it with works. For the one who truly believes is the one who practices in action what he believes. Concerning those who retain faith in name only, Paul says the contrary: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him.”

[Col. 0900D] By faith we understand that the ages were ordered by the word of God, so that visible things came to be from invisible things. Since certain Hebrews were still weak and had indeed begun from faith, but were being made fainthearted by the sufferings of their tribulations and were bearing less patiently the evils inflicted upon them, the Apostle first encourages them from his own example, saying, “Recall the former days”; then from divine Scripture, which says that “the righteous person lives by faith”; and finally by reasoning, demonstrating that faith is the substance of things that do not appear. Now, however, he begins to speak of their ancestors, wonderfully setting them forth as an example, because just as all of them were saved through faith, so we too are all saved through faith. For when the soul finds a companion in the same sufferings, it rests and breathes again. This ordinarily happens in faith, and in tribulation of whatever kind. The human race is exceedingly fragile and excessively hesitant in thought; therefore consolation from the faith and patience of those who came before is necessary.

The Apostle therefore encourages them by means of the fathers, but first from the common principle, saying: “It is manifest that God did not make these things from things that already existed, but visible things from invisible things, existing things from things that did not exist.” By reasoning we cannot discover how he made everything from nothing, or visible things from invisible things, because we were not present when they were made. How, then, is this held as certain? Clearly, it is a matter of faith to believe it. For by faith we believe that the ages were ordered—that is, perfected or made—because the things that are seen were made not from visible things, [Col. 0901B] but from invisible things.

Here “invisible things” may be understood as the unformed matter of which it is said at the beginning of Genesis: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” By the name “heaven,” however, we must not understand this bodily heaven called the firmament, but the angelic nature and the spiritual heavens. By “earth” is understood the unformed matter from which all bodily things were afterward made; at that time they were in a certain sense invisible, when darkness was over the face of the abyss. From invisible matter, visible things were made when everything was divided and distinguished according to its appearances and forms.

What he says about visible things being made from invisible things can also be understood in another way. Before the world was formed, it existed invisibly in the wisdom of God; yet through the completion of the work it became visible to human eyes. When he says that the ages were perfected by the word of God, by “ages” we must understand all things made in time, or the ages of the Word of God the Father, in accordance with what John says: “All things were made through him” (John I). The ages, as Ovid Naso says, are so called from *sequi*, “to follow,” because they follow one another and revolve back into themselves, as Varro testifies. They may also be called ages from the point at which the variety of time began to exist.

By faith Abel offered to God a far greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained the testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks. He places first the one who suffered evil, and suffered it from his brother, setting forth an example proper to them. For they too had suffered the same things from their fellow tribesmen. Therefore he encourages them: just as Abel was unjustly killed by his brother and did not refuse persecution, so they too should not refuse to suffer unjustly at the hands of their fellow tribesmen and brothers.

“Far greater,” that is, a greater sacrifice, Abel offered to God than Cain—not because that sacrifice was greater in material things, but because Abel brought to the benevolent God whatever he had that was better, with a good disposition through faith. From that point onward his possessions were multiplied, and we understand that by this he pleased God. He did this through faith, because he believed that what he offered with good will was pleasing to God, and believed that he would be rewarded by him.

God also bore witness to his gifts, either because fire descended from heaven, as Theodotion records: “The Lord was inflamed over Abel and over his gifts”; or through the statement by which he was praised and proved righteous by the Lord in the Gospel. For the Lord said in the Gospel (Luke XI): “Amen, I say to you, the blood of all the righteous that has been shed upon the earth will be required, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah.”

Through that sacrifice he still speaks, although now dead, as it is said: “The blood of Abel cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. IV). Or “he still speaks” means that, although Abel’s body was killed, his glory could not be killed with him. While his glory is proclaimed throughout the world, while his praise is on everyone’s lips, while everyone admires him, he still speaks every day, although dead. For whoever admonishes others by his example to be righteous speaks in some manner.

By faith Enoch was translated so that he would not see death, and he was not found, because God translated him. Enoch pleased God through faith, which was adorned with good works, believing that by it he would altogether please God. Therefore he was translated into the earthly paradise, from which Adam had once been expelled—namely, so that he would not experience temporal death until the time appointed by God had run its course.

In what condition or state he now exists in paradise is not for us to inquire. This, however, must be believed: he rests there without any distress, pain, or labor. And just as he lives without any assault of the flesh or any trouble, so, unless the human being had first sinned, after the full number of the elect had been completed he would have been transferred from the earthly paradise to the heavenly paradise. The cause of his being transferred was that he pleased God; but the cause of his pleasing God was his faith. For if he had not believed that God would repay him with a reward, how could he have pleased him? Before his translation he had the testimony that he pleased God, since Scripture says that “Enoch walked with God,” obeying his will.

For without faith it is impossible to please God. Enoch believed that if anyone believed that God exists and approached him, he would receive a reward. Since faith is therefore the foundation of all good things, no one can please God without faith. The one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.

Whoever approaches God by believing must believe that he is God—that is, that he always possesses being, in accordance with what he himself said to Moses (Exod. III): “I am who I am”; and, “He who is has sent me to you.” He must also believe that, for those who seek him through good works, in accordance with what the Psalmist says, “Seek the Lord, and be strengthened” (Ps. CIV), he is the eternal and true rewarder.

By faith Noah, having received an oracle concerning things not yet seen—that is, concerning the rains—and fearing, prepared an ark for the salvation of his household. Through it—that is, through faith—he condemned the world, specifically by comparison with his better faith and conduct, and he was appointed heir of the righteousness that comes through faith.

By faith he believed God that he would bring waters upon the earth, when God said to him (Gen. VI): “The end of all flesh has come before me, and I will bring water upon them. Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood,” and the rest that follows. Therefore he was saved with his entire household, that is, his family.

No completed experiment of work or reasoning contributed anything in this matter. “Others were marrying,” says the Lord in the Gospel, and the weather was clear; thousands of signs of the Flood were nevertheless appearing. Yet Noah feared, and through faith, fearing things not yet seen, built an ark for the salvation of his family. Through that faith he condemned the world by comparison with his own faith, which the world refused to possess. For he showed them to be worthy of this punishment: even over the span of a hundred years, they refused to be corrected by the construction of that ark.

Through faith, moreover, and not through the law, he was appointed heir of righteousness, since he alone held the faith of the fathers, which the others learned from him. He is called heir of the kingdom of heaven, or heir of the world, because through his offspring the world was restored; and he appeared righteous because he believed God.

By faith Abraham, the one now called Abraham, obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. It is as though he were saying: Abraham too pleased God through faith. As soon as God said to him, “Go out from your land and go to the land that I will show you, and I will give it to you and to your offspring” (Gen. XII), he believed God and went out to the place to which God had commanded him, not knowing where he was going.

The place and dwelling of that land were unknown to him; and insofar as he walked, he walked by faith. Or “not knowing where he was going” means that he had no one to imitate.

By faith he lived in the land of promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise. “Tent” is a diminutive of *casa*, “house”; here it is used for tents and tabernacles in which Abraham lived with Isaac and Jacob like travelers and pilgrims, teaching them the faith of God, since they were fellow heirs of his promise.

For the promise made to Abraham was made to Isaac and Jacob, and to all who are fellow heirs together in the promises made to Abraham. To Abraham it was said: “In you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII); and, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI). To Isaac, he said: “God, fulfilling the oath that I swore to your father Abraham, will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give all these regions to your descendants” (Gen. XXVI). To Jacob also he said: “I am God Almighty. I will cause nations to grow and multiply from you; I will give you the land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac” (Gen. XXXV).

See how all are fellow heirs in the promises made to Abraham. It should also be noted that Abraham’s faith is doubled because of the greatness of his faith; hence he is called the head of faith. For just as he went out from his land by faith, not knowing where he was going, so by faith he remained and dwelt in his own land as in a foreign one. He saw his son living there as a stranger; he saw his grandson; he saw himself wandering in a foreign land, [Col. 0904A] and he was not troubled.

Although it had been said to him, “I will give it to you and to your offspring”—not “to you through your offspring,” but “to you and to your offspring”—neither he, nor Isaac, nor Jacob possessed this promise; rather, their succession did. And because, when he obeyed God and went out from his land, he was not called Abraham but Abram, the Apostle said, “Consider”: “By faith the one now called Abraham, who was then called Abram, lived in the land of promise as in a foreign land.” At first he was called Abram, and afterward Abraham.

For he was awaiting a city having foundations, whose architect and founder is God. The heavenly city is said to have foundations because of its stability and firmness. Whoever has once found a place in it can never be disinherited or torn away from it. Therefore, he says, they lived by faith in the land of promise as in a foreign land because they did not attend to the promises made concerning the earthly land, but sought the future rest. They showed themselves worthy of greater things; therefore he did not permit them to receive these things, because he wanted to give them greater ones.

By faith Sarah herself, although barren, received power to conceive offspring, and she gave birth beyond the proper time of life, because she considered him faithful who had made the promise. A question arises here: Why does he say that Sarah received by faith the power to conceive, when she was reproved by the angel for laughing out of unbelief? Her laughter was not laughter of joy and complete faith, whereas Abraham’s laughter was one of joy and complete faith.

The question is resolved as follows: Although she first doubted, afterward she was strengthened in faith by the angel’s words. The cause of her doubt was removed, and faith was introduced. She received power to conceive because she was already dead with respect to age and was barren. There were two obstacles: one of time, for she had already grown old; the other of nature, for she was barren. But she received power to receive and retain the seed.

Women ordinarily become barren chiefly for two reasons: either because they do not have the power of heat in the womb by which they can prepare the seed—which also happens in old age, when the womanly functions fail—or because the womb is closed even in youth, so that the seed does not reach the places of conception. Against these conditions God gave power: that is, against barrenness, stability, [Col. 0904D] and old age. The seed reached the place of conception sufficiently; and after it had arrived, he gave the woman firmness for childbirth. Thus, through the firmness of faith, the infirmity of the womb was strengthened, and everything became possible for the believer.

Therefore, from one man—and him as good as dead—there arose descendants, as numerous as the stars of heaven and as the sand on the seashore, which is innumerable. “For this reason,” he says, because both Abraham and Sarah possessed true faith, innumerable peoples arose from the one body of Abraham and Sarah. By these words he wished to show that Sarah did not give birth only to Isaac, but to more descendants than any fertile woman.

He says that those two had one body because Genesis says, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II). He adds further, “and from this body, as though dead,” saying that they were born not from a dead life but from dead seed. An old man can indeed still discharge semen, but it nevertheless lacks the firmness necessary for begetting children, unless perhaps with a young woman, as happened in other cases.

“As the stars of heaven,” he says, “or the sand of the sea.” This is spoken hyperbolically. By the stars of heaven are to be understood the good—Abraham’s children from both peoples through faith. By the sand of the sea, however, are understood the reprobate, Abraham’s children from the Jewish people according to the flesh, who, always seeking earthly things, are weighed down by the burden of sins. And although the stars of heaven, the sand of the sea, and even those designated by these images are innumerable to human beings, they are nevertheless numerable to God, to whom all things are open.

According to faith—that is, with faith—all these died without receiving the promises, but seeing them from afar, greeting them, and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth. Those who say such things—namely, that they are strangers upon the earth—show that they are seeking a homeland. If they had remembered that land from which they had gone out, so as to desire to return to it, they would certainly have had time to return. But now, because they do not wish to return to the place from which they came out, but remain in a foreign land like pilgrims, they seek a better one, that is, a heavenly one.

Two matters here deserve inquiry. Since he had said above that Enoch was translated so that he would not see death and was not found, here he says that all these died according to faith. And since he had also said that they did not receive the promises, but saw them from afar, above he said of Abel that he obtained the testimony that he was righteous; of Enoch, that he was translated; and of Noah, that he was saved from the condemnation of the world. As for Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, there is no doubt that they received many promises concerning both Christ and the land of promise.

These two matters require the following solution. When he first said, “All these died with faith,” this must be understood to mean that all of them died except Enoch alone, whom we know to have been translated. When he added that they did not receive the promises, it is clear that they received them in some respects, but not in others. Enoch received the promise that he would not see death; Noah received salvation; and many others received promises as well.

But these things were for them only certain foretastes and initial tastings of future realities, not the fullness of the promises. For God grants us not only the things that are to come, but also the necessities of this life, as he said to his disciples: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these temporal things of life will be added to you insofar as they are beneficial” (Matt. VI).

In this respect, because in the present age they earned in part the praise of righteousness, did not perish with the wicked, and were rich in temporal goods, although they were pilgrims—as we read of Abraham, that he was rich in silver and gold—they received certain foretastes of the promises. [Col. 0906A] But because they did not obtain the full promise of the heavenly homeland, they are said, as it were, not to have received the promises. Nevertheless, they saw the promises from afar, the promises that the Lord Christ proclaimed when he came, saying: “Whoever leaves house or brothers or sisters or father or mother for my sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX).

Those who lived before the Lord’s coming did not obtain this promise, although they had left all their possessions, just as the apostles did. Or they did not obtain the promises concerning the Lord’s coming: although he had been promised to them, they did not see him present in the world.

They also greeted those same promises—that is, they desired and longed for them—as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X). He says “greeting” by a metaphor drawn from travelers by sea: when they see from afar the desired cities before entering them, they anticipate them with a greeting and make them familiar to themselves.

They looked upon these promises in faith, welcomed them with desire, and confessed in speech that they were strangers, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “I am a sojourner with you, as all my fathers were” (Ps. XXXVIII). “Sojourner” derives from *peregre*, that is, from traveling a long distance. We say *peragrare*, “to travel through,” meaning “to walk throughout.” For those who lived in tents and bought burial places with money were clearly pilgrims, to such an extent that they did not even possess a place in which to bury their own people. Therefore, the first virtue is to be a stranger and sojourner in this world, to have nothing in common with the kings of this age, but to be removed from them like a pilgrim—

Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God. For he prepared a city for them. “Therefore,” he says, because they believed in God and presumed nothing for themselves from earthly things in order to place their hope in them, almighty God is not ashamed to be called their God. For he himself says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Deut. III)—namely, through faith and the merit of their life.

Just as God is glorified when he is called the God of benevolent and excellent people who worship virtue, so, conversely, he is put to shame and blushes in the deeds of the wicked if they invoke him. Hence he says through the prophet: “Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations” (Isa. III). Those men, however, were so distinguished in virtue and so full of confidence that God was not put to shame, but rather glorified, when he was called their God.

In general, God is called the God of earth and the God of heaven; indeed, he is also the God of the nations, and not only of the nations but of the whole world, because he himself created all things. But he is not called the God of those saints merely through creation; he is called their God as a friend. So even now the Lord God is called the God of Christians.

“He prepared,” he says, “a city for them”—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem. For this reason he did not give them an inheritance in the present age; or, alternatively, for this reason he is not ashamed to be called their God, because he predestined them to reign with him in the heavenly city.

[Col. 0907A] By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he was offering his only-begotten son, the one in whom he had received the promises, to whom it had been said, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called,” reasoning that God was able even to raise him from the dead.

What is the meaning of the fact that blessed James, mentioning Abraham in his epistle, praises him above all for his works, while the blessed Apostle praises not his works but his faith with the greatest care? Blessed James rightly praises him for his works, because he knew that Abraham was also perfect in faith. He was writing to those who appeared to have faith, but did not adorn that faith with good works.

Blessed Paul, however, was writing to those who appeared to possess the good works of the law but did not have perfect faith. Therefore he rightly recalls Abraham’s faith more attentively, so that they might strive to imitate him; or certainly so that he might show that those who wish to be Abraham’s children must possess both faith and works. Thus one rightly praised him for faith, and the other likewise praised him for works.

“By faith,” he says, “Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested.” Although he had no freeborn son except Isaac, and in him had received the promise that he would become the father of many nations, he was not therefore disobedient to God. Although he heard something contrary a second time, when God said to him, “Offer your son Isaac to me” (Gen. XXII), after he had already heard, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI), he did not doubt the promises. He believed that God could raise Isaac from the dead and multiply from him a multitude of peoples.

Therefore he immediately wished to offer his son, because he believed that God would promptly raise him again. But so that no one could say that Abraham had another son from whom he hoped the promise would be fulfilled, the Apostle says: “He even offered his only-begotten son”—the same Abraham who had received the promises concerning him.

Why, then, did God test him? Did he not know that Abraham was strong in faith and approved? Certainly he knew. He tested him not so that he himself might learn, but so that he might demonstrate him to others and make his strength manifest, as he himself showed by saying: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. XXII)—that is, “I have caused others to know that you fear the Lord.”

Hence he also received him in a parable. *Parabola* is a Greek word; in Latin it is called a likeness or figure. He received him in a parable from death when he said to him, “Do not stretch out your hand over the boy” (Gen. XXII), because Isaac was saved when the ram was killed.

Isaac was killed with respect to the father’s intention; afterward God restored him to the patriarch in a parable—that is, in a figure and likeness of Christ’s passion. Everything that was then enacted in Abraham occurred in likeness of what the true Abraham—namely, God the Father and creator of all nations—had determined to do for us at the end of the age. Abraham bore the figure of God the Father, while Isaac bore the figure of Christ.

Abraham, as Scripture says, carried fire and a sword, because God the Father in a certain manner carried the sword of the passion when he permitted Christ to be killed. Hence the Son says to him in the psalm: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck”—that is, whom you permitted to be struck (Ps. LXVIII). And God the Father says through Zechariah: “I will strike the shepherd” (Matt. XXVI)—that is, “I will permit him to be struck.”

The fire that Abraham carried signifies the heat and fervor of God’s supreme love, by which he loves us; concerning this it is said: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world” (John III). For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son to God as a victim, so God the Father handed over his only-begotten Son for us all.

Isaac himself carried the wood upon which he was to be placed, because Christ too carried upon his shoulders the wood of the cross on which he was to be crucified. The ram signifies the flesh of Christ. Isaac was offered but not killed; only the ram was killed, because Christ was offered in his passion, but his divinity remained impassible.

By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning future things. He blessed them concerning future things because he believed that everything would afterward happen to them according to what he had invoked upon them, and in blessing them he wished for the things that were to come. This may also be understood in another way: he blessed them concerning future mysteries, because Jacob bore the figure of Christ or of the Christian people, while Esau bore the figure of the Jewish people.

By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped the top of his staff. We read in Genesis (chap. XLVIII) that, when Joseph heard that his father was ill, he came to him and brought his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, for a blessing. Jacob, possessing faith and believing that everything would happen to them according to what he had been inspired by God to desire for them, blessed them.

He is said to have blessed each of them because he poured his own blessing upon each and placed the younger before the elder, since he foresaw that events would occur in this way. What follows—“and he worshiped the top of his staff,” that is, Joseph’s staff—can be understood in two ways.

Jacob, inspired by the prophetic Spirit, understood that Joseph’s staff signified the kingdom of Christ. By its top, that is, the summit of the staff, he understood the power and honor of Christ’s kingdom, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Your staff is a righteous staff, the staff of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV). Therefore he did not worship the staff as a god according to the rite of the nations who worshiped idols; rather, in the staff he worshiped Christ, whose kingdom and power he foresaw as being prefigured in it.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, perhaps he worshiped Joseph’s staff according to the custom of that time, because he saw Joseph as lord of the whole land of Egypt—namely, for the same reason that Esther is read to have worshiped the staff of Ahasuerus (Esth. V).

By faith Joseph, when dying, spoke of the departure of the children of Israel and gave instructions concerning his bones. He spoke of the departure of the children of Israel, believing that everything God had promised to their fathers was true, especially what he had said to Abraham: “Know beforehand that your offspring will be foreigners in a foreign land, and they will mistreat them for four hundred years. Nevertheless, I will judge the nation whom they serve, says the Lord, and afterward they will return to the land of their fathers” (Gen. XV).

Joseph would certainly not have given instructions concerning his bones unless he had hoped with full faith for their return to the land of promise. For when he visited them, he said: “The Lord will visit you after many days; carry my bones away from here with you” (Gen. L).

Not only did the tribe of Joseph carry their father’s bones with them through the desert into the land of promise, but the other tribes did so as well. They carried with them the bones of all the patriarchs and buried them at Shechem, which came into the possession of the tribe of Joseph.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, together with Sarah, Rebecca, and Leah, were buried in the double cave of Mamre or Arbe, which Abraham had bought from the sons of Heth; Adam and Eve were also resting there in burial. Perhaps someone may ask why all those holy fathers preferred to be buried in the land of promise rather than elsewhere. The answer is that they did not do this out of concern for tombs, but rather because, through the Holy Spirit, they foresaw that the Lord would redeem the human race in that land. With the greatest desire they wished to be buried there together with him, so that when he rose, they might rise together with him.

We, however, ought not to become fainthearted wherever we are buried, since we do not know where the bodies of many martyrs lie gloriously in the earth.

By faith Moses, after he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that he was a beautiful child and did not fear the king’s edict. Moses was not hidden through his own faith, since he could not yet speak, but through the faith of his parents—his father and mother. Believing that almighty God could free and protect him, they guarded him for three months.

Afterward, when they could not conceal him because of his crying, they placed him in a basket of papyrus and set it among the reeds of the river. The king’s edict was that all the male children should be thrown into the river.

But what does it mean that they did not fear the king’s edict? If they did not fear it, why did they guard the child? They feared it in that they did not dare to keep him openly; but they acted as though they did not fear it in that they did not throw him into the open river. Instead, they placed him in a basket and set him among the river reeds, hoping and trusting that almighty God would protect him. Their trust was therefore reckoned to them as though they had not feared.

How, then, did they hope to save the child except through faith? “They saw,” he says, “that he was a beautiful child.” From the moment of his birth, a great grace of beauty had evidently been infused into him—not through nature producing a handsome infant, but through the gift of divine grace. This grace also moved that barbarous Egyptian woman, the daughter of Pharaoh, to love him, take him, and nourish him.

By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to possess the enjoyment of sin for a time. He considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of the Egyptians. For he was looking toward the reward.

It is as though he were saying to those to whom he was writing: None of you has abandoned a broad and splendid royal palace, or royal treasures, as Moses did; indeed, he not only despised them but renounced them. Having preferred heaven, he did not wish to admire the beauty of the Egyptian kingdom. He chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasure of temporal sin.

He considered it a sin to remain in the king’s palace, enjoying temporal happiness while abandoning his brothers in tribulation. He judged it a sin, I say, not to suffer affliction with the others. If Moses judged it a sin not to suffer grievously with others, how great a heap of sins will those have who abandon the assembly of the faithful?

“You suffer,” he says, “for yourselves; but Moses chose this not only for himself. Looking toward the reward, he chose it also for others, so that he might receive a greater recompense. He voluntarily cast himself into such dangers, although he could have lived piously and enjoyed worldly goods.”

“He considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of the Egyptians.” He calls it the reproach of Christ because Moses endured reproach for Christ, who is of one essence with the Father according to his divinity. Or he calls it the reproach of Christ because it was the kind of reproach Christ endured from his relatives.

Just as Christ endured reproach from those whom he had come to redeem, when they said to him, “You have a demon” (John VIII), and inflicted evils upon him even to the passion, so Moses endured reproach from his brothers, whom he wished to free. One of them said to him: “Who appointed you ruler or judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” (Exod. II.)

Similarly, whenever anyone suffers reproach from members of his household or from those to whom he has rendered a benefit, he suffers the reproach of Christ. “He was looking,” he says, “toward his reward”—and toward the reward of the whole people. Thus, whenever someone suffers adversity, he ought to recall what reward he will consequently receive from the Lord.

By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; for he endured the invisible One as though he were visible. We read in Exodus that when a certain Hebrew who was injuring his brother said to Moses, whom Moses wished to rebuke, “Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Moses fled at these words, because Pharaoh, having heard this, sought to kill him.

But since it is clear that he fled to Midian, what does blessed Paul mean when he says, “not fearing the king’s anger”? If he did not fear, why did he flee? His flight was therefore an act of faith: he believed that God would deliver him, and he displayed outwardly a fear that he did not possess inwardly. For that reason it is reckoned to him as though he had not feared.

He did not wish to remain there because he did not want to appear, out of a desire for boasting, to be throwing himself into obvious danger and tempting the Lord his God—something altogether diabolical. Holy men, so long as they have something they can do, ought not to tempt God; rather, they ought to imitate their Lord, who often gave way to the Jews, observing what he himself commanded: “When they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X).

Moses’ flight, therefore, was entirely outward, since inwardly he relied most firmly upon God’s help. Hence the Apostle says “the invisible One,” saying that he endured God as though he were present. This means: He trusted so completely in God’s help and was so secure in his protection that he looked upon almighty God, who is invisible by nature, as always present.

By faith he celebrated the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them. By the faith through which Moses believed that the people would be saved by that blood, he celebrated the Passover and the sprinkling of blood with which he smeared the doorposts, so that the angel who was destroying the firstborn of the Egyptians might not afflict the Israelites. It was as though he said to them: “If the blood of the typical lamb, in the midst of Egypt and amid such great devastation, preserved unharmed the Jews whose doorposts were sprinkled with that blood, how much more will the blood of the man who is the Lamb—that is, Christ—save us, whose doors, that is, whose foreheads, are fortified by the sign of Christ’s Passion” [Col. 0911B]. For the angel feared that blood, understanding that the Lord’s death was present there, and for that reason did not touch the doorposts, although what was being done was itself nothing; what was accomplished through it, however, was great. The doorposts of the Israelites were smeared with the lamb’s blood so that the destroying angel would not dare to inflict death; faithful peoples are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s Passion as a protection of salvation, so that they may be delivered from destruction.

By faith they crossed the Red Sea as though through dry land; when the Egyptians attempted this, they were swallowed up. It was as though he said to those for whom he was writing these things: “We must hold faith so firmly that whenever our mind is tossed about in some despair, even then we should trust that we will be delivered, even if we come as far as death and all hope for us is abandoned.” What hope could they have had [Col. 0911C]? On one side there was the sea; on another they were enclosed by very high mountains; on the third side there were enemies. If they tried to flee, they would either perish in the sea or fall into the hands of the Egyptians. Yet, because they had faith, they overcame everything. For by the faith through which Moses believed God, he struck the sea at his word and divided it into twelve sections, in accordance with what is said in the Psalms. Believing that they could cross the sea on dry ground, all those tribes entered; but the tribe of Judah entered first, in accordance with what is read in Hosea: “Judah,” he says, “was leader with God in the sea.” Thus that sea was a wall for the Hebrews on their right and on their left, providing them with a dry path; but it drowned the Egyptians. Hence the Apostle says that, when the Egyptians attempted it, they were swallowed up. For by this it became evident that it was water, because living men were absorbed in it; and by this it became evident that it was not an illusion but a reality: the Egyptians experienced it and were swallowed up.

Allegorically, the Red Sea is baptism, consecrated by the redness of Christ’s blood. The Hebrews who went out from Egypt and crossed the Red Sea are the faithful, who, abandoning the darkness of unbelief, passed through the font of baptism. Pharaoh and the Egyptians died in the sea because in the baptismal font the devil died, losing the power that he possessed. Original and actual sins also died there, if any had previously existed.

By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days [Col. 0912A]. It was not the sound of the trumpets that cast down the stones of the walls, but the faith with which they believed God cast them down. We read that, at the Lord’s command, Joshua ordered the ark of God to be carried around Jericho for seven days, while trumpets sounded. On the seventh day, when they had blown the trumpets, the walls of Jericho fell; this is not without a great mystery.

Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” represents this world, because just as the moon diminishes through its monthly phases, so this world falls through its daily declines. In the ark the Church is represented; in the bronze trumpets, strong preachers are signified. Joshua, who led the ark around the city, is Christ, who governs his Church throughout this world.

Therefore the Israelites, carrying the ark, went around this city of Jericho for seven days while the bronze trumpets sounded, and its walls fell through the presence of the ark and the sound of the bronze trumpets. For in this age, which unfolds through the succession of seven days, the ark is carried—that is, while the Church moves around the world in response to the voices of the preachers. As at the sound of trumpets the walls of Jericho fell, so the proud of this world, its rulers, and the arrogant obstacles of unbelief fall, until at the end of time the last enemy, death, is destroyed [Col. 0912B].

By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, because she received the spies in peace. In this passage the blessed Apostle offers great consolation and encouragement to everyone: if an unbelieving and idolatrous prostitute was saved by faith alone, how much more will those be saved who have not fallen into graver crimes [Col. 0912C]. It is as though he plainly said: “It is disgraceful if you are more unbelieving than a prostitute. She merely heard human beings announcing these things and immediately believed; you hear not only human beings but also the voices of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, and in addition you recognize the very Son of God sent to you.”

Rahab attained the result of faith. While all the others were perishing, she alone was saved. Rahab, whose name is interpreted as “enlarged,” represents the Church, which has been enlarged from east to west and from north to south and possesses the breadth of charity, so much so that it even pours out prayer for its enemies.

And it is rightly said that she lived among foreign and alien peoples in the desires of the flesh and devoted herself to prostitution, because before the Lord’s coming the Church was alienated from God, living according to the desires of the flesh and devoted to prostitution and idolatry. But after the true Jesus sent two spies to her—that is, Peter and Paul, or the two Testaments—she became faithful, abandoned the prostitution of idolatry, and was thereby saved; and she is saved daily so that she may not perish with the unbelievers [Col. 0912D].

Up to this point he has spoken about the lawgiver and the ancient fathers. Now he is going to speak about the judges who came after Joshua, mentioning only their names because of the brevity of his discourse: those who fought by faith and conquered many nations.

And what more shall I say? For time will fail me as I tell the story. That is, the time allotted for writing the Epistle will fail me if I wish to recount all the deeds of those whom I have mentioned up to this point, or what I can relate about their successors: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets who through faith conquered kingdoms [Col. 0913A].

Although he mentions all of them collectively, the point is that the deeds of each were performed through the same faith: all of them together conquered kingdoms through faith. Gideon, having received a sign from the Lord through the three hundred men who drew water with their hands—of whom the Lord said to him, “By these you will overcome Midian”—and also through the fleece that was wet and dry, filled with faith, struck down Zebah and Zalmunna and gained victory over his enemies.

Allegorically, Gideon, whose name is interpreted as “going around in the womb,” signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who, through the mystery of the Incarnation, was placed in the Virgin’s womb and, through the fullness of divinity—which fills all things—went around the whole world, because by filling all things he encompasses all things [Col. 0913B].

The three hundred men who drew water with their hands, received fire in jars, went out against Midian, and, when the jars were broken, made the fire shine forth and blew the trumpets, while the enemies were simultaneously put to flight, represent the holy preachers. They possess faith in the holy Trinity and are marked with the sign of the Lord’s Passion. This is indicated by the letter tau, the letter T, whose numerical value expresses three hundred and which among the ancient Jews had the form of a cross.

The jars, which are vessels made either of cast material or of clay, signify the frail bodies of those same preachers, about which that eminent preacher says: “We have [Col. 0913C] this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Corinthians IV). The sound of the trumpets expresses the voices of the preachers. When the jars were broken, therefore, the fire shone forth and the enemies were put to flight.

The Midianites represent this age, because after the holy martyrs depart from this world, they increase through miracles. Thus, shaken by the power of miracles, the enemies are put to flight—either by being brought under the faith or by ceasing their persecutions, overcome by fear of the signs.

Nor is it without mystery that, when Gideon prayed, the fleece was wet at first while the whole earth was dry; but afterward the fleece was dry while the whole earth was wet. The fleece represents the Jewish people, while the earth represents all the nations. Therefore it was rightly that the fleece was wet at first while the earth remained dry, because when the Jewish people had been moistened by the dew of heavenly wisdom before the Lord’s coming, all the nations were dried up by the drought of faith and wisdom [Col. 0913D]. Again, after the Lord’s coming, when all the nations had been moistened by the dew of wisdom, Judaea perished in dryness.

Barak (Judges IV) is Lapidoth, the husband of Deborah. By the faith through which he believed the prophetess, he overcame Sisera and all his chariots. Samson, by the faith through which he believed, obtained from God what he prayed for; dying, he killed more men than he had killed while alive. For he said: “Lord God, remember me and restore my former strength to me now, my God, so that I may take vengeance on my enemies and receive one vengeance for the loss of my two eyes” (Judges XVI).

Jephthah had faith when he fought against the Ammonites and when he offered his daughter, although in this [Col. 0914A] he acted foolishly, thinking that he could please almighty God by shedding human blood. He vowed that, if the Lord gave him victory over the Ammonites, he would sacrifice to him whoever first came out to meet him from his household. And he did so. For his daughter came out to meet him, and after she had lamented her virginity, he killed her (Judges XI).

But one may ask why the custom arose that every year the virgins of the Hebrews should mourn Jephthah’s daughter. The reason appears to be that, when they see her mourned by her own daughters, no one will dare to leap into such folly and such sacrilege as to shed human blood for God.

David, filled with faith, went out against the Philistine and killed him (I Samuel XVII). And because he believed God, he earned many promises concerning Christ. Samuel, the prophet and priest, possessed [Col. 0914B] perfect faith. Through it he anointed David king at the word of the Lord, and by killing Agag, king of Amalek (I Samuel XV), they practiced righteousness, because what they believed in their hearts they completed in their deeds. By adorning that same faith, they attained the promises concerning Christ or concerning the heavenly homeland.

For Abraham received a promise concerning Christ, when the Lord said to him: “In your seed, that is, in Christ, all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XXII). David also received many promises, to whom the Lord said: “When you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed who will come forth from your loins, and I will establish his throne upon your throne” (II Samuel VII). And elsewhere: “I will place upon your seat one from the fruit of your loins” (Psalm CXXXI). And again: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, [Col. 0914C] his seed shall remain forever” (Psalm LXXXVIII).

They stopped, that is, closed, the mouths of lions, as did Samson, David, and Daniel when he was thrown into the pit.

They quenched the force of fire, as when the three young men, Daniel’s companions, were thrown into the furnace of blazing fire at the command of Nebuchadnezzar, while Chaldaean madness raged; yet it caused them no harm (Daniel XIII).

They escaped the edge of the sword, that is, they repelled the strength of their enemies from themselves by fighting bravely, as did Joshua, Gideon, David, and other kings and leaders of the Jews.

They recovered from weakness, as did Job and Hezekiah, who, when he had fallen sick to the point of death, was restored to his former health by the Lord’s favor for a period of fifteen years (IV Kings X). By the term “weakness” we can understand the evil of captivity, from which they were delivered when the Lord willed it, Cyrus commanded it, and Ezra and Nehemiah carried it out [Col. 0914D].

They became strong in war, as did Joshua, the successor of Moses; Samson, who killed many of the Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey (Judges XV); David the king; and Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers. In their time six thousand Jews also killed one hundred thousand enemies, and three thousand who had been sent to Antioch in aid of Demetrius killed one hundred and twenty thousand.

They put the camps of foreigners to flight. They did this frequently. Camps are so called from *castrare*, “to castrate,” because in them lust is castrated. It is not the military custom for men to take wives or other women with them among the nations into battle. Once, however, two rulers of the earth went to war accompanied by their wives: Darius, namely, and Antony; but both fell there. Darius was overcome by Alexander, while Antony was overcome by Octavian Augustus [Col. 0915A].

Women received back their dead through resurrection. He means those women whose sons were raised by Elijah and Elisha. They received them after their resurrection, or restoration to life—not as husbands, but they received alive those whom they had lost in death.

Others were stretched out, refusing deliverance, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Many of the saints were stretched out—that is, extended on a cross and bound with ropes, as was the blessed Andrew. Or they were stretched out by being tied to the tops of two trees and torn apart, or even extended upon the limbs of untamed horses; thus they were torn apart or, in another sense, stretched out [Col. 0915B]—that is, beheaded. All these things are seen to have been accomplished in the holy martyrs.

They did not accept deliverance—that is, release in the present, in order to escape their torments—so that they might obtain a better and more glorious resurrection in the future. For the greater the torments someone endures for God in the present, the more glorious he will appear in the resurrection.

Others experienced mockeries and scourges, and in addition bonds and imprisonments. “Mockeries” are so called from play, that is, ridicule. First the holy martyrs were mocked and derided; then they were afflicted with scourges. Thus bound with chains, they were placed in prisons; finally they were killed by various and elaborate torments.

They were stoned, as were Naboth; Jeremiah, in Egypt, by the remnant of the exiles; Ezekiel, in Babylon; and many others in the New Testament [Col. 0915C].

They were sawn apart. Here the plural number is used in place of the singular. For we read of no saint in the Old Testament being sawn apart except the prophet Isaiah, whom King Manasseh had sawn with a wooden saw; Manasseh had married Isaiah’s daughter.

They were tested, as Abraham and many others were—not for deception but rather for testing, specifically the testing of which it is said: “The Lord your God is testing you,” that is, proving you; for God is not a tempter of evils (James I).

They died by the killing of the sword, as did Uriah and Josiah, and many others.

They wandered about in *melotae*, in goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and afflicted. Here [Col. 0915D] we must understand Elijah and others who acted in this way, and who, afflicted everywhere by poverty and tribulations, endured everything through faith so that they might attain the rewards of heavenly desires. Every deprivation and want is called distress, by which a person is pressed—that is, afflicted—whether by hunger or by some other lack.

Some say that a *melota* is a kind of garment made from goatskins, hanging down from one side. Because of its roughness, Egyptian monks are said to use this kind of clothing. Elijah too is read to have used it. Others, however, say that it is a kind of garment made from the skins of a badger. The badger is an animal called *taxus* or *meles*, accustomed to live in underground caves; its hide is said to be hairy, and the name of this garment is derived from it: from *meles*, *melota* [Col. 0916A].

Of whom the world was not worthy. Here, under one meaning, by “the world” we can understand lovers of the world, who desired earthly things alone and were far removed from love of their Creator. For that reason they were not worthy to have such companions as those whose great deeds the Apostle described above.

Alternatively, by “the world” may be understood everything contained in heaven and earth—gold, silver, gems, and every precious thing—and, in addition, the reprobate themselves, deceived by love of worldly possessions. The world, therefore, was not worthy of these saints; that is, even if the whole world were reduced to a price, it could not rightly be compared with one of them, nor, even if all those things could have been offered as a price, could they have bought such a man [Col. 0916B].

To mention the memory of a few out of the many: how could a man such as Moses be compared with anything? When he wished, he divided the sea; when he wished, he brought its waters back; when he wished, he caused manna to descend from heaven; he brought water out of a rock, and performed countless other deeds (Deuteronomy VIII). Or how could the price of the world be compared with a man such as Joshua, his successor, who, when he wished, made the sun and moon—those two great lights—stand still in one place, saying: “Sun, stand against Gibeon, and moon, against the valley of Aijalon, do not move”? (Joshua X.)

Perhaps someone may say: “They could not be bought because they could not be found.” That is certainly true, because no one like them could be found in the whole world; and even if such people could have been found, they could in no way have been compared with anything of value [Col. 0916C]. For what the whole world could not accomplish, one of them accomplished by a word.

When the whole world had suffered drought for three years and six months in the time of Elijah and had been unable to obtain rain, at Elijah’s word the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain fell upon the face of the earth.

They wandered in deserts, on mountains, in caves, and in the hollows of the earth. Here he wishes Elijah, the outstanding prophet, to be understood, as well as the sons of the prophets who were driven into hiding in the time of Ahab and Jezebel because Jezebel wanted to kill them. At that time Obadiah fed them by fifties in caves and in the hollows of the earth. Hence he deserved the gift of prophecy, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward.”

And all these, though approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us [Col. 0916D].

Who are those who were approved by the testimony of faith, if not all those mentioned above? Their faith, so clear and praiseworthy, has been recalled: stars of the firmament, earthly human beings and heavenly angels, living stones and shining pearls. Their deeds confirm their faith, because without faith it is impossible to please God.

They were therefore approved by the testimony of faith—that is, through holy conduct, which faith produced; they were found worthy of praise, for their faith was declared by their pure works. Yet although they were so perfect, they did not receive the promise [Col. 0917A].

Someone may say: “What benefit did they gain from serving God, if they remain without a reward to this day?” Far be it from the hearts of the faithful to believe that they remain without a reward. While still clothed in mortal flesh, they received a great reward: namely, to see and know God and to perform many wonders. Now they rest in soul, enjoying with ineffable joy the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom.

But let us see what John says about them in his Apocalypse, and thus it will become clear what promise they did not receive. John says: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God that they possessed, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?’ And white robes were given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be complete” (Revelation VI) [Col. 0917B].

At present the souls of the saints each possess a single robe, rejoicing in their immortality and exulting in the happiness they enjoy. They will possess two robes when, at the general resurrection, they receive immortality and incorruption in the body, which at present they possess only in soul.

This, then, is the promise they have not yet received, concerning which Isaiah says: “In their land they shall possess double,” namely, after the general resurrection. And truly it is fitting that those who served God in body and soul should receive their reward in both body and soul.

The following words—“since God had provided something better [Col. 0917C] for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us”—that is, so that they should not attain perfection, are expressed in human fashion. For example, some children returning from the field might say to their father: “Father, we worked today and endured the heat of the sun” (Matthew XX); it is time for you to give us refreshment. And he might answer them: “Wait a little until all your brothers who worked with us in the same way arrive; then you will feast with them in the fullest measure.”
