In the same way almighty God, so to speak, acted when he did not grant the elect immortality in the body, so that there might be greater glory and greater desire when all, on the day of judgment, receive their two robes. This is what the words mean: they should not attain perfection without us, who are still pilgrims here, in the resurrection of the bodies [Col. 0917D].

## CHAPTER XII

Therefore, since we too are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every burden and the sin that encircles us, and with patience let us run the race set before us.

By “a cloud of witnesses” he means the multitude of patriarchs, prophets, and the other faithful who were witnesses to perfect faith and also witnesses to the Son of God, whom they foretold as coming into the world. They are rightly called a cloud because of the height and abundance of their merits.

For just as a cloud is illuminated by the sun and filled with its warmth, and afterward warms the earth and often drenches it with rain, while at other times it sends forth flashes of lightning, so those holy fathers, warmed and illuminated by the true Sun, warm and illuminate human hearts by their example. In their own time they sent down rain through their words and flashed with miracles [Col. 0918A].

So great a cloud of witnesses has been placed before us as an example, so that we may strive to imitate their faith and works. Therefore let us lay aside every burden of vices through repentance, as well as the sleep of laziness and weak thoughts.

By adding, “and the sin that encircles us,” he shows that the Jews were tempted by the devil on every side, devoted to carnal desires, and abounding in many sins.

“Let us run with patience toward the race set before us,” so that just as they patiently endured the adversities of this age, so we too may endure them. He does not say that we should add something to our course, but that, remaining in the same course, we should run toward the race appointed for us, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “I have run the way of your commandments” (Psalm CXVIII).

In the present age we have been placed in a contest against the vices of the flesh, against demons, and against false brothers. We must run patiently, or complete this contest, so that we may reach the promised reward of the contest [Col. 0918B].

Let us look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, disregarding its shame.

Just as children look to their parents and disciples to their teachers in the diligent performance of work and in contests, shaping their minds according to their [Col. 0918C] teachers and receiving certain rules from them through observation, so we too, if we wish to run and to learn how to run well toward Jesus Christ, the author and perfecter, should look to him. He said to us: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew XI). And elsewhere: “If they persecuted me,” he says, “they will also persecute you” (John XV); and: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?” (Matthew X.)

Let us look to Christ and receive in him an example of patience. He said: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew XXIV).

For he himself is the author and perfecter. He is the author of faith for us because he infuses faith into us. We cannot believe unless he comes first to us. Hence he says to his faithful: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV) [Col. 0918D].

He himself is the perfecter, or fulfiller, of faith because he grants us completion or perfection, so that we may persevere in faith. Or he is the perfecter of faith in this respect: he gives the will and the ability to accomplish the good by which faith itself is adorned. For faith without works is not perfect; it is dead (James II).

In him we all possess perfection, for he endured the cross for the joy set before him. The Son of God, setting before himself—that is, establishing in his own presence—the joy of the resurrection and ascension into heaven, and of all the glory that he received after the resurrection, endured the cross because he saw that it would ultimately benefit him.

“Disregarding its shame”: that is, counting the disgrace [Col. 0919A] as nothing, because he endured that dishonor without embarrassment or shame. It was a very great joy for him to suffer for us, so that he might fulfill the will of God the Father, for which afterward he received power over every creature.

Hence he says: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke XXII). If, then, he who had no necessity of being crucified was crucified for us, how much more fitting is it that we should endure everything bravely?

For this reason the Lord appeared in the flesh: to awaken human life by admonition, to kindle it by providing an example, to redeem it by dying, and to restore it by rising again. For this reason he will die, to teach us to regard as nothing the glory bestowed by human beings.

And he sits at the right hand of God’s throne—that is, in the prosperity of eternal life and in the fullness of the Father’s majesty [Col. 0919B]. If there were no other promise or exhortation from God, this one example alone ought to suffice: here the Apostle sets Christ before us to persuade us to endure every adversity patiently, so that we may deserve to sit with Christ in glory.

Consider him who endured such opposition from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary or faint in your souls. The Apostle wished to indicate by the single term “opposition” all the adversities that Christ endured from the Jews: blows, mockery, spitting, slaps, insults, and death itself.

“Remember,” he says, “Christ, who endured such great and such grievous things from sinners, although he had committed no sin, so that you who are recognized as transgressors and sinners may not grow weary and faint in your souls [Col. 0919C], but, by imitating him, may endure similar things patiently.”

Christ endured opposition against himself—that is, he allowed them to act against him as they wished, contradicting them in nothing. He urges them not to faint in tribulations, since they had not yet reached martyrdom and the shedding of blood.

Hence he adds: “You have not yet resisted unto blood, struggling against sin.” It is as though he said: “Even if you have lost your earthly possessions, stripped by your fellow citizens, you have not yet suffered death. You still remain alive.”

He resisted unto blood, fighting against sin, who fought for the truth of faith against unbelievers even unto death, as the holy apostles and their successors did. For unbelief is the greatest sin. When someone wishes to deceive either by flattery or by threats, and fights for the faith against unbelievers, he is certainly struggling against sin.

This may also be understood of every sin: namely, evil suggestion, perverse will, and impure desire. Whoever resists these by refusing to consent to them is fighting against sin [Col. 0919D].

And you have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as sons, saying: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him.”

The Wisdom of God the Father, speaking through Solomon, among other things also uttered this through his mouth, which the blessed Apostle has now adopted as an example, urging the Jews not to faint in tribulation because they were being reproved by the Lord for the sake of testing [Col. 0920A].

He says: “My son, do not neglect”—or, “do not treat negligently”—the discipline of the Lord. Discipline is so called from *discere*, “to learn”; it can also be called correction of conduct. When someone is afflicted by hardships and tribulations, he should not grow weary or faint, but should endure patiently, reflecting that he is being corrected by the Lord.

For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives.

The Apostle presents these testimonies so that, just as sons are scourged by their parents so that they may become worthy to enter into their paternal inheritance—and for this reason they are often ordered to stand all night in the cold and are hardened in various ways—so these people too may endure God’s corrections with a cheerful spirit, so that they may become fit to reach the true inheritance of the eternal homeland [Col. 0920B].

For many serve the Lord in prosperity, yet fall away in adversity. Such people have not yet been perfectly tested so as to gain possession of the inheritance. Hence the Apostle, having taught them to live well in prosperity, urges them not to faint under correction. For the son whom the Lord loves, so that he may establish him as an heir of the kingdom of heaven, he chastises in various and different ways and scourges either through illness, poverty, persecution, or torments.

It should be noted, however, that not everyone who is scourged is a son, but every son is scourged. Which of the saints do we read has reached the inheritance of eternity from this world without divine scourging? Therefore, the less we should murmur against the scourge by which we are chastised, the more certainly we perceive in it the affection of paternal love.

Hence he himself says: “Those whom I love, I reprove and chastise” (Revelation III). Yet many were scourged, such as Antiochus and Herod—not so that they might be received into the inheritance, but so that it might be shown in part here what evils they would suffer after death [Col. 0920C].

Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as to dearly loved sons; one must understand: so that you may seize possession of the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. It is as though he said: “It is better for you to pass into the heavenly inheritance through discipline and correction, which are administered with paternal affection, than to be outside discipline and thus descend to the punishments of hell” [Col. 0920D].

Do you think that God hates you and has abandoned you because of the things you have suffered? If you had not suffered these things, then you would have had greater reason to think so. For if he scourges every son whom he receives, the one who is not scourged is certainly not among the sons.

By these words he shows them that the very thing by which they thought themselves abandoned gave them greater reason to believe that they were loved by him. For what son is there whom his father does not correct? A master of a household may sometimes neglect the children of others, but he chastises and corrects his own, lest harmful negligence overwhelm them.

There is no wise father who does not correct delinquent children; sometimes he even reproves those who are doing good, so that they may be kindled to better things. Hence Eli, because he did not correct his sons, [Col. 0921A] did not deserve to leave them as heirs of the priesthood after him (I Samuel I).

But if you are outside discipline, in which all good sons, or the holy Fathers mentioned above, have shared, then you are illegitimate and not sons. Whoever remains outside the Lord’s discipline, in which all good sons who belong to the heavenly inheritance have shared, is an illegitimate son and does not belong to the paternal inheritance, because he is not the son of a free woman. Beware lest you be illegitimate sons. For all unbelievers and negligent people who despise the Lord’s discipline are regarded as illegitimate and not sons.

Furthermore, we had fathers who instructed us, and we revered them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? In other words, we should consider that, since we had fathers who instructed us and feared them, we ought much more to obey God, the Father of spirits, and live in eternal glory. The Father of spirits, or Creator of souls, is almighty God, because he first created all things from nothing, and thereafter fashioned human bodies and those of other animals from the elements; but he created, and continues to create, the human soul from nothing. We must not think that the soul is a part of the Godhead, since the Godhead is uncreated, whereas the soul is created.

He therefore calls almighty God the Creator of souls, rather than of bodies, although he is the Creator of all things, because our body is formed from both paternal and maternal seed, while the soul is always created by God from nothing. “If,” he says, “we feared our earthly fathers, by whom we were instructed for a time so that we might become worthy to be their heirs, how much more ought we to obey and submit to the Creator of souls, so that we may live with him in the glory of eternal blessedness?”

There is not only a difference between them because of the distinction between their persons—for these fathers are earthly, whereas he is heavenly—but also because of the very purpose of their discipline and instruction. They do not instruct us for the same purpose or in spiritual matters, but for what seems good to them, as the Apostle makes clear when he says: “Those fathers of the flesh, from whose seed we received our bodies, instructed us for a few days according to their own will; but this one, namely the Father of spirits, instructs us for what is useful,” that is, for the salvation and benefit of our soul, “so that we may receive his sanctification.”

Earthly fathers instruct us so that we may be useful to them according to their own will, which is not useful in every respect. Almighty God, however, trains us for everything beneficial, so that we may attain salvation for our souls and receive his sanctification—that is, so that we may be holy in a certain manner, just as he himself is holy, according to what he says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XI). For this purpose, I say, he instructs and disciplines us: to make us worthy of his gifts.

Every nation, after all, instructs its sons according to its own will. Thus it was customary for the Romans to train their sons in military matters, and for the Greeks to educate theirs in letters.

[Col. 0922A] Now every discipline, while it is being undergone, seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

Every discipline, he says, both human and divine, when it is being learned, does not appear to be a discipline of joy but of sorrow. He called all discipline both divine and human because whatever is learned is called discipline. It does not appear at present to be a discipline of joy but of sorrow because the person undergoing it is very often beaten and constrained; he suffers ill repute, endures cold, and bears every kind of labor for the sake of the task being undertaken.

But when he has reached perfection, he rejoices and is glad, and receives a most welcome reward, as the Apostle says: “Afterward, when it has reached the summit of perfection, that same discipline will yield the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it,” that is, those tested and perfected by that same discipline. He calls the fruit “most peaceful” because it is the most welcome and acceptable recompense received by those who are trained and tested through that discipline.

For example, Roman recruits who were trained in military discipline first endured many hardships and later rejoiced, possessing sovereignty over the whole world. The same is to be understood of those who are afflicted under divine discipline and who are destined to receive eternal rewards, such as the holy apostles, martyrs, and teachers of the Church.

Therefore, raise your drooping hands and strengthen your weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray but rather be healed. Why “therefore”? Because the reward of recompense is given for discipline, and joy follows; or, alternatively, so that you may be able to receive the heavenly inheritance with the good sons. Raise your hands, which have drooped from good works and grown sluggish through the idleness of laziness, and your weakened knees, so as to perform good works.

By “feet” and “knees” we should understand good works, just as we do by “hands”; by “paths,” however, we should understand the intellect and intention of the mind. The meaning is: Perform such works as possess a perfect understanding, and let them be done with good intention. “Walk straight,” he says, “so that lameness does not increase further, but rather may be raised to a state of uprightness.”

He commands that drooping hands and weakened knees be raised, just as Isaiah also orders: “Strengthen the slack hands and make firm the feeble knees” (Isa. XXXV, 3), so that what is lame may not go astray—that is, so that one who hesitates may not stray from the path of uprightness in faith and good works, but rather may be healed from sins by believing rightly in God. It is as if he were saying: Whoever does not believe rightly should believe more firmly and steadfastly, so that in every way he may find healing for his soul. By these words he touches upon their hesitations, so that they might believe in God without any doubt.

Pursue peace with all people—he means, with good people—and holiness, without which no one will see God. There are indeed many things that display the form and character of Christianity, but mutual affection and peace, which unites the hearts of all people, are greater and better than everything else. Therefore the Truth itself says: “I leave you peace” (John XIV, 27); and again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid. XIII, 35). For this reason the Apostle says: “Pursue peace with all good people.”

By “peace” we are to understand love and concord. “Holiness” means purity of mind and body. It is as if he were saying: Love all good people as yourselves, and maintain chastity—or purity—of mind and body within yourselves, because without peace and holiness no one will see God. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

Take care that no one is lacking the grace of God. What does “take care” mean? It means attending and considering carefully, so that none of you, he says, may be deprived of the grace of God. He speaks to them as to travelers who remain on a long journey in a group and company, and to whom the person in charge ordinarily says: “See that no one remains behind who does not continue with us.”

It is as if he were saying: I do not require only that you yourselves obtain grace and enter the heavenly homeland; you must also look after the others. By “the grace of God” he means faith, hope, and charity, through which a person is worthy to find the grace of God, since whoever possesses these also possesses the other virtues. Or by “the grace of God” he means the remission of sins, which is freely given to us by God in baptism.

“See,” he says, “that none of you is alienated from the grace of God, which is given in baptism, or from perfect faith and the other virtues, lest some root of bitterness spring up and hinder, and through it many be defiled.” He calls the root of bitterness an evil will and perverse intention, from which the bitter fruit of sin proceeds. Just as a bitter root cannot produce sweet fruits but only those like itself—that is, bitter ones—and just as a sulfurous spring does not send forth water fit for drinking, so an evil will and perverse intention produce evil actions and the bitterness of sin. Through these the path of ascent to the heavenly homeland is obstructed, and through that evil will, from which the seeds of wickedness proceed, many are defiled.

For a little leaven corrupts the whole lump, and through a single sin of unbelief all the works that might have been good are corrupted; through a single sinner many are defiled. The root of bitterness may specifically be understood as the sin of unbelief, although, as we have said, it also refers to an evil will and wicked intention. He appropriately called sin bitter, because nothing is more bitter than it once it has been committed. Those who are tormented by the sorrow of conscience after committing a transgression know this by experience, and are consumed by dreadful bitterness to such an extent that the bitterness of the offense sometimes overturns the understanding and reason themselves, as we read concerning Cain, who fell into despair.

Let there be no fornicator or profane person like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright. Esau is called a fornicator because, against the will of his father and mother, he took foreign wives (Gen. XXXVI). Properly speaking, “profane” means irreligious, as if it meant “far from the sanctuary and temple of God”; here, however, it is used for a glutton, or for one who sells what is useful in exchange for what is worthless. This suits Esau well, for he was a glutton and gourmand, selling his birthright for cheap food—namely, red lentils.

Here “birthright” means the honor and dignity of the priesthood. Before the priesthood of Aaron, which was established by God in the Law, all firstborn sons were priests, as was Shem, who was also Melchizedek and the firstborn son of Noah. It was a great dignity to possess the birthright, since the firstborn also received the larger share of their father’s property and inheritance, and their clothing was richer and more splendidly adorned.

Thus we read in Genesis that Rebecca, taking Esau’s very fine garments, which she had at home, put them on Jacob and brought him to his father (Gen. XXVII). When Isaac perceived the smell and fragrance of his garments, he said: “See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field” (ibid.).

Since, therefore, there were among the Jews certain followers of Esau in fornication and gluttony, the Apostle recalls Esau’s deed to their memory, urging them to beware of all such people, lest anyone become like him, who for the pleasure of temporal things went so far as to sell his birthright. Through his own negligence and greed he sold the honor he had received from God, and for a small thing lost great glory. He who had been first became last, while he who had been second remained first.

For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected—he means, by God. The account in Genesis (ibid.) relates that Esau, returning from the field, learned that his brother had forestalled him in receiving his father’s blessing. He said with tears and a great cry: “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me also.” Isaac replied: “I have made him your lord; and now, my son, what can I do for you?” (ibid.).

At last, overcome by his cries, Isaac gave him a blessing concerning the riches of this world and that he would abound in the things produced by the earth, saying: “In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above shall your blessing be” (ibid.).

It is therefore evident that when he wished to inherit his father’s blessing—that is, to receive the dignity of the priesthood, which he had already lost, together with his father’s holiness and the spirit of prophecy—he was, because of his sins, brought to the point where he was rejected by God and deprived by his brother of his father’s blessing.

Hence what follows: “For he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.” Why did he find no place for repentance—that is, forgiveness through repentance—which he sought with tears? Because he did not seek it as he ought. Those tears were tears of indignation over his lost honor and of resentment against his brother, rather than of true humility and repentance. Thus he said: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and then I will kill my brother Jacob” (ibid.).

Therefore, although he sought it with tears, he could no longer reach that place of blessing as his brother had. He ought to have repented as we read that Peter did: after denying the Lord, he went outside and wept bitterly (Luke XXII). His great sin was forgiven because he performed repentance as he ought.

For you have not approached a tangible and accessible fire, and darkness, and storm, and tempest, and the sound of a trumpet, and a voice of words. It is customary for those who make comparisons to diminish and weaken one side so that the excellence of the other side may stand out. So too the Apostle now shows, by comparison with the things that occurred in the Old Testament, that our things are greater and brighter, gentler and better, and worthy of greater admiration.

He now distinguishes between Christ and Moses, between the Gospel and the Law, between heaven and Mount Sinai, and between the sprinkling of legal blood and the cleansing of Christ’s blood. These things are much better than those were. There the shadow rested; here the truth is held and revealed.

“You have not approached,” he says, “a tangible and accessible fire”—that is, you have not approached the visible and palpable light of fire that could be handled by bodily sight, as we read concerning the ancient Jewish people, but rather the invisible and incomprehensible God. These things are said to have occurred on Mount Sinai when the Law was given: fire, whirlwind, darkness, storm, the sound of a trumpet, and a voice of words. “The Lord God was seen on Mount Sinai” (Ex. XIX–XX).

A whirlwind is a powerful wind that carries away straw and whatever is light, enveloping it in the dust of the earth; it often even lifts up heavy objects. Darkness is the obscurity of smoke and fire. A storm is tempest and rain. These things occurred when the Law was given so that the hearts of the Jews, inclined toward sin, might be shaken and so that they would not dare transgress the Law.

There was also an earthquake, so that, struck with complete terror, they might take refuge with the God of heaven. Darkness, like the obscurity of smoke, signifies the obscurity of the Law itself. The whirlwind, or agitation of the winds, signifies the threat of the Law, which says: “If anyone does this or that, let him be put to death.” The storm signifies its vengeance. The sound of the trumpet signifies the presence and coming of almighty God, concerning which the same Apostle says elsewhere: “At the command and voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God he will descend from heaven” (I Thess. IV, 16). By the trumpet is understood the very voice of the angels. We must not suppose that the angels rebuked them with a bronze or horn trumpet.

The voice of words is also understood not to be the voice of almighty God himself, but of the angels. Through a subordinate creature—that is, through an angel—God spoke to Moses. That it was not God’s own voice the Lord demonstrates in the Gospel when he says to the Jews: “You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form” (John V). And that Moses spoke with an angel, not with the Lord, blessed Stephen shows in his sermon to the Jews: “This is the Moses who was with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai.”

The Gospel, however, was not given amid trembling or threats, but with paternal affection. The Lord spoke to the faithful as to sons. When he ascended the mountain and, among other precepts of life, presented the eight Beatitudes to them, no signs appeared or were seen by which they might be terrified, as happened when the Law was given.

It follows: “Those who heard the sound of the trumpets and the angels excused themselves, so that the word might not be spoken to them”—that is, so that he might not speak to them. They could not endure what was being said to them; that is, they could not bear the voice of the angel because of fear. Hence they also said to Moses: “Speak to us yourself, and let the Lord not speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. XX).

They had been struck with overwhelming fear, seeing the whole of Mount Sinai smoking, along with storms, thunder, and the sounds of trumpets (ibid.). “And if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned”—he means, with hailstones sent down from heaven. For the Lord had commanded: “Let the children of Israel keep far from the mountain, because if a human being or any beast approaches the mountain, it shall be killed with hailstones.” [Col. 0926B] What was seen was therefore so terrifying—he means, that they did not dare either to hear or to approach the mountain.

Moses said: “I am terrified and trembling.” If Moses was terrified, what should be said of the others? But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

This depends on what was said above: You did not approach the tangible and accessible fire of Mount Sinai, but you approached Mount Zion; the other statements were inserted parenthetically. By Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” and by Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” he wishes the heavenly homeland to be understood, namely the Church above, which consists of angels and righteous human beings, and which is approached by faith and desire.

“You have approached Mount Zion,” he says—that is, the city of the living God, Jerusalem—by faith and desire. You have approached the assembly, or multitude, of many thousands of angels, joined to them in faith and destined to be joined to them again in glory, according to what the Lord says: “The elect will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

And you have approached the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. By the Church of the firstborn we should understand the apostles, who were the first to believe, and to whose faith these people have been joined by believing; their names are written in the memory of almighty God, according to what the Truth himself said to them: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

And you have approached God, the judge of all—that is, the Lord Jesus, who says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). Through him God the Father will judge not only the Jews but all human beings.

And you have approached the spirit of perfected righteous people. By “the spirit of the righteous” he calls the Holy Spirit, by whom all are sanctified in baptism and receive from him the remission of all sins. They are rightly called “perfect,” because they will then exist as perfected righteous people when they have been cleansed from every defilement.

Or by “the spirit of perfected righteous people” he means the souls of the saints who have proved acceptable to God, to whom those people had been joined by faith and desire.

You have also approached Jesus, the mediator of the New Testament. The Lord Jesus is our mediator because he is at once human and God. Just as Moses was mediator between God and the people, conveying God’s words to the people and then the people’s words back to God, as he himself says: “I was the mediator between the Lord and you” (Deut. V, 5), so the Lord Jesus conveyed to us the words of God the Father and now conveys ours to him, continually interceding for us, while also confirming the New Testament for us through his passion.

You have also approached the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel. Following the language of the Law, he signifies Christ’s cleansing by the term “sprinkling,” since the cleansing that took place through blood was called sprinkling. They therefore approached Christ’s blood, or cleansing—that is, his passion—because they were cleansed through faith in his passion.

The blood of Christ speaks better than Abel’s blood because Abel’s blood demanded vengeance against his brother’s murderer, whereas Christ’s blood implored life and forgiveness for his persecutors, when he said to the Father: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

Or it speaks better because it makes us proclaim that Jesus himself is the Son of God, through whose passion we have been redeemed and through whose baptism we have been washed; and because through his blood we have been made sons of God.

See that you do not refuse the one who speaks. This means: Beware lest you despise Jesus speaking through his Gospel, since he sits at the right hand of the Father, observing what each of us does (Luke XXIV). For if those people did not escape when they refused the one who spoke on earth, much less shall we escape if we turn away from the one who speaks to us from heaven.

It is as if he were saying: If your fathers did not escape the vengeance of almighty God when they transgressed his commandments, which were given to them through Moses or through an angel—both of whom spoke on earth—much less shall we be able to escape his vengeance if we despise the commandments given through the Son.

They heard him speaking on earth; we hear him from heaven. Because of the unity of person that the Son of God possesses in two natures, he is said to speak to us from heaven. On earth he appeared to speak through his humanity, but he was on earth and in heaven through his divinity. Hence he himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III). Likewise, while the Gospel is preached on earth, he himself speaks to us from heaven. Therefore he must be heard much more than Moses.

It follows: “Whose voice then shook the earth”—he means, when the Law was given—“but now he promises, saying: Once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.” The one who then shook Mount Sinai by his command, and the earth around it where the people were standing, when he gave the Law to Moses, now promises that not merely part of the earth, nor the whole earth alone, but also heaven will be shaken.

Therefore, the greater the works he promises to accomplish, the more greatly he is to be feared. Although there have often been earthquakes in different places and regions of the world, there has not been one throughout the whole world; and although the earth has been shaken, heaven has not. Hence he rightly says that this will happen once, on the day of judgment, showing that the heavens and earth will never again be shaken.

Therefore it also follows: “And the phrase ‘once more’ indicates the removal of things that can be shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.” This shaking of heaven and earth refers to their renewal and improvement. As the day of judgment approaches, the earth will indeed endure a shaking, but heaven and earth alike will be moved and changed from their present form into a better one, according to what the Apostle says elsewhere: “The form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII).

When its form has been changed, its substance will remain, and afterward there will be a new heaven and a new earth. Here, however, understand “heaven” not as the starry or ethereal heaven, but this aerial heaven, from which birds are also called “birds of heaven.”

Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom—he means, now in hope, but one that we shall possess in reality—we have grace, through which we may serve God acceptably with fear and reverence.

The unshakable kingdom is the heavenly Church, which consists of angels and righteous human beings. This Church is the kingdom of God, and almighty God is the kingdom of the Church. We receive this kingdom now in hope, but then we shall possess it in reality, when Christ hands the kingdom over to God the Father.

It is called an unshakable kingdom because, if heaven and earth will remain unshakable after their transformation, much more will the elect, after the resurrection, receive unshakable immortality in the body and unchangeability in the soul, reigning eternally with God. They themselves will be the unshakable kingdom of almighty God, and their kingdom will be the contemplation of the holy Trinity.

Since we shall receive this unshakable kingdom in reality, the Apostle urges us to have grace, through which we may serve God in a way pleasing to him. By “grace” he means right faith, certain hope, perfect charity, and holy conduct. Through these we must serve God with fear, fearing him as God and judge of all, and with reverence, loving him as Father. We must fear him lest we be disciplined here and afterward separated from rest.

## CHAPTER XIII

For our God is a consuming fire. Almighty God is called fire, not because he consumes the material that he made, but because he consumes what a human being has drawn upon himself externally—namely, the rust of sins. He does not consume what he himself made, but what human wickedness has introduced.

This fire also performs another action: it sets human hearts aflame with the love of God. Concerning this fire the Truth says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII, 49). The earthly hearts of people are called “earth,” because, while they are always occupied with lowly thoughts and earthly desires, they are trampled by evil spirits as though they were earth.

But the Lord casts fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he sets the hearts of carnal people aflame with love of God and neighbor. This is why almighty God is called fire: because he consumes the rust of sins and sets human hearts on fire with charity. But one may still ask why he is compared with fire. The answer is that, just as fire lies hidden in flints and rocks, so almighty God remains in his creation, though he is not seen.

Let brotherly love remain among you. This means: Love everyone as yourselves, remembering that you have one almighty God as Father and one Church as mother—or that you were begotten from one father, Adam, and one mother, Eve.

And do not forget hospitality. He did not say, “Be hospitable,” but, “Do not forget hospitality.” Before they had been stripped of their possessions, they had been very devoted to hospitality; but after they had been deprived of most of their property, they had again become excessively tight-fisted. Therefore the Apostle urges them to fulfill the duty of hospitality according to their means, saying to them: “Do not consign your former hospitality to oblivion.”

Hospitality should be practiced with a cheerful mind and joyful spirit, according to what blessed Peter says: “Be hospitable to one another without complaining” (I Pet. IV, 9). And elsewhere: “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7).

It follows: “For through this some have pleased God by receiving angels as guests,” as Abraham did, who deserved to receive the promise concerning a son, and Lot, who was delivered from the destruction of Sodom. Therefore the Judge of all will say on the day of judgment: “As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

Remember those in chains as though you were chained with them; that is, just as you would wish help to be given to you and yourselves to be remembered if you were imprisoned in a jail, so remember those who are held in bonds for the faith of Christ, as though you yourselves were chained with them.

And remember those who suffer—as though you too were still dwelling in the body. Since you still remain in the body and know by experience what those who suffer require, remember those who labor in teaching and holy conduct, supplying them with food and clothing, just as you would wish to be remembered if you were suffering in the same way.

For, because you remain in a mortal body, you know by experience, as they do, that “a human being’s life upon earth is a warfare” (Job VII, 1), and that “a human being is born to labor, as a bird is born to fly.”

Let marriage be held in honor among us, as pleases God, and let the marriage bed be undefiled. “Marriage” is so called from *connubere*, “to marry.” At that time there were some who condemned marriage, saying that conjugal union was unclean and that no one could rise pure from a spouse’s bed.

Therefore the blessed Apostle not only permits legitimate marriage, whose purpose is the love of children rather than the satisfaction of lust, but also says that it pleases God. An honorable marriage is to take a wife lawfully out of love for children, to abstain from her at appointed times, and not to have several wives, since at the beginning, as Scripture says, “God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them,” and he said to them: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I).

It is also said in what follows that the two would become one flesh. The marriage bed of such a union is undefiled—that is, legitimate intercourse without fornication, and an undefiled bed from which the participants rise undefiled, not carrying away from it the stain of sin.

Thus blessed Matthew the Apostle says in one place that legitimate marriage and an undefiled marriage bed possess, in a certain sense, the uncleanness of the mingling of seed, but do not possess the stain of sin. It is better to take a legitimate wife than to commit fornication with prostitutes or to violate another man’s wife.

But if the marriage is not legitimate, nor entered into for love of children but for the satisfaction of lust, and if there are several wives, then the marriage is no longer honorable, nor is the marriage bed undefiled. For God has judged fornicators and adulterers.

To fornicate is to defile oneself in any manner and to satisfy lust; to commit adultery is to violate another person’s marriage bed. Hence an adulterer is so called as one who violates another’s marriage bed.

But will almighty God judge—that is, condemn—only fornicators and adulterers, leaving aside murderers, sacrilegious people, thieves, and those involved in various other crimes? Certainly not. Why, then, did the Apostle specifically say that fornicators and adulterers would be judged? Evidently because there was no hesitation concerning murderers, sacrilegious people, robbers, parricides, and others weighed down by the burden of sins: there was no doubt that they were to be condemned.

But at that time there were some who doubted concerning fornicators and adulterers, saying that God had made males and females for the purpose of intercourse and that it was therefore not a sin to sleep with any woman. This is entirely far from the truth.

Therefore, when the Apostle had first said that honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage bed please God, he immediately added: “For God will judge fornicators and adulterers,” showing that fornicators and adulterers are justly judged. If marriage has been permitted, then fornicators are justly subjected to punishment and adulterers are justly punished.

Let your conduct be without avarice, and be content with what you have. “Conduct” means an honorable life and good living. He did not say, “Do not possess riches,” but, “Let your conduct”—that is, your life and way of living—be without avarice.

An avaricious person is called one who is greedy for gold, because he is stingy in giving and covetous in receiving, with a hand closed for giving and extended for receiving. Concerning this, a certain wise man gave the warning: “Let your hand not be extended to receive and closed when giving.”

Perhaps, after they had been stripped of their own possessions by unbelievers, they desired to gather riches again by withholding alms. Therefore the Apostle warned them that their conduct should be without avarice, content only with the necessities presently available and not anticipating the future, in accordance with what he had urged elsewhere: “Having food and clothing, with these let us be content” (I Tim. VI).

And lest they perhaps say, “What shall we do if the support we need should happen to fail us?” he added consolation by presenting testimony from the book of Joshua. Almighty God himself said: “I will not abandon you or forsake you.” After Moses’ death the Lord said to Joshua: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. Be strong and courageous” (Dan. X); “I will not abandon you or forsake you.”

This example applies to Joshua, but likewise to every elect person who has placed his hope in God. For he in no way lies if we place our hope in him.

Thus—he means, he is with us—so that we may confidently say: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.” Here the word “man” means not only any fleshly adversary but also the ancient enemy, who is called “man” by taking his name from his function, because he deceives human beings, just as Christ is called a lion because of his strength.

Therefore the Prophet says: “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man” (Ps. CXXXIX)—that is, from the devil. In all our tribulations and temptations, then, we ought to cry out this verse of the Psalmist or the Apostle, saying: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me”—that is, what any enemy or adversary can do.

Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith. All prelates and teachers, insofar as they preach good things and perform good works, are to be heard and imitated. But insofar as they either do not preach rightly or live badly, they are neither to be heard nor imitated.

For example, if someone preaches rightly and lives well, he is to be heard and imitated. If he does neither, he is not to be heard or imitated. But if he preaches rightly, even though he lives badly, he is not to be despised so that he is not heard.

Therefore the Lord said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII).

Since these people had good leaders—namely, the holy apostles and their successors—the Apostle urges them to remember them and their way of life, considering their outcome—that is, their perseverance to the end in right faith and good works—and to imitate their faith, meaning their steadfastness in goodness.

Since their way of life had a good end, he therefore says: “Imitate their faith.” By “faith” he means their steadfastness and perseverance.

Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, he himself also throughout the ages. These words belong to what precedes, where he testified that God had said: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” They could have replied that this did not pertain to God’s promise, because it was not promised to us, but rather God made this promise to Joshua. To this the Apostle responds: “Do not lose heart, for just as this promise pertains to Joshua, so it pertains to you, because Jesus Christ, being of one essence with the Father, was himself at that time, is himself now, will himself be so, and will remain so throughout the ages.” Do not suppose that he who existed then does not exist now. The same one who was yesterday will also be the same throughout the age. “Yesterday” signifies past time; “today,” the present; “the ages,” the future without end—as though he were saying: Before the ages, throughout the ages, and after the ages, he will always remain, as the Prophet says of him: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Heb. I).

Do not allow yourselves to be led away by various and foreign doctrines. Various and foreign doctrines are the new teachings of heretics, [Col. 0932A] by which simpler people are led away and separated from the truth of the faith; they are also the superstitions of the Jews, who teach that one must abstain from certain foods forbidden by the Law, while allowing others. Since, therefore, there were among them some who were carnally minded and who, through observance of and distinctions among foods, led certain people astray, drawing them away from the evangelical doctrine, which says that “all things are clean to the clean” (Tit. I), the Apostle addresses them so that they would not be led away by that foreign doctrine. He makes this clearer by adding: “For it is good that the heart be established by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those who have walked in them.” “It is good,” he says, “and perfect to establish and strengthen the mind in the grace of the New Testament, so that you may have perfect faith, believing that all things are clean to the clean, rather than establishing yourselves in distinctions and observances [Col. 0932B] of foods, calling some foods clean and others unclean—observances that have benefited nothing those who have lived by them.” After the Lord’s coming, all those things that were enacted symbolically came to an end, and especially after the Lord said: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person”; rather, “all things are clean to the clean.” For God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. It is better to retain faith together with perfect conduct than to dispute about distinctions among foods, rejecting what God created clean. For there is one perfect observance: to abstain from sins. Abstaining from foods is of no benefit if one does not abstain from sins. For although they devoted themselves to such observances, [Col. 0932C] it benefited them nothing if they did not have faith. Insofar as they kept the Law, it benefited them; insofar as they did not eat certain foods, they gained no benefit whatever.

We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat. The Apostle refers the legal custom to a spiritual and mystical meaning. The commandment of the Law was that on the tenth day of the seventh month after the Passover feast—namely, the feast of the offering—they should take a calf and a goat and sacrifice them outside the camp. The high priest was to carry the blood of those animals into the Holy of Holies, praying there alone for the people; their flesh, however, was to be carried outside the camp and burned there, and no one serving the tabernacle was permitted to eat from it. Spiritually, those two animals—the calf and the goat—prefigured the Lord the Savior. For he is the calf whom the loving father sacrificed at the return of the prodigal son; he is also the goat who was offered for sinners. That high priest, too, who entered the Holy of Holies with the blood of those animals to pray for the people, bore the type of the true High Priest, who entered the inner regions of the heavenly homeland with the blood of his passion, praying for his faithful. Those animals were sacrificed within the camp, but their flesh was burned outside the camp, because our Redeemer was likewise sacrificed in Jerusalem, as though within the camp, by the words and judgment of the children of Israel; but his flesh was burned outside Jerusalem on the cross [Col. 0933A] by the fire of his passion. For when he was condemned to death, while the Jews were crying out (Matt. XXVI), “He is guilty of death! Crucify him, crucify him!”, he was, so far as they were concerned, in a certain sense sacrificed. Mark the Evangelist, wishing to show that this was so, says: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark XV)—namely, with their tongues. For at the sixth hour he was raised upon the cross outside Jerusalem, and there his body was consumed by the fire of his passion.

That Jewish altar which was made outside the camp, where the flesh was consumed, is the altar of the Church, where the body of Christ is consecrated daily. We therefore have the altar of the Church, where the Lord’s body is consecrated, and those who serve the tabernacle of their body have no authority to eat from it: namely, fornicators, adulterers, drunkards, [Col. 0933B] the unclean, those who sow discord among brothers, and all who serve the pleasures and desires of their flesh. “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. XI).

For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the Holy Place by the high priest as a sin offering are burned outside the camp. How these things pertain to God has, I think, been explained sufficiently. But since he himself is the head of all the elect, through the flesh of those animals all the elect may be understood—those who are outside the camp, that is, outside the way of life of worldly and carnal people, who put to death the members of their bodies together with their vices and desires, or who, as martyrs for Christ’s name, endure every adversity; who, set aflame by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, consume in themselves whatever is fluid [Col. 0933C] and lustful, and burn equally with the love of devotion to God and neighbor.

They are consumed outside the camp in two ways: either when, as we have said, they put to death their members together with their vices and desires, or when, following the example of the Lord’s passion, they undergo martyrdom and receive the palm of martyrdom, in accordance with the exhortation of blessed Peter: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. II). Their blood is brought into the Holy Place by the high priest when their praiseworthy life is presented to God the Father through the true Priest, Jesus, who is our advocate and intercedes for us. And it is appropriately understood as blood, because “the life of a human being is in the blood.” Or their blood is brought into the Holy Place when their souls are carried to the heavenly realms in triumph over their passion [Col. 0933D]. They are also rightly consumed upon the altar, because the holy martyrs accomplish all these things in faith, by which they believe that they will be rewarded by God. Those things consecrated upon this altar are not permitted to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle, because those who live carnally and are held fast by love of this world dare not approach what the holy martyrs fulfill by enduring in perfect faith.

Therefore—that is, to fulfill the mystery—Jesus, in order to sanctify through his blood the people who believe in him, suffered outside the gate. As the book of the Gospels testifies, saying: “Outside the gate of Jerusalem he suffered in the place of the beheaded, which was called [Col. 0934A] Calvary” (Matt. XXVII). Thus, in order to convert the shadow and figure into the reality that had been prefigured concerning himself and his members, and to redeem and cleanse by his blood the people who believed in him, the Lord suffered outside Jerusalem.

Let us therefore go out to God outside the camp, bearing his reproach. Since the Lord suffered for us, the Apostle exhorts us to imitate him, saying: “Since he himself suffered outside the camp in order to sanctify us, let us go out to him outside the way of life of carnal people, putting to death our members together with their vices and desires, and let us imitate his passion by enduring martyrdom for him.” To bear his reproach means to suffer the same things that he suffered. His cross appears to the pagans to be his reproach, but to us it is sanctification and redemption. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, despising present things, loving future things, scorning visible things, and desiring and loving eternal things. He continues:

For we have no enduring city here, but we seek the one that is to come. It is certain that in this world we cannot have an eternal dwelling or a city that always remains, since the world and its desire will pass away. Therefore we ought, with our utmost efforts, to strive toward the heavenly city of Jerusalem, whose inhabitant is God, who will remain eternally.

Through him, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise—that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name [Col. 0934C]. Through him, that is, Christ, we ought to offer God the Father a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving for all the good things received from him. He calls thanksgiving the fruit of the lips because those same acts of thanksgiving merit the fruit of rewards. Hence the Apostle says that “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). They offered cattle, therefore, but we offer none of these things; rather, we ought to offer God thanksgiving alone. Concerning this sacrifice the Psalmist says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. XLIX).

And do not forget beneficence and fellowship. For by such sacrifices God is won over. A beneficent person is called generous and devoted to almsgiving. From this comes the term “beneficence,” meaning generosity in almsgiving. “Do not forget,” he says, “beneficence and fellowship”—that is, generosity in almsgiving and fellowship, through which you ought to share and distribute to others from your resources. Even if others have seized your possessions, do not forget to give alms from what you have, as the Prophet says: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL). By such sacrifices and gifts of alms, God is won over and his favor obtained. Hence the Prophet says: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI). One should not consider the poor person who appears to receive, but rather the one who commanded the giving. The alms given to the poor on earth are received by God in heaven. And do not consider what you are to receive: you gave earth, but he will return heaven; [Col. 0935A] you gave temporal things, and you will purchase eternal ones.

Obey your leaders and submit to them. One must obey all prelates and preachers insofar as their teaching and conduct are holy and devout. But if they stray from the way of righteousness, like the scribes and Pharisees, let us not do what they do, but what they say—unless, perhaps, they have become contrary in the faith. For if they have become contrary in the faith, they must not only be avoided but also fled from. But if they teach well while differing from Christ in their conduct, let us hear him speaking about such people in the person of the scribes and Pharisees: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do everything whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works, [Col. 0935B] for they say and do not do” (Matt. XXI).

For they keep watch, as though they were going to give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning. All prelates and leaders must indeed be obeyed, unless they have strayed from the truth of the faith; but especially those who keep watch—that is, those who watch without interruption in preaching, in good example, and in concern for external matters, being solicitous about how they will give an account for them. Therefore we ought to be subject to our leaders, who are concerned for us, since they will give an account for us, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning—that is, so that they may care for us with gladness and cheerfulness, not with complaint and disturbance of mind. For the bad conduct and disobedience of subjects often provoke the minds of prelates to bitterness, so that they become more sluggish and sorrowful regarding their progress [Col. 0935C]; or we ought to obey them so that on the day of judgment they may give an account for us with joy, confident of their reward, and not groaning, anxious about our condemnation. For this is not beneficial to you: namely, that they should care for you with groaning or give an account for you with sadness.

Pray for us. Here he destroys the pride and arrogance of mind of certain bishops who, inflated by the appearance of pride, disdain to ask their subjects to pour out prayers for them. If, therefore, he who was called by the Lord to become the teacher and master of all nations did not disdain to ask that his subjects—whom he had acquired for the Lord—should pray for him, how much more do those filled with envy, robbery, and other vices need the assistance of their subjects’ prayers? He continues: “For we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to conduct ourselves well in all things.” The Apostle was accused by the Jews of not loving his own people as he loved the Gentiles, and therefore he addresses them gently and imploringly, showing that he had goodwill toward all people, that is, toward both Jews and Gentiles. “We are confident,” he says—I and my companions—“that we have goodwill toward all people, desiring to conduct ourselves well toward both Jews and Gentiles.” Do not bring forward accusations or disparagements, for our conscience reproaches us in nothing [Col. 0936A] and does not condemn us for lacking goodwill toward you.

But I urge you all the more to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly. It is indeed my will to come to you; therefore I earnestly urge you to pray for me, so that my desire to come to you may quickly be fulfilled. It should be noted that he first asked them for the assistance of their prayer, and then, not simply but with complete intention and every possible effort, he pours out a devout prayer to the Lord for them, saying:

Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great Shepherd of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant. The “God of peace” in this passage is understood as God the Father, from whom true peace proceeds, who loves peace, and who reconciled us completely to himself through the blood of his Son. He brought the great Shepherd of the sheep back from the dead—that is, from the tomb, which is properly the place of the dead—raising him on the third day, in accordance with what the Son himself prayed when approaching his passion: “Father, glorify your Son” (John XVII), that is, “Raise your Son.” And what does God the Father say to him in the psalm? “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery” (Ps. LVI), that is, the choir of all virtues. The Son replies: “I will awake at dawn” (ibid.).

God the Father therefore brought his Son back from the dead, that is, from hell or from the tomb, in accordance with what the psalm had foretold: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV). And, so to speak, the Son himself raised himself by the power of the Word. For just as the whole Trinity created that man in the Virgin’s womb, so the whole Trinity brought him back from the dead, since those three Persons act indivisibly. The Lord Jesus is the great Shepherd who leads his sheep to the pastures of life and the pleasant green meadows of paradise. He is the Shepherd who says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John X). His sheep are the elect, of whom he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life” (ibid.).

May he fit you—that is, prepare you—and make you perfect in every good thing, so that you may do his will, himself doing in you what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen. “May the God of peace,” he says, “fit you for every good thing,” that is, make you suitable in right faith, in teaching, and in perfect conduct, [Col. 0936D] so that you may fulfill his will, while he himself does in you what is pleasing to him. For you can have no good thing from yourselves unless he goes before and follows after you, in accordance with what the psalm entreats, saying: “His mercy will go before me, and his mercy will follow me” (Ps. LVIII). The Apostle also says elsewhere: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. II). He accomplishes all these things through Jesus Christ in prayer, because through him we were made and redeemed, and through him whatever good we have is supplied to us. To him—that is, to God the Father and to Jesus Christ—be glory throughout all future ages. Amen. “Amen” is a confirmation, equivalent to “let it be,” or “it is truly so, as he has said.”

[Col. 0937A] But I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation. For indeed I have written to you only briefly. Note that he called the whole Epistle one “word,” and did not say, “I ask you to bear patiently the word of admonition,” because they were fainthearted, but “the word of consolation”—that is, a word of comfort and exhortation. For I have not written much to you, but little, compared with what I would say to you if I were present, fearing that I might be a burden to you.

Know that our brother Timothy has been released. Timothy was the blessed Apostle’s fellow bishop and assistant in preaching. He says that Timothy was released by him and sent out for preaching, or perhaps from Athens, where the Apostle had left him. It may also be understood that Timothy had been held in prison and was then released. With him—that is, with Timothy—if he comes more quickly, I will see you. He wishes to make them gentler by saying that he is ready to come to them.

Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Just as he had written this Epistle generally to all the Hebrews, so he wished all generally to enjoy good health, not only the prelates but also all their subjects, whom he calls saints because they had been holy in baptism [Col. 0938A]. At the same time, he flatters them by greeting them honorably, so that they might recognize that he loved them—not merely outwardly, but with complete affection of mind. The brothers from Italy greet you. In these words he very clearly indicates to us that he wrote this Epistle at Rome, which is situated in the Italian region, and, as the teachers think, that he was at that time in prison.

Grace be with you all. Amen. Grace means something freely given. Here, however, by the name “grace” we must understand perfect faith together with the performance of good works; also the remission of sins, which the elect receive at the time of baptism; and the gift of the Holy Spirit, which is given both in baptism and through the laying on of the bishops’ hands. All these things are given freely by God. The Apostle therefore prays that those to whom he was writing might possess them all. Let us also pray to the Lord in devout supplication that, through the intercession of his outstanding Apostle, he may make us possessors of these things in the present, and that, keeping with complete integrity the faith he taught and adorning it with good works, we may, with Christ as our guide, deserve to attain the contemplation of the heavenly vision. Amen.

[Col. 0937]

THE SEVEN BOOKS OF THE EXPOSITION OF HAYMO, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT, ON THE APOCALYPSE OF BLESSED JOHN.

(According to the edition published at Cologne in the year 1531, by Eucharius, under the supervision of Godefrid Hittorp.) (G)*

PREFACE OF HAYMO.

[Col. 0937C] We read in ecclesiastical history that blessed John was banished by the most impious Caesar Domitian to the island of Patmos, carried into exile, and condemned to the mines because of his unconquerable preaching of the Gospel, so that there perhaps he might keep watch over the secret recesses of the marble quarries, dig the earth, or perform similar tasks imposed by imperial commands, as we read happened in the passions of the holy martyrs. There, the more he was thought to be bound by human custody, the more he deserved—transcending the limits of humanity—to see heavenly things. To him, who was denied the ability to travel beyond the confines of the earth, permission was granted to penetrate heavenly secrets. And the more he was deprived of human comfort, the more divine assistance was present to him.

There he deserved to see this prophecy concerning the condition of the present and future Church. Among the other books of the New Testament it is called a prophecy, as is said below: “Blessed is he who reads the words of this prophecy.” But the difference between this prophecy [Col. 0938C] and that which was revealed before the Lord’s coming is as great as the difference between servant and master, between Law and Gospel, between God and human being. For what those earlier prophets saw as coming from afar, this prophet shows to have already been accomplished in large part and to be in the process of being accomplished in the present. For just as blessed John the Baptist is regarded as greater than all the prophets because what they foretold he pointed out with his finger, so this prophecy is greater than all the others, because what the ancient prophecy foretold would be revealed, this prophecy shows to have been revealed.

In this revelation nothing historical is to be understood, as the very words themselves, if examined carefully, demonstrate. For it is impossible, to mention only a little of much, that he literally saw horses in a vision whose riders wore breastplates of fire, hyacinth, and sulfur. Our fathers said that three kinds of visions are to be understood. The first is bodily, such as when [Col. 0939A] with the eyes of the body we see heaven and earth, the sun and the moon, and other things of this sort.

The second is spiritual. It occurs in ecstasy—that is, in an excess of mind—whether men are awake or asleep, when they do not perceive bodily things but, seeing likenesses of bodily things, foresee future mysteries in them. This kind of vision is common to the righteous and the reprobate, as when Nebuchadnezzar saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands, and Pharaoh saw seven fat cows and seven full ears of grain, and so forth. Yet neither understood what he had seen unless Daniel revealed the mystery of the vision to the one and Joseph to the other. Nor is it surprising that the reprobate need an explanation of such obscurities, since Daniel himself, not understanding what the four winds that contended on the great sea signified, approached one of those standing there and asked him about all these things [Col. 0939B].

The third kind is intellectual. It does not occur through bodily things or through likenesses, but the truth itself is manifested in the minds of those who see. This belongs properly to the elect. In this way the prophets spoke, because they saw and understood the things they said. Hence they were called “seers,” as the history of the Books of Kings makes clear when it says: “For he who is called a prophet today was formerly called a seer.” Thus the prophecies seen by the prophets themselves are called visions: hence “The Vision of Isaiah,” “The Vision of Amos,” and the others. Because this vision is intellectual, it is considered more subtle than the others.

John spoke through this kind of vision, since divine power showed him such great mysteries in his mind. This revelation itself took place through an angel, but the angel bore the figure of Christ, who spoke through him, just as the one who formerly spoke to Moses did. Hence Moses sometimes says that God spoke to him, and at other times that an angel did.

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0939]

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0939B]

The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ. The sense would be clearer if he had added a verb and said, “This is the Apocalypse”; but we frequently find in the divine Scriptures this manner of expression, in which a verb is omitted. Thus Solomon does not say, “These are the proverbs of Solomon,” or “These are the words of Ecclesiastes,” but simply, “The Proverbs of Solomon” and “The Words of Ecclesiastes, king of Jerusalem.” Isaiah likewise says, “The Vision of Isaiah,” without any verbal support. So do the others. By speaking in this way, they have taught that such sentences contain the necessary implied words.

For example, when we read, “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ,” we must supply, “This is.” “Apocalypse” is a Greek word, and in Latin it is called “revelation” or “manifestation,” because in it the condition of the present and future Church was manifested to blessed John and, through him, to the Church. Which God gave him to make known to his servants. Here too the expression would be clearer if he had said, “which”; but this manner of expression also frequently occurs in Scripture. Thus we find: “I have fought the good fight” (2 Tim. IV), instead of “I have fought with a good fight.”

This revelation of the Lord Jesus Christ, which he received from God in order to make manifest through his revelation to his servants the things that must shortly take place, designates both his natures in these words: his divine nature, in that he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, reveals all the mysteries; and his human nature, in that he received from the Father and the Holy Spirit—and also from himself—the commission to manifest through his revelation to his servants the things that must shortly take place.

For in this passage “God” is understood as the whole Trinity. From it the man assumed by the Word of God received the commission to reveal these mysteries to his servants; and here the very form of a servant is proclaimed as mistress of servants. He manifested them to his servants—that is, to those who follow his commandments. Elsewhere he says to them: “When you have done everything that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unworthy servants’” (Luke XVII). The heavenly revelation is not opened to servants of the Mosaic Law, that is, to Jews, nor to philosophers devoted to worldly wisdom, but to those subject to divine grace. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI).

Things that must shortly take place. These words encompass two things: namely, that those things which must be brought to an end should soon reach their conclusion, and that those things which must be begun should soon take their beginning. Nevertheless, these things will in no way receive an end. Therefore the torments that pass away are not to be feared, but those that endure forever are to be feared. Nor should fleeting joys be sought, but joys that remain in an unchanging state.

“Shortly,” that is, in the present time. For all the time of the present life, compared with eternity, is like the tiniest moment of a single hour. Hence John himself also says in his Epistle concerning this very long period: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John II). Christ therefore reveals to John—that is, to his Church—both the things that quickly pass away and the things that quickly arrive, so that when it sees itself afflicted or prospering temporally, it may consider the brevity of this period: how quickly joys and tribulations pass away with time, and how quickly those same things that will remain without end draw near. Thus it should not envy the prosperity of the wicked, but rather rejoice in its own adversities.

And he signified. Here we must understand “signified” as deriving not from “display” but from “sign”; thus “he signified” means “he sealed,” for a sign is called a seal. At this point a question arises: why is this said, when later we find the angel saying to John, “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book” (Rev. XXII)? It must be known that Holy Scripture is closed by a sign to the impious but opened to the faithful. Riches are not locked under a seal for faithful servants, but for thieves and robbers. By saying, therefore, “he signified,” he taught that the revelation was closed to unbelievers but opened to the faithful through spiritual exercise. Hence Daniel is told: “Go, because the words are closed and sealed until the appointed time” (Dan. XII).

Sending it through his angel to his servant John. This angel appeared to blessed John in the figure of Christ. Since the Son is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, revealing all things, he also filled that angel; dwelling inwardly in them, he spoke through him to John. John himself bears the figure of the Church, as we shall see below. Christ appeared to him—as has been said—not in his own nature, but through an angel, just as he formerly appeared to the fathers [Col. 0941B].

When the ministry for which he had come was completed, he was also seen by human beings for as long as was necessary, until he ascended into heaven on the fortieth day. Thereafter he did not wish to appear through the substance he had assumed from us. Therefore we must not seek his bodily presence, but rather believe that he is everywhere in divine majesty. Thus the whole Son of God, through his divinity, was in the angel; whole and entire, he remained with the Father and the Holy Spirit in heaven. This is attributed to no other than that incorporeal and simple nature which is wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, wholly without place in place, and wholly without parts in parts.

What is surprising, then, if after his incarnation an angel appearing in the likeness of the Son of Man is mentioned, as we find below [Col. 0941C], when even the angels who appeared to the holy fathers long before his coming are called men? In this connection blessed Ansbertus Ambrosius says: “It may also be believed that, after his ascension, the Lord appeared to the blessed Apostle Paul not in his own nature, but rather only through an angel in that form in which he is accustomed to be recognized by human beings. This may also be proved from the fact that, if blessed Paul, newly converted, had seen him in his own substance, it would follow that he would have appeared to the disciple whom he loved above all and who had been devoted to him from youth, not through an angel but by himself.”

The phrase “sending it through his angel to his servant John” follows the custom of the holy Fathers, who in their writings speak of themselves as though of another person. Thus we find: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job,” and so on, [Col. 0941D] ending with “turning away from evil” (Job I). Also: “Moses was a very meek man above all who dwelt on the earth” (Num. XII). John himself often does the same in his Gospel: “This is the disciple whom Jesus loved.”

Who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ. John bore witness to the word of God when he said (John I): “In the beginning was the Word”; and, “All things were made through him”; and, “He was the true light that enlightens everyone,” and the other things that follow in that passage concerning the divinity of the Word. He bore witness to Jesus Christ when he said: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). In saying these things we do not divide the Persons, but show both natures.

When he says “whatever he saw,” we must supply: whatever he knew concerning the incarnate Word of God, whether in his divinity or in his humanity. He saw one thing with the eyes of the body and another with the eyes of the mind: with the eyes of the mind he saw the divinity, and with the eyes of the body the humanity. He saw him begotten by the Father before all the ages and creating all things with the Father. He saw him born at the end of time from a mother for our salvation; then suffering, buried by a righteous man, raised from the dead, and exalted to the right hand of the Father; and thereafter coming to judgment. He saw all these things and bore witness, and we know that his testimony is true.

But what John did, the Church also does daily—the Church of which he was a member and in whose figure he saw this Apocalypse. From its mouth his testimony does not depart, because it continually [Col. 0942B] adheres to his teaching.

Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this prophecy and keeps what is written in it. For the time is near. In these words two kinds of persons are included: teachers, who read and explain to others, and hearers, who hear, retain, and fulfill in practice what is written in it. Although this book contains many profound mysteries, it nevertheless includes many things which, even when kept according to the letter, provide great benefit and salvation to those who observe them.

They keep what is written in it who do not violate the faith of Christ and the Church, who avoid what is forbidden and fulfill what is commanded, fear the punishments that have been threatened, and love the heavenly promises. From this it is clearly gathered how great its authority and excellence are, since among all the books of the New Testament this alone is called a prophecy, and whoever observes it is declared blessed.
