To this is added: “For the time is near”—namely, the time of judgment, when he will repay each person according to his works. It is as though he were saying: “Blessed is the one who, having been imbued with the mysteries of the faith, keeps what is commanded in them and does not presume to do what is forbidden, because the time of observance does not impose long delays, and the day of recompense in a certain sense stands at the door.”

John to the seven churches that are in Asia.

There are two Asias, namely Greater and Lesser Asia. Lesser Asia fell by lot to blessed John; in it are seven metropolitan cities, of which Ephesus is the chief. But when Greater Asia is joined to Lesser Asia, they occupy almost half the world. To this vast region almighty God, in his mercy, appointed blessed John as preacher; and therefore he directs his prophecy particularly to the churches of Asia.

What he says to the seven churches of Asia, he certainly says to the whole Church. Although it is one, it is comprehended by the number seven, by which universality is often signified, according to the saying: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. 118:164). This may also be because of the innumerable gifts that she receives from the Holy Spirit, who, although one Spirit, fills the whole world—that is, the universal Church. The Spirit is also called sevenfold by the prophet because he is said to have rested upon the Lord on account of his sevenfold, that is, manifold, gifts, which he grants to the faithful.

The Church, then, is one, just as the Spirit is one. Hence she is called *catholic* in Greek, that is, universal, and she has been filled with the gift of the sevenfold Spirit. Thus we read in Zechariah (Zech. 4) of a lampstand wholly of gold, with seven vessels and seven lamps above it. Isaiah also recalls that the sevenfold Church is joined to Christ, saying: “Seven women shall seize one man on that day, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread’” (Isa. 4), and so forth.

This one man is Christ, whom the sevenfold Church embraces, saying: “We shall eat our own bread”—that is, we shall eat your body, given to us by God; we shall be adorned with the garments of virtues. Only let your name be invoked over us; take away our reproach, so that you may be our husband, lest the Jews reproach us by saying that we have no husband.

Thus Solomon also says (Prov. 9) that Wisdom “cut out for herself seven pillars,” and “cut out seven pillars and made a house,” because by the sevenfold Spirit she separated the hard hearts of the Gentiles from the love of the present age, filled them with that Spirit, and raised them for the strength of the heavenly building.

The Church is rightly comprehended by this number seven, which consists of three and four. She is spread throughout the four regions of the world, yet with steadfast mind and faith observes the faith of the holy Trinity. Each human being also contains the mystery of this number, since each is a member of this Church: he consists of four bodily humors, is endowed with four virtues, and loves God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his will. For he is vigorous spiritually through three things and bodily through four. In the love of God he is spiritually stirred by three qualities; bodily, he is composed of hot and cold, moist and dry matter.

Asia is interpreted as “exaltation.” Exaltation is understood both in a good and in a bad sense; it is not always taken as a vice, but sometimes designates the heights of the virtues. It is used in a good sense in Isaiah (Isa. 58; 60): “I will set you as the pride of the ages. I will raise you above the heights of the earth.” The heights of the earth are riches, honors, and dignities. Above these heights almighty God placed Peter, Paul, and the others who laid the first foundation of the Church.

For just as, when someone climbs a mountain, he looks down upon the things beneath him to the extent that he directs his steps farther toward the heights, so the one who strives to fix his attention on the highest things despises earthly things more greatly as he is raised higher toward heavenly things. What he previously believed to be above him while placed below, after advancing through ascent he recognizes as beneath him.

The Church abides in this good exaltation, because, trampling upon all earthly things, she dwells in heaven in mind, saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

If we wish to understand exaltation in the contrary sense as well, we do not thereby depart from sound understanding, because many have been cast down from their pride and humbled by the grace of Christ. Since they too are members of the Church, this revelation pertains to them. We recognize this fulfilled in Paul, who was first a proud persecutor of the Church and afterward became a most devout preacher. Every day, by inward grace, Christ calls his Church from among the proud and exalted and makes her most gentle and humble.

## Grace to you

Grace is so called because it is freely given—not a payment rendered, but forgiveness freely bestowed. This grace must be understood here especially in the sense that, without any merit on the part of human beings, God sent his Son, who redeemed us by his blood and brought us to adoption as children of God.

Hence it follows: “and peace,” because through his passion he reconciled the human race to God the Father. It should be noted that the text does not say “peace and grace,” but places grace first and then adds peace, because no one can come to the peace of reconciliation unless the grace of mercy has preceded him. Since we are able to come to God’s peace, we have arrived there through God’s grace.

More generally, everything we receive from God—whether in faith, in works, in abstinence, in fasting, or in other matters—is given to us freely by God, solely through his mercy.

It must be asked here why, in this gift of grace, after the Son and the Holy Spirit have been named, the person of the Father is passed over in silence. When he says, “from him who is, and who was, and who is to come,” he indicates the Son in these words. This is proved especially by what follows: “who is to come,” namely, for judgment, to render to each according to his works. “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

He alone, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, possesses true being, because he is always unchanging. Hence the Psalmist says: “But you are the same” (Ps. 101:28). Angels exist as well, but they have undergone change, when one of them fell through pride. Human beings exist, but they are changeable, as the first man was changed: from just he became unjust, from good impious, from immortal mortal.

Every creature, compared with eternity, is changeable and is, as it were, nothing. Therefore the one who is always the same is said in a special sense to possess being.

He “was,” because before he was born in time from the blessed Virgin, he made all times together with the Father, according to the saying: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3).

He “is to come” for judgment, according to the promise of the angels: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Since these expressions appear to apply only to the Son, and since the Church of the righteous receives this grace from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—for where there is inseparable unity, there is also inseparable operation—what does it mean that mention is made only of the Son or the Holy Spirit?

It must be understood that it is the custom of holy Scripture that whenever one person of the Trinity is mentioned, the whole Trinity is understood together. Therefore, when we read that grace is given to the faithful in the person of the Son, we must understand the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together in that giving.

Again, since there is one Spirit who fills the whole world, why does John introduce seven spirits in this revelation? Clearly, it is because of the sevenfold—that is, manifold—operation of the Spirit. In the property of his nature he is simple; in the distribution of his graces he is manifold.

Hence Solomon speaks of the same Spirit as both one and manifold. “And from the seven spirits who are before his throne.”

God’s throne consists of the holy angels and righteous human beings, in whose minds he rests through faith. Thus it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 7:27). The Holy Spirit is before this throne because, as we have said, he rests in the memory of the saints, possesses them, directs their works, and kindles them to love God and their neighbors. To him also remission of sins especially belongs, which takes place in baptism through the work of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord says to the apostles: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20:22–23).

Why the spirits are called seven has been explained above.

## And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness

Because he was about to say more about Christ, he again introduces his person, saying: “And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness,” that is, the truthful one, because he bears witness to the Father, saying to the Jews: “The Father who remains in me does his works” (John 14:10); and: “This is eternal life, that they may know you” (John 17:3); and: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16); and: “I have not come of myself” (John 7:28); and many similar statements.

But just as the Son is the faithful witness, so also are the Father and the Holy Spirit. For the Father speaks concerning the Son, bearing witness to him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). The Son himself bears witness concerning the Spirit when he says: “It is the Spirit who gives life” (John 6:63); and: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8); and: “The Paraclete himself will teach you all things” (John 14:26).

The Holy Spirit also bears witness concerning the Son, that he is the truth, as it is written: “It is the Spirit who testifies, because Christ is the truth” (1 John 5:6); and the Son himself says: “He will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

Therefore it must be understood that just as these three are one, so their testimony is one, although one is revealed through the testimony of another.

The Son is specially called the witness because, in bearing witness to the truth, he went even to the death of the flesh. For although the whole Church bore witness to Christ through her preachers, those who die for Christ’s name are specially called witnesses.

## The firstborn from the dead

The first man was created under such a condition that, if he had not sinned, he would have remained immortal. But because he sinned, he died and returned to his mother, that is, to the earth from which he had been formed. The Lord said to him: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return, from which you were taken” (Gen. 3:19). Formed from the clay of the earth into a living soul, he had come forth alive, as it were, from his mother’s womb.

After that man became mortal, he begot mortal and sinful children, all of whom, when dead, return to their mother. Therefore, when God came in the flesh, he died under the same law and was buried in the womb of his mother.

But because on the third day he rose from the dead, thereafter to live eternally, and death would no longer rule over him, he rightly had to be called “the firstborn from the dead.” Although others rose before him, such as Lazarus, they did not rise to live eternally; they died again and paid the debt of the flesh. Therefore they are not reckoned as having risen or lived.

He, then, is rightly called the firstborn from the dead, because he rose from the dead in such a way that he would never again die.

This may also be understood in another way. All the elect who mortify themselves, killing within themselves vices, sins, and the pleasures of the flesh, are dead to sin and live to God. Christ is rightly called their firstborn, because he committed no sin and displayed the mortification of carnal life.

## And the ruler of the kings of the earth

All the elect who do not allow the tyranny of vices to rise up within them are called kings of the earth, but subject those vices to the judgment of the law. The “kings of the earth” may also be understood specially as preachers, who restrain the hearts of carnal people from wickedness and rule upon the earth as kings, while in no way setting themselves above good and spiritual men.

Hence Peter confesses himself equal to Cornelius (Acts 10), whereas he strikes down the soul of Ananias with the sword of the word (Acts 5).

It must be understood that the preachers of the Church desire to rule even over carnal people in such a way that they display compassion toward human nature and uprightness toward vices. Their prince, then, is Christ, who is “King of kings and Lord of lords.” Concerning him it follows:

## Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood

The passions that the Son of God endured for us show with what love he loved us. Concerning this love the Apostle says: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her” (Eph. 5:25). He also exhorts the faithful to imitate this love, saying: “Walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us” (Eph. 5:2).

He who is beautiful loved us who were ugly; he who is merciful loved the impious; he who is without sin loved sinners. He did not love us as we were, but as he made us by that very love. Hence it is added: “and washed us from our sins in his blood.”

This love is ineffable and incomprehensible. When scarcely anyone would die even for a righteous person, Christ, at the appointed time, died for the impious, so that he might offer us to God—indeed, the righteous for the unrighteous.

When we were stained by sins, he washed us with his blood, so that he might present to himself a Church without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind. He also turned the blood of his passion into a mystery of cleansing for us, so that, baptized in faith in his death, we might be cleansed from all sins.

Hence the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3).

There is also a second baptism, the pouring out of tears, by which publicans and sinners are baptized every moment: thus Mary was cleansed after many tears for her crimes, and Peter after the Lord’s threefold denial.

## And he made us a kingdom and priests for God and his Father

By this statement all the elect are shown to be priests, those who above were called kings. Since the head of the faithful is both king and priest, the members of the head are appropriately called kings and priests. Peter says to them: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9).

They themselves are kings, priests, sacrifice, and altar. As kings, they restrain the tumult of carnal pleasures rising up against them; as sacrifice, they offer to God the sacrifice of praise and mortification; and they mortify their bodies with respect to the desires of the present age, so that they may become a living offering.

The Only-Begotten of the Father, then, who is king and priest, made his elect kings and priests. He established them as kings of the earth and showed them to be priests by their very works.

The expression “for God and his Father” does not indicate two natures or two persons, but one. According to the rule of understanding stated above, the Holy Spirit is also understood there together with them.

“To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

This refers specifically to the Son, who made us and willed us to become priests; yet here we also receive the love of both, which is the Holy Spirit.

## Behold, he comes with the clouds

The Lord will come to judgment in a cloud, because he ascended into heaven in a cloud. Thus the angels said to the apostles: “Why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Clouds are often mentioned in sacred Scripture. We read in Exodus that almighty God brought the children of Israel out of Egypt in a cloud. The cloud also filled Moses’ tabernacle and Solomon’s temple, and in the Lord’s transfiguration a cloud overshadowed Moses and Elijah.

The saints too will come to judgment in clouds, according to the Apostle’s saying: “We shall be caught up to meet Christ in the clouds” (1 Thess. 4:17).

That cloud which illuminated the children of Israel and surrounded the Egyptians with darkness signifies the Lord’s clemency, which illuminates the perfect and blinds the reprobate. Thus, when the Lord comes to judgment, he will appear gentle to the righteous, whom he will also illuminate by bringing them to behold his majesty; but he will appear terrifying to the reprobate, whom he will place in the dark prison of hell.

Concerning this it is said in the Gospel: “Throw the useless servant into the outer darkness.” To some he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father”; to others: “Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil” (Matt. 25:30, 34, 41).

The fact that the Egyptians and the children of Israel could not approach one another signifies what Abraham answered the rich man: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke 16:26).

Sometimes the cloud also signifies Christ’s body, as in the saying: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt” (Isa. 19:1). He ascended upon a light cloud and came into Egypt when, assuming the flesh of our humanity, he appeared in the world without the burden of sin.

Clouds in the plural signify holy preachers, who rain down words and flash with miracles. Concerning them the prophet says: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6), that is, upon the vineyard.

With these clouds—with the multitude of the saints—the Lord will come to judgment, because he will dwell in their hearts. Hence it is written: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14).

## And every eye will see him

In accordance with customary modes of expression, let us understand “every eye” here as meaning every human being. Every eye, that is, every person who will then rise, will see him bodily, whether for life or for death. This does not refer to animals, whose life is in their blood and which cease to exist when they die. The eye will see, but it is the eye of human beings.

Another translation says: “Every eye will see him such as they despised him, and such as they refused to believe him to be.” Then the saying will be fulfilled: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6).

“And those who pierced him”—the implied verb is “will see him”—namely, the Jews who crucified him with their tongue, as Mark says (Mark 15:25): “It was the third hour, and they crucified him,” crying: “He is guilty of death.”

Pilate’s soldiers also will see the one whom they crucified while mocking him. But they will see him not so that they may despise him as before, ridicule him, insult him, and rejoice; rather, they will see him so that they may tremble, groan, mourn, and grieve.

Hence it is added: “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.” This means all the reprobate who desire earthly things and dwell upon the earth through desire, exalting themselves by honors and living in luxury. To them the Lord says: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24).

Above all, those who pierced him will mourn over him. The wretched will grieve more because they are losing such a Lord than because they have fallen into the most atrocious torment.

## Even so: Amen

What is *etiam* among the Latins is *amen* among the Hebrews. Both are adverbs of affirmation. Therefore he says: “Even so, amen,” as though he were repeating: “It is true, it is true, and it cannot be changed,” because all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.

Know with certainty that this will take place, since he confirms it with such a sentence.

## I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end

Here it is clearly shown that the angel who announced these things to John bore in himself the person of God, when he says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.”

John himself, who tells these things to us, likewise speaks in this manner. So also does Paul say: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Cor. 13:3), and David: “Attend, my people, to my law” (Ps. 77:1).

Among the Greeks, Latins, and Hebrews, *alpha* is the beginning of the letters. What is A among us is *alpha* among the Greeks and *aleph* among the Hebrews. *Omega* is the final letter among the Greeks.

What “Alpha and Omega” means he makes clear when he adds: “The beginning and the end.” He is the beginning before whom there is no one, and the end after whom there is no one; or he is the beginning from whom all things take their origin and the end in whom all things are brought to completion; or he is the beginning because “in the beginning was the Word,” and the end because “the Word became flesh.”

Hence he himself says through Isaiah: “Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none” (Isa. 43:10).

That John—or rather the angel speaking in the person of God—says this is made clear when he adds: “The Lord God says, who was, and who is, and who is to come, the Almighty.” This has already been explained above.

## I, John, your brother

Up to this point we have the preface to the following book; from here the narrative begins.

He speaks to the churches of Asia, showing himself their equal. For the sake of humility he says: “I, John, your brother and sharer in the tribulation and kingdom and patience in Christ Jesus.”

Here two things must be joined together: tribulation and patience. Tribulation and patience pertain both to the head and to the members, but the kingdom pertains only to the head.

John was Christ’s partner in tribulation and patience. Just as Christ suffered reproaches, mockery, blows, and scourging, so blessed John is read in the Acts of the Apostles to have been scourged; and he was cast by Domitian into a vessel of boiling oil, and finally was separated from human society.

He was also a partner in patience. Just as Christ patiently endured his passion and loved his crucifiers, praying for them and saying: “Father, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60), so blessed John loved those who inflicted evils upon him and prayed for them.

The kingdom properly pertains to the head, who is the everlasting kingdom of his saints. He will give his elect no other kingdom than himself. To them he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34), as though he were saying: “Come, members; reign after tribulation in the head, because I am your kingdom.” Concerning this kingdom he himself says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21).

Finally, it should be considered that John says he shares in three things: tribulation, kingdom, and patience. The kingdom stands in the middle of these, and it cannot be possessed unless tribulation has exercised one from this side and patience has defended one from the other. In this passage he represents all the faithful.

## I was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ

Here he confirms his account in four respects: by person, when he says, “I, John”; by place, when he shows that he was exiled on the island of Patmos; by cause, namely, why he suffered these things—because of the word of God; and by time, that is, on the Lord’s Day.

“I was on the island called Patmos.” The history is well known: blessed John was exiled to the island of Patmos because of the word of God, to which he bore witness by saying: “In the beginning was the Word”; and because of the testimony he bore to Jesus Christ, namely, that he was true God and true man. For him to whom the earth was denied, heaven was opened.

Patmos is interpreted as “strait.” There the sea is especially turbulent; a strait is so called because it is narrower. Therefore, through the name of this island, the distress of the passion that blessed John suffered is not inappropriately expressed, just as did the others whose person he represented.

For the more the saints are afflicted in the present life, the more the heavenly mysteries are revealed to them. Hence Paul, placed in prison, said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

The wicked also endure punishments, since murderers are killed and confined in prisons. But punishment does not make saints; justice does. Often the righteous endure similar things, but the righteous are crowned because of justice, whereas the unjust are condemned because of iniquity.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” (Ps. 42:1).

Therefore John rightly says that he was exiled because of the word of God and the testimony of Christ, not because of murder or other crimes. He was one of those to whom the Lord says: “Blessed will you be when people hate you, exclude you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of me” (Luke 6:22); and elsewhere: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

Everyone who suffers for this reason—that he preaches the divinity and humanity of the Son of God—will be blessed, and to such people the heavenly mysteries will be revealed when they come to the vision of their Creator.

## I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day

Here it is clearly demonstrated that blessed John saw this vision not bodily, but in the Spirit. Yet he was not in a dream; he was carried away in ecstasy, as Ezekiel was. While Ezekiel was sitting in his house and the elders of Judah were sitting before him, he was carried in mind to Jerusalem.

Thus, as has been said, when John saw this revelation he neither saw, heard, felt, nor understood anything through the body, nor did he entirely abandon the flesh itself. Rather, his spirit, which was to be instructed, was taken up by the instructing Spirit, so that it might behold lofty and mystical things.

It should be noted that he says he was carried away not on the Sabbath, nor on the sixth day, but on the Lord’s Day. The character of things is often shown according to the character of the times.

Thus Abraham, in the fervor of his faith, saw angels at midday; Lot, at the destruction of Sodom, saw them in the evening; Adam saw them after midday; and Solomon, who would not preserve wisdom, received it at night.

So here the Lord’s Day clearly signifies the faith that had already been made manifest throughout the world when blessed John saw these things. The Apostles had already gone forth and preached everywhere, and the bodily rest of the Sabbath had already passed into spiritual rest.

The Church whom blessed John signified, having mortified the works of the flesh, was already rising into the light of the Spirit. All the elect are in the Lord’s Day, because they rejoice in the joys of the future resurrection.

## And I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet, saying to me: What you see, write in a book

Just as, being in the Spirit, he saw spiritual things, so the voice that he heard was spiritual. He had been led outside the body through contemplation, and therefore what was behind him must be understood accordingly.

He did not see these things through the body, as though he could see something behind the body. Rather, his “face” signifies the very power of contemplation, which was extended toward the things he saw; his “back” signifies forgetfulness of present things, from which he had been led away by the Spirit and was now seeing beyond them.

Therefore, intent upon heavenly things, he heard a voice concerning those things that he had forgotten, so that he might turn the face of his mind toward them and write down what he saw for the benefit of his hearers.

Thus the saints have behind them all the joys of the present life, while they extend themselves toward what lies before them, considering all temporal things as nothing while they contemplate the joys of the future life, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Forgetting what is behind, I stretch myself toward what is before, pursuing the prize of the eternal calling” (Phil. III).

He is told: “What you see, write in a book,” as though he were told: “What you are going to see.” For he had not yet seen anything; he had merely been raised up to see.

He calls the book his memory—that is: “Store in your mind the things you see, and make them known also to others.” That books signify human hearts and conscience is testified by Daniel, who says: “The Ancient of Days sat, and the books were opened, and another book, which is the book of life” (Dan. 7:9–10).

The faithful are likewise told to remember in their hearts what they see—that is, what they understand—and to strive to make it known to others.

This voice is rightly called “great,” whether it is understood as being in John or in the Church, because it speaks not of mediocre things but of the highest. It is also called like a trumpet because it sounds through the mouths of preachers, to whom Isaiah says: “Cry out; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1).

It is also fitting that the voice John heard—and, in him, the Church—is called like a trumpet, which receives sound from within without external noise and emits it outwardly. John first heard silently in his heart what afterward sounded outwardly in his voice. The divine voice sounded one way to the prophets, and they afterward spoke in another way.

God spoke to them in their hearts without the sound of a voice; they afterward spoke, forming the words with the tongue of the flesh.

## And send it to the seven churches

That is, to the universal Church, because, as was said above, the totality of the faithful is expressed by the number seven. What he says to one of them he certainly says to all the churches.

Hence he says below: “Let the one who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. 2:7).

## To Ephesus

Ephesus is interpreted as “my will” or “my counsel.” By this name the whole Church is generally signified, in whom the will of God is found through faith, hope, charity, and the other good works.

Therefore she herself, desiring that not her own will but God’s will be done in her, says daily in prayer that God’s will, not her own, may be done in her.

To her the Lord says through the prophet: “You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate, but you shall be called ‘My will is in her’” (Isa. 62:4).

She is also rightly called “my counsel,” because she follows not her own counsel but that of her God, hearing Solomon’s words: “Hear counsel and receive instruction, so that you may be wise at your end” (Prov. 19:20); and again: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent” (Sir. 32:19).

This is contradicted to the reprobate: “You have despised all my counsel” (Prov. 1:25); and elsewhere the Lord says: “My will is not in you” (Mal. 1:10).

It must be understood that “will” pertains to charity, by which the holy Church does not serve the Lord under compulsion of fear, but willingly submits herself to the Creator, saying with the Psalmist: “Freely I will sacrifice to you” (Ps. 53:8).

“Counsel,” however, pertains to correction. Although some may wish by every means to remain in their crimes, through God’s mercy a word of correction comes to them, so that, rejecting error, they may receive the counsel of salvation.

Thus Saul was corrected. His counsel had been to erase the name of Christ from the earth, but from a wolf he became a lamb.

The holy Church receives the counsel of Christ because she guards herself from sins and, in order to attain perfection, follows his counsel when he says to a certain man: “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21).

## To Smyrna

Smyrna is said to mean “their song.” Whose song could this be except that of the elect? It is the same song of which the Psalmist says: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. 95:1).

These words, however, are not spoken only to one church; they apply generally to the universal Church. The apostles belonged to her members, and the Lord said to them: “I give you a new commandment” (John 13:34).

She sings a new song by loving God and neighbor, since the one who fulfills this commandment sings it. She also sings a new song when she celebrates the mystery of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection.

She will sing it more perfectly in the future, when she sees in reality what she now sees in hope, and the saying will be fulfilled: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord” (Ps. 84:5).

Hence Ezekiel says (Ezek. 2:9–10) that he saw a book in which were written a song, lamentations, and woe. Whoever wishes to sing the song there—that is, the new song—must have lamentation in the present life by mourning his own sins and those of others.

But whoever in the present life has despised lamentation will undoubtedly have woe in the future, so that while some have woe without end, these may sing “Alleluia” without limit and live forever.

## To Pergamum

Pergamum is interpreted as “division of horns.” Horns signify kingdoms, as appears in the book of Daniel and in Zechariah.

The horns of Christ, then, are understood as the saints who will come to his kingdom. But just as Christ’s horns are his members, to whom he will give an everlasting kingdom, so the horns of the devil are his members, who will be condemned with him.

Between these horns—that is, between the righteous and the reprobate, and between the kingdom of Christ and that of the devil—the holy Church makes a division, separating the good from the evil and the proud from the humble by the judgment of her sentence, saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:14).

Concerning these horns the Psalmist also says: “I will break all the horns of sinners, but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. 75:11).

Thus the kingdom of Christ is distinguished from that of the devil: the kingdom of Christ is raised up through humility, while the kingdom of the devil is cast down through pride.

## To Thyatira

Thyatira is said to mean “illuminated.” By this name the Church in general is signified, for she has been illuminated by the one who illuminates every human being coming into this world.

To her the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). Concerning her Isaiah says: “The people who walked in darkness” (Isa. 9:2).

## To Sardis

Sardis sounds, in the Latin language, like “for the prince of beauty,” with “fitted and adorned” understood. To whom does this refer except the one of whom the Psalmist says: “You are the most beautiful of the sons of men” (Ps. 45:3), and in the Song of Songs: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved” (Song 1:15)?

The Church is fitted and prepared for this prince of beauty through the adornments of virtues. Hence the Psalmist says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Ps. 45:10); and in the Song of Songs: “We shall make golden ornaments for you” (Song 1:11).

## To Philadelphia

Philadelphia is said to mean “saving God’s inheritance.” The Church herself is called the inheritance, concerning which the Father says to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8).

Concerning her the wicked tenants, seeing the heir, said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21:38).

She is God’s field; she is also his vineyard. Through her preachers she strives to save herself in such a way that she may please God in faith and works and never depart from his will.

Laodicea. Laodicea is rendered in our language as “a tribe pleasing to the Lord,” or “they were in vomit.” Scripture often uses the word “tribe”; hence: “For there the tribes of the Lord went up” (Ps. CXXI). The Church is likewise divided into these three orders—priests, soldiers, and cultivators—just as there were, perhaps, three such orders among the Jewish people, as there were among the Romans: senators, soldiers, and farmers. This tribe is called pleasing to the Lord, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Who loved us and washed us from our sins.” And the Lord himself says: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III). But the phrase “they were in vomit” refers to the reprobate, who are mixed together with the good, like grain with chaff on the threshing floor. By their presence they burden the saints, like harmful foods. Therefore they must be expelled from the body of Christ. Such were the heretics, who were expelled from the Church, concerning whom John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (John II); and the Psalmist: “Expel them, for they have provoked you, O Lord” (Ps. V). In their person it is also said in the following words of this prophecy: “Because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III).

And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me. Here it is plainly evident that John heard not a bodily but a spiritual voice, because he says that he turned not in order to hear, but in order to see. This is recognized as impossible according to the bodily senses, for a voice can never be seen. But he, carried away in spirit to contemplate sublime things, both heard and saw the same reality, because there to hear is to see, and to see is to hear. The Church also, which is represented in John, sees the voice behind her, because she considers in the Law and the Prophets the mysteries that she sees fulfilled in herself as having been foretold. For it is written in Genesis: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II)—namely, Christ and the Church. Hence Paul says: “But I speak of Christ and of the Church” (Eph. V).

And I turned and saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like the Son of Man. The seven golden lampstands signify precisely what the seven churches signify, that is, the universal Church, filled with the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit, since their words provide both the light of knowledge and the fire of love.

Yet it is not unfitting that she is represented by seven golden lampstands. The Church has a golden color because she shines with divine wisdom, of which it is written: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” She has a lamp because she shines by word and example, in accordance with what Paul says: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. II). She also possesses length through the long-suffering of hope and perseverance, as the Lord says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

Since a lampstand is produced by hammering, it aptly corresponds to the Church, which in this world is afflicted by various pressures. Amid these the Lord offers her consolation, saying: “When you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not consume you” (Isa. XLIII); and through the Prophet: “I will turn my hand toward you, and I will smelt away your dross until it is pure” (Isa. I).

John rightly sees one like the Son of Man in the midst of the seven golden lampstands, because Christ, who presides over his Church and protects her by presiding over her, is in the midst of his elect, according to the saying: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII); and elsewhere: “Rejoice and praise, O dwelling-place of Zion, because great is the Holy One of Israel in your midst” (Isa. XII).

It must be observed that he does not say simply that he saw the Son of Man, but one like the Son of Man. For that angel—as has often been said—was acting in the person of Christ. He is therefore called not the Son of Man himself but one like the Son of Man, because, having conquered death, he dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him. Or certainly he is called one like the Son of Man because, although he assumed our flesh, he did not commit sin, but appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh. It is proper to human beings not to be free from sin; and therefore, because he himself committed no sin, the Psalmist says: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. II).

Clothed in a long robe. The poderis is an ankle-length garment, since the Greeks also call feet *podas*. By the poderis, therefore, we should understand the flesh of Christ, which the true priest offered when he offered himself to the Father on the gibbet of the cross as a living and holy sacrifice, a pleasing fragrance. This garment reaches to the ankles because he loved his own to the end, as John says: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John XIII).

Or by the poderis we may understand the universal Church, which is the Lord’s garment, according to what is said to her by the prophetic voice of the Father: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these things as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX); and Paul says to the faithful: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (I Cor. I). This garment extends to the feet because it will reach, at the end of the age, even to the final members of the faithful who are to be born.

And girded about the breasts with a golden sash. In the Old Testament we read that the Lord appeared to Daniel girded at the loins, as he himself testifies: “I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a certain man clothed in linen, with his loins girded” (Dan. X). Here, however, the angel is shown to John girded not at the loins but at the breasts.

The girding of the loins signifies the restraint of lust; hence: “Let your loins be girded.” The angel appearing to Daniel is therefore rightly reported to have been girded at the loins, because the Scripture of the Old Testament condemns the act of lust. But to John he is rightly shown girded at the breast, because the New Testament also condemns impure thoughts, saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). For thoughts move within the breast.

When it is said to the faithful, “Let your loins be girded,” we must understand that whoever has not yet restrained the fornication of the flesh still belongs to the old human being.

We may also understand this in another way: the two breasts signify the two Testaments; the golden sash signifies the Church of the elect, who is rightly joined to the angel at the breasts, because through observance of both Testaments the Church is united to Christ in the bond of love—that is, in love of God and neighbor. Or certainly the angel is girded at the breasts because from the two peoples one Church of the elect is united to Christ through the bond of charity.

His head and his hair were white like white wool and like snow. In the book of Daniel we read (Dan. VII) that the Ancient of Days sat, whose garment was white as snow and whose hair was like pure wool. There those words signify the eternity of the Father, as is shown in what follows, when the person of the Son is then mentioned. The same Daniel says: “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming with the clouds of heaven, and he came as far as the Ancient of Days” (ibid.), that is, as far as God the Father.

Here, however, the whiteness of the angel’s head and hair signifies the whiteness of the innocence of the Son of God. This whiteness is fittingly expressed through wool: wool is the clothing of sheep, and he himself is the sheep of whom Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he will be led to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII), because, as the Apostle says: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (I Pet. II).

By the head we understand Christ himself, of whom Paul says: “The head of the man is Christ” (I Cor. XI); and again: “He is the head of all the churches” (Eph. I). By the hair, those who are more perfect and adhere more closely to their head; they too possess the whiteness of wool because they imitate the simplicity and innocence of their head, who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI); and to whom he says: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. X).

Snow signifies the newness of the resurrection. Thus the Lord expressed the brightness of the future resurrection through the snowy whiteness shown to the three disciples, when his face shone like the sun and his garments became like snow. For this reason the angel who testified to his resurrection, appearing to the women, symbolically displayed white garments like snow.

And his eyes were like a flame of fire. The Lord’s eyes signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning which Zechariah says: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III); and later John says that he saw a Lamb as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.

They are rightly called flames, because they kindle us to the love of God and illumine us with divine knowledge. Concerning this fire the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). By the angel’s eyes may also be understood the more eminent and spiritual men in the Church, namely the apostles, to whom the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V). They not only shine but also burn, since their words provide both the light of knowledge and the fire of love.

The divine utterances may likewise be understood through the eyes, for it is written: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. CXVIII); and concerning Joseph: “The word of the Lord inflamed him” (Ps. CIV).

And his feet were like aurichalcum, as if burning in a furnace. The Lord’s feet sometimes signify the stability of eternity; sometimes his humanity, through which the knowledge of divinity came to us; sometimes the preachers, concerning whom it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Rom. X); sometimes the traces of his imitation; and sometimes the final members.

Here, however, they properly signify his members, who will be tested by the fire of tribulation in the time of Antichrist. For just as aurichalcum is brought from bronze to the color of gold through many processes, so they will be burned by the tribulation of the final time, so that they may be tested like the purest gold.

And just as Antichrist will be more savage than all persecutors, so they will be stronger than all the martyrs who came before. For this furnace signifies the most powerful tribulation, concerning which the Lord says: “Then there will be such tribulation as has not been, nor will be” (Matt. XIV).

Another translation reads “aurichalcum of Lebanon.” Since that mountain is said to be in Judea, this clearly indicates that the final members of Christ’s body will then be harassed more fiercely by the furnace of tribulation in those regions where their Lord was crucified by the impious Jews.

And his voice was like the voice of many waters. Above we read that he heard the angel’s voice like a trumpet; now it is like the voice of many waters, because at first he sounded through a few preachers, concerning whom the Lord says: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. IX), and afterward resounded through the ministry of many peoples. For many waters are peoples, as we read below. What was first proclaimed by a few preachers, the whole world afterward proclaimed.

The voice like that of many waters may also be understood as charity, which is the source and origin of all spiritual gifts, as the Lord himself makes clear when he says: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII). Hence on the great day of the feast he himself stood and cried out: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink; and from his belly will flow living waters” (John VII).

It is as though he said: Let the one who thirstily desires understanding of the Scriptures come to me; when he comes, let him drink the Spirit of charity, for God is charity. The singular voice of Christ is therefore rightly said to be like the voice of many waters, because although charity is one, when it fills the mind it kindles it in many different ways to innumerable works of virtue.

[Col. 0957A] And he held seven stars in his right hand. What the seven stars are, the angel himself explains below, saying: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches.” He had already included the same meaning above in the seven lampstands, that is, the universal Church, or all teachers. For what is said to the individual angels is plainly referred to all. The Lord himself makes this clear: although he says of each one, “Write to the angel of that church,” he concludes at the end: “Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. II).

Stars shine at night, and so do lampstands. Therefore the person of the Church is not inappropriately expressed in these words, and especially that of the teachers, who shine by word and deed in the night of this age and show others an example of holiness and light. To them the Lord says: “Let your light shine before men, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Christ’s right hand is understood here as the highest blessedness and prosperity of the future life, which now remains in hope but will then exist in reality. The saints already stand in this right hand, because in God’s predestination it is already certain who will be placed at the right hand when the sheep are separated from the goats. They will by no means have a place on the left, because no unhappiness or adversity will harm those to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXIII), and so forth.

Concerning this right hand the Lord says to the Church through the Prophet: “Do not fear, for I have helped you, and the right hand of my Just One will receive you” (Isa. XLI).

And from his mouth came a sword sharp on both sides. The sword sharp on both sides signifies the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. Hence Paul says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). This sword proceeds from his mouth, in accordance with what the Lord himself says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV).

It is said to be sharp on both sides because on one side it cuts away sins of action and on the other sins of thought. For the Old Testament says: “You shall not kill; you shall not steal” (Exod. XX; Deut. V). But the New Testament says: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment”; and: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

The word of God is also called a sword sharp on both sides because it separates the good from the evil. Hence the Lord himself says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). For he came to set a father against his son and a daughter against her mother, and so forth.

Or the sword is called double-edged because it forms the imperfect externally according to the letter and teaches the perfect inwardly according to the mystical meaning. A simple person hears there, “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill,” and so forth, and resolves in his heart to keep these commands. In doing so, through the word of God he cuts himself away from carnal pleasures, so that by keeping the commands of the divine word he may be saved.

The wiser person considers higher mysteries when he hears: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I), and so forth. Raised up by these mysteries, he desires nothing in this world, because he already longs to enjoy the presence of the one whose greatness is proclaimed so fully in the divine utterance.

[Col. 0958A] And his face was shining like the sun in its strength. Because Christ and the Church are one person—namely, head and members—we may understand his face as the saints, though not as they are now, but as they will be later, when they attain the vision of their Creator. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII).

We should not understand this as referring to the visible sun, since then it too will possess a much greater light, according to the prophetic saying: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun like the light of seven days” (Isa. XXX). Rather, we should understand it as referring to the one of whom it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. IV).

If the saints will possess a greater light than this visible sun, how much more excellent and sublime, we may suppose, will be the brightness of the head, from whom the members will be illumined!

When John spoke here of the sun, he therefore added: “Like the sun shining in its strength,” namely, when at midday it shines at the center of the sky with such brilliance that human sight cannot endure the splendor of its light. He displayed this brightness on the mountain before the three disciples, when his face became like the sun.

For, as blessed Hilary says, he shone a hundred times more brightly; but the Evangelist had no created thing more splendid to which he could compare that same brightness. Therefore he says that his face shone like the sun. And as the Lord then appeared, so he will come to judgment.

Here one may ask: If the Lord is to come with such brightness at the general resurrection, why did he not appear to the disciples in the same brightness after his resurrection? The answer is that after his resurrection he concealed the brightness of his face from the disciples so that they might either endure it or recognize him. If he had not done this, mortal eyes could not have seen him.

For if, while he still bore a mortal body, they could not endure the brightness of his face when he was transfigured on the mountain, how much less could they have endured it if, after his resurrection, he had manifested his brightness not merely like the sun but with the sun shining sevenfold?

Why should we say this only of the Lord, when even we, wretched mortals, cannot endure the brightness of holy souls shining with the eternal sun?

Moreover, the statement that the sun or moon will possess a greater brightness after the day of judgment pertains to the fall and restoration of the first human being. After the human being sinned by transgressing God’s command, he entered darkness; and therefore the sun itself, which had been created to serve humanity, also lost most of the brightness of its light.

But when humanity has been restored and renewed after the general resurrection, the sun too will be renewed, and it will shine sevenfold—that is, much more brightly than it does now. Hence afterward it will suffer no setting, as Isidore testifies, lest the impious enjoy the brightness of its light.

Alternatively: the sun has a rising and a setting, and therefore it is fittingly compared with Christ, who had a rising when he was born in time from his mother and a setting through death. His face, moreover, signifies his manifest presence in the flesh, which was hidden when he set upon the cross; but when he rose again from the dead, it began to shine in its strength, namely through the multitude of miracles and the preaching of the teachers.

The Psalmist also speaks of his setting: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting” (Ps. LXVII). He ascended above the setting because from where he set, from there he rose.

When John said these things, Christ had already risen, had already turned toward setting, and was already shining again in his strength—that is, he had already been born in the flesh, suffered, and been raised, and his birth, passion, and resurrection had already become radiant throughout the world. Therefore the angel’s face shone not simply, but like the sun in its strength.

And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. John here signifies the entire multitude of the elect, while the angel represents the person of the head alone. Here the Lord’s feet signify neither, as above, the eternity of his divinity, nor the preachers, nor finally the other members, but only the signs of his passion and humility, since he humbled himself even unto death.

John falls at the angel’s feet when the holy Church imitates the traces of his passion, according to Peter’s words: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II), mortifying herself with vices and desires.

She falls at his feet because, when she considers her Redeemer dead, she immediately dies to the world and humbly prostrates herself in order to imitate his footsteps. John is rightly said to have fallen at the angel’s feet not dead but as though dead, because the elect, while imitating the traces of Christ’s passion and dying to the world, nevertheless live to God.

Hence the Apostle says: “I live, yet it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II); and again: “I appeal to you to present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Rom. XII), and so forth. A sacrifice is slain and yet is living, because although the saints mortify themselves with vices and desires, they do not wholly depart from the body.

Or they become as though dead when they mortify themselves, because they already live in the hope of the future resurrection, according to the Apostle’s saying: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; and when Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory” (Col. III).

And he placed his right hand upon me, saying: Do not fear. In sacred Scripture one expression does not always bear one meaning. Above we read that the right hand signifies the highest blessedness and prosperity of the future life, in which the saints already stand through God’s predestination.

The right hand is not to be understood in that way here, as in the preceding verse. The feet do not contain the earlier mysteries within themselves, but signify only the examples of Christ’s imitation and passion. Thus here we should understand the angel’s right hand as the holy preachers. Hence Moses says: “At his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. XXXIII), as though he were saying: The doctrine of the Holy Spirit is in the holy preachers.

It should be noted that John does not say what the angel did by placing his right hand upon him—whether he lifted him from the ground or drew him down to the ground. But from the book of Daniel (Dan. X) we learn that he lifted him from the ground, for Daniel says that the angel, who was girded with refined gold and whose body was like chrysolite, placed his right hand upon him and raised him onto his knees.

The angel therefore places his hand upon John, who lies at his feet as though dead, and raises him when Christ extends the help of consolation to his self-mortifying Church through his preachers. The Apostle Paul was placed, as it were, as Christ’s right hand upon the hearts of the faithful, which were weighed down by pressures and anxieties, when he lifted them up by offering consolation and saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

The Church is not raised from the earth in such a way that she is completely removed from all afflictions. Rather, when she hears such words and others like them concerning the sufferings inflicted upon her, she lifts her heart toward the joys of the heavenly homeland. Such is the saying of the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. X); and elsewhere: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

The words “Do not fear” are rightly added there, as though it were said to the Church of the elect: In the struggle of suffering, raise the hearing of your mind toward future rewards, and, having received confidence from above, boldly drive human fear far away.

I am the first and the last and the living one; and I was dead, and behold, I am living for ever and ever. Here it appears most clearly that the angel who appeared to blessed John bore the figure of Christ. These words apply to no one other than Christ, who was born, suffered, was buried, and was raised.

He is the first, in whom all things were made; he is the last, through whom all things were restored. He is the first, who was born before the ages: “In the beginning was the Word.” He is the last, because he was born at the end of the times: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

“I was living,” he says, either before all ages in the essence of divinity or before death in the flesh. “And I was dead,” meaning after the birth of the flesh. “And behold, I am living for ever and ever” after the resurrection, as the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, will never die again; death will no longer rule over him” (Rom. VI).

In this passage we should understand that great consolation was offered to blessed John, who lay as though dead, when he was told: “I was living and was dead, and I am living for ever and ever.” Nothing could be more fitting than that he should hear the Lord, who was like him in death, speaking in this way while he himself lay as though dead.

It was as though Christ said both to him and to all the faithful: Do not fear suffering for me, since you are members, when I, who am the head, did not hesitate to die for you. For just as I live after death, so you too will live when raised from the dead by the head.

Therefore observe that after death your life lives—the life that consists in the head—and shows you the example of rising one day to glory, provided that now you do not withdraw from the body through empty fear.

And I have the keys of death and of hell. The keys signify eternal and judicial power. Hence it was said to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI). We must not understand childishly that there are keys in heaven in the same way as there are keys at a door; rather, the keys signify the power of binding and loosing.

So here too the name of keys indicates eternal power. Hence elsewhere it is said: “He who opens and no one shuts; he shuts and no one opens” (Rev. III).

Death is understood as the devil, because through the devil’s envy death entered the world. Hell, moreover, means his members who are destined for the punishments of hell.

The Son of God therefore possesses the keys of death and hell because, by his hidden unlocking, he grants the devil or his members power to rage in persecution against the saints, and again, whenever he wills, he causes all their temptation to cease.

The devil was confined by these keys when the Lord said to Job: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man?” The tempter replied: “Does Job fear God for no reason? Have you not fenced him in, and his house, and all that he possesses?” and so forth up to: “Stretch out your hand, and surely he will bless you to your face” (Job I–II).

The Lord unlocked the key for him when he gave him power to tempt Job, saying: “Behold, he is in your hand” (Job II). Having received this power, he went out and struck Job with a grievous ulcer (ibid.). But afterward he was restrained and shut up under the key, when that very temptation benefited blessed Job unto glory, all his possessions were restored to him twofold, and the same temptation increased the accumulation of the tempter’s condemnation.

By these keys he had been released when, shaking Peter with fear, he compelled him to deny God. He was shut up again when the Lord looked upon Peter, and Peter wept bitterly and washed away the stains of his threefold denial with the bitterest tears.

By these keys too he had been released when he had bound Mary to himself through many crimes; but he was shut up when many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much.

With these keys opened he had been released when he tempted Paul, to whom, lest the greatness of his revelations should exalt him, a thorn in the flesh was given.

By these keys of divine judgment he is released each day when he is permitted to weary the elect with temptations, and again restrained when he is permitted to intensify those temptations not beyond measure but according to a limit, in accordance with the saying: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure” (I Cor. X).

Write, therefore, what you have seen, what is, and what must take place after these things. Here John represents the order of preachers, to whom it is said: “Write what you have seen,” that is, what you have understood concerning me in the Law and the Prophets, so that you may keep it in your heart and disclose it for the benefit of others.

Or, if we refer these words specifically to the apostles, they are told to write the miracles of Christ that they saw, proclaim them to others, and through them draw others to faith in Christ. These things have also now been fulfilled in me, and those things must take place afterward in my members.

Since he had already been told above that he must write what he had seen, and now by a repeated command he is again urged to write, the repetition of the word removes negligent sluggishness from the diligence of preachers, so that what they are repeatedly admonished to do may be fulfilled without delay. It continues:

The mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches. A sacrament is a mystery in which one thing is seen and another understood, as, for example, in Christ’s body, where, although bread is seen, the true flesh is present. Hence the priests themselves say: “May the sacraments that we have received, O Lord, benefit us for the salvation of body and soul.”

Thus here too there was a sacrament, because the universal Church was expressed in the seven stars and the seven lampstands. What is signified by the seven stars is also signified by the seven lampstands: the whole Church, or more particularly the holy teachers, who are rightly represented both by stars and by angels, because in the night of this age they shine through the purity of their lives and, ministering heavenly things to others, become angels of truth.

To them Paul says: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the firmament of heaven.”

This too must be understood: the one angel is the seven, and the seven are the one, because what he says to one pertains to all, and what he says to all is likewise referred to each individual.

The same angel who appeared to blessed John explained some things but left others marked with signs. He did this so that our reading of the book would not become worthless to us and so that we would also have places in which to exercise our understanding.

He explained some things because, if the book were entirely closed to us, we would become weary of reading it, since we could not reach its inner mysteries. Again, if he opened everything to us, it would be easy for us to understand, and for that reason we would read it with less diligence.

The angels to whom he wrote, as we shall find in what follows, are not understood as heavenly spirits, since it is absurd to believe that there is anything in the heavenly spirits deserving of reproach. Rather, they are the faithful who stand in the Church, concerning whom it is written: “The angels of peace will weep bitterly” (Isa. XXXIII); and Malachi says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Mal. II), because he is “the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

The holy teachers of the Church are called angels because, as was stated above, the stars and lampstands shine in the night of this age, and by ministering heavenly things to others they become angels of truth. Paul says that they shine like lights in the firmament of heaven in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, through the purity of a sincere life.

It continues:

CHAPTER II.

And to the angel of the church of Ephesus write:

“These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.”

Ephesus is interpreted as “will” or “my counsel,” which also particularly suits that church, in which was the will of God, [Col. 0963A] as we shall find below, when the same angel says: “I know your works”; and the counsel of correction appears in what follows: “I have something against you, because you have abandoned your first love.” This also applies generally to the whole Church. For what is said to the angel—that is, to the priest of that church—is said in him to the whole church; and in the church of the Ephesians, to the universal Church of the faithful.

For by the seven stars which he held in his right hand are understood all the saints, who are already held in the presence of God in the predestination of eternal blessedness. They are likewise signified by the seven lampstands, in whose midst Christ walks, because he distributes among them, individually, the gifts of his grace: to one, the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of speech; to another, hospitality; to another, abstinence, contemplation, and other things of this kind, which one and the same Spirit accomplishes (I Cor. XII). Although he is present everywhere, while he bestows on them the grace of his gifts he walks daily, as it were, in the midst of the lampstands.

Or certainly, by the hand we can understand the clemency of his divinity, which no one can escape, because “all the ends of the earth are in his hand.” In this right hand are the good and the wicked. The good are restrained, lest they pass beyond the measure of the virtue they have received through empty glory, or fall into the enticements of vices; while the wicked are restrained by this right hand of power, so that they cannot harm as much as they wish, but, like servants under the authority of their Lord, may beat the children with a measured scourging.

There are therefore some to whom the Lord comes through the faith they possess, and sometimes through good will. But because they again drive him out through reprehensible conduct and fall into vices, he cannot remain there; therefore he walks on and passes over to the elect, with whom he remains for a long time and dwells in their hearts. He makes the reprobate feel the presence of his coming; but because their works do not follow their faith, he does not remain with them at all, but passes from them to the hearts of the elect, in whom he dwells through the works of virtue.

This is indicated by the dove sent out from the ark. Flying over the waters of the flood, when it found nowhere to rest its foot, it returned to the ark. Hence in the Gospel he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). In these words he shows that he comes to those in whom he does not find a dwelling.

It is therefore rightly said: “Who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.” It is as though it were said openly: He moves about among the elect and the reprobate with the word of exhortation until he finds someone with whom he may make his dwelling through works of virtue. Or certainly, when for a time he abandons one of the elect, who must be tested by the innermost examination of discernment, in temptation, and in his loving favor accompanies another whom he rescues from temptation, he appears to move about in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.

“I know your works and your labor and your patience.”

This does not apply specially but generally to all the elect, whose works, labor, and patience are known to God. To know, in God’s case, means to choose. Thus in the books of Moses it is frequently said to the people: “God knows you out of all the nations,” that is, “He has chosen you”; and to Moses himself: “I know you by name” (Exod. XXXIII), that is, “I choose you specially above the rest.”

Sometimes “to know” is said of making people know; hence: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him or not,” that is, “to make you know.” And to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. XXIV), that is, “I have made you know.” God is also said to know, and by that knowledge the power of divine subtlety is understood, to which all things are naked and open, according to the saying: “You have known all things, the last and the ancient” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

In these expressions concerning the churches, therefore, we must understand God’s knowing according to the character of the passages. Christ therefore says to the Church: “I know your works,” that is, “I approve and choose them”; or, “I know your works,” that is, “I make you know the reward of your works” [Col. 0964A] and your labor.

Because a person who works labors, labor is rightly added after works of virtue, since the holy Church, just as it is great in works, is also great in labor. Its patience is especially praised: it patiently endures all labors, sincerely loves those whom it bears while they act wickedly, and perseveres in this to the end of life, according to the saying: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, XXIV).

Works and labors are common to the good and the wicked; true patience, however, is a singular gift bestowed from heaven. If it is lacking, many works and many labors are suddenly reduced to nothing. True patience is that which both bears with the evils of one’s neighbors calmly and sincerely loves those whom it bears while they act perversely.

“And you cannot endure the wicked”—understand, willingly—and here “I know” must be supplied, as above.

In this life the good and the wicked are mixed together. Therefore, since it cannot be otherwise, the wicked must be endured by the good. They ought to hate in them the fact that they are wicked, and they ought to love them because they are human. Hence David says: “I have hated the unjust” (Ps. CXVIII)—not because he hated the nature of the unjust, but the works of injustice.

Sometimes, therefore, the weak attempt to escape the perversities of the wicked and their company by withdrawing bodily, not knowing how impious it is, because of the perversity of the wicked, to abandon the unanimity of the saints. If they devoted themselves to patience, then, since there is no other place available, they would find within themselves a place where they could escape them.

“And you tested those who call themselves apostles and are not.”

In the time of blessed John, false apostles arose—that is, heretics: Marcion, Ebion, and Cerinthus in Asia, wishing to corrupt the true faith and preaching that Christ was less than the Father. They were certainly false apostles, in accordance with the meaning of the word, since “apostle” means “one sent.” But these were not sent by Christ, but by the devil. They transformed themselves into apostles of Christ and claimed that they had been sent by him, although they belonged not to the truth but to false doctrines.

Concerning such people the Lord says through the Prophet (Jer. XXIII): “They themselves came, though I did not send them.” He therefore says: “You tested those who call themselves apostles and are not,” that is, “You tested their faith and teaching.” “And you found them liars.”

There are two kinds of testing; here, however, testing pertains to examination, as also in the passage: “He tests us for ten days” (Dan. I). So too the holy Church tests—that is, examines—the hearts of individuals daily, so that those who do not hold the true faith may either be corrected or expelled from the fellowship of the Church, as the heretics were expelled.

These men—that is, Ebion and the others—were hidden before they were examined, but they were tested both by blessed John and by the angel of his church. Because they were found to be perverse teachers, they were condemned under anathema and expelled from the Church. Likewise Sabellius, Photinus, and the other robbers, who had not entered the bosom of the Church through the door, remained concealed until they were tested by the pastors of the Church.

“And you have patience,” by patiently enduring the perversity of those who inflict evils upon you. “And you have endured for my name’s sake and have not grown weary.”

It is as though the Church of all the elect were told: Because you have had patience in everything, you have therefore endured the torments inflicted upon you by the impious; for if you had not had patience, you would have failed amid so many adversities. And because you possess patience, you do not succumb, since you endure these things not for earthly glory but for my name’s sake.

“But I have this against you: you have abandoned your first love.”

Above he spoke to the saints; now he speaks to the reprobate, because, as was said above, just as the good and wicked are mixed in the present life, so the divine word addresses them together: “I have,” he says, “this against you”—that is, against the reprobate who are in you—“because you have abandoned your first love,” that is, faith in God and love of him. You have surrendered yourself to secular and earthly pleasures, just as a woman abandons her first love for her husband and joins herself to an adulterer.

When first love is rejected by some, worldly desire is immediately introduced, and it happens, in a pitiable way, that the former does not even return to memory once the latter has fully possessed the mind. “Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen,” that is, from what grace you have been separated, you who were formerly joined to me and shone with the splendor of holiness.

“And repent,” because you abandoned me and received earthly love as a woman receives an adulterer, “and do the first works,” that is, return to the love of your former husband. “But if not, I am coming to you, and I will show you the presence of my wrath, and I will move your lampstand from its place [Col. 0965D], unless you repent,” that is, “I will move you from the place of your virtue and from the fellowship of the faithful.”

It should be noted that he does not say, “I will cast the lampstand out of its place,” but only, “I will move it.” For although someone may sin, nevertheless, if he performs perfect repentance, he will not lose his former dignity or rank. Thus, although Peter denied Christ, he did not lose his apostolic rank.

But let us express this by way of an example. If any person commits a grave sin in the sight of human beings, he is moved from his place; yet if he quickly rises again through repentance, he has not been moved in the sight of God. Although through sin he may appear to have been moved in the sight of human beings, nevertheless, because he was destined to rise again in God’s presence, he has not been moved, since he will not hold a place of lesser holiness if he has performed perfect repentance.
