Let it therefore be said to the unrepentant person who refuses to return to God: “I will move your lampstand from its place unless you repent,” as though it were said: “After your fall into crimes, you will by no means receive the gift of holiness from me unless you take care to soften your heart through repentance.”

“But you have this”—understand, “something good”—“that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.”

Again in this passage he turns his speech toward the person of the faithful, saying: “You hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans.” Nicolaus was one of the seven deacons who were chosen and ordained by the apostles. While the others remained in their ministry, he departed from their faith and teaching.

When he was reproved because he had a very beautiful wife and was excessively jealous of her, he replied, in order to excuse himself from this suspicion: “I do not care what she does; whoever wishes may use her.” Hence she was made available for common use. Many of his followers began to imitate this deed; they also ate food sacrificed to idols and mixed their own foods with those of the gentiles.

They likewise said that this world was made not by God but by certain rulers, contrary to what is said in Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). These deeds of the Nicolaitans are rejected by the good and detested like dung.

Let us see whom these people signify spiritually in another way. Nicolaus is interpreted as “foolish people.” By this name the gentiles are represented, who are foolish because they refuse to believe the true Wisdom, that is, Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the gentiles foolishness” (I Cor. I).

For these people commonly use wives, eat food sacrificed to idols, and assert that the founders of this world were human beings—that is, Jupiter, Saturn, and the rest. Although they are considered gods by those people, they were nevertheless human beings and reigned on this earth, though they lived shamefully.

Nicolaus also signifies heretics who, because they do not hold a true understanding of the Wisdom of God the Father, who is the Son, are foolish according to God, although they may appear wise according to the world. When Arius and his followers assert that Christ is a creature, they are foolish and senseless, because, by confusing the substance of the Trinity, they deny that Christ is God. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. LII).

Two of their deeds are especially noted, because they are often called both idol-worshippers and fornicators. Since they do not have the true faith, the error which they follow is itself charged against them as the worship of idols. They are also fornicators because they serve the uncleanness of the flesh, and for this especially they perish.

The Jews too are foolish because they refuse to believe in Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father, and vainly boast that they have the Father, whose Son they pursue with hatred; for whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father either.

But if we examine carefully, we also find Nicolaitans within the holy Church: namely, those whom we see storing up treasure in earthly love. For what could be more foolish than to concentrate one’s entire mind on storing money in a place where it is not possible to retain it forever? Hence the Lord exhorts his disciples, saying: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matt. VII).

That person is counted among this number of fools who, when he said, “I will destroy my barns and build larger ones, because I have nowhere to gather my fruits” (Luke XII), heard from the Lord: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and the things you have gathered, whose will they be?” (Ibid.)

These profits of foolish people, who seek only earthly things, produce in them the offspring of every vice, because, according to the Apostle, “the root of all evils is greed” (I Tim. VI). Through it one person is driven to robbery, another to false testimony, another to perjury, and others to the remaining crimes. It also led Judas to the point that he handed the Lord himself over to death.

Through this greed the covetous person makes his soul a commodity and becomes an idolater, loving the creature more than the Creator. What the Apostle says about the gluttonous, “whose god is their belly” (Phil. III), can similarly be understood of the covetous, whose god is a coin of gold or silver.

These are the deeds of the Nicolaitans—that is, of foolish people, namely pagans, other unbelievers, and false Christians—which the Lord, and those who belong to him, are shown to hate.

It should be noted that the Lord says he hates not the nature but the works of human beings. Hence he does not say: “You hate the Nicolaitans, whom I hate,” but: “You hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.” A human being must be loved, but his evil work must be hated.

“Let the one who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

Since at the beginning of this address the Lord commanded that it be written to one angel and to one church of Ephesus, whereas here he does not invite one angel or one church to hear the Spirit’s words, it is perfectly clear that what he says to one, he says to all. In one angel and one church of the Ephesians, he depicts the unity of the Church.

Whenever this brief admonition is given, whether in this book or in the Gospel, what follows or precedes it must be understood spiritually. For it is not the ear of the body that is required here, but that of the heart; unless someone possesses this ear, he cannot grasp the words of the Spirit.

Thus, when the Lord spoke to the crowds in parables, although all who were present had ears, he warned the apostles, saying: “I speak to you who hear.” It is as though he said: “I open the words of heavenly mysteries to those whom I know to perceive them with the same inward ear of the heart.”

The ear of the flesh passes over into hearing, but the hearing of the heart is vigorous both in hearing and in understanding.

It must also be observed that although at the beginning of these addresses the angel speaks on behalf of the Son of God—or, more precisely, the Son of God speaks through the angel—he does not say here: “Let the one who has an ear hear what the Son of God says,” but “what the Spirit says.” For the Son’s words are the words of the Holy Spirit. By this name the whole Trinity is also understood, concerning which it is said: “God is Spirit.”

Therefore, while Christ speaks, the Father and the Holy Spirit speak equally in him, because just as they are inseparable in unity, so they speak inseparably; and they teach the unity of the saints.

It must be known, moreover, that in this revelation, as in what follows, it is openly shown that sometimes the Son speaks in his own person, which applies to him alone, while at other times he speaks in the person of the Trinity. Therefore each address must be considered carefully, to determine which statements are to be referred only to the humanity of the Son of God and which to the whole Trinity.

“To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.”

The tree of life is the Wisdom of God the Father, as Solomon attests when he says: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, and whoever holds her is blessed” (Prov. III). The Apostle likewise testifies that Christ is the power of God and the Wisdom of God.

She is rightly called the tree of life because she grants eternal life to her faithful, whom in the present she satisfies with her body and in the future will satisfy with her contemplation. Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI).

She is rightly called the tree of life because in the present life she defends her elect from the heat of vices by the shade of her protection, and in future blessedness she offers food of eternal contemplation to those who desire it.

Let it therefore be said: “To the one who conquers the incitements of his flesh, the temptations of demons, and the adversities of wicked people, I will give to eat from the tree of life”—that is, “I will give myself to him as his reward when I have led him to my contemplation.”

Paradise is understood either as the present Church, in which his faithful daily eat his body and drink his blood, or as eternal life, which is Christ himself, as the Lord says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

When he says that he has a God, in whose paradise he asserts that this tree exists, he speaks according to the humanity which he assumed for us. Those, therefore, who conquer the pleasures of sin in this paradise of the Church worthily attain the reception of the sacraments of the body and blood, and will reach the contemplation of God. They will receive the tree of life itself as their reward, because he himself is the tree of life that gives, and he himself gives from the tree of life to those who conquer, and he himself is the fruit of the tree that he gives.

[Col. 0968D] And to the angel of the church of Smyrna write:

Smyrna is interpreted as “their song.” A song pertains to joy, which plainly suits the faithful, to whom the Lord speaks in the person of this church. For these words are not spoken to one person alone, but rather to the unity of the saints.

“These things says the first and the last.”

The first, namely, before whom there was no one; the last, through whom all things were restored.

“Who was dead and lives.”

Although he was dead through weakness, as the Apostle says (II Cor. XIII), he lives through the power of God. This is the first and the last: he who always lives in his substance, existing as the first, was dead in our humanity at the end of time, being born as a human being.

[Col. 0969A] “I know your tribulation.”

“I know,” that is, “I approve and choose.” Although tribulation is here expressed in the singular, it is nevertheless understood as manifold and of every kind. Hence the Psalmist says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII).

The holy Church, in whose person the divine word speaks here to the church of Smyrna, endures many tribulations outwardly, when it receives from adversaries insults, chains, prisons, and other torments of this kind; or when it is invisibly tormented inwardly by demons; or when, exhausted by fasts, prayers, and vigils, it nearly succumbs under its own burden.

It is also afflicted and troubled by itself when the flesh resists the spirit. The Lord knows and approves all these tribulations, and in the future he will deliver them from all of them, when he takes every tear from their eyes.

“And your poverty”—understand, “I know and approve.”

“But you are rich toward God,” according to the saying: “As having nothing, yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI).

It is remarkable how the elect can be both poor and rich. This can be understood in two ways. Many saints were rich in this world, such as Abraham, David, and many others; yet they were as though possessing nothing, because, despising earthly riches, they recognized themselves as pilgrims while already holding heavenly riches in their minds. After meeting their own needs and those of their families from what they possessed, they spent the remainder for the uses of the poor.

Or certainly, they were poor in material things, as were the holy apostles, but rich in faith, already possessing heaven through hope. To them the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. III).

Let it therefore be said: “I know your poverty, but you are rich,” as though it were said: “From the very thing by which you consider yourself poor through humility of spirit, you are proved rich in every respect.”

One and the same elect person is both poor and rich: poor, as still a pilgrim; rich, as destined one day to become a citizen; poor in earthly dwelling; rich in blessed predestination.

“And you are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.”

This does not pertain only to one church of the Smyrnaeans, but generally to the whole Church throughout the world. In individual places and throughout the entire world it is blasphemed by the impious, who call themselves Jews and are not, because “Jew” is interpreted as “one who confesses,” but they are a congregation [Col. 0969D] of Satan.

Whoever truly confesses Christ is a Jew. Concerning such people the Lord says: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father” (Mark VIII; Luke XII). Therefore the expression of the name “Jew” signifies the confession of our Mediator; and consequently all who are reckoned by the name of Christianity are spiritually called Jews.

The Jews generally lost this name when they denied Christ, saying: “We do not know where he is from” (John IX). They always blaspheme the Church of God, sometimes openly and sometimes secretly, but always in their hearts.

The false Christians also belong to their company: they have the Christian name, but they do not have the works of Christianity. Concerning them Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus I).

The Church is therefore blasphemed by false Jews because the words of the elect are judged by the reprobate; for the sayings and deeds of the righteous are always contrary to the thoughts of the reprobate.

Although such people remain within the bosom of the Church, in life and conduct they divide themselves into many synagogues of Satan, because, as many vices as they serve, so many divisions they produce within themselves.

Such people falsely appropriate the name of Jews to themselves. Inflamed by the fires of zeal, they have often become accustomed to blaspheming the Church more severely than those who have never approached its fellowship to commit insults.

But until the weeds are finally separated from the wheat, none of these people should be abandoned. All must be admonished; all must be endured, after the example of our Redeemer, who endured the sacrilegious and impious traitor Judas until the suffering of death.

He exhorts the Church to bear with their evils, and, as though adding powerful weapons, he says:

“Fear none of those things which you are about to suffer.”

That is: Whatever injuries and harms you suffer from false Jews, false brothers, or pagans, do not fear them, because they pass away. This is what he says to the faithful in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X).

“Behold, the devil is about to send some of you into prison, so that you may be tested, and you will have tribulation for ten days.”

It is now clear that different persons are being addressed through one angel. First the divine voice spoke as though to one person: “Fear none of those things which you are about to suffer.” Now it adds, as though speaking to many: “Behold, the devil is about to send some of you into prison,” and so forth.

By the name of prison every tribulation of sufferings is understood, which the saints endured from the devil. Through his members he torments them in different ways, shutting them in prisons and afflicting them with diverse and varied tribulations.

He does not say, “The devil is about to send you into prison,” but “some of you,” because this does not pertain to the whole body of the angel, which consists of saints and reprobates. Rather, he wishes those to be understood who emerge victorious from the tribulations inflicted upon them: they are troubled so that they may be tested, and tested so that they may be crowned.

Let it therefore be said: “Behold”—that is, in the present time—the devil is about to send, through his members, such as Nero, Domitian, and the others, “some of you into prison,” that is, into various afflictions, “so that you may be tested,” so that after the testing you may become victorious and be crowned, according to the saying: “Blessed is the person who endures temptation” (James I). “And you will have tribulation for ten days.”

By the ten days during which the Church is troubled, the whole present time is understood, in which the commandments of the Decalogue are necessary. For just as, for example, any emperor who sends soldiers against enemies equips them with every kind of weapon, so almighty God, sending his elect into battle in this world against demons and wicked people, equips them with the commandments of the Decalogue, armed with which they can resist them.

As long as they possess the Decalogue, they are necessarily stationed in battle array. Hence it is rightly said: “You will have tribulation for ten days.” It is as though it were said: Do not seek rest in the battle of the present life as long as you are armed like soldiers with the ten commandments against the enemy’s temptations, whether open or hidden. For there is no place for joy where the whole life of a human being is temptation.

Some people say—as blessed Bede does—that the ten temptations refer to the ten persecutions of the gentiles, and they suppose that these extend from Nero Caesar to Diocletian. Those who say this may see for themselves how it is so.

This number ten can also be understood in another way. It is clear to all readers that the first human being was principally tempted and overcome by the serpent in paradise through three temptations; afterward, when the second human being was tempted in these same three ways, the serpent succumbed: avarice, vainglory, and desire. Against these principal temptations the Church fights daily.

The number seven refers to the present time, which revolves through seven days. Since this threefold temptation cannot be absent from the whole course of this life, in which the other vices chiefly exercise their dominion, and since this mortal life itself unfolds through cycles of seven days, the principal tribulation of the Church is rightly expressed by the number ten days.

For when this threefold temptation is applied to the seven days, the number ten is completed. Let it therefore be said concerning the elect: “You will have tribulation for ten days,” as though he said: Until the present life comes to an end, revolving through seven days, you will have a struggle against various temptations, in which these three chiefly hold dominion.

“Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.”

Here he openly shows to whom the ten days extend: namely, to the whole period during which the elect must preserve the faith. This is said both generally to the whole Church and specially to every faithful soul.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X). Be faithful, therefore, until death, and amid many pressures and innumerable disasters always look toward the triumph of victory.

Because he was going to say this, he had first stated above: “These things says he who was dead and lives.” It is as though he said: Do not lose faith in the King, because if you fight alongside me throughout the whole time of battle, after death you will be crowned with me; you will also receive a share in reigning.

Now is the time for battle; then will be the time for crowning. Hence it is also said below (Rev. III): “Whoever conquers, I will make him sit on my throne, just as I conquered and sit with my Father on his throne.”

Let the one who has the ear of the heart and understanding of mind hear and understand that what has been said applies to him, and what the Spirit says to the churches:

“Whoever conquers the devil’s temptations and the incitements of his flesh will not be harmed by the second death,” that is, by eternal damnation.

In sacred Scripture three deaths are often mentioned: one, the death of sin; another, the death of the flesh; and the third, the punishment of eternal damnation. The latter death is called here the second, not the third, because the discussion concerns only those deaths which cause harm—namely, the death of sin and the death of eternal punishment. In comparison with these, the death which is common to all should not be called death.

Hence the Apostle calls those who are dead according to the flesh “sleeping,” saying: “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep” (I Thess. IV).

The first death, therefore, which causes harm, is sin. To this death, which can cause harm, no other death follows except eternal damnation. Therefore, leaving aside the intermediate death, which does not cause harm, the other death—which causes harm after sin—had to be called the second.

Let it therefore be said: “Whoever conquers will not be harmed by the second death.” That is, whoever in this time overcomes the death of sin, which kills souls, will not arrive at the harm of that death which follows it and endlessly torments both bodies and souls. This death always kills and never extinguishes completely.

In the word “harmed,” corruption through misery should be understood. For only what is subject to corruption can be harmed.

And to the angel of the church of Pergamum write:

Pergamum is interpreted as “division of horns.” This plainly suits the Church, in which the good and the wicked exist together, and which, by judging, makes a distinction between the good and the wicked, so that the horns of sinners may be broken and the horns of the righteous exalted.

“These things says he who has the double-edged sword.”

The *rhomphaea* is a sword sharpened on both sides. By the name of sword, sacred Scripture is understood, as the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

This sword of the Old and New Testaments is rightly said to be sharpened on both sides, because on one side it cuts away sins of action, and on the other sins of thought. For the Old Testament says: “If anyone commits adultery, he shall be put to death” (Lev. XX); but the New says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V), and many things similar to these.

Or certainly, it is called sharp on both sides because, just as a two-edged sword divides flesh and separates limb from limb, so the sword of God’s word separates the good from the wicked. Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X), and so forth.

Or it is called sharp on both sides for this reason as well: it instructs the simple through the historical meaning and the perfect through allegory.

I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. This is also said generally to the universal Church, which, mingled with the reprobate, knows that throughout the world she is exercised by Satan’s temptations. For just as all the elect are the dwelling place of God, [Col. 0972D] so all the reprobate are the dwelling place of the devil; in their midst the Church dwells, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. II). And in the Song of Songs it is said: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song II). Thus the praise of the elect grows all the more and is spread everywhere, since amid the wicked they preserve works of innocence.

Hence Holy Scripture praises Lot (Gen. XIX), because he was just in sight and hearing, dwelling among those who daily afflicted his soul by their unjust deeds. Hence also the Church says of the elect: “They surrounded me like bees” (Ps. CXVII). For the bee carries honey in its mouth but hides poison in its tail. So indeed those who contrive frauds put sweetness first, so that they may infect others with bitterness.

“And you hold fast my name”—that is, you honor the name of Christianity with an undivided faith, even in a time of tribulation. “And you did not deny my faith,” though pressed down by the afflictions of the faithless.

“And in those days Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you.” It is not easy to see what sort of Latin construction this is, unless perhaps it is understood through suppressed words. If he had said, “You did not deny my faith in the days of Antipas, my witness, who was killed among you,” the meaning would be plain and easily understood. But when it says, “You did not deny my faith, and in the days Antipas, my witness,” and so forth, the sentence is obscure. Therefore suppressed words are necessary, so that we may pronounce the sentence in this way: “And you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith; and in those days in which Antipas, my faithful witness, existed, who was killed among you, you did not deny my faith.”

The same is found in the Psalm: “Do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak against God with iniquity” (Ps. LXXIV). If it immediately added, “For God is judge,” the sentence would seem clear. But since it inserts in the middle, “For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains,” and then adds, “For God is judge,” the sentence is rendered obscure. Either, then, this construction arose through the fault of copyists, or certainly, as was said, it has, according to the custom of Scripture, certain necessary parts of speech understood.

But let us now examine the meaning. There was a certain martyr who was killed in the church of Pergamum; through him, of course, all the martyrs are understood—those who suffer in this world either by open or by hidden martyrdom. For just as all are found in one Church, so all Christ’s martyrs are found exalted in one martyr by the proclamation of praise.

When he says that his witness was killed among the saints, this must be understood not as meaning that he was killed by them, but that he was killed among them—namely, by those in whom Satan dwells, that is, by the reprobate who are Satan’s dwelling place. In their person he immediately adds:

“But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to fornicate.” These words do not concern the one to whom it was previously said, “You hold fast my name,” and so forth, but those who were mingled with the reprobate, whom the angel of Pergamum—that is, the bishop of that city—allowed to teach perversely. The historical account is clear (Num. XXII): Balaam was summoned by Balak to curse the children of Israel. He refused to curse them and even wished to become like them in death. But afterward, overcome by gifts, he gave counsel for the destruction of that same people.

He foresaw that the minds of the children of Israel were ready for fornication. Therefore he advised Balak to place beautiful women before them, so that, enticed by their appearance, they might rush into illicit embraces, and, beguiled by their blandishments, eat from the sacrifices of Peor; by this deed, plainly, having been abandoned by God, they would fall before them. And this counsel was fulfilled against the children of Israel, and they were easily deceived. Then wrath went out from the Lord and struck twenty-three thousand of them, until Phinehas, moved by zeal for God, exercised vengeance upon the adulterers.

These things were then done at the instruction of an impious diviner and magician; and the same thing takes place particularly in the church of Pergamum, but generally throughout the world. Balaam, therefore, is interpreted as “vain people”; Balak as “one who strikes down”; Israel as “a man who sees God.”

Balaam, then, signifies heretics, who do not possess within themselves the weight of virtues and faith, and therefore are vain. Balak, who is called “one who strikes down,” signifies the princes of this world. This name fittingly applies to them, because, without doubt, while the princes of this earth always seek to be superior to others, if they see anyone striving to rise to the summit of his dignity, they strike him down to the ground with all their strength—that is, they cast him down into lowliness.

Often, at the persuasion of heretics, they fight against the Israelites—that is, against men who see God—so that they may eat from sacrifices offered to idols and fornicate away from God by following the heretics’ wicked doctrines. For when they put certain persuasive and sweet things first in their false teachings, they wish, as it were, to seduce them by beautiful women, so that they may eat food sacrificed to idols—that is, follow the teaching of idols, full of every impurity—and fornicate there, that is, abandoning the doctrine of truth, cleave to the lies of perverse teachers in the most ardent fire of lust.

Alternatively, Balaam, who, as we said, is interpreted as “vain people” and signifies demons wandering through empty things, and Balak, who is called “one who strikes down,” signifies our flesh, which often strikes down the soul by drawing it toward perverse deeds, although the soul ought to see God with its whole mind. This occurs through women, that is, through the pleasures and delights of this age, by love of which the soul, often enticed by the snares of demons, is drawn into consenting to the use of illicit things. Israel signifies the soul contemplating God.

With Balaam teaching, then, Balak sent lovers of pleasure before the children of Israel, so that by their persuasions they might eat from the sacrifices and fornicate with them. For when the flesh is delighted by the persuasions of unclean spirits, it brings the enticements of those desires before the mind’s sight, and by love of them—as has been said—it is swept into consent.

“So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” What has been said above about the deeds of the Nicolaitans, or what they signified by their actions, is sufficient. “So you also,” he says, “have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans”—that is, just as there are among you those who follow the teaching of Balaam, so there are those who follow the teaching of the Nicolaitans. This is said to those who were imitators of them, and they are also urged to repentance when it is said:

“Repent likewise”—namely, from the deeds of the Nicolaitans, just as from the deeds and teaching of Balaam.

“But if not, I am coming to you, and I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth.” Above, he had already urged the angel to repent because he allowed certain people to hold the teaching of Balaam or of the Nicolaitans. Therefore, when he says, “But if not, I am coming to you,” and then adds, “I will fight against them,” this must be understood as though he were saying, “I will fight with you.” These words concern both those who followed the aforesaid teaching and those who did not correct them. For the one who teaches wickedness and the one who silently allows wickedness to be taught are bound by equal guilt.

To such people the Lord says, “I am coming to you”—that is, I will make you experience the coming of my wrath and my vengeance—“and I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth”—that is, I will condemn them with the sharp judgments of my words. For the sword of God’s mouth signifies his word and powerful commands, as Paul testifies when he says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

“Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” Whatever he says to one of them, he certainly wishes all the churches to hear.

“To the one who conquers his own desires and the temptations of demons, I will give the hidden manna”—that is, I will give myself to him, who am the living bread descended from heaven, and who therefore became man so that man might eat the bread of angels.

That bread, the manna once given to the children of Israel in the wilderness, signified this. Those who ate it spiritually, such as Moses, Aaron, and Joshua, although they died in body, were immortal in mind. But those who understood nothing there beyond what they saw died an eternal death. Concerning them the Lord says to the Jews: “Your fathers ate manna and died” (John VI).

So now also those who worthily receive the body and blood of the Lord receive life there; but those who eat it unworthily eat and drink judgment upon themselves. This manna promised here to the faithful they now receive in the sacrament through faith; at some time it will be received in truth through spiritual participation. What now remains hidden will then be manifest.

Therefore, “To the one who conquers, I will give the hidden manna”—that is, after the labors of this life have ended, I will grant him the contemplation of myself. Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI).

For manna is interpreted as “What is this?” We do not say “What is this?” except concerning something we have not previously seen. This manna now remains hidden, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man—what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

[Col. 0975D] “And I will give him a white stone, and upon the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” A stone is a precious gem, also called a carbuncle, because, when placed in darkness, it is said to shine like a burning coal.

By this stone Christ himself is understood, who shone amid the darkness of this age when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Hence it is rightly called white, because he appeared among human beings pure, without any darkening by sin, and by the light of his divinity illumined the darkness of our mortality.

He says, then, “I will give the victor a golden stone”—that is, I will give him myself, who triumphs over the world and the author of death, so that he may be my brother and a participant in the kingdom in [Col. 0976A] glory. Hence John says: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John I), so that, just as he himself is the Son of God by nature, so they may be sons by grace.

In this grace of adoption a new name is also given—that is, the name “Christian,” previously unheard of. The faithful are called Christians from Christ, just as Israelites are named from Israel, and Jews from Judah. Concerning this name the Lord himself previously spoke through the prophet Isaiah to his Church: “You shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord will name” (Isa. LXII).

This name is on the stone because it began from him from whom all Christians are named. And this name is given only to victors—that is, to all those predestined to eternal life, who adorn the dignity of this name by their deeds. Hence it follows: “Which no one knows”—understand, worthily—“except the one who receives it.”

For “to know” is here used in the sense of experiencing the power of this name. In the same way, women are said not yet to have known men—that is, they have not yet experienced a man’s bed. No one, therefore, knows this name except the one who receives it—that is, no one defends the power and dignity of this name by conduct and life except one who was previously predestined by God, so that he might not only be called a son of God but also be one.

To know the name of Christ pertains to keeping the commandments. In contrast, John says of any reprobate: “Whoever says, ‘I know God,’ and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him” (I John II). No one, therefore, knows this name except the one who receives it—that is, the one who has been predestined by God to be rightly called and to be a Christian.

This stone may also be understood as fiery charity. It has whiteness because it is a garment covering the blackness of sins, and fire because it is the love by which God and humanity are loved. A white stone is therefore given to those who conquer, so that they may love God and their neighbor. A name is given upon the stone so that they may fulfill that love in the new commandment. For it is written: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII). The power of this name is known only by the one who receives it—that is, by the one who keeps it in the new commandment entrusted to the disciples.

“And to the angel of the church of Thyatira write.” Thyatira, as was said above, is interpreted as “illuminated,” signifying the universal Church, which has been illuminated through Christ, [Col. 0976D] who is the true light enlightening every person who comes into this world. Therefore, although the divine word seems to speak to one particular Church, it generally concerns the whole Church.

“These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire.” Here it is openly shown whose type the angel bore, the one who displayed these things to blessed John, when he declares that his words are the words of the Son of God, saying: “These things says the Son of God, whose eyes, existing like a flame of fire, are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which illuminate the whole body of the Church.”

Or else the eyes are the divine utterances concerning which it is written: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. CXVIII), and again: “Your utterance is thoroughly refined by fire” (ibid.). Or the eyes of the Lord may also be understood as the teachers, who illuminate us by their teaching and example and provide the light of knowledge.

“And his feet are like aurichalcum.” The Lord’s feet are either the holy preachers, through whom he traverses the world, tested by the fire of tribulation, or else his final and last members, who fall in the ultimate persecution.

“I know your works”—that is, I approve your good deeds, since I freely bestowed on you the ability to perform them. In this passage the person of the universal Church is introduced.

“And your charity and faith”—understand, “I know,” in the same way as your works: your charity, by which you love God with your whole heart and your neighbor as yourself; and your faith, by which you believe God to be three in persons and one in majesty.

Here the order is inverted: works are mentioned first, then charity, and afterward faith, although the proper order is first to believe, then to love what one believes, and afterward to perform what faith and love have taught.

To these praises of the Church it adds: “And your ministry and your patience.” The ministry is understood as that by which they ministered to the Churches, offering works of mercy to those in Jerusalem who possessed nothing of their own, as the Apostle urged them (Gal. II), so that they would remember the brethren. Patience is understood in this way: they willingly endured all the adversities of this age for Christ, so that, persevering to the end, they might be saved.

“And your last works are more numerous than the first.” As regards the appearance of the Church, her works are rightly said to be more numerous than the first, because the Church was initially established by easier and lighter commandments. Hence the apostles imposed only four requirements upon those who believed (Acts XV): that they abstain from what had been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what had been strangled, and from fornication.

Afterward, when the multitude of the Church had grown, the point was reached at which they left everything for Christ and aimed at the summit of perfection: they gave their possessions to the poor and left brothers, sisters, fathers, mothers, and wives. From this also the monastic life took its beginning.

Or this may certainly refer to the day of judgment, when, as the most savage persecution increases in the time of Antichrist, a greater strength of action will shine forth in the Church, while Jews and Gentiles alike, established in the faith of Christ, will labor twice as much as they do now.

“But I have a few things against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet, and she seduces my servants and teaches them to fornicate and to eat what has been sacrificed to idols.” No interpretation permits these words to refer to those whom he had previously praised with such great commendation. Rather, he turns his speech from the general body of the elect to the portion of the reprobate, which is understood in the teachers who, through their negligence, allow fornication and idolatry to exist in the Church under the Christian name.

But let us now examine the meaning. Jezebel was the wife of Ahab, king of Israel, both an idolater and a fornicator, and she also persecuted the servants of God. Yet this woman did not live until the coming of the Lord, for we read that she was trampled under the hooves of horses. But because there were people in the same Church who imitated her evil deeds, the mother herself of fornications, Jezebel, is marked out in them.

For just as all the elect, living one life, form one body of Christ, so all the reprobate make themselves one body of the devil. Thus it comes about that preceding members are found joined to those who follow, and those who follow to the preceding members. Hence it is written: “Woe to them who have gone in the way of Cain” (Jude I); and John says: “Now many antichrists have arisen” (I John II).

It may also be that this woman existed at that time, as some affirm and another translation indicates, in the same Church—namely, the wife of that angel—who taught the servants of God to eat what had been sacrificed to idols and to fornicate. From the likeness of this particular woman, the speech is figuratively transferred to the general Jezebel of the whole world.

The fornication of this Jezebel is understood in four forms. First, it occurs in the mind, concerning which it is written: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). Second, it occurs when the will of the mind is carried into effect; hence Paul says: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (I Cor. VI).

The third kind of fornication occurs when we worship images in place of God. Concerning this the Lord speaks through the prophet against Jerusalem, saying: “She committed adultery with wood and stone” (Jer. III).

The fourth kind occurs when earthly riches are desired immoderately and the creature is loved more than the Creator. Of this Paul also says (Eph. V): “And avarice, which is the service of idols.”

Three kinds of this fornication now flourish in the Church of this world: in the desire for bodily lust, in the actual performance of obscene intercourse, and in avarice for earthly prosperity. Nor has the fourth kind, which consists in the worship of images, been completely extinguished.

It should be noted that Jezebel calls herself a prophet, and for this reason seduces the servants of God. Many imitate this deed: being devoted to riches, and not wishing to be alone, they urge others to enjoy the pleasures they desire, saying that if God had wanted this not to happen, he would not have made male and female, nor fashioned bodily members suitable for such use.

“It is foolish, therefore, to abstain from such pleasure, which is enjoyed not only by other beasts or birds but even by flies.” While they say these things, it sometimes happens that they compel the flesh to take pleasure and draw it into consent to lust. Thus they reach the evil deed, to such an extent that, as time passes, having no reverence for modesty, they proclaim before others with praise what they have shamefully done.

Hence Jezebel is rightly called “a flow of blood,” or “flowing,” or “a dunghill.” Women, as blessed Jerome says in his books on the prophets, suffer a flow of blood each month, because when the monthly period arrives, excess blood is expelled. The name “blood,” however, signifies sins; hence David says: “Deliver me from bloods, O God” (Ps. L)—that is, from the sin of adultery and murder.

Jezebel is therefore called “a flow of blood” because the reprobate immediately bring into effect by their actions the evil will that they previously conceived, as soon as the time arrives for carrying out their iniquity. And when the deed of the desired pleasure is brought to completion, the mind becomes more anxious than it had been, increases the flames of lust in the heart, and casts itself entirely into bodily pleasure; thus, so to speak, the whole fluid melts together.

This is why Jezebel is called “flowing.” Because they turn an evil deed into a habit of sinning, and consequently express an opinion of themselves without any reverence, the same Jezebel is rightly called “a dunghill.” For from the filth of the lust they have perpetrated they emit far and wide the stench of an evil reputation. Hence the prophet says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I).

For beasts to rot in dung is, as blessed Gregory says, for any lustful person to end his life in the mire of desire. To such people the Psalmist’s words also apply: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII).

By the third kind of fornication, too, many who pursue these things customarily deceive the faithful. For certain illnesses or events in life they invite them to trees, springs, and other such places, saying: “By doing this I escaped such-and-such a danger, and by doing that I obtained such-and-such prosperity.” While they do these things, they invite the servants of God, as it were, to spiritual fornication.

But in another form of fornication also the reprobate deceive many: by their perverse persuasions they draw certain people away from the love of God and compel them to serve earthly desires. Therefore woe to those who fornicate as often as they desire earthly things more than heavenly things, and love the creature more than the Creator.

“And I gave her time to repent, and she does not wish to repent of her fornication.” Job says of such people: “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it in pride” (Job XXIV). For whoever sins and lives is tolerated by divine mercy while doing evil, so that he may turn back from his iniquity.

Therefore, the longer such a person is awaited and refuses to repent, the more tightly he will be bound by the chains of his guilt and punished by a just judgment. Hence the saying: “The child shall die at a hundred years, and the sinner at a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. LXV).

But we must ask: since in the preceding verse the negligent preacher, sluggish in exhortation, was told, “I have against you that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet, and she seduces my servants,” why does it not add, “I gave you and her,” or, under one expression, “I gave you both time to repent”?

The answer is that in the angel the whole body of the Church is included, and when he is rebuked, the rebuke pertains to those who are guilty. Therefore, from the particular class of preachers who had previously been reproved, the speech returns to the generality of the people and, within it, rebukes as though secretly the reprobate portion of that class for its impenitence—the same portion that he had rebuked openly above.

This is so that the part represented by the holy preachers earlier might not seem joined to the part represented by the reprobate. Thus, in perverse teachers, one and the same angel is openly reproved in particular for the guilt of silence and secretly rebuked in general for hardness of mind. But in the holy teachers he is neither openly reproved in particular nor secretly rebuked in general.

For when the divine voice says, “I have against you that you permit Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet, and she seduces my servants,” the silence of preachers who are sluggish in exhortation is revealed. But when it adds, “And I gave her time to repent, and she does not wish to repent of her fornication,” it passes from the particular to the general and comprehends both the particular and the general together under one expression.

“Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her will be in the greatest tribulation, unless they repent of their deeds; and I will kill her children with death.” What Jezebel is, those who commit adultery with her are; and her children, begotten from fornication, are also the same: one body of Satan.

But because reprobates succeed reprobates, the genus is divided into species, so that it may be shown through what successions the whole body of the devil progresses and through what increases it grows together.

The completed state in which Jezebel is placed with all her followers is understood as boldness and security in sinning. This universal harlot is placed on a bed not so that she may rest, but so that she may languish with fever and suffer delirium, to the point that she now says or does things that others would be ashamed to hear.

Often, by God’s just judgment, because of past sins, people rush into greater crimes. While they sin boldly and without fear, they rest as though on a bed—that is, in the security of sinning. God is said to place them in this security because, by a just judgment, he permits them to be placed there. The same meaning is found in the saying: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. X)—that is, he did not soften it.

So here also it says, “I place her on a bed”—that is, I will not draw her back, but, because of her past sins, I will permit her to sin freely and without fear. “And those who commit adultery with her”—that is, with themselves, since it was said above what the harlot is—“will be in the greatest tribulation.” This means that they will be brought, through the increase of their sins, to the greatest tribulation of Gehenna.

For the punishments of sins are, in a sense, the very increase of vices. This will happen unless they repent of their deeds. For when certain sinners refuse to repent of the crimes they have committed, they rush into other crimes, even more serious ones. Hence Paul says of certain people who knew God but did not glorify him: “Therefore God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. I).

“And I will kill her children, her imitators, with death.” We must not understand here the ordinary death by which the just also die, but the death that follows the death of the body: the soul’s condemnation, that is, everlasting damnation.

The bed onto which Jezebel is threatened with being cast may also signify eternal punishment, to which the wretched and reprobate will be handed over for torment. “And those who commit adultery with her”—that is, those who imitate her fornication in whatever way—“will be in the greatest tribulation” after the death of the flesh, where their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished. This is because they neglect to repent until sudden destruction overtakes them.

Moreover, according to the preceding interpretation, the children are understood either as imitators of evil people or as their perverse works. These will then be given over to death, when, after temporary joy, the wretched sinners will be handed over to be tormented by everlasting punishments for these deeds, having reached the death of their souls through the impunity of their crimes.

By contrast, the elect are afflicted here so that afterward they may rejoice. To them the prophet says: “Israel, I will no longer be angry with you, because my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezek. XIV). And in this Apocalypse: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. I).

The wicked prosper for a time, destined to be punished by eternal death; the elect are afflicted for a short while, destined to be strengthened by everlasting goods. He therefore says, “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline”—through bodily scourges, through the loss of temporal possessions, and through various and diverse afflictions of body and soul.

He also permits those whom he despises to remain on a bed—that is, in the security of sinning. The almighty God does this like a father who has two sons. He permits one to be his own master, allowing him to sleep, eat, drink, and do whatever else he wishes, because he intends to deprive him of his inheritance.

But, by contrast, he excommunicates the other, afflicts him with blows, sometimes makes him stay awake throughout the night, and makes him stand with his feet bound, because he wishes to make him his heir.

In this way God reproves and disciplines his elect, to whom he will give the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, so that, after the labors of this life have ended, they may attain the eternal possession. But he permits the reprobate to be masters of their own will and to rest on the bed of security, where afterward they will all be condemned with their wicked fathers. There will be great tribulation there, which no tongue of flesh can express; there every person who is failing does not perish, and the dying always live.

And all the Churches shall know that I am the one who searches hearts and kidneys. In the kidneys the delight of carnal desire is signified, because the seed of human conception proceeds from the loins. In the heart, however, thoughts are expressed, which proceed from the heart. As the Lord says: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, thefts” (Matt. XV), and so forth. Since in the preceding verse the Almighty had said that idolaters and adulterers would be condemned to death, not openly but secretly, he now demonstrates the faith of the Church, which believes even what it has not seen. For the Church of the faithful knows that God knows all things; although he may seem to tolerate the reprobate, nevertheless, secretly, in his foreknowledge, he already condemns them. Thus he says: “All the Churches shall know that I am the one who searches kidneys and hearts,” that is, I behold the deeds and thoughts of each person. Human beings may indeed know our works and words, but to God even our thoughts are manifest, because he sees what each person thinks or takes delight in. Hence that most wise orator says: “You alone know the hearts of all the children of men” (2 Chron. VI). When he comes to judgment, he will condemn not only works but also the very slightest thoughts of the heart. Accordingly, through the Prophet (Isa. LXVI), he says: “Behold, I am coming to gather together the works and thoughts of each person.” [Col. 0981D]

This statement—that in the vengeance of the reprobate God is said to be the searcher of kidneys and hearts—may also appropriately be understood in this way: what the Church now holds by certain faith, it will see in the future through the experience of events. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord shall be known when he executes judgments” (Ps. IX)—not because he was previously unknown through faith, when he judged secretly, but because then he will be known through the experience of his judgments. [Col. 0982A]

“And I will give to each of you according to his works.” Here it is clearly shown that above he comprehended everything under the name of fornication, since this sentence foretells not the future condemnation of one work but of many. Manifest crimes will be punished, and hidden ones also; therefore we are compelled here to confess fornication in every form, which above we understood as fourfold. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. LXXII). Let it therefore be said: “And I will give to each of you according to his works”—to the just, namely, the reward of labor; to the impious, the punishment of eternal condemnation. Here there is nothing further that ought to be explained, but much that ought rather to be feared. For it is also said here through prophecy that Noah, Daniel, and Job alone would save their own souls, but would not deliver son or daughter.

“But I say to you and to the others who are in Thyatira: those who do not have this teaching, who have not known the depth of Satan.” [Col. 0982B]

Above he had rebuked the reprobate; now he turns his word toward the elect. Therefore he rightly says: “I say to you and to the others,” that is, to the just who above were not included among the number of the reprobate.

“Those who do not have this teaching”—that is, those whom the wicked persuasion of Jezebel does not incline toward evil action, so that they imitate the wicked. “Who have not known the depth of Satan”—that is, they have not imitated his pride. For they are said not to know Satan’s depth in the same way that sacred Scripture says that women did not know men when they had not yet experienced a man’s bed, or as we say in ordinary speech that a truthful person does not know how to lie.

The depth of Satan is understood as pride, because, swelling up against God, he wished to become like the Most High. For this reason, when he fell to the earth, he cast down with himself many legions of angels who consented to him. Man knew his depth when, by imitating him, he desired to become like God, according to the promise of the deceiver: “On whatever day you eat, you will be like gods” (Gen. III). Those also knew this depth who eagerly sought to raise a tower as far as heaven. [Col. 0982C]

But the elect do not possess knowledge of Satan’s depth, because in all things they humble themselves, following the footsteps of the Redeemer, who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). For they attend to what the Lord says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV). Therefore, having received wise counsel from this, they seize the path of humility, by which they may ascend to the summit of exaltation, as some say:

“Nevertheless, I do not lay upon you any other burden; only hold fast what you have until I come.”

This is said of those who, puffed up against the Son of God and knowing Satan’s depth, were striving to drag those who had believed in Christ from among the nations toward the ceremonies of the old law. Of them Luke says (Acts XV): “Certain men who had come down from Judea were teaching the brothers that unless you are circumcised according to the law of Moses, you cannot be saved.” For this reason they also sent Barnabas and Paul to the apostles in Jerusalem, from whom they learned that it was sufficient for the Gentiles to abstain from what had been sacrificed, from blood, from what had been strangled, and from fornication. [Col. 0982D]

When certain people from among the Gentiles said to them, “Unless you are circumcised according to the law of Moses, you cannot be saved,” Peter said: “Why do you seek to impose upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts XV). Of those who were saying these things, the Lord here says to the Church: “I do not lay upon you any other burden”—that is, observance of the old law, as those who belong to the synagogue of Satan do—but I permit you to remain under a light burden. Therefore, hold fast what you have: the light burden to which you have been called; do not cast it away.

Concerning this burden, that is, the grace of our Redeemer, Peter says: “We believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid.). The Lord himself invites his faithful to this burden, saying: “Take my yoke upon you” (Matt. XI), and so forth. A little later: “For my yoke is easy,” and so on. Thus he calls from burden to burden, but from a heavy one to a light one—that is, from law to grace, through which the law is not only fulfilled but also surpassed. [Col. 0983A]

Yet while saying this, we tie a question for ourselves. If, according to the foregoing statement of blessed Peter, the law is unbearable, how can it be surpassed? We must understand that the same law is unbearable in the observance of carnal precepts, but is fulfilled in the keeping of spiritual commandments, which are comprised in the ten words of the two tablets. In the action prefigured by those victims, however, it is surpassed, because in comparison with those things that are now performed in truth, they appear exceedingly insignificant; they could not be fulfilled by their hearers, since only the letter was outwardly proclaimed.

For in the Old Testament some precepts concerned a life to be represented figuratively, namely, the offerings of carnal victims; others concerned a life to be lived, and in these the law is fulfilled by believers through the ten words of the law. In the commandments of the figuratively represented life, the law is indeed unbearable according to the letter, but according to the spirit it is surpassed. When the Lord, having completed this statement, concludes by saying “until I come,” he clearly shows that, until the time of restoration, the Church remains under grace, and that the burden of the law is by no means to be added to the shoulders of believers, contrary to the falsehood of the Jews. [Col. 0983B]

“And whoever conquers the desires of the flesh and the temptations of demons, and whoever keeps my works until the end”—that is, perseveres in my faith until the end of life—“to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod, and they will be shattered like a potter’s vessel, just as I also received from my Father.” [Col. 0983C]

The Son of God must not be understood to have received this authority over the nations through his divinity, since he is equal to the Father, but through the form of his humanity, by which he was made lower even than the angels. According to this humanity he says in the Gospel: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XVIII). According to this humanity, the Father is also said to address him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II). But concerning the authority which he has with the Father before all ages, Daniel bears witness, saying: “His authority is an eternal authority, which shall not be taken away” (Dan. VII).

The authority, therefore, which Christ, having become man in time, received from the Father, he promises to give to his elect—but in himself, from whom the whole body is governed and to whom the whole body of the Church clings. Since he himself is the head of the elect, while the elect are his members, what the head itself possesses the members also appear to possess by hereditary right. [Col. 0983D]

Let it therefore be said: “To the one who conquers I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod.” The apostles first received this authority, and afterward their successors, to whom authority to bind and loose was given. It must be understood, however, that when preachers receive authority over others, they first rule themselves. They restrain themselves from what is unlawful just as they strive to restrain their subjects.

Their rule is also expressed by the iron rod, which possesses uprightness but no softness, because holy preachers know neither to spare themselves nor others against justice. They strive to direct the path of justice equally in themselves and in others. Hence it is said to their head: “Your rod is a rod of uprightness, the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV). What this means is immediately explained when it is added: “You have loved justice and hated iniquity.”

By contrast, the rod of certain rulers in the Church is soft and crooked—indeed, it is the alteration of justice itself. When both flock and shepherd sin equally, yet the shepherd, who is foremost, gently pats himself while harshly imposing temporal penance upon his subjects, he plainly carries a soft and pliable rod. Conversely, the Lord admonishes, saying: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Matt. VII), because every prelate ought equally to spare himself and the flock subject to him, and equally to correct himself and the flock subject to him. [Col. 0984A]

The nations who believe in Christ are rightly compared with earthen vessels, because in the frailty of the flesh they contain the treasure hidden from the ages. Hence Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. IV). That the vessels are said to be shattered at the touch of the rod can be understood in two ways: some are broken apart so that they may be changed into the pursuit of a better life; others so that they may perish eternally. Thus one and the same rod rules those predestined to life, while it destroys and shatters those foreknown for death.

This is why the Lord commands Jeremiah to go to the potter’s house, and there, showing him a vessel that had been spoiled and then refashioned by the potter into something better, says: “Can I not do with you, house of Israel, just as this potter does? says the Lord. Behold, as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand” (Jer. XVIII). Elsewhere, too, it is said to the same potter of the human race: “Turn the impious, and they will not exist” (Prov. II)—that is, after their overthrow they will remain not impious but pious. By contrast, elsewhere it is said: “You will destroy them, and you will not build them up” (Ps. XXVII). [Col. 0984B]

“And I will give him the morning star. Let the one who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.”

According to the literal sense, he calls the morning star *Lucifer*, which, rising, by its rising shows the sun’s approach. Spiritually, the morning star is understood as Christ, who, rising from the dead, drove away the darkness of this age, filled the whole world with the light of faith, and illumined the darkness of our mortality with the radiance of his light. Concerning this star Peter says to the faithful: “Until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. I).

In sacred Scripture, whenever the morning star is placed in the singular, the man Christ is represented by it. When morning stars are introduced in the plural, angelic creatures are signified. Hence: “When the morning stars praised me together” (Job XXXVIII). When stars are mentioned simply and without qualification, teachers of the Church are sometimes expressed by them; hence: “Those who are learned will shine like the stars of the firmament” (Dan. XII). [Col. 0984C]

Thus Christ, appearing alive after death, became the morning star for us, because, while providing in himself an example of resurrection, he indicated what light would follow. Therefore he professes that he will give the morning star to those who conquer—that is, himself and the glory of the future resurrection. This will be fulfilled when those who are in the tombs hear the voice of the Son of God, and when he transforms the body of our humility, conforming it to the body of his glory (Matt. V; Phil. III). For when the darkness of mortality has been cast down as the resurrection shines, there will appear, as it were, a morning star, which will reveal the perfect day of eternity.

## CHAPTER III

“And to the angel of the Church of Sardis write.”

As stated above, Sardis is interpreted as “to the prince of beauty,” with “apt” and “adorned” understood. Here too it must be said that, just as we discussed at length above, what is said to one Church certainly applies to all. [Col. 0985D]

“These things says the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars.”

The Son of God has seven spirits, namely, the sevenfold Spirit, equal to him in the nature of unity. Hence Isaiah (chap. XI): “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest,” he says, “upon the humble: the spirit of wisdom and understanding.” He also has seven stars, that is, the sevenfold Holy Spirit, as a servant under the authority of his power. And although the Son of God is of one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is rightly said to possess the sevenfold Spirit, because every grace of that Spirit is bestowed through Christ upon believers.

“I know your works: you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead. Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die.”

He shows that this person is partly already dead and partly still alive: dead, that is, in respect of crimes, but alive in respect of good works. Let it therefore be said: “You have a name that you are alive, but you are dead.” It is as though he were saying: You think that you live because you are engaged in certain good works. But understand that you cannot live if vices have prevailed over the virtues by which you seem to live. [Col. 0986A]

For there are some who devote themselves to almsgiving and care for the poor, but do not restrain their hands from robbery. Others devote themselves to generosity in almsgiving, restrain their hands from robbery, and hold themselves back from committing adultery, but, driven by the goads of anger and envy, seek to extinguish the life of others. So too in similar cases, while they think themselves alive through certain good works, many die through a single crime. Of such people James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James II).

A kindly exhortation is directed to them when it is said: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die.” It is as though he were saying: If you wish to live in those things which you have done well, awaken through repentance from those things which you have done badly; for if you remain dead in those things, you will in no way live in these. Hence the Psalmist admonishes, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). [Col. 0986B]

In the statement “strengthen the rest that were about to die,” it is also shown that if someone awakens perfectly from the sleep of sin through the lament of repentance, he does not, once alive, lose those works which he performed well even while dead. Thus he gives them life by awakening from the sleep of sin. For it is said: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die,” as though it meant: If you revive in that part in which you are dead, strengthen the rest that still live within you, lest they die.

These words can also be understood in another way. There are many who guard their life from every crime and also serve the virtues, yet seek human praise. Therefore, because a right intention does not precede in thought, every work that follows in outward display is wrong. Through what proceeds outwardly into public view, they are considered alive by human beings; therefore they have a name that they are alive. But through what lies hidden within, they are reckoned dead before God. [Col. 0986C]

Hence the devout admonition follows: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die.” It is as though he were saying: If you wish to live, beware of seeking praise from human beings, lest exaltation spoil the intention of your work. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Take heed that you do not perform your righteousness before human beings” (Matt. VI).

“I do not find your works complete before my God.” The works of the person who performs virtues given to him by the Lord but stains them with vices are not complete before God; nor are the works of the person who, through pride, seeks human glory for the good things he performs outwardly. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be luminous” (Matt. VI). “But if it is evil, your whole body will also be dark.”

All these matters, which we have examined under a twofold interpretation, can also be understood of those who boast that they possess the remaining virtues without charity. It should be noted, however, that the only-begotten Son of God—one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit—says that he has God according to the humanity which he assumed from us and for us. According to this humanity he also cried out upon the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Col. 0986D]

“Therefore keep in mind how you have received and heard.”

This sentence accords with each of the senses of the preceding interpretation. It can apply to those who flourish in the other virtues but waste away through a single crime; and to those who guard their life from every crime but seek human glory from it; and also to those who, without the mother of the virtues, which is charity, may produce the fruits of action but do not bring them to perfection.

Let it therefore be said: Keep in mind how you received from the holy preachers, and how you heard, that “if anyone keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all” (James II). Or keep in mind that a wicked intention must not precede works of virtue—namely, that you must not seek human glory—if you wish the works themselves to reach the reward of recompense. Or keep in mind how you received and heard that, even if you abound in all the virtues, if you do not have charity, you are nothing. [Col. 0987A]

Hence the Apostle says: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. XIII).

“And keep”—that is, keep what you received and heard from the holy preachers. “And repent”—so that you may wash away, with the groans of tears, what you have understood wrongly, and fulfill through the execution of works what you received from the preachers.

Therefore, if you do not keep watch, I will come to you like a thief, and you will not know when I will come.

The person who keeps watch holds the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the divine light. The person who keeps watch preserves through action what he believes. The person who keeps watch drives negligence and sluggishness away from himself. The person who keeps watch both providently desires what is good and cautiously avoids what is evil. The person who keeps watch seeks not human praise from what he does, but the glory of God. [Col. 0987B]

Therefore, if you do not keep watch so as to do everything solely out of love for the Creator; if you do not shake off from yourself the lethargy of negligence; and if you do not strive to await the coming of the heavenly Judge, I will come to you like a thief—that is, suddenly and unexpectedly. Hence it follows: “And you will not know when I will come.”

For just as a thief, arriving unexpectedly, slaughters those who are sleeping and plunders their possessions, so the heavenly Judge either comes daily and individually upon certain reprobates unexpectedly, destroying them, unrepentant, by the sentence of punishment and cutting them off from the happiness of the present age; or he will do this universally on the day of judgment, when he comes suddenly to judgment, condemns all the reprobate, and destroys their deeds like a most powerful robber. As he himself says in the Gospel: “If the householder had known at what hour the thief would come, he would surely have kept watch and would not have allowed his house to be broken into” (Matt. XXIV). And he added by way of admonition: “Therefore you also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (ibid.). [Col. 0987C]

“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, because they are worthy.”

By “names” we should understand the people themselves. He uses the word “names” in order to show that he knows not only the number but also the names of his elect. He knew Moses by name and writes the names of his saints in heaven, as he himself says to them: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

“You have a few names”—that is, a few people in comparison with the others who serve crimes and the uncleanness of the flesh—“who have not defiled their garments,” that is, the garment of baptism, the garment of immortality and innocence. These are plainly the garments from which the devil stripped the first human being in paradise when, through consent to sin, he laid him low before himself.

Man was adorned with these garments when, through the sacrifice of the fattened calf, the younger son, reconciled to his father, deserved to be clothed again in the first robe. Hence Paul says: “Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the one who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Col. III). [Col. 0987D]

The person who does not stain his garments with filth is the one who, after the sacrament of baptism, does not commit mortal sin. But because few are those who keep themselves undefiled from the knowledge of crime after baptism, it is first said: “You have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments.”

It is then added concerning them: “And they will walk with me in white, because they are worthy.” They will walk with him in white who imitate his innocence and holiness as far as they are able. Christ goes before by giving examples; the elect follow by imitating his examples. Hence Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. II). What follows—“because they are worthy”—means, by implication, because they are clean, or because they are worthy of that dignity. [Col. 0988A]

But are those who stain their life with the spots of crimes after baptism to be despaired of? Certainly not. If they repent, they wipe away the stains of their former life through the weeping of tears, which is a second kind of baptism. For just as there are two kinds of martyrdom, so there are two baptisms.

These garments are therefore preserved spotless in some and made white again after stains in others. Some, as has been said, commit no crime after the water of the washing; others wipe away the crime they have committed through the tears of repentance. The former must be admonished not to introduce the same stains of crime continually after baptism; the latter, to whom this has happened, must be exhorted to wash away those stains without delay in streams of tears. Hence it is said in this same Apocalypse: “Blessed is the one who keeps his garments, lest he walk naked” (Rev. XVI). [Col. 0988B]

“The one who conquers will thus be clothed in white garments.” In other words: The one who has fought bravely with the enemy to receive the garments and has conquered in the struggle will shine once again clothed in those same garments, like those who either kept them spotless or washed them after they had been stained.

This exhortation can also be applied to those who are still held under the yoke of the devil’s domination and have not yet been clothed with faith. They are urged to conquer—that is, to believe in Christ—because “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John V). Thus, by renouncing the ancient enemy through the washing of regeneration, they may receive from the one in whom they have believed the purity of heavenly life.

“And I will not erase his name from the book of life.” This means: I will write his name in the book of life. For “I will not erase” is said as though it meant “I will write.” By contrast, concerning the reprobate who do not conquer, it is said: “Let them be erased from the book of the living” (Ps. LXVIII). Explaining this, he adds: “And let them not be written among the just.” [Col. 0988C]

The book of life in which the elect are written must be understood as the predestination of Almighty God, because all the saints were foreknown and predestined before all ages and ordained for life, as it is written: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. II).

Therefore, the names of the reprobate are said to be erased from this book of life in the sense that, on account of the merit of their reprobation, they are by no means written in it.
