Similarly, Pharaoh’s heart is said to have been hardened by the Lord, meaning that the hardness of his heart was not softened by grace.

Let it therefore be said of the victor: “I will not erase his name from the book of life.” This is equivalent to saying: I know that he will be victorious; I keep his name written in heaven.

“And I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels.” Christ will confess before his Father the name of the person whose works he approves in the present. This confession will be fulfilled before the Father and his angels when he says to those placed at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV). It will then be brought forth publicly in praise, when the same Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X), and before his angels. [Col. 0988D]

## “And to the angel of the Church of Philadelphia write.”

Philadelphia, according to Bede’s interpretation, means “brotherly love.” By this name the universal Church is designated, which lives in love of God and neighbor and is shown to be loved by the Lord. It says: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI), and so forth.

Alternatively, according to Ansbertus Ambrosius, Philadelphia means “saving the Lord’s inheritance.” By this name the Church herself is also expressed, since she saves herself when she advances in faith and good works and never departs from the will of her Creator. For she is the Lord’s inheritance, concerning which the Psalmist records the Father’s voice to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II). [Col. 0989A]

“These things says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens. I know your works”—that is, I choose your works. “Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut.”

For this reason he principally and uniquely calls himself the Holy and True Lord: although we call certain people among human beings holy and truthful, in comparison with him no one is holy and true, because he himself is holiness and truth. Hence it is written: “Behold, among the holy ones no one is immutable” (Job XV). Likewise the Apostle says: “Every human being is a liar; God alone is truthful” (Rom. III:4).

We must understand the key of David as the incarnation of Christ. For according to the flesh he descended from the stock of David. The door which this same key opens or shuts is understood as the mediator himself between God and human beings, through whom we enter into eternal life, which he himself is. He teaches this when he says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X), and so forth. [Col. 0989B]

Thus he himself is called both the key and the door, just as the shepherd is called both the doorkeeper and the door. Therefore, when the key of David opens the door, he certainly opens himself, who was born according to the flesh, suffered, and was raised on the third day.

This door was previously closed to all except the prophets and holy Fathers, who through the Holy Spirit knew of his coming. Now, however, it has been opened to all who believe in Christ, while it remains closed to unbelievers. No one can close this door to the person to whom Christ himself wishes to open it.

Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when the Jews threatened the beaten disciples not to speak in the name of Jesus, once he opened their mouths no one could shut them. Therefore they answered: “We cannot fail to speak of the things that we have seen and heard” (Acts IV). [Col. 0989C]

The apostles had attempted to open this door, which had been closed to the Asians; but because, when he closes it, no one opens it, the Spirit of Jesus prevented them from speaking the word of God in Asia.

Alternatively, we can understand this door as sacred Scripture, which Christ himself opens to the faithful who believe in him, and no one shuts. He shuts it to the Jews who remain in unbelief, and no one opens it. Our Redeemer first opened this door when, after his resurrection, he opened the understanding of the two who were walking on the road so that they might understand the Scriptures, and taught them what had been written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms and had been fulfilled in him.

“Because you have little strength, and you have kept my word, and you have not denied my name amid the distresses and disturbances of this age.”

He shows the reason why the Church deserves these gifts: she trusts not in her own strength but in the grace of the eternal King. “And you have kept my word”—that is, the word of faith—“and you have not denied my name amid the distresses and disturbances of this age.” [Col. 0989D]

The saints are said to have little strength amid the disturbances of this age, although they possess much, because they presume that they can do much through Christ but little through themselves. Hence they say: “In God we shall perform valorous deeds, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing” (Ps. LIX).

When the Apostle Paul had said that he had labored more than all the apostles, he immediately added, as guardian of his humility: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV). And elsewhere: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV).

Thus it is said: “You have little strength,” as though it meant: You think that you have little strength, but in this you have great strength: because, through my giving, you hold fast the word of my faith and have not denied my name. Therefore, through me, you have been able to do much, because you did not fear in the virtues bestowed upon you.

Alternatively, holy Church has little strength in the present in comparison with the strength she will have in the future, when she will be afflicted by neither sorrow nor labor. [Col. 0990A]

“Behold, I will make those from the synagogue of Satan—who say that they are Jews, but are not, and lie—come.”

This has already been partly fulfilled in those Jews who, enlightened through the grace of Christ, have been given to the universal Church—that is, gathered into the unity of its faith. It will be fulfilled generally at the end of the age, when, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

For the present, in the synagogue of Satan—that is, in the assembly of the devil—they say that they are Jews, that is, confessors, but they lie, because every day they blaspheme Christ in the synagogues. For “Jew” means “confessing,” and therefore the expression of the name “Jews” is a confession of Christ. [Col. 0990B]

They say that they are Jews, but they lie, because, as the Apostle says (Rom. II): “It is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh, but the one who is a Jew inwardly; and circumcision is not of the flesh but of the spirit.” They lost the dignity of this name when, denying Christ, they said: “We do not know where he is from” (John IX).

“Behold, I will make them come with the steps of faith and worship before your feet.” That is, I will make them venerate your works and, by venerating them, imitate them. At present, because they do not believe, they not only do not venerate the works of the Church but also despise them.

“And they will know that I have loved you.” They will then know that Christ loves his Church when they themselves have become one Church with her. Hence, through the Prophet, it is said to Jerusalem: “The children of those who humbled you will come to you bowed down, and all those who slandered you will worship the traces of your feet, and they will call you the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel” (Isa. LX). [Col. 0990C]

“Because you have kept the word of my patience, I also will keep you from the hour of temptation which is to come upon the whole world to test those who dwell on the earth.”

The word of patience is what the Lord himself demonstrated by his example when, placed upon the cross, he prayed for his persecutors. Christ’s bride sets this word of patience before herself in every oppression and distress. For this reason, above all, he promises that he will preserve her from the hour of temptation.

The hour of temptation is understood as the whole present age, in which, although the Church is exercised by various temptations, she is not overcome. Concerning this temptation we pray daily to be delivered, saying: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. VI; Luke XI)—that is, into the fall of deception by which those who dwell on the earth are tempted: those who love earthly things, burn with worldly desires, and are overcome. [Col. 0990D]

The elect, however, whose way of life is in heaven, are tempted so that, having been tested, they may be crowned, not so that, having been led astray, they may be condemned.

We can also refer this hour—which is said not to have come already or to be present, but to be future—more appropriately to the times of Antichrist. Then that temptation will come which will examine not parts of the world but the whole world at once; from one side torments will rage, and from the other miracles will persuade. Hence the Lord rightly says concerning that time: “Then there will be tribulation such as has not been, nor will be” (Matt. XXI). The elect will be delivered from that temptation—that is, they will not be deceived—precisely because they are elect. [Col. 0991A]

I am coming soon. Lest the elect, when they see themselves worn down by the tribulation of temptation, should succumb, the Lord promises that he will come quickly to reward them. For everything that passes happens quickly; and therefore all present time hastens more rapidly toward its end from the very point at which it seems, as it were, to grow, and from the point at which it appears to receive increase it suffers decline.

Hold fast what you have—that is, the conduct and faith of heavenly life, through which you may attain the glory of the kingdom—so that no one may take your crown. This statement shows how, when the reward is taken away from some who are proud by the just judgment of God, it is mercifully given to others. Since the number of God’s elect is fixed, when some lose through their negligence the reward promised to them, others are substituted in their place, lest their position remain empty. Thus, for example, the Gentiles were substituted in the place of the Jews, who persisted in unbelief. Therefore each person who stands must take care lest, by pride or in any other way, he fall, lest another take his crown. But whoever has fallen through some lapse should rise, so that he may attain the promised crown.

“Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will go out no more.” No one doubts that the Church is the temple of God’s elect, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. III). The blessed Apostle Peter likewise speaks to the faithful: “And you, as living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses” (1 Pet. II).

The pillars of this temple are not only those who are more perfect, according to what Paul says—“Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars” (Gal. II)—but also their hearers, who triumph over the ancient enemy and possess strength through steadfast action. Therefore the Church itself is generally called by the Apostle “the pillar and foundation of the truth.”

The Lord therefore says: “Whoever conquers”—that is, the devil’s temptations, worldly desires, and the pleasures of the flesh—“I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.” In other words, I will make him strong in good works, so that he fears no loss, but by the strength of his steadfastness—that is, by his example and teaching—supports the Church.

As for the words, “and he will go out no more,” it is clearly understood that earlier, in the preceding members of the human race, he had gone out—namely, in that younger brother who, after leaving his father’s house, departed into a distant region and there dissipated his property by living wantonly with prostitutes. The Church had withdrawn from the unity of faith and action in order to build a tower; but, recalled by the slaughter of the fatted calf, it will go out no farther—that is, it will not be separated from the grace of Christ.

We may also understand this concerning both kinds of people. The first man, created in the image of God, was placed amid the delights of paradise, like a certain pillar of happiness. But when he heard the devil’s voice, he went out from the happiness of paradise into the misery of the world, and from rest into labor. When he fell, we also fell together with him; when he went out, we too went out with him. Hence the saying: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke X). Seeing this man’s misery, the author of the human race brought him and his offspring back, through the outpouring of his blood, to the place from which he had departed. This restoration is to be understood not only of those who, already stripped of their bodies, rejoice in heaven in visible form, but also of those who, while still dwelling in the flesh, walk by faith and rejoice on earth in hope.

They will go out no more from this joy of hope, because they are established in the heavenly glory of the saints—those who are shown to have lost it and gone out in the first Adam. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John VI). And the Psalmist says: “He is my God and my salvation; I shall not be moved any more” (Ps. LXI).

Let it therefore be said: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God”—as though it were said: I will bind the number of the elect, whom I foresee as conquerors, by the commands of my commandments into the building of the heavenly homeland; and because that building consists of the elect themselves, I will make it firm with unyielding love. “And he will go out no more”—that is, he will not be torn away from the common happiness of the heavenly homeland by any persuasion or terror of the enemy.

As for the fact that the Son of God says that he has God, as we have already said above, this must be understood according to the form of his humanity, in which he is shown to be lower not only than the Father but also than himself.

“And I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of the new Jerusalem, which comes down from heaven from my God.” The pen with which this name is inscribed is understood as the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which we become sons of God. For this is what he means by saying, “I will write upon him the name of my God”: I will make him a son of my God, so that, just as I am a son by nature, so he may be one by grace.

That this happens through the Holy Spirit Paul makes clear when he says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV). “And the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.”

When he says, “and the name of the city of the new Jerusalem,” understand: I will write it upon the one who conquers. This is to be understood in the sense that, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, he will deserve fellowship with God among the number of the saints.

Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” is said to descend from heaven from God in its head, to whom it is united by faith, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John III), and so forth. Or certainly it descends from heaven in the sense that whatever it possesses in faith and good works it has received from God above, according to the Apostle James: “Every good gift” (James I), and so forth.

It is rightly called new, because through the washing of regeneration and the Spirit of love it is stripped of the oldness of the earthly man and clothed with heavenly newness. Hence Paul says: “Having stripped off the old man with his deeds, put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Col. III). And elsewhere: “The old things have passed away; behold, everything has become new” (2 Cor. V).

“And my new name”—understand: I will write it upon the one who conquers—so that, from me who am called Christ, he may in time be called a Christian; that is, one anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit. He received this new name not according to his divinity, in which he has always remained equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, but according to the form of a servant, which in time the grace of the Holy Spirit anointed. From his own name he gave us this privilege, that we are called Christians after him. Concerning this name the prophet Isaiah says: “And he will call his servants by another name” (Isa. LXV)—that is, by the Christian name.

From this comes our dignity; from this our exalted position; from this we are called kings, priests, and Christians. Wherever the name of salvation sounds most clearly, there at last let this book receive its fitting conclusion.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0993]

## CHAPTER III FOLLOWS

[Col. 0993C]

“And to the angel of the Church of Laodicea write.” Laodicea is interpreted as “a tribe beloved by the Lord,” or “they were in the vomit.” Both interpretations indeed apply to the Church of the Laodiceans. In it there were some fervent in spirit and devoted to the love of God, and others lukewarm, and therefore like harmful food that must be vomited out.

These words, however, which are spoken to the Church of the Laodiceans, apply generally to the Church, in which good and evil are mixed together: some are loved by God, while others are rejected from the mouth of God.

First, however, we must consider the fact that John is told, “Write”—that is, commit it to writing for the benefit of future believers. Or what is said to him applies to the whole order of preachers, to whom “write” is said: that is, commit it to your mind, or store it in the minds of your hearers who listen. Books signify both the saints and the Lord himself. Hence the words: “The books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life” (Rev. XX). Therefore he says, “Write,” namely in the hearts of good hearers: carefully inscribe what you understand.

“These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness.” Amen is a Greek word, interpreted in Latin as *verum*, “true,” or *fideliter*, “faithfully.” None of the translators transferred this word into another language; it is found in the same letters among all peoples. The truth, however, is Christ himself, who says in the Gospel: “I am the truth” (John XIV).

Therefore, especially in the Gospel, he confirms his speech with this oath, as though saying: Because I am unchangeable truth, I demonstrate this through this particle of speech. He alone is, in a singular sense, the Amen—that is, eternal truth. And so, in order that this truth might be shown to be unchangeable and eternal, the word itself has not been altered by any translator.

Concerning him it is also added: “the faithful witness.” But were there not other faithful witnesses—that is, true ones? Jacob bore witness to Christ, saying: “The ruler will not fail from Judah” (Gen. XLIX), and so forth. Moses also said: “Your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. X). So too Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the others, all of whom were certainly faithful or true witnesses, because they proclaimed true testimony concerning Christ.

Why, then, does the Lord say this especially of himself, when there are also many true and faithful witnesses? Because he alone is truly the witness who is never changed. For just as he is called holy in a special sense, although there are many other saints, so, in comparison with him who is without sin, human beings are unjust. Although these people are saints, nevertheless, because they are merely human, they cannot be without sin and sometimes they lie. Christ, however, is holy and true in his very essence, because he committed no sin—that is, no lie ever proceeded from his mouth.

Christ is a witness who bore testimony to himself and to the Father, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X). Likewise the Father himself said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III). The Holy Spirit also bears witness, concerning whom the same Lord says to the apostles: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV).

“He is the beginning of God’s creation”—that is, from him all creation received its beginning. For everything that exists in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses, was made through the word of God. Since therefore all things were made through him, it is certainly evident that he himself is before all things. Yet the Father did not precede the Son in time or origin, just as the sun’s ray does not precede its heat, nor fire its radiance. The Father always existed, and the Son was always with him; the Son was not created by the Father but begotten.

He is therefore called the beginning of all creation because from him all things have the beginning of their existence. Hence, when the Jews asked who he was, he answered: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John VIII). Paul likewise says: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Col. I). And lest we should think that he was created, he immediately added: “In him all things were established.”

He is therefore the firstborn of all creation, from whom and through whom every creature arose.

The Arians say that the Son of God is a creature in his divinity, denying that he existed before Mary; but they lie. The Son of God is himself Wisdom, as Paul says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” And the Apostle says to God the Father: “You made all things in wisdom” (1 Cor. I).

Since he is the Father’s Wisdom, and they affirm that he was created in time, they consequently say that there was a time when he did not exist. They say this because Solomon, speaking of Wisdom itself, says: “The Lord possessed me,” or “created me,” according to another translation, “at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII).

If this is true—something which it is impious even to imagine—then God the Father was foolish before he begot his Wisdom. Certainly they cannot deny that he is the Wisdom of God, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. I). Therefore to those most foolish men, devoid of reason, it must be said: If God was foolish, how did he establish all things so wisely? And how did he create us, if before he was created he was without wisdom, being foolish and unaware of what he was doing?

Wisdom, therefore, was not created by the Father. Before all things were made, she was with the Father. Nor did God the Father beget the Son from another substance, but from himself, just as a plan is generated in the mind.

When Solomon says in the person of Christ, “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways”—that is, at the beginning of his actions, before he made anything—this is to be understood as meaning that God the Father possessed the whole of creation, both human and angelic, in his Wisdom, through which he established everything, whether in heaven or on earth.

But if we read, as it is found in certain books and in another translation, “The Lord created me,” this is to be understood in the sense that, before he made anything, he predestined his Wisdom to become incarnate, so that by his passion and death he might redeem the human race and restore it to its homeland. Thus, at the beginning of his actions, he possessed or created for himself in divinity his Wisdom, equal to him, when he later willed to assume flesh.

Sacred Scripture often narrates things that are future as though they had already happened. For the Apostle also says of us that God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I). If, then, according to the Apostle’s teaching, almighty God chose all the elect before the foundation of the world, what is surprising if, in his predestination, before he made anything, he ordained the very head of the elect to be the head of the elect? Concerning him the Apostle says: “So that he himself might hold first place in everything” (Col. I).

“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth.”

It is clear that cold or hot things can be eaten and drunk, but the lukewarm our body cannot endure because of vomiting. This, then, is how we should understand what the Lord says here: “Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth.”

The cold are the Jews or pagans, bound by that icy rigidity of which it is said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). For the north wind is cold, and the devil is the north wind. In the Song of Songs it is said to him: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song IV). “Rise, north wind”—that is, depart, devil. “Come, south wind”—let the Holy Spirit come, who by his arrival may warm and illumine human hearts, so that they may bring forth works of virtue.

The hot are those who remain fervent in spirit in the love of God and neighbor. The lukewarm are those who are neither altogether unbelieving nor eagerly striving toward Christ.

There are also some who were previously cold and subject to many crimes, but the Holy Spirit often touches the hearts of such people. Inflamed by him, they become fervent. The more they remember that they were sinners, the more they desire to love their liberator, as their iniquity recedes and their charity catches fire. Concerning such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV).

There are also some established within the holy Church who guard their life from every crime but nevertheless do not rise to the performance of any good. Such people are neither cold nor hot, because it is not enough to avoid evil unless one also strives to do good, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI).

Such people, trusting in their own works, are accustomed to say: “Look, I do not seize what belongs to others; I commit no unlawful act; I do not commit adultery or murder, nor, finally, do I do any similar evil. It is enough for me not to do evil; therefore I also use my own possessions confidently.” While saying this, they do not give their own possessions to the needy. And one who holds on to plunder does not fear holding on to avarice, nor does he remember that the rich man was not condemned because he seized what belonged to others, but because he did not distribute what belonged to himself.

There are also others who do not seize what belongs to others and distribute what belongs to themselves, but do this not out of love for God and neighbor, but for empty display, so that they may be praised by human beings. This is what the scribes and Pharisees did: when they gave alms, they had a trumpet sounded before them. Such people too are recognized as neither hot nor cold, because those who relieve the poverty of the poor ought to do so with the love of charity. They hear the Apostle’s words: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor” (1 Cor. XIII), and so forth.

There are also others who abandon the wealth of earthly possessions and come to a monastery, assuming the religious habit. Then, becoming sluggish, they believe that this alone can suffice for their salvation: that they have abandoned their possessions and, while wearing the religious habit, commit none of the various crimes. For this reason they sleep, drink, and live securely. While doing this, they are lukewarm. It would have been better for them to remain in the world, where they might recognize their sins and, at some point, moved by God’s mercy, devote themselves to good works, than to remain in a monastery and thus cease from good works.

There are also others who have lived in monasteries from childhood, abound in good works, and remain fervent in spirit, but toward the end of their lives become sluggish and lukewarm. For all such people it would certainly be better either to be perfectly good or altogether evil than to be neither good nor evil.

Therefore it is added: “Because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth.” No one is found to be hot who was not previously cold, because no one is good who was not once evil. “All have sinned and lack the grace of God” (Rom. III).

The lukewarm can arise from the hot or from the cold. One person, converted from the coldness of unbelief, does not advance to the perfect fervor of righteousness; another turns his mind and actions away from the very heat of righteousness in which he had previously burned.

For, as has been said, we know that cold or hot things are easily taken into the body, whereas the lukewarm is expelled from the mouth itself with great nausea and vomiting. The mouth of God is the holy preachers. Hence the prophets often said: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken this,” because such holiness was in them that God dwelt in their hearts and spoke through them.

The evangelists and the other teachers are therefore the mouths of God. Through their ministry God daily transfers into his body, which is the Church, the hot—that is, the fervent, whenever they are made still better through divine preaching—and the cold, that is, unbelievers, whenever Jews or pagans are converted to his faith and joined to the number of the saints.

Concerning this eating, it is said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts X, XI). But they do not convert the lukewarm, because such people despise their words while growing sluggish in their security. The preachers cease to exhort them and abandon them like unfruitful land, because they see that they cannot at all be restored to a better life. For it is easier to bring any pagan to the faith of Christ than to call any one of such people back from sluggishness to fervor of spirit.

“Because you say, ‘I am rich.’” Many say this: “I am rich in faith,” because the Lord says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI). “And I have become wealthy,” because I teach correctly and do not serve evil works.

Another says: “I lack nothing,” because, believing correctly, he not only does not commit evil but also does various good things, although not for God’s sake. Therefore it is added: “You do not know that you are miserable,” because you deceive yourself, thinking that you are saved by faith alone, although it is written: “Faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself” (James II).

“And miserable,” because you do not understand that you are deceiving yourself.

“Poor,” because you do not have the works by which you might be enriched in heaven, nor do you possess right understanding.

“Naked,” because you have been stripped of virtues.

“Blind,” because you do not have the light of knowledge.

But because the Lord is merciful, he also exhorts such people to return to fervor, when he adds:

“I advise you to buy from me gold refined and tested by fire.” By gold refined by fire—that is, tested by fire—we should understand the Lord Jesus Christ, who was tested by the fire of his passion: spat upon, scourged, mocked, and finally crucified and killed. Yet he endured all these things patiently and prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII).

Therefore it is said to anyone: “I advise you to buy.” Buy gold—that is, if you wish to abound in virtues, strive to imitate Christ, whether when you are scourged by God or when you endure evils inflicted by your neighbors, so that you too may become gold refined in the fire of tribulation, according to the Psalmist: “You tested us, O God; you examined us by fire as silver is examined” (Ps. LXV). And again: “We passed through fire and water.”

“So that you may become rich”—that is, so that you may abound in many virtues—“and may be clothed in white garments, and the shame of your nakedness may not appear.” In this passage the garments are understood as the innocence of baptism and the adornments of virtues: faith, charity, and the other good works by which the shame of nakedness—that is, the lukewarmness of your former way of life—is covered.

We may also understand by gold tested in fire the charity that enriches whoever possesses it, because it makes him abound in all virtues. It is the root of all good things, and it is tested by fire because it is truly kindled through the love of the Spirit. Whoever possesses it will be clothed in white garments, because, purified from the blackness of sins, he will be adorned with many virtues through that same charity, which covers a multitude of sins. Charity is called white because it knows neither the stain of sin nor any duplicity.

“And anoint your eyes with salve, so that you may see.” By the salve, which comes from the earth and removes the dust of the earth from the eyes, we should understand the Lord Jesus Christ, who was born from the earth—that is, from the Virgin Mary—according to the words: “Our God worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXVII).

“Anoint your eyes with salve”—that is, imitate the poverty of the Son of God, who, although he was rich, became poor for us, to such an extent that he did not have, as foxes do, a place where he could lay his head. Therefore he was born in a lodging, wrapped in the cheapest cloths, and placed in a manger, because there was no room for him in the inn.

“Anoint your eyes with salve, so that you may see”—that is, because earthly pleasures had closed and blinded the eyes of your mind, consider the poverty of your Redeemer, and so awaken to the future rewards of the saints. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

Or certainly, by the salve with which the eyes are illumined we may understand the divine utterances, through which the eyes of the mind are enlightened, according to the words: “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII).

“Anoint your eyes with salve”—that is, apply the divine commandments to the eyes of your mind, so that you may see the light of the virtues whose absence you suffer, and, seeing it, hasten to cover that nakedness by good works, so that afterward you may see God. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. V).

When anyone, through heavenly inspiration, recalls to mind by reading and hearing what the Lord has commanded throughout the individual pages of Scripture, he surely sees how much he lacks in virtues—or, indeed, whether he possesses none at all. Thus, as though through the anointing of salve, he is restored to clearer sight, while he is inwardly illumined by the word of God.

But one kept for necessary uses is tamed by yoke and reins, goaded with spurs, and struck with blows. And to a sick person whose life is thought to be hopeless, a physician does not deny anything his mind desires, even when it is contrary to his health; rather, he grants it. But when recovery is thought possible, everything desirable to his mind that is contrary to his health is entirely forbidden.

“I reprove and discipline those whom I love.” In many ways almighty God, merciful and compassionate, reproves and disciplines those whom he loves. Therefore his words and blows must be willingly endured.

Sometimes he does this through scourges; sometimes through hidden and divine inspiration; sometimes through various effects of tribulations and anxieties. Hence Solomon says: “The Lord reproves the one whom he loves” (Prov. III), and “he scourges every son whom he receives.”

The Lord does this—if human things may be compared with divine things—in the manner of a most loving father who has two sons. One of them he wishes to make his heir, and he scourges him in various ways: sometimes he excludes him from food or drink; sometimes he makes him stand immobile all night with his feet bound; he subjects him to unceasing insults; and sometimes, as though he were a stranger, he subjects him to another’s service.

The other, whom he does not intend to make his heir, he allows to follow his own will. He grants him permission to eat and drink and gives him free steps to walk wherever he wishes.

So too almighty God afflicts the righteous with countless torments and various tribulations, so that afterward they may rest in heaven and receive the inheritance of eternal blessedness. Conversely, he allows the reprobate to remain in their pleasures, according to the words: “He gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (Rom. I).

The reprobate, who are now devoted to the desires and pleasures of the world, await eternal punishments. But the righteous, who are now worn down by temporal scourges, will be freed from eternal punishment, because a calf prepared for slaughter is allowed to feed more freely in the pastures.

Although the Lord acts in many ways, there are specifically five ways in which human beings are scourged by him.

Sometimes it is to increase their merits, as with Job and Tobit.

Sometimes it is to preserve their virtues, as with Paul.

Sometimes it is so that past sins may be corrected, as with the paralytic, to whom it was said: “Behold, you have been made well; see that you do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

Sometimes it is not so that they may be corrected, but so that they may perish in a twofold destruction, as with Antiochus and Herod, concerning whom it is said: “Crush them, Lord, with a twofold destruction” (Jer. XVII).

Sometimes it is so that God’s glory may thereby be made manifest, as with Lazarus and the man born blind.

But whatever way the elect are scourged, they are made better by the scourge. Therefore the exhortation follows: “Be zealous, then, and repent.”

A zealous person may be diligent, envious, or an imitator. Here the word is used for imitation. There were indeed members of the same Church of the Laodiceans whom Christ had scourged. Therefore he exhorts the others to imitate them, as though saying:

When you see some among you being scourged, imitate their patience, patiently enduring scourges in the present so that afterward you may deserve fellowship. And repent because of what you said: “I am rich and lack nothing,” and so forth.

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.” Since almighty God fills heaven and earth everywhere through the presence of his divinity, what should we understand by the door in this passage except the understanding of the heart?

The Lord stands at the door and knocks when he illumines the human heart either through inward inspiration or through the teaching of preachers. Whoever guards his admonitions in action hears him knocking.

“If anyone hears my voice”—whether by reading the divine utterances himself or by having them explained by others—“and opens the door of his heart to me,” so that he brings to completion in action what he understands, “I will enter in to him”—that is, I will illumine his hidden places—“and I will dine with him, and he with me.”

He speaks of this in the Gospel, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

If we ask what the food of Christ is, by which we refresh him, he himself makes it clear when he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV).

Therefore we read in the Gospel that, as his passion drew near, he said to his disciples: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV). And as though someone might ask, “Why then will you die?” he immediately adds: “But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do just as the Father commanded me, rise; let us go” (John XIV).

He fulfilled the Father’s will when he went forth for us to the passion of death.

A supper is called a common meal, because *κοινόν* (*koinon*) in Greek means “common.” Thus the head dines with the members, and the members with the head, because Christ died for the elect, and the elect die with him, so that they too may fulfill the Father’s will.

Christ feeds us because he illumines us by his faith. We in turn feed Christ because we gladden him by our faith and action.

Let it therefore be said: “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me”—as though it were said:

Whoever, by acting and loving, carries out my words, and expands himself to receive the sweetness of my divinity, I will touch through inward grace, illumine him, and dine with him, and he with me. For in doing the Father’s will, each will rejoice: I in his compassion, and he, incorporated into my sufferings, in mine.

“Whoever conquers, I will make him sit with me on my throne.” A throne is the seat of a judge. By the throne, judicial power is signified, in which the saints will come to judgment with their head.

Let it therefore be said: Whoever conquers the devil’s temptations, and the desires of his flesh, I will make him sit on my throne—that is, I will make him reign and judge in the judgment—“just as I conquered the devil and sat with my Father on his throne.”

He himself conquered the devil, because, as we read in the Gospel, the devil tempted him in three ways, but was overcome by him. Hence the angels came and ministered to him (Matt. IV).

He conquered the Jews who handed him over to death when, after three days, he rose again, death having been defeated, to be victorious forever.

He also sits on the Father’s throne—that is, he remains coequal and coeternal with him in the same power.

No one should be disturbed by the fact that one throne signifies judicial power, since in the Gospel we read that the Lord said to the disciples: “You who have followed me” (Matt. XIX), and so forth. In the following parts of this book we also read of twenty-four thrones, since twelve multiplied by two produces twenty-four.

In this number all the patriarchs and apostles, and all the perfect, who will come with the Lord to judgment, are included. For in the twelve patriarchs all the perfect fathers of the Old Testament are included; through the twelve apostles, all those of the New Testament; just as through the twelve tribes of Israel all the nations are included.

One throne is therefore mentioned in the singular because of the one judicial power. Twelve are mentioned because of the perfection of the elect who will judge. Twenty-four are mentioned because of those who, made perfect in both Testaments, will come with the Lord to judgment.

But since it is clear that not all who conquer will sit with the Lord in judgment, but only those who are more perfect, it is rightly asked why the Lord promises here: “Whoever conquers, I will make him sit on my throne.”

To make this clearer, let us set two people before us as an example. One suffered for Christ; the other conquered only the devil, the incentives of the flesh, and worldly conduct, and so attained eternal blessedness. Will they therefore be equal in the future, since they did not conquer equally in the present? Certainly not, because “star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. XV).

Nevertheless, we must understand that what such people and the others will not possess in themselves, they will possess in their superiors. Those who will not judge personally will nevertheless judge through their leaders.

For such great charity will exist among them that each person will count as his own whatever he sees in another. Therefore what he does not have in himself he will have in another. Thus all the elect will possess power in their leaders, just as the whole human body has the power to speak through the mouth, to see through the eyes, to hear through the ears, to smell through the nostrils, and to work through the hands, although the individual members have their own functions. What one member does not have in itself, it has in another.

But before the Church reaches this dignity, in the meantime, humbled in this pilgrimage, she groans and does not seek the summit of exaltation, since throughout the whole life of the saints she bears the name of humiliation.

Whoever has an ear—that is, understanding of heart—let him hear, that is, let him understand what the Spirit says to the churches. Here it is plainly shown that what was said to each individual church applies generally to all the churches. It should be noted, however, that the angel does not say, “Let him hear what the Son says to the churches,” although he appeared specifically in the person of the Son, but rather, “what the Spirit says.” Under this name the whole Trinity is understood, because, since they have one substance, they also have one operation and one utterance. That the whole Trinity is signified by the name “Spirit,” the Lord makes clear in the Gospel, saying: “God is spirit, and those who adore him must adore him in spirit and in truth” (John 4). At times, however, the Son of God speaks specifically of his divinity. Thus we have: “The Son of Man must suffer, be crucified, die, and be buried” (Matthew 26), which pertains to him alone, although even these things cannot be said without the Spirit. Here he speaks in the person of the Godhead. Therefore the words of the Son are the words of the Father and of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER IV

“After these things I saw.” It is customary for the ancient prophets to describe the times of their visions by the names of kings and by the number of years, months, and even days. Thus Ezekiel says: “In the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me.” Likewise Daniel says, “in the third year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar,” and so forth. This new prophet, however, does not at all describe the time of his prophecy by periods—that is, by years or months—but mentions only a single day when he says: “I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.” From this it is understood that he saw this entire prophecy in a single day. Therefore the phrase “after these things I saw” should not be referred to a succession of times, but to the order of the visions. That is, after he had seen the things described above, he also saw the things that follow. He saw this not with bodily sight but with the mind, as we shall see later.

“And behold, a door was opened in heaven.” In this passage heaven signifies the Church. For the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah 1). Solomon likewise says: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7). If, then, the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom—which is Christ, according to what Paul says (1 Corinthians 1), namely, that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God—and if heaven is the seat of God, then certainly the Church is the heaven in which he himself sits.

In this heaven, that is, in the Church, there is this open door, namely Christ, who says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved,” and so forth, “and will find pasture” (John 10). For no one comes to the Father except through him, through whom one enters into faith. One passes from faith to sight, and the pastures of eternal refreshment are found.

This door was previously closed, because before his coming his mysteries were hidden from everyone except the prophets. Enlightened by the Holy Spirit, they saw his incarnation, passion, death, and resurrection. These same mysteries had already been revealed throughout the world through the preaching of the other apostles.

John saw this door in two ways. He saw all these things with bodily eyes, since he adhered to him and saw his miracles when he raised the dead, gave sight to the blind, and accomplished similar works in his presence. Finally, when he died, John received his virgin mother into his care. Or he saw them with the eyes of the mind, as this prophecy clearly shows.

“And the first voice which I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me, saying…” The first voice which John heard signifies the Old Testament, in which the mysteries of Christ and of the Church were foretold. For everything which he recognized in this prophecy as already fulfilled or soon to be fulfilled had previously been announced in the Law, the Prophets, and the other Scriptures of the Old Testament.

This voice is rightly said to have been like the voice of a trumpet, because it sounded through the mouths of preachers, to whom it is said: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58). The Jews also used trumpets in battle, and sacred Scripture admonishes us in battle, while we fight against the devil’s temptations and against the incitements of our flesh.

But let us see what the voice itself said: “Come up here,” that is, to the door. For all the Scripture of the Old Testament invites us to contemplate the mysteries of Christ. Thus we have the saying of Micah: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and all nations shall flow to it” (Micah 4).

This mountain is Christ, whom Daniel saw cut out without hands; it grew and filled the whole earth (Daniel 2). The house of Jacob, moreover, is the Church of the faithful. Therefore for John to ascend to the open door is for the Church to flow together to the mountain, that is, to Christ.

Let it then be said to John, and in him to the entire company of teachers: “Come up here,” not by bodily steps, but by the steps of the mind and of faith, and see in Christ everything already fulfilled which was previously announced by the prophets.

“And I will show you what must take place soon”—that is, in the present age, which, compared with eternity, is a moment as brief as an hour. It should be understood, however, that when it says, “I will show you what must take place soon,” it does not deny that these things already existed; rather, it declares that henceforth they would endure. For the dignity of the Church had already been exalted when John saw these things, and the statement shows that it would continue until the end of the age, when it will come with the Lord to judge.

“After these things I was immediately in the Spirit.” This should not be understood to mean that his spirit was removed from his body and that he then saw this vision. Rather, as was already said above, he saw all this with the mind. The power of the Holy Spirit raised his mind to contemplate heavenly mysteries. He saw and heard nothing through the body; instead, seized by the Holy Spirit in ecstasy—that is, led by him—he saw and heard these things, retaining them spiritually in his hearing so that he could write them down and transmit them to posterity.

If we wish to refer this to the elect, it declares the spiritual character of their conduct, to whom Paul says: “You are not in the flesh, but in the spirit.” And elsewhere: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5).

“And behold, a throne was set in heaven.” If the Church is the seat, as was said above—the soul of the just being the seat of wisdom—and heaven is also the Church itself, we must see how the throne is in heaven. We can explain it simply in this way: although the Church, which is the seat of God, still exists in this flesh, it already inhabits heaven in mind. In accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

Alternatively, the present Church, which still journeys in the body far from Christ, is in heaven in mind, since it already reigns with him. But it is better to examine these words more subtly; this will be clearer from the example of the Old Testament, in which we read that eight souls were saved at the time of the Flood in the ark. In that passage the eight souls signify the multitude of the faithful, while the ark signifies the universal Church.

Thus, just as there the ark is the eight souls, and the eight souls are the ark—that is, the universal Church—so here the throne is heaven, and heaven is the throne. Therefore it is said, “A throne was set in heaven,” as though one were to say, “The Church in the Church.”

“And upon the throne was one seated.” It is customary in this prophecy sometimes to understand God the Father by the one seated, and sometimes God the Son. It intends the Father to be understood as the one seated where it says: “I saw in the right hand of the one seated a book opened,” calling the right hand of the one seated the Son, through whom all things were made, while understanding the one seated himself to be God the Father.

Here, however, by the one seated we must understand the Lord Jesus Christ, as the following words will clearly teach. Above we read that he saw one like the Son of Man walking in the midst of seven golden lampstands; here, however, he is said to have seen him seated. The Lord walks in the midst of his elect when he spreads among them the gifts of his grace; he sits when he judges the merits of each one. Concerning this it follows:

“And the one who was seated was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius.” That is, his countenance and face were like the appearance of jasper and sardius.

By the jasper stone, which certainly has a green color, we should understand the brightness of the divinity of the Son of God. In the contemplation of this there is the fullness and supreme refreshment of all the saints. Hence the saying: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will find pasture” (John 10). For this will be the reward of the elect: the face of God, in whose vision they will be satisfied in every way. Hence: “My sheep will hear my voice, and I give them eternal life” (ibid.).

The sardius stone resembles red earth, and therefore it signifies the humanity of the Son of God, which was drenched in the redness of blood at the time of his passion. Hence the angels ask: “Why is your garment red, and your vestments like those of one treading the winepress?” (Isaiah 63).

Thus the one who has greenness in the splendor of divinity also has redness in humanity, through which he recalled Adam—whose name is interpreted as “red clay”—to heavenly things. One thing is green and another is red; yet these are not two but one, because one man and God consists of two natures. He is perfect God and perfect man. Therefore what is green in him belongs to power, while what is red belongs to mercy. By what is green he created us; by what is red he redeemed us.

We may also understand the Church through these stones. It has the greenness of jasper because it remains in contemplation of God, and therefore already considers the prosperity of this world as nothing while it clings to the pastures of eternal greenness. To it the Song of Songs says: “You who dwell in the gardens, your companions listen for you; let me hear your voice” (Song of Songs 8).

It also has the sardius, a stone which, as we said, is red in color, because the elect are warned by the frailty of humanity lest they become exalted by the vision of divine things. Thus, when Daniel or Ezekiel gazed upon divine mysteries, the angel said to him, “Son of man,” as though saying: “You behold the brightness of heavenly grace, yet remember that you are human and have descended from the stock of sinful humanity; therefore, from human weakness, you are red earth.”

“And there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.” Greek Ἶρις is called arcus in Latin, “bow.” A bow appears on a rainy day and is a sign of reconciliation, as the Lord said to Noah at the time of the Flood: “I will set my bow in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant” (Genesis 9).

What, then, should we understand by the bow except the Lord Jesus Christ? If this is carefully considered, the effect of the rainbow itself seems to indicate it. For a ray of the sun enters a rain-bearing cloud, and thus the bow is formed; this is entirely fitting for Christ. He is the sun in respect of divinity, concerning whom it is written: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise.” The ray of this sun—that is, the brightness of eternal light—entered the cloud when he assumed flesh in the Virgin’s womb.

Of this cloud the prophet says: “Behold, the Lord ascends upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt” (Isaiah 19). This cloud, that is, the Lord’s flesh, is rightly called rain-bearing because of the multitude of his teachings.

The bow is a sign of reconciliation, because all our salvation and reconciliation consist in Christ. Hence the angels announced peace at his birth, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). And as he ascended to the Father, he said to his disciples: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14).

Thus, if one letter is added to *iris* in Greek—namely, *i*, so that it is called *irini*—the word itself expresses this, because εἰρήνη means “peace.” The rainbow, therefore, was around the throne because he is the crown and protection of his saints.

There are also two principal colors in the rainbow: green, that is, watery, and red. In these are clearly signified the water of baptism and the blood of redemption, or the grace of the Holy Spirit. Through these two things we are cleansed from all sins. The whole Church is surrounded by these two mysteries, and through them it is renewed into the newness of God’s grace.

Alternatively, by these two colors we may understand two judgments: one which took place through water, and another which will take place through fire.

Or by the rain-bearing cloud we may understand the saints, who rain through their words and flash through their miracles. Enlightened and illumined by the brightness of heavenly light, they turn the justice of the Creator toward mercy through their most devout supplications, like Moses, who, interceding for the people of Israel, said: “Either forgive them this sin, or erase me from your book” (Exodus 32).

As for what follows—“like the appearance of an emerald”—since the emerald is a green-colored stone, through this stone, just as above through the jasper, the divinity of the Son of God is expressed, through whom the whole Church is cleansed and governed.

“And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones were twenty-four elders seated.” In the Gospel the Lord attests to only twelve thrones, upon which he says that the twelve apostles will sit in judgment: “You will sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). Why, then, does John mention twenty-four? Clearly, because of the twofold Testament, the Old and the New.

They are called twelve because of apostolic dignity, and twenty-four because of the fathers of both Testaments, who will come with the Lord to judgment. For in the twelve tribes of Israel all nations are understood. In the twelve apostles all the perfect are understood, all who have followed the apostles’ example in the present life, just as in Peter the other apostles and preachers received the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

There is also one throne, as we read above—that is, one judicial power—and there are twenty-four because of the number of the prophets, the apostles, and the other faithful. They will be seats in whose hearts God will sit; they themselves will also sit, because they will judge others. Hence the Psalmist says: “There they sat, the seats in judgment” (Psalm 121).

Concerning them it further follows: “Clothed in white garments.” This pertains not only to the apostles but generally to all who preserve the garments of baptism unstained by capital sins. Those who have been baptized have put on Christ, according to the Apostle’s saying: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3). They have white garments if they preserve the sacraments of baptism inviolate.

“And on their heads were golden crowns”—understand, “I saw.” Victors receive a crown when they triumph over their enemies; therefore, not without reason, the crowns of the saints signify the kingdom and reward of those who triumph over the author of death. But just as they judge in him, so through him they possess victory, for he says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16).

The same Church may also be represented under another interpretation by the twenty-four elders. This number consists of six and four, because four times six is twenty-four. Six refers to work, because God Almighty completed all his works in six days, and on the sixth day and at the sixth hour he redeemed humanity. Four refers to the four books of the holy Gospel.

Since the holy Church, whether in the Old Testament or in the New, recalls and venerates God’s work and preserves the books of the holy Gospel, it is rightly comprised in the twenty-four elders. Or, certainly, this is because of the twenty-four books of the Old Testament, which it uses according to canonical authority, and in which it recognizes that the New Testament and the things fulfilled in it were foretold.

Hence the Evangelist says concerning the two thieves who were crucified with the Lord: “This happened so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says: ‘And he was reckoned among the wicked’” (Mark 15; Isaiah 53).

“And from the throne proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps.” The throne of God is the Church of the elect itself, from which flashes of lightning proceed—that is, signs of miracles—concerning which it is said: “Your flashes of lightning illumined the world” (Psalm 76). They are rightly compared with flashes, because they terrify and illuminate.

Flashes also descend from clouds, and the saints themselves are clouds: they rain through their words and flash through their miracles. They also emit voices and thunderclaps, that is, words of preaching and warning, saying: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 19). Hence: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Psalm 76).

Since he says that from the seat proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps, although these pertain not to a seat but to clouds, he wishes the seat itself to be understood as the cloud from which rain, flashes, and thunder proceed.

“And seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven Spirits of God.” Seven spirits are spoken of, although there is one Spirit, because of the sevenfold grace which is said to have rested upon the Lord, as the prophet says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11).

The Holy Spirit is rightly compared with lamps, because he kindles the saints with the love of God and illumines them with the light of faith, lest they fall into the pit of error. *Lampas* is Greek; in Latin it is called *flamma*, “flame.” It shines nowhere except before the throne, because those who are outside the Church, such as heretics, cannot possess the Holy Spirit.

Hence it is also stated in the canons that if such people wish to be joined again to the Church through right faith, they are to receive the imposition of the bishops’ hands, so that they may thus receive the Holy Spirit whom they have lost.

“And before the throne there was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal.” He calls the laver “the sea”; for we read that Solomon made the sea, that is, the laver. By the sea we should understand baptism, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all were baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10).

It is compared with glass, which is a transparent material, because of the purity of faith demonstrated in baptism, when those being baptized profess that they believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The glassy sea shines within and without, because one believes with the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation.

It should be noted that the same sea is said to resemble crystal. Crystal is born from water and hardens into stone through intense cold; so the saints are brought through the tribulation of the present life to firmness.

Before the throne, therefore, are the seven Spirits of God and the glassy sea resembling crystal, because only in the Church does the Holy Spirit burn, and the baptism of the Trinity is bestowed. Thus the faith of the elect is manifested, their life is refined, and they are cleansed from the filth of vices.

“And in the midst of the throne, and around the throne, were four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind.” There is no doubt that these living creatures signify the Lord Jesus Christ and all the saints, especially the four Evangelists, who are said to be in the midst of the throne and around it because, beginning from Jerusalem, they reached the ends of the earth through preaching.

Jerusalem is in the middle of the world, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “I have set her in the midst of the nations, and lands around her” (Ezekiel 5).

By the eyes of the living creatures the mysteries of the divine Scriptures are signified. The living creatures are therefore full of eyes, because as many as are the words of Scripture, so many are, as it were, the lights of the saints by which they illumine the hearts of their hearers.

They have eyes in front and behind because they speak both of what has happened and of what is to happen. This part of the expression is sometimes used for the past, as in: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8). At other times it is used for the future, as in the Apostle’s saying: “Forgetting what is behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3).

The living creatures are therefore full of eyes in front and behind because they perfectly contain all the mysteries of the Old and New Testaments, which principally explain the causes of three times: the past, the present, and the future. Some mysteries they announce as foretold, others as already fulfilled, and others as still to be fulfilled: namely, the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation as foretold; the dispensation of that same Redeemer as already fulfilled; and the separation of the righteous and the wicked as still to be fulfilled.

These eyes agree with one another, because what shines in the Old Testament shines brilliantly in the New.

Alternatively, the living creatures have eyes in front and behind because all the elect continually contemplate their Redeemer as judged in the first advent of his humility and as one who will judge in the second advent of his majesty. Moreover, when any of the elect, instructed by the words of the Evangelists, recalls and mourns past sins and carefully guards against what may follow, he has eyes in front and behind.

Many things can be said about this, but, seeking brevity, we omit them.

“And the first living creature was like a lion, and the second living creature like a calf, and the third living creature had a face like a man, and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle.” It is very remarkable that John arranges these living creatures in a different order from Ezekiel, placing the lion first, whereas Ezekiel placed the human face first.

The answer is that prophecy does not preserve the order of history. If it did, it would no longer be prophecy but history. This is easily understood from the books of the prophets. To give one example for all, it should be observed that the same prophet Ezekiel, after saying above that the word of the Lord came to him in the twenty-sixth year, later, speaking against Pharaoh king of Egypt, says that the same prophecy came to him in the eleventh year.

The Holy Spirit spoke through the prophets as he wished and when he wished. Therefore one should not look for an order of discourse there as in the book of Genesis, or of Kings, or in the other historical books.

Ezekiel therefore places the human face first, that is, Matthew, preserving the order of history. Matthew is understood by the man because he describes the humanity of the Son of God in time, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.”

Then Mark is understood by the lion, because he begins with a cry, like a lion, saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

Third he places the calf, that is, Luke, who began with the priesthood, saying: “There was in the days of Herod the king a certain priest.” He also dwells especially on the temple, and therefore ends his Gospel in this way: “They were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.”

In fourth place he places the eagle, which signifies John, who began with divinity, since Christ was first born as man, then preached and uttered a terrible voice like a lion, then suffered like a calf, and afterward ascended to heaven like an eagle. Thus in this order the order of history is preserved.

John, however, places the lion first because Christ had already risen from the dead. The peoples did not believe in Christ because he was born as a man or because he suffered as a calf, but because he rose from the dead as a lion.

Hence Paul says: “Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way,” as though he were saying: “We no longer contemplate a dead man among the living creatures, but a lion living eternally after death.” Hence we read below: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5).

Jacob also speaks of him in the person of Judah: “You have gone up to the prey, my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who will rouse him?” (Genesis 49).

Those who discuss the nature of beasts say that the lion does not sleep with his eyes closed. Thus Christ died in his humanity, yet remained awake and impassible in his divinity. A sleeping lion is also born and is awakened by the voice of its father; so Christ was awakened by the voice of the Father, according to the Psalm: “Awake, my glory” (Psalm 56), and so forth.

Since belief arises from the fact that he rose, John rightly placed the lion first. In the order of sequence, therefore, the man and the calf are first, but in power the lion is first. The lion is the king of beasts, and therefore Mark is not inappropriately understood through it.

He places the calf second, which, as was said, signifies Luke, because the calf was a sacrifice of the priests and was offered in the temple; Luke himself also dwells especially on the temple in his narrative.

Third he places the man, that is, Matthew, who describes the temporal birth of Christ.

Fourth he places the eagle, that is, John, who, with eyes dazzled, transcending every height of heaven and even the choirs of angels, beholds the divinity of the Son of God, saying: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1).

These four living creatures signified the four rivers of paradise flowing in the Church from the one fountain, Christ. Likewise, they signify the four rings of the ark by which the Church is carried.

These four living creatures also signify the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who was born as a man, suffered as a calf, rose as a lion, and ascended above all the heavens as an eagle.

They also signify all the saints. For each elect person, insofar as he lives rationally according to the will of God, is a man, because man is a rational animal. Insofar as he endures the adversities of this age with equanimity, he is a lion, according to what is written: “The righteous is confident as a lion, without fear” (Proverbs 28). Insofar as he mortifies himself with his vices and desires, he is a calf. Insofar as he seeks heavenly things through contemplation of the mind, he is an eagle.

“And the four living creatures each had six wings.” The wings of the living creatures signify the two Testaments, by which the Church is borne up to heavenly things. But although there are two Testaments, the spiritual wings of the same Church, because of the twofold Testament represented in the twelve tribes of Israel or in the twelve apostles, are multiplied twelvefold by the number two, yielding twenty-four wings. For twice twelve is twenty-four.

Alternatively, the number twelve consists of the parts of seven, namely three and four. Or we may say that three times four, or four times three, makes twelve; this is a sacred number because of the twelve apostles.

In the number three the faith of the Holy Trinity is understood; in the number four, the four parts of the world. Let the number twelve, therefore, be multiplied by two, and twenty-four results. By this number the whole company of the elect is expressed: through them the faith of the Holy Trinity is preached throughout the four quarters of the earth, and the whole world is lifted up to heavenly things.

We can also understand these six wings in another way. The first wing signifies the natural law; the second, the law of Moses; the third, the Prophets; the fourth, the Gospel; the fifth, the Apostolic Epistles; and the sixth, canonical authority, or the teaching of Catholic men—Jerome, Augustine, and the other holy Fathers.

By these wings the holy Church is raised daily and lifted up to heavenly things.

Alternatively, the number six pertains to all the work of Christ, which was accomplished or is being accomplished in six days and in the six ages of this world.

The four, therefore, pertain to our nature, which consists of four bodily humors. The saints therefore use four sets of six wings, because as long as they remain in this life they can comprehend only those things which are accomplished through the six ages of this world.

Hence Isaiah says that the cherubim are described as covering their head and feet with wings, because the saints cannot know either what existed before the foundation of the world or what will take place after the end of the age.

Ezekiel adds that “the likeness of the four was one,” because they teach one faith to the four quarters of the world. The four are also found in the one Gospel, as is clearly shown by the harmony of its text.

“And around them and within, they are full of eyes.” These living creatures, as was said above, signify all holy preachers. They are full of eyes around and within because by their preaching they illumine both those who dwell in the midst of the Church and those who live at the ends of the earth.

Or they are full of eyes around and within because they instruct the simple through the letter and the more perfect through spiritual understanding. Paul had eyes, as it were, outwardly when he said to certain people: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (1 Corinthians 3). He had eyes, as it were, inwardly when elsewhere he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2).

Or they are full of eyes around and within because they preserve themselves pure in thought and in deed, while instructing others through perfection of faith and works. The Psalmist briefly comprehends both aspects when he says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed around with golden fringes of varied ornament” (Psalm 44).

The Church diligently strives to cleanse the interior of its heart in the sight of God, and is also proved to preserve its exterior irreproachable, so that in both respects it may be beautiful outwardly to others and inwardly to itself.

Or they are full of eyes around and within because they manifest outwardly with the mouth the faith they possess in the heart, according to the saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

“And they had no rest day or night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.” The whole Church, which is signified in these living creatures, does this day and night, because in prosperity as well as in adversity, and even continually, it strives to offer praise to its Creator.

It should be noted that when the holy living creatures say three times, “Holy, holy, holy,” they return to the singular number when they say, “Lord God Almighty.” For although there is a Trinity in persons, there is unity in majesty. He was before all ages and is immutable, as the Psalmist says: “But you are the same” (Psalm 101). And he is to come in judgment, to repay each one according to his works.

At this point a question arises: why, after the holy living creatures have mentioned the Trinity, do they add, “who is to come”? Our faith holds that at the judgment only the person of the Son will be seen, because he will judge in the form in which he was judged; and “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

It should be understood, however, that although the person of the Son alone will be seen in judgment, the Father and the Holy Spirit will nevertheless be present there with him in the unity of divinity. The very nature of the invisible Trinity will judge the wicked through the humanity assumed by the Son.

“And when the living creatures gave glory, honor, and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, who lives forever and ever…” In this passage the living creatures do not signify the universal Church in general, as above, but only the four Evangelists. They give glory, honor, and blessing to Almighty God when they refer to him everything they have received from God.

They gave glory and honor to God when they said, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty,” because in these words they preached and praised his divinity, magnificence, eternity, and lordship.

But what they did, they certainly admonish us also to do: to praise God for everything we have received from him, so that whatever we possess in the glory of faith and honor, in the work of virtue and hope, and in the blessing of heavenly reward, we may refer to him.

The Apostle Paul says: “Glory and honor to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and to the Greek” (Romans 2). This does not mean that the good, or that glory, comes from the Jew, the Greek, or the Gentile, but from God, since he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). And the Apostle says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift” (James 1), and so forth.

It is likewise commanded that whoever glories should glory in the Lord.

By the one seated upon the throne we should understand Christ, as above, presiding over his Church.

Twenty-four elders fell down before the one seated on the throne, and they worshiped the one who lives forever and ever. The twenty-four elders signify the universal Church, both in its leaders and in its subordinate peoples. The twenty-four elders fall down: they humble themselves and refer all their good to him, saying: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113). They presume nothing on the basis of their own merits, but know that they possess all their good from him. Hence it follows: “For they worshiped the one who lives forever and ever.” They worship him when, on the basis of their own merits and works, they seek not their own grace but his. [Col. 1012D]

“Casting their crowns before the throne.” Since victors receive a crown, we should rightly understand here by the crowns the triumph and victory of the saints. To place the crowns before the throne therefore means to fall on one’s face and worship.
