The elect cast their crowns before the throne because whatever virtue and strength they possess, they attribute inwardly in the secret of their mind to the one from whom they received the strength to conquer the devil and the temptations of their flesh.

This was prefigured when, as the Lord was coming to Jerusalem, the crowd that went out to meet him is said to have spread before the feet of the she-ass on which he sat the palms that signify victory. What is signified by the branches of palms spread along the road is signified by the crowns placed before the throne.

[Col. 1013A]

“Casting their crowns before” the throne, they say:

> “You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power.”

Christ received glory when he rose from the dead on the third day; honor when, on the fortieth day after his resurrection, he was raised to the right hand of the Father’s majesty; power when all things were subjected to him, as he himself testifies, saying to his disciples: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

> “For you created all things, and because of your will they existed, and they were created [Col. 1013B].”

It is as though they were saying: “For this reason everything that is accomplished by those who belong to you must be ascribed to you, because, in order that they might exist and accomplish what is yours, they received from you the ability to do so.”

But what follows is remarkable: “Because of your will they existed, and they were created.” If they existed, how were they created? They existed in the predestination of almighty God, and they were created in visible operation. Those things that previously existed without time in the will of the craftsman were created in time according to the way they had been arranged in the Creator’s art.

John also sets forth something similar in his Gospel. After saying, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1), he immediately added: “What was made in him was life.” The apostle Paul says of the elect: “He chose us,” he says, “before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1), and so forth.

## CHAPTER V

“And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a book written within and on the outside, sealed with seven seals.”

By the one seated in this passage we should understand God the Father; by his right hand, the Son, through whom all things were made [Col. 1013C]. Of him the Psalmist says: “The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly” (Ps. 117), and so forth.

The book in the right hand of the one seated signifies the Old and New Testament. It is rightly said to have been in the right hand of the one seated, because the principal intention of sacred Scripture pertains to Christ: it contains the account of his birth, death, resurrection, ascension, and second coming for judgment. Concerning all these things, examples present themselves to those who seek them.

The Old and New Testament are called one book because neither the New can be separated from the Old nor the Old from the New; rather, whatever was foretold in the Old is established as fulfilled in the New. The Old Testament is the announcement and veil of the New, while the New is the revelation and fulfillment of the Old.

The book is rightly said to be written within and on the outside [Col. 1013D]: on the outside, with reference to the Old Testament; within, with reference to the New; or on the outside, with reference to the face of the earth; within, with reference to allegorical meanings.

Alternatively, “within and on the outside” may be understood because one Testament promises the earth, saying: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land,” and many other passages; while the other promises the inward blessedness of the heavenly kingdom, when it says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

This book is also shown to be sealed with seven seals—that is, sealed with seven seals. The number seven, as has often been said, refers to totality. By the seven seals, therefore, we should understand the fullness of the obscurity and mysteries that lay hidden in the Old Testament.

Hence Habakkuk says: “God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from [Col. 1014A] the shadowed and densely covered mountain.” The shadowed and densely covered mountain of Lebanon signifies the books of the Old Testament, covered by the figures of allegories. The Lord is said to come from them because he is known to have been foretold there.

Alternatively, the number seven refers to the sevenfold Holy Spirit. The book is sealed with seven seals because all Scripture was both given and opened through the grace of that same Spirit. Hence the Law is read to have been written by the finger of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit. When the Lord rose from the dead and opened the understanding of the disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures, he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20).

We may also understand by the seven seals the seven modes of expression on which all Scripture rests. We speak either:

1. In the indicative, as in: “I am the Lord [Col. 1014B] your God, teaching you what is profitable” (Isa. 48).

2. In the promissive, as in: “I will show you, O man, what is good” (Mic. 6), and so forth.

3. In the imperative, as in: “Hear, O Jacob, my servant”; and: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6).

4. In the optative, as in: “Would that you had attended to my words” (Isa. 48).

5. In the subjunctive, as in: “If you hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples” (Exod. 19).

6. In the infinitive, as in: “To understand and to know the Lord is understanding.”

7. In the impersonal form, as in: “Who will declare the mighty deeds of the Lord?”

The expression of sacred Scripture itself is thus sevenfold, contained, as it were, beneath seven seals of understanding, since it is distinguished according to these seven modes.

When we inquire into the Scriptures, the first text that presents itself is that of a deed simply narrated. It comprehends only those scriptural statements that signify nothing mystically but unfold the circumstances of events in a straightforward manner [Col. 1014C], as in: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6).

The second kind that presents itself is an allegorical deed. Although it narrates something that happened, the deed is nevertheless regarded as wholly allegorical, and for this reason it is not commonly encountered. Thus, throughout all the borders of Israel, a girl is sought for King David and found to be so warm that she heats the limbs of the aged man suffering from cold, yet does not arouse him to lust when he has been warmed. By her is signified wisdom, which does not grow old even in the aged but instead kindles them with the fire of divine love.

This mode also includes the fact that the Israelite people were healed in the desert from the bite of serpents by looking at a bronze serpent. By that serpent our Redeemer [Col. 1014D] is understood, suspended on the cross; he liberates us from the bite of the devil and grants the faithful the remedies of blessed immortality.

If these matters are examined literally, they will for the moment seem absurd. But when they are applied to mysteries, they convey great sacraments.

The third mode is both historical and allegorical. In this mode it is written that Abraham had two sons, who, as the Apostle writes (Rom. 4), signify the two Testaments.

This mode also includes the passage in which Isaac, prepared by filial devotion, is said to have carried the wood for himself, singularly signifying Christ’s Passion. The Father delivered Christ for all, and allowed him to carry his own cross.

In the same way, the woman formed from the side of the sleeping [Col. 1015A] man signified the Church, which was to be built from the side of Christ hanging on the cross.

The fourth mode is that in which the divinity of our Creator is disclosed to us in sacred writings, sometimes literally and sometimes mystically.

Literally, for example, when he says to Moses: “I am who I am,” and: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3).

Mystically, for example, when almighty God says that he creaks like a wagon loaded with hay, thereby indicating that he bears the heavy sins of human beings; or when Isaiah describes the Lord as seated upon a high and elevated throne, signifying the angelic powers whom he has subjected to himself for whatever he wills.

The fifth mode is that of parables. It is formed both by the narration of words and by the enactment of deeds. It is so varied and hidden that it not only [Col. 1015B] admits many things that cannot be understood literally, but also, in certain passages where it intends to narrate mysteries, takes testimony from history and alters the very literal action.

This mode is formed by verbal parables, among which is the passage: “The trees went forth to anoint a king over themselves” (Judg. 9), and so forth. Trees cannot walk or appoint a king for themselves; rather, something else is conveyed metaphorically through such scriptural expressions by means of an appropriate signification.

As has been said, the text of the literal account is sometimes altered for the sake of mystical understanding. Thus, in the title of Psalm 33, it says: “A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed,” although the event took place before Achish, king of Gath, as the Book of Kings [Col. 1015C] recounts (1 Kings 21).

When Abimelech is substituted for Achish, it plainly indicates that, through the interpretation of the name itself, a deeper mystery is to be penetrated. Abimelech is interpreted as “the kingdom of my father,” signifying the Jews, before whom the true David, the strong-handed Lord Jesus Christ, changed his appearance when, appearing in the form of a servant, he humbled himself even to death on a cross.

> “We saw him without form or beauty, and his appearance was as though hidden and despised; therefore we did not esteem him” (Isa. 53).

“Abimelech dismissed him, and he departed,” because Christ, having been by no means received by the Jews, passed over to the Gentiles with the apostles. Hence Paul says to them:

> “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you; but since you rejected it, behold, we turn [Col. 1015D] to the Gentiles.”

At other times this same mode, in parables of deeds, conveys a prophecy of future works through the very sins of human beings and the transgressions of adulterers. This is shown to have occurred in David, who took Uriah’s wife, whom he had desired after seeing her from the roof, and killed him with the sword (2 Kings 11).

In this passage David signifies Christ, who, mercifully looking from heaven upon the Church in his predestination—she who was to be cleansed by the washing of water in the word—desired her providentially in order to join her to himself, once justified, as her lawful spouse.

But for David to be joined to Bathsheba, her husband Uriah is killed. For the Church of the righteous to cling to her heavenly Bridegroom, the power of the ancient enemy is broken and cast down to be trampled [Col. 1016A] under the feet of the elect. Hence the Lord says to them in the Gospel:

> “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon all the strength of the enemy” (Luke 10).

The sixth mode concerns the Savior’s two comings. Here vigilant discernment must be exercised, lest the first be taken for the second or the second for the first. The Jews, ignorant of this distinction, remain afflicted by the blindness of ignorance, not knowing what pertains to his first coming and what to his second.

The first therefore claims the place of humility. Thus: “God will raise up for you from among your brothers a prophet like me” (Acts 7), and elsewhere: “After these things he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3), together with other passages of this kind.

The second, however, occupies the places of exaltation and terror. Thus we read: “God will come openly.” And then: “They will see the Son [Col. 1016B] of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty” (Mark 13).

For this reason he himself says through Malachi: “I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers” (Mal. 3).

The seventh mode retains the twofold character of the commandments: the commandments concerning the life that must be lived and those concerning the life that is to be figured.

The commandments concerning the life that must be lived remain to this day, as in: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12), and other such commandments, which are still commanded to be observed by evangelical authority.

The figures of the life that was to be represented have passed away, such as circumcision, the sabbath, and the offering of sacrifices. As has been said, when the shadow ceased, these are performed spiritually in the truth.

But since this book is said to have been written within and on the outside, we must examine, of these [Col. 1016C] seven modes, which should be regarded as within and which as outside.

The first, therefore, the historical and simple mode, retaining nothing mystical in itself, is wholly outside.

The second, the allegorical mode, is entirely within.

The third, containing within itself the twofold form of both, is assigned partly to the outside and partly to the inside.

The fourth, concerning God, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by alteration, must be understood in both senses as within. “The peace of God surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4), and no one can adequately comprehend his mercy, which has narrated many things about itself figuratively.

The fifth, extending through parables of words, sometimes imitating the literal action and often foreshadowing either a prophecy of works or the secrets of spiritual meanings through the sins and adulteries of human beings, must in every respect be regarded as within [Col. 1016D].

The sixth, concerning the Savior’s two comings, is evident outside in clear testimonies, while it lies hidden within in certain testimonies, so that it may both remove doubt and exercise the faithful.

The seventh, finally, is outside in the commandments concerning the life that must be lived, but lies hidden within in the commandments concerning the life that is to be figured.

We know these modes, hidden before the time of Redemption, to have been revealed through Christ and in Christ at the time of the Redeemer himself. From these modes Saint Ambrose speaks at length in a brilliant and beautiful style.

“And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice: ‘Who is worthy to open the book and to loose its seals?’”

Who is this angel? Clearly, any teacher of the Old Testament. “The lips of the priest guard [Col. 1017A] knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

The angels of the Old Testament—that is, the holy prophets and patriarchs—were anxiously asking who could unlock the law so that it might be understood spiritually.

But when he says, “Who is worthy to open the book and to loose its seals,” is the order reversed? First he says that the book is to be opened, and then that its seals are to be loosed, although the seals must be loosed first and the book opened afterward.

This nevertheless happened in that order because the Lord first opened the book—that is, by becoming human he fulfilled in himself the Scripture of the Old Testament. Hence he himself says: “I did not come to destroy the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5).

Then, finally, rising from the dead, he unlocked the seals when he opened to his disciples what had been written [Col. 1017B] about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

“And no one was able, whether in heaven”—that is, among the angels—“or on earth”—that is, among human beings—“or under the earth”—that is, among souls already separated from the body—“to open the book,” that is, to unlock the mysteries of the Scriptures, because the fullness of time had not yet arrived, when the herald of the law was demanding that such things be fulfilled.

But what is said—“nor to look upon it”—is remarkable, since John had earlier said of himself: “I saw in the right hand of the one seated a book.” If no one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth could look upon the book, how could he see it? Where was he, or was this granted to him alone which was permitted to none of humankind or the angels?

Here, however, “to look upon” is used in the sense of “to comprehend [Col. 1017C] worthily.” For what angel or human being can comprehend how that unbounded and life-giving Spirit was formed within a virgin’s womb? How could he, after the resurrection, possessing a true and tangible body, enter among the disciples through solid walls with the doors shut?

No one, therefore, could comprehend by the reasoning of the mind how these things were accomplished by the Son of God, just as it is written: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53).

“And I wept greatly because no one was found worthy on earth to open the book or to look upon it.”

It may be asked: since, by the time blessed John saw these things, the book mentioned above had already been revealed through the mysteries of the birth, Passion, resurrection, ascension, and sending of the Holy Spirit, why does he say that he wept because no one had been found who could open the book? [Col. 1017D]

It must be understood that blessed John does not weep in his own person but in the person of the fathers of the Old Testament. They wept while longing for the coming of the Son of God into the world. One of them said:

> “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come down, so that the mountains might tremble before your face” (Isa. 64).

Hence the Lord also said in the Gospel to his disciples:

> “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see” (Matt. 13), and so forth.

“And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep. Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and loose its seven seals.’”

By this elder we should understand any father of the Old Testament who, while foretelling the coming [Col. 1018A] of the Son of God, offered consolation to the others. One of them said:

> “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah,” and so forth.

And again:

> “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49).

In saying these things, he plainly showed that the book was to be unlocked through the coming of the Son of God. Hence it follows: “Behold, the Lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered,” and so forth.

He is called a lion by way of signification because, victorious, he rose from the dead. He is called a Lamb because he was offered in sacrifice for us on the cross.

“From the tribe of Judah,” because David descended from the seed of Judah, and blessed Mary was from David’s line; for this reason he is called the Root of David, in accordance with what Isaiah says (chap. 11):

> “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.”

“Behold,” he says, “the Lion has conquered.” What did this Lion—that is, Christ—conquer? The devil, the world [Col. 1018B], death, and hell.

For this reason he opened the book and loosed its seals: when he came into the world, he fulfilled all that had previously been foretold about him.

No one should be troubled by the fact that he does not say “he will conquer,” since these are the words of the fathers who preceded him. Sacred Scripture often uses the past tense in place of the future, as in: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 11).

“And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain.”

As was said above, the throne is the same as the four living creatures, and the elders are likewise the same as the four living creatures; the throne, the living creatures, and the elders together signify the whole Church, in whose midst Christ is, according to the passage:

> “Behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst” (Zech. 2).

Earlier John says that he saw one like the Son of Man walking in the midst [Col. 1018C] of seven golden lampstands. Then he says that he saw one seated; now he adds that he saw a Lamb standing. This is to be understood as follows:

The Lord walks when he bestows the gifts of his mercy upon his elect: to one, the grace of tongues; to another, interpretations of utterances.

He sits when he judges the deeds of individuals.

He stands when he assists those who are struggling. To stand is to assist; hence Stephen saw him standing in heaven amid the hands of those who were stoning him.

He is rightly seen in the Church not as slain but as though slain, because although he died through weakness, he lives through the power of God. Or certainly Christ stands in the midst of his elect as though slain because he dies daily in his elect, who put themselves to death with their vices and desires.

“Having [Col. 1018D] seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.”

What is signified by the seven horns is also signified by the seven eyes, namely, the Holy Spirit, as he himself makes clear when he adds: “which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.”

Although there is one Spirit, as it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1), the seven eyes or seven horns are spoken of on account of the sevenfold character of his grace.

He is rightly represented by seven eyes because he illuminates his elect as he moves throughout the whole earth, as Zechariah says.

But this should be considered: horns are on the head and rise above the flesh. Therefore, by the horns may be understood the more eminent people of the world, who greatly surpass [Col. 1019A] others and cling to Christ the Head, in whom they have also received a kingdom.

Kingdoms are likewise signified by horns, as we read in Zechariah, because the four horns are the four principal kingdoms.

For this reason Paul, seeing that certain members rise above the others through the gift of the Holy Spirit, says: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8). In other words, he says: “You are not enclosed like the other bones of the body, but rise like horns above flesh and bones.”

“And he came and took the book from the right hand of the one seated on the throne.”

Since the Father, the Holy Spirit, and the Son are of one substance in divinity, why does he say that the Lamb took the book from the right hand of the one seated?

This is because the one who became a Lamb as though slain—the man assumed from the Word of God—received the book not only from the Father and the Holy Spirit but also from the divinity of the Word, by which it assumed him [Col. 1019B].

He took the book because he fulfilled in deed the things that had been foretold about him.

“And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb.”

The Lamb opened the book when he fulfilled in deed the things that had long before been foretold about him. Therefore all the saints, recognizing him as truly their God, about whom so many mysteries had been foretold, fall down—that is, they think humbly of themselves and imitate him.

Hence it follows:

> “Each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.”

A harp consists of wood and strings, but the strings are stretched in different ways. By the wood, therefore, we should understand [Col. 1019C] the cross of Christ; by the strings, the flesh of the saints.

The strings are stretched upon the wood because the saints imitate Christ’s cross and Passion, in accordance with the words of the apostle Peter: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example” (1 Pet. 2), and so forth.

Yet they are stretched in different ways because not all suffer equally: one is crucified, another beheaded, another burned, and another stoned. They endure torments of this kind in different ways, yet all produce one sound because all confess one faith.

And just as Christ died for them, so they die for him.

By the bowls we should understand the breadth of their charity. Hence they are rightly said to have been full of aromatic spices. Incense signifies pure prayers [Col. 1019D]. Therefore the Psalmist says:

> “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140).

It is fitting, then, that the bowls are placed after the harps, because the Lord first suffered and through his suffering displayed the breadth of his charity when he prayed for those who crucified him, saying:

> “Father, do not hold this sin against them, because they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

The saints have harps because they imitate Christ’s Passion; they also have bowls because they pray not only for their friends but even for their enemies, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Stephen, who knelt and prayed, saying:

> “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7).

The prayers of the saints are compared with aromatic spices because no prayer can be more pleasing [Col. 1020A] than one poured out for an enemy, so that the Lord’s command may be fulfilled, which says:

> “Love your enemies,” and so forth.

“And they will sing a new song, saying: ‘You are worthy, O Lord, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood.’”

The new song is the New Testament, in which a new reality is contained: his incarnation, Passion, death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and sending of the Holy Spirit. In it also the whole Law and the Prophets are comprehended under the twofold commandment, as he himself says:

> “I give you a new commandment” (John 13).

Of this song the Psalmist says:

> “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 93).

The holy Church sings this song because she continually recalls these things and recognizes that he accomplished such things [Col. 1020B] for her.

She also confesses this by her very actions: in his name she is reborn in the baptismal font; she puts herself to death with her vices and desires; in hope and faith she rises with him; she is lifted up to heavenly things; she is enriched by the gift of the Holy Spirit; and she professes that she will come with her Head to judgment.

But let us hear what the living creatures and the elders themselves say:

> “You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive the book,” and so forth.

The Lord received the book and loosed its seals when, having become human, he fulfilled in deed the things that had been foretold about him.

Hence we read in the Gospel that, after tasting vinegar, he said:

> “It is finished” (John 19),

meaning everything that had to be accomplished in him, even unto death.

It is as though they were saying: “In comparison with our victories, your victory alone [Col. 1020C] is judged worthy, because through your singular Passion we have been redeemed from the prince of death and from the curse of the Law.”

If anyone doubts that the whole Church can be comprehended in the four living creatures or the twenty-four elders, as was said above, let him attend to their words, in which they say: “You redeemed us for God,” because we were held captive by the devil.

“From every tribe,” that is, from every order. For, as was said above, tribes are so called from the three orders.

“And language,” because although there are seventy-two languages, from all of them those who had been predestined have been gathered into the faith.

“And people,” because there are more peoples than languages: one language may be spoken by many nations, as by Romans, Italians, Franks, Burgundians, Aquitanians, and Goths, although each nation possesses certain particular characteristics.

What [Col. 1020D] he adds, “and nation,” is the same as what he had said earlier: “and people,” because there is no human race that is not included in the Church. For there is no distinction of persons with him, but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him (Acts 10).

And he redeemed these people not at a cheap price but with his own blood. Hence the Apostle says:

> “You were bought at a great price” (1 Cor. 6).

“And you made us a kingdom and priests for our God, and we shall reign upon the earth.”

All the elect are called kings because they do not allow the tyranny of vices to rise up within them. They restrain the desire for sexual excess, extinguish the fire of anger, and crush other temptations of this kind that seek to rise up within them.

They are also called priests [Col. 1021A] because every day they offer themselves upon the altar of the heart as a contrite sacrifice, so that they may become a living offering, putting themselves to death with their vices and desires.

Hence Paul says:

> “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12).

When they do this, they are kings upon the earth, because they restrain carnal and earthly desires and, as though reigning over the earth subjected to them, rule by the law of virtue.

The Church of the elect, then, just as she was redeemed by Christ, has received in him who redeemed her the power to open the book.

“And I saw and heard the voice of many [Col. 1021B] angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders.”

John shows most clearly here that this entire vision was spiritual when he says: “And I heard the voice of many angels.” A voice cannot be seen; “to see” is used in the sense of “to understand,” just as we read in Exodus: “The people saw the voices,” that is, they understood them (Exod. 20).

We too customarily ask someone to whom we wish to show something whether he “sees,” that is, whether he understands what we are saying.

John’s entire seeing and hearing, therefore, took place in the Spirit, and for that reason it was spiritual.

In this passage, the living creatures, the throne, and the elders signify the same thing as the angels, namely, all the saints. Not only are those who teach others called angels—such as bishops, priests, and others—but also all righteous people who strive to make known to others the good that they understand.

John himself says in his Gospel that “to all who believed in him, he gave power to become children of God [Col. 1021C]” (John 1), and the Psalmist says: “I have said: You are gods” (Ps. 81).

The Lord likewise says in the Gospel: “But you, who are gods, whom do you say that I am?” (Matt. 15).

If the saints are called children of God, and not only children of God but also gods, what is surprising if they are called angels?

Of these angels Isaiah says: “The angels of peace will weep bitterly”; and Zechariah says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

These angels are around the throne and the living creatures because they themselves are the throne and the living creatures; they are also the angels and the elders.

We may likewise understand these angels as the heavenly spirits who stand around the Church and guard her, in accordance with the Apostle’s words:

> “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit [Col. 1021D] salvation?” (Heb. 2).

There is no doubt that these angels also rejoiced at the restoration of the human race, although previously they regarded human beings as strangers to their fellowship.

Hence, when the Lord was born, there was present a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will” (Luke 2).

Whether this is said of holy human beings or of heavenly spirits, an innumerable multitude is indicated when it follows:

> “And their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice.”

If he had given a definite number, expressing their total, and had said ten thousand or one hundred thousand, or something of that kind, he would plainly have indicated a finite number.

We read something similar in the Book of Daniel [Col. 1022A], which says:

> “Thousands of thousands ministered to him” (Dan. 7).

The innumerable number of angels signifies the numerable multitude of the elect. As many holy human beings will ascend into heaven as angels remained there after the devil perished, because those saints will occupy places in all the orders of angels.

> “The Lamb who was slain is worthy to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing.”

He who is called a lion because of his strength is called a lamb because of his innocence and simplicity, and because he was offered in sacrifice.

He is worthy to receive power, so that the same power and strength that are in the Word may also be in the man assumed, so that God and man may be capable of all things.

And divinity, because “in him the whole [Col. 1022B] fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2).

And wisdom, so that just as the Word, begotten by the Father before the ages, knows all things, so that man joined to the Word in the unity of person may know all things, and nothing may be hidden from him.

For he is the power of God and the wisdom of God, as the Apostle says:

> “Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13).

Hence the Apostle says:

> “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him now no longer in that way.”

When, after the power, wisdom, and divinity already mentioned, strength is added, the statement is repeated, since power and strength are the same.

Then follows: “And honor and glory and blessing”—that is, he is worthy to receive honor in the resurrection, glory in the ascension [Col. 1022C], and blessing because, raised to the right hand of the Father’s majesty, he is blessed, that is, praised, by all his creation.

For it is fitting that the humanity of the Son of God, which endured such torments—after spittings, blows, death, and burial—should rise again, be placed at the Father’s right hand, and be praised, worshiped, glorified, and blessed by every creature.

“And every creature that is in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and those that are in the sea and that are in it, is worthy to receive.”

That is, his humanity is worthy to possess all things in heaven—that is, among the angels—in earth, among human beings, under the earth, in hell, and in the sea, together with what is in it.

This is what the Lord himself says when, rising from the dead:

> “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

And the Apostle says:

> “At the name [Col. 1022D] of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2).

We may also understand the sea allegorically as this world, in which the one hundred and fifty-three fish were enclosed, signifying the number of the elect.

“And I heard every creature saying to the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb: ‘Blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever.’”

“Every creature”—that is, the living creatures, the elders, and the angels—I heard saying this to the one seated on the throne, God the Father, and to the Lamb, his Son.

Although only the persons of the Father and the Son are mentioned in this passage, the Holy Spirit is understood there as well. For where the Son and the Holy Spirit are, there without doubt the Father is also included.

Thus the holy Church now does generally what is represented in these [Col. 1023A] living creatures, elders, and angels: she praises her Creator, to whom alone are due honor, blessing, praise, and glory forever and ever.

And the four living creatures were saying, “Amen.” And the twenty-four elders fell down and worshiped the one who lives forever and ever. As has often been said, the living creatures are the same as the elders, that is, the entire body of the Church. Therefore the elders also answer “Amen” with the living creatures, and the living creatures worship and fall down with the elders. For one and the same Church, represented under different names, both praises God together and confirms by the interposed “Amen” that the faith is true; and the one whom it exalts with a genuine proclamation of praise, it humbly worships by falling down. What this falling and this worship signify, we have already explained above. What follows.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1023B]

And I saw when the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals. The opening of the seal is the revelation of the mystery. Indeed, by the seven seals, as was said above, the fullness of the hidden mysteries is signified—mysteries that lay concealed before the Lord’s coming. Although these were many and foretold in many ways, as the Apostle says, “In many parts and in many ways God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets” (Heb. 1), they can nevertheless all be comprehended in three ways: namely, by speech, by action, and by work. For example: “Behold, I come” is speech; “In the head of the book it is written of me” is the recognition of the preceding speech, demonstrating Christ, of whom the prophet says, “Behold, the one desired by all the nations will come” (Hag. 2). [Col. 1023C] For in the opening of Genesis it is also said of him that in the beginning—that is, in the Son—God made heaven and earth. The same Son reveals this about himself in the Gospel, saying to the Jews, “I am the beginning, who also speak to you.”

By action, when it follows: “That I may do your will, my God.” The same Son also showed that this work was his own when he says in the Gospel, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 4). To put it briefly, the Lamb opened the seven seals for us when, for our salvation, as had been promised concerning him in the Holy Scriptures, he willed both to be born and to die, to rise from the dead, and also to ascend into heaven; and he foretold that he would come for judgment. Hence, after rising from the dead, he opened the disciples’ understanding so that they might understand everything concerning him that was contained in the Holy Scriptures, saying that “it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead” (Acts 17). For this reason also he promised the disciples that he would send the Holy Spirit, who would teach them everything and announce to them what was to come.

And I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as though with a voice like thunder, “Come and see.” In this passage one living creature signifies the primitive Church from the Jews, concerning whom it is written that in one day three thousand believed, then five thousand, and afterward many thousands. John, however, signifies the Church that follows. Therefore the angel says to John, “Come and see,” because the primitive Church invites the succeeding Church by its teaching and preaching, saying: “Come to the faith,” namely, of Christ—not with bodily steps, but by faith and the mind—and, passing from the mystical language of the Law and the Prophets to an understanding of knowledge, see those things that were foretold earlier now openly fulfilled. Hence the saying, “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. 44). Hear what was foretold; see what has been fulfilled.

And behold, a white horse, and the one seated upon it had a bow, and a crown was given to him. By the white horse we must understand the Lord’s body, cleansed from every sin; by its rider, the divinity of the Word, which now indeed mounts this horse when the Word of God joined flesh and soul to himself within the Virgin’s womb. Hence he himself speaks through the Psalmist to God the Father: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. 72), and so forth.

By the bow, the two Testaments are signified, from which proceed as many arrows as there are divine utterances. For people are killed by arrows, and by these arrows of the divine Scriptures the reprobate are killed so that they may die to sin and live to God. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your arrows are sharp” (Ps. 44), and so forth. The Church had been struck by these arrows when she said: “The watchmen who go around the city found me; they struck me and wounded me.”

By the crown that was given to him, we can understand the faith of all the nations dwelling throughout the circuit of this world. For he rose from the dead, was preached by the apostles, and was believed by the whole world.

And he went forth. From where, unless from the opened seal—that is, from the revealed mystery of the Scriptures? [Col. 1024C] He went forth from the seal when, as had been foretold, he was incarnate; that is, when the Word became flesh. He went forth conquering the devil, first in himself, so that afterward he might conquer him in his members.

We may also understand by the white horse, in general, the universal Church, which was made white in baptism and over which Christ presides. She says in Psalm 50: “You will sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” More particularly, the order of preachers is expressed in the white horse, of which Habakkuk says (ch. 3): “Mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.” They are rightly called the Lord’s horses, because the Lord, presiding over them, went throughout all the nations through their preaching and gathered them to his faith, when “they went forth and preached everywhere.” Concerning this sitting also the Lord says: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

Therefore the rider who was seated had a bow, because through the preaching of teachers, by the judgments of the divine Word, Christ struck the hearts of the gentiles and killed their vices and sins, so that the health of virtues might rise again.

The crown, according to this interpretation, can be understood in two ways: either as the victory of the saints over the devil and the persecutors of this world, or as the multitude of faithful subjects for whom they receive the reward of the eternal kingdom, as the Apostle says to his hearers: “What is my joy or crown of rejoicing? Are you not my crown?” (Phil. 4). [Col. 1025A]

This order of preachers went forth from Judea with its rider—that is, with Christ, who said to them: “Go into the whole world”—first conquering the devil in himself, so that afterward he might conquer him in others whom he had drawn from idolatry to the worship of Christ.

And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying, “Come and see.” And another horse went forth, a red one. Just as above by the white horse we understood Christ’s body—that is, the holy Church, cleansed from sin through baptism and Christ’s passion—so in this passage by the red horse we must understand the entire body of the devil, that is, all the reprobate. For just as Christ is the head of all the faithful, and all the faithful are his body, in whom he dwells through faith, so the devil is the head of all the reprobate, and all the reprobate are his body, in whom he dwells.

The red horse, therefore, is the body of the ancient enemy, bloodied by sins and drenched in the blood of the slaughter of souls. That blood signifies sins, as the Psalmist makes clear when he says: “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God” (Ps. 50). For the reprobate are bloodied by sins and also defiled by murders. Hence through the prophet the Lord says to certain people (Isa. 1): “When you cry out to me, I will not hear you; for your hands are full of blood.” This is why later the beast upon which the prostitute sits is said to be scarlet.

And the one seated upon it was granted the power to take peace from the earth. Power was given to the devil to take peace from the earth when he is permitted to do this by God’s just judgment. The meaning is like that of the statement: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 11).

It must be noted, however, that he takes peace not from heaven but from the earth. Heaven signifies the saints, to whom the Lord, as he was about to ascend to the Father, says: “I give you my peace” (John 14). From these the devil cannot take peace, because they are heavenly and trample upon the earth, having as their inhabitant the prince of peace, of whom Paul says: “He is our peace” (Eph. 2).

From the earth—that is, from earthly people—he takes peace, making them discordant and sowing divisions among them like the separations of weeds, because they are earth: that is, they pursue earthly and transitory things without restraint. Concerning this it is further added: “And that they should kill one another, and a great sword was given to him.”

We must not understand the sword as bodily, but as spiritual, by which not so much bodies as souls are slaughtered. This sword signifies evil persuasion, perverse speech, and wicked deception. With this sword the devil kills people in two ways: when he secretly suggests evil through himself, or when he openly persecutes the righteous through his members. Hence we read in the Gospel: “When the devil had put it into the heart of Judas to betray the Lord” (John 13). First, by the sword of evil persuasion he persuaded him in his soul to betray the Lord; afterward he persuaded him to kill himself. Thus that wretched man, despairing, hanged himself with a noose.

Likewise, he spoke to the woman through the serpent, saying: “Why did God command you not to eat from the tree of life?” (Gen. 3). Through her he killed Adam. This is what is meant here by the statement that people should kill one another.

Through his members also he slaughters many, both by spiritually separating them from the faith and by bodily removing them from this light, as through Nero, Domitian, and others. Concerning such people the Psalmist says: “They have sharpened their tongues like a sword” (Ps. 63); and again: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56).

And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying, “Come and see,” and behold, a black horse. By the black horse the entire body of the devil is understood, just as above by the red horse: a body darkened by the blackness of sins, always suffering hunger because it desires to devour others and transfer them into the belly of its wickedness. And just as their head never says, “Enough,” so these too are never satisfied.

Hence it is rightly added: “And the one seated upon it had a balance in his hand.” Merchants customarily carry a balance in their hands; they trade in what pleases them and weigh what they give and receive. But the devil is a very evil merchant, who gives cheap things in order to take away precious ones.

The balance, therefore, signifies his perverse persuasion, because he seeks to bargain away the life of many so that he may satisfy his hunger. To accomplish this, he first withholds the nourishment of the Word of God from those to whom he promises temporal things. Having taken the slain into his body, he increases rather than removes the hunger of his wickedness. He gives certain cheap and temporal things and takes away precious and eternal things, just as he gave Adam the apple and through him received the whole world in his descendants.

[Col. 1026C]

And I heard a voice, as it were a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying: “Two pounds of wheat for a denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and the oil.” This voice heard by John is understood as the voice of almighty God, when, after the nations had been gathered to the faith, the Lord restrained the ancient adversary from harming the elect and taught the Church how she could escape his assaults, saying: “Repent” (Matt. 3), and so forth.

He also commanded the apostles, as they went forth, to baptize all nations and to teach them to turn from the worship of idols to the true worship of God. Then the devil lost his wheat, barley, wine, and oil—that is, all the faithful—and began to eat straw, drink grape-wine residue, and consume olive dregs.

Hence the voice itself added, saying: “Two pounds of wheat for one denarius”—understand: “It is worth this.” But these words must first be considered according to the literal sense. “Two pounds of wheat” is understood as two sextarii, and “three two-pound measures of barley” as six sextarii. The one seated on the black horse—that is, the devil—is commanded not to touch the wheat or the barley, because two sextarii of wheat, that is, one two-pound measure, are worth one denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley are likewise worth one denarius.

But let us now see what these things signify. Although the whole Church is wheat, according to what the Apostle says, “One bread, one body; we are many in Christ” (1 Cor. 10), here we must understand the wheat especially as the preachers of both Testaments. They are ground by the tribulation of the present life, baked by the fire of suffering, and made into Christ’s most beautiful bread, imitating the one who says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies,” and so forth.

Thus one two-pound measure, consisting of two sextarii, because a person ordinarily has a vessel that holds two sextarii, signifies one Church gathered from two peoples into one, according to the saying: “I have other sheep that are not from this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10). It is comprehended under the number two because of the two Testaments, or because of the twofold commandment of love.

The two-pound measure of wheat is worth a denarius because all the saints have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “You were bought at a great price” (1 Cor. 6). Or by the denarius we can understand the Lord Jesus Christ himself, whom they will receive as their reward. Those laboring in the vineyard received a denarius.

Alternatively, by the denarius eternal life is understood, which will be given to all the elect when they hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25).

The three two-pound measures of barley signify subject and simple hearers, who are comprehended under the number three because they are adorned by faith in the Holy Trinity.

The wheat and the barley are therefore one, because although one person surpasses another in strength and dignity, all have nevertheless been redeemed by the one blood of Christ. Even if one labors more and another less in the Lord’s vineyard, all alike receive one denarius after their labor. Although there will be a diversity of dwelling places, there will nevertheless be one reward, because all together will possess the one God, and what one does not possess in himself he will certainly possess in another, because God will be all things in all.

“And do not harm the wine and the oil.” What was signified above by the wheat is understood here by the wine, and what was signified above by the barley is now understood by the oil—that is, all the saints in the universal Church.

They are rightly represented by wine and oil, because just as wine and oil are produced from many grapes and olives pressed in the winepress, so they are pressed by many tribulations in this life and stored in the chambers of the Lord’s cellar. They are wine because they have been baptized in faith in the Lord’s passion. Afterward they received the oil of the Holy Spirit. Divine power therefore forbids the ancient enemy to harm them by persuading them to sin.

[Col. 1027D]

And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying, “Come and see.” And behold, a pale horse. Those who were designated above by the red and black horse are also designated here by the pale horse: all the reprobate, who will come to the pallor of eternal death, since pallor properly belongs to the dead.

It is no wonder that death is expressed by the pallor of the horse, since the rider himself is also called Death. Hence it follows: “And the one seated upon it was named Death.” By this name the devil is understood, because through the devil’s envy death entered the world. He sits upon those who are pale—that is, those who possess works of death. Although they themselves are dead, they also seek to extinguish others.

Hence it follows: “And hell followed him.” These people are rightly called hell, because just as hell never says, “Enough,” but continually widens its bosom to receive souls, so they enlarge their minds to pursue earthly things and cannot acquire as much as they desire. Therefore they follow the devil—that is, they imitate him, who is the head of all wickedness. Hence it is written: “They imitate him who belong to his side” (Wis. 2).

The author of death, therefore, about to wage war against the living, sits upon the pale horse, because through the service of those whom he has already spiritually killed he seeks to extinguish the life of the elect.

And power was given to him over the four parts of the earth, to kill with the sword. Here it is openly demonstrated that almighty God has placed angels over individual nations according to their merit. Just as he appointed a good angel, Michael, over the good—hence the saying, “I have no helper except Michael, your prince”—so he placed evil angels over the wicked. Therefore the four angels appointed over the four principal kingdoms were not good but evil.

Power was given to him over the four parts of the earth—that is, over all the reprobate who dwell in the four parts of the earth: east, west, north, and south.

Or by the four parts of the earth we can understand the four principal kingdoms, namely, the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Medes and Persians, the Macedonians, and the Romans.

Alternatively, we can understand the four parts of the earth over which the devil received power as heretics, pagans, Jews, and false Christians. Over these four parts of the earth—that is, over earthly people who inhabit the earth through their desires—the devil has power, and with them he fights against Christ’s one Church.

He cannot divide the Church because she is united by the faith of Christ, according to the saying: “My dove is one” (Song 6). Those others are found divided, whereas these are found united.

He killed those parts of the earth with the sword of evil suggestion, as was said above, and with the famine of hearing the Word of God. Concerning this famine the Lord says through the prophet Amos (ch. 8): “I will send a famine upon them, not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the Word of God.”

Here a question arises: If God sends this famine, what sin does the devil commit? The question is easily resolved, because what God does by just judgment, the devil does through persuasion and evil intention.

“And with death”—understand: it was granted to him to kill people, spiritually and inwardly.

“And with the beasts of the earth.” The beasts signify savage and bestial people, through whom the devil killed many, such as Nero, Domitian, and the other persecutors of the holy martyrs. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts” (Titus 1); and elsewhere: “If, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus” (1 Cor. 15).

And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain. In Moses’ tabernacle there were two altars: one, covered with bronze, outside under the open sky, where sacrifices were burned; the other inside, before the veil, on which only blood and incense were placed, and which was covered with gold.

When the veil was torn, the ark that had been within the Holy of Holies was joined to the golden altar, so that there was no longer any separation between the altar and the ark.

By these two altars two peoples are signified. One is represented by the outer altar, namely, the carnal people among the Jews, who think that they can be saved and justified only through the works and sacrifices of the Law.

By the golden altar, which was inside, the other people are signified: the spiritual fathers of both Testaments, who do not think that they can be saved solely through the Law or the works of sacrifices, but rather through faith in the coming Christ. For just as the spiritual teachers understood the Law, so also did those prophets, patriarchs, and others act.

We can clearly prove this from the words of David, who, knowing that he could not be cleansed from adultery by the sacrifices of the Law, said: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.” Considering that this could not be done, he adds: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. 50).

It must be understood that the golden altar under discussion was formerly before the ark, but a veil hung before both this altar and the one that divided the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. Within the Holy of Holies was the ark, in which there were only the two tablets written by the finger of God. By this ark Christ is signified, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

After the true high priest came and tore the veil, the ark and the altar became one, because the head and the members—that is, Christ and the Church—are one body.

This altar is therefore mentioned here when it says: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain.” There are no longer two altars but one, because Christ has been joined to his body.

For he is the altar, the priest, and the sacrifice. He is the priest because through him we direct our offerings to God the Father. Hence priests, wishing to be heard by the Lord in each prayer, conclude their prayers in his name, saying: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.”

He is the altar because he offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross. Therefore there are no longer two altars but one, after the true high priest entered the Holy of Holies with a part of his body. Just as they are already with him in reality, so these others are with him in hope.

Thus the souls of the slain are themselves the altar, and yet they are beneath the altar, because they cannot be made equal in every respect to their head: he is God, they are human beings; he is Lord, they are servants.

Therefore they are the altar, joined to their head; and they are beneath the altar because they are not equal to him in every respect.

Alternatively: those who are the altar are beneath the altar—that is, beneath themselves—because they have not yet reached the glory to which they will come when they will be like the angels of God.

Their desire is still divided, because they await the resurrection of their bodies. And just as they served Christ with body and soul, so they will be rewarded with body and soul, because this is truly fitting.

Therefore, because they have not yet reached the dignity to which they will come, they are beneath themselves, since afterward they will be greater. But when they have come to such glory, they will no longer be beneath themselves but within themselves.

This can be understood by the following example. Let us suppose that someone was raised in a monastery and afterward made abbot. As long as such a person lives under his superiors, he is, as it were, beneath himself; but once he has been elected abbot, he is no longer beneath himself but within himself.

In the same way, the souls of the faithful will no longer be beneath themselves when their souls rejoice together with their bodies in immortality.

The souls of the slain are called the souls of martyrs. For there are two kinds of martyrdom in this world. One is open, occurring in the body, as Peter, Paul, and the others were martyred. The other is hidden, when the saints endure insults, mockery, and abuse from the wicked.

Concerning these two kinds of martyrdom the Lord says to the sons of Zebedee: “Are you able to drink the cup that I shall drink?” (Matt. 20); and afterward: “You will drink my cup.” One of them was beheaded, while the other ended his life in peace; nevertheless, he was not without martyrdom, because he endured many insults and adversities for Christ.

Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 5) that he was flogged with the others when they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, on account of the Word of God and the testimony they bore.

This is the Word of which John says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). Because they had that Word in their hearts, they also produced testimonies with their mouths, according to the saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

Or, because they carried the Word of God in heart and mouth, they displayed their testimony in their works, refusing to worship idols. For this they were killed, either by open martyrdom or by hidden martyrdom, when their persecutors called them impostors and hypocrites.

And all those who had endured open or hidden martyrdom cried out, saying with a loud voice: “How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?”

A question arises here: Why do the saints, already dwelling with the Lord, ask vengeance upon their enemies, when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke 6)?

It must be understood that those saints, already standing in the presence of their Creator, see his will. Therefore they receive from him what they know he wishes to do, and from him they drink what they thirst for from him.

They ask vengeance upon their enemies in two ways, and this out of charity: so that those who are predestined to eternal life may be converted from evil to good; and so that those who, as God foreknows, are to be damned may die and cease from sinning, so that afterward they may suffer a lesser punishment in hell, where each person will endure the magnitude of punishment according to the quality of his works.

To ask this is indeed an act of charity and mercy.

It must not be thought that they emit a bodily voice as we do, drawing air through the organ of the throat into the bellows of the belly. Their voice is their desire. And each one cries out all the more loudly the more intensely he burns with desire.

Concerning this the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. 9). They ask vengeance upon the reprobate because they desire the day of the final judgment to come and await the resurrection of their bodies.

And individual white robes were given to them. By the white robes we must understand the reward of baptism, the prize of martyrdom, the recompense of eternal things, and the joy of the heavenly homeland.

Before the resurrection, therefore, the saints each have one robe, because they still enjoy eternal blessedness in the soul alone. Later they will receive two, when, having received their bodies, they will be unchangeable in soul and incorruptible in body.

Concerning this Isaiah says: “In their land they will possess double” (Isa. 61).

And they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be completed. This statement is a divine inspiration by which the power of patience is poured into their desiring minds as they await the day of judgment, so that they may endure all things patiently while awaiting the number of those who likewise will be killed for Christ and afterward reign with them.

Thus those who desire to receive their bodies rejoice in the number of the brothers who are to be gathered.

In this way almighty God speaks to the saints, as a householder with many children might reply to each one returning from the field and asking him for food: “Your refreshment is indeed prepared, but wait for your brothers, so that when you have all been brought together, you may all eat and feast together with joy.”

Those who are to be killed just as they were—either by open or by hidden martyrdom.

And I saw when he had opened the sixth seal, and a great earthquake occurred. What should we understand by the earthquake in this passage except the most powerful persecution that will occur in the time of the Antichrist?

Therefore he rightly did not simply say, “An earthquake occurred,” but added, “A great earthquake occurred,” because, as the Lord says, the tribulation at that time will be such as has not been and will not be since human beings began to exist.

And the sun became black like a sackcloth garment. Sinners and the guilty are clothed in sackcloth. The sun signifies Christ, of whom it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. 4). Concerning him the wicked will also say, groaning: “The sun of righteousness did not shine for us.”

The sun will therefore become like sackcloth when those in whose hearts Christ will shine are considered worthless and are killed by the ministers of the Antichrist as though they were sinners and guilty.

Alternatively, the sun signifies the preachers themselves, to whom the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). They will then become like sackcloth because they will conceal before the wicked whatever light and virtue they possess.

The sun will also be darkened in those who, shaken by fear or softened by enticements, will deny Christ and fall into the darkness of error.

And the whole moon became like blood. The moon signifies the Church, which will then become entirely like blood, because the persecution of the Antichrist will rage against the Church not in one place only but in every region of the world.

And the stars of heaven fell upon the earth. Heaven is the holy Church, of which the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne” (Acts 7), and Solomon says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 2).

The stars of heaven, therefore, are the saints who shine amid the darkness of this life like stars in the firmament. They will then fall from heaven when, under that extremely severe persecution, they depart from the faith—those who previously seemed to shine through right faith and righteous works.

They will fall upon the earth because they will cling to earthly pleasures and, through that earthly love, will plunge into iniquity.

Hence it follows: “As a fig tree casts its unripe figs when it is shaken by the wind.” Although in the Gospel the fig tree signifies the synagogue, here it specially signifies the whole Church, from which those who had been fruitless and empty of good works will then fall.

The early fruit of the fig tree is called the first-season fig. Before it reaches maturity, it falls to the earth when shaken by the wind. So also those who have not yet reached the maturity of good works and are empty will, shaken by the wind—that is, by the final persecution—fall to the earth, namely, into earthly pleasures.

That wind is rightly called great because, as was said above, that persecution will seize even the elect.

And heaven withdrew like a scroll being rolled up. What is heaven is also the scroll, that is, the holy Church. For while she has God as her inhabitant, she also has the law of God written—not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of a fleshly heart.

It must be observed that the Church herself is said to withdraw like a rolled-up scroll. What is contained inside a rolled-up scroll is not seen except by those to whom it is voluntarily opened.

In this way the saints of that time will reveal themselves to their own people and conceal themselves from outsiders, as we read in the passions of the holy martyrs. John addresses the members of this Church, saying: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4).

The Church will withdraw in her elect from the reprobate, not by bodily departure but by faith and action, according to the saying: “Go out from her midst, my people, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isa. 52).

And every mountain and island was moved from its place. By the mountains in this passage we must understand the distinguished saints established in the Church, who rise above the others, just as mountains surpass the level ground. To them belongs what the Lord says through the prophet: “I will raise you above the heights of the earth” (Isa. 58).

They will be moved, not so as to depart from the faith, but as they withdraw in body, mind, and action from association with the reprobate, hearing what the prophet says, as was mentioned above: “Go out from her, my people.” This refers to Babylon, which signifies sins and the association of the wicked.

The islands likewise signify the churches, because just as islands are beaten by waves, so the churches are beaten by the waves of the persecutions of this life. Concerning them the prophet says: “The islands will wait for me and will hope in my arm” (Isa. 51). They too will be separated, like the mountains, when they are divided from the wicked by faith and action.

And the kings of the earth, the princes, the tribunes, the rich, the strong, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains. Kings are those who know how to rule their bodies well, so that they do not grow arrogant through vices or succumb to poverty.

Princes are holy people of lesser dignity, who, unlike kings, do not resist all things, but nevertheless resist certain things through the virtues granted to them.

Tribunes are those with still less power than princes; nevertheless, insofar as they prevail, they fight against the vices of the flesh.

The rich are called rich not in possessions but in good works. Hence the Apostle urges people to become rich in good works.

The strong are strong not through bodily power but through courage of spirit.

The slave is one bound by marriage. The free person is one released from marriage and from sins.

All these, caught in the final persecution, will flee and hide themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains—that is, they will seek the aid of holy men and angels. To these mountains, when seized by the final persecution, the Lord urges people to flee in the Gospel, saying: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains” (Matt. 24).

And they will say to the mountains and rocks—that is, to the angels and human beings. They are rightly called mountains because they despise earthly things and contemplate heavenly things. They are rightly called rocks because they are strengthened by Christ, who is the rock.

“Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of the one seated upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb”—that is, bend your hearts toward mercy and help us, through your compassionate intercessions, to escape the wrath of the judge.

For the great day of their wrath has come—that is, the condemnation of the rejected. And who will be able to stand? That is, no one. For if the saints will then fear his wrath, and the angels too will be shaken with fear, who among us will endure, when even the righteous will scarcely be saved? Concerning this time the prophet says: “That day is a day of wrath” (Zeph. I).

We can also understand these things in the opposite sense. For mountains often signify the proud in sacred language, as in Isaiah: “Raise a signal upon the mountain covered with darkness”; by these words Balthasar understood it to mean one covered by the cloud of unbelief and impiety. Islands, moreover, are called those who are tossed by the waves of worldly affairs and are unstable. Such people will be moved from good to evil, from faith to unbelief, so that they may fulfill their desire. Even in a time of peace they not only seize the possessions of outsiders, but also rejoice at the death of their relatives and convert their goods to their own uses.

“Kings,” “princes,” and “tribunes,” according to the rank of their degrees, signify all the rejected: namely, men of greater dignity, those of middling rank, and those of lesser rank. When they fear losing their kingdoms and honor, and see the Antichrist and his members reigning, they will pass over to them and be moved to evil, so that they may be spared by them and not lose their riches. The rich, likewise, are those who are rich in sins: they will be able freely to fulfill every evil they desire and will not need the assistance of others in wrongdoing. We likewise understand “the strong” as strong in evil, whether for producing drunkenness or for overthrowing the faith of others.

“Slaves” are those who serve sin, because “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin.” “Free” means free from righteousness—that is, from another’s righteousness. Hence Paul says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. VI).

All these, with the future judgment threatening, will run for the aid of demons, since in despair they will not dare approach any of the saints, saying: “Fall upon us, and hide us from the wrath of him who sits upon the throne”—that is, “Free us now, because until now we have trusted in you.”

## CHAPTER VII

“After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth.” The four angels standing over the four parts of the earth are princes, set over the four principal kingdoms: namely, those of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, Medes and Persians, Macedonians and Romans. Over these four parts of the earth stood four wicked angels, because they had bent those kingdoms toward the rule of their own service.

“Holding the four winds of the earth, so that they would not blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree.” What the four angels are, the four winds also are: namely, four demons holding supremacy over the four kingdoms. Accordingly, in the book of Daniel we read that four winds were fighting upon the great sea, and four beasts were rising from the earth; these are the aforesaid four kingdoms of the world.

The angels were therefore holding the four winds—that is, themselves in their members. Since the devil and all the wicked are one body, he himself is plainly understood both in the angels and in the winds. The angels were holding the four winds of the earth so that they would not blow upon the earth, because the four demons set over the individual kingdoms held all the subject peoples in such subjection that no one dared to breathe any regional breath against them, or mutter against them, or blow forth the word of truth against idols by saying: “They are not gods, which are made by human hands, but images, useful for nothing.”

By “earth” the diversity of provinces is signified; by “sea,” the countless number of islands. By “trees,” moreover, individual human beings are understood, because the interpretation moves from the whole to the particular. For those demons held all the people dwelling in these four kingdoms bound to their service.

“And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God. And he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees.”

The other angel signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is written: “His name shall be called the angel of great counsel” (Isa. IX). He ascended from the rising of the sun because on the third day he rose from the dead and by his resurrection illuminated the whole world through evangelical teaching. Hence the Psalmist says: “He who ascended above the setting sun—the Lord is his name” (Ps. LXVII).

He therefore came from the rising of the sun and commanded the four angels not to harm the earth and the sea, because, rising from the dead, he forbade the demons to injure those predestined to eternal life. Thus he also subjected those four kingdoms to himself and brought them to the knowledge and worship of the one God. Hence Nabuchodonosor saw a stone cut from the mountain, which struck the statue on its iron feet and crushed together the gold, silver, and bronze. Gold signifies the kingdom of the Assyrians; silver, that of the Medes; bronze, that of the Persians and Macedonians; and iron signifies the kingdom of the Romans.

For Christ, born from the Jewish stock without marital intercourse, through the preaching of the apostles struck the extremity of the Roman kingdom. Then he crushed all the aforesaid kingdoms of the world that had been subject to it. But the stone grew and was raised up into a kingdom that will never be destroyed.

Hence what follows is also said: “Until we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads.” Here it must be observed that although John earlier says that he saw one angel, that angel now speaks in the plural, saying: “Until we seal”—that is, “I and my apostles.” For what the apostles did, Christ himself did, since he dwells in them, according to the saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

This seal, by which all the servants of God are sealed upon their foreheads, is the seal of the holy cross, which the faithful bear in the Church in two ways: in body and in soul. In the body, because they are sealed upon the forehead in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. In the soul, because they imitate Christ’s passion, crucifying themselves with vices and desires.

Hence in the Old Testament it was commanded that they place blood from the lamb upon both thresholds, because this outward sign profits nothing unless one also receives it inwardly: “For faith, if it has no works, is dead.” Therefore he says: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads,” as though he were saying: “Do not injure those who were ordained for eternal life before all ages.” Hence the Apostle says: “He chose us before the foundation of the world for adoption as sons of God” (Eph. I).

“And I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel.” In this passage a finite number is used for an infinite one. It does not refer only to the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, but to the whole Church, which is comprehended in this number through its elect; the nature of the number itself also demonstrates this.

For three signifies the highest good, namely, the holy Trinity. Four is likewise sacred because of the four books of the Gospel, or because of the four rivers of paradise, or also because of the four parts of the world, or the four principal virtues. Thus, whether three is multiplied by four or four by three, twelve results. This number too is sacred because of the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles.

The number one thousand signifies perfection, because it is often used for totality. Hence: “The word that he commanded for a thousand generations” (Ps. CIV). Since, then, the Church is gathered from all generations through knowledge of the Trinity, watered by the four rivers of paradise, and extended throughout the four parts of the world, it is rightly represented by twelve thousand.

But if it is to be perfected in what it has believed, it is necessary that the number twelve thousand be joined to a fourfold solidity. Let twelve thousand therefore be multiplied by four, and let forty-eight thousand result.
