Then, so that what it has believed may attain to contemplation of the Trinity, let forty-eight thousand again be multiplied threefold, and let it produce one hundred and forty-four thousand.

The number one hundred, which is transferred from the left to the right, also signifies the general number of the saints, who, found in the perfection of their works, are to be placed on the right.

“From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed.” This passage plainly shows that we should not understand a carnal descent here, because the sons of Jacob are not placed in this catalogue according to the order of their birth. Judah, who is placed first here, was in fact born fourth. Gad is third here, whereas there he is found eighth. The same must be observed concerning the others.

Why this was done is made clear by the interpretation of the names themselves. Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praising.” In him the Church is comprehended: it does penance for past sins and does not cease praising the Creator. For *confiteor* is an equivocal word, used both for confession and for praise. Hence the Lord says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI). And the Psalmist says: “I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart” (Ps. CXXXVII).

Ruben is said to mean “seeing a son.” In this passage he signifies the Church itself, which sees sons—that is, good works. Hence: “May you see the sons of your sons.” The “sons of sons” are understood as the reward of works.

This lineage is therefore spiritual, because in Judah the beginning of confessions comes first, and in Ruben the growth of virtues follows. If Ruben were placed first, the order of his birth would be confused. For first, through confession, we withdraw from evil; then we advance to the good that follows, so that we may be formed in what is upright and pleasing.

After Ruben, Gad is rightly placed. His name is interpreted as “temptation,” because temptation commonly tests those who act well. Hence it is said to someone: “Because you were acceptable to the Lord, it was necessary that temptation test you.” And because those who are girded with divine strength against the same temptations stand firm, Gad is rightly called “girded.” Hence the Psalmist says: “You girded me with strength for battle” (Ps. XVII).

And because the saints pray with the door shut and, as far as they can, conceal their works from human favor, so that he who sees in secret may repay them, it is also rightly fitting that Gad be called “a robber.” Since the temptation inflicted crowns those who have been tested, after Gad there fittingly appears:

“Aser,” who is interpreted as “blessed.” Hence: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation” (James I).

Certain of this promise, the saints not only patiently endure the evils inflicted upon them, but, even when placed amid tribulations, do not depart from the breadth of charity. Therefore after Aser comes Nephthalim, which is interpreted as “breadth.” For they run by that commandment of which the Psalmist says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII).

And because, advancing through this exceedingly great commandment of love, they consign the things behind them to forgetfulness and stretch forward toward what lies ahead, and recognize that they are pilgrims in this life—and therefore confess themselves to be beggars—Manasses is rightly placed after Nephthalim. His name is interpreted as “one who has forgotten,” or “necessity.” “One who has forgotten,” because they leave behind the one thing that lies behind them; “necessity,” because they have not yet reached the things they desire. Hence the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. XXIV).

Accordingly, Simeon is also well placed after Manasses. His name is interpreted as “he heard sorrow,” because the desire of those who ask to be dissolved and to be with Christ is often delayed, though it is not taken away. It is therefore also necessary that they retain the meaning of the name “habitation,” which Simeon likewise seems to signify: those who mourn in the tabernacle of corruption ought to rejoice in the dwelling of eternal rest, knowing that when their earthly dwelling is dissolved, they have an edifice in the heavens, a house not made with hands.

Levi follows him. Levi is called “added,” because such people, already trampling upon all earthly things, add to themselves commandments that are not requirements, such as virginity, the distribution of half of one’s goods or possessions, and other things of this kind, which are added not by command but by counsel.

To such people it rightly belongs that Issachar is joined after Levi; Issachar is interpreted as “reward.” Such people are owed the reward of recompense, of whom Jeremiah says to one: “Let your voice cease from weeping, for there is a reward for your work” (Jer. XXXI).

Those who live in this way and labor solely for the reward of eternal life sometimes undergo temptations. Hence after Issachar there is rightly placed:

“Zabulon,” who is interpreted as “habitation of strength.” Such people do not succumb to temptations, but “strength is made perfect in weakness.” The Apostle says of such people (Heb. XI): “They recovered strength from weakness. They became strong in battle,” because their body, which enemies consider weak and through which they prepare the soul’s destruction, is found to be unconquered.

Even when they are persecuted by the wicked, they do not cease to expend upon their enemies the talent of the divine word entrusted to them. Therefore Joseph, who is called “increase,” is rightly placed after Zabulon, because they do not hesitate to distribute the money entrusted to them to their enemies, so that they may bring back an increase of profit from it.

And because all these are to be placed at the right hand of the eternal King—being found among virgins, the continent, and those well-married in these twelve stages of spiritual progress—Benjamin is rightly placed after them all. He is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” They are, as it were, generated from his right hand, since they are protected in this age by his power.

Nor should it be passed over why Dan was expelled from this catalogue, although he is found in the other books, like the other brothers. Manasses, who was not a son of Jacob but was born of a foreign mother—that is, of Aseneth, daughter of Putiphar, priest of Heliopolis—takes his place.

To this it must be said that the Antichrist will be born from Dan, according to Jacob’s saying: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way,” and so forth, “until his rider falls backward” (Gen. XLIX). Dan is therefore removed from this passage to show that the Antichrist is to be expelled from the number of the saints.

Alternatively: Dan is interpreted as “judgment passing over the Hebrews,” because, after the truth appeared, all their sacrifices and victims passed away, and the truth arose through Manasses—that is, through the Gentile people, who consigned idols to forgetfulness.

When the priesthood that had gone before as a figure was completed, the true priesthood immediately arose in the Church according to the order of Melchizedek. Concerning this the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, the days are coming, and I will complete a covenant over the house of Judah” (Jer. XXXVIII). And the Apostle says: “What is becoming obsolete and growing old is near to disappearance.”

For when the Lord had already come, the priesthood of the Jews had been turned into old age and was declining toward senility; therefore it soon perished when the true priest, Christ, arrived. Thus, in the sixth place, Manasses is rightly established in place of Dan, who was expelled from it, because, in the sixth age of the world, when the Lord Jesus Christ came, the Jewish people lost the priesthood and every good thing, and in its place Manasses—that is, the Gentile people—was received and adopted as a son.

And just as Dan was expelled from this spiritual catalogue, so all the rejected will be expelled from the fellowship of the saints on the day of judgment.

“After this I saw a great crowd, which no one could number.” That is, after I heard the number of the faithful who are included in the twelve tribes of Israel, I saw a crowd that no one could number. The number of the elect is finite with God, but infinite among human beings. Therefore the statement, “which no one could number,” must be referred to human beings.

“From every nation and tribe and people and language.” When he says “from every nation” and then adds “and tribe,” he shows that, under the name of all nations, the faithful of all tribes are included, and conversely, under the name of tribes, the faithful of all nations are included.

The holy Church is divided into three orders: the prelates, the married, and the continent. The number mentioned earlier therefore should not be understood as finite but as infinite.

“Standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb.” By the throne, as has often been said, the Church is understood, for it is the seat of God, according to the saying: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. V).

The Church stands before the throne—that is, before itself—because it watches over itself and provides for itself, lest it do anything unbecoming. It stands when it strengthens its mind in the solidity of love and faith. Hence the Psalmist says: “He established my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX).

It also stands in the sight of the Lamb, because, confident in its conscience, it wishes all its works to be seen by God, by whom it will be rewarded. Hence one of those standing there said: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (IV Kings III).

“Clothed in white robes.” By the white robes understand the sincerity and purity of baptism, the cleansing of hidden and open martyrdom, and the washing of the fountain of tears.

Before the Mediator’s coming, the hearts of the human race were spattered with the stains of sins; afterward they were whitened in the three ways mentioned above. Many preserve these robes clean after the washing of baptism because they commit no mortal crime. Others are defiled by various wicked acts, but, so that they may return to their former beauty, they whiten themselves through hidden or open martyrdom, with groans and tears. Thus all the faithful possess the robes described above.

“And palms were in their hands.” Palms signify the triumph of victory; hands signify the power of action. The elect therefore have palms in their hands when, in whatever way, they triumph over the ancient enemy and the pleasures of this age.

Or understand “hands” as power. That power is signified by hands is shown in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “No one can snatch my sheep from my hand” (John X)—that is, from my power. For we have received power to become children of God, as blessed John says: “To all who believed in him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.”

We have palms in our hands—that is, victories—when through good works we triumph over the devil and the incitements of the flesh. The sum of this victory rests, of course, in the head of the members.

“And they cried out with a loud voice, saying.” Let us understand the loud voice not as a noise of the voice but as the highest desire of the saints. Hence: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. X). When Moses said nothing outwardly but only prayed inwardly with a groan, the Lord said to him: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. XIV).

“Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” Whatever salvation is granted to human beings, whether in body or in soul, must be attributed to him. Hence the Psalmist says: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. III).

“Salvation to our God”—that is, to God the Father—“and to the Lamb”—that is, to the Son of God, who sits upon the throne and is called the Lamb because of his innocence and his sacrificial offering.

Just as here he introduces the Father and the Son sitting, while the Holy Spirit is understood, so earlier, where he mentioned only the Son, the Father and the Holy Spirit are likewise understood. We read something similar in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

For this is the practice of divine Scripture, as was said above: wherever it sets down the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit is understood with them. He sits upon the throne—that is, upon the Church, which is the seat of God—and by dwelling in the hearts of the faithful he reigns there.

“And all the angels stood around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures.” What the thrones are, the elders are; and what the elders are, the four living creatures are also. Here there is a genus within a genus, as we read above concerning the ark and the eight souls.

The Church is expressed in different ways because of its various offices. Since the Lord, reigning in the Church, examines all things individually, he is rightly represented by one throne. Since the Church itself, made judgment over others in its head, judges, it is rightly represented by the elders. Since, through faith, it already clings in some members to green pastures, while in others it enjoys them through hope, it is fittingly represented by the living creatures. Since it announces what is to come by preaching, it is openly represented by angels. Since it is gathered from different nations, it is rightly represented by the crowd.

Therefore the author of this revelation, wishing to show that this innumerable crowd consists of the angels themselves, mentions only their fall. For it is not fitting that human beings should stand stiff-necked while angels worship.

Here, then, we understand the angels to be the elect themselves, who are represented by the twenty-four elders. They are rightly called angels because they announce eternal life. The elect, as we have said, are angels; sometimes they are introduced standing, sometimes sitting. Standing, as here; sitting, as there: “There they sat upon thrones for judgment” (Ps. CXXI). And: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

They are around the throne because they surround the Church on every side with teaching, prayer, and example.

“And they fell upon their faces before the throne.” This fall is a sign of humility, because the elect attribute whatever good they have not to their own merits but to the grace of God, from whom all good things are received, according to the saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I).

And note that the elect fall upon their faces, whereas the rejected fall backward. The elect look ahead to what awaits them in the future; the rejected, however, neglect to foresee what will follow them in the future.

“And they worshiped God, saying: Amen, blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving, honor and power and strength to our God forever and ever. Amen.”

Although all these things pertain to the holy Trinity, who is one and true God, they are nevertheless referred especially to the person of the incarnate Word. By this authority the mouths of the unbelieving Jews are closed.

They say: “Your Christ was merely a man.” But we say in opposition that he was neither a liar: he was God and man, one truth. This is what “Amen” expresses, for *amen* means “true” or “faithfully.”

They also say: “A curse is fitting for one who was crucified, because ‘cursed is the man who hangs upon a tree’” (Deut. XXI). We, on the contrary, say that blessing belongs to no one more fittingly than to him who took away from us the curse of the law and caused the blessing of Abraham to reach the Gentiles.

They also say: “Glory does not befit a dead man, but only the living God.” We, on the contrary, say that glory should be ascribed to no one more than to him, because, remaining in his divinity, he is the author of eternal light; having died for a time in his humanity, he rose on the third day through the glory of the Father, shares in that glory, and lives and sits at the right hand of God the Father.

They likewise say: “Your Christ is not that wisdom which reaches mightily from end to end, since he was born a little child from our sister, and as a human being advanced in wisdom with the passage of time.”

We, on the contrary, say: “That wisdom did not suffer any diminution in the assumed humanity, since, insofar as he was human, he advanced in wisdom. Rather, this humanity, taken up by that wisdom, remained one wisdom—the wisdom by which the world was made, and by which the human being created from the earth was restored and raised from earth to heaven.”

They say: “No thanksgiving is owed to him for the salvation of souls, because he could not save his own.” We, on the contrary, say: “Thanksgiving is owed to no one more fittingly than to him who, in order to bring salvation to our souls, wished by his own power to lay down his soul. If he had not wished to do so, he would never have laid it down.”

They also say: “No reason permits the honor of divinity to be ascribed to one who was mocked with insults and deemed worthy of contempt.” We, on the contrary, say: “For this reason he is more worthy of honor from us, because he endured unworthy things for our sake.”

They likewise say: “Christ was not eternal power and strength, because he could become weary from a journey.” We, on the contrary, answer: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. I). For his weakness overthrew the strength and power of the whole world.

“And one of the elders answered and said to me: These who are clothed in white robes—who are they, and from where have they come? And I said to him: My lord, you know.”

Why does he say “answering” when no question has preceded? He speaks according to the customary manner of Scripture, which often, when no one has asked a question, presents a statement in the voice of one answering. Hence in the Gospel we read that Jesus, answering, said: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI). Elsewhere we read that the angel, answering, said to the women: “Do not be afraid” (Matt. XXVIII), although no question from the women had preceded.

In this revelation, however, the response of one elder differs from those examples because this is interrogative, whereas the others are declarative. What, then, do we understand by one elder, except the order of the prophets, the unity of all preachers?

The twenty-four elders, because of the number of the two Testaments, which is expressed by doubling the number twelve in the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, are frequently mentioned here. In one elder, however, the unity of those same Testaments is represented. Or certainly the elder himself, the elder of the elders—the Lord, namely, of the preachers—is signified.

The elder asks so that John may inquire; by inquiring, hear; by hearing, understand; and by understanding, kindle himself to imitate what he asks about. Finally, those clothed in white robes are shown to him, so that he may desire such a habit and such a garment.

Immediately, however, he asks who they are or from where they have come, so that, if he wishes to enter their number, he may, upon hearing who they are and from where they have come, strive to be like those whom he sees and hasten to come from the place from which he knows that the others have come.

What the white robes are has been said a little earlier. Let it therefore be said: “These who are clothed in white robes—who are they, and from where have they come?” It is as though the holy preachers, or the Lord of the preachers, were saying to pious hearers:

“Are all who were chosen before the foundation of the world lovers of the world? Are they followers of their own pleasures? Have they walked along the road of pleasure?”

When John, speaking on behalf of good hearers, answered one of the elders, “My lord, you know,” that elder immediately continued on behalf of the Lord or his preachers:

“These are those who have come from the great tribulation, and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

His voice, of course, cries and preaches such things throughout this entire age through the mouths of teachers. Thus, by saying “they have come,” he encompasses the sum of the three times—past, present, and future—in place of “they have come, they are coming, and they will come.”

“From the great tribulation”—that is, from the adversities of this age, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations” (Acts XIV); and the Psalmist: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII).

The saints endure great tribulations: the sword has cut the throats of some; the gallows of the cross has fastened others; water has swallowed others who were subjected to it; devouring flame has consumed others.

Nor do only those who endure bodily tortures of this kind belong to this glory. So too do those who, in a time of peace, desire to live piously in Christ and endure for Christ the reproaches and mockery of others; those who fast, devote themselves to vigils, multiply their prayers, and kill their own wills with the sword of the commandment.

Thus they whiten their robes—that is, their bodies—in the blood of the Lamb when they imitate the example of Christ, their head: either by suffering for him, by patiently enduring the insults inflicted by others, or by putting themselves to death with respect to vices and desires.

“Therefore they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple. And he who sits upon the throne will dwell over them.”

It is as though it were said: “For this reason they belong to the number of the elect; for this reason they are the throne of God; for this reason they are the temple of God; for this reason they offer him holy service in his temple: because they are clothed in such garments and appear washed in the blood of the Lamb.”

They are presided over by the Creator as a throne; they are inhabited by him as a temple; and they are shown serving God before the throne in the temple, because they themselves are simultaneously the temple and throne of God.

For what he said, “He sits upon the throne,” he repeated by saying, “He dwells over them,” thereby showing that they are both throne and temple.

They serve day and night—that is, they preserve the uprightness of faith and action in prosperity and adversity. Day signifies prosperity, while night signifies the adversity of this age. Yet the saints serve God in both, because neither prosperity nor adversity can incline them away from the blessed discipline and free service of their Creator. And this takes place in the Church—that is, in themselves.

“They will hunger no more, nor thirst any more; neither will the sun fall upon them, nor any heat, because the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will rule them and will lead them to the fountains of the waters of life.”

The reason is given why they will not hunger or thirst, and why they will not suffer the sun—that is, heat—when it says: “Because the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will rule them,” and so forth.

“They will hunger no more, nor thirst,” he says. The saints will no longer suffer hunger because they will be filled by the presence of him who is the living bread descended from heaven. Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI).

They will not endure thirst either, because he himself is the drink of life. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord rules me,” and so forth, through: “He led me beside the waters of refreshment” (Ps. XXII).

“Neither will the sun fall upon them, nor any heat”—that is, no adversity, distress of tribulation, or trouble of persecution and temptation will weigh upon them, because they will be sheltered by his shadow. To him the Psalmist says: “Shelter my head in the day of battle” (Ps. CXXXIX).

The names “sun” and “heat” often signify the tribulation of persecution. Hence, concerning the seeds sown in the Gospel, the Lord himself says that what fell upon the rock withered when the sun rose and was scorched by the heat.

“But the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will rule them”—that is, Christ, standing in the midst of his Church, will govern them. “And he will lead them to the fountains of the waters of life”—that is, to the contemplation of the holy Trinity.

Hence the Psalmist says: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). This is as though he were saying: “In your fountain we shall see the fountain.”

The Holy Spirit too is called a fountain, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink, and living waters will flow from his belly.” Why is a fountain of waters introduced, rather than simply a fountain, unless because the simplicity of gifts is expressed by this statement?

There is one fountain because of the unity of nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It is a fountain of waters because of the abundance, as we have said, of graces.

He will therefore lead them to the fountains of the waters of life—that is, to behold the majesty of the holy Trinity. When hunger and thirst have been driven away, they will neither suffer the sun nor the heat of vices and will not be burned by the heat of disturbances.

“And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” Almighty God, in a marvelous affection of compassion, sometimes shows himself as a father and sometimes as a mother, because he wipes away the tears of his weeping children.

As a father, he recalls his children who have turned away, saying: “Return, returning children, and I will heal your apostasies” (Jer. III). Transcending even the compassionate entrails of a mother, he says: “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have pity on the child of her womb? Even if she should forget, I will not forget you” (Isa. XLIX).

Behold, he loves as a father; behold, he has compassion even beyond a mother; and he wipes the tears from the eyes of the elect.

It must be noted, however, that God promises to wipe away every tear. For the tears of the elect are various. One weeps because he has done evil, or because he has not done good. Another because he endures the harsh blows of correction. Another because he is assailed by vices. Another because he remains a long time in exile from the kingdom.

In this way the weeping of the saints is varied in this life. It will then be wiped away completely, when, at the appointed time of joy, eternal happiness follows, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. III). And elsewhere: “Again I will see you, and your heart shall rejoice” (John XVI).

Then he will indeed wipe away every tear, because nothing adverse will be able to happen to them by which they might be saddened even slightly.

## CHAPTER VIII
And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour. Heaven—as we have often said—is called the Church of the righteous. When it withdraws from the multitude of bodily affairs and seeks the seclusion of a certain inner secret through contemplation, restraining the tumult of thoughts and entering into the secret of inward quiet, it prepares, as it were, a kind of silence for God in the mind. But because in this life contemplation is by no means carried out perfectly, and the tumult of thoughts intrudes upon the resisting mind, it is rightly said that silence occurred for about half an hour. If it had been perfect in this life, it would not have been said to occur for “about half an hour,” which signifies imperfection, but rather for a whole hour, which demonstrates perfection. Thus silence occurs in heaven for about half an hour when, in this mortal life, the mind of the elect both perceives something of the rest above and yet is unable to remain long in what it has perceived.

And I saw seven angels standing in the presence of God, and seven trumpets were given to them. The order is reversed in this passage, because first an angel comes before the altar, holding a golden censer in his hand, and only then do the seven angels receive seven trumpets. By the seven angels are understood the preachers of the universal Church. They are rightly called angels because they announce eternal life to us, of whom it is written: “The angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isa. XXXIII). They are also rightly expressed by the number seven, because they are filled with the sevenfold Spirit. They rightly end in the number seven because they are placed over the whole body of believers; for the number seven signifies both universality and perfection. Hence: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII).

They are also said to stand in the presence of God because, having trampled upon all earthly pleasures, they cleave to the contemplation of God and consider his will—he who is nowhere absent—and accomplish in deed what they know to please him. Hence Paul says: “We speak as from God, in the presence of God, in Christ” (II Cor. XII). And Elijah: “The Lord lives, in whose presence I stand” (III Kings XVII).

By the seven trumpets, too, is understood the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments, because of the sevenfold Spirit through whom all Scripture was dictated and disclosed to those who understand it. Scripture is compared to a trumpet because it announces great things. Hence it is said to the preachers themselves: “Cry aloud; lift up your voice like a trumpet.” They were given to the angels by the angel—that is, by Christ, who gave all teachers an understanding of the divine books in both Testaments. Thus it follows:

And another angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer. This other angel who stood before the altar is understood as the man Christ God, of whom the prophet says: “His name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel” (Isa. IX). He is the messenger of the Father’s will, who came and stood before the altar with a golden censer, to show that he is the true high priest of the good things to come. It is the ministry of a priest to stand beside the altar and carefully burn incense prepared with aromatics. He is the angel of angels and the high priest of high priests.

Moreover, before the altar—that is, before the whole Church, which is kindled by the fire of divine love and offers the true sacrifice, namely, a contrite heart, to the Lord, sacrificing itself so as to become a living and rational offering—before this altar stands the angel, that is, the true high priest, through whom we send all our gifts to God the Father. Hence priests make mention of him in each of their prayers, so that they may be heard through him, saying: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Therefore one must observe how John described these things when he said: “He came and stood.” Coming pertains to his humanity, through which he had to pass from one place to another; standing pertains to his divinity, through which he is present everywhere, according to the saying: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXXIII). He therefore came to us through his humanity, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” while through his divinity—according to which all things were made—he exists everywhere.

Holding a golden censer. What should we understand by the golden censer in which fire is placed, if not the Lord’s body? He received the censer when he joined our mortality to his divinity. The censer is rightly called golden because in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The Word and the man are one wisdom, concerning which it is written: “Receive wisdom as gold.”

We may also understand by the golden censer, in which incense is burned, the Church, which, kindled by the fire of divine love, directs pure prayers to God, saying with the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL). She herself is also filled with wisdom, which she received from her own head.

And many incense offerings were given to him. What the incense offerings signify has already been stated, and here it is clearly revealed when it continues: “That he might offer them with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne.” The incense offerings are given to that angel so that he may offer them upon the altar—that is, upon himself—to God the Father, through whom the saints direct their prayers and all their works to the Father, according to what is written: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the expiation for our sins” (I John II).

And the smoke of the incense rose from the prayers of the saints out of the angel’s hand. Just as smoke is produced from burned aromatics, so the power of compunction is generated from devoted prayer. But it rises from the angel’s hand before God because, through our Redeemer, the things entrusted by the faithful reach God the Father.

Since fire is placed in the censer so that smoke may be produced from it, it is clear—as has been said—that by the censer both the Lord himself and his whole body are understood. Into this body the fire of the Holy Spirit is sent, concerning which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). Kindled by this fire, the elect direct the smoke of compunction to God through Christ, and they are inflamed with love of God and of neighbor.

And the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar. The angel took the censer when the Lord joined human nature to himself within the Virgin’s womb, or when he first chose disciples in Judea. For he did not fill his body from another spirit, but from himself, from whom the Church was filled; while the others were filled according to measure, him the fullness of the Spirit filled.

And he cast it upon the earth. This can be understood in two ways. First, he sent the Holy Spirit upon the earth—that is, into the hearts of the apostles—when, rising from the dead at the time of his resurrection, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John X). Then he sent the same Holy Spirit upon the earth—that is, into the hearts of the Gentiles who believed in him through the preaching of the apostles. He first did this among the Jews, whom he himself gathered to his faith; then among the Gentiles, for whose salvation he sent the apostles, who, by believing in him, deserved to receive the Holy Spirit.

And there were thunderclaps, voices, flashes of lightning, and earthquakes. When the apostles preached, these thunderclaps occurred—that is, threats and terrors such as: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. VII). And: “Then the king will say to those who are on his left: Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

There were also voices of exhortation, such as: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). And: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII). There were flashes of lightning and terrors of miracles, by which the faithful and those predestined to life were enlightened. Others, however, were blinded, attributing these things to the devil rather than to God. The earthquakes signify persecutions against believers, through which they are tested.

And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound the trumpets—that is, all the preachers of the universal Church who possessed knowledge of the two Testaments prepared themselves to sound the trumpet, namely, to make the doctrine of the Gospel resound.

The elect prepare themselves to preach in two ways. First, before bringing the word of preaching into public, they consider how to adapt the word to each person according to the qualities of each: how to address servants, masters, superiors, subjects, the simpler, and the more perfect. Thus Paul exhorted kind masters to show mercy to their servants, knowing that the common Lord of all is in heaven. He also admonished servants to render what was due to their masters, serving not merely for the sake of being seen.

Or certainly they prepare themselves because they first do what they are going to preach. First they display it in themselves by their deeds, and afterward also by their words, so that the simple may be instructed by the example of their conduct, while the more perfect may be instructed by the word of exhortation. For the Lord did this as well, according to what Luke says: “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts I).

And the first angel sounded the trumpet. What the first angel is, so are those who follow, because what one is, all seven are—that is, the whole Church of the saints.

And there came hail and fire mixed with blood. By hail the anger of almighty God is signified, as it is written: “The anger of the Lord descends like hail.” By fire, however, is understood the hatred and envy of the reprobate against the saints. As soon as the apostles began to preach hail—that is, God’s vengeance—the reprobate were inflamed with zeal and hatred, which is signified by fire.

That blood follows the fire pertains to the condemnation of the reprobate, because those who persecuted the true preachers will perish like murderers shedding human blood. The Lord says: “Whoever hates his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. V). And John: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III).

It is not surprising that the elect find mercy from the very source from which the reprobate incur anger, as the Apostle says: “To some we are an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life” (II Cor. II). And Simeon says of the Lord himself: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke II).

And it was cast upon the earth, and a third of the earth was burned, and a third of the trees was burned, and all the green grass was burned. By the earth earthly people are signified, upon whom the anger of almighty God falls.

When it is said that a third of the earth was burned, these words seem to sound as though more of the elect remained in two parts than perished in the third. But this is not so, because it is written: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” In the two parts, therefore, all the good are included, divided according to the dual number: superiors and subjects, preachers and hearers. Of these it was said above: “Blessed is the one who reads and hears the words of this prophecy.”

In the third part are all the reprobate: heretics, pagans, Jews, and false Christians. Upon all these came hail—that is, the anger of God—and the fire of eternal condemnation, together with blood, namely, vengeance for murder and for the other sins signified by blood, according to the saying: “Deliver me from bloodguilt” (Ps. L).

Yet the earth here means the same as the trees, namely, the totality of the wicked. They are the earth because they seek earthly things; they are also trees, wavering in instability, concerning whom the Apostle says: “These are autumn trees, fruitless, uprooted, twice dead.”

The statement that all the green grass was burned is a repeated assertion, referring to the third part, as above—that is, to the part of the wicked who are grass, namely, seductive and pleasure-loving people who follow their lust. Concerning such people the prophet says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL). In contrast, those who are nourished by the bread of God recline upon the grass, because they restrain all carnal pleasures within themselves.

And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea. The great mountain is the devil, who raises himself to the height of pride. Hence, at the beginning of his creation, he also wished to become like the one of whom it is written: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the top of the mountains,” saying: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. II and XIV).

Or he is called a mountain for this reason: at the end of time he will enter the lost man and show himself to be like God, according to what the Apostle says: “He will oppose and exalt himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (II Thess. II).

He burns with fire—that is, he is tormented by wickedness and envy. For this reason he deceived the first man: he envied him the place that he himself had lost. He was cast into the sea—that is, into the world—and began to dwell in the hearts of the reprobate.

When, therefore, the angel sounded the trumpet, the great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea, because, when the Church preached through her teachers, the devil was driven out from those who had been predestined to eternal life and was compelled to return to his own. This does not mean that he had not previously been in them, but that, after being rejected by these people, he began to be condemned all the more in the reprobate.

And a third of the sea became blood. What happened in the sea appeared similar to what once happened in Egypt at the departure of the children of Israel. By the water turned into blood, carnal wisdom is understood. It is turned into blood when it persuades people to commit evil openly—not only those outside the Church, but also heretics and false Christians, who, desiring to follow their own wills, attempt to defend themselves through their wisdom and empty philosophy.

Hence it is written: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III). Thus the wisdom of the flesh is turned into the perversity of error. The third part of the creatures that died in the sea, according to the interpretation already given, signifies heretics, false Christians, pagans, and Jews. Although they live bodily, they are dead in soul, and in this world they have been turned into blood—that is, into the perpetration of evil deeds, which, as we have said, are signified by blood.

And a third of the ships perished. Ships are understood in both a good and a bad sense. In a good sense, as we read in the Gospel, where the Lord entered a ship and crossed the strait (Mark VI). In a bad sense, as here. The third part of the ships is understood as those heretics and others who are carried along without a helmsman and are therefore beaten and submerged by the waves of the sea of this age.

And the third angel sounded the trumpet, and a great burning star fell from heaven like a torch. What the first angel is, so are the second, the third, and the others: the preachers of the universal Church. But because they succeed one another, just as martyrs succeed apostles, and confessors and virgins succeed martyrs, they are distinguished in this way as the first, second, third, and the rest.

The one signified by the star is also signified by the mountain: namely, the ancient enemy. He was created among the other bright lights of heaven, but now retains only his former name—not because he shines, but because he transforms himself into an angel of light. In heaven the great star is called Lucifer, which shines more brightly than the others. Through Isaiah it is said to him: “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning!” (Isa. XIV). And because he also shone more brightly than the other stars, that is, the angelic spirits, he is rightly called not simply a star but, with the addition, a great star.

He fell from heaven—that is, from the fellowship of the angels—according to the saying: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke X). Because, after he fell, he envied the human race, he deserved to be called a burning torch, for he burns with envy and has consumed the whole world. Hence: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Rom. V).

And it fell upon a third of the rivers and upon the springs of waters. What the rivers are, the springs also are. Rivers arise from springs and then run toward the sea. The many waters are many peoples. Therefore, here the rivers and springs themselves signify heretics and the others included in the third part, into which the devil fell when he envied the human race and sowed the doctrine of error through them. The meaning is as if he had said: “Upon a third part of human beings.” Hence it continues:

And the name of the star was Wormwood. By wormwood, which is an extremely bitter herb, is understood the perverse doctrine of the heretics. Through their falsehood they have turned the sweetness of faith into the bitterness of perfidy, error, and conduct, because all their conduct and doctrine have been turned into bitterness.

The ancient enemy, cast out from the elect, attacks the reprobate through falsehood and infects them with poison. By falsehood we must understand not only the harm of perverse belief but also that of evil conduct. What the holy Church teaches in the sacred writings as agreeing with the true faith, heretics, Jews, and philosophers turn into a perverse dogma; and what the former use for the growth of virtues, Catholics living perversely use as an incentive to vice.

Although the former understand many things concerning the Lord, and the latter perform certain beneficial actions, everything is nevertheless exceedingly bitter: the words of the former sound bitter, and the deeds of the latter cry out bitterly.

And many people died from the waters that had been made bitter. That is, many perished from the faithless and bitter doctrine of the heretics. They had many disciples, who followed their examples and doctrine; all these died, not so much by bodily death as by the death of the soul.

And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and a third of the sun, a third of the moon, and a third of the stars were struck, so that a third of them was darkened, and a third of the day did not shine, and likewise a third of the night. By the sun, moon, and stars in this passage we must understand the Church. A third of her is darkened, while two parts remain in brightness: the good superiors and subjects, the teachers and the hearers.

The Church herself is called by the name of the sun, as it is said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Song of Songs III). The same Church is also called by the name of the stars, according to what the Apostle says: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. II).

As long as the heretics were in the Church, they were thought to be, as it were, light. But as soon as their error was exposed and their faith was examined and recognized by Catholics, their blindness became known, and they were darkened because they were cast out of the Church.

For example, when a blind man is placed in a ray of sunlight, because he has diseased eyes, his blindness is immediately revealed. The little light he seemed to possess is lost. So too, as soon as they were placed before those examining them, their error became known. Those who had previously seemed to shine through faith began to be darkened and were expelled from the Church because of their unbelief.

When it says, “A third of the sun was struck,” and so forth, the striking of the sun must be referred to the day, while that of the moon and stars must be referred to the night. In the sun is signified the open error of the heretics; in the moon and stars, the hidden error, because some deceive those whom they can through open persuasion, others through secret persuasion in concealed places.

It should be noted that it does not say, “A third of them was struck and darkened,” but, “It was struck so that it might be darkened.” It was struck for this purpose, namely, that afterward it might be darkened. They were first wounded secretly in the mind, and afterward darkened when they were openly expelled from the Church and anathematized.

But lest their destruction be attributed to God, the statement about the aforementioned lights—“A third of them was struck so that it might be darkened”—should be understood in the same way as it is said that Pharaoh’s heart was hardened by God, namely, that it was not mercifully softened by him. The sun is not at fault because its rays bring blindness to diseased eyes; rather, this must be attributed to the defects of the eyes, which grow dark because of the light.

Almighty God, however, often uses our evils well and is accustomed to bring many things about through them. He stirred up teachers against the error of schismatics to defend the truth of the faithful. For undoubtedly they would not have devoted themselves with such diligence to expounding the Scriptures if the falsehood of error, resisting the truth, had not grown. Hence it is written: “There must be heresies” (I Cor. XI).

And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice: “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell upon the earth,” because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet. What is signified by the angels is also signified by the eagle—that is, the universal Church, or more specifically the teachers—who fly through the midst of heaven, namely, who run through the midst of the Church. The Church is called heaven because it is the dwelling place of God.

When John says, “I saw and heard the voice of one eagle,” he undoubtedly shows that in spiritual vision seeing is hearing, and hearing is seeing. The three woes signify the eternal condemnation contained in the voices of the three angels who follow.

That he says he saw and heard the voice of one flying eagle—not the voices of the four preceding angels, but of the three following angels who were about to sound their trumpets—and of an eagle mourning, clearly indicates that the Church of the elect does not cease both to mourn and to preach the blows of various future calamities, as though the Church herself were saying: “Throughout the whole period of the present life I see myself mourning and at the same time preaching the destruction of the reprobate.”

The one eagle flying through the midst of heaven rightly signifies the Church, which stands in the unity of faith and, having trampled upon the desires of earthly pleasures, is lifted toward heavenly things by inward contemplation. Her members say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

She rightly flies through the midst of heaven because, through the elect, she possesses the whole world on every side. Her preaching is called not simply a voice but, with the addition, a loud voice, because it resounded throughout the whole world, as was said concerning her first preachers: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Rom. X). Or certainly “loud voice” refers to the boldness of great freedom.

It should also be noted that, lamenting, it announces that woe will come not upon those who inhabit heaven but upon those who inhabit the earth—that is, upon those devoted to earthly desires and pleasures.

## Chapter IX

And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth. As was said above, this star signifies the devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light. Appearing to certain people, he says that he is Christ, as he did to blessed Martin.

He falls from this heaven—that is, from the number of the angels—or from heaven, that is, from the Church, every day when some are converted from paganism to the faith, or when those born of Christian parents are regenerated in the baptismal font and renounce the devil, all his works, and all his pomps. He falls upon the earth, that is, upon those who are earthly. For he has no power in heaven, that is, among the saints.

And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it. What is signified by the abyss if not the perverse hearts of the reprobate, darkened by sins? Concerning this abyss it is said in Genesis: “Darkness was over the face of the abyss” (Gen. I).

By the pit, however, heretics are understood, because through their perverse and profound doctrine they plunge people into the depths of the earth. The key of the pit of the abyss signifies the power of the devil, who rules over heretics, pagans, and the other unbelievers.

We read that keys were given to Peter—that is, the power of binding and loosing. Thus, in this passage, the key given to the devil signifies the power that he exercises over the reprobate. It is said to have been given to him because it was not taken away, just as Pharaoh’s heart was hardened—that is, not softened.

And he opened the pit of the abyss. He himself inspires the heretics to bring forth the darkness of their doctrine in order to deceive those whom they can. He does this because it occurs at his instigation.

Or by the key we may understand carnal power, namely, the kings and rulers of this age whom the heretics joined to themselves. They would not dare to say such great and such things unless they were supported by temporal power.

And smoke rose from the pit. That is, the doctrine of the wicked heretics was revealed. It is rightly compared to smoke because it lacks the light of truth. What provides light to the saints in sacred Scripture pours blindness upon the heretics, who also do not cease to obscure the light of faith for others.

Like the smoke of a great furnace. The great furnace is the final persecution that will occur in the time of Antichrist. From it smoke will emerge—that is, an opposing doctrine that will turn the minds of the perishing into darkness. The smoke of the pit is compared to it because just as error exists now and will spread even more widely, so then it will be sown by the impious. Hence it says: “There will be tribulation such as has not been and will not be.”

Here a question arises: Why is the smoke of the pit said to be like the smoke of a great furnace? If the tribulation will then be such as has never been, how is it now like the doctrine of the Antichrist? One must understand that the persecution and false doctrine of the Antichrist and of the others will be similar in one respect and dissimilar in another.

They will be similar in the persecution of the saints and in the error of falsehood; but they will be dissimilar in this respect: then they will perform miracles, although they will be false teachers, whereas these cannot do so. That persecution will therefore be more terrible because it will deceive through both means.

And the sun and the air were darkened. That is, the Church, because what is signified by the sun is also signified by the air. This is to be understood as occurring in a third part of it, namely, in all the reprobate, as above.

From the smoke of the pit—that is, from the doctrine of the heretics—locusts went forth upon the earth. These are the disciples of error who arose to deceive the earthly hearts of human beings.

Locusts neither have straight steps, as certain animals do, nor flight like birds. Thus the disciples of the heretics, or the heretics themselves, possess neither a straight faith, by which they might fly and seek heavenly things with the saints—concerning whom Isaiah says: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX)—nor straight steps of conduct, by which they might say with the Psalmist: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Ps. XXXIX).

Locusts leap and gnaw every green thing, because those people are lifted up through boastfulness and kill whatever souls they can find that possess the greenness of faith.

And power was given to them, as scorpions have power over the earth. The power of the scorpion to harm lies in its tail. With it the scorpion strikes and spreads its poison. The scorpion is also gentle in the face but strikes secretly with its tail.

Such are the heretics, who mix false things with true so that they may more easily deceive their hearers. Thus, through the poison of evil doctrine, they deceive the simple, of whom the Psalmist says: “Their throat is an open grave” (Rom. III). Sacred Scripture also testifies that the prophet who teaches falsehood is himself the tail.

And it was commanded them not to harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God upon their foreheads. It was said above that all the green grass was burned, which is understood as referring to its third part.

Therefore, here grass is taken in a good sense. It signifies infants, who cannot receive solid food but, like animals, delight in the surface of the letter. To them the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ; I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III).

By every green thing are understood those who are making progress, who are now able to understand and grasp what John says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I).

Trees, moreover, signify all the perfect, strong, and steadfast in faith, because such people can endure the winds of temptations and persevere with firm stability. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. XCI).

Here too, however, a part must be understood from the whole, as above. While two parts remain in the Church, the locusts are prohibited from harming them, and the third perishes.

Hence it immediately continues: “Except those people who do not have the seal of God upon their foreheads,” implicitly meaning those who are unworthy. For not only are those outside the Church excluded—pagans and Jews—but also false Christians, who bear the seal on their bodies, have been baptized, and remain in the Church, yet stain by their deeds the faith they appear to possess and are therefore harmed.

Such is the meaning of the saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI). Many receive the same sacraments, yet Christ does not dwell in them, because they eat and drink not for salvation but for their own judgment; therefore they are guilty of the body and blood of Christ.

Elsewhere the same meaning is expressed: “No one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” Yet many confess him only with words, while, having the appearance of piety, they deny its power; they profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds.

And it was given to them that they should not kill them. This refers back to the preceding things: the grass, every green thing, and the trees, which we understood in a good sense and from whose death and harm the locusts were forbidden.

But that they should torment them for five months. By five months is understood the whole present age, from the Lord’s ascension to the end of the world, during which heretics and the other unbelievers and impious people rage against the Church.

Since the number five pertains to the five bodily senses, the whole present age is rightly understood by five months, because the impious can harm the saints only for as long as they possess the five bodily senses.

And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person. Just as a scorpion spreads its poison from behind, so those reprobates harm people through things that quickly pass away and are left in the present, and are therefore called “the things behind.” They do this through the power of this age, either crushing people by threats or seducing them with advantages.

And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. These days in which the elect will seek death are understood as extending from the Lord’s ascension to the end of the world. More specifically, this will occur in the time of Antichrist.

Here we understand “people” to mean priests and the superiors of churches. When they see such a great dogma of depravity arise at that time—as has already occurred in part in the times of the heretics—they will seek death, desiring to remain in the contemplation of God, to be dead to the world and to all the activities of the age, and to live for God.

But when they seek this, death will flee from them, because the unbreakable bond of governance will bind them. They will not be able to abandon the flock entrusted to them at the mouths of wolves, lest the losses of the flock return upon them and it be counted as sin against them if, for the sake of their own quiet, they allow the flock to wander or perish.

And they will desire to die, and death will flee from them. As has been said, holy men desire, amid the scandals of this age, to cleave to God through contemplation in a secluded way of life. Yet, for the sake of the gain of others, they labor in the struggle through various occupations.

Thus they live unwillingly, but they bear their postponed death with equanimity for the salvation of others, attending to the Apostle’s saying: “Let no one seek his own interests, but those of others” (I Cor. XIII).

And the likenesses of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. All heretics are compared to horses because of their swift movement everywhere: they will suddenly fill the whole world. They are compared to locusts because of their emptiness.

They go forth to battle because they fight against the sound faith of the elect. And just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these will resist the truth. Although they cannot withstand the preachers rationally, they nevertheless always resist the truth irrationally.

And upon their heads were what looked like crowns resembling gold. It was said above concerning the elders that they had golden crowns upon their heads, signifying the triumph of their victory.

These, however, do not have crowns, but certain shapes resembling crowns; nor are they golden, but like gold—as though they were some fabrication of falsehood. They pretend to be victorious and worthy of reward, but they possess neither crowns nor gold, because, as the Apostle says, while they have the appearance of piety, they deny its power.

And their faces—understand, the faces of the locusts—were like human faces. Because a human being is a rational animal, their rationality is understood by the human faces. Although they are deceivers, they nevertheless say many true things; they are dialecticians and know the other liberal arts.

And they had hair like women’s hair. A woman’s hair is recognized by its flowing length. Hence the Apostle says: “If a woman lets her hair grow long, it is a glory to her” (I Cor. XI). By the hair of women, therefore, we should understand their effeminate and wanton minds, because they are men who please themselves and pursue their own pleasures. Or, by the faces of men and the hair of women, both sexes are understood, because they deceived not only men but also women. Since the heretics leap like locusts, rush about like horses, and yet resist the truth in everything, their teaching is rightly described as stench. Thus women themselves also defended them, such as Constantine’s sister, who recalled Arius from exile; and Justina, who defended the same Arian doctrine against Ambrose; and many others. The locusts therefore have human faces and women’s hair, so that in heretical perfidy both sexes may, so to speak, applaud, support, and defend themselves all the more wickedly. The women’s hair may also signify those whom the heretics deceived—minds readily seduced and pliable through feminine softness.

And their teeth—understand, the locusts’ teeth—were like lions’ teeth. Lions’ teeth have a natural capacity for tearing and producing stench. Such were the heretics, who killed human souls and spread an evil reputation about themselves. And just as it is fitting for Christ’s good preachers that “we are the good odor of Christ” (II Cor. II), so, conversely, for these there will be stench instead of a sweet odor. [Col. 1054D]

And they had breastplates like iron breastplates. By the breastplates are shown the hardened and stubborn hearts of perverse people, because just as a man is protected by a breastplate so that he may not be wounded by the blows of weapons, so they protect themselves by their obstinacy, lest the arrow of truth reach their hearts; and thus they defend their perfidy as the faithful defend the truth. In this way, devoted to falsehood, they disdain to obey the truth. It should be noted how apt the comparison of heretics is in each individual feature: in the locusts they are marked as exalted and vain; in the scorpions’ tails, as venomous; in the horses, as wanton and vain; in the human face, as cunning through simulation; in the women’s hair, as disorderly in character; in the lions’ teeth, as foul; and in the iron breastplates, as perfidious in heart. [Col. 1055A]

And the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots of many horses running into battle. What was signified above by the tails is here signified by the locusts’ wings—that is, the power of the heretics, or the doctrine that they choose for themselves. Their sound is also rightly said to be like that of chariots of horses running into battle. For when chariots come out from the stables, they customarily proceed divided and separated from one another until, arriving at the place of combat, they join together and fight with a common purpose. So too heretics divide among themselves and put forward errors opposed to one another. For example, Photinus denies that Christ existed before Mary, but says that he took his beginning from her and possessed a true body. Arius, on the contrary, says that he was born before the ages and is a creature. [Col. 1055B] Likewise, the others devise various errors of falsehood that are greatly opposed to one another. Yet although they disagree among themselves, they fight with one accord against the unity of the Church.

And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings in their tails, and their power was to harm human beings for five months. By the tails, as was said above, temporal power is understood, through which they do harm by joining the rulers of this age to their error. But what had been omitted above concerning the scorpions’ tails is added here when it says: “And there were stings in their tails.” What the sting in the locusts’ tails is, Paul explains when he says: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin” (I Cor. XV). It is therefore clear that all their power is error and sin. The statement that follows—“their power was to harm human beings for five months”—is a repeated sentence, by which the present life is expressed again. Above, the locusts are said to have received power to torture human beings for five months without killing them. Here, however, they are said to have the ability to harm human beings for the same number of months. This is to be understood there of the good, but here of the wicked: they torture the former but do not kill them; the latter they do not torture but kill by harming them. [Col. 1055D]

And they had over them as king the angel of the abyss. That is, the devil, who is the prince of all the reprobate. He is king over all the sons of pride—not because he created or governs human beings, but because he exercises dominion over those whom he makes his servants through sin. His name in Hebrew is *labbadon*, in Greek *apollyon*, and in Latin his name is “Destroyer.” In certain manuscripts it is found written *abadon*, with an initial *a*; but this is written falsely and is due to a scribal error. The initial letter should be *l*, and it should be pronounced *labbadon*, as blessed Jerome says in his Hebrew interpretations.

What *labbadon* means in Hebrew is expressed by the Greek *apollyon* when it is added that in Latin his name is “Destroyer.” For in these names the devil is understood, because he destroys human beings—that is, he sends them outside their heavenly homeland. They will hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). The unjust, to whom this will be said, will indeed be destroyed—that is, they will be expelled from all fellowship with the saints. [Col. 1056A]

For we read in the Gospel that what had been written above the Lord’s cross was written in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin, because those three languages were then in use: “This is Jesus, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII). So here too the name of the devil, who at the end of time will enter the lost human being and falsely claim to be Christ, is expressed in three languages. He is rightly called “Destroyer,” because just as the name “Gatherer” belongs to Christ, so the name “Destroyer” belongs to the devil. Hence: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. XII).

“One woe has passed, and behold, two more woes are still coming after these.” We read above that the eagle flying through mid-heaven foretold three future woes. One of these is described in the preceding account as having passed, or in the tribulation that occurred in the time of the holy martyrs; but two are still said to remain to be narrated, or to be fulfilled at a later time under Antichrist. [Col. 1056C]

And the sixth angel sounded his trumpet, and I heard one voice from the horns of the golden altar that is before the sight of God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: “Release the four angels who are bound in the great river Euphrates.” The altar signifies the Church, from which the smoke of compunction is directed to God. The altar is rightly called golden, because the Church of the righteous is certainly illumined by eternal wisdom, of which Solomon says: “Receive wisdom as gold.” It is also rightly said to be before the sight of God, because it is always illumined by heavenly regard; hence it is said in the Psalms: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII). All the preachers are the horns of this altar. Thus in the Old Testament we often read that blood was placed upon the horns of the altar: by this were signified the holy martyrs who were to be drenched in their own blood.

We should understand the one horn of the altar specially mentioned here as the Lord Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings. He commanded the sixth angel—that is, the whole Church—to release the four angels, by whom the four principal kingdoms, their four powers, and the entire body of the devil are understood. The Church releases the four angels—that is, all the demons in their head—from whom she heard through Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI). [Col. 1057A]

The number four is often used for totality. Thus at the end of the age the elect are said to be gathered by the angels from the four winds of heaven. Or it is said to him, “Release them,” meaning: preach that they will be released at the time of Antichrist. For now they are bound, because they cannot harm as much as they wish, since the Lord came and took their power away from them. Here we should consider how fiercely they would rage if they were released, since even now, while bound, they rage so greatly.

The same applies to what is said in the Gospel about the fig tree, when the Lord says to the gardener: “Cut it down,” meaning: preach that it will be cut down. For the apostles did not cut down the Jews, but foretold that they would be cut down by the Romans. By the river Euphrates, in which the angels are bound, secular power is understood, because the devil dwells and reigns chiefly in the rulers of this age. Euphrates is a river of Babylon, which, divided into many streams, enters Babylon. The Medes and Persians divided this river into many channels and entered Babylon through its riverbed. This river is often understood negatively. Here, however, as we have said, it signifies secular power, in which the devil is foretold to be bound until the final persecution, since he is permitted to harm the impious as much as he wishes until the final persecution arrives. [Col. 1057B]

And the angels were released—the text says “were released” in place of “will be released”—that is, the demons and the entire body of the devil. They had been prepared for the hour and day and month and year, in order to kill a third of humankind. By “hour,” understand half a year; by “day,” “month,” and “year,” three years, during which Antichrist will rage against the good. That period can be understood by “hour, day, month, and year” because an hour gradually completes a day, days complete months, and months certainly complete a year. The demons are prepared to kill a third of humankind because they are always awaiting an opportunity to harm. Hence it was not without reason said earlier of the locusts that they were like horses prepared for battle. The third part is to be understood as above.

And the number of the cavalry was twenty thousand times ten thousand. And I heard their number. In this number the whole multitude of demons and human beings is understood. Therefore, in this passage we should understand the horsemen as demons, who preside over the wicked and dwell in their hearts. “Twenty thousand times” means nothing other than twenty thousand. The same applies to the saying: “I do not say to you, Peter, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII). This means nothing other than seventy-seven. When a number is expressed by a noun, as, for example, when one says “seven times seventy,” the sum is multiplied and becomes four hundred ninety. But when the words are used adverbially, nothing other than the number itself is meant. Thus we read in Genesis: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken for Lamech” (Gen. IV). [Col. 1057D]

“Twenty thousand times,” therefore, signifies all the reprobate; “ten thousand” signifies all the saints, who keep the ten words of the law. And because there are more reprobate than righteous, a doubled number of the reprobate is set against the single number of the righteous. Of the elect themselves it is said: “The chariots of God are ten thousand.” The number of the reprobate is also doubled because it consists of wicked spirits and reprobate human beings. Against the single and very small number of the righteous is set the innumerable multitude of faithless human beings and demons. [Col. 1058A]

And so I saw horses in the vision—understand, as I had said, and recorded it—and those seated upon them had breastplates of fire-colored, hyacinth-colored, and sulfur-colored material. By those seated upon the horses are understood demons, or teachers of error—namely, heretics and the powerful of this age, over whom the devil presides, just as Christ presides over the elect. Of these it is written: “You will mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.” In those demons, or teachers of error, all the reprobate are understood; and by the breastplates, punishments and eternal torments are signified, from which the wretched will not be freed by any prayer. For they will say in hell, groaning: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” But for that reason they will not find mercy; rather, they will hear: “I do not know you.” The demons will endure these unavoidable punishments, and so will all the reprobate. [Col. 1058B]

He used “hyacinth-colored” in place of “smoky,” for smoke comes forth from fire. The color itself also indicates this, since hyacinth holds the appearance of air: in hell there will be an inextinguishable fire. There will also be smoke that blinds the wretched, so that they can no longer see the true light. And “sulfur-colored,” that is, putrid. For there will be a twofold punishment there, of heat and cold. Hence Job says: “They pass from excessive heat to the waters of snow” (Job XXIV). There will also be an intolerable stench, by which they will be tormented, scorched by fire and sulfur and consumed by worms.

And the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads. For, as was said above, they kill souls and emit from themselves the stench of an evil reputation. By the heads of the horses, however, the authors of errors are understood. They are strong enough to crush the weak, and although they pretend to be a good odor, they are found to be filled with stench. As we recalled above, the mouth of a lion both tears bodies apart and emits a natural stench. [Col. 1058C]

And from their mouths came forth fire and smoke and sulfur. By these three plagues a third of humankind was killed—by the fire, smoke, and sulfur that came forth from their mouths. Fire, smoke, and sulfur proceeding from their mouths killed a third of humankind, because the preaching of the wicked prepares eternal punishments for their followers. This is rightly called the torment of the impious, by which the multitude of the wicked arrives at that punishment. It is a kind of figurative expression in which what is procured is shown through the thing that procures it.

Fire comes forth from their mouths because, on account of their doctrine, all these things will come upon those who receive it. When they have fallen into that punishment, they will experience how bitter a death it is: to be burned perpetually by fire and yet never utterly die; to suffer smoke continually and never see the light; to be perpetually filled with stench and never enjoy any sweetness. Their doctrines are therefore wholly dreadful, since by them one arrives at such things. [Col. 1058D]

For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails. Through their perverse preaching they deceive by persuasion, and, supported by temporal powers, they are exalted through the things that are behind. By the tail, as was said above, earthly power is expressed, which rejoices in temporal things. These must be set aside by all who strive toward the things that lie ahead. In the mouth, however, what is done through the mouth is understood. Their power, therefore, is in their mouths and in their tails, because those whom they cannot deceive through the perversity of error they deceive through the rulers of this age.

Hence it is added: “For their tails are like serpents, having heads, and with them they do harm.” We read in Genesis that the devil, assuming the form of a serpent, deceived the woman through the evil fraud of persuasion. Such too are these teachers of error, who by their perverse doctrine deceive those whom they can. And because those whom they cannot overthrow through the perversity of error they oppress through worldly power, their tails are rightly said to be like serpents. [Col. 1059B]

“Having heads”: by these the rulers of this age are signified. The heretics join themselves to these so that they may overthrow Catholics from the faith. Hence another translation has: “Their tails are like dragons.” For by dragons, which are almost more monstrous than all other beasts, the power of the world is plainly signified. Ezekiel (ch. XXIX), speaking in the person of the Lord to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, demonstrates this when he says: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh, great dragon.” And Jeremiah (ch. LI), speaking in the person of Jerusalem concerning Nebuchadnezzar: “He devoured me, he consumed me, he swallowed me like a dragon.” Supported, therefore, by the patronage of rulers, the teachers of error do more harm than they would if they persuaded by speech alone. [Col. 1059C]

And the rest of the human beings—that is, the pagans—who were not killed by these plagues.
