That is, they were not deceived by the heretics so as to die in soul, and they did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons and golden, stone, and wooden images, which can neither see nor hear nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts. Understand that they too will perish in fire, sulfur, and smoke. It is as though he said: These people too seem to belong to the number mentioned above.

The heretics deceived only Christians and Jews, not pagans. But because the pagans did not know God, although they could have done so through the natural law, they will likewise be condemned. Here we must consider by what punishment those deserve to be punished who, possessing knowledge, faith, and understanding of God, despise all these things, if even those will be condemned who possessed none of them and will perish solely because they did not know God through the natural law.

Although they ought to have considered and recognized that they should worship and adore the Creator of heaven and earth and of all things, they abandoned the Creator and began to worship the works of their own hands—golden, stone, and wooden images—which can neither see nor hear, because there is no spirit in them. And they did not repent of their murders, by which they killed many and poured out and offered the blood of their sons and daughters to demons; nor of their twofold fornication, so as to cease either from the impurity of the flesh or from idolatry; nor of their thefts, because each stole from the others whatever he could. [Col. 1060B]

Concerning the conduct of these unrepentant people, the purpose of the present work does not permit us to say more, especially since this book, having been extended at length, awaits the completion of its appointed end. [Col. 1060C]

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1059]

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 1059C]

And I saw another strong angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow was upon his head. The angel is Christ, the messenger of the Father’s will. And because a new messenger of eternal life had come, he announced new things, promised new things, and bestowed new things upon his faithful. Hence he is also called through the prophet the angel of great counsel. The members of this priest are also those of whom it is written: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge” (Mal. II).

In the fact that John says he saw another angel, there is no difference in the subject, but only an order of vision and the customary method of recapitulation. He saw another angel because he repeated another vision to be explained under another understanding. He is called strong because he came to wage war against the aerial powers. Concerning him the Psalmist, in the person of the angels, says (Book III): “Who is this king of glory?” And, answering, he says: “The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII).

But since the Lord is everywhere, according to the statement, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII), and since there is no place outside heaven and earth, how did he descend from heaven? To this we must undoubtedly answer that his descent was nothing other than the incarnation of his humility. The angel appeared clothed with a cloud because the Lord, clothed in flesh, appeared among human beings. Concerning this the prophet says: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt” (Isa. XIX). He ascended upon a light cloud when he assumed flesh without the burden of sin.

The head of the angel is understood as the divinity of the Son of God, according to the statement: “The head of Christ is God.” The rainbow, as we said above, is called in Greek *iris* and in Latin *arcus* (“bow”), because it appears in the cloud in various colors. Since the time of the flood it has been placed as a sign of reconciliation between God and human beings. A bow is formed in heaven when a rain-bearing cloud is illumined by the rays of the sun, because when the brightness of eternal light—and the Sun of justice—assumed flesh, reconciliation was made with the world.

There are also two principal colors in the rainbow, namely blue and fiery red, through which two judgments are signified: in one, the preceding flood; in the other, the subsequent fire. The mysteries of baptism may also be represented by the rainbow: we are baptized with water in remembrance of the passion of the Son of God, and thus receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). [Col. 1061A]

The rainbow was therefore upon the angel’s head because the reconciliation of the Son of God consisted in the power of the Word. And his face was like the sun. Since knowledge of a human being is in the face, the incarnation of the Son of God is understood through the angel’s face, because unless he assumed flesh, no human being would know him. The Psalmist desired this manifest knowledge in the face when he said: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX).

Christ’s face does not shine like this visible sun, but far more brightly, since it is also said of the elect: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII). The elect will indeed be like the angels, but not so like them as to be equal to the Son of God. When he was transfigured on the mountain before the three disciples, he already displayed in himself the future members of his body.

Christ is not compared to the sun without reason. The sun has a rising and a setting. Hence Solomon says: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; there it rises again, circles toward the south, and turns toward the north” (Eccl. I). The sun rose when Christ was born. It came to its setting when he died for us. Thus it returned to its rising, because his humanity is shown to have returned from the suffering of death to the glory of resurrection. There it rises again and circles toward the south, because, rising from the dead, he illumined the hearts of the disciples with the warmth of faith and the Holy Spirit. Those in whom the Sun of justice pours a greater warmth of the Spirit are rightly called “the south.”

As it circles toward the south, it turns toward the north, because through the preaching of the apostles it is brought to gather the Gentiles, in whom that cold wind held sway which, lifted up in pride, is said first to have declared: “I will set my throne in the north.” What follows—“The Spirit goes forward, surveying all things”—pertains to the fact that the whole world is shown to be filled with preaching. Hence: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel; your lightning flashes have illumined the world” (Ps. LXXVI).

“And it returns to its circles,” because after the gathering of the Gentiles, the multitude of the Jews will also be illumined; and when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved. The members of the Redeemer may also be understood through the angel’s face—not as they now are on earth, but as they will be in heaven. Hence: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun.” Since the Lord and the Church are one person, it is not inappropriate that the Church herself is said to shine like the sun in the angel’s face. [Col. 1061D]

And his feet were like pillars of fire. By the angel’s feet the preachers are understood, in whom the incarnate wisdom of God walked throughout the whole world. Concerning them it is said: “They went forth and preached everywhere.” And again it is said of them: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Rom. X). They are aptly compared both to pillars and to fire, because, like pillars, they bear the building of the Church placed upon them, and, kindled by the Holy Spirit, they inflame the hearts of their hearers with the love of God through preaching.

Since they are sent to preach, they are rightly called feet; since they kindle those to whom they preach with the love of God, they are rightly called fire; and since they are built into the structure of the Church, they are appropriately called pillars. That they are pillars Paul testifies when he says: “Peter and James and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave the right hand to me and Barnabas” (Gal. II). Hence the Psalmist also says: “I have established its pillars” (Ps. LXXIV). [Col. 1062A]

And he had in his hand an open book. Above we read that he saw a book sealed with seven seals, by which the Old Testament is signified, filled with manifold obscurity. Here, however, the open little book signifies the New Testament, which is opened in the hand of God—that is, revealed through his operation. That hand is the work of our salvation. And because secrets were known to have lain hidden in the earlier book, it is appropriately signified that the grace of the New Testament has now shone forth revealed in the open little book. For he himself, appearing in the flesh—which is understood through the angel’s face—opened the things that had lain hidden by being born, dying, rising from the dead, and ascending into heaven.

And he placed his right foot upon the sea, and his left upon the earth. By the right foot are signified those members who are broken by no adversities and lifted up by no successes: the apostles, martyrs, and others who have power to tread upon every force of the enemy. Such people are set upon the sea—that is, upon this world—because they endure all the persecutions of the wicked and do not succumb.

By the left foot, however, which is placed upon the earth, confessors are understood, such as Remigius, Germanus, Martinus, and the others who lived in a time of peace and did not undergo public martyrdom, because they are established upon the earth—that is, upon the solidity of faith. God arranged the alternation of times within the Church, setting the stronger members upon the waves of the sea and the weaker upon the solidity of the earth. Thus also the rulers of this age, wherever the onset of war is stronger, prepare the strongest soldiers. [Col. 1062C]

And he cried out with a loud voice, like a lion when it roars. When a lion roars, all beasts are afraid, and he displays his own strength. Christ, called a lion on account of his strength, cried out, either through himself or through his preachers, when he said: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III). And again: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV). By this voice he demonstrated his strength, subduing many to himself and striking bestial and savage people—beasts, so to speak—with fear.

What Christ did, his apostles also did: they preached eternal torments to sinners and converted savage people to his faith through their teaching. And when he had cried out, the seven thunders spoke their voices. What are the seven thunders except the universal Church, filled with the sevenfold Spirit in its preachers? Hence the lion rightly cried out first, and afterward the seven thunders spoke, because Christ preached first; then the apostles and the other teachers, proceeding at his call, preached everywhere. [Col. 1063A]

The seven thunders are rightly said to speak their voices, because holy preaching did not admit into its doctrines the fables of the Jews, the empty songs of the philosophers, or the craftiness of the heretics. Rather, as it was delivered according to its proper meanings, it diffused itself into the hearts of its hearers through the holy preachers.

The holy apostles may also be understood specifically in the seven thunders. They thunder in the wheel of this age because they speak lofty, profound, obscure, and terrifying things. Their number is composed from the parts of the number seven: the even four and the odd three. Whether three is multiplied by four or four by three, the number twelve is reached, because through the twelve apostles the faith of the Holy Trinity thundered throughout the four-part world. They were sent to preach the three highest things through the four lowest. [Col. 1063B]

And when the seven thunders had spoken their voices, I was about to write. And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: “Seal what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it.” Earlier John had heard: “What you see, write in a book.” He therefore wished to write what he had heard from the seven thunders, but he was told: “Seal”—that is, place seals upon—what the seven thunders had spoken, and do not write it.

Here it is rightly asked why this is said to him, since in John all teachers are represented, and they certainly ought not to seal up the divine words so that they would not be made manifest for the benefit of others. We must answer that what we mark with a seal we do not wish to be known to everyone, but only to intimates and to those whom we know with certainty that we can trust. What we say openly and do not seal, however, we bring to the knowledge of many.

John—and in him the entire order of teachers—is told not to write what the seven thunders spoke because the divine words are not to be revealed to everyone. They must be concealed for a time, lest the Lord’s command be violated: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII). They should also be distributed discreetly to the simple, according to each person’s capacity, because some receive the drink of milk, while others are able to receive solid food. [Col. 1063D]

Hence the Lord himself says to his disciples: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI). And again: “Blessed is the faithful and prudent servant who gives his fellow servants their measure of grain at the proper time” (Luke XII). Let John therefore be told: “Seal what the seven thunders spoke, and do not write it.” And let this be said through him to the entire choir of teachers: Conceal the mysteries of God’s words within the secrecy of your mind in such a way that either those who ought not reach their knowledge do not reach it, or those who ought to know them receive that knowledge with discretion and moderation.

And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth raised his hand toward heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever. Although the Lord forbids swearing in the Gospel, saying: “Do not swear either by heaven or by earth, but let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; anything beyond this is from evil” (Matt. V), what does it mean that he himself, raising his hand toward heaven, swears by him who lives forever and ever?

We must know that human beings are rightly forbidden to swear because they often fail in their oaths. God would not have restrained human beings from swearing if he had known that sin was absent from it. God, however, can swear, since he never lies. His oath is every word he speaks, because whatever he says is fulfilled without any ambiguity.

By the angel’s hand, as we said above, the operation of the Son of God and the dispensation of human redemption are understood. The angel raised his hand toward heaven when the Son of God raised to the right hand of the Father the flesh that he had assumed for us. Hence it is written: “I will raise my hand to heaven and swear by my right hand,” as though he said: I will raise to heaven the flesh assumed by the Word, and through both natures—the nature of the Word and that of the human being—I will confirm whatever is to come.

He swore by him who lives forever and ever—that is, by God the Father—when he showed that he and the Father are one, saying: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV). He also referred all his works to God when he said: “The Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works.”

Concerning him it is also added: “Who created heaven and the things that are in it”—that is, the sun, the moon, and the other stars—“and the earth and the things that are in it”—that is, human beings, beasts, birds, and everything down to the smallest worm—“and the sea and the things that are in it”—namely, whales and fish of various kinds. [Col. 1064C]

Here the perfidy of the heretics is condemned, since they do not hesitate to assert that some things were made by the good God and others by the prince of darkness.

But when he adds, “because there will be time no longer,” he creates a question for us, especially since the Psalmist says of the reprobate: “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him, and their time will be forever” (Ps. LXXX). If the time of the wicked will be forever, how will time now no longer exist?

To this we must answer that for the righteous there will be no time—that is, no mutability—because they will be unchanging in mind and incorruptible in body. Time is the succession of days and nights. Therefore time will no longer exist there where there is no variation of anything whatsoever. The righteous will remain unchanging, because they will abide in eternal brightness and unfailing light. Hence the Psalmist says: “By your ordinance the day endures” (Ps. CXVIII).

The wicked, however, will have time, because they will continually be changed through various torments and will pass from the waters of snow into excessive heat. What the Lord denies concerning the righteous, therefore, the Psalmist affirms concerning the unjust.

But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet—that is, when the holy Church begins to proclaim her final preaching—the mystery of God will be accomplished [Col. 1065A]. That is, whatever is now hidden will be brought to completion, because “accomplishment” here does not signify abolition but perfection. The mystery is that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. 2); it will then be accomplished—that is, perfected—when good things have been given to the righteous and the punishments previously prepared have been imposed upon the unrighteous, just as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets. For the prophets’ entire concern was principally with the Lord’s coming and the consummation of the age. Therefore, what was foretold beforehand through them will then be brought to completion.

And I heard again a voice from heaven speaking with me and saying: “Go and take the book from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth.” The angel who holds the open book is Christ, and the one who invites John to go to the angel is also Christ. For he himself holds the book open, because he revealed all that had been hidden in the Old Testament concerning his birth, passion, death, and resurrection. Therefore, that voice which came to John is understood as nothing other than the inward inspiration by which God inspires the hearts of the faithful to approach him, in accordance with the saying: “Approach him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33) [Col. 1065B]. For what is said to John is certainly said to all who, with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of the Lord. Such people have the little book open; therefore they are told to approach the angel, not with bodily steps but with the steps of faith and the mind.

Nor is it surprising if Christ himself speaks of himself as though of another, since even the saints in Scripture very often, whenever they speak of great things concerning themselves, speak as though of another. Hence the statement: “Moses was a very meek man, more than all who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. 12). And Job: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, a simple and upright man, turning away from evil” (Job 1). And John himself: “This is that disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 13). It is also fitting that the voice itself sounded not from earth but from heaven, because the one who is from earth speaks of earth [Col. 1065C]. But what follows—“standing upon the sea and upon the earth”—has been explained above.

And I went to the angel, saying to him that he should give me the book. The saints’ readiness follows the commanding voice of God in action, for they go to the angel—that is, they approach Christ in faith and devotion—asking him to give them the book, from whom the mouths of the mute are opened and the tongues of infants are made eloquent. Hence James says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him” (Jas. 1) [Col. 1065D].

And he said to me: “Take the book and devour it.” To devour the book once received is to store Scripture away in the hidden bowels with eagerness. Here it must be noted that he does not say, “Take it and drink it,” but “devour it,” that is, eat it eagerly. For sacred Scripture is drink in some passages and food in others. In more obscure matters, which cannot be understood without exposition, it is food, because it is taken in as though by chewing, reading, and ruminating. But in clearer matters, which can be understood without exposition, it is drink; for we swallow drink without chewing. We therefore drink what is clearer and more evident, which we are able to understand even without exposition.

And although the holy apostles, and John himself, clearly understood the mysteries of God, they nevertheless still needed exposition as to how those mysteries pertained to him. Therefore John is by no means told, “Drink,” but “Devour,” as though it were said more plainly: “Work through it and understand it”; that is, first chew it, and then swallow it. This is what the holy fathers did—Augustine, Gregory, and the others whose expositions we now use [Col. 1066A].

And he will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey. The order in this passage is inverted. First food is taken into the mouth, and only afterward is it carried down to the lower parts of the belly. All this will be explained in what follows.

And I took the book from the hand of the angel, and devoured it, and it was in my mouth as sweet honey. And when I had devoured it, my belly became bitter. Who else are represented by the mouth of the Church except the holy preachers, who meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night and can say: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 118)?

By the belly, worldly people are understood—those who serve their belly and their pleasures—of whom the Apostle says: “Their god is their belly” (Phil. 3) [Col. 1066B]. Such people sometimes eagerly receive divine words through the mouth of preachers; but because they serve earthly pleasures, the word of God, which had been like sweet honey to them in the mouth of their teachers, becomes bitter in their belly. This happens, for example, when they hear: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his house, nor his field”; and: “If anyone does not hate his father, or mother, or wife, children, and daughters, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). And again: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9). The divine words become bitter to them because they despair of being able to do these things, wishing instead to serve their own pleasures.

Alternatively: For the holy preachers themselves, God’s word is sweet in the mouth—for preaching, meditation, and exposition. But when they are compelled to fulfill by their deeds what they teach in words, it is turned into bitterness for them. The word is likewise sweet in the preachers’ mouth, as we have said, for reading and exposition; but when, on account of their preaching itself, they are despised, afflicted, and tormented in various ways, it is turned into bitterness in their belly, because they are inwardly distressed both by the affliction and by the condemnation of those who despise them. Hence the Apostle says: “I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart” (Rom. 9) [Col. 1066C].

That the belly signifies the secret place of the heart is shown by Jeremiah. When he had said, “My belly, my belly, I am in pain,” he immediately added: “The senses of my heart are troubled within me” (Jer. 4). For it would not pertain to the salvation of the people if he were declaring that he suffered pain in a bodily belly; rather, he said that his belly was in pain because he experienced affliction of mind [Col. 1066D].

Or certainly, the book that has been received and eaten is turned into bitterness when a teacher, seeing penitents converted through his preaching, is joined to them in the affection of his mind and, with the Apostle, suffers with those who suffer and weeps with those who weep.

Or certainly, it is sweet to us when it promises the joys of the heavenly homeland; but it is bitter when it imposes the austere commandments by which we reach that same homeland. It is sweet to hear: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). But it is bitter: “Unless you become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18). Likewise, it is sweet to hear: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). But it is bitter: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2). It was sweet for the apostles to hear: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones” (Luke 22). But it was bitter for them to hear: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be the servant of all” (Matt. 23) [Col. 1067A].

And he says to me: “You must prophesy again concerning peoples and nations and languages and many kings.” John brought forth almost everything—or rather, everything—that was set forth in this book not specifically in his own person but generally in the person of the elect. But what is narrated in this verse he teaches to apply both to his own person and to that of others.

When he saw these things, he had been exiled to the island of Patmos; therefore he is told: “You must prophesy again concerning peoples and nations and languages and kings.” It was as though the divine voice said to him: “You will not die on this island, as you suppose. You will prophesy again, and with your own hand you will write this Apocalypse that you have seen, and you will teach it to others. Nor will you announce only this prophecy; for the instruction of the faith of the saints, you will write the Gospel in greater depth than the others” [Col. 1067B].

He says “again” because he had evidently already done this before kings and nations. For this reason he was sent by Domitian, that most impious Caesar, into a cauldron of boiling oil and was then carried into exile to the same island, where he also saw this Apocalypse. When he had already advanced in age and thought that he would soon depart from the world to Christ, Domitian was killed and everything carried out by his command was annulled. John returned to Ephesus, where he handed over the aforementioned Apocalypse to the churches to be read [Col. 1067C].

But when Ebion, Valentinus, and Cerinthus were barking against Christ, he was moved by the prayers of the bishops and, after proclaiming a three-day fast, also wrote the Gospel. Thus he preached to so many peoples and nations because his preaching reached the knowledge of many.

But what is attributed specifically to him is assigned generally to preachers, in whose person he says: “You must prophesy again concerning peoples,” because, when others depart to Christ, the Church of the elect does not cease to preach again through subsequent preachers. We should understand “to prophesy” as “to preach,” just as Paul says: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge” (1 Cor. 14) [Col. 1067D].

Or certainly, John is commanded to prophesy again for this reason: so that what the teachers of the Church preach with their mouths, they may proclaim again through their deeds. For those who announce the words of life to believers must also not cease to proclaim life through their works.

## CHAPTER XI

And a reed like a rod was given to me. These words apply to John, but they likewise apply to the entire order of preachers. By the reed we must understand what is made with a reed, namely, divine Scripture, because the ancients wrote with reeds. Therefore the reed is rightly said to be not empty but like a rod [Col. 1068A].

In the rod, the uprightness of sacred Scripture is understood. In it there is no falsehood and no error, as there is in the books of philosophers, Jews, and heretics, whose teaching is full of falsehood. Sacred Scripture, however, is straight in every respect, and therefore is rightly compared to a rod, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “Your rod is a rod of uprightness, the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44).

Alternatively: Kings carry a rod in their hands as a sign of their power, by which their royal authority is expressed. Therefore the reed—that is, divine Scripture—is rightly compared to a rod, because it promises a kingdom to those who observe it, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5), and many similar things. And this kingdom, which heavenly preaching promises, perseveres in inflexible righteousness.

After the reed had been given to him, the divine voice says to him: “Rise”—that is, for the office of preaching—and do not lie prostrate in the depths of vices. For, as was said above, what is said to John applies to all preachers of the truth, who must proclaim again through their deeds what they preach in words [Col. 1068B].

And measure the temple of God and the altar. The temple of God is the Church herself, to whom the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3). The altar within the temple signifies the more eminent faithful in the Church—that is, virgins, the continent, and those who renounce the world. Just as the altar is in the temple, so the life of religious persons exists within the body of the faithful, in whom above all the continual and unfailing fire of holy compunction remains.

What follows—“and those who worship in it”—is as though one should supply: “Measure those who worship in the temple and at the altar.” By this statement those are indicated who worship the Father in spirit and in truth, as the Lord says [Col. 1068C].

Therefore it is said to the entire order of teachers: “Rise to better works; measure the temple, the altar, and those who worship in it.” That is, announce the word of God to each profession and order according to its dignity and place. For example, say to virgins: “Blessed are you who have rejected marital union; therefore you will have fellowship with the angels. You who have no bridegroom on earth will have in heaven Christ the Bridegroom, God and man, living forever.”

Say also to those who have renounced the world: “Blessed are you who, not forgetful of the Gospel commandment, have left all earthly things for Christ and followed him, from whom you will receive an unfailing treasure in heaven.”

And say to the continent: “Blessed are you who, after lawful marriage, pursue continence and strive to be numbered among those of whom it is rightly said: ‘For they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes’” (Rev. 14).

Or let us understand the altar generally as the holy Church, in which the sacrifice of praise and the incense of prayer are offered daily to God. “Measure the temple and the altar”: that is, speak the word according to each person’s capacity, entrusting simpler things to the simple and high and profound things to the perfect [Col. 1068D].

But cast out the court that is outside the temple, and do not measure it. This is a truly remarkable expression: he commands that the court be cast out which is shown to be outside. For how can it be cast outside if it is not inside? But this is like the statement: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living”—that is, “Let them not be written in it.” Thus here also it is said: “Cast out the court,” that is, do not count it as being inside [Col. 1069A].

By the court that is outside are understood heretics, pagans, and Jews, for whom there is no entrance into the Holy of Holies. Of them Paul says: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 5). Therefore let it be said: “Do not measure the court that is outside,” that is, do not count such people among the number of the saints, because it has been given to the nations.

That is, they will perish in a common punishment and will be counted among those who worship idols, because they too appear to worship images, holding falsehood in place of truth. The Jews say that they believe in God the Father, but they lie, because whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father; and whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. They therefore worship falsehood, because they do not adore the truth [Col. 1069B].

Heretics also profess various errors concerning the Lord. Since they depart from the truth, they are regarded as similar to the nations. For example, Sabellius says that the Father and the Son are the same person; because he refuses to understand two persons in the Father and the Son, he is like—and even worse than—the pagans.

Photinus likewise asserts that Christ is a mere human being and that he did not exist before Mary. He is like the nations, who confess that they worship an image of a dead man, since he says that Christ was merely human and denies that he is God. Therefore such people and those like them, whether they wish it or not, pass into the number of those who worship images of dead human beings, especially since what they hold is false in every respect.

Likewise, those who destroy by their works the faith they possess are counted among the unbelievers.

And they will trample upon the holy city—that is, the courts themselves—for forty-two months. The holy city was formerly called Jerusalem, in accordance with the Gospel statement: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose and appeared to many in the holy city” (Matt. 27). Nevertheless, here the reference is not to that city but rather to the Church, of whom it is written: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86) [Col. 1069C].

They trample this city—that is, the courts, namely heretics, pagans, Jews, and false brothers—both by word and by torment. But just as flint, when trodden under human feet, may be polished but cannot be crushed, and is polished all the more the more it is trodden, so the holy Church is made stronger and more brilliant by the persecution of the faithless. Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12).

The forty-two months may specifically refer to the period of three and a half years, when the Church will be trampled and oppressed more bitterly by the impious under Antichrist. For forty-two months are contained in three and a half years. By this number also the entire present age may be understood, on account of the six ages of the world and the seven days by which all present time revolves. Six times seven makes forty-two [Col. 1069D].

Alternatively: We read in the Old Testament that the people of Israel entered the promised land at their forty-second encampment. Since everything happened to them in figure, this journey certainly also pertains to us, who linger on the journey through the desert and strive toward the homeland of promise after the baptism of the Red Sea, in which Pharaoh was drowned with his armies—that is, the devil with all original sins [Col. 1070A].

Therefore, what was previously enacted there figuratively through forty-two encampments, here is expressed through a figurative use of the word “months.” The city is trampled for forty-two months because, for as long as it passes through the journey of the present life, the Church endures persecution from the impious.

And I will give to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy—that is, I will grant that they prophesy—for 1,260 days. Here also, both in the number of days, which together make three and a half years, and in the coming and prophecy of the two witnesses, persecution and the reign of Antichrist are clearly indicated. Concerning these two witnesses, the Lord says through the prophet Malachi: “Behold, I will send you Enoch and Elijah, so that they may turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers” (Matt. 4) [Col. 1070B]. And the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Elijah, when he comes, will restore all things” (Matt. 17).

These two, therefore, when they come, will prophesy—that is, preach—because, as was said above, “to prophesy” is sometimes used for “to preach.” For 1,260 days—that is, three and a half years—after which they will be killed by Antichrist.

They will be clothed in sackcloth, because the repentance that they preach with their mouths they will also display in their clothing, just as blessed John did, who was clothed in camel’s hair.

But in these two witnesses the entire Church is included in its preachers. Throughout the whole period of this life she prophesies and preaches the mysteries of the Son of God, whether now or in the final times. The Church is fittingly represented in two witnesses on account of the two Testaments by which she is strengthened; or because she consists of two peoples and is given life by the two commandments of love; or also on account of the two kinds of martyrdom [Col. 1070C].

In the sackcloth the humility of the saints is expressed. Although they are teachers, they confess that they are sinners, for sackcloth is appropriate to the guilty. Or certainly, because the life of the saints will appear contemptible to the reprobate, they are said to be clothed in sackcloth. This is what is said in this same Apocalypse: “The sun became black like a sackcloth made of hair” (Rev. 6).

These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth. Specifically, the two—namely Enoch and Elijah—are called two olive trees on account of the anointing of the Holy Spirit with which they have been imbued. They are also called lampstands because they will shine and show the light of truth to others both in word and in deed [Col. 1070D].

Generally, all the saints of the Church are included in these two, having received the Holy Spirit at the time of baptism and through the laying on of the bishops’ hands. They are called two olive trees, although there is one olive tree, namely the universal Church, in accordance with the statement: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51), on account of the two Testaments, or the love of God and neighbor, or the two kinds of martyrdom.

Likewise, although the same Church is one lampstand on account of the unity of faith, it is called two lampstands on account of the mysteries mentioned above.

They are fittingly said to stand before the Lord of the earth, because the saints are shown to cling inwardly to their Creator through deep contemplation, and, continually considering his will, they do those things in which they do not offend their Creator [Col. 1071A]. Hence Elijah says: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (1 Kings 17). And Paul: “As from God, before God, we speak in Christ” (2 Cor. 12).

This may also be understood in another way of these two witnesses, who stand before the Lord of the earth: namely, that they have been transferred to paradise, where Adam once was before he sinned, and, removed from our sight, enjoy the brightness of the vision of God.

And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire will come out of their mouth and devour their enemies. This has already been fulfilled in part, when, as we read in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 1), fire came down from heaven at Elijah’s command and consumed the captains of fifty together with their fifty men [Col. 1071B].

But just as these words apply specifically to those two, so they also apply generally to all the saints. By fire holy preaching is signified, because it kindles the hearts of its hearers to the love of God. From this fire, therefore, the good are perfected, while the wicked perish. Hence Paul says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God”; and: “To some we are an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2).

When the saints proclaim good things before the wicked, they harm them even against their will, because they turn the good things they hear into their own condemnation. And when they persecute the saints, who announce life to them, they are devoured by this fire—that is, by the doctrine proceeding from their mouths—because on account of their contempt and persecution of the saints they are driven toward eternal punishments [Col. 1071C].

And if anyone wishes to injure them, he must be killed in this way—namely, by the sentence of the word of God.

Or certainly, the fire proceeding from the witnesses’ mouths kills their enemies because the holy Church strikes those who think contrary to Christ and persist in evil with the thunderbolt of anathema.

If we wish to understand this also in a good sense, the holy Church in her teachers devours her enemies with the fire of her mouth when, through the word of exhortation and the administration of illumination, she summons them to love of herself, so that hostility may die and they may live by the grace of love, with the coals of love heaped upon their heads, in accordance with Solomon’s saying.

These have power to shut heaven with clouds so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy; and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague whenever they wish. We recognize that this was also literally fulfilled in Moses and Elijah, since one of them turned the waters of the Nile River into blood because Pharaoh’s heart had been hardened. The other closed heaven so that it would not rain for three and a half years [Col. 1071D].

For when the impious king Ahab was reigning—he who killed the saints of God and, in addition, worshiped idols—and when all the people of Israel had abandoned the God of their fathers and worshiped Baal, and Elijah had been unable to recall them to the worship of God, he said in anger: “The Lord lives: there shall be neither dew nor rain for you except according to the word of my mouth” (1 Kings 17). And so it happened until the people performed repentance and he again obtained rain by his petition [Col. 1072A].

Moses also struck the land of Egypt with every plague whenever he wished—that is, until he delivered the children of Israel from the Egyptians’ servitude.

Spiritually, the saints themselves are called heaven. They are also called clouds, concerning which it is written: “And I will command the clouds not to rain upon it rain” (Isa. 5). They therefore shut heaven—that is, themselves—not so that heaven’s rains issue forth in no way at all, but so that they do not rain upon the earth that produces thorns and thistles.

They rain, therefore, upon the perfect, but hide their rain from the impious, because they reveal their preaching to the good and to those willing to receive it, but conceal it from those who despise and mock it. Hence the saying: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7).

And they have power over the waters to turn them into blood. Water signifies Scripture. Hence the statement: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Prov. 18). They therefore turn water into blood when they provide an occasion for those who understand what has been rightly spoken in a wrong manner, and when they turn the teaching they have received into their own destruction [Col. 1072B].

The saints are said to do this because they announce the divine words to those who despise them, desiring to instruct them and recall them to God’s will.

They also have power to strike the earth with every plague whenever they wish, because it is in their power to speak whenever they wish and again to be silent whenever they wish: to speak, that is, to the faithful, and to be silent before the unbelieving. Therefore, whenever they close the divine mysteries to unbelievers, they strike them with an incurable plague [Col. 1072C].

Whenever, however, they disclose God’s mysteries to the faithful, they draw some toward death and others toward life. What benefits some unto salvation becomes for others a cause of death; and when they form words before the impious, they offer the blood of carnal understanding by which they may die.

It must be noted that he does not say, “They will have power,” but “They have power,” so that we may understand this to have been said not only of the two—Enoch and Elijah—who are to come, but also of the preachers of the Church in the present time.

And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that ascends from the abyss will make war against them, and will conquer them and kill them. This testimony is not to be referred to the actual reign of Antichrist, but to the preceding period in which they will preach, before he begins to reign [Col. 1072D].

At the revelation of the beast, the testimony of those who teach that he is not Christ but the devil must be finished—that is, perfected and completed. They will proclaim to Jews and nations that Christ has already come in former times and, through his passion, redeemed the human race. Therefore they will be killed by him, having been seized by him.

This is what follows: “The beast that ascends from the abyss will make war against them.” By the name “beast” is signified not only that condemned man himself but also the devil who dwells in him, who will be exalted and lifted above everything that is called God or worshiped, as well as his entire body.

That lost man will therefore ascend from the abyss—that is, from the multitude of faithless Jews, who are deep in impiety by birth and grow in it through the stages of their lives—in accordance with the statement: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path” (Gen. 49) [Col. 1073A].

For the devil will ascend from the abyss—that is, from the hearts of the reprobate in whom he dwells—and will enter that condemned man, so that through him he may perform signs and be so exalted as to sit in the temple of God as though he were God.

His entire body, together with its head, will ascend from the abyss, because by God’s divine judgment it will be permitted to rage. “The judgments of God are a great abyss” (Ps. 35). From there he will ascend from which he will be permitted to rise into pride.

He will make war against God’s witnesses, both bodily and spiritually. He will display all the things that were fulfilled in earlier martyrs: rods, clubs, leaden balls, red-hot iron plates, iron claws, beasts, fires, prisons, and whatever similar kinds of torture there may be [Col. 1073B].

Again, those whom he cannot conquer in this way he will try to overcome through teachings. He will offer gifts, utter sweet words, and employ false miracles. By both means, raging, he will turn many from the straightness of the faith toward error—deceiving some through terrors and others through persuasion.

But when it is said, “He will conquer them,” this does not concern the saints, who cannot be conquered and who can be killed before they can be separated from the faith. Rather, a certain portion of the wicked is understood, a portion joined to the body of Christ, which is said to be capable of being conquered either by terrors or by flatteries.

But the statement, “He will kill them,” pertains to the saints, whom he will kill in various ways but will not be able to overcome. Among them will also be Elijah and Enoch themselves, who in no way will be overcome by the beast either through terrors or through flatteries [Col. 1073C].

Among those who will be conquered are included false Christians, Jews, heretics, and pagans.

If we ask what the weapons of the Church are, they are certainly faith and innocence, the two commandments of love, and also the two Testaments. With these she fights; with these she proves victorious, even when she dies.

And their bodies lay in the street of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified. Literally, he calls Jerusalem the great city, which was called the great city of God. But after it killed its Lord, it is no longer called the great city or Jerusalem, but Sodom and Egypt [Col. 1073D].

Although persecution will rage everywhere, the Church’s affliction will nevertheless be more savage and bitter where the Lord is handed over to crucifixion and where the head of the wicked will appear, namely Antichrist. In its street the bodies of the saints are specifically said to lie, so that, where the principal struggle will be, the bodies of the dead may there perish in great numbers.

This also signifies that the Jewish people in particular will cling to Antichrist until, through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, those who are to be saved from among them return to Christ.

That city is fittingly called Sodom and Egypt, because it is recognized to have pursued the works of the Sodomites and the abominations of the Egyptians. Hence Isaiah says to them: “Hear, rulers of Sodom” (Isa. 1).

More deeply, by the great city in which the bodies of the saints will lie, the whole world is understood, because at that time the saints will be killed in every part of the world [Col. 1074A]. Hence it is fittingly said: “Where their Lord was killed.” For the fact that the Lord suffered outside the gates of that city signified that Christ would suffer in his members throughout the whole world.

Thus there is the great city called Babylon, in which the devil reigns, just as there is the city of Christ, Jerusalem, in which Christ himself reigns. The former began with Cain, while the latter began with Abel.

“Sodom” is interpreted as “mute,” and “Egypt” as “darkness.” By these names are included those who, shaken by excessive fear, will not dare to confess the faith of Christ in the time of Antichrist. Blinded by the darkness of unbelief and held in the darkness of sins, they will deny him.

Moreover, they will trample upon the holy city—that is, they will oppress it. The bodies of many will lie there, both those who have died and those who are afflicted by various tribulations, namely hunger, nakedness, prisons, and other unheard-of tortures [Col. 1074B].

And people from the nations, tribes, languages, and peoples will see their bodies for three and a half days. The persecution of the saints that will take place among all nations is also plainly shown when it is said that all peoples, tribes, and languages will see their bodies for three and a half days—that is, three and a half years, during which Antichrist will reign.

Here “day” is used for “year,” just as in the Old Testament, where we read that the spies who explored the land for forty days caused the people to murmur. Therefore they remained in the desert for forty years, when the Lord said to Moses: “I have assigned you a day for a year” (Num. 14) [Col. 1074C].

Likewise, to Ezekiel it was commanded that he lie upon his left side for 390 days; and it was said to him: “I have assigned you a day for a year” (Ezek. 4). The captivity of the ten tribes, which would last 390 years, was signified by these days.

And they will not permit their bodies to be placed in tombs. By the bodies we must understand whole persons: not only those who have been killed but also those who, worn down by various pressures, will lie there and be trampled [Col. 1074D].

It is customary for sacred Scripture sometimes to signify the whole person by the soul and sometimes by the body. By the soul, as in the statement: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Acts 7). By the body, as Mary says in the Gospel: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John 20), when she was seeking only the body that had been placed in the tomb, while his soul, together with the divinity of the Word, had descended to the underworld.

But such savagery will then exist, and that persecution will be so monstrous, that the reprobate will not be satisfied after killing them. To increase their wickedness, they will not even allow them after death to be placed in tombs. We read that this was also done during the persecution of the holy martyrs; it will then happen to an even greater degree, in proportion to the greater severity of the persecution.

Alternatively: The bodies of the dead are placed in tombs so that they may rest there and await the final day. Hence a certain wise man says: “Their bodies were buried in peace.” At that time, therefore, they will not permit them to be placed in tombs—that is, they will not allow them to rest as the bodies of the dead rest—but will torment them with various and carefully devised tortures [Col. 1075A].

A tomb is also so called because it “reminds the mind” (*monumentum*, from *monere*, “to remind”); for when we contemplate the tombs of the saints, who gave their bodies for Christ, we are reminded to offer them veneration. Therefore they will not permit them to be placed in a tomb—that is, they will not permit them to be venerated—but, as though they were worthy of mockery, they will allow them to lie in the streets, where they may be devoured by beasts.

And the inhabitants of the earth will rejoice over them, and they will celebrate, and they will send gifts to one another. Those who inhabit the earth are rightly so called: rejoicing at the destruction and death of the saints, they do not know how to raise their minds either to contemplate the rewards of the elect or to consider their own punishments. At the end of time, when the Church has been handed over into the persecutors’ power, such people, seeing the bodies of Enoch, Elijah, and the other martyrs lying unburied, will rejoice at the humiliation and death of those who reproved them for their evil lives and sins. And they will send gifts to one another—that is, blessings and temporal presents, or mutual congratulations in words—as though celebrating a festival.

Because these two prophets tormented those who inhabit the earth. As was said above, this occurred through the consumption of spiritual fire, the withholding of saving rain, and the changing of waters into blood. Although the wicked now rejoice throughout the whole period at the tribulation and humiliation of the righteous, delighted when they have done evil and exulting in the worst deeds, nevertheless their exultation over the affliction or death of the righteous, and through their own cruelty, will then be longer and greater. But when they say, “Peace and security,” sudden destruction will overtake them. Hence this too is appropriately added:

“And after three and a half days.” That is, sudden destruction will come upon those who say, “Peace and security,” and then grief, when they are saying “joy”—namely, after the forty-five days mentioned in the book of Daniel and in Isaiah.

“The spirit of life from God will enter them.” It will not be an alien spirit that enters them; rather, each person will receive his own soul. “And they stood.” In place of “they will stand,” because the past tense is used here for the future. “Upon their feet.” How far in the future this will be, after those forty-five days, God alone knows. The saints are rightly said to stand, because they will already be unchangeable in mind and incorruptible in body.

“And great fear fell”—that is, will fall—“upon those who saw them.” In place of “will see,” meaning upon all the reprobate who killed them. There they will recognize in glory those whom they persecuted in the present life, and they will fear when they see them glorified, awaiting the sentence of divine vengeance. Or else the saints themselves, when they see one another glorified, and see heaven burning, hell opened, and demons moving throughout this air, will fear when they see the Lord coming to judgment with a multitude of angels. But, as the Lord says, “the powers of heaven will be shaken” (Matt. 24); how much more, then, will human beings be shaken? Concerning them he adds further:

“And they heard a loud voice saying to them, ‘Come up here.’” This voice calling them to ascend into heaven is the same of which the Apostle says: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thess. 4). “Come up here,” he says—that is, ascend to God and to your head, because you are his members, and he is now about to repay each one according to his works. Therefore do not linger on earth, lest you be involved in the punishments of the wretched.

“And they ascended into heaven in the cloud, and their enemies saw them.” We read in the Gospel that the Lord will come to judgment in a cloud. Thus the angels who witnessed his ascension said: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven”—that is, in the same flesh and in a cloud (Acts 1). Therefore, just as Christ will come in a cloud, so also will all the saints. Hence he himself says: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24). The Apostle likewise says: “But we who are alive will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4)—not in the air, but in heaven.

If anyone, considering this statement of Paul’s, asks how the general sentence pronounced upon the first man is to be fulfilled—the sentence in which God said to him, “You are earth, and to earth you will go”—he should know that God’s sentence is true, as is Paul’s, because human beings will be found alive, and Paul speaks these words in their person. Yet he should also know, as blessed Augustine says, that in the very rapture into the clouds they will taste death, even if only for a moment. They will therefore return to earth, because for the body to return to earth means that, when the soul departs, the body remains—and the body is certainly earth.

Thus we confidently say that in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, within the very clouds, those who are found alive at the Lord’s coming will receive the spirit of life; nevertheless, as has been said, they will taste momentary death. The wicked, in fact, will remain on this earth, while the elect will be raised to glory. In that glory their enemies will see them and will realize that those whom they judged and condemned unjustly are judging justly.

“And in that hour there was a great earthquake.” While speaking about that very judgment, he suddenly turned to events that will occur earlier—that is, to the persecution of Antichrist, of which he had spoken shortly before—and he calls it the hour that he had previously expressed as three and a half days. What wonder if that persecution is called one hour, when the whole present age is called one hour, according to what John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2)?

The earthquake therefore signifies that most violent persecution. Hence it is rightly called not simply an earthquake but a great earthquake, because then there will be a tribulation such as, as the Lord says, has not been and will not be. For this reason the angel also says to Daniel: “There will come a time such as has not been since nations began to exist.”

“And a tenth of the city fell, and seven thousand human names were killed in the earthquake.” This passage is explained in the Gospel, where the Lord says that a certain woman who had ten drachmas lost one of them. There are nine orders of angels, but man was created as the tenth, to fill the place vacated by the devil. This tenth part perished in those who consented to and believed in Antichrist. Yet not the whole tenth part perished, but a portion of the tenth part—namely, among heretics, pagans, Jews, and false brothers.

The city is called Jerusalem because it consists of angels and human beings. The city whose tenth part fell is that part which, not reaching the nine orders of angels, does not hold the place of the tenth order with the elect. Although the number of those who are lost is infinite, it is comprehended under a finite number when it says: “Seven thousand human names were killed in the earthquake.” The number seven is often used for the whole; therefore, by the seven thousand human beings are understood all the reprobate who died in soul under that persecution.

“And the rest, who remained in the faith”—that is, those who returned to the faith after their denial, or those who were converted from error to true teaching and persevered in that same faith—“were cast into fear, and they gave glory to the God of heaven.” This means either that, because he governed them and granted them strength, they did not fall, or that, after their fall, they were mercifully raised up again.

**[Col. 1077C] The second woe has passed, and behold, the third woe is coming soon.** Above, the flying eagle announced three future woes, two of which have already occurred in the exposition, while the third still remains. The first woe recounts the battle of the locusts; the second, the release of the four angels, extending to this point, where many things concerning the coming of Antichrist are said by recapitulation; the third begins here and extends to the predetermined point, namely, the condemnation of all the reprobate together with their head.

**And the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices arose in heaven, saying: “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever.”** In the seventh angel nothing other than the Church is understood, as above in the other angels—not now preaching as previously, but standing in the presence of its Creator. This is what the angel standing above the sea and the earth swore earlier by him who lives forever and ever: that time would be no more, but that in the days of the seventh angel the mystery of God would be completed.

When the seventh angel sounds the trumpet, loud voices arise in heaven—that is, in the Church of the elect itself. These voices are nothing other than the great desire of the saints, praising God and sounding forth thanksgiving, saying: “The kingdom of this world,” over which the ancient enemy ruled, “has become the kingdom of our Lord God”—that is, of the Father—and of his Christ, his Son. The Father and the Son will reign, together with those who are understood in the name of the Father and the Son, with the whole Church of the elect, forever and ever.

The Son of God received this authority through his humanity, although through his divinity he possessed all things with the Father. Hence, rising from the dead, he himself says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

**And the twenty-four elders**—that is, the preachers—who sit in the presence of God on their thrones, that is, in judicial authority, according to the saying: “Behold, the Lord will come with the elders of his people.” They fell upon their faces, referring everything of their own to him who says: “Apart from me you can do nothing.” They sit in the presence of God because in everything they do or say they always regard God as present to them.

**And they worshiped God, saying: “We give thanks to you, Lord God almighty, who are unchangeable and who were before the ages with the Father.”** Here it should be observed that he does not add, “who are to come,” as above. They show that he is already present in the judgment in which all these things will take place, and they do not proclaim him as still to come.

**“You who have received your great power.”** This refers to the time when, rising from the dead, you subjected all the kingdoms of the world to your authority—and this in your humanity, because your power is unfailing in your divinity. “And you have reigned, you reign, and you will reign.”

**And the nations were angry,** because they see their worship reduced to nothing; hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry.” **And your wrath has come,** that is, the time of your vengeance, when you will break the necks of the enraged peoples.

**And the time of the dead.** This means that those who are dead through sin may die through everlasting condemnation. In these thanksgivings they comprehend the Lord’s two comings: the first, humble and hidden, when, rising from the dead, he subjected the world to himself; the second, exalted and manifest, when he will be angry with the wicked and avenge his servants.

The elect do not rejoice because the reprobate are condemned, but because the time has come when the wicked receive just condemnation and they themselves receive a worthy recompense for their good works. The wicked will be condemned first, and then the righteous will be rewarded; the bodies of the righteous cannot attain the kingdom unless the condemnation of the reprobate has preceded it.

When he says, “You were angry,” this should not be understood as though God becomes angry in the same way as a human being. Rather, he will appear so to the reprobate whom he condemns. In each person’s conscience he will be such as that person sees him: in the minds of the elect he will appear benevolent, and in the minds of the reprobate, angry.

**“To judge and to reward each one: your servants the prophets and the saints.”** These words seem to suggest that the merit of the elect preceded the reward they are to receive. For nothing is repaid unless it is owed. But this is not so, because it is written: “Who has first given to him, that he may be repaid?” (Rom. 11). And elsewhere: “By grace you have been saved, and this is not from yourselves, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2).

It must therefore be understood that, in order that we might give something to God, we first received it from him. His mercy goes before us so that we may will, and follows after us so that we may act. Hence the Psalmist says: “His mercy will go before me, and his mercy will follow me” (Ps. 20, 58). Thus what we have received belongs to God, because he gave it, and to us, because we received it from him. Therefore, when the Lord repays a reward, he himself rewards his own gifts in the elect.

With this understanding we say each day: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 5). If it is ours, why do we ask that it be given? It becomes ours by our receiving it, although it was not ours by possession.

It is asked why, after naming the prophets and the other saints, the apostles have been omitted. It should be understood that the apostles are included among the prophets, since they are prophets: they announce beforehand both the punishments of the reprobate and the rewards of the saints. The Lord himself says of them: “Behold, I am sending prophets to you.” And to John it was said: “You must prophesy and preach to the nations.” Since not all who are saints are prophets, the prophets will be rewarded, and these others will also be rewarded.

**“And those who fear your name, the small and the great.”** Those who fear his name—that is, who reverence his name and therefore fear to sin—will receive their reward with the small and the great. The great are those who, with the help of divine grace, are able to do the good they understand. The small are those who cannot fulfill what they understand, because they do not even have the opportunity.

For example, someone established in a monastery wishes to show mercy to his brothers and also wishes to offer others the word of preaching and instruction; but because he has not been called to this, he cannot accomplish in action what he understands and desires. Such people are therefore counted among the perfect. Consequently, no one should despair because of imperfection, even though perfection has not been granted to everyone.

For this reason the Church says to her bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out perfume; therefore the young women have loved you greatly” (Song 1). And because the number of such young women is found to be exceedingly great, Solomon says later: “The young women are without number” (Song 4).

**“And the time has come to destroy those who corrupted the earth.”** Those who corrupted the earth—that is, who stained their flesh with various vices and sins, or who stained others by evil example and teaching—will be destroyed, that is, separated from the land of the living and from the inheritance of the saints, condemned to the exile of eternal damnation.

**And the temple of God in heaven was opened.** Heaven is the Church, which is the seat of God. The temple in heaven is understood as the body of Christ, concerning which he himself says to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Evangelist explains this by adding: “He was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 5).

This temple was opened by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven. For the body itself is the temple of God, because the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in it. The temple is in heaven because these mysteries are preached and preserved in the Church.

Or the temple was opened when, as we read in the Gospel, his side was pierced by a lance. By saying that the temple was opened in heaven, John wished, according to this interpretation, that it be understood as opened in his presence, since he knew himself to belong to the number of those concerning whom it had been written: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

**And the ark of the covenant was seen in his temple.** What is signified by the temple is also signified by the ark—that is, the Church of the saints. It is a genus within a genus, as the eight souls were in the ark. It is called the ark of the covenant because it possesses knowledge of the two Testaments, not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts.

There is the urn containing manna—that is, the body of Christ, in which is the true bread that came down from heaven. There is Aaron’s rod, by which the priesthood is signified, because that priesthood preceded it in figure. For it signified the royal priesthood now exercised in the Church.

This ark was carried by four rings because it is instructed by the four Gospels. When the temple was opened, the ark was seen: when he died and his side was pierced by the lance, the Church was built through the mystery of blood and water. As a figure of this event, the woman is described at the beginning as having been fashioned from the side of the sleeping man.

**And there were flashes of lightning, voices, thunder, an earthquake, and great hail.** By the flashes of lightning are understood the miracles by which the minds of unbelievers were struck and, their powers of pride immediately broken, submitted themselves to humility. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will multiply the flashes of lightning, and you will trouble them.”

By the voices are understood preaching and exhortation. It is rightly said that the flashes of lightning come first and the voices follow, because the holy preachers first performed miracles and then, by speaking, invited their hearers to believe new things. Thus Peter first healed the paralytic at the Beautiful Gate, and then instructed the minds of the Jews in the faith through the word of exhortation.

The thunder signifies the threat of the terror of divine judgment. Thunder follows the voices so that those who perhaps despise miracles and disregard words may be shaken by the terror of judgment.

The earthquake signifies the persecution that was stirred up against the saints. Hence hail rightly follows the earthquake: hail signifies those who stir up persecution. Hail crushes the crops of the earth, and it is itself crushed; thus the hail completely disappears, and afterward the earth bears fruit again.

In the same way, while the rulers of this age persecuted and afflicted the saints, they themselves were likewise shattered and reduced to nothing, either in their power or through conversion to something better. For many of those who persecuted the Church of God were converted to the faith of Christ and began to suffer what they had previously inflicted on others.

Moreover, when the wicked perished—or when those who had been predestined were converted to the faith—the Church began to bear fruit in good works and to grow in faith.

# CHAPTER XII

**And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet.** This is the sign of which Ahaz was admonished to ask from God, either in the depths below or in the heights above. But when he said, “I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord,” the prophet, turning to the house of David, said: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son.”

It was indeed a great sign when a virgin conceived and gave birth, and after giving birth remained a virgin. This happened in heaven—that is, in the Church, of which the Lord’s mother was also a member.

**A woman clothed with the sun,** that is, surrounded by the divinity of the Most High. Hence the angel says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). This is the divinity of which Paul says that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

In this passage the blessed Mother of God represents the person of the Church. Not everything narrated here can correspond literally and specifically to the blessed Virgin; rather, according to the mystical account, it applies generally to the Church of the elect, in which this sign occurs every day, because Christ is conceived and born in her every day.

She is herself the mother, and she is also the son. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Mark 3). For when she creates new peoples every day, Christ is born in them.

She is also clothed with the sun—that is, surrounded by Christ, concerning whom it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. 4). Hence Paul says: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). Concerning this sun the wicked will say in hell: “The sun of righteousness did not shine for us” (Wis. 5).

By the moon, which is changeable, since from the beginning it grows until the full circle and thereafter wanes until the thirtieth day, all the changeable things of this world are signified. Therefore both the blessed Mother of God and the whole Church have the moon beneath their feet, because they despise all temporal things, regarding all that is changeable as nothing, and hold heavenly things in the gaze of the mind, saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

Alternatively, in this woman we can understand the more perfect members of the Church, who, in accordance with the Lord’s counsel, left all their possessions and followed Christ. By the moon, however, the simple are signified, those who labor for the use of others in planting, building, and farming. Those who are perfect have such people, as it were, beneath their feet, because they are far removed from the merit of the perfect. Nevertheless, the simple will not lack a reward, even though they do not equal the perfect in every respect, provided they faithfully fulfill their ministry.

**And upon her head a crown of twelve stars.** Since by the woman, as we have said, the Church is understood, by her head the Lord Jesus Christ is understood. Paul, speaking of God the Father, says of him: “He gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body.”

In the twelve stars the twelve apostles are signified. Through their preaching they drive away the darkness of unbelief and illuminate their hearers with the light of truth. Hence the angel says to Daniel: “Those who are learned and instruct many will shine like stars for everlasting ages.”

Upon her head is a crown of twelve stars—that is, of the twelve apostles—through whom all the nations surrounding this world believed in Christ, and through whom the head first carried victory over the whole world.

**And, being pregnant, she cried out in labor and was in anguish to give birth.** This cannot be applied literally to blessed Mary, who, just as she conceived without pleasure, so gave birth without pain; she could not have experienced the pangs of childbirth, since she contracted no sin of lust in conception.

According to the mystical meaning, however, this refers to the Church, which is called a woman—not because of an effeminate spirit, but because through preaching and spiritual washing she does not cease daily to give birth to spiritual children. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of the Father …” and so forth, up to “is also my mother.”

The Church is reckoned as mother and as son: when she brings anyone to the faith, she is mother; when she regenerates someone in the baptismal font, she is mother. But in those who come forward for baptism and confess that they believe in Christ, she is son. Hence Paul says: “Through the Gospel I begot you.”

Concerning this woman the Lord says: “When a woman gives birth”—that is, when she wishes to give birth—“she has sorrow, because her hour has come.” Just as a woman is afflicted and tormented while in labor, so the holy Church, while she is in this world and sees her own people afflicted and troubled in various ways, is sorrowful, afflicted, and tormented. She cries out to God, asking to be delivered, lest, overcome by tribulations, she succumb.

But when she reaches the time or hour at which the final members of the body are born into eternal light, then the anguish and cry of labor will cease.

**And another sign appeared in heaven: and behold, a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns.** By the dragon, as we have already said above, the devil is understood. He openly never ceases to devour whomever he can. Because he has harmed human beings for a long time, he is called great on account of the multiplicity of his snares.

He is red because of murder, since he was a murderer from the beginning—that is, from the time when he killed the first human being. Heaven is understood as the Church itself, which above was signified by the woman. The dragon is in heaven because, even in the Church, the devil does not cease to harm those whom he can. He does not possess heaven; rather, he opposes heaven.

By the dragon’s seven heads all the kings subject to him are understood—those who fight against the sevenfold Church. By the ten horns all the kingdoms subject to him are understood. That kingdoms are signified by horns is shown by Zechariah and Daniel, both of whom say that they saw four horns, which are four principal kingdoms.

With these horns—that is, with the power of this world and the kingdoms subject to him—the devil fights against those who observe the ten commandments of the law.

**And upon his heads were seven diadems.** What is signified by the heads is also signified by the seven diadems: namely, all the power of this world that adheres to him and, through plausible deception, fights against the seven churches and against the sevenfold Spirit.

**And his tail swept away a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth.** By the dragon’s tail, as was also said above, evil teachers are understood. For the prophet who teaches falsehood is himself a tail. The tail may also be understood specifically as Antichrist, who will utter every falsehood, having the devil dwelling in him, concerning whom the Lord says: “He did not stand in the truth.”
