For example, if the apostle John had been lifted up on a cross as Peter was, and if what is said of Peter is true—namely, that he had a wife—then John would certainly surpass him, because the former would be a virgin while the latter would not. Hence such a person can neither sing that song with John nor follow the Lamb wherever he goes. They were purchased from the earth. At what price? Clearly, by the precious blood of Christ, whose love lifted them from the earth and made them celibate.

These are those who were not defiled with women—that is, who were not polluted or stained with women in mind and body. For it is of no benefit to be a virgin in body if someone happens to be corrupt in mind. [Col. 1106D] They are virgins. Therefore: These follow the Lamb wherever he goes—that is, they imitate him. To follow Christ is to imitate him. Hence he himself says: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John 12)—that is, let him imitate me. These follow Christ because, just as he is a virgin, so they preserve virginity. And because in the present they follow him more closely than others, in the future they will adhere to him more familiarly. The other faithful, who have lost bodily virginity, will also follow him—not wherever he goes, but wherever they are able. This multitude of saints, although it will not be able to sing that song, will nevertheless be able to hear it and rejoice together in so great a gift.

[Col. 1107A] These were purchased from among all as firstfruits for God and the Lamb. For just as the finest lamb is chosen from a large flock, and just as firstfruits are chosen from many fruits, so these are chosen from the multitude of the elect; offering themselves as firstfruits, they produce a hundredfold harvest.

And no deceit was found in their mouth. Here a question arises: why does John say this, when the Psalmist says, “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115), while God alone is truthful? The matter is resolved as follows: every human being, insofar as he is from himself, is a liar; but insofar as he is truthful, he is from God. Thus, when the Lord asked his disciples, saying, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And he said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah” (Matthew 16). Behold, a human being truthful—indeed, most truthful—in confessing the Son of God. But from where is he truthful? Not from himself, but from God the Father who is in heaven. [Col. 1107B]

But when the Lord elsewhere foretold the punishment of his passion, Peter answered: “Far be it from you, Lord; you will not die. I will die for you.” Behold, a lying human being. But from where is he a liar? Clearly, because he does not understand the things that are of God, but those that are of human beings. Therefore every human being, insofar as he is from himself, is a liar; insofar as he is from God, he is truthful.

But since these things apply to all the saints, why is it said specifically of virgins alone: “No deceit was found in their mouth”? Without doubt, because in comparison with others only virgins are called truthful. Nor is it surprising that those are called truthful in a special way who appear, through virginity of mind and body, to cling more closely to the Truth, who is Christ. For they are without blemish. This too must be understood in a similar way: [Col. 1107C] although the saints also are without blemish—that is, without corruption, since they have already been cleansed of every sin—in comparison with God they are liars and stained.

And I saw another angel flying through the midst of heaven, having an eternal Gospel. The first angel is the Lamb himself, about whom the preceding discussion was given, for he is the messenger of the Father’s will. By the other angel, however, the order of preachers is understood. He is called “another,” not because Christ and his preachers are not one—for he is the head and the elect are members—but because in the narrative they are not one person. For this angel is the same as the one who follows, namely, the order of preachers. But because one succeeds another, one is mentioned after another.

[Col. 1107D] The angel flies through the midst of heaven: that is, holy preachers proceed swiftly through the Church, preaching Christ. He flies through the midst of heaven because, in contemplation of mind, they seek heavenly things, clinging not to earthly things but inviting even the peoples subject to them toward heavenly things by word and writing. Concerning these flying preachers Isaiah says (chapter 60): “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” They fly like clouds because, lifted from earthly desires on the wings of virtues, they rain down words and flash with miracles. They are like doves at their windows because, although they see outward things, they desire nothing earthly, but continually contemplate eternal joys.

[Col. 1108A] This angel is also said to have the eternal Gospel because what the Gospel promises will remain eternally. Through what it announces, what is announced is expressed. To evangelize those sitting upon the earth, and upon every nation, tribe, language, and people, saying with a loud voice. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Gospel must be preached throughout the whole world, and then the end will come.”

“Fear the Lord”—that is, revere his name—“and give him honor”—that is, worship him and submit to him—“because the hour of his judgment has come, to repay each person according to his works. And worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea, and the fountains of waters.” It is as though he were saying: Do not worship Antichrist, who will prevail over human bodies only for a time, but worship him who, after killing the body, has power to cast the soul into Gehenna.

[Col. 1108B] And do not worship him who, filled with the spirit of deception, is thought to be the creator of the creature, but rather him of whom Daniel says (chapter 7): “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” And the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name,” and so forth, “until: Our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2). “Give him honor,” he says, “and not Antichrist, who is known to be opposed to honor in the mark, the name, and the number of his name.” In heaven, earth, and sea, every creature is shown to have been created in time.

[Col. 1108C] And another angel followed him, saying: “Fallen, fallen is that great city Babylon, which made all the nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication.” In that this angel is said to follow the first, the succeeding order of preachers imitates him. The angel rightly follows the angel because he announces the same thing. The first said: “Because the hour of his judgment has come”; the second says: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” (Isaiah 21).

By the name Babylon, the confusion of worldly conduct is understood. There are two cities in this world: Jerusalem, which has Christ as king, and Babylon, which has Nebuchadnezzar—that is, the devil—as king. One began with Abel, the other with Cain; one is the body of Christ, the other the body of the devil.

[Col. 1108D] When the holy preachers say, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon,” the past tense is used for the future. “Fallen,” that is, for “she is about to fall,” or “she will fall into eternal condemnation”—the condemnation by which the devil and all his members will be damned when they hear: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25).

But the fact that the angel—that is, the order of preachers—proclaims the ruin of the faithless city by repeating the announcement serves to confirm the matter. Or certainly, he now shows that all their glory will perish together with the reprobate themselves, in accordance with: “The world and its desire will pass away” (1 John 2). It is as though he were saying: Both worldly glory and those who love it have fallen together.

[Col. 1109A] This city is called great because of the innumerable multitude of the reprobate, or because of the enormity of their vices. The wine of fornication means all the vices and sins by which the reprobate defile others. Above all, however, the philosophers and rulers of this age intoxicate all their subjects with the wine of error, and thus take away their understanding, so that, abandoning the Creator, they serve the creature. For fornication is also used specifically for idolatry. Hence: “You will destroy all those who fornicate away from you” (Psalm 72). This Babylon—that is, worldly conduct—made all the nations drink from the wine of its fornication, because the entire mass of vices is held in the pursuit of temporal glory. On account of all those whom they intoxicate with the wine of error and sins, they will be punished.

[Col. 1109B] And a third angel followed them, saying with a loud voice. Three angels are placed here because they announce the faith of the Trinity; nevertheless, as has been said, what the first is, the following are also—that is, the order of preachers. With a loud voice, because by the freedom of their speech they show that they despise the beast and regard him as nothing.

If anyone worships the beast—that is, the devil—and his image—that is, Antichrist—and receives his mark on his forehead—that is, his faith in his mind—or on his hand, so as to imitate his works—

He too will drink of the wine of the wrath of God mixed with unmixed wine in the cup of his wrath. Let us see who have the mark of the beast on their forehead and hand, and who have it only on their hand.

The Jews have it on their forehead and hand, because they believe in him and will receive him, according to: “Another will come in his own name; him you will receive.” They also imitate his works by blaspheming Christ and serving the most wicked deeds.

[Col. 1109C] False Christians, however, have his mark on their hand: they profess that they know God, but deny him by their actions. Since they deny Christ by their works, they are without doubt of Antichrist, and therefore carry his mark on their hand.

For this reason it is also said here that false Christians, who imitate Antichrist in their works, will likewise be condemned, just as the Jews who follow him in faith and deed.

What the wine is, the cup is—that is, the vengeance and wrath of almighty God that will come upon those who worship and imitate Antichrist. For when we put wine into a cup, we do not say, “Behold, the wine and the cup,” but simply either “wine” or “cup.” He therefore placed “wine” and “cup” in order to show that what was in the cup, mixed with unmixed wine, was turbid in comparison with the unmixed wine. For we call unmixed wine pure.

[Col. 1109D] In this cup, therefore, the dregs are mixed with the unmixed—that is, pure—wine. By the unmixed wine, the vengeance of divine judgment upon the righteous is understood: they are scourged in the present so that afterward they may be glorified. By the dregs, the condemnation of sinners is expressed: they will be condemned at the final judgment. For the wine is above, while the dregs lie hidden at the bottom, because the saints are punished in the present and divine judgment rages openly against them, as it were. But the reprobate will be condemned at the end, because now they are abandoned without the scourge.

The reprobate will drink what remains at the bottom—that is, the dregs—and the elect will not drink it. The reprobate, after the wantonness of pleasure, will be condemned to eternal torments, while the elect, after temporal discipline, will be raised into the power of the kingdom.

[Col. 1110A] Therefore, if anyone worships Antichrist or receives his image on his forehead or hand, he will not at present receive scourges, as one intoxicated with wine, but in the future he will be punished with everlasting vengeance, as one intoxicated with dregs.

And he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the saints. Although there are in hell so many and such countless torments that they can neither be described nor estimated, all torments are briefly comprehended in these two. There will be fire—not to give light, but to burn the bodies of the wretched. There will also be sulfur, which will both feed the fire and produce an intolerable stench. Thus stench will arise from fire, and fire from stench, although either of these alone—the fire or the stench—could suffice for the torment of the wretched.

[Col. 1110B] Sulfur, as we have said, has stench, while fire has heat. Those who now burn with the stench of the flesh toward perverse desires, serving lust above all, rightly deserve afterward to perish in fire and sulfur, so that through just punishment they may learn what they have done through unjust desire.

By the angels in whose presence they are said to be tormented, not only angelic spirits but also the Church of the elect is signified. This will happen so that, when the righteous behold the torments of the impious, they may increase in the praises of God, through whose mercy they escaped what the wretched suffer. In themselves they see the good for which they have been freely rewarded, and in the others they behold the punishment from which they mercifully escaped. Thus the torment of the wicked will contribute to the increase of the elect.

[Col. 1110C] It is added: “And in the presence of the Lamb.” This does not mean that they will see him thereafter, since it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.” Rather, they will be terrified by such fear that almighty God will seem always to be present to them and always to inflict upon them the wrath of his vengeance. Hence Job says: “Leave me, therefore, that I may mourn a little for my sins, before I go to the land where the shadow of death and everlasting horror dwell” (Job 20).

And the smoke of their torments will rise for ages of ages. Great smoke is an indication of great flames. Although without the nourishment of wood, the fire of the reprobate will nevertheless be corporeal; therefore he says that its smoke will be everlasting. Since he sees the reprobate burning in fire without end, he says that the smoke of their torments rises for ages of ages.

[Col. 1110D] Here the error of Origen is openly destroyed: he said that after a thousand years the reprobate would return to life, while the righteous would return to punishment. Otherwise what the Truth says is false: “These will go into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into everlasting life” (Matthew 25).

If anyone wishes to ask why the reprobate will be tormented without end for a temporal sin, it must be said that the strict Judge, when he comes, will weigh not deeds but wills. For, if it were possible, the reprobate would always desire to live in this life, so that they would never cease to sin. Therefore those who never wished to be without sin will never be without punishment. There will be no end to the vengeance of the wicked, since they never wished to have an end to their crimes.

[Col. 1111A] For if, as they say, the punishments of the reprobate are eventually to end, then the joys of the righteous must also eventually end. If this is not true, then neither is that which he threatened true, nor is that which he promised true.

But they say: “For this reason he threatened sinners with eternal punishment: to restrain them from committing sins, since he ought to threaten his creature with eternal punishments, but not inflict them.” We answer them quickly: If he threatened falsely in order to correct people from injustice, then he also promised falsely in order to summon them to justice.

[Col. 1111B] And they have no rest day or night, who worshiped the beast and his image, and whoever received the mark of his name. “Day and night” signifies continuous time, or also alternations of punishments, in accordance with: “They will pass from excessive heat to the waters of snow” (Job 24). Hence: “Their time will be for ages.” The wretched will fail without cessation, and there will always be something to torment them, because what has failed will continually be restored for torments.

Here—that is, in the present life—is the patience of the saints. As they consider the joys of the saints and the punishments of the reprobate, they patiently endure everything so that they may be saved at the end. They keep the commandments of God—that is, the legal precepts—such as: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Matthew 22), and “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not steal” (Luke 18), and other commandments of this kind.

[Col. 1112A] And I heard a voice from heaven saying: “Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.” This voice pertains both to John himself and to all the faithful who await eternal recompense. Write it in your heart and in the hearts of your hearers, or commit it to writing so that it may reach posterity: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”

This statement can be understood in two ways. “Blessed are the dead to the world who die in the Lord,” living by virtues—that is, those who, full of faith and other good works, depart from this world. Or: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord”—that is, those who, imitating their head, do not fear undergoing temporal death for him, so that they may live eternally with him.

“From now on,” says the Spirit—that is, the whole Trinity, which is God—“so that they may rest from their labors.” What is said above, “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord,” applies to all the elect. But what follows, “From now on the Spirit says that they may rest from their labors,” pertains especially to prelates, who labor in various ways because they are seen to have the flock of God entrusted to them. To their person the Lord specifically said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25).

[Col. 1112B] For their works follow them—that is, the reward of their works will follow them, when each person receives according to his labor. Because the reward follows the work after the work has been done, the work itself of the elect is said to accompany them. Where the end of the work is announced, there at last let the end of this book be.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1111]

### CHAPTER XIV FOLLOWS

[Col. 1111C]

And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one seated like a son of man—“I saw” is understood. By the white cloud, the flesh and soul of our Redeemer are understood, which the stain of sin did not darken. Concerning this cloud the prophet says: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt” (Isaiah 19). He ascended upon a light cloud and came into Egypt when he took on the flesh of our mortality and was born and appeared in this world.

He saw one seated upon the cloud because Christ, by the power of his divinity, presides also over his humanity. Or certainly, by the white cloud the Church is understood, cleansed from sins in the font of baptism. Through the faith of Christ and his baptism she is cleansed from all sins, in accordance with: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15). Christ presides there, and by his sitting protects and governs the Church like a hen protecting her chicks.

Why is he called not simply a human being but one like a son of man? This was said above: having risen from the dead and transcended the limits of humanity, he no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6). The cloud and the one seated upon the cloud are also one—that is, the head and the members. Hence, when the Lord sits upon the cloud, the cloud itself certainly sits with the Lord.

He had upon his head a golden crown, by which the victory of Christ is signified: [Col. 1112C] he first triumphed over the devil and bestowed upon his Church the triumph of victory. We also read above that the angel had twelve stars upon his head. There Christ is understood through the angel, the twelve apostles through the twelve stars, and through them the entire order of preachers, by which Christ is crowned—that is, adorned and surrounded—and from whose fellowship he rejoices in his head, that is, in his mind.

And in his hand he had a sharp sickle—that is, in his power he had judicial authority or dignity, which Christ himself also gave to his faithful, saying to the disciples: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

The sickle may also be understood as divine preaching, which the Lord elsewhere calls a sword, saying: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10). Why is divine preaching called a sword? Because through it the good are separated from the wicked, as members are separated from members.

[Col. 1112D] Christ has this sickle in his hand—that is, in his activity—because what he taught in words he first fulfilled in deeds, in accordance with: “The first account I composed, O Theophilus, concerning all that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts 1). Wishing to instruct the preacher how he ought to preach, the Lord first displayed in himself the model of the Word.

[Col. 1113A] He also entrusted this sickle—that is, divine preaching—to his Church, saying to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28). The sickle is sharp because it swiftly separates a human being from earthly desires and from the company of the wicked.

And another angel came out of the temple. The same one who was signified by the first angel—that is, Christ—is signified by the other angel; but because of the order of the visions he is called another, although he is the same. He came out of the temple—that is, from his invisible majesty—when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1). For, although invisible in his nature, he took on flesh and a soul in the virginal womb and became visible in our substance.

[Col. 1113B] Hence the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2). And the Lord himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). The Son is the temple of the Father; the assumed human being is the temple of the Word; and the Church is the temple of the Father and the Son. Concerning her Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3). He therefore came out of the temple when he appeared visibly to human sight.

Crying out with a loud voice to the one seated upon the cloud. In this passage, the one signified by the cloud is also the one signified by him seated upon the cloud. It is a genus within a genus, as was said above concerning Noah’s ark and the eight souls.

The one seated upon the cloud is therefore the Church in her preachers, to whom Christ speaks by commanding: “Send forth your sharp sickle”—that is, divine preaching—“against the Jews.” For this is what he himself says to them: “Go only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 10).

And reap—that is, separate the Jews from earthly understanding or from earthly desires, so that they may no longer receive things carnally: “If you are willing and hear me, you will eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1).

[Col. 1113C] Because the hour has come to reap—that is, the time foretold through the mouths of the prophets has arrived, and what must now be gathered is the spiritual understanding and faith of Christ.

Because the harvest of the earth has withered—that is, the hearts of the peoples have been prepared to believe, and therefore it is time for them to be cut away from the earth and gathered into the faith of almighty God. Concerning this harvest he himself says in the Gospel: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matthew 9).

[Col. 1113D] And he who was seated upon the cloud sent his sickle upon the earth, because at the voice of Christ they began to preach first to the Jews, until they drove them from their territories. Hence Paul and Barnabas said to them: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first,” and so forth (Acts 5).

And the earth was reaped—that is, all who had been foreordained to eternal life were gathered. Concerning them it has already been written: “If the number of the children of Israel were like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Romans 9).

And another angel came out of the temple that is in heaven. Above he had said that an angel came out of the temple; now he took care to indicate where this temple had been seen. This angel too is Christ. Here, however, we should understand “heaven” simply as the dwelling place of the heavens, where the temple is—that is, the holy angels in whom God dwells.

[Col. 1114A] For if he deigns to dwell in human beings, even sinners, in accordance with: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6), how much more in angels, who are without sin! They themselves are the temple of God because they are continually in his contemplation.

He therefore came out of the temple that is in heaven, not because he withdrew from the contemplation of the angels, but because, by assuming flesh, he appeared visibly to human beings. He too had a sharp sickle—that is, judicial authority, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). Or, as was said, in the sharp sickle [the source reads “in the sharp face”; materially uncertain], heavenly preaching is understood, which divides father from son and son from father, and so forth, as the Lord says in the Gospel—that is, it separates the reprobate from the good.

[Col. 1114B] And another angel came out of the altar. The one who is above is also signified by this angel—that is, Christ, the messenger of the Father’s will. The altar is the same one who is also the high priest, namely Christ, through whom we direct our gifts to God the Father, asking to be heard through Christ.

All the elect are also an altar, to whom the Apostle says: “I appeal to you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12). The angel therefore came out of the altar—that is, Christ was chosen uniquely as prince from the entire multitude of the faithful.

He has authority over the fire. The fire is the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12). He also descended upon the elect in tongues of fire.

[Col. 1114C] Hence it is rightly asked how the angel, who is understood to be Christ, can have authority over the fire—that is, over the Holy Spirit—since he is of one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For God the Father did not, as the heretics say, create the Son from certain subsisting things, nor did the Son himself create the Holy Spirit as something lesser than himself. Since they have one divinity, they also have one essence; and therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance, one power, and one majesty.

But the Son of God has authority over the fire in this respect: no angel or human being receives the Holy Spirit except through the Son. Hence, after rising from the dead, he breathed upon them and said to his disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). And elsewhere: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16).

[Col. 1114D] And he cried out with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle—that is, to the order of preachers, who have divine preaching within them—saying: “Send your sickle and harvest the clusters of the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe.”

What was signified above by the ripe grain is here signified by the clusters of the vine of the earth: namely, all the faithful. Its grapes are ripe—that is, the peoples have been prepared to believe. Then the Lord gave this command, when, appearing to his disciples after his resurrection, he said to them: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 27), and so forth.

And the angel sent his sickle upon the earth, because they went forth and preached everywhere. And he harvested the clusters of the vine of the earth—that is, he separated human beings from earthly understanding and from their former error, and joined them to the unity of faith.

And he cast them into the great vat of the wrath of God. What is understood by the vat—or, as another translation has it, the winepress—if not the distress of human tribulation, [Col. 1115A] into which all, good and evil alike, are cast?

In this tribulation the saints are threshed like grain, so that they may be separated from the chaff and stored in the heavenly granaries. They are also trodden underfoot like grapes in a winepress, so that, pressed free of the grape-skins, they may be enclosed in eternal storehouses.

He therefore sent the sickle and the clusters he had harvested into the winepress, because the holy Church, having been sent to preach, handed over to great tribulations those whom she had separated from earthly love or from their former error. By these tribulations they are afflicted by the impious and tormented in various ways.

Hence the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory” (Romans 8); and elsewhere: “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations.”

[Col. 1115B] It is called the vat of the wrath of God because these tribulations occur on account of human sins. For if the first human being, in whom all sinned, had not sinned, no human being would be cast into the vat—that is, no one would endure these distresses of tribulation. But after he sinned, he was expelled from paradise and cast into the vat of tribulation.

This vat is called great because of the most bitter torments of the elect, by which they are afflicted in the present life. For what greater pressure of distress and tribulation could there be than to crucify a human being, as Peter was crucified, or to be burned, as Lawrence was? The unjust therefore afflict the just temporally, so that afterward merciful God may spare them eternally.

And the winepress was trodden outside the city. By the container, let us understand what is contained, that is, by the winepress, those who are in the winepress. The city, however, outside which they were trodden, is the Church. If, then, as was said above, the winepress signifies the tribulation in which both the good and the wicked are afflicted, what does it mean that they were now trodden outside the city? For if the city itself is being trodden, how are they trodden outside the city?

But it must be understood that here he returns from the general to the particular and speaks only in the person of the reprobate, about whom he will say more in what follows. This is immediately made clear when he adds: “And blood came out of the winepress as far as the horses’ bridles.” For when the saints are pressed, they do not yield blood from themselves, but the purest wine, which is stored in the Lord’s storehouses. The reprobate, however, because they seemed to be within the Church but were not, were cast into the winepress and yielded blood—that is, unbelief. [Col. 1115D]

For blood is understood in different ways in sacred discourse. Sometimes it signifies the propagation of the human offspring, as in the passage: “As many as believed in him, he gave them power to become children of God, who were born not of bloods but of God” (John 1). Sometimes it signifies adultery and murder, as in: “Deliver me from bloods, O God, my God” (Psalm 50). Sometimes it signifies other sins, as in: “Blood touched blood” (Hosea 4). Blood touches blood when sin is added to sin. Sometimes it signifies unbelief, as here, and in Exodus, where the waters are reported to have been changed into blood.

Blood therefore came out of the winepress—that is, the sin of unbelief came out of the pressure of tribulation. The wine that comes forth from the good grapes, which is stored [Col. 1116A] in the Lord’s storehouses, is not mentioned. Instead, blood is said to come forth from wild grapes or, so to speak, winter grapes—that is, from the reprobate, who, mixed together with the grapes, do not reach maturity, but, touched by some tribulation or weighed down by the distress of persecution, immediately withdraw from the faith. Infected with the error of perfidy, they slide outward. For this reason they are said to be trodden outside the city, while the elect remain within, drunk with the wine of faith.

Such was Porphyry, and many others who yielded to persecutions, departing from the faith of Christ and becoming reprobate. And because in this way not only the least of people but also rulers perish, he rightly adds: “as far as the horses’ bridles.” By horses, subjects are understood; by bridles, rulers and prelates, who ought to have governed others [Col. 1116B]—such as Julian the Apostate and emperor. It is as though he said: The temporal affliction was so great that it led even those who seemed to govern others into unbelief. Thus blood is said to have reached as far as the horses’ bridles, as though it were plainly said: Temporal affliction prevailed to such an extent that it stained even those who seemed to govern the peoples with the blood of unbelief.

“For one thousand six hundred stadia.” A *stadium* is a Greek term for a measure in Latin. It is also said to derive from *stando* (“standing”), because Hercules, running one hundred and twenty-five paces in a single breath, stopped there. By this measure the Greeks measured the places in which they held games; there, while playing, walking about, and engaging in amusements, they strolled.

In the one thousand six hundred stadia, therefore, the entire multitude of the reprobate is included, which consists in the four regions [Col. 1116C] of the world, because of the four quarters of this world. For four times four hundred makes one thousand six hundred. In the number one hundred, the totality of something is often understood. The number four, however, pertains to the four regions of the world. Therefore, in the one thousand six hundred, all the reprobate are designated—those who run through the four parts of this world amid the vanities of pleasures and proceed along the broad way that leads to death. For this reason their totality is comprehended by that number.

But what has been said of the first coming may also be referred to the second. No one who considers what the Lord says about the time of the harvest and about the reapers is unaware that the future judgment will be carried out through angels. For he says: “The harvest is the consummation of the age, and the reapers are angels.” The parable of the weeds also agrees with this passage, as does the statement that “the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind,” from which they chose the good into vessels—without doubt, the angels—and cast the wicked outside. But what they will do by the office of their ministry, Christ and the Church will do by their authority.

Let it therefore be said of the angel who had a sharp sickle in his hand—that is, judicial power. For the sickle gathers within itself whatever it cuts, since no one can escape the examination of divine judgment. We are within it, no matter where we try to flee. Rightly, therefore, the Judge who is to come is said to hold a sickle, because when he confronts all things with power, he surrounds everything by cutting it.

Hence the Psalmist says: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Psalm 138), and elsewhere: “Neither from the rising of the sun nor from its setting” (Psalm 74), and so forth—the implied meaning being that there is no place for fleeing, since God is the Judge. It is as though he said: There is no route of escape anywhere, because the one who judges is everywhere.

A recapitulation of what precedes: “And another angel came out of the temple,” because at the judgment he will appear to human beings in human form from the secrecy of his divinity. “Crying out with a loud voice to the one seated upon the cloud.” As was said above, what is called the cloud is the angel to whom Christ cries—that is, the Church—which, because of the unity of its Head, is also said to sit upon the cloud, that is, upon itself. For it would not have been appropriate to say, “The angel who sat upon the cloud cried out to the same cloud.” Therefore he changed the cloud—that is, the Church—into the name of an angel. Nevertheless, what is the cloud is also the angel sitting upon the cloud.

“Send forth your sickle.” This is what the Lord himself says elsewhere to the apostles, and through them to all the perfect: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

“For the hour has come to reap”: that is, the time is at hand when the elect must be rewarded and the reprobate condemned by God’s just judgment.

“For the harvest of the earth has withered”: that is, the end of each person has arrived, when both the chaff—that is, the reprobate—will be handed over to the fire, and the grain will be stored in the Lord’s granary.

“And he who sat upon the cloud sent his sickle into the earth,” and so forth: that is, the Church, sitting with the Lord in the authority of judgment and distinguishing between the good and the wicked, will examine all things.

“And another angel came out of the temple that is in heaven,” and so forth. The one who has the reaping sickle also has the vintage sickle. The one who said to the reaper, “Reap,” also said to the vintager, “Gather the vintage.” For what the standing grain is, the clusters also are; and what the chaff is, the grape-stems are likewise. The rest has been said above.

“He gathered the entire vintage of the earth”: that is, he collected all from the earth, both good and wicked, grain and weeds. And he stored the pure wine—that is, the saints—in the Lord’s storehouse; but the grape-stems—that is, the reprobate—he cast into the winepress of the wrath of God.

By the winepress of the wrath of God, the condemnation of hell or the sentence of divine judgment is understood. The reprobate will be cast into that winepress when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire.” If the term “winepress” did not designate hell, the prophet would certainly not have said: “All the slain and those falling by the sword, who went down uncircumcised to the farthest land, and bore their disgrace with those who go down into the pit.” And the Psalmist says: “You have saved me from those descending into the pit” (Psalm 29).

Therefore, what follows—“great”—is not, according to this interpretation, to be referred to the winepress but to the devil, who is called great because of the boastfulness of his pride. The great one—that is, the devil—with his entire body, he will cast into the winepress of God’s wrath, when all the reprobate, as has been said, are condemned with the devil and his angels.

“And the winepress was trodden”: that is, those who were in the winepress were trodden. They were overwhelmed in eternal death, not now so that they might be cleansed, but so that they might utterly perish. “Outside the city”: that is, outside the fellowship of the saints, with whom the reprobate will then have no communion at all. [Col. 1118A]

“And blood came out of the winepress as far as the horses’ bridles.” By the blood that comes out of the winepress—that is, the sentence of the strict Judge—vengeance is understood: vengeance for the blood and for all the vices on account of which the wicked will be condemned. It reaches as far as the bridles because the sentence of divine judgment will include not only subjects but also kings and rulers themselves, who have served bloodshed and various vices.

As for what follows, “for one thousand six hundred stadia,” in this number, as was said above, the entire multitude of the reprobate is expressed, those who pursue the breadth of this life throughout the fourfold world.

## CHAPTER XV

“And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wondrous.”

Whoever attends carefully to the understanding of the holy Fathers easily recognizes that this Apocalypse cannot at all be taken according to the letter. Heaven, therefore, as has often been said, is the Church, of which the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Acts 7); and elsewhere: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom.” For the Church itself, despising all earthly things, flies upward through the desire of the mind toward heavenly things. Hence Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3); and again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2).

In this heaven—that is, in the Church—John saw a sign, and that sign was great and wondrous. What the sign was, however, he explains when he adds that he saw seven angels. “Having the seven last plagues.” Since the number seven is often used for totality, on account of this time which revolves through seven days, by the seven angels the same thing is understood as by heaven: the universal Church. But because the author of the history frequently returns from the general to the particular, in this passage let us understand by the seven angels all preachers in particular, of whom it is written: “The angels of peace will weep bitterly” (Isaiah 33), and elsewhere: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge” (Malachi 2), and so forth.

What the seven plagues are is made clear in what follows, when those same angels are said to have received seven bowls full of the wrath of God. For the bowls are the same as the angels—that is, the holy preachers. They have seven plagues, namely, knowledge of the whole of Scripture, by which the hearts of the good are wounded for salvation and the hearts of the wicked for destruction.

Some hear the angelic preachers say in the divine discourse: “Neither the greedy, nor adulterers, nor the others whom the Apostle names, will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). Fearing the fire of Gehenna, they are wounded in heart and return to God through the lamentations of repentance. In this way the saints are wounded for their salvation. Hence the holy Church itself says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love,” and again: “The watchmen who go around the city found me; they struck me and wounded me” (Song of Songs 3).

Conversely, when the reprobate hear these things, they despise the words of the preachers. What is salvation for the former is condemnation for the latter.

At this point a question arises: Why does he say that the angels have the seven last plagues, when from the beginning of the world to its end we find that some are wounded for salvation and others for death? The first man, placed in paradise, received a command from God not to touch the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. If he had kept that command, it would have benefited him unto life. But he despised the command, and what had been given to him for life was turned into death. Thus, through a salutary command, he was wounded and died. [Col. 1119A]

God also gave Moses the legal commandments, saying: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20), and other things of the same kind. Some who kept them, such as Moses, Joshua, and many others, had life in them. Others, however, despising them, were wounded, because they lost both their present and their future life.

When the Lord himself preached, some believed in him and some did not. Those who believed in him were saved by doing penance for their former sins; those who refused to believe were condemned. Hence he himself says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15). Hence also this saying: “Whoever believes will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16).

The apostles likewise, when preaching, became for some “the aroma of life unto life,” but for others “the aroma of death unto death” (2 Corinthians 2).

It is the same now. For example, the angel preaches: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Deuteronomy 5), and other things of this kind. Some person hears this and finds it burdensome; he does not wish to hear the angel’s counsel. Therefore he despises his word and does what seems right to him. What could have benefited him for salvation, if he had been willing to believe it, is thus turned into his condemnation.

Likewise, some pagan hears the angel say: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). He hears and refuses to believe; therefore he is wounded by that divine preaching itself, in which he is already declared condemned.

Since these plagues, as was said, have existed from the very beginning of the world, what does John mean when he says that he saw angels having the seven last plagues? It means that then the condemnation of the unbelief of the reprobate will be greater, when, while Elijah and Enoch preach, few will listen to them, whereas many, following unbelief, will cling to Antichrist. Hence he adds: “For in these the wrath of God is completed”—that is, it will be completed. For Christ will immediately come to judgment after their final preaching, and the wicked will be condemned for their unbelief and obstinacy of mind, by which they abandoned Christ and, moreover, killed the servants of God.

“And I saw something like a glassy sea mixed with fire.” Those who have the seven bowls and the seven plagues are the ones who stand upon the sea. The sea signifies baptism, as Paul testifies when he says: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10).

It is called glassy because of the purity of faith manifested in baptism, when they confess that they believe in God the Father, his Son, and the Holy Spirit, as Paul says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

But the sea itself is mixed with fire, and by this it has been coagulated. In the fire, the Holy Spirit is understood, or also the passion of our Redeemer. For through the grace of the Holy Spirit the faithful are baptized in remembrance of the Lord’s passion. Hence John says of this same Redeemer: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (John 1); and Paul says: “As many of us as were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6).

The sea was coagulated by fire because, through the power of the Holy Spirit, the faithful are strengthened, so that they do not waver or, through any frost of persecution, become soft. Of this water the Psalmist says: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing,” and so forth, continuing to: “He led me beside the waters of refreshment” (Psalm 22).

“And those who conquered the beast and its image”—that is, Antichrist—“and the number of its name.” Those who did not believe that he was the sun or the light, I saw, it is understood, standing upon the glassy sea. [Col. 1120B]

Who are those who stand upon the glassy sea? They are those who hold to what they professed in baptism and preserve the grace of baptism undefiled, abstaining from all more serious crimes.

“Having the harps of God.” They themselves are harps, because they mortify themselves in remembrance of the Lord’s passion. For, as was said above, there is wood and there are strings in a harp. In the wood the cross is understood; in the strings, the hearts of the saints, who mortify themselves with their vices and desires. Of these Paul says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5).

“And singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying”: In the song of Moses, the Old Testament is understood; in the song of the Lamb, the New Testament. This must be understood from what follows, for they reveal what the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb are when they add:

“Great and wondrous are your works, Lord God almighty.”

The pages of both Testaments testify to this with harmonious voice: the works of almighty God are great and wondrous. Moses also recounts how God made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; how the Spirit of God was borne over the waters; and how he saw the bush burning without being consumed. He also tells of the rod changed into a serpent, the waters of Egypt changed into blood, Egypt struck with ten plagues, and the sea divided at the entry of the children of Israel. Then he tells of the bitter waters sweetened by the addition of wood, of water brought forth from the rock for the thirsty people, and many things like these [Col. 1120D] that are commemorated in the Old Testament, that is, in the song of Moses.

In the New Testament likewise, great and wondrous works of God are recounted. Who could worthily explain how great a work it is that God became man; that he who is the food of all is nourished with a woman’s milk lest he die of hunger; that he who fills heaven and earth is enclosed within the body of one virgin? Who is sufficient to speak of or contemplate these things and those like them worthily?

Yet while divine compassion endured all these things, while he raised the dead and healed the sick, finally—and this is especially wondrous—it came to pass that life died, power became weak, and he endured many things like these, until, after the triumph of the resurrection, he was exalted above all [Col. 1121A]. These works of God the holy angels—that is, all preachers—proclaim; all of them recount these things to their hearers.

We too, if not worthily, nevertheless according to our measure, ought to do this, saying: “Great and wondrous are your works, Lord God almighty. Although you were the Word abiding in the beginning with the Father, in a new order you put on humanity; you died for us, were wondrously raised, were lifted above the heavens, and will come again for judgment.”

“Your ways are just and true, King of the ages.”

We read in Genesis that almighty God withdrew from the whole human race after he had destroyed it with the waters of the flood, but clung to Noah and his sons because they were found to be righteous. Then, lifted up in pride after they had multiplied, they wished to build a tower against God; and there all the nations withdrew [Col. 1121B] from the worship of God except the offspring of Abraham.

Almighty God therefore abandoned them and clung to Abraham and his seed, who worshiped him for a long time. But after the Son of God came to them, they denied him, saying: “We do not know where he is from” (John 9), and, “He has a demon” (Matthew 11). Hence they handed him over to death. He withdrew from them and passed over to the Gentiles.

These are the just and true ways of almighty God, because it is just before the Almighty that he remain with those who cling to him through faith and love, but abandon those who withdraw from him. By the ways of God we must understand his actions, which are just, because God can do nothing unjustly. For when he condemns some and mercifully frees others, he is recognized as a just Judge toward the former and as merciful toward the latter.

Let us place two sinners before our eyes, so that this may become clearer. Both hear the divine commandments, which contain rewards for the just and punishments for the reprobate. One of them, by God’s mercy, is pierced with remorse, does penance, and is saved; the other, persisting in his crimes, is condemned by God’s just judgment on account of his sin.

Therefore “just ways”—that is, actions—are just because God is a just Judge, and in one person his mercy appears, while in the other his justice appears. For if he did not condemn the reprobate, he would seem—God forbid—to approve iniquity. Therefore, whoever presumes to flatter himself on the basis of God’s mercy should also see that he is a just Judge.

Those who triumph well over the beast rightly say in praise of the Lord: “Your ways are just and true, King of the ages.” It is as though they said: Even when you lead the Gentiles, upon whom you ought to have inflicted wrath, to mercy, you do not cease to be just. And when, in anger, you reject the Jews, to whom you had promised to give a reward for observing the law, you in no way lose your truth.

“Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify your name?”

The meaning is this: Since your judgments are now known to be true, and since, without any preceding merits of human beings, you free whom you will while duly punishing others for their sins, what Jew or Gentile will not fear you? That is, who will not reverence your name? And who will not glorify your name, according to the saying: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise” (Psalm 47)?

“For you alone are merciful”: because, through gratuitous compassion, you predestine and save some who deserved death, bringing them to life.

“For all nations will come by the steps of faith and of the heart,” because the Jews denied you.

“And they will worship in your presence”: that is, with a pure heart, which you alone see. Concerning this worship the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “The hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4).

“For your judgments have been revealed.”

At this point a question arises: Why do those triumphing over the beast say, “Your judgments have been revealed,” when the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Romans 11)?

The question is resolved as follows. No one can comprehend the subtlety of God’s judgments—namely, why he wills one thing to happen and another not to happen. For who can say why God, who previously allowed the Gentiles to walk freely in their own ways, took the Jews to himself and then, rejecting the Jews, called the Gentiles?

His judgments are nevertheless revealed in this respect: they are just. For everyone who knows the truth understands that whatever God has done is just.

“After these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of the Testimony in heaven was opened.”

The tabernacle and heaven are one thing, namely, the Church. In this heaven the temple was opened, as was said above: the mysteries of Christ were revealed in the Church—his birth, death, passion, and resurrection, and other things of this kind.

The Church itself is called the tabernacle of the Testimony because it possesses the tablets of the two Testaments. It also contains within itself the ark, the Lord Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and [Col. 1122C] knowledge; and the urn, namely, the Lord’s body, in which is the true bread that descended from heaven. There too is the rod of Aaron, which had blossomed—that is, the spiritual priesthood, which prefigured the true priesthood of the Church.

John says that the temple of the tabernacle of the Testimony in heaven was opened, although, as he had said, the tabernacle and heaven are one, as though dividing a genus into its parts, just as was said above concerning the ark and the eight souls.

“And seven angels having the seven plagues came out of the temple.”

In the seven angels, as has often been said, all preachers are understood, because the number seven is used for totality. These have seven plagues—that is, the fullness of doctrine—by which, as was said above, the hearts of some are wounded for salvation and the hearts of others for destruction.

The temple from which the angels came out signifies the secrecy of their hearts. For when holy preachers devote themselves to contemplation, they make themselves strangers to all the world’s activities; and when they meditate upon the divine words, they dwell, as it were, in the temple—that is, in the secrecy of their minds.

But they must not devote themselves to their own concerns in such a way that they abandon the needs of others. When they again come out into public life, to preach, to shape the conduct of carnal people, or to administer temporal matters, they come forth, as it were, from the temple.

Thus, while longing for inward things, they sit in the temple, and, while not neglecting the care of their neighbors, they come out from the temple. For example, a teacher or any person may be about to go out in public to deliver a sermon to the people. First, while sitting, he gathers himself within himself, considering what he ought to say, to whom he ought to speak, and how he ought to speak; how he should begin the sermon and how he should end it.

Behold: while he dwells within the secrecy of his mind in this way, he remains, as it were, in the temple. But when he proceeds to preach and publicly brings forth what he had considered in his mind, he comes out, as it were, from the temple—that is, from the secrecy of his mind.

“Clothed in a pure and shining stone.”

That is, adorned with and clothed in the Lord Jesus Christ, according to the saying: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3). He is rightly called the stone with which the elect are surrounded, because he is an impenetrable wall. He is pure because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2). He is called shining because he is the brightness of eternal light and the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world.

Or, if we read “clothed in pure stones,” as is found in certain manuscripts, these stones designate the virtues: hope, faith, charity, chastity, humility, and others of this kind, with which the faithful are adorned.

Another translation has “clothed in pure linen,” by which purity of life and chaste innocence are understood. For linen grows from the earth and is brought to the brightness of beauty through much labor, because chastity, or a pure life, is acquired through much labor and mortification of the flesh. Concerning these garments Solomon says: “Let your garments always be white” (Ecclesiastes 9).

“And girded about the breasts with golden belts.”

By the belt with which their breasts were girded, the bond of chastity is shown. This signifies that in the New Testament not only the act of lust but even the thought itself is restrained by the strength of the mind. The Old Testament says: “Whoever commits adultery shall be punished”; but the New says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5).

Or certainly, by the golden belt the bond of charity is understood, because the saints bind one another not through fear of punishment but through charity, by the love of God alone. Or again, by the golden belts wisdom is signified, concerning which it is written: “Receive wisdom as gold.” The breasts of the angels are girded with golden belts because the hearts of the elect are filled with heavenly wisdom; they themselves continually praise God and call others to praise him.

“And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls, full of the wrath of the living God, who lives for ever and ever.”

Above we read that he saw four living creatures, which signify both the four Evangelists and all the saints, or even the Lord himself, who became man by being born temporally from a virgin. He became a calf in his passion, in which he offered himself to God upon the altar of the cross; he became a lion when he rose from the dead on the third day; and an eagle when he ascended into heaven on the fortieth day.

This one living creature—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—gave the seven angels seven bowls. What the seven angels are, the seven bowls also are: holy preachers filled with divine preaching. For in order that they might be angels—that is, messengers of eternal life—they became bowls filled [Col. 1124A] with the word of wisdom.

But because it would have been absurd and less fitting to say, “One living creature gave seven angels seven angels,” he varied the expression, saying: “One living creature gave seven angels seven bowls.”

Alternatively, by the living creature that gave the seven angels seven bowls we may understand the order of the elect—the apostles and the others—who gave bowls to their successors, that is, entrusted divine preaching to them. For they not only baptized them but also ordained them and caused them to sit in their place, as Peter did with Clement, Linus, and Cletus. To them he also handed on the power of binding and loosing that he had received from the Lord, and compelled them to sit in his chair.

This too is done every day, when, through the laying on of hands, bishops of souls are established in the cities.

The bowls they receive are rightly described as golden, because, in order that they may fulfill the office of preaching, they are enlightened from heaven by the radiance of wisdom.

But since above he said of the elders that they held bowls full of fragrances, what does it mean that here it is said of the angels that they received seven bowls full of the wrath of the living God, who lives for ever and ever? They are the same angels as the elders, because in their teaching the salvation of the elect is complete, while the condemnation of the reprobate is also complete; from the same source from which the former receive life, the latter receive death.

Hence the Apostle says: “To some we are the aroma of life unto life, to others the aroma of death unto death” (2 Corinthians 2). For this reason the Lord himself is said to be appointed for the falling of some and for the rising of others.

[Col. 1124C] And the temple was filled with smoke from the majesty of God and from his power. In this passage, “temple” signifies the weak hearts of simple-minded brothers, to whom it seems unjust that almighty God permits the wicked to reign in this life and to prosper in every honor, wealth, and bodily health, while, on the contrary, he allows his saints to be crucified, stoned, burned, and to end their present life through various torments, nor can they ever have rest in the present life. For example, Nero, the most impious emperor, who even transformed a male into a woman, ruled the whole world. Peter, however, chief of all the apostles, was seized and crucified by him. Paul too, father of all the nations, who labored more than all the others, was beheaded by him.

Smoke signifies [Col. 1124D] the blindness of ignorance with which the hearts of such unbelievers are filled. They do not know how to consider that God is going to give them an inheritance as sons, and therefore he permits them to be afflicted for a time, so that shortly afterward they may rejoice with him without end. And this is done by the majesty and power of God. Great indeed is God’s power in this matter, since he can endure a wicked man’s being emperor and lord of the whole world, and his chosen suffering evils at that man’s hands.

And no one of such people, it is understood, could enter the temple—that is, no one could investigate the subtlety of the judgments of almighty God—until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed; that is, until all the preaching of the Church had reached its end. When the seven plagues of the seven angels have been completed, [Col. 1125A] that is, when all the Church’s preaching has reached its conclusion and Christ has come to judgment to repay each person according to his works, then these judgments of almighty God, which are now hidden, will be revealed. Then the reprobate, who here flourish in honor and dignities, will be led to punishment, while the just, who in this world endured the torments and punishments inflicted by them, will be raised to the kingdom.

In the person of such people the Psalmist says: “I considered this in order to understand it; it is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny.” The saints who have golden bowls enter the temple of God, because they consider and perceive the judgments of almighty God and recognize that everything is just. Thus they know both the torments of those who are exalted in the present [Col. 1125B] and hold dominion, and the rewards of those who are humbled and endure the rule of other men. Therefore “no one” must be understood of those who attempt to criticize the judgments of almighty God.

The same applies to John’s statement about Christ: “No one accepts his testimony.” And to the Psalmist’s statement: “There is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13). In what follows, the same John says: “Whoever accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.” For there are some whose “no one” accepts Christ’s testimony, such as the wretched Jews; and again, there are some who accept his testimony and know that God is true.

Thus, in this passage too, “no one could enter the temple” is to be understood in this way.

Alternatively: the temple signifies the hearts of the holy [Col. 1125C] elect, while smoke signifies contrition of heart, because the hearts and breasts of sinners are pierced with compunction, even to their inmost depths and to tears. The temple is filled with smoke when the hearts of certain criminals are filled with the lament of repentance.

For example, some sinner hears a preacher speaking wisely and learnedly, saying what the Apostle says: “Neither adulterers, nor the unclean, nor fornicators, nor others of this kind will possess the kingdom of God.” As each sinner hears and considers what immense torments of hell threaten him, he is pierced in heart and gives forth smoke—that is, contrition of heart—when he confesses his sin with tears.

Smoke precedes a great fire, because from the confession of sin and contrition of heart arises the fire of charity. First [Col. 1125D] a person confesses his sin; afterward he begins to love the Lord his God and his neighbor very greatly. And this is done by the majesty and power of God, because God by his power enlightens the heart of the person who repents; he is the one who produces confession of sins in human hearts.

Therefore the Psalmist also sings: “Confession and magnificence are before him.” And elsewhere: “He touches the mountains, and they smoke” (Psalms 110, 103)—that is, he pierces the minds of worldly and proud people by the regard of his mercy, and they utter the laments and weeping of repentance.

But although this is so, no one can enter the temple—that is, no one can be certain about his conscience, whether he has obtained forgiveness and remission of his sins. For he does not know [Col. 1126A] whether he is worthy of hatred or of love until the seven plagues of the seven angels are ended—that is, until all the preaching of the holy Church has reached its term and conclusion, when Christ will come to repay every human being according to his works.

## CHAPTER XVI

“And I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels: Go and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth.”

This voice is the voice of almighty God. It is rightly called loud because it commands great things. The temple, as has often been said, is the holy Church. The seven angels are all holy preachers. The voice comes from the temple to the angels because Christ speaks from the Church to the preachers, since they themselves are the Church.

[Col. 1126B] He therefore says: “Go, pour out upon the earth the bowls of the wrath of God which you have received.” This is what he himself says to his disciples, as to the first angels: “Go to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 10). Elsewhere we read that he sent them ahead of him into every place where he himself was going to come.

Why, however, are they called bowls of the wrath of God? This was stated above: from the same source from which some receive the pardon of reconciliation, others receive the wrath of retribution. By “earth” are signified earthly hearts of human beings. The angels therefore pour out a bowl upon the earth when the holy preachers speak against earthly people.

Hence it follows:

“And the first went and poured out his bowl upon the earth.”

A question arises here. If they were commanded to pour out their bowls upon the earth, why is it that, as though transgressing the command, one poured his bowl upon the earth, [Col. 1126C] another upon the sea, another upon the rivers and springs of waters, another upon the sun, another upon the throne of the beast, another upon the great river Euphrates, and another upon the air? As far as the literal meaning is concerned, they seem to transgress the command, but they do not do so with regard to the mystical meaning. For what is the earth is also the sea and the rest: that is, the entire body of the devil together with its head.

Likewise, what is one angel is the seven, and what are the seven is the one. For just as Christ together with his head is one—because he himself is the head and the elect are the members, and the members are nothing other than the head—so the devil and all the wicked are one body, bound together by the unity of wickedness.

Although “earth” may be understood as the entire multitude of the reprobate, concerning which it was said to the devil in the beginning, “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Genesis 3), nevertheless in this passage we can understand “earth,” upon which the first bowl was poured, specifically as the Jewish people.

Concerning this earth Job says: “The earth from which bread came forth in its place was consumed by fire.” That is, the Jews, from whom the divine utterances proceeded, were slain in their own place by the sin of unbelief and the fire of envy.

Thus the angel poured out his bowl upon the earth because the apostles, at Christ’s command, began to preach the remission of sins, beginning from Jerusalem. Christ himself, who is the prince of the angels, also preached in that same land. Since they refused to believe in him, they were condemned in the sin of their unbelief.

Hence it follows:

“And a grievous and most malignant sore came upon the people [Col. 1127A] who have the mark of the beast and upon those who worshiped his image.”

This sore is not of the body but of the mind. It is the sin of unbelief, by which the Jews were wounded because they refused to believe in Christ. Hence the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse” (John 15). By this sore the Jews died.

The unbelieving among the nations also appear to die from it, but the Jews more grievously than the nations, because they had the law, received knowledge of God, and heard him himself preaching in the flesh. The Gentiles possessed none of these things, unless they despised the preaching of Christ that they heard through the apostles. Therefore they too will be condemned, but the others more harshly.

For this reason it is written: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged.” Therefore he did not simply say that a grievous or a most malignant sore had occurred, but joined the two terms, “grievous and most malignant,” to magnify the size of this wound—as though he were saying, “irremediable and deadly”—by which alone, even if other sins are absent, any person who is wounded is judged worthy to be punished with eternal penalty.

And because he describes the final blindness of the Jews, who are going to receive Antichrist in place of Christ, in accordance with the saying: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive,” he rightly calls those who seem to bear the mark of the beast and worship his image people most grievously wounded by Christ’s preaching.

The mark of the beast, as was said above, is understood as his faith. The Jews already bear this mark, believing in him and awaiting him, ready to receive him with complete devotion of heart. Then they will openly receive the one whom they now hold with their entire desire. They also worship his image—that is, Antichrist himself—now through their desire and longing, but then they will be prostrate before him in mind and body.

Indeed, it is fitting that those who, swollen with pride, reject the fattened calf should receive the kid: that is, those who despise Christ should receive Antichrist. We should therefore understand this specifically of them, although it also appears generally applicable to unbelieving Gentiles.

For the Jews themselves will have many, indeed innumerable, followers among the unbelieving Gentiles in receiving Antichrist, just as the apostles had many imitators in the faith of Christ.

Moreover, it should be known that just as the Jews and Gentiles, because they despise the preaching of the Church, will receive Antichrist as one wound added to another, so the reprobate established within the holy Church, because they confess Christ rightly but deny him by their works, should, when the moment of persecution approaches, lose the profession that they carry only on their tongues. They will bear the mark through denial of the faith, the mark that they had long secretly borne in the works of their hands, and they will openly follow the same Antichrist after whom they had long secretly walked.

“And the second angel poured out his bowl upon the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead man.”

In the sea there is water. Therefore it must first be considered what the water is, and [Col. 1128A] then how it was changed into blood. The law of the Old Testament is water, subsequently changed into living water through Christ’s wedding.

Scripture was given to the Jews as sweet water, by which they could be saved if they believed in the Christ promised to them. But they turned that same Scripture into the bitterness of unbelief by denying Christ and handing him over to death, and into blood—that is, into a carnal understanding.

Thus the sea became blood, just as blood truly exists in the body of a dead man, because they genuinely turned the law to their own destruction, since they always wished to understand it carnally and never passed over to its spiritual meaning.

But those are shown to perish through this pollution more dangerously who, to their own condemnation, are reported to have denied Christ before Pilate, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27).

“And every living soul died in the sea.”

Here a part is understood from the whole. For not everyone dies under the carnal meaning of the law, since many now, by God’s grace, understand spiritually those things that happened to them in figure.

The same applies to the saying: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13). For in this sea—that is, in sacred Scripture—is contained the life of the 153 fish that were caught in the apostles’ net.

For the fish being caught in the apostles’ net means that, among the elect, the waters are by no means changed into blood. Therefore “every living soul died in the sea” must be understood only of those who attend to nothing in the law except the letter, like the Jews, [Col. 1128C] who, above all, have not been dead since the time when the faithful began to live through spiritual meanings.

“And the third poured out his bowl upon the rivers and upon the springs of waters, and they became blood.”

What the first angel is, so are the second and the third, and finally all of them—that is, all the preachers. By the rivers and springs of waters, however, the Gentiles are signified, just as above by the sea.

A river tends downward from its beginning and pours into the sea. In the same way, the Gentile world, overtaken by unbelief, ran toward death. Yet among their philosophers the Gentile world received its bowl—that is, sacred Scripture and knowledge of God.

For example, Plato, placed in Egypt by Jeremiah, learned that almighty God made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them. But he turned this bowl into blood—that is, into the depravity of error—when he said that the heavenly beings, that is, the angels, made the rest, namely the lesser creation.

Virgil too learned from Daniel’s book about the four kingdoms preordained by God, one of which is golden. But he turned this into blood when he attributed it to Saturn and Jupiter and called them the founders of those kingdoms.

Hence the teacher of the nations says: “To think according to the flesh is death,” and again: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God.”

“And I heard the angel of the waters”—that is, the messenger of the peoples, since, as we read below, many waters are many peoples—“saying: You are just, who were holy.”

The past tense is used here [Col. 1129A] for all three times: past, present, and future. “You who were holy, you are just, and you will be.” This justice is manifested in what follows: “because,” he says, “you judged these things, since they poured out the blood of the saints and prophets, and you gave them blood to drink.”

For it is just before you that, because they poured out the blood of your saints, they themselves should drink blood. That is, they should suffer retribution for the blood they shed, and those who, while good things were being announced to them, not only failed to listen but also cruelly killed the announcers should by no means come to knowledge of you.

This is to be understood both of the Jews and of the Gentiles. The Jews poured out the blood of the holy prophets: they killed Ezekiel, cut Isaiah to pieces, and stoned Jeremiah. Therefore Stephen also reproached them in the dispute he had with them, saying: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One.”

The Gentiles likewise poured out much blood of holy martyrs: Nero crucified Peter, beheaded Paul, and killed many others. All these later drank blood by God’s just judgment—that is, they suffered the retribution for bloodshed—either in the present, as did the Jews and Nero, so that they would lose both the present and the future life, or, condemned in hell, when they were handed over to eternal torments.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The blood of all the saints will be required from this generation of reprobates, blood which has been poured out upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah.”

Alternatively: “the blood of the holy [Col. 1129C] prophets” is understood as their spiritual meaning. Therefore whoever pours out the blood of the prophets or of the other saints—that is, whoever turns their spiritual meaning into an earthly understanding—will drink blood, that is, will suffer the retribution for bloodshed.

This means that he will lose whatever appears to be vital in him and will remain in a carnal understanding, by the just judgment of God. For they are worthy. It is fitting that the one who refused to drink spiritual wine should be made drunk with the corruptions of vices as with blood.

“And I heard another”—the word “word” is understood—“saying: Yes, Lord God almighty, your judgments are just and true.”

He did not say, “I heard another one saying,” lest we understand another angel; rather, “I heard another saying” means that another word was repeated by him.
