For the same [Col. 1129D] angel who had spoken the preceding words added this statement as well, saying: “Yes, Lord God almighty, your judgments are just and true,” because it is just that those who poured out blood should drink blood—that is, suffer the retribution for bloodshed.

This can be understood specifically of heretics, from whose mouths an abundance of words seems to flow like rivers. But these people, who pour out the blood of saints and prophets, having been turned into blood, drink blood. For when they change the words of the law, the utterances of the prophets, and the sayings of the apostles into false meanings, then, when the moment of persecution arrives, they lose the very name of Christ, which they falsely held, by openly serving the vices of the flesh.

Let it therefore be said: “You are just, who were holy, who judged these things,” [Col. 1130A] and so forth—as though it were saying: Since they perverted the words of the law, the utterances of the prophets, and the sayings of the apostles, and thereby, as it were, killed the prophets, it is fitting that through temporal scourges—which previously they trampled underfoot—they should drink before human beings the very blood that they shed and with which they stained their own souls. That is, they should publicly deny your name, which they falsely worshiped, and presume to repeat the corruptions of the flesh, which they had restrained as though for the sake of empty glory.

“And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun.”

The sun has various meanings in sacred Scripture, and it is used both in a good and in a bad sense. Sometimes it signifies Christ, concerning whom it is written: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise” (Zechariah 3). Sometimes it signifies the tribulation of the present life, in accordance with what is said in the parable of the seed that was sown: some fell upon the rock, and as soon as the sun rose, it withered.

Here, however, let us understand the sun as that condemned man himself who, in the last days, will falsely present himself as the sun of righteousness, although the thickest darkness and the shadow of death are in him.

The angel therefore pours out his bowl upon the sun when the preachers proclaim the word of preaching against Antichrist and his ministers.

“And it was given to him to afflict people with heat and with fire.”

This may be referred to both. Heat signifies the severe persecution by which Antichrist will afflict people—that is, the saints who have remained in the faith, such as Elijah and Enoch. It was given to him by God—that is, he was permitted to afflict people with heat and fire, with an exceedingly powerful persecution such as never was and never will be, as the Lord says in the Gospel.

Hence it follows:

“And the people were scorched with great heat.”

For, as was said, there will then be a tribulation such as has not been and will not be, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led astray (Matthew 24).

Alternatively: those who will be tortured will afflict with heat—that is, with great anger and distress—those by whom torments have been inflicted upon them. For their persecutors will be able to kill them before separating them from the faith of Christ; when they see them unconquerable, they themselves will burn with a great heat of anger, indignant at those whom they see remaining steadfast amid their torments.

This too happened in the persecution of the holy martyrs, but then it will happen with much greater force, in proportion to the severity of the tribulation. These people—that is, the reprobate—will be more severely tortured [Col. 1130D] in soul than the saints in body. The saints will revive amid their torments, while the others will gnash their teeth. The saints will praise God, while the others will become almost lifeless.

Thus they will afflict people who are wise according to human standards: they will make them consumed by the flames of envy and malice, while they remain unconquerable unto death.

Hence it follows: “And they blasphemed the name of the Lord, who has power over these plagues.”

When they see the saints patiently and firmly persevering in the faith unto death and joyfully going to their martyrdom, they will blaspheme the Lord. He is said to have power over these plagues because he removes them from whomever he wishes and, by just judgment, permits them to fall upon whomever he wishes, in accordance with the saying: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exodus 11).

“And they did not repent.”

Why did they not repent? Because they could not. Why could they not? Because they did not wish to. And why did they not wish to? Because they could not.

Blessed Ansbertus Ambrose says something else: “If I were asked a thousand times why they did not repent, I would not answer.”

“That they might give him glory”—that is, that they might recognize themselves as sinners and praise the just judgments of God. For the one gives glory to God who both accuses himself for his iniquities and praises God’s just judgments. On the contrary, it is the habit of the wicked to defend their iniquities and criticize the judgments of God.

“And the fifth angel poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast, and his kingdom became dark.”

What is the throne of the beast is his kingdom—that is, the entire body of the devil: evil rulers together with the peoples subject to them. The devil is called a beast because, whether lying in wait secretly or raging openly, he attempts to attack the Lamb—that is, the body of Christ.

When he says, “His kingdom became dark,” it is as though he were saying, “It was not illuminated,” because they do not deserve to be enlightened on account of their preceding merits. They too have been wounded by the darts of their preceding offenses, by which their hearts are wounded.

Hence it follows: “And they gnawed their tongues because of the pain.”

According to the literal sense, this cannot in any way stand: how could one person tear another’s tongue when he is gnawing his own because of his pains? Thus, when it says that they gnawed their tongues because of the pain, it is as though it were saying: Each one tore apart both his own tongue and another’s. But “they gnawed” means nothing other than this: openly and in the light they uttered blasphemies against Christ, encouraging one another to confess Antichrist as justly worthy of confession and to blaspheme Christ as unjustly.

Therefore it adds:

“And they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their wounds.”

After saying that they gnawed their tongues because of the pain, and then adding that they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains, it shows that gnawing their tongues means blaspheming the God of heaven through mutual encouragement.

This pain is insensible: it is the sin of unbelief, which unbelievers suffer without perceiving their own pain, just as madmen endure injury and think themselves healthy. Because they refused to withdraw from the sin of unbelief, they fell into such wickedness that they blasphemed the God of heaven.

This blasphemy occurs in two ways: by the voice and by the hardness of the heart. Although blasphemy of the mouth is destructive, hardness of heart is still more destructive.

“And they did not repent of their works.”

It is as though it were said: The pain arising from the wound of blasphemy so violently crushed them that they could not rise at all to fruitful repentance, because, hardening themselves, they did not wish to return to repentance.

“And the sixth angel poured out his bowl upon that great river Euphrates, and dried up its waters.”

The Euphrates is a river of Babylonia, which, as is said, upon entering Babylon divides into many streams. This river is often used in a bad sense. Hence the saying: “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Psalm 126). Jeremiah too says: “The sacrifice of the Lord of hosts is in the land of the north, by the great river Euphrates.”

By the great river Euphrates, therefore, the power of this world is expressed, together with the whole multitude of the wicked, against whom the holy preachers speak without ceasing. This river is divided into many streams because the multitude of the wicked is divided among many crimes. Some are murderers, some adulterers, and others stained by various crimes.

Its water will be dried up because the ability to sin will be taken away. When the reprobate have been condemned with the devil and his angels, every opportunity for sinning will be removed. Nevertheless, an evil will will remain, because, if it were possible, they would wish to live eternally, sin eternally, and eternally persecute and afflict the saints.

Therefore the Lord will by no means say to those who are rejected, “Depart from me, you who have worked iniquity,” but rather, “you who work iniquity,” as though he were saying: “You who still possess the will to practice evil.”

Hence the Psalmist says: “The sinner watches the just and seeks to put him to death.” For if it were possible, just as Nero killed Peter in this life, so he would wish to kill him in the judgment.

Let it therefore be said of the angel: “He poured out his bowl upon the river Euphrates and dried up its water.” It is as though it were said: When the preaching of heavenly life was offered, it stirred the reprobate to such great wickedness that, although no opportunity to practice evil remained for them, an iniquitous will nevertheless remained.

“That the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun.”

These kings are understood as the saints, who rule themselves and others well and restrain the movements of their flesh by ruling them. They are said to come from the rising of the sun because they are called by the Lord, who is the true sun of righteousness.

But in order that the way may be prepared for these kings, the water of the Euphrates is first dried up. For unless the wickedness of the evil had first reached completion, they would by no means appear for judgment. These kings pass through them when they judge their wickedness after it has been completed; and when every opportunity for sinning has been removed, those who are to judge them will themselves be rewarded after their condemnation.

First these people will hear: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” Then the others will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matthew 25).

Another translation has: “That the way might be prepared for the King who comes from the rising of the sun,” namely Christ, concerning whom the Prophet says: “Behold, a man whose name is Rising.” For when he comes to judge, the way will now be prepared for the one of whom this was said.

“And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet.”

What the dragon is, the beast and the false prophet are also: that is, the devil together with his entire body. Nevertheless, because of the distinction of persons and of the powers that have greater authority within that body of the wicked, they are mentioned separately: the dragon, that is, the devil; the beast, Antichrist; and the false prophet, the teachers of that condemned man together with the peoples subject to them.

From the mouth of all these three come forth three spirits, which is nothing other than one spirit. Such is the unity of wickedness among all the demons [Col. 1133A] that, although they are many in power and wickedness, they are nevertheless reduced to one because they attack human beings in different ways.

Thus one is called the spirit of falsehood, another the spirit of fornication, and a third an unclean spirit. He is said to have seen three unclean spirits according to their number, namely, the parts of the same body.

The unclean spirit is rightly so called because of the grave sins by which it has been defiled and by which it does not cease to defile others. But because head and members are one—that is, the devil and all the wicked—the very ones who are unclean spirits are the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet.

Therefore the spirit came forth from the mouth of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet—that is, from themselves—to open blasphemy against Christ and open persecution against his saints. For now, while they remain hidden and do not dare to rage openly, they rest, as it were, within themselves.

But when the devil has entered the lost man, then they will come forth to open blasphemy, as we have said, and to persecute the saints.

Nor is it without significance that these spirits are said to have come forth in the form of frogs. Frogs cause annoyance to people, make a racket, take away their peace, and wallow in mud. Such will be the ministers of Antichrist. They will seem not to speak but rather to make a racket with chattering voices. They will also remove all rest from the elect when they pursue them everywhere with great severity, and will wallow in mud—that is, in the filth of sins.

“For they are spirits of demons performing signs.”

The demons themselves will perform signs through those whom they inhabit, [Col. 1133C] either true signs by God’s permission or false ones, by which the reprobate will be deceived through God’s just judgment. Thus the magicians once appeared to raise people from the dead, as Simon did in Nero’s presence.

The Lord also speaks of this in the Gospel: “In those days false Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will perform great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led astray” (Matthew 24).

But it is not without reason that those who perform signs are said to proceed in the form of frogs. For we read in the history of the Old Testament that, when Moses performed signs, the magicians did likewise up to the sign of the frogs.

For example, first Moses threw down his staff, and it was changed into a dragon; the magicians did the same by their incantations, although Moses’ staff swallowed their staffs. [Col. 1133D] Then he changed the waters of the Nile into blood; they too did the same with the waters of the cisterns that the Egyptians had dug for themselves, since they did not wish to drink from the river water.

Moses also caused frogs to rise over the land, and they too were permitted to do this by their magical arts. But when gnats came forth after the staff struck the dust of the earth, the incantations that had already prevailed three times completely vanished. Therefore, having been defeated, they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 11).

So these too will reach the sign of the frogs, but there they will fail and, defeated, become still, because their foolishness—that of the condemned man and the false prophets—will become manifest, just as theirs did. Hence the Apostle says: “As Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these too will resist the truth” (2 Timothy 3).

But these signs, as was said, will either be true, by God’s permission, or false, by which the reprobate will deserve to be deceived on account of their former sins. Therefore they are not said to perform them in the presence of the saints but in the presence of human beings, as was said above—that is, in the presence of those who do not understand the things of God but the things of human beings.

In the presence of the elect, however, they will appear mute, and they will not be able to proceed beyond the appointed sign of the frogs.

“And they go out to the kings of the whole earth to gather them for battle on the great day of almighty God.”

That one devil is signified by the three unclean spirits is shown by this going forth, concerning which it is written elsewhere: “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out and deceive the kings and the nations that are upon the four corners of the earth” (Revelation 20).

Here “kings” must be understood in a bad sense: the rulers and wealthy people of this world, who are members of Antichrist.

How, then, do they go out to them if they themselves are the people in whom the demons dwell? They go out to them through those same people—that is, toward open blasphemies and to stir up persecution.

Hence it follows:

“To gather them for battle against God and his saints.”

Where will he gather them? Will they come together in one place, so that those who are in the West will travel to the East, or again from the East to the West? No. They will be gathered into one agreement and one evil will. Because of the unity of their wickedness this is said: what one does, the others also do.

The day [Col. 1134C] on which they will be gathered for battle is understood as the final persecution, when the devil and his members will fight openly against Christ through blasphemies and against his Church through persecutions.

He is waging war even now, but secretly, because he is bound. If he does so much while bound, how much do we suppose he will do when released? Then he will gather them for battle, when he raises up the most grievous persecutions against them.

Therefore that day is rightly called both great and God’s day, because then the victorious Lamb, together with his own, will fight against the most savage beasts.

Behold, I am coming like a thief. We can understand this coming both as daily and as universal. For Christ comes daily like a thief whenever a person dies suddenly by an unforeseen death, while he is not expecting it. On the day of judgment also he will come like a thief, that is, suddenly, because when they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will overtake them. Blessed, however, are those who, whether they pass through death daily or, at that time, come to the general resurrection, are found prepared. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Keep watch, lest when the Lord comes suddenly he find you sleeping” (Mark XIII); and elsewhere: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (I Thess. V).

Therefore it is added here also:

> Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked.

He keeps watch who holds the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the heavenly light; he keeps watch— as blessed Gregory says—who preserves through his works what he believes. These garments, which vigilant care is admonished to preserve, are the sacraments of baptism. He preserves his garments who does not repeat baptism. He also guards his garments who strives to fulfill what he promised in baptism. These are the garments of immortality and innocence from which the first man had been stripped in paradise; but through the slaughtered fatted calf—that is, through the Passion of the Son of God—he receives these same garments again in baptism. Whoever, therefore, does not stain himself with graver sins preserves these garments. If, however, through the obstruction of sins and the compulsion of bodily frailty, it should happen that they are lost, there is still a second baptism by which he may be cleansed, namely, the spring of contrition and of tears. Concerning this twofold baptism the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Ps. XXXI)—in the baptism of the first regeneration—“and whose sins have been covered,” through contrition of heart.

There is also another kind of garment with which the elect are clothed, namely charity, concerning which James says: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (James V). This was the garment from which the man whom the king cast out from the wedding feast had been stripped, as the Gospel testifies, saying: “The king entered to see those reclining at table” (Matt. XXII). Blessed, therefore, is the one who guards his garments—that is, the faith he received in baptism, the innocence of life, charity, and the other virtues—lest he walk naked; that is, lest, stripped of these things, he be shamefully condemned with the devil. And they will see his shamefulness; that is, his sin will be evident to everyone.

And he will gather them into the place that is called in Hebrew Armageddon. He returns to what he had passed over above concerning the unclean spirits who went forth to summon the kings of the whole earth to battle. And because one should be understood in the three, he returns from the plural number to the singular, saying: “He will gather them into the place that is called in Hebrew Armageddon.” The same is true of that passage in the Gospel when, as the Lord was freeing a man from a legion, he questioned it as though it were one, saying: “What is your name?” The united unity itself answered him: “My name is Legion.” And by adding, “We are many,” it showed that the unity consisted of many.

Armageddon is interpreted as “the uprising of unjust witnesses,” or “a mountain of robbers,” or “a rounded mountain.” All the ministers of Antichrist are unjust witnesses. They are rightly called unjust because they unjustly confess Christ to be Antichrist, and unjustly confess Antichrist to be Christ. At the uprising of the unjust witnesses Antichrist will gather them, because he will draw them over to his side for this purpose: that they may utter words of blasphemy and iniquity against Christ. Those concerning whom the Lord says in the Psalm belong to the number of these unjust witnesses: “Unjust witnesses rose up against me, and iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. XXVI).

Armageddon is also called “a mountain of robbers.” Christ is called a mountain by the faithful, in accordance with what is found in the prophet Isaiah: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. II). And: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the summit of the mountains” (Mic. IV), that is, Christ, who surpasses all the elect in merit. And just as Christ is called a mountain by the faithful, so Antichrist will be called a mountain—that is, “Christ”—by robbers, namely by his ministers, who steal right faith from the hearts of the faithful.

Antichrist is also called a rounded mountain because of the multitude of peoples adhering to him, or because all whom he entices by perverse seduction are called rounded: in his body he displays various errors, while on one side he rages openly and on another deceives by fraud. For he sends forth, as it were, a single rounded mass of combatants against the elect when he afflicts them through temporal power. But when his insane power is despised, he sends forth a stronger force, pretending through miracles and false signs to ensnare them.

And the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air. The seventh is also the first, because all are understood in one; and, as was said above, in the seven angels all the preachers of the Church are represented. They pour out their bowls into the air, that is, they spread their preaching against the demons who move throughout this air, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

> And a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying: It is done.

This voice is understood to be the voice of almighty God. The temple and the throne are one, namely the holy Church, which the Lord both presides over by inhabiting it and inhabits by presiding over it. He inhabits it as a temple and presides over it as a throne. From the one seated on the throne and dwelling in the temple this voice proceeds, because by his judgment all things are brought to completion. “It is done,” he says; that is, the kingdom of Antichrist is ended, and the condemnation of the reprobate is complete.

What follows—

> And there were flashes of lightning, and voices, and thunder,

together with the other things that follow, comprises a recapitulation of the same period of persecution. The flashes of lightning signify the miracles that the ministers of Antichrist will perform in order to strike terror into people. The voices are called their exhortations, by which they will persuade people to believe that Antichrist is God. Thunder, however, signifies the threats and tortures by which they will deceive many. The great earthquake signifies a great and exceedingly powerful persecution. Hence it is said: “Such an earthquake as never was,” that is, one so great “since human beings came upon the earth.” The Lord also makes this clear when he says in the Gospel: “Then there will be tribulation such as was not from the beginning of the world” (Mark XIII).

We can also refer these things to a good interpretation, namely to the preachers of truth, who will fulfill all these things spiritually, to strengthen the hearts of the elect and terrify the minds of the reprobate. Their miracles are flashes of lightning, illuminating the faithful and terrifying unbelievers; their exhortations to piety are voices; the threats of future judgment are thunder; and the earthquake signifies the movement of those who, through their preaching, are moved from unbelief to faith.

And the great city was divided into three parts. From the beginning of the world to the end of the age, two cities appear to be built, one belonging to God and the other to the devil: one beginning with righteous Abel and extending to the last of the elect; the other taking its beginning from the wicked Cain and ending with the last of the reprobate. Here, however, the great city is understood as the city of the devil, called great because of the multitude of peoples or the enormity of its crimes.

This city is declared in this passage to be divided into three parts—not as though it had not previously been divided and were to be divided only then, but so that it may be clear of what kinds of people it consists: pagans who still remain in the error of heathenism; heretics and Jews, who are counted as one; and false Christians, who now lie hidden in the bosom of the Church.

> And the cities of the nations fell.

Here a genus is divided into its species. What was signified above by one city is now signified by the many cities of the nations. For Babylon the one city is what the many cities of the nations are, just as the one Church is what the seven are. And when it says, “The cities of the nations fell,” this means what is said below: “Babylon fell, fell.” Although it falls daily in the reprobate, it will nevertheless be condemned generally at the end of the age and will fall when it hears from the Lord: “Go into the eternal fire.”

And Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath. Almighty God does not suffer any forgetfulness, nor does he remember because he is immutable; rather, divine speech accommodates itself to human frailty when it attributes human emotions to God, just as fathers and mothers often accommodate themselves to their children by lisping, so that they may be more easily understood by them.

It must be understood, however, that almighty God in one respect now forgets the elect, and in another remembers them. When he does not reward them in the present for their good deeds, he appears to forget them; when he purifies their evils through scourges, he remembers them. At the future judgment, however, it will be otherwise. He will remember their good deeds in order to reward them; but their evils, because they have been punished here through scourges, he will consign to oblivion. Thus, what he now forgets he will then remember, and what he now remembers he will then forget.

The opposite will happen to the reprobate. In the present almighty God remembers them so that, if they do anything good, they may be rewarded in the present; but he does not remember them so as to make them endure scourges for their crimes. At the future judgment he will remember them so that they may be handed over to eternal fire for their sins; but he will not remember them so as to grant them a reward for any good work.

Therefore it is rightly said here: “Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath.” By the cup of indignation, infernal punishment is understood, which will be given to all the reprobate when they are condemned together with their head. In this punishment there will be innumerable torments: fire, cold, immortal worms, intolerable stench, and other things of this kind, together with the thickest darkness, concerning which it is written: “Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness.”

And every island fled, and the mountains were not found. These signify the saints, who are battered on every side by the waves of this life and, rising above the earth, seek heavenly things in mind together with the Apostle. Hence the Psalmist says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains”; and elsewhere: “The mountains surround him” (Ps. CXXII, CXXIV); and the Prophet: “The mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the summit of the mountains” (Mic. IV).

These people flee from association with the wicked, not bodily, because they cannot do so, but mentally. Bodily they dwell in the midst of sinners, but in mind they remain far removed from their fellowship. Through the Prophet it is said to them: “Go out from her”—that is, from Babylon—“my people, and do not touch the unclean thing” (II Cor. [sic]). What they will then do bodily, when they are wholly separated from the wicked, they do now mentally, because by their merit they are far removed from the wicked life of those people.

“They were not found,” that is, they were not found in the society of the wicked through a sharing of life.

And great hail, like a talent, came down from heaven upon the people. There are three kinds of talent: one of one hundred and twenty pounds, another of seventy-two, and a third of fifty. Here, however, mention is made only of the middle talent, which contains seventy-two pounds.

What else should we understand by hail than the sentence of almighty God? Hence it is written: “The wrath of the Lord descends like hail.” It is rightly mentioned as a talent, because the sinful reprobate from the seventy-two languages will be condemned, and no one predestined to death will escape this death. The wrath of the hail itself is said to be of a talent’s weight because of the magnitude of the vengeance. This wrath, moreover, is inflicted only on account of the preceding guilt.

Sin therefore precedes in human beings, and because of its merit the hail descends from heaven. As it descends, the great blow wounds the reprobate, because the wrath of the strict judge itself brings this about: those who do not quickly wipe away the sin they have committed by the hand of repentance fall into another and worse sin. For from that judgment arises the subsequent fault by which the blinded mind is led to fall into something worse and become bound by another sin.

The sin that arises from sin is therefore no longer merely sin; it is simultaneously sin, a wound, and the punishment of sin, because almighty God, by a just judgment, darkens the heart of the sinner so that, through the merit of the preceding sin, he may also fall into another. The one whom he did not wish to free, he struck by abandoning him.

To make this clearer, let us state it by way of example. The Jewish people, becoming proud of the law of God that they had received, reached, through the swelling of their heart, the evil of denial. If they had repented of the pride with which they had swollen, it would have been merely a sin. But because through that swelling they proceeded to the denial of Christ, it is not only sin but simultaneously sin and the cause of sin, because it generated another sin from itself.

Through this same cause they fell into the punishment of sin: those who refused to receive the Christ promised to them will at some time receive Antichrist, as the Lord himself says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive.”

Thus, in the swelling produced by their observance of the law, the public contempt of Christ through the reception of Antichrist is sin, a wound, and the cause of sin. It is sin in itself; it is the wound of sin because the preceding guilt of pride inflicted it; and it is the cause of sin because from itself it generated the subsequent guilt by which the devil is to be worshiped in Antichrist.

And people blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail. It is as though he said: The wrath of the strict judge brought it about that those who did not receive the truth so as to be saved should, through the operation of terror, render service so as to perish.

To blaspheme God because of the plague of the hail means, because of the merit of preceding sin and with the wrath of the heavenly judge permitting it, to incur the wounds of blasphemy. Thus it is said: “People blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail,” as though it were said: They blasphemed for this reason, because they incurred the wounds of that very blasphemy from the hail, or through the hail. By the hail is expressed the exceedingly powerful tribulation that will occur in the time of Antichrist.

For, suddenly changing his subject, while he had been speaking of the condemnation of the reprobate upon whom the wrath of God descends, he returns to the time of Antichrist. At that time the affliction of the hail will be so great that many, fearing the punishments set before them, will withdraw from the faith of Christ and blaspheme God because of the plague of the hail.

Now, since it is said that the end of these plagues is about to come, and since this book should also be concluded with an appropriate ending, the meaning is that the torments will be exceedingly powerful and severe. “For it became exceedingly great,” so that nothing like it had occurred before and nothing like it would occur afterward, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then there will be such tribulation as has not been, nor will there be afterward” (Mark XIII).

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 1139]

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 1139B]

And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great prostitute.”

The angel in this passage represents Christ, who is the messenger of the Father’s will; John, however, represents the Church. What the angel says to John is said daily by Christ to the whole Church. It should be observed here that the angel comes in order to teach John, while that same John is invited to come in order to be taught.

The angel comes to John—that is, Christ comes to the Church—whenever, either through inward inspiration or through the teaching of the apostles and the other saints, Christ invites her to contemplate the torments prepared for the reprobate by the just judgment of God.

“Come,” he says, by the steps of faith and understanding, “and behold the condemnation of the great prostitute,” that is, “consider the condemnation of the reprobate.” John comes when the holy Church gives assent and, understanding the words of the teachers or admonished by divine inspiration, considers the punishments that will come upon the reprobate.

Moreover, the prostitute here is understood as Babylon, that is, the entire multitude of the reprobate. Alternatively, the angel who invites John may be understood as the preceding order of teachers, represented by the apostles, martyrs, and other leaders of the Church; and John as the Church that follows them.

The angel therefore invites John to come and see the condemnation of the faithless city, because those teachers who came before strove to show the condemnation of all the reprobate to their followers, so that, when they see the wicked flourishing in this life and themselves in want, they may desire nothing from the prosperity of the wicked while considering the evils that threaten them. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “Many walk, of whom I often told you” (Phil. III).

There are two cities in this world with their kings, as was said above: Jerusalem and Babylon, with Christ and the devil. One of them is established upon a firm rock, while the other is founded upon sand; and therefore one remains—the city of Christ—while the other falls—the city of the devil.

It is called a prostitute because, just as a woman prostitutes herself when she brings in a stranger in place of her husband and invalidates the covenant of her former bridegroom, so the entire multitude of the wicked has done and continues to do when, abandoning the Creator, it prostitutes itself to demons for violation. It abandons its God, who is the husband of the soul, and joins itself to an adulterer, namely the devil, by worshiping idols, loving earthly things more than heavenly things, or serving the uncleanness of the flesh.

And because the human race perishes chiefly through carnal lust, which is the mother of all vices, that multitude of the wicked is called a prostitute.

Who sits upon many waters. Since, as we read below, many waters are many peoples, sitting upon many waters means nothing other than reigning over many peoples, because the lust of the flesh rules over many and drags many into its misery, although it does so in different ways.

Hence, when the Lord speaks to blessed Job about the devil, he says: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job XL). The seed of intercourse is in the loins of men, but in the navel of women. Therefore, when the devil deceives men, he is said to have strength in his loins; but when he deceives women, in the navel.

That the seed is in the loins of men God makes clear when he says to the faithful: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII). Paul also speaks of Levi, who was still in the loins of Abraham when Abraham offered tithes to Melchizedek. That it is in the navel of women the Prophet makes clear when, under the figure of a prostitute, he says to Jerusalem: “On the day of your birth,” he says, “your navel was not cut” (Ezek. XVI). To cut the navel on the day of birth is, at the time of conversion, to cut away the lust of the flesh.

Because, therefore, the devil deceives both sexes, he is rightly said to have strength and power in the loins or in the navel. It must be understood, however, that he does this in different ways because of the different causes involved, as was said above.

For example, there are some who have vowed their virginity to God, such as monks, canons, and others placed in the ecclesiastical order. If they are later corrupted after being enticed by carnal desire, they sin more grievously than if they had never professed such a state. There are married people who abandon their own marriage bed, violate another’s, and commit adultery; these sin more grievously than those who do not have wives of their own. There is a similar kind among those who commit incest with relatives or sisters, as Ammon did with his sister Tamar. There are also others—and this is more wicked and more grievous—who, abandoning the natural use of woman, unite themselves with males or with beasts.

Although the human race offends God in many ways, it acts more gravely in none than in this, which is against nature. Since fornication, the mother of all vices, exercises power over the reprobate, the prostitute rightly sits upon many waters.

This fornication pertains to the lust of the flesh; spiritual fornication, however, pertains to the lust of the eyes, and in these two every sin is committed, in accordance with the saying: “Everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes” (I John II).

Concerning this spiritual fornication the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. LXXII). In brief, let us say: Whoever desires earthly things more than heavenly things, and the things that are in the world, commits fornication.

With whom the kings of the earth fornicated. Those who are the kings of the earth are themselves also the prostitute; but because of the distinction between rulers and subjects, she is divided into kings and inhabitants of the earth, although the kings themselves are inhabitants of the earth, that is, lovers of earthly things and servants of lust.

Those kings, therefore, fornicated with the prostitute—that is, with themselves—by seeking earthly honors and pleasures and pursuing the uncleanness of the flesh. For the more they eat and drink, the more they indulge in lust. Thus they make themselves the very body of the prostitute, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Do you not know that those who cling to a prostitute become one body with her?” (I Cor. VI).

And those who inhabit the earth were made drunk with the wine of her prostitution. By the kings, wicked rulers are understood; by the inhabitants of the earth, their subjects, who are made drunk with the wine of fornication, that is, are filled with every sin. The kings are understood as the authors of wickedness, while the inhabitants of the earth are understood as their imitators.

The incentives of the flesh and of fornication are rightly compared with the wine of drunkenness. A person drunk with wine becomes so insensible that he does not fear danger not only to his soul but even to his life; hence he throws himself boldly into death. In the same way, lust removes a person’s sense and rational understanding, so that he does not fear the condemnation of hell. Therefore he boldly does evil even against his conscience and does not fear being condemned for his sin, which he cannot foresee, because the sin itself removes his rational sense.

And he carried me away in spirit into a desert. Here it is clearly shown that blessed John did not see all these things bodily, but in spirit and through the understanding of his mind.

In sacred speech, “desert” sometimes signifies heaven, sometimes the hearts of the saints, sometimes almighty God, and sometimes the hearts of the reprobate.

Heaven is signified by “desert,” as in the Gospel: “Which one of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the desert and go to seek the one that had gone astray?” (Matt. XII). For humanity deserted heaven when it sinned.

The hearts of the saints are signified, as in: “Behold, I have withdrawn, fleeing, and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV), that is, in the secrecy of the mind. The saints remove themselves from all the cares of this age and become a desert with respect to these anxieties, remaining free in the solitude of their minds from the affairs of the world.

Sometimes “desert” signifies God, as in Jeremiah: “Who will give me a lodging in the solitude of travelers?” (Jer. IX).

It also signifies the hearts of the reprobate, as in: “How the city full of people sits solitary” (Lam. I). If it is solitary, how is it full? Or if it is full, how is it solitary? It is solitary because it is without God.

Hence John also says: “The voice of one crying in the desert: Make straight the way of the Lord” (John I). Those whom almighty God does not inhabit by grace are rightly called a desert.

In this passage, however, we should understand the desert as the hearts of the reprobate, empty because of the absence of divinity. The angel represents Christ, as above; John represents the Church. She is led into the desert whenever, either through inward inspiration or through the preaching of teachers, she is drawn to consider the merits of the reprobate and, because of their perverse works, sees their future condemnation as just.

And I saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast. He calls the one whom he had shortly before called the prostitute—a name signifying the entire assembly of the wicked—a woman. The beast signifies the devil, upon whom all the reprobate sit, running through various vices at his prompting. Just as the city of God is built upon Christ, so that city of the reprobate is built upon the devil.

She is rightly called a prostitute, to show in what respect the kingdom of the devil prevails most greatly. She is also rightly called a woman, because sin took its beginning from a woman, through whom, as Scripture testifies, we all die.

This woman sits upon the beast because, driven by the devil, she is borne headlong into sinning. For example, when someone goes to kill a servant of God or to burn down a church—as those who in our time have joined themselves to pagans are now doing—the devil carries him, while the devil himself is the one upon whom that person sits.

The designation “scarlet beast” refers both to the devil and to his entire body: either because it has been bloodied by innumerable sins, or because of the blood of the saints that they shed, or also because of the words of the divine Scriptures wrongly understood.

Concerning it he adds:

> Full of names of blasphemy.

It is as though he said: No part of it is free from blasphemies, because by voice and deed alike it blasphemes God and his servants. This will happen even more after that condemned man begins to reign who will say that he is Christ, although he is Antichrist. Then his entire body will blaspheme God to the greatest degree, because he will say that all those who came before him were opposed to him, asserting that Christ was Antichrist, and that Christ’s apostles were false apostles and ministers of Antichrist. Whatever we now hold in truth, he and his members will entirely deny and declare to have been a lie.

Having seven heads and ten horns. By the seven heads, as was said above, all the wicked kings who existed from the beginning of the world to the end of the age are understood, because the number seven commonly signifies totality. By the ten horns, however, all the kingdoms subject to the devil and Antichrist are understood. Hence Daniel says: “The fourth beast will be a fourth kingdom on earth, which will be greater than all kingdoms” (Dan. VII). The ten horns of that kingdom will be ten kings, whom this Apocalypse mentions in the seven heads and ten horns of the beast.

Those kings and kingdoms themselves are also part of the beast, because they blaspheme Christ by voice and deed. Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus, who came in the flesh, is not from God; and this is the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is coming, and now he is already in the world” (I John III); and elsewhere: “Now many antichrists have arisen.”

It is not surprising if the seven heads signify the same thing as the ten horns, since the woman who is the prostitute, the many waters, and the beast are shown to constitute one entire body. Because of the diversity of its crimes, the beast itself is divided now into seven heads and now into ten horns: it deceives by fraud and oppresses by force—by power, that is, through open authority; by signs and false wonders; and by the deceit of iniquity through the hypocrisy of simulated virtue.

We should also understand this generally of the whole body of the wicked, although some refer it to Nero, asserting that he is to be resurrected from the underworld and receive his kingdom again.

And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold, and with a precious stone and pearls. Purple is the garment of kings, and it is dyed with the blood of sea fish. What, then, should we understand by the purple with which the woman was clothed except the appearance of rule? What the Church possesses in truth, these people will possess in imitation.

The Church has purple and scarlet—that is, royal dignity—because she has Christ as king and also has many kings arising from herself, since the Church herself reigns through Christ. For she is a chosen and royal race.

But this woman, the prostitute—that is, the entire multitude of the wicked—says that she has purple although she does not; that is, she pretends to have kings, such as Nero, Domitian, and the other leaders of the wicked who possessed the riches of this age, which entice the minds of the wicked. But such men were not kings, because they could govern neither themselves nor others well. Rather, they themselves served vices and drew others by their example into the practice of vice.

The Church also has a garment gilded with gold, that is, charity, or wisdom, concerning which it is written: “Receive wisdom as gold”; and the Psalmist says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Ps. LXIV).

Thus this prostitute, although utterly foolish, still, in her disregard of the future prosperity that ought to follow for her, declares herself wise and boasts in the books of philosophers and in the wisdom of human speech.

The precious stone and pearls signify the virtues of the saints: faith, hope, charity, humility, gentleness, and other such qualities with which the faithful are adorned. Although the Church alone possesses these ornaments, this perverse woman attempts deceitfully to appropriate them to herself. She therefore pretends to possess what she does not have, so that those whom she cannot draw into error by power she may deceive through simulated holiness and plausible fraud.

Having a golden cup in her hand, full of the abomination and uncleanness of her fornication. The prostitute herself is a golden cup because of the simulated holiness that she displays outwardly, although inwardly she is full of every iniquity and abomination. Hence Jeremiah says: “Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord” (Jer. LI).

Through hypocrisy she pretends to possess the gold of simulated holiness, so that she may more easily invite anyone to drink the uncleanness of her fornication. To such people the Lord says: “Woe to you, who are like whitewashed tombs” (Matt. XXIII).

To abominate is to cast away. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “The Lord will abominate the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V). This woman, therefore, is full of abomination—that is, full of works of wickedness for which she deserves abomination, meaning rejection. This is immediately made clear when it adds: “and the uncleanness of her fornication.” Here fornication, which is the root of all evils, is placed for all sins.

And on her forehead was written a name: Mystery, Babylon the great, mother of fornications and of the abominations of the earth. By the forehead of Babylon, the manifestation of her deeds is signified. Hence the Lord says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII).

Because Babylon—that is, the multitude of the reprobate—through hypocrisy pretends to be what it is not, displaying itself as a golden cup although it is full of iniquity and abomination, lest the superstition of error deceive the unwary under the cloak of pretense, those who are attentive are made cautious by the inscription on its forehead, since “Babylon”—that is, “confusion”—is written there.

We must therefore consider why the name itself is called a mystery. A mystery is said to be a hidden matter in which one thing is seen and another understood. The works of Babylon are on the forehead for some and in mystery for others. For the simpler, who cannot foresee or understand them, they are a mystery, because what is done inwardly by the multitude of the reprobate is hidden from them. For the more perfect, however, she displays her name on her forehead, because they easily recognize all her works.

Therefore her name is indeed on her forehead, but nevertheless it is written as a mystery, because for some it is displayed openly, while for others it is concealed in mystery.

Babylon is called great because of the multitude of the reprobate or the enormity of their crimes.

“Mother of fornications,” that is, the root of all evils. Sin began from a woman, who received the seed of the devil as from an adulterer—that is, his perverse suggestion—and gave birth to sin by despising the Lord’s command. She later also deceived her husband and thus transmitted the seed of sin down to us.

Both, therefore, became parents of sin, because the adulterer and the prostitute were deemed worthy to become one body.

Alternatively, “mother of fornications” is understood as the preceding generation, which through perverse imitation and evil example left behind wicked imitators. For just as the descendants of the righteous are called imitators of the good—whence it is said, “The generation of the upright will be blessed”—so the descendants of the impious are called their imitators. Therefore Babylon is called the mother of fornications in relation to the authors of transgressions.

And I saw a woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. What John saw, the whole Church sees, for he represented it. He therefore says: “I saw a woman,” that is, an assembly of evil people, “drunk with the blood of the saints,” that is, filled with vengeance for the blood of the saints, “and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” In this verse both the Jews and the Gentiles are included: the former shed the blood of the prophets, while the latter shed that of the apostles and the other martyrs. Therefore both Jews and Gentiles will suffer vengeance for the blood that was shed. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, all the blood shed upon the earth will be required, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, from this most wicked generation” (Luke 11).

Or certainly, as was said above, “the blood of the prophets” is understood spiritually as their meaning. Those who do not fear to distort it into a carnal meaning by interpreting it wrongly, as the Jews do, will suffer vengeance for the blood that was shed, when they lose whatever vitality they possess. And I was astonished when I saw her, with great astonishment. In the same way, when the saints daily consider the condemnation of all the reprobate, they wonder why the wretched do not consider the torments that threaten them.

And the angel said to me: “Why are you astonished?” The Church is likewise told by Christ through inward inspiration: “Why are you astonished at the torments and punishments of the reprobate, which will come upon them by the just judgment of God? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her.” That is: “I will show you what that woman signifies and what the beast signifies, and I will also reveal their condemnation.” The beast “has seven heads and ten horns,” that is, all the reprobate kings and all the kingdoms subject to him.

The beast that you saw was and is not. The beast is the devil, as has often been said. He was in this world from the beginning of the age, and there held the chief power until the Lord’s coming; in the hearts of human beings he wickedly exercised the authority of dominion. But after Christ came and, by his death, destroyed the dominion of death, he took away the devil’s power and cast him out. Therefore he is now “not,” because, in comparison with his former power, his present power is nothing. He was therefore in the earlier members, but is not in the later ones.

And he is about to rise from the abyss—that is, he will be born from the depth of the Jews’ faithlessness, in accordance with: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way” (Genesis 49). It should be noted that he says “he will rise,” because from his very infancy he will be exalted, lifting himself above everything that is called God or worshiped. And he will go into destruction, that is, into everlasting condemnation, in accordance with: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2).

This we should also understand generally of the whole body of the wicked, although some refer it to Nero, asserting that he will be raised from the dead and will receive a future kingdom. And the inhabitants of the earth will wonder. By “the inhabitants of the earth” the reprobate are understood: they inhabit the earth in mind and cling to earthly things through the desire of their hearts. When they see the devil whom they believed in condemned—for this especially concerns those who will receive the Antichrist as God—they will wonder and say to one another: “Was this our hope?” (Isaiah 20.) Turning to him, they will say: “Behold, we were deceived when we thought you were the Christ; now we see you being condemned.”

Their names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. [Col. 1146B] The book of life is the right of divinity, that is, the foreknowledge and predestination of almighty God. Those who will follow the Antichrist are not predestined to life, that is, foreordained to it, because none of those whom God predestined from the beginning of the world to be saved will perish. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the likeness of his glory” (Romans 8). For God knows to whom he will say, “Go into the eternal fire,” and to whom, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 21).

Seeing the beast, that is, the devil, who was in great power before the coming of the Son of God—and is not, because his power was taken away, as was said above, through the passion of the Son of God; or “was,” because he has already appeared in his members, and “is not,” because the head of those members has not yet appeared by himself.

[Col. 1146C] This is the meaning: “Let the one who has wisdom”—that is, understanding is necessary for him in this passage—“let the one who has wisdom,” that is, intelligence, understand. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. It has frequently been said that, under one figure, a general category can often be found, as here. For what is called the beast is also called the seven heads, the seven mountains, and the seven kings: that is, the entire party of the wicked, which consists in its leaders, as though in kings, and in the peoples subject to them.

Five have fallen. In the five kings understand the five bodily senses, which govern our infancy. By nature we desire things that are soft to the touch, love flavorful things, seek melodious and harmonious sounds, delight in fragrant things, and enjoy what is beautiful to the sight. We reject in every way the things opposed to these: bitter, discordant, foul-smelling, rough, and ugly things. But when mature age arrives, these five kings mentioned above cease, and another king succeeds them—either understanding or error.

These are also the five husbands of whom the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “You have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband” (John 4), because error rules over you. What we have said about each individual can also be understood generally of the human race, because these five senses govern each one of us, and also the whole human race, in tender age. When mature age arrives, either legitimate understanding, the true husband, succeeds, or the adulterous one, which is error.

This is the king of whom the divine word speaks: “One,” it says—as though it were saying: “They have reached mature age in understanding, and yet they have chosen to let their error rule over them.” This is the king of the whole body of the devil, whoever is such a person. Hence the Apostle says of certain people who know God and yet follow error: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Romans 1), and so forth.

What follows—“the other has not yet come”—pertains to the remaining body of the Antichrist, or to the Antichrist himself. Although he now reigns in his members, he will reign more fully and openly through himself. Concerning him it follows: “And when he comes, he must reign for a short time,” that is, for three and a half years. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “If those days had not been shortened, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the elect they will be shortened” (Matthew 24).

And the beast that was and is not is itself the eighth, and is from the seven. The beast that was in the earlier members of the devil—in those who preceded and those who followed—will be joined to the body of the one that is not yet but is to come, as we have said, at the end of time; that is, it will be joined to the Antichrist. It will be the seventh because it is of the same kind, and it will be the eighth because it surpasses sevenfold the wickedness and hypocrisy of the devil’s members, those who now exist or formerly existed.

He called it “the eighth,” although it will be the seventh, for no other reason than to show that the Antichrist will then reign seven times as powerfully in his body, when he has been released, as he now does. Likewise, when the Lord spoke in the Gospel of one evil spirit, to show that one is equivalent to seven, he immediately added: “Then,” he said, “it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself” (Luke 11). He would not have said “seven others” unless he had wished seven to be understood also in the one.

And he goes into destruction. He says this of the same body of the devil, which will certainly perish with its head when the day of judgment comes, as the Lord says: “Go into the eternal fire,” and so forth.

And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom. In the time of the Antichrist there will be ten kingdoms on earth, as the book of the prophet Daniel testifies. But, as Daniel himself says, there will be a fourth kingdom on earth that will be greater than all the kingdoms, devour the whole earth, and trample and crush it. The ten horns of that kingdom [Col. 1147D] will be ten kings. Of these, he will kill three—namely, the king of Egypt, the king of Africa, and the king of Ethiopia—while the others will submit to him.

They will receive authority as kings for one hour after the beast. “One hour” is understood as three and a half years, during which they will reign with their head. “After the beast” means that they will be second to him in honor and dignity, having received these from the head himself.

Those kings already reign in their grandfathers and great-grandfathers, that is, in people like themselves; yet, compared with that final power, they have not yet received the kingdom fully. So too with the kingdom of the Church: it existed in the world before the Redeemer’s coming, but then rose to greater prominence when its head appeared in the flesh. They will receive this authority after the beast, that is, in subjection to him as members, and as his subjects.

These have one purpose: against Christ and his members, so that they may deny Christ and confess the Antichrist. But the innocence of the Lamb will destroy the purpose of the beast, in accordance with: “The Lord scatters the plans of the nations” (Psalm 32).

And they will hand over their power and authority to the beast, that is, they will attribute to him whatever strength and might they possess, saying: “We give you thanks, because whatever we have, we have received from you.”

They will fight against the Lamb, in word and deed, in order to separate the faithful from his faith. And the Lamb will conquer them, because he will give steadfastness to his own, so that they may be killed before they can be separated from the faith of Christ, who says: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world” (John 16). Or he will conquer them when he condemns them together with their head, the devil.

For he is Lord of lords and King of kings. As though he were saying: “Although the reprobate will lose the glory of the children of God, they will not escape his dominion; they will always endure him as Lord.” For he uses them for the benefit of the saints, even when he is fighting against their faithlessness. In this sense Nebuchadnezzar is called the servant of God, and the evil spirit is also called the Lord’s spirit: evil, of course, in itself; but the Lord’s spirit because it was created by God and subjected to his power.

And those who are with him are elect, called, and faithful; “therefore,” it is understood, “they surpass kings.” They are elect in God’s predestination before the foundation of the world, called through the preaching of the apostles, and faithful through the performance of good works.

[Col. 1148C] And he said to me: “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples, nations, and languages.” Here what had been stated above is explained: namely, that the beast sits upon many waters. These many waters, as is said here, are many peoples from all nations, peoples, and languages, deceived by the devil, especially through lust, which is the mother of all evils. The prostitute sits upon the waters because the lust of vices holds the kingdom of dominion over the reprobate. Or certainly, because the kingdom of the ancient enemy is raised up in the arrogance of pride from the multitude of peoples, the prostitute is therefore said to sit upon many waters.

And the ten horns that you saw on the beast—these will hate the prostitute. Since the kingdoms designated by the horns are, as was said above, the beast, that is, the entire body of the devil, and since the beast itself is the prostitute, that is, the entire multitude of the reprobate, the ten horns, or the beast, will hate the prostitute. This means that the reprobate will hate themselves.

This can be understood in three ways. When the reprobate do evil deeds, they hate themselves, because it is written: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.” For by the very thing through which the reprobate love themselves—by following their desires—they are shown to hate themselves. Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul, because by loving his soul wrongly he hates justice, and therefore prepares his soul to receive the misery of future hunger.

In another way, the kings and the beast will hate the prostitute because the lovers of this age persecute one another with hatred. If someone sees another rising to a height that he himself cannot reach, he pursues him with hatred, since among the proud there are always quarrels. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “Envying one another, hating one another” (Galatians 5).

Or certainly, when the wretched see themselves placed before the judgment and condemned, they will hate themselves because they sinned and did not repent after sinning. But it will do them no good then to hate the evil they committed, when they will be unable to be free from that evil.

And they will make her desolate. This means that they will make themselves strangers to God on account of their past sins. God, who dwells in peace and charity, will no longer dwell with them. Hence we read that Jeremiah cried out in a lamenting voice: “How the city full of people sits solitary!” (Jeremiah 9.)

And they will make her naked, understood from what precedes. The garments of the faithful are the sacraments of baptism, charity, and innocence. But all who repeat baptism, or stain themselves with more serious crimes, or violate the laws of charity, strip themselves of these garments.

There are also some who are naked of these garments even in the present age, such as the Jews and pagans, who have neither been baptized nor kept the commandment of charity. False Christians, although they appear to possess these garments, will nevertheless be found naked with them at the judgment, because they lost by evil living what they had possessed. Thus all will be found naked together, because the body of the reprobate is constructed from openly unbelieving people and false brothers.

And they will eat their own flesh. The prophet Isaiah speaks of the reprobate, saying that “their fire will not be quenched and their worm will not die” (Mark 9). They will therefore eat their own flesh, because they will always be fed with punishments, and worms will always consume them; yet they will never come to an end, although they will continually perish.

While they eternally provide food for worms, they will, as it were, eat their own flesh with fire, because they will endure the punishment of their own flesh. They eat their own flesh, devoted to eternal punishment, but with another’s teeth, not their own—namely, with the teeth of immortal worms, which they themselves sharpened for devouring through their iniquities.

And they will burn her completely with fire, because by serving evil works they themselves prepared for themselves the eternal fire in which they would be tormented, and by their own will they cast themselves headlong into those same fires through their wicked actions. Thus, by kindling with their iniquities, as with pieces of wood, the fire by which they are burned, they themselves consume themselves.

In ordinary speech, what happens to them is therefore attributed to the reprobate, just as we say that someone killed himself if, although able to avoid the danger of death, he did not avoid it; or that someone set himself on fire if he willingly threw himself into the fire.

For God put it into their hearts to do what pleased them. Often almighty God, angered by people’s preceding sins, permits them to do things by which they offend him still further. Hence it is said of certain people who did not receive the truth: “For this reason God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is improper” (Romans 1). It is also said that he hardened Pharaoh’s heart, which did not deserve to be softened.

Therefore God put it into the hearts of the unbelievers, because of their preceding unbelief, to do what pleased them. What this was, he immediately makes clear when he adds: “To give their kingdom to the beast.” They give thanks to it and attribute their honor and strength to it, as though they had received from it everything they possess.

But it was not God’s will—for he wills no injustice, and to him the Psalmist says, “You have loved justice and hated iniquity”—that the reprobate, fighting against God, should hand over their kingdom to the beast. Rather, the merits of their preceding iniquities demand that, having been permitted by God to go astray, the reprobate should walk in error, so that they may not be saved by the mercy of the one who spares, but condemned by the justice of the one who punishes.

As though he were saying: “Because their merits demand it, God permitted their hearts to be darkened in such a way that they would act thus, and for so long, until the words of God are fulfilled”—that is, until all that was previously foretold is completed in deed.

Here a question arises: why are God’s words said to be fulfilled when the Lord himself says in the Gospel, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24)? We should understand that God’s words are fulfilled in one respect, but do not pass away in another. They are fulfilled so that what was promised may be completed in deed; they do not pass away because what they declare endures eternally. The word of God sets forth judgments that will remain forever.

It was foretold concerning Christ that, when he comes to judgment, he will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left. The King will say to those at his left: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth, until he says to them: “Depart from me, you who practice iniquity” (Matthew 7).

These words of God will be fulfilled when he comes to judgment and says to the reprobate: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil,” and so forth. “Then these will go into eternal punishment” (Matthew 25).

He also promised that the saints would be placed at his right hand and that he would give them glory. These words of God will be fulfilled when they hear: “Come, blessed of my Father,” and so forth.

Thus it is said, “until the words of God are fulfilled,” as though it were being said: “Until the good and the evil receive what the utterances of God promise.”

And the woman whom you saw is the great city, that is, the whole multitude of the wicked, which has a kingdom over the kings of the earth. For the multitude of the wicked is especially lifted up in pride through kings and the rulers of this age. Thus it is said that the great city has power over the kings of the earth, as though it were being said: “The kingdom of this age itself reigns over all who possess the power of pride.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

And after these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven. These words may seem to mean that some interval occurred in this revelation between the visions, but that is not so. Blessed John saw all these things on one day, namely, the Lord’s Day. Thus he says, “I saw another,” as though he were saying, “I saw another vision.”

It was therefore one angel who revealed these visions, but because of the different vision he says that he saw another angel. We too say of someone: “You seemed to me a different person when you were saying this or that; now you appear different when you are speaking differently.”

“After these things,” he says—that is, after the preceding vision—“I saw another angel descending from heaven.” This angel is Christ, who is the messenger of the Father’s will and who daily announces eternal life to his faithful.

Here the question arises how John saw him descend from heaven, since the Son of God, in the substance of his divinity, is everywhere with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what he says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth.” And again: “Outside heaven and earth there is no place where the Lord is not.”

But he descended from heaven not by passing from one place to another, but when he assumed soul and flesh in the virginal womb, so that he who was invisible in his own nature could be seen in our nature. His descent, therefore, is nothing other than the assumption of flesh. Concerning him Paul says: “Although he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2).

Having great power. This power can be referred to both his natures, namely, the divine and the human. In him this power existed eternally through his divinity, before all ages, because just as he created all things with the Father and the Holy Spirit, so with the Father and the Holy Spirit he possessed all things.

This power was also given to him in time, when, after the triumph of the resurrection, authority in heaven and on earth was given to him, so that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (ibid.). For concerning this power he himself says after rising from the dead: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth.”

But concerning the power that he possesses with the Father before the ages, Daniel says: “His power is an everlasting power.” And the earth, that is, the Church of the elect, was illumined by his glory, that is, by his power. For he dispelled from the hearts of the faithful the darkness of unbelief, ignorance, and sins—he who is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world.

Hence it is written: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen” (Isaiah 9). He also says of himself: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9). And elsewhere it is written of him: “The light came into the world, and people loved darkness more than light” (John 3).

Because this angel came to destroy the power of the devil, he is rightly called strong, since he is shown to have come stronger than the strong and mightier than the powerful. Because he came to empty human wisdom of its power, the earth is rightly declared to have been illumined by his glory, as though it were being said: “Against the swelling power of the world, great power has appeared; against the darkness of false teaching, the light of true knowledge has appeared.”

This angel may also be understood as the first order of preachers, which existed in the apostles and apostolic men. Christ, who is the angel of great counsel, spoke through them. Hence John is called “the voice of Christ crying out.” Paul also says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13.)

This angel is said to have descended from heaven because whatever the holy preachers possess, whether in teaching or in conduct, was given to them from heaven. Hence James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1).

He also has great power, which he received from his head, when it was said to Peter, the chief of preachers: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 23).

And the earth, that is, the Church, was illumined by his majesty, because through its preaching the whole world, surrounded by the darkness of unbelief, was filled with the light of faith. This happened when they preached everywhere, beginning from Jerusalem and reaching to the ends of the whole earth, for the earth failed before their tongue did. Hence the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” and so forth (Psalm 18).

And he cried out in a loud voice, saying. By the loud voice we understand the preaching of Christ, who says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” This voice, proceeding from the Lord himself and afterward through the apostles, filled the whole world with its cry. This voice was strong because it destroyed the very strong gates of the kingdoms of the Gentiles.

“Babylon has fallen, has fallen.” After she raised herself up in pride. Hence: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Psalm 72). Or she has already fallen in the presence of God. The Lord knows who belong to Babylon, and they will fall into everlasting condemnation. They had also already fallen in their head from heaven, for through pride he fell irreparably from that heavenly building.

And she has become a dwelling place of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean bird. In the literal sense, this is said of Babylon, which was captured by the Medes and Persians after Baltassar was killed. People did not live there for long afterward, because it was reduced to everlasting desolation, and a road was built through it [the transmitted “viaque est pro ca” is evidently corrupt]. Where once there were the most beautiful and distinguished habitations of human beings, there are now habitations of demons and beasts; dragons, serpents, and birds of various kinds dwell there.

That Babylon signified this other Babylon, which consists of a multitude of reprobate people, in whom there is a prison of every unclean spirit, because demons are held enclosed there in the hearts of wicked people as though in prisons. They are called unclean because of the filth of all the sins in which they move.

They are also the unclean birds that range through this air until the day of judgment, awaiting their condemnation, in accordance with what Jude says: “The angels who did not keep their first estate he has handed over to be tormented under the darkness of this air until the day of judgment” (Jude 6).

Or we may understand the unclean birds as frivolous and proud people who dwell in that same Babylon. Thus the evil spirits are called demons because of their wickedness; unclean spirits because of the enticements of the flesh; and birds because of the exaltation of the mind.

Isaiah speaks at greater length about these birds and beasts: “All the beasts,” he says, “will play there; it will be a dwelling place of dragons and a pasture of ostriches; demons will meet with onocentaurs, and hairy creatures will call to one another” (Isaiah 34).

And all the nations drank from the wrath of her fornication. That is, all the nations will suffer vengeance for her sins.
