And the kings of the earth who fornicated with her. This means the rulers of this age, who fornicated with themselves by loving earthly things more than heavenly things, or by pursuing the uncleanness of the flesh or worshiping idols. They too will suffer vengeance for their blood, since they are the leaders of the wicked and therefore belong to the company of the Babylonians.

And the merchants of the earth became rich from the power of her luxuries. They are called merchants of the earth because they make their souls available for sale and do not fear committing sins, provided that they can acquire for themselves the honors and dignities of this age.

They became rich from the power of her luxuries, that is, from the ambition of worldly display—not through virtues but through sins. These are the merchants who exchange their souls for temporal abundance in an unhappy bargain.

It should be noted that in this passage three persons among the reprobate and three kinds of sinners are included, through whom all the wicked and all sins are signified: namely, the subject nations, their kings, and the merchants. These are the leaders and rulers who make their souls available for sale in order to acquire counties, bishoprics, and the other dignities of this age.

There are also three kinds of vices from which all sins proceed: lust, gluttony, and greed. Under the name of fornication, the lust of pleasures is signified; under the power of luxuries, the appetite of gluttony; and under enrichment, the greed of the merchants.

And I heard another voice saying: “Come out of her, my people.” This voice is understood as the voice of almighty God, who daily cries out, urging the elect, either through the teaching of the faithful or through inward inspiration, to come out of Babylon.

But the voice that reaches the ear through the service of preachers is heard by the good and the evil alike; the voice that reaches the heart is heard by the righteous alone. He therefore says: “Come out of her, my people”—not bodily, because you cannot do so, but mentally.

He immediately makes this clear when he adds: “And do not share in her sins.” In the present life, the good dwell bodily among the evil, but in character and conduct they are far removed from their company. Therefore the voice of God warns them to come out of her in mind, character, and life, not in body, and not to share in her sins, lest they also become partners in her punishments.

If they are partners in guilt, they will be alike in torment. But if they are separated from the life of the wicked, they will be separated from their punishment. We can prove this in Lot, who dwelt bodily in the midst of the wicked but was far removed from their way of life in mind. Therefore, while the others perished, he alone deserved to be delivered.

And do not receive any of her plagues. As though he were saying: “For this reason, see that you do not share in her sins, lest, when her sins have been completed, you begin to suffer together with her.” Since you were unwilling to have a life like theirs in sins, you will not receive an equal vengeance with them. Yet this will happen not through our merits but through the mercy of the Savior himself.

For her sins have reached as far as heaven. The sins of those who refuse to repent reach as far as heaven, because they rise up against God, who dwells in heaven. If it were possible, they would wish to evade his just judgment. They turn the time given to them for repentance into an increase of guilt; and the longer they are awaited, the more severely they will be struck.

Therefore Babylon rightly does not come to her plagues until her sins reach heaven. Those who refuse to turn from their wickedness and are still awaited so that, by committing further offenses, they may be struck more severely, will not be condemned until their sins are complete. Hence the Apostle says: “To fill up their sins always” (1 Thessalonians 2).

These things are said particularly of the individual members of Babylon. In general, however, the sins of that same body reach heaven at the end, when it rises up in pride against God in its final and complete form—when its members are joined together and its head, the Antichrist, is joined to them, and the enormity of its transgression shows that there is nowhere further for it to go in sinning.

Thus the voice that says, “Come out of her, my people, and do not share in her sins,” now strikes the ears of the elect throughout the whole of time; but then it will cry out more urgently, when, with her sins already touching heaven, the faithless city has arrived at the appointed punishments on the very day of judgment.

Let it therefore be said: “Come out of her, my people,” and so forth. As though it were being said: “Do not be afflicted with the reprobate city by eternal blows. While a little time still remains, flee participation in her sins, for the end is already approaching when sins will receive their due conclusion.”

And the Lord God remembered her iniquities. God is said to remember, not because he ever suffers forgetfulness, but Scripture speaks in our manner, accommodating itself to our weakness, as was said above. He appears to consign the good deeds of the righteous and the acts of the wicked to oblivion when he permits these to be afflicted, while allowing those to flourish in honors and dignities.

Conversely, at the judgment he will appear to remember the deeds of the good when he rewards them for their good works; and he will consign the good deeds of the wicked to oblivion, since they receive their reward in the present. When they say to him, “Did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?” (Matthew 7), he will say to them: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25).

Repay her as she herself repaid you. Here the divine word addresses the company of teachers, to whom Babylon—that is, the multitude of the reprobate—has inflicted evil.

It should be noted that he did not say, “Do to her as she did to you,” but, “Repay her as she repaid you.” If he had said, “Repay her as she did to you,” the meaning would be clear. The Church, through its leaders, will judge all the reprobate, to whom the Lord says: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

But because almighty God often purifies the good through the evils inflicted by the reprobate, the faithful are told: “Repay her as she repaid you.” As though it were being said: “Just as she previously exercised my vengeance upon you, so you exercise my vengeance against her.”

And double double things according to her works. That is, punish her in body and soul; or certainly, hand her over to a double punishment, namely, heat and cold. In hell the reprobate will be tormented in soul and body and tortured by a double punishment.

Although the wicked sinned in time, they will be punished eternally, because when God comes to judgment he will judge not only the deeds but also the inclinations and wills of each person. The reprobate would wish, if it were possible, to live eternally so that they could always sin. Therefore they will always endure torments, since, if it were possible, they would always desire to commit sins.

In the cup in which she mixed for you, mix a double measure for her. What does the cup signify except the torment of suffering with which the reprobate afflicted the martyrs in the present life? He therefore says: “In the cup in which she mixed for you, mix a double measure for her.” That is: just as she inflicted the affliction of tribulation upon you, so you now inflict torments upon her and condemn her by your judgment.

In proportion as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her. All this had already been said above. But because different persons are signified according to their differing circumstances—one sinning more, another less—it is as though he were saying: To the extent that anyone has given himself over to temporal glory and joy, and has surrendered himself to pleasures, to that extent give him torment and mourning; that is, allot to each according to the work of his deeds. [Col. 1155C] For the sake of distinguishing punishments, this same wicked city received as much as it deserved; nevertheless, no punishment will be lacking for her: she who sinned temporally will be tormented by eternal punishments.

Because in her heart she says, “I sit as queen”—that is, “I have been established in honor and dignity,” just as a queen sits in glory and honor—“and I am not a widow,” because “I have a husband, and through his loss I shall not see mourning.” This harlot, that is, the city of the reprobate, speaks in this way while she glories in wicked princes and the kings of this age, such as Nero and Domitian. Exalted by their great riches and honors, she thought that she would reign and live with them eternally and never lose them, so that she would mourn at their loss, as women ordinarily mourn when they lose their husbands.

Or otherwise: just as the Church has her own husband, namely Christ, as the Apostle says, “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI), so the harlot, that is, the city of the reprobate, has been joined in adultery to a husband, namely the devil, by whom she thinks herself ruled and with whom she reigns in this world. While she delights in present luxuries, she does not guard against eternal punishment; overflowing only in temporal pleasures, she places her life in them, never thinking that she will lose temporal life, so that she herself may suffer the mourning which the reprobate endure in everlasting punishment.

Alternatively, the souls of the elect have their own husband, namely spiritual understanding, by which they are governed toward eternal salvation, so that, through the innermost examination of discernment, they despise all earthly things and yearn for those above. By contrast, the harlot moves toward destruction with an erroneous understanding, while she boasts that by spiritual understanding she arranges the innermost matters of her heart. This passage is connected with what precedes, where it is said that five kings have fallen and one remains. The number five pertains to the five bodily senses. When these fall away in a person after infancy, error arises in unbelievers, but in the faithful rational understanding arises, and this is the husband of the faithful. The reprobate, however, possess not this understanding but an erroneous one, as though it were their husband.

Hence the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband” (John V). As if he were saying: “You do not have rational understanding, but error rules you.” Since the wicked city therefore lacks rational understanding, she falsely thinks that she has a husband, saying: “I am not a widow, because I possess understanding of mind, and I shall not see mourning”; as though, supported by understanding and virtues, she would remain in joy.

Therefore in one day her plagues will come—or in one hour, namely at the time of judgment. For Christ will come suddenly to judgment, when he is not expected, to repay each according to his works. What these plagues are he reveals when he adds: death and mourning. We can understand these plagues by contrast, that is, by considering the rewards which the saints will receive.

First, let us consider what bodily death is. Bodily death is the absence of the soul; the death of the soul is the absence of God, because “the soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. XVIII). The elect, possessing God, will have life, according to the saying: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII). Therefore they will live forever, because they will remain in the presence of life. When the reprobate lose this life—that is, God—they will incur death, because they will share in the one whose name is Death, as we read above.

The saints will rejoice and sing praises to their Creator, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. C). But for the wretched there will be mourning, according to the saying: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn” (Luke VI). Because they delighted in present pleasures and refused to fear future vengeance, rejoicing when they had done evil, they will descend in a short time to hell and mourn with everlasting grief.

And famine. The face of almighty God will be present to the company of the just, and in his sight they will be satisfied by eternal refreshment, according to the Psalmist: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI). When the reprobate have lost God, who is the refreshment of the saints, they will endure eternal famine.

Finally, they will be consumed by fire, when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Because the Lord is strong who will judge her. The Lord is therefore called strong who will judge her because he cannot be bent by anyone’s prayers. She will be tormented eternally because no angel or human being will dare, be able, or desire to oppose God when he has delivered his strong sentence of condemnation against the reprobate.

[Col. 1157A] And the kings of the earth will weep and mourn over her. The weeping of the kings can be understood in two ways. Kings are used here in a negative sense and signify the reprobate who are rich in this age, placing their hope in earthly things; and they themselves are kings, just as Babylon is the harlot-city. Therefore, when it says, “who fornicated with her,” it means nothing other than that they fornicated with themselves, loving earthly things more than God or serving the uncleanness of the flesh.

And they lived in luxury—that is, in honors and dignities, eating and drinking and following their own desires. Thus, on the day of judgment, when all the worldly glory in which they trusted has perished, they will weep and mourn, with only regret for their former life remaining, saying: “What did our pride profit us, or what did the boasting of our riches bring us? All things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. V).

Or we may understand this as referring to the present age, in which the survivors among the reprobate, seeing the glory of the world decline—whether through the slaughter of pagans or through the destruction of various peoples—weep and lament because their love and glory are passing away. They will mourn the destruction of those who lost their riches together with their life, and they fear that similar things may happen to them. Hence it follows: Seeing the smoke of her burning.

By the smoke of that city is understood the diminution of temporal possessions. When the wicked see this, considering, as has been said, the slaughter of some and even the devastation of peoples, they weep and mourn because their glory is perishing and this present tribulation precedes eternal fire. Just as smoke is an indication of flames, so present tribulation seems to be a sign of things to come. Thus, when such people observe present tribulations and also look upon the punishment that follows, they weep and grieve, fearing that similar things may happen to them: that is, that they may be stripped of the world’s glory and deprived of present goods and an abundance of pleasures.

Standing far off, because of fear of her torments. At the judgment they will certainly not be able to do this, when ruin will seize all their falls together. In this life, however, they stand far off—not bodily, since after a short time they will pass into their company, but in spirit, while each person fears for himself what he sees another suffering through accusations [Col. 1157D] and power. If it were possible, he would wish to be separated both from their torments and from their dispossession, so that he might always possess temporal things and not pass to hell; he would always wish to live so that he might always be able to sin.

But let us hear what they say about the destruction of the world. For they say: Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city. They weep because it has happened that they have lost both riches and life together. For if they could, they would have wished always to live in luxury and never to lose this wretched life. Babylon is called great because she extends throughout the whole world, both because of the multitude of the reprobate and because of the enormity of their crimes. She is also called strong, not in good but in evil and in the persecution of the saints, whom she afflicted and killed in various ways.

For in one hour your judgment has come. Concerning this hour the Apostle John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II), namely the period from Christ’s Passion to the end of the age. Throughout this entire hour—that is, throughout the whole present time—the reprobate are condemned. Their judgment comes to each one when, daily stripped of their bodies, they are condemned in hell. And because in the present time they are also temporally tormented for the crimes they have committed, Babylon is rightly said now to be smoking, so that eventually she may be burned by the everlasting flames of torment.

And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her. Who these merchants are has already been stated above: those who make their souls available for sale and do not fear losing them, provided only that they can acquire honors and dignities. Or merchants are those who travel from place to place, never allowing themselves even a little rest, in order to accumulate for themselves the glory and riches of this age. When they see certain places laid waste by disaster, consumed by the sword, and plundered by hostile invasion, they lament because the glory of the world in which they rejoiced is perishing.

For no one will buy their merchandise anymore. Thus they say: When the glory of all things has perished, there will be no merchandise for us to buy, nor anyone to buy our merchandise, so that we may be enriched by its price. They grieve because unwillingly they are now losing what they possess, and they do not love what they could willingly possess forever.

[Col. 1158C] Merchandise of gold and silver, precious stone and pearl, fine linen, purple, silk, and scarlet, every kind of thyine wood, every vessel of ivory, every vessel of precious stone, bronze, iron, and marble—“no one will buy any of it anymore” is understood. Here it is plainly shown that the reprobate grieve over the loss of those things which pertain to the five bodily senses. They attend to nothing except enjoying what they perceive outwardly through the five bodily senses. Thus they mourn when things that are pleasant to the bodily senses or useful for external purposes ordinarily fail, because they regard all their prosperity as consisting in these things.

Gold, silver, and the rest are referred to the sense of sight, and carnal people desire them with greater ardor in proportion as they are rarer than other things. If we wish to understand these things spiritually, let us first inquire how they signify the riches of the elect, which never perish, and then show in what ways the opposing party strives deceitfully to appropriate them.

Gold signifies radiant wisdom, concerning which it is written: “Receive wisdom as gold.” By the name of silver, sacred utterances are signified. Of these the Psalmist says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire” (Ps. XI).

When the word “stone” is used in the singular, the Savior of all is signified by it, concerning whom it is written: “Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (I Pet. II). When it is used in the plural, the members of that same Redeemer are represented by it; to them the Apostle Peter says: “You yourselves, as living stones, are being built into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II).

By the name “pearl,” in the singular, the Lord Jesus Christ is signified; in the plural, his apostles are signified. Concerning these it is said in this same Apocalypse: “The twelve gates are twelve pearls, one for each” (Apoc. XVIII).

In fine linen, the justifications of the saints are understood; in purple, martyrdom; in silk, virginity; in scarlet, true charity; in thyine and precious wood, enduring steadfastness; in ivory, the beauty of virtues; in bronze, strength and long-suffering, or certainly the sonority of preaching; in iron, the sharpness of subtlety; in marble, unconquered humility.

The beast, or the harlot-city, plausibly boasts that all these things are often possessed under a veil, when in gold and silver she displays the teaching of philosophers and heretics. In precious stone and pearl she presents false Christs, false prophets, and founders of heresies. In fine linen she presents injustice covered under the pretext of justice. In purple she veils the killing of heretics beneath the mantle of Christ’s martyrs. In silk she conceals corruption of mind beneath bodily integrity. In scarlet she masks simulation of charity with cruelty. In thyine and precious wood she hides obstinacy of mind beneath enduring steadfastness. In ivory she covers the ugliness of vices with a pretense of virtues. In bronze she conceals enduring and resounding infidelity beneath the covering of very powerful preaching. [Col. 1159C] In iron she engraves the cunning of deception beneath the sharpness of assistance. In marble she sets forth a snare hidden beneath the likeness of humility and false submission.

Because all these things, veiled under the pretext of false religion, are confounded and removed toward destruction, the world is rightly described as flourishing among the reprobate while being deprived of those same riches.

And cinnamon, amomum, spices, ointment, incense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle, sheep, horses, chariots, slaves, and human souls. From what precedes, “no one will buy merchandise anymore” is always understood. Some of these pertain to smell, while others pertain simultaneously to smell and touch. Cinnamon, amomum, various spices, and incense are referred to smell; ointment is referred simultaneously to touch and smell.

But let us inquire, as we began, how the opposing party appropriates those things which these species signify for good, and over whose removal she bitterly laments. By cinnamon and amomum, the fragrance of virtues is signified, whence the Church says: “Like cinnamon and amomum, giving forth fragrance, I gave an aroma.” Hence Paul says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II).

By the various spices and incense, the prayers of the saints are expressed. Thus, in the Song of Songs, in the voice of the Bridegroom in praise of the Church, it is said: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and incense, and from every powder of the perfumer?” (Cant. V). And through the Psalmist it is said: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. C).

By the name of ointment, the very divinity incarnate is understood. To him it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Cant. I). And elsewhere: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices” (ibid.).

Now, if we consider how the opposing party says that these things are fraudulently possessed, and over whose removal she seems to be grievously afflicted, then in cinnamon and amomum she presents the stinking life of heretics, to be imitated under the guise of the fragrance that proceeds from the virtues of the saints. Concerning them, by contrast, it is said: “It shall be instead of a sweet fragrance, a stench” (Isa. III). In the various spices she offers the contrived diligence of hypocrites in prayer, veiled in the likeness of those who pray well. In ointment she displays the harshness of pseudo-Christians covered beneath the veil of Christ’s gentleness.

When the authors of these simulations have been removed, the world is described as weeping bitterly, just as Nero wept after Simon Magus had been killed, and just as the heretics became sorrowful at the death of Arius, whom they nevertheless did not cease to imitate, although he had been condemned.

Wine, oil, fine flour, and wheat pertain to taste. These entice the throat in such a way that the things they truly signify sweeten the palate of the elect’s heart, while the things assumed from their false imitation are believed to be pleasant by the minds of the reprobate.

By new wine the New Testament is signified. It intoxicates the minds of its hearers and makes them insensible to the desires of the world; hence the Lord is said to have made wine from water at the wedding. What else is signified by oil but the anointing of the Holy Spirit? Thus, in the voice of the Psalmist, it is said to our Redeemer: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

By fine flour and wheat, the flesh of our Redeemer is expressed, by which the faithful are daily healed. When the faction of the reprobate city, overshadowed by the beast’s seduction, thinks that it possesses these things, it grieves all the more if it happens to lose them, in proportion as they seem to signify great wealth. For they grieve at having lost wine and oil when they have lost grape-skins and olive refuse. They lament that they have lost fine flour and wheat when they have lost weeds and chaff.

They think that the preachers of the true faith, filled with spiritual doctrine, inspired by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and nourished for life by heavenly sacraments, have been taken away, while they would rejoice—indeed, if they could, they would wish—that the seducers of wicked heresy, infected by corrupted doctrine, full of demonic spirit, and condemned through the abuse of divine sacraments, had been removed from the world.

Cattle, sheep, horses, and the rest are suited to external uses, since they help human beings either in riding or in carrying burdens. The chariot mentioned here was a type of vehicle among the ancients, perhaps still resembling rural wagons, prepared for the wealthy of this age to sit in. It is also called by another name, a carriage. Such vehicles are sold and merchandise is acquired from them, as we read in the Book of Kings that a chariot came out of Egypt and was sold for six hundred shekels of silver.

When he said, “and the merchandise of slaves”—with “no one will buy anymore” understood—it is rightly asked why he adds, “and the merchandise of human souls.” Can slaves indeed be sold or bought without souls? Certainly not; but something else is understood in these words.

There are some slaves who are sold only in body, while their souls remain free, such as those who are sold to Christians: they are slaves in body, but through right faith they are free in soul. Thus Joseph was sold. Although he was a slave in body, he was free in soul, and therefore his mistress could not draw him into sin. Such people are not sold in soul, because they are distributed for a price only with respect to their external condition of servitude, while the freedom of the soul remains inwardly.

Many, however, are taken captive in both soul and body, such as those who are sold to pagans or Jews. For those who buy them circumcise them according to their law and make them slaves not only in body but also in soul, so that masters and slaves alike are bound by the bond of servitude. On account of these two kinds of sale, therefore, the divine discourse made a distinction between the merchandise of slaves and the merchandise of human souls.

Each of these individual species also signifies the elect, whom the same beast deceitfully displays as her possessions and whose loss she laments. Cattle signify the elect, who say with the Psalmist: “I have become like cattle before you” (Ps. LXXII). Sheep likewise represent the saints, to whom the Lord says: “Behold, I send you like sheep among wolves” (Matt. X). And to Peter he says: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI).

There is also no doubt that horses signify preachers, since the prophet says: “You sent your horses into the sea.” By the name of chariots we likewise know that the same preachers are signified, as Elisha testifies when Elijah ascends and he cries out: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer” (IV Kings II, XIII).

By the name of slaves the elect themselves are expressed, those who subject themselves to God’s service with the whole desire of their mind, knowing that they stand under his power. With the Psalmist they say: “As the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters … so our eyes are upon the Lord our God” (Ps. CXXII).

By contrast, when the world has been laid waste by the judgments above, the beast’s faction laments that it has lost cattle, sheep, horses, and chariots—that is, strong and innocent men to carry the burdens of their own people—when it has lost the weak for every good work and the harmful for evil. It mourns that it has lost those who are outwardly dead to the world, while inwardly it has wickedly lost those same people alive.

And the fruits desired by your soul have departed from you. This also happens when enemies rise from one kingdom against another kingdom and not only plunder cities but also devastate all the trees of the region and burn them with fire. These things pertain both to sight and to taste. Hence we read in Genesis that the woman saw that the tree was beautiful to look at and pleasant for food; she took its fruit and ate, and she gave some to her husband.

It should be noted that although people ordinarily take greater pleasure in other, more important things, he says only “the fruits desired by the soul.” This shows that a person is greatly offended not only in greater matters but also in the smallest things when they are desired immoderately and beyond what is proper.

In sacred Scripture, fruits signify the virtues of the saints, as in the saying: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of apples” (Cant. IV). The beast’s faction therefore says that it possesses by simulation everything which the Lamb possesses in truth.

And all the fat things—that is, the thick things—and the splendid things have perished from you, and they will no longer find them. These seem to be referred to taste, or to gluttony. Thus all the things which the reprobate pursue according to the five bodily senses they lament when the world perishes, because they know how to think of nothing except what they observe outwardly.

When they see others pass through death [Col. 1162B] and affliction from this life, they themselves, surviving them, lament the destruction of those who have left behind the world’s joy, fearing that similar things may happen to them. These things also signify something good, as do the others, since they reveal the simulation of the wicked. For when the Psalmist says, “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. LXII), he shows that fatness signifies the virtues of souls. This fatness appeared in the preachers of the new life, and the faction of the reprobate grieves that it has lost it among the heretics. Hence it follows:

Merchants of the earth, about whom enough has been said above: those who have become rich, not through virtues but through sins. They will stand far off from her, not bodily, as was said above, but in mind, unwilling to follow them. Because of fear of her torments, they will weep and mourn, saying: [Col. 1162C] “Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, clothed in fine linen”—“garment” is understood—“and purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold, precious stone, and pearls, because in one hour such great riches have been laid waste.”

Those who above are called kings are now called merchants: they exchange their souls in an unhappy trade for earthly profits. Hence it is said below: “Your merchants were the princes of the earth.” In the city, however, human beings devoted to riches and surrendered to pleasures are understood. For a city is not clothed with gold, silver, or the other materials, but rather the people who dwell in it are.

When some perish together with their earthly possessions, their survivors, as we have mentioned above, mourn because their glory appears to be perishing; and they stand far off because they do not wish to become their companions either in the loss of earthly goods or in the punishments to which they believe them to be passing. The one hour in which he declares that such great riches have perished is understood as the brief period from the Lord’s Passion to the end of the age. Concerning this John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II).

And every shipmaster, and all who sail to distant places, and sailors, and those who work upon the sea, stood far off and cried out when they saw the place of her burning. Those who above are called merchants are here called shipmasters and sailors. Surely those sailing the sea will not be able to be present so as to see the burning of the city? Rather, all the devotees of this age are expressed by them, fearing for themselves when they see the ruin of their hope.

They are said to see the place of her burning through the smoke of the fire—that is, through the present distress of tribulations they taste in advance the knowledge of future punishments. All this has been explained more fully above and is therefore touched upon briefly here.

They say, weeping: What is like that great city? “City” is understood. As if they were saying: No city can be compared with her in greatness and honor. The eyes of carnal people know nothing great except what they can see with bodily eyes, and therefore, by comparison with the present life, they even despise heavenly things.

They love the world more than God; they love children more than angels. They regard earthly pilgrimage as their home instead of the heavenly homeland. They consider bodily health the highest happiness; they prefer gold, silver, and stones to the crowns of life. Therefore, by comparison with present joys, they believe that nothing exists beyond them and say: “What is like that great city?” As if they were saying: Nothing. Concerning them it is further added:

And they threw dust from the earth upon their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning. By “head,” sacred Scripture often understands the ruling power of the mind. By “earth,” earthly desire is signified. For the reprobate to throw dust from the earth upon their heads is to corrupt the eyes of their minds with earthly love, so that they cannot look upon heavenly things.

The reprobate therefore lament the ruin of the great city, yet they do not cease desiring earthly things. While they gaze immoderately upon earthly possessions, they blind their eyes, as it were, with the dust of the earth, so that they cannot behold the joys of the heavenly homeland.

Alternatively, by the heads of the reprobate we may understand their princes. When the reprobate see themselves already placed at judgment and condemned, they will put the dust of the earth upon their heads—that is, they will reproach the faces of their princes, by whom they were seduced into loving earthly things, for which they will then perish. They will say: “Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, in which all who have ships on the sea became rich from her merchandise.”

Many merchants in this age grow rich from goods transported by ship not only from one place to another but also from one region to another. For example, this happened in Solomon’s time, when fleets went to Ophir once every three years and brought back forty talents of gold and many other commodities which could not be found in the land of Israel. It still happens today; thus cloaks and various ornaments are brought into these regions from the land of the Greeks.

For in one hour she has been laid waste—that is, when the day of judgment suddenly arrives. Observe that they lament not only the loss of riches but also the sudden and unforeseen ruin of this age.

Rejoice over her, heaven, and holy apostles and prophets. A question arises here. Since the Lord commands in the Gospel, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Luke XXVI), what does it mean that here heaven, apostles, and prophets are urged to rejoice?

It must be understood that they are not commanded to rejoice over the destruction of the reprobate, but rather over God’s just judgment. Thus, after saying, “Rejoice, heaven, and apostles and prophets,” he immediately adds: “For God has judged your judgment concerning her.” They are also commanded to rejoice because their reward will come after the condemnation of the reprobate. The elect will not be lifted up to glory before the reprobate are condemned and cast into hell, because it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.”

They rejoice, therefore, because they agree with the just Judge. They would not agree with him if they did not rejoice over his just judgment. They also rejoice because, when the wicked perish, their own glory draws near. Hence, when the Lord had explained to his disciples the ruin of the perishing world, he immediately added: “When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke XXI).

As if he were saying: When you see from the desolation of the world that its end is approaching, look up and raise your heads—that is, make your hearts joyful—because, while the world with which you are not friends is coming to an end, the redemption which you have sought is drawing near.

In “heaven, apostles, and prophets,” the whole Church is included, proceeding from the beginning of the age to its end. “For God has judged your judgment concerning her”: this is the judgment of which we read above, that the souls of the saints beneath the altar of God cried out, saying: “How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Apoc. VI).

“He has judged our judgment”: that is, he has justly condemned her who unjustly condemned us. She who inflicted temporal death upon us will now experience the eternal punishment of Gehenna.

The blessed Ansbertus Ambrosius also refers all these things to those who, terrified by these evils and considering what awaits them, flee from this contrition to fruitful repentance.

And one strong angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: With this force that great city Babylon will be cast down, and she will no longer be found. This angel is the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the messenger of the Father’s will. Concerning him the Prophet says: “He shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel.”

When he says that he lifted up a great millstone, it is as though he were saying: “He lifted up a great mill.” He is rightly said to have been one angel, because there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism. He is rightly called strong because he came to overthrow the powers of the air. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII).

By the mill, the revolving nature of this age is understood, in which much flour—that is, many temporal thoughts and cares—is produced. The millstone signifies the weight of sins contracted in the same activity, by the one who brings about what is brought about.

Concerning this mill, the Lord says about those placed at the end of this age: “There will be two women grinding; one will be taken and the other left” (Luke XVII). Concerning this mill it is also said: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be cast into the depths of the sea” (Matt. XVIII).

This is understood not only of scandal but of all more serious sins, on account of which the reprobate will be cast into the sea—that is, into the depths of hell. And this is done through the angel, that is, through Christ, because, as he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

With this force—that is, with this speed—that great city will be cast into the sea and will no longer be found. Just as this stone quickly passes into the depths of the sea, so the whole assembly of the reprobate will quickly be cast into the depths of hell and will no longer be found in the fellowship of the Church.

In this Church the good are presently together with the wicked, because just as this life stands midway between heaven and earth, so it contains within itself the citizens of both sides. Then, however, all the wicked will be separated and will no longer be found in the company of the good.

And the sound of harpists and musicians, and of flute players and trumpeters, will no longer be heard in you. From the things he had mentioned above, which pertain to the five bodily senses, he now adds things which he likewise predicts will be taken away from the world. All these things are sought with delight by the princes of this age, but then they will be taken away from them, because they will have no delight, being established in torment and tortured by eternal punishments.

He shows through all these things that whatever is perceived with sweetness through the five bodily senses will utterly pass away from this age.

And every craftsman, such as a smith, carpenter, or jeweler, and every craft will no longer be found in you; and the sound of the mill will no longer be heard in you; and the light of the lamp will no longer shine for you; and the voice of the bridegroom and bride will no longer be heard in you.

As if he were saying: Everything that pertains to use and pleasure will be taken away from the wicked. Why this happens is then supplied as the reason. “For your merchants,” he says, “were the princes of the earth.” These are the merchants mentioned above, who exchange their souls in an unhappy trade in order to acquire temporal honors.

Therefore, because Babylon seeks earthly things, uses temporal goods, and is deprived of them by God’s just judgment, she is plunged into condemnation to eternal punishments. The wicked city consists of the kings and merchants of the earth themselves: they make their souls available for sale and are raised up in pride by the arrogance of their exaltation.

Because by your sorceries—that is, your evil deeds—all the nations went astray. Here it is revealed that just as the Church extends among all the nations of the world, so does Babylon. Above all, however, he shows through these words that the princes of this age serve avarice, by whose examples the rest of the multitude is corrupted.

And in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all those who were slain on the earth.

The divine discourse sometimes speaks to Babylon as though to a second person, and sometimes about Babylon as though about a third person. For earlier it says: “No craftsman and no craft will ever again be found in you,” and so forth; similarly now it says: “And in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, who were slain on the earth.” In these words it is shown most plainly that the whole body of the devil must be understood in this city [Col. 1166A]. The blood is said to have been found there—that is, vengeance for blood—which will come upon the whole wicked generation, in accordance with the saying: “The blood of all who has been shed upon the whole earth will be required from this generation.” It must also be understood that those are found to have shed the blood of prophets and saints who were not afraid to twist their words into a meaning other than that in which they were spoken.

## CHAPTER XIX

After this—that is, after the vision just mentioned—I heard in my mind, as it were, a loud voice of many trumpets in heaven saying: “Alleluia.” John here represents the Church, which hears these voices every day [Col. 1166B], because it itself sends them forth. When he says, “After this,” it does not indicate a difference of time, as has been stated, but an order of narration.

This loud voice is the great desire of the saints. It is rightly called loud because the saints speak great things and accomplish great things. The multitude of trumpets is the great assembly of the faithful. Yet although they are many, they utter one voice, because everything they say consists in the concord of one faith.

These are the trumpets of the preachers by which, when they went around Jericho for seven days, its walls fell down. This is mystically fulfilled in the Church, in which, throughout seven days—that is, throughout the whole period of this life—while the preachers sound the trumpet of doctrine, every stronghold of the unbelievers collapses.

“Alleluia” is a Greek expression; in Latin it is said: “Praise the Lord” [Col. 1166C]. Hence, where our books have, “Praise the Lord, children,” the Greeks have *Alleluia*. The saints therefore resound with “Alleluia,” because they themselves praise the Lord in word and deed and exhort others to do the same. The most powerful fathers who came before us did this; we too, though little ones of weak understanding, are permitted to say it.

But now let us hear what they say: “Alleluia, praise and glory and power belong to our God.” For to say “alleluia” means to say “praise,” because every heavenly and earthly creature ought to praise God. And “glory,” that is, honor and exultation. And power belongs to our God because he conquered the devil and granted his chosen ones the power to conquer. To them he says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI).

Because his judgments are true and just.

By these judgments, namely, he judged that those who shed blood should drink blood—that is, should endure vengeance for blood. Hence the Psalmist says: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Psalm CXVIII) [Col. 1166D].

Who judged the great prostitute—that is, the whole multitude of the wicked—who corrupted the earth, that is, herself, by her prostitution. This means through the uncleanness of the flesh, or through the worship of idols, or even through the love of earthly things more than heavenly things.

And he avenged the blood of his servants from her hand. For just as they shed their blood, so he also shed their blood. Or we may understand the shedding of blood spiritually, as above. They shed the blood of the saints because they corrupted the spiritual meaning. And because they poured out what was vital in the divine utterances and turned it into a carnal meaning, they themselves lose whatever vitality they possess [Col. 1167A].

And again they said: “Alleluia.” The repetition of a statement is a confirmation. For the Church continually praises God with unceasing devotion; in its person the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII).

Two deeds of the prostitute are recalled here: namely, that she corrupted the earth—that is, herself—by evil works, and that she shed the blood of the saints, for which she will endure the fire of Gehenna eternally.

And the smoke of her torments rises for ever and ever. This smoke signifies not the tribulation of the present age but the eternal one. Therefore it must be observed that he does not say, “It will rise,” but “It rises,” because the wicked city is condemned daily in each individual reprobate [Col. 1167B] and is led down to the punishments of hell, just as Jerusalem daily passes into the heavenly homeland in each of the elect.

Here, then, the flame of eternal punishment is signified by smoke, because the wretched will be tortured forever. This passage is directed against those who say that the reprobate will return to glory after many years, contrary to the Lord’s sentence, by which he will say to them: “Go into eternal fire” (Matthew XXV). For whatever is eternal has no end. This is what is said here: “Its smoke rises for ever and ever,” because the torments to which the wretched will then be handed over will not come to an end.

And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God, who sits upon the throne, saying: “Amen, Alleluia” [Col. 1167C].

What the twenty-four elders signify, the four living creatures also signify: namely, the entire Church of the elect. Because it examines the deeds of those subject to it, it is rightly represented by elders; because it seeks the pastures of eternal verdure, it is fittingly represented by living creatures.

In the number twenty-four, as stated above, all the fathers of both the Old and the New Testament are shown, because of the doubled twelve; enough has already been said above about the nature of that number.

The falling of the elders and the living creatures does not refer to ruin but to humility. They fall before the one sitting on the throne—that is, before God, who presides over his Church—because, humbling themselves, they attribute to him whatever they possess in faith and works, since they received these things from him [Col. 1167D] who says: “Without me you can do nothing.”

Thus, while worshiping, they say: “Amen,” that is, “It is true,” because praise, glory, and power belong to our God, who judged the great prostitute. For it is just that the one who shed the blood of the saints should drink blood—that is, should endure vengeance for blood. Therefore he is to be praised, because whether on account of the enticements of pleasures or on account of the shedding of blood, he condemns and punishes the reprobate only justly.

“Amen” is interpreted as “true”; “Alleluia,” “praise the Lord.”

Although the throne and the twenty-four elders are one Church, they are distinguished in this way: the Church is, in general, from Christ as one throne, and, in particular, Christ mystically sits upon thrones in those of its members who are more eminent [Col. 1168A]. Therefore, exhorting one another, they say: “Alleluia,” that is, “Praise the Lord.”

And a voice came out from the throne, saying: “Praise our God, all his saints.”

We read that this was done not once but a second time in the preceding utterance, and here it is again commanded. But so that this praise may always continue without failing, the members are instructed by mutual exhortation to praise him all. For the throne itself consists of the servants of God.

When, therefore, a voice came out from the throne and entered their ears a second time, surely the servants were uttering a word of exhortation to their fellow servants.

But in what follows—“and you who fear God”—a question arises: why are those who fear God commanded to praise him, when John himself says in his Epistle: “Because fear has punishment,” and so forth: “The one who fears is not perfect in love” [Col. 1168B]. Elsewhere too it is written: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus XV).

But it must be understood that there are two kinds of fear: that of servants and that of sons. Servants fear lest they be beaten by their masters; sons fear lest they offend the eyes of a loving father and be deprived of their inheritance. Thus the reprobate fear in one way, and the righteous in another.

The reprobate fear that they may be condemned in hell for their sins; the righteous fear that they may commit some sin and offend the eyes of their Creator. Those who fear with this fear are therefore commanded to praise God. Of this fear the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Psalm XVIII).

Little and great.

The little are those who cannot penetrate the deeper mysteries. To them the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as little ones in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Corinthians III) [Col. 1168C]. Nor can they fulfill the Lord’s command, in which he says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew XIX).

The great, however, are those of whom the Lord himself says: “Whoever does and teaches, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V). All these praise God, and they stand together in the Church, in accordance with the saying: “The small and the great are there”—that is understood to mean, in the kingdom—“the children of love.”

And I heard a voice like that of a great trumpet, and like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of great thunderclaps, saying: “Alleluia.”

The great voice of the songs is the great devotion of the saints. It is rightly compared to a trumpet because it proclaims great things. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” [Col. 1168D].

The voice of many waters is the voice of many peoples, for many waters are many peoples, as we read above. In the voice of great thunderclaps, the terror of judgment is expressed. Great thunderclaps issue forth when they announce the terror of divine judgment to the wicked.

All, therefore—that is, preachers and their subordinate hearers—exhorting one another, say: “Alleluia,” that is, “Praise the Lord.”

For the Lord our God Almighty has reigned.

As though they were saying: “We must praise him together for this reason: just as the devil reigned over us from the beginning of the world, so Christ himself has reigned over us from his coming. And us, who were formerly the devil’s kingdom, he transferred into the kingdom of his glory,” dying and rising from the dead on the third day [Col. 1169A].

His power is shown especially in this: the one who at the beginning wondrously formed humanity was able, at the end of the ages, to restore even more wondrously the one who had perished. In all these things, both his power and his mercy are displayed.

Let us rejoice and exult and give him glory.

This is not the voice of outsiders—that is, of Jews or pagans, who are far from the faith of Christ and from the fellowship of the faithful—but the voice of all the saints, exhorting one another to rejoice and exult and to give glory to God Almighty. By his mercy alone, without any merits of preceding good works, he brought them to such great dignity.

For the marriage of the Lamb has come.

In sacred Scripture we often read that the union of Christ and the Church is called a marriage. Thus it says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a marriage for his son” (Matthew XXII) [Col. 1169B].

Christ is the bridegroom and the Church the bride, because he betrothed her to himself both through faith and through the grace of baptism. Christ therefore gave this bride a pledge, namely faith, hope, and love. Through these, throughout this entire period, she is joined to him; in the future she will be united to him in reality.

And his wife has prepared herself.

He speaks of two things: the bride and the wife. For now the holy Church is a bride; but when she has been brought to the embrace of her husband and sees in reality what she now sees in hope, then she will be a wife.

It is customary in sacred Scripture sometimes to call brides wives and bridegrooms husbands, and again to call wives brides and husbands bridegrooms. Thus, after the Evangelist had earlier said of the Lord’s mother, “When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph,” he added shortly afterward: “Joseph her husband [Col. 1169C], being righteous and unwilling to expose her, intended to dismiss her secretly.” And the angel said to him: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matthew I), although she was not yet actually his wife.

The same is true of the saying: “If a betrothed girl is found in the countryside and a man lies with her, let him be put to death, because he has humbled his neighbor’s wife” (Exodus XXII).

A man and a wife, a bridegroom and a bride, are likewise mentioned when Joel says: “Let the bridegroom come forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room” (Joel II).

When he says, “His wife has prepared herself,” this is understood not of the preparation now taking place through faith, but rather of that preparation of which the Lord says: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him. Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. Then the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him into the marriage feast” (Matthew XXV) [Col. 1169D].

This is the union when the one who was called the bride passes into the status of wife. Although this union and preparation are to occur at the end of the age, they are reported as already accomplished in God’s predestination. Therefore all the righteous long for this form of union and, exhorting one another, say: “Let us rejoice and exult and give him glory.”

It may also be understood in this way: when the Church reaches that place, it will say these words. Foreseeing that this will certainly happen, the Spirit narrates it as though it had already occurred.

And it was granted to her to clothe herself in shining and pure linen [Col. 1170A].

He himself explains what the linen is when he adds: “For the linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.” The righteous deeds of the saints are accomplished through faith, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Having been justified by faith, let us have peace with him.” They are also accomplished through the grace of baptism, through generosity in almsgiving, and through love, which covers a multitude of sins.

And because the Church does not possess these virtues from herself but receives them from God, it is therefore said: “It was granted to her”—by God, of course, from whom every good thing is bestowed—in accordance with the saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I). Hence Paul also says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Corinthians IV.)

In this life the Church is clothed through faith and love [Col. 1170B]; in that life she will be clothed by love alone, which is declared to be the greatest of these. All righteous deeds especially consist in this love, on account of which everything is done through faith.

It is rightly called shining and pure linen, because then the conscience of the elect, which here has been adorned with faith, hope, and love, will not be darkened by any stains of sin.

And he says to me: “Write.”

That is, write it in your heart, or also write it in a book so that it may reach posterity. For what is said to John is said to the whole Church, whose representative he then was.

Blessed are those who have been invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.

These words are not spoken of the marriage taking place in the present, to which many seem to enter through faith and baptism. They are not blessed for that reason, because they stain by their works the faith they appear to possess. Hence it is written: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XX) [Col. 1170C].

Rather, this is understood of the marriage into which only the good will enter, where no one will be found worthy to be cast out for lacking a wedding garment, but all, clothed in white robes, will rejoice eternally with Christ.

Many enter the present marriage only to leave it, but whoever enters that marriage even once will never leave it again.

Blessed—that is, happy—are those who in God’s foreknowledge and predestination have been invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb, that is, to that heavenly banquet above: to fellowship with the angels and holy human beings. There will be refreshment for holy souls, namely the immediate presence of almighty God.

Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm XVI) [Col. 1170D].

Of this supper it is also said in the Gospel: “Blessed is the one who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke XIV). At this supper the Lord himself will serve his faithful, in accordance with the saying: “He will gird himself, make them recline, and come by and serve them” (Luke XII).

It is rightly called not a banquet but a supper, because it will be fulfilled at the end of the age. After the midday meal, supper remains; after supper, no banquet remains. Therefore those who, after the end of the present life, come to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation are truly invited to the supper of the Lamb.

And he says to me: “These are the true words of God.”

That is: God is truthful and never lies; these words that I am telling you are God’s words, and therefore what I have foretold as future will certainly come to pass [Col. 1171A].

God’s words come to a human being when the Word of God itself reveals them inwardly in the hearts of the faithful through inspiration, without the sound of a voice.

And I fell before his feet to worship him, and he says to me: “See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus.”

Because John saw the angel as greater than himself, he wished to fall down and worship him. Here the angel and John each assume their own persons. For when the angel earlier said, “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last,” he showed that in that passage he was sent in the figure of Christ. But here, considering his own person, he forbids himself to be worshiped.

It should also be noted that this same angel is said to have feet, because, when he came, he assumed a body from the air [Col. 1171B].

He says, “See”—that is, take care not to do this—“because I am your fellow servant.” I and you have one Lord, and I am not superior to you in anything except doctrine, which I have been sent to teach you. Nor am I merely your companion; I also declare myself the equal of all your brothers, namely faithful human beings, who hold the testimony of Jesus—that is, the faith of Jesus.

Here it should also be considered that, although we often read in the Old Testament of angels being worshiped by human beings, we never read that they were forbidden to be worshiped. But after the Lord raised the assumed human being above the heavens, the angel feared to be worshiped by a human being whom he recognized as reigning above himself.

Because he tells him that he must not worship the angel, he also shows whom he ought to worship [Col. 1172A], adding: “Worship God.” As though he were saying: “Do not worship me, who speak these words to you, but the one in whose person I appear to you.”

For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. Whatever the spirit of prophecy has spoken is a testimony to Jesus, to whom the Law and the Prophets bear witness. Thus, when Moses and Elijah appeared with him on the mountain at his Transfiguration in the same majesty, it was shown that he has testimony from the Law and the Prophets.

Hence the Lord himself says to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John V). For all Scripture was given through the Spirit. Therefore the spirit of prophecy is the testimony of Jesus, because all Scripture bears witness to Jesus.

Thus, after rising from the dead, he said to his disciples [Col. 1172B]: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (John I).

And when he was baptized, the Holy Spirit also bore witness to him that he was the Son of God, when it descended upon him in the form of a dove. The spirit of prophecy therefore bears witness to Christ, because everything narrated by the Law and the Prophets appears to have been spoken about him.

But it is not those who believe merely verbally the things said about him who have this testimony of Jesus, for faith, if it has no works, is dead. Rather, those have it who possess the faith that works through love—that is, those who adorn by their works the faith they possess.

But since the whole substance of faith proclaimed about Christ is concluded here, let the length of this book at last be brought to its proper end.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1171]

## CHAPTER XIX FOLLOWS

[Col. 1171C]

And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse.

As has very often already been said, heaven is understood as the Church of the elect, of which it is written: “Heaven is my throne.” Solomon says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” Paul, however, confirms that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

This heaven was closed when the apostles and the other faithful were not permitted to speak freely, and had not yet reached all the nations by preaching. This heaven was closed when, compelled by fear, the apostles were shut in a room and concealed themselves in silence because of fear. Then the Lord came while the doors were shut, stood in their midst, and said to them: “Peace be with you.”

But after he ascended into the heavens, he opened this heaven [Col. 1171D], because on the tenth day after his Ascension he sent them the Holy Spirit. Set aflame by it, they began to speak in various languages the mighty works of God. Those who previously had not dared to confess Christ in their own language afterward preached him publicly in innumerable varieties of languages.

By the white horse we must understand the body and soul of Christ; by the rider of the horse, the divinity of the Word, which presides over his humanity.

The divinity mounted this horse [Col. 1172C] when, by assuming human flesh and a human soul, the Word of God united them to himself. But although a horse is one thing and a rider another—a horse being an animal and a rider a human being—this does not apply to the Lord, in whom there are not two persons but one, although in two substances.

For just as a human being, consisting of soul and flesh, is regarded as one person, so he himself, consisting of soul, flesh, and divinity, is one Christ, consisting in one and the same person of two substances.

The horse over which the divinity of the Word uniquely presides is rightly described as white, because no obscurity of sin is found in that assumed human being. Hence it is written: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (I Peter II).

With heaven opened, the white horse and its rider are seen, because, as the Church preaches, Christ’s humanity and his divinity are revealed to the nations.

Of his divinity it is further added [Col. 1172D]: “And the one who sat upon it was called Faithful and True.”

Faithful, because whatever he promises he will undoubtedly fulfill; true, because he is himself the truth of the Father, who never lies, and he judges with justice—that is, he repays each person according to his works. For the one who is just in all things cannot judge otherwise.

Therefore those who regard him as merciful and faithful in his promises [Col. 1173A] must consider that he is true and just. For this reason he leaves no unrepentant person unpunished, nor does his mercy save anyone who has not been converted; and he fights in his elect.

He first conquered the devil by himself, because he came to defeat the powers of the air; then he conquers daily through his members. So that the faithful may become victors, they are aided by Christ, without whom they can do nothing.

He judges, therefore, as king of the ages; he fights because in his members he is always waging war against the attacks of demons and wicked people.

And his eyes were like a flame of fire.

The eyes of this rider are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence it was said above that John saw the Lamb as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes [Col. 1173B], which are the seven spirits of God sent throughout the world.

These eyes are rightly called like a flame of fire because they illuminate us for faith and kindle us to love of God and neighbor. Or by the Lord’s eyes we may understand the divine utterances, which likewise illuminate us and kindle us to love of God.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Psalm CXVIII); and again: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm XVIII).

And upon his head were many diadems.

Because the Lord grants the crowns of victory to many of the elect, he is said to have many diadems upon his head, with which the multitude of saints is crowned.

For since he is the head of all the elect and the elect are his members, from the one who made him head the members also receive their crowns. He himself grants crowns of victory to each victor [Col. 1173C], yet—as has already been said—he himself conquers in all.

Alternatively: God is the head of Christ, in accordance with what the Apostle says. The Word and the Father, with the Holy Spirit, are one God.

Therefore, on the head of Christ—that is, in God the Father—there are many diadems, because everything is referred to him, from whom, according to the Apostle, all things are shown to exist. The Son is not from himself but from the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. From the one from whom all things come, therefore, are the many diadems in him.

All the elect therefore have crowns in the head of Christ, because they are crowned by the Father after victory.

But in what follows [Col. 1173D]—“having a name written which no one knows except himself”—a very difficult question arises: can the Son know something that the Father or the Holy Spirit does not know?

Certainly not. For those whose substance is inseparable also have inseparable knowledge. Therefore what the Son knows, the Father knows, and the Holy Spirit knows as well. Accordingly, when the Son is said to know something, the whole Trinity is taught to know it.

And when the Father alone is said to know something, he is understood to know it together with his Wisdom, who is Christ, and with the Spirit of his Wisdom. Whatever the Holy Spirit is said to know, he is wholly believed to know together with the Father and the Son, whose Spirit he is.

For when the Lord says in the Gospel: “But concerning that day no one knows except the Father,” this is not to be understood as though the Father knew something which the Son did not know. The Son is the Father’s Wisdom. Rather, the Son is said not to know in the sense that he makes human beings not know [Col. 1174A], just as he is said to know in the sense that he makes human beings know something.

Thus it says: “The Lord your God tests you, so that he may know”—that is, so that he may make you know—“whether you love him or not.”

When the apostles asked him about the day of judgment and he did not disclose that day to them, he is said in this way not to know the day, because he made them not know it. For he cannot be ignorant of the day from whom every day was made; nor can there be any time hidden from him through whom all times were made.

The Father therefore knows the Son’s name, because the Son was begotten from him; the Holy Spirit also knows it, because he proceeds from both.

But do human beings not know this name as well? For the same John says later: “His name is called the Word of God,” and again: “He had written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” [Col. 1174B].

If blessed John knew his name, what does it mean when he says: “No one knows his name except himself”? Surely John was not someone who could know the name of God?

The sense must be supplied: no outsider knows his name except he himself together with his body, which is the Church. Not the Jews, who blaspheme him in their synagogues; not heretics, who think wrongly about him; not pagans, who refuse to believe in him; nor indeed false Christians, who destroy by their works the faith they possess.

Rather, Christ himself together with the Church—which has been granted to know that name in him—knows his own name.

This is like the statement he makes elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III) [Col. 1174C]; that is, Christ together with his body, which is the Church.

And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood.

The garment sprinkled with blood signifies the flesh of the Redeemer, stained with the blood of his Passion. Concerning this garment Isaiah, speaking in the person of the angels addressing the Lord, says: “Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one treading in the winepress?”

He answered them: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man with me from the nations” (Isaiah LXIII).

Alternatively, the Lord’s garment stained with blood may be understood as the Church, which in the holy martyrs has been drenched with their own blood. For in Scripture the Lord’s garment often signifies the Church.

Hence the Psalmist, speaking in its person, says: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my garment they cast lots” (Psalm XXI) [Col. 1174D].

All the elect are God’s garment, in accordance with what is said to him by the Father: “As I live, says the Lord, you will be clothed with all these.”

And his name is called the Word of God, because the same one who appeared as a human being in time in order to suffer was God in the beginning and was with God.

He is called the Word of God because through him God the Father made all things, in accordance with the saying: “He spoke, and they were made.” If he spoke, then surely he spoke through the Word, through whom he made all things.

Hence the same John says in his Gospel: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

For through this Word God the Father also wished to announce himself to the world. Of him it is written: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). Although the Word was invisible [Col. 1175A] in its own nature, it became visible by assuming flesh in our nature.

And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses.

By this army is understood the multitude of the faithful. Heaven too is the Church, as has very often been said.

Thus the armies that are in heaven are said to follow Christ when the armies themselves are heaven, just as people are said to enter battle in a camp when the camp itself consists of those who are prepared for war.

The multitudes of saints are rightly called armies because in this age they wage war and continually remain in combat against their enemies: namely, evil spirits, wicked people, and also the vices of the flesh.

The white horses on which they sit are their bodies, cleansed from every sin [Col. 1175B]. For each holy soul’s horse is its own body, which knows both how to restrain itself from unlawful things with the bridle of continence and, in turn, how to release itself through the impulse of love for the practice of good works.

They follow Christ because they imitate his purity and chastity, putting to death their vices and desires, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” and so forth (Colossians III).

It was said above concerning the virgins that one hundred and forty-four thousand follow him wherever he goes. Therefore it must be understood that others also follow him: namely, martyrs, confessors, and good married people, while virgins do so in a special way.

The higher the rank, the smaller it is in number.

Clothed in white and clean linen.

That is, adorned with the innocence of chastity and purity. It has already been stated above what the linen is: the righteous deeds of the saints.

And from his mouth proceeds a sword [Col. 1175C] sharp on both sides.

The sword is understood as sacred Scripture, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI).

The Lord himself speaks of this sword in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace but a sword” (Matthew X). For just as flesh is cut by a two-edged sword and limbs are separated from limbs, so by the sword of God’s word the good are divided from the wicked and the faithful from the unfaithful.

This sword is also understood in both Testaments, because on one side sins of action are cut away and on the other sins of thought.

It proceeds from the mouth of God, in accordance with what the Lord himself says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew IV) [Col. 1175D].

By this sword the faithful are wounded for their salvation, but the unfaithful and the contemptuous for their condemnation. Hence the Apostle, who was one of those who carried the sword of God’s word, says: “To some we are the aroma of life leading to life, and to others the aroma of death leading to death” (II Corinthians II).

Therefore it follows: “So that with it he may strike the nations.”

The nations in this passage do not signify wicked nations, as above, but good ones, because of what follows.

And he himself will rule them with an iron rod.

Of these nations the Father says to him through the Psalmist: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm II).

The iron rod signifies inflexible and unconquerable power. He will rule the nations with an iron rod—that is, with the strength of his kingdom, or with inflexible justice.

Hence the Psalmist [Col. 1176A] says to him: “The rod of your kingdom is a straight rod.” And, as though explaining what this rod is, he adds: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.”

And he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of almighty God.

Christ died because of the sins of the human race, by which it deserved God’s wrath. No one would live unless he had died. For if the first human being had not sinned, he would have remained immortal.

But because he despised God’s commandments, he immediately incurred God’s wrath and died. The Son of God mercifully assumed that death for us. In that death he was trodden, yet he himself trod it, because, rising from the dead, he crushed it by his powerful strength.

Alternatively, by the winepress we may understand the tribulation of the present life. The Lord treads the winepress—that is, those who are in the winepress, namely all the elect, whom he purifies through the hardships of this life [Col. 1176B].

Hence the Apostle says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” And Solomon says: “God chastises every son whom he receives.”

For just as grapes are crushed in the winepress so that storerooms may be filled with wine, so the elect are crushed by the afflictions of suffering so that they may be stored in the heavenly dwellings.

And because the elect patiently endure the wrath of God that is owed to sinners, they are rightly now called the wine of the fury of God’s wrath. They endure God’s wrath on account of the sins for which, as has been said, God was angry with the first human being, and they become wine stored in the Lord’s cellars.

But the grape skins—that is, all the reprobate—although they are pressed in the same way, are thrown outside and separated from their company.

The elect are the wine of fury only so long as they are crushed in the winepress like grapes and separated from the grape skins [Col. 1176C]. But once they have entered the eternal storerooms, they cease to be the wine of fury, because the treading of the winepress comes to an end.

And on his garment and on his thigh he has written: “King of kings and Lord of lords.”
