By the Lord’s garment, as we said above, is understood that body which the Word of God the Father assumed through a soul in the Virgin’s womb. By the thigh, however, the propagation of the flesh is signified. Thus Abraham, when he sent his servant to take a wife for his son from his father’s household, said to him: “Put your hand under my thigh, and swear to me by the Lord of heaven and earth” (Gen. 34). For he foresaw that the Lord of heaven would be born from his thigh, by whom he adjured the servant. Jacob likewise said: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49).

In his garment, therefore—that is, in his human body—and in his thigh—that is, in his carnal descent—he has written that he is King of kings and Lord of lords. Hence Matthew describes his genealogy through kings, namely through David and his descendants. When we read his words and recognize and believe that he truly descended from David’s stock, we acknowledge him as the true king; and, believing, we read in the Lord’s thigh that he himself is the King of kings. For the promises concerning his incarnation were made chiefly to David, among them this one:

“When you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up from your seed what will come forth from your loins, and I will establish his kingdom forever. He shall be my son, and I will be his father” (2 Sam. 7).

The kings whose king Christ is are all the saints who rule themselves and others well. To them Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). They are also rulers who exercise authority over their subjects, having received power in the apostle Peter, to whom the Lord says: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16).

Alternatively, by the Lord’s garment the Church is understood: Christ washed her in the baptismal font and betrothed her to himself, since she had neither spot nor wrinkle. By the thigh, however, all Christians are understood who, believing in Christ, have become children of God, according to John’s statement: “But to all who believed in him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1). In his garment, therefore, and in his thigh—that is, in the hearts of his elect—he has written that he is King of kings and Lord of lords.

And I saw another angel standing in the sun.

As has often been said, the angel is understood to be Christ, of whom the Prophet says that he will be called “the angel of the great counsel.” He is called another because he displays another vision, in the manner described above, where we say that a person is “another” when he changes the preceding manner of speaking addressed to us.

In sacred Scripture the sun has various meanings. At times it signifies the Lord himself, as it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4). At times it signifies the tribulation of persecutions, as the Lord says concerning the seeds that fell upon rocky ground, that when the sun rose they were scorched. At times it signifies something manifest, as when Nathan, speaking on the Lord’s behalf, said to David: “You acted in secret, but I will act in the sight of this sun” (2 Sam. 12), that is, openly. This was fulfilled when Absalom entered his father’s wives’ chambers in the sight of everyone. The Psalmist speaks in the same sense: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18), as if he were saying: He has displayed the mystery of the assumed humanity in the light of manifestation.

Thus, in this passage, the sun signifies the disclosure of a manifest vision. Christ therefore stands in the sun—that is, in manifest light and in the faith of the peoples—because his glory has spread throughout the whole world. He rose from the dead, was preached by the apostles, and is now believed throughout the world; and he stands in this light of faith.

And he cried out with a loud voice to all the birds that were flying through the midst of heaven.

Birds likewise are sometimes placed in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense, and therefore they must be understood according to the qualities of the passages in which they occur. They are used in a bad sense when the Lord speaks of the seeds that were sown and eaten by birds. They are used in a good sense when the Gospel says:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which is the smallest of all vegetables. But when it has grown in the ground, it becomes larger and is made into a great tree, so that the birds of heaven dwell in its branches” (Matt. 13).

The mustard seed is the Lord Jesus Christ, who at the time of his Passion appeared contemptible and less than all human beings, as though he were nothing. But after he rose from the dead, he became a great tree, so that the birds of heaven dwell in its branches—that is, in the teachings of the Gospel. These birds are the saints who rest there. They are called birds of heaven because in mind they seek heavenly things, so that they can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

He therefore calls birds those who live a heavenly life. They are rightly said to fly through the midst of heaven, because they do not cling to earthly things, but, as has been said, seek heavenly things in their minds and travel everywhere preaching. This is what he means by “through the midst of heaven,” that is, through the midst of the Church. Concerning them Isaiah says: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60).

The angel cries out to the birds—that is, he speaks to them through inward inspiration—saying:

“Come and gather for the great supper of almighty God.”

What is meant by a supper, except a banquet of eternal refreshment? He therefore calls the birds to the supper—that is, all the saints to the feast of the coming kingdom—saying: Come by believing and doing good. “Gather for the supper of almighty God,” that is, for the common banquet of eternal refreshment.

That you may eat the flesh of kings and the flesh of tribunes and the flesh of the mighty, and the flesh of horses and of those who sit upon them.

This is why he said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10), that is, kill unbelief in human beings and transfer it into your body, which is the Church.

By flesh in this passage the whole human being is understood. For sometimes in Scripture the whole human being is understood by “soul,” as in the statement: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3). For neither did souls enter Egypt without bodies, nor can flesh without souls see the Son of God; rather, by the name of flesh or soul the whole human being is understood—that is, the whole by a part.

So here also, when it says, “that you may eat the flesh of kings and tribunes,” various classes of people who are converted to Christ are included. There are kings in the Church, and there are tribunes—that is, counts and other more distinguished nobles—and there are mighty, extremely warlike men who have been converted to Christ.

By horses are designated those who were formerly pleasure-seeking and stained by lust, of whom the Prophet says: “They became like stallions let loose, frenzied after women” (Jer. 5). In the Psalms the Lord himself also warns, saying: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31).

By the riders we may understand the founders of heresies. Since they excel the carnal in knowledge of the sacred utterances, they sit, as it were, upon irrational animals, and by right of power abuse them for every kind of crime. But sometimes holy men convert such persons to the faith of Christ through their teaching and draw them toward the goodness of the Church; thus, as though slaughtering them, they eat them.

And the flesh of all, both free persons and slaves, and of the small and the great.

The freed persons are virgins in the flesh. The slaves, however, are those bound by marriage, to whom the Apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. 6), that is, you were strangers to righteousness.

By the small are understood the ignoble common people and the multitude of the populace. By the great, however, are understood the philosophers and the rich of this age.

From all these the great banquet of the supper is prepared. It has indeed been prepared from the rising of the holy Church, but it will be prepared more abundantly at the end of time, when not only the Gentiles but also the Jews will hasten forward and be converted to Christ. Hence we may refer these words particularly to that time.

The angel in the sun is therefore understood to be Elijah and Enoch, preaching Christ in open light. Although they will endure the persecutions inflicted by Antichrist, they will nevertheless preach Christ steadfastly and openly, saying to all the birds—that is, to all the saints, their fellow preachers:

“Come to the great supper of almighty God,” that is, to the assembly of the Church and the eternal refreshment of all the faithful.

This supper is rightly called great because at that time both Gentiles and Jews who have been predestined to eternal life will believe and come to this supper, so that they may eat the flesh of kings and of the others—that is, so that people from every condition and class may be converted to the faith of Christ and transferred into his body, which is the Church.

And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to make war against the one who sat upon the horse and against his army.

As was said above, the beast sometimes signifies the devil, the prince of evil men; sometimes Antichrist; and sometimes the entire body of the devil. In this passage the beast is understood to be the devil together with the man he has assumed.

The kings and their armies signify rulers together with their subjects devoted to evil. These wage war against Christ and his faithful, fighting with blasphemies and reproaches, tribulations and miracles. Although from the very advent of the Lord the devil and his members have begun the battle of conflict against the Church, he will fight more powerfully at the end of the age, when, released by divine judgment, he will rage with his own strength, when he attempts to disturb the camps of the saints through signs and miracles.

Then the beast, the kings, and their armies will fight against Christ and his army, because the reprobate will be established against the Church with one desire and one will, when the ancient enemy raises himself up in secular power through the condemned man. Then the reprobate will rise with unanimous cruelty against the Church together with their head, and in this persecution no member of the wicked will differ from the will of his head.

And the beast was seized.

This means “will be seized,” since the past tense is here placed for the future.

And with it the false prophet, who performed signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image.

The beast is understood to be Antichrist; the false prophet, wicked teachers. What signs the false prophet will perform has been said above, since many things are included under one heading, among them that he will cause fire to descend from heaven.

He says “before the beast” because wherever those ministers of Antichrist may be, they will do what they know pleases him as though they were always standing in his presence and were seen by him. By these signs he will subject those who received the mark of the beast—that is, those who believed in him—and those who worshiped his image, like the Jews, who await his coming with joy and veneration and will receive him when he comes.

In accordance with this the Lord says to them: “I came,” he says, “in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive.” Enough has been said about all these matters above; therefore they are briefly repeated here.

These two—that is, the head and the body—were cast alive into the lake of burning fire and sulfur.

This can be understood in two ways. Those whom Christ, when he comes for judgment, finds alive in the flesh will be cast alive into the lake of burning fire. After briefly tasting death, they will immediately rise again and be condemned with the devil and his angels. Although they will taste the momentary death of the flesh, they will rise again in the twinkling of an eye; they are called not dead but alive.

Alternatively, those who live and are cast into the lake of fire are those who knowingly do evil. To make this clearer, let us give an example: suppose that two men are placed before us, one dead and the other alive. If you touch the dead man, he does not feel it; if you touch the living man, he feels it. Often in Scripture the dead are used for those who do not know, and the living for those who know.

The pagans are therefore dead, and, as though ignorant and dead, they descend into hell, as it is written: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged.” The living, however, are those who possess the faith of Christ; but when they destroy it by their works, they descend alive into hell, because they sin knowingly. They will certainly be tormented more severely, because “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is required will be beaten with many blows.”

Finally, we must consider how terrifyingly the place of punishments is described as a lake of fire and sulfur. It is called a lake because of the thickest darkness in which it submerges the wretched. It is fire because it burns them up. It is sulfur because it both submerges and burns those whom it receives, and fills them with continual stench.

And the rest—that is, the faithful who have been converted to Christ—were killed by the sword of the one seated upon the horse, which proceeded from his mouth.

Having recounted the condemnation of the reprobate, he returns to those who have been converted to Christ. They were killed and died to the world and to sin by the sword of the word of God, so that they might live.

And all the birds—that is, all the saints—were filled with their flesh.

The satiety of the elect is the joy and gladness they experience at the progress of the faithful. But because some are slaughtered by the sword of the word of God for salvation, as was said above, while others are slaughtered for condemnation, we may also understand these dead who were killed by the sword of the one seated upon the horse as those who pass into hell before the Lord’s second advent. The birds—that is, the demons—rejoice over them, for they are filled with great joy when they lead their imitators to destruction. Thus they are satisfied by the damnation of those whom they offered themselves as authors of error.

These birds do not come when summoned to the slaughter of the supper; rather, like ravens and kites, they come so that, if anything dead or useless has been cast away by the faithful, they may consume it.

If it is said that the good birds—that is, holy preachers—are filled with the flesh of the reprobate, meaning that they rejoice more greatly at their deliverance when they behold the punishment of the impious, this must be understood in a particular sense, as though it said: The elect are inwardly satisfied by the sweetness of contemplation in proportion as they outwardly behold the torments of the reprobate, from which they have escaped by divine mercy.

Hence Isaiah says: “And they shall remain unto the fullness of vision for all flesh” (Isa. 66). The condemnation of the reprobate is, as it were, food for the elect, because the more continually they behold their torments, the more fully they enjoy the joys of divine contemplation. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him” (Ps. 51).

Because they drank in the pleasures of the world as though they were water, burned with the fires of envy, and defiled the dwelling of their bodies with the stench of lust, they are rightly said to be cast into the lake of burning fire and sulfur with the one whom they had as their instigator in committing these things.

But when he does not say “they will be cast” but “they were cast,” he follows the authority of Scripture, which customarily uses the past for the future. Thus we have the statement: “They dug my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21). By an anticipatory narration, we understand with complete certainty that what is still future at the end of time has been placed in the past.

## CHAPTER 20

And I saw another angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand.

He now returns to what came before, namely to the events that occurred before the second advent of Christ. For in this prophecy the historical order is not preserved.

This angel is the same one mentioned above, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who is called by the Prophet “the angel of the great counsel.” But where does he descend, since he is everywhere? For he himself says through the Prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Since there is no place outside heaven and earth, his descent is nothing other than the assumption of humanity. Hence the Apostle says:

“Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the likeness of human beings and being found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2).

He descended from heaven because, having become human, he was made for a little while lower than the angels.

By the key of the abyss is understood the discernment by which almighty God sometimes permits the reprobate to rage against the Church as far as he knows to be useful; and again, lest they harm others as much as they wish, he takes away from them the means of going forth and causing harm.

The abyss, deep and dark, signifies the hearts of wicked people. Just as a door is opened by a key and then closed again, so the devil or his members are sometimes permitted to rage, and sometimes are forbidden to go forth.

By the chain is expressed the inescapable power of God, which encircles and embraces all things. He has it in his hand—that is, in the power of the Word through whom all things were made. Through this power he himself performed mighty works and miracles; through it God the Father also worked all things, heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible.

In this hand—that is, in the power of his Word—he possesses both the force of discernment by which he regulates all things according to his governance and the inescapable power by which he encircles and embraces all things.

And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan.

How this was done he himself reveals when he says in the Gospel:

“When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, his possessions are at peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he binds the strong man and takes away all his weapons, and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11).

Appearing in the humility of the flesh, he first bound the strong man; then he made those who had been vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy.

Dragon, serpent, devil, and Satan are several names, but they signify one and the same enemy. He is called dragon because of his malice in causing harm; serpent because of his cunning in deceiving; ancient because of the wicked and practiced designs by which he has not ceased to cause harm from the beginning.

He is also called devil, that is, “flowing downward,” because every day he falls away from the hearts of the faithful. Because he opposes Christ and the Church, he is called Satan, that is, “the adversary.”

And he will bind him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss.

The number one thousand is used in Scripture for the perfection of a matter. Hence the phrase: “The word that he commanded for a thousand generations” (Ps. 104). According to secular wisdom also, it is perfect, because it consists of ten multiplied by itself. Ten times ten makes one hundred. This figure is no longer square but plane. Ten times one hundred makes one thousand, and this number, rising in height, produces a solid figure.

Therefore, because of its perfection, this number signifies the whole of the present time, from the Lord’s Passion to the end of the age. Here, however, the whole is placed for a part, because the thousand years express however much time belongs to the Church—that is, up to the reign of Antichrist.

During this time the devil is bound in the abyss—that is, in the hearts of unbelieving and perverse people—where he lies hidden and reigns until the advent of Antichrist. Then he will be released from his prison and proceed to open blasphemies and persecutions.

But it is remarkable that he is said to be cast into the abyss when he was already there. The reason is that, as has often been said above, after he was expelled from the faithful, he began to dominate his own more fiercely.

And he shut it—that is, he prohibited him from going forth, so that he could not extend the steps of his wickedness elsewhere except where God’s hidden and just judgment permits.

And he set a seal over him—that is, he sealed him, so that even those whom he holds under himself might remain hidden from him.

For the devil is sealed in this respect: neither the devil himself nor his members can know which of those whom he holds or has lost belong to the number of the elect; only the one by whom he is confined knows this. Sometimes some who seemed to belong to him suddenly pass into the number of the elect; at other times some who had escaped his dominion return to the one whom they had abandoned.

Peter himself was under his power when he denied Christ, and David when he committed adultery and murder together. But a seal was placed over him because he could not foresee that each of them would return to life through repentance and obtain God’s mercy.

Since, therefore, he does not know who belong to him and who belong to Christ, those who are under him are also kept confined, as though under a seal. Thus it comes about that he cannot fully know who are his, nor can we know who belong to Christ. Instead, what follows says:

“so that he might no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years are completed.”

A difficult question arises here. If he was bound for this reason, so that he might no longer deceive the nations, how does he fight daily against so many people and deceive them by causing them to rush into vices?

But we must understand that the nations now believing in Christ, even if he appears for a time to deceive them, are not deceived in such a way that those who are to be saved according to God’s predestination perish eternally. Therefore the whole is to be understood by a part—namely, that part which cannot be deceived.

These are the nations concerning which the Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations” (Ps. 2).

After this—that is, after the thousand years—we are again to understand the whole by a part, as above, because three and a half years still remain from the thousand years. He must be released for a short time—that is, for three years. But even then he will not be able to deceive those predestined to life; rather, he will deceive those whom he held deceived before he was released.

For just as now, while bound, he is restrained from harming the faithful, so then, when released, he will be crushed by the power of divine strength so that he cannot deceive them.

The thousand years, insofar as they concern the elect, signify the whole period of this life, up to the end of the age. Insofar as they concern the reprobate, they extend to the advent of Antichrist. Then he will seem to go out to deceive, because, by comparison with that deception, the deception now taking place is denied to be deception.

If someone asks why God wished to release for a short time the one whom he had once bound, blessed Ambrose answers: “If you ask me, I reply quickly: so that both the power of God and the devil’s weakness may be revealed.” The power of God is shown in this, that the saints remain steadfast in faith even amid scourges and the hardships of tribulations. The devil’s weakness is shown in this, that he is conquered even by girls and infants.

If he were never released, his malicious and cruel power would be less apparent, and the most faithful patience of the holy nations would also be less tested. He will therefore be released for a short time and rage against the elect with all his strength, so that God’s power may become known in them, since they will not be overcome by so great an assault, and so that he may be ashamed of his weakness and his own inability, as though God were reproaching him: “See how weak you are, since you are conquered by girls.”

And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given to them.

*Thronus* in Greek is called *sedes* in Latin. By the thrones the universal Church is signified. By those seated upon them are understood the holy preachers, namely the twelve apostles and all who have imitated their perfect life. To these thrones the Psalmist also says: “There they sat, the thrones” (Ps. 121).

They are thrones because God sits in their hearts, and they will sit in judgment because they will judge the deeds of others. They will come with the Lord to judgment, according to what he himself says to them: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

Even now they sit and judge, because they received power in the apostle Peter, to whom, together with the others, it was said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven,” and so forth (Matt. 16). Judgment was given to them—that is, the power of binding and loosing.

The question arises why above he mentions one throne in the singular, saying: “Behold, a throne was set in heaven” (Rev. 4), whereas here thrones are mentioned in the plural. This does not refer to that general judgment, but to the present time, in which they judge between the good and the wicked.

And the souls of those who had been beheaded.

“You saw” is understood. By the souls of those who had been beheaded is understood the fullness of all the saints, whether those who are spiritually dead in soul or those who were physically slaughtered for the Lord through the glory of an immense martyrdom.

For the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God.

They were killed for this one reason: because they confessed Christ as God and human being and refused to worship the devil. “Jesus” is the proper name of the assumed human being, and it is interpreted as “Savior,” because he will save his people from their sins. “The word of God” signifies the divinity of the Son of God, in which he is equal to the Father.

They were therefore killed for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God—that is, for faith in his humanity and divinity.

But why are the souls of those who were beheaded said to have been seen especially, since they alone will not reign with Christ? Clearly, this is because of the greater rank of their dignity. There will indeed be virgins, married people, and others there, but those who endured martyrdom for Christ’s name will possess greater glory.

Concerning these it is further said:

And those who did not worship the beast or its image—that is, Antichrist—nor received its mark upon their foreheads.

That is, in faith, as the Jews do.

Or upon their hands.

That is, in works, as do not only the pagans who perform the devil’s works, but also false Christians, who destroy by their works the faith they possess. Enough has been said about them above.

We may also understand the image of the beast as the entire body of the devil—that is, all the reprobate who imitate him. The righteous do not worship this image because they imitate the reprobate in nothing.

For they neither worship the beast nor receive its mark upon their foreheads or hands, because they do not follow either the unbelief of the Jews who await Antichrist, the doctrine of heretics, or the error of the Gentiles. Hence the Apostle warns: “Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6).

They do not worship the image of the beast—that is, they do not imitate the pretense of the reprobate, who profess the confession of faith with their mouths but live unbelievingly.

And they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

The saints reign with Christ both in the present life and in the future. Therefore, by the number one thousand we understand both the present and the future life, because the kingdom of the saints will not end on the day of judgment but will receive increase.

They already reign through faith, and also in those who pass daily from this life through the clear vision of God. But they will reign more fully when they are brought together into the kingdom, and “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15).

Hence the same John says in his Epistle:

“Beloved, now we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed.

Just as above the saints are understood to be those who will always reign with Christ, so here the reprobate are understood to be those who will never live. He says “the rest” because the saints also die in the present life, according to Paul’s statement: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” and so forth (Col. 3). Again he says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (ibid.).

These people therefore die to sin and for that reason will live with Christ forever. The rest of the dead, however, who are dead in soul through sin, did not live—that is, they will not live. Since they do not live here through faith and action, there they will not live through resurrection.

Such people, although living here, are dead in soul; and they pass daily toward death when, departing from this life, they are condemned in hell. In the future they will die when they rise again—not in order to live afterward, but in order to receive bodies and pass again into everlasting death.

And they will not live until the thousand years are completed—that is, throughout all future time those wretched dead will remain dead and will never be able to live, having been separated from life. They were dead before, but on the day of judgment their death will not receive an end; it will receive increase, because throughout the whole period represented by the thousand years they refused to hear the voice of the Son of God so that they might live.

The Lord reveals these two deaths in the Gospel. Concerning the present death, by which the saints rise in soul to life after sin, he says:

“The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5).

Concerning the other death he says:

“Then all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God. And they will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life.”

Since, therefore, the reprobate here—that is, in the first resurrection—do not wish to return from the death of sin to life, they will certainly pass in the second resurrection, which is of the flesh, into the second death together with that flesh.

Thus the elect will pass from the life of righteousness to the life of blessedness through the resurrection of the flesh; and the reprobate will pass from the death of sin to the punishment of death through that same resurrection of the flesh.

This is the first resurrection. He would never say “first” unless there were also a second. The first resurrection, therefore, is that which takes place in the soul: to return from unbelief to faith and to rise from vices to virtues.

The second will take place on the day of judgment, when they will rise with their bodies to live forever. For just as there are two deaths—one of the soul and the other of the body—so there are also two resurrections: one that takes place here in the soul, as we have said, and another that is awaited in the future in the body.

Concerning this resurrection, which takes place in the present through baptism, the Apostle says to the faithful: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. 3).

Blessed—that is, happy—and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection, that is, the one who rises here in soul.

Happy is the person who, while still living in the body, rises from the death of the soul, because when the resurrection of the flesh arrives, he will live in eternal joy. The one who rises from the death of his mind in this life will afterward rise happily in the flesh.

And the second death has no power over them.

That is, it has no power over them as it does over the reprobate, concerning whom enough has been said above: “The rest of the dead did not live,” and so forth.

Because those who first strove to rise from the death of the soul have no second death—that is, eternal condemnation—in them, as has been said above, just as there are two resurrections, so likewise there are two deaths.

But they will be priests of God the Father and of his Christ—that is, of the Son—and they will reign with him for a thousand years.

These words do not apply only to bishops and presbyters, but to all the faithful, whoever are members of Christ, the true king and priest. To them the apostle Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 3).

They are kings because they rightly rule the movements of carnal thoughts both in themselves and in their subjects. They are priests because they put themselves to death so that they may become a living sacrifice. Concerning them the Prophet says: “These are the sons of Zadok, who approach from the sons of Levi to the Lord to minister to him” (Ezek. 40).

They are therefore priests and kings in the present. Nevertheless, their priesthood and kingdom will not receive an end on the day of judgment, but an increase, when they will offer themselves wholly to God and be set over all kingdoms.

By contrast, the reprobate, who receive their reward here, will be stripped of all things. In the thousand years during which they will reign with Christ, the whole future period is understood, as was said above. They will never be separated from the glory of that kingdom, as the heretics wished; rather, they will reign with Christ forever.

In accordance with this the Lord says: “These will go into eternal life” (Matt. 25).

And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison. He now returns to describe the times of Antichrist. By “the thousand years completed” he understands a part from the whole. For he will be released in such a way that three years and six months will remain. Above, the thousand years are understood as the entire period from the Lord’s coming to the end of the age; here, however, they extend only to the reign of Antichrist, when he will be released from his prison—that is, from the hearts of the reprobate, in which he is now bound, lest he rage as much as he wishes. Or he will be released from prison because he will arise from the perversity of the Jews’ unbelief. In accordance with the saying: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way” (Gen. XLVI), and so forth.

And he will go out—that is, into open blasphemies and persecutions. And he will seduce many nations, Gog and Magog, which are at the four corners of the earth. Certain people speak variously about these nations, judging them to be northern peoples, namely the Getae and Massagetae, [Col. 1187A] who inhabit the island of Scanza. But if the devil were going to seduce only these two nations, it would in no way be said that he went out to seduce many nations that are over the four parts of the earth, since these peoples inhabit not four parts but only one part of the world.

Others also say that these nations were enclosed by Alexander the Great in the regions of Macedonia, where they multiplied so greatly that they produced twenty-four kingdoms from among themselves. But even these, if that were true, could not occupy all the parts of the world. Therefore this opinion is human, not divine. For in these two nations the entire multitude of the reprobate is understood: those who are over the four parts of the earth, that is, over the East, West, North, and South. In this passage it is shown [Col. 1187B] that the faith of the saints will be found in all the parts of the world before the end of the age. In accordance with what the Lord says: “The Gospel must be preached throughout the whole world, and then the end will come”; and likewise, that the multitude of the wicked will rage throughout all the parts of the world. Since the faithful will be everywhere, therefore the unbelievers will pursue them everywhere.

Gog is interpreted as “roof,” and Magog as “from the roof”—as though one were to say, “a house proceeding from a house.” By the roof, therefore, the hearts of the reprobate are understood, in which the devil now lies hidden. In accordance with what we read above, that he is shut up in the abyss. The devil, however, is “from the roof,” as though proceeding from the hearts of the reprobate. Thus he is now in the roof, and then he will proceed from the roof. The devil is now covered over in them, but in the times [Col. 1187C] of Antichrist he will come out from the roof as if uncovered, because what he now does secretly he will then do openly.

Or certainly the nations themselves are the roof, because in them the devil is now covered and confined; and they will be “from the roof” when they burst forth into open persecution. He will therefore come out into open persecution in order to seduce Gog and Magog—that is, all his members. This seduction will incite all the reprobate to wage war against Christ. And he will gather them for battle—not into one place, but into one agreement and one evil will, by which he will make them all united. Their number is like the sand of the sea. We read in Genesis that God said to Abraham: “I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore” (Gen. XVII). [Col. 1187D] In the stars the saints are understood; in the sand of the sea, all the sterile and fruitless reprobate.

And they went up—that is, the devil and his members, Gog and Magog—over the breadth of the earth. Here the Church of the saints is shown as destined to spread throughout the whole world. In accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations” (Luke XXIV). And again: “They will preach this Gospel throughout the whole world, and then the consummation will come.”

Therefore, just as the Church will be everywhere, so persecution will also be everywhere; and there will be no place in which there is a saint whom the wicked will not persecute.

And they surrounded the camp of the saints. The saints are called a camp [Col. 1188A] because they are always fighting against the devil and his members. Thus it is said: “They went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints”—as if it were said: Throughout the entire inhabited earth they confined the Church of the elect in distress.

He rightly says, “they went up,” namely against the elect, swelling with pride and imitating their head, who says: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). He ascends above the heights of the clouds, whereas they ascend over the breadth of the earth, because the head is raised especially against God, while the members are raised generally against the elect.

And the beloved city. The Church itself is the city loved by God, of which the Lord says: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V). And the Psalmist says: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI). [Col. 1188B]

And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them. By the sudden fire we should understand the sudden destruction of Antichrist or of his members. Hence Paul says: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (II Thess. II). And in the Gospel the Lord himself says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (I Thess. V).

For just as this world is now full of people, so it will be at the coming of the Son of Man. And so, when the Lord suddenly comes to judgment, as fire—that is, as a sentence of condemnation—he will descend suddenly from heaven and devour the wicked, not only in body but also in soul. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be at the coming of the Son of Man” (Luke XVII). [Col. 1188C]

Alternatively: Above we read of the holy preachers that fire coming out of their mouths devoured their enemies. For fire seems to descend from heaven when, as a result of the preaching of the divine word, the reprobate’s spite of envy increases. Thus the very preaching that is life to the righteous is everlasting condemnation to the reprobate. Hence Paul says: “To some we are an odor of death leading to death, and to others an odor of life leading to life” (II Cor. II).

And the devil who was seducing them, whether through himself or through his members, was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast—that is, Antichrist—was also thrown.

And the false prophet. Here the past tense is used for the future: “was thrown” in place of “will be thrown.” By the lake of fire into which the devil was thrown, the depth of hell is understood, in which the wicked, condemned together with their head, will be wrapped in perpetual darkness. [Col. 1188D] For although there is fire there, it will not be for giving light, but for burning the bodies of the wretched. The bodies of the reprobate will be fuel for the fire. Therefore the fire itself will also be unquenchable, because the bodies, being immortal, will always keep it burning.

Sulfur both feeds fire and generates stench, because, as has been said, there will be perpetual fire there and intolerable stench. Hence it follows: “And they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.”

Since there is always darkness in hell, in accordance with the saying, “Throw the useless servant into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXV), what does it mean when it says here, “They will be tormented day and night”? It should be understood that “day” and “night” are not used here to indicate the alternation of day and night, but the changing forms of punishment, namely heat and cold. [Col. 1189A]

By contrast, it is said of the saints that “time will be no more”—that is, there will be no change. Explaining this, Paul says: “We will all rise, but we will not all be changed” (I Cor. XV). Among the elect there will be no alternation of anything; just as they will be immortal in body, so they will also be unchanging in mind. The reprobate, however, although immortal in body, will suffer corruption, because they will be eaten by worms; and they will endure change of mind, continually failing and yet never reaching an end of their failing. This mutability of punishments is therefore expressed here by “day and night.”

Alternatively, we may refer “day” to the glory of the righteous and “night” to the punishment of the reprobate. Those who will be in hell will therefore be tormented day and night, remembering the good deeds of the righteous and their own evil deeds. [Col. 1189B]

And I saw a great white throne. The throne is the Church, over which Christ presides both uniquely and universally. It is called great because the Church consists of a multitude of peoples and is spread throughout the parts of the world. It is white because, through the font of baptism, it is washed from every stain of sin.

And the one seated upon it. “I saw” is understood. This signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who dwells in the hearts of the faithful. In accordance with the saying: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Cor. VI).

From whose presence earth and heaven fled. This is what the Lord says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV). Heaven and earth will pass away, not in the sense that they will cease to exist, but in the sense that they will be changed. In accordance with what Paul says: “The form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII). [Col. 1189C]

For then there will be a new heaven and a new earth. They will flee from the judge’s presence in the form they now have and will display the beauty they now conceal. Hence in this same Apocalypse it is said: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. XXI). For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.

Fire will accompany the Lord’s coming, occupying as much of the air as the water of the Flood occupied when it rose fifteen cubits above all the mountains that were under the whole heaven. In this connection it should be known that certain people, considering divine Scripture less carefully, first said that heaven and earth would pass through fire before judgment took place. Others, however, assert that the resurrection will take place first, followed by the renewal of heaven and earth. [Col. 1189D]

But both these groups were deceived by an insufficiently careful interpretation, as Paul makes clear when he says: “The day of the Lord will make it manifest, because it will be revealed in fire” (I Cor. III). And the Psalmist says: “Fire will burn before him, and a mighty tempest will surround him” (Ps. XLIX).

For the Lord will come to judgment at the same time, the dead will rise, and the elements will be dissolved by fire. When God judges through fire, and the fire has enveloped the adversaries and cast them into hell, while sending the elect beforehand into the kingdom, then the new heaven and earth will appear. We gather this also from an example familiar to us: after the revolutions of the winter days, we see spring shine above with more abundant sunlight and glow below with the variety of flowers. [Col. 1190A]

Hence, in the Gospel, the Lord also compares the kingdom of heaven to summer.

And the place—the place, that is, of the former vision—was not found among them. It is as though he said: “The form passes away; nature remains.” Hence Paul says: “The form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. III).

We may also understand heaven as the souls of the saints and earth as their bodies. At that time they will receive not only incorruption of body but also unchangeableness of mind, when, passing away from the form they now have like earth and heaven, they will be changed into a more beautiful state. The place of their former corruption and mutability will not be found in them. It will be as though they were no longer the same people but others, as they pass from the oldness of the first corruption into the newness of the second regeneration. [Col. 1190B]

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. The great are those of whom the Lord says: “Whoever does and teaches, he will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). The small are those who preserve simplicity of life and are not capable of grasping higher mysteries. All are generally included here: all who will come to judgment, whether for glory or for condemnation.

Alternatively, by “great and small” we may understand the kings and rulers of this world together with their subjects. All these—the righteous and the more perfect together with the simpler, and the rulers of this world together with their subjects—will stand on the day of judgment. The former in order to be rewarded, the latter in order to be condemned.

And books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life. The opened books are the two Testaments, which will be opened at the judgment, when each of the elect will plainly see what he has fulfilled from them and what he has neglected. The other book, which is the book of life, signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who grants life to his faithful. In him the books—that is, the two Testaments—will be opened, because in him all the actions of the righteous will be examined. [Col. 1190C]

Alternatively, the opened books signify the works of the righteous, which will be made manifest to all at the judgment. Their works are now hidden, because, wishing to avoid human favor, they perform all their deeds in secret; but then they will be revealed in the clear light. Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord will come and bring to light the things hidden in darkness, and will disclose the purposes of hearts; then each one will receive his praise from God” (I Cor. IV).

The books may also be understood as consciences, which will be mutually revealed to each person, because whatever one person thinks will easily be understood by another.

And the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works. That is, they were judged from both Testaments, according to what they did or did not do in accordance with them. [Col. 1190D]

Alternatively, the reprobate will also be judged by comparison with the works of the saints. It will be as though, in the unfolding of the books, they were reading the good they refused to do, considering the lives of the righteous, by comparison with which they are condemned. Therefore it is advantageous for them, in the present life, to consider their deeds and to change their worse habits through conversion.

For whoever wishes to understand fully what he is like must surely look upon those unlike himself; and he should measure himself against the pattern of the good, seeing how disfigured he is because he has abandoned the good. [Col. 1191A]

And the sea gave up the dead who were in it. This will happen before the books are opened and the dead are judged from them according to their works. As far as the literal sense is concerned, the sea, the rivers, and all pools will give up their own dead who are held in them. To whom will they be given except to life? For then all will rise, whatever death may have destroyed them by and wherever they may have been hidden.

In a deeper sense, the sea—that is, this world set in fluctuation—will give up its dead, producing both the good and the wicked in general. In accordance with what the Apostle says: “For we will all rise.”

Alternatively, by the dead whom the sea will give up we may understand those who will be found alive at the Lord’s coming; they will indeed suddenly be made dead and restored to life. [Col. 1191B]

And death and hell gave up the dead who were in them. Death signifies the devil, of whom Paul says: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II). Hell signifies all the devil’s members.

Alternatively, by death we may simply understand the death of the flesh, while by the name “hell” the places of darkness are signified. Thus both death and hell will give up their dead—that is, the devil and all his members.

Or again, all the places of hell will then restore to life all whom they hold bound through the death of the body.

After all had risen, each one was judged—that is, “will be judged”—according to their works. This means that each will receive according to his work.

[Col. 1191C] And hell and death—that is, all the devil’s members together with their head—were thrown into the lake of fire. This means into the deep condemnation of hell.

Hell rightly signifies all the reprobate. Either because those who dwell there are one house together with the hell in which they dwell; or because, imitating the devil’s works, they are never satisfied with evils, just as hell never says, “Enough.”

And whoever was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire. This means whoever was not predestined to life before the foundation of the world. He was thrown into the lake of fire. For, as was said above, the book of life signifies the right of divinity—that is, God’s foreknowledge. Whoever has not been foreordained in it will be thrown into the lake of fire. This means that he will be joined to the society of the reprobate. [Col. 1191D]

When it says, “whoever was not found,” this means nothing other than “not foreordained.” The elect, however, are written in this book; they were foreknown and foreordained before the foundation of the world. Hence the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined” (Rom. VIII). And elsewhere: “He chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I).

## CHAPTER XXI

And I saw a new heaven and a new earth. In the predestination of almighty God, future things have already come to pass. Therefore he says here that he sees a new heaven and a new earth, and he adds: “For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” How this is to be understood, whether according to the literal sense or spiritually, was explained above. [Col. 1192A]

The first heaven and the first earth passed away—that is, they were changed through renewal and departed from their former form. In accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “The form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. III).

But regarding what follows, “and the sea is no more,” it is uncertain whether this can be understood literally—that is, that the sea, together with the rivers, will dry up—or whether it is said only in a spiritual sense. For the earth subsists through the joining of the waters, since it contains waters beneath, outside, and above itself, lest it perish through natural dryness; for unless it were tempered by waters, it would be reduced to ashes.

Therefore we cannot easily say whether, through that immense heat, the sea together with the rivers will be dried up, or whether it too will be changed into something better. Even if this happens through God’s power, the earth, though dry, will be able to subsist sufficiently. [Col. 1192B]

There are, in fact, four elements, of which two are to be changed for the better, as is said here and as the Lord manifests in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away”—that is, they will be changed. Whether the sea or fire will pass away, that is, be changed, God knows, although here we read: “And the sea is no more.” And elsewhere: “The light of the lamp will not shine in her.” How these things will happen, we shall know better when we have arrived there.

And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God. This holy city is the Church. It is called a city because it is inhabited by many and extends into the four parts of the world, having God as its inhabitant. Hence Paul says: “God’s holy temple is what you are” (I Cor. III). [Col. 1192C]

It is called holy because it is sanctified daily through baptism. It is also called Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” because it labors for this purpose: to receive the vision of God in the heavenly places.

It is called new because it is stripped of the oldness of sin. The perpetration of sin belongs to the old Adam. Therefore, when the Church is cleansed from original sin, it comes from the oldness of sin into newness. Hence the Apostle says: “Strip off the old man and put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Col. III).

This city is said to descend from God because, from its beginning, it descended together with its head, with whom and through whom it ascends upward. Hence the same Lord says: “No one has ascended into heaven,” and so forth. [Col. 1192D]

Alternatively: It is said to descend from heaven because the grace by which God made it the Church is heavenly, in accordance with the saying: “I, the Lord, am the one who makes you.” Whatever it possesses in faith, hope, love, the other virtues, and baptism has been given to it from above. Hence James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I).

Prepared—that is, adorned with faith and the other virtues—so that it might deserve to become a bride, as a bride adorned for her husband.

He says two things, “bride” and “husband,” in which “wife” is implied, because it is customary for Holy Scripture to call bridegrooms “husbands” and brides “wives.” Thus we read: “Let the bridegroom come out from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room” (Joel II); and Zipporah says to Moses: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me” (Exod. IV). In the Gospel it is also said by the angel: “Joseph, her husband” (Matt. I). And in the Law: “If a man finds a girl betrothed in the field and lies with her, he shall die, because he humbled his neighbor’s wife” (Deut. XXII). [Col. 1193A]

The holy Church is therefore now a bride through faith, hope, and love; but then she will be a wife when she reaches the embraces of her husband—that is, the contemplation of almighty God. This is indeed accomplished daily in individual elect persons, but it will be completed generally at the end, when all together hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXX), and so forth.

He calls her adorned—that is, composed with every virtue—in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Ps. XLIV).

And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying. By the throne here the angels and holy human beings are understood, in whom the Lord dwells. Therefore this loud voice is understood as the voice of almighty God. It is called loud because it speaks of great things, saying: [Col. 1193B]

“Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings.” Great indeed is the grace of God, that human beings should become the tabernacle of him whose greatness the world cannot contain. “The tabernacle of God is with human beings,” that is, the human beings themselves are God’s tabernacle.

John here represents the figure of the holy Church, which hears the voice saying, “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings,” when, through inward inspiration, it recognizes itself to be God’s tabernacle.

And he will dwell with them—that is, with those who have deserved to be God’s tabernacle. Hence he himself says to the apostles: “Behold, I am with you all the days” (Matt. XXVIII).

And they will be his people. In accordance with the saying: “Israel is my inheritance.” [Col. 1193C]

And God himself will be with them. Dwelling in their faith and love, as he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.”

And the almighty God is their God, with whom he deigns to dwell. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV). And he himself speaks in the Law, saying: “You shall give no possession to the sons of Levi, for I am their inheritance.”

For when a person departs from God through sin, he is not God’s people and does not possess God. But when he returns to God through repentance, he is God’s people, because he possesses God and is possessed by God.

[Col. 1193D] And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. These words do not concern the present life, which is full of grief and tears, but the future, when all grief will be taken away from the faithful and everlasting joy will be possessed. In accordance with the saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. V).

We should consider why he says that every tear will be taken from the eyes of the saints, when it would have been sufficient to say, “He will wipe away a tear from their eyes.” It should be understood that there are various kinds of tears by which the elect are afflicted in this life. [Col. 1194A]

Sometimes they weep because of fear of punishments, lest they be deservedly handed over to retributive penalties on account of their iniquity. Sometimes they weep because of love and fellowship with the heavenly citizens. For after they have obtained forgiveness of sins, they begin to weep again—not because they fear condemnation, but because they are delayed from the kingdom.

At other times they lament the sins of others, as Samuel wept for Saul because the Lord regretted that he had made him king over Israel; and as Paul wept for the Corinthians, who, after fornication and idolatry, had not repented.

The Lord will therefore wipe away every tear from the eyes of the elect, because they will neither be constrained by fear of punishments nor delayed from the kingdom, which they will possess immediately; nor will they weep over the sins of others, because, once the reprobate have been condemned by God’s just judgment, no one will thereafter be able to sin. [Col. 1194B]

And death will be no more. After we have all risen from the dead, death will no longer exist among the elect—not death of body or of soul. The first man was created in paradise under this condition: that, if he did not sin, he would remain immortal and, once the number of the elect was complete, would pass from the earthly paradise to the heavenly homeland without the intervention of death. Yet he was created in such a way that, if he sinned, he could die.

This death, which he incurred through sin, was destroyed by the Lord’s death. Therefore it will have no place among the elect after we have all risen to life, having become such that thereafter we can neither die nor sin.

Nor will there be mourning in that Church, because, as was said above, it arises in the present life in many ways. Nor will there be any more crying or pain. [Col. 1194C]

In this passage “crying” means the complaint of evil suggestion. Before the human being sinned, he was in great peace and possessed all his members as subject to him, with none resisting him in any way. But after he sinned, he immediately felt the cry of evil suggestion rising up against him; and, seeing the woman, he desired her. By God’s just judgment it consequently happened that the one who refused to be subject to God could not have his members subject to him.

We all continue to endure this cry. Paul shows that he labored under it when he said: “I see another law in my members” (Rom. VII), and so forth. For this cry is always present, because the flesh always resists the spirit.

But when this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality, the cry that did not allow the elect to rest in this life will cease to rage against them. There every evil suggestion will cease; there there will be no pleasure of the flesh. [Col. 1194D]

Nor will there be pain after this, because the flesh of the elect will no longer produce thorns and stings of sins over which they ought to grieve.

For the former things have passed away, because in the present age they endure all these things; but when heaven and earth have been renewed, then the elect will be renewed and will in no way endure their former sufferings.

And the one seated on the throne—that is, almighty God, who presides over his Church—said: “Behold, I make all things new.” Namely, the things spoken of above, among which heaven and earth will also be renewed.

And he said to me: “Write.” Write them in your heart, or also commit them to writing, so that they may come to the knowledge of those who come afterward. But what is said to John pertains to the whole Church, which seems to write the words of God on the tablets of flesh that are hearts. [Col. 1195A]

These words, divinely shown to you from the beginning of this book, are completely faithful and true, because they proceeded from the true God. It is as though he said: Let the words they speak be impressed more firmly in the memory of the heart, since they are spoken concerning the entire fullness of faith and the entire confidence of hope.

And he said to me: “It is done.” This means “It will be done”: all the things spoken above will be fulfilled, whether concerning the reward of the righteous or the condemnation of the reprobate. Because all these things will certainly be completed in their proper time, they are confirmed by the voice of almighty God as though they had already happened; in his presence all future things remain present. Hence the saying: “He made the things that are to come.”

“I am α and ω, the beginning and the end.” This does not mean that he has a beginning in time or an end, but that all things received their beginning from him and will resume their end in him. Enough has been said about these matters above. [Col. 1195B]

But by the fact that the Lord, now for the third time in this Apocalypse, repeats his name through the angel, saying, “I am α and ω,” he indicates two things to us. One is that we should understand that what is contained in this revelation belongs properly neither to the angel nor to John. The other is that we may know that he himself is God before the ages and human at the end of the ages.

“I will give the thirsty the fountain of the water of life freely.” To the thirsty—that is, to those who hunger for righteousness—the fountain of water is promised. Of them the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V).

The fountain of living water signifies the inseparable Trinity. The Father is a fountain, the Son is a fountain, and the Holy Spirit is a fountain. Hence the Psalmist says: “With you is the fountain of life.”

To those who thirst for God, therefore, he will give himself as a reward; in contemplating him there will be refreshment of eternal satisfaction. Desiring to be satisfied from this fountain, the Psalmist said: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Ps. XLI). Of this fountain he says: “Whoever drinks will have life.” For by possessing God he will have eternal life, which is God. Hence he himself says: “This is eternal life” (John XVII), and so forth. [Col. 1195C]

This fountain is given freely to the faithful—that is, without any preceding merits of human beings.

Whoever conquers the devil’s temptations, the incitements of his flesh, and the adversities of wicked people will possess the things spoken of above: almighty God, and immortality and incorruption of the flesh.

“And I will be his God”—that is, eternal satisfaction and reward. “And he will be my son”—those who, by believing in God, become faithful sons of God: here through faith, but there through manifestation.

Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (I John III). [Col. 1195D]

But for the timid, the unbelieving, the accursed, and murderers. We may understand as timid those whose will was to believe in Christ, but who, seeing the various kinds of torments prepared for the faithful, withdrew from faith in Christ, shaken by fear. Some, even after the faith of Christ and baptism, withdrew from the faith, whether shaken by terrors or enticed by blandishments, because they feared the punishments. [Col. 1196A]

Their portion will be in the lake that burns—that is, in everlasting condemnation.

There are also timid people within the peace of the Church, who are afraid to do good because they fear rulers and worldly people. Of such it is said: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. LI).

With the unbelieving—that is, with the pagans; and with the accursed—that is, with unbelieving Jews or false Christians, who are accursed by God, that is, utterly abominable. Hence the saying: “The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V). [Col. 1196B]

And with murderers—that is, those who kill a human being in any manner, or who cut their own throats through hatred. Hence the saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III).

And with fornicators—that is, with those who serve idols, or pursue the uncleanness of the flesh, or love the creature more than the Creator, and love riches beyond measure. Hence Paul says: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Gal. V).

And with poisoners—that is, magicians who practiced incantations. Or by “poisoners,” that is, evildoers, we may understand those who dominate others through human power. Hence in the Gospel: “The kings of the nations lord it over them” (Matt. XX), and those who have authority over them are called poisoners—that is, evildoers.

And with idolaters, who venerate images of dead human beings, or even representations of certain things, in place of God.

And with all liars. Having named above, in order, the individual originators of the vices, he added at the end, “and with all liars.” By saying “all,” he shows that there are many kinds of lies. For blessed Augustine says that there are eight kinds of lies; nevertheless, there is no lie free from sin. Hence it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I). And again: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V). [Col. 1196C]

Some say that there is no sin if they utter a lie for the sake of truth or justice, as we read happened in Egypt concerning the midwives. When they returned to Pharaoh and were reproached for preserving alive the infants whom they had been ordered to kill, they lied, saying: “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women; they themselves have skill in midwifery” (Exod. I).

Hence Scripture also reports: “Therefore God built them houses.” Was that lie, then, for which they received a reward from God, not a sin? It was indeed a sin, but it was cleansed through an act of mercy. Thus God built dwellings for them—that is, he gave them a multitude of children—because they had preserved the lives of other people’s children. [Col. 1196D]

We likewise read of Rahab the prostitute, who hid Joshua’s messengers and replied to those searching for them: “I admit that they came to me, but when the gate was being closed, they went out together” (Josh. II).

Because she performed an act of mercy toward them and delivered them from death, she later deserved to attain knowledge of the one God and to be counted among the Israelites, since that sin of lying was cleansed by an act of piety and mercy. It would have been worse if she had handed them over to death than that she denied them and lied. [Col. 1197A]

One point, however, we must retain: no kind of lie remains without punishment unless it has been loosened through repentance or some work of piety. For of all those listed above, their portion will be in the lake of fire and sulfur—that is, in the deep condemnation of hell, where fire and sulfur are together.

This is the second death, that is, of body and soul. The first death takes place in the soul through sin; the second is understood as taking place in soul and body.

It follows:

And one of the seven angels who had the bowls full of the seven final plagues came. By the seven angels, as was said above, either the universal Church is understood, or all preachers, because of the sevenfold Spirit by which the Church is instructed and teachers are educated. For it has often been said that the number seven signifies totality, since all present time revolves through seven days. Therefore, one of the seven angels who came to John is understood as the Lord Jesus Christ, who, according to the prophet, is the angel of great counsel—that is, the messenger of the Father’s will. He is one of the angels because he is the head of all the elect, and through the assumption of humanity he was joined to them in the Virgin’s womb. He therefore came through the mystery of the Incarnation, although he was everywhere through the power of his divinity.

These angels—that is, the preachers whose head is Christ—have bowls full of the seven final plagues. This means that they are filled with divine preaching, by which some of their hearers are wounded unto salvation, while others are wounded unto their own destruction. The plagues are rightly called “final,” because they are sent in the final hour of this age—that is, from the Lord’s Incarnation until the end of the world.

And he spoke with me, saying, “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” John in this passage signifies the Church, to whom God speaks through hidden inspiration in the mind, saying, “Come”—with the steps of faith and the steps of love—“and I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” That is, he will reveal to you yourself what you now are through faith and what you will later be, when you come to the contemplation of God. He uses two expressions, “bride” and “wife,” because she who is now a bride through faith and love will then be a wife when she comes to the embrace of her husband. God is the Church’s husband; hence Solomon says, “There is no man in his house” (Prov. 7).

And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain. Here it is clearly shown that John did not behold this vision with bodily eyes, but in the spirit—that is, he was lifted up with the eyes of his mind to contemplate heavenly mysteries. The great and high mountain to which he says he was lifted is understood as Christ. Of him Daniel says, “Because the stone cut from the mountain without hands grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan. 2). He himself also says of himself, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 8). This mountain is great because it fills the whole world. It is high because he is man and yet is also true God.

Of this mountain Isaiah says, “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared upon the summit of the mountains”—that is, Christ, the ruler of all the elect. Why, then, are both an angel and a mountain understood as Christ, while the Church is understood in John? The angel leads John to the mountain: that is, Christ establishes his Church upon himself. Christ is therefore rightly called both angel and mountain, because, appearing as a messenger to the Church, he invites the elect to their heavenly homeland, and by bearing that same Church upon himself, he raises it to heavenly things.

And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem descending out of heaven from God and possessing the glory of God. The city is the Church, having God as its inhabitant. It is called holy because it is sanctified daily through baptism. It is called Jerusalem because it labors for this purpose: to arrive at the vision of the heavenly homeland. It descends from heaven because everything good that it possesses has been given to it from heaven through God’s grace. Hence James says, “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 3).

Or, as was said above, it will descend from heaven in its Head, because he joined it to himself in the virginal womb. Hence the Apostle says, “Christ betrothed the Church to himself, not having spot or wrinkle.” It possesses the glory of God because it is illumined by the Son of God, who “enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Hence he also says to the apostles, “I am the light of the world” (John 8).

Thus it follows: “And its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone.” This is said because, while he illumines his elect, he nourishes them with the pasture of eternal freshness. The jasper stone is green in color, and therefore the vision of the holy Trinity is not inappropriately understood through the jasper stone, since the souls of the saints desire to attain it, as living creatures seek out whatever is green. Hence he himself says, “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10): he will enter through faith and go out from faith into hope, and he will find pastures of eternal satisfaction. Therefore the Psalmist says, “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me there in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22).

“Like crystal.” By crystal, however, the reward of heavenly recompense is understood, which will be fulfilled in the very vision of God. For water is, as it were, changed into crystal when the contemplation of God itself becomes the reward of those reborn from water and the Spirit. Indeed, if we carefully consider what the jasper signifies, crystal signifies the same thing, because the reward of the saints will be nothing other than the present face of God.

And it had a great and high wall. The wall of the Church is Christ, of whom Isaiah says, “On that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: ‘Our city of strength is Zion, the Savior; he will place a wall in it’” (Isa. 26). He is also great, of whom the Psalmist says, “The Lord is great in Zion” (Ps. 98). He is also high because he has been exalted by the Father above all things and has also been established as God through his humanity. He himself is the wall—that is, the defense and protection—of his Church.

Or, more generally, the wall is understood as the Church itself, which is called a wall because of the firmness of its faith and the constancy of its virtues. This wall is great because the Church consists of many believers and is extended through the four regions of the world. It is also high because, while it inhabits the earth in body, it possesses heaven in mind.

Hence it is appropriately added: “Having twelve gates.” By the twelve gates, the twelve apostles are understood. Through the twelve apostles, moreover, the entire order of teachers is understood, through whose ministry we enter the Church. They baptize us and, by teaching the faith of the Church, introduce us through its gates.

Of these it is further said: “And at the gates twelve angels.” That is, all teachers subordinate to the apostles, such as priests and the other leaders of the Church’s lesser orders. Even if they are unable to accomplish great things, they nevertheless do not cease to announce to the faithful people the lesser things they have received. Of them it is written in Zechariah, “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and the law is sought from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

Thus twelve angels stand at the twelve gates, because the teachers of the Church follow the faith and footsteps of the apostles.

“And names written upon them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.” We must not understand the sons of Israel carnally as the twelve sons of Jacob, whose life was reprehensible, as Scripture makes clear. Rather, we must understand the spiritual fathers descending from his offspring, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets. Their names are written upon the gates because their memory is contained within the faith of the apostles. What these men announce as having happened, those others foretold as going to happen. Since, therefore, they announce the same things that the prophets foretold, they show that they have their memory implanted in their hearts.

Alternatively, in the twelve sons of Israel we may understand all nations, just as in the twelve apostles we understand the entire order of preachers. The names of the twelve sons of Israel are therefore written on the twelve gates because all nations stand within the faith and love of the apostles. Hence Paul says, “You are our letter, written in our hearts” (2 Cor. 3).

Three gates on the east. By the east, the Jewish people are understood, from whom Christ arose, the true sun of righteousness, enlightening the hearts of believers. There the three gates were first, because the faith of the holy Trinity was first announced among them by the prophets and other righteous people who, enlightened by the Spirit, came to know the faith of the holy Trinity.
