Hence Isaiah says that he heard the cherubim crying, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. 4). But because one majesty is understood in the Trinity of persons, after saying “Holy, holy, holy” in the plural, they attend to the unity of substance and add, “The Lord God of hosts.” Similarly, the Psalmist, first saying, “May God the Father bless us; may God the Son bless us; may God the Holy Spirit bless us,” turns the Trinity of persons toward the unity of majesty, saying, “And may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66).

Three gates on the north. By the north, the Gentiles are understood, placed in the condition of unbelief and ignorance, as our ancestors were. There too are three gates, because the Gentiles, instructed through the teaching of the apostles and the other preachers, received the faith of the holy Trinity.

The three gates on the east are rightly mentioned first, and those on the north afterward, because the Jews believed first and the Gentiles afterward. The latter had previously been in the north, which is the coldest and harshest wind, and they had the devil, who says, “I will set my throne in the north.”

And three gates on the south. By the south we understand the radiance of faith, which shines throughout the whole world. Since the sun is fixed in the south, that is, at the center of the sky, it illumines the entire world, signifying Christ, who illumines the whole Church with the light of his radiant faith.

There are therefore three gates on the south, because the faith of the holy Church is illumined by the splendor of the holy Trinity, having been baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

And three gates on the west. By the west we understand the final age of the world, in which, through Elijah, Enoch, and the other preachers, the same faith of the holy Trinity will be spread throughout the four quarters of the earth, embracing Jews and Gentiles alike. The number twelve of the gates, comprehended under the number three through the four parts of the world, pertains to the ministry of the twelve apostles, through whom the faith of the holy Trinity has been spread throughout the four quarters of the earth.

And the wall of the city had twelve foundations. The wall itself is the city, which has twelve foundations because it rests upon the teaching of the apostles and prophets. The foundation of these foundations is Christ, of whom Paul says, “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3).

When “foundation” is spoken of in the singular, Christ himself is understood, upon whom the entire building of the Church is established. When it is spoken of in the plural, the patriarchs, apostles, and other teachers are understood. Hence the same Apostle says, “You are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2).

Thus the apostles and the other teachers are understood as the foundation, founded upon the one foundation, Christ. For he is the foundation of foundations, just as he is the King of kings and Lord of lords.

This is also why, after the foundations have been named, the name of the Lamb is not omitted, but he says: “And on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.” On these foundations—that is, on the faith of the patriarchs and apostles—are the names of the twelve apostles, because whoever undertakes governance in the Church holds the apostles’ place, imitating their teaching and actions.

To make this still clearer, let us say that the foundations are the patriarchs and prophets, on whom the names of the twelve apostles are written, because the apostles possessed the faith which those men also possessed. The apostles believed that Christ had come in the flesh; the patriarchs and prophets foretold that he would come.

Hence the Psalmist says, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86). The mountains themselves are the patriarchs and prophets, upon whom the teachers of the New Testament are founded, because they imitate their faith. They are, as it were, foundation upon foundations, since those mountains themselves are recognized as foundations.

And the one who spoke with me had a golden measuring reed, in order to measure the city. Here the angel bore the figure of the Son of God, because he orders all things by measure and number. By the reed we should understand divine preaching, because writing is done with a reed; therefore Scripture is rightly understood through the reed, the agent standing for the thing produced.

With this reed—that is, with divine speech—God touches and illumines the hearts of the faithful. In them he weighs and measures the deeds and progress of each person, giving to one the word of wisdom and to another kinds of tongues, and so forth. This measuring reed is called golden because of the splendor of divine wisdom, which in many passages is represented by gold. Hence it is said, “Receive wisdom as gold.”

With this reed, therefore, he measures the city—that is, the universal Church—and its gates, that is, the teachers and leaders of the Church, and the wall of the city, in which nothing other than the city itself is understood.

And the city was laid out as a square. In a square figure, one side is not greater and another smaller; rather, all four sides extend together at equal length. By these four sides we should understand hope, faith, love, and works, which are equal, because each believer hopes as much as he believes, loves, and acts.

Likewise, he hopes as much as he believes, loves, and acts; he loves as much as he believes, hopes, and acts; and he acts as much as he believes, loves, and hopes.

The Church is rightly said to be laid out as a square, because it is strong through faith, patient through hope, broad through love, and effective through works. Each of the faithful also possesses faith, by which they believe what they cannot see—namely, the one God who is three in persons and one in majesty. They possess hope because they hope to attain what they do not yet see. They also possess love, that is, love of God and neighbor. To these virtues, so that their life may be perfect, works are added, without which faith is dead. Hence the apostle James says, “Faith without works is useless” (James 2).

Alternatively, by the four sides of the city we may understand the four principal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. These must exist in the elect in such a way that none exceeds another.

Prudence is knowledge of what should be desired and what should be avoided. Temperance must be joined and made equal to it, because prudence is not perfect unless a person strives to restrain himself and withdraw from the pleasures of this age. Once he has done this, he must possess fortitude, so that he may accomplish in action what he understands. Finally, he must possess justice, so that he may regulate his actions in such a way that he does not appear to himself excessively just or wiser than is appropriate.

Its length is as great as its breadth. He repeats what was said above, because a square figure is equal on every side. Its length is therefore as great as its breadth, because faith is as great as hope, love, and works. For as much as we believe, so much do we love; as much as we love, so much do we presume in hope; and insofar as we are raised toward heavenly things through hope, so far are we extended through love toward God and neighbor. To that same extent we strive to adorn faith, hope, and love with works.

Likewise, each person is as prudent as he is temperate, strong, and just; as temperate as he is prudent, strong, and just; as strong as he is prudent, temperate, and just; and as just as he is prudent, temperate, and strong.

And he measured the city with the golden reed, twelve thousand stadia. The city is already understood as the Church, and the reed as evangelical teaching. By the twelve thousand stadia, all those laboring in the Church are represented. A stadium is understood through what takes place in a stadium—that is, the place of labor and the reward of those who labor. Hence Paul says, “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?” (1 Cor. 2).

The elect therefore labor in the stadium, that is, in the labor of the present life, so that they may receive the prize of heavenly recompense. The sum of the elect is also expressed by twelve thousand. The number twelve is considered perfect because it consists of ten and two: ten pertains to the ten commandments of the law, and two to the two commandments of love, upon which the whole law and the prophets depend.

Alternatively, it is considered perfect because it is composed from the parts of seven, namely three and four. Three refers to faith in the holy Trinity; four refers to the four Gospels.

The number one thousand is likewise shown to be perfect because the square of the number ten produces a complete number: ten times one hundred is one thousand. The number one thousand is therefore perfect. Hence it is said, “The word which he commanded for a thousand generations,” by which the totality of generations is expressed.

Since, therefore, the number twelve or the number one thousand is used in sacred speech to signify perfection, the fullness of their perfection is rightly expressed in twelve thousand—those who fulfill the Decalogue with love of God and neighbor, preserve faith in the holy Trinity, and do so according to the authority of the four Gospels.

God Almighty measures these people with the reed because he weighs out the teaching of knowledge to each according to the capacity of his understanding. Nevertheless, he shows all whom he touches in the things they have received to be perfect. Each person possesses through love in another what he has not received in himself, so that from many members one body may be formed. Or, as was said above, to one is given the word of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, and so forth.

Although these gifts are not equal—since, as the Lord says, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14)—all will nevertheless receive the reward of heavenly recompense. When our wondrous Creator and Dispenser grants to one what he denies to another, he does not therefore appear to depart from the measure of the reed.

Whoever attempts to do more than he has received usually loses what he has, because he hastens boldly to seize what he cannot attain. We also use the ministries of our bodily members properly when we preserve their distinct functions. We see light with our eyes, but hear sound with our ears. If someone abandons these functions by confusing their order, he does not rise to what belongs to another.

And its length and breadth and height are equal. This is the solidity of the square figure of which he said above, “The city was laid out as a square.” Length pertains to faith, height to hope, and breadth to love, of which it is written, “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118).

Alternatively, length pertains to patience, height to contemplation, and breadth undoubtedly signifies love, which is so broad that it reaches not only to friends but even to enemies, according to the command: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6).

The length, breadth, and height of the city are therefore equal, because to the extent that the mind is patient through long-suffering, it is broad through love; and to the extent that it is patient through long-suffering and broad through love, it is also high through contemplation. Each person is raised to higher things through contemplation insofar as he humbles himself by enduring the evils of his neighbors.

The length, breadth, and height of the Church are therefore equal, because insofar as it is patient amid adversity and widened through love toward all, to that same extent it is high through contemplation.

And he measured its wall, one hundred and forty-four cubits. This number contains the square of twelve: twelve times twelve makes one hundred and forty-four. The number one hundred signifies perfection. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever has left house, or brothers or sisters, and so forth, will receive a hundredfold” (Matt. 19)—that is, he will attain perfection of mind, so that he will no longer wish to recover what he once lost.

The number forty is also considered perfect in sacred Scripture for many reasons: either because of the Lord’s fast, completed over forty days, or because of the Decalogue and the four Gospels, in which the perfection of the Decalogue is contained. The number four is likewise consecrated because of the four rivers of paradise, the four books of the Gospel, the four regions of the world, or the four principal virtues.

Since the cubit is a measure of the hand, the cubit rightly expresses the work of the hand. The wall, moreover, is the city itself. The angel therefore measured the walls of the city at one hundred and forty-four cubits because Almighty God weighs and considers how much each of the elect labors, through the authority of the four Gospels, in the Decalogue, and what perfection of mind they attain, so that they may reach the fellowship of the angels.

Hence it follows: “The measure of a human being, which is that of an angel.” At the literal level, this shows that the angel who displayed these things to John appeared in human form. At the level of higher understanding, however, the measure of a human being, which is that of an angel, is rightly understood as the angel himself who measures the Church, because the glory of angels and human beings will be equal in heavenly blessedness.

Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel, “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 12). Or the measure of a human being is called that of an angel because as many angels as remained in heaven after the fall of the archangel, so many human beings will ascend from earth into heaven.

And the structure—that is, the building—of its wall was of jasper stone. Jasper is green in color and signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the refreshment of the living creatures who are saints. In the contemplation of Almighty God will be the supreme perfection and eternal satisfaction of the elect, according to the Psalmist: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22).

Alternatively, through the jasper stone the elect are represented, whose faith never withers but remains green in its works. The city’s structure is therefore made from jasper stone because Christ’s foundation is first established in the Church, upon which all the faithful are also placed, according to the Apostle: “Coming to him, a living stone, you yourselves are built up like living stones into spiritual houses” (1 Pet. 2).

For just as, in the construction of a wall, great square stones are first placed, carrying those set above them, while those stones in turn carry others, and the whole building is constructed in this way until the final stone is reached—which, although carried by all, carries no one—so in the foundation of the Church the apostles were placed first, then the martyrs, then confessors, virgins, widows, and the other saints. They all carry one another, most willingly enduring the sufferings of their own minds, according to the Apostle’s command: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6).

Alternatively, they sustain one another by their example, and this continues until the end of the age, when the last elect person will be placed at the final summit of this building. Although he will be carried by all who preceded him, he will have no one whom he can carry, because in him the whole building of the Church will be completed.

Christ, however, will be both the foundation and the consummation of the Church; he is its beginning and its end.

And the city itself was pure gold, like pure glass. By gold, heavenly splendor is understood, concerning which the Lord says, “Receive wisdom as gold.” In glass, purity of heart is understood. For if a vessel is made from other metals, whatever is placed inside it is not visible from outside. In glass, however, everything placed within is wholly visible from without. Therefore glass signifies the purity of heart of all the saints, which will be made mutually manifest to everyone in heavenly blessedness.

These words cannot refer to the present Church, in which the consciences of individuals are hidden from one another, but to the future Church, when the Lord comes and “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness,” and the consciences of all will be revealed to everyone. Whatever anyone has thought will be wholly visible to another, and each person will then be perceptible to another just as he can now be perceptible to himself.

Or, as was said, gold signifies heavenly wisdom, while glass signifies purity of faith. For in glass, as was said, whatever is placed inside is wholly visible outside. Thus the purity of faith is signified: the saints hold it in their hearts and manifest it also with their mouths. Nothing is done within through hypocrisy that is not displayed outwardly through the pure confession of mouth and deed.

And the foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone. The foundations of the city—that is, of the Church—are the patriarchs, prophets, and other preachers, upon whose teaching and examples the structure of the Church stands. These foundations are adorned with every precious stone—that is, with every virtue: faith, hope, love, hospitality, fasting, abstinence, and the other works of good actions.

Alternatively, understand the precious stones as all those who imitate the patriarchs, prophets, and preachers, who have been placed in the city’s building and adorn the city itself through their conduct and life. Concerning these stones the Lord says through the prophet, “Behold, I will set your stones in order and will lay your foundations in sapphires” (Isa. 54).

Hence it follows: “The first foundation was jasper.” As was said above, this stone is green in color, and therefore not inappropriately signifies the Lord, who is the food and refreshment of all the elect. He is the first foundation of the Church because, as the Apostle says, “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3). It also signifies the elect, whose faith will never wither but will always persevere in the greenness of its works.

The second, sapphire. The sapphire stone is by nature not at all precious, but in its mystical significance it is found to be exceedingly splendid. It retains a sky-blue color and therefore signifies the saints who seek heavenly things with their minds, saying with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

The third, chalcedony. By nature, chalcedony is much less valuable than sapphire, but in mystical meanings it too is found to be very precious. It is of an exceptionally strong nature, so much so that it resists the tools of every sculptor. Therefore it signifies the saints who are utterly unconquerable amid the adversities of this age. One of them says, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8). And again, “I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels, and so forth, will be able to separate us from the love of Christ” (ibid.). Such people are rightly established in the foundation of the Church because they provide others with examples of fortitude. Hence the same Apostle says to his hearers, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 8).

This stone also resembles a pale, glowing lamp, and in this it signifies the humility of the saints, who are considered pale in the present life because they are despised, scorned, and regarded as nothing. Nevertheless, they shine in a dark place and show others the light of knowledge and ardor. Hence it is said of one of them, “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5): burning in faith and love, shining in word and deed.

The fourth, emerald. Emerald is a precious stone by nature, but it is still more precious as a figure of the elect. This stone possesses such greenness that it surpasses the greenness of all plants and even makes the surrounding air appear green. If its mass is sufficiently large, it also reflects the images of those who look at it.

There are many kinds of this stone, but the most precious emeralds are found in Scythia, a deserted region. They are guarded, however, by griffins—terrible and fierce animals with the body of a lion but feet, beak, and wings like an eagle. Thus they run across the earth like lions and fly through the air like birds.

These beasts guard that desert region and preserve the stones—not because they turn them to their own use, but because they take them away from human beings. The Arimaspi, men with one eye, wage war against them and carry away the stones.

This contains a beautiful mystery. The emerald stone, which, as we have said, possesses extraordinary greenness, signifies Christ, who will give his faithful the pastures of eternal refreshment. The desert in which the stones are found signifies the hearts of the saints, who withdraw far from earthly things and the cares of this world so that they may serve the Lord in the quiet of their inmost hearts. Hence one of them says, “Behold, I have gone far away by fleeing, and I remained in solitude” (Ps. 54).

The emerald stone is found in their hearts because Christ dwells in them. But griffins are present—that is, evil spirits—who strive to take Christ away from the faithful. They do not possess him themselves; rather, out of envy, they take him away from human beings.

But there are also Arimaspi with one eye, that is, the elect possessing one eye of the mind. They fight with the griffins—that is, with evil spirits—and seize Christ for themselves, Christ who is the precious stone.

Just as the Lord is signified by this stone, so are the elect, whose faith never withers. They too are placed in the foundation of the Church, because they instruct others by both example and teaching and strengthen them in the doctrine of Christ.

### Fifth, the sardonyx

Sardonyx is composed of sardius and onyx. There are many varieties of it, but the more precious kind is distinguished by three colors, like the arrangement of a fingernail: in its lower part it has a black color, in the middle a red one, and in the upper part a white one. Or, alternatively: its first part is black, its middle white, and its upper part red. It signifies the saints, who appear black—that is, despised, contemptible, and abominable—but who, having nevertheless been renewed through the grace of Christ, are continually illumined by him with the radiance of faith, so that, when necessity presses, they do not fear to pour out their own blood through the service of charity, not only for their friends but even for their enemies themselves. This is signified by the red color.

Hence, in the Song of Songs, the Church says: “Do not look at me, that I am dark, because the sun has discolored me” (Song I). Therefore the Apostle Paul says: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, yet our inward person is renewed from day to day” (II Cor. IV).

### Sixth, the sardius

Sardius has the appearance of red earth, and therefore signifies the saints, who, although they are led to understand and behold sublime things, nevertheless always strive to recognize their own frailty, remembering that they are children of Adam, whose name is interpreted as “red earth.” They continually recall who they are and from where they have come—namely, from the fragile root of sinful humanity—so that they may not be puffed up by the gift of heavenly grace that they have received.

Hence Ezekiel, who often beheld heavenly mysteries, is called “son of man”; and Abraham says: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII). The Psalmist likewise says: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust; man is like grass, his days are [like grass]” (Ps. CII).

This stone is fittingly placed sixth, since it seems to retain the appearance of red earth, because the first man was also created on the sixth day, and it was said to him: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III).

### Seventh, the chrysolite

Chrysolite shines like gold and appears to emit from itself certain fiery sparks. By its appearance are signified those who shine with the light of heavenly wisdom and pour their virtues and judgments upon their neighbors, like sparks, through words of exhortation; by these they kindle others to the love of God and of neighbor.

### Eighth, the beryl

Beryl has two colors, green and pale. It represents the life of those who cling to the contemplation of eternal blessings and who, because of their concern for the administration of their brothers’ affairs, return, as it were, to pallor. While they strive to serve their brothers in external matters through the active life, those who shortly before had been green in the contemplation of God become pale again through their administration of temporal affairs in the exercise of human charity.

### Ninth, the topaz

Topaz contains within itself the colors of all stones; hence it also received its name, because *pan* in Greek means “all” in Latin. Kings can possess nothing more precious than this in their treasures. It is born on an Egyptian island called Topazion.

It signifies the saints filled with every virtue, shining with many virtues as though with many colors.

### Tenth, the chrysoprase

Chrysoprase is golden and green in color, as its very name makes clear, and it differs little from beryl. It signifies the elect, resplendent with wisdom and continually striving toward heavenly things through the greenness of faith.

### Eleventh, the hyacinth

Hyacinth resembles water suffused with a ray of sunlight. In this it signifies the elect, filled with wisdom—not human wisdom, by which the children of this age are wiser than the children of light, but divine wisdom, signified by the rays of the sun entering the water.

### Twelfth, the amethyst

Amethyst is sprinkled with three principal colors: purple, violet, and rose. By this are signified the saints, who bear a heavenly state of life on earth and are destined to attain in heaven both their reward and coevality with the angels. Hence the Lord says: “They will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. XXII). This is signified by purple, which is the garment of rulers.

In the violet, which is a humble plant yet possesses an excellent fragrance, their humility is expressed together with the fragrance of a good reputation. In the rose color, charity is understood—charity that flourishes in them to such an extent that they even rush forward to suffering and martyrdom, not only for their friends but also for their enemies themselves.

Hence the Lord says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

“And the twelve gates are twelve pearls, one at each gate.” As far as the literal sense is concerned, this means that the city has twelve gates, and that each gate was made from a single pearl—that is, each gate was formed from one gem. Again, at each gate there were twelve pearls, which together number one hundred and forty-four.

A single gate, or a single pearl, is understood to signify the Lord Jesus Christ, who, just as he is called the foundation of foundations, may also be called the pearl of pearls. This is the pearl that the merchant bought after selling everything.

By the twelve gates are understood the holy apostles and the other preachers, who open for us the gate of the Church. Hence the Psalmist says: “Open for me the gates of righteousness” (Ps. CXVII). Immediately he adds one gate, which signifies the Lord uniquely, as has been said, without whom no one comes to the Father: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. CXVII).

Earlier we read that the angel measured the walls of the city as one hundred and forty-four cubits. This number is repeated here when twelve pearls are described at each of the twelve gates, because the number twelve multiplied by twelve completes the number one hundred and forty-four, in which the entire multitude of the saints is contained.

“And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.” Earlier it was said that the city itself was made of pure gold, like transparent glass; here the street of the city is said to consist of the same materials.

By the walls of the city are understood those in the world who are stronger and more exalted; by the street, which is so called because *platon* in Greek means “broad” in Latin, are understood the simple, who are subject to them and dwell in the breadth of charity.

The street of the city is said to be made of pure gold, just as the walls are said to have been, because although there is a difference in merits—just as in this life one person is found holier than another, so in that blessedness one is found more exalted than another—nevertheless each person will possess in another, through the love of charity, what he does not possess in himself.

Hence it is said through blessed Job: “The small and the great are there”; and the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV).

Gold signifies the splendor of eternal recompense, while glass expresses the purity of their hearts, which will then be made manifest to each of them in one another. The street, therefore, is adorned with the same materials as the walls, because although those who are subject do not have as much glory as the rulers and teachers of the Church, nevertheless, as has been said, each will possess in another, through the ardor of charity, what he does not possess in himself, when, as the Apostle says, “God will be all in all” (I Cor. XV).

Hence it follows:

“And I saw no temple in it. For the Lord God almighty is its temple, and the Lamb.”

The present Church is the temple of God, according to what the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III). Yet it also has a bodily temple, namely, a place of prayer, where the faithful assemble to hear the divine words and celebrate Christ’s sacraments.

That heavenly city, Jerusalem, however, will no longer have a visible temple, because the Lord God almighty, the Father, and the Lamb—that is, the Son of God—are its temple. Hence Paul says: “For Jesus did not enter into dwellings made by human hands”; and elsewhere: “Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, entered once for all into the holy place through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by human hands, that is, not of this creation” (Heb. IX).

This temple—that is, the whole Trinity—the Church now possesses through faith; then it will possess it through manifest vision, when God will be all in all and in him. For then the Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, will be the temple of the Church: he will dwell in the Church by governing it, and the Church will dwell in him by resting in him.

In that dwelling—that is, in divine protection—it will flourish in three qualities: there it will have blessed existence, perfect knowledge of the holy Trinity, and chaste love of the one whom it has come to know. In these three qualities of blessedness the whole sum of blessedness consists.

“And the city does not need the sun or the moon to shine upon it.” This Jerusalem, which exists in the present age, enjoys the light of the sun by day and the light of the moon by night. That heavenly Jerusalem, however, will need none of these, because it will possess the true light, which will illumine not only bodies but also the minds of individuals.

Hence it follows: “For the glory of God will illumine it.” God himself, who now illumines the minds of the faithful through faith, will then illumine them much more when they have been found worthy to see him face to face. Hence he himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

“And its lamp is the Lamb.” A lamp pertains to fire. The present Church needs a lamp—that is, it needs to be illumined by bodily fire. That Church will no longer need to enjoy such a lamp, because its light is the Lamb, that is, the vision of Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Of the Son himself it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “For he is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. VII).

This light cannot be seen in the present age. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII).

“And the nations will walk by its light.” Christ is the light of the Church. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Arise, be illumined, Jerusalem, for your light has come” (Isa. LX).

It is sufficiently clear that these words should be referred not to the reward of the future age but to the labor of the present. For then the saints will no longer labor in walking; after their labor they will live in blessedness and rest. Now, therefore, they walk by its light—that is, by faith in Christ and by the other virtues—in order that afterward, having reached their heavenly homeland, they may rest in that light, namely, in the contemplation of God himself.

“And the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it.” The kings of the earth are understood to be all the righteous who strive to govern themselves well together with those subject to them. Of them it is said: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever he wills, he turns it” (Prov. XXI).

These kings—that is, all the righteous—will bring their glory and honor, which are one and the same thing, into that heavenly Jerusalem, because there they will receive all their recompense and prosperity, and all their joy and exultation. The more they are afflicted and despised in the present life, the more they will be exalted there.

By contrast, the reprobate, who possess their glory and honor in the present age and indulge themselves in the prosperity of this world, will remain empty there. Hence the Lord says: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation here” (Luke VI).

Because the saints do not love the glory of this age in the present life—the glory that belongs to the reprobate—they bring their glory to eternal blessedness, where they will be exalted and rewarded. To one of them the Lord will say: “You shall be over ten cities”; and to another: “You shall be over five,” as he himself reveals in the Gospel.

Alternatively: The kings of the earth are understood to be the apostles and the other preachers, who are rightly called kings because of the governance of the souls whom they rule. They will bring glory and honor into that city—that is, all those whom they acquired for Christ through their preaching and teaching.

Hence Paul says to certain people: “You are our glory on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Cor. I). These people are rightly called the glory and honor of kings, since for their sake those same kings are crowned.

“And its gates shall not be shut by day.” There will be great security in the heavenly Jerusalem, where there will no longer be any ambushes of the enemy. Therefore its gates will not be shut, because there will be perpetual day there, which night will not follow.

Hence it follows: “Night shall not be there.”

But let us see how the gates are shut in the present life. These gates are understood to be the preachers, through whose ministry we enter the Church. When the gates of a city are shut, they do not allow those entering to pass. Thus the gates are figuratively shut when the holy preachers drive the devil away from the hearts of the faithful and deny him access, while they teach the faithful how to resist his temptations.

Hence Peter says: “Your adversary, the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; resist him, firm in faith” (I Peter V).

He says there that its gates will not be shut because, once the fear of night has been removed, perpetual day will shine upon the elect. It will no longer be said there: “Watch and pray” (Mark XIII), which pertains to the night of adversity, but: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV), which is brought into the security of day.

“And they will bring the glory and honor of the nations into it.” There is no doubt that the very people who above are called the kings of the earth—that is, the holy preachers—will bring the glory and honor of the nations into that city. When the multitude of the faithful has been gathered, they will introduce into the heavenly homeland with themselves those whom they brought to faith through preaching.

Great glory and great honor of the nations will be brought into that city, because it will be adorned for the most part by the nations themselves.

“Nothing defiled, nor anyone who does what is abominable, shall enter it.” In this city, the defiled—that is, those stained by vices—and those who do what is abominable, that is, sin, enter together with the good, because just as this life stands midway between heaven and earth, so it contains within itself the citizens of both realms.

But into that city, where only the good will be, nothing defiled and no one who does what is abominable—that is, sin—will enter, because there will be no mixture of the wicked there, but only the fellowship of the good. Only the good will reign with Christ, with whom and in whom they will happily remain in that same heavenly Jerusalem.

“And falsehood”—you must understand, falsehood too shall not enter it—that is, no one who still commits the offense of lying. For, as was said above, no falsehood is without sin.

“Except those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.” Only those will enter the heavenly Jerusalem who, in the foreknowledge of God, were known and predestined for this before all ages. The Lamb’s book of life is understood to be the power of almighty God, as was said above, because he knows all things before they come to be.

## CHAPTER XXII

“And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb.”

The river of living water is understood as the doctrine of the Old and New Testaments. That water signifies holy preaching Solomon teaches when he says: “Deep water is words from a man’s mouth, and a rushing torrent, a spring of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII). The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII).

Although the doctrine of the Old and New Testaments is one, it is expressed in the plural because it proclaims the unity of faith, yet reaches many hearers and is spread through the mouths of many.

It is rightly called a river of living water because it gives life to those whom it irrigates and invites them to eternal life. It is therefore rightly compared to shining crystal because of the purity of faith that is received in baptism. Those whom it gives life by vivifying, it brings to the water of baptism; and it makes them both radiant through the purity of faith and exceedingly strong through its power.

The throne of God the Father and of the Lamb, that is, of the Son of God, from which it proceeds, is the Church of the faithful, to whom Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III), because Christ sits in their hearts with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Since their power is inseparable, their throne also is inseparable.

The water therefore proceeds from the throne of God because preaching is spread through the Church itself.

“In the middle of its street,” that is, in the middle of the Church itself. This doctrine irrigates not only the strong but also the simple, who are signified by the street.

“And on both sides of the river was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month.” This cannot be understood literally, so that the tree should be on both sides of the river, unless perhaps it was placed in the middle, with its branches spread out on either side.

Spiritually, however, it should be understood that the tree is on both sides of the river. The tree of life is Christ, the wisdom of God the Father, concerning whom Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is the one who holds her fast” (Prov. III).

Hence also in the Book of Genesis we read that there was a tree of life in the middle of paradise. That tree signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who grants eternal life to those who worthily eat of him.

The tree is therefore on both sides of the river because the Old and New Testaments proclaim Christ. What is foretold in the Old Testament as future is revealed in the New as fulfilled.

By the twelve months in which Christ himself, who is the tree of life, produces his fruits, the twelve apostles are understood. He himself says of himself and of those apostles in the Gospel: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?” (John XI), calling himself the day and the twelve apostles the hours.

And because days are made from hours, and months from days, what is signified simply by the twelve hours is also signified by the twelve months: namely, the twelve apostles, through whom Christ brings forth his fruit—that is, miracles, preaching, and heavenly works.

Hence we read in the Gospel that, having gone forth, they preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them. Hence Paul also says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII).

“Each”—you must understand, each tree—“yielding its fruit.” What is understood through the months is also understood through the trees, which proceed from the one trunk: namely, the twelve apostles, and in them all the saints, who never cease continually to render the fruit of their faith and works.

“And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” If the branches of the trunk signify the apostles, the leaves of the tree signify the apostles’ disciples, who reach the healing of the nations, instructing them by their example and teaching and leading them to true healing of mind.

If, however, we wish to refer these things to the heavenly Jerusalem, let us understand the river of living water as the contemplation of the holy Trinity, in which there is the fullness of eternal refreshment, according to the Psalmist’s words: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is made manifest” (Ps. XVI).

Above, too, we read, with the Lord himself speaking: “I will give the thirsty freely from the fountain of living water.” Pointing out that he himself is the fountain, the Psalmist says: “The children of men will hope in the protection of your wings. They will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV).

In this fountain there is perpetual life, because whoever is able to reach the contemplation of God, possessing eternal life—that is, possessing God—will himself also live forever.

This river is said to be bright as crystal because through its contemplation it will lead to the firmness of immortality and unchangeability. The river is also rightly said to proceed from the throne of God and to flow into the street of the city.

What is the throne is also the street of the city, namely, the whole Church in general; but it is distinguished in this way because of the persons of different kinds within it. Since it satisfies with the abundance of its vision those whom it governs by possessing them, it rightly overflows from the throne like a fountain, so that each inhabitant may draw from it according to his strength and receive according to his merits.

Although the same vision is possessed simultaneously by all, it is nevertheless distributed to each according to the merits of the individuals.

“And on both sides of the river was the tree of life.” What was previously signified by the fountain of living water is now also signified by the tree placed on both sides of the river: namely, the contemplation of the holy Trinity, which satisfies both the angelic and the human nature on either side. The drink of this vision is so manifold that whatever anyone then desires becomes this same vision, when, as the Apostle says, “God will be all in all” (I Cor. XV).

Nor is this surprising, since even the manna given from heaven to the children of Israel—by which eternal satisfaction is represented—tasted to each person according to what he delighted in, in accordance with the testimony of Scripture.

By the months in which the tree itself produces fruit, eternity is understood: by the years, as in “your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI); by the months, as in Isaiah: “Month after month” (Isa. LXVI); by the day, as in: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII); and again: “According to your ordinance, the days endure” (Ps. CXVIII).

The tree of life therefore yields fruit through twelve months, because the reward of blessed immortality itself, which is signified by the fruits and in which the elect rejoice, has no limit but remains without end.

“Each tree yielding its fruit.” They will yield their fruit in this respect: they will receive the reward of their works.

“And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” The leaves of the tree are understood as the praises of the saints, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Ps. LXXXIII). These praises will advance the healing of the nations, when the perpetual praise of the Creator, filling their hearts, allows no weariness, fatigue, or sadness to remain in them.

“And no curse shall be in it any longer.” In the present Church there is a curse—namely, the race of human beings who received the curse in Cain. In that fellowship of the saints there will be no curse; rather, the whole Church of the elect will be blessed in its inhabitants when they hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

“But the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it.” Earlier he had set down one throne, from which he also said that he had seen the river of living water flow. Now, however, he introduces thrones in the plural, saying: “The thrones of God will be in it.”

Yet this too signifies many thrones as one: namely, the whole Church of the elect, which is expressed as one throne because of the unity of faith and as many because of the diversity of the nations. Hence above twenty-four thrones were also reported to have been seen.

“And his servants will serve him.” Since the Lord says to his disciples: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John XV), how does Scripture here call those who have already become immortal servants? Or, if they will then attain the liberty and glory of the children of God, having already been freed from the slavery of corruption, how are they said to serve in that eternal rest?

We should understand that, because they will no longer labor in any struggle but will be cherished in eternal rest, they will be free and subject to no servitude. Even now they are not servants of fear but of love.

There are two kinds of servitude. A servant fears being beaten by his master; a son, however, fears being deprived of his father’s inheritance by offending in some way the eyes of his loving father. The former serves through fear, the latter through love.

By this servitude the elect serve almighty God here, taking every precaution lest they offend him in any sin. There, however, they will serve him by praising and glorifying him, according to the words: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Ps. LXXXIII).

“And they will see his face.” That is, they will possess perfect knowledge of him. This should not be understood childishly, as though we were to think that God has a face that can be seen by bodily eyes. Rather, because knowledge is present in the face of a human being, the face that the elect are said to see here signifies nothing other than knowledge of the holy Trinity.

Hence it is written: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III). The saints will see God in such a way as the angels now see him, concerning whom the Lord says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

How this vision is to be understood has been sufficiently explained above. Blessed Ansbertus Ambrosius, following the statements of other teachers, says that many speak of this by opening the eyes of the mind, declaring that the nature of God is to be contemplated, just as charity is seen. For if our outward person cannot see our inward person, how much less can it behold God, who is far more subtle than our soul?

They will therefore see him with the mind—that is, as has been said, they will possess perfect knowledge of him—so that what the Lord says may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Let the rest be investigated from his abridgment.

“And his name will be written on their foreheads.” By the forehead, as was said above, faith is expressed. But since there will then be neither faith nor hope, what does it mean that the elect are said to have God’s name on their foreheads?

We should understand that faith is placed here for the reward of faith, which will be the contemplation of almighty God. When the Church has received what it believed through faith, it will rightly be seen to bear the reward of faith itself on its forehead as a title of glory.

“And night shall be no more.” This means either the succession of time or the tribulation of distress, which is often represented by night. He had already said this above, but by repeating the statement he shows how greatly that light should be desired, which he emphasizes so often in his discourse.

“And they will need no lamp-light or sunlight.” Now human weakness is made fit to perform the works of the day by the rest of night, and it also uses a lamp at night for consolation. But then, when God will be all in all, and he is the true light illuminating everyone, there will be no need of the light of a lamp or of the light of the sun.

Hence it follows: “For the Lord God will illumine them.”

If, however, we understand night as ignorance, and the lamp or sun as the preaching of the divine word, then at that time there will be neither the night of ignorance nor the preaching of doctrine, because, as Isaiah says: “A man shall no longer teach his neighbor, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all shall know me, from the greatest to the least” (Jer. XXXI).

Rather, all who cling to eternal wisdom will shine with perfect knowledge.

“And they will reign with their head forever and ever.”

“And he said to me.” There is no doubt that it was the angel who showed him these things who said: “These words”—namely, the words that were spoken or shown to you from the beginning of the book—“are most trustworthy,” because whatever has been said to you will truly be fulfilled. “And they are true,” because they have been spoken by the true God.

What is said to John also pertains to the universal Church, to which the truth of these words is revealed through inward inspiration. Therefore no one should become so foolish as to doubt in any way the truth of what is proclaimed with such solemn testimony.

“And the Lord God, the spirit of the prophets, sent his angel to show his servants the things that must soon take place.” He himself who spoke through the prophets sent his angel to show John—and through him to the whole Church—the things that must soon take place.

By the name “spirit” the whole Trinity is understood. It sent the angel, who was indeed an angel by nature but bore the person of the incarnate Word alone. Hence at times he speaks in the person of Christ, saying: “I am the first, I am the last” (Isa. XLIV), and so forth. At other times, mindful of his own nature, he forbids John to worship him.

It should be noted that at the beginning of this book he said and indicated that he was sending his angel to his servant John. Here, however, he does not say that the things that must soon take place are to be shown to one individual, but to servants in the plural.

By these words he shows that he looked not specially to John alone but, through John, generally to the benefit of all, because what is said to John applies to all the faithful of the Church.

What are the things that must soon take place? The reward of the saints and the condemnation of the reprobate. Hence it follows:

“Behold, I am coming quickly,” namely, to repay each person according to his merit. Although the span of this present life may appear to be of some length, nevertheless all the time of the present life, compared with eternity, is regarded as momentary. Therefore he declares that he is coming quickly, so that the things that must take place may soon be fulfilled.

“Blessed”—that is, happy—“is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book,” preserving what has been written in it, so that he may be found worthy of eternal recompense.

“And I, John”—you must understand, blessed am I—“who heard and saw these things.” And after I had heard and seen them, I fell before the feet of the angel who was showing them to me, in order to worship him.

“And he said to me: ‘See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers the prophets, and of those who keep the words of the prophecy of this book.’”

Here, as above, John and the angel resume their proper persons. So that no one might doubt John’s authorship of the book, John brings forward his authority, saying: “I, John, who heard and saw these things.”

The angel also resumes his own person and forbids John to worship him, saying: “See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers.”

From these words it was sufficiently established above that the angel had assumed an ethereal body and therefore is said to have feet, and that he feared being worshiped by a human being after the coming of the Son of God, since he knew that a human being was already above him. We read nothing of this kind in the Old Testament, where we frequently read of angels being worshiped by human beings without being forbidden.

But it is very strange that John wished to worship the angel a second time, contrary to the angel’s prohibition. For the angel had already forbidden him to worship him in a similar manner and had taught that the one God should be worshiped.

To this it may be answered that either, struck by the great astonishment of the visions, he had forgotten what he had heard above, or else this may be a repetition of the earlier statement.

“Worship God.” That is, offer the reverence of honor not to a creature but to the Creator.

Notice, moreover, that the angel often foretold future things to John, and that many things in this book are also found to resemble the words of the prophets. Whole verses of Isaiah, Zechariah, and other prophets are found there. Thus we have: “They will see the one whom they pierced” (John XIX).

“And he said to me: ‘Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.’” Why did he say here, “Do not seal”—that is, do not seal up or close—the words of this book, when in the middle of this discourse John was told: “Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it”?

The reason is that divine mysteries are to be sealed, closed, and hidden from the wicked and the contemptuous. Hence we read: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII), and: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (ibid.). Divine words, however, are to be revealed to the faithful.

Hence the Lord says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables” (Luke XI).

Thus, with respect to unbelievers, it is said: “Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it”; but with respect to the faithful: “Write what you see,” and, “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.”

Alternatively, what is said to John at the beginning of this revelation—“Write what you see and what you are about to see”—what is said in the middle—“Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken”—and what is said at the end—“Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book”—may be understood in this way.

The Holy Spirit foresaw that at the first period some would arise in the Church who would receive the Lord’s word with joy and eagerness. Then there would also be some in whom iniquity would abound and charity grow cold, who would despise the word of God rather than receive it. Finally, as judgment approaches, there will be those—not only Gentiles but also Jews—who will receive the word of God with the greatest eagerness, while it is preached by Elijah and Enoch and by the other preachers.

Therefore, because at the first and last periods there were, or will be, faithful people who receive the word of God with joy, it is rightly said at the beginning of this book: “Write what you see,” and at the end: “Do not seal the words of this prophecy.”

But because in the middle period there are many who despise the word of God, it is appropriately said in the middle as well: “Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write it.”

“Because the time is near.” This pertains to what he previously said: “Do not seal the words of this prophecy.” The time in which these things are to be fulfilled extends from the time of Christ’s resurrection to the day of judgment, when each person will be repaid according to his works.

Of this very brief time the same John says in his Epistle: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II).

Whoever does harm, let him continue to do harm; and whoever is in filth, let him continue to defile himself. This is a permissive, not an optative, mood; [Col. 1217A] for often almighty God permits a person, on account of past sins, to fall into worse ones. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me,” and so forth, up to: “They shall walk according to their own devices” (Psalm 80). In this statement it is plainly shown that the guilt of disobedience came first, and that because of it they were permitted by God to walk in their own desires. Hence Paul says of certain people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks.” Therefore God handed them over to a depraved mind, so that they might do what is not fitting (Romans 1).

Let it therefore be understood: “Whoever does harm”—with “to himself” implied—that is, whoever does not wish to hear the words of God, “let him continue to do harm,” that is, let him remain unrepentant and be joined to his past sins. And whoever lives in the filth [Col. 1217B] of vices, let him continue to defile himself, that is, let him slide into worse things. For when someone is granted a time for repentance yet remains unrepentant, he turns the very remedy of grace into an increase of guilt. Since he does not wish to abandon evil in order to live, he increases that by which he will die. Of such people Paul says: “So that they may always fill up their sins” (1 Thessalonians 2).

And let the righteous person be justified still further through faith and through works. And let the holy person be sanctified still further. In accordance with the saying: “The saints shall go from strength to strength.” For the elect are always advancing in virtue, because each day they begin anew and, as time passes, add virtues to virtues.

Behold, I am coming soon—that is, to judge. And my reward is with me, to repay each person according to his works. This saying urges both the elect to advance toward better things and [Col. 1217C] the reprobate to turn away from evil, lest they perish without excuse. These words require no exposition, since they explain themselves.

I am the α and the ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. The first, before whom there is no one; and the last, after whom there is no one. The beginning, from whom every creature received its beginning; and the end, because everything is brought to completion in him. Alpha pertains to the dignity of the Word, omega to the humanity assumed at the end of time. He is therefore alpha, that is, the beginning who remains with the Father. He is also omega, that is, the end, born in time from his mother. Hence Paul says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10).

Nor should “beginning” be referred to him in the sense that, as the heretics wished, he began to exist in time; rather, it pertains to the order [Col. 1217D] of creatures, which received their beginning from him. Concerning alpha, John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and all things were made through him” (John 1). Concerning omega, which among the Greeks is the end of the letters, just as alpha is the beginning: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). In these words the whole substance of Christian salvation consists: namely, that in one and the same Christ both perfect divinity and true humanity are to be believed.

Blessed are those who wash their robes—that is, their bodies and their life—in the fountain of baptism and in the tears of repentance, and through observance of God’s commandments. So that their power may be in the tree of life—that is, in the Lord Jesus Christ. Those who have this will certainly possess everything in their head. [Col. 1218A] Hence, after he had said above, “I will give the thirsty person the water of life freely,” he immediately added: “Whoever conquers will possess these things.”

And through the gates—that is, by the gates—let them enter the city, namely, through the apostles and the other teachers, that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem. For through whose ministry we now enter the Church, through their mouths and their absolution we shall enter the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 1218B] Concerning these gates the Psalmist says: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (Psalm 117). Immediately he identifies one principal gate, to which these others also belong, adding: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.” For this gate signifies Christ, who says: “I am the door, says the Lord; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). Whenever any one of the faithful enters the way into the kingdom of heaven through the mouths of preachers, he certainly enters through him who speaks through their mouths.

Outside are dogs—that is, Jews, heretics, and the other unbelievers who bark against the Church. And sorcerers—that is, evil-doers or magicians—and the immoral, that is, those who sin shamelessly. And murderers, who kill people in various ways. And those who serve idols, that is, those who worship certain images in place of God, or who love earthly things more than God. And everyone who loves a lie and practices it.

For many practice falsehood, yet do not love falsehood, since they do not lie out of zeal for and love of sinning. They cleanse such a lie through an act of mercy, as was said above concerning the Hebrew midwives. But just as these people, in such lying, do not escape destruction unless a resolve [Col. 1218C] to amend follows, since Scripture says, “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5), so also those who are ensnared by deceit through zeal, will, and love must be punished with a heavier penalty. All those mentioned above will be outside—that is, they will be excluded from the entrance of the heavenly Jerusalem—when they hear: “Depart from me, you accursed” (Matthew 25).

I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches. This had already been said above. In these words it is plainly shown whose figure John assumed in this revelation. Nor do the things said to him pertain only to John himself, but to all the churches, which are comprehended above under the number seven, in which the one catholic—that is, universal—Church is signified.

I am the offspring and root of David. [Col. 1218D] This means nothing other than: I am from David’s very nature. For the blessed Mother of God descended from the stock of David, and therefore the Son of God himself is the son of David. Hence, when he asked the Jews, “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” he received this answer from them: “David’s.” And he said to them: “How then does David call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand’?” (Matthew 22.)

According to his divinity, therefore, he is the Lord God of David; according to his humanity, however, he is not another, but this same offspring and root of David, that is, of David’s nature. Alternatively: I am the root of David because David received his beginning from me. And I am the offspring and root of David because from him, at the end of time, I assumed the substance of flesh.

The splendid and morning star. [Col. 1219A] According to the literal sense, he calls Lucifer the splendid and morning star; while it illuminates the final hours of the night, it declares that morning will soon arrive. Christ himself is the splendid star, because he is the true light that enlightens every human being (John 1). And rightly “morning,” because he rose in the morning and drove away the darkness of the whole world, and after the final resurrection, having conquered mortality, showed us the brightness of the eternal day, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Romans 13).

And the Spirit—that is, the whole Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and the bride, that is, the holy Church, say to every believer: “Come to God,” namely, with the steps of faith and the strides of love, in accordance with the saying: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33). The Spirit, that is, God, [Col. 1219B] says this through hidden inspiration in the hearts of the faithful. The bride, that is, the holy Church, invites her hearers to the heavenly homeland through open preaching.

And let whoever hears—whether through hidden inspiration or through the preaching of teachers—the voice of God say to every other believer: “Come,” through right faith and through works appropriate to faith. For whoever has already been called by God must also call another, lest he go alone to the reward. For even one who is going to the bath, as blessed Gregory says, wishing to have companions, urges others to go with him.

And let whoever thirsts for righteousness—that is, for almighty God—come, that is, draw near to him, so that he may receive eternal satisfaction. Let whoever wishes receive the water of life freely; that is, let whoever desires to enjoy the contemplation of God, in which [Col. 1219C] there is refreshment with eternal satisfaction, strive to live rightly, so that afterward he may be able to attain to that vision of God.

But since the Apostle says, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9), how does the one who wills receive the water of life freely? It must be understood that mercy first precedes us, so that we may will; then our will also follows through that same grace, so that we may act. Concerning this Paul says: “He who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2).

Therefore, whoever thirsts—that is, whoever desires eternal delights through the grace of God that precedes him—let him strive toward them with the strides of love. And whoever wills—that is, whoever has been changed from unwilling to willing, not through his own merits but through the gratuitous will of God—let him draw up the water of eternal delight.

I therefore testify—that is, I solemnly charge and bear witness—to everyone [Col. 1219D] who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to the things contained in this book any [Col. 1220A] error, God will bring upon him the plagues written in this book, so that after countless torments he may arrive at eternal condemnation.

At the time when blessed John wrote these things, heretics arose in the Church—namely Valentinus, Ebion, and Cerinthus—whom he also calls Antichrists in his Epistle. Therefore he addressed this warning to them, lest through the perversity of error they dare to add anything to this book, just as, for example, Arius attempted to remove from his book the words: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). Photinus likewise said: “I grant Jesus his beginning from Mary.”

And if anyone removes from the words of this book of prophecy either its meaning or even its words against his own conscience, as Arius did with the Gospel, as was said above, God will remove his share from the book of life—that is, [Col. 1220B] he will not be written in the memory of God’s foreknowledge—and from the holy city, that is, from the heavenly Jerusalem and the fellowship of holy angels and human beings, and from those rewards that are written in this book.

Nevertheless, this must be understood: this is not said concerning those who sincerely believe what they say, but concerning those who speak wrongly about God against their own conscience.

He says, “The one who bears witness to these things”—with “words” understood—and therefore it is made clear how true they are, because the Lord Christ himself bears witness to them. Hence it follows: “Yes,” that is, “Let it be so,” so that all the things said above may be fulfilled. “I am coming soon,” to judge and repay each person according to his works.

Amen, that is, it is true, because what [Col. 1220C] has been foretold will undoubtedly be fulfilled. Come, Lord Jesus. The whole Church speaks these words through John, desiring Christ to come to judgment. Hence each day in the Lord’s Prayer it humbly asks: “Your kingdom come.” And also: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved.”

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

In this passage John represents the preachers, who, knowing that a person cannot be justified through the law but through grace, desire that this same grace may always remain with the Church. Note, moreover, that this book took its beginning from grace and placed its conclusion in grace, because we are saved by God’s preceding grace and justified by his following grace. Hence Paul too, following the custom of this expression, arranged his Epistles [Col. 1220D] to the churches so that he would begin with grace and place the conclusion in grace.
